<meta>This page is the formal dedication of the work. ### TO THE REVEREND FATHER IN CHRIST AND LORD, LORD GUILLAUME BRI-
### ÇONNET, BISHOP OF LODÈVE, JACQUES LEFÈVRE D'ÉTAPLES SENDS ETER-
### NAL GREETING IN CHRIST GOD.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'N' with scrolling foliage and a floral motif on a criblé (dotted) background.</image-desc>

IT IS NOT hidden from you, most wise father—you who are accustomed to take the greatest delight in those things that come from Providence—that when a farmer plows a field, spending whatever labor he can upon it, if a small plant rises up and brings forth abundant fruit, that is a gift of God. <note>Lefèvre uses this agricultural metaphor to argue that while human effort (like writing or farming) is necessary, the actual "fruit" or spiritual benefit belongs entirely to God.</note> Indeed, there is no one among the faithful who would now doubt this or deny it. If, therefore, the earth which the tracks of cattle trample is made fertile by divine favor, how much more the rational earth of human minds, which lies open to divine entrances and which divine footsteps traverse? But the earth which is not cultivated, and which does not feel the heavenly rain: if it brings forth anything, it is not fit for human use, but rather consists of thorns, briars, and thistles, or herbs without any utility. In almost this same way, whatever human minds produce that do not feel the divine ray usually harms more than it helps, nor does it provide any life-giving food for the mind.

For the offspring of minds destitute of heavenly favor are thistles, briars, and burrs. And almost everything is full of such things: both among those who have written about human affairs and those who have written about divine ones. I except those who did not set out to write of themselves, but were driven by a divine impulse. For that impulse tends toward things sublime and luminous. Human minds, however, are sterile of themselves. If they believe they are capable, they are being presumptuous; and if they produce anything, it is unfruitful, heavy, obscure, and rather a hindrance to the mind than a life-giving food, consistent with the soul and life. Therefore, if the perceptible earth brings forth fruit suited to the human body, it is a most manifest sign of a heavenly gift; but even more so if the human mind produces an offspring conducive to the life and salvation of souls.

Therefore, in such matters, one ought not to pay attention to the mind itself, nor the human craftsman (whoever he may be whom God has chosen as his instrument), but especially to the heavenly grant and the divine Giver himself. For this reason, most kind father, I would wish most earnestly to entreat you and all who are about to read the Epistles of the <term>divinely-speaking Paul</term> <note>original: "diuiniloqui Pauli." This term emphasizes that Paul’s words are not his own, but God speaking through him.</note> arranged in this volume, that they attend not so much to Paul himself as to the grace of Paul and the Giver of that grace. And they ought to attend to human authors so much the less when they happen to read any commentaries, if they perceive signs of spiritual life and true nourishment for the soul. Instead, they must understand the power from above that makes the depths fertile; they must recognize the true Author, and once recognized, follow him with as much purity of mind and piety as they can muster. For one approaches him by these steps alone: he who works all things in all. <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 12:6.</note>

If, however, they perceive no life-giving nourishment for the mind, the field of the human mind has not felt the dew of the Holy Spirit, nor has it been soaked by the rain of the Holy Spirit; rather, it has produced a useless sprout from itself, according to the divine word: "Cursed," he says, "is the earth in your work; it shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you." <note>original: "Maledicta (inquit) terra in opere tuo: spinas & tribulos germinabit tibi." A quote from the Latin Vulgate, Genesis 3:17-18, describing the fall of man.</note> Therefore, what we have from the <term>second generation</term> <note>This refers to the "new birth" or spiritual regeneration in Christ, contrasted with the "first birth" or natural state of fallen humanity.</note> is not our own, but the work of divine blessing. In this, therefore, let us look to the divine blessing as the craftsman; in that other [the first birth], let us look to the curse of the first birth. The work of the latter is to be avoided just as the work of the blessing is to be pursued.

And although it must be pursued, those who exercise themselves around what is already planted, watered, and already possessing growth from God are not to be esteemed any less. Yet a great grace can be in all these and around all people. Those who attend to this grace prepare themselves to receive grace. For what does the Distributor of graces want except to pour grace into those who are prepared, just as a bright light pours into eyes capable of seeing? Those who understand these Epistles to be a gift of God, and that what has been added [the commentary] is a gift of God, will profit. And they will profit not from themselves, but from grace. But truly, those who perhaps look to a worldly craftsman—indeed, even to Paul himself, who is now above the world—as if these Epistles were his own work and not the result of a higher <term>energy</term> <note>original: "energiæ." Lefèvre uses this term to mean the active, working power of God within a person.</note> operating in him divinely: if they approach the reading with their own sense, they are likely to receive little fruit from it. And being puffed up by the sense of their own flesh, judging many things perversely, they will vanish into vanities and become sick in mind to the same extent.

If anyone is granted to see that this is so, it is no small thing. May Christ be present, the author of divine gifts, granting grace to all, preserving what is given, and increasing what is preserved: so that no one may judge by their own sense, nor be presumptuous in judging. For Paul is only an instrument. "You seek," he says, "a proof of Christ speaking in me." <note>original: "Experimentum (inquit) quæritis in me loquentis Christi." A quote from 2 Corinthians 13:3.</note> For this is the doctrine of Christ, not of any other person. Accordingly—

<summary>This page contains a dedication by Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples to Bishop Guillaume Briçonnet, asserting that the following biblical commentaries are products of divine grace rather than human intellect. Lefèvre warns readers to look past the human authors to the Holy Spirit to find true spiritual nourishment.</summary>
<keywords>Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples, Guillaume Briçonnet, St. Paul, Epistles, Divine Grace, Holy Spirit, Commentary, Biblical Interpretation, Humanism, Lodève</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the dedication to Bishop Guillaume Briçonnet. Lefèvre d'Étaples transitions from theological reflections on the source of wisdom to a technical explanation of the book's layout, specifically how he has integrated Greek textual insights alongside the traditional Latin Vulgate and how he has handled chapter divisions and reference canons.</meta>

# EPISTLE.

of which those who are studious will draw waters in joy from the fountains of the Savior, as the divine oracle contains. <note>A reference to Isaiah 12:3: "With joy you will draw water from the wells of salvation."</note> This is the part of the doctrine of which it is said in Hosea: *I desired the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.* <note>Hosea 6:6. Lefèvre emphasizes internal spiritual knowledge over outward ritual.</note> If Paul is the sole instrument of this divine knowledge, what can any who come after him be—if indeed they can be called anything—except a very small and thin sub-instrument, even less and lower than every instrument? Yet it is a great thing to be a sub-instrument in this way, even though it is less than a sub-instrument, for it far exceeds human strength.

¶ Those, therefore, who approach the reading of these things piously: not Paul, nor anyone else, but Christ and His most good Spirit will ensure they profit in piety. But those who approach presumptuously and proudly: not even Paul, nor any other, but He who *resists the proud and gives grace to the humble* will repel them. <note>original: "superbis resistit & humilibus dat gratiam" — James 4:6 and 1 Peter 5:5.</note> Sweet is the manna that thickens from the dew of heaven, and sweet the honey gathered from the same flowers; but sweeter than all is the gift of God to those to whom He Himself grants a taste.

¶ But enough for such small things; let the pious readers be sufficiently warned by us. To them, first through the grace of the Savior, we present the divine-speaking Epistles of Paul in the **Vulgate edition**, to be read at first glance. And alongside them: the **understanding from the Greek** corresponding to them. <note>Lefèvre provided two versions of the text side-by-side: the traditional Latin and his own translation based on Greek manuscripts.</note> After which, as fourteen epistles of the blessed Paul are received into the use of the churches, so also fourteen books of commentaries are appended. This is done with such diligence that the first corresponds to the first epistle, the second to the second, and so on. And in all: chapter to chapter, and number to number. All things are marked in the Greek fashion, so that the harmony and mutual correspondence of all may easily be open. A small number above at the side, on the left of the reader, shows the chapter of the epistle. 

It must be noted, however, that each of these epistles among the Greeks is written in a continuous flow, and not divided by manifest readings and chapter rubrics as among the Latins. Instead, numbers are only placed in the margin, corresponding to the places where the Latins have their chapter divisions. For it is not the custom of any writers that when a letter is sent, it is sent divided by rubrics and such separations <term>discapedinibus<gloss>divisions or gaps</gloss></term>, but woven with a continuous thread and described continuously. In which way there is no doubt that Paul—expert in all things—both wrote and sent them. Therefore, we too have noted the sections in this way: through marginal numbers at the side of the text, now on the right, now on the left. The tiny numbers in the same parts are for the sake of the commentaries and canons. 

But perhaps that will seem less worthy of note to some. Now, however, let me return to demonstrate a few things regarding the rest. ¶ The larger number high up in the middle of the margin toward the right shows the number of the epistle. For the Epistle to the Romans is the first, the two to the Corinthians are the second and third, and so on in order, as they are usually arranged in the books of the Latins. And in the same part high up at the far side, the name of the epistle is read—for example, whether it is to the Romans, to the Corinthians, or to whichever others it was written. 

And because our ancestors, both Greek and Latin, prefixed <term>canones<gloss>reference tables or indexes</gloss></term> to these epistles—and it is still easy to find them in many ancient codices: among the Greeks, **Eusebius** and **Ammonius**; among the Latins, **Priscillian**—we also have prefixed others. We omitted those of Priscillian, not only because they are found corrupted everywhere, but also because their numbers did not harmonize with ours. These new canons relate to the contents of the epistles, the articles of faith, and arguments against heretics; all these things, clearer than light, will be easily seen in their places. 

¶ Whether readers do so or otherwise matters little. For a servant ought to have no care, much more so a sub-servant—and less than a sub-servant—whether others approve or reprove, as long as his labor is accepted by the one Lord of all and his sovereign Lord. May Christ the Lord, more than Lord and sovereign Lord, accept our labor.

¶ Some will perhaps wonder not a little that we have dared to add a Greek understanding to the translation of Jerome, judging it to be done too insolently. They will not so much accuse as condemn me for rashness and audacity. To whom we bear no ill will. For they would do so justly if the matter were as they suspect and as many are now persuaded. But they will grant us good favor when they clearly understand that we have dared nothing against the translation of Saint Jerome, but rather regarding the **Vulgate edition**, which existed long before Jerome, that blessed and glorious light of the Church, and which he himself censures, plucks at, and convicts along with us, calling it the "Old" and "Vulgate" edition. <note>Lefèvre makes a scholarly distinction: he isn't correcting St. Jerome, but rather the "Old Latin" version that existed before Jerome's revision, which Jerome himself had criticized.</note>

¶ Therefore, most holy prelate, for the innumerable benefits with which you have long since heaped upon me and daily heap, and for the great conveniences for study you grant me, I can respond with no other thing, nor be of any other use to you, except to acknowledge you in every place as my unique benefactor. Nevertheless, do not disdain to receive these first fruits of divine blessing, our labor on the most blessed Paul—offered first to God—as his sacred priest <term>antistes<gloss>prelate or high priest</gloss></term> and vicar. Accept them not as our gift, but as something offered to God. Welcome Paul as a guest; let in the herald of Christ, the legate of Christ for the life of all nations, the super-worldly orator. Whom you have otherwise requested so greatly as a traveler...

# TO THE REVEREND FATHER IN CHRIST AND LORD, LORD GUILLAUME BRIÇONNET, BISHOP OF LODÈVE, JACQUES LEFÈVRE D’ÉTAPLES <note>original: "Iacobus Faber Stapulensis." Lefèvre was a pioneering French humanist and theologian whose work paved the way for the Reformation.</note> SENDS ETERNAL GREETING IN CHRIST GOD.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'N' featuring a bird perched among ornate floral and leaf patterns.</image-desc>
It does not escape you, most wise father—you who are accustomed to take the greatest delight in those things which come from Providence—that when a farmer plows a field, expending whatever labors he can upon it, if a seedling rises and brings forth abundant fruit, that is a gift of God. Indeed, there is no one among the faithful who would now doubt this or deny it. If, therefore, the earth which the tracks of cattle tread upon is made fertile by divine favor: how much more the rational earth of human minds, which is open to divine entrances, and which divine footsteps traverse? Moreover, the earth which is not cultivated, and which does not feel the heavenly rain: if it produces anything, it is not fit for human uses, but is thorns, briers, and thistles, or weeds without any utility. In nearly this same way, if human minds give birth to anything that does not feel the divine ray, it usually harms more than it profits, nor does it provide any vital food for minds. For the offspring of minds destitute of heavenly favor are thistles, thorns, and burs. And almost everything is full of such things: both among those who have written concerning human affairs, and those who have written concerning divine ones. I except those who have approached writing not from themselves, but driven by a divine motion. For that motion tends toward things sublime and luminous. Human minds, however, are sterile of themselves. If they believe they are capable, they are presumptuous; and if they give birth to anything, it is fruitless, heavy, dark, and a food contrary to the mind rather than vital, soul-nourishing, or conducive to life. Therefore, if the sensible earth produces fruit suited to the human body, it is a most manifest sign of a heavenly gift. But truly much more so if the human mind brings forth an offspring leading to the life and salvation of souls. Therefore, in such matters one ought not to look at the mind itself, nor the human artisan (whoever he may be whom God has chosen as His instrument), but especially at the heavenly grant and the divine Giver Himself. Wherefore, most kind father, I would wish most earnestly that you and all who are about to read the Epistles of the divine-speaking Paul arranged in this volume be exhorted: that they look not so much at Paul himself as at the grace of Paul, and the Giver of that grace. And they ought to look at human authors so much the less when they perhaps read any commentaries whatsoever, if they perceive signs of spiritual life and true pasture for the soul. Rather, they must understand the power from above that makes fertile the depths; they must recognize the true Author, and once recognized, follow Him with whatever purity of soul and piety they can muster. For He is approached only by those steps—He who works all things in all. They perceive no vital nourishment of the mind if the field of the human mind has not felt the dew of the Holy Spirit, or has not been soaked by the holy rain of the Spirit; but instead has brought forth a useless sprout from itself, according to the divine word. *Cursed,* He says, *is the earth in your work: it shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you.* <note>A reference to Genesis 3:17–18. Lefèvre uses the Fall of Man to explain intellectual failure.</note> Therefore, what we have from a fertile generation is not our own, but is the work of divine blessing. In that blessing, therefore, let us look to the divine Artisan. But in the other, let us look to the curse of the first birth. The work of the latter is to be fled just as the work of the blessing is to be pursued. And even in that which is to be pursued, the human author (as it is worthy to say) is not to be gazed upon. For this ought to be most thoroughly proven: *neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase.* <note>1 Corinthians 3:7.</note> So much less are those to be esteemed who exert themselves regarding what is already planted, watered, and already possesses the increase of God. Nevertheless, great grace can be in all these things and around all people. Those who attend to this grace prepare themselves to receive grace. For what does the distributor of graces wish but to pour grace into those who are ready, just as a bright light enters capable eyes? Those who understand these Epistles to be a gift of God, and that which has been added to be a gift of God, will profit. And they will profit not from themselves, but from grace. But truly, those who perhaps look at the worldly artisan—or rather, who look at Paul himself, who is now above the world, as if these Epistles were his work and not the work of a higher energy operating divinely in him—approaching the reading with their own sense, they are likely to receive little fruit from it. And puffed up by the sense of their own flesh, judging many things in a distorted way, they will vanish amidst vanities and be equally sick in mind. If it is granted to anyone to see that this is so, it is no small thing. May Christ be present, the author of divine gifts, granting grace to all, preserving what is given, and increasing what is preserved: so that no one may judge by his own sense, nor be presumptuous in judging. For Paul is only an instrument. *You seek,* he says, *proof of Christ speaking in me.* <note>2 Corinthians 13:3.</note> For this is the doctrine of Christ, not of anyone else. Therefore—

Proin <note>Catchword: "Therefore" or "Henceforth."</note>

# THE EPISTLE.

<note>original: "STOLA." This is the conclusion of the word "EPISTOLA" (Epistle/Letter) from the previous page's footer.</note>

If they devote themselves to this study, they will "draw waters with joy from the fountains of the Savior" <note>A reference to Isaiah 12:3.</note>, as the divine oracle contains. This is the part of the doctrine of which it is said in Hosea: **"I desired the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings."** <note>original: "Scientiam dei volui potius quam holocausta." Hosea 6:6.</note> For if Paul is merely the instrument of this divine knowledge, what could any later writers be—if they can even be called anything—except a very small and thin *sub-instrument*, even smaller and lower than any instrument? Yet it is a great thing to be a sub-instrument in this way, even though it is less than a sub-instrument, for it far exceeds human strength. Therefore, those who approach these readings piously will find that not Paul, nor any other, but Christ and His most good Spirit will provide that they may grow in piety. But for those who approach presumptuously and proudly: not even Paul, nor any other, but He who **resists the proud and gives grace to the humble** <note>1 Peter 5:5 / James 4:6</note> will repel them. Sweet is the manna that thickens from the dew of heaven, and sweet the honey gathered from flowers; but the gift of God is sweeter than all to those to whom He grants its taste. But enough of such small things; let the pious readers be sufficiently warned by us.

To these readers, first, through the grace of the Savior, we present the epistles of the divine-speaking Paul in the **Vulgate edition** <term>Vulgate: the "common" Latin translation of the Bible used by the Church</term> to be read at first glance, and from the same region, the meaning corresponding from the **Greek**. After these, just as fourteen epistles of the most blessed Paul are received in the use of the churches, so also fourteen books of commentaries are placed below. This is done with such diligence that the first corresponds to the first epistle, the second to the second, and so on. And in all of them, chapter corresponds to chapter and number to number, and all things are marked in the **Greek manner** <note>original: "græco more." Referring to the use of Greek letters as numerals.</note>, so that the mutual agreement and correspondence of all parts may be easily seen. 

A small number high on the side in the reader's left-hand region shows the chapter of the epistle. It should be noted, however, that each of these epistles is written among the Greeks in a continuous flow and not divided into obvious sections and chapter rubrics <note>Rubrics: headings or instructions typically written in red ink.</note> as among the Latins; instead, numbers are simply placed in the margin in the region where the Latins have their chapter sections. For it is not the custom of any writers that when a letter is sent, it is sent divided by rubrics and such gaps, but woven with a continuous thread and written continuously. In which manner there is no doubt that the skillful Paul both wrote and sent them all. For this reason, we also have noted the sections through marginal numbers at the side of the text, now on the right, now on the left. The tiny numbers in those same parts are for the sake of the commentaries and **canons** <term>Canons: here meaning reference tables or indexes to help find specific topics or passages</term>. But perhaps that will seem less worthy of notice to some. 

Now, however, let us return to showing a few things of the rest. A larger number high up in the middle of the margin toward the right shows the number of the epistle. For the Epistle to the Romans is the first, the two to the Corinthians are the second and third, and so on in that order in which they are usually arranged in the books of the Latins. And in that same part high up at the far edge, the name of the epistle is read—for example, whether it is written to the Romans, or to the Corinthians, or to any others. And because our ancestors, both Greek and Latin, prefixed **canons** to these epistles—and it is still easy to find them in many ancient codices <note>Codices: ancient manuscript books.</note>, namely **Eusebius** and **Ammonius** <note>Eusebius of Caesarea and Ammonius of Alexandria, famous for creating cross-reference systems for the Gospels.</note> among the Greeks, and **Priscillian** among the Latins—we also have prefixed others. However, we omitted those of Priscillian <note>Priscillian of Avila (4th century), whose "canons" were popular but who was also a controversial figure often associated with heresy.</note> not only because they are found to be corrupted everywhere, but moreover because their numbers did not agree with ours. We have prefixed others regarding the contents of the epistles, articles of faith, and against heretics, all of which will be seen very easily in their places, clearer than light. 

And in all these things, some will perhaps approve of our diligence. Whether they do so or otherwise matters little. For a servant should have no care, much less a sub-servant and something less than a sub-servant, whether others approve or rebuke, provided that his labor is acceptable to the one Lord and Over-Lord of all. May Christ—Lord, and more than Lord, and Over-Lord—therefore accept our labor. Some will also perhaps wonder not a little that we have dared to add "Greek understanding" to the translation of **Jerome** <note>St. Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the primary translator of the Latin Vulgate.</note>, judging it to have been done too insolently; they will not so much accuse me of temerity and audacity as condemn me. I feel no anger toward them. For they would indeed do so justly if the matter were as they suspect and as many are now persuaded. But they will grant us good favor when they clearly understand that we have dared nothing against the translation of Saint Jerome, but rather against the **Vulgate edition**—which existed long before that blessed and glorious light of the Church, Jerome, and which he himself censures, plucks at, and convicts, and which he calls the "old and common edition." 

Therefore, O most keen Prelate <note>Addressing Bishop Briçonnet.</note>, since I can respond to you in no other way for the innumerable benefits with which you have long overwhelmed me and daily overwhelm me, and for such great advantages for study which you grant me—being able to be of no other use to you than to acknowledge you in every place as my unique benefactor—nevertheless, do not disdain to receive these first-fruits of our labor on the blessed Paul, offered first to God. You, His consecrated priest and vicar, receive them not as our gift, but as something offered to God. Admit Paul as a guest; let in the herald of Christ, the legate of Christ for the life of all nations, the super-worldly orator. Him whom you once so greatly requested as a traveler...

# TO THE REVEREND FATHER IN CHRIST AND LORD, LORD GUILLAUME BRIÇONNET, BISHOP OF LODÈVE, JACQUES LEFÈVRE D’ÉTAPLES <note>original: "IACOBVS FABER STAPVLENSIS." Lefèvre was a leading French humanist and theologian who sought to reform the Church from within through a return to original biblical texts.</note> WISHES ETERNAL SALVATION IN CHRIST GOD.

<image-desc>A large ornamental historiated initial 'N' featuring a scholar or saint seated at a reading desk within a classical room, surrounded by dense foliate and architectural motifs in a woodcut style.</image-desc>

It does not escape you, most wise father—you who are accustomed to contemplate deeply those things which come from divine providence—that when a farmer plows a field, spending whatever labor he can upon it, if a seedling rises and brings forth abundant fruit, that is a gift of God. There is no one among the faithful who would now doubt this or deny it. If, therefore, the earth trodden by the feet of cattle is made fertile by divine favor, how much more the <term>rational earth</term> <note>Lefèvre uses the metaphor of "rational earth" to describe the human mind or soul, which possesses the capacity for reason but remains barren without divine intervention.</note> of human minds, which is open to divine entry and trodden by divine footsteps? 

However, the earth that is not cultivated and does not feel the heavenly rain—if it produces anything at all—is not fit for human use; instead, there are thorns, briars, and thistles, or weeds without any utility. In nearly this same way, if human minds produce anything that does not feel the divine ray, it usually harms more than it profits, nor does it provide any vital nourishment for minds. For the offspring of minds destitute of heavenly favor are thistles, thorns, and burs. Almost everything is full of such things, both among those who have written about human affairs and those who have written about divine ones. 

I exclude those who approached writing not of themselves, but urged by a divine impulse; for that impulse tends toward things sublime and luminous. Human minds, however, are sterile of themselves. If they believe they are capable on their own, they are presumptuous; and if they produce anything, it is fruitless, heavy, dark, and rather contrary to the mind than a vital nourishment, suitable for the soul and life. Therefore, if the physical earth brings forth fruit accommodated to the human body, it is a most manifest sign of a heavenly gift. But truly much more so if the human mind brings forth offspring conducive to the life and salvation of souls. 

Therefore, in such matters, one ought not to look at the mind itself, nor the human craftsman (whoever he may be whom God has chosen as His instrument), but chiefly at the heavenly grant and the divine Giver Himself. For this reason, most kind father, I would most earnestly pray that you and all who are about to read the <term>Epistles of the divine-speaking Paul</term> <note>The letters of St. Paul the Apostle, which form a central part of the New Testament.</note> arranged in this volume, would look not so much at Paul himself as at the grace of Paul and the Giver of that grace. 

And they should look at human authors so much the less when they perhaps read any commentaries, if they perceive signs of spiritual life and true food for the soul. Instead, they must understand the power from above fertilizing the depths; they must recognize the true Author, and having recognized Him, follow Him with as much purity and piety of soul as they can. For one approaches Him only by these steps—He who works all things in all people. 

But if they perceive no vital nourishment for the mind, then the field of the human mind has not felt the dew of the Holy Spirit, nor has it been moistened by the rain of the Holy Spirit; rather, it has produced a useless sprout from itself, according to the divine word: **"Cursed,"** He says, **"is the earth in your work; thorns and thistles shall it bring forth for you."** <note>original: "Maledicta (inquit) terra in opere tuo : spinas & tribulos germinabit tibi." A quotation from Genesis 3:17-18.</note> Therefore, what we have from a fertile generation is not our own, but the work of divine blessing. 

In that blessing, therefore, let us look to the divine Craftsman. In the other, however, let us look to the curse of the first birth, whose work is to be avoided just as the work of blessing is to be pursued. And although it is to be pursued, the human author (to speak worthily) is still not to be looked upon; for this ought to be most thoroughly proven: that **"neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the growth."** <note>original: "neq; qui plantat esse aliquid / neq; qui rigat / sed qui incrementũ dat deus." 1 Corinthians 3:7.</note> 

So much the less should those be esteemed who exert themselves regarding things already planted, watered, and already having the growth of God. Yet great grace can be in all these things and concerning all people. Those who attend to this grace prepare themselves to receive it. For what does the Distributor of graces wish except to pour grace into those who are prepared, just as a bright light is poured into eyes capable of seeing? 

Those who understand that these Epistles are a gift of God, and that what has been added is a gift of God, will profit. And they will profit not from themselves, but from grace. But truly, those who perhaps look to the worldly craftsman—indeed, even those who look to Paul himself, who is now above the world, as if these Epistles were his own work and not the work of a higher energy operating divinely in him—approaching the reading with their own sense, will receive little fruit from it. Being puffed up by the sense of their own flesh and judging many things with distortion, they will vanish into vanities and will only fall ill in their minds. 

If it is granted to anyone to see that this is so, it is no small thing. May Christ be present, the Author of divine gifts, granting grace to all, preserving it when given, and increasing it when preserved, so that no one may judge by his own sense or be presumptuous in judging. For Paul is only an instrument. **"You seek a proof,"** he says, **"of Christ speaking in me."** <note>original: "Experimentum (inquit) quæritis in me loquentis Christi." 2 Corinthians 13:3.</note> For this is the doctrine of Christ, not of any other. Therefore...

STOLA. <note>original: "EPISTOLA" (The Letter). This header is a continuation of the title from the preceding page.</note>

...of which those who study it will be partakers: they will draw waters in joy from the fountains of the Savior, as the divine oracle contains. This is the portion of doctrine of which it is said in Hosea: *I desired the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.* <note>original: "Scientiam dei volui potius quam holocaustum." A reference to Hosea 6:6, emphasizing that inner spiritual knowledge is superior to external ritual.</note> If Paul is merely the instrument of this divine knowledge, what can any who come after him be—if they can be called anything at all—except a very small and thin <term>sub-instrument</term> <note>Lefèvre uses the word "subinstrumentum" to humbly describe his own role as a commentator who merely assists the primary "instrument," St. Paul.</note>, even smaller and lower than any other instrument? Yet it is a great thing to be a sub-instrument in this way, even if one is lesser than a sub-instrument; it is a role that far exceeds human strength.

¶ Therefore, those who approach these readings with piety will find that it is not Paul, nor anyone else, but Christ himself and his most benevolent Spirit who will grant them progress in godliness. But for those who approach with presumption and pride: it will not be Paul, nor anyone else, but the Lord himself who will repel them—He who *resists the proud and gives grace to the humble.* The manna that forms from the dew of heaven is sweet, and the honey gathered from the flowers of that same dew is sweet; but the gift of God is sweeter than all things to those whom He allows to taste it.

¶ But enough for now of such brief words; let the pious readers be sufficiently warned. To them, first by the grace of the Savior, we present the Epistles of the divine speaker Paul in the <term>Vulgate edition</term> <note>The "Vulgate" refers to the common Latin translation of the Bible used by the Western Church. Lefèvre presents it alongside his own "Greek-aligned" version for comparison.</note> to be read on the first side, and directly across from it, the understanding of the same Epistles corresponding to the Greek. Following these—just as the fourteen Epistles of the most blessed Paul are received for use in the churches—so too fourteen books of commentaries have been added. This has been done with such care that the first book corresponds to the first Epistle, the second to the second, and so on. In all of them, chapter corresponds to chapter and number to number, and all are marked in the Greek fashion so that the agreement and mutual correspondence of all parts may be easily seen. A small number at the top of the margin on the reader's left side shows the chapter of the Epistle. However, it should be noted that each of these Epistles is written in a continuous flow among the Greeks and is not divided into obvious sections and chapter headings as it is among the Latins; rather, numbers are merely placed in the margin adjacent to the places where the Latins have their chapter divisions. For it is not the custom of any writer, when an epistle is sent, to send it divided by headings and such gaps; instead, it is woven with a continuous thread and written down as a single flow. There is no doubt that Paul, who was skilled in all things, wrote and sent them in this way. Therefore, we too have noted the sections by marginal numbers at the side of the text, sometimes on the right and sometimes on the left. The very tiny numbers in those same parts are for the sake of the commentaries and the <term>canons</term> <note>Canons were cross-referencing systems or indices used in early Bibles to help readers find related passages or themes.</note>. But perhaps this will seem to some to be a matter hardly worthy of note.

¶ Now let us return to point out a few things regarding the rest. A larger number at the top in the middle of the margin on the right shows the number of the Epistle. For the Epistle to the Romans is first, the two to the Corinthians are second and third, and they follow in this order according to how they are usually arranged in Latin books. In that same part at the very top edge, the name of the Epistle is read—for example, whether it is written to the Romans, to the Corinthians, to any others, or to an individual. And because our ancestors, both Greek and Latin, prefixed "canons" to these Epistles—which can still be easily found in many ancient manuscripts, such as those of Eusebius and Ammonius among the Greeks, and Priscillian among the Latins—we also have prefixed others. We omitted those of Priscillian, not only because they are found to be corrupt everywhere, but also because their numbers did not agree with ours. We have added others so that the contents of the Epistles, the articles of faith, and arguments against heretics might all be seen quite easily in their places, clearer than the light of day.

¶ In all these matters, some will perhaps approve of our diligence. Whether they do so or otherwise matters little. For a servant should have no care—all the more so for a "sub-servant" and one less than a sub-servant—whether others approve or reproach him, provided only that his labor is accepted by the one Lord of all and his <term>Supreme Lord</term> <note>original: "superdomino." Lefèvre uses this term to emphasize Christ's absolute sovereignty over all earthly masters and scholars.</note>. Therefore, may Christ the Lord, who is more than Lord and the Lord above all, accept our labor.

¶ Some will also perhaps wonder not a little that we have dared to add a "Greek understanding" to the translation of Jerome, judging this to have been done too insolently. They will not so much accuse me as they will condemn me for recklessness and audacity. I hold no anger toward them. Indeed, they would be right to do so if the matter were as they imagine and as many have now been persuaded. But they will grant us their kind pardon when they clearly understand that we have dared nothing against the translation of Saint Jerome, but rather against the "Vulgate edition." This edition existed long before Jerome—that blessed and glorious light of the Church—and he himself mocks, picks apart, and refutes it, calling it the "old and common edition." <note>Lefèvre is defending his use of the Greek text to correct the Latin. He argues that the common Latin Bible of his day was not actually Jerome's superior translation, but an older, flawed version that Jerome himself had tried to fix.</note>

¶ Therefore, most fierce protector, since I can respond in no other way to the innumerable benefits with which you have long overwhelmed me and continue to overwhelm me daily, and for the great advantages for study which you grant me—since I can be of no other use to you than to acknowledge you in every place as my unique benefactor—do not disdain to receive these first fruits of divine blessing, our labor upon the most blessed Paul. Offered first to God, may you, his sacred prelate and vicar, receive them—not as our gift, but as something offered to God. Welcome Paul as a guest; bring in the herald of Christ, the legate of Christ sent for the life of all nations, the other-worldly orator. Love him, whom you have so often and so greatly desired while he was a stranger.

# A DEFENSE SHOWING THAT THE OLD INTERPRETATION OF THE EPISTLES OF THE BLESSED PAUL WHICH IS READ EVERYWHERE IS NOT THE TRANSLATION OF JEROME.

<image-desc>A large square woodcut initial 'Q' featuring white interlaced vine and leaf patterns (knotwork) against a dark, cross-hatched background.</image-desc>
Because in the letter prefixed a little while ago we
already said that we have added nothing to the
translation of Jerome (for we would not have
presumed to do so), it now seems appropriate that
we should show—with everyone's good favor—that
the "Vulgate" edition <note>In this context, "Vulgate" refers to the "common" or widely used Latin version of the Bible, which Lefèvre argues predates Jerome's work.</note> of the epistles of the most blessed Paul, which the churches use everywhere, is not by Jerome, but existed before him. For in this way, those who follow will proceed with a more tranquil mind; they will be satisfied, having perhaps suspected the opposite or having already been persuaded of it. And perhaps they will love me, whereas they might have hated me had this not been revealed. Or they might even commend me, where they might have detracted. Although we do not seek commendation so much as that our labor might benefit many, to the glory and honor of Him for whose grace we undertook it, and who inspired our labor. For He is worthy, and more than worthy, of all honor, praise, and knowledge. ¶ But by what means can we more conveniently show that that <term>ἐκδοσιν</term> <note>original: "ekdosin" (edition or publication)</note>—that is, the common edition—is not Jerome’s, than from Jerome himself? Let him seem to weave the defense for himself against those who think otherwise, rather than any other person doing so. Truly, as far as it concerns me, I am drawn to this defense and apology only unwillingly and forced by the opinion of others. For I would wish there were never a need for it. Nevertheless, we must gird ourselves for it using the words of the holy Jerome. We must show him to be our lord, protector, and defender, though some think us his adversary. ¶ Indeed, if the holy Jerome cites the translator of this edition as another person, calls him "the Latin translator," and names the interpretation itself "the common edition," does it not excellently follow that the translation is not Jerome's? If he frequently finds fault with the Latin translator and accuses him of ignorance—if he even more frequently taxes the statements of that edition—who will deny, who will hesitate to say that holy Jerome both denies that he was the translator and refutes that edition as being his own?

<margin>
JEROME
</margin>
Yet, I believe it remains hidden to no one that holy Jerome does this, provided they have been diligent and careful in reading his commentaries on the epistles of the most blessed Paul. So that these things may appear more clearly, shall we now hear the holy Jerome? Let all faith in me be cast away unless he himself testifies to the same most openly. For in the first book of his commentaries on Paul's Epistle to the Galatians, where in the second chapter of the epistle it is read according to the common edition: *And I conferred with them the gospel which I preach among the Gentiles* <note>original: "Et contuli cum illis euangelium quod praedico in gentibus." Galatians 2:2.</note>. Jerome says: "Where the Latin translator above had said 'I acquiesced'—in that place where it is written: *immediately I did not acquiesce to flesh and blood* <note>original: "continuo non acquieui carni et sanguini." Galatians 1:16.</note>—in the present passage he has translated it as 'I conferred' rather than 'I acquiesced.'" And in the first book of the commentaries on the Epistle to the Ephesians, where in the first chapter of the epistle I read: *who is the pledge of our inheritance, unto the redemption of acquisition* <note>original: "qui est pignus haereditatis nostrae / ĩ redẽptionẽ acquisitionis." Ephesians 1:14.</note>. Jerome says: "The Latin translator put 'pledge' [pignus] for 'earnest money' [arrabone]. However, 'earnest money' does not mean the same thing as 'pledge'." Behold, therefore, how he cites the Latin translator: not as...

himself, but as if speaking of someone else. ¶ But that he names this very version we are discussing the "Vulgate edition" <note>original: "vulgatam æditionem." In the first book of commentaries on Ephesians: twelve times. In the second: five times. In the third: eight times. In the commentaries on the Epistle to Titus and Philemon: frequently. Wherefore I think sufficient satisfaction has been given to the suspicion of those who condemn us—as if we had dared to add our own new understanding from the Greek to the translation of Jerome, and not only added it, but frequently criticized it in our examinations as being translated with little justice. ¶ But you will say: "Everyone holds the Vulgate edition to be Jerome’s." ¶ We refute that they hold this; on the contrary, every learned man and whoever is endowed with sound judgment knows well that it is not Jerome’s work, seeing as he refutes, rebukes, and condemns it, as is already sufficiently clear from what has been said, and is more clearly evident to those reading his commentaries. ¶ "But," you say, "that edition is never found without Jerome’s letters and prefaces." ¶ And that, moreover, is false. For in several ancient manuscripts, it is found with the prefaces and letters of others, which they ascribe either to Isidore <note>St. Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636), a later scholar whose work was sometimes confused with Jerome's.</note> or to someone else even more ancient. Shall it therefore be the translation of anyone whose prefaces and short letters are prefixed to it? And how, if it belongs to one, shall it belong to anyone else? And if it belongs to each one, how shall it belong to another? For it follows excellently: the translation belongs to him whose prefaces are attached. But the prefixed prefaces are recognized as Isidore’s. Therefore, it is Isidore’s translation, not Jerome’s. But even if we concede this last point, by which we refute the preceding one, we do so for the same reason that we refute it being Jerome’s: because the prefixed prefaces are recognized as Jerome's. ¶ But again, you persuade yourself from Jerome that it is Jerome’s. For at the end of the book which he composed *On Illustrious Men*, he wrote about himself in this manner:
<margin>JEROME</margin>
"I have restored the New Testament to the Greek faith; <note>original: "græcæ fidei reddidi." This means Jerome aligned the Latin text with the original Greek authority.</note> the Old I have translated according to the Hebrew." Now, in the New Testament, the Epistles of Paul are contained. Therefore, he translated them. And if he translated them, what other translation could it be, except that which is called the Vulgate edition and which is in the use of the churches? ¶ Rather, on the contrary, you ought to have argued from the words of the most blessed and equally most learned Jerome: Holy Jerome restored the New Testament, in which these Epistles are also contained, to the Greek faith. But the Vulgate edition overflows with such manifold faults that it has not so much been "restored to the Greek faith" as it stands in need of being restored. Therefore, it is not Jerome's. Unless one were to say it was restored to the Greek faith according to its merit. Which is both false, and he himself shows it to be false. ¶ But perhaps you will add: "He translated it first, and then corrected that translation in his later writings." ¶ O stubborn head, and peevish caviller, a most wicked sophist! Do you not see that you do an injury to the holy man in order to defend your own error? Do you not see that you charge a man who was both most holy and most learned not only with ignorance, but moreover with presumption and the audacity of rashness—one who presumed to translate before he knew how? If he had first been the translator of the Vulgate edition, would he say of himself: "The Latin translator, deceived by the ambiguity of the word, translated 'prudent' instead of 'chaste,'" as was said a little above he had stated in his commentaries on the Epistle to Titus? If so, he betrays his own ignorance. If he translated it and conceals it, pretending it was another translator, he strikes his own error onto another. Both of these are far removed from Jerome, who was as learned as he was holy...

### DEFENSE: THAT THE OLD TRANSLATION OF THE EPISTLES OF BLESSED PAUL WHICH IS READ EVERYWHERE IS NOT THE TRANSLATION OF JEROME.

<image-desc>Large woodcut ornamental initial 'Q' featuring complex interlaced knotwork and vine patterns contained within a square double-line border.</image-desc>

Because in the letter prefixed just before this I already stated that we have added nothing to the translation of Jerome (for we would not have presumed to do so), it now seems appropriate that we should demonstrate—with the good favor of all—that the "Vulgate edition" <note>original: "vulgatam æditionem." Here referring to the standard "common" Bible text of the time.</note> of the epistles of the most blessed Paul, which the churches use everywhere, is not Jerome’s, but existed prior to him. In this way, the reader may approach what follows with a more tranquil mind; for those who perhaps suspect the opposite, or are already persuaded of it, will be satisfied. Perhaps they will even come to love me, though they might have hated me had this not been revealed. Or they might even commend me, though they would have disparaged me. However, we do not seek commendation so much as that our labor might benefit many, to the glory and honor of Him for whose sake we undertook it, and who breathed life into our work. For He is worthy, and more than worthy, of all honor, praise, and knowledge.

¶ But how can we more conveniently show that that <term>edition</term> <note>original: "εκδοσιν" (ekdosin), the Greek word for "edition" or "version."</note>—that is, the Vulgate edition—is not Jerome’s, than from Jerome himself? It is better that he should seem to weave this defense for himself against those who feel otherwise, rather than anyone else. Truly, as far as I am concerned, I am drawn into this defense and apology only unwillingly and compelled by the opinions of others. I wish there were never a need for it. Nevertheless, we must gird ourselves for it using the words of the holy Jerome, so that I may show him to be our master, guardian, and defender—he whose adversary people think we are.

¶ Indeed, if the holy Jerome cites the translator of this edition as another person, calls him "the Latin translator," and names the translation itself "the Vulgate," is it not excellently proven that the translation is not Jerome’s? If he frequently goads the Latin translator and accuses him of ignorance—if he frequently critiques the said edition—who will deny, who will hesitate to say that the holy Jerome denies being the translator and rejects that edition as his own?

¶ And yet, I believe it is hidden from no one that the holy Jerome does exactly this—provided one has been diligent in reading his commentaries on the epistles of the most blessed Paul. To make this appear more clearly, let us now hear the holy Jerome himself. Let all faith in me be cast away unless he himself testifies to this most openly.

<margin>
JEROME
</margin>
For in the first book of his commentaries on Paul's Epistle to the Galatians, where in the second chapter of the epistle it reads according to the Vulgate edition: "And I conferred with them the gospel which I preach among the Gentiles" <note>Galatians 2:2</note>. On this, the holy Jerome says: "Where the Latin translator previously had 'acquiesced' <note>original: "acquieuit"</note> in that place where it is written, 'immediately I did not acquiesce to flesh and blood' <note>Galatians 1:16</note>; in the present passage he has translated it as 'conferred' <note>original: "contuli"</note> rather than 'acquiesced'." And in the first book of his commentaries on the Epistle to the Ephesians, where in the first chapter of the epistle it reads: "Who is the pledge of our inheritance, unto the redemption of acquisition" <note>Ephesians 1:14</note>. Jerome says: "The Latin translator put 'pledge' <note>original: "pignus"</note> for <term>earnest-money</term> <note>original: "arrabone." Lefèvre is highlighting Jerome's linguistic critique of the translator's choice.</note>. However, 'earnest-money' does not mean the same thing as 'pledge' sounds." See, therefore, how he cites a Latin translator: not as if speaking of...

¶ We refute that "everyone" holds this; rather, every learned person and those of sound judgment know well that it is not Jerome's work, seeing as he refutes, rebukes, and condemns it—as is already clear enough from what has been said, and shines even more brightly to those who read his commentaries. ¶ "But," you say, "that edition is never found without Jerome's letters and introductions." ¶ That, moreover, is false. For in quite a few ancient manuscripts, that version is found with the introductions and letters of others, which they ascribe either to **Isidore** <note>likely St. Isidore of Seville</note> or to some other even older author. Would it then be the translation of anyone whose introductions and letter are prefixed to it? And how, if it belongs to one, could it belong to anyone else; and if it belongs to any one person, how could it belong to another? It happens excellently that the translation belongs to him whose introductions are prefixed. But the prefixed introductions are recognized as Isidore's. Therefore, it is Isidore's translation, and not Jerome's. But even if we concede this last point, by which we refute the preceding one: by that same logic we refute that it is Jerome's, because Jerome's prefixed introductions are recognized <note>Lefèvre is using his opponents' logic against them: if headers prove authorship, then headers by others prove it isn't Jerome's</note>.

<margin>JEROME</margin>
¶ But again: you persuade yourself from Jerome's own words that it is Jerome's. For at the end of the book he composed *On Illustrious Men* <note>original: "De viris illustribus"</note>, he wrote of himself in this manner: "I restored the New Testament to the Greek faith; the Old I translated according to the Hebrew." Now, the Epistles of Paul are contained in the New Testament; therefore, he translated them. If he translated them, what other translation could it be but that which is called the Vulgate edition and which is in the use of the churches?

¶ Rather, you ought to have argued the opposite from the words of the most blessed and learned Jerome. Holy Jerome restored the New Testament (in which these Epistles are contained) to the Greek faith. But the Vulgate edition swarms with such manifold faults that it has not so much been "restored to the Greek faith" as it "struggles to be restored." Therefore, it is not Jerome's. Otherwise, it would have been restored to the Greek faith in a manner worthy of his status. Which is false, and he himself shows it to be false.

¶ But perhaps you will add: "He translated it first, and then corrected that translation in his later writings." ¶ O stubborn head, and peevish caviller, most wicked sophist! Do you not see that you do an injustice to the holy man just to defend your own error? Do you not see that you attribute to this most holy and learned man not only ignorance, but moreover presumption and the audacity of rashness—that he presumed to translate before he knew how? If he had been the previous translator of the Vulgate edition, would he say of himself, "the Latin translator, deceived by the ambiguity of the word, translated 'prudent' instead of 'chaste,'" as was said a little above he wrote in the commentaries on the Epistle to Titus? If so, he betrays his own ignorance. If he translated it and conceals it, pretending it was another translator, he pins his own error on someone else. Both of these are alien to Jerome, who was as learned as he was holy.

### A DEFENSE THAT THE OLD TRANSLATION OF THE EPISTLES OF THE BLESSED PAUL, WHICH IS READ EVERYWHERE, IS NOT THE TRANSLATION OF JEROME.

<image-desc>A large square woodcut decorative initial 'Q' containing intricate interlacing vine patterns and knotwork in a style reminiscent of manuscript illumination.</image-desc>

Because in the preface placed just before this, we have already said that we added nothing to the translation of Jerome (for we would not have presumed to do so), it now seems appropriate that we show, by everyone's good grace, that the common edition of the epistles of the most blessed Paul—which the churches use everywhere—is not by Jerome, but existed before him. For in this way, readers will approach what follows with a more tranquil mind, being satisfied even if they perhaps suspected the opposite or were already persuaded of it. And perhaps they will love me, whereas they might have hated me had this not been revealed; or they might even commend me, where they might have detracted. Yet we do not seek commendation so much as that our labor might benefit many, to the glory and honor of Him for whose grace we undertook it, and who has breathed life into our work. For He is worthy, and more than worthy, of all honor, praise, and knowledge. ¶ But how can we more conveniently show that that <term>ekdosin</term> <note>original Greek: ἔκδοσιν, meaning an "edition" or "published version"</note>—that is, the common edition—is not Jerome's, than from Jerome himself? For he seems to weave his own defense against those who think otherwise better than anyone else could. Nevertheless, we must gird ourselves for it using the words of the holy Jerome, so that I may show him to be our master, guardian, and defender—the very man they think we are opposing. ¶ Indeed, if the holy Jerome cites the translator of this edition as another person, calls him "the Latin translator," and names the translation itself "the Vulgate" <note>meaning the "common" or "widely circulated" version</note>, does it not excellently prove that the translation is not Jerome's? If he frequently finds fault with the Latin translator and accuses him of ignorance, and if he even more frequently critiques the aforementioned edition, who will deny it? Who will hesitate to say that the holy Jerome denies being the translator and refutes that edition as his own? And yet, I believe it escapes no one that the holy Jerome does exactly this—at least, no one who has been diligent in reading his commentaries on the epistles of the most blessed Paul. So that these things may appear more clearly, let us now hear the holy Jerome himself. Indeed, let all faith in me be cast aside unless he himself testifies to this quite openly. a.iiii.

but as if speaking of another person.

<margin>JEROME</margin>
¶ But that he calls this version we are discussing the "common edition" <note>original: "vulgatam æditionem"</note> is most clearly evident from the third book of his commentaries on the same epistle <note>referring to Galatians</note>, where we find it written thus: "And those who are Christ’s have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires." <note>Galatians 5:24</note> And this (he says) is so noted, if we follow the common edition: reading "have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires." In this manner, he calls it the "common edition."

<margin>JEROME</margin>
¶ And although he is not usually wont to cite the Latin interpreter without rebuking both him and the edition we use everywhere, in certain places he is known to do so even more openly. As in the second book of his commentaries on the same epistle to the Galatians, where in chapter five we read: "You are made void of Christ, you who are justified in the law; you have fallen from grace." <note>Galatians 5:4</note> For here (says the holy Jerome) "it is not as in the Latin, where it is badly translated as 'you are made void of Christ'; rather, 'you have ceased from the work of Christ' is better understood." And in the third book of commentaries on the same epistle, where a little later in the same fifth chapter, we read thus in the common edition: "A little leaven corrupts the whole lump." <note>Galatians 5:9</note> The same Jerome says: "It is poorly held in our manuscripts that 'a little leaven corrupts the whole lump'; the translators have rendered their own sense rather than the words of the Apostle."

<margin>JEROME</margin>
And in the epistle to Titus where in the first chapter we read: "But hospitable, kind, prudent, sober." <note>Titus 1:8</note> Jerome says again: "The Latin translator, deceived by the ambiguity of the word, translated 'prudent' instead of 'chaste'." <note>The Latin word *pudicus* (chaste) was confused with *prudens* (prudent).</note> Behold how he openly insults and argues against both the translator and the edition! Who, therefore, unless lacking in mind and reason, would say this translation belongs to Jerome? Would he rebuke himself, and say that he himself had translated differently and indeed foolishly, when the Greek source is perfectly sound?

¶ Indeed, if anyone wishes to look accurately, he will find that in the three books of commentaries on the epistle to the Galatians, the Latin translator and our common edition are noted nineteen times, if not more. In the first book of commentaries on Ephesians: twelve times. In the second: five times. In the third: eight times. In the commentaries on the epistles to Titus and Philemon: frequently. Therefore, I think enough has been done to satisfy the suspicion of those who would condemn us, as if we had dared to add our own <term>understanding</term> <note>meaning a new interpretation or translation</note> from the Greek to the translation of Jerome—and not only added it, but frequently criticized it in our examinations as being translated with little justice.

¶ But you will say: "Everyone holds that the common edition is Jerome’s."

¶ We refute that "everyone" holds this; on the contrary, every learned man and those who possess sound judgment know well that it is not Jerome's work, seeing as he refutes, contradicts, and condemns it, as is already clear enough from what has been said, and shines even more clearly for those who read his commentaries.

¶ "But," you say, "that edition is never found without Jerome's letters and prefaces."

¶ And that, furthermore, is false. For in quite a few ancient manuscripts, it is found with the prefaces and letters of others, which they ascribe either to Isidore <note>Saint Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636 AD), a famous scholar-bishop of the early Middle Ages.</note> or to someone else even more ancient. Shall it then be the translation of anyone whose prefaces and letters are attached to it? And how could it belong to any one person if it belongs to many, and if it belongs to everyone, how shall it belong to another? It is excellently argued that the translation belongs to him whose prefaces are attached. But the prefaces attached are known to be Isidore’s. Therefore, it is Isidore’s translation, and not Jerome’s. But while we concede this last point, we refute the preceding one by the same reasoning: we refute that it is Jerome's simply because Jerome's prefaces are seen to be attached.

¶ But again: you persuade yourself from Jerome's own words that it is Jerome's. For at the end of the book he composed *On Famous Men* <note>original: "de viris illustribus"</note>, he wrote of himself in this manner:

<margin>JEROME</margin>
"I have restored the New Testament according to the Greek source <note>original: "græcæ fidei"</note>; I have translated the Old Testament according to the Hebrew." Since the epistles of Paul are contained in the New Testament, he therefore translated them. And if he translated them, what other translation could it be but that which is called the common edition, and which is in use in the churches?

¶ On the contrary, you should have argued from the words of the most blessed and learned Jerome. The holy Jerome restored the New Testament (in which these epistles are contained) to the Greek source. But the common edition swarms with such manifold faults that it is not so much "restored to the Greek source" as it "cries out to be restored." Therefore, it is not Jerome's. Unless you claim that it was restored to the Greek source with due dignity—which is false, and he himself shows it to be false.

¶ But perhaps you will add: "He translated it first, and then corrected that translation in his later writings."

¶ O stubborn head, peevish caviller, and wicked sophist! Do you not see that you do an injustice to the holy man just to defend your own error? Do you not see that you charge a man who was both most holy and most learned not only with ignorance, but furthermore with the audacity of presumption and rashness, as if he presumed to translate before he knew how? If he had been the first translator of the common edition, would he say of himself: "The Latin translator, deceived by the ambiguity of the word, translated 'prudent' instead of 'chaste'," as was said a little above that he wrote in his commentaries on the epistle to Titus? If he speaks of himself, he betrays his own ignorance. If he translated it and pretends he did not, feigning that someone else was the translator, he strikes another for his own error. Both of these are far removed from Jerome, who was as learned as he was ho—

He systematically dismantles the common belief that the presence of Jerome's prefaces proves his authorship, suggesting the translation may actually be by Isidore of Seville.</summary>

<meta>The author continues to argue that the common Latin Bible (the Vulgate) used by the Church was not actually the work of Saint Jerome. Having previously shown that Jerome criticized the "common edition," the author now uses Jerome’s own letters and logical proofs to show that Jerome’s actual translations were either lost, distinct from the common text, or merely "corrections" rather than new translations.</meta>

# APOLOGIA

...it is entirely foreign to such a most holy man—indeed, a hero and more than a man. ¶ But come now, consider this: how could that unlearned translation have been so easily received by the entire church, while that learned and polished one, which restored the New Testament to the Greek standard <note>original: "fidei græcę reddidit," literally "rendered to the Greek faith/source," referring to textual accuracy</note>, has not yet been received? How did it gain such strength so suddenly that, while Jerome was still writing, it was already called the "Vulgate" <note>the common or popular version</note>? And this was at a time when the holy Jerome suffered so many rivals (though it was beyond the merit of such a holy man), even in Rome, the head of all churches, so much so that he himself, due to the envy of his rivals, was driven of his own accord into exile and wandering in distant places. ¶ And as for your contention that he translated the epistles of Paul: you can by no means conclude that from his own words. For he testifies that he translated the Old Testament. But regarding the New Testament, he does not say he translated it, but that he "restored it to the Greek standard." This is equally done by one who compares and emends texts. For instance, Jerome himself emended the old edition of the Psalter <note>The Book of Psalms</note> twice, by a collation <note>comparison</note> of Greek manuscripts (as he testifies when writing to Paula and Eustochium). 

<margin>JEROME</margin>
And what is this "emending," if not restoring it to the Greek standard? If he translated it, why did he not openly disclose it in this case rather than in the others? He says: "I translated 28 homilies <note>sermons</note> on Jeremiah and Ezekiel from Greek into Latin. I translated one book by Didymus on the Holy Spirit into Latin. I translated the Old Testament according to the Hebrew standard." Behold! When he translates, he says openly that he has translated or turned a work from Greek into Latin. Therefore, it is not clear from his own words that he translated the New Testament, and even less so the divine epistles of the Apostle Paul. ¶ But suppose he *did* translate it. Does it immediately follow then that the translation used everywhere by the churches is Jerome’s? What <term>analytical thinker</term> <note>original: "analyticus"</note>, I ask, would recognize this as a compelling form of argument based on known and pre-confessed facts? What <term>logician</term> <note>original: "dialecticus"</note> would admit this as his own from the established premises? By what <term>complex syllogism</term> <note>original: "epicheremate"</note> is this concluded? By what <term>logical inference</term> <note>original: "symparafinate"</note> is it gathered? By what <term>corollary</term> <note>original: "Porismate"</note> is it supported? What if Ambrose translated it: would it then also be Ambrose’s? And yet it is not Ambrose’s, as can be recognized by anyone looking at the Ambrosian text. ¶ And we should not believe that Ambrose translated it, but rather that he emended some places of the common edition from the Greek, so much so that the edition existed before Ambrose, and therefore before Jerome. Indeed, Jerome even attached his own commentaries to that translation commonly used by the Latins, which, in the course of commenting, he frequently refutes. ¶ Add further that those who held weight and authority in the church at that time did not greatly require this in the canonical scriptures. 

<margin>AUGUSTINE</margin>
This is most clearly evident from Aurelius Augustine writing to Jerome. He says: "Regarding the translation of the holy canonical scriptures into the Latin tongue, I would prefer you not to labor, except in the manner in which you interpreted Job: so that by applying signs, the difference between your interpretation and that of the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament</note>—whose authority is most heavy—may be apparent." These are the words of the holy Augustine. In this, you prove Jerome: that he marked the translation of Job from the Greek with an <term>obelisk</term> <note>a mark (†) used to indicate words in the Greek not found in the Hebrew</note> where it was superfluous compared to the Hebrew; and where it was lacking, he added to it, likewise marking what he added with an <term>asterisk</term> <note>a mark (*) used to indicate additions</note>. How then would the churches, by universal use throughout all nations (which is the most difficult thing of all to do), have received a changed version which the highest authorities and those of the first rank did not approve? Therefore, they did not receive it then. And when they might have received it later, and when the practice of all churches might have been changed everywhere, is not easy to find. Nevertheless, we do not deny that the writings of Jerome (as many as have been found) are approved. But if he translated the epistles of Paul, if the catholic epistles of the apostles, if the gospels, if the acts of the apostles: these have not yet emerged into the light for the public use of the churches; nor even his complete revisions of those scriptures. ¶ This is easy to recognize from his epistle to Sunia and many other writings of the same Jerome. ¶ What then: have they perished? Perhaps; unless time, that great discoverer of things, restores them to our descendants. The Book of Job, of which the blessed father and doctor of the church Augustine speaks and which he approves, is not in the use of the churches. How much less, then, those not equally approved? However, I found that book of Job in one place where aged decay was consuming old volumes thrown together in a heap without any order. Having found it, I immediately entrusted it to be transcribed by my companion, Ioannes Solidus <note>John Solidus, a Polish humanist and physician</note>, a young man from Krakow who had come to our studies, a very dear friend to me and a most ready writer. And what wonder is it if it is not held, even if he either translated or emended it? For even the "Gospel according to the Hebrews," 

<margin>JEROME</margin>
which was recently translated by me into the Greek and Latin tongue—and which Origen often uses—he <note>Jerome</note> reports after the resurrection of the Savior: "But when the Lord had given the linen cloth to the servant of the priest, he went to James and appeared to him." Behold, he translated into the Latin language that gospel whose testimony he uses both in his commentaries on the epistles and on Matthew. But who can produce it now? Nor would I easily believe those things which he prepared for the New Testament, whether they be translations or restorations to the Greek standard. For how many distinguished men have written in Italy, and perhaps in Germany, Britain, Gaul, and Iberia, whose writings Italy lacks, and...

...those very places in which they wrote? If we desire the things which our own domestic hearth produces, what wonder is it if we desire those things which Jerusalem and Bethlehem—the most blessed cradles of Christ, the author of life—produced, even if they were born in another world almost cut off from us? And though this is so, we should be far more grieved that we do not feel the benefit of the most blessed Jerome’s translations, or his restoration of the New Testament to the Greek standard <note>original: "fidem græcam," referring to the reliability or authenticity of the Greek source texts</note>, and of these divine epistles of Paul, than it should be our heart's desire to have shown the opposite. Although I also claim that this has been done quite clearly, without ambiguity, and without a cloak of words for the sake of truth; yet everyone will be less able to remain in doubt if we briefly note the places which Jerome marks as faulty in both the Latin interpreter and the Vulgate edition. First: in the Epistle to the Galatians. Then: in the Epistle to the Ephesians. Following that: in the Epistle to Titus. And finally: in the Epistle to Philemon. For we have not seen his commentaries on any more than these. All of these will be easily perceived from the list set before your eyes.

¶ In his commentaries, the holy Jerome either censures or directs all these things: sometimes criticizing the Latin interpreter, sometimes the Vulgate edition <note>In this context, the "Vulgate" refers to the common version of the Bible circulating in the Middle Ages, which the author argues has been corrupted over time</note>. We have shown this all the more diligently so that the public error—introduced by the nature of the translations we use everywhere—might be thoroughly uprooted from the minds of men who have been persuaded by false, common rumors, and so that this false persuasion might have no further hiding places. And though our purpose was to show this regarding the common translation of the epistles of the blessed Paul (which we have done), we grieve nonetheless that it is so, and that we do not instead possess the translation made by Jerome himself. 

Whosoever wishes to carefully observe these same commentaries of the holy doctor of the Church, Jerome, upon this passage, "and might cleanse to himself a people acceptable" in the second chapter of the Epistle to Titus (I leave aside other passages from his other commentaries on other books of Holy Scripture, of which there is a manifold witness and a rich abundance, for the sake of brevity), will clearly understand from this that not only the translation of the epistles, but even the translation of the Gospels which the churches now use, is not the <term>Hieronymian</term> <note>meaning 'belonging to Jerome'</note> work. 

Wherefore it is all the more to be lamented that such great and illustrious labors of that most blessed man and holy doctor of the Church—which he himself had undertaken for the public benefit of all the pious and the studious—have perished, if indeed they have perished for us and for posterity. But if this be the case, and if Christ our Lord—the true light, and the only true and never-failing light—should illuminate anyone of posterity to restore to us what has perished, which was once restored by Jerome, then that person (whoever he may eventually be) must not be attacked with envy or any ill-will, but the grace of Christ must be honored in him. To whom alone all honor is due, all glory and thanksgiving, in all things and above all things, forever and ever. Amen.

### THE END OF THE APOLOGY: THAT THE VULGATE EDITION OF THE EPISTLES OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PAUL IS NOT BY JEROME.

# CANONS OF THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS.

### CHAPTER I.
<margin>1</margin> ¶ Concerning the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; that Christ is of the seed of David; concerning his resurrection from the dead.
<margin>2</margin> ¶ Concerning thanksgivings for present and past goods; concerning prayer for future things.
<margin>3</margin> ¶ Concerning the fruit of the Gospel in every nation, among both the wise
<margin>4</margin> and the unwise. ¶ Concerning not being ashamed of the Gospel, because it leads to salvation: both for the Gentiles and the Jews; that the future life shall be from faith.
<margin>5</margin> ¶ Concerning divine vengeance against those who have knowledge of God and live unjustly; how creation reveals the Creator and accuses the unjust.
<margin>6</margin> ¶ Concerning the ungrateful, the presumptuous, and those who vainly judge themselves to be wise: how they are deserted by God and, left in their own darkness, miserably rave and vanish
<margin>7</margin> into utter absurdities. ¶ How idolatry originated from this. ¶ How those
<margin>8</margin> abandoning God—who is supreme holiness, purity, perfection, and truth—are engulfed in all manner of uncleanness, bodily harm, and
<margin>9</margin> falsehood. ¶ From this, sins against nature bubble up; against which all creation seeks vengeance from God.
<margin>10</margin> ¶ That such persons lack no vice of flesh or mind: they are worthy of eternal death.

# CANONS. CHAPTER II.
<margin>II</margin>
<margin>11</margin> ¶ That the wicked who rebuke the unjust are not excused.
<margin>12</margin> ¶ That neither they, nor those who are rebuked, shall escape the true judgment of God.
<margin>13</margin> ¶ Concerning the kindness of God, His long and merciful expectation, concerning repentance, the obstinate, those who work well and those who work ill; concerning eternal life, glory, honor, and the incorruptibility of the good; concerning the
<margin>14</margin> eternal punishments of the wicked. ¶ That God will judge all: both those before the Law, those under the Old Law, and those under the New Law. God gave these laws not primarily just so they would be known, but so that those hearing them might act according to them; for they are like the
<margin>15</margin> prescriptions of a physician. ¶ Concerning the law of nature: how God engraved it into minds from the very beginning of creation for

<column-break/>

Rom.
1
2
