</margin>
<margin>16</margin> acting according to it until the final day, even if it does not suffice for life, for faith completes it; for life is from faith. ¶ That the Jewish law did not benefit—but even hindered—the one who knew it but acted contrary to it, leading to the dishonoring of God. And so it is for every law: for the one who knows it and does the opposite.
<margin>17</margin> ¶ Concerning circumcision: how God accepted it as valid based on obedience to the law and action.
<margin>18</margin> ¶ Similarly also concerning uncircumcision in the New Law; how both flesh and the "letter" <note>original: "litera"; referring to the literal or outward observation of the law</note> were attached to circumcision, and now the spirit is attached to uncircumcision.

# CANONS. CHAPTER III.
<margin>III</margin>
<margin>20</margin> ¶ That the Jews were the first to believe the words of God.
<margin>21</margin> ¶ That because of the unbelief of some, the old law of God was no less true; the same must be thought of the New Law (because it is far truer and more eminent than the old).
<margin>22</margin> ¶ That the justice of God is recognized even in the injustices of the wicked.
<margin>23</margin> ¶ In the lying works of men, God manifests Himself more abundantly as truthful (which is good) to His own glory, by punishing lying deeds more severely; however, evil must not be done so that such good things may result.

<margin>26</margin> the law pointed out. ¶ That justification from God happens in the whole world, among every people and nation following
<margin>27</margin> faith in Christ. ¶ Concerning the remission of sins, justification freely given and through the sole grace of our Lord Jesus Christ. For it is grace that justifies as a "formal cause" <note>original: "forma"; in philosophy, this is the essential nature that makes something what it is</note>, not works; just as whiteness makes a swan white, and not its flight or its sitting in a lake. God, however, justifies as the "efficient cause" <note>original: "efficiens"; the agent or force that brings an effect into being</note> and the giver of grace; for He is just, and thus justifies, like the sun which, being heat-giving, heats things.
<margin>28</margin> ¶ That one must not glory in works, but in God and His grace through faith in our Lord Jesus Christ.

In his commentaries, the holy <term>Jerome<span>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD) was the scholar traditionally credited with translating the Bible into Latin (the Vulgate).</span></term> either criticizes or corrects all these things: sometimes rebuking the Latin translator, other times the common <term>Vulgate<span>The "Vulgata" or common version of the Latin Bible used by the Western Church for centuries.</span></term> interpretation. We have demonstrated this all the more diligently so that the widespread error—introduced by the style of translations we commonly use—might be completely uprooted from the minds of men, who have already been persuaded by false common rumor. We hope that this false persuasion might no longer find any place to hide.

It was our purpose to show this concerning the common translation of the epistles of the most blessed Paul, and we have done so. Yet we grieve that this is the state of things, and that we do not instead possess Jerome's own original translation. Anyone who is willing to carefully study the commentaries of that holy teacher of the Church, Jerome, on this passage—"and he might cleanse for himself an acceptable people" in the second chapter of the Epistle to Titus—will clearly understand. (I leave aside other passages from his other commentaries on various books of Holy Scripture, of which there is a rich abundance of evidence, for the sake of brevity). 

From these examples, one will see that not only the translation of Paul's epistles, but even the translation of the Gospels which the Church now uses, is not actually the work of Jerome. This is why we must grieve even more: that such great and illustrious labors of that most blessed man and holiest doctor of the church, which he undertook for the public benefit of all the faithful and the studious, have perished—if indeed they have perished for us and for those who come after us. 

But if this is the case, and if Christ our Lord—the true light, and the only true and unfailing light—should enlighten someone in the future to restore those things which have been lost to us (though they were once restored in the past), that person must not be attacked with envy or ill will. Instead, whoever they may be, the grace of Christ must be honored in them. To Him alone all honor is due, all glory, and thanksgiving, in all things and over all ages of ages. Amen.

---

->MOST BLESSED PAUL THE APOSTLE<-
->IS NOT BY JEROME.<-

In his commentaries, the holy Jerome <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD) was the scholar traditionally credited with the Vulgate translation of the Bible.</note> either critiques or directs all these things: sometimes rebuking the Latin translator, at other times the common <term>Vulgate</term> <note>The standard Latin Bible used by the Roman Catholic Church.</note> translation. We have shown this all the more diligently so that the public error—introduced by the logic of the translations we commonly use—might be thoroughly uprooted from the minds of men who have been falsely persuaded by common rumor, and so that false persuasion might have no further hiding places.

It was our purpose to demonstrate this regarding the customary translation of the epistles of the most blessed Paul (which we have done), grieving nonetheless that it was so, and that we did not instead possess the translation of Jerome himself. Whoever wishes to diligently observe these same commentaries of the holy doctor of the church, Jerome, upon this passage, "and might cleanse for himself an acceptable people" in the second chapter of the Epistle to Titus (I leave aside other passages from his other commentaries on other books of Holy Scripture, of which there is manifold evidence and rich abundance, for the sake of brevity), will clearly understand from the same that not only the translation of Paul’s epistles, but even that of the Gospels which the Church now uses, is not Jerome's work.

Therefore, it is all the more to be lamented that such great and clear labors of that most blessed man and holiest doctor of the Church—which he had undertaken for the public benefit of all the pious and the studious—have perished, if indeed they are entirely lost to us and to posterity. But if this be so, and if Christ the Lord—the true light, and the only true and unfailing light—should enlighten any of our descendants to restore those things which are lost to us, though once restored in the past: he must not be pursued with envy or any ill will, but in him (whoever he may eventually be) the grace of Christ must be honored. To Him alone be all honor, and all glory, and thanksgiving, in all things, and above all, for ever and ever. Amen.

<margin>76</margin> ¶ Concerning the sadness of Paul: on account of the memory of his ingratitude toward such great love of God and Christ. ->II<-

<margin>1 Corinthians 9 & 10</margin>
Regarding the preaching of the gospel: bringing along a faithful wife, and not working with one’s own hands for food while preaching—even if one were neither to eat nor drink from the proceeds of preaching, nor lead around a "sister-wife" <note>original: "vxorem sororem," a reference to a Christian wife or a woman assisting in ministry</note>, but instead worked manually to provide for a living and to meet bodily needs.

<margin>62</margin>
¶ Because the necessity of preaching the gospel was imposed upon him, whether he was willing or unwilling, just as Jonah’s preaching was to the Ninevites. He carried this out willingly, and beyond what was commanded, he added this: that he did it without cost or burden to his listeners.

<margin>63</margin>
¶ He considers it a great reward for himself: that he can provide the gospel through his own labors without the expense or burden of others; that he becomes the servant of all, so that he might win everyone for Christ; accommodating himself to the Jews as a Jew, to those under the law as one under the law, and to those without the law as one without the law, so that he might acquire everyone for Christ, eventually becoming himself a sharer in the gospel.

<margin>64</margin>
¶ Because the faithful are placed in this world as if in a racing stadium, they must run with all their strength toward the crown of immortality.

<margin>65</margin>
¶ Because Paul himself ran toward that crown not as if toward something uncertain, but by constantly chastising himself through preaching, labor, and the exhaustion of his body: lest while he urged others to the race, he himself might not likewise receive that crown. When this crown is received by one, it does not prevent another from receiving the same. For the crown of immortality is like the flame of a candle, which all other candles may take for themselves while the original flame remains whole and unharmed; so it is for those who reach the crown of immortality by running.

<margin>X</margin>
### CANONS CHAPTER X.

<margin>66</margin>
¶ What the cloud, the sea, the manna, the drink from the rock, and the punishments following the desires for carnal food, idolatries, and fornica-

<column-break/>

-tions, and the grumblings of the children of Israel, prefigured for us.

<margin>67</margin>
¶ That we must be vigilant: lest we fall away from the spirit. For God does not allow us to be tempted beyond human strength; and when temptation is present, he helps us to overcome if we struggle with all our might, and he provides a happy outcome.

<margin>68</margin>
¶ Concerning the fleeing of idolatry. Concerning the communion of the cup of the Lord, and the heavenly bread, which is the body and blood of Christ. Under the "fleeing of idolatry," every vice is prohibited. For the greedy man, worshipping riches, is like a worshipper of Dis <note>The Roman god of the underworld and wealth</note>. The lustful man, worshipping the act of fornication, is like a worshipper of Venus. The glutton is like a worshipper of Ceres. The drunkard is like a worshipper of Bacchus. The ambitious man is like a worshipper of Jupiter and Juno. The angry man and lover of slaughter is like a worshipper of Mars. And those living in this way still obey these demons through the work of idolatry, even if not through public sacrifices and offerings.

<margin>69</margin>
¶ Because those living in such a way cannot participate in the cup of the Lord and the union with his holy and undefiled body. Instead, they provoke God to a jealousy of vengeance, from whose hand no one can be rescued.

<margin>70</margin>
¶ Not everything that is within our power should be done: but only that which is beneficial to us, and which builds up <term>edifies</term> others.

<margin>71</margin>
¶ Concerning the great liberty which has been given to us in Christ. However, it is not always to be used when it does not build up, or when it offends the conscience of another. When we use it, it must be used in all things with thanksgiving for the glory of God, seeking to please everyone for their benefit and holy edification.

->II<-

<margin>1 Cor. 14</margin>
The spiritual things of God are to be desired: and the gift of prophecy <note>The author uses "prophecy" here in the sense of inspired preaching or the interpretation of Scripture for the community.</note> more so than that of tongues, because it is a more universal gift for edification <note>original: "ædificationem charisma"</note>.

<margin>97</margin> 
¶ By the gift of tongues, a person edifies himself, praising and magnifying God in that tongue, though it remains unknown to others. By the gift of prophecy, he edifies the church and the entire assembly. 

<margin>98</margin> 
¶ That the gift of tongues alone is a small thing; but when combined with the gift of interpretation, it is greater and more excellent. 

<margin>99</margin> 
¶ That one speaking from a gift but without an interpreter is like a flute or a harp <note>original: "tibiæ aut citharæ"</note> sounding some divine praise or song that is not intelligible to those listening. 

<margin>100</margin> 
¶ That one speaking from a gift is considered a "Barbarian" <note>original: "Barbarus". In the classical and biblical context, this refers to someone speaking a language that the listener does not understand.</note> by those who do not understand him. Thus, it is often not the fault of the speaker, but the ignorance of the listener, that an injustice is done to the Spirit of God. Ignorance and presumption among men often cause similar offenses regarding other gifts. 

<margin>101</margin> 
¶ That the gifts of the Spirit are to be requested not for the sake of curiosity, but for edification. If anyone is given a tongue to speak and a spirit to pray, he ought to ask—for the sake of both his own and others' edification—for the grace of interpretation and the gift of understanding, so that he can pray both in spirit and in mind, and help others by interpreting what he speaks in the spirit. And so it is regarding other gifts. 

<margin>102</margin> 
¶ That we ought not to be children in our minds; rather, we should have senses that are worthy of God, perfect, and manly. But in matters of malice and cunning, we should be like little children. 

<margin>103</margin> 
¶ That the gift of tongues was given as a sign to unbelievers, so that they might repent upon seeing it; but prophecy is given for believers. 

<margin>104</margin> 
¶ That the gift of prophecy can be less easily condemned or despised than the gift of tongues. 

<margin>105</margin> 
¶ That each person should turn his own gift, as the Spirit of God deigns to bestow it, toward the work of edification. 

<margin>106</margin> 
¶ That in the administration and exercise of these gifts, order must be maintained, and confusion and disorder avoided. 

<margin>107</margin> 
¶ That one possessing a gift should yield his place to another who also has a gift. All the more so if the one who is to be 

<column-break/>

<margin>108</margin> 
believed has a superior gift; and there should be no pride <note>original: "tumor", literally a swelling or puffed-up state</note> or contention among those possessing the gifts of the Spirit. ¶ That it is not permitted for women to speak in the public assembly <note>original: "cōtione", a public gathering or sermon</note> of the church. 

<margin>109</margin> 
¶ That the gifts of the Holy Spirit are not to be forbidden; rather, all of them (whenever they are present by His grace) are to be admitted honorably and without confusion.

### CANONS OF CHAPTER XV.

<margin>110</margin> 
¶ That Paul received the Gospel by the gift of the Holy Spirit: concerning the death of Christ for our sins, His burial, His resurrection on the third day, and His appearance after the resurrection. 

<margin>111</margin> 
¶ That the grace of God made him—a former persecutor and entirely unworthy in himself—into an apostle; and that the grace of God worked more abundantly in him than in the others.

### CANONS. CHAPTER XII.

61 ¶ That one must not boast, neither in prosperity nor in adversity; and concerning Paul being caught up into Paradise. <note>original: "de raptu Pauli in Paradisum" — referring to the "Third Heaven" experience described in 2 Corinthians 12:2-4.</note>
62 ¶ The saints, to whom God does magnificent things and reveals secrets, ought not to commit and manifest these to everyone. This is because many do not know how to give glory to God, but instead attribute to men what they owe to God, as if these men were something of themselves.
63 ¶ Concerning the pressures according to the flesh <term>secundum carnem: referring to physical suffering or worldly opposition</term> which the evil one stirred up against Paul, who was so wonderfully comforted according to the mind by divine infusions and revelations. Paul overcame these pressures of the evil one not by his own strength, but by that which is most sufficient for all: the grace of Christ.
64 ¶ The more the pressure increased beyond human strength, the more abundant was the grace of God delivering him. Thus, Paul was then stronger than he was when outside of those pressures; and in his weaknesses, he boasted in the abundance of God’s grace.
65 ¶ Paul became "foolish" for the sake of the Corinthians who were thinking carnally. <note>original: "carnaliter sapientibus" — those focused on worldly status rather than spiritual truth.</note> Yet for the spiritual, he was always truly sober and wise in divine things.
66 ¶ A spiritual man ought not to be broken or discouraged from doing good and wishing well by the disobedience or neglect of others. Thus, the malice of the wicked should not overcome the impulse to provide and impart good things.
67 ¶ In spiritual people, there is no deceit, even if those of the world <note>original: "terreni" — the "earthly" or worldly-minded.</note> suspect deceit.
68 ¶ When good men are forced to punish the wicked, it brings about a certain humiliation, dejection, and sadness for them before God. Also concerning the place of repentance after sins have been committed.

<margin>XIII</margin>

### CANONS. CHAPTER XIII.

69 ¶ If warnings do not benefit those who sin, one must act with threats. If they are not corrected by threats, having been convicted by witnesses, they must be punished for the deed.
70 ¶ The power by which the wicked are punished is from God. This power is weak neither in itself nor in those who punish, but is firm, powerful, and valid.
71 ¶ God must be prayed to, even by those who punish,

<column-break/>

<margin>2 Corinthians</margin>

73 ¶ One must strive toward perfection and the consolation of the Spirit. And one must believe that very thing which the saints teach.

# CANONS OF THE EPISTLE
# TO THE EPHESIANS
# CHAPTER I.

1 ¶ A greeting in God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ.
2 ¶ That thanksgiving must be offered in recognition of the immense benefits of God: such as the fullness of blessing with which we have been blessed in Christ; the election before the foundation of the world to a spiritual and immaculate <note>pure or stainless</note> life; the adoption in Christ and through Christ the Lord; redemption and the remission of sins through His blood; and similar ineffable <note>too great to be expressed in words</note> benefits of His mercy and 3 grace. ¶ Because those who believe in Christ are sealed with the Holy Spirit to receive the inheritance of the promise, for the eternal 4 praise of God. ¶ That thanks must be given to God upon hearing of the holy conduct of others, and God must be prayed to, so that He might increase His graces in them for a more perfect knowledge of Himself, and the excellence of His divine gifts for loving, venerating, and worshiping Him. Concerning the resurrection of Christ and His seating at the right hand of God, above all principality and power, and every name that can be named. Because

<column-break/>

Christ is the head of the church: the church is indeed the body and the fullness of Christ, who nonetheless fills all things in all people. For what would He not fill, who is the infinite fullness: above all things, beneath all things, outside all things, within all things, surrounding and nourishing, sustaining and supporting, gathering and collecting, binding together, fastening, and uniting all things?

<margin>II</margin>
# CANONS OF CHAPTER II.
5 ¶ Concerning the former error of life, in which we served the flesh and the spirit of the power of the air, the prince of darkness <note>referring to the devil or spiritual forces of evil</note>. He still rules over those who are carnal <note>focused on worldly or physical desires</note> and not firmly persuaded in faith. From him, the grace and mercy of God, which is rich toward all, has liberated us by putting our sins to death and bringing the dead to life in the resurrection of a new life, making us sit together in the heavenly places. This was to show the surpassing riches of His grace and kindness toward us: saved by grace in His beloved Son, by receiving faith in the Son of God, and not from our own works. Thus, no one should be ungrateful toward God, 6 boasting in their own works. ¶ Because it is fitting for us to be mindful of this great and unthinkable grace toward us: that Christ is our peace, reconciling both the Gentiles <note>non-Jewish people</note> and the Hebrews, who were perpetually like two opposites carrying on hostilities against each other. He made them one, having destroyed the enmities through the death of His cross, preaching peace to all—both those who were near and those who were far off—making everyone sons of the eternal Father, and creating access to Him through Himself. 7 ¶ Because we are citizens with the saints and members of God's household: built upon the firm rock, Christ, the foundation of the apostles and prophets, and made a holy temple to God in the Holy Spirit.

<margin>III</margin>
# CANONS OF CHAPTER III.
8 ¶ So that the temple of God might be built from the Gentiles, sanctified by the Holy Spirit, Paul did not fear prisons, chains, and all the losses of this present life; for even that sublime mystery of God...

**Q**uathat before the apostles, it had not been revealed that the Gentiles <note>Non-Jewish people</note> were to be incorporated into the Son of God, and were to be co-heirs of the promises of Abraham and his children. For the opening of this mystery to the Gentiles by God the Father, who created all things through Jesus Christ, Paul was appointed as a minister.
<margin>10</margin> ¶ That one must not succumb or lose heart in the tribulations of the upright; and in what manner the good and holy pray for confirmation, faith, love, and the knowledge of the great graces of God, which are to be bestowed on others by God, for glory, and for the giving of thanks throughout all generations of the ages.

<margin>IIII</margin> ->CANONS. CHAPTER IV.<-

<margin>11</margin> ¶ That the faithful are to be exhorted to walk worthily in the calling of the faithful, to think humbly, toward gentleness, toward patience, toward mutual support, toward the bond of peace, and the unity of body and spirit. For the Lord of all is one over all, through all, and in all. One faith, and one baptism.
<margin>12</margin> ¶ That each person has as much grace as Christ gives; and concerning his descent into the lower regions <note>original: "ad inferos," a reference to the Harrowing of Hell, the belief that Christ descended to the realm of the dead before his resurrection</note>.
<margin>13</margin> and his ascent to the heavens. ¶ Concerning the various degrees of Christ's graces granted for the building up of his body <note>The Church</note>; in the building of which, charity and love glue and connect all parts together, so that nothing is dislocated or gapes open.
<margin>14</margin> ¶ In the manner that the Gentiles walk: the faithful must not walk thus. For they [the Gentiles] walk according to the flesh, according to the "old man" <note>The sinful nature prior to conversion</note>; these [the faithful] must walk according to the spirit, according to the man of the new creation, in justice and true holiness.
<margin>15</margin> ¶ That the passions of the flesh are to be set aside or continually repressed.
<margin>16</margin> ¶ That where there are works of darkness, an entry is given to the devil; whom it is necessary to exclude by the performance of work with the hands, by holy speech of the mouth, and by the holy operation of every part of the body and soul. For the doing of these things, the gifts of Christ are not lacking.

<margin>18</margin> ¶ That the followers of fleshly and irrational passions will not inherit the kingdom of God.

<margin>20</margin> ¶ Concerning the horrific and wicked deeds of those who dissuade from the truth of God; which horror and unspeakable foulness they do not even recognize because they are in darkness, sleeping and dead. Nevertheless, Christ is ready to awaken and raise them from the dead and enlighten them, so that they may see their horror, if they wish to come to their senses.

# CANONS OF THE EPISTLE TO THE PHILIPPIANS.
### CHAPTER I.

<margin>Philippians 1 2 I</margin>
1 ¶ **A** greeting in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
2 ¶ **T**hanksgiving to God for the holy conduct of the Philippians, and a prayer to God: that He may increase grace in them until the day of the Lord's coming, to the glory and honor of God.
3 ¶ **T**hat from persecutions and the endurance of those who suffer, the faith of Christ grows. In this matter, however it may happen, one must rejoice; because Christ is the life of the faithful who live, and for those who die, He is life and gain. Therefore, the state of those passing from this present dark life is better.
4 ¶ **T**hat God’s kindness again brings forth the life of the good for the salvation of others. Therefore, one must never cease from exhorting others to lead a life in the service of Christ according to their dignity, neither being softened by prosperity nor cast down by adversity.

<margin>II IV</margin>
### CANONS OF CHAPTER II.
5 ¶ **T**hat one should be of the same mind, in one love, in unanimity, in humility of feeling, in mutual subjection, and by imitating the humility of Christ. Though He was God and equal to God, He humbled himself, becoming obedient even unto death—indeed, a death of the greatest humiliation and the shame of the cross. Now He is exalted above all things, possessing a name before which they bow: those in heaven, those on earth, and those in the underworld.
6 ¶ **T**hat it is God who works in the faithful both the will and the deed; we ought to run along with and cooperate with this according to our manly strength. For the good shine among the wicked in this world like stars in the sky.
7 ¶ **T**hat a concern and desire takes hold of the saints: to know the state

<column-break/>

of those who are absent in their Christian conduct.
8 ¶ **T**hat even in the absence of a pastor, those who are absent should be confirmed in the faith through the presence of others who have been committed to them.

<margin>III</margin>
### CANONS OF CHAPTER III.
9 ¶ **T**hat one must especially beware of those who wish to pull people from spiritual things toward fleshly things: from confidence in the grace of Christ through faith, to confidence in works.
10 ¶ **T**hat in this life the heavenly prize <term>brauium</term> <note>original: "brauium," a prize or reward given to the winner of a race or contest</note> is not fully grasped; rather, one must always run toward the things ahead and never slip back toward evil, so that at the end of the race—which is the boundary of this life—we may receive the ineffable gift of the divine grant and the immortal palm of our race.
11 ¶ **T**hat just as Paul and the saints did, so we must run, imitating Christ, fleeing the enemies of the cross, and meditating on the future goods from the gift of Christ. He will transform the bodies of our mortality and make them conform to the splendor of His glory.

<margin>IIII</margin>
### CANONS OF CHAPTER IV.
12 ¶ **T**hat one must stand firm in the Lord.
13 ¶ **T**hat it is necessary to be concerned not only for men, but also for the sanctity and every assistance of women. By thinking on gentleness and the approaching end of life, one should pray without anxiety, making petitions and giving thanks to God. For the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, is that which can save both hearts and minds.
14 ¶ **T**hat all truth, honesty, justice, purity, and everything lovable and praiseworthy is to be pursued, so that the God of peace may dwell with us.
15 ¶ **T**hat regarding the work of mercy to be shown to the poor, the Philippians finally agreed with the apostle; for this, he gives thanks to God. For he who understands this is like a green tree. He who does not is like a dead tree, bearing no fruit.
16 ¶ **T**hat regarding benefits received, it is never fitting for us to be ungrateful or forgetful toward either God or men. Furthermore, thanks for benefactors must be poured out abundantly.
17 ¶ **A** greeting and a prayer for the grace of Christ, which is more desirable than any other good. Wi-

<margin>Colossians 1 2</margin>
### CHAPTER I.

<margin>I</margin>
1 ¶ **A** greeting in the grace and peace of God our Father and of our Lord Jesus Christ.
2 ¶ **T**hat thanks must be given to God when the good conduct of others is heard of; moreover, prayers should be added: that God may grant perseverance and the increase of every grace. Furthermore, thanks and prayers are to be poured out for one’s own benefits and the divine graces surrounding oneself, with continual meditation on the redemption and remission of sins granted to us in the beloved Son of God.
3 ¶ **T**hat Christ is the image of the invisible God; that He was born before every creature, visible and invisible <note>original: 'genit⁹ prior omni creatura', a reference to Christ's eternal nature</note>; that through Him and in Him all things were established. That He who is the beginning of all things is the head of the church. That He is the first of those rising again in a true and perfected resurrection, in whom all fullness dwells, through whose blood all things, both heavenly and earthly, have been reconciled.
4 ¶ **A**ll who persevere in faith and the hope of the gospel, having been reconciled to God through the blood of His Son, are established by Christ as holy, immaculate, and irreproachable in His sight. Also, that Christ suffers in His holy members <note>referring to the suffering of believers</note> so that the church, which is His body, may be saved. Paul was appointed by Christ for this mystery, hidden for so many ages, to be opened to the nations.

### CANONS OF CHAPTER II.
<margin>II</margin>
5 ¶ **C**oncerning the zeal, care, anxiety, and struggle of Paul: so that all might know the mystery of God, for the pious and for Christ, which is the holy gospel in which all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden away.
6 ¶ **T**hat

<column-break/>

<margin>Colossians 2 3</margin>
one must especially beware of the persuasion of the eloquence of the ungodly, and of those philosophizing emptily about divine matters.
7 ¶ **T**hat the fullness of divinity dwells in the body of Christ, and that the faithful are filled with divinity, derived into them from the head, who is Christ. Concerning the spiritual circumcision of our flesh from sins in Christ, and our death, burial, and co-resurrection in baptism.
¶ **T**hat the handwritten record of our obligation <note>original: 'chirographum', a legal bond or debt-note representing sin</note> was taken away from the prince of darkness, fixed to the cross of Christ and deleted, after the evil powers were stripped of the human race (which they were miserably holding as slaves and captives).
8 ¶ **T**hat since the truth is present: no one is to be judged or accused if they no longer care for the shadow of truth <note>referring to the Jewish ceremonial laws as 'shadows' of the reality found in Christ</note>.
9 ¶ **T**hat the worship and veneration of angels must be fled from.
10 ¶ **T**hat such curious doctrines are neither to be touched, nor tasted, nor handled; all of these lead to corruption, pretending to be hidden wisdom while actually containing vain madness and superstition.

### CANONS OF CHAPTER III.
<margin>III</margin>
11 ¶ **W**e who have risen with Christ ought to seek the things that are above, where Christ sits at the right hand of the Father; to feel those things that are above, not those upon the earth and below. To care for the hidden life by which we live with Christ, not the manifest earthly life. For the hidden life shall be made manifest eternally, and the manifest life shall pass away and disappear like smoke.
12 ¶ **T**he members of the flesh, which are harmful affections, are to be mortified upon the earth; and those works of harmful affections, because of which the wrath of God, vengeance, and retribution come upon the earth.
¶ **T**hat the old man must be completely stripped off, and the new man put on, who is created according to the image of God, according to the image of the Son of God, and in Christ, Christ.
13 ¶ **T**hat every spiritual gift <note>original: 'charisima'</note> and every work of virtue is an ornament of the new man, such as mercy, kindness, humility, gentleness, patien—

# CANONS OF THE FIRST EPISTLE TO THE THESSALONIANS CHAPTER I.
1 ¶ A greeting in the grace and peace of God the Father and of the Lord Jesus Christ. 
2 ¶ The giving of thanks and prayer to God: for the faith, hope, and charity of others. 
3 ¶ That for the grace of the salvation of others, God gives the word, the power, and the ability to perform signs in the Holy Spirit.

<margin>Chapter 2</margin>
## CANONS OF CHAPTER II.
4 ¶ What sort of people those ought to be to whom the preaching of the Gospel of Christ is entrusted. 
5 ¶ That far from

<column-break/>

such people should be flattery, greed, and the desire for glory. 
6 ¶ That they should be as little a burden as possible: but of the same mind as a nurse is toward her own children. 
7 ¶ That it is better to work with one's hands for a living than to live off what is distributed, even for those who instruct others toward the blessed life with all their effort. 
8 ¶ That God works in those who receive His word. 
9 ¶ That the Jews killed the Lord Jesus and their own prophets, and persecuted the apostles of God, and prohibited the word of salvation from being brought to the Gentiles, whence the wrath of God came upon them even to the end. 
10 ¶ That in persecutions they are to be comforted: and even, if possible, visited in person by a friend—I do not mean an ordinary friend, but one of Christian and spiritual friendship.

<margin>Chapter 3</margin>
## CANONS OF CHAPTER III.
11 ¶ He who cannot help in person during times of necessity should help through another faithful person, lest those afflicted by pressures should succumb to temptations. 
12 ¶ That upon hearing of the faith and love of others, one should rejoice in spirit and in God, and pray that nothing be lacking for the perfection of their faith and love. 
13 ¶ In all things to be done: the holy help of God the Father and of our Lord Jesus Christ is to be invoked, both concerning oneself and concerning others.

<margin>Chapter 4</margin>
## CANONS OF CHAPTER IV.
14 ¶ That one must walk and please God, just as the holy apostles handed down how one should walk and please Him; and God provides the increase of grace. For they themselves know the will of God: not those who, according to human wisdom, pre-determine how life is to be lived and how one must walk and please. 
15 ¶ That the will of God is our sanctification: that each person should keep the temple of God—both body and soul—in honor and sanctification, and in all the justice of God. 
16 ¶ He who despises the precepts of the apostles despises not man but God, who poured them out through the Holy Spirit. ¶ That brotherly love, that is, the love of those reborn and spiritual brothers, is the command of God. 
17 ¶ That for a Christian man, to work with his own hands...

### CANONS <note>Summaries or Rules</note> OF CHAPTER V.

<margin>20</margin> ¶ That the day of the Lord will arrive suddenly, like a thief in the night. 
<margin>21</margin> ¶ That the children of Christ are children of the light and of the day; therefore they must not sleep, nor perform the works of night and darkness. <margin>22</margin> ¶ That mutual exhortation for building one another up <note>original: 'aedificationem'</note> must not be neglected. 
<margin>23</margin> ¶ Those who lead in the exhortation and teaching of Christ are to be held in greater honor and love, and are to be obeyed peacefully. The unruly are to be warned, the faint-hearted comforted, the weak assisted, and patience must be maintained toward all. Evil is to be returned to no one for evil; one must always rejoice in the spirit, pray constantly, give thanks in all things, and not quench the spirit. Prophecies are not to be despised; all things must be examined, the good held fast, and one must abstain from every evil. 
<margin>24</margin> ¶ That good things are to be prayed for on behalf of others, from whom the benefit of prayers should also be requested.

<margin>2 Thessalonians 1</margin>
### CHAPTER I.

¶ Greeting in the grace and peace of God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

<column-break/>

<margin>2 Thessalonians 1:1, 2, 3</margin>
¶ Thanks must be given to God for the increase of faith and the multiplication of love for one another, and there should be rejoicing for patience in persecutions and pressures, through which people are made worthy of the kingdom of God. 
¶ That the justice of God will give rest on the day of judgment to those pressured and troubled for the faith; when He shall take vengeance in a flaming fire upon those who did not know God, and who did not obey the Gospel. 
<margin>4</margin> ¶ That prayer must be made for all the faithful: that God may make them worthy of His calling, and fulfill every good will and work, so that the name of our Lord Jesus Christ may be glorified.

<margin>II</margin>
### CANONS OF CHAPTER II.

### CHAPTER I.

1 ¶ Salvation in grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ.
2 ¶ It is the duty of bishops <note>original: 'Episcoporum'</note> to keep watch: so that doctrines are not taught differently in various places, and that they are not fables, argumentative, or contentious.
3 ¶ Nothing should be permitted to be taught which opposes love from a pure heart, a good conscience, and sincere faith.
4 ¶ The Old Law: a law for the sick, which is not imposed upon the righteous man, for he is healthy. The Gospel: the law for the healthy <note>This reflects a common Reformation-era distinction between the Law, which exposes sin/sickness, and the Gospel, which provides spiritual health.</note>.
5 ¶ The benefits of God and His immense graces must be kept in memory, against our imperfections and ingratitude.
6 ¶ Christ came: so that He might save through His grace the sinners believing in Him, who otherwise by themselves and their own works would have perished forever.
7 ¶ That there is only one King of ages; immortal, invisible, God who is wise in Himself, to whom honor and glory is owed for ages of ages.
8 ¶ The graces of God must be stirred up, and a good conscience must be maintained.

<margin>II</margin>

## CANONS OF CHAPTER II.

8 ¶ The faithful people are to be instructed: toward prayers, orations, supplications, and thanksgivings for all men, for kings and whoever is placed in power, so that all may spend their present life in peace, tranquility, in all piety and honesty. For this is the will and good pleasure of our Savior God.
9 ¶ One must believe in one God, and one mediator, Jesus Christ: who

<column-break/>

9 gave Himself as a redemption for all. ¶ Instruction of men: and that men ought to pray in every place, lifting up pure hands to God, defiled by no crime, nor by anger, nor by any other lust whatsoever.
11 ¶ Instruction of women: regarding their adornment, teaching, subjection, and silence.

## CANONS OF CHAPTER IIII.

15 ¶ Prophecies: concerning future apostates and heretics regarding marriage and abstinence from foods.
16 ¶ It is the duty of bishops: to nourish the people with words of faith and sound Gospel doctrine.
17 ¶ Fables: are to be avoided in teaching the people. For such things are more fitting for doting old women—though they do not even suit them—than for a bishop and a teacher of the people.
18 ¶ Every exercise of a bishop: ought to be toward piety and the worship of divinity. For this exercise has the promise of the present and future life. Therefore, the bishop who neglects this and exercises himself in other things loses both the present and future life.
19 ¶ It befits a bishop most of all men, in every turn of fortune, to hope in the living God, who is the savior of all, but especially of the faithful.

21 ¶ A bishop ought to attend to sacred reading, exhortation, and doctrine, and by no means neglect the gifts of God within him. Doing so, he saves both himself and the people entrusted to him. By doing otherwise, he drowns both himself and the entrusted people in the abyss <note>original: 'barathrum'; a deep pit or hell</note>.

### CANONS <note>Rules or summaries</note> CHAPTER V.

<margin>V</margin>
<margin>22</margin> In what way a bishop <note>original: 'episcopus'</note> must conduct himself toward the elderly, the young men, the old women, the young girls, the widows, and every station of life: holily, chastely, and blamelessly.
<margin>23</margin> ¶ The command concerning widows who have children or grandchildren: those who are able to manage the care of the household affairs.
<margin>24</margin> ¶ Who is: a true widow.
<margin>25</margin> ¶ Who is a widow: not a true one, but dead to Christ.
<margin>26</margin> ¶ That it is the bishop's concern to command such things: so that everyone may provide irreproachable care for their household and domestic servants.
<margin>27</margin> ¶ Which widow: is to be supported from the sacred funds.
<margin>28</margin> ¶ That younger widows: are not to be supported from the sacred funds.
<margin>29</margin> ¶ For younger widows: second marriages are permitted for the procreation of children.
<margin>30</margin> ¶ That the church is not to be burdened in providing for widows: except for true widows.
<margin>31</margin> ¶ Elders <note>original: 'Presbyteros'</note> who lead well by example and word: are to be honored with double honor, both earthly and spiritual.
<margin>32</margin> ¶ Accusations against elders—that is, the seniors—are not to be easily admitted: unless sufficient witnesses are present.
<margin>33</margin> ¶ Where they are convicted of having sinned: they are to be rebuked in front of everyone to strike terror into others.
<margin>34</margin> ¶ These things, under the threat of divine oath, every bishop must observe, and he must attempt nothing by his own personal opinion: but judge according to preceding judgments and the forms handed down to the saints, doing nothing through favor or the patronage of others.
<margin>35</margin> ¶ A bishop should not easily lay hands <note>original: 'manus... imponere'; referring to the rite of ordination</note> on others to be consecrated: lest he admit unworthy men into the service of the eternal King, and be held guilty for their unworthiness and wicked lives.
<margin>36</margin> ¶ Above all, it befits a bishop to cherish good testimony.
<margin>37</margin> ¶ He must care for his health with honorable sobriety: so that he may be of use to the people in the service of Christ.
<margin>38</margin> ¶ He must show himself to be good not only openly, but also in secret: because neither good nor evil things will remain hidden in the end, whatever may have come before them.

<column-break/>

<margin>1 Timothy 6</margin>

### CANONS CHAPTER VI.

<margin>VI</margin>
<margin>39</margin> ¶ Instruction for faithful servants who have unbelieving masters.
<margin>40</margin> ¶ Instruction for the servants of faithful masters.
<margin>41</margin> ¶ That a bishop must teach in this way. He who does otherwise: is vain and proud, holding nothing of the knowledge of God. And therefore, knowing nothing, he loves battles and contentions over words: from which innumerable evils gush forth.
<margin>42</margin> ¶ It befits a bishop especially to be far removed from the greed for gain: and to be far from those who, with every intention, sweat for profit, thinking that piety consists of gain and increasing those secular goods which they claim belong to the church. But having food and the means to be clothed according to the dignity of his position: he should be content.
<margin>43</margin> ¶ Those who strive to become rich in this world: how many evils follow them. For that greed: is the root of all evils.
<margin>44</margin> ¶ That every bishop should flee gain and avarice. Why should he spend his whole days on the preservation, gain, increase, or interest <note>original: 'fenori'; often used for usury or financial lending</note> of the earthly goods of the church? This is the devil's mousetrap and the nets of a decorated excuse <note>original: 'phaleratae excusationis'; literally "harnessed" or "ornamental" excuses that look good but are deceptive</note>; this is a fake and lying piety. But let him pursue justice, piety, true faith, love, patience, and gentleness; let him fight the good fight of faith; let him lay hold of eternal life, mindful of the good confession made at his anointing.
<margin>45</margin> ¶ To keep the commandment immaculate: every bishop is bound by a divine oath until the end of the world.
<margin>46</margin> ¶ Instruction for the rich of this age.
<margin>47</margin> ¶ The bishop: must overturn all profane novelties and all heresies. Farewell in grace. May Christ, who deemed us worthy, make us overcome every evil: so that doing His will without end, we may be able to praise Him without end.

### CANONS <note>Summaries or rules of interpretation</note> OF THE EPISTLE TO THE HEBREWS.
#### CHAPTER I.

1 That God, who in the old law revealed himself through the prophets in many forms and in separate parts, has in the new law revealed himself in a uniform and singular way through the Son.
2 That the Son is the radiance of his glory and the exact representation <note>original: 'character'</note> of the Father's essence <note>original: 'substantiae'</note>, sustaining all things, powerful in all things, performing the purification of sins through himself, and sitting at the right hand of the majesty of God on high: being as excellent as his name, which is higher than the names of angels.
3 Which names of Christ are more excellent and more venerable than the names of angels.

<margin>II</margin>

### CANONS OF CHAPTER II.

4 That without comparison, the Gospel must be attended to more closely and fixed in the heart than the old law was.
5 That God did not wish to subject the world to the old law, which was given through the arrangement of angels, but rather the Hebrew people. However, to the new law, given through the Son, he subjected the entire world.
6 That it matters not if all do not obey the Gospel; nevertheless, all are bound to be subject to the Gospel—those who obey, unto salvation; those who do not obey, unto eternal condemnation.
7 That only the passion of Christ was fitting, through which the entire human race could be redeemed and satisfaction made for transgressions.
8 That Christ willed to be a true man and a brother to other men for this mystery of redemption: so that the devil might be conquered by a man, he who had once conquered the human race.
9 That he did not take on the nature of angels, but the seed of Abraham; he was not made an angel, but was made man. He experienced all the weaknesses and temptations that humans do (with sinlessness alone as his companion), so that having become the high priest <note>original: 'pontifex'</note>, mediator, and advocate for men before God, he might show compassion in mercy for human infir-

# CANONS OF THE EPISTLE TO THE HEBREWS.
## CHAPTER I.
<margin>I</margin>
<margin>1</margin>
That God in the Old Law showed himself in many forms and in various parts through the prophets; but in the New Law, he does so uniformly and uniquely through his Son.
<margin>2</margin>
That the Son is the brightness of glory and the exact representation of the Father’s substance <note>original: *character paternæ ſubſtãtiæ*</note>, sustaining all things, all-powerful, performing the cleansing of sins by himself, sitting at the right hand of God’s majesty in the high places: a name as excellent as he is, higher than the names of angels.
<margin>3</margin>
That the names of Christ are more excellent and more venerable than the names of angels.

<margin>II</margin>
## CANONS / CHAPTER II.
<margin>4</margin>
That we must pay incomparably more attention to the Gospel and fix it in our hearts than was required for the Old Law.
<margin>5</margin>
That God did not wish to subject the whole world to the Old Law (which was given through the arrangement of angels), but only the Hebrew people. However, to the New Law, given through the Son, he has subjected the entire world.
<margin>6</margin>
That it matters not if some do not obey the Gospel; nevertheless, all are obligated to be subject to the Gospel. Those who obey find salvation; those who do not find eternal condemnation.
<margin>7</margin>
That the passion of Christ alone was fitting: through which the entire human race could be redeemed and satisfaction made for transgressions.
<margin>8</margin>
That Christ willed to be a true man and a brother to other men for the mystery of redemption: so that the devil, who had conquered the human race, might be conquered by a man.
<margin>9</margin>
That he did not take on the nature of an angel, but the "seed of Abraham" <note>The lineage of the biblical patriarch Abraham</note>; he was not made an angel but was made man. Having experienced all things that men do—weakness and temptations (yet remaining without sin)—he was made a high priest <term>pontifex</term>, mediator, and advocate for men before God, so that he might have mercy and compassion on human weaknesses 

<column-break/>

and temptations.
<margin>III</margin>
## CANONS / CHAPTER III.
<margin>10</margin>
That we must continually look to Christ, our high priest before God.
<margin>11</margin>
The honor given to Christ is above that of Moses, just as the creator is above the creature.
<margin>12</margin>
Moses was a servant in another's house; Christ is the Son and Lord in his own house.
<margin>13</margin>
The heart must not be hardened in the Law of Christ as hearts were hardened under the Law of Moses.
<margin>14</margin>
That everyone in the time of grace ought to examine themselves diligently, lest there be any unbelief within them; and if there is, it must be washed away.
<margin>15</margin>
That those who hardened themselves in unbelief under Moses did not enter the promised land but died in the desert.

<margin>IIII</margin>
## CANONS / CHAPTER IIII.
<margin>16</margin>
Those who harden their hearts in the time of grace shall not enter the land of the living (which is the rest of the Lord), but shall perish in the desert of this world.
<margin>17</margin>
For the faithful of Christ, a true rest of God and a true Sabbath-keeping <note>original: *ſabbatisimus*, referring to a holy state of rest</note> has been left behind, into which they shall enter.
<margin>18</margin>
That whoever enters that rest has completed all his labors; there shall be no more labor, nor pain, nor grief. Regarding the all-powerful efficacy of the Word of God: which leads us to that rest.
<margin>19</margin>
For those who hold fast to the confession of faith: the throne of grace and mercy of our great high priest—who experienced all our weaknesses except for sin—must be approached with confidence.

**21** ¶ That the understanding of the mystery and the pattern of Christ's priesthood, according to the likeness of the priesthood of Melchizedek, belongs to those who are mature <note>original: *perfectorum*</note> and those who can be nourished by solid food, not to infants <note>original: *paruulorum*</note> who can only accept the nourishment of milk and are unable to understand anything that is difficult or sublime.

<margin>VI</margin>
### CANONS FOR CHAPTER VI.

**22** ¶ For those wishing to grasp the mysteries of God: the mind must be raised to higher things, not turned back toward the basic rudiments of faith. ¶ That he who has been restored to life through baptism, if he afterwards falls back into death from which he had been restored: he cannot be restored again by baptism to the life he has lost. <note>The author is summarizing the difficult passage in Hebrews 6 regarding the impossibility of a second repentance after apostasy.</note>

**23** ¶ Those who frequently receive the graces of God and do not produce the fruit of life are close to a curse, bearing the sign of the accursed.

**24** ¶ Good works are the signs of God’s blessing.

**25** ¶ We ought to imitate those who held the signs of blessing within themselves: those who through faith, hope, and unshaken, expectant patience obtained the promises of God, like the faithful Abraham.

**26** ¶ Regarding the promises of God, and the immutable counsel and oath of God. No one should doubt or despair of the promises: but hope in them must be held fast like a firm anchor, especially since our forerunner has already entered the heavens for us: the eternal high priest <note>original: *pontifex*</note>, mediator, and advocate according to the order of Melchizedek.

<margin>VII</margin>
### CANONS FOR CHAPTER VII.

**27** ¶ Who Melchizedek was: what his names signify, his condition, and whose likeness he bore.

**28** ¶ That Melchizedek came in a likeness greater than Abraham: and his priesthood is greater than the priesthood of the Mosaic law.

**29** ¶ That the authority of blessing showed Melchizedek to be better and superior to Abraham.

**30** ¶ That the life of the priest Melchizedek is recorded, but not his death: this was a likeness of the eternal priesthood of Christ.

**31** ¶ That the priesthood of Aaron

<column-break/>

<margin>Hebrews 7, 8, 9</margin>
did not bring things to completion: therefore there was a need for another to complete them, and by his existence, the law also was transferred.

**32** ¶ That Christ arose from the tribe of Judah and not from the priestly tribe: receiving a priesthood not from priests, but one above the priestly office. It is not a temporal office from men, but one above men, eternal and indissoluble.

**33** ¶ Not without reason was there an abrogation <note>original: *abrogatio*; a formal repeal</note> of the prior priesthood and law, but for the latter there is none. Therefore, the first was without an oath, as something imperfect and changeable; the second was with the protestation of an oath, as something perfect and immutable.

**34** ¶ That the priests of the prior priesthood were mortal, and therefore many. The priest of the later priesthood is immortal, and therefore one. Those priests could save neither themselves nor others; this one, living forever, can save all who come to him.

**35** ¶ Such a high priest was necessary if the world was ever to be, or could be, saved.

<margin>VIII</margin>
### CANONS FOR CHAPTER VIII.

**36** ¶ A summary <note>original: *Epilogus*</note> of several points already stated.

**37** ¶ That since Christ is a priest and high priest forever: he has that which he continually offers to God for his people—not the kind of offering the priests made in shadow and faint traces (for those were mere types), nor the kind now offered on earth covered by sacred veils, but the naked and open truth.

**38** ¶ That the testament of Christ is a completed testament. The old was not completed, for the old has perished; the new remains forever.

<margin>IX</margin>
### CANONS FOR CHAPTER IX.

**39** ¶ Which justifications and which tabernacles the Old Testament had in symbol, and what was contained within each tabernacle.

**40** ¶ Who entered into the first and who into the second tabernacle of the old law, and how frequently that entry was repeated.

**41** ¶ That Christ, once and for all with his own blood, entered the tabernacle [not made] by hand...

## COMMON ANNOTATIONS FOR THE ABOVE CANONS.

<margin>1</margin> ¶ These are the methods, uses, and practices of the above canons. For example: the "elements" (that is, the small numbers on the side) of the first canons, which belong to the fourteen Epistles, show the arguments of similar parts through matching numbers.

<margin>2</margin> ¶ The larger numbers placed on the side, outside the position of the others, designate those sections which the Latins are accustomed to call the "chapters" of the Epistles.

<margin>3</margin> ¶ The larger numbers located at the top in the header itself designate the number of the Epistle—namely, which Epistle it is that the canons are placed under, whether the first, the second, or whichever other it may be.

<margin>4</margin> ¶ And at the top side, the name of the Epistle is seen, such as "To the Romans," "First to the Corinthians," "Second to the Corinthians," and so on in this manner.

<margin>5</margin> ¶ And the numbers immediately following the name of the Epistle indicate how many canons—and from how many chapters—the margin of that side contains. These instructions are for understanding the method.

<margin>6</margin> ¶ Therefore, the one who reads the Epistles: if they read the canon for any element of the Epistle, they will have the argument of that part, providing a brief and summary understanding. Indeed, for those who have been somewhat prepared beforehand, those canons possess the full power of a complete commentary. This pertains to their usefulness.

<margin>7</margin> ¶ Furthermore, if you seek the argument or meaning of any part of any Epistle—for example, the sixth Epistle which is "To the Philippians," specifically this little part: *Nevertheless, you did well sharing in my distress,* <note>original: "attamen probe fecistis communicantes pluræ meæ" - a reference to Philippians 4:14</note> right up to the salutations with which that Epistle is closed—and you require the argument: look at the "element" of that small part (that is, the number 16). Seek that number 16 in the table of canons where "VI" is seen inscribed at the top as if on a lintel. The canon for that number will reveal the argument of that passage to you: namely, that it never befits us to be ungrateful or unmindful of benefits bestowed upon us, whether toward God or toward men; moreover, that thanks should be poured out abundantly to God on behalf of benefactors. The example: Paul, who is grateful and mindful for the benefits received from the Philippians, and moreover gives thanks to God for them, holily praying for an increase of all good things for them. For when Paul gives thanks for some people, he teaches us that thanks should be given for similar reasons; when he prays, he teaches that we must pray. And in general, the actions of the saints [serve as our guide]...

...our instructions are for carrying out similar things; and if there are things they avoid and flee, our warnings are for fleeing similar things. And as has already been said regarding this part: so you will also find the argument you require for any small part of any of these 14 Epistles of Paul. <margin>8</margin> And this follows the practice of the first canons <note>The "Canons" here refer to a structured cross-referencing system or index common in early Bibles to help readers find related themes across different letters.</note>. <margin>9</margin> In the second canons, which pertain to the articles of faith: the inscriptions at the top show what the subjects below designate. <margin>10</margin> The numbers at the top refer to the fourteen epistles. <margin>11</margin> The numbers in the small spaces of the grid lines show the location in the epistle marked above from which the article is taken. <margin>12</margin> However, if the number indicating this is placed on the line of the article, it belongs to the upper number, <margin>13</margin> suggesting one of the first seven epistles. <margin>14</margin> If it is in the lower line where the article is not marked at the head of the intervals but is understood: <margin>15</margin> it belongs to the lower number of epistles and indicates one of the latter seven. From these, the method, utility, and practice of the second canons are immediately clear. <margin>16</margin> A nearly identical method, utility, and practice are found in the table of the third canons, which are against heretics. At the top are placed only the first and capital letters of the epistles, except for the epistle to Philemon, from which no argument against heretics is drawn. To complete the number of fourteen, the epistle to the Hebrews is placed twice, represented by the capital letter H with its number 14 placed above it. In the spaces of the intervals: numbers marked with a preceding dot belong to one of the first seven epistles, designated by the letter and the number placed at the top. Numbers in those same middle intervals marked with a following dot belong to one of the latter seven epistles—specifically the one figured in the second row of capital letters at the top with its assigned numbers. Both sets of numbers show from which place and from which epistle the refutation and argument against the heresy and heretic marked in the corresponding section are taken. The rest, I believe, is plain enough and sufficiently clear.

### A PANEGYRIC ON THE LIFE OF THE BLESSED PAUL, FROM POPE DAMASUS.
<note>Pope Damasus I (c. 305–384 AD) was known for his Latin poetry and for commissioning the Vulgate translation of the Bible.</note>

> Long ago Saul, zealous for the teachings of his ancestors,
> Wishing to put his fathers' laws before the Lord,
> Refused to believe the holy prophets had sung of CHRIST.
> While, blind, he tore the pious womb of his holy mother <note>An allegory for the early Church.</note>,
> Burning to cut down the people with constant slaughter.
> After the darkness: he began to know the true light.
> Having been tested, he felt what the glory of CHRIST could do.
> As he received the voice and light of the Lord into his senses,
> He was instructed in conduct, following the commands of CHRIST.
> As one washed clean, he pleased as Paul by a holy name:
> (A marvel of faith in things) suddenly carried beyond the ether.
> It was given to him to know what the rewards of life could be.
> The third light of heaven held him as he went to paradise.
> He enjoys the conversations of the Lord; he keeps the secrets.
> He is commanded to preach the truth to nations and peoples.
> Tossed by the sea, he lived through night and day in the deep;
> Yet it is a wonder that he alone overcame such labor.
> Lashings, chains, hunger, stones, and the fury of wild beasts,
> The filth of prison, rods, torments, shackles,
> Shipwreck, tears, the dire venom of the snake,
> And the stigmata: he exults to carry the marks of CHRIST in his body
> And teaches the believers how they may conquer death.
> Worthy of God: you live through all ages as a master.
> In these brief verses (I confess), most holy teacher:
> I, Damasus, wished to show your triumphs.

And so, with these things having been tasted beforehand, and having invoked the favor of JESUS CHRIST—praying that this very thing may be auspicious, salvific, and life-giving to many—let us approach the intended work.

### THE EPISTLE.

For I am not ashamed of the gospel. For it is the power of God for the salvation of everyone who believes: to the Jew first and to the Greek. For the righteousness <note>original: "iustitia"; while often translated as "justice," in a Pauline context it refers to "righteousness" or being made right with God.</note> of God is revealed in it from faith to faith, as it is written: "The just man lives by faith." For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and injustice of those men who hold the truth of God in injustice. Because that which is known of God is manifest in them. For God has manifested it to them. For his invisible things from the creation of the world are understood and seen through those things that were made; also his eternal power and divinity, so that they are without excuse. Because when they had known God, they did not glorify him as God, or give thanks; but they became vain in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened. For saying themselves to be wise, they became fools. And they changed the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of an image of a corruptible man, and of birds, and of four-footed beasts, and of serpents. For which cause God delivered them up to the desires of their heart, unto uncleanness, to dishonor their own bodies among themselves. For they changed the truth of God into a lie: and worshipped and served the creature rather than the creator, who is blessed forever. Amen. Therefore God delivered <margin>D</margin> them up to shameful passions. For their women changed the natural use into that use which is against nature. And likewise the men also, leaving the natural use of the woman, burned in their lusts one toward another, men with men working filthiness, and receiving in themselves the reward which was fitting for their error. And as they did not like to have God in their knowledge, God delivered them up to a reprobate sense, to do those things which are not convenient: being filled with all iniquity, malice, fornication, avarice, wickedness; full of envy, murder, contention, deceit, malignity; whisperers, detractors, hateful to God, contumelious, proud, haughty, inventors of evil things, disobedient to parents, foolish, dissolute, without affection, without covenant, without mercy. Who, having known the justice of God, did not understand that they who do such things are worthy of death: not only they that do them:

But do you think this, O man, you who judge those who do such things and do them yourself: that you shall escape the judgment of God? Or do you despise the riches of his goodness and patience and long-suffering? Do you not know that the goodness of God leads you to repentance? But according to your hardness and your impenitent heart, you treasure up for yourself wrath in the day of wrath and of the revelation of the just judgment of God: who will render to each according to his works. <margin>B</margin> To those indeed who, according to patience in good work: seek glory and honor and incorruption for eternal life. But to those who are from contention and who do not yield to the truth, but believe iniquity: wrath and indignation, tribulation and anguish upon every soul of man who works evil, of the Jew first and of the Greek <note>Erasmus uses the term "græci" (Greeks) here to reflect the original Greek text's specific phrasing.</note>. But glory and honor and peace: to everyone who works good, to the Jew first and to the Greek. For there is no acceptance of persons before God. For whoever sinned without the law: shall perish without the law. And whoever sinned in the law: shall be judged through the law. For not the hearers of the law are just before God: but the doers of the law shall be justified. For when the nations <note>original: "gentes"; referring to the non-Jewish nations.</note> who do not have the law naturally do those things which are of the law: those not having a law of this kind are a law to themselves. They show the work of the law written in their hearts: their conscience rendering testimony to them, and between themselves their thoughts accusing or even defending, in the day when God shall judge the secrets of men according to my gospel through JESUS CHRIST. But if you are surnamed a Jew, and rest in the law, and glory in God, and know his will, and approve the more useful things, being instructed through the law, you trust yourself to be a leader of the blind: a light of those who are in darkness, an instructor of the foolish, a teacher of infants...

<summary>This page contains the transition from Romans Chapter 1 to Chapter 2, where Paul argues that those who judge others for their sins are equally guilty before God, who judges all—both Jews and Gentiles—impartially based on their deeds and conscience.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the theological argument from the end of Chapter 5, contrasting the legacy of Adam with the legacy of Jesus Christ. On the previous page, the author established that just as sin entered the world through one man (Adam), life and grace enter through one man (Christ). Here, the text concludes that comparison and moves into Chapter 6, addressing the practical implications of grace—specifically, why a person under grace should no longer live in sin.</meta>

# EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS
<page-num>5</page-num>

->text<-

<columns>2</columns>

Therefore, just as through the offense of one <note>Adam</note> judgment came upon all men unto condemnation: so also through the righteousness of one <note>Christ</note> it came upon all men unto the justification of life. For just as through the disobedience of one man, many were made sinners: so also through the obedience of one shall many be made righteous. Moreover, the law entered <note>original: "subintravit"; meaning it was introduced alongside the existing situation</note>: so that sin might abound. But where sin abounded: grace superabounded. So that just as sin reigned unto death: so also grace might reign through righteousness unto eternal life through JESUS CHRIST our Lord.

<margin>A VI</margin>
**W**hat shall we say then? Shall we remain in sin, so that grace may abound? Far from it. For we who are dead to sin: how shall we still live in it? Or do you not know, brothers: that as many of us as were baptized into CHRIST JESUS, were baptized into his death? For we were buried together with him through baptism into death: so that just as CHRIST rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we also might walk in newness of life. For if we have been planted together <note>original: "complantati"; an image of being grafted into a plant</note> in the likeness of his death: we shall be also in the likeness of his resurrection. Knowing this: that our old man was crucified together with him, so that the body of sin might be destroyed, so that we should no longer serve sin.

<margin>B</margin>
For he who is dead: is justified <note>or "freed"</note> from sin. But if we are dead with CHRIST: we believe that we shall also live together with CHRIST. Knowing that Christ, rising from the dead, now dies no more: death shall no longer have dominion over him. For in that he died to sin, he died once: but in that he lives, he lives to God. So also you: reckon yourselves to be dead indeed to sin: but living to God in CHRIST JESUS.

<margin>C</margin>
Therefore do not let sin reign in your mortal body: so that you should obey its lusts. Neither offer your members <note>referring to parts of the body or faculties of the soul</note> as weapons of wickedness to sin: but offer yourselves to God, as those living from the dead, and your members as weapons of righteousness to God. For sin shall not have dominion over you. For you are not under the law: but under grace. What then? Shall we sin: because we are not under the law, but under grace? Far from it. Do you not know, that to whom you offer yourselves as servants to obey: you are the servants of him whom you obey.

<column-break/>

Therefore, just as through the offense of one judgment came upon all men unto condemnation: so also through the righteousness of one it came upon all men unto the justification of life. For just as through the disobedience of one man, many were made sinners: so also through the obedience of one shall many be made righteous. Moreover, the law entered: so that sin might abound. But where sin abounded: grace superabounded. So that just as sin reigned in death: so also grace might reign through righteousness unto eternal life through JESUS CHRIST our Lord.

What shall we say then? Shall we remain in sin, so that grace may abound? Far from it. We who are dead to sin: how then shall we live in it? Or do you not know: that as many of us as were baptized into CHRIST JESUS, were baptized into his death? We were buried therefore with him through baptism into death: so that just as CHRIST rose from the dead through the glory of the Father: so we also might walk in newness of life. For if we have been planted together in the likeness of his death: we shall be also in the likeness of his resurrection. Knowing this, that our old man was crucified together: so that the body of sin might be destroyed, so that we should no longer serve sin. For he who is dead: is justified from sin. But if we are dead with CHRIST: we believe that we shall also live together with CHRIST, knowing that CHRIST, rising from the dead, dies no more, death no longer has dominion over him. For that which died to sin: died once. But that which lives: lives to God. So also you: reckon yourselves dead indeed to sin, but living to God in CHRIST JESUS our Lord.

Therefore do not let sin reign in your mortal body: so that you should obey its lusts. Neither offer your members as weapons of righteousness to sin <note>The Latin here contains a likely scribal error "iustitiae" (righteousness) where "iniquitatis" (wickedness) is expected based on the parallel column; however, the instruction remains a warning against serving sin.</note>: but offer your own selves to God, as those living from the dead: and your members as weapons of righteousness to God. For sin shall not have dominion over you. For you are not under the law: but under grace. What then? Shall we sin because we are not under the law but under grace? Far from it. Do you not know that to whom you offer yourselves as servants to obey: you are the servants of him whom you obey.

...[the commandment] which was for life, was found to be for death. For sin, having taken the opportunity through the commandment, deceived me and through it killed me. <summary>In this passage from Romans 9, Paul explores the doctrine of divine election, arguing that God's promises to Israel are fulfilled through a chosen spiritual lineage rather than mere physical descent. He uses the examples of Jacob, Esau, and Pharaoh to illustrate God's absolute sovereignty in showing mercy or hardening hearts as He sees fit.</summary>

**Technical Vocabulary**
*   **Epistle to the Romans:** The letter written by Paul to the early Christian community in Rome.
*   **Grace:** <note>original: *gratia*</note> Unmerited favor or a gift from God.
*   **Election:** <note>original: *electio*</note> The act of God choosing individuals or a group for a specific purpose or salvation.
*   **Israel:** The people of the covenant; the Jewish nation.
*   **Abraham:** The patriarch of the Jewish people.
*   **Baal:** A Canaanite deity; here used to represent idolatry.
*   **Elijah:** <note>original: *Helia*</note> A major prophet of Israel who felt alone in his faithfulness.
*   **Benjamin:** One of the twelve tribes of Israel.
*   **Christ:** <note>original: *Christus*</note> The "Anointed One" or Messiah.

<summary>Paul explains that while many in Israel rejected the Gospel, God has preserved a faithful remnant by grace. He argues that Israel's temporary "stumbling" has opened the door for the Gentiles to receive salvation, which will ultimately serve to stir Israel back to God.</summary>

(so far as it depends on you) having peace with all men. Not defending yourselves, most dearly beloved, but give place to wrath. But as much as is in you, having peace with all men; not avenging yourselves, beloved, but yielding to wrath. For it is written: Vengeance is mine; I will repay, says the Lord. For this: you shall not commit adultery, you shall not kill, you shall not commit theft, you shall not covet. And if there is any other precept, it is briefly enclosed in this saying: namely, you shall love your neighbor as yourself. Love works no evil to a neighbor. The fullness of the law, therefore, is love. ¶ And let us be knowing of this time: that it is now the hour for us to rise from sleep. For now our salvation is nearer than when we believed. The night has passed; but the day has approached. Let us therefore cast off the deeds of darkness and put on the weapons of light. As in the day, let us walk becomingly: not in hangovers and drunkenness, not in bedrooms and immodesty, not in strife and envy. But put on the Lord JESUS CHRIST: and do not make care for the flesh into lusts.

[...of] God: that I may be a minister of JESUS CHRIST among the Gentiles / celebrating <note>original: "celebrans"</note> the gospel of God / so that the offering of the Gentiles may be well accepted / sanctified in the Holy Spirit. I have indeed cause to glory in CHRIST JESUS : in those things which pertain to God. For I do not dare to speak of anything except those things : which CHRIST has performed through me toward the obedience of the Gentiles / in word and deed / in the power of signs and wonders / in the power of the spirit of God. So that from Jerusalem and roundabout even to Illyricum <note>A Roman province on the eastern Adriatic coast, encompassing parts of modern-day Croatia and Albania.</note> : I have fulfilled the gospel of CHRIST. Thus I have been ambitious to preach / not where CHRIST was named : lest I build on another's foundation. But as it is written: Those to whom it was not announced concerning him : shall see. And those who have not heard : shall understand.
<margin>126</margin> Because of which I have been hindered many times : from coming to you. But now having no more place in these regions : I have felt a desire for many years to set out for you. When I set out for Spain : I will come to you. For I hope that while passing through / I may see you : and be accompanied by you there / after I have first been partially satisfied by your company.
<margin>127</margin> But now I am setting out for Jerusalem : to minister to the saints. For if the Gentiles have participated in their spiritual things : they ought also to minister to them in fleshly <note>meaning material or physical</note> things.
<margin>128</margin> Therefore when I have completed this / and assigned this fruit <note>the financial gift</note> to them : I will set out through you for Spain.
<margin>129</margin> I know indeed that when I come to you : I will come in the fullness of the blessing of the gospel of CHRIST. Now I beseech you, brothers, through our Lord JESUS CHRIST / and through the love of the Spirit : that you strive with me in prayers to God for me. That I may be delivered from the unbelievers who are in Judea : and that my ministry in Jerusalem may be well accepted by the saints. So that at last in joy I may come to you by the will of God : and may rest with you. Now may the God of peace be with you all. Amen.

[...of] God / that I may be a minister of CHRIST JESUS among the Gentiles / sanctifying <note>original: "sanctificans"</note> the gospel of God / so that the offering of the Gentiles may become accepted and sanctified in the Holy Spirit. # EPISTLE [TO THE ROMANS]
