# EPISTLE

<page-num>XI 55</page-num>
<header>2 Timothy</header>

Make every effort to come to me quickly. For Demas has abandoned me, loving this present world, and has departed for Thessalonica; Crescens for Galatia, Titus for Dalmatia. Luke alone is with me. Pick up Mark and bring him with you, for he is useful to me for ministry. But Tychicus I have sent to Ephesus. When you come, bring the cloak <note>original: "phelonem"; a heavy circular garment used for travel or protection against the cold</note> that I left at Troas with Carpus, and the books, especially the parchments. Alexander the coppersmith <note>original: "aerarius"; a metalworker, here identified as an antagonist of Paul</note> has shown me much malice; may the Lord repay him according to his works. You also should watch out for him, for he strongly opposed our words. At my first defense, no one stood by me, but everyone abandoned me. May it not be held against them. But the Lord stood by me and gave me strength, so that through me the preaching might be fulfilled and all the nations might hear; and I was rescued from the mouth of the lion <note>A metaphor for extreme danger, possibly referring to the Roman Emperor Nero or the threat of the arena</note>. And the Lord will deliver me from every evil work and will save me for his heavenly kingdom. To him be glory forever and ever. Amen. ¶ Greet Priscilla and Aquila, and the household of Onesiphorus. Erastus remained at Corinth. But I left Trophimus sick at Miletus. Make every effort to come before winter. Eubulus greets you, as do Pudens, Linus, Claudia, and all the brothers. The Lord **JESUS CHRIST** be with your spirit. Grace be with you. Amen.

### VULGATE EDITION. THE EPISTLE OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PAUL TO TITUS.

<margin>A <insert>I</insert></margin>
<image-desc>An ornamental woodcut initial 'P' featuring a scholar or saint seated at a writing desk within an arched interior, framed by classical architectural elements.</image-desc>
**P**aul, a servant of God and an apostle of **JESUS CHRIST**, according to the faith of God’s chosen ones and the knowledge of the truth which aligns with piety <note>original: "pietatem"; here meaning a life of devotion and religious duty</note>, in the hope of eternal life, which God, who does not lie, promised before the ages began. But in his own time, he has manifested his word through the preaching which was entrusted to me according to the command of God our Savior: To Titus, my beloved son according to our common faith, grace and peace from God the Father and **CHRIST JESUS** our Savior.

<margin>B</margin>
For this reason, I left you in Crete: so that you might set right those things that are lacking, and appoint elders <note>term: "presbyteros"; the Greek word for "elders," referring to local church leaders</note> throughout the cities, just as I directed you. If anyone is without reproach, the husband of one wife, having faithful children who are not accused of riotous living or insubordination. For it is necessary for a bishop <note>term: "episcopum"; literally an "overseer" or guardian of the community</note> to be without reproach, as God’s steward: not arrogant, not quick-tempered, not given to wine, not a striker <note>meaning a person prone to physical violence</note>, not greedy for shameful gain. Instead, he must be hospitable, kind, prudent, sober, just, holy, and continent <note>meaning self-controlled or disciplined</note>, holding fast to that faithful word which is according to sound doctrine, so that he may be able to exhort with healthy teaching and to convict those who contradict it.

<margin>C</margin>
For there are many who are even disobedient, vain talkers, and seducers—especially those of the circumcision <note>This refers to Jewish converts who insisted that Christians must still follow the ritual laws of Moses, such as circumcision</note>—who must be rebuked. They subvert entire households, teaching things they ought not for the sake of shameful gain.

### UNDERSTANDING FROM THE GREEK. THE EPISTLE OF THE MOST BLESSED APOSTLE PAUL TO TITUS.

<image-desc>An ornamental woodcut initial 'P' depicting a figure (likely Saint Paul) holding a book and a sword, the traditional attributes of the apostle, set against a dark background with white vine-work patterns.</image-desc>
**P**aul, a servant of God and an apostle of **JESUS CHRIST**, for the faith of God’s chosen ones and the recognition of the truth, which is according to piety in the hope of eternal life, which the non-lying God promised before the ages began. But in his own proper times, he has manifested his word in preaching, which I was entrusted with according to the command of God our Savior: To Titus, my true son <note>original: "peculiari filio"; emphasizing Titus as a legitimate or "special" spiritual heir</note> through our common faith, grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and the Lord **JESUS CHRIST** our Savior.

For this reason, I left you in Crete: so that you might correct the failings and appoint elders city by city, in the manner that I ordained for you. If anyone is guiltless <note>original: "isons"; a transliteration of the Greek word meaning innocent or blameless</note>, the husband of one wife, having faithful children who are not accused of riotous living or insubordination. For it is necessary for a bishop to be guiltless, as a steward of God: not stubborn, not quick-tempered, not given to wine, not a striker, not a seeker of shameful gain. Instead, he must be hospitable, a lover of good things, modest, just, holy, temperate, embracing the faithful word which is according to doctrine, so that he may be able both to exhort in sound teaching and to refute those who speak against it.

For there are many who are also not submissive, vain talkers, and deceivers of minds—especially those who are from the circumcision—whose mouths must be stopped. They subvert entire households, teaching things they ought not for the sake of shameful gain.

XII 56 Titus

<margin>4</margin> ¶ One of them, their own prophet, said: “Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy bellies <note>original: "ventres pigri"; an ancient idiom referring to those who are idle and gluttonous</note>.” This testimony is true. For this reason, rebuke them sharply so that they may be sound in faith, not paying attention to Jewish fables and the commands of men 
<margin>5</margin> who turn away from the truth. ¶ To the pure, all things are indeed pure. But to those who are defiled and faithless, nothing is pure; instead, both their minds and their consciences are defiled. They claim to know God, but by their works they deny Him, since they are abominable and 
<margin>6</margin> unfaithful, and unfit for any good work. But as for you, speak the things that befit sound doctrine. ¶ Let the older men be vigilant, chaste, modest, sound in faith, in 
<margin>7</margin> love, and in patience. ¶ Likewise, let the older women be in holy behavior <note>original: "in statu sacredecentes"; meaning a demeanor that reflects a sacred or religious life</note>, not slanderers, not enslaved to much wine, but good teachers; let them wisely teach the younger women to be lovers of their husbands, to love their children, to be modest, chaste, self-controlled at home, kind, and subject to their own husbands, so that the word 
<margin>8</margin> of God is not blasphemed. ¶ In the same way, exhort the younger men to be self-controlled; in all things showing yourself to be an example of good works, in doctrine showing integrity, chastity, immortality <note>or "sincerity"</note>, and sound, 
irreproachable speech. Do this so that the adversary may be put to shame, having 
<margin>9</margin> nothing evil to say against us. ¶ Slaves should be subject to their own masters in all things, being well-pleasing and not talkative <note>original: "contradicentes"; literally "speaking against"</note>, not committing 
theft, but showing all good faith, so that they may adorn the doctrine of our 
<margin>10</margin> Savior God in all things. ¶ For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to all people, instructing us that, having denied ungodliness and worldly desires, we should live modestly, justly, and piously in this present age, waiting for the blessed hope and the appearance of the glory of the great 
God and our Savior **JESUS CHRIST**. He gave himself for us so that he might redeem us from all iniquity and might cleanse for himself a special people, eager 
<margin>11</margin> for good works. ¶ Speak these things, and exhort and rebuke with all authority. Let no one despise you.

<column-break/>

A certain one of them, their own prophet, said: “Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy bellies.” This testimony is true. <margin>D</margin> For this reason, rebuke them harshly, so that they may be sound in faith, not attending to Jewish fables and the mandates of men who turn themselves away from the truth. All things are pure to the pure. To the defiled and faithless, however, nothing is pure, but both their mind and conscience are defiled. They confess that they know God, but in their deeds they deny Him, since they are abominable and untrustworthy, and unfit for any good work. <margin>A</margin>
<margin>II</margin> But you, speak what befits sound doctrine. That the older men be sober, modest, prudent, sound in faith, in love, and in patience. Likewise, that the older women be in holy attire <note>original: "in habitu sancto"</note>, not false accusers, not enslaved to much wine, but teaching well so that they may teach prudence. That the younger women love their husbands and cherish their children; being prudent, <margin>B</margin> chaste, sober, having care for the home, kind, and subject to their husbands, so that the word of God is not blasphemed. Likewise, exhort the younger men to be sober. In all things show yourself as an example of good works: in doctrine, in integrity, in gravity, and with sound, irreproachable speech. Do this so that the one who is an opponent may be afraid, having nothing evil to say about us. That slaves be subject to their masters, <margin>C</margin> pleasing them in all things, not talking back, not stealing, but in all things showing good faith, so that they may adorn the doctrine of our Savior God in all things. For the grace of God our Savior has appeared to all men, teaching us that, denying ungodliness and worldly desires, we should live soberly, justly, and piously in this age, waiting for the blessed hope and the coming of the glory of the great God and our Savior **JESUS CHRIST**. Who <margin>D</margin> gave himself for us, so that he might redeem us from all iniquity and cleanse for himself an acceptable people, a follower of good works. Speak these things and exhort, and rebuke with all authority. Let no one despise you.

## VULGATE EDITION. ¶ THE EPISTLE OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PAUL TO THE HEBREWS.

<image-desc>Large woodcut initial 'M' depicting two robed figures, possibly saints or apostles, standing within the interior spaces of the letterform.</image-desc>

# EPI.
### A IIII

With whom was he angry for forty years? Was it not with those who sinned, whose corpses were cast down in the desert? And to whom did he swear that they would not enter into his rest, except to those who were disobedient? And we see that they could not enter into his rest because of unbelief.

<margin>A</margin> Therefore, let us fear, lest perhaps while the promise of entering into his rest remains, any of us should seem to fall short. For indeed, the good news was announced to us just as it was to them; but the word heard did not profit them, because it was not mixed with faith by those who heard it. For we who have believed shall enter into rest, as he said: "As I have sworn in my wrath: they shall not enter into my rest." <note>original: "si introibunt"; a Hebrew idiom where "if they shall enter" implies a strong negative "they shall certainly NOT enter."</note> And indeed the works were finished from the foundation of the world. For he spoke in 

<margin>B</margin> a certain place concerning the seventh day thus: "And God rested on the seventh day from all his works." And in this place again: "They shall not enter into my rest." Since therefore it remains for some to enter into it, and those to whom it was first announced did not enter because of unbelief: again he defines a certain day, "Today," saying through David, after so long a time, as it was said above: "Today if you will hear his voice: do not harden your hearts." For if Joshua <note>original: "Iesus"; the Latin and Greek name for both Joshua and Jesus is the same. In this historical context, it refers to the successor of Moses who led Israel into Canaan.</note> had given them rest, he would never have spoken of another day after that. Therefore, there remains a Sabbath rest <note>original: "sabbatismus"; a specific term for a divine or spiritual Sabbath-keeping.</note> for the people of God. 

<margin>C</margin> For he who has entered into his rest has also rested from his own works, just as God did from his. Let us hasten therefore to enter into that rest, so that no one may fall into that same example of unbelief. For the word of God is living and effective, and sharper than any two-edged sword, and reaching even to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intentions of the heart. 

<margin>D</margin> And there is no creature invisible in his sight: but all things are naked and open to the eyes of him to whom we must give account. Having therefore a great high priest <note>original: "pontificem"; literally a "bridge-builder" between humanity and the divine.</note> who has passed through the heavens, JESUS the son of God: let us hold fast to the confession of our hope.

<column-break/>

With whom, however, was he angry for forty years? Was it not with those who sinned: whose limbs were destroyed in the desert? To whom indeed did he swear that they should not enter into his rest: except to those who were disobedient? And we see that they could not enter because of unbelief.

Let us fear therefore, lest perhaps while the <gloss>16</gloss> promise of entering into his rest is left behind: someone from among us might seem to be neglected. Since indeed the news was announced to us: just as it was also to them. But the word of hearing did not profit them: where those who heard were not united by faith. For we who have believed shall enter into rest: as he said. "As I have sworn in my wrath: they shall not enter into my rest," namely, the works having been completed from the foundation of the world. For he spoke in a certain place about the seventh day thus. "And God rested on the seventh day from all his works." And in this again. "They shall not enter into my rest." 

Since therefore <gloss>17</gloss> it remains that some should enter into it: and those to whom it was first announced did not enter because of unbelief: again he determines a certain day, "Today," in David: after so much time (as was said) saying. "Today if you will hear his voice: do not harden your hearts." For if Joshua <note>original: "Iosue"</note> had provided rest for them: he would never have spoken of another day afterwards. Therefore there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God. 

For he who has entered <gloss>18</gloss> into his rest: he also has rested from his works: just as God did from his own. Let us hasten therefore to enter into that rest: lest anyone fall into the same example of unbelief. And no creature is hidden in his sight: but all things are naked and exposed to his eyes: of whom we speak. 

Having <gloss>19</gloss> therefore a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, JESUS the son of God: let us hold fast the confession.

# XIIII 60 Heb.

**For we do not** have a high priest <note>original: "pontificem"; the Latin word for a bridge-builder, used here to describe the High Priest as a mediator between God and humanity.</note> who cannot sympathize with our weaknesses: but one who was tempted in all things just as we are, yet without sin. Let us therefore approach the throne of grace with confidence: so that we may receive mercy and find grace in time of need.

<margin>20</margin> **For every** high priest is appointed from among men for those things which pertain to God, so that he may offer both gifts and sacrifices for sins. Being able to sympathize with those who are ignorant and wandering: because he himself is also surrounded by weakness. And because of this, he ought to offer for sins just as much for himself as for the people. And no one takes this honor upon himself: but he who is called by God, just as Aaron was. <note>Aaron was the brother of Moses and the first High Priest of Israel.</note>

So also CHRIST did not glorify himself to become a high priest: but it was he who spoke to him, "You are my son, today I have begotten you." As he also says in another place: "You are a priest forever, according to the order of Melchizedek." <note>Melchizedek was a mysterious king and priest mentioned in Genesis who had no recorded lineage, making him a symbol of an eternal priesthood.</note> Who in the days of his flesh offered up prayers and supplications with a strong cry and tears to him who was able to save him from death: and he was heard because of his reverence. And though he was the Son: he learned obedience from the things he suffered. And having been made perfect: he became the cause of eternal salvation for all who obey him, having been called <margin>21</margin> by God a high priest according to the order of Melchizedek.

Concerning him we have much to say, and it is not easy to explain in speaking: since you have become dull in hearing. For whereas for the time you ought to be teachers: you still need us to teach you what are the basic elements <note>original: "elementa principij"; the rudimentary ABCs or first principles.</note> of the words of God. And you have become like those in need of milk: and not solid food. For everyone who partakes of milk: is unskilled in the word of righteousness. For he is a babe. But solid food is for the mature: who by reason of use have their senses trained to the discernment of good <margin>22</margin> and evil.

But CHRIST, appearing as the high priest <note>original: "pontifex"</note> of the good things to come, through a greater and more perfect tabernacle, not made with hands—that is, not of this creation—entered once for all into the sanctuary, not through the blood of goats or calves, but through his own blood, having found eternal redemption.
<margin>D</margin> For if the blood of goats and bulls, and the ashes of a heifer, being sprinkled, sanctify those who are defiled for the cleansing of the flesh: how much more shall the blood of CHRIST, who through the Holy Spirit offered himself unblemished to God, cleanse our conscience from dead works to serve the living God? And for this reason, he is the mediator of a new testament <note>covenant</note>: so that, death intervening for the redemption of those transgressions which were under the former testament, those who are called may receive the promise of an eternal inheritance.

### 14 Hebrews

For JESUS did not enter into holy places made by hands, which are merely patterns of the true ones, but into heaven itself, so that he might appear now before the face of God on our behalf. Nor was it so that he should offer himself often, as the high priest <note>original: "pontifex"</note> enters into the sanctuary <note>original: "sancta"</note> every year with the blood of another. Otherwise, he would have had to suffer frequently since the beginning of the world. But now, once, at the completion of the ages, he has appeared for the destruction of sin through his own sacrifice. And just as it is appointed for men to die once, and after this the judgment: so also CHRIST was offered once to exhaust <note>or "take away"</note> the sins of many. He will appear a second time without sin to all those waiting for him for salvation.

<margin>G</margin>
<margin>A (X)</margin>
¶ For the law, having a shadow of the good things to come, and not the very image of the things themselves, can never make those who approach perfect through the same sacrifices which they offer continuously year after year; otherwise, would they not have ceased to be offered? This is because the worshipers, once cleansed, would no longer have a conscience of sin. But in these sacrifices, a remembrance <note>original: "commemoratio"</note> of sins is made every year. For it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins.

<margin>B</margin>
Therefore, when entering the world, he says: "Sacrifice and offering you did not want, but you have prepared a body for me. Holocausts <note>term: burnt offerings; from the Greek 'holokaustos', meaning 'burned whole'</note> and offerings for sin did not please you. Then I said: Behold, I come. In the heading of the book <note>original: "In capite libri"; likely referring to the opening of the scroll of the Law</note> it is written of me, that I should do your will, O God." Saying above, "because sacrifices and offerings and holocausts for sin you did not want, nor were they pleasing to you"—which are offered according to the law—then he said, "Behold, I come to do your will, O God." He takes away the first that he may establish the second. By which will we are sanctified through the offering of the body of JESUS CHRIST once for all.

<margin>C</margin>
And every priest indeed stands daily ministering, and often offering the same sacrifices which can never take away sins. But this man, offering one sacrifice for sins, sits forever at the right hand of God, waiting from then on until his enemies are placed as a footstool <note>the text cuts off at 'sca-' for 'scabellum'</note>

# EPISTLE TO THE HEBREWS
## Chapter 12

<margin>C</margin> God offers himself to you as to sons. For what son is there whom the father does not correct? If you are without discipline, of which all are made partakers: then you are illegitimate <note>original: "adulteri," literally "adulterous" but here meaning children born out of wedlock</note> and not sons. Furthermore, we indeed had the fathers of our flesh as instructors: and we revered them. Shall we not much more obey the Father of spirits: and live? And they indeed for a short time <note>original: "in tempore paucorum dierum," literally "in a time of a few days"</note> instructed us according to their own will: but He does so for that which is useful in receiving his holiness. Now all discipline in the present indeed seems not to be of joy, but of sorrow: but afterward it will return the most peaceful fruit of justice to those who have been exercised by it. <margin>D</margin> Therefore, lift up your drooping hands and weakened knees: and make straight steps with your feet, so that no one who is limping may go astray: but rather be healed. Pursue peace with all and holiness: without which no one shall see God. Looking carefully lest anyone lack the grace of God: lest any root of bitterness springing up should hinder you, and through it many be defiled. Lest there be any fornicator or profane person like Esau: who for one meal sold his birthright. For you know that afterward, desiring to inherit the blessing, he was rejected. <margin>E</margin> For he found no place for repentance, although he had sought it with tears. For you have not come to a tangible and accessible fire, and whirlwind, and gloom, and storm, and the sound of a trumpet, and the voice of words: which those who heard excused themselves, lest the word be spoken to them. For they could not bear what was being said: and if even a beast touches the mountain, it shall be stoned. <margin>F</margin> And so terrible was that which was seen. Moses said: I am terrified and trembling. But you have come to Mount Zion, and the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to the company of many thousands of angels, and the church of the firstborn who are written in heaven, and to God the judge of all, and to the spirits of the righteous made perfect, and to Jesus the mediator of a new testament, and to the sprinkling of blood speaking better

<column-break/>

God is offered to you as to sons. For who is the son whom the father does not correct? But if you are without correction, of which all are made partakers: then you are bastards <note>original: "nothi," a legal term for children born outside of a valid marriage</note> and not sons. Furthermore, we indeed have the fathers of our flesh as correctors, and we revere them: shall we not much more be subject to the Father of spirits and live? And they indeed corrected us for a few days according to what seemed good to them: but He according to what is useful for receiving His holiness. Now all correction in the present indeed seems not to be for joy but for sadness: but afterward, to those exercised by it, it will return the peaceful fruit of justice. <margin>74</margin> Wherefore, lift up your drooping hands and weakened knees, and make straight paths for your feet: lest that which is lame be turned aside, but rather be healed. <margin>75</margin> Pursue peace and holiness with everyone, without which no one shall see God: watching lest anyone be deprived of the grace of God: lest any root of bitterness springing up disturb you, and by it many be defiled. <margin>76</margin> Lest anyone be a fornicator or impure like Esau: who for one meal sold his birthright. For you know that afterward, wanting to receive the inheritance and the blessing, he was rejected. For he found no place for repentance, even though he sought it with tears. <margin>77</margin> For you have not come to a mountain that can be touched, and to a burning fire, and thick cloud, and darkness, and whirlwind, and the sound of a trumpet, and the voice of words: which those who heard asked that the word should not be added to them. For they did not bear what was commanded: and if a beast touch the mountain, it shall be stoned. And so terrible was that which appeared. Moses said: I am fearful and trembling. But you have come to Mount Zion, and the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and the assembly of many thousands of angels, and the church of the firstborn written in the heavens, and to God the judge of all, and the spirits of the righteous made perfect, and to Jesus the mediator of the new testament, and to the blood of sprinkling speaking better

Therefore, receiving an unshakable kingdom, let us have grace, through which we may serve God pleasingly with fear and reverence. For our God is a consuming fire.

# COMMENTARIES ON THE EPISTLES OF THE MOST BLESSED PAUL THE APOSTLE
## BOOK ONE, WHICH IS ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS, CHAPTER 1

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial letter 'P' depicting a seated figure at a desk, likely St. Paul, within an ornate frame featuring architectural elements and floral patterns.</image-desc>

<margin>I</margin>
**PAUL**, an apostle worthy of God: at the head of his epistle to the Romans: sets forth a holy greeting, encompassing nine points. He places his name in the first position: as is usually done. He says he is a servant of Jesus Christ; a called apostle; set apart for the gospel of God; that God had previously promised the gospel through the prophets in the holy scriptures concerning his son; the son of God incarnate from the seed of David. Our Lord Jesus Christ is defined and declared to be the son of God by power, by the holy spirit, and by the resurrection from the dead. [Paul says] he received grace from our lord Jesus Christ the son of God and an embassy <note>original: "legationem," referring to his mission or apostleship</note> for his name to bring about the obedience of faith among the nations. In the ninth point, he completes the greeting. He greets them, therefore, in this manner. **¶** Paul, a servant of JESUS CHRIST, called to be an apostle, set apart for the gospel of God, which he had promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy scriptures concerning his son, who was made from the seed of David according to the flesh, defined as the son of God in power through the spirit of holiness, by the resurrection from the dead, JESUS CHRIST our lord, through whom we have received grace and apostleship for his name toward the obedience of faith in all nations, among whom you also are the called of JESUS CHRIST: to all who are at Rome, beloved of God, called to be saints, grace to you and peace from God our father, and the lord JESUS CHRIST. <margin>1</margin>

<margin>1</margin>
**¶** This is just as if the word were understood to be said: "I, Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ, a called apostle, say: let grace and peace from God our father and our lord Jesus Christ be to you all living in Rome, beloved of God, and called to holiness." But come, let us discuss a few of those nine things contained in this greeting. First, regarding the name of Paul: Origen <note>a prominent early Christian scholar from Alexandria (c. 184–253 AD)</note> felt that Paul had two names <note>original: "binomiū," meaning binomial or two-named</note>. Because he was a Hebrew, he had the Hebrew name Saul. But because he was also born a Roman citizen, he had the Roman name Paul from the beginning, which is quite close to the Hebrew. This also happened with John Mark; indeed, one reads of both in the Acts of the Apostles, for "John" and "Saul" are Hebrew, but "Mark" and "Paul" are Roman clan names <note>original: "gentilitia," names belonging to a Roman *gens* or family line</note>, just as in Marcus Regulus, Marcus Antonius, Paulus Emilius <note>Aemilius Paullus, a famous Roman general</note>, or Paulus Sergius. For thus Luke has it in the Acts: *Having taken along John, who was surnamed Mark.* And again: *But Saul, who is also Paul: filled with the holy spirit, looking at him, said.* Therefore, since Paul recognized himself to be the apostle to the Gentiles, in writing to them he rightly places the Roman name first and calls himself Paul, he who was also called Saul.

<margin>2</margin>
<margin>2</margin>
**¶** But he calls himself a servant of Jesus Christ. In what sense is "servant" <note>original: "seruus," which can mean servant or slave</note> used here? I think it is used in almost the same way that philosophers use it. For Paul does not seem to have been without experience or ignorant of philosophy or any human discipline; but in divine matters, the Holy Spirit made him more eminent than all others. In the sacred scriptures, he is that "little Benjamin in ecstasy of mind" <note>a reference to Psalm 68:27 (Vulgate 67:28), often interpreted as a prophecy of Paul, who was from the tribe of Benjamin</note>. Philosophers, however, are accustomed to call a man a servant who is not his own, but belongs entirely to another; who does not live for himself, does not work for himself, does not produce for himself, but for his master. Therefore, since Paul is the freest of all men, he calls himself a servant of our lord Jesus Christ: he testifies that he is not his own, but entirely Jesus Christ's; that he does not live for himself, but for Jesus the Lord. He teaches us that in all things Christ the Lord must be looked to, and every work must be done for his sake, just as he himself always looks to the Lord in all things and always does everything for his sake. And this service to Christ surpasses all liberty: it is far more eminent than the liberty of kings. It is called "service" through an abundance of good, not through a defect. It is as much superior to philosophical liberty as an earthly master surpasses an earthly servant, and indeed much more. I would rather be—and truly be able to be called—a servant of Christ, than be in reality the supreme ruler of Asia, Africa, and Europe. This service is spiritual; but that which the philosophers knew is fleshly. This is illuminated; that is blind. This is heavenly; that is earthly. Therefore, it is not without reason that the name of service here is said to imitate the meaning used by philosophers in a proportional way: namely, as much as the spirit can bear a proportion to the flesh. But truly, he who does not know how to transfer [this meaning] from the flesh to the spirit (having left the flesh behind) will be an unfit listener to Paul’s mysteries. For this is an excellent title: where liberty coincides with eminent service, and it is fitting for a Christ-like apostle. But it should be noted: when he says...
<margin>3</margin>

It connects the "Communion of Saints" from the Creed to the Greek concept of the Eucharist.</meta>

<header>COMMENTARY</header>

...in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit; teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you. And behold, I am with you always, even unto the end of the age. Regarding the **Communion of Saints** (for I call it the "Holy Assembly" <note>original: "Synaxin," a Greek term for a liturgical gathering or the Eucharist</note>, as the primitive fathers also called it—such as the sacred Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-century Christian philosopher</note> in his *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, where he says: <term>Communion and assembly are uniquely and singularly called as one</term> <note>original Greek: "ἐνιαίως ἀφηγόρευται κοινωνία καὶ σύναξις"</note>. And Paul, in his first epistle to the Corinthians, also calls it "Communion," as will be discussed in chapter 10 of the second book of these commentaries): regarding the communion of saints, then, it is written in John: "Unless," he says, "you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in you. He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life." Likewise, regarding the **Remission of Sins**, in John: "Whose sins you remit," he says, "they are remitted to them; and whose you retain, they shall be retained." Regarding the **Resurrection of the Flesh and Eternal Life**, in the same author: "All who are in the tombs," he says, "shall hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who have done good shall come forth unto the resurrection of life; but those who have done evil, unto the resurrection of judgment."

And elsewhere: "This is the will of my Father who sent me: that everyone who sees the Son and believes in him should have eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day." You see, therefore, how the justice of God is revealed in the gospel from faith to faith, for the salvation of everyone who believes. From this, it is easy to understand that if we obtain salvation and eternal life through faith, then those who unhappily pass through this course of their momentary trial without understanding—or rather, refusing to understand—will perish through infidelity and be punished with eternal death. For whoever is without faith is impious. But suppose one has faith that God exists, yet lives wickedly; what of such people? *Truly, their portion is with the unfaithful.* Therefore, Paul adds:

<margin>.</margin> For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven upon all the impiety and injustice
<margin>.</margin> of those men who hold back the truth in injustice; because the knowledge of God is manifest to them,
<margin>.</margin> for God has manifested it to them. For his invisible attributes, from the creation of the world, are clearly seen
<margin>.</margin> being understood through the works themselves, namely his eternal power and divinity. (But you may ask: what is that "wrath of God from heaven" which is shown upon those who believe God exists and [acknowledge] his eternal power and divinity, yet live wickedly? That wrath of God from heaven is the sword, famine, plague, and similar avenging scourges, as is said through Isaiah: *My sword is drunk in heaven*; and through Jeremiah: *Behold, I will send upon them the sword and famine and plague.* And the "truth of God" is the recognition and knowledge of God; those who know him but act wickedly "hold back the truth"—that is, the knowledge of God—in injustice. But who is there who does not know? Who can be excused? Since the power and divinity of the Creator are sufficiently declared and understood from the very condition of the world, its structure, and its visible ornament through the works themselves, just as it is written elsewhere: *For from the greatness and beauty of the creatures, their Creator can be known and seen.*)

Therefore, Paul joins this: <margin>5</margin> <margin>.</margin> So that they are without excuse. Because, although they knew God,
<margin>.</margin> they did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but they became vain in their thoughts,
<margin>.</margin> and their foolish heart was darkened. Claiming to be wise, they became fools. (What does it mean that they "became vain in their thoughts," except that they held thoughts and knowledge about God in a useless and empty way? For they did not achieve the end they ought to have. This is what it means to be frustrated and to "vanish." For thoughts and knowledge of God are granted to us so that we may glorify him and give thanks—because he has deigned us worthy of the knowledge of himself. But they did not do so; rather, they turned away entirely from that goal. And what did they do? Paul adds, saying:

<margin>7</margin> <margin>.</margin> And they changed the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of an image of corruptible
<margin>.</margin> man, and of birds, and of four-footed beasts, and of serpents. (Truly a great folly: to transfer the glory and worship due to the immortal God onto mortal man, or rather, onto something even less
<margin>.</margin> than man—for [they transferred it] into an image of a man, and into images of birds, beasts, and
<margin>.</margin> serpents—and to transfer the name of God to those things, calling them "God." Origen, in his work *Against Celsus*, clearly describes this regarding the Egyptians. "Among the Egyptians," he says, "magnificent temples, groves, and massive gateways are seen. Admirable shrines are moreover covered with proud hangings. But when one reaches the inner sanctuaries themselves: a crocodile, a dog, a goat, a monkey, or something of this sort is seen being worshiped." Just as one of the saints <note>likely referring to a Christian poet or father</note>, noting those who practiced such things, skillfully sang in this manner:

> *There are those ready to travel by the shorter crossroads:*
> *They worship cheap garden-herbs in the gardens of the Nile.*
> *Daring to place leeks and onions as gods among the clouds,*
> *And to set garlic and Serapis above the stars of heaven.*
> *For Isis and Serapis, and the monkey with the great tail,*
> *And the crocodile are the same as Juno, Laverna, and Priapus.* <note>The author equates Egyptian gods with Roman gods to mock their absurdity</note>
> *These you worship, O Nile; but these you also adore, O Tiber.* <note>Tiber refers to Rome, implying that even the Romans have adopted these foreign follies</note>

<summary>This page provides a theological commentary on Romans 1:18-23, contrasting the true "Communion of Saints" with the "vanity" of those who, despite seeing God's power in nature, turned to the idolatrous worship of animals and plants. It uses historical references from Origen and satirical poetry to mock Egyptian and Roman paganism.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the first chapter of St. Paul's Epistle to the Romans. Having established the failure of the pagans to acknowledge God through creation, the author now explains the divine "abandonment" that follows, shifting from theological error to moral decay.</meta>

<page-num>69</page-num>
<header>Romans</header>

### I

<margin>§</margin>
But those who dismiss God in this way: is it not just that they should be dismissed by God? That, serving their own lusts, they should be driven to madness by the mockery of demons—whom they served in these sorts of fabrications after abandoning God? For this reason, they are certainly forsaken by God, as
<margin>Paul.</margin>
Paul clearly reveals: <margin>›</margin> ¶ *Therefore, God also gave them up to the desires of their hearts, unto impurity: so that they might dishonor their own bodies among themselves, they who exchanged the truth of God for a lie, and worshipped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever. Amen.* <note>original: Romans 1:24–25</note>
<margin>›</margin> ¶ What does "and God gave them up" mean, except that God dismissed and permitted them? And since God is holiness and supreme purity, what remains but that those who dismiss Him should be impure and unclean? And the more they dismiss Him, the more impure and unclean they become, gravitating toward impurity. And because nature does not provide this (for God is holy in all His works), they seek it most especially in those things which are "against nature." And because the demons have dismissed God even more, they are therefore more impure and more inclined toward impurity—specifically that which we have said is against nature. Is it not true, then, that those who desert God and are like demons will be impure, and will love that impurity which is against nature? Certainly. And this is the most certain sign that they have deserted God and have been forsaken by God. This is what Paul most clearly suggests when he says: <margin>For</margin> ¶ *For
<margin>this reason</margin> this reason, God gave them up to shameful passions. For even their women exchanged the
<margin>natural</margin> natural use for that which is against nature. In the same way, the males also, leaving the
<margin>natural</margin> natural use of the woman, burned in their lust for one another; men working
<margin>shamefulness</margin> shamefulness with men, and receiving in themselves the reward of their error that was fitting.* <note>original: Romans 1:26–27</note>
¶ Behold the precipices and impurities into which those who abandon God fall—and indeed, even far greater ones which the Apostle skillfully left unspoken. For he knew among whom the holy people to whom he was writing were living. And why is it that the demon of this impurity—I mean that which is against nature—the chief author and inventor, sometimes mingles himself as a <term>succubus</term> <note>a demon taking a female form to have sexual contact with men</note> to men and an <term>incubus</term> <note>a demon taking a male form to have sexual contact with women</note> to women? Is that not against nature? It is even more so than if a human were to mingle with a beast. And because of the admission of an incubus, in our own times God permitted all the virgins of a single cloister to be openly tormented by demons. This happened because of the crime of one person, even though the others were virtuous and entirely ignorant of that wickedness; God was showing that it is better to be tormented by demons than to consent to a sin against nature. He showed, moreover, that the strictest and most severe justice must be carried out regarding such people, because on their account even the innocent—both communities and entire regions—are punished or even utterly overthrown. Because of this, earthquakes destroy cities, flames burst forth laying waste to everything, or fire descends from heaven; the fruits of the earth perish, as do the cattle, and all the labor of the farmers comes to nothing; and after these things, souls undergo eternal punishment. O judges of cities, be vigilant, lest this evil creep in—especially at this time, when so many and such great monsters appear which portend I know not what horror, and where the devil seems to have some power to sow such unspeakable and monstrous poison. Cut it back while it is new, while its strength to do harm is still weak. It is a <term>Hydra</term>, it is an <term>Echidna</term> <note>mythological multi-headed monsters; the Hydra grew two heads for every one cut off unless seared with fire</note>. Hercules destroyed the Hydra with flames so that it would not grow to an immense size. See to it that if you do not carry out justice, the justice of God from above does not destroy you, you who are unwilling to save that which is perishing as a whole. Keep God before your sight; otherwise, if you do not, it will happen to you as it happened to those who did not wish to keep a constant memory of God before them. And what was that? Certainly, just as they forgot God,
<margin>10</margin> so God forgot them. This is easily understood from these following words of Paul, who says: <margin>›</margin> ¶ *And as they did not see fit to acknowledge God, God gave them
<margin>›</margin> up to a depraved mind, to do those things which are not fitting; being filled with all injustice, fornication,
<margin>›</margin> wickedness, greed, malice; full of envy, murder, strife, deceit, depraved habits; whisperers,
<margin>›</margin> detractors, hateful to God, insolent, proud, arrogant, inventors of evil things,
<margin>›</margin> disobedient to parents, foolish, dissolute, without affection, untrustworthy,
without mercy. Who, knowing the justice of God—that those who do such things are worthy of death—not only do them, but also consent to those who do them.* <note>original: Romans 1:28–32</note> ¶ What does "they did not see fit to acknowledge God" mean, except that they did not try, they did not strive to retain the knowledge of God, and to have God present in all their actions? Therefore, as if by contrast, God—forgetting them—dismissed them to a depraved mind; that is, a mind attempting nothing rightly, experiencing nothing that is good. Since they had been unwilling to experience that which was their supreme good. Therefore, by contrast, those who strive to retain the knowledge of God in all their actions, and to keep Him always before their eyes, do what is fitting. They are full of justice; they flee fornication and all wickedness; they are pure and good, generous, benevolent, innocent friends, peaceful, simple, of good character, patient, slandering no one, pious and beloved by God, just, humble, not ambitious, providing good things, obedient to parents, wise, modest, possessing love, faithful, merciful, recognizing God as the rewarder of the good and the avenger of the evil, and acquiescing to good things and not to evil. ...with God as spectator, who in truth sees all things and from whom nothing can be hidden. <margin>A</margin>
### EXAMINATION of certain points concerning the letter.

<margin>1</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *In the holy scriptures concerning his son, who was made from the seed of David according to the flesh, who was predestined the son of God in power according to the spirit of sanctification from the resurrection of the dead, JESUS CHRIST our Lord.* <note>original: Romans 1:3–4</note>
<margin>2</margin>
<margin>3</margin>
<margin>4</泊> ¶ The phrase *who was made* etc. is not found in Paul <note>The author likely means the specific word order or phrasing in the Greek original differs</note>. And the word *appointed* <note>original: "destinatus"</note> rather than *predestined* <note>original: "praedestinatus"</note> is the better reading. This is also noted by the translator of Origen’s commentaries on this epistle: for though (he says) "predestined" is commonly found in the Latin codices and copies, yet according to the truth of the translation, "appointed" should be written, not "predestined." For he who already exists is *appointed*, while he who does not yet exist is *predestined*. He then adds that those who do not yet exist can be predestined. But He who is, and always is, is not *predestined* but *appointed*. Thus says that author, whom some believe to have been Jerome. From this and countless other points, it is clear that this [Vulgate] edition is not by Jerome, but is much older. <note>Humanist scholars often argued that the standard Latin Bible was not the work of St. Jerome, but an older, less accurate version.</note> What the old translator calls *in virtue*, we can call *in power* or *might*; for that is what Paul’s vocabulary designates. The phrase *according to the spirit of sanctification* could be more correctly stated as *through the spirit of holiness*. For the same word which the old translator renders as *sanctification* is translated as *holiness* in Psalm 29 and Psalm 144, and indeed quite fittingly. Yet truly, whether they say *Holy Spirit*, *spirit of holiness*, or *spirit of sanctification*, they mean the same thing. And because this phrase *from the resurrection of the dead* sometimes signifies the resurrection of those who have died (as in the letter to the Corinthians: *star differs from star in brightness, so also is the resurrection of the dead*), but sometimes signifies the *resurrection from the dead*—which is the sense Paul uses here—meaning the same as that pillar of the Church, the apostle Peter, when he says: *Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who according to his great mercy has regenerated us into a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead*. Therefore, lest the <term>homonymy</term> <note>Words that sound or look the same but have different meanings.</note> deceive anyone, we thought it better to put *from the resurrection from the dead*, which is neither homonymous nor ambiguous, and conveys the sense the apostle intended. It is also better to use the ablative case, saying *by the Son of God, Jesus Christ our Lord, having been made, appointed, or defined*. For it is held in this understanding by Paul. And all these things refer back to what he had said: *concerning his Son*. Thus we should read: *in the holy scriptures concerning his son, born of the seed of David according to the flesh, defined as the Son of God in power through the spirit of holiness, by the resurrection from the dead, Jesus Christ our Lord.* For when the old translator changed the grammatical case and said *who was predestined according to the spirit of sanctification from the resurrection of the dead of Jesus Christ our Lord*, he both changed the meaning and made the speech less fitting. He ought to have subsequently changed the remaining dependent words into the direct case, or expressed them all in the ablative. <margin>5</margin> **Paul:** *In the holy scriptures concerning his son, who was born of the seed of David according to the flesh, who was designated Son of God in power according to the Spirit of holiness by his resurrection from the dead, Jesus Christ our Lord.* <note>original: ἐν γραφαῖς ἁγίαις περὶ τοῦ υἱοῦ αὐτοῦ, τοῦ γενομένου ἐκ σπέρματος Δαβὶδ κατὰ σάρκα, τοῦ ὁρισθέντος υἱοῦ θεοῦ, ἐν δυνάμει, κατὰ πνεύμα ἁγιωσύνης, ἐξ ἀναστάσεως νεκρῶν, ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν.</note> <margin>6</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Through whom we have received grace and apostleship for obedience to the faith in all nations for his name.* ¶ In Paul, it is found as *unto the obedience of faith*. And the phrase *for his name* refers back to *apostleship*. Therefore, the Latin phrasing is more intelligible if it is joined directly to it, avoiding the <term>hyperbaton</term> <note>A figure of speech where the natural order of words is disrupted, often by placing words far apart that belong together.</note>. For the sense is: *through whom we have received the apostleship for his name*, that is, in his place and name; and this is the same as what he says to the Corinthians: *we act as ambassadors for Christ*. **Paul:** *Through whom we received grace and apostleship, for obedience among all the nations, for the sake of his name.* <note>original: Δι’ οὗ ἐλάβομεν χάριν καὶ ἀποστολὴν, εἰς ὑπακοὴν ἐν πᾶσι τοῖς ἔθνεσιν, ὑπὲρ τοῦ ὀνόματος αὐτοῦ.</note> And it should be noted that Paul was accustomed to using frequent hyperbatons. If these are preserved in translation, they disturb the Latin speech and render it more obscure and less intelligible. For this reason, where they occur in these epistles, we will slightly change the word order to avoid this figure of speech, following the Latin custom of speaking. If we cannot conveniently avoid it, we will occasionally repeat the word from the preceding phrase to which the following phrase refers. ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *To all who are at Rome, the beloved of God, called to be saints.* ¶ It should rather be said, *to all you who are at Rome*. This is both because Paul is speaking to the Romans, and because of the immediately preceding phrase *among whom are you also, the called of Jesus Christ*, and the immediately following *grace to you*. But since Paul speaks using a participle—as if we were to say "to all those existing at Rome"—the old translator resolved the participle using the third person when he should have used the second. He committed a <term>barbarism</term> <note>A grammatical error or unpolished use of language.</note> which Jerome would never have made if he had translated the epistle. **Paul:** *To all those being in Rome, beloved of God, called saints.* <note>original: πᾶσι τοῖς ὀυσιν ἐν ῥώμῃ ἀγαπητοῖς θεοῦ, κλητοῖς ἁγίοις.</note> Where also note:

...where Paul so often repeats "called," "of the called," "to the called." The term is a noun, *kletos* <note>original: κλητὸς</note> (as has already been mentioned), not a participle, and this word designates those who have been summoned, called forth, and invited.

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Grace to you and peace from God the Father and our Lord JESUS CHRIST.* <note>Romans 1:7</note>

¶ It should be read, following Paul, as: *from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.* Paul: *grace to you and peace from God your Father [and] the Lord Jesus Christ.* <note>original: χάρις ὑμῖν καὶ εἰρήνη ἀπὸ θεοῦ πατρὸς ὑμῶν κυρίου ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ</note> But here some hesitate: should it rather be said "from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ," or "and [from] the Lord Jesus Christ"? It is as if we were saying: "grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Father of the Lord Jesus Christ." Truly, they should have understood from the first epistle to Timothy—where it says *grace and mercy and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord*—and from the epistle to Titus—*grace and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our savior*—that Christ’s name here is to be referred back to the implied verb and preposition of the blessing, not to the word "Father," and it should be said "and [from] the Lord Jesus Christ."

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *For God is my witness, whom I serve in my spirit.* <note>Romans 1:9</note>
<margin>A
2</margin>
¶ Rather: *whom I worship in my spirit.* Paul: *for God is my witness, whom I worship in my spirit.* <note>original: μάρτυς γάρ μου ἐστὶν ὁ θεὸς ᾧ λατρεύω ἐν τῷ πνεύματί μου</note> From this, "I worship" (*latreuo*) and "worship" (*latria*) <note>The author is distinguishing between *latria* (worship due to God alone) and *dulia* (service/veneration)</note> are interpreted as "I worship" and "worship" or "cultivation." In the sacred scriptures, these terms are almost exclusively attributed to God alone, as in Luke: *You shall adore the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve*, where the same word *latreuseis* <note>original: λατρεύσεις</note> is found. If this did not signify a service peculiar to God but a common one, it would not say "and him alone shall you serve," which is the same as saying "and him alone shall you worship." Therefore, whenever Paul uses these words *latreuo* and *latria*—which ought to be specific to God—we will use the Latin *colo* (I worship), *cultus* (worship), or *cultura* (cultivation/veneration), so that a "common" service is not understood. I say "common" regarding both God and men, which in the sacred scriptures is signified by the words *douleuo* and *doulos* <note>original: δουλεύω, δοῦλος</note>, that is, "I serve" and "servant" or "slave." For these are used for both God and men. Of God: *Serve the Lord in fear* <note>original: δουλεύσατε</note>. And: *For your servant keeps them* <note>original: ὁ δοῦλος</note>. And Paul later: *for he who serves Christ pleases God* <note>original: ὁ δουλεύων</note>. *Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ* <note>original: δοῦλος</note>. Regarding men, however, to Timothy: *those who have faithful masters, let them not despise them because they are brothers, but rather let them serve* <note>original: δουλευέτωσαν</note>. *Servants, obey your masters according to the flesh* <note>original: οἱ δοῦλοι</note>. Thus, by interpreting *latreuo* and *latria* as "worship" and "worshiping," and *douleuo* and *doulos* as "serve" and "servant," the illusion of ambiguity is avoided—an ambiguity which does not exist in the Greek. But the old translator <note>A reference to the author/editor of the Vulgate, traditionally St. Jerome</note> often confuses these: making many words in Latin out of one word in Paul, and rendering many of Paul's words as a single one in Latin. Yet, he ought to have striven to render many to many and one to one as far as possible. Still, I would not want this to be thought of as said from a desire to blame or find fault. For I believe the old translator was some holy man in the Church, or perhaps a martyr of Christ, whose authority was so great that the Church did not prefer even Jerome or anyone else over him.

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Beseeching if by any means at last I may have a prosperous journey.* <note>Romans 1:10</note>
¶ In Paul, it is not "to have a prosperous journey," but rather "I shall be prospered" or "it will turn out well," or if you prefer to follow Latin custom and use the subjunctive, "that I may be prospered" or "that it may turn out well." For this is how they usually interpret *euodothesomai* <note>original: εὐοδώθησομαι</note>. Paul: *Praying if somehow now at last I shall be prospered.* <note>original: Δεόμενος εἴ πως ἤδη ποτὲ εὐοδωθήσομαι</note>
<margin>B
2</margin>
¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *That I may impart to you some spiritual grace for your strengthening, that is, to be comforted together in you.* <note>Romans 1:11–12</note>
¶ Rather, based on Paul, it should read: *that I may impart to you some spiritual gift.* And the logic of Latin speech rather requires saying *that is, for the sake of being comforted together in you*, by resolving the infinitive "to be comforted" into a gerund, so that it may be seen to aptly explain the phrase "for your strengthening." And when he says "for the sake of being comforted together in you," it is as if we were saying "that I may be comforted together with you." But this latter form is more common in Latin, so we have used this explanation. Paul: *that I may impart some spiritual gift to you for your strengthening; that is, to be comforted together in you.* <note>original: ἵνα τὶ μεταδῶ χάρισμα ὑμῖν πνευματικὸν εἰς τὸ στηριχθῆναι ὑμᾶς. τοῦτο δὲ ἐστὶ συμπαρακληθῆναι ἐν ὑμῖν</note>
<margin>B
3</margin>

¶ Here there is a hyperbaton <note>A rhetorical figure where the natural word order is disrupted</note>. The phrase *that I might have some fruit in you* should be referred back to the earlier phrase *I purposed to come to you*. To understand this in the Greek sense, I have repeated the last words of that earlier part. Where they do not repeat them, however, the phrase *and I was hindered until now* can be read as a parenthesis. <note>original: πολλάκις προεθέμην ἐλθεῖν πρὸς ὑμᾶς καὶ ἐκολύθην ἄχρι τοῦ δεῦρο, ἵνα τινὰ καρπὸν ἔχω</note>

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *So as much as is in me, I am ready to preach the gospel to you who are in Rome also.* <note>Romans 1:15</note>
¶ What the old translator rendered with a concrete term, "is ready," we have translated with an abstract term. For the Greeks, including Paul, frequently use neuter concrete nouns where Latins more fittingly use abstract ones. As in the following chapter: *Do you not know that the goodness of God leads you to repentance?* <note>Romans 2:4</note> where "the good" <note>original: τὸ χρηστὸν</note> is a neuter concrete noun, as if you said "the kind thing," and in many other places. Paul 9: *So, as much as is in me, I am ready to preach the gospel to you who are in Rome also.* <note>original: οὕτω τὸ κατ’ ἐμε πρόθυμον, καὶ ὑμῖν τοῖς ἐν ῥώμη εὐαγγελίσασθαι; Romans 1:15</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *I am not ashamed of the gospel.* ¶ **Of Christ:** Paul 19: *For I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ.* <note>original: οὐ γὰρ ἐπαισχύνομαι τὸ εὐαγγέλιον τοῦ Χριστοῦ; Romans 1:16</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *For it is the power of God.*

<margin>A</margin>
¶ We have preferred to say "authority" <note>original: potestas</note> rather than "virtue" <note>original: virtus</note> since the Greek here has *dynamis* <note>original: δύναμις</note>. This is to prevent "virtue" from being seen to signify what the Greeks call *arete* <note>original: ἀρετὴ; moral excellence</note>. For the gospel is a certain divine power for saving everyone who believes. Paul: *for it is the power of God.* ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *To the Jew first and to the Greek.* ¶ I have preferred to say "and to the Gentile" here. For the holy Jerome is the authority—in the second book of his commentaries on the Epistle to the Galatians where he explains this—that *Hellen* <note>original: ἕλληνα</note>, when spoken absolutely, is aptly translated as "Gentile." For he says: "Whoever of you were baptized in Christ have put on Christ; there is neither Jew nor Greek." He says that for "Greek," we ought to understand "Gentile," because *Hellen* signifies both a Greek person and an ethnic person, that is, a Gentile. Furthermore, the old translator <note>The "Vetus Interpres," referring to the translator of the Vulgate</note>, where we read in Galatians: "But neither was Titus, who was with me, being a Gentile, compelled to be circumcised," and in Colossians: "There is neither male nor female, Gentile nor Jew," has in both places translated *Hellen*—which he called "Greek" here—as "Gentile." I say this is the case when it is spoken absolutely. For sometimes a specific meaning is known by addition; as when it was said earlier, "to Greeks and to barbarians." By this addition "and to barbarians," he used the word *Hellen* as a specific name for the Greek nation, which was distinguished from barbarian and unlearned nations because of their study of wisdom and more elegant manners. Paul: *to the Jew first and to the Greek.*

<margin>B 5</margin>
¶ **The old edition:** *But the just man lives by faith.* ¶ It should be read as "will live." Paul: *But the just man will live by faith.* <note>original: ὁ δὲ δίκαιος ἐκ πίστεως ζήσεται; Romans 1:17</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Who hold the truth of God in injustice.* The word "of God" is included here, even if it does not prejudice the understanding. Paul: *of those who hold the truth in unrighteousness.* <note>original: τῶν τὴν ἀλήθειαν ἐν ἀδικίᾳ κατεχόντων; Romans 1:18</note>

<margin>C 5</margin>
¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Because that which is known of God is manifest in them; for God has manifested it to them.* <note>Romans 1:19</note> ¶ "That which is known" is a concrete neuter. This (as has been said) is translated more intelligibly and more suitably to Roman speech through an abstract noun, which we have also done. For the "knowledge of God" <note>original: Notitia enim dei</note> refers back to what he had previously called "truth," and the latter part clarifies the former. And where it is said with a preposition "in them," Latin usage prefers it to be said without the preposition. Indeed, that it is the same for Paul to say "is manifest to them" and "is manifest in them," he hints at through the following part, where he speaks without the preposition: "God has manifested it to them." Paul: *Because that which is known of God is manifest in them, for God has manifested it to them.* <note>original: διότι τὸ γνωστὸν τοῦ θεοῦ. Φανερόν ἐστιν ἐν αὐτοῖς, ὁ θεὸς γὰρ αὐτοῖς ἐφανέρωσεν</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *For the invisible things of him, from the creation of the world, are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made.* <note>Romans 1:20</note> ¶ "Creation of the world" <note>original: creatura mundi</note> here signifies the condition, the fabric, and the adornment of the mundane workmanship (according to Athanasius). And what the old translator says—"by the things that are made"—should rather be said with the single word "works." Paul: *For his invisible things from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by his works.* <note>original: τὰ γὰρ ἀόρατα αὐτοῦ ἀπὸ κτίσεως κόσμου τοῖς ποιήμασι νοούμενα καθορᾶται</note>

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *His eternal power also and divinity.* Paul 9: *his eternal power and divinity.* <note>original: ἥτε ἀΐδιος αὐτοῦ δύναμις καὶ θειότης</note> That is, "his eternal power and divinity." And this mode of speaking in Paul is usually explanatory; for he is explaining those "invisible things of God." It would have been better to translate it in this way, for the conjunction "and" <note>original: que</note> implies an explanation rather than "also." But lest there be any ambiguity, we have expressed the explanatory particle.

<meta>This page continues the philological analysis of the Epistle to the Romans, specifically focusing on the transition from the end of Chapter 1—listing the vices of the pagans—to the beginning of Chapter 2, which addresses the self-righteousness of those who judge others while committing the same sins. The author continues to compare the Greek source text with the Latin Vulgate (referred to as the "old translator").</meta>

<header>I 71</header>

<margin>Romans</margin>
*That they might do those things which are not fitting: filled with all iniquity, malice, fornication.* ¶ When the old translator changed the infinitive "to do" <note>original: "facere"</note> into the subjunctive "that they might do" <note>original: "ut faciant"</note>, it followed that he should have changed the subsequent accusatives—"filled," "full," "hateful," <note>original: "repletos/plenos/odibiles"</note> and the rest—into the nominative case to follow the rule of correct speech. Therefore, it seemed more just to us to change the infinitive into the gerund "of doing" <note>original: "faciendi"</note>, which does not depart from the nature of the infinitive, while maintaining a more suitable form of speaking. And in Paul, the word for "malice" follows the word for "fornication." Paul: *to do things not fitting, having been filled with all unrighteousness, sexual immorality.* <note>original: "ποιεῖν τὰ μὴ καθήκοντα, πεπληρωμένους πάσῃ ἀδικίᾳ, πορνηρίᾳ"</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:**
*Who, although they had known the justice of God, did not understand that those who do such things are worthy of death; not only those who do them, but also those who consent to those doing them.* ¶ Here the old translator changed Paul’s meaning, and what Paul affirms, the translator in some way denies. For Paul has: *who, knowing the justice of God—that those who do such things are worthy of death—not only do these things, but also consent to those acting.* It is easy to see, therefore, that this negation, "did not understand," <note>original: "non intellexerunt"</note> was added in the Vulgate edition. For Paul, in that earlier part, denies nothing, but affirms. But how could they "know the justice of God" and yet "not understand" that those who do such things are worthy of death? To know the justice of God and to not understand this very thing are surely in conflict. For what is it to know the justice of God, if not to understand the law of God forbidding such things, whether written down or carved into our hearts? And in this phrase, *not only those who do them, but those who consent to those doing them,* the indefinite pronoun "who" <note>original: "qui"</note> is twice superfluous. For the old translator leaves indefinite what Paul defines; that is, he speaks indefinitely where Paul is specific. But who would attribute these errors to Jerome? Therefore, this entire passage should be struck through with a triple obelus <note>a symbol used by ancient scholars to mark a passage as doubtful or spurious</note>. Paul: *who, knowing the righteous decree of God, that those practicing such things are worthy of death, not only do them, but also give approval to those practicing them.* <note>original: "οἵτινες δικαίωμα τοῦ θεοῦ ἐπιγνόντες ὅτι οἱ τὰ τοιαῦτα πράσσοντες ἄξιοι θανάτου εἰσὶν, οὐ μόνον αὐτὰ ποιοῦσιν, ἀλλὰ καὶ συνευδοκοῦσι τοῖς πράσσουσι"</note> But now let us move on to the rest. ->Chapter II.<-

<margin>11</margin>
There are those who, recognizing the justice of God—that those who do the indecent things named above are worthy of death—nevertheless do them and consent to those doing them; and they themselves are without excuse. But you will say: "If they do those things, yet do not consent to those doing them but instead judge, accuse, and rebuke them, will they then be excusable?" Not at all. For in that which they judge others worthy of death, they condemn themselves by the same logic as being guilty of the same punishment, since they do the same and similar things as those they judge. Regarding these, Paul says: ¶ *Therefore you are inexcusable, O man, whoever you are who judges. For in that which you judge another, you condemn yourself; for you who judge do the same things.* ¶ Here, the argument from similarity convinces them that they are without excuse. But it is also not difficult to gather that they are inexcusable by a syllogism <note>a logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two premises</note>. For we know that the true judgment of God and the just condemnation of death is against all who do such things. They themselves do such things. Therefore,
<margin>12</margin>
they are justly condemned to death; they are thus not excusable. You understand this from Paul, who adds: ¶ *But we know that the judgment of God is according to truth against those who do such things. And do you think, O man, you who judge those who do such things and yet do the same, that you will escape the judgment of God?* ¶ It is rightly understood and concluded: "you will not escape." But perhaps you will say: "God tolerates it and does not punish me." But it does not follow from this that "therefore you will escape." Rather, it follows that you will be punished more severely unless you repent. For the fact that God tolerates you, that He does not punish you but delays and waits for the punishment, is a sign of His ineffable kindness, which does not want to destroy you but to save you and lead you to repentance. Yet you despise the riches of God's kindness. For you do not know (as even the pagans themselves confess) that divine wrath proceeds with a slow step toward vengeance, but compensates for the lateness of the vengeance with the severity of the punishment. Or if you hold the pagan writers in low esteem,
<margin>13</margin>
listen at least to the apostle of God saying: ¶ *Or do you despise the riches of His kindness, and patience, and long-suffering, not knowing that His kindness... according to your hardness and impenitent heart, you treasure up for yourself wrath on the day of wrath and revelation, and of the righteous judgment of God? Who will render to everyone according to his works: to those who, through the patience of good work, seek eternal life: glory, and honor, and incorruptibility. But to those who are contentious, and who do not believe the truth but believe iniquity: there will be fury and wrath. Tribulation and anguish will be upon every soul of man who works evil, the Jew first and also the Gentile. But glory and honor and peace to everyone who works good, to the Jew first and also the Gentile. For there is no respect of persons with God.* ¶ The "day of wrath and revelation and of the righteous judgment of God" is the Day of Judgment, in which all will stand before the judgment seat of Christ. Regarding this, the prophet Zephaniah <note>original: "Sophonias"</note> says: *That day is a day of wrath, a day of tribulation and anguish, a day of calamity and misery, a day of darkness and gloom, a day of cloud and whirlwind, a day of the trumpet and alarm against the fortified cities and against the high corners.* Behold the day of wrath. But the same is called the "day of revelation" because all things will be naked and open. Judgment (says Daniel) was set, and the books were opened. The same is called the "day of the righteous judgment of God." For even the prophet...

The text emphasizes that God's patience is meant to lead to repentance, but those who judge others while sinning themselves are "treasuring up wrath" for the Day of Judgment.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the analysis of Paul’s Epistle to the Romans, specifically Chapter 2. The author is moving from the condemnation of universal sin to the mechanism of God’s judgment, exploring how both those with the written Law (Jews) and those without it (Gentiles) are held accountable through the "law of nature" and conscience.</meta>

<header>COMMENTARY</header>

[The Psalmist] cries out: *You are righteous, O Lord, and your judgment is right* <note>original: "Justus es domine: & rectum iudicium tuum"</note>; you render to each according to their works. And what He renders to each, whether for good or for evil, Paul has expressed. For to the good, there will be glory, honor, immortality, and the unfailing security of peace; but to the evil, by contrast, there will be confusion, ignominy, eternal death, and an unfailing scourge. We ought to have a great eagerness for doing good and fleeing evil, since whoever performs good—whether they have the Law or not—shall not lack the reward for their work before God. Conversely, if they perform evil, all shall find destruction and everlasting ruin. This is what Paul adds, saying:

<margin>14</margin>
¶ *For whoever has sinned without the law shall also perish without the law; and whoever has sinned under the law shall be judged by the law. For it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law who shall be justified.* ¶ Understand these things as referring to the written Law. But how shall those who do not have the Law be "doers of the Law"? Clearly from this: that whoever is capable of using reason has the **law of nature** <term>lex naturae: the inherent moral sense of right and wrong believed to be planted by God in all humans</term> inscribed in their hearts. For what else is the written Law, containing the Ten Commandments, but an expression of the law of nature? This you will easily understand from what Paul adds next. But let us first observe that when Paul says, "it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law who shall be justified," it is not to be understood that anyone can be justified by works alone. Indeed, Paul does not say the doers of the law *are* justified, but *shall be* justified. For works do not justify anyone; rather, if works are good, they prepare one for receiving God's justification.

For just as illumination comes from the sun, so justification, glorification, immortality, and **Christ-likeness** <note>original: "Christiformitas"</note> come from God. And just as the opening of the pupil is not the sun's illumination itself, but only a certain preparation for illumination and for a kind of "sun-likeness" of the eye, so the performance of good works is not justification, but a preparation for divine justification and **God-likeness** <note>original: "diuiniformitatem"</note>. And just as someone who does not open their pupil is not illuminated by the sun, in this same way, if someone does not perform good works, they will not be justified by God. This defect in justification does not depend on God, but on us, when we are turned away and unprepared to receive divine justification. For if someone willfully turns away from the sun and closes their eyes so as not to see the sun’s light, this lack of light proceeds not from the sun, but from the one who turned away and rendered themselves incapable. For what does the sun want but to illuminate? And what does God want but to justify? Since He is more righteous than the sun is bright—indeed, He is **justice itself** <note>original: "ipsa per se iustitia"</note>.

Truly, there is a righteousness of works, and he who fulfills what God commands is righteous; but this righteousness (as well as that which the philosophers speak of) is nothing but a shadow <note>original: "vmbria"</note> of that divine righteousness of which Paul speaks. Conversely, evil works do not make one's ultimate state miserable by themselves; rather, they prepare one for the ultimate misery of the "outer darkness," where there is gnashing of teeth, horror, mourning, the ghastly masks of demons <note>original: "laruæ"</note>, deformity, and the devouring of flames. For it was then that the famous rich man first knew what extreme misery was, when he cried out: *Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus*

<margin>15</margin>
*that he may dip the tip of his finger in water to cool my tongue, because I am tormented in this flame.* <note>Luke 16:24</note> But now back to Paul. For Paul adds: ¶ *For when the Gentiles, who do not have the law, do by nature the things of the law, they, not having the law, are a law unto themselves; who show the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience bearing witness to them, and their thoughts accusing or even defending one another, until the day when God shall judge the secrets of men, according to my gospel through JESUS CHRIST.* ¶ See how those to whom the Law was not given have the "work of the law" written in their hearts through the rectitude of the mind. This is known from the testimony of conscience and from silent thoughts either accusing or defending them—and this continues until the day of judgment. They are accused if some evil is committed—such as if parents are dishonored, if adultery or murder is committed, or if false testimony is given—with their own conscience witnessing that it is evil. They are defended if good is performed, such as supporting parents and neighbors, or abstaining from another's property. In defense, there is security and joy; in accusation, insecurity and sadness. Therefore, there is always security, honor, and peace for everyone who works for the good, to the Jew first and then to the Greek (that is, the Gentile).

¶ And again: *For when the Gentiles, who do not have the law, naturally do those things which are of the law, they, not having the law, are a law unto themselves; who show the work of the law written in their hearts.* Since divine power and divinity have been visible to every nation from the very creation of the world, through its beauty and magnificence, should we think that even in these times some can be saved without the handed-down Law? Although the secret judgments of God must be left to God alone, perhaps someone might respond: if we consider certain regions of the "unknown world" <note>original: "ignoti orbis"</note> to which the Gospel has not yet been brought or heard, where the inhabitants love God through the law of nature (having known Him through the magnificence of His works) and cherish their neighbors as their peers and honor their parents...

<summary>The author explains Paul’s argument that Gentiles are accountable to a "law of nature" written in their hearts, which acts as a precursor to divine justification. He uses analogies of the sun and the eye to argue that while good works do not "earn" salvation, they prepare the soul to receive God's light.</summary>
