<meta>This page continues the commentary on the second chapter of Paul’s Letter to the Romans. The previous page discussed how the "law of nature" is written on the hearts of all people, even those without the written Mosaic Law. This page explores the specific implications for people in newly discovered lands and the responsibilities of those who possess the Law.</meta>

<header>I 72</header>
<sig>Ko.</sig>

...what they would not want done to themselves, they should avoid doing to others <note>This refers to the "Golden Rule," which the author views as the core of natural law.</note>, and they should do the other things which the **divine law** <term>lex divina: the moral requirements of God, distinguished here from "ceremonial" rites like specific sacrifices</term> (excepting the ritual of ceremonies) commands. If by some chance of their nature they transgress these decrees, they should repent and sigh toward Him whom they believe to be the Parent of the world and the author of such great beauty and providence, and by a natural instinct, they should pray for pardon. I say that to believe such people will be saved is neither unworthy of divine piety (whose mercy fills the earth) nor contrary to the apostolic sentence. 

However, since other factors exist, the glory of those to be saved who received the Law, and around whom the divine rites were properly performed, will be far more eminent—just as the glory of the sun is more eminent than the other stars. 

If you should say: "Without faith it is impossible to please God" <note>original: "Sine fide impossibile est placere deo" — Hebrews 11:6</note>, he will respond that they had faith, as those who recognized God from His works and glorified Him. If you further object that it is written: "He who believes and is baptized shall be saved; but he who does not believe shall be condemned" <note>original: "Qui crediderit & baptizatus fuerit: salvus erit..." — Mark 16:16</note>, he will admit this is true, but will point out it is also written: "Go into the whole world and preach the gospel to every creature" <note>original: "Euntes in mundum universum: prȩdicate euangelium..." — Mark 16:15</note>. This command is immediately joined to the previous one; therefore, one must first go and first preach the Gospel. Only then, where it has been heard and preached, will he who does not believe undoubtedly be condemned. Yet at the start of this question, it was assumed that no one had yet gone to them, and no one had yet preached. 

But perhaps he will add: if even in an **unknown world** <note>A reference to the Americas or other lands recently reached by European explorers.</note> for many centuries some have observed the Jewish Sabbaths and ancient justifications, and God had not yet signaled to them through any angel, prophet, or apostle that the **Messiah** had already come, nor that the figures of the Old Law had ended with the presence of the Truth (just as darkness ends with the presence of light), they should not be deprived of the fruit of their piety simply because they were still "Judaizing." 

If you then ask: "So perhaps the **Tartars** <note>Historically referring to the Mongol or Turkic peoples of Central and Northern Asia.</note> at this time are saved under the law of nature?" he will immediately deny it. For they have heard the Gospel and seen the signs of the Gospel, yet they rejected them. But it ought not to be so for the world that has been unknown until now; rather, day by day that oracle is fulfilled: *Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world* <note>original: "in omnem terram exiuit sonus eorum" — Psalm 19:4 / Romans 10:18</note>, according to the times of visitation and the all-knowing divine dispensation, which knows what time is suitable for each. For this reason, in these times, He has uncovered unknown regions of the world so that Christ the Lord, King of all ages, may be announced everywhere. 

Therefore, we all ought to pray that He sends apostles into these new harvests, to whom He may grant the power to perform true signs of apostleship; and let no one arrogantly take this honor for himself, according to the word of Christ the Lord saying: *The harvest indeed is plentiful, but the laborers are few. Pray therefore the Lord of the harvest to send laborers into his harvest.* <note>original: "messis quidem multa est..." — Matthew 9:37-38</note> And blessed are those whom He deems worthy of such honor, whose praises Europe, Asia, Africa, and all the unknown regions of the earth may continually sing; and by singing, may they attain their salvation along with us. Let us and them alike be changed into a spiritual person who envies no one’s happiness. 

But will those who do not consent to evildoers but rebuke them—and not only rebuke them but, being enlightened, teach others to do good—yet themselves perform evil, will they be excused? Such were the Jews, who possessed an understanding of the Law. Not at all. Therefore Paul adds:

If, therefore, the uncircumcised keeps the righteousness of the law: will not—

<margin>19</margin> —his uncircumcision be counted as circumcision? And will not that which is by nature uncircumcision, if it fulfills the law, judge you who through the letter and circumcision are a transgressor of the law?
<margin>¶</margin> Certainly, for one who is uncircumcised in the flesh but circumcised in the spirit, uncircumcision will be counted as circumcision—far more so than that circumcision which is according to the letter and in the flesh. And the uncircumcision which is by nature (for we are all born uncircumcised, having the head of the genital organ covered by the thin skin called the **prepuce** <note>The author uses a literal anatomical description here: "glandem genitalis organi cuticula contectum... quae praeputium appellatur."</note>) will condemn carnal circumcision. And wherever you follow Paul regarding the "uncircumcision of the law," if you understand it as the "uncircumcised person," you do not err. And when he says "that which is by nature uncircumcision fulfilling the law will judge you who through the letter and circumcision are a transgressor," it is as if he said: "the one who is uncircumcised by nature, yet fulfills the law, will judge and condemn you, a transgressor of the law despite having the written letter and circumcision." But these things are not at all difficult to understand. Soon the Apostle implies that there is a double kind of Jew and a double circumcision, saying: <margin>¶</margin> "For he is not a Jew who is one outwardly; neither is that circumcision which is outward in the flesh. But he is a Jew who is one inwardly; and circumcision is that of the heart, in the spirit, not in the letter; whose praise is not from men, but from God."
<margin>5 ¶</margin> He implies there is a double kind of Jew. One is a Jew according to the flesh; the other, according to the spirit. According to the flesh is he who is circumcised only outwardly and in the body. But according to the spirit is he who is circumcised in the hidden and secret place of the heart. And just as the first has a small part of the flesh removed and yet clings to the flesh and its passions, so the second has all carnal passions removed and clings to the spirit and the God of the spirit. In the sacred scriptures, this man is understood as the true **Jew** <note>The author is playing on the etymology of the name Judah/Jew, which means "praise" in Hebrew (Yudah).</note>; the other is one in name only. This one is spiritual; the other, carnal. This one is in secret; the other, in the open. This one belongs to God; the other, to men. This one is heavenly; the other, earthly. This one is called a Jew in heart and spirit; the other, in flesh and letter. According to the prophecy of **Zechariah**, God chose this "Judah" as his possession. "The Lord," he says, "will possess Judah as his portion in the holy land" <note>Zechariah 2:12</note>. But according to **Isaiah**, God destroyed the other. For he says, "**Jerusalem** has fallen, and Judah has collapsed, because their tongue and their deeds are against the Lord, to provoke the eyes of his majesty" <note>Isaiah 3:8</note>. This one is praiseworthy: "Judah," he says, "your brothers shall praise you" <note>Genesis 49:8</note>. The other does not deserve praise: "Those who call you blessed," he says, "deceive you and destroy the way of your steps" <note>Isaiah 3:12</note>. This one is seeing; the other, blind. This one confesses; the other denies.

<meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous page regarding the distinction between the outward observance of the Law (the "letter") and the internal transformation of the believer (the "spirit"). The author transitions here from a theological reflection on circumcision to a technical grammatical analysis of the Latin Vulgate text of Romans chapter 2.</meta>

I 73 Ro.

For through rebellion (says the Lord through Jeremiah) the house of Israel and the house of Judah have rebelled against me. They have denied the Lord and said, "He is not." Since therefore "Judah" and "Jew" are interpreted as "one who confesses" <note>The name Judah (Yehudah) is traditionally derived from the Hebrew root meaning to praise or confess</note>, and yet a Judah and a Jew according to the <unclear>flesh</unclear> deny the Lord, whereas a Judah and a Jew in heart and spirit confess the Lord and also praise Him from their heart: it is established that the latter is, by the thing itself and in truth, a Jew and called so, while the former is a Jew in name only. In a similar way, circumcision is twofold: that of the flesh, and that of the heart. Circumcision of the flesh: the trimming away of the foreskin stretched over the organ of generation. Of the heart: the cutting away of carnal affections. The former adheres to the flesh; the latter to the spirit. The former is carnal; the latter is spiritual. The latter is commanded and commended by God; this is what the sacred scriptures preach and mean. Concerning this, it is said in Deuteronomy: "The Lord your God will circumcise your heart, so that you may love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul." And concerning the same, He commands through the prophet Jeremiah: "Be circumcised to the Lord, and take away the foreskins of your hearts." This is circumcision in the spirit; the other is in the letter. This is hidden; that is manifest. This is the truth; that is the sign and shadow of it. This is done by God; that by man. Through this, we are known as children of God according to the spirit; through that, as children of Abraham according to the flesh. For the former is a sign of the name of sonship; the latter is a sign of sonship to God. Those having the former possessed the land of the Canaanites; but those having the latter shall inherit the kingdom of heaven. And this Jew and that, and this circumcision and that, differ from each other as much as spirit and flesh, heaven and earth, light and darkness, new and old; so much so that they almost correspond as opposites throughout. Yet to spiritual men, and those who see the utterances of God in the light of the Gospel, carnal things are manifest symbols of spiritual things. And we who follow Christ Jesus ought to be truly Jews in secret and in spirit, and truly circumcised in heart; indeed, we alone can be such. And no one who follows Christ is uncircumcised and unclean, as the prophet Isaiah says: "He shall no longer add to pass through you, the uncircumcised and the unclean," because the Lord has comforted His people; the Lord has prepared His holy arm in the eyes of all nations, and all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God. To whom be honor and glory forever and ever. Now to the examination of the letter.

# EXAMINATION of several points regarding the literal text.

<margin>A 11</margin>¶ The Vulgate edition: "For which cause you are inexcusable, O man, everyone who judges." <note>Romans 2:1</note> ¶ Lest it should lack a vocative case among the Latins, it seemed more fitting that this particle be translated as "whosoever" in this manner: "For which cause you are inexcusable, O man, whosoever you are who judge." Paul: "Therefore you are inexcusable, O man, everyone who judges" <note>original Greek: Διὸ ἀναπολόγητος εἶ ὦ ἄνθρωπε, πᾶς ὁ κρίνων</note>. ¶ The Vulgate edition: "For you do the same things **which** you judge."
<margin>2</margin>¶ It should be read as "you **who** judge" <note>the author is correcting a neuter plural "quæ" to a masculine singular "qui"</note> in the masculine singular, not the neuter plural. Paul: "For you do the same things, you who judge" <note>original Greek: τὰ γὰρ αὐτὰ πράσσεις ὁ κρίνων</note>. ¶ For you do the same things as the one judging, that is, you who judge.

<header>COMMENTARY</header>

<margin>25</margin> This is the speech of their law. It is therefore directed to them, and in the first place. Paul hints at this, saying:
¶ Now we know that whatever the law says, it speaks to those who are under the law: so that every mouth may be stopped, and all the world may become subject to God. Because by the works of the law, no flesh shall be justified in his sight. For through the law comes the knowledge of sin. <note>Original: "per legem enim cognitio peccati." This is a central Pauline theme: the Law identifies what is wrong but does not provide the power to do what is right.</note>
"That every mouth may be stopped": let no one, neither Jew nor Gentile, boast that they have been justified by themselves or by their own works. For none of them were justified by the works of the law—neither the Gentiles by the law of nature nor the Jews by the written law. Instead, both Gentiles and Jews are justified by the grace and mercy of God, so that the whole world may be subject, indebted, and bound to God. Let no one attribute the honor of their justification to themselves, but to God. For while a person prepares himself with the help of the works of the law, God is the author of justification. Indeed, the "works of the law" are common to both Jews and Gentiles; but the Gentiles had them written only in their hearts, while the Jews also had them delivered by God on the tablets of the law. Thus, neither the Gentiles nor the Jews could offer an excuse when they transgressed them. Truly, the Jews had even less excuse, for they had a greater knowledge of what constituted sin. This was even through the written law—"for through the law comes the knowledge of sin"—not unlike how a doctor's instructions provide knowledge of the things that aggravate a disease. And since all, both Jews and Gentiles, are found guilty before God in those works, "by no means shall all flesh be justified by the works of the law in his sight."

But suppose you ask: what if someone kept the works of the law throughout their life? From those works, he would indeed be <term>just</term><note>The Latin 'iustus' implies being in a right legal standing or "righteous."</note>, but by a "legal righteousness"—legal, I say, according to either the law of nature or the written law. But by this, he is not yet justified, not yet possessing that righteousness from which he might have eternal life. For God alone is the one who grants this righteousness through faith, who justifies unto eternal life by grace alone. That first kind is called the righteousness "of the law"; this second kind, "of faith." That is of "works"; this is of "grace." That is human; this is divine. Man is the author of the former; God is the author of the latter. The former justifies regarding earthly and transitory goods; the latter justifies regarding divine and eternal goods. The former prepares; the latter completes. Therefore, the former is the way; the latter is the goal. The former is a shadowy footprint and a sign; the latter is light and truth. The former makes sin known so that sin and death may be fled; the latter makes grace known so that grace and life may be pursued.

Let us strive, therefore, to have the former, but let us especially sigh for the latter. It is of this latter righteousness (as if of both) that the sacred authors especially speak, while the philosophers speak of the former. Many know and attend to the former; few to the latter. <margin>26</margin> And when you hear "righteousness" and "justification" in Paul, understand it especially in this way. Concerning which he himself adds:
> **B**ut now the righteousness of God has been manifested without the law, being witnessed by the law and the prophets; even the righteousness of God through faith in JESUS CHRIST, unto all and upon all those who believe. For there is no distinction.

"But now" is understood as being after the coming of Christ and the announcement of Christ. And this "righteousness of God" was witnessed in the law. For the righteousness of God is the righteousness of faith, concerning which we have a testimony in Genesis: "Abraham believed God," it says, "and it was reckoned to him as righteousness." <note>Genesis 15:6</note> It was also witnessed in the prophets, such as that passage in Isaiah according to the <term>Septuagint</term><note>The ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, often used by the New Testament authors.</note> edition: "Behold, I place in Zion a chief cornerstone, tested, elect, and precious; and whoever believes in him shall not be put to shame." <note>Isaiah 28:16</note> And for this righteousness and justification of faith, it matters nothing whether one is a Jew or a Gentile, a Greek or a Barbarian. This is from the mercy of God alone, who wants all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth; and they ought to give glory to God alone. For from themselves and <margin>27</margin> their own works they cannot be saved—from which they more frequently deserve damnation than salvation. Paul opens this up in this manner:
> **F**or all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God; being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in CHRIST JESUS. Whom God set forth as a <term>propitiation</term><note>Original: "propiciatorium." This refers to the "Mercy Seat," the gold cover of the Ark of the Covenant where blood was sprinkled to atone for sins.</note> through faith in his blood, to show his righteousness for the remission of past sins through the forbearance of God; to show his righteousness at this time, that he might be just and the justifier of him who has faith in JESUS.

¶ But what is this, "whom God set forth as a propitiation through faith," except that God placed him before himself as a conciliation and peace between himself and sinners? For he himself is our peace. Thus, for us who have faith in the redemption through his blood, he shows his righteousness—namely, that of faith and grace—by forgiving us our sins which we committed before having faith. Nay, even if we who have faith stumble through some evil error, our sins are not forgiven except by that "propitiation" placed before God for us, and by the blood of redemption interceding for us, poured out upon the wooden altar in the great sacrifice. All these things are given to us freely, for "he has trodden the winepress alone." <note>Isaiah 63:3</note> And as Isaiah says: "He has borne our infirmities and carried our sorrows. The Lord laid on him the iniquity of us all. The discipline of our peace was upon him, and by his bruises we are healed." <note>Isaiah 53:4-5</note> And who is such a sinner that, if he turns to consider such great kindness of God and calls upon him from the heart, he would not obtain pardon through such a great mediator? And when the apostle says "justifying him who has faith in Jesus," he shows that this righteousness and justification is from God and not from men. Therefore, no one [should boast] in himself and in his...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Epistle to the Romans, specifically focusing on the conclusion of chapter 3. The author expands on the previous argument that the Law serves to expose sin, leading to the necessity of justification through faith in Christ rather than through human effort or the Mosaic Law.</meta>

<header>Ro. 75</header>
<sig>k.iiij.</sig>

<margin>28</margin>
No one should boast in their works as if they could be saved by them; instead, one must boast in God alone, in the wounds of Christ, and in his blood. For this reason, Paul adds a section in the form of a dialogue:

<margin>»</margin>
Where then is boasting? It is excluded. By what law? That of works? No, but by the law of faith. <note>Original: "Ubi est ergo gloriatio? Exclusa est. Per quā legem? factorū? Non, sed per legem fidei." Romans 3:27.</note>

<margin>»</margin>
For we maintain that a man is justified by faith apart from the works of the law. Is God the God of Jews only? Is he not also the God of the Gentiles? Yes, of the Gentiles also. Since there is one God, who will justify the circumcised by faith and the uncircumcised through faith. Do we then nullify the law through faith? Far from it! On the contrary, we uphold the law. <note>Original: "Arbitramur igitur iustificari hominem sine operibus legis... sed legē statuimus." Romans 3:28-31.</note>

¶ Circumcision—that is, the Jews—was justified by the faith of Abraham. And the uncircumcised—that is, the Gentiles—are justified through the faith of Christ. But because Christ is greater than Abraham, so the justification through the faith of Christ is greater than the justification from the faith of Abraham. It justifies not only the uncircumcised, but the circumcised as well. Christ’s justification is universal; Abraham’s was particular. Christ’s is true; Abraham’s was a shadow. Christ’s is perfect; Abraham’s was imperfect, even receiving its own justification from Christ’s. For the faith of Christ justifies the circumcised; therefore, their justification from the faith of Abraham was not perfect. Yet, circumcision never adds anything to the justification of Christ, for it is already perfect. Anyone who believes that the justification of circumcision (which is from the faith of Abraham) is necessary for Christ's justification would surely believe that Christ’s justification is imperfect and lacking—a thought that is wicked and impious to hold.

But perhaps you will ask, since Paul says, "we maintain that a man is justified apart from the works of the law": has anyone ever been justified without the works of the law, whether I mean the written law or the law of nature? If I say that countless people have, I would perhaps not be lying. It is certain that regarding the Gentiles, and even the tax collectors who fled to the grace of baptism, having only faith in Christ and a confession of his holy name: as soon as they emerged from the holy bath, they were justified. And if they had died immediately upon emerging, who doubts they would have escaped into the life of the blessed, even without works? We hold the same view regarding baptized infants.

<image-desc>A block of approximately three lines of text has been heavily redacted with thick horizontal ink strokes, making the original words illegible.</image-desc>

But perhaps someone will say: if we are not justified by the works of the law, then we work in vain. Not at all in vain! For if we do not work when the capacity and opportunity for working are present, we lose the grace of justification; and much more so if we perform contrary and vicious works. Therefore, we must perform whatever good we can, even earnestly, so that we may retain our justification—and not only retain it, but so that it may increase within us. If a mirror turned toward the sun's radiance receives the sun's image, the more it is polished and wiped clean, the more the received image of the sun is increased. But if it is neglected, if it is rendered impure and filthy, that solar brightness perishes. So it is with justification in those who are lazy or who lead an impure life. Therefore the Apostle also says: "While we have time, let us do good to all." <note>Original: "dum tempus habemus/ operemur bonum ad omnes." Galatians 6:10.</note> Nor should you believe it is enough that you were once justified if you have faith. It is not so.

---

Our ancestors in the early church also used to <term>catechize</term> <note>From the Greek 'katecheo', meaning to instruct by word of mouth, specifically for those preparing for baptism.</note>—that is, they instructed the <term>neophytes</term> <note>Literally "newly planted"; those recently converted or newly baptized into the faith.</note> in the faith regarding what they should do before the bath of regeneration and what they should do after. They did this so that the converts might be found prepared as a dwelling place for the incoming Trinity, and so that, having been further sanctified by the Trinity, they might preserve that dwelling in purity and brightness through subsequent good works. For thus he had commanded through both his prophet and his herald, he who wishes to justify the whole human race: "Prepare," he says, "the way for the Lord; make his paths straight." <note>Isaiah 40:3 and Matthew 3:3.</note> And the Lord himself promises his arrival, saying: "If anyone loves me, he will keep my word; and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our home with him." <note>John 14:23.</note> It is fitting, therefore, that the lodging for such a great guest—namely, the eternal Lord—should be prepared in advance with both good works and faith. Therefore, the law of works is not destroyed by faith; rather, that law is established, of which faith is the summit, claiming for itself the highest place in justification.

<margin>A</margin>
May Christ Jesus, the author of faith, who is blessed forever, deign to grant this to us. Amen.

Our ancestors in the early church also used to catechize—that is, they instructed the neophytes <note>New converts to the faith.</note> in the faith—regarding what they should do before the washing of rebirth and what they should do after. This was so they might be found prepared as a dwelling place for the incoming Trinity; having been further sanctified by it, they were to preserve that dwelling in purity and brightness through subsequent good works. For so the One who wishes to justify all of humanity had commanded through both the prophet and His messenger: "Prepare," he said, "the way for the Lord; make his paths straight." And the Lord Himself promises His coming, saying: "If anyone loves me, he will keep my word; and my father will love him, and we will come to him, and make our home with him." It is fitting, therefore, that the lodging for such a great guest—namely, the eternal Lord—be prepared in advance with both good works and faith. Therefore, the law of works is not destroyed through faith, but that law is established, of which faith is the summit, claiming for itself the highest place in justification. May the author of faith, Jesus Christ, blessed forever, deign to grant this to us. Amen.
<margin>20</margin>
Now, however, we move to the examination of the text.

### ¶ EXAMINATION of certain points regarding the text.

¶ The Vulgate edition says: "First, indeed, because the oracles of God were entrusted to them." <note>Original: "Primū quidem quia credita sunt illis eloquia dei." Romans 3:2.</note> ¶ Here I would prefer to say "chiefly" or "especially" rather than "first," lest...

<summary>This page argues that justification comes through faith in Christ rather than the works of the Law, using the metaphor of a polished mirror to explain how good works maintain and reflect the "light" of divine grace. It emphasizes that while faith initiates justification, active virtue is required to preserve the soul as a dwelling for the Trinity.</summary>

Let the first be understood as a numeral, and let the second or whichever subsequent cause be sought, which Paul does not immediately subjoin. ¶ And the relative pronoun "them" after "entrusted" is superfluous; for it has nothing to refer back to. If it is added for the sake of clarity, it seems better to say "to him" or "to that one," so that it refers aptly to the Jew. Paul says: "For first, they were entrusted with the oracles of God." <note>Original Greek: "πρῶτον μὲν γὰρ ὅτι ἐπιστεύθησαν τὰ λόγια τοῦ θεοῦ." Romans 3:2.</note> <margin>A 21</margin> ¶ **Vulgate edition:** "Does their unbelief make the faith of God void?" ¶ This should not be spoken in the past tense, but in the future: "will it make void?" Paul says: "Will their unbelief nullify the faith of God?" <note>Original Greek: "μὴ ἡ ἀπιστία αὐτῶν τὴν πίστιν τοῦ θεοῦ καταργήσει." Romans 3:3.</note> The word <term>katargeō</term> <note>Original Greek: "καταργέω"</note> means to empty, to take away, to dissolve, or to make void. ¶ **Vulgate edition:** "But God is true." It should be spoken as an imperative: "But let God be true." Paul says: "But let God be true." <note>Original Greek: "γινέσθω δὲ ὁ θεὸς ἀληθής." Romans 3:4.</note> ¶ **Vulgate edition:** <margin>A 22</margin> "But if our iniquity commends the righteousness of God, what shall we say? Is God unjust?" ¶ It is more correct to say: "if our unrighteousness commends the righteousness of God." For in this way, there is a better contrast: unrighteousness corresponds to righteousness. For name is opposed to name, and thing to thing, and this is how it corresponds in Paul's writing. Likewise, it is also more correct to say: "is God unrighteous?" Paul says: "But if our unrighteousness establishes the righteousness of God, what shall we say? Is God unrighteous?" <note>Original Greek: "εἰ δὲ ἡ ἀδικία ἡμῶν, θεοῦ δικαιοσύνην συνίστησι, τί ἐροῦμεν; μὴ ἄδικος ὁ θεὸς;" Romans 3:5.</note> Truly, the ancient translator <note>The "old translator" refers to the traditional author of the Vulgate, often identified with St. Jerome.</note> took very little care with these things, though they contribute both to the proper use of language and to a clearer light of understanding. ¶ **Vulgate edition:** "Otherwise, how shall God judge this world?" ¶ It is sufficient to say: "how shall God judge the world?" Paul says: "Otherwise, how shall God judge the world?" <note>Original Greek: "ἐπεὶ πῶς κρινεῖ ὁ θεὸς τὸν κόσμον;" Romans 3:6.</note> <margin>B 23</margin> ¶ **Vulgate edition:** "And not as we are blasphemed." ¶ It would be clearer if the verb "is" were expressed, and we said: "and it is not as we are blasphemed," that is, it is not as we are said to speak in an execrable manner. And for this reason, we have explicitly included the verb "is." Paul says: "And not as we are slandered." <note>Original Greek: "καὶ μὴ καθὼς βλασφημούμεθα." Romans 3:8.</note> <margin>B 24</margin> ¶ **Vulgate edition:** "What then? Do we excel them? Not at all. For we have charged that Jews and Greeks are all under sin." ¶ The relative pronoun "them" is superfluous, nor is there anything to which it aptly refers. And "pre-accused" should be said rather than "charged"; it designates that we have stated the cause beforehand. Paul says: "What then? Are we better? Not at all. For we have already charged both Jews and Greeks, that they are all under sin." <note>Original Greek: "τί οὖν; προεχόμεθα; οὐ πάντως. προῃτιασάμεθα ἰουδαίους τε καὶ ἕλληνας, πάντας ὑπὸ ἁμαρτίαν εἶναι." Romans 3:9.</note> But where did he say before that the Gentiles were under sin? Where the Jews? The Gentiles, certainly, from this passage: "who, when they knew God, did not glorify him as God," up to this very place where the Jew is named, where he pre-accuses and shows beforehand that the Jews are under sin. Indeed, he subjoined a general confirmation of this same matter from Psalm 13. <note>Psalm 14 in modern numbering. The author is referring to the "None is righteous" passage cited in Romans 3:10-18.</note> And this is not said concerning original sin, but regarding the sin of transgression against the works of the law. <margin>C 25</margin> ¶ **Vulgate edition:** "And let all the world be made subject to God." ¶ It can also be said from Paul's text: "let all the world be liable or become liable to God," like a bound debtor, constrained, or obligated; for he who is justified owes his justification to God. For he did not justify himself, nor did his works justify him, but God—by the grace and mercy of God, through the mediation of the faith of Jesus Christ, which he received. Paul says: "and let all the world become liable to God." <note>Original Greek: "καὶ ὑπόδικος γένηται πᾶς ὁ κόσμος τῷ θεῷ." Romans 3:19.</note> <margin>C 26</margin> ¶ **Vulgate edition:** "Unto all and upon all who believe in him." ¶ The phrase "in him" is superfluous according to the Greek. However, it seems to have been added for a more exact understanding; it would be sufficiently understood through what was previously stated: "through the faith of Jesus Christ." Nevertheless, its addition does not cause harm. Paul says: "unto all and upon all those who believe." <note>Original Greek: "εἰς πάντας καὶ ἐπὶ πάντας τοὺς πιστεύοντας." Romans 3:22.</note> <margin>D 27</margin> ¶ **Vulgate edition:** "And they lack the grace of God." ¶ It should read "glory." There are even ancient manuscripts that have "glory." And that word "lack" implies a deprivation, as if we said: "and they are deprived of the glory of God." Paul says: "and fall short of the glory of God." <note>Original Greek: "καὶ ὑστεροῦνται τῆς δόξης τοῦ θεοῦ." Romans 3:23.</note> ¶ **Vulgate edition:** "Whom God proposed as a propitiator." ¶ It should read "propitiatory." <note>The <term>propitiatory</term> (Latin: *propitiatorium*) refers to the "mercy seat" or the lid of the Ark of the Covenant where atonement was made.</note> Indeed, ancient manuscripts also have "propitiation," which is more suitable to what is called a "propitiatory." This is the same word Paul uses here, which is interpreted in Chapter 9 of Hebrews. Paul says: "Whom God set forth as a propitiation." <note>Original Greek: "ὃν προέθετο ὁ θεὸς ἱλαστήριον." Romans 3:25.</note> ¶ **Vulgate edition:** "In the sustaining of God for the showing of his righteousness." ¶ More correctly: "of his own righteousness," as in Paul: "for the showing of his own righteousness for the remission of preceding sins." And the word <term>anochē</term>, <note>Original Greek: "ἀνοχή"</note> which the ancient translator here renders as "sustaining," he renders as "patience" in the second chapter, where he says: "Do you despise the riches of his goodness, and patience, and longsuffering?" Truly, the word <term>anochē</term> properly signifies endurance and tolerance, which is also "patience." For patience is named from *patior* [to suffer], just as it signifies that very thing which I bear and tolerate. Paul says: "in the forbearance of God, for the demonstration of his righteousness." <note>Original Greek: "ἐν τῇ ἀνοχῇ τοῦ θεοῦ, πρὸς ἔνδειξιν τῆς δικαιοσύνης αὐτοῦ." Romans 3:25-26.</note> ¶ **Vulgate edition:** "Since he himself is just and the justifier of him who is of the faith of JESUS CHRIST." ¶ Paul here only has: "who is of the faith of Jesus." The word "Christ" is missing. Paul says: "to be himself just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus." <note>Original Greek: "εἰς τὸ εἶναι αὐτὸν δίκαιον καὶ δικαιοῦντα τὸν ἐκ πίστεως ἰησοῦ." <margin>Romans</margin>

...no less than the Gentiles themselves are justified. And not only for the Jews against the Gentiles, but also for the Gentiles against them: the occasion for boasting and contending has been removed. Paul: **Where then is the boasting?** <note>original Greek: "ποῦ οὖν ἡ καύχησις;" Romans 3:27</note> The Vulgate edition: **Seeing that it is one God who justifies the circumcision by faith and the uncircumcision through faith.** <margin>Romans 3</margin> Latin authors use the causal conjunction "since" <note>original: "quandoquidem"</note> more often than "because" <note>original: "quoniam quidem"</note>. And "he will justify" <note>original: "iustificabit"</note> should be said, rather than "he justifies" <note>original: "iustificat"</note>; for faith does not immediately justify—neither Abraham’s nor Christ’s—but faith precedes, and then justification follows, as He alone wills and knows who justifies, to whom alone the glory of justification and thanksgiving is due forever. Paul: **Seeing it is one God who will justify the circumcision by faith and the uncircumcision through faith.** <note>original Greek: "ἐπείπερ εἷς ὁ θεὸϛ ὃϛ Δικαιώσει περιτομὴν ἐκ πίστεως καὶ ἀκροβυστίαν Διὰ τῆϛ πίστεωϛ." Romans 3:30</note> Now let us pass to what follows.

->CHAPTER IV.<-

<image-desc>Large woodcut initial 'P' containing a figure (likely Saint Paul) seated at a desk or lectern, framed by decorative architecture.</image-desc>

**P**aul gives the primary and closest roles to faith in justification, and does not want us to trust in works (as some think), as if they could be justified by them, or as if one who performs works is made justified because the works themselves justify. It is not so; rather, the glory of justification must be given to God who justifies, not to the works. Those people look back at themselves; Paul, however, looks toward God. They glorify themselves; Paul glorifies God. They boast in themselves and are puffed up; Paul boasts in God and humbles himself within. They are surely impious; Paul is pious. They are carnal; Paul is spiritual. Human knowledge weighs them down as they lean on carnal sense; divine knowledge raises Paul up, as he surrenders his own sense and leans <margin>29</margin> upon the Spirit. Paul attributes all things and all praise to God; they attribute it to man. <margin>Romans 4. What then shall we say that Abraham our father according to the flesh [found], etc. For if Abraham was justified by works, etc.</margin> Therefore, Paul adds, **What then shall we say that Abraham our father according to the flesh has found?** <margin>19</margin> **For if Abraham was justified by works, he has something to boast about, but not before God.** <margin>29</margin> For if Abraham had performed the work and his own works had justified him, this praise would be his, not God’s. But when we say that God justified Abraham by faith, this glory of justification belongs to God, not to Abraham.

But perhaps you will say here: "Yet James the Apostle says that Abraham was justified by works." For he says, <margin>James 2</margin> **Abraham our father, was he not justified by works when he offered his son Isaac upon the altar?** This in no way opposes what the Spirit-speaking Paul denies. For Paul denies that Abraham was justified by works in the way believed by those who trust in the works of the law—as if righteousness comes from works and the works themselves justify. Instead, he says that he was rather justified by God through faith. This is also the view of the divine James, who says, <margin>James 1</margin> **Every best gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights.** With Him there is no change, nor a shadow of turning; that is, there is no sign or evidence of His changing or turning. For who would deny that justification is a perfect gift? And he does not want us to be justified by works either, as those want who trust in works as if works justify. But he himself joins works to faith as aids for obtaining or preserving justification. For he says, <margin>James 2</margin> **Do you see that faith worked together with his works, and by works was faith made perfect?** And faith which works do not precede, accompany, or follow, he calls "dead," just as we would call a man "dead" whom no action, no sense, and no breath accompanies. But if we see someone acting or feeling, we know that he lives; and if we perceive any spirit—that is, breath, inhaling or exhaling—we still have a sign of life. So works, which are the same as the works of the royal law (for so he calls it, containing the Ten Commandments), are signs of faith—and indeed of a living faith, which justification follows, just as illumination follows a healthy eye turned toward the sun; it retains its justification.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Romans Chapter 4, specifically expanding on the nature of Abraham's faith and the distinction between a reward earned through labor and the gift of grace given through faith.</meta>

<header>COMMENTARY</header>

¶ **For what does the scripture say? Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness.** <note>original: "Credidit Abraham deo: & reputatum est illi ad iustitiam." Romans 4:3</note>
¶ Therefore, God’s justification followed the faith and belief of Abraham. But because justification is not owed to works, the Apostle declares what follows by saying: ¶ **Now to the one who works, the wages are not credited according to grace, but according to debt. But to the one who does not work, but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is credited as righteousness.** <note>original: "Ei autem qui operatur: merces non imputatur secundum gratiam..." Romans 4:4-5</note> Just as David also speaks of the **blessedness of the man to whom God credits righteousness without works: Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered. Blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not imputed sin.** <note>original: "Beatitudinem hominis cui deus reputat iustitiam sine operibus..." Citing Psalm 32:1-2 (Vulgate Psalm 31)</note> ¶ If anyone were justified by works in this manner, justification would be a debt, and it would not be God's gift and grace. For a debt is one thing, and grace is another. For grace is a gift bestowed without any debt whatsoever. But he who says that justification is a debt takes away all grace from God, and makes men ungrateful toward God, and therefore unworthy of justification. For if you dig in a garden and receive a coin as a daily wage for your work, what grace do you owe to the one who pays you? For he paid what he owed. He did you no favor; you were deserving, and he gave you what you deserved. Therefore, let us not say that we are justified by works in this way. Those who say this look at themselves and attribute merit to themselves. They think what is grace is a debt. They are ungrateful, puffed up, and boasting in works.

But let us say that anyone is justified by faith, so that we may see justification as God’s gift and grace, not a debt. For when the ungodly is justified by God, who does not see that justification is God’s gift and grace? For what works does the ungodly perform to which justification is owed? But did not he who said, **"I said I will confess my injustice against myself, and you forgave the ungodliness of my sin,"** <note>original: "dixi confitebor aduersum me iniustitiam meam..." Psalm 32:5</note> believe that it was God who could justify the ungodly, and that justification was grace, not a reward for works? Certainly. From the same 31st Psalm <note>Modern Psalm 32</note>, Paul cites another testimony for the same purpose. And in truth, whether one works or does not work, sighing because of the offense committed against God: through turning to God by faith, justification is by God's grace alone. Those who say these things do not look at themselves, but at God. They do not attribute merit to themselves, nor justification as a deserved wage; but they speak of it as it truly is—grace. They are not ungrateful, but with a perpetually burning affection, they give thanks to the God who justifies for such an ineffable gift that can be earned by no one. They do not boast, they do not swell with pride; but they humble themselves before God with a total prostration of mind and devotion, knowing themselves to be debtors of infinite thanksgivings.

To recognize this piety, to possess this humility, to look not at ourselves but at God’s beneficence, the divine Apostle raises us up when he says we are not justified by works, but according to the purpose of God’s grace. For he wants the grace of justification to be imparted to us by God, provided we turn ourselves to Him and do not trust in ourselves, but in His goodness alone, and in the gift of the grace of His purpose and good will. For He says through Isaiah: **Seek the Lord while he may be found. Call upon him while he is near. Let the ungodly forsake his way, and the unjust man his thoughts, and let him return to the Lord, and he will have mercy on him; and to our God, for he is great in forgiving.** <note>original: "Quaerite dominum dum inueniri potest..." Isaiah 55:6-7</note> ¶ If God has granted some to perform good works, let them not look at themselves but at God; let them not think they are justified by those works, but when they have done all things, let them say as it truly is: **"We are unprofitable servants; we have done what we ought to have done."** <note>original: "serui inutiles sumus..." Luke 17:10</note> What does "we are unprofitable" mean, if not "undeserving"? It is the Lord’s goodness, it is the Lord’s grace, it is His mercy, that what has been done for us is not our merit, nor the Lord’s debt, but the gift of His over-abounding goodness, and a gift alone. And blessed forever be that super-eminent goodness, inaccessible to all thought, which is so great that it can owe nothing, but only give. For what can the All-Good and All-Beneficent owe? And to whom does He owe all things? For whatever is held is held from Him; He has nothing from anyone; He has nothing; He is the possessor of all, and all things are His.

And if justification were owed to the works of the law, it could belong to very few. But he who understands justification to be the grace of God—who justifies not from merits, but who dismisses the sins of hearts turned toward Him (for He alone gazes upon the hearts of all)—sees that justification can extend itself to <term>perplurimos</term> <note>original: "perplurimos," meaning the vast majority or very many</note>. And he who judges by works saves few and damns many, and becomes a rash judge. For judgment does not belong to him, but to God. For He alone is the one who justifies, and who has the power to send into Gehenna. But he who attends to the grace of God keeps silent and does not pass judgment. For it would be foolish to wish to confine the infinite grace of God within the narrow straits of human judgment, or rather, human rashness. Therefore, justification—which is common to both those who work and those who do not, and even to those committing acts contrary to the works of the law—can be most wide-reaching and extend to <term>perplurimos</term>, to both the circumcised and the uncircumcised, to both the good and the bad who repent of their malice through the sighs of the heart.

Accordingly, Paul asks: <margin>31</margin> ¶ **Is this blessedness then only in the circumcision, or also in the uncircumcision? For we say that faith was credited to Abraham as righteousness. How then was it credited? While he was in circumcision, or in uncircumcision? Not in circumcision, but in uncircumcision.** <note>original: "Beatitudo igitur haec: in circumcisione..." Romans 4:9-10</note> ¶ The Jews erred vehemently, not believing that anyone could be justified without circumcision and the works of the law. Paul refutes and enlightens them. For...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the fourth chapter of the Apostle Paul's Letter to the Romans. It builds upon the previous discussion regarding faith versus works by examining the specific historical example of Abraham.</meta>

->I<-
->Ro.<-

Abraham was neither circumcised, nor justified by the works of the law: but by believing in God he was justified. For when Abraham did not yet have any offspring, the Lord led him outside and said to him: "Look up at the heavens and count the stars if you can." And He said to him: "So shall your offspring be." <note>original: "Suspice coelum : & numera stellas si potes. & dixit ei. sic erit semen tuum." Genesis 15:5</note> Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness. Later, he fathered a son by Hagar while still uncircumcised <term>in praeputio; literally 'in the foreskin,' referring to the state of being a Gentile or uncircumcised</term> when he was 86 years old. Indeed, Abraham was 99 years old when he circumcised the flesh of his foreskin. These things are well known from the history in the Book of Genesis. Therefore, the <term>justification</term> of grace is common to both the circumcised and the uncircumcised alike. Nor is the salvation of men by the grace and gift of God confined to such narrow limits as the Jews used to think. And circumcision, which the Hebrews think justifies a person, does not justify; rather, it is a sign of the righteousness that comes from faith. Similarly, the works that follow faith are the signs of a living faith, just as our breath and breathing are the signs of life. For justification is the life of faith: if it is present, faith is alive; and because it lives, it has "vital signs," which are works.

<image-desc>A rectangular area containing four lines of text has been completely obscured by a repeating sequence of decorative woodcut blocks featuring floral or scrollwork patterns.</image-desc>

<margin>32</margin>
¶ **And he received the sign of circumcision as a seal of the righteousness of the faith** <note>original: "Et signũ accepit circuncisionis: signaculũ iustitiæ fidei"</note> **which he had while still uncircumcised. This was so that he might be the father of all who believe without being circumcised, so that righteousness might be credited to them as well. And that he might be the father of circumcision, not only to those who are of the circumcision, but also to those who follow in the footsteps of that faith which our father Abraham had while still uncircumcised.** ¶ I believe these words carry a clear meaning. But the author <note>referring to Paul</note> also uses another line of reasoning: because justification comes from the same source as the promise made to Abraham. Now, the promise was made to Abraham because he believed God—as is known from Genesis—and not because of his works. For Abraham was seventy-five years old when the Lord said to him: "Go out from your land, and from your kin, and from your father's house, and come into the land that I will show you, and I will make you into a great nation. I will bless you and make your name great, and you will be a blessing. I will bless those who bless you, and I will curse those who curse you; and in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed." <note>original: "Egredere de terra tua... & in te benedicetur omnes cognationes terræ." Genesis 12:1-3</note> Therefore, Abraham went out, just as the Lord had commanded him. Is not Abraham's departure from his land, his kin, and his father's house a sign of his faith? Truly, works are certain indicators of faith. But regarding the earthly promise, we read in the same history of Genesis: "Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness." And He said to him: "I am the Lord who brought you out of Ur of the Chaldeans, to give you this land so that you might possess it." See how the promise was not made to Abraham because of the works of the law, but only because he believed God. Truly, anyone who says that the offspring of Abraham received the earthly inheritance because of works makes faith empty and takes away the promise. For if it were owed to works, neither faith nor the promise would be necessary; whether faith or a promise existed or not, one would receive it simply because it was earned. To say, therefore, that the offspring of Abraham received the earthly inheritance and justification from the works of the law is to make faith void and to abolish the promise which the sacred words commend. For this is how Paul explains it:

<margin>33</margin>
¶ **For the promise to Abraham or his offspring, that he would be the heir of the world, was not through the law, but through the righteousness of faith. For if those who are of the law are heirs, faith is made void and the promise is abolished.** <note>original: "Non enim per legem promissio Abrahæ... exinanita est fides / & sublata est promissio." Romans 4:13-14</note> ¶ And it is so far from the truth that the children of Abraham received justification and the worldly inheritance from the law or works of the law, that they actually incurred a curse and wrath because of the law. They even lost that land which had been promised to Abraham's faith, being scattered and winnowed through all the nations. For they did not keep the law, but transgressed it, just as Paul says: ¶ **For the law brings about wrath. For where there is no law, there is no transgression.** <note>original: "Lex enim iram operatur. ubi enim non est lex: neq; præuaricatio." Romans 4:15</note>

<margin>34</margin>
¶ It follows, therefore, that from the justification of faith and the promise made to Abraham—by gift and by grace—the children of Abraham's faith (whoever they may be) receive justification. They receive the promise not only of an earthly and worldly inheritance (which was a figure or "type" of the heavenly inheritance and the land of the living) but the land of the living itself and a heavenly dwelling. For the promise of God is firm, as He is faithful and true. His grace is firm, and the faith of Abraham was firm. However, the law and our works are weak. God's promise is vast. He says: "In you all the families of the earth shall be blessed," and again, "In your offspring all nations shall be blessed." God's grace is vast, for He is rich toward all; and faith is commanded to all the ends of the earth. But the law and the works of the law are narrow. Justification would therefore be weak and narrow if it were from the works of the law. But now, since it is from faith, grace, and the promise of God, it is most firm and most vast. For this reason, Paul rightly concludes:

<margin>35</margin>
¶ **Therefore it is by faith: so that the promise may be firm according to grace for all the offspring—not only for those who are of the law, but also for those who are of the faith of Abraham, who is the father of us all, as it is written: 'For I have made you a father of many nations' before the God in whom you believed, who gives life to the dead and calls into being things that do not exist as though they were.** <note>original: "Ideo ex fide: vt secundum gratiam firma sit promissio... qui viuificat mortuos / & vocat ea quæ non sunt tanq̃ sint." Romans 4:16-17</note> ¶ From the 17th [chapter] of the history of Ge[nesis]...

<summary>This page analyzes Romans 4, arguing that Abraham was justified by faith long before he was circumcised or given the law. It concludes that the promise of God is universal and based on grace, making faith the essential requirement for both Jews and Gentiles.</summary>

### COMMENTARY

<margin>36</margin>
...this testimony is taken from Genesis. However, because Paul frequently cites testimonies differently than we have them written, some believe that a more secret understanding of the law was written down by Ezra, and that Paul was not ignorant of this. Because he reveals the spirit of the letter more clearly, both here and in the following passages, he occasionally introduces testimonies from that source—details which would not escape the more diligent searchers of the divine words. Jerome indeed was aware that Ezra had left those books behind, though perhaps he had not seen them; therefore, he thought the Apostle did not cite testimonies to the letter, but according to their spiritual meaning. And it is true that the Apostle cites according to the meaning; yet some also maintain that this meaning had been written down, even if that scripture has not reached us, just as many other things cited by the apostles have not. To show how firm the faith of Abraham was, he adds:

> ¶ Who against hope believed in hope, that he might become the father of many nations, according to what was said: "So shall your offspring be." And he was not weakened in faith, nor did he consider his own body already dead (since he was about a hundred years old) or the deadness of Sarah’s womb. In the promise of God he did not waver through distrust, but was strengthened in faith, giving glory to God, being fully assured that what He had promised, He was also able to do. Therefore, it was credited to him as righteousness. <note>Paul is summarizing the narrative of Genesis 15 and 17, emphasizing that Abraham’s "hope" was based on God's character rather than physical possibility.</note>

¶ So also we—when the conversation turns to righteousness and justification, or the obtaining of the promise of the eternal inheritance—ought to have faith like the faithful Abraham. We should give glory to God, recognizing that these things come from God and not from ourselves or our own works. We should praise His grace, which is the savior of all, and His omnipotent truth and faithfulness, for He truly and faithfully fulfills every promise of His grace to the faithful. For what was said—that "it was credited to him as righteousness"—while true of Abraham, was not written for him alone. It was written for us as well, so that we might have firm faith in God, understanding that He justified Abraham by His grace. But it is also for us who believe in Him: that out of the abundance of His goodness He will justify us, and much more so than Abraham. For He has already given His only-begotten Son to atone for our sins and raised Him to immortality for our justification. Before the coming of Christ, neither were sins perfectly blotted out, nor was anyone perfectly justified to receive eternal life; rather, <margin>37</margin> only certain preparatory things preceded. These things—the blood of Christ and the resurrection—have been enacted in truth. Paul testifies to all this in this manner, saying:

> ¶ Now it was not written for his sake alone that it was credited to him, but also for those to whom it will be credited—for those of us who believe in Him who raised Jesus our Lord from the dead, who was handed over for our sins and was raised for our justification.

¶ Those who lived before the coming of Christ were not yet redeemed before His arrival; they were not yet able to obtain full and consummate <term>justification; the theological state of being made "right" or "just" before God</term>. But all who enter this life after His coming—after His life-giving death that takes away sins and His resurrection that fully justifies—all these are redeemed, and all can obtain full and consummate justification. Therefore, to the Author of such great gifts be praise, honor, and thanksgiving forever and ever.

<margin>A 29</margin> ¶ AN EXAMINATION of several points regarding the literal text. ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *For if Abraham was justified by works, he has glory.* ¶ **From the Greek:** rather "boasting" <note>original: "καύχημα" (kauchēma)</note>. Paul writes: <note>original: "εἰ γὰρ Ἀβραὰμ ἐξ ἔργων ἐδικαιώθη, ἔχει καύχημα"</note> (If for Abraham from works was justified, he has a boast). And wherever this word *kauchēma* is placed, we prefer to add the noun "boasting" for the sake of the Greek understanding. But where *doxa* <note>original: "δόξα"</note> appears, we use the name "glory." This is so that the ambiguity in the Latin vocabulary does not deceive readers, since such ambiguity is not found in the Greek.

<margin>A 30</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Reward is not imputed according to grace.* ¶ It could have been said "is not credited" <note>original: "reputatur"</note> according to grace, just as the ancient translator had said a little earlier: *Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness.* And a little later: *Faith is credited to him as righteousness.* For both here and there, Paul uses the same word *logizomai* <note>original: "λογίζομαι" (logizomai), meaning to reckon, count, or credit</note>. Paul writes: <note>original: "ὁ μισθὸς οὐ λογίζεται κατὰ χάριν"</note> (The reward is not credited according to grace).

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *His faith is credited as righteousness according to the purpose of the grace of God.* ¶ This phrase "according to the purpose of the grace of God" is not currently found in the Greek codices. However, it does not hinder the understanding. Paul writes: <note>original: "λογίζεται ἡ πίστις αὐτοῦ εἰς δικαιοσύνην"</note> (his faith is credited as righteousness). And he immediately adds: <note>original: "κατάπερ καὶ Δαβὶδ λέγει"</note> (just as David also says).

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *To whom God accepts righteousness without works.* ¶ The ancient translator could have said: *to whom God credits righteousness without works.* For the same word which the ancient translator here renders as "accepts" <note>original: "accepto fert"</note>, he had translated a little before as "credits" <note>original: "reputor"</note>. Paul seems to use this word sometimes in the passive and sometimes in the active voice for the convenience of the passage. The ancient translator uses such a variety of interpretations for one and the same word that he sometimes translates it as "imputed," sometimes "credited," sometimes "accepts," and many other things. Truly, when that word occurs, we will not vary the translation regarding the Greek meaning, just as Paul did not vary the word, so that we do not seem to introduce a different meaning. Paul writes: <note>original: "ὁ θεὸς λογίζεται δικαιοσύνην χωρὶς ἔργων"</note> (God credits righteousness apart from works).

<margin>B 31</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Does this blessedness then remain only for the circumcised, or also for the uncircumcised?* Neither the word "only" nor "remains" is found in Paul’s text, but...

->I.<-

<margin>B 32</margin> The substantive verb <term>is</term> <note>original: "est"</note> could be understood as implied, as if we were to say: "Is this blessedness then in the circumcision, or also in the uncircumcision?" Paul: **"Does this blessedness then come upon the circumcision, or also upon the uncircumcision?"** <note>original Greek: "ὁ μακαρισμὸς οὗτος οὖν ἐπὶ τὴν περιτομὴν ἢ καὶ ἐπὶ τὴν ἀκροβυστίαν"</note> ¶ The Vulgate edition: **"The seal of the righteousness of the faith which is in the uncircumcision."** ¶ The verb is not expressed in the Greek. But if it had to be expressed, it seems it should have been done through the past tense rather than the present; one should say "the faith which **was** in the uncircumcision." Paul: **"a seal of the righteousness of the faith which [was] in the uncircumcision."** <note>original Greek: "σφραγι̃δα τη̃ς δικαιοσύνης τη̃ς πίστεως τη̃ς ἐν τη̃ ἀκροβυστίᾳ"</note> ¶ The Vulgate edition: **"Not to those only who are of the circumcision."** ¶ In Paul's text, the particle "only" is joined with "circumcision," not with "those." This is so it may be understood as: "not to those who are of the circumcision **only**." Paul: **"to those not of the circumcision only."** <note>original Greek: "τοι̃ς οὐκ ἐκ περιτομη̃ς μόνον"</note> ¶ The Vulgate edition: **"But to those who follow the footsteps of the faith which is in the uncircumcision of our father Abraham."** ¶ As before, the past tense should be understood rather than the present; or it should be expressed through the past tense for a clearer understanding of the Latin phrasing. For in the Greek, the verb is not expressed but is understood. Paul: **"but also to those who walk in the footsteps of the faith of our father Abraham which [was] in the uncircumcision."** <note>original Greek: "ἀλλὰ καὶ τοι̃ς στοιχοι̃σιν ἴχνεσι τη̃ς πίστεως τη̃ς ἐν τῇ ἀκροβυστίᾳ του̃ πατρὸς ἡμω̃ν ἀβραάμ"</note> ¶ "But also to those who follow the footsteps of the faith which [was] in the uncircumcision of our father Abraham." Because if the verb "was" is expressed—by saying "the faith which **was** in the uncircumcision of our father Abraham"—it seems more appropriate and corresponds better to what Paul intends: that faith was credited to Abraham for righteousness while in uncircumcision, not in circumcision. Also, we explain it more appropriately through the past tense to designate that he was justified in uncircumcision a long interval of time before circumcision was given to him.

<margin>C 33</margin> ¶ The Vulgate edition: **"That he might be the heir of the world."** ¶ You may ask: where was the inheritance of the world promised to Abraham? It seems the answer can be: in Genesis 13, where it is held: "And the Lord said to Abraham after Lot was separated from him: 'Lift up your eyes and look from the place where you are now, to the north and the south, to the east and the west: all the land which you see I will give to you and to your offspring forever. and I will make your offspring like the dust of the earth.'" Therefore, all regions of the earth—south and north, east and west—were promised to Abraham and his offspring, as the inheritance of the world. From this, it is understood that the "offspring of Abraham" refers not only to the Jews who inhabited Judea, but also to all the faithful wherever they may be among the nations. Truly, these latter are the children of Abraham's faith; the former are children of the flesh. And it is not only Judea that must be understood as the land of promise, but also this land which we tread upon in Europe. Indeed, the entire world is the land of promise. Paul understood and opened this up wonderfully when he said the inheritance of the world was promised to Abraham. Therefore, those who strive to make people faithful, in whatever places of the earth they live, seem to serve the divine promise, so that the inheritance of the world may fall to the children of Abraham. And as long as they are not yet faithful, they are not the offspring of Abraham; but through faith first, they are raised up as the offspring of Abraham. In this way, John [the Baptist] did not call the hardened and unfaithful Jews "children of Abraham," but said: "For I tell you that God is able to raise up children for Abraham from these stones." Therefore, faith truly makes children of Abraham, not the flesh.

<margin>D 35</margin> ¶ Therefore, it is faithfulness, not carnal kinship. ¶ The Vulgate edition: **"The promise to all the offspring, not to him who is of the law only, but also to him who is of the faith of Abraham."** ¶ Here, it would have been better to say "to that which" <note>original: "ei quod"</note> twice. For "to him" <note>original: "ei"</note> refers back to "offspring" <note>original: "semen"</note>, which is a neuter noun. Paul: **"the promise to all the offspring, not to that [offspring] of the law only, but also to that of the faith of Abraham."** <note>original Greek: "ἐπαγγελίαν τω̃ πᾶντι τω̃ σπέρματι. οὐ τω̃ ἐκ του̃ νόμου μόνον. ἀλλὰ καὶ τω̃ ἐκ πίστεως ἀβραάμ"</note> ¶ The Vulgate edition: **"And calls those things which are not as though they are."** ¶ Thus in Greek: **"and calling the non-existent things as existent."** <note>original Greek: "καὶ καλου̃ντος τα μὴ ὄντα ὡς ὄντα"</note> Or: "who calls those things which are not as though they were." And this word "The Caller" <note>original: "ὁ καλῶν"</note>—that is, "he who calls," which descends from the verb *kaleo*—and its derivatives are frequently used by Paul; it signifies the same as "summons," "invites," and (if I may say so) in a certain way "allures." As in the Epistle to the Galatians: "But when it pleased Him who set me apart from my mother's womb and called me through His grace." <note>original Greek: "καὶ καλέσας διὰ τη̃ς χάριτος αὐτου̃"</note> Therefore, according to this meaning, "He who calls those things which are not as though they were" means: He summons, invites, and with exuberant kindness allures things which do not exist as though they did. They do not exist in themselves, but they are always present to God, to whom all things are always present. For He who fills infinity fills the world, being present everywhere in the world. And He who fills eternity fills all time as well, and is present to all time and all temporal things. And great and incomprehensible is the kindness of God, who called, summoned, and invited us to His righteousness even before we existed, as if His providence did not abandon us whether we were or were not. And when the mysteries were being performed for our first fathers, He was providing for us and inviting us to His righteousness. "Now it was not written," says the most blessed Paul, "for his sake alone, that it was credited to him as righteousness; but for our sake also, to whom it will be credited as we believe in Him who raised JESUS our Lord from the dead."

<margin>E 36</margin> ¶ The Vulgate edition: **"According to what was said to him."** ¶ The small word "to him" is redundant; it is not found in the Greek. Paul: **"According to what was said."** <note>original Greek: "κατὰ τὸ εἰρημένον"</note> ¶ The Vulgate edition: **"So shall your offspring be, like the stars of heaven and the sand..."**

Paul: **"So shall your seed be."** <note>original Greek: οὕτως ἔσται τὸ σπέρμα σου</note> And he immediately adds: **"and not being weak in faith."** <note>original Greek: καὶ μὴ ἀσθενήσας τῆ πίστει</note> And if the old translator’s Greek manuscript did not have this, it was added by someone to supplement the understanding, although it should have been sought from the history in Genesis, where it is read: "Look up at the heaven, and count the stars if you can," and he said to him, "So shall your seed be." ¶ The Vulgate edition: **"Now it is not written only for him."** ¶ Paul: **"But it was not written for him alone."** <note>original Greek: οὐκ ἐγράφη δὲ δι’ αὐτὸν μόνον</note> Where "alone" is clearly recognized as being added to "him." Therefore, we have followed this understanding and this law of translation along with the old translator. ¶ The Vulgate edition: **"Who raised JESUS CHRIST our Lord from the dead."** ¶ The Greek does not have "CHRIST." <margin>38</margin>Through the death of Christ our sins are deleted—that is, they are dismissed and forgiven by Christ on our behalf. And they are also dismissed and forgiven in us through the same, as often as we fall into error and, with repentance as our guide, recur to him through true faith. And through his resurrection, after the dismissal of sins, <term>justification</term> <note>The process by which a person is made righteous or "right" with God.</note> is granted to us in him—that is, to him for our sake. This is followed by peace with God and reconciliation, so that we may receive an eternal inheritance with Christ. This inheritance we possess in this world through hope, but in the next through the enjoyment of eternal goods. For in Christ is the remission of all sins; in Christ is the justification of all; in Christ is the reconciliation of all. And therefore Paul adds: ¶ **Therefore, being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord JESUS CHRIST, through whom we have access by faith into this grace in which we stand, and we glory in the hope of the glory of God.** ¶ Truly great is this grace: the justification received by us from Christ. For in Christ it is supreme and universal, but in us and in each individual it is a particular justification, in which we must especially stand. It is also a great occasion for glorying and exulting in the spirit: the expectation of the glory of God in the immortality of life. But the Apostles and Paul did not only glory in that certain hope of the glory of God, but also in tribulations, as it is written: "And they went rejoicing from the presence of the council because they were counted worthy to suffer reproach for the name of Jesus." For they recognized that tribulations produced patience in them, as they bore those trials with an even and joyful mind for Christ's sake. Patience, in turn, made them "proven," just as gold is proven when it does not yield to the violence of fire but endures, becoming more beautiful and (so to speak) more joyful. This proof much more increased their hope. For hope has no consequence of shame. For just as despair destroys, shames, and takes away life, granting death; so hope saves, defends from shame, and, taking away death, grants life. Add to this that through these things they were made like Christ and were imitators of Christ, who was troubled, most patient, proven, and hoping above all others. Troubled: "A man," he says, "has trampled me; fighting all day, he has troubled me." <note>A reference to Psalm 56:1.</note> Most patient: "You are," he says, "my patience, O Lord; my hope from my youth." <note>A reference to Psalm 71:5.</note> Proven: "You have tested my heart," he says, "and visited me by night; you have examined me with fire, <margin>39</margin> and no iniquity was found in me." <note>A reference to Psalm 17:3.</note> Likewise, hoping: "But I," he says, "will always hope, and I will add to all your praise." <note>Psalm 71:14.</note> And again: "In you, O Lord, have I hoped; let me never be put to shame." <note>Psalm 31:1.</note> And for that reason, Paul subjoins: ¶ **And not only that, but we also glory in tribulations, knowing that tribulation works patience; and patience, proof; and proof, hope; and hope does not confound.** ¶ Here is the wonderful order of these three virtues in Paul: faith, hope, and <term>charity</term>. <note>In this context, "charity" (Latin: caritas) means divine, selfless love rather than just giving to the poor.</note> Faith is first; second is hope; and third is charity. From faith comes hope; and hope immediately has the charity of God as its companion. For if you do not believe—if you do not have faith—you do not hope. If you do not hope, you do not love. But if you both believe and hope, you immediately love. And the charity of God is the perfection and consummation of the other two, faith and hope. This charity was abundantly poured out upon the apostles and <margin>40</margin> divine Paul through the Holy Spirit. Hope, he says, does not confound. And he adds the reason, saying: ¶ **Because the charity of God is poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who is given to us.** ¶ If there were hope without charity, it would be empty and would confound, as it would find death rather than life. Therefore, let us imitate the glorious apostles, having firm faith, which is followed by the hope of attaining the glory of God, in which we should exult in mind. And let us not only exult in the hope of glory, but also by bearing tribulations with equanimity, [proving] our testing through patience...
