<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Epistle to the Romans, specifically focusing on the beginning of Chapter 5. It transitions from the discussion of Abraham's faith to the fruits of justification: hope, charity, and the role of Christ’s death in reconciling humanity to God.</meta>

79 Ro.

->I<-

acknowledging and increasing our hope: let us pray that charity <note>or "love"; original: charitatem</note> be added to this hope through the gift of the Holy Spirit. ¶ And how should we not hope? How should we not possess the love of God? For while we were still weak and powerless to return to health, Christ died at that time for us, the ungodly. Now, hardly anyone would be willing to die for a just man, though there might be some who would dare to face the danger of death for the sake of a good person or to achieve some great good. But we were not just; we were unjust and impious. Nor did Christ seek his own benefit or advantage by dying for us. For he sought no advantage for himself, since what he held from the Father was greater than all things. ¶ **"What my Father gave me,"** he said, **"is greater than all."** <note>A reference to John 10:29</note> And in this, he showed his great and inexpressible love toward us, to increase hope and charity within us: that he died for us while we were still sinners, even at that very time. What then of now? Shall we not (whom he has redeemed, justified, and reconciled to the Father) much more be saved through him, having been snatched from eternal damnation? ¶ Ought we not much more to hope, to burn with charity, and to exult in God through Christ our Lord, who loved and loves us so much and has bestowed such unimaginable benefits? If the death of the Son of God reconciled enemies, will not his immortal life much more save those who are now reconciled and made his friends? These are arguments from the lesser to the greater.

<margin>41</margin>
For this is how Paul has it:
> For while we were still weak, according to the time, Christ died for the ungodly. For hardly does one die for a just man; perhaps for a good man someone might dare to die. But God proves his charity toward us: because while we were still sinners, Christ died for us. Much more, therefore, being now justified in his blood, we shall be saved from wrath through him. For if, while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son: much more, being reconciled, we shall be saved in his life. And not only that, but we also glory in God through our Lord JESUS CHRIST, through whom we have now received reconciliation.

¶ But from where would we receive reconciliation, except from a preceding enmity toward God? And from where did this enmity between us and God hang? The Apostle reveals that it was from sin. For through the sin of the first parent, death entered into the whole world, and enmity was established between him and God. And in this manner, death passed into all men—those who sinned in the same way he sinned and died because of their own sin—and it passed likewise into those who did not sin, just as if they had transgressed like Adam. For even Abel and infants who did not sin died in the same way as Adam. And sin reigned from Adam until the giving of the Law, and it reigns after the Law was given. For whoever did not love God and neighbor before the Law—and all the more if they despised or hated them—was sinning; whoever brought shame or dishonor upon father and mother, whoever committed murder, whoever snatched the property of others, and things of that kind. However, there is this difference: that sin before the giving of the Law (even if it was sin) was not imputed <note>or "accounted/reckoned"</note> as sin. But after the Law was given, sin was imputed and recognized to be sin. It is just like something unhealthy before and after a doctor’s order: it remains unhealthy, such as for those suspected of leprosy: dairy products, fresh fish, and pork. But this is the difference: that the unhealthy thing is not reckoned as unhealthy before the order, even if it is harmful and unhealthy; but after the doctor’s order, its unhealthiness is not ignored, but is reckoned and known to be unhealthy. And Paul suggests all these things when he says:

<margin>42</margin>
¶ Therefore, just as through one
> man sin entered into the world, and through sin, death; so death passed into all men, in which all have sinned. For until the Law, sin was in the world; but sin was not imputed when there was no law. But death reigned from Adam until Moses (even over those who did not sin) in the likeness of the transgression of Adam, who is a form <note>or "type"</note> of the one to come.

¶ There were two Adams. The first was the transgressor of God’s command, cast out of paradise. The second was the perpetual observer of God’s mandate, taken up into paradise. The first was the author of sin and death for men; the second was the grantor of justification and life. The first: the old. The second: the new. The first: earthly. The second: heavenly. And the earthly was a "type" <note>term: *typus* — a prophetic figure or foreshadowing</note> of the heavenly—that is, a certain figure and shadowy likeness representing him in some things by a direct law of proportion and analogy, but in many other things by contrast. For just as the old Adam was taken from the virgin earth <note>A common theological idea that Adam was made from earth that had not yet been "corrupted" by tilling or the curse</note> and the second from virgin flesh; and as God breathed the breath of life into the mud formed into a man, so the power of the Most High overshadowed the Virgin with the Holy Spirit; and as the old Adam slept in the garden and Eve was formed from his side, so while the Lord slept on the cross, the Church was formed from his opened side. These things correspond correctly to the Analogy, and the first Adam is a "form of the one to come"—that is, of Christ and the incarnate Word of God. But in that Adam was a transgressor and Christ innocent, that the former was disobedient and the latter obedient, that the former was the author of death and Christ of life, that the former was earthly and the latter heavenly—that first one was the type and figure, while this one is the truth. These and countless other such things show the first Adam and...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Epistle to the Romans, specifically analyzing the comparison Paul makes between Adam and Christ in Chapter 5. It builds on the previous discussion of justification by explaining why Christ's power to save is logically and ontologically superior to Adam’s power to bring death.</meta>

<header>COMMENTARY</header>

The second point is to respond from the opposite perspective, which is what Paul's sentiment achieves. For the offense belongs to the first Adam, while grace and the gift belong to the second. These are opposites and they correspond from opposite positions: for the offense (inasmuch as it is a privation, a negation, and a "non-being" <note>original: *non ens*; a philosophical term meaning sin is the absence of good rather than a positive substance</note>) is weak and ineffective. Grace, however, is a quality <note>original: *habitus*</note>, an affirmation, and a valid and effective "being" <note>original: *ens*</note>. Who, therefore, does not see by this manifest argument: if the offense of the first Adam, being weak and feeble, could hurl many into death, how much more can the grace and gift of Christ the Lord—the second and true Adam, who is the true and living image of God—provide life to many? This grace and gift of Christ is, indeed, strong, valid, and effective. Let us therefore flee to the grace of Christ, which is most powerful for saving, and infinitely more powerful to save than the sin of Adam or our own sin is to damn. For it is as much more powerful as "something" is more powerful than "nothing." Let this hope animate us and convert us, burning with love for him who is both willing and so powerful to save. Sin and the gift (understand grace and the gift to be the same thing) do not have equal power. For sin came through one who sinned, but the gift through one who did no sin. From one sin came judgment unto condemnation, but the gift from many sins leads unto justification. How powerful, then, is the gift! How powerful is grace for saving and justifying, which countless sins are not strong enough to resist! Therefore, the gift and sin are not equals. Let us therefore aspire to the grace of Christ, which resists countless sins; and whoever possesses it can struggle against infinite sins, just as light can drive away infinite darkness. For anyone who does not feel this efficacy of the grace of Christ is blind, denying the power of light over darkness and believing that the "nothing-power" of darkness is stronger than light. If, therefore, by the offense of one, death reigned over many through that one, how much more by a much more powerful right shall life reign through the one, Jesus Christ, for those receiving the abundance of grace, the gift, and justification? For this one is truly the strongest; whereas that one <note>Adam</note>, since he fell, is weak and feeble. Grace, the gift, and justification are valid; sin and death are weak and ineffective. And although a human being, looking at himself and within himself, cannot overcome sin and death (just as the body cannot drive away darkness), yet when he looks at the grace of Christ, he sees that—not indeed by himself, but by the grace of Christ in him—he can put to flight both offense and death just as the sun's radiance drives away the shadows from a dark place. You will easily understand all of Paul's reasoning if you know how to follow the analogy of opposites, and to attribute (as is right) the more powerful parts to Christ for saving, and the weaker parts to Adam for damning. And certainly, they are as much weaker as man is less powerful than God. The parts of grace are more powerful for giving life, while the parts of sin are weaker for bringing death. The Apostle gathers these points through a most certain reasoning, which no one will fail to recognize as most valid, unless they are entirely ignorant of good logic <note>original: *dialectice*</note>. But—

<margin>43</margin>
> now let us hear how Paul, being ignorant of no discipline, neither divine nor human, argues nobly. For he says: ¶ "But not as the offense, so also is the gift. For if by the offense of one many died, much more has the grace of God and the gift, in the grace of one man Jesus Christ, abounded unto many. And the gift is not as it was through one who sinned. For judgment was from one unto condemnation: but grace is from many offenses unto justification. For if by the offense of one, death reigned through one: much more shall those receiving the abundance of grace, and of the gift of justice, reign in life through **JESUS CHRIST.** Therefore, just as through the offense of one it was unto condemnation for all men: so also through the justice of one it is unto justification of life for all men. For as by the disobedience of one man, many were made sinners: so also by the obedience of one, many shall be made just."

¶ Behold the offense of one, to which the stronger grace of the one is opposed. That one was Adam: mortal and earthly. This one is Christ: immortal and God. Offense leads to death;
<margin>40</margin>
much more does life follow grace. Offense brings the condemnation of all men to death; grace brings the absolution and justification of all men to life. Behold, to the disobedience of one, a stronger obedience is opposed. The sin of many followed the disobedience of that one; much more frequently does the justice of many follow the obedience of this one. If these things do not follow, it is not due to any insufficiency of this grace, justice, or obedience, but because of our own perversity—we who are unwilling to be participants in such great and powerful grace, justice, and obedience. It is just as if some captives thrown into chains either distrusted or scorned to be participants in a ransom, even though someone had come who possessed a most bountiful ransom for everyone. He possesses within himself the redemption of us all; a redemption sufficient not only for us, but even for redeeming countless worlds. And so that it might be known how strong and valid his grace is, it was given at the time when offenses were at their strongest. For although there were offenses before the Law, they were not recognized as offenses. But through the Law, they were known to be offenses. And men sinned not through ignorance, but knowingly, and therefore more seriously. The Law was given first and primarily so that, knowing evils, they might flee them; and secondly, so that by not doing what it commanded, they might sin more gravely. The latter was a matter of occasion;
<margin>44</margin>
the former a matter of intention. And therefore Paul adds: ¶ "But the Law entered in, that offense might abound. But where offense abounded, grace did superabound: so that as sin reigned..."

...as sin reigned unto death: so also may grace reign through righteousness unto eternal life through JESUS CHRIST our Lord. ¶ The law indeed slipped in: so that (not by intention, but by occasion) the offense might abound. The one giving the law is like a physician. The law represents the prescriptions, revealing all things that are harmful and unhealthy, as well as all things that assist health. Those receiving the law are like the patients in a hospital. If they follow the cravings of their disease—having been warned about many harmful and unhealthy things they were previously ignorant of and did not desire—they may begin to desire and use them. By this occasion, and not by the physician's intention, they will become more gravely ill. Such is the case with those who transgress the law. This is how the first parent <note>referring to Adam</note> sinned. For God wished to protect and save him through a command. For He knew what was to come: that the enemy would lure him into eating from a fruit harmful to him, or perhaps he might have eaten it through ignorance, whereby he would have incurred bodily death and harmful affections. He did not obey the physician and God, and by this occasion, he offended more seriously. For the tree was good and fulfilled its place in the number of the universe, just as fire is good, or as hemlock is good while fulfilling its own nature; but fire is bad for you if you touch it, and hemlock is bad if you eat it. And when Paul argues from opposites, he sometimes adds more to one part of the opposition than to the other; if you understand the same amount in the other part, you do not err. For example, when he says: "so that just as sin reigned in death: so also grace may reign through righteousness unto eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord." In the second part, he adds "through righteousness" and "through Jesus Christ our Lord," which are not placed in opposition in the first part. Therefore, if you understand the whole by expressing the opposites—"as sin reigned through unrighteousness unto eternal death through Adam: so also grace reigns through righteousness unto eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord"—you will not err, and you will see the opposites set against one another individually: reign (namely, a tyrannical one) against reign; sin against grace; unrighteousness against righteousness; eternal death against eternal life; Adam against Christ. Whoever does this in other passages will be greatly helped in understanding. For Paul frequently expresses fewer things while intending more. Christ restored the kingdom, grace, righteousness, and eternal life—things more magnificent than those which Adam had lost for himself and for us. To Him be honor and glory forever and ever. <meta>This page continues the theological commentary on the Epistle to the Romans, specifically focusing on the contrast between Adam and Christ in chapter 5. <meta>Archival mark "5" in pencil at top left corner</meta>

responding from the opposite side. This is what Paul’s opinion pursues. For the first **Adam** <note>original: "Adę"</note> belongs the transgression; to the second belongs grace and the gift. And these are opposites, and they respond as opposites. For transgression (being a <term>privation</term> <note>the absence or lack of a good that should be present</note>, a negation, and a "non-being") is weak and ineffective. Grace, however, is a state of being, an affirmation, and a valid and effective "being." Who, therefore, does not see by manifest argument: if the transgression of the first Adam, being infirm and weak, could plunge many into death, how much more can the grace and gift of Christ the Lord—the second and true Adam, who is the true and living image of God—how much more, I say, can the grace and gift of Christ, being strong, valid, and effective, provide life to many?

Let us therefore flee to the most powerful grace of Christ for salvation, which is infinitely more powerful for saving than Adam’s sin or our own can be for damning. For it is as much more powerful as "something" is more powerful than "nothing." Let this hope animate us and convert us, burning with love toward him who wills and is so powerful to save. Sin and the gift (understand "grace" and "gift" as the same thing here) do not have equal strength. For sin came through one who sinned; the gift came through one who did not sin. From one sin came judgment unto condemnation, but the gift from many sins leads to justification. How powerful, then, is the gift, how powerful the grace for saving and justifying, which countless sins are not strong enough to resist! Therefore, the gift and sin are not equal.

Let us therefore aspire to the grace of Christ, which resists countless sins. Whoever possesses it can struggle against infinite sins, just as light can drive away infinite darkness. For he who does not feel this efficacy of Christ’s grace is blind, denying the power of light in the darkness and believing the "nothing-power" <note>original: "nichilopotentiam"</note> of darkness to be more valid than light. If, therefore, by the transgression of one, death reigned over many through that one, how much more by a more valid right shall life reign through the one, Jesus Christ, for those receiving the abundance of grace, of the gift, and of justification? For this one is the strongest; but that one <note>Adam</note>, because he fell, is weak and infirm. Grace, the gift, and justification are valid; sin and death are weak and ineffective. And although man, when he looks at himself and within himself, cannot overcome sin and death—just as a body cannot drive away darkness—yet when he looks to the grace of Christ, he sees not himself, but the grace of Christ in him. It can chase away transgression and death just as the sun’s beam chases the shadows from a dark place. You will easily understand all of Paul’s reasonings if you know how to follow the analogy of opposites, and to attribute the more powerful parts to Christ for saving (as is right) and the weaker parts to Adam for damning. And certainly they are as much weaker as man is less powerful than God. The parts of grace are more powerful for giving life, while the parts of sin are weaker for bringing death. The apostle collects these points by a most certain reasoning, which no one will fail to recognize as most valid unless they are utterly ignorant of good <term>dialectics</term> <note>the formal art of logical argument and investigation</note>. But now, let us hear how Paul—ignorant of no discipline, neither divine nor human—nobly argues. For he says:

¶ Behold the transgression of one, to which the stronger grace of the other is opposed. That one: Adam, mortal and earthly. This one: Christ, immortal and God. Transgression: death follows. And much more does life follow grace. Transgression: the condemnation of all men to death. Grace: the absolution and justification of all men to life. Behold, to the disobedience of one, a stronger obedience is opposed. The sin of many followed that man’s disobedience; much more frequently does the righteousness of many follow this man’s obedience. If this righteousness does not follow, it is not because of any insufficiency of grace, righteousness, or obedience in him, but because of our own perversity—we who are unwilling to be participants in such great and powerful grace, righteousness, and obedience. It is just as if some captives thrown into chains either distrusted or despised being part of a redemption, even though someone arrived who possessed the most copious ransom for everyone. He himself holds within himself the redemption of us all; it is sufficient not only for us, but even for redeeming countless worlds. And so that it may be known how strong and valid his grace is, it was given at the time when transgressions were at their strongest. For although there were transgressions before the Law, they were not recognized as transgressions. But through the Law, they were known to be transgressions. And men did not sin through ignorance, but knowingly, and therefore more gravely. And the Law was given first and principally so that they might flee known evils; secondarily, so that by not doing them, they might sin more gravely. The former was the intention; the latter was the occasion. And therefore Paul adds:

<meta>This page continues the theological commentary on Romans 5. It concludes the analogy of the Physician (God) and the Law (medicine) and begins a scholarly "Examination" of the biblical text, comparing the standard Latin Vulgate translation against the original Greek to ensure theological accuracy.</meta>

[sin reigned] unto death: so also might grace reign through righteousness into eternal life through JESUS CHRIST our Lord.

## I

**T**he Law indeed slipped in: so that (not by intention, but by occasion) transgression might abound. He who gives the law is the physician. The law consists of the prescriptions: revealing everything harmful and unhealthy, as well as everything that aids health. Those receiving the law are the sick. <margin>2</margin> If these patients follow the cravings of their disease—having been warned of many harmful and unhealthy things which they previously ignored and did not desire—and they then begin to crave and use those very things: they will become more gravely ill by occasion, though not by the physician's intention. So it is with those who transgress the law. In this way, our first parent <note>Adam</note> sinned. For God wished to protect and save him through a command. For He knew it would happen that the enemy would entice him to eat of the fruit that was harmful to him, or perhaps he might have eaten it through ignorance, whereby he would have incurred bodily death and harmful affections. He did not obey the physician and God: and by occasion, he failed. For the tree was good, and it filled its place in the number of the universe—just as fire is good, and just as hemlock is good, fulfilling its own nature—but fire is bad for you if you touch it, and hemlock is bad if you eat it. 

And when Paul argues from the opposite side, he sometimes adds more to one part of the opposition than the other: but if you understand the same amount in the other part, you do not err. For instance, when he says: "so that just as sin reigned in death, so also might grace reign through righteousness into eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord." In the second part, he adds "through righteousness" and "through Jesus Christ our Lord," which are not placed as opposites in the first part. Therefore, if you understand the whole thing this way, expressing the opposites—"that just as sin reigned through unrighteousness into eternal death through Adam, so also grace reigns through righteousness into eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord"—you will not err, and you will see the opposites more clearly, point by point. Kingdom (for it is a tyrannical one) against kingdom. Sin against grace. Unrighteousness against righteousness. Eternal death against eternal life. Adam against Christ. And he who does this in other matters will be greatly helped toward understanding. For Paul often expresses fewer things while intending more. And Christ repaired the kingdom, the grace, the righteousness, and the eternal life more magnificently than the things Adam had lost for himself and for us. To Him be honor and glory forever and ever. Now to the examination.

<margin>A 38</margin> ¶ EXAMINATION of several points regarding the literal text. **The Vulgate edition** <note>The standard Latin Bible of the time</note>: "Therefore, being justified by faith, *let us have* peace." ¶ **From Paul** <note>referring to the Greek text</note>: it should rather be said "we *have*" in the present <term>indicative</term> <note>a mood of a verb that expresses a fact or certainty, rather than a wish or command</note>. And he speaks of the apostles, the disciples, and himself, as is clear from the progression when he says: "the love of God is poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who is given to us." It follows that those justified and reconciled to God are those who *possess* peace, not those still wishing for what they already have. We should therefore read "we have," not "let us have." Paul: <note>original Greek: δικαιωθέντες οὖν ἐκ πίστεως εἰρήνην ἔχομεν</note> "Therefore, being justified by faith, we have peace." 

¶ **The Vulgate edition**: "And we glory in the hope of the *children* of God." ¶ **From Paul**, we should read: "and we glory in the hope of the *glory* of God." Why? Because "children" is an addition and superfluous. For what is there in which we ought to glory and exult more than in the hope of attaining the glory of God, solely from His goodness? Paul: <note>original Greek: καὶ καυχώμεθα ἐπ᾿ ἐλπίδι τῆς δόξης τοῦ θεοῦ</note> "and we exult in the hope of the glory of God." 

<margin>41</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition**: "For why did Christ, when we were still weak according to the time..." ¶ **Paul does not have** "for why," but "still" or "even," confirming on our part that a great occasion for love and affection ought to be held, although that immense love of God anticipated us by loving us first. But does not that public light of the world <note>the sun</note> anticipate the eyes so that they may see? So also does divine love anticipate us, so that we may love Him. And because of that very kindness of anticipation, we ought to love Him all the more fervently. It converted us even when we were completely fleeing and turned away, so that we might recognize such great goodness; it saves even the unwilling and pursues those fleeing lest they perish. Therefore, it should be read: "For while yet Christ..." And in what follows, "when we were still weak," the word "still" should be removed from this spot and it should read: "Christ, when we were weak." For Paul says: <note>original Greek: ἔτι γὰρ χριστὸς ὄντων ἡμῶν ἀσθενῶν κατὰ καιρόν</note> "For while we were still weak, or we being weak." For that "still" (as was already said) ought to be placed at the beginning, in place of this "for why." Where it says "according to the time," understand it as "at that time," connecting it to what follows, so that you understand it as "at that time He died for the ungodly." 

¶ **The Vulgate edition**: "While <margin>B 41</margin> we were still sinners according to the time." ¶ In this place, the phrase "according to the time" is superfluous; it is not found in the Greek. And if it were placed there, it seems it should refer to what follows (as was said), not what precedes, so that it would read "at that time Christ died for us." That is, during that time and in that season. Paul: <note>original Greek: ὅτι ἔτι ἁμαρτωλῶν ἡμῶν</note> "that while we were yet sinners," and immediately there follows "Christ for us." 

¶ **The Vulgate edition**: "Therefore as through one man sin entered into *this* world." ¶ <margin>5</margin> It was enough to say "into the world." Paul: <note>original Greek: Διὰ τοῦτο ὥσπερ δι᾿ ἑνὸς ἀνθρώπου ἡ ἁμαρτία εἰς τὸν κόσμον εἰσῆλθεν</note> "Therefore, just as through one man sin entered into the world." 

¶ **The Vulgate edition**: "And through sin death; and so death passed into all men." ¶ "And so into all": the conjunction "and" seems superfluous.

and it should be read in this way: "and through sin, death; so death passed into all men." <note>original: "et legēdū hoc modo. & per peccatū mors: ita ī oēs homines mors pertrāsiit."</note> Paul writes: "and through sin, death; and so death passed unto all men." <note>original Greek: "καὶ διὰ τῆς ἁμαρτίας ὁ θάνατος, οὕτως εἰς πάντας ἀνθρώπους ὁ θάνατος διῆλθεν."</note> And here, the phrase "so into all men" acts as the second part of the comparison. ¶ The **Vulgate edition** <note>The standard Latin Bible of the time</note> says: "In whom all have sinned." <note>original: "In quo oēs peccauerūt."</note> In Greek, this is "on account of which all sinned." <note>original Greek: "ἐφ’ ᾧ πάντες ἥμαρτον."</note> This phrase "on account of which" <note>original: "ἐφ’ ᾧ"</note> or "in whom" is ambiguous; it is unclear whether it is neutral—signifying "in that in which"—implying that just as Adam incurred death in the sin which he committed (this being the first entry of death into the world), so all who have sinned have incurred death in that in which they sinned—that is, in their own sin and because of their own sin. Yet Paul does not seem to mean that everyone sinned in this way, as he immediately adds: "death reigned from Adam until Moses even over those who did not sin." Therefore, those who did not sin and yet died did not die "in that in which they sinned," but rather in the "likeness of the transgression of Adam." Christ is the fount of all justification; Adam is the sinkhole <note>term: "sentina" — literally the bilge-water or cesspool, used here to contrast a pure fountain with a collection of filth</note> of all transgression. The likeness of Christ is life. The likeness of Adam is death. All who obtain salvation do so in the likeness of Christ; all who die do so in the likeness of Adam. There are, however, some who die both in that likeness and through their own specific fault. And this sense seems more in line with the Apostle’s intention. Others understand "in whom" in the masculine sense, referring to the one man, Adam; they understand it as: "in whom (namely, in the one man Adam) all have sinned." In that case, it means nothing other than that Adam's sin was universal, binding all his posterity to death, just as Christ's righteousness is universal, releasing all his posterity from death and restoring them to life. Thus all the children of Christ have worked righteousness in Christ. But to say they worked righteousness in Christ is not to say that they themselves performed the work, but that Christ performed a universal work of righteousness. Likewise, for all to have sinned in Adam is not for them to have committed a specific sin, but that Adam committed a fault of universal obligation. Is it not universal if it is common to both Adam and all his children? Certainly, it is universal. And the righteousness of Christ is far more universal, just as the capacity of heaven is wider than the narrowness of the earth. For the sin of Adam is like the whole earth, while the righteousness of Christ is like the vastness of the heavens. ¶ Blessed are they who are received into that vastness, and wretched are those who flee from it. He who understands that this obligation <note>A legal or moral debt</note> in the posterity of Adam is called "sin" by many will grasp the meaning of these difficult passages. He will see that few are exempt from this obligation: Christ alone by his nature; others by grace—some to a greater degree, some to a lesser—such as Enoch, Elijah, the Virgin Mother of God, and the Beloved Disciple. <note>The author lists figures traditionally thought to have been spared the full "debt" of death or original sin</note> And though Christ died, he did not die from the obligation of Adam; rather, though he was not bound, he died for those who were bound, so that he might free us from that obligation. And though the Blessed (or most Blessed) Virgin died, she did not die from the obligation of our first parent, but in imitation of her Son, so that in this too she might be "Christ-formed" and might console all the righteous who follow, who die in a Christ-like manner by imitation, and no longer out of the obligation of Adam. And this is the death of the righteous; they are all the more happy because they imitate the death of Christ and are sharers in the future resurrection. Even if Enoch and Elijah should die one day, they will die by no other death. But here we must close the floodgates, lest we rush into the vast sea of original sin and be forced to follow an opinion other than the Apostle's. Truly, there is a very wide gap between the Apostle’s way of discussing this and that of others. ¶ The **Vulgate edition**: "But sin was not imputed." <note>original: "Peccatum autē non imputabatur."</note> 
<margin>Chapter 42</margin> Paul’s word is "was not reckoned." <note>original Greek: "οὐκ ἐλλογεῖται"</note> This is better translated as "was not reckoned" rather than "imputed," as the translator almost always does elsewhere. For when we read "sin was not imputed," people understand it to mean "not imputed by God," just as in the passage: "Blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not imputed sin." But when it is said "sin was not reckoned," the understanding immediately follows that sin was not *reckoned by them* (namely, those who were sinning) to be sin—even though it was indeed sin and was being imputed by God. It is like a man who uses unhealthy things: he sins, even if he does not know he is sinning, and his physician reckons it against him; but he reckons it much more after he has given instructions and forbidden the unhealthy things. So, after the law was given by the Physician of Souls—the most merciful and most good God—those who sin will be beaten with many stripes. <note>A reference to Luke 12:47-48</note> Paul 
<margin>13.</margin> writes: "but sin is not reckoned." <note>original Greek: "ἁμαρτία δὲ οὐκ ἐλλογεῖται"</note> ¶ The **Vulgate edition**: "But death reigned from Adam until Moses, even over those who did not sin in the likeness of the transgression of Adam." ¶ The phrase "in the likeness of the transgression of Adam" seems to be said through *hyperbaton* <note>term: "hyperbaton" — a figure of speech where the natural word order is disrupted for emphasis</note> and should be referred back to the earlier part in this way: "but death reigned from Adam until Moses in the likeness of the transgression of Adam, even over those who did not sin." If it stays in its current place, it should be set off by an intervening parenthesis. But the holy **Ambrose**, because he understood it without hyperbaton or parenthesis, applied a different meaning, perhaps wishing to suggest that every man has sinned, but not "in the likeness of the transgression of Adam." He refers this "likeness of the transgression of Adam" to the act of "having sinned." And he speaks of Adam's sin as a particular sin. But who else bit the fruit in paradise? Who can compare it to idolatry—a type of sinning in which not all have sinned? But because Paul speaks of Adam as the opposite of Christ, and concerning...

Adam’s sin as universal, just as Christ’s justice is universal; therefore, the phrase understood through **hyperbaton** <term>hyperbaton: a rhetorical device where the natural word order is disrupted or transposed for emphasis or style</term> (which is very frequent in Paul’s usage) is more fitting to Paul's meaning. Paul [says]: "Nevertheless, death reigned from Adam until Moses, even over those who had not sinned in the likeness of the transgression of Adam." <note>original Greek: "ἀλλ’ ἐβασίλευσεν ὁ θάνατος ἀπὸ ἀδὰμ μέχρι μωϋσέως καὶ ἐπὶ τοὺς μὴ ἁμαρτήσαντας ἐπὶ τῷ ὁμοιώματι τῆς παραβάσεως ἀδάμ."</note>
<margin>C 43</margin> ¶ The **Vulgate edition** <note>The standard Latin Bible of the time</note>: "And not as through one sin, so also the gift." <note>original: "Et non sicut per vnum peccatum ita & donum."</note> ¶ It should be read: "not as through one who sinned [is] the gift." Paul [says]: "and not as through one who sinned is the gift." <note>original Greek: "καὶ οὐκ ὡς Δι’ ἑνὸς ἁμαρτήσαντος τὸ δώρημα."</note> For this word *hamartēsantos* is masculine, signifying a "sinner" or "one who has sinned." This is also the case in the **Ambrosian text** <note>A Latin commentary on Paul traditionally attributed to St. Ambrose, though now often assigned to "Ambrosiaster"</note>: "and not as through one who sinned." ¶ And the phrase "so also" is superfluous for the literal interpretation, but was added by the translator for clarity. What Paul is saying is: the gift is not like the one who sinned. For a sinner is weak and powerless, and from him comes the fault; but the gift is from a just man, who neither sinned nor could sin. He is not only powerful, but omnipotent. Is it any wonder then if one grace is effective in destroying countless faults? For darkness cannot enter into light, but light enters into darkness. Yet in the absence of light, darkness multiplies. There is also another interpretation given regarding the letter and the sense of the translator. ¶ The **Vulgate edition**: "For judgment [came] from one unto condemnation: but grace from many [offenses unto justification]." <note>original: "Nam iudicium ex vno in condemnationem : gratia autem ex multis."</note> ¶ The translator could have said: "but the *gift* from many," to more clearly and openly suggest the declaration of the preceding text where we use the word "gift." For Paul uses **charisma** <term>charisma: a Greek word for a free gift or favor bestowed by God</term> here, which the translator elsewhere renders as "gift," as seen shortly before: "But not as the offense, so also the gift." Paul [says]: "but not as the transgression, so also the gift." <note>original Greek: "ἀλλ’ οὐκ ὡς τὸ παράπτωμα , οὕτως καὶ τὸ χάρισμα."</note> Truly, these four [Greek words]—**charisma**, **dōrēma**, **dōrea**, and **charis**—the first three of which are usually translated as "gift" and the fourth as "grace," you may take as meaning the same thing in Paul's writing. Paul [says]: "For the judgment was from one unto condemnation, but the gift was from many [transgressions]." <note>original Greek: "τὸ μὲν γὰρ κρίμα ἐξ ἑνὸς εἰς κατάκριμα , τὸ δὲ χάρισμα ἐκ πολλῶν."</note> ¶ The **Vulgate edition**: "Much more the abundance of grace, and of the donation, and of justice." <note>original: "Multo magis abundantiam gratiæ/ & donationis/ & iustitiæ."</note> ¶ Here the translator could have said "of grace and of the gift of justice," removing the conjunction "and." Paul [says]: "of grace and of the gift of justice." <note>original Greek: "τῆς χάριτος καὶ τῆς δωρεᾶς τῆς Δικαιοσύνης."</note> Just as a little before he translates the same word *dōrea* as "gift," when he says: "much more the grace of God and the gift, in the grace of one man Jesus Christ." Where Paul has: "much more the grace of God and the gift in grace of the man Jesus Christ." <note>original Greek: "πολλῷ μᾶλλον ἡ χάρις τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ ἡ δωρεὰ ἐν χάριτι τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ."</note> ¶ The **Vulgate edition**: "So also through the obedience of one." <note>original: "Ita & per vnius obedientiem."</note> ¶ The translator could have said "obedience" in a way that more appropriately matched the word "disobedience" mentioned earlier as its opposite. Paul [says]: "so also through the obedience of the one." <note>original Greek: "οὕτως καὶ Διὰ τῆς ὑπακοῆς τοῦ ἑνός."</note> And why, if here he translates *parakoēs* as "disobedience," does he not also translate *hypakoēs* as "obedience," creating a manifest opposition just as Paul did? Add to this that the same word, *hypakoēn*, which Paul uses here, he elsewhere translates as "obedience," such as in this Epistle to the Romans <note>The author attributes this quote to Romans, but it is actually Hebrews 5:8</note>: "he learned obedience from the things which he suffered." Where Paul says: "he learned obedience from what he suffered." <note>original Greek: "ἔμαθεν ἀφ’ ὧν ἔπαθεν τὴν ὑπακοὴν."</note> But these things will perhaps seem of little importance. However, to speak appropriately should not seem a light matter to anyone who is truly wise. But now to what follows.

### CHAPTER VI

<margin>45</margin> Shortly before, the blessed Paul said: "where sin abounded, grace did more exceedingly abound." Those who did not understand could have said: "therefore, let sin abound in us, so that grace may superabound in us; let us persevere in sin so that we may receive the abundance of grace." Paul excludes this insane impiety, saying: ¶ "What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid." ¶ He gives the reason and reveals the **sacrament** <term>sacrament: here used in the sense of a 'sacred mystery' or the inward spiritual meaning of an outward act</term> when he adds: ¶ "We who are dead to sin, how shall we live any longer therein? Know you not that all we who are baptized in **CHRIST JESUS** are baptized in his death? For we are buried together with him by baptism into death; that as **CHRIST** is risen from the dead by the glory of the Father, so we also may walk in newness of life." ¶ We have a twofold birth in this world: one from Adam, and another from Christ. From the former, we are born children of the flesh, of wrath, of sin, of obligation, and of death. From the latter, we are born children of the spirit, of glory, of grace, of redemption, and of eternal life. From the former, we are children of man and slaves; from the latter, we are children of God and free. Adam and all his children are one body of sin, with Adam as the head. Christ and all his children are one body of justice, with Christ as the head. In the former, the death of obligation and the worst kind of death reigns, as it is written: "The death of sinners is the worst." <note>Psalm 34:21</note> In the latter, there is a death of imitation, and it is the best, of which it is said: "Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints." <note>Psalm 116:15</note> And this precious death first occurs for us in the sacred veils, in holy baptism, where we are transferred from the body of sin into the body of justice.

<meta>This page continues the theological exploration of Romans 6, moving from the comparison of Adam and Christ to the specific mechanism of how a believer transitions from the "body of Adam" to the "body of Christ" through the sacrament of baptism.</meta>

<page-num>6</page-num>
<header>COMMENTARY</header>

from the body of Adam: into the body of Christ, which cannot happen unless we die to sin and live to righteousness. This death occurs in us through the washing of the font <note>original: "ablutionem lauacri," referring to the baptismal bath</note>: signifying the most precious blood of Christ’s death through the crosses with which we are marked, representing the cross of Christ. It is as if we have died together with Christ in a mystery and been crucified with Him. We are immersed three times, suggesting the three-day burial with Christ, being buried with Christ in a mystery. Finally, we emerge entirely. This emergence is a sign of Christ’s resurrection and of our own final resurrection, as if we have already risen in a trace <note>original: "in vestigio," meaning an earthly reflection or foreshadowing of the real thing</note> and will rise in the truth of the resurrection at the end. And this is our second birth. The first was fleshly; this is spiritual. That was old; this is new. And the life which we lead after this emergence and in this birth ought to be a trace and an imitation of that life which we expect from the gift of God after the final resurrection. But what is that life, if not that continuous, beatific vision of God and the eternal praise of His ineffable goodness? Thus, all our conduct after baptism ought to be in the contemplation and praise of God—though currently seen through a mirror and in riddles <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 13:12: "For now we see through a glass, darkly."</note>—while that future life will be in truth. And because this regeneration of the font is but a trace, there must be another, truer one. It is that of which the Lord says: "In the regeneration, when the Son of Man shall sit on the throne of his majesty, you also shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel." <note>Matthew 19:28</note> We must not, therefore, flee back to the body of sin and death like apostates and fugitives. This is what those do who return to sin after baptism, not understanding the holy birth that has taken place within them, nor that they are a bright dwelling place of God. Oh, if only men understood the great sacrament of the King’s piety <note>original: "pietatis regisacramentum"</note> within themselves! They would see the body of sin destroyed daily; Christ the Lord destroyed the "head" of that body so that the rest might be more easily destroyed. For Adam was the head of the body of sin, whom Christ the Victor led out from the kingdom of death into the kingdom of life. He not only spared that captive, but having destroyed sin and restored righteousness, He clothed him in a splendid robe of immortality. Therefore, the body of sin is now headless <note>original: "acephalum," from the Greek for "without a head"</note> and like a trunk without a head. Why, then, do all the members not run to where the head is? For it is with Christ the Lord, who "led captivity captive." <note>Ephesians 4:8</note> He bestowed such great gifts upon them: where those who have died to sin through baptism—which is the sign and representation of Christ's death—are brought in:

<margin>46</margin>
so that as new members of the body of Christ’s righteousness, they might carry in themselves the symbol of His glorious resurrection, as Paul testifies, saying: ¶ "For if we have been planted together in the likeness of his death, we shall be also in the likeness of his resurrection. Knowing this, that our old man is crucified with him, that the body of sin might be destroyed, that henceforth we should not serve sin. For he that is dead is justified from sin." <note>Romans 6:5–7</note> ¶ Our **old man** is the man of the first birth, the fleshly man, the man of sin, and a member of the body of sin. But our **new man** is the man of regeneration and the second birth, the spiritual man, the man of grace, and a member of the body of righteousness. The former lives for sin and is dead to righteousness; the latter, conversely, is dead to sin and living for righteousness. And just as air shimmering with light can be said to be "living" to the light and "dead" to the darkness, so the new man is living to righteousness and dead to sin. He, therefore, who is dead to sin is justified from sin—just as air "dead" to darkness is purified from darkness by the light. And just as air, as long as it contains darkness, cannot be called "dead to darkness" alongside the sun, nor "living to the light" simultaneously with the sun: so if we have sin, we cannot be called "dead with Christ" and "living for righteousness with Christ." For what does it mean to be dead with Christ, if not to be dead to sin and to live for righteousness? And if we wish to emulate the truth of the sacred signs performed upon us: having died once to sin and living for righteousness, we must never again allow death to dominate us. For Christ died only once:

<margin>47</margin>
and once He rose, He never dies again. Death no longer has dominion over Him. Paul magnificently introduces these mysteries, saying: ¶ "Now if we be dead with Christ, we believe that we shall also live with him: Knowing that Christ being raised from the dead dieth no more; death hath no more dominion over him. For in that he died unto sin, he died once: but in that he liveth, he liveth unto God. Likewise reckon ye also yourselves to be dead indeed unto sin, but alive unto God through Jesus Christ our Lord." <note>Romans 6:8–11</note> ¶ Certainly, those who are dead to sin live to God in Christ Jesus our Lord, in the body of Christ Jesus our Lord. For they are members of His body. And just as a hand lives in you, so those who are dead to sin live in Christ, living for righteousness and for God. And if they are dead to sin, they are dead to the flesh and living to the spirit. How then shall they work sin in

<margin>48</margin>
the flesh to which they are dead, and not rather perform the works of the spirit to which they live? Surely that is contrary to the nature of this sacred birth and beyond reason. And therefore, Paul adds: ¶ "Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body, that ye should obey it in the lusts thereof. Neither yield ye your mem-

<note>Extensive handwritten interlinear and marginal annotations in Latin, written in multiple directions, commenting on the text below which has been struck through.</note>
<unclear>For if anyone is under the law, he is subject to sin; but he who is under grace is not liable to sin. But because someone might say: "If we are under grace and are not held by the law, it is permitted to sin," Paul responds to this: If he sins, he is a servant of the law, because he who sins is under the law. But he who is under grace is subject to righteousness. [Additional glosses in upper margin]</unclear>

~~¶ What then? Shall we sin because we are not under the law, but under grace? God forbid.~~

<margin>49</margin>
> you are [under] the law: [you are] under grace. What then? Shall we sin because we are not under the law, but under grace? God forbid. ¶ A sick man is "under the law," that is, under the physician’s care; a healthy man is not. Yet just as it is foolish to say a healthy man must be sick because he is not under a physician, so it is surely absurd to say we must sin because we are not under the law. On the contrary: because someone is healthy, he does not fall sick, and therefore he is not under a physician. In the same way, because someone is under grace, he must not sin, and therefore he is not under the law. But to be under grace and to sin is impossible; they do not allow for one another at the same time, any more than health and sickness. For he who is under grace is subject to righteousness, just as he who is healthy is subject to health. And he who sins is subjected to sin, just as he who is sick is subjected to sickness. But how can it be that someone is simultaneously healthy and sick—or rather, simultaneously 
<margin>50</margin>
living and dead? For righteousness is life, and sin is death, or something closely related to them.
¶ Therefore, Paul adds the reason for this impossibility, saying: ¶ Do you not know that
> to whom you yield yourselves as servants to obey, his servants you are whom you obey; whether of sin unto death, or of obedience unto righteousness? But thanks be to God: that whereas you were the servants of sin, you have obeyed from the heart that form of doctrine which was delivered to you. Being then made free from sin, you became the servants of righteousness. ¶ All sinners who came to Christ were servants of sin. But when they were received by Christ into his own body, they were freed from sin and made servants of righteousness. Just as those who are restored to health from a heavy lethargy <note>original: "veterno," a medical term used here to describe a coma-like spiritual stupor</note> serve health once they are freed from disease. And this service is pleasing, joyful, and desirable—one that coincides with freedom. The other kind, however—serving sin, serving disease—is harsh, sad, and intolerable; it is a service that is only a wretched slavery. Life follows the former; death follows the latter. The former brings joy, gladness, and no confusion <note>original: "confusio," in the sense of being confounded or put to shame</note>; the latter brings mourning, grief, and every shame <note>original: "erubescentia," literally a reddening of the face or blushing from guilt</note>.
It is shameful even to speak of this [the state of sin] and to make a comparison with that [the state of grace]. However, because those who were weak better understand the benefits of health by looking at the works of the sick (by way of contrast) due to their own infirmity: therefore Paul, having first asked for pardon, leads them by the hand from the works of the service of sin to recognize, by contrast, the works of the service of righteousness, saying: ¶ I speak 
<margin>51</margin>
> in human terms because of the infirmity of your flesh. For as you yielded your members to serve uncleanness and iniquity unto iniquity: so now yield your members to serve righteousness, unto sanctification <note>original: "sanctificationem," the process of being made holy</note>. ¶ This is just as if he were making an open contrast and said: "As you yielded your members to serve uncleanness and unrighteousness unto unrighteousness: so now yield your members to serve cleanness and righteousness unto righteousness." But he 
<margin>52</margin>
deliberately turned the phrasing. For what divine thing did Paul know? That other way was simpler and more humble. And he adds: ¶ For when you were the servants of sin, you were free from righteousness. What fruit had you then in those things of which you are now ashamed? For the end of those things is death. But now being made free from sin, and become servants to God, you have your fruit unto sanctification, and the end everlasting life. For the wages of sin is death; but the grace of God is eternal life in CHRIST JESUS.

<summary>This page uses a medical analogy of health and sickness to explain that a Christian under grace cannot remain in sin, arguing that righteousness and sin are as mutually exclusive as life and death. It concludes with the famous contrast between the "wages of sin" (death) and the "gift of God" (eternal life).</summary>

<header>COMMENTARY</header>

...to our Lord. ¶ Those who are servants of sin: they do not live for themselves / they do not bear fruit for themselves / but for sin and death / being exempt from righteousness. If these people return to their senses <note>The author uses the verb *resipiscunt*, implying a change of mind or "coming to" after being senseless.</note> toward righteousness, having been made healthy, they feel shame for the acts of their previous life, no differently—and indeed much more so—than someone who, having been restored to a healthy life from a state of severe madness <note>original: *amentia*</note>, is ashamed of his deeds done while insane. There is no fruit from that life: but its end is death / and eternal destruction. But those who are servants of God and of righteousness: they live for God / they bear fruit for God / their fruit is sanctification / their end is eternal life. This is what God gives in Christ our Lord to all His members: so that just as the Head is glorious, the members may be glorious / just as the Head is immortal, the members may also be immortal. Therefore, to Him from whom and in whom all things are given to us, to our King and our head: all honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

¶ EXAMINATION of certain points concerning the literal text. ¶ The Vulgate edition <note>The standard Latin Bible of the time.</note> says: *For we who are dead to sin.* ¶ The word "For" <note>original: *enim*</note> is superfluous. Paul wrote: *we who died to sin* <note>original Greek: ὅιτινες ἀπεθάνομεν τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ</note>. And "to sin" is in the dative case / both here and elsewhere: whenever it is joined with the words "died" or "lives." And this applies to other words joined with them: such as "he lives to righteousness" / "he lives to God." "He is dead to righteousness" / "he is dead to God." "He lives to sin" / "he lives to death." "He is dead to sin" / "he is dead to death." For indeed, he who lives to righteousness: is dead to sin. And he who lives to sin: is dead to righteousness. He who lives to death: is dead to God. And he who lives to God: is dead to death. For this is Paul's way of speaking: it is neither unlearned nor irrational. For sin / transgression / death: these are like tyrants. But Righteousness / grace / Christ / God: these are like kings, or rather, most truly Kings and Lords. Furthermore, we speak in a very appropriate way using the dative case: "The male servant is dead to his master." "The female servant is dead to her mistress." And this is said when they are no longer of any use to them. "The male servant lives for his master" / "the female servant lives for her mistress": when they are of use to them. And the more useful they are: the more they live for them. In this same way we speak regarding those things found in Paul. And just as the best servant, living for his master, is dead to himself (for if he lived for himself: he would work for himself / he would bear fruit for himself / and he would look out for and act on his own behalf) and the best female servant, dead to herself, lives for her mistress: so no one can be a good servant of God unless, being dead to himself, he lives for the Lord. For he who lives for himself: is dead to the Lord. And thus "living for oneself" and "living for the Lord" fight against each other: so that they can never exist at the same time. But "dying to oneself" and "living for the Lord" go together: and this is what it means to live for righteousness / to live for God / and finally to live eternally. And this "death of self" is a precious death in the sight of the Lord, which harmonizes with life. "Living for oneself" and "dying to God" also go together: and this is finally to die eternally / a life harmonizing with death. 

But wait, if someone is dead to himself, does he immediately live for God? Not necessarily. For he who serves greed / who serves lust / who delights in slaughter / doing all things because of greed / because of intemperance / because of slaughter: though dead to himself, he lives for those sins / he works for them / and will eventually receive the wages <note>original: *stipendia*</note> of his tyrants, which are eternal punishments. Hence it happens that "dying to oneself" and "dying to God" do not just fight against each other in the way that "living for oneself" and "living for God" do. For "dying to oneself" and "dying to God" can coexist in the servants of sin: but in those who are righteous, they are opposites. It also happens that the lover of self, who is "living for himself," stands in the middle between those "dead to themselves" who truly live, and those "dead to themselves" who are truly dead. It does not follow that if someone is "dead to himself," it can be immediately concluded: "therefore he is dead [spiritually]." For it can happen that such a person is most alive, as Peter and Paul were "dead to themselves" yet most truly living. Indeed, no one is truly alive who is not dead to himself. Nor can it be immediately concluded: "he is dead to himself, therefore he lives." For Judas / walking with bare feet / often lying on the bare ground with Christ / and enduring many hardships: he was dead to himself. But he did not live. For he lived for greed and for death. But this is not living: it is simply perishing and dying. Therefore, the death which is opposed to death-as-death: is life. And the life which is opposed to life-as-life: is death. But the death of sin is opposed to the death of righteousness: but as a death which is opposed to death-as-death. Therefore, the death of sin is life. And the life of sin is opposed to the life of righteousness: but as a life which is opposed to life-as-life. Therefore, the life of sin is death. And from this it is known that the "death of self" for those who are righteous harmonizes with life. For it is opposed to the death of righteousness. And "living for oneself" harmonizes with death. For it is opposed to the life of righteousness. But in the wicked, the "death of self" is death, being likewise opposed to the life of righteousness. And he who understands these modes of speaking / and these turns of opposition / penetrates the sacred understanding of Paul's words far more easily. But this must also be noticed: that the ablative case <note>In Latin, the ablative often indicates the "means" or "instrument" (by/from), while the dative indicates the "recipient" or "reference" (to/for). The author is arguing that Paul uses the dative to show a relationship of service, not just a state of being.</note> is not joined to these same words with equal fitness / and if they were joined, the meaning would be changed. For we do not say "dead by righteousness" in the same way we say "dead to righteousness" / nor "living by death" as we say "living to death." For what else would that be: than saying something is black by whiteness, or white by blackness? But nothing is blackened by whiteness, nor whitened by blackness. Therefore, nothing dies by righteousness: nor lives by death. Since if we say appropriately that someone lives by righteousness and dies by death: these express the cause / the former...

<summary>The author explains the transformation from sin to righteousness as a shift in "ownership," using a philological analysis of Paul's use of the dative case to describe living "to" or dying "to" a master. He distinguishes between the physical self-denial of someone like Judas and the true spiritual "death to self" practiced by the Apostles.</summary>

that form of doctrine into which you were delivered. And interpreters ought to attend to this / so that they do not change the meaning / but convert the speech according to the property of the language into which they are translating. For frequently / that which is said fittingly in one language: if you translate it into another while preserving the phrasing of that first language / it will be awkward and unsuitable. As in this place, what is fitting in Greek: is not so much so in Latin / unless it is brought back to the custom of the language. Those who have read Jerome's little book *On the Best Method of Translating* <note>original: *Hieronymi de optimo genere interpretandi*. A famous letter by St. Jerome (Letter 57) defending his practice of translating "sense-for-sense" rather than "word-for-word."</note> are not ignorant of this. <margin>D 25</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition.** *For when you were the servants of sin / you were free from righteousness.* <note>original: *liberi fuistis iustitiæ*. The author is debating the grammar of the Latin "iustitiæ," which can be read as a dative ("to/for righteousness") or a genitive.</note> The translator could have said: *for when you had been servants of sin / you were free from righteousness* / using the ablative case. For where he said *essetis* and *fuistis* <note>Latin forms of "you were."</note>: Paul has the same word in both places, <note>original Greek: ἦτε (*ete*)</note> which the translator also interpreted as *fuistis* a little above. Where he said *but thanks be to God that you were the servants of sin* <note>original Greek: ὅτι ἦτε δοῦλοι τῆς ἁμαρτίας (*hoti ete douloi tes hamartias*)</note>, and "free" here designates a privation <note>A "privation" means the absence or lack of something; here, being "free from" righteousness means lacking it entirely.</note>. And "of righteousness" is in the dative case: which by the law of Latin speech / ought to be translated as an ablative. And *you were free to righteousness* is the same as if we were to say / *you were exempt and non-participants in righteousness.* And that "free" designates a privation: Paul suggests quite clearly / when he adds shortly after: *but now being made free from sin.* And what is *freed from sin*: unless it be released from the slavery of sin? What is *free from righteousness*: unless it be freed from righteousness / released and made a non-participant in the slavery of righteousness? And Paul has that whole sentence thus:
19. *For when you were the servants of sin, you were free from righteousness.* <note>original Greek: ὅτε γὰρ δοῦλοι ἦτε τῆς ἁμαρτίας, ἐλεύθεροι ἦτε τῆ δικαιοσύνῃ (*hote gar douloi ete tes hamartias, eleutheroi ete te dikaiosyne*)</note> <margin>¶</margin> **The Vulgate edition.** *But the end, eternal life.* It should rather be said *into eternal life.* Paul: <note>original Greek: εἰς ζωὴν αἰώνιοv (*eis zoen aionion*)</note>. <margin>¶</margin> **The Vulgate edition.** *But the grace of God: eternal life.* Rather / *but the gift of God: eternal life.* Paul: <note>original Greek: τὸ δὲ χάρισμα τοῦ θεοῦ ζωὴ αἰώνιος (*to de charisma tou theou zoe aionios*)</note>. But we have said that both "gift" and "grace" signify the same thing. But now we must return to the explanation of the letter.

### CHAPTER VII.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'S' containing an illustration of two figures, likely a man and a woman in a landscape, representing the theme of marriage or union discussed in the text.</image-desc>

The Synagogue <note>In this allegorical context, "Synagogue" refers to the Jewish people or the Old Covenant community.</note> was a bride: and she had Moses as a husband. The Law of Moses: was that very law / by which the Synagogue was bound to her husband. The handmaid was the gathering of the nations <note>The Gentiles.</note> who did not have a husband: but being deserted / bound by no law to a husband / she committed adultery and fornicative acts. For having left God: she was joined to idols. But the mercy of God cleansed the handmaid: and from a handmaid / made her a free woman. And from her / for the most part, the Church was made: which is a bride / and has Christ as a husband. Indeed, the Gospel law: is the law of Christ by which the bride, the Church, is bound to her husband Christ. But because the handmaid could not have a husband unless she died / and rose into a better and uncontaminated life: therefore before she can have Christ as a husband / she dies in baptism / and likewise all the stains of her ancient habit are wiped away. And from death she rises again into a new and most bright life. No longer a handmaid: but a free woman. No longer a slave: but a mistress / who has a husband. And therefore the sins of her other life: are in no way reckoned to her. She has no sign of it / no trace. If she is called a handmaid of righteousness / a servant of righteousness / a handmaid of Christ / a servant of Christ: this is true liberty / and true mastery / and she is truly free and a mistress. But because she is still a young girl and so small: she is educated in the law of her husband / until, as an adult, she may run from the narrow places of this world into the most ample bridal chamber of heaven to meet her husband. Where she may enjoy her husband: in the delights of paradise. Let her enjoy, I say, her husband: whose vision brings beatitude / whose embrace is the highest chastity / whose touch is the highest purity / and whose union is eternal life. But when the Synagogue had a husband: she was subject to the law of her husband / and this / either as long as the husband lived / or as long as she herself lived. But let it be that Moses, the husband of the Synagogue / lived for the law of the flesh until Christ the Lord mortified both the flesh and the law of the flesh on the cross / until he descended to the lower regions / and had Moses as a companion of his resurrection, whom he also had at the transfiguration: then certainly Moses no longer lived for the law of the flesh / but for the law of righteousness. Because if he did not then live for the law of the flesh: he was dead to it. Therefore from that time the Synagogue was a widow / and without a husband: nor any longer / bound to any man. And it was plainly permitted to her: having left the law of her husband / to marry another husband / who was also far more noble than Moses. But oh, foolish widow: who believes she has a husband / when she has none. Let it be that she has one. If she herself dies / and returns from death into life: she is no longer bound to the first / no longer tied to his law / but is free to take whom she will. But whom would she rather prefer: than him who wiped away all her filth / than him who raised her from death to life / than him who is immortal and is strong and able in all things. Whose prior husband / would even have been glad: to be able to adore the furthest prints of his feet. This husband is immortal: and he makes the bride immortal. And therefore this law: between the husband and the bride is indissoluble. But Moses was a mortal husband: and the Synagogue a mortal bride. And therefore the law: between the Synagogue and Moses / was dissoluble / now on one side / now on both. And certainly now it is dissolved on the part of the husband: nor are the Jews any longer bound to the law of the flesh / although they believe themselves to be bound / because they believe that Moses still lives for the law. For if he still lives for the law—

...he would have died. But because he lives: he is dead to the law / to the law (I say) of the flesh. Blessed Paul was not ignorant of this. And recognizing the widowhood of the **Synagogue** <note>The author uses "Synagogue" here to represent the Jewish people under the Old Covenant, following a common medieval allegorical tradition.</note>: in the analogy of a woman whose husband is dead / he calls her to another, to Christ the Lord / and he calls her sweetly indeed in great charity / saying:

<margin>53</margin>
> ¶ Do you not know, brothers (for I speak to those who know the law), that the law rules over a man for as long as he lives? For a woman who is under a husband is bound to the law while her husband lives / but if the husband has died: she is released from the law of the husband. Therefore, while her husband lives: she will be called an adulteress / if she belongs to another man. But if her husband has died: she is set free from the law / so that she is not an adulteress if she belongs to another man.

¶ He did not want to say openly to the Synagogue: "Moses your husband is dead." Why? So that you are no longer liable to his law. He feared that the bride, understanding this only emotionally, might be consumed by grief / and not understanding this "precious death," she might mourn / whereas she ought especially to rejoice. But concerning the man and the woman / in a **parable** (as it seemed) he wove this for her. For he who dies in this covenant: lives / and even more than lives. For the Savior says: *He who believes in me: even if he has died, he shall live. And everyone who lives and believes in me: shall not die for eternity.* And leaving behind the talk of the husband / that is, the spouse and **Moses** in the parable / who through grace was already saved: he had died to the law. He then passed to the death of the bride who had already received **baptism** / and therefore was dead both to sin and to the law through the body of Christ. From the body of Adam / of sin / and of the law: she was transferred into the body of Christ / of grace / and of the spirit. And from that death she had returned to the life of the spirit and of grace. And therefore she was no longer liable to the law of her former husband: both by reason of the husband who had died / and by reason of herself, who from death / had passed into a new life. Therefore he adds, saying:

<margin>54</margin>
> ¶ Therefore, my brothers, you also have been made dead to the law through the body of **CHRIST**: so that you may belong to another, who rose from the dead / that we may bear fruit for God.

<margin>55</margin>
¶ Under the law: they bore fruit for Moses / for the flesh / for the body of Adam and of sin / and finally for death. For all those under the law descended to the underworld. But under grace they ought to bear fruit for God / for the spirit / for the body of Christ and for justice / and finally for eternal life. For all who live under this grace (as is fitting): fly away to the seat of perpetual life in heaven. The most holy Paul reveals this with these words:

> ¶ For when we were in the flesh: the passions of sins which were through the law / worked in our members / so that they might bear fruit for death. But now we are loosed from the law / in which we were held as we were dying: so that we may serve in the **newness of the spirit** / and not in the **oldness of the letter**.

¶ **Newness of the spirit**: the law of grace and spiritual things. **Oldness of the letter**: the old and carnal law. He who understands it literally / as if there were no figure: walks carnally. But he who understands it allegorically / figuratively / and as a type of another: walks and understands spiritually. And he sees grace conspiring with the law: but as a shadow with its own truth. And the passions of sins / that is, harmful and irrational desires: were occasionally excited through the law in our members / just as the precepts of a **physician** <note>original: *medici*. The author uses the metaphor of a doctor to explain that the Law itself is good, but the "patient" (humanity) reacts poorly to its prohibitions.</note> forbidding many things to a sick man / often occasionally excite passions in the sick person to desire more wickedly those things which are forbidden. Whence it happens that he becomes much more sick and sometimes meets his death. But are the physician's precepts therefore bad? Not simply / but bad occasionally. Not because of him who gave them: but by the occasion of him who received them. For he who gave those precepts: gave them for health and life / even if he who received them / made them an occasion for himself for a more serious infirmity and death. So it is also with the law. For it is good: and for the sake of the good; but for those weak in the flesh it is occasionally harmful / showing that those things which are evil, are evil. As Paul clearly opens up, saying:

<margin>56</margin>
> ¶ What shall we say then? Is the Law sin? God forbid. But I did not know sin: except through the law. For I did not know lust: unless the law said / you shall not covet. But sin, taking the occasion: through the commandment worked in me all manner of lust.

¶ The one giving the law: is like the physician. The one receiving: like the sick man. The Law: like the physician's precepts / showing what is healthy and what is unhealthy / forbidding the latter and commanding the former. Sin: like the disease. Therefore the Law is simply good / and very good. Which he confesses / who said: *The law of your mouth is good to me: above thousands of gold and silver.* But that it is occasionally bad: the Lord suggests through **Ezekiel** saying: *I gave them precepts that were not good: and judgments in which they shall not live.* <note>original: *Ego dedi eis præcepta non bona*. A reference to Ezekiel 20:25.</note> Therefore the law was given to them for salvation. But because it was a law of the flesh / namely so that the infirmities of the flesh might be healed / and they themselves were weak in the flesh: therefore occasionally the passions of the infirmity of the flesh were increased through the law. Just as if a doctor forbids a man with **dropsy** <term>dropsy: an old medical term for edema, a condition characterized by an excess of watery fluid in the body's tissues</term> to drink: the appetite for drinking is increased all the more by the precept. So that it seems from the precept / which nevertheless forbids it: that appetite is harvested. So also the passions of sins seemed to be in them through the law: and that too is occasionally true / but they are primarily and causally from sin / and from the weakness of the flesh. Therefore the Law is by its own nature for salvation: not because it can make salvation perfect. For perfect salvation is through grace: not through the law / or the works of the law. Yet those who did the works of the law: as it is written / lived in them. He says: *Keep my laws and judgments: which...*

that form of doctrine: into which you were handed over. And interpreters ought to attend to this: that they do not change the meaning, but should convert the speech according to the property of the language into which they are translating. For frequently, what is said fittingly in one language, if you translate it into another while preserving the phrasing of the original language, will be clumsy and unsuitable. Just as in this place, what is fitting in Greek is not quite so in Latin, unless it be reduced to the custom of the language. This is not unknown to those who have read Jerome’s little book *On the Best Kind of Translating* <note>Jerome's *De Optimo Genere Interpretandi* (Letter 57) is a foundational text for Western translation theory, advocating for "sense-for-sense" rather than "word-for-word" translation.</note>.

<margin>D 25</margin> **Vulgate edition.** *For when you were slaves of sin, you were free of righteousness.* The translator could have said: *when you were slaves of sin, you were free from righteousness* <note>The author is debating whether "righteousness" should be in the dative or ablative case in Latin to better capture the Greek sense of being "separate from" it.</note>. For where it says *essetis* [you were] and *fuistis* [you have been], Paul has the same word in both places, *ἦτε* <note>original: ἦτε (ēte)</note>, which the translator a little above translated as *fuistis*. Where he said, *but thanks be to God that you were slaves of sin*—*ὅτι ἦτε δοῦλοι τῆς ἁμαρτίας* <note>original: ὅτι ἦτε δοῦλοι τῆς ἁμαρτίας (hoti ēte douloi tēs hamartias)</note>—and here "free" designates a privation <note>meaning a lack of something, or being "free from" the influence of righteousness while enslaved to sin.</note>. And "of righteousness" is in the dative; which, by the law of Latin speech, ought to be translated as an ablative. And it is just as if we were to say "you were free from righteousness," as if we were to say you were "immune and non-participants in righteousness." And that "free" designates a privation, Paul suggests quite openly when he adds a little later: *but now having been set free from sin.* And what is "set free from sin" but being loosed from the slavery of sin? What is "free of righteousness" but being "liberated from righteousness," loosed and made non-participants in the service of righteousness? And Paul has that whole sentence thus: *ὅτε γὰρ δοῦλοι ἦτε τῆς ἁμαρτίας, ἐλεύθεροι ἦτε τῇ δικαιοσύνῃ* <note>original: ὅτε γὰρ δοῦλοι ἦτε τῆς ἁμαρτίας, ἐλεύθεροι ἦτε τῇ δικαιοσύνῃ; Translation: "For when you were slaves of sin, you were free in regard to righteousness."</note>.

**Vulgate edition.** *The end indeed, life eternal.* It should rather be said *into eternal life*. Paul wrote *εἰς ζωὴν αἰώνιον* <note>original: εἰς ζωὴν αἰώνιον (eis zōēn aiōnion)</note>. **Vulgate edition.** *But the grace of God: life eternal.* Rather, *the gift of God: life eternal*. Paul wrote *τὸ δὲ χάρισμα τοῦ θεοῦ ζωὴ αἰώνιος* <note>original: τὸ δὲ χάρισμα τοῦ θεοῦ ζωὴ αἰώνιος (to de charisma tou theou zōē aiōnios)</note>. But we have said that both "gift" and "grace" signify the same thing. Now, however, we must return to the explanation of the letter.
