The "oldness of the letter" is the old and carnal law. He who understands it literally, as if it were not a figure, walks carnally. But he who understands it allegorically, figuratively, and as a type of another, walks and understands spiritually. He sees that it agrees with the law of grace, but as a shadow agrees with its own truth. <margin>56</margin> the good, but to those weak in the flesh it is occasionally harmful, showing those things that are evil to be evil. ¶ And

The Law is like the doctor's prescriptions, showing what is healthy and what is unhealthy, forbidding the latter and commanding the former. Sin is like the disease. Therefore, the Law is simply good, and very good. This is confessed by the one who said: *The law of your mouth is good to me, above thousands of gold and silver.* <note>Psalm 119:72</note> But the Lord also suggests that it is occasionally "evil," saying through Ezekiel: *I gave them precepts that were not good, and judgments in which they shall not live.* <note>Ezekiel 20:25</note> Therefore, the law was given to them for salvation. It is just as if a doctor forbids a dropsical man <note><term>dropsical</term>: suffering from edema or "dropsy," an old medical term for swelling caused by excess fluid. Thus it seems from the command—which nonetheless troubles him—that the appetite is within him. So also the passions of sins seemed to be in them through the law. And that is also occasionally true, but they are primarily and causally from sin and from the weakness of the flesh. Therefore, the Law is by its own nature for salvation—not that it can produce perfect salvation. For perfect salvation is through grace, not through the law and the works of the law. <meta>This page continues the commentary on Romans 7. It moves from the analogy of marriage to a botanical analogy of a seed, explaining how the Old Law served as a necessary but incomplete "hidden" life that had to pass away for the "perfected" life of Grace to flourish.</meta>

HEADER: COMMENTARY

...the man who does them shall live by them. <note>original: "vivens homo vivet in eis," referencing Leviticus 18:5 and Romans 10:5.</note> ¶ **B**ut that "living by the law"—living in those commandments—is not a perfected life, but rather a certain inception toward a perfected life. It is similar to the life of a seed compared to the life of a plant; for the plant to exist, the seed must cease to be and (so to speak) die. Unless (says the Truth) <note>A common medieval and Renaissance title for Christ, referencing John 14:6 ("I am the Way, the Truth, and the Life").</note> a grain of wheat falling into the earth dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it is certain that the plant will rise and bring forth much fruit. ¶ **S**o it is for one who lives by the law, who performs the works of the law while living in them: he must die to the law so that he may live by grace, which is the completed life, and which God alone gives—not the law, and not works. Therefore, "living in those things" is a certain preparation for the completed life, just as the life of the grain prepares for the completed life found in the plant. And just as the life of the grain is dark and buried in the soil, so too is the life which comes from the law and works dark. Those who lived that life and in those works descended to the underworld. <note>original: "descendebant ad inferos." This refers to the "Limbo of the Fathers," where the righteous of the Old Testament were believed to wait for Christ's resurrection.</note> Yet they lived this dark life as if under the soil, feeling no pain among the spirits of the dead, but awaiting a better and luminous life which Christ, the King of Ages and Lord, brought to them. They immediately ceased to live that life of the law, now living a luminous life—the life which is from grace and belongs to the region of light. ¶ **F**or how could they live in darkness and light at the same time? But do you not notice that when there is no sickness, there is no need for a doctor’s prescription? So it is that when there is no sin, there is no need for the law. Just as children have no need for the law because they do not yet have sin—they are not yet sick in the flesh—but like Adam, they first begin to be sick in the flesh when they have the sense of good and evil. Then the <term>concupiscence</term> <note>Disordered desire or the tendency toward sin.</note> of their infirmity will rise. Then the law is needed to forbid evil and command good. If they follow the law, they shall live to the law, eventually to receive the optimal life of grace; if they do not follow it, the law—which was good—will occasionally lead them to the "death" of the law, and subsequently to the death of the "outer darkness," which is the opposite of the best life. ¶ **T**herefore, before 
<margin>57</margin> the time of the law, they were dead to sin, and sin was dead in them. But when the time comes when the law is needed, sin is awakened. Paul suggests this when he says: ¶ 
> For without the law, sin was dead. I was once alive without the law; but when the commandment came, sin revived and I died. And the commandment, which was meant for life, I found to lead to death. For sin, taking opportunity through the commandment, deceived me and through it killed me. Therefore the law indeed is holy, and the commandment holy and just and good. Was that which is good, then, made death to me? Far from it! But it was sin, so that sin might appear as sin, working death in me through what is good, so that sin might become sinful beyond measure through the commandment. 

¶ **A** disease declares itself most clearly to be a disease the more it strives after forbidden things and flees from recommended ones. It takes opportunity from the doctor’s prescriptions—which were good and healthy—to kill more quickly and become (so to speak) a "more diseased disease." And so it is with sin. ¶ **B**ut when a sickness like a fever causes heat, what will the law of the fever, given by the doctor, command? Without a doubt: to cool down. If it causes coldness like a paralysis, must one not apply heat? ¶ **A**nd since sin is an infirmity of the flesh, what will the law of sin be like, given by He who understands transgressions? Will it not be spiritual? ¶ **F**or spirit and flesh are opposites, just like heating and cooling. And thus the spirit heals the infirmity of the flesh, just as heat heals a frozen paralysis. ¶ **A**nd as heat is a friend to life and cold a friend to death, so the spirit is always a friend to life, while the flesh is a friend to death. ¶ **A**nd as it is death for those born in the cold to live without heat, so the flesh of those who have reached the time of the spirit is dead without the spirit. Sin dwells in the flesh; the spirit in the mind. Sin, I say, dwells in the flesh—but in that flesh which is "earth," feeling the curse of Adam. But the flesh which does not feel the curse does not sprout thorns and thistles and harmful lusts. Therefore, as sin is the infirmity of the flesh, so the spirit is the health of the mind. The latter is implanted by God in every mind; the former is sown from Adam into all flesh that has not been preceded by a blessing. <note>This refers to the concept of Original Sin being passed down through the lineage of Adam.</note> ¶ **F**or Christ took on flesh, but without Adam’s infirmity. For that flesh which was in the Virgin had been preceded by every blessing. ¶ **A**nd just as the flesh which follows the spirit and the mind is cured of Adam’s infirmity, so that which follows the spirit dies to Christ's flesh, <note>This passage seems to contrast the fallen flesh with the redeemed flesh of Christ.</note> and the mind grows sick from the contagion of the flesh. The flesh which is not delighted by the spirit is likened to the weak flesh; it does not feel the sting of lusts, experiencing only innocent passions, such as thirst, hunger, cold, heat, weariness, sorrow over evils, joy over good things, and the like. In such a state, the flesh bears the likeness of Christ’s flesh; and even more so does the spirit bear the likeness of the Spirit, who lives by the grace and spirit of Christ. ¶ **B**ut why is there such a great battle between the law of the flesh (which is nonetheless spiritual) and us, to whom it was given for health? ¶ **W**hence does this happen? Because we are carnal—traded, conceived, born, and (so to speak) acquired by our parents under sin, under the lusts that take their origin from sin and the infirmity of the flesh. Because the flesh does not understand the good, nor does it want it (for these belong to the mind and spirit), and we work with the flesh and not what the mind understands. The will, by its own nature, wants the good, but we work with the flesh—but a weak flesh; and there, the infirmity seems to work rather than the flesh itself. For a healthy flesh, rivaling the flesh of Christ, would never work in such a way, just as a healthy woman would never act like one in labor...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Romans 7, moving from the botanical analogy of the seed to a medical analogy of a patient. It specifically addresses the "infirmity" of the flesh and discusses the Virgin Mary's exemption from original sin through the "blessing" of God, referencing St. Anselm of Canterbury.</meta>

...sick, gnawing on coals, chalk, or perhaps raw meat. <note>original: "ægra, carbones, cretam aut crudas fortasse carnes rodens." This describes a medical condition where a patient craves non-food items, used here as a metaphor for the soul's disordered desires under sin.</note> But now let us hear Paul <margin>58 ,</margin> speaking and telling of this infirmity.

¶ For we know that the law is spiritual; but I am carnal, sold under sin. <note>Romans 7:14. The author uses "negotiatus" (traded or sold), emphasizing being a slave to a transaction of sin.</note>

¶ But come now, if someone is "sold under sin"—such that his birth comes from a man and a woman, which can scarcely be understood without lust <note>original: "concupiscentia," the theological term for disordered desire or "inclination toward sin."</note>—will he not immediately have the flesh of sin upon being born? I should not think it necessary. For the infirmity of the flesh arises from the curse that Adam incurred: "Cursed," he said, "shall be the earth in your work." <note>Genesis 3:17</note> Therefore, health shall come from a blessing. If, then, God blesses the earth from which someone's flesh is taken, even before they are conceived, then surely that person will be both conceived and born without any infirmity. I mean infirmity of any kind, both potential and actual. But is a curse more powerful—so that no man may be conceived without sin—than a blessing, so that someone may be conceived without sin? That seems unlikely. For a blessing aligns with *being*, which can do all things; while a curse aligns with *non-being*, which can do nothing. But did not the Savior of the world, when he came into the world and wished to take flesh without sin, bless his earth <note>A common metaphor for the Virgin Mary's womb.</note> even before that flesh was formed from which he would take his own? Just as he had predicted long before through the prophet saying: "Lord, you have blessed your land." <note>Psalm 85:1</note> Whoever believes this, believes on the side of the blessing; and those who attend to the blessing, I judge to be children of the blessing. Those who think otherwise fix their eyes on the darkness of the curse. And this Virgin, the daughter of blessing and the mother of all blessing, seeing that some would raise an unfortunate problem against her blessing in the future, anticipated it shortly before it happened. She ordained that her blessed conception be celebrated through an angel, meeting the ill-omened error that was to come with great kindness for the salvation of many—an error which, like a whirlwind, was set to entangle many. As a sign of this (as I believe), a most violent storm at sea was calmed. Those who were to announce that this holy conception should be celebrated were snatched from a fate of death that was already looming and imminent. Saint Anselm, the faithful bishop of the people of Canterbury, committed this event to memory. <note>The author refers to a popular medieval legend that St. Anselm of Canterbury (c. 1033–1109) established the Feast of the Immaculate Conception following a miraculous rescue at sea.</note> Therefore, this Virgin was not a daughter of Adam's obligation, but of Christ's grace; not of Adam's infirmity, but of God's blessing. It is not the case, then, that if someone is "sold under sin"—if someone is conceived from a man and a woman—that they immediately have the flesh of sin; rather, it is those whom the blessing has not healed. For certainly the children of lepers are conceived and born with leprosy, but only potentially, which manifests itself in its own time and becomes actual. In the same way, all children of Adam are both conceived and born with the sin of the flesh—not actual sin, but potential, which in its own time puts forth its strength in the body and rouses multiple lusts <note>original: "concupiscentias"</note> against the spirit. I say *all* children of Adam: those whom blessing and grace either did not anticipate at all or did not heal. But as for those who still have this infirmity of the flesh and act according to it, hear Paul <margin>59 ,</margin> revealing their condition when he says:

> "For that which I work, I do not know. For I do not
> do that which I want; but that which I hate, I do. If then
> I do that which I do not want, I consent to the
> law, that it is good. But now it is no longer I that work it,
> but the sin that dwells in me. For I know
> that in me, that is, in my flesh, there dwells no
> good thing. For to will is present with me; but how to
> work that which is good, I find not." <note>Romans 7:15-18</note>

¶ In the analogy of a sick man—one who is healthy in mind but violently ill in body—and from the understanding added to this text, the things Paul says are easily understood, which otherwise present a difficult understanding. Therefore, understand "good" as "healthy" and "evil" as "sick." Understand the "law of God" and the "law of the mind" as the "doctor's orders." Understand the "law of sin which is in the members" as "that which the infirmity commands and seeks." Understand the "inner man" as the "healthy mind," and the "outer man" as the "sick body." Furthermore, understand one who is in control of his mind but laboring heavily in his body and obeying the body's infirmity. This explains what was said before and also what follows.

<margin>60 ,</margin> ¶ "For the good that I want, I do not; but the evil which I do not want, that I do. Now if I do that which I
> do not want, it is no more I that work it, but sin that dwells in me. I find then a law,
> that when I want to do good, evil is present with me. For I delight in the law of God according to the
> inner man: but I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my
> mind, and bringing me into captivity to the law of sin which is in my members. Unhappy man that I am!
> Who shall deliver me from the body of this death?" <note>Romans 7:19-24</note>

¶ Paul represents in himself the carnal man who feels the infirmity of the flesh and the law of the members, which takes the mind captive to fulfill the desires of carnal infirmity—that is, sin. In reality, he was not such a man, but lived entirely according to the spirit. Yet he transforms himself into the weak for the sake of the weak, so that he might win the weak over. But he himself had also been weak at one time; he knew by whom he had been healed, and he gives thanks to God through the Lord, the Savior of all, from whom he obtained healing. Renewed into the life of the spirit and delivered from this death of the body, he shows to everyone that they can be saved through Him. If they serve with the flesh, they will serve the law of sin and death which is in the members; but if they serve with the spirit and mind, they will serve the law and life. And so he says:

<margin>61 ,</margin> ¶ "I give thanks to God through JESUS CHRIST our Lord. Therefore, I myself with the mind serve the law of God; but with the flesh, the law of sin." <note>Romans 7:25</note> ¶ He who serves with the mind and spirit serves the law of God; he who serves with the flesh serves the law of sin. But can it be...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Romans 7, moving from the discussion of the Virgin Mary's exemption from original sin to the internal conflict between the spirit and the flesh. The author continues to use medical metaphors (fever and improper cravings) to explain how the "law of the flesh" operates in opposition to the "law of God."</meta>

...that one and the same person should serve the law of God and the law of sin simultaneously in both mind and flesh? Not at all. For God and sin, being and non-being, life and death are opposites, and it is impossible to serve two such contrary masters at the same time. Therefore, the phrase *I myself serve the law of God with my mind, but with my flesh the law of sin* <note>Romans 7:25</note> includes a specific condition in its meaning. It refers to the "law of sin" which is in the limbs, not the "law of sin" that was given *against* sin—such as the Mosaic Law—for these two would be contrary to each other. For example: suppose someone becomes angry. The law of this desire <note>original: "concupiscentiæ," referring to disordered human desire or "lust"</note> which is born from sin and the weakness of the flesh is to seek revenge and take vengeance. The Law of Moses, however, says: *do not seek revenge nor be mindful of injuries.* <note>Leviticus 19:18</note> Or suppose one sees a beautiful woman and, from the weakness of the flesh, desire arises. The law of this desire is to mingle and commit fornication. The Law of Moses says the opposite: *you shall not commit adultery.* For if you follow the law of desire, sin is completed; and sin, when it is completed, generates death. 

It is just as if you are burning with an unbearable fever: the "law" of this unbearable heat is to drink cold liquids. If you drink, you complete the disease, and it brings forth death for you. And so it is with other desires which follow the weakness and sickness of the flesh. Therefore, these desires are "sickly" regarding the pursuit of good and healthy things, just as the cravings of those with a fever are sickly regarding the pursuit of what is wholesome. For this reason, some of the philosophers have not inappropriately called these types of desires "sicknesses of the soul" <note>original: "a grimoniae," likely a corruption of "aegrimoniae" (distresses or sicknesses of the mind)</note>; the more vehement they are, the more dangerous they become, and the more they reveal the weakness of the flesh. ~~A reproach of the authors for all~~

<margin>A 53</margin>
# **EXAMINATION of several points regarding the literal text.**

¶ **The Vulgate Edition:** *But if her husband be dead, she is loosed from the law of her husband.* <note>Romans 7:2</note> ¶ The word "her" <note>original: "eius"</note> is superfluous, though it does not hinder the understanding. Paul's Greek: *εαν δε αποθανη ο ανηρ, κατηργηται απο του νομου του ανδρος* [but if the husband dies, she is released from the law of the husband]. ¶ **The Vulgate Edition:** *But if her husband be dead, she is set free from the law of her husband.* ¶ Neither "her" nor "husband" <note>referring to a second instance of the word "vir"</note> are present in Paul's Greek. Yet they do not obstruct the meaning. Paul's Greek: *εαν δε αποθανη ο ανηρ, ελευθερα εστιν απο του νομου του μη ειναι* [but if the husband dies, she is free from the law so as not to be (an adulteress), etc.]. And because "free" is used for "set free," there is nothing inconsistent there; indeed, it seems to make the Latin phrasing more suitable.

¶ **The Vulgate Edition:** *if she be with another man.* Twice the old translator <note>The "old translator" refers to the traditional author of the Vulgate, Jerome.</note> translates it this way, whereas Paul sometimes says *εαν γενηται ανδρι ετερω* [if she becomes (belongs) to another man] and sometimes *γενομενη ανδρι ετερω* [having become (belonging) to another man]. In Latin usage, this means "if she belongs to another man." In this way, the translator should have rendered it more accurately, so that it would correspond to what is interpreted a little later: *that you may belong to another who has risen from the dead,* where the Greek has *εις το γενεσθαι υμας ετερω τω εκ νεκρων εγερθεντι*. Otherwise, he should have said, as before, "that you may be with another who has risen from the dead."

¶ **The Vulgate Edition:** <margin>B 55</margin> *Passions of sins.* <note>Romans 7:5</note> ¶ Paul has *τα παθηματα των αμαρτιων*. There are those who prefer to interpret *pathemata* here as "affections" <note>term: affectus — emotional disturbances or mental states</note> which disturb and cloud the mind and soul, which others also call "passions" <note>original: "παθη" (pathe)</note>, claiming this is more proper Latin. We do not disagree with them; and we should translate *pathemata* sometimes as "affections" and sometimes as "passions" depending on the suitability of the passage. For instance, here it should be "affections," but in the following chapter "passions," where Paul has: *λογιζομαι γαρ οτι ουκ αξια τα παθηματα του νυν καιρου* [For I reckon that the sufferings (passions) of this present time are not worthy]. For the word *pathema* is a "homonym" <note>term: homonymum — a word with multiple meanings</note> among the Greeks; it must be understood according to the location and the subject matter, and translated by us accordingly.

¶ **The Vulgate Edition:** *But now we are loosed from the law of death.* ¶ According to Paul, we should read "dying," not "of death." Paul: *νυνι δε κατηργηθημεν απο του νομου αποθανοντες* [but now we are released from the law, having died]. This can have a double sense. One is: *we, dying* to the flesh and to sin, are loosed from the law; this can be understood regarding the literal text. The other is that "dying" refers back to the following phrase, so the sense is: *but now we are loosed from the law in which we, dying, were held.* This is how the old translator understood it. For what is the "law in which we, dying, were held" except the "law of death"? For the sake of this, we have also referred it back to the following phrase.

¶ **The Vulgate Edition:** *But sin, taking occasion by the commandment, wrought in me all manner of concupiscence.* <note>Romans 7:8</note> ¶ Paul has: *but sin, taking an occasion.* Paul: *αφορμην δε λαβουσα η αμαρτια*. And this is less ambiguous than if we say "the occasion having been taken," lest anyone...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Romans 7, specifically focusing on the relationship between the Law and sin, before transitioning into Chapter 8. The author meticulously compares the standard Latin Bible (the Vulgate) with the original Greek text to clarify Saint Paul’s meaning regarding human frailty and divine grace.</meta>

<margin>B 55</margin> ...one might wrongly understand <note>original: "male intelligens"</note> and think that he who gave the Law took the opportunity through that Law to lead men into sinning. This would be an impious error; rather, when it is said, "the opportunity being taken, sin taking [it]," it is clearly recognized that this is an opportunity *for* sin, and there is no doubt by whom this opportunity is made. For since God made a good tree, and when he gave the commandment to Adam—which was a good and life-giving commandment—he did not give him an opportunity for sinning. Instead, the wickedness of the ancient serpent took the opportunity from this to lead Adam into sinning. The same is true of the Law given later.

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *But I am dead.* <note>original: "Ego autem mortuus sum"; Romans 7:9</note> ¶ It should rather be read: *But I was dead.* Paul [says]: *But I died.* <note>original: "ἐγὼ δὲ ἀπέθανον"</note> Which is true; for he was dead to sin when he was a little child and lived without the Law. Yet he carried a potential weakness in his flesh, which in its own time was bound to break out into action, unless it were healed by obedience to the Law and, especially, by the grace of God.

<margin>C 57</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *For sin, taking opportunity.* <note>original: "Nam peccatum occasione accepta"; Romans 7:11</note> ¶ It should rather be read as was said before: *For sin, taking an opportunity.* Paul [says]: *For sin, having taken the starting point.* <note>original: "ἡ γὰρ ἁμαρτία ἀφορμὴν λαβοῦσα"</note> Why it is said this way rather than that way is for a specific cause.

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *That sin might become sinning beyond measure.* <note>original: "Vt fiat supra modū peccans peccatum"; Romans 7:13</note> ¶ "Sinning" is used here as a noun. Paul [says]: *that sin might become a sinner to the extreme.* <note>original: "ἵνα γένηται καθ' ὑπερβολὴν ἁμαρτωλὸς ἡ ἁμαρτία"</note> It is as if he said "so that through excess, sinning might become a female sinner," and this signifies an increase in weight and gravity. It is as if one said "weakness weak beyond measure" or "grave sin exceeding measure."

<margin>C 58</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Sold under sin.* <note>original: "Venūdatus sub peccato"; Romans 7:14</note> Paul has: *traded under sin.* <note>original: "πεπραμένος ὑπὸ τὴν ἁμαρτίαν"</note> This signifies being "dealt" under sin. But because traders sell, buy, and acquire, the translator said "sold." He could perhaps have said it more intelligibly: *acquired.* Truly the Prophet who said, "Behold, I was conceived in iniquity" <note>Psalm 51:5</note>, was saying he was traded under sin and acquired. That word "sold" <margin>C 56</margin> makes the sense more obscure.

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *For not the good that I want do I do: but the evil which I hate, that I do.* <note>Romans 7:15</note> ¶ The words "good" and "evil" are not found in Paul's [original Greek], yet they do not hinder the understanding. Paul [says]: *For not what I want do I perform, but what I hate, that I do.* <note>original: "οὐ γὰρ ὃ θέλω τοῦτο πράσσω, ἀλλ' ὃ μισῶ τοῦτο ποιῶ"</note>

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *But now, no longer I.* <note>Romans 7:17</note> ¶ Where this translator <margin>C</margin> inserts "and" and says "now no [longer]," Paul has "not yet" <note>original: "οὐκ ἔτι"</note>, which we said before is usually translated as "not also" or something similar. Paul [says]: *I no longer work it out.* <note>original: "οὐκ ἔτι ἐγὼ κατεργάζομαι αὐτό"</note>

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *For to will is present with me: but to perform the good I find not.* <note>Romans 7:18</note> ¶ Where this translator says "to perform," Paul has "to work out" <note>original: "κατεργάζεσθαι"</note>, a verb which the translator renders a little later as "to operate" or "to work." Where he says, "now no longer I work that out," Paul [says]: *I no longer work it out.* <note>original: "οὐκ ἔτι ἐγὼ κατεργάζομαι αὐτό"</note> <margin>D 61</margin> And he could have said earlier: *but to work the good I find not.*

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *The grace of God through JESUS CHRIST our Lord.* <note>Romans 7:25</note> ¶ It should be said: *Grace [be] to God*, or rather, *I give thanks to God*, as Paul has it: *I give thanks to God through Jesus Christ our Lord.* <note>original: "εὐχαριστῶ τῷ θεῷ διὰ Ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν"</note> For "eucharisto" is a verb meaning "I give thanks." Now let us apply our pen to the following things.

->**CHAPTER VIII.**<-

<margin>62</margin> If we live by the spirit, if we live by the mind: we serve the law of God. But if by the flesh: we serve the law of sin. But he who serves the law of God: in what can he be condemned? Certainly in nothing. Therefore Paul adds: ¶ *There is therefore now no condemnation to those who walk in CHRIST JESUS not according to the flesh, but according to the spirit.* <note>Romans 8:1</note> ¶ He says "In Christ Jesus" because no one can live by the spirit unless he has obtained it by the grace of Christ. And therefore, if you wish to live by the spirit or the mind: look to Christ and his grace, not yourself, not your own works, even though you ought to work according to your strength. Your works will not free you from the weakness of the flesh, even if they prepare you; rather, it is the grace of Christ, and the law of the spirit of life, and his grace. For the Law of Moses commanded, but it could not confer the spirit and grace. Therefore it was weak to heal because of the weakness of the flesh. But the Law of Christ both commands works and, moreover, gives the spirit and grace, which is far more powerful for healing than works. For works are supporting aids <note>original: "adminiculantia"</note>, but grace is that which perfects and consumes. Therefore Paul adds: <margin>63</margin> ¶ *For the law of the spirit of life in CHRIST JESUS has freed me from the law of sin and death. For what was impossible for the law, in which it was weakened through the flesh, God sent his own son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and concerning sin, he damned sin in the flesh, so that the justification of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk not according to the flesh, but according to the spirit.* <note>Romans 8:2-4</note> ¶ Christ took flesh in the likeness of sinful flesh, but not having the weakness of the flesh—that is, sin—in any way. We, however, have the flesh of sin, and feel the weakness of sin <margin>everywhere</margin>. And this is true flesh; but Christ's flesh was <insert>truer as flesh</insert> because it was entirely healthy; <unclear>our</unclear> flesh is entirely <unclear>in some way</unclear> corrupted and sick. But when we are made members of the body of Christ: through his grace and through his flesh, to which our flesh is united, he mortifies sin—that is, the weakness of the flesh—in our flesh. But you will say: How is our flesh united to his flesh? Certainly, as often as we receive his most holy body: flesh [is united] to flesh and his spirit to our sp[irit]...

# COMMENTARY

[We are] united so that we may be one body and one spirit in him, and that we may walk not according to the flesh but according to the spirit. Nevertheless, if you walk according to the flesh of Christ—that is, according to innocent affections and innocent passions—you do not sin. For example: bearing the tribulations of the body patiently, defending against nakedness and harm with necessary clothing, preserving life with necessary food and drink, and refreshing or restoring the weariness of the body with sleep (as is fitting). If, however, you add excess or curiosity <note>original: "curiositatem"; in a theological context, this often refers to a disordered or vain desire for sensory pleasure or useless knowledge</note> to these things, these do not pertain to the flesh of Christ's body, but to the flesh of sin. And when you hear "flesh" named simply, understand it for the most part as the flesh of sin which opposes the spirit, and whose wisdom <note>original: "prudentia"; often translated as "mindset" or "outlook" in modern versions of Romans 8</note> is contrary to the way of the most wise, and whose law is contrary to the law of God. For its wisdom is this: to diligently find ways to carry out those things to which its own weakness, along with its lusts, drives it.

<margin>64</margin>
¶ Wherefore Paul adds:
> ¶ For they that are according to the flesh, mind the things that are of the flesh: but they that are according to the spirit, the things that are of the spirit. For the wisdom of the flesh is death: but the wisdom of the spirit is life and peace. Because the wisdom of the flesh is an enemy to God: for it is not subject to the law of God, neither can it be. And they who are in the flesh cannot please God.

¶ If the wisdom of the spirit is life and peace in the spirit, then the wisdom of the flesh is death and continuous war in the flesh. And if the wisdom of the flesh is an enemy to God, the wisdom of the spirit is a friend to God. Furthermore, if the spirit is subject to the law of God, the flesh cannot be subject to the law of God. For the spirit obeys the law of God, but the flesh by no means does so. And if those who are in the flesh—who live by the flesh—cannot please God, then surely those who are in the spirit and who live by the spirit will please God. Those who are not ignorant of <term>dialectical places</term> <note>Methods of logical argument and categorization used in classical rhetoric and philosophy</note> immediately see that these things must be so, and they see countless such things which, in Paul’s divine way of philosophizing, correspond by opposites. And how could the flesh be subject to the law of God, since it is judged by the law of sin? For the law of God is the law of the spirit, the law of life, the law of the healthy. And we see the sick, who cannot live by the law of the healthy until they themselves are healed. So also the flesh, until it is healed, cannot live by the law of God, nor be subject and obedient to it. But those who are not in the flesh but in the spirit—who do not live by the flesh but by the spirit—belong to the law of God and please God. They live by the spirit through the grace and righteousness of Christ; they are dead in the body because it was subject to sin, yet they possess the spirit of Christ. Though the body is dead, it has nevertheless been made a member of Christ, which Christ will also raise in truth from the dead, conformed to his own body

<margin>65</margin>
unto the immortality of life. Such were the faithful Romans in the primitive church, to whom Paul speaks these things:
> ¶ But you are not in the flesh, but in the spirit, if so be that the spirit of God dwell in you. Now if any man have not the spirit of Christ, he is none of his. And if Christ be in you, the body indeed is dead because of sin; but the spirit liveth because of justification. And if the spirit of him that raised up Jesus from the dead dwell in you; he that raised up Christ from the dead shall quicken also your mortal bodies, because of his spirit that dwelleth in you.

¶ But come now, do our bodies, having been made members of Christ, live in another way? They ought to live in the likeness of Christ’s resurrection. Because he rose spiritually, therefore the body in itself ought also to be dead. However, by imitation and spiritually it should live, because it is restored in the imitation of the resurrection. Truly, because this is an imitation and not yet the fullness <note>original: "veritas"; literally "truth" or "reality" of the event</note> of the resurrection, the weakness of potential sin still remains, which returns to action unless a conversion to the spirit and the grace of God takes place. Then we miserably serve the flesh and sin again, and we die a worse death in the flesh—the flesh which had been dead to sin by imitation and had risen to the life of the spirit. We therefore owe everything to the spirit and nothing to the flesh, which did not live in itself but in the spirit. For the flesh in itself is death, just as the spirit in itself is life. And therefore,

<margin>66</margin>
Paul exhorts both the Romans, and us in the Romans, by the price of the great God, against this sin:
> ¶ Therefore, brethren, we are debtors, not to the flesh, to live according to the flesh. For if you live according to the flesh, you shall die: but if by the spirit you mortify the deeds of the flesh, you shall live. For whosoever are led by the spirit of God, they are the sons of God. For you have not received the spirit of bondage again in fear; but you have received the spirit of adoption, in which we cry: Abba (that is, Father). For the spirit itself giveth testimony to our spirit, that we are the sons of God.

¶ "The spirit itself." Understand this as the Holy Spirit, who moved the disciples and apostles to call upon God by the name of "Father." As he says through the Evangelist: *But as many as received him, he gave them power to be made the sons of God, to them that believe in his name, who are born not of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God.* <note>John 1:12-13</note> But also the Lord himself gave us this confidence to call God "Father." They received, therefore, the spirit of liberty and veneration. For sons—whether by nature or by adoption—are free. They owe veneration to a parent, not slavish fear. Certainly, in the Old Law, the spirit did not move the fathers to approach God by the name of "Father," but to invoke him as "Lord" <note>original: "dominum"; implying a master-servant relationship</note>. In this, they are designated as having been servants, and having received servitude in fear. For when they thought of the "Lord," they thought of command and power, not [of fatherly love].

The author emphasizes that the New Law moves believers to call God 'Father' through the Spirit, whereas the Old Law was characterized by the fear and servitude of a 'Lord.'</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Epistle to the Romans, specifically Chapter 8. The previous page discussed the "wisdom of the flesh" as death and the "wisdom of the spirit" as life. This page explores the transition from a "servile fear" of punishment to a "filial love" as adopted children of God, and the cosmic expectation of the restoration of all creation.</meta>

...to those who do [wrong], inflicting punishment; thus, out of hatred for lashes and punishments, the fear of God arose in them. This is **servile fear** <note>original: "servilis timor"; the fear of a slave who obeys only to avoid the whip, rather than out of love</note>, which does not arise from the spirit of Christ, nor was it given to us by Christ. But Christ has freed us from that servitude and that fear of servitude, and he has changed servitude into **filial adoption** <note>original: "filiale adoptionem"; being brought into a family as a true son or daughter</note>. He has converted the fear of servitude into the love of veneration.

Therefore, let us fear God, but let this fear proceed from love. If you think of God as Father, what else do you think of but his ineffable kindness toward you, his supreme care for you, and his supreme providence? You think of him wanting you to be his own heir and a co-heir with Christ—who is a Son by nature, while you are one by adoption. How, then, considering such great kindness from the eternal Father, do you not love him? And out of the vehemence of love, how do you not fear to offend him? Why would you not gladly endure all things for his sake, whether they be prosperous or adverse? 

If he who is Son by nature—and in whom you are adopted—conducted himself toward the Father in this way (for whose love he endured so many and such great things so that you might be adopted), will you not imitate the true and natural Son of God, whether the things that happen are joyful or hard and adverse? Therefore, Paul added:

> ¶ And if sons, heirs also; heirs indeed of God, and joint-heirs with Christ: yet so, if we suffer with him, that we may be also glorified together. For I reckon that the sufferings of this time are not worthy to be compared with the glory to come, that shall be revealed in us.

For it is necessary for adopted sons to imitate the true Son: who came not to do his own will, but the will of the Father; who came not to be served, but to serve; who came not for the honors and delights of this world, but to endure dishonor and troubles. "We saw him," (it says) "and there was no sightliness; and we desired him, despised and the most abject of men, a man of sorrows and acquainted with infirmity." <note>This is a reference to the "Suffering Servant" in the book of the prophet Isaiah, chapter 53.</note> 

But eternal glory followed these contempts, these sorrows, and these infirmities. So, if by imitating him we do not do our own will but the Father’s; if we do not wish to rule and be served, but to serve for his sake; and if we are filled with joy to endure the contempt, sorrows, and pressures of the world in imitation of him—then a glory similar to the Son's will follow this modest pilgrimage of our earthly dwelling. But if we live otherwise, an eternal confusion will follow this modest and momentary stay of ours. 

Yet how great is the kindness of God toward us! He makes the heavens, the sun, the moon, the stars, the elements, and the entire **cosmic machine** <note>original: "machina mundi"; a common Renaissance term for the universe viewed as a complex, divinely-ordered structure</note> of the sensible world serve us. It remains subject to vanity, change, and corruption for a time, until the adopted sons receive the kingdom of God in immortality. This will happen when the number of the saved is fulfilled, and all rise in immortality, and mortal things are changed into immortality. Then the "machine" of things itself will change; it will be transformed from a corruptible and mutable state into an incorruptible and immutable one, and from a sensible state into a spiritual one. 

Just as the sensible machine served the children of God in a sensible and suffering way while they were sensible and subject to suffering—indeed, even serving the true Son of God when he was sensible and subject to suffering—so too, for the spiritual, impassible <note>original: "impassibilibus"; meaning they can no longer suffer or be harmed</note>, and immortal children of God, the machine of the world shall be made spiritual and impassible. It will exist for the glory of the Creator, and having performed every mortal duty, it will rest in a glorious end. Then that which was said in the mystery of the Holy Revelation will be fulfilled: "I saw a new heaven and a new earth. For the first heaven and the first [earth] passed away." And again: "And he who sat on the throne said: Behold, I make all things new." <note>Quotes from the Book of Revelation 21:1, 5.</note> 

This is the expectation of the sensible machine: every part of it seems to groan and suffer pain for as long as it takes to be restored to that best, spiritual, and immutable state. And this expectation of divine ordinance is a form of hope, but the long delay is a kind of sad and involuntary affection for the machine itself. Yet it is voluntary in its expectation and obedience to God, who subjected it to corruption for a time. How, then, could the sufferings of this time be worthy of the future glory that shall be revealed? 

<margin>68</margin>
As Paul—the divine man who is conscious of divine secrets—says, the entire machine of the world waits for this, adding:

> ¶ For the expectation of the creature waiteth for the revelation of the sons of God. For the creature was made subject to vanity, not willingly, but by reason of him who hath subjected it in hope. Because the creature itself also shall be delivered from the servitude of corruption, into the liberty of the glory of the children of God. For we know that every creature groaneth and travaileth in pain, even until now.

And it is not enough that every sensible creature endures anguish and labors so that the children of God may be brought forth in a perfect birth into the life of immortality; but even all the saints and the souls of the saints groan and sigh for that final and most perfect birth of immortality. For this reason, those plaintive voices of the souls of the saints are believed to reach that place: "How long, O Lord, holy and true, dost thou not judge and revenge our blood on them that dwell on the earth?" To whom it was said: that they should rest yet for a little time, until the number of their fellow-servants and their brothers be fulfilled. 

<margin>69</margin>
For what nature, by its own instinct, does not strive to be in its best state? Therefore, it is not only the sensible machine that strives for this best state, but as Paul says:

> ¶ And not only it, but ourselves also, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, even we ourselves groan within ourselves, waiting for the adoption, the redemption of our body.

And because he who hopes is both certain and unshakeable...

It also explains that the entire physical universe (the "cosmic machine") groans in expectation, waiting to be transformed and perfected alongside the glorified children of God.</summary>

# COMMENTARY
### Page 8

...is united, so that we may be one body and one spirit in him, and walk not according to the flesh but according to the spirit. Nevertheless, if you walk according to the flesh of Christ—that is, according to innocent affections and innocent passions—you do not sin. For example: patiently bearing the tribulations of the body, defending against nakedness and harm with necessary clothing, preserving life with necessary food and drink, and refreshing or repairing the weariness of the body with sleep (as is fitting). 

But if you add excess or curiosity to these things, these do not belong to the flesh of the body of Christ, but to the "flesh of sin" <note>original: "carnem peccati"</note>. And when you hear "the flesh" named simply, understand it for the most part as the flesh of sin which opposes the spirit; its wisdom <note>The Latin *prudentia* here refers to the "mindset" or "way of thinking" of the flesh.</note> is contrary to the wisdom of the spirit, and its law is contrary to the law of God. For its wisdom is this: to diligently find ways to carry out those things toward which its own weakness, with its desires, impels it—which is sin. But the wisdom of the spirit is to do those things which are pleasing to God, and toward which divine virtue moves us. Therefore, Paul adds:

<margin>✝ 64</margin>
> For those who are according to the flesh, savor the things of the flesh; but those who are according to the spirit, savor the things of the spirit. For the wisdom of the flesh is death; but the wisdom of the spirit is life and peace. Therefore, the wisdom of the flesh is an enemy to God; for it is not subject to the law of God, nor can it be. And those who are in the flesh cannot please God.

If the wisdom of the spirit is life and peace in the spirit, then the wisdom of the flesh is death and continual war in the flesh. And if the wisdom of the flesh is an enemy to God, the wisdom of the spirit is a friend to God. Furthermore, if the spirit is subject to the law of God, the flesh cannot be subject to the law of God. For the spirit obeys the law of God, but the flesh by no means does. And if those who are "in the flesh"—who live by the flesh—cannot please God, then surely those who are "in the spirit" and live by the spirit will please God. 

Those who are not ignorant of dialectical topics <note>A reference to classical logic and rhetoric, where opposites are used to prove a point.</note> immediately see that these things must be so, as well as countless other such things which correspond through opposites in Paul’s divine way of philosophizing. And how could the flesh be subject to the law of God, when it is subject to the law of sin? For the law of God is the law of the spirit, the law of life, and the law of the healthy. We see that the sick cannot live by the law of the healthy until they themselves are healed. So also the flesh, until it is healed, cannot live by the law of God, nor be subject or obedient to it. 

But those who are not in the flesh but in the spirit—who do not live by the flesh but by the spirit—are subject to the law of God and please God. They live in the spirit through the grace and righteousness of Christ, and they are dead in the body because it was subject to sin; yet, possessing the Spirit of Christ, the dead body has been made a member of Christ. In truth, Christ will raise this body from the dead, conforming it to his own body for the immortality of life. Such were the faithful Romans in the primitive church, to whom Paul speaks:

But if the spirit of him who raised JESUS from the dead dwells in you, he who raised CHRIST from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies because of his spirit dwelling in you.

But come now, our bodies, having been made members of Christ—do they live in some way? They ought to live in the likeness of Christ’s resurrection. Because he rose spiritually, the body must be dead in itself and corporally, yet live by imitation and spiritually; because in the imitation of the resurrection, there is a return to life. 

Truly, because this is an imitation and not yet the reality of the resurrection, the potential weakness of sin still remains. Unless there is a conversion to the spirit and the grace of God, it returns to action <note>The original text repeats a sentence here, likely a printing error: "Verum quia hæc imitatio eſt... redit ad actum."</note>, and we miserably serve the flesh and sin again, and we die a worse death by the flesh—which had been dead to sin by imitation and had risen to the life of the spirit. We therefore owe everything to the spirit and nothing to the flesh, which does not live in itself but in the spirit. For the flesh in itself is death, just as the spirit in itself is life. And therefore, through this sin, Paul, the herald of the great God, exhorts both the Romans and us in the Romans:

<margin>66</margin>

For you have not received the spirit of servitude again in fear, but you have received the spirit of adoption, in which we cry out: Abba, that is, Father. For the spirit itself bears witness to our spirit that we are the children of God.

He says through the Evangelist: "But as many as received him, he gave them power to become the sons of God, to those who believe in his name, who were born not of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God." In this, they are designated as having been servants, having received servitude in fear. For when they thought of the "Lord," they thought of command and power, not...

...has an indubitable hope: for he seems to already possess in hope that which he awaits without doubt. The most blessed

best intercessor acting for him. And indeed, the Holy Spirit made that prayer in him, which he

is the conformity to the Son of God, in which God glorifies his own, whether in this or in the other age. For 
is it not glorious to be conformed to Christ, or rather to be **Christ-formed**? ¶ These are the fore-
<margin>72</margin> known, these are the predestined, these are the called, these are the justified, these are the glorified. Paul, relating these 
<margin>></margin> divine secrets to us, says: ¶ *But he who searches hearts knows <term>what</term> <note>original: "q̃" (quid/quae)</note> is the wisdom of the Spirit, because 
<margin>></margin> he pleads for the saints according to God. And we know that for those who love God, all things 
<margin>></margin> work together for good—for those who are called according to his purpose. For those whom he foreknew, 
<margin>></margin> he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, so that he might be the firstborn among many 
<margin>></margin> brothers. And those whom he predestined, he also called. And those whom he called, he also justified. And those 
<margin>></margin> whom he justified, he also glorified.* ¶ **Purpose**: this is the fore-knowledge and prescience of God, 
about which more will be said in the following chapter. But how is Christ the firstborn among 
many brothers? It is certainly to be understood that there are three births. The first is of the flesh. The 
second of the spirit. The third of immortality. The first occurs when anyone is born into the world. The second: in 
baptism. And the third: in the final resurrection. By the first birth, Christ was born in 
original justice; and according to this, he is not the firstborn. For Adam also was born in original 
justice, as was Eve, and the glorious Virgin. Nor according to this is Christ called "brother," but 
the son of Adam and the son of the undefiled Virgin. By the second birth: he was born in the Jordan, receiving 
the testimony of the Father (*This is my beloved Son in whom I am well pleased*) and of the Holy 
Spirit descending and remaining upon him. And according to this birth: he is the firstborn 
among many brothers, the first of all those reborn in the Holy Spirit. According to this 
he is called "brother," both the brother of the reborn Virgin Mary, and of the apostles, and of the disciples, and of all 
people everywhere reborn in the sacred font of baptism. For to whom would the Son of God be called "brother," 
if not to the children of God? For by this birth alone are all called "children of God." And this birth of Christ, 
this regeneration of baptism, contains the truth of all others and sanctifies 
everyone. He is also the firstborn from the dead. For he was the first of all to rise into the immortality of life, 
attaining the third and final birth most fully in the resurrection. And if others 
rose with him, he nevertheless holds the primacy and the honor of the firstfruits. But you might say: "Did 
John not baptize long before Christ?" You speak truly: they were being baptized in water, in a figure and symbol of the 
truth, but they were not yet being reborn. *I indeed* (says John) *baptize you with water; 
but one mightier than I is coming, whose sandal strap I am not worthy to untie; 
he will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire.* And the Lord said: *Unless one is reborn of 
water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God.* And if anyone should say: the Holy Spirit...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Romans 8, shifting from the role of the Spirit in prayer to the security of the believer in God's love, the status of the Virgin Mary, and the triumphant conclusion of the chapter's argument on divine election.</meta>

# I

The Holy Spirit descended into the Virgin Mother of God <note>original: "deiparam virginem"</note> before Christ was born, as it is written: *The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you.* And she was full of grace, and blessed among all women, and the Lord was always with her. This we freely confess; but it was not through regeneration <note>new birth or spiritual rebirth</note>. Indeed, after Christ, she was the first of all those regenerated: this most blessed and most happy Virgin—and as she is always Virgin, always holy—was reborn from water and the Holy Spirit. You see, therefore, how Christ is without controversy the firstborn among many brothers (as the most holy Paul revealed), whom He called in His foreknowledge, pre-defined, justified, and glorified. It is truly a great glory to be the sons of God, to be the brothers of Christ—those who are not ignorant of these immense benefits of God toward them. Let no one ascribe anything to themselves; let no one look to themselves, but to God; let no one trust in themselves, but in God alone. These are the benefits of God. It is God who chooses us. And how can we not trust in Him who chooses us, who loves us, who wants to give us all things, who gave us His own Son and willed that He be sacrificed for us all?

<margin>73</margin> Therefore, Paul—the interpreter and orator of God’s vehement kindness toward us—adds:

¶ What then shall we say to these things? If God is for us, who is against us? He who did not spare even His own Son, but handed Him over for us all, how will He not also, with Him, give us all things? Who will accuse those who are against God's elect? It is God who justifies. Who will condemn? CHRIST JESUS, who died, or rather, who rose again, who is also at the right hand of God, and who also pleads for us.

¶ It is a most certain proof of God’s great love for us that He handed over His own Son for us all; that He accuses and rebukes the adversaries of the elect; that Christ Jesus, who died for all—or rather, who rose for the glory of all—condemns the adversaries. But also declaring His own love and charity toward us, He continually intercedes, requests, and pleads for us as a mediator at the right hand of the Father. And why would He not plead now, since while He was on earth, whatever He did, whatever He asked, He did and asked for us? Even then He pleaded with the Father for us, asking the Father and saying: *Holy Father, keep them in your name, those whom you have given me, so that they may be one as we are.* And again: *I do not ask for these only, but also for those who will believe through their word, so that all may be one, as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be one in us.* ¶ Oh, infinite sea of charity! Not that by which we love God, but by which God the Father and the Son love us. Why then do you distrust?

<margin>Ro.</margin>
<margin>74</margin> Why do you fear that God does not love you? You surely fear that the wave of the sea might fail. Therefore, looking upon this ineffable charity of God and Christ, Paul exclaims:

¶ Who shall separate us from the love of CHRIST? Shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or hunger, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword? As it is written: *Because of you we are being put to death all day long; we are counted as sheep for the slaughter.* But in all these things we are more than conquerors through Him who loved us.

¶ Do not fear, therefore, that God does not love you, whether you are in tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or hunger, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword. For He always loves you. And as for the fact that you conquer and overcome vices, His love for you does this. It is not the love with which you love Him (for all love of a creature is weak and infirm, though it is still pleasing and acceptable to God), but the effective and most strong love of God. He says, "we overcome through Him who loved us." Behold, he does not look at his own love, but at the love of Christ and God. That love he praises, that love he extols, that love he honors. O fools, and those with a crooked mind <note>original: "incuruata mente"; a metaphor for a soul turned inward on itself or distorted by pride</note>: learn to look to God, not to yourselves, and then God will work in you. You will work rightly. You will love rightly. You will understand all things rightly and not obliquely. Why do you attribute to your own weakness what is owed to divine strength? Trust in divine love, not in your own. Can you perhaps surpass God in loving? For you who love—and love happily indeed—bring forth a spark of His love. As the holy Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, an early Christian mystical philosopher whose works were highly regarded in the Renaissance</note>, infused with divine light, says: "He follows those who turn away and recoil from Him with an amorous pursuit <note>original: "amatorie sequitur"</note>; and He strives and begs that those whom He seeks with such force of love do not desert Him."

<margin>75</margin> Can Paul not say, then, with exceeding truth?

¶ For I am certain that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature will be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in CHRIST JESUS our Lord.

¶ The charity of God, by which He loves us in Christ Jesus His most blessed Son, conquers all things. It is stronger than all things, stronger than all angels—whether the highest, the middle, or the lowest—stronger than the depths of hell <note>original: "infernis"</note>, which it has despoiled and despoils daily; stronger than the world and every creature. Therefore, Christ is the reason for such great love toward us; and because of Him we are loved by God with such insuperable and inescapable love. Let us, therefore, prepare our whole heart to love Him in return <term>redamandum</term> <note>to love back; a reciprocal love responding to God's initial love</note> who loves us so much, and because of whom we are loved so much. And thus, let there be all love, all honor, and thanksgiving forever. Now let the present work turn itself to examination: and the labor is indeed sweet under the inspiration—

<meta>catchword: [of God as the author], labor.</meta>

The author also clarifies the Virgin Mary's unique status as the first to be spiritually reborn after Christ.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philological and theological commentary on the eighth chapter of Romans. # COMMENTARY

<margin>A 62</margin> ¶ EXAMINATION of several points concerning the literal text. **The Vulgate edition:** *Who now walk according to the flesh.* ¶ This entire phrase, "but according to the spirit," is missing here and ought to be added immediately. **Paul** <note>original Greek: "mê kata sarka peripatousin alla kata pneuma"</note> writes: *who walk not according to the flesh, but according to the spirit.* ¶ **The Vul-**
<margin>A 63</margin> **gate edition:** *For the law of the spirit of life in CHRIST JESUS.* ¶ And this is indeed correct, but "spirit" is in the genitive case <note>meaning it indicates possession: "the law belonging to the spirit"</note>. **Paul** <note>original Greek: "ho gar nomos tou pneumatos tês zôês en christô iêsou"</note> writes: *For the law of the spirit of life in Christ Jesus.* 
<margin>A 64</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *For they who are according to the flesh, savor the things of the flesh; but they who are according to the spirit, feel the things of the spirit.* ¶ The word "feel" <note>Latin: "sentiunt"</note> is superfluous in this place. For after "spirit," no verb is held in the original. It would be more appropriately placed above in the 
<margin>B 65</margin> position of the word "savor" <note>Latin: "sapiunt"</note>. **Paul** <note>original Greek: "hoi gar kata sarka ontes ta tês sarkos phronousin; hoi de kata pneuma ta tou pneumatos"</note> writes: *For those who are according to the flesh set their minds on the things of the flesh; but those according to the spirit, the things of the spirit.* ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *If however the spirit of God dwells in you.* ¶ The translator creates an ambiguity here, where Paul seems to confirm his statement without doubt. For a little before he had said: "but you are not in the flesh, but in the spirit," and he adds <note>original Greek: "eiper pneuma theou oikei en hymin"</note>: *since indeed / certainly / the spirit of God dwells in you.* ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *But the spirit lives because of justification.* ¶ The translator could have said: *because of righteousness.* **Paul** writes <note>original Greek: "dia dikaiosynên"</note>: *because of righteousness.* Usually, the translator everywhere converts *dikaiosynên* as "righteousness" and *dikaiôma* as "justification." But that matters little, except that it is better to show consistency in translating. ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *who raised*
<margin>C 66</margin> *JESUS CHRIST from the dead.* ¶ "Jesus" is not found here in Paul, but only "Christ." **Paul** <note>original Greek: "ho egeiras ton christon ek nekrôn"</note> writes: *he who raised the Christ from the dead.* ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *But if by the spirit you mortify the deeds of the flesh.* ¶ It is now read as "the acts of the body." **Paul** writes <note>original Greek: "ei de pneumati tas praxeis tou sômatos"</note>: *but if by the spirit [you mortify] the actions of the body.* But these differences do not hinder understanding. ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *But you have received the spirit of the adoption of sons, in which we cry, Abba, Father.* ¶ "The adoption of sons" is expressed by a single word <note>original Greek: "huiothesias"</note>, and it is enough to translate it as "adoption." Indeed, by Latin custom, this word sufficiently shows the understanding of "sons." And where it says "Abba, Father": here "Father" is in the nominative case <note>used for a subject or a title</note> and is not in the vocative case <note>used for direct address</note>; it is an explanation of what is meant by "Abba."
<margin>C 67</margin> **Paul** writes <note>original Greek: "all’ elabete pneuma huiothesias en hô krazomen abba ho patêr"</note>. ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *If however we suffer with him, that we may also be glorified.* ¶ This can also be an assertion, and perhaps it would have been better for the translator to turn it thus: *since indeed we suffer together, so that we may also be glorified together* / or *that we may be conglorified.* It is as if he says: certainly we suffer with Christ for this purpose, so that we may also be glorified with Christ, although the sufferings of this time are not to be compared to the future glory that will be revealed in us. **Paul** writes <note>original Greek: "eiper sympaschomen hina kai syndoxasthômen"</note>. I would have preferred to say "we suffer together" <note>simul patimur</note> rather than "we suffer with him" <note>compatimur</note> (as was said) because "to suffer with" <note>compatior</note> among Latin speakers often signifies "to pity." Paul does not intend that meaning here. For he does not speak of compassion and affection, but of the pressures and tribulations which they endured for Christ and in imitation of Christ. This is what it means to suffer with Christ. However, these pressures and persecutions
<margin>D 68</margin> which they bore for Christ were as nothing compared to the future glory which they expected by God's gift and grace. ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *For the expectation of the creature.* ¶ Here the word is *ktisis*, which we previously said refers to the "creation of the world"—that is, this visible fabric, the divine and sensible workmanship. If Origen <note>An early Christian theologian (c. 184–253 AD)</note> had grasped this understanding, he would not have 
<margin>D 69</margin> fallen into such futile suspicions regarding this passage; it is better not to have seen what he saw in his book *On First Principles*. ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *And not only that.* ¶ "That" <note>Latin: "illa"</note> is superfluous, even if it does not hinder understanding. **Paul** writes <note>original Greek: "ou monon de"</note>: *And not only [so].* ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *And we ourselves groan within ourselves, expecting the* 
<margin>E 71</margin> *adoption of the sons of God.* ¶ "Of the sons of God" is superfluous. We ourselves sigh within ourselves, expecting the adoption. ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *And in like manner the spirit also helps our infirmity.* **Paul** speaks in the plural: "our infirmities."
<margin>E 72</margin> **Paul** writes <note>original Greek: "tais astheneiais hêmôn"</note>. ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *But he who searches hearts knows what the spirit desires.* **Paul** has <note>original Greek: "ho de ereunôn tas kardias oiden ti to phronêma tou pneumatos"</note>: *But he who searches the hearts knows what is the prudence of the spirit*—namely, the one who moves these ineffable and unutterable groanings in the hearts of the elect in this manner. For He knows what this workmanship of the spirit signifies and what it intends for itself. ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *And we know that to those who love God, all things work together for good.* **Paul** has the verb "cooperates" in the singular <note>original Greek: "synergei"</note>. And it can be referred back to the Spirit, of whom he had spoken a little earlier. So that the sense is: *To those who love God, the Spirit works all things together for good.* For he said before: "the spirit helps our infirmities," "the spirit asks for us, stirring up unutterable groanings in us," "the spirit asks for the saints according to God's will." And what does the Spirit do? Truly, to those who love God, the Spirit works all things together for good. He helps the weak, He helps those who pray, and whatever good we do, He so helps us that He Himself seems to do it rather than we. Thus He leads us, thus He moves us.

# THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

->.8.I<-

He works in all our actions: just like a nurse with a year-old infant, who seems to do the walking rather than the infant itself. I would not deny, however, that if "all things" is understood as the subject, it could be translated in the plural "all things work together" <note>Latin: "cooperantur"</note>. For in Greek, neuter plural subjects are aptly joined with singular verbs. This was the sense understood by the old translator <note>referring to the author of the Vulgate</note> and many others after him. Yet the sense mentioned above <note>that God is the subject who "works all things together for good"</note> seems to be drawn from the sequence of the discourse, and that sense is also more divine and worthier of Paul.

**The Vulgate edition:** *To those who are called to be saints according to his purpose.* ¶ The word "saints" is superfluous.
<margin>F. 72</margin> **Paul** <note>original Greek: "tois kata prothesin klêtois ousin"</note> writes: *To those who are called according to his purpose.* ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *For whom he foreknew, he also predestined.* ¶ He could have said: *Because whom he knew before and defined beforehand.* **Paul**
<margin>F.</margin> <note>original Greek: "hoti hous proegnô kai proôrisen"</note> writes: *Because whom he foreknew and foreordained.* ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *And whom he justified, them he also magnified.* ¶ He could have translated: *these he also glorified.* **Paul** <note>original Greek: "toutous kai edoxasen"</note> writes: *these he also glorified.*
<margin>73</margin> **The Vulgate edition:** *Who also did not spare his own son.* ¶ The word "his" <note>Latin: "suo"</note> is superfluous. For "his own" <note>Latin: "proprio"</note> is the same as saying "his." Nor is it found in Paul. **Paul** <note>original Greek: "hoste tou idiou huiou ouk epheisato"</note> writes: *Who did not spare his own son.* ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *How has he not also with him given us all things.* ¶ One should rather say "will give." **Paul** <note>original Greek: "charisetai"</note> writes: *will freely give.* ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Who shall accuse against the elect of God.* ¶ Even if the Greek phrasing represents it this way, for the sake of Latin understanding it seems it should be expressed differently, in this manner: ¶ *Who shall accuse those who oppose the elect of God?* or in some other similar way, adding a few words for clarity. For God does not accuse the elect; rather, He accuses those who oppose them. ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Who is he that condemns?* ¶ The translator ought to have said "will condemn," just as he previously said "will accuse," or "who is the one condemning" as in the Greek. **Paul** <note>original Greek: "tis ho katakrinôn"</note> writes: *Who is the one condemning?* And then the verb "will be" is understood. ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Who is at the right hand of God, who also intercedes for us.* ¶ It should read "who even is at the right hand of God." **Paul** <note>original Greek: "hos kai estin en dexia tou theou"</note> writes: *who is even at the right hand of God.* And where he says "intercedes" <note>Latin: "interpellat"</note>, he previously said "requests" <note>Latin: "postulat"</note>. For the word in Paul's text is the same in both places: *entynchanei* <note>original Greek: "entynchanei"</note>. Perhaps "requests" is better, as it signifies to intercede, to act as a patron, and to ask reasonably. For "to intercede" <note>Latin: "interpellare"</note> more commonly means to interrupt a speech. However, whether we say "requests" or "intercedes," let us always understand the same meaning as Paul.
<margin>G. 74</margin> **The Vulgate edition:** *Who therefore shall separate us from the charity of CHRIST.* ¶ "Therefore" is superfluous. **Paul** <note>original Greek: "tis hêmas chôrisei apo tês agapês tou christou"</note> writes: *Who shall separate us from the love of Christ?* There are those who think these words were spoken concerning Paul's own love toward God, as if he were in a state of ecstasy. It is true that Paul’s love for God was great. But here he seems to commend not his own love, but rather God’s love toward us. "In all these things (he says) we overcome through him who loved us." And this sense is more divine. Furthermore, even if he were speaking of his own ecstatic love, he would not join himself to others by saying "who shall separate **us**?" but would rather have said "who shall separate **me**?" For Paul is not accustomed to looking at himself. ¶ If he does sometimes look at himself, he speaks of himself not sublimely or immodestly, but humbly. And whoever understands this is greatly enlightened to walk through his writings according to Paul's great and habitual piety toward God. Otherwise, those who do differently deceive themselves, thinking of Paul in human terms, whereas he should be understood far more divinely and above human sense. May God, therefore (with Paul as our intercessor), enlighten us to understand these holy epistles not humanly but divinely, not carnally but spiritually, as is right and fitting. ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Tribulation, or distress, or hunger, or nakedness, or danger, or persecution, or the sword.* ¶ The words are rearranged here. For in Paul, "persecution" is placed before "hunger." **Paul** <note>original Greek: "thlipsis, ê stenochôria, ê diôgmos, ê limos, ê gymnotês, ê kindynos, ê machaira"</note> writes: *Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or hunger, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword.* ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *But in all these things we overcome because of him who loved us.* ¶ It should read: *through him who loved us.* And so Paul has it. **Paul** <note>original Greek: "Dia tou agapêsantos hêmas"</note> writes: *Through him who loved us.* ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Neither things present, nor things to come, nor fortitude, nor height, nor depth.*
<margin>G. 75</margin> ¶ "Fortitude" is superfluous; nor does it have any corresponding word in the original. **Paul** <note>original Greek: "oute enestôta, oute mellonta, oute hypsôma, oute bathos"</note> writes: *neither things present, nor things to come, nor height, nor depth.*

<margin>CHAPTER IX.</margin>

### [Decorative Initial C]

Considering the love of God and Christ toward us to be so wonderful, so inseparable, and so insuperable, Paul—further considering that he had been a persecutor of such a kind and vehemently loving Christ out of zeal for his brothers according to the flesh, even to the point that he wished to be an **anathema** <term>anathema: a person cursed or cut off from the community</term> from Christ for them and for the paternal traditions—cannot help but be affected by the greatest sadness and continual pain of heart, as one who reflects that he was so ungrateful toward such great kindness. Therefore, it is not Paul’s love that is so inseparable and insuperable by every creature, but rather Christ's love toward us, who even lovingly sought out his persecutor and embraced his adversary.
