<meta>This page transitions from the conclusion of the commentary on Romans chapter 8 to the beginning of chapter 9. It focuses on the intense sorrow St. Paul feels for his fellow Israelites and begins a deep theological exploration of divine election, specifically why God chose Jacob over Esau.</meta>

<page-num>9</page-num>
<header>COMMENTARY</header>

<margin>76</margin> speaking. And Paul testifies to this with a great and powerful attestation, saying:
> ¶ I tell the truth in **CHRIST JESUS**; I do not lie, my conscience bearing me witness in the Holy Spirit: that I have great sadness and continuous grief in my heart.

¶ And what is the cause of such great sadness and continuous grief? He adds, saying:
> ¶ For I wished that I myself were anathema <note>original: "anathema"; meaning "accursed" or "separated"</note> from **CHRIST** for my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh, who are Israelites.

And in another place, when he recalls himself with sad remembrance:
> I am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the church of God. But by the grace of God, I am what I am.

And he does not only deplore that out of ignorant zeal he wished to be separated from Christ, but
<margin>77</margin> that the Israelites, his brothers according to the flesh, are ungrateful toward such great divine benevolence and love. He adds this point, saying, "for they are Israelites."
> ¶ Whose is the adoption, and the glory, and the covenants, and the giving of the law, and the worship, and the promises. Whose are also the fathers, from whom is **CHRIST** according to the flesh, who is over all things, God blessed forever. Amen.

¶ Great is the love and benevolence of God toward the Jews, whom He willed to adopt and glorify. And in no other nation did the Lord appear bodily, as He Himself said: *I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.* The covenants were given to them as agreements. Concerning the Old, the Scripture says:
> Our Lord made a covenant with us in Horeb <note>Mount Sinai</note>.

But concerning the New:
> I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah; not according to the covenant that I made with your fathers.

And the first legislation was given to them by Moses; the second by Christ. Just as it was written: *out of Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem.* "Latria," that is, worship <note>original: "Latria id est cultus"</note>, was given to them so that they might worship the God they desired, while others worshipped not God, but demons; for it says, *all the gods of the gentiles are demons.* And that the promises were made to them, almost all the prophets are witnesses. Moreover, their fathers were Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, from whom Christ the Lord willed to descend according to the flesh; for according to His divinity, He had an eternal origin from the Father. And if other things seem small, this is nonetheless a great argument for His love toward them: that Christ, who is God blessed over all things, deigned to take flesh from them. But you will say: If the promises concerning Christ were made to them, and they did not receive Him (as it is written, *He came unto His own and His own received Him not*), has the word of God therefore become void? Not at all. For those are understood to be the children of the promise who would emulate the faith of Abraham, and not only those who
<margin>78</margin> descend from Abraham according to the flesh. And those are the true Israelites, and children, and the seed of Abraham: not by flesh, but by spirit. Therefore Paul adds:
> ¶ But it is not as though the word of God has failed. For not all who are of Israel are Israel. Nor because they are the seed of Abraham are they all children; but "in Isaac shall your seed be called," that is, it is not the children of the flesh who are the children of God, but the children of the promise are counted as the seed. For this is the word of promise: "At this time I will come, and Sarah shall have a son."

¶ This is known from the history of Genesis. But also that Rebecca, the mother of Jacob and wife of Isaac, received the word of promise concerning one of the sons—namely, Jacob—the same sacred history makes manifest:
> Rebecca went, it says, to consult the Lord. Who, answering, said: "Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples shall be divided from your belly, and one people shall overcome the other: and the elder shall serve <margin>79</margin> the younger."

Behold the promise that Esau himself would serve Jacob. Therefore, not only did Sarah have the word of promise, but also Rebecca. For this reason Paul adds: ¶ From one (understand "son") <note>The text here seems to clarify the lineage through Isaac</note> Rebecca from one, who had a bed, our father Isaac. ¶ Not only that, but Rebecca also had the word of promise. And that Jacob and the people who descended from him were made master, while Esau and his people were made servants, this was done not by the choice of human knowledge, but by the choice of divine foreknowledge. Not by human will, but by divine will. Not by their works, but by divine mercy and justice. For as divine knowledge is to be preferred to ours, so is God's election to ours, and the divine will to our will. And it is just that that immense wisdom of God and His immensely good will should be the rule of all things, ordering all things, being honored and coming before all else. That Jacob is loved, the reason is divine wisdom and that surpassingly good will of God. Could the works of Jacob be so great that they were the reason for God to love him? Would you prefer those works to goodness itself and infinite mercy? Indeed, I do not deny that Jacob’s works were good and that his will was good, but I make the mercy of God and God’s "super-good" will the cause. And that He holds Esau in hatred, the reason is divine justice. I do not deny that Esau’s works were evil and his will was evil. Truly, that evil of will and works he had not from God, but from himself and his own accord. For God helped and enlightened both toward the good, as they were instructed for a blessed life by the same parents—and indeed holy parents on both sides. And one [Jacob] emerged good and obedient of his own accord; while the other [Esau] emerged evil, reluctant, and disobedient of his own accord. And these things God always foreknew...

<margin>80</margin>
For this reason Paul adds:
> ¶ For when they were not yet born, nor had done anything good or evil—so that God's purpose according to election <note>original: "prothesi"; refers to God's pre-set plan or purpose</note> might stand, not based on works but on Him who calls—it was said to her: The elder shall serve the younger. As it is written: **JACOB** I loved, but **ESAU** I hated.

¶ It was said to her, that is to **REBECCA**: "The elder shall serve the younger." This is the promise, and it is written (as mentioned) in Genesis. But the addition, "Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated," is found written at the beginning of the prophet Malachi. But is God therefore unfair or unjust if, out of His purpose and foreknowledge, He loved Jacob and hated Esau? By no means; rather, He is just in both. In Jacob, who was good, He showed His **MERCY**. In Esau, who was harsh and wild, a follower of his own passions, He showed His **JUSTICE**. In the former, His love—so that He might turn everyone toward goodness and piety; in the latter, His hatred—so that He might deter everyone from evil. And a person always has God as a helper toward the good, whatever they may do, whether good or evil. But when one performs a good work, they cooperate with God; when they do evil, they act without God and against divine help. It is no different than if a good father helps his two sons with his resources, education, advice, and encouragements to live happily: one son, obeying the father, performs good works; the other, being disobedient, does evil. He who does good cooperates with the good father. He who does evil acts without the father and against the father’s help. So it is with God, and much more so: He had given everything for the good to both Jacob and Esau, just as He gives to every mortal. But does not the one who gives, and gives for this purpose, help as far as He is concerned? Truly, when someone performs a good work and is accepted by God, it is not because of the work itself, nor from their own will, but they are accepted out of God’s compassion and will. For God's will is infinitely 
<margin>81</margin> good, while ours is finite and (so to speak) of no goodness at all. From whom is it, therefore, that every acceptance and every justification comes from the will of God? Paul suggests this when he says:
> ¶ What shall we say then? Is there injustice with God? God forbid. For He says to **MOSES**: I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will show compassion to whom I show compassion. Therefore, it is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy.

¶ This testimony to Moses is now found written in Exodus: "I will have mercy on whom I will, and I will be gracious to whom it shall please me." See how mercy and compassion are to be attributed to the divine will and good pleasure, not to works or to our own will. But if mercy and compassion are to be referred to the divine will, are not justice and vengeance as well? And just as mercy and compassion help the righteous toward the good, do not God's justice and worthy 
<margin>82</margin> vengeance likewise not prevent the wicked from evil? For what else does Paul mean when he adds:
> ¶ For the Scripture says to **PHARAOH**: For this very purpose I have raised you up, that I might show my power in you, and that my name might be declared throughout all the earth. Therefore, He has mercy on whom He wills, and whom He wills, He hardens.

¶ For what does "whom He wills, He hardens" mean, except "whom He wills, He leaves behind," or "upon whom He wills, He takes vengeance and manifests the power of His justice"? And for this reason, He does not prevent them from acting according to their own will. For He made free will <note>original: "liberum arbitrium"</note> for both angels and humans so that, from the liberty of those who work well, His mercy and grace might be known; while from those who work poorly, His justice and power might be known. This testimony concerning Pharaoh is taken from the history in Exodus, where we now read God announcing to Pharaoh: "For now, stretching out my hand, I will strike you and your people with a plague, and you shall perish from the earth. But for this cause have I placed you: to show my strength in you, and that my name may be told in all the earth. Still you retain my people and do not wish to let them go." For this reason, although God was able (for what is He not able to do?), He did not prevent Pharaoh from acting according to the own lust of his soul and resisting His will by refusing to release the people, so that His justice and the power of His just vengeance might be known to him, and God might be known throughout the whole world to be just and powerful. ¶ But if Pharaoh had obeyed Him (which indeed he could have done, had he not disregarded God), His mercy would have been known to him. Therefore, free will is given to everyone for two ends: for mercy and for justice. For mercy, to the one doing good (for which one always has divine help); but for justice, to the one doing evil (which indeed happens from oneself and in respect to oneself). For as wax turned toward the hearth <note>original: "focum"; the fireside or heat source</note> melts, but when moved away, it hardens and stiffens of itself and in itself: so that which turns toward God softens toward the good, but that which turns away, in itself and of itself, grows cold and hardens. For every mind is wax, and God is the sun. ¶ If God is said to harden those who turn away, it is just as when the sun hardens wax. For both happen by absence and accidentally on the part of God and the sun; but essentially <note>original: "per se"</note> it happens from the thing that is hardened. Therefore, as far as God is concerned, "to harden" is "to leave behind." But as for the one who—

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Romans 9, moving from the analogy of the sun and wax to Paul’s famous metaphor of the potter and the clay. It addresses the human impulse to question divine justice regarding election and "hardening."</meta>

# COMMENTARY

is hardened: to be confirmed in evil by one's own will. But as wax softens: this happens by itself through the sun; so too when we perform a good work: God works through Himself and softens us toward the good. Truly, God made both the wax capable of liquefying and us capable of working good. But neither is the wax able to liquefy of itself, nor are we sufficient to work good from ourselves: so that we do not glorify ourselves, but rather God, from whom all good comes. But you will say: If God has mercy on whom He wills, and whom He wills He hardens, why then are the hardened further accused? For that is the will of God, which nothing can resist. Indeed, why are they punished, when they are what God wills them to be? This is an argument of impiety, and of those daring to rise up against God their maker and say: "Why have You made us thus?" Paul deters the unrefined and the foolish from this kind of impious contention against God. For it is not appropriate for the wise and the upright, who do not admit such thoughts—or immediately kill them off as if they were poisonous serpents. For these are the breaths of the ancient serpent, corrupting the soul. Paul, I say, deters them by the analogy of the potter and the potter's vessels, saying:

> §3. You say to me then: why is he still accused? For who resists his will? On the contrary, O man, who are you to answer back to God? Does the thing formed say to him who formed it: why did you make me thus? Or does the potter of the clay not have power from the same lump to make one vessel for honor, and another for dishonor?

This is Paul's first "dilution" <note>original: "dilutio"; a rhetorical term for dissolving or answering an objection</note> of the question, intended especially for the unrefined: namely, that one must not impiously argue against God, whether He acts toward this person for mercy or toward that person for His justice. It pleases God to have mercy, and it pleases God to punish. But life is in His will, and wrath is in His indignation. Indeed, even when He punishes He is merciful, and when He shows mercy He is just. But you, when you sin, do not wish to be accused; you do not wish to be punished. Truly, you are accused because you sin of your own accord, and divine help was ready to assist your weakness so that you might not sin; and you are punished because God is just, and you sin not by His will, but by your own. For He wants you to be good, and always assists you toward this. Your own will is the cause of your sin and your hardening through itself, and not God's will—unless perhaps you wish to speak of a "cause" by accident or permission, but that is not being a "cause." For God wants all people to be saved—much more than a father wants his own children to be, since He made and created us. And how could He want us to sin, when the divine word says of Him: "You are not a God who wills iniquity"? If, therefore, you sin, you sin against His will; if, however, you act well, you act according to His will. For He wants you to act well, but freely; therefore He does not introduce necessity upon you to act well, and much less to act poorly. How then does the impious man speak against God, saying "if he has mercy on whom he wills and whom he wills he hardens, who resists his will?"—as if, if someone is evil, God wants him to sin by necessity. For He wants him to sin neither by necessity nor freely. And it is as if, if someone is good, He wants him to be good by necessity. That He certainly does not want; yet He wants him to be good freely, and assists him toward that very thing. Why then does God harden some, why does He abandon them, why does He will to harden or abandon? Truly, as a father finally deserts incorrigible children after long waiting, and shows in them his power and worthy vengeance: so also God does with the obstinate and the stubborn, whom He finally deserts for this reason. For waiting would benefit them nothing; rather, it would increase their punishment. And He has mercy on others, and wills to have mercy, as a father does for children of obedience, or those who repent from disobedience. So also God wills to have mercy on the obedient and the repentant, that He may show in them the riches of His glory, as in the vessels which He prepared for His glory. And from this, God's mercy is known on the one hand, and God's justice and power on the other. And

§4. This is the second "dilution" which Paul applies to the question concerning hardening, speaking in this manner:

> What if God, willing to show his wrath and make his power known, endured with much patience the vessels of wrath prepared for destruction? ¶ And regarding mercy, connecting it in this way: And that he might make known the riches of his glory on the vessels of his mercy, which he prepared for glory—us, I say, whom he also called, not only from the Jews but also from the Gentiles, just as he says in Hosea: I will call those who were not my people "my people," and her who was not beloved "beloved." And it shall be in the place where it was said to them "you are not my people," there they shall be called children of the living God. ¶ So we now read in the prophet Hosea: I will have mercy on her who was without mercy, and I will say to "not my people" "you are my people," and he himself shall say "you are my God." And again: And it shall be in the place where it is said to them "you are not my people," it shall be said to them "children of the living God."

And from this passage of Hosea ("I will call my not-people my people" and "my not-beloved beloved"), a third, deeper dilution of the question is understood in Paul, intended for the more learned. Because in God, "willing" and "not-willing" absolutely coincide. Wherefore both election and non-election, knowledge and non-knowledge, do not signify any change in God, but in us.

It concludes by citing the prophet Hosea to show how God’s mercy extends to the Gentiles, reframing election as a change in humanity rather than a change in God.</summary>

In us, therefore, there is election; and conversely, in the Jews, election is now called non-election, and their calling is called rejection. They say this change occurs regarding us and regarding them, but truly no change occurs in God. That there was an election of the Jews is testified by Moses, who said to them: "The Lord your God has chosen you to be a special people to Himself out of all the peoples who are on the face of the earth" <note>original: "Te elegit dominus deus tuus: ut sis ei populus peculiaris de cunctis populis / qui sunt super terram"; Deuteronomy 7:6</note>. And regarding their rejection, Jeremiah says: "In casting us off, You have rejected us; You are vehemently angry against us" <note>original: "Proiiciens repulisti nos: iratus es contra nos uehementer"; Lamentations 5:22</note>. And thus He rejected, cast out, and threw them away, so that even if they are multiplied like the sand of the sea, only a small remnant shall be saved. This is because so few now come to Christ, acknowledging the justice of God by which it is necessary for them to be saved. As Paul brings forward the prophecy of Isaiah concerning them, saying: ¶ "But Isaiah cries out for Israel: 'Though the number of the children of Israel be as the sand of the sea, a remnant shall be saved. For He is the one who finishes and abbreviates the word in justice: because a short word the Lord will make upon the earth'" <note>original: "Si fuerit numerus filiorum Israel tanq̄ arena maris: reliquiæ saluæ fiēt... sermonem abbreviatum faciet dominus super terram"; Romans 9:27-28 quoting Isaiah 10:22-23</note>. And as Isaiah predicted: "Unless the Lord of Sabaoth <note>The "Lord of Hosts"</note> had left us a seed, we would have become like Sodom, and we would have been made like Gomorrah." ¶ The one who finishes and abbreviates the word in justice is Christ the Lord. The "abbreviated word" <note>original: "Verbum abbreviatum"</note> is the Gospel and the law of the spirit. The "seed" left to the Jews, because of which God did not utterly destroy them, is Christ the forever-blessed, who deigned to be born from them according to the flesh. And still, for the sake of Christ—whom they nevertheless persecute and blaspheme as much as they can—life is granted to them among the nations, as it is written: "The breath of our mouth, Christ the Lord, was captured in our sins; to whom we said: 'In Your shadow we shall live among the nations'" <note>original: "Spiritus oris nostri Christus dominus: captus est in peccatis nostris / cui diximus: in vmbra tua uiuemus in gētibus"; Lamentations 4:20, interpreted here Christologically</note>. Great is the dignity of Christ, and an incomparable honor to the Jews, if only they understood. Behold, the Jews were once chosen, but now rejected; once a people, now not a people.

In us, election and reprobation <note>Rejection or condemnation</note> imply a wide opposition and can never coincide. But (as has been said) it is different in God. And whoever writes regarding the coincidence of things that do not coincide, and rises from contracted <note>Limited or specific</note> things to an absolute notion, has an open field to philosophize piously about the foreknowledge and predestination of God. But our ways of understanding, the "otherness" of contradiction, cannot reach that absolute state. Yet in this "untouchable touch" <note>original: "mattingibili attactu," likely "inactingibili" (unattainable); a Cusan concept of grasping the infinite through a realization of its transcendence</note>, the perfected person knows through every limited understanding; and here, ignorance is superior to knowledge. In eternity, there is nothing that God foreknew or predestined as "before" or "after," but He always knows and defines in the same way and immutably; never otherwise than now. And if it is said "before," "prior," "sooner," or anything similar—such as "before I formed you in the womb"—this does not refer to God's duration, but to the priority or posteriority of the creature. Therefore, "knowing" and "foreknowing" in God are entirely the same, as are "defining" and "predefining" and other things of that kind. And because those who were once foreknown, predefined, and chosen are now unknown, reprobate, and rejected: it is their own error and turning away that causes this. But even so, divine mercy recalls them: "Return, O rebellious Israel, says the Lord, and I will not turn my face away from you; for I am holy, says the Lord, and I will not be angry forever" <note>Jeremiah 3:12</note>. Truly, those who were known at the first, unknown in the middle time, will be known in the final time; and they shall return to the Lord, as it is written of them in Hosea: "The children of Israel shall sit for many days without a king, without a prince, without sacrifice, without an altar, without an Ephod, and without Teraphim; and after these things, the children of Israel shall return and seek the Lord their God and David their king; and they shall tremble before the Lord and His goodness in the last days" <note>Hosea 3:4-5</note>. And why they are rejected in the middle time, their ignorance causes, which turning away and infidelity accompany. For they believe they can achieve justice by the works of the law, and they neglect faith. But the Gentiles believed that they could not achieve the justice of God by works, but that it is bestowed by the grace and mercy of God: having attained the justice of God's grace. And they believe and work, not because those works justify them, but because He whom they obey justifies them—He who commands them to believe.

It harmonizes the concept of divine predestination with human error and the eventual restoration of Israel.</summary>

# COMMENTARY
<meta>catchword: ri</meta>

<margin>§6</margin> to see and to work, faith nevertheless (as has been said) is closer to justification than works. Paul indicates this in this manner: ¶*What then shall we say? That the Gentiles, who did not follow after righteousness, have attained to righteousness, even the righteousness which is of faith. But Israel, following after the law of righteousness, has not come unto the law of righteousness. Why? Because they sought it not by faith, but as it were by the works of the law. For they stumbled at the stumbling-stone, as it is written: Behold, I lay in Zion a stumbling-stone and a rock of offense: and whosoever believes in him shall not be confounded.* <note>The author is quoting Romans 9:30-33, which contrasts the Gentiles' acceptance of Christ through faith with the Jews' rejection of Him based on their adherence to the Old Testament Law.</note> ¶This oracle is taken from Isaiah, although it is now read a little differently. <note>original: "Esaia"; referring to Isaiah 8:14 and 28:16.</note> This stone, and this rock, is Christ the Lord: a stone of offense and a rock of scandal to those who reject Him, to those who do not believe; but truly a stone of salvation and a rock of glory to those who receive and believe in Him. But did not the Jews reject Him when they cried out: *Take him away, take him away, crucify him, his blood be upon us and upon our children*? Did they not reject Him when Pilate asked them, *Shall I crucify your King?* and they furiously cried out: *We have no king but Caesar*? Do they not reject and deny Him daily? Yet He rejects no one coming to Him; rather, unmindful of every offense and injury, He receives them as a son. How, therefore, can one who returns to such a sea of mercy—even if previously destined for death—not be destined for life? But you are not predestined to life because you wish it, but because God wills it; for that infinitely good will is the cause of your life, and of your election and destination. And to understand this is great tranquillity of mind: the mind rests in its own salvation, attending to God and not looking back at itself. For that immensely good will of God is the salvation of all, and the most tranquil harbor of rest, the giver of all grace and life. To whom be honor and glory from every creature. Amen.

### <margin>A 79</margin> ¶EXAMINATION of several points regarding the literal text.

¶The Vulgate edition: *For I myself wished to be anathema from CHRIST for my brethren.* <note>The Vulgate is the late-4th-century Latin translation of the Bible that became the Catholic Church's official version. "Anathema" refers to being cursed or cut off.</note> ¶It matters nothing whether it is said *I wished* or *I was wishing*. <note>original: "optaui" or "optabam"</note> For the Latins are accustomed to interpret those past tenses of the Greeks sometimes by the imperfect and sometimes by the perfect tense, insofar as they seem to fit the understanding better. And there are those who think this was said by Paul out of zeal: as if he himself desired to lack the fellowship of Christ—and not only the fellowship of Christ, but to be cursed by Christ (for that is what *anathema* <note>original: "anathema", from Greek "ἀνάθεμα"</note> seems to signify)—provided that his brothers according to the flesh might be converted, recognize, and confess Christ. So Moses desired to be an anathema from God out of zeal for his brothers when he said: *Forgive them this guilt: or if you do not, blot me out of your book which you have written.* <note>Reference to Exodus 32:32.</note> But it seems rather that Paul is giving the cause of his sadness, as has been explained: namely, that he wished to be an anathema from Christ. And Jerome says: *anathema* is properly Hebrew; and the Greeks say *anathematizo* <note>original: "ἀναθεματίζω"</note> for "I devote" or "I curse." Whence it is certain that *anathema* signifies detestation and execration. Paul: *For I myself was wishing to be an anathema from Christ.* <note>original: "ηὐχόμην γὰρ αὐτὸς ἐγὼ ἀνάθεμα εἶναι ἀπὸ τοῦ χριστοῦ"</note> ¶The Vulgate edition: *Who have the adoption of sons.* ¶It is <margin>A 77</margin> enough to say: *whose is the adoption.* Paul: *whose is the adoption.* <note>original: "ὧν ἡ υἱοθεσία"</note> ¶The Vulgate edition: *And the testament, and the law-giving, and the service, and the promises.* ¶It should be said in the plural: *testaments.* And it can also be said no less fittingly: *the worship and the promises.* Paul: *and the testaments and the law-giving and the worship and the promises.* <note>original: "καὶ αἱ διαθῆκαι καὶ ἡ νομοθεσία καὶ ἡ λατρεία καὶ αἱ ἐπαγγελίαι"</note> <margin>B 78</margin> ¶The Vulgate edition: *Not as though the word of God hath failed.* ¶Paul has: *But it is not as though the word of God has fallen away.* <note>original: "οὐκ οἷον δὲ ὅτι ἐκπέπτωκεν ὁ λόγος τοῦ θεοῦ"</note> Not so, however, that the speech of God has failed. ¶The Vulgate edition: *For all are not Israelites that are of Israel: neither are all children because they are the seed of Abraham.* ¶From Paul it should read: *for not all who are from Israel are Israel; neither because they are the seed of Abraham are they all children.* Paul: *for not all those from Israel are Israel; nor because they are the seed of Abraham are they all children.* <note>original: "οὐ γὰρ πάντες οἱ ἐξ ἰσραὴλ, οὗτοι ἰσραὴλ. οὐδ᾿ ὅτι εἰσὶν σπέρμα ἀβρααμ, πάντα τέκνα"</note> <margin>C 79</margin> ¶The Vulgate edition: *And not only she, but Rebecca also, having had Isaac our father by one cohabitation.* <note>original: "concubitu"</note> ¶That word "she" is superfluous. By "one" it is understood "of the sons." Paul does not have "cohabitation" but *koitēn* <note>original: "κοίτην"</note>, that is, having a bed or a marriage-couch. And that participle "having" can be interpreted not inharmoniously by the imperfect tense; for it designates both the present and the imperfect. And that *koitē* <note>original: "κοίτη"</note> signifies a bed: thus in Psalm 4: *Be sorry in your beds.* <note>original: "ἐπὶ ταῖς κοίταις"</note> And in Psalm 35: *He has meditated iniquity on his bed.* <note>original: "ἐπὶ τῆς κοίτης αὐτοῦ"</note> And in Psalm 149: *They shall rejoice in their beds.* <note>original: "ἐπὶ τῶν κοίτων αὐτῶν"</note> Luke 11: *And my children are with me in bed.* <note>original: "καὶ τὰ παιδία μου μετ᾿ ἐμοῦ εἰς τὴν κοίτην εἰσίν"</note> But even the old translator a little later in chapter 13 interprets the same word as "bed," where Paul has *not in beds and wantonness* <note>original: "μὴ κοίταις καὶ ἀσελγείαις"</note>. It is a wonder, therefore, that here he both confused the understanding and joined things that should not be joined. For "from one" <note>original: "ἐξ ἑνὸς"</note> and "bed" <note>original: "κοίτην"</note>, a genitive and an accusative, could not be joined. Moreover, Paul abstains from such expressions that could not come forth from a virginal mouth, speaking everywhere very holily and modestly. Thus Paul has this whole sentence: *And not only so, but also Rebecca, having a bed from one, Isaac our father.* <note>original: "οὐ μόνον δὲ, ἀλλὰ καὶ ῥεβέκκα ἐξ ἑνὸς, κοίτην ἔχουσα ἰσαὰκ τοῦ πατρὸς ἡμῶν"</note> <margin>C 81</margin> <margin>§</margin> ¶The Vulgate edition: *I will have mercy on whom I have had mercy: and I will show mercy to whom I will have mercy...*

The author argues for more precise and modest language in describing biblical events, specifically regarding Rebecca and the "marriage bed."</summary>

<meta>This page continues the linguistic and theological analysis of the Epistle to the Romans, specifically focusing on the transition from the end of Chapter 9 into Chapter 10. The author compares the Latin Vulgate translation with the original Greek text to provide a more precise interpretation of Paul’s arguments on divine mercy and the "stumbling" of the Jewish people.</meta>

Romans.

# I

<margin>81</margin> Paul: *I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I have compassion.* <note>original: "ἐλεήσω ὃν ἂν ἐλεῶ καὶ οἰκτειρήσω ὃν ἂν οἰκτείρω."</note> I will have mercy on whomever I have mercy: and I will be merciful to whomever I am merciful, or as it is understood from the literal Greek: it has been interpreted.

<margin>82</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate Edition:** *Why does he yet find fault?* Paul: *Why does he yet blame?* <note>original: "τὶ ἔτι μέμφεται."</note> The verb *memphetai* <note>original: "μέмφομαι"</note> which Paul uses here signifies to complain, to accuse, to blame, to rebuke, and similar things. But here it is used impersonally. Therefore, it should rather be interpreted by one of these terms: lest anyone think, when it says "why does he yet complain?" it is the same as saying "why is he yet questioned?" when it is not that: but rather "why is he yet accused, blamed, and rebuked—the one who sins and is hardened in evil?"

<margin>83</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate Edition:** *O man, who are you to reply against God?* ¶ It would be better to say "on the contrary." *O man, who are you that replies on the contrary against God?* <note>original: "Ὦ ἄνθρωπε σὺ τίς εἶ, ὁ ἀνταποκρινόμενος τῷ θεῷ." The author notes that "antapokrinomenos" implies a back-and-forth or contradictory response.</note>

<margin>d</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate Edition:** *The thing formed to him who formed itself.* ¶ The word "itself" is superfluous. Paul: *The thing formed to him who formed [it].* <note>original: "τὸ πλάσμα τῷ πλάσαντι."</note>

<margin>84</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate Edition:** *What if God, willing to show his wrath.* It is better to say "If indeed" rather than "What if." Paul: *If indeed.* <note>original: "εἰ δὲ."</note> For when "What if" is said, the meaning is hardly drawn out.

<margin>F</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate Edition:** *Vessels of wrath fitted.* ¶ Should be read as "having been prepared." Paul: *prepared.* <note>original: "κατηρτισμένα."</note>

<margin>85</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate Edition:** *I will call not my people, my people; and her not beloved, beloved; and her who had not obtained mercy, one who has obtained mercy.* ¶ The phrase "and her who had not obtained mercy, one who has obtained mercy" is superfluous here. And because of the prophecy of Hosea where we have it translated as "not my people, my people," I would prefer the first part to be interpreted as "people" <term>populum</term> rather than "common folk" <term>plebem</term>, lest "beloved" should seem to refer to the common folk as an adjective. Paul: *I will call the "not-my-people" my people, and the "unbeloved" beloved.* <note>original: "καле́σω τὸν οὐ λαόν μου λαόν μου, καὶ τὴν οὐκ ἠγαπημένην ἠγαπημένην."</note> And he immediately adds: *And it shall be in the place.* <note>original: "καὶ ἔσται ἐν τῷ τόπῳ."</note>

<margin>86</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate Edition:** *Sons of the living God.* ¶ It can be said "of the one who lives." Paul: *of the living [one].* <note>original: "ζῶντος."</note>

¶ **The Vulgate Edition:** *For he will finish the work, and cut it short in equity.* ¶ "Work" <term>verbum</term> is in the accusative case. "Finishing" and "cutting short" are masculine nominatives. However, by changing the participle into a verb, or by expressing the substantive verb, the meaning becomes clearer. Paul: *For he is completing the word and cutting it short in righteousness.* <note>original: "λόγον γὰρ συντελῶν καὶ συντέмνων ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ."</note> "Completing the speech and cutting it short in justice," where the verb is understood. And since the old translator had interpreted the Greek *logon* <note>original: "λόγον"</note> as "discourse" <term>sermonem</term>, the expression would have been less ambiguous.

<margin>87</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate Edition:** *But as it were by works. For they stumbled at the stone.* ¶ "Of the law" is missing from "by works." Paul: *by the works of the law.* <note>original: "ἐξ ἔργων νόμου."</note> And "stumbled" means "they resisted" or "they rejected." Paul: *For they struck against the stone.* <note>original: "προσέκοψαν γὰρ τῷ λίθω."</note> They resisted the stone, or they rejected it. For I would believe that the word *proskoptō* <note>original: "πρόσκοπτω"</note> signifies this not poorly. It also means "I strike against" and "I fall upon." But the former sense is clearer than the latter.

### CHAPTER X

<image-desc>A large decorative letter 'V' featuring a scholar or prophet figure sitting in a natural landscape, surrounded by ornate vine-like patterns.</image-desc>

The Jews struck against the stone of offense which they resisted and which they rejected, preferring to follow the righteousness of the law which does not truly justify, rather than Christ who completes the law and who truly justifies. Therefore, they are not among the number of the elect; nor (if we look at them in isolation) can they be. Yet they can be if we look to God, who calls those who are "not-elect" as "elect." Paul, not being ignorant of this, intercedes for them before God with the full will of his soul so that they might be saved and found among the number of the elect. He prays that the zeal of God which they have—in guarding the given law, believing they are justified by the works of the law—they might convert to a true zeal for the righteousness of God. This happens by believing in Christ, and by understanding and expecting righteousness not from the works of the law, but through the faith of Jesus Christ, by the grace and gift of God. ¶ He who understands in this way and has zeal for righteousness, understands according to true science and recognition, and is zealous for God's righteousness. But those who act in the other way—namely, being zealous for righteousness in the Jewish manner from the works of the law—they neither understand nor are zealous according to recognition, but according to ignorance. They neither obey nor are subject to the righteousness of God, which justifies unto eternal life. Paul testifies that he desires this light of knowledge and this righteousness for them, saying: ¶ *Brothers, the desire of my heart and my prayer to God for Israel is for their salvation. For I bear them witness that they have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge. For they, being ignorant of God's righteousness and seeking to establish their own righteousness, have not submitted themselves to the righteousness of God. For CHRIST is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes.* ¶ And what else did the Lord signify than that he himself is the end, the fulfillment, and the consummation of the law, when he said: *Do not think that I have come to abolish the law or the prophets; I have not come to abolish but to fulfill.* Indeed, when the Savior says, "I have not come to abolish the law," he hints that works are not to be excluded from salvation. Rather, he teaches that they are to be observed even more exactly than the law itself expressed. But when he says "to fulfill," he suggests that those works are not the consummation and completion, but he himself is. And it is a completed righteousness which he gives—not which works provide. And there is a righteousness of the law which is acquired from works. But if you compare this to the righteousness of God, which is given to the righteous through the faith of Christ, you hold—

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Epistle to the Romans, moving from the distinction between the Law and Mercy into a deep dive on Chapter 10. Commentary.

<image-desc>Decorative header with the text "COM." inside a circular frame with vine-like flourishes.</image-desc>

[shadows] you compare to light. <note>original: "bras luci comparas." Likely continuing the word "tenebras" (shadows/darkness) from the previous page.</note> And there is the life of the law and the life of the justice of God, but they differ as much as living for God differs from living for the law, or living for the truth differs from living for the shadow. The justice of God is the truth; the justice of the law is the shadow. 
<margin>88</margin>
Moses wrote the justice of the law; Christ gave the justice of God. The former is the beginning; the latter is the completion. This is what Paul adds, saying:

¶ *For Moses writes of the justice which is from the law: that the man who does these things shall live in them.*

¶ So Moses has it in **Leviticus**: *I am the Lord your God, keep my laws and judgments: which a man doing shall live in them.* <note>Reference to Leviticus 18:5.</note> But it is one thing to live *in* them—that is, to live for the law—and another to live for God. For the fathers, before Christ had come, lived in them and lived for the law. But when Christ came and drew them out of the darkness in which they were living the life of the law, they began to live for God. For that life was absorbed as if it were not life at all by that most excellent life of God and Christ, just as a tiny light is absorbed by a most excellent light. And so one must think regarding the justice of the law and the justice of God, which cannot be possessed without faith in Christ.

<margin>89</margin>
Moses revealed this faith in Christ to them in an enigma <note>The author uses "enigma" to mean a prophetic riddle or a veiled truth.</note>—that he would descend from the heavens and return from the underworld, along with his justice. Paul adds to this in this way:

¶ *But regarding the justice which is from faith, he speaks thus: Do not say in your heart: who shall ascend into heaven? This signifies the descent of CHRIST. Or who shall descend into the abyss? This signifies the bringing back of CHRIST from the dead.*

¶ Paul wonderfully understood that the words of Moses, which he wrote in **Deuteronomy** (that is, the "Second Law"), were enigmatic. For the first law figured the justice of the law, and the second law figured the justice of God. And indeed, what would he not have understood, he who spoke through the Holy Spirit? I say he understood through this: that when Moses said, "do not say in your heart who shall ascend into heaven," we must understand that Moses, in the Second Law, was hinting through a riddle that Christ had descended from the heavens so that he might open that justice of God in the Gospel, which is truly the "Second Law." And by this which he said, "or who shall descend into the abyss," we must likewise understand that Moses in the Second Law was hinting through a riddle that Christ had returned from the abyss of the underworld. The Gospel, truly the Second Law, makes this clear: 
<margin>90</margin>
and that eternal life is granted to believers from the underworld—that is, from perpetual death.

And that which Moses mentions in passing, Paul interprets as the word of faith, saying:

¶ *But what does it say? The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart. This is the word of faith which we preach. Because if you confess with your mouth the Lord JESUS, and believe in your heart that God has raised him from the dead, you shall be saved. For with the heart one believes unto justice, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation. For the scripture says: Everyone who believes in him shall not be confounded. For there is no distinction between Jew and Gentile. For the same Lord is over all, rich toward all who call upon him. For everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved.*

¶ We ought to have the word of faith both in our mouth and in our heart. In the mouth, certainly, for our own salvation and the salvation of others. For what else are we doing when we have it in our mouth but working for the salvation of those who hear? And what else when we have it in our heart but cooperating with God for our own justification? Therefore, it should never depart from the heart or the mouth. From the heart, so that we may always be justified; and from the mouth, so that we may save others as ministers and co-workers of God, increasing the justice of God within us. For we increase it—not that God flows into us differently, more strongly, or more intensely—but insofar as by doing good things, we are made more capable of receiving the grace of God and the infusion of his justice. 

For the sun shines equally upon the diseased eye, the healthy eye, and even the blind eye; but by the blind it is not received, by the diseased it is received only a little, and by the healthy it is received more fully—not because the sun is more intense in itself. In the same way, the identical and unvarying light of God's justification always shines upon everyone, wishing to be received even by the unfaithful. And it is received, provided the blindness of infidelity is removed. If it is not received while one is unfaithful, even though the light knocks at the door of the unfaithful, the cause is not the light itself, but the one who is not capable of receiving it, just as a blind eye cannot receive light. Truly, the blindness of the mind is like cataracts of the eyes, which can indeed be removed. Once removed, the eye gradually becomes more capable of light. 

Oh, the supreme mercy of God in bestowing life upon everyone, and indeed bestowing it most eagerly! For what does supreme life desire but to give life? And supreme justice, but to justify? For it can do nothing else of itself but give life and justify whatever is capable of it. And how is anyone made capable? Through faith. For faith removes the blindness of the mind, the obstacle to the capacity for divine justice. And through what is faith obtained? Through the confession of the word of God with the mouth and through preaching. But how can that preaching be had? Through divine infusion, and through the sending of those filled by God throughout the whole world. All these things divine goodness provided 
<margin>91</margin>
so that he might justify all, so that he might make all capable of his justice. Hence Paul joins:

¶ *How then shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? Or how shall they believe him whom they have not heard? And how shall they hear without a preacher? And how shall they preach unless they are sent? As it is written: How beautiful are the feet of those who preach peace, of those who preach good things.*

¶ This oracle is read in **Isaiah**, and in the prophet **Nahum**. In Isaiah: *How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of those announcing...*

He emphasizes that God's grace is universally available like sunlight, but requires faith—fostered by preaching—to be received.</summary>

of the one announcing and preaching peace: announcing good things, preaching salvation. In Nahum: *Behold upon the mountains: the feet of him who brings good news and announces peace.* <note>Reference to Isaiah 52:7 and Nahum 1:15.</note> But someone might say: If hearing the words of those bringing the good news of Christ is so peaceful, so healthy, and so good, why then did not all who heard it obey the Gospel? I said: "Behold, here I am, behold, here I am" to the nations that did not call upon my name. I have stretched out my hands all day to an unbelieving people, who walk in a way that is not good, following their own thoughts.* And thus that insurmountable goodness of God always acted: so that the word of God could not be hidden from Israel, whether they had remained obedient in their own land, or had lived cast out among the nations in disobedience. But even if hearing profited them little, he strives to save them by the example and imitation of the faithful Gentiles—who did not know God, yet received the one whom Israel used to worship. O happy Israel, if it would only attend to the great care and piety of God toward itself! For he does not wish to destroy them through dispersion, but to save them. And no less happy are the Gentiles, if they continually glorify the mercy and grace of God, which reached them for life before they even knew or desired it. ### EXAMINATION of some points regarding the literal text.

<margin>87</margin>
¶ <term>The Vulgate edition</term> <note>The standard Latin Bible used in the Western Church.</note>. *The prayer to God is made for them unto salvation.* ¶ Paul has: *to God is for Israel unto salvation*, or *for salvation*, which is the same thing. Paul: *The prayer which is to God for Israel is for salvation.* <note>original Greek: "ἡ δέησις ἡ πρὸς τὸν θεὸν ὑπὲρ τοῦ ἰσραὴλ ἐστὶν εἰς σωτηρίαν."</note> ¶ <term>The Vulgate edition</term>. *For they have a zeal of God: but not according to knowledge.* ¶ "Indeed" [quidem] is superfluous. And where the interpreter says "knowledge," Paul rather has "recognition" [cognitionem]. Paul: *that they have a zeal for God, but not according to recognition.* <note>original Greek: "ὅτι ζῆλον θεοῦ ἔχουσιν, ἀλλ’ οὐ κατ’ ἐπίγνωσιν."</note> ¶ <term>The Vulgate edition</term>. *And seeking to establish their own*, the word "justice" is missing. Paul: *and seeking to establish their own justice.* <note>original Greek: "καὶ τὴν ἰδίαν δικαιοσύνην ζητοῦντες στῆσαι."</note>
<margin>B 88</margin>
¶ <term>The Vulgate edition</term>. *For Moses wrote that the justice which is of the law, the man who does it shall live in it.* ¶ According to Paul, it should read: *writes*. The word "that" [quoniam] is superfluous in the place where it is; but it could be placed before "who" and after "does." And immediately "it" [ea] is missing in the plural. And it should say at the end: *in them* [in eis], not *in it* [in ea], so that it does not seem to refer back to "justice" as a relative pronoun. Paul: *For Moses writes of the justice which is from the law, that the man who has done those things shall live in them.* <note>original Greek: "μωυσῆσ γὰρ γράφει τὴν δικαιοσύνην τὴν ἐκ τοῦ νόμου ὅτι ὁ ποιήσας αὐτὰ ἄνθρωπος ζήσεται ἐν αὐτοῖς."</note> Moses writes of the justice which is of the law, which the man who does those things shall live in them.
<margin>B 89</margin>
¶ <term>The Vulgate edition</term>. *Who shall ascend into heaven? That is to bring CHRIST down; or who descends into the abyss? That is to call CHRIST back from the dead.* ¶ "That is" [id est] and "this is" [hoc est] are the same term in Paul: *this is*. <note>original Greek: "τοῦτ’ ἔστιν"</note> Therefore the old interpreter should have translated it the same way in both the first and second place, by saying "this is." ### COMMENTARY

...you compare shadows to the light. And there is a life of the law, and a life of the justice of God. But they differ as much as living for God differs from living for the law, or living for the truth differs from living for a shadow. The justice of God is the truth; the justice of the law is a <margin>88</margin> shadow. Moses wrote of the justice of the law; Christ gave the justice of God. The latter is the completion; the former, the beginning. Paul adds this, saying: ¶ *For Moses writes of the justice which is from the law: that the man who does these things shall live in them.* ¶ <note>Reference to Romans 10:5 and Leviticus 18:5.</note> This is what Moses has in Leviticus: *I am the Lord your God; keep my laws and judgments, which if a man does, he shall live in them.* But it is one thing to "live in them" (to live for the law) and another to "live for God." For the fathers, before Christ had come, lived in those laws and lived for the law. But when Christ came and drew them out from the darkness in which they lived the life of the law, they began to live for God. For that life was absorbed as if it were "non-life" by that most excellent life of God and Christ, just as a small light is absorbed by a most excellent light. And this is how one must think of the justice of the law and the justice of God, which cannot be possessed without the faith of Christ. 

Moses revealed this faith of Christ to them in a riddle <note>original: "in aenigmate"</note>—that He would descend from the heavens and return from the underworld, bringing His <margin>89</margin> justice. Regarding this, Paul adds: ¶ *But of the justice which is from faith, he speaks thus: Do not say in your heart: Who shall ascend into heaven? This signifies the descent of CHRIST. Or, who shall descend into the abyss? This signifies the bringing back of CHRIST from the dead.* ¶ Paul wonderfully understood that the words Moses wrote in Deuteronomy (that is, the "Second Law") were enigmatic. For the first law figured <note>In the sense of "acted as a prefiguration or type."</note> the justice of the law, and the second law figured the justice of God. And indeed, what could he not have understood, he who spoke through the Holy Spirit? I say he understood that when Moses said, *Do not say in your heart, who shall ascend into heaven?*, we are to understand that Moses, in the Second Law, was enigmatically suggesting that Christ descended from the heavens to open that justice of God in the Gospel, which is truly the "Second Law." And by saying, *Or who shall descend into the abyss?*, we are likewise to understand that Moses suggested Christ returned from the abyss of the underworld. The Gospel, which is the "Second Law" in truth, makes this clear: <margin>90</margin> it bestows eternal life from the underworld—that is, from perpetual death—upon those who believe. 

And what Moses adds in passing, Paul interprets regarding the word of faith, saying: ¶ *But what does it say? The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart. This is the word of faith which we preach. Because if you confess with your mouth the Lord JESUS, and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved. For with the heart one believes unto justice; but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.* ¶ For the Scripture says: *Everyone who believes in him shall not be confounded.* For there is no distinction between Jew and Gentile. For the same Lord of all is rich toward all who call upon Him. For *everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved.* 

We ought to have the word of faith both in our mouth and in our heart. In the mouth, certainly, for our own salvation and that of others. For what else do we do when we have it in our mouth, than work for the salvation of those who hear? And what else do we do when we have it in our heart, than cooperate with God for our own justification? Therefore, it should never depart from the heart or the mouth. From the heart, so that we are always justified; from the mouth, so that as God's ministers and coworkers, we may save others, increasing the justice of God within us. We "increase" it not because God flows into us differently, more strongly, or more intensely, but insofar as by doing good things, we are made more capable <note>In the sense of having more "capacity" to receive.</note> of God's grace and the infusion of His justice. 

For the sun shines equally upon a bleary eye, a healthy eye, and even a blind eye; but it is not received by the blind one, it is received only a little by the bleary one, and more fully by the healthy one—not because the sun is more intense in itself. Thus, the same and invariable light of God's justification always shines upon everyone, wishing to be received even by unbelievers. And it is indeed received, but only once the blindness of unbelief is removed. If it is not received when one is an unbeliever and it knocks at the unbeliever's door, the cause is not the light itself, but the one who is not capable of it, just as the blind eye is not capable of light. Truly, the blindnesses of the mind are like cataracts of the eyes, which can indeed be removed. Once they are removed, the eye gradually becomes more capable of light. 

¶ It is the supreme mercy of God to bestow life upon all, and to bestow it most eagerly. For what does "Supreme Life" desire, if not to give life? And "Supreme Justice," if not to justify? For it can do nothing else of itself than to give life and justify whatever is capable of it. And how does anything become capable? Through faith. For faith removes the blindness of the mind, which is the obstacle to the capacity for divine justice. And through what is faith obtained? Through the confession of the word of God with the mouth, through preaching. But how can that preaching be had? Through divine infusion, and through the sending of those filled <note>original: "infusorum"</note> by God throughout the whole world. Divine goodness provided all these <margin>91</margin> things so that He might justify all, and make all capable of His justice. Accordingly, Paul adds: ¶ *How then shall they call upon him in whom they have not believed? Or how shall they believe him whom they have not heard? And how shall they hear without a preacher? And how shall they preach unless they are sent? As it is written: How beautiful are the feet of those who evangelize peace, who evangelize good things!* ¶ This oracle is read in Isaiah and in the prophet Nahum. In Isaiah: *How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of the one who announ—*

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Paul's Epistle to the Romans, Chapter 10. ...of the one announcing and preaching peace: of the one announcing good, preaching salvation. <note>Refers to Isaiah 52:7 and Nahum 1:15.</note> In Nahum: *Behold upon the mountains: the feet of him who evangelizes and announces peace.* But someone might say: "If hearing the words of those evangelizing about Christ is so peaceful, so healthy, and so good, why then have not all who heard obeyed the Gospel?" For example, the Jews, in whose entire land the Gospel was preached, and among whom Christ performed the very things that are preached and announced. Even if they had not heard it in their own land, it could not have remained hidden from them even in foreign lands. For the Gospel was preached in every part of the world where they were dispersed, so that even in this way they might come to their senses and be saved; so that those who refused to receive their salvation in their own home might, being provoked by the Gentiles, attain justice through faith. 

And all these things were foretold to them by the oracles of the prophets: that they would not believe in their own land, and that they would be provoked to believe by foreigners and in foreign lands. When they see these things being fulfilled before their eyes for nearly fifteen hundred years, it is a wonder that the scale of infidelity does not fall <margin>92</margin> from their eyes so that they might finally recognize Christ, their life, and glorify Him along with the Gentiles—for to recognize Him alone is salvation and life. And therefore Paul says: ¶ *But not all have obeyed the Gospel; for Isaiah says: Lord, who has believed our report?* ¶ <note>Romans 10:16 quoting Isaiah 53:1.</note> Why is it a wonder if not all obeyed? For Isaiah had foretold this. What does *Who has believed our report?* mean, except "only a few, and not all"? And this speech is directed especially to the Jews. 

For of the Gentiles he had foretold: *He shall sprinkle many nations; kings shall shut their mouths at him.* And: *Those to whom it was not told of him, have seen; and those who heard not, have contemplated.* For the prophets were not telling those things to the Gentiles, but to the Jews; and the Jews heard them. But the Gentiles, once the apostles were sent, saw through faith what had not been told to them, and what they had not heard before. And <margin>93</margin> their faith was immediately planted by the hearing of the word of God. The Jews (as was prophesied of them) did not grasp it. Which is also what Paul says, adding: ¶ *Therefore faith is from hearing, and hearing through the word of God. But I say: Have they not heard? Yea, verily, their sound hath gone forth into all the earth: and their words unto the ends of the world. But I say: Hath not Israel known? First, Moses saith: I will provoke you to jealousy by that which is not a nation; by a foolish nation I will anger you. But Isaiah is bold, and saith: I was found by them that did not seek me: I appeared openly to them that asked not after me. But to Israel he saith: All day long I have stretched forth my hands unto an unbelieving and contradicting people.* ¶ <note>Romans 10:17-21, quoting Psalm 19, Deuteronomy 32, and Isaiah 65.</note>

This oracle is read thus in Isaiah 65: *They sought me who before did not ask; they found me who did not seek me. I said: Behold, here I am, behold, here I am to the nations that did not call upon my name. I stretched out my hands all day to an unbelieving people, who walk in a way that is not good, following their own thoughts.* And thus that insurmountable goodness of God always acted: so that the word of God could not be hidden from Israel, whether they had remained obedient in their own land, or dwelt scattered among the Gentiles as outcasts for their disobedience. But even if hearing profited them little, He strives to save them by the example and imitation of the faithful Gentiles—who did not know God, yet received Him whom Israel used to worship. O happy Israel, if it would only attend to the great care and piety God has for it! For He does not wish to destroy them by their dispersion, but to save them. And no less happy are the Gentiles, if they continually glorify the mercy and grace of God which reached them for life, even though they were neither knowing nor willing. Therefore, let the grace and mercy of God—which seeks the Jews and has already reached the Gentiles—be known by every nation and people, and once known, let it be forever and eternally praised, loved, and glorified. Amen.

<margin>A 87</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *The prayer to God is made for them unto salvation.* <note>original: "Obsecratio ad deū fit pro illis in falutem"</note> ¶ **Paul has:** *to God it is for Israel unto salvation,* or *toward salvation,* which is the same thing. **Paul:** *the prayer to God on behalf of Israel is for salvation.* <note>original Greek: "ἡ δέησις ἡ πρὸς τὸν θεὸν ὑπὲρ τοῦ ἰσραὴλ ἐστὶν εἰς σωτηρίαν"</note>

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *And seeking to establish their own.* <margin>B 88</margin> The word *justice* is missing. **Paul:** *and seeking to establish their own justice.* <note>original Greek: "καὶ τὴν ἰδίαν δικαιοσύνην ζητοῦντες στῆσαι"</note>

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *For Moses wrote that the justice which is of the law, the man who does it shall live in it.* ¶ According to Paul, it should be read: *writes.* The word *that* (quoniam) is extra in the place where it sits, but it could be placed before *who* or after *does.* And immediately following, the word *them* (ea) is missing in the plural. And one should say at the end: *in them* (in eis), not *in it* (in ea), so that it does not appear to refer back to "justice" as a relative pronoun. **Paul:** *For Moses writes of the justice from the law, that the man having done these things shall live in them.* <note>original Greek: "μωυσῆς γὰρ γράφει τὴν δικαιοσύνην τὴν ἐκ τοῦ νόμου ὅτι ὁ ποιήσας αὐτὰ ἄνθρωπος ζήσεται ἐν αὐτοῖς"</note> <margin>B 89</margin> *For Moses writes of the Justice which is of the law, that the man who has done those things shall live in them.*

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Who shall ascend into heaven? that is, to bring Christ down; or who has descended into the abyss? that is, to call Christ back from the dead.* ¶ The phrases *that is* (id est) and *this is* (hoc est) are represented by the same term in Paul: *this is.* <note>original Greek: "τοῦτ' ἔστιν"</note> Therefore, the old interpreter ought to have translated it the same way in the first and second instance, saying *this is.* And when he says *this is*: just as...

### CHAPTER XI.

<margin>D</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative drop cap initial "D" featuring floral patterns and a mythical bird-like creature.</image-desc>
**That** God has not rejected the Hebrew people is indicated by this: that many of the Hebrews received the faith of Christ. Indeed, at a single preaching of Peter—as is read in the Acts of the Apostles—souls were added, about three thousand. And Paul, finally, by the mercy of God, was chosen as a "vessel of election" for the salvation of the nations: who was both a Hebrew and of the tribe of Benjamin. He did not, therefore, reject them; rather, they are the people of God. And as many as wished to receive the faith of Christ were called the chosen of God and the foreknown. Who, in comparison to the other Hebrews, were certainly few and small in number, and were as the "remnant of Israel." The others, however, were cast away and unknown; but only their own voluntary and stubborn turning away caused them to be called cast away and unknown. They were perishing, and the others were being saved. Truly, those who were being saved—whose number is known to God (for the number of those who perish is unknown, and they themselves are unknown; for to them it is said: *I know you not, whence you are. Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth*)—those who, I say, were being saved, were saved by the election, grace, and will of God, not by their own, even if they wished to be saved. For who would not wish to be saved? Indeed, even those who perish wish to be saved; but our will, our choice, and our works are ineffective for this very thing: whereas God’s election is most effective and most powerful. Indeed, it alone is what can both effect and grant salvation to us.

<margin>94</margin>
Therefore, when we are converted, our conversion does not make us chosen, but the will, grace, and election of God does, even if we are never called "chosen" unless we are converted. Understand "converted" and not "turned away." Which things Paul also suggests, saying: ¶ *I say then: Has God rejected his people? God forbid. For I also am an Israelite, of the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin. God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew. Or do you not know what the Scripture says in Elijah, how he pleads with God against Israel, saying: Lord, they have killed your prophets, and overturned your altars; and I am left alone, and they seek my life. But what does the divine response say to him? I have left for myself seven thousand men who have not bowed the knee to Baal.* So then, at this time also, there is a remnant made according to the election of grace. ¶ In the third book of Kings <note>Known in modern Bibles as 1 Kings 19.</note> this supplication of Elijah to God against Israel and the divine response to him is read. And when he says: *I have left for myself seven thousand men,* he signifies the election of those who were left behind. Here and at any time, whoever are saved, it is the election of God and grace that saves, not works, even if works are joined to salvation. For he declares that works were joined when he says: *who have not bowed the knee to Baal*—they were not bowed before an idol, but rather before the true God

<margin>95</margin>
whom they adored. But was that election, that grace, owed to their works? How so? If it were owed, it would no longer be grace, but a debt. For it is contradictory for something to be called a debt and a grace, just as a gift and not a gift [are contradictory]. For grace is a gift; a debt is not a gift. Therefore, Paul adds: ¶ *And if by grace, then it is no more of works; otherwise grace is no [longer]*

...grace would no longer be grace. And if it is from works, it is no longer grace, because a work would no longer be a work. ¶ For this discourse in Paul recurs from the opposite perspective: it is by grace, therefore not from works; it is from works, therefore not from grace. It is grace, therefore not a work; it is a work, therefore not grace. For "work" implies a debt, while "grace" implies not a debt, but the abundance of goodness freely sharing itself with those who are prepared and capable of receiving it. He who confesses grace honors God and looks toward God; he who seeks what is owed to him <note>Original Latin: "debitum," referring to a legalistic claim of merit</note> wishes to be honored himself and looks toward himself, and claims that the infinite light is a debt owed to the darkness. Therefore, we cannot attain salvation from works, but we attain it by God’s election and grace. And those who seek it from works remain blind, attributing to works what is owed to grace, and to themselves what is owed to God. Instead, He immediately turned Himself to the Gentiles, so that they might confess His grace and faith, through which they were made safe. Paul, the interpreter of God's sublime goodness, invites us to this, saying: ¶ *What then? Have they stumbled so that they might fall? God forbid! But by their offense, salvation has come to the Gentiles, so that they might be lead to jealousy of them.* ¶ But perhaps someone might say: "Therefore, if Israel had not offended, but had understood the grace of God in their own land, there would be no salvation for the Gentiles." This is not the case at all. For if everyone had received Christ, the salvation of the Gentiles was already decreed by God through the grace of Christ, just as the prophet Isaiah says: *He shall give the nations in his sight, and he shall obtain kings.* And again: *He shall bring forth judgment to the nations.* And elsewhere: *The nations shall walk in your light, and kings in the brightness of your rising.* And the same: *I come with all nations and tongues, and they shall come and see my glory, and I will set a sign among them, and I will send those who have been saved from among them to the nations: to the sea, to Africa, to Lydia, to Italy, to Greece, and to the islands far off, to those who have not heard of me and have not seen my glory, and they shall announce my glory among the nations.* And therefore, if a few chosen Hebrews sent to the nations through the whole world became the cause of the salvation of the nations, how much more—if all the Hebrews had been chosen—would the salvation of men have been accomplished both more quickly and more conveniently? For everyone would have assisted in such a great and admirable salvation. But many of them even stood in the way. If the salvation of men was accomplished while they were offending, what would it have been if they were not offending? What if they possessed the righteousness of God? If a few are known [to produce a result], then by a much stronger reason 
<margin>98</margin>
the opposite is true: that it would have been more for the salvation of men. And the response is understood: it would have been much more. For thus "righteousness" would correspond to "offense," and "fullness" to "diminishing," as opposites. But Paul, relying on both human and divine wisdom, did not wish to form the <term>epicherema</term> <note>A complex rhetorical syllogism where a premise is immediately followed by its proof.</note> so openly in the manner of orators, leaving it to be easily understood by the reader who is even slightly skilled in dialectic and rhetoric. <margin>></margin> your [kinsmen]! Their loss is their death. Therefore, their discovery <note>original: "inventio," referring to the restoration of the Jewish people</note> will be life from the dead. And this is no disgrace to the Gentiles: if Paul, while he is the Apostle to the Gentiles, should make some of the Jews—from whom he descended according to the flesh—safe and extract them from death unto life. What wonder is it then if he strives to lead them to salvation, who are known to be holy both from their root and from their remnants—namely, the first believers?

And as for the fact that they were broken off: they were not broken off and cast away because of the nature of that nation, nor their worship of God, nor their origin, but because of their unbelief. And because the Gentiles are grafted in and stand: it is not from their nature, nor from the worship they had previously received, nor from their root (for the greatest part of them descended from Ham <note>In the table of nations in Genesis, Ham was traditionally viewed as the ancestor of various non-Hebrew peoples, often associated with those outside the covenant</note>), but they are grafted in by faith and they stand by faith. If they desert faith, they are broken off and fall away. And if those [the Jews] receive faith, they are grafted in again and shall stand.

The Gentiles: by nature and origin, profane. The Jews: holy. The Gentiles: uncultivated. The Jews: cultivated. The former: demonic. The latter: plucking the pastures of the true God. The former: joined to the holy ones against nature. The latter: joined according to nature. For the Gentiles, as Gentiles, cannot be numbered among the holy; but the Jews, as Jews, could be. The Gentiles are sustained in the root of the Jews, not the Jews in the root of the Gentiles, as it is written: **T**here shall arise a root of Jesse, who stands as a sign for the peoples; him the Gentiles shall entreat. This root sustains all nations.

Therefore, the Gentiles have no reason to exalt themselves against the Jews, nor any ground to boast. Rather, in all things they ought to admire and glorify the mercy and grace of God, who looked upon them when they were so miserable and dead and brought them to life. They should be humbled within themselves, boasting only in the mercy of God (which is prepared for all). Concerning this matter—lest they be puffed up or become proud in themselves, but rather be humbled before God and fear (as is right)—
<margin>100 ></margin> Paul admonishes the Gentiles, saying: ¶ **I**f the firstfruits are holy, so is the whole batch <note>original: "massa," referring to the lump of dough from which the firstfruits are taken</note>; and if the root is
<margin>></margin> holy, so are the branches. ¶ **A**nd if some of the branches were broken off, and you, being a wild olive, were grafted in among them and became a sharer of the root and the richness of the olive tree: do not boast against the branches.
<margin>></margin> ¶ **B**ut if you do boast: you do not carry the root, but the root carries you. But you will say: The branches were broken off so that I might be grafted in. Well said. They were broken off by unbelief, but you stand by faith. Do not be proud in your thoughts, but fear; for if God did not spare the natural branches, fear lest perhaps he also not spare you.
<margin>></margin> ¶ Jeremiah suggests that the community of the Hebrews is aptly called an "olive tree," speaking of it thus: *The Lord called your name a rich, beautiful, fruitful, and fair olive tree.* And this spiritual grafting is miraculous and opposite to physical grafting. For in physical grafting, a fertile branch is grafted onto a wild one; the grafted branch does not take its condition from the root but keeps its own nature—indeed, it is even made more fruitful by the infertile root. But in the spiritual grafting of which Paul speaks here, it happens in the opposite way. For that which is grafted in does not retain its own nature, but follows the fruitfulness and condition of the root, having nothing from itself but everything from the root.

<margin>></margin> ¶ **I**f, therefore, the grafting of the nations were similar to physical grafting, they might perhaps have something in themselves to boast about. But since it is the opposite, they have no reason to boast in themselves, but only in the root. For the root in which the church is planted, along with all the children of the church, is Christ. If you make the church a bride, Christ is the bridegroom; if the church a body, Christ is the head; if the church a temple or a city, Christ is the cornerstone, the mountain, and the foundation. If the church is an olive tree, Christ is the root which carries it, makes it fruitful, and waters it.

And if we look closely at this spiritual olive tree, the Jews have the first part as those who are natural; the Gentiles have the second part as those who are grafted branches. This gives us great cause both for loving and for fearing. For loving: when we consider God's kindness toward us—not natural branches—who grafted us into the holy olive. For fearing: when we consider the severity of God's justice and rigor toward the Jews—the natural branches of the olive—whom he cut off from the holy olive. He did this for us because of faith, and for the Jews because of unbelief. How then shall we not fear—we who are not natural branches—lest if we fall from faith, we be cut off and lopped away? And how can we not see that if the Jews are found faithful,
<margin>101 ></margin> they shall much more than we be grafted into their own and natural olive tree? Reasoning from the lesser to the greater necessarily concludes this. Therefore Paul adds: <margin>></margin> ¶ **S**ee therefore the kindness and severity of God: toward those who fell, severity; but toward you, kindness, if you remain in that kindness; otherwise, you also will be cut off. And even they, if they do not remain
<margin>></margin> in unbelief, will be grafted in. For God is powerful enough to graft them in again. For if you were cut out of a
<margin>></margin> natural wild olive tree and, contrary to nature, were grafted into a good olive tree, how much more shall they, who are according to nature, be grafted into their own olive tree. <unclear>V...</unclear>
