<margin>102</margin> Truly even the Hebrews—when all the nations have received the faith of Christ (for this is indeed destined to happen one day)—will themselves receive the faith of Christ and be saved, though they are now rejected. This mystery, which is to say a hidden and secret thing, Paul reveals by saying:
> For I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, of this mystery, lest you be wise in your own conceits: that blindness has happened in part to Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles comes in; and so all Israel shall be saved, just as it is written: There shall come out of Zion the one who shall deliver and turn away impiety from Jacob. And this is my covenant with them, when I shall take away their sins.

¶ Regarding that conversion of the nations and the return of the Jews, we read thus in Isaiah: *They shall fear the name of the Lord from the west, and his glory from the rising of the sun, when he shall come like a violent river which the spirit of the Lord drives, and the Redeemer shall come to Zion.* And to those who return from iniquity in Jacob, says the Lord: *This is my covenant with them: My Spirit which is in you, and my words which I have placed in your mouth, shall not depart from your mouth, nor from the mouth of your offspring, says the Lord, from now and forever.* Then the children of Israel will leave behind the "letter" <note>The "letter" refers to a literal or legalistic interpretation of the Old Testament Law.</note> and receive the "spirit," and the Gospel shall not depart from their mouths or the mouths of their offspring for eternity. Indeed, because they did not receive the Gospel, they are now enemies; but the Gentiles, because they did receive it, are friends. In comparison to the Gentiles, the Jews are enemies, yet they are beloved for the sake of the fathers. Shall I say for the sake of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob? Yes, but even more so for the sake of Christ and the holy apostles who descended from them, and whom 
<margin>103</margin> God chose and loved in the fathers. He does not repent, nor does He cease to choose and to love. Because of this, the Apostle adds: ¶ *As concerning the Gospel, they are enemies for your sake; but as concerning the election, they are beloved for the fathers' sakes. For the gifts and the calling of God are without repentance.* 

¶ Behold, the Hebrews are both "enemies" and "beloved." You must understand that love and hatred are not different things within God; rather, these terms describe a change in us, not in God. Once God has loved, He always loves and never ceases to love. But if you turn away, that which is love in God becomes hatred toward you. For from God there is always love; from you alone comes the hatred. Hence, it is more proper to say that God loves rather than that He hates anything (as it is written): *For you love all things that exist, and you hate none of the things which you have made; for you would not have fashioned or made anything if you hated it.* <note>A reference to the Wisdom of Solomon 11:24.</note> For the latter [hatred] regards what is foreign, while the former [love] is substantial and intimate. The same applies to His calling, choosing, giving, and the bestowing of grace, of which there is no regret with God, as the Apostle has made clear. 

And marvelous is the wisdom of God: He allows those whom He sees trusting in their own "health" <note>Here "health" is a metaphor for self-righteousness or spiritual pride.</note> to fall ill—and indeed to fall violently ill—so that He may heal them most perfectly, and so they may recognize Him as the only source of perfect health. Thus, they cease to trust in their own health and trust only in the health that is His gift. And those who think they "see" the path to righteousness, but do not, He allows to fall into blindness so that He may illuminate them most perfectly. Thus, those who "saw" but did not truly see might, conversely, "see" after being blind. 

Truly, unbelief is a great blindness, which the Gentiles first fell into while the Jews believed. For the Gentiles did not believe that the Jews worshiped the true God; but through this unbelief, they were healed by the mercy of God, recognizing and confessing that it is God's mercy and grace alone which truly heals souls. But now that the Gentiles are healed and seeing, the Jews have fallen into blindness. Just as the Gentiles did not believe in the God the Jews worshiped, so now the Jews do not believe that the Gentiles have obtained mercy. God permitted this so that He might at last heal them most perfectly, and they might realize that while they "saw," they did not truly see, but only thought they did. They will learn that God's mercy alone is what makes the blind truly see and the sick perfectly healthy, as it is written: *The Lord gives light to the blind.* Thus, at last, both Gentiles and Jews—made perfectly whole after extreme infirmity—will with one voice celebrate the mercy of God, the true savior of all. For He has opened their eyes and made them truly healthy, forever performing healthy works. For it pleased that highest and most admirable Wisdom for the world to be saved in this way. Those who were first sick were first healed; 
<margin>104</margin> and those who were first healthy began to be sick so that they might be healed most perfectly, and thus all might be saved. 

¶ Paul concludes this, saying: ¶ *For as you also once did not believe God, but have now obtained mercy through their unbelief, so also they now do not believe your mercy, that they also may obtain mercy. For God has concluded all in unbelief, that he might have mercy on all.* ¶ O the depth of the riches and the wisdom...

It highlights the divine strategy of allowing all people to fall into the 'sickness' of unbelief so that they may eventually be 'healed' by universal mercy.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the final verses of Romans 11, moving from the theological praise of God’s wisdom to a detailed philological examination of the Latin Vulgate translation compared to the original Greek and Hebrew sources.</meta>

...of the wisdom and knowledge of God? How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor? Or who has first given to him, that it should be repaid to him? For from him and through him and to him are all things. To him be glory forever. Amen. <note>original: "pientię et agnitionis dei... Ipsi gloria in sæcula. Amen." This is the famous "Doxology" that concludes Romans 11:33-36.</note> 

That which **Paul** brings forward—*For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor?*—seems to be borrowed from **Isaiah** or from the Book of Wisdom. If it is from the Book of Wisdom, it is established that the book held authority and was older than the apostles. Therefore, we should not listen to those who think that book belongs to **Philo**, who was a contemporary of the apostle or even later, and who possessed no such wisdom, as is clear from his books. But as **Tertullian** says: even if the book is **Solomon’s**, written when he was pure and overflowing with untainted grace and full of wisdom (for that wisdom was given by God) and living innocent of crime, the Jews do not accept it because it contains too clear a testimony concerning the Just One—that is, **Christ**—and the manner of his condemnation through their envy. 

And **Jerome** seems to have been too credulous of a certain faithless Jew in preparing the introduction to that book—at least if it is truly his; I believe it is more worthy of the ash-heap than the Bible. My zeal for God and the truth compels me to speak this way. And would that **Jerome**, otherwise a holy and admirable man, had never consulted the Jews when he prepared the introductions to the sacred books—men who strive to bring about the abrogation of faith, to diminish authority, and to extinguish the Spirit. 

Regarding the writing of this book: When a certain virgin named **Elizabeth**, veiled for God from her tender years and who from her youth experienced divine ecstasies <term>occupations; original: "occupationes," referring here to being "occupied" or seized by divine presence</term> and conversations with angels, once asked an angel whose writing it was, the angel replied to her: "It was pronounced by the Holy Spirit through the Wise One." But who is called "The Wise One" by antonomasia <term>a rhetorical term for using a title in place of a proper name</term> if not **Solomon**? Whom should we believe: the angel or the Jew? 

And certainly, it should never be doubted that it is **Solomon’s**, even if the Jews deny it. But enough on this testimony. And when he adds at the end, *From him, through him, and to him are all things*, it is a confession of the super-divine Trinity. "From him" suggests the Father; "through him" the Son; and "to him" <note>original: "in ipsum," literally "into him"</note> the Holy Spirit. He shows that "from him" is the power from which all things come; "through him" the wisdom through which all things are made; and "to him" the goodness toward which all things are turned. And when he adds, *To him be glory forever*, it is a confession of the divine Unity. Therefore, to the super-divine Trinity and Unity be all honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

## EXAMINATION of several points regarding the literal text.

**The Vulgate Edition:** *The Lord has not rejected his people, whom he foreknew.* <note>Romans 11:2</note> Although he says "the people" (*plebem*) here, a little earlier the old translator rendered it "the populace" (*populum*) when he said, *Has God rejected his populace?* For in both places **Paul** has the Greek word *ton laon* <note>original: "τὸν λαόν"</note>. And it would have been better to translate "foreknown" (*praegnovit*) here than "prescient" (*praescivit*), although they are one and the same. **Paul** writes: *God has not rejected his people, whom he foreknew.* <note>original: "οὐκ ἀπώσατο ὁ θεὸς τὸν λαὸν αὐτοῦ, ὃν προέγνω"</note>

**The Vulgate Edition:** *How he intercedes with God against **Israel**.* The same word used here was used in the eighth chapter; it requires the old translator to have interpreted it more correctly where he said: *But the Spirit himself requests for us.* It is more correct, I say, than "intercedes" here and a little further down, unless there are those who prefer to defend this word over that one. **Paul**: *how he appeals to God against Israel.* <note>original: "ὡς ἐντυγχάνει τῷ θεῷ κατὰ τὸν ἰσραήλ"</note>

**The Vulgate Edition:** *But what does the divine response say to him?* The word "divine" is superfluous <note>It is not in the original Greek</note>. **Paul**: *But what does the oracle say to him?* <note>original: "ἀλλὰ τί λέγει αὐτῷ ὁ χρηματισμός"</note>

**The Vulgate Edition:** *The remnants according to the election of the grace of God are made safe.* The words "of God" and "made safe" are superfluous and are not found in **Paul**. **Paul**: *There has come to be a remnant according to the election of grace.* <note>original: "λεῖμμα κατ’ ἐκλογὴν χάριτος γέγονεν"</note>

**The Vulgate Edition:** *But if it is by grace, it is no longer from works; otherwise grace is no longer grace. What then?* If it is "by grace," the word grace is in the ablative case. However, an entire sentence is missing before "What then?", namely: *But if it is from works, it is no longer grace, otherwise work is no longer work.* And where it says "no longer" (*iam non* or *non iam*), the Greek has *ouk eti* <note>original: "οὐκ ἔτι"</note>, which as stated above means "no further," "not yet," "not also," "no longer," and similar things. **Paul**: *But if by grace, no longer from works, since grace no longer becomes grace. But if from works, it is no longer grace, since work is no longer work.* And immediately after, **Paul** adds: *What then?* <note>original: "τί οὖν"</note>

**The Vulgate Edition:** *God gave them a spirit of compunction.* **Paul** brought this from the oracle of the prophet **Isaiah**, which goes like this: *Go, and say to this people: Hear, you who are hearing, and do not understand; and see the vision, and do not know. Blind the heart of this people, and make their ears heavy, and close their eyes; lest perhaps they see with their eyes... and I should heal them.* <note>Isaiah 6:9-10</note> But because *katanysis* <note>original: "κατάνυξις"</note>, which they usually translate as "compunction," can be taken in a good or a bad sense—in a good sense as here: *be pricked in your beds* <note>original: "ἐπὶ ταῖς κοίταις ὑμῶν κατανύγητε," Psalm 4:4</note>, when the pain of evil deeds or thoughts stings back—in a bad sense as in this place: when we struggle against the good, as if fighting back and stinging those who prick us toward good things. In the good sense it means to repent; in the bad sense it means to sting back and kick back. Therefore, **Paul’s** speech is more intelligible if it is said that God gave them a "spirit of back-stinging" or "recalcitrance," lest ambiguity and...

...taken in a positive sense, it might deceive the reader. And when it says *he gave*: understand this not as something God did *per se* <note>Latin: "through himself" or directly</note> but *per accidens* <note>Latin: "by happenstance" or indirectly</note> and by way of permission. For God was pricking them and moving them toward the opposite: both through the prophets and through the holy scriptures, through virtues, signs, and through the manifestation of His holy presence; but they themselves kicked back against all divine help and struggled against it. And this is the **spirit of compunction** <note>The "spirit of stupor" or "remorse" mentioned in Romans 11:8; the author argues God allowed this state rather than causing it.</note> which God permitted for them, bearing himself toward them as a devoted father toward disobedient sons, whom the more he strives to help—now with advice, now with chastisement, now with mercy—the more he finds them kicking and struggling against their own good. Therefore, if the father removes that spirit of recalcitrance so that he himself seems to give it to them, that is not *per se*, but *per accidens*. He gives and acts incidentally, and he permits it (because they are free), rather unwillingly than willingly. So too did God act toward the Jews. For the very help against which they kicked shows that God was not the one making them do what they did. Therefore, He did not wish for them to have that resistant spirit. <margin>B 8 9</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Let their table become a snare before them.* <note>Romans 11:9</note> ¶ The phrase *before them* is found in Psalm 68, but here in Paul it is not found. **Paul:** *let their table become a snare* <note>original Greek: "γενηθήτω ἡ τράπεζα αὐτῶν εἰς παγίδα"</note>. However, the word *doxazo* <note>to glorify or honor</note> has multiple meanings. Sometimes it means "I glorify" or "I honor and make famous," while other times I think it means "I estimate," "I judge," or something similar. Therefore, the understanding of this passage could also be: *I judge it to be my duty.* Thus you may understand Paul’s meaning: "Indeed, as long as I am the apostle to the Gentiles, I judge it to be my duty if by any means I might provoke my own flesh to jealousy and speak of a servant’s zeal for God." <margin>C 16 100</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *And if the offering be holy.* ¶ The word *aparche* <note>Greek: ἀπαρχὴ</note>, which the old translator here renders as "offering" <note>Latin: delibatio</note>, is almost everywhere else usually translated as "firstfruits." This is what the translator did in the preceding eighth chapter, where he says: *But we ourselves, having the firstfruits of the Spirit* <note>original Greek: "ἀλλὰ καὶ αὐτοὶ τὴν ἀπαρχὴν τοῦ πνεύματος ἔχοντες"</note>. And there is no need for more examples, because wherever they translate it as "firstfruits," this word is found. Truly, he understood these "firstfruits" according to the spirit, which are also called "remnants" and "offerings." Therefore, the old translator seems to have followed the meaning more paraphrastically than by the law of strict translation. <margin>17</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *But you, being a wild olive, were grafted in among them, and became a partner of the root and the fatness of the olive.* <margin>D 101</margin> ¶ **Wild olive** <note>Latin: oleaster</note> signifies a wild and uncultivated olive tree. *Grafted in*: others use *insitus* <note>implanted</note>. Hence they prefer to call it an "implanting." What he translated as "fatness" would be more Latinate if called "richness" or "abundance." **Paul:** *But you, being a wild olive, were grafted in among them and became a sharer of the root and the fatness of the olive.* <note>original Greek: "σὺ δὲ ἀγριέλαιος ὤν ἐνεκεντρίσθης ἐν αὐτοῖς καὶ συγκοινωνὸς τῆς ῥίζης καὶ τῆς πιότητος τῆς ἐλαίας ἐγένου"</note> <margin>22</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *See therefore the goodness and the severity of God.* ¶ Both here and subsequently, one should say "kindness" <note>Latin: benignitatem</note> rather than "goodness." **Paul:** *See then the kindness and the severity of God.* <note>original Greek: "ἴδε οὖν χρηστότητα καὶ ἀποτομίαν θεοῦ"</note> For **kindness** seems to correspond more as an opposite to **severity**, which speaks of the rigor of justice—not that these indicate a contradiction in God, but in us. For in God, mercy and justice, kindness and severity, coincide; but the same thing in God is called severity toward the wicked and kindness toward the good. This is what the most divine Paul expressed when he said: *Toward those indeed who fell, severity; but toward you, kindness.* <margin>E 25 102</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *That you may not be wise in your own conceits.* ¶ In Paul, it is more accurately said as *prudent*. Paul does not want us to rely on our own prudence and say that the Jews have been abandoned by God and will never be saved. They are indeed abandoned, but not entirely—only in part. For he knows through the Holy Spirit and through the prophets that the Jews will be saved in the end, when the Gospel has been preached through all the nations and received. Then, from the two peoples, there shall be one flock and one shepherd, Christ the Lord, the ever-blessed. O blessed eyes that shall see these things! For they shall undoubtedly see them, to the praise and glory of the eternal King and to the salvation of innumerable souls. To this end, the glorious kings **Ferdinand of Spain** and **Manuel of Portugal** <note>Ferdinand II of Aragon and Manuel I of Portugal, contemporary monarchs known for their religious zeal and military campaigns.</note> seem even now to be cooperating, for in recent years they have carried out Christian battles, not so much for the cause of destruction as for the acquisition of souls. ### COMMENTARY

...rather in their unbelief than because of their belief, for even if all had believed, the nations <note>the Gentiles</note> would nonetheless have obtained mercy. For Christ was the expectation of the nations; indeed, he was the universal lawgiver to be sent to both Jews and Gentiles alike, whereas Moses was a specific lawgiver. Christ is the universal savior in truth; Moses was a specific one in figure and shadowy imitation. <margin>•</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *For God has concluded all things in unbelief.* <note>Romans 11:32</note> ¶ It should read "all people." Paul says: *For God has shut up all together in disobedience.* <note>original Greek: συνέκλεισε γὰρ ὁ θεὸς τους πάντας εἰς ἀπειθειαν</note> For he made a circle. First, the Jews were faithful and the Gentiles unfaithful; second, the Gentiles are faithful and the Jews unfaithful—unfaithful indeed unto "disobedience," <note>original Greek: ἀπείθειαν</note> that is, a stubborn unbelief and an extreme sickness (so to speak). And so the Gentiles previously labored under such stubbornness and infidelity in the worship of idols. But from such extreme incurability, the mercy of God heals and saves by grace, which alone can do this. <margin>•</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments, and unsearchable his ways!* <note>Romans 11:33</note> <margin>•</margin> ¶ "Height" <note>Latin: *altitudo*</note> is a word with two meanings, signifying both depth and sublimity. What Paul says here signifies depth. Therefore, lest it be believed he said the same thing as if he had said "height," <note>original Greek: ὕψος</note> it seems more correct that the translator should have said "O the profundity." <note>original Greek: ὅ βάθος</note> And perhaps even better: "O the depth," so that the particle "O" is understood more suitably as an exclamation, not an address. <margin>•</margin> And where it says *and unsearchable his ways,* it is better as "un-traceable his ways," so that the negation is more readily understood. For among grammarians, "to investigate" <note>Latin: *investigate*</note> and "investigable" tend more toward affirmation than negation. And why do I say grammarians? This is true even in the sacred books, such as in the first book of Kingdoms <note>Modern 1 Samuel 20:12</note> concerning Jonathan: *If I shall have investigated the intention of my father tomorrow or the day after, and if there is anything good for David and I do not immediately send to you and make it known to you, may God do these things to Jonathan.* <margin>•</margin> In Chronicles <note>Latin: *paralipomenis*</note>: *Do you not perceive that his servants have come to you to explore, and investigate, and search your land?* <note>1 Chronicles 19:3</note> Nowhere in the sacred books do you find "investigate" that does not affirm. <margin>•</margin> How then can "investigable" <note>Latin: *investigabile*</note>—coming from the same origin—not be more affirmative? But the sacred scriptures use "unsearchable" <note>Latin: *investigabili*</note> in that negative way. Perhaps they do not use it so much as the ancient translators misused it. For the sacred letters in their origins clearly negate, as Paul says: *O the depth of the riches, and wisdom, and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments, and untraceable his ways!* <note>original Greek: Ὦ βάθος πλούτου, καὶ σοφίας, καὶ γνώσεως θεοῦ ὡς ἀνεξερεύνητα τὰ κρίματα αὐτοῦ, καὶ ἀνεξιχνίαστοι αἱ ὁδοὶ αὐτοῦ.</note> <margin>•</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *For who has known the sense of the Lord?* <note>Romans 11:34</note> It should rather have been translated: *the mind of the Lord.* Paul says: *For who has known the mind of the Lord?* <note>original Greek: τίς γὰρ ἔγνω νοῦν κυρίου</note> <margin>•</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *For from him, and through him, and in him are all things. To him be glory forever and ever.* <note>Romans 11:36</note> <margin>•</margin> ¶ They say "from" refers to the efficient cause, "through" to the form, and "in" to the end <note>the final purpose</note>. The first act is Three and One: One because it is first and simplest; Three because it is the producer of all, the form of all, and the end of all. Indeed, every substantial act imitates this in its own way, triply and unitedly—which even the philosophers do not deny. For this reason, it seems it should rather be said: "and *unto* him" <note>Latin: *in ipsum*</note>; for all things are for the sake of the end, that is, toward the end and because of the end. "Of the ages" at the end of the phrase is an abundance from the original model. Paul says: *For from him and through him and unto him are all things: to him be glory unto the ages. Amen.* <note>original Greek: ὅτι ἐξ αὐτοῦ καὶ δι' αὐτοῦ καὶ εἰς αὐτὸν τὰ πάντα, αὐτῶ ἡ δόξα εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας. ἀμήν.</note>

<margin>105</margin> **T**he mercy of God saves you: those who ought to live by the spirit, for God and Christ, and mortify the flesh and its lusts. And this mortification is a living and holy offering, and a rational worship <note>Latin: *rationabilis cultura*</note> which is offered to God. Paul vehemently exhorts us to do this through the mercies of God. For by what could he better exhort us than by the mercy through which alone we are saved? <margin>•</margin> He exhorts us, therefore, in this manner, saying: ¶ *I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, that you present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing to God, which is your rational worship. But just as a fertile land does not exist where there are noxious weeds, so the gifts of God do not bear fruit except in a humble mind. <margin>•</margin> Therefore, one must take the greatest care lest pride occupy the mind, which is the enemy of humility and is like a noxious weed <note>Latin: *lolium*—specifically tares or cockle</note> preventing the gifts of God and the heavenly harvest from bearing fruit. <meta>This page continues the commentary on the Epistle to the Romans, moving into the practical applications of Chapter 12. Having established the theological foundations of faith in previous chapters, the author now addresses the "order of the Church" and how individual believers should behave as members of one body.</meta>

Ro. 97

# I

...more than is right or than one's own rank and duty require, such a person seems wise to himself and feels it: he is arrogant and proud, and he does not maintain humility according to the measure of faith. But it is necessary for all the faithful to know that they are one body, whose head is Christ. Therefore, every understanding in all people ought to flow from Christ. And he who is not of Christ does not have the understanding of the Head <note>Christ is the head of the mystical body, the Church</note>, <margin>107</margin> but the understanding of a stranger. And just as one limb never usurps the function of another limb, so one rank in the church ought never to usurp what belongs to another. Otherwise, it is to be proud, to feel more than is right, and to confuse the order. Rather, the lower ranks should be content with the duties of the lower, the higher with the higher, the sacred with sacred matters, and the secular with secular matters. They should help one another in their respective functions, just as the members of the body help each other, love each other, and work together. Paul reveals this to us, saying:

<margin>A</margin>
> ¶ For just as we have many members in one body, but all members do not have the same function, so we, being many, are one body in CHRIST, and individually members of one another. Having gifts that differ according to the grace that was given to us.

¶ In these differing gifts, what else is understood but the order of gifts? Because of ignorance and pride—or rather, a prideful ignorance and an ignorant pride—Christ, the giver of gifts, does not want this order to be confused. But who does not see this order being miserably confused every day? We see it when secular men wish to be the dispensers of sacred matters, and conversely, those dedicated to sacred offices handle temporal matters too greedily. We see it when <margin>A</margin> every lowest person dares to speak against a superior and usurp the superior's office, which is to criticize the behavior of those below them and to instruct them in the spiritual life. But on the contrary, the superiors are criticized by the lowest, and they themselves do not correct those beneath them. Is this not a confusion of the order and the gifts of God? Paul enumerates seven such gifts and offices of God here. First: the gift of prophecy, from which one is called a prophet. Second: the gift of ministry, from which one is called a minister. Third: the gift of teaching, from which come teachers. Fourth: the gift of exhortation, from which come exhorters and preachers. Fifth: the gift of distribution, from which come the liberal, the munificent, and the magnificent. Sixth: the gift of presiding, from which come leaders. Seventh: the gift of mercy, from which come the merciful. He who is not a prophet should not claim the work of a prophet. He who is not a deacon <note>original: *diaconus*</note> should not minister. He who is not a teacher—that is, one who does not have the gift of understanding eloquence—should not teach. He who is not endowed with the grace of exhortation should not preach. And so it goes for the rest. In the first rank are those gifted by God with understanding for the future direction of the church. In the second: deacons and the ministers of the duties of faith. In the third: bishops. In the fourth: preachers. In the fifth: those relieving the needs of others and the costs of divine worship by their own expense. In the sixth: primates and princes. In the seventh: the executors of works of charity toward the sick, the hungry, the thirsty, the naked, the stranger, and the burying of the dead, having also received this grace from God. Paul enumerates these seven, <margin>108</margin> saying:

> ¶ Whether prophecy: according to the analogy <note>original: *analogiam*, meaning proportion or rule</note>, that is, the reason of faith. Whether ministry: in ministering. Whether he who teaches: in doctrine. Whether he who exhorts: in exhortation. He who contributes: in simplicity. He who presides: in diligence. He who shows mercy: in cheerfulness.

¶ Furthermore, he enumerates twenty-four things that ought to be common to every state of life. 1: love without pretense. 2: hatred of evil and clinging to good. 3: brotherly charity. 4: mutual honor. 5: dutiful diligence. 6: fervor of spirit. 7: service to the Lord. 8: joy in the hope of eternal goods. 9: patience in affliction. 10: zeal for prayer. 11: helping the needs of the saints. 12: hospitality, which is the receiving of strangers. 13: the blessing of persecutors. 14: the blessing of all and the cursing of none. 15: joy from the joy of others, or sadness from their sadness. 16: unity of mind. 17: humility. 18: the renouncing of one's own wisdom. 19: for evil, returning not evil but good. 20: the example of a good life. 21: peace with all as far as is proper. 22: not being angry and not seeking revenge. 23: doing good to <margin>109</margin> enemies. 24 and last: always overcoming evil with good. The most blessed apostle encompasses all these things in these precepts:

> ¶ Let love be without hypocrisy. Hate what is evil, clinging to what is good. In brotherly love, be kindly affectionate to one another. In honor, anticipating one another. In zeal, not lazy. Fervent in spirit. Serving the Lord. Rejoicing in hope. Patient in pressure <note>original: *pressura*, meaning tribulation or affliction</note>. Constant in prayer. Communicating to the needs of the saints. Following hospitality. Bless those who persecute you. Bless and do not curse. Rejoice with those who rejoice, and weep with those who weep. Be of the same mind toward one another. Do not think high things, but associate with the humble. Do not become wise in your own eyes. Repaying no one evil for evil. Providing good things before all men if it is possible. As much as is in you, having peace with all men. Do not avenge yourselves, beloved, but give place to wrath. For it is written: Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord. If therefore your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him a drink; for by doing this you will heap coals of fire...

### EXAMINATION of several points regarding the literal text.

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercy of God.* <note>Romans 12:1</note> ¶ Paul says "mercies" in the plural. Paul: *I beseech you therefore, brethren, through the mercies of God.* <note>original Greek: "παρακαλῶ ὀυν ὑμᾶς ἀδελφοὶ Διὰ τῶν ὀικτιρμῶν τοῦ θεοῦ"</note> For this is how they usually translate "mercies" <note>original: "ὀικτιρμῶν"</note>, as in Psalm 24: "Remember your mercies" <note>original Greek: "μνήσθητι τῶν ὀικτιρμῶν σου"</note>, and frequently elsewhere.

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Your reasonable service.* ¶ Theologians maintain that "latria" <note>a technical term for the highest form of worship</note> is the cult or worship that is owed to God alone. And therefore, to signify this, wherever Paul uses "latria," we prefer to translate it as "worship" or "cultivation." For he commands us to worship God rationally. But how shall we worship rationally, unless when praying and adoring, we present our bodies—dead to vice and alive to righteousness—as a living sacrifice, holy (that is, pure and clean), and well-pleasing to Him? Paul: *To present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God, which is your rational worship.* <note>original Greek: "παραστῆσαι τὰ σώματα ὑμῶν θυσίαν ζῶσαν ἁγίαν εὐάρεστον τῷ θεῷ, τὴν λογικὴν λατρείαν ἡμῶν"</note>

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *But be transformed in the newness of your sense.* ¶ It should rather be said, "of your mind." Paul: *but be transformed by the renewing of your mind.* <note>original Greek: "ἀλλὰ μεταμορφοῦθε τῇ ἀνακαινώσει τοῦ νοὸς ὑμῶν"</note>

<margin>A 106</margin>
¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *To all who are among you, not to be more wise than it behooves to be wise: but to be wise unto sobriety.* ¶ Regarding what he says about "being wise" <note>Latin: "sapere"</note>, we have said that the Latin custom is to translate this rather as "to feel" or "to think." And if the first and last parts are turned into gerunds, the speech seems more suited to the Latin style. And where the old translator said "unto sobriety," Paul rather has "unto modesty." Paul: *not to think too highly beyond what one ought to think, but to think unto being modest.* <note>original Greek: "μὴ ὑπερφρονεῖν παρὸ δεῖ φρονεῖν, ἀλλὰ φρονεῖν εἰς τὸ σωφρονεῖν"</note> For *sophronio* and *sophrosyne* <note>Latinized forms of the Greek verbs for acting with a sound mind</note> signify being modest and modesty. Although Jerome refers this passage of interpretation to "chastity" <note>original Greek: "ἀγνεῖαν"</note>, it does not seem to fit the meaning quite so appropriately.

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *And to each as God has divided the measure of faith.* ¶ It is more suited to the Latin language if the word "as" is placed before "to each."

<margin>B 107</margin>
¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Each one members of another.* ¶ The old translator could also have said: "but each in turn members." Paul: *but each one members of one another.* <note>original Greek: "ὁ δὲ καθεῖς ἀλλήλων μέλη"</note>

<margin>108</margin>
¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Or ministry in ministering.* ¶ Paul has "in ministry." Paul: *or ministry in the ministry.* <note>original Greek: "εἴτε Διακονίαν ἐν τῇ Διακονίᾳ"</note>

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Or he who teaches in doctrine.* ¶ Paul: *or the one teaching in the teaching.* <note>original Greek: "εἴτε ὁ Δάσκων ἐν τῇ Διδασκαλίᾳ"</note> This is the same thing as what the old translator put. Truly, to grasp the meaning—which depends on the preceding phrase, "having gifts according to the grace given to us that differ"—one can understand "having the gift" as being implied. Paul understood this from the preceding passage, and it does no harm if it is understood in the following parts, even if not expressed.

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *He who exhorts in exhorting.* ¶ Paul has "in exhortation." <note>original Greek: "εἴτε ὁ παρακαλῶν ἐν τῇ παρακλήσει"</note> For it responds to the preceding: "in ministry," "in doctrine," and to the following: "in simplicity," "in solicitude," "in cheerfulness." And what he says here, "he who exhorts," is the same word that the translator rendered at the beginning as "I beseech." For there Paul has "I beseech" <note>original Greek: "παρακαλῶ"</note>, but here its participle "exhorting" <note>original Greek: "παρακαλῶν"</note>. From this you understand that this "beseeching" is nothing other than a certain exhortation granted by divine gift. For who was superior to Paul in divine exhorting?

¶ **He who gives, in simplicity.** ¶ But who is the one giving in simplicity? I would consider him to be the one who gives for the sake of God alone. For if he looks to himself or something else, he is already divided; he gives not in simplicity, but in duplicity. For he teaches the spiritual man to think not of himself, but of God alone. For what need is there for him to look to himself or his own salvation, as if anxious for himself, when the Lord forbids us to be anxious for ourselves? Let him therefore leave this care to God, to whom alone it belongs to save, and let him give in simplicity, never divided from God. And although he does not think of it, he will achieve his own salvation far better. For the Lord is anxious for us when we do all our things for His sake in simplicity, casting upon Him all care, all hope, and the entirety of our providence, while still working whatever good we can. For the Lord is Master, and we are servants. He is indeed the Lord, but of infinite goodness and wisdom. Even a temporal master hates lazy servants; he even esteems those who are anxious for themselves and serve him for the sake of hope of reward less than those who serve in simplicity, thinking nothing of themselves but only of the master himself, committing the whole of their providence to the goodness and wisdom of their master. Shall we not therefore commit our providence to infinite goodness and wisdom, not thinking of ourselves nor being anxious for ourselves, in simplicity (whether in giving, or in anything else)...

<margin>C</margin>
If you were leading a flock of sheep, you would be diligent and careful lest any sheep perish through your negligence. Otherwise, you would have to give an account to the master of the house. How much more diligent ought he to be who leads the flock of Christ, lest anyone perish through his negligence? Otherwise, he must give an account to Christ, the eternal King. Peter led, so did Paul, and so did other saints. ¶ **He who shows mercy: with cheerfulness.** ¶ He who shows mercy: he gives either to the weak, or the hungry, or the thirsty, or the naked, or the imprisoned, or those suffering other necessities of life. ¶ He who does this by the gift of God, does it with cheerfulness, as it is written in another place: *God loves a cheerful giver.* <note>2 Corinthians 9:7</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition: Rejoice with those who rejoice.** <note>original: "Gaudere cum gaudentibus"</note> Latin reason seems to require that we express this rather through a gerund <note>referring to a specific grammatical form in Latin</note>. ¶ **The Vulgate edition: Being of the same mind one toward another.** <note>original: "Idipsum inuicē sentientes"</note> ¶ Where the old translator says "that same thing" <note>original: "idipsum"</note>, we say more appropriately "the same." Paul: *providing good things in the sight of all men.* <note>original Greek: "προνοούμενοι καλὰ ἐνώπιον πάντων ἀνθρώπων"</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition: Not defending yourselves, dearly beloved.** <note>original: "Non vosmetipsos defendentes charissimi"</note> ¶ It should rather be said: "not avenging," beloved. Paul: *not avenging yourselves, beloved.* <note>original Greek: "μὴ ἑαυτοὺς ἐκδικοῦντες ἀγαπητοί"</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition: Revenge is mine and I will repay.** <note>original: "Mihi vindictā & ego retribuā"</note> ¶ It should be said: "vengeance" in the nominative case. And Paul added: *Vengeance is mine, I will repay.* <note>original Greek: "ἐμοὶ ἐκδίκησις, ἐγὼ ἀνταποδώσω"</note> ¶ **For doing this: you shall heap coals of fire upon his head.** ¶ What does this mean? If, because of the Lord's command, you love your enemy—if you do good to him and he does not depart from his enmity and hatred—your love and your good deeds will be the cause of his more heavy punishment from God, who says: *Vengeance is mine; I will repay.* And your love and your benefits toward him, while he remains hardened in hatred, will be for him on the day of retribution and vengeance like coals of fire and ignited torments cast upon his head. However, you ought not to feed or give him drink when he is in need for the purpose of heaping punishments on him, but for the sake of God who commands it. Or, if you know your enemy is angry, do it so that you may reconcile him to yourself, and once reconciled, restore him to God, and thus save your brother. For this is to live spiritually and in simplicity before God. And this sentiment of the most blessed Paul is supported by what is said in Proverbs 25: *If your enemy is hungry, feed him. If he is thirsty, give him water to drink. For you shall gather coals upon his head, and the Lord will reward you.*

## CHAPTER XIII

<margin>D</margin>
The Apostle, worthy of God, has set forth the gifts and offices common to all superiors; now he instructs those who are inferior, and under one general duty—subjection, which is obedience—he encompasses all things that belong to inferiors. For he who does not obey is not subject. And there are two supreme powers in the republic of the faithful: one ecclesiastical, which is called Papal; and the other secular, which is called Royal. In the first, there ought to be one monarch to maintain sacred matters in the best state: and this is the Supreme Pontiff <note>the Pope</note>. And in the second, there should be one monarch for the governance of secular affairs and for conducting Christian wars against the enemies of religion: and this is the Emperor of the Christians. And all patriarchs, primates, archbishops, bishops, and other ecclesiastical dignities and orders ought to obey the sacred monarch in holy institutions insofar as he is the Supreme Pontiff—not, however, insofar as he is the particular bishop of some specific place. Likewise, all Christian kings, dukes, nobles, and all orders of the secular militia ought to obey the secular monarch for the sake of conducting the wars of Christ, not as the king of some particular kingdom, but as the monarch and supreme Emperor of the Christians. And the synagogue of the Hebrews, as a figure of the Church, had monarchs for sacred matters: Aaron, Eleazar, Phinehas, and their successors, the high priests of the Hebrews. For secular affairs and the conduct of wars, it had monarchs: Moses, Joshua, Othniel, and the other emperors of the Hebrews who succeeded them. Nor should these offices be confused. Because even in sacred matters, the secular monarch ought to obey the sacred monarch and his decrees. And conversely, the sacred monarch should leave to the secular monarch the authority for the governance of temporal affairs and the conduct of the wars of Christ. And subjects who resist this ordination resist God. And as has been said of these two powers, so it is to be understood of other high authorities. For instance, in sacred matters: those who are under patriarchs should obey them as patriarchs. Those under primates: as primates; under archbishops: as arch-

...archbishops. Those under bishops: obey them as bishops. And in secular matters, those under <term>kings</term><note>Latin: *regibus*</note>: obey them as kings. Those 
<margin>110</margin>
under <term>dukes</term><note>Latin: *ducibus*</note>: obey them as dukes. Those under nobles: obey them as nobles. And so it is for every eminent order, as Saint Paul holy admonishes us, saying: <margin>, , , , ,</margin> **Let every soul be subject to the higher powers. For there is no power except from God; and the powers that be are ordained by God. Therefore, whoever resists the power resists the ordinance of God; and those who resist shall bring judgment upon themselves.** <note>A translation of Romans 13:1-2</note> ¶ If the powers that be are ordained by God, it follows that those which are not ordained are not from God. And therefore they are not "powers," but rather <term>lapses</term> and <term>disorders</term> <note>original: "prolapsiones & inordinationes"</note> of power. For example, if a secular person claims for himself the power to ordain sacred things, or if, contrary to the <term>sacred order</term> <note>referring to the clergy</note>, one claims the authority to wage war and the management of secular affairs. For this is a disorder: it is not power, but the weakness and lapse of power. And what if the priests and fellow-confessors who are under a bishop refuse to obey? Do they not resist the divine ordinance? Or shall they have the power to pull away the yoke of obedience from the highest power, and cling only to the supreme power? Is that "ordained"? And if it is not ordained, it is not from God. Is it not necessary for lower things to be formed in the likeness of higher things, and for the sacred order of the lower to imitate the higher? If the angels refused to obey the archangels, but wished to cling in obedience only to God, would they not fill heaven with confusion? And would they not, through this pride, fall from heaven even faster than Lucifer, the head and inventor of pride and the first disorder? Have not these others also fallen from the sacred ecclesiastical leadership through disorder and pride? What if episcopal duties were handed over to an order to which they are not owed as an inferior, and that person dared to abuse them rather than use them, and yet desired the same strict obedience for himself which he denied to his superior? It is almost just that he who denies obedience according to the divine ordinance should himself be denied the obedience he lusts after outside of that divine ordinance. For it is not a divine ordinance that the lowest things should cling to the highest without a middle <note>The author argues against "jumping" ranks in a hierarchy, a key concept in medieval political and religious thought</note>. This is not unknown to those who have read the <term>sacred hierarchy of Dionysius</term> <note>referring to Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-6th century theologian whose works on celestial and ecclesiastical hierarchies were foundational for medieval thought</note>. What if, in the governing of secular affairs, dukes refused to obey kings, and nobles refused to obey dukes, and every lower power dragged away the obedience due to the superior, but wanted their own obedience to be immediate to the supreme monarch—as if, because one order is superior to another, there should be no obedience between them? Would not a great confusion be brought into the secular government? A monarch ought not to introduce such confusion, for his power is "ordained," and this would be "disorder." Therefore, it does not come from power. A man can do what he can do by power, but not what he does by "non-power"; for that is not "being able" <note>Latin: *posse*</note>, but "not being able" <note>Latin: *non posse*</note>. What then? Can a secular monarch exempt an inferior from a superior, such as a duke from his king? Certainly he can. For he can make a duke a king, and raise his dominion into a kingdom. In the same way, the supreme Sacred Hierarch <note>likely referring to the Pope</note> can lead a lower order to equality with a higher one, such as creating a priest and fellow-confessor of a bishop into a bishop himself, or an archbishop into a [higher] archbishop, and so on. And when subjection is removed in this way, and they gradually adhere more closely to the highest order, no disorder occurs; and all things (as long as they are done for the sake of dignity) preserve the imitation of the divine. But you will say: "It is necessary for the lower orders to pull away the yoke from the immediate power and cling directly to the supreme power; otherwise, the lower and subject ones will suffer many difficult and hard things from that immediate power, whether in sacred or temporal matters." But one must not, for that reason, resist the divine ordinance. Do you not know, by the authority of the Apostle <note>Saint Paul</note>, who is God's legate in this matter, that those who resist that ordinance will receive judgment—that is, God's condemnation? It is wickedness that makes you pull away from the yoke; you will be subject to manifold punishment and damnation because you do not obey the ordinance of God, because you confound the sacred leadership, because you rashly insert yourself into the highest ranks without any order, and because you wish to sin more licentiously without your sins being rebuked. Or if they are rebuked, they are not rebuked by the one who ought to do it. For you wish to obey someone whom you never see (so that you do not fear him), and who does not know your deeds (so that he cannot correct them). And therefore, those evil and hard things which you fear from the immediate power—whom you were bound to obey by divine ordinance—you do not escape; instead, you fall into a heavier evil by introducing confusion and disorder into the established leadership. But if you now wish, having become more well-advised, to escape these evils and the confusion of the divine ordinance (which is worse than these evils) in both types of power, follow Paul when he says: 
<margin>111</margin>
<margin>, , , , , ,</margin> **For rulers are not a terror to good works, but to the evil. Do you wish not to be afraid of the power? Do that which is good, and you shall have praise from the same. For he is the minister of God to you for good. But if you do that which is evil, be afraid; for he bears not the sword in vain. For he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that does evil.** <note>A translation of Romans 13:3-4</note> ¶ By "wrath," understand "vengeance." Therefore, an ordained power shines before the good toward good and love; but before the evil, toward punishment and terror. It praises the good and promotes them to higher things; it blames the evil and thrusts them down to lower things. And just as subjects who do not obey resist the divine ordinance, so too do the powers that do not lead rightly, or who become sluggish against the divine ordinance, or who pervert it. But you will say...

<summary>This page discusses the necessity of following hierarchical order in both church and state, arguing that power is a divine ordinance and resisting one's immediate superior creates a "disorder" comparable to the fall of Lucifer. It uses the theology of Pseudo-Dionysius to justify why lower ranks must not bypass middle authorities to reach the supreme monarch or hierarch.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the divine origin of authority, moving from the general principle that all power comes from God to the specific problem of how to respond to "violent" or unjust rulers, and finally to the unifying principle of Love as the fulfillment of the Law.</meta>

<header>Romans</header>

There are certain violent powers, and sometimes those who preside are violent. Must we also obey them? Yes, not only out of fear of the punishments they inflict because they are violent, but also out of fear for our conscience, lest we resist the divine ordinance. For when earthly goods are abused, by divine ordinance, harsh and violent powers are often set over people to take away those earthly things in which they have sinned. Thus, the greedy, the luxurious, those belching from excess, the blasphemous, and men with such abominable habits, must be governed harshly. This is so that adversity may turn back to God those whom earthly prosperity had turned away. And because you do not know how to distinguish what is of God and what is of men: therefore (as long as it is not a sin to obey),
<margin>112</margin> even if it is troublesome and heavy, do not resist, do not murmur, but obey for the sake of God from whom is all power in heaven and on earth. And lean upon Paul saying: ¶ **Therefore be subject of necessity, not only for wrath, but also for conscience.** For this reason you also pay taxes. For they are God's ministers, serving for this very purpose. ¶ "For wrath" (as has been said) means for the sake of vengeance and fear of punishment. For harsh and violent powers are the clients of divine justice and (so to speak) exist as certain <term>lictors</term><note>original: "lictores"; in ancient Rome, these were officials who carried out the sentences of magistrates, often including corporal or capital punishment.</note> of the wicked. Under secular justice, if they are not obeyed, a heavy penalty follows; how much more so under divine justice. Other powers, being milder, educate their subjects to do God's justice voluntarily, like certain revered and honorable magistrates. To these, what else is owed but honor and love? Yet, obedience is owed to all in common. Wherefore
<margin>113</margin> Paul adds: ¶ **Render therefore to all their dues: tribute to whom tribute is due; custom to whom custom; fear to whom fear; honor to whom honor. Owe no man anything, but mutual love.** ¶ Justice commands us to render to each what is his own; and the powers, which are her ministers, watch over this very thing so that it may be done. So in every creature, God declares Himself just, granting to each nature what is its own and what is appropriate. It is necessary, therefore, that he who does not wish to incur wrath and worthy vengeance should imitate the just parent <note>referring to God</note>. But what is the shortest path by which we may imitate Him and be made just? Love <note>original: "dilectio"</note>. And why is this a wonder? For love and affection is the leader and the <term>charioteer</term><note>original: "auriga"</note> of God's justice. For He says:
<margin>114</margin> "You have not established or made anything while hating it." <note>A reference to Wisdom 11:24: "For thou lovest all things that are, and abhorrest nothing which thou hast made."</note> So too for human justice: love is the leader and the principle. Hence Paul says: ¶ **For he who loves another has fulfilled the law. For this: you shall not commit adultery, you shall not kill, you shall not steal, you shall not covet; and if there be any other commandment, it is summed up in this saying: namely, you shall love your neighbor as yourself. Love works no evil to a neighbor; therefore love is the fulfillment of the law.**
¶ When he says, "For he who loves another has fulfilled the law," he understands this as the love which is <term>charity</term><note>original: "charitas"; the author distinguishes between general love and the divine virtue of charity.</note>. For love (as one of the saints says), so that it may be called charity, reaches out to another: first toward God, second toward the neighbor. And on this twin love, according to the saving speech of the Gospel, hang all the law and the prophets. The love of neighbor depends upon the love of God, for the former is a certain likeness of the latter. And the other commandments depend upon the love of neighbor. Nor is there perfect love of God without love of neighbor. For how can you perfectly love the Truth if you do not love its image? And as John, the beloved disciple of God, says: "He who does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?" For every person is your neighbor, having been formed with you according to the divine image; and all the more so if, through regeneration and the reformation of that image <note>referring to baptism and spiritual renewal</note>, he has become a brother to you. Nor is this love a perfect love without the love of God; for a likeness receives its perfection from the truth. Therefore, perfect love toward another is that which includes the love of God and does not exclude charity for the neighbor. And regarding this, Paul also said: "He who loves another (namely, God and neighbor) has fulfilled the law." And at the end he added: "therefore love is the fulfillment of the law." But you will understand these things more easily if we set down the ten commandments, which are understood by the name of the Law, in this manner:

> 1. You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, all your soul, and all your strength.
> 2. And your neighbor as yourself.
> 3. Keep the Sabbaths holy.
> 4. Honor your father and mother.
> 5. You shall not kill.
> 6. You shall not steal.
> 7. You shall not commit adultery.
> 8. You shall not bear false witness.
> 9. You shall not covet your neighbor's wife.
> 10. Nor any other thing whatsoever.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Epistle to the Romans, specifically focusing on the transition from the legal requirements of the Decalogue to the transformative power of Christian love (charity) and the urgency of spiritual awakening.</meta>

<header>COMMENTARY</header>

You see that love contains the first and second commandments. But from the love of God, the love of neighbor hangs and follows. Likewise, the Sabbath observance, all ceremonies, and the observation of divine worship follow from it. For if you love God with all your heart, all your mind, and all your strength, you will love your neighbor, whom He commanded to be loved as yourself; and you will sanctify the celebrations which were commanded for His honor. Furthermore, you will honor your father and mother, and you will not kill, nor commit adultery, and so on for the rest. For how could you perfectly love someone in this way—with your whole mind and all your strength—if you held his commands in contempt? That is truly impossible. Therefore, he who has the charity <note>The Latin *charitas* implies a selfless, divine love rather than just "feeling good" about someone.</note> of God does not sin. For he can do all things, and he fills all things with goodness. Yet this is not within our own power, unless it is granted from above. For how could a low and cold nature grow warm, unless heat descended from above? But also, how could it be capable of being warmed, unless that highest Nature willed to warm it? God, therefore, wills to fill every person with His love, provided that the person themselves wills to be warmed.

Now, one wills to be warmed when they dispose and prepare themselves as much as they are able to receive that ray of divinity. In this, one helps themselves most strongly through the love of neighbor—which is exactly what Paul intended to emphasize in this passage. For upon the love of neighbor hangs the fulfillment of the 4th, 5th, 6th, 7th, 8th, 9th, and 10th commandments. <note>The author uses the traditional numbering where the 4th commandment is honoring one's parents.</note> For if you love your neighbor as yourself, how will you not honor your father and mother, both of whom you hold not only as neighbors, but as more than neighbors? And if you love your neighbor, you will not kill him, you will not steal his goods, you will not defile him with adultery, you will not speak false witness against him, you will not covet his wife, nor his daughter, nor his male servant, nor his female servant, nor his house, nor his field, nor anything that is his. In short, love works no evil toward a neighbor, because it observes everything that God commands. He who observes these things is found prepared to be capable of receiving divine love. You see, therefore, how the love of neighbor helps you to receive divine love; and when that divine love arrives, the love of neighbor will be made perfect. For previously it was not perfect, even if it tended toward perfection and served as a useful support for receiving divine love. Conversely, he who lacks love for his neighbor performs evil and wicked deeds against him. He dishonors father and mother, who hold the first and most powerful place among neighbors. He does not shrink from slaughter. He commits theft. He commits adultery, indulges in gluttony, and gets drunk. He speaks false witness, he strives, he is envious. He covets his neighbor's wife <unclear>neighbor's</unclear> so that he might violate the laws of the marriage bed, reveling in bedrooms and impurities. He snatches the possessions of another if he can, following the desires of the flesh and never the spirit, receding far away from divine love, without which there can be no salvation. ❧ And these are the works of darkness. Those who perform these things sleep in sin, never rising to the works of light. For the Light is Christ, who rises for the just; and filling their hearts with His divine light, He ignites them with perfect charity, by which they are able to fulfill the works of light and the divine law.

<margin>115</margin>
> Therefore, the most blessed apostle exhorts us in this way, saying: ❧ **And let us be mindful of this time: because it is now the hour for us to rise from sleep. For now our salvation is nearer than when we first believed. The night has passed, and the day has drawn near. Let us therefore cast off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light. Let us walk honestly, as in the day: not in gluttony and drunkenness, not in chambering and impurities, not in strife and envying; but put on the Lord JESUS CHRIST, and make no provision for the flesh in its lusts.** ❧ The "Night" is infidelity; the "Day" is fidelity. "Sleep" is being held back in sin; "Waking" is being occupied in good works. "Works of darkness" are works of sin. "Works of the flesh" are works of infidelity. "Works of light" are works of the justice of God. "Works of the spirit" are works of faith. "Our salvation" is the life of the world to come. The closer we are to our earthly dissolution, the more we approach that life. This is the prize <note>original: *bravium*; a term for the prize given to the winner of a race.</note> of our course—not a debt owed, but something set forth freely and bestowed freely. Therefore, the more we approach the end of our course, the more we ought to be vigilant in integrity. We are in the day—the day of both faith and knowledge. And if he who walks in the physical day strives to appear adorned and honorable, and does this for the glory of the world, should we not much more, as we walk in the spiritual day, strive to appear spiritually adorned and honorable? We should do nothing of the works of darkness, being clothed in the armor of light against the malignant powers of the night, leading a Christ-like life, so that we may truly be seen to have "put on" Jesus Christ. To Him be all honor and power, forever and ever.

### EXAMINATION of certain points regarding the literal text. ❧ **The Vulgate Edition:** *Those things which are from God, are ordained.* ❧ Paul is speaking here only about powers (authorities). Therefore, even if the statement is universally true, for the understanding of Paul’s intent, it should have said "they [the powers] are ordained." Indeed, Paul explicitly included the noun "powers," saying: <note>original Greek: "αἱ δὲ οὖσαι ἐξουσίαι ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ τεταγμέναι"</note> *but the powers that be are ordained by God.* ❧ **The Vulgate Edition:** *They acquire damnation for themselves.* ❧ Paul speaks of this in the future tense in this way: <note>original Greek: "οἱ δὲ ἀνθεστηκότες"</note> [those who resist...]

<meta>This page continues the philological and moral commentary on Paul’s Epistle to the Romans, moving from the end of Chapter 13 into the beginning of Chapter 14. The previous page discussed the primacy of charity as the fulfillment of the Law.</meta>

# Romans

...they will receive judgment for themselves. <note>Greek: ἑαυτοῖς κρίμα λήψονται</note> Those who resist: they will receive judgment for themselves.

<margin>A 111</margin>
¶ **Vulgate edition.** For rulers are not a terror to good conduct, but to bad. ¶ Paul speaks in the plural. "For rulers are not a terror to good works, but to bad." <note>Greek: οἱ γὰρ ἄρχοντες οὐκ εἰσὶ φόβος τῶν ἀγαθῶν ἔργων, ἀλλὰ τῶν κακῶν</note> For rulers are not a terror to good works, but to bad. However, Latin usage requires it to be translated instead as: For rulers are not a terror to good works, but to bad. <note>The commentator notes that the Latin dative case *bonis operibus* is more idiomatic than the Vulgate’s genitive.</note> That is, rulers are not a terror to those who do good, but to those who do evil.

<margin>B 111</margin>
¶ **Vulgate edition.** For he is God's servant to you for good. ¶ The ancient translator <note>Referring to the author of the Vulgate</note> should have said "handmaid" <note>Latin: *ministra*</note> rather than "servant" <note>Latin: *minister*</note>, as he had previously spoken of "it" <note>Referring to the concept of Authority</note>. For this confirms what he had said about authority. Truly, he did this for the sake of clarity: <term>Diakonos</term> <note>Original: Διάκονος</note> is of common gender, meaning both a male servant and a female handmaid. Here, however, he took one gender for another, not paying attention to what it refers to: "to the authority," <note>Greek: πρὸς τὴν ἐξουσίαν</note> which is feminine in Greek. But Paul is found to use the common gender as a masculine, as in chapter 15 of this epistle where he says: "Now I say that Christ Jesus was a servant of the circumcision." <note>Greek: Διάκονον γεγένησθαι περιτομῆς</note> Yet he also uses it as a feminine later in this same epistle, in chapter 16, where he says: "I commend to you Phoebe our sister, who is a servant." <note>Greek: Διάκονον</note>

<margin>113</margin>
¶ **Vulgate edition.** For he is God's servant: an avenger for wrath. ¶ Here too the ancient translator should have said: "For she is God's handmaid," for the same reason as just before.

<margin>C 114</margin>
¶ **Vulgate edition.** For he who loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law. ¶ We should not say "neighbor" here, but "another." Paul: "for he who loves another." <note>Greek: ὁ γὰρ ἀγαπῶν τὸν ἕτερον</note> For loving "another" pours out further and more broadly than loving a "neighbor." For the former refers to God and neighbor, while the latter refers to the neighbor alone.

¶ **Vulgate edition.** For you shall not commit adultery. ¶ It is better to say: For *this*, you shall not commit adultery. Paul: "for this: you shall not commit adultery." <note>Greek: τὸ γὰρ οὐ μοιχεύσεις; the commentary highlights the Greek article *to* which points to the specific command.</note>

¶ **Vulgate edition.** In this word it is restored: you shall love your neighbor. ¶ In Greek it is "recapitulated," <note>Greek: ἀνακεφαλαιοῦται</note> that is, it is summarily contained and comprehended. Paul: "it is recapitulated in this word, namely: you shall love your neighbor." And when it says "in this," <note>Greek: ἐν τῷ</note> it has the force of saying "namely," lest we repeat "in this" twice.

¶ **Vulgate edition.** Love of neighbor works no evil. ¶ Following Paul, we should say: "to a neighbor." And the word "neighbor" seems to look forward to what follows, not backward. As if we were saying "love works no evil to a neighbor," which is universally true of love—both for God and for neighbor. Paul: "love works no evil to a neighbor." <note>Greek: ἡ ἀγάπη τῷ πλησίον κακὸν οὐκ ἐργάζεται</note>

<margin>C 115 D</margin>
¶ **Vulgate edition.** And knowing this time. ¶ The word should be understood appropriately according to Paul's custom, who frequently uses participles for verbs, so that we might say "and let us be knowing this," or "let us know this time," that it is now the hour for us to rise from sleep.

¶ **Vulgate edition.** As in the day let us walk honestly. ¶ "As" <note>Latin: *Sicut*</note> is one word, not two; unlike how people usually write "so that" <note>Latin: *sic vt*</note>. Therefore, to remove this ambiguity, we have explained it by "as if." Paul: "let us walk becomingly as in the day." <note>Greek: ὡς ἐν ἡμέρᾳ εὐσχημόνως περιπατήσωμεν</note>

¶ **Vulgate edition.** Not in revelries and drunkenness. ¶ In "revelries," Paul says <term>komois</term> <note>original: κώμοις</note>; this word signifies the lust of banquets, boldness, and all immodesty. Furthermore, the Holy Athanasius interprets "revelries" as lascivious songs following excessive luxury of wine and more profuse drinking. It is certain that these things should be most foreign to a Christian and spiritual man. For you should not believe anyone to be a true Christian who is not also spiritual, unless perhaps in name only—a name which is never denied to anyone once they have been washed in the sacred waters <note>That is, baptized</note>.

¶ **Vulgate edition.** And make no provision for the flesh in its desires. ¶ Since the ancient translator had previously spoken using the imperative mood, "put on the Lord Jesus Christ," it followed that he should use the same mood to say "do not make." For Paul does not change the mood, and the connecting particle demanded this. Paul: "and make no provision for the flesh unto lusts." <note>Greek: καὶ τῆς σαρκὸς πρόνοιαν μὴ ποιεῖσθε εἰς ἐπιθυμίας</note>

->CHAPTER XIV<-

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'V' showing a figure, possibly a prophet, seated in a landscape, within a square decorative frame.</image-desc>Just as some people are strong in body, others weak, some healthy, and others sick; so in mind some are strong and healthy, others weak and sick. But those strong and healthy in body help the weak and infirm in body; much more should those strong and healthy in mind help the weak and infirm in mind. Now, the strength and health of the mind is a strong and healthy faith. The weakness of faith, however, is an infirmity of the mind. Therefore, when we see those weak in faith, we ought to receive and support them, yet not by judging their thoughts. For just as many who are strong and sound in body often abstain from many things like the infirm, but not for the same reason as the infirm; so many strong and sound in mind abstain from many things—from which the infirm also abstain—yet for a different reason and thought. For while the latter abstain from wine and from meats fearing they might be harmed or that it might be a sin for them to use them, the former abstain from the same things without fearing harm, and without fearing...

<meta>This page continues the philological and moral commentary on Paul’s Epistle to the Romans, specifically Chapter 14. The previous page discussed the authority of the state and the debt of love; this page focuses on the freedom of the Christian conscience regarding food and holy days, and the importance of not acting against one's own convictions.</meta>

...keep it to yourself: have it also before God. **Blessed is he who does not condemn himself in what he approves**, but he who wavers: if he eats, he is condemned, because it is not from faith. For everything that is not from faith: is sin. ¶ It is not enough that someone holds a certain faith within himself: but he must also hold it before God in love and for the salvation of his neighbor, just as it is written: "Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven." <note>Matthew 5:16</note> And when you do anything—whether you drink, or eat, or approve of anything else—that is, whether you attempt to do or to omit something: the Apostle calls you blessed if, out of the fullness of faith, you do not judge yourself to be doing evil, or do not doubt, or do not hesitate <note>Original: *haeres*, literally "get stuck" or "hesitate"</note> that you are sinning in that very thing you attempt. But if you judge that you are doing evil and sinning: as for example, if you judge that you are sinning if you eat of some food, and nevertheless you eat it, you sin and are condemned as one liable to sin, because it is not from a healthy faith; or if it is from faith: it is from a wandering <note>Original: *erronea*</note> faith. And indeed, everything which in this manner is not from a healthy faith: is sin. Truly, when someone, out of weakness of faith and feeble knowledge, hesitates and doubts whether doing something is a sin, and does not doubt that omitting it is not a sin: he ought to commit himself to that which is certain, and flee the uncertain. Therefore, in that case, he ought to omit it and not act. And conversely, if he doubts that omitting it is a sin, but in no way doubts doing it, but knows it to be good: then he ought to do it, and by no means omit it. However, it rarely happens that both—doing and omitting—are doubtful in this way; but if it should happen: by seeking the counsel of another more illuminated in faith, he must either do it or omit it. Also, if you discern that what you attempt to do is a scandal to your neighbor and you nevertheless do it: you judge yourself in what you attempt and you sin, because you do not act from faith, but against faith. If you attempt a food which you know kindles the lust of desire, which you are not accustomed to restrain, or a drink which you know will cast you into drunkenness: you judge yourself in what you attempt and discern, and you sin. And you do not act from the faith which you ought to have as a leader and model in all things. For every such thing: is sin. But now to the examination.

<margin>A 116.</margin>
EXAMINATION of several matters concerning the literal text. ¶ **Vulgate edition.** **Now take up the one who is weak in faith.** ¶ It is enough to say: "the one weak in faith." And that word "take up" <note>Latin: *assumite*</note>: signifies to take into protection, or to help. Paul: "Receive the one who is weak in faith." <note>Greek: τὸν μὲν ἀσθενοῦντα τῇ πίστει προσλαμβάνεσθε</note> ¶ **Vulgate edition.** **For another believes he may eat all things.** ¶ Rather, "one indeed believes" <note>Latin: *hic quidem credit*</note>: as is the custom to speak in partitions. And the word "he" <note>Latin: *se*</note> is superfluous. And this little part, "believes to eat all things," should be said more suitably to the custom of Roman speech as: "believes all things are to be eaten." <note>The author is correcting the Latin grammar to better reflect Greek/Classical style.</note> Paul: "One indeed believes he may eat all things." <note>Greek: ὃς μὲν πιστεύει φαγεῖν πάντα</note> ¶ **Vulgate edition.** **But he who is weak: let him eat vegetables.** ¶ Paul does not command or order this: but says it through the <term>indicative</term> <note>The mood of a verb used for statements of fact, rather than commands.</note>, "he eats." And in the plural: "vegetables" <note>Latin: *olera*</note>. Paul: "But the one who is weak eats vegetables." <note>Greek: ὁ δὲ ἀσθενῶν λάχανα ἐσθίει</note> For some Jews who had come to Christianity and were at Rome: were very scrupulous regarding foods, and in their weakness of faith: they even made some of the Christians from the Gentiles weak regarding foods, as those who less understood the faith of Christ and the sense of the Scriptures. Paul says these people are to be taken into protection here; for the scrupulous and those of a fearful conscience: are to be helped, and if it can be done, healed. For they would be healed: if they tasted the true understanding of the Scriptures.

<margin>A 118.</margin>
¶ **Vulgate edition.** **For another judges between day and day: but another judges every day.** ¶ Because there is a partition here, it can be said as was stated: "One indeed judges a day between a day," or "besides a day," "but that one judges every day." Paul: "One indeed judges one day above another; another judges every day." <note>Greek: ὃς μὲν κρίνει ἡμέραν παρ᾽ ἡμέραν, ὃς δὲ κρίνει πᾶσαν ἡμέραν</note> ¶ **Vulgate edition.** **Let everyone abound in his own sense.** ¶ It can equally be said: "Let each one be satisfied in his own mind," or "in his own sense." Paul: "Let each be fully convinced in his own mind." <note>Greek: ἕκαστος ἐν τῷ ἰδίῳ νοῒ πληροφορείσθω</note> ¶ **Vulgate edition.** **He who observes the day: observes it for the Lord. And he who eats: eats for the Lord.** ¶ After the phrase "he who observes the day observes it for the Lord": an entire similar negative phrase is missing, namely: "and he who does not observe the day, to the Lord he does not observe it." However, some prefer that where it says "observes" <note>Latin: *sapit*</note>: it should be translated as "regards" <note>Latin: *sentit*</note>. Paul: "He who regards the day, regards it for the Lord; and he who does not regard the day, to the Lord he does not regard it. And he who eats, eats for the Lord and gives thanks to God." <note>Greek: ὁ φρονῶν τὴν ἡμέραν κυρίῳ φρονεῖ, καὶ ὁ μὴ φρονῶν τὴν ἡμέραν κυρίῳ μὴ φρονεῖ, καὶ ὁ ἐσθίων κυρίῳ ἐσθίει καὶ εὐχαριστεῖ τῷ θεῷ</note>

<margin>B 119.</margin>
¶ **Vulgate edition.** **For in this CHRIST died and rose again: that he might rule over both the living and the dead.** ¶ It should rather be said "he was dead" <note>Latin: *mortuus fuit*</note>: just as the Lord says of himself in the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation 1:17-18</note>, "I am the first and the last, and the living one, and I was dead: and behold I am living forever and ever." If he is living: how did he die? That one who is living is dead: no one will concede, not even those whom the phantoms of sophistry disturb. In the Greek, the past tense is clearly designated, as if we said "he was dead" or "he met death": and so openly that it is the same in the word "he rose again." Wherefore the ancient translator <note>The author of the Vulgate</note> ought to have made the past tense clear there as well. Truly, even after "he rose again": the word "he lived" was omitted. Paul: "For to this end Christ both died, and rose, and lived again, that he might rule..." <note>Greek: εἰς τοῦτο γὰρ Χριστὸς καὶ ἀπέθανεν καὶ ἀνέστη καὶ ἔζησεν ἵνα καὶ με...</note>
