<meta>This page continues the philological analysis of the Epistle to the Romans, transitioning from the end of Chapter 14 into the beginning of Chapter 15. The author compares the Latin Vulgate translation against the original Greek, focusing on nuances of verbs and the placement of the final doxology.</meta>

Romans.
I

<margin>and that he might rule over the dead and the living <note>Original Greek: ϗ̄ νεκρῶ̄ν ϗ̄ ζώ̄ντων κυριεύσῃ (Romans 14:9)</note></margin>
<margin>120</margin> ¶ The Vulgate edition: *I know and trust in the Lord JESUS.*
It ought rather to be said: "I am persuaded" or "I have been made certain in the Lord Jesus." For that is what the word <term>peithomai <note>original: πείθομαι; to be won over or convinced</note></term> means, which Paul uses here. Indeed, the old translator <note>The author of the Vulgate</note> in the following chapter translates it as "I am certain," where he says: "I myself am certain of you, my brothers." Similarly, in the second epistle to Timothy, he translates the same word as "I am certain," where it is read: "I know him in whom I have believed, and I am certain that he is able to keep my deposit until that day." Paul says: *I know and have been persuaded in the Lord Jesus.* <note>Original Greek: οἶδα καὶ πέπεισμαι ἐν κυρίῳ ἰησοῦ (Romans 14:14)</note>

<margin>C 121</margin> ¶ The Vulgate edition: *For whom CHRIST died.* <note>original: mortuus est</note>
¶ It should be said (as seen previously): "He was dead" <note>original: mortuus fuit</note>. Paul says: *for whom Christ died.* <note>Original Greek: ὑπὲρ οὗ χριστὸς ἀπέθανεν</note> But you will say that "dead" is now a noun and now a participle. When it is a noun, it is not aptly said of Christ that "he is dead" <note>implying a current state</note>, but when it is a participle, there is perhaps nothing jarring in saying "he who died"—not now, but once in the past. You speak truly; but it is better explained by "was [dead]," so that ambiguity is removed and every absurd interpretation is avoided. Just as in Paul's writing, neither through ambiguity nor through the fantasy of an absurd understanding is anything [wrongly] contained. What of the fact that when the Latins join those participles with present verbs, they use the participles for the present, and with past verbs for the past? Truly, if it happens that we speak otherwise at some point, we shall follow the custom of the old translator and the now-accepted phrasing (as if "is dead" and "was dead" were the same).

¶ The Vulgate edition: *Therefore let not our good be blasphemed.*
¶ It should be said: "your good." Paul says: *your good.* <note>Original Greek: ὑμῶν τὸ ἀγαθόν</note>

¶ The Vulgate edition: *For he who in this serves CHRIST, pleases God.*
¶ In *these things*, it should be said—namely in righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit. Paul says: *for he who in these things serves Christ is pleasing to God.* <note>Original Greek: ὁ γὰρ ἐν τούτοις δουλεύων τῷ χριστῷ εὐάρεστος θεῷ</note>

¶ The Vulgate edition: *Nor in which your brother is offended.*
¶ "Let us guard" is not found in Paul; but only "those things which are of mutual edification," and that refers back to the preceding verb "let us follow" or "pursue," which is the same thing. Paul says: *and the things of edification for one another.* <note>Original Greek: καὶ τὰ τῆς οἰκοδομῆς τῆς εἰς ἀλλήλους</note>

<margin>D 122</margin> ¶ The Vulgate edition: *But all that is not from faith is sin.* And he immediately adds: *but we who are stronger.* Paul used the verb <term>proskoptei <note>original: προσκόπτει; to strike against or stumble</note></term> in place of a passive; it should be read as "stumbles." Paul says: *nor in that which your brother stumbles.* <note>Original Greek: μηδὲ ἐν ᾧ ὁ ἀδελφός σου προσκόπτει</note>

¶ Truly, in the Greek copies, immediately after "everything that is not from faith is sin," there is added this praise and thanksgiving: *To him who is able to strengthen you according to my gospel and the preaching of Jesus Christ, according to the revelation of the mystery kept secret for long ages but now manifested* <note>Original Greek: τῷ δὲ δυναμένῳ ὑμᾶς στηρίξαι κατὰ τὸ εὐαγγέλιόν καὶ τὸ κήρυγμα ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ, κατὰ ἀποκάλυψιν μυστηρίου χρόνοις αἰωνίοις σεσιγημένου, φανερωθέντος δὲ νῦν</note> and the rest that follows. That is: "Now to him who is able to confirm us according to my gospel and the preaching of JESUS CHRIST, through the revelation of the mystery kept silent in worldly times, but now manifested according to the scriptures of the prophets, by the command of the eternal God, made known for the obedience of faith among all nations, to the only wise God, through JESUS CHRIST, to whom be glory forever. Amen." And this thanksgiving is at the end of the epistle <note>Romans 16:25-27</note>; I do not know whether it was translated by the [original] translator or by someone else. We have also reserved it to be placed in that spot because of the custom of the Latin copies. However, wherever it is placed, it is worthy and full of the Apostle's piety. We ought always to be mindful of it, whether in the beginning, the middle, or the end. Therefore, to the only wise God be all praise and honor, glory, and thanksgiving forever.

### CHAPTER XV.

<image-desc>A large decorative historiated initial 'L'. The scene inside the woodcut depicts a bearded man in robes kneeling in a landscape, looking upward toward the heavens in a prayerful pose. In the background are hills and some architectural structures.</image-desc>

<margin>123</margin> **M**ost people <note>original: Plerique</note> (as has been said) abstain from many things, believing it to be a sin where there is no sin. But those who are sound and strong recognize that it is not sin, and they are able to use those things. The former do not, because they are held back by that weakness for a long time. For he who judges [it to be sin]: if he uses it, he condemns himself. Nevertheless, those who are sound ought not to boast in this and despise the weak, or please themselves by always doing whatever is permitted to them, especially if they know it hurts the weak person. Truly, if one knows that by using it he can benefit the weak person, let him use it; if he knows that by abstaining he benefits him, let him not use it. For neither using nor not using is a sin; but to harm a brother and hurt him is a sin.

¶ Which Paul also adds, saying: ¶ *But we who are strong ought to bear the weaknesses of the weak, and not to please ourselves. Let each of us please his neighbor for his good, for edification. For even CHRIST did not please himself; but as it is written: The reproaches of those who reproached you fell upon me.*

¶ He adds the reason why no one should please himself—that is, always freely doing what is permitted without sin: the imitation of Christ. For even he was permitted, without sin, both to use riches and to flee the troubles of poverty, and to turn away from the reproaches and insults that were cast upon him, and all the other hard things he endured for us. He says, "I am poor and in labors from my youth." And this which the most blessed apostle brings forward is from Psalm 68 <note>Psalm 69 in modern bibles</note> where it is now read: *The reproaches of those who reproached you fell upon me.* And it follows: *And I covered my soul in fasting, and it became a reproach to me. And I made sackcloth my clothing...*

COM.

[Page 101]

[If you] have faith within yourself: have it also before God. Blessed is he who does not judge himself in what he approves. But he who wavers, if he eats, is condemned, because it is not from faith. For everything that is not from faith is sin. ¶ It is not enough that someone has a certain faith within himself; he must also hold it before God in the love and salvation of his neighbor, just as it is written: *Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven.* ¶ And when you do something, whether you drink or eat, or whatever else you approve—that is, whether you attempt to do or to omit something—the apostle calls you blessed if, out of the fullness of faith, you do not judge yourself to be doing wrong, or do not doubt, or hesitate that you are sinning in that very thing you attempt. If, however, you judge that you are doing wrong and sinning—as for example if you judge that you sin if you eat of some food, and yet you eat—you sin and are condemned as one liable for sin, because it is not from a sound faith; or if it is from faith, it is from an erroneous faith. And indeed, everything that is not from sound faith in this manner is sin. Truly, when someone, out of weakness of faith and feeble knowledge, hesitates and doubts whether doing something is a sin, and yet does not doubt that omitting it is not a sin: he ought to commit himself to that which is certain and flee the uncertain. Therefore, in that case, he ought to omit it and not act. Conversely, if he doubts that omitting it is a sin, but in no way doubts that doing it is good: then he ought to do it and by no means omit it. However, it rarely happens that both—doing and omitting—are doubtful in this way. If that should happen, after taking counsel from another who is more enlightened in faith, he must either do it or omit it. Also, if you discern that what you attempt to do is a stumbling block to your neighbor, and yet you do it: you judge yourself in what you attempt, and you sin, because you are not acting out of faith, but against faith. If you attempt a food which you know kindles the desire of lust, which you are not accustomed to restrain, or a drink which you know will cast you into drunkenness: you judge yourself in what you attempt and discern, and you sin; and you are not acting from the faith which you ought to have as a guide and model in all things. For all such is sin. But now to the examination.

### EXAMINATION of several points concerning the letter.

¶ The Vulgate edition: *Now take up the one who is weak in faith.* <note>original: "Infirmum autem in fide assumite" (Romans 14:1)</note> ¶ It is sufficient to say: "weak in faith" <note>the author suggests a simpler Latin phrasing "infirmum fide" over "in fide"</note>. And that "take up" signifies "take into protection" or "help." Paul says: *the one being weak in faith, receive.* <note>original Greek: τὸν ἀσθενοῦντα τῇ πίστει προσλαμβάνεσθε</note> ¶ The Vulgate edition: *For another believes he eats all things.* <note>original: "Alius enim credit manducare se omnia" (Romans 14:2)</note> ¶ Rather, here "one indeed" <note>original: "cuidem"</note> believes, as is the custom in speech involving divisions <note>referring to the Greek structure "one... but another..."</note>. And "himself" <note>original: "se"</note> is superfluous. And this phrase "believes he eats all things" is more suitably said according to the custom of Roman speech as "believes all things are to be eaten." Paul says: *one indeed believes [he may] eat all things.* <note>original Greek: ὃς μὲν πιστεύει φαγεῖν πάντα</note> ¶ The Vulgate edition: *But he who is weak, let him eat vegetables.* <note>original: "Qui autem infirmus est : olus manducet"</note> ¶ Paul does not command or order this <note>using the subjunctive/imperative</note>, but says "he eats" <note>original: "manducat"</note> through the indicative; and in the plural: "vegetables" <note>original: "olera"</note>. Paul says: *but the one being weak eats vegetables.* <note>original Greek: ὁ δὲ ἀσθενῶν λάχανα ἐσθίει</note> For some Jews who had come to Christianity and were at Rome were very scrupulous concerning foods and weak in faith; and by their weakness, they also made some Christians from the Gentiles weak concerning foods, such as those who less understood the faith of Christ and the sense of the scriptures. Paul says these are to be taken under protection here. For the scrupulous and those of fearful conscience are to be helped, and if possible, healed; for they would be [healed] if they tasted the true understanding of the scriptures.

<margin>
A
118.
</margin>

¶ The Vulgate edition: *For one judges a day between a day: but another judges every day.* <note>original: "Nam alius iudicat diem inter diem : alius autem iudicat omnem diem" (Romans 14:5)</note> ¶ Because there is a division here, it can be said as was mentioned: "One indeed judges a day over a day," or "beyond a day," while "another judges every day." Paul says: *one indeed judges a day over a day, but another judges every day.* <note>original Greek: ὃς μὲν κρίνει ἡμέραν παρ᾽ ἡμέραν, ὃς δὲ κρίνει πᾶσαν ἡμέραν</note> ¶ The Vulgate edition: *Let everyone abound in his own sense.* <note>original: "Vnusuquisq̃ in suo sensu abūdet" (Romans 14:5)</note> ¶ It can equally be said: "let everyone be satisfied in his own mind" or "his own thought." Paul says: *let each in his own mind be fully assured.* <note>original Greek: ἕκαστος ἐν τῷ ἰδίῳ νοῒ πληροφορείσθω</note> ¶ The Vulgate edition: *He who regards the day, regards it for the Lord. And he who eats, eats for the Lord.* <note>original: "Qui sapit diem : domino sapit . & qui manducat : domino manducat" (Romans 14:6)</note> ¶ After the phrase "he who regards the day regards it for the Lord," a whole similar negative phrase is missing, namely: "and he who does not regard the day, does not regard it for the Lord." However, some prefer that where "regards" <note>original: "sapit"</note> is said here, it should be translated as "is minded" or "perceives." Paul says: *the one being minded of the day, is minded for the Lord; and the one not being minded of the day, for the Lord is not minded; and the one eating, eats for the Lord and gives thanks to God.* <note>original Greek: ὁ φρονῶν τὴν ἡμέραν κυρίῳ φρονεῖ, καὶ ὁ μὴ φρονῶν τὴν ἡμέραν κυρίῳ μὴ φρονεῖ · καὶ ὁ ἐσθίων κυρίῳ ἐσθίει καὶ εὐχαριστεῖ τῷ θεῷ</note>

119.

¶ The Vulgate edition: *For in this Christ died and rose again: that he might rule over both the living and the dead.* <note>original: "In hoc enim CHRISTVS mortuus est & resurrexit : vt & viuorum & mortuorum dominetur" (Romans 14:9)</note> ¶ It should rather be said "he was dead" <note>original: "mortuus fuit"</note>, just as the Lord says of himself in the Apocalypse: "I am the first and the last, and the living one, and I was dead; and behold, I am living forever and ever." If he is living, how "is he dead"? <note>The author is critiquing the Latin tense; "mortuus est" can mean "he is dead," whereas "mortuus fuit" clarifies the past action.</note> No one will concede that he who is living is dead, not even those who are troubled by the phantasms of sophistry. And the past tense is clearly designated in the Greek, as if we were to say "he was dead" or "he met death"; and it is just as clear in the word "he rose again." Therefore, the old translator <note>the author of the Vulgate</note> should have made the past tense clear there as well. Truly, even after "he rose again," the word "he lived" <note>original: "vixit"</note> was omitted. Paul says: *for unto this Christ both died and rose and lived, so that also...* <note>original Greek: εἰς τοῦτο γὰρ Χριστὸς καὶ ἀπέθανεν καὶ ἀνέστη καὶ ἔζησεν ἵνα καὶ...</note>

<meta>This page continues the philological analysis of the final verses of Romans 14 and begins the commentary on Chapter 15. # Romans

...and might be Lord of both the dead and the living. <note>original: "ϗ νεκρῶν ϗ ζώντων κυριεύση"</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *I know and am confident in the Lord Jesus.* <note>Romans 14:14</note>
<margin>120</margin> It should rather be said, "I am persuaded" or "I have been made certain" in the Lord Jesus. For that is what the word *pepeismai* <note>original: "πέπεισμαι"</note> which Paul uses here, signifies. And the ancient translator <note>The "ancient translator" usually refers to the traditional author of the Vulgate.</note> in the following chapter translates it as "I am certain," where he says: *I myself also am certain of you, my brothers.* Similarly, in the second epistle to Timothy, he translates the same word as "I am certain," where we read: *I know whom I have believed, and I am certain that he is able to keep that which I have committed unto him.* <note>2 Timothy 1:12</note> Paul: *I know and am persuaded in the Lord Jesus.* <note>original: "οἶδα καὶ πέπεισμαι ἐν κυρίω ἰησοῦ"</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *For whom Christ died.* ¶ It should be said (as seen previously) "he has been dead" <note>original: "mortuus fuit"</note>. Paul: *for whom Christ died.* <note>original: "ὑπὲρ οὗ χριστὸς ἀπέθανεν"</note> But you will say that "dead" is now a noun and now a participle. When it is a noun, "Christ is dead" <note>original: "mortuus est"</note> is not aptly said, but when it is a participle, perhaps it is not absurd to say "he who is dead"—not now, but formerly. You speak truly, but that "formerly" is better explained by "was" <note>original: "fuit"</note>, and thus ambiguity is removed, along with every absurd interpretation. Thus also in Paul, neither ambiguity nor the fantasy of an absurd interpretation is contained. What then? Since the Latins join those participles with present tenses, they use participles for the present, and with past tenses for the past. But if it happens that we sometimes speak otherwise, we shall follow the custom of the ancient translator and the now-accepted speech (as if "has died" <note>original: "mortuus est"</note> and "was dead" <note>original: "mortuus fuit"</note> were the same). ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Therefore, let not our good be blasphemed.* ¶ It should say "your good." Paul: *your good.* <note>original: "ὑμῶν τὸ ἀγαθόν"</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *For he who in this serves Christ pleases God.* <margin>¶</margin> It should say "In these," namely in righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit. Paul: *For he who in these things serves Christ is pleasing to God.* <note>original: "ὁ γὰρ ἐν τούτοις δουλεύων τῶ χριστῶ εὐάρεστος τῶ θεῶ"</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *And let us keep those things which belong to mutual edification.* ¶ "Let us keep" is not found in Paul; rather, it refers only to "those things which are for mutual edification," and it is traced back to the preceding verb <margin>D 122</margin> "let us follow" or "let us pursue," which is the same thing. Paul: *and the things of edification for one another.* <note>original: "καὶ τὰ τῆς οἰκοδομῆς τῆς εἰς ἀλλήλους"</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Nor in which your brother stumbles.* ¶ It seems Paul used the word *proskoptei* <note>original: "προσκόπτει"</note> for the passive; or it should be read as "is offended." Paul: *nor in that by which your brother stumbles.* <note>original: "μηδὲ ἐν ᾧ ὁ ἀδελφός σου προσκόπτει"</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *But everything that is not from faith is sin.* And he immediately adds: *We who are stronger ought to...* ¶ However, in the Greek copies, immediately after "everything that is not from faith is sin," this praise and thanksgiving is added: *Now to Him who is able to strengthen you according to my gospel and the preaching of Jesus Christ, according to the revelation of the mystery kept secret for eternal ages, but now manifested...* <note>This is the Doxology usually found at Romans 16:25-27.</note> and the rest that follows. That is: *Now to Him who is able to confirm us according to my gospel and the preaching of Jesus Christ, through the revelation of the mystery kept silent in secular times, but manifested now, according to the scriptures of the prophets, by the command of the eternal God, made known for the obedience of faith among all nations, to the only wise God: through Jesus Christ, to Him be glory forever. Amen.* And this thanksgiving at the end of the epistle—I know not whether it was translated by the [original] translator or by another. We have also reserved it to be placed in that location <note>i.e., at the end of Chapter 16</note> because of the custom of the Latin copies. Wherever it may be placed, however, it is worthy and most full of the Apostle's piety. And we ought always to be mindful of it, whether at the beginning, the middle, or the end. To the only wise God, therefore, be all praise and honor, glory, and thanksgiving forever.

### CHAPTER XV.

<note>The decorative initial P depicts a pastoral landscape with classical or biblical figures near buildings.</note>

Many (as has been said) abstain from many things, believing it to be a sin where there is no sin; but those who are healthy and strong recognize that it is not, and they are able to use those things. However, they should not do so at first as long as the others are held by that weakness. For he who judges [it a sin], if he uses it, condemns himself. Nevertheless, those who are healthy ought not to glory in this and despise the weak, or always do whatever is permitted to them merely to please themselves, if doing so harms the weak. Indeed, if he knows that he can benefit the weak by using it, let him use it; if he knows he can benefit him by abstaining, let him not use it; since neither using nor not using is a sin, but to harm a brother and hurt him is a sin. Which Paul also adds, saying: <margin>123</margin> ¶ *But we who are strong ought to bear the infirmities of the weak and not to please ourselves. Let each of us please his neighbor in what is good for edification. For even Christ did not please himself; but, as it is written: The reproaches of those who reproached you fell on me.* ¶ He adds the reason why no one should please himself—that is, always freely doing what is permitted to him without sin: the imitation of Christ. For it was also permitted to Him, without sin, both to use riches and to flee the troubles of poverty, and to turn away from the reproaches and insults that were imposed, and all other hardships which He endured for us. *I am poor,* He says, *and in labors from my youth.* <note>Psalm 87:16 in the Vulgate numbering</note> And that which the most blessed Apostle brings forward is from Psalm 68 <note>Psalm 69 in modern Bibles</note>, where we now read: *The reproaches of those who reproached you fell on me.* And it follows: *And I covered my soul with fasting: and it was made a reproach to me. And I made sackcloth my garment...*

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the final verses of Romans 14, focusing on the relationship between faith, conscience, and the act of eating. It then transitions into a philological "Examination" (EXAMINATIO) where the author compares the Latin Vulgate translation against the original Greek text to propose more accurate readings.</meta>

# COMMENTARY

...you have within yourself: keep it also before God. Blessed is he who does not judge himself in that which he approves. But he who wavers, if he eats, is condemned, because it is not from faith. For everything that is not from faith is sin. ¶ It is not enough for someone to have a certain faith within themselves; it is also necessary to have it before God in the love and salvation of one's neighbor, just as it is written: *Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.* <note>Matthew 5:16</note> And when you do something, whether you drink, or eat, or attempt any other thing you approve—that is, to do it or to omit it—the apostle calls you blessed if, out of the fullness of faith, you do not judge yourself to be acting wrongly, or do not doubt, or do not hesitate that you are sinning in the very thing you attempt. However, if you judge that you are acting wrongly and sinning—as for example, if you judge that you are sinning if you eat from a certain food, and nevertheless you eat—you sin and are condemned as one guilty of sin, because it is not from a healthy faith. Or, if it is from faith, it is from an erroneous faith. And yet, everything that in this way is not from a healthy faith is sin. Truly, when someone, out of weakness of faith and feeble knowledge, hesitates and doubts whether doing something is a sin, and does not doubt that omitting it is not a sin: they ought to commit themselves to that very thing which is certain and flee the uncertain. Therefore, in that case, they ought to omit it and not act. Conversely, if one doubts whether omitting it is a sin, but in no way doubts doing it—but rather knows it to be good—then they ought to do it and in no way omit it. However, it rarely happens that both—doing and omitting—are doubtful in this way. But if it should happen, after seeking the counsel of another more enlightened in faith, one must either do it or omit it. Also, if you discern that what you attempt to do causes a scandal <term>scandalum: a stumbling block or an action that leads another into sin</term> to your neighbor, and nevertheless you do it: you judge yourself in what you attempt, and you sin, because you do not act from faith, but against faith. If you attempt a food which you know kindles the craving of lust, which you are not accustomed to restrain, or a drink which you know will cast you into drunkenness: you judge yourself in that which you attempt and discern, and you sin. And you do not act from the faith which you ought to have in all things as a leader and model. For every such thing is sin. But now, to the examination.

<margin>A 116,</margin>
¶ EXAMINATION of several points regarding the literal text. ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Now receive him who is weak in the faith.* <note>Romans 14:1</note> ¶ It is sufficient to say: *weak in faith.* And that word "receive" <note>original: "assumite"</note> signifies: take into protection, or help. Paul says: *the one who is weak in faith, receive.* <note>original: "τὸν μὲν ἀσθενοῦντα τῇ πίσει προσλαμβάνεσθε"</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *For another believes he may eat all things.* ¶ Rather, "this man indeed believes," as is the custom of speaking in partitions <note>Partition: a rhetorical device dividing a subject into parts, here "this man... that man."</note>. And "himself" <note>original: "se"</note> is superfluous. In this small part, "believes to eat all things," it should be said more suitably to the custom of Roman speech: *believes all things are to be eaten.* Paul: *who indeed believes to eat all things.* <note>original: "ὃς μὲν πιστεύει φαγεῖν πάντα"</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *But he who is weak, let him eat herbs.* ¶ Paul does not prescribe or command here, but speaks through the indicative: *he eats.* And in the plural: *vegetables.* Paul: *but the one being weak eats vegetables.* <note>original: "ὁ δὲ ἀσθενῶν λάχανα ἐσθίει"</note> For some Jews who had come to Christianity and were at Rome were very scrupulous concerning foods and weak in faith. And by their weakness, they even made some Christians from among the Gentiles weak regarding foods, as those who less understood the faith of Christ and the sense of the Scriptures. Paul says these men are to be taken into protection. For the scrupulous

<margin>A 118,</margin>
and those of fearful conscience are to be helped and, if it can be done, healed. For they would be healed if they tasted the true understanding of the Scriptures. ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *For one judges a day between a day: but another judges every day.* ¶ Because there is a partition here, it can be said as was stated: *This man indeed judges a day between a day,* or *beyond a day, but that one truly judges every day.* Paul: *who indeed judges day by day, who but judges every day.* <note>original: "ὃς μὲν κρίνει ἡμέραν παρ' ἡμέραν , ὃς δὲ κρίνει πᾶσαν ἡμέραν"</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Let every man abound in his own sense.* ¶ It can equally be said: *let each one be satisfied in his own mind* or *his own sense.* Paul: *each in his own mind let him be fully assured.* <note>original: "ἕκαστος ἐν τῷ ἰδίῳ νοῒ πληροφορείσθω"</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *He who tastes the day, tastes for the Lord. And he who eats, eats for the Lord.* ¶ After the phrase "he who tastes the day, tastes for the Lord," an entire similar negative phrase is missing, namely: *and he who does not taste the day, for the Lord he does not taste.* <note>The author notes the Vulgate omitted the phrase "he who regards not the day, to the Lord he doth not regard it."</note> Some prefer that where "tastes" <note>original: "sapit"</note> is said here, it should be translated "perceives" or "thinks." Paul: *The one thinking the day, for the Lord he thinks, and the one not thinking the day, for the Lord he does not think, and the one eating, for the Lord he eats and gives thanks*

<margin>B 119</margin>
*to God.* <note>original: "ὁ φρονῶν τὴν ἡμέραν κυρίῳ φρονεῖ , καὶ ὁ μὴ φρονῶν τὴν ἡμέραν κυρίῳ μὴ φρονεῖ , καὶ ὁ ἐσθίων κυρίῳ ἐσθίει καὶ ἐυχαριστεῖ τῷ θεῷ"</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *For in this Christ died and rose again: that he might rule over both the living and the dead.* ¶ It should rather be said "he was dead" <note>original: "mortuus fuit"</note>, just as the Lord says of himself in the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation</note>: *I am the first and the last, and living, and I was dead: and behold, I am living forever and ever.* <note>Revelation 1:17-18</note> If he is living, how "is he dead"? No one will grant that "he who is living is dead," not even those whom the phantoms of sophistry disturb. In the Greek, the past tense is clearly designated, as if we were to say "he was dead" or "he met death"—and it is so clearly open as in the word "he rose again." Therefore, the old translator ought to have made the past tense clear there as well. Truly, even after "he rose again," the word "he lived" was omitted. Paul: *for unto this Christ both died and rose and lived, that also...* <note>original: "εἰς τοῦτο γὰρ Χριστὸς καὶ ἀπέθανεν καὶ ἀνέστη καὶ ἔζησεν ἵνα καὶ..."</note>

<meta>This page continues the philological "Examination" (EXAMINATIO) of the Epistle to the Romans, specifically focusing on the final verses of Chapter 14. It then transitions into the commentary for Chapter 15, discussing the responsibilities of the "strong" in faith toward the "weak."</meta>

Ro:

# I

<margin>C 120</margin> ...he might be Lord of the living. <note>original Greek: ς, κρῶν ζώντων κυριεύσῃ</note> ¶ Vulgate edition: **I know and am confident in the Lord JESUS.**
It ought rather to be said, "I am persuaded" or "I have been made certain" in the Lord Jesus; for that is what the word *peithomai* <note>original Greek: πείθομαι</note> which Paul uses here signifies. Indeed, the old translator <note>The "old translator" refers to the traditional author of the Latin Vulgate, often identified as St. Jerome.</note> in the following chapter translates it as "I am certain" where he says: "I myself also am certain of you, my brothers." Similarly, earlier and in the second epistle to Timothy, he translates the same word as "I am certain" where it is read: "I know whom I have believed, and I am certain that he is able to keep that which I have committed unto him against that day." Paul: "I know and am persuaded in the Lord Jesus." <note>original Greek: οἶδα καὶ πέπεισμαι ἐν κυρίῳ ἰησοῦ</note> ¶ Vulgate edition: **For whom**
<margin>121</margin> **CHRIST died.** ¶ It should be said (as seen before) "has died" or "was dead." Paul: "for whom Christ died." <note>original Greek: ὑπὲρ οὗ χριστὸς ἀπέθανεν</note> But you will say that "dead" is now a noun and now a participle. When it is a noun, it is not aptly said "Christ is dead," <note>The author is debating the nuance between "is dead" (a state) and "has died" (an action).</note> but when it is a participle, perhaps nothing sounds wrong in saying "he who has died"—not now, but formerly. You speak truly: but that "formerly" is better explained by "was dead," and thus ambiguity is removed, along with any absurd interpretation. This is also true in Paul’s writing, so that no fantasy of ambiguity or absurd understanding is contained therein. What then? When the Latins join those participles with present tenses, do they use participles for the present and with past tenses for the past? Truly, if it happens that we sometimes speak otherwise, we shall follow the custom of the old translator and the now-accepted phrasing (as if "is dead" and "was dead" were the same). ¶ Vulgate edition: **Therefore, let not our good be blasphemed.** ¶ It should say "your good." Paul: "your good." <note>original Greek: ὑμῶν τὸ ἀγαθόν</note> ¶ Vulgate edition: **For he who in this serves CHRIST: pleases God.** ¶ It should say "In these things," namely: in justice, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit. Paul: "For he who in these things serves Christ is pleasing to God." <note>original Greek: ὁ γὰρ ἐν τούτοις δουλεύων τῷ χριστῷ εὐάρεστος θεῷ</note> ¶ Vulgate edition: **And let us keep those things which are of mutual edification.** ¶ "Let us keep" is not found in Paul; rather, only "the things which are for mutual edification," and this refers back to the preceding verb "let us follow" or "pursue," which is the same thing. Paul: "and the things of edification
<margin>D 122</margin> toward one another." <note>original Greek: καὶ τὰ τῆς οἰκοδομῆς εἰς ἀλλήλους</note> ¶ Vulgate edition: **Nor in that which your brother stumbles.** ¶ It seems Paul used the word *proskoptei* <note>original Greek: προσκόπτει</note> as a passive; or it should be read "is offended." Paul: "nor in that which your brother stumbles." <note>original Greek: μηδὲ ἐν ᾧ ὁ ἀδελφός σου προσκόπτει</note> ¶ Vulgate edition: **But all that is not from faith: is sin.** And immediately he joins to this: **But we who are stronger.** ¶ However, in the Greek manuscripts, immediately after "all that is not from faith is sin," this praise and thanksgiving is joined: "Now to him who is able to strengthen you according to my gospel and the preaching of Jesus Christ, according to the revelation of the mystery which was kept secret since the world began, but now is made manifest..." <note>original Greek: τῷ δὲ δυναμένῳ ὑμᾶς στηρίξαι κατὰ τὸ εὐαγγέλιόν μου καὶ τὸ κήρυγμα ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ. κατὰ ἀποκάλυψιν μυστηρίου χρόνοις αἰωνίοις σεσιγημένου, φανερωθέντος δὲ νῦν</note> and the rest that follows. That is: "Now to him who is able to strengthen us according to my gospel and the preaching of JESUS CHRIST, through the revelation of the mystery kept silent in secular times but now made manifest, according to the scriptures of the prophets, by the command of the eternal God, made known to all nations for the obedience of faith; to the only wise God: through JESUS CHRIST, to him be glory forever. Amen." And this thanksgiving at the end of the epistle: I know not whether it was translated by the [original] translator or by someone else. We have also reserved it to be placed in that location <note>The author refers to placing the doxology at the end of Chapter 16, as is common in Latin Bibles.</note> due to the custom of the Latin manuscripts. Wherever it may be placed, however, it is worthy and most full of the apostle’s piety. And we ought always to be mindful of it, whether at the beginning, in the middle, or at the end. Therefore, to the only wise God: be all praise and honor, glory, and thanksgiving forever.

## CHAPTER XV.

<image-desc>Decorative initial P featuring a figure, possibly a scholar or saint, seated in profile within a landscape containing trees and architectural elements.</image-desc>Many (as has been said) abstain from many things, believing it to be a sin where there is no sin. However, those who are healthy and strong recognize that it is not a sin and are able to use those things. But the former cannot, so long as they are held by that infirmity. For he who wavers, if he uses it, condemns himself. Nevertheless, those who are healthy ought not to boast in this, nor despise the weak, or always do whatever is permitted for their own
<margin>123</margin> pleasure, if doing so harms the weak person. Indeed, if one knows that by using a thing they can benefit the weak, let them use it. If they know that by abstaining they benefit them, let them not use it. Since neither using nor not using is a sin, but to harm a brother and wound him is a sin. This is what Paul adds, saying: ¶ **But we who are strong ought to bear the infirmities of the weak, and not to please ourselves. Let every one of us please his neighbor in that which is good for edification. For even CHRIST did not please himself; but, as it is written: The reproaches of those who reproached you fell on me.** ¶ He adds the reason why no one should please themselves—that is, always freely doing what is permitted without sin—which is the imitation of Christ. For it was permitted to him also, without sin, to use riches, to flee the hardships of poverty, and to decline the reproaches and insults that were heaped upon him, and all the other hard things he sustained for us. "I am poor," he says, "and in labors from my youth." And this which the most blessed apostle brings forward is from Psalm 68 <note>Psalm 69 in modern numbering.</note> where we now read: **The reproaches of those who reproached you fell on me.** And there follows: **And I covered my soul with fasting: and it was made a reproach to me. And I made sackcloth my garment.**

...and I became a proverb to them. **For these things were written for our instruction: so that we might imitate Christ the Lord, not pleasing ourselves, but considering the salvation of others (for he endured these things so that he might heal us from the sicknesses of death), so that the truth of the scriptures might leave us an example, consolation, and the hope of true goods.** <note>original: "Haec enim ad nostram doctrinam scripta sunt... vt nobis exemplum / consolationem / & verorum bonorum spem veritas scripturarum relinqueret."</note> This is what Paul adds in this way: ¶ For whatever things were written before were written for our instruction, that through patience and the comfort of the scriptures we might have hope. ¶ To this reason for why the scriptures were left to us, he adds a petition <note>original: "imprecationem"—usually a curse, but here used in the sense of a solemn prayer or invocation.</note> of a holy and pious heart, which may God through his mercy make effective in these times throughout the whole world; and may all nations everywhere glorify God—that is, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ—with one mind and one mouth. This is Paul’s holy petition: ¶ Now may the God of patience and consolation grant you to be like-minded toward one another, according to CHRIST JESUS, that with one mind and one mouth you may glorify the God and Father of our Lord JESUS CHRIST.

¶ Truly, it cannot happen that all are of one mind and glorify God with one harmonious voice unless there is mutual love among them all. Moreover, mutual love cannot exist unless the strong take up the care and protection of the weak, the rich of the poor, the prudent of the ignorant, and the wise of the foolish; just as Christ, for the glory of God, took up our protection in all things. I say "our" protection: both of the Jews and of the Gentiles. Of the Jews indeed, by showing that the promises of God were true for them through the seal of circumcision; <note>The "seal of circumcision" refers to the ritual marking the covenant between God and the Jewish people.</note> but of the Gentiles, <margin>126</margin> by showing that they were called through the mercy of God alone to glorify God. Paul also adds this, saying: ¶ Wherefore receive one another, even as CHRIST also received you to the glory of God. Now I say that CHRIST JESUS was a minister of the circumcision for the truth of God, to confirm the promises made to the fathers. And that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy; as it is written: For this cause I will confess to thee among the Gentiles, O Lord, and sing unto thy name. And again he says: Rejoice, you Gentiles, with his people. And again: Praise the Lord, all you Gentiles; and laud him, all you people. And furthermore, Isaiah says: There shall be a root of Jesse, and he that shall rise to reign over the Gentiles; in him shall the Gentiles hope. ¶ These testimonies are taken from Psalms 18 and 117, <note>The text lists Psalms 17 and 116, following the numbering found in the Latin Vulgate.</note> and Isaiah 11. Again, here, according to his usual piety, he prays for good things for the faithful, saying: ¶ Now the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, that you may abound in hope, through the power of the Holy Spirit. ¶ To this holy and pious petition, he adds a commendation of the Roman faithful, so that by <margin>128</margin> the praise and commendation of the apostle, they might be made more eager in faith and in the love of God and neighbor. This is the praise given to the Romans by the most blessed apostle: ¶ And I myself also am persuaded of you, my brothers, that you also are full of love, filled with all knowledge, able also to admonish one another. ¶ And would that this praise could truly be said now, both of the Romans and of others who confess the name of Christ with their mouths. But where love is extinguished, religion is likewise extinguished. For we have come to those times of which he himself prophesied. For in the last days, he says, perilous times shall come; and men shall be lovers of their own selves, covetous, boasters, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, unthankful, unholy, without natural affection, truce-breakers, false accusers, incontinent, fierce, despisers of those that are good, traitors, heady, high-minded, and lovers of pleasures more than lovers of God; having a form of godliness, but denying the power thereof. <note>The author is quoting 2 Timothy 3:1-5 to lament the moral decay of his own era.</note> These, alas, are our times. But may God, through his great mercy, quickly rekindle the extinguished spark in the hearts of men, so that faith and love may appear revived, and the praise of the apostle may be owed to them, and the worship due to God may be paid. What do these earthquakes portend? What do so many wars? What do the openings of the earth? What do the appearances of monsters and portents? What do these persecutions and scourges of the church portend, if not at last some arrival of warmth after such freezing cold? May God and the Holy Spirit send warmth into the world—and send it quickly—which is so necessary for the reviving of souls. But what humility is found in his deeds! For Paul, full of the Holy Spirit, in whom Jesus Christ speaks, excuses himself to the Romans <margin>130</margin> for the boldness of his writing, while also subjoining the reason for his boldness—that is, his confidence—surely condemning all the proud by his own humility. And he says: ¶ Nevertheless, brothers, I have written the more boldly unto you in part, as putting you in mind, because of the grace that is given to me of God, that I should be the minister of JESUS CHRIST to the Gentiles, ministering the gospel of God, that the offering up of the Gentiles might be acceptable, being sanctified by the Holy Spirit. I have therefore whereof I may glory through JESUS CHRIST in those things which pertain to God. For I will not dare to speak of any of those things which CHRIST has not wrought by me, to make the Gentiles obedient, by word and deed, through mighty signs and wonders, by the power of the Spirit of God. So that from Jerusalem, and round about unto Illyricum, <note>Illyricum was a Roman province located in the western Balkans, along the eastern coast of the Adriatic Sea.</note> I have fully preached the gospel of CHRIST. Yea, so have I strived to preach the gospel, not where CHRIST was named, lest I should build upon another man’s foundation.

...but as it is written: **To whom he was not announced, they shall see; and those who have not heard shall understand.** ¶ This is the reason why the apostle says he took up such boldness: to have written to the Romans. And he glories—not in himself, but in the grace of Christ and the power of the Spirit—which worked so many and such great things through him. All the places from Jerusalem round about as far as Illyricum were filled with the gospel, both by performing signs and wonders, which he does not rashly or arrogantly attribute to himself, but to Christ the Lord and to the Holy Spirit working through him. He himself was only the organ and instrument of Christ and the Holy Spirit, like a pipe is to a flute player. <note>original: "vt fistula tibicini"—a common metaphor in early Christian writing to describe the relationship between God and the human author.</note> And the people of Illyricum, to whom he had preached the gospel of Christ, are the Dalmatians. <note>Dalmatia was a Roman province on the eastern coast of the Adriatic Sea.</note> Geographers who are not unskilled know how vast and immense the distance is from Jerusalem to there, especially for those who, in the manner of Paul, would complete that journey by traveling in a circuit: passing from Jerusalem through Caesarea, Sidon, Seleucia, Pieria, Cilicia, Lycaonia, Antioch, Pamphylia, Lycia, Caria, and Ephesus; from there also crossing from Asia through the various dangers of the Aegean Sea into Europe, traversing Attica, Boeotia, Achaia, Thessaly, Epirus, Apollonia, and Macedonia, which now borders Illyricum, separated only by mountains. Truly, Luke described his pilgrimage more exactly in the Acts of the Apostles. And that oracle—**to whom he was not announced, they shall see**—is taken from Isaiah 52. Then the apostle gives the Romans the reason for what he had written at the beginning of the epistle:

<margin>130</margin>

But now, having no more place in these regions, and having had a great desire for many years to come to you, when I set out for Spain, I will come to you. For I hope to see you as I pass through, and to be**

For if the Gentiles have shared in their spiritual things, they ought also to minister to them in carnal things.** ¶ That "communion" or contribution which Macedonia and Achaia made was a pious alms collected by the community, which they liberally bestowed upon the needy saints who were in Jerusalem. For there were many poor people in Jerusalem, especially after the apostles went out from Judea to the Gentiles. For as it is written in Acts, as many as were owners of fields or houses brought the price of what they had sold and laid it at the feet of the apostles, and it was distributed to each as anyone had need. However, those from the Gentiles who believed did not follow Christ by leaving everything behind in such great poverty. Therefore, the apostle was very concerned that mercy be shown to the saints who were in Jerusalem and Judea (many of whom had seen Christ the Lord, the author of life and Lord of glory, in the flesh), lest they perish from hunger and nakedness among the other unbelievers—the killers of Christ the Lord—who still raged against them with all cruelty because of Christ. But what he would do after this remarkable work of mercy, having provoked the Romans to similar works of mercy by the example of the Macedonians and Achaians and by his own concern and piety for the

needy, he suggests by saying: ¶ **When therefore I have completed this, and have delivered to them this fruit, I will go by way of you into Spain.** ¶ For he knew that Spain, in the western part, was the end of the world, that is, the *inhabited world*. <note>original: "τῆσ οἰκουμένησ" (tēs oikoumenēs)—the Greek term for the civilized or inhabited world.</note> And for that reason, he desired that this oracle be fulfilled through him in that region: **Their sound went out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.** But you will say: "Did the apostle Paul ever actually set out for Spain?" I believe so, indeed. Sophronius, the Patriarch of Jerusalem, also left this in writing. <note>Sophronius (c. 560–638 AD) was a monk and theologian who became Patriarch of Jerusalem.</note> For he writes that Italy, Gaul, and Spain were illuminated by the passage of the most blessed Paul. He relates that when Paul was received as a guest in Spain in the house of a certain illustrious man named Probus, and Xantippa, the wife of the same Probus, was diligently observing and admiring the modesty of her guest, it happened by divine will that while she was thus intently gazing at the face of the stranger, there appeared on Paul's forehead, as if written in golden letters: **Paul the Apostle, preacher of Christ.** Since she had heard many things about the apostle from prior fame and had long desired to be able to see his face, she collapsed at Paul’s feet, overcome equally by joy and amazement, and with tears. Having been taught the mysteries of Christ, she was reborn in Christ along with her husband and household, being joined to the kingdom of eternal blessedness. It is also handed down that Philotheus, the prince of that region, adhered to Paul and became a confessor of Christ. ¶ How happy are they who exchange an earthly kingdom for an eternal one! But Paul also knew from the Holy Spirit that he would come to the Romans in the abundance of the blessing of the announcement of Christ, provided he was delivered from the Jews, the persecutors of Christ, the apostles, and the disciples. Therefore, he also gave them this sign...

...signifies: likewise he implores the support of their prayers, so that they might not be frustrated of such a great good. Rather, he asks that they themselves might be participants in all the good things which he was about to do in that offering <note>The "offering" refers to the collection of money Paul was bringing to the poor Christians in Jerusalem.</note> which he was about to make to the saints: God well-accepting both the one offering and that offering through their prayers, and God bestowing grace so that he might set out toward them. For he attributes all things to God, as the one who is the most universal <margin>133</margin> providence of all. Yet we ought to dispose ourselves as much as we can to receive that providence. ¶ Which we understand from these things which Paul adds in this manner: ¶ **But I know that when I come to you, I shall come in the fullness of the blessing of the gospel of CHRIST. Now I beseech you, brothers, through our Lord JESUS CHRIST and through the love of the Spirit, that you strive together with me in prayers to God for me, that I may be delivered from the unbelievers who are in Judea, and that my ministry in Jerusalem may be well-acceptable to the saints; that at last I may come to you in joy by the will of God and may rest with you. Now may the God of peace be with you all. Amen.** ¶ For what greater thing could the most blessed apostle pray for the Romans, unless that every good thing be with them? For with whom God is, truly every good thing is undoubtedly with them. ¶ May he also deign to be present with us, and to bestow that grace upon us, so that we may be able to praise, honor, and glorify him for eternal ages with all the saints, perpetually and without end. Amen. But now we must hasten to the examination.

<margin>A</margin> ¶ **EXAMINATION of several points concerning the text.** ¶ **The Vulgate Edition:** <margin>123</margin> *We who are stronger (firmiores) ought to bear the infirmities of the weak (infirmorum).* ¶ In Paul's writing, it is not "stronger" and "weak," but rather "the able" (validi) and "the powerless" (inualidorum). Paul says: <note>original Greek: Ὀφείλομεν δὲ ἡμεῖς οἱ δυνατοὶ τὰ ἀσθενήματα τῶν ἀδυνάτων βαστάζειν — "We who are powerful/able ought to bear the weaknesses of those without power."</note> ¶ **The Vulgate Edition:** *Let each of you (vestrum) please his neighbor.* ¶ It should be said "each of us" (nostrum) in the first person. For Paul has it thus, and it is the more correct speech; it follows from him having said "we ought." <margin>A</margin> And the word "his" is superfluous. Paul says: <note>original Greek: ἕκαστος δὲ ἡμῶν τῷ πλησίον ἀρεσκέτω — "Let each of us please his neighbor."</note> <margin>124</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate Edition:** ¶ *For whatever things were written (scripta sunt), were written (scripta sunt) for our instruction.* ¶ Rather, "written before" or "previously written." <margin>B</margin> Paul says: <margin>125</margin> <note>original Greek: ὅσα γὰρ προεγράφη... προεγράφη — "Whatever was written beforehand... was written beforehand."</note> ¶ **The Vulgate Edition:** *Now may the God of patience and solace (solacij) give you the same mind toward one another.* ¶ What the old translator <note>The "old translator" refers to the author of the Vulgate, traditionally St. Jerome.</note> here renders as "solace," he had rendered just a little bit earlier as "consolation." Why then, when Paul uses the same word, is the translation varied? And regarding what he added, "give you the same mind toward one another," it should rather have been said "grant that you feel the same way mutually." Paul says: <note>original Greek: ὁ δὲ θεὸς τῆς ὑπομονῆς καὶ τῆς παρακλήσεως δώη ὑμῖν τὸ αὐτὸ φρονεῖν ἐν ἀλλήλοις.</note>
¶ **The Vulgate Edition:** *That you may with one mind and one mouth honor (honorificetis) God and the Father of our Lord JESUS CHRIST.* ¶ It should rather be said "Unanimously" and "glorify" (glorificetis). And when we say "and the Father of our Lord," the "and" is used explanatively, as if we were saying "that is, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ." Paul says: <note>original Greek: ἵνα ὁμοθυμαδὸν ἐν ἑνὶ στόματι δοξάζητε τὸν θεὸν καὶ πατέρα τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ.</note> <margin>B</margin> And where it says in Greek "in one mouth," Latin speech <margin>126</margin> is more customary without the preposition "in." ¶ **The Vulgate Edition:** *Wherefore receive (suscipite) one another, as also CHRIST received (suscepit) you unto the honor of God.* ¶ "Receive" and "received" are the same word that the old translator previously translated in the preceding chapter as "take up" (assumite) and "took up" (assumpsit). We have said that this signifies both taking under one's protection and helping. And it should be said "into the glory (gloriam) of God" rather than "into the honor." Paul says: <note>original Greek: διὸ προσλαμβάνεσθε ἀλλήλους καθὼς καὶ ὁ χριστὸς προσελάβετο ὑμᾶς εἰς δόξαν θεοῦ.</note> ¶ **The Vulgate Edition:** *For the truth of God to confirm the promises of the fathers: but that the Gentiles might honor God for (super) mercy.* ¶ What the old translator here calls "for" (super), he previously translated as "because of" (propter) when he said "because of the truth." Therefore, it is better in both places to say "for" (pro) or "on account of" (ob). And where he translated "honor," it should rather have been said "glorify"; it refers back to the verb "I say." It is as if Paul had resumed: "I say that the Gentiles glorify God on account of mercy." Even if we say "for mercy," it means the same thing. Paul says: <note>original Greek: ὑπὲρ ἀληθείας θεοῦ εἰς τὸ βεβαιῶσαι τὰς ἐπαγγελίας τῶν πατέρων, τὰ δὲ ἔθνη ὑπὲρ ἐλέους δοξάσαι τὸν θεόν.</note> <margin>C</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate Edition:** *And I will sing (cantabo) to your name.* <margin>126</margin> ¶ Rather "I will sing a psalm" or "play the harp." Paul says: <note>original Greek: καὶ τῷ ονόματί σου ψαλῶ.</note> ¶ **The Vulgate Edition:** *That you may abound in hope and in the power of the Holy Spirit.* ¶ The connective particle "and" is <margin>127 128</margin> superfluous. Paul says: <note>original Greek: εἰς τὸ περισσεύειν ὑμᾶς ἐν τῇ ἐλπίδι, ἐν δυνάμει πνεύματος ἁγίου.</note> ¶ **The Vulgate Edition:** *Filled with all knowledge, so that you are able to admonish one another (alterutrum).* <margin>D</margin> ¶ More correctly "mutually" or "each other." Paul says: <margin>129</margin> <note>original Greek: πεπληρωμένοι πάσης γνώσεως δυνάμενοι καὶ ἀλλήλους νουθετεῖν.</note> ¶ **The Vulgate Edition:** *That I may be a minister of CHRIST JESUS among the Gentiles, sanctifying (sanctificans) the gospel of God.* ¶ Paul says "Jesus Christ" [reversing the order], and "celebrating a sacred rite" or "making it solemn and famous" rather than "sanctifying." Paul says: <note>original Greek: εἰς τὸ εἶναί με λειτουργὸν ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ εἰς τὰ ἔθνη ἱερουργοῦντα τὸ εὐαγγέλιον... — ierourgounta implies performing a priestly or sacred service.</note>

<margin>Ro.</margin>
<note>original: "ἱερουργέω"</note> of God. For it signifies "to minister" <note>This refers to Paul’s description of his ministry as a sacred or priestly service.</note>, to solemnize and celebrate sacred rites. ¶ **Vulgate Edition.** That the offering of the Gentiles might become acceptable and sanctified in the Holy Spirit. ¶ The copulative particle <note>The word "and".</note> is superfluous here. **Paul:** <note>original: "ἵνα γένηται ἡ προσφορά τῶν ἐθνῶν εὐπρόσδεκτος ἡγιασμένη ἐν πνεύματι ἁγίω"</note> that the offering of the nations might become well-pleasing, sanctified in the Holy Spirit. ¶ **Vulgate Edition.** I have therefore glory in CHRIST JESUS toward God. ¶ If Latin usage allowed it, one should rather say: "I have therefore boasting in Christ Jesus in those things which pertain to God." For *doxa* is translated as "glory," but *kauchesis* is more correctly "boasting" or "glorying." **Paul:** <note>original: "ἔχω οὖν καύχησιν ἐν χριστῶ ἰησοῦ τὰ πρὸς τὸν θεόν"</note> I have therefore boasting in Christ Jesus in those things which pertain to God—as if we were saying "unto those things toward God." ¶ **Vulgate Edition.** For I do not dare— ¶ It should be said in the future tense: "I will dare." **Paul:** <note>original: "τολμησω"</note> I will dare. ¶ **Vulgate Edition.** In word and deeds and in the power of signs, in the power of the Holy Spirit. ¶ It should rather be said "in word and work in the power of signs" without the connecting particle. And "Spirit of God," not "Holy Spirit." **Paul:** <note>original: "λόγω καὶ ἔργω ἐν δυνάμει σημείων καὶ τεράτων ἐν δυνάμει πνεύματος θεοῦ"</note> in word and work, in the power of signs and wonders, in the power of the Spirit of God. ¶ **Vulgate Edition.** so that from Jerusalem and round about as far as Illyricum I have fulfilled the gospel of CHRIST. ¶ It seems more fitting for the Latin language to translate "gospel" in the ablative case <note>i.e., "filled these places WITH the gospel"</note>; <margin>E 129</margin> as if we were saying "from Jerusalem round about as far as the regions of Illyricum I have filled those places with the gospel of Christ." For what is suitable in one language often cannot be maintained in another due to the specific properties of that language. ¶ **Vulgate Edition.** Thus I have preached this gospel, not where CHRIST was named. ¶ Paul does not have "I have preached," but rather that he was "desirous of that honor" <note>Paul uses a word implying a holy ambition or desire for honor.</note> so that he might preach and announce Christ where he had not been heard. And this "ambition" and "desire for honor" is of the best kind. And would that in our own time many such could be found, seeking and (if I may say so) affecting honor, which is nothing other than to consider it an honor. For thus he used "striving for honor" <note>original: "Φιλοτιμούμενον"</note> in a positive sense. **Paul:** <note>original: "οὕτως δὲ φιλοτιμούμενον εὐαγγελίζεσθαι, οὐχ ὅπου ὠνομάσθη χριστός"</note> thus striving for honor to evangelize, not <margin>130 E</margin> where Christ was named. ¶ **Vulgate Edition.** And they who have not heard shall understand concerning him. ¶ "Concerning him" is superfluous in this place. **Paul:** <note>original: "καὶ οἷς οὐκ ἀκηκόασι, συνήσουσι"</note> and those to whom it was not told shall understand. ¶ **Vulgate Edition.** For which cause I was hindered very much from coming to you, and <margin>F 130</margin> have been prevented until now. ¶ It should rather be said: "many times" or "concerning many things." And that whole part "prevented until now" is not found in the Greek, even in the more reliable manuscripts. **Paul:** <note>original: "διὸ καὶ ἐνεκοπτόμην τὰ πολλὰ τοῦ ἐλθεῖν πρὸς ὑμᾶς"</note> Wherefore also I was hindered many times from coming to you. ¶ But now, having no more place in these regions. ¶ Understand this as if we say: "but now having no more work or business in these regions." For that way of speaking was suited to Paul and that time. ¶ **Vulgate Edition.** But having a desire to come to you from many years now past: when I shall begin to set out for Spain. ¶ From Paul we only have "from many years." If, or when, I set out for Spain. And "as if" <note>original: "ὡς ἂν"</note> or as some manuscripts have "as if" <note>original: "ὡς ἐὰν"</note> seems to be used for "when" <note>original: "ὅταν"</note> or "whenever" <note>original: "ὅτεαν"</note>. However, he uses the present indicative "I go/set out" <note>original: "πορεύομαι"</note>; the Latin language more easily admits the present subjunctive. Not that the Apostle's speech is not far more beautiful and eminent. ¶ **Vulgate Edition.** I hope that passing by I may see you: and by you I may be brought on my way there. ¶ In Paul, "that" is not present. Rather: "for I hope, passing through, to see you." However, it is the custom of Latin speakers to turn the participle into a gerundive; and the use of the future infinitive is rare. And that "being brought on my way" which Paul calls "escorted" <note>original: "προπεμφθῆναι"</note> signifies to be honorifically accompanied and sent forward. **Paul:** <note>original: "ἐλπίζω γὰρ διαπορευόμενος θεάσασθαι ὑμας καὶ ἀφ᾽ ὑμῶν προπεμφθῆναι ἐκεῖ"</note> for I hope, passing through, to see you and by you to be escorted there. ¶ **Vulgate Edition.** If I shall first have enjoyed you: but now I shall set out for Jerusalem. ¶ It should rather be said: "If I shall first have been filled or satisfied by you." <margin>F 131</margin> And "I set out" is in the present indicative. **Paul:** <note>original: "ἐὰν ὑμῶν πρῶτον ἀπὸ μέρους ἐμπλησθῶ. νυνὶ δὲ πορεύομαι εἰς ἱερουσαλήμ"</note> if first I am filled by you in part. But now I set out for Jerusalem. ¶ **Vulgate Edition.** For it has pleased those of Macedonia and Achaia to make a certain contribution. ¶ It should rather be said: "For it pleased Macedonia and Achaia." It is the same word which the old translator immediately resumes and translates as "it pleased" when he says: "For it pleased them, and they are their debtors." And what he translates as "contribution," rather means "communion" or "fellowship." **Paul:** <margin>F 133</margin> <note>original: "εὐδόκησαν γὰρ μακεδονία καὶ ἀχαΐα κοινωνίαν τινὰ ποιήσασθαι"</note> for it pleased Macedonia and Achaia to make a certain fellowship. ¶ **Vulgate Edition.** For if the Gentiles have been made partakers of their spiritual things. ¶ Rather: "if the nations have been made partakers." **Paul:** <note>original: "εἰ γὰρ τοῖς πνευματικοῖς αὐτῶν ἐκοινώνησαν τὰ ἔθνη"</note> for if the nations shared in their spiritual things. <margin>G 133</margin> ¶ **Vulgate Edition.** I shall come in the abundance of the blessing of CHRIST. ¶ It should read "in the abundance," or rather "fullness of the blessing of the gospel of Christ." For "of the gospel" is missing. **Paul:** <note>original: "ἐν πληρώματι εὐλογίας τοῦ εὐαγγελίου τοῦ χριστοῦ ἐλεύσομαι"</note> I shall come in the fullness of the blessing of the gospel of Christ. ¶ **Vulgate Edition.** Through the charity of the Holy Spirit: that you help me in your prayers for me to God: ¶ "Holy" and "your" are not found in Paul. And that word "help" signifies to "help in a fight"—that you should strive with me against the unbelieving Jews, in prayer...

### CHAPTER XVI.

<image-desc>A decorative initial letter 'I' featuring a scholar or saintly figure seated at a desk, engaged in writing or study, framed by classical architectural elements.</image-desc>

**IN** this part, the apostle salutes twenty holy men by name and eight women; all of whom were in Rome for a long time before him, announcing Christ and forming the Roman people toward the worship of true piety. The men are Aquila, Epaenetus, Andronicus, Junias, Amplias, Urbanus, Stachys, Apelles, Aristobulus, Herodion, Narcissus, Rufus, Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermas, Patrobas, Hermes, Philologus, Julias, and Nereus. The women are: Prisca—or as some manuscripts have it, Priscilla, who was also the wife of Aquila—Mary, Tryphaena, Tryphosa, Persis, Olympa, the mother of Rufus, and the sister of Nereus. But before he salutes them, he commends Phoebe, a faithful woman, a courier <note>original: "tabellariam"</note> of his letters from Corinth, and a minister <term>minister <gloss>deaconess or servant</gloss></term> of the church of Christ which was in the port of Corinth.

<margin>134</margin>
For they maintain that Cenchreae was a port in Corinth. And the apostle, never omitting the duties of charity and instructing us by his own example to do the same, speaks thus: "I commend to you Phoebe our sister, who is a minister of the church which is in Cenchreae, that you may receive her in the Lord as becomes the saints, and assist her in whatever matter she may have need of you. For she herself has assisted many, including myself." After this commendation of a faithful and obedient woman toward the servants of Christ—for his own kindness was not feigned or superficial but true—he commands them from the heart to favor those whom he knows are burning with the love of Christ. Thus the Romans might know whom they ought to hear and to whom they might safely entrust themselves in faith, saying:

### EXAMINATION of several points regarding the literal text.

<margin>A</margin> ¶ **Vulgate edition.** To the church which is in Cenchreae: that you may receive her in the Lord worthily of the saints. ¶ In Paul, it is "in Cenchreae." And for "worthily," it should rather be said "by the merit of the saints" or "in accordance with the dignity of the saints," <margin>135</margin> of whom Phoebe was a minister. **Paul:** <note>original: "τῆς ἐκκλησίας τῆς ἐν κεγχρεαῖς, ἵνα αὐτὴν προσδέξησθε ἐν κυρίῳ ἀξίως τῶν ἁγίων"</note> of the church in Cenchreae, that you might receive her in the Lord worthily of the saints. ¶ **Vulgate edition.** Salute Prisca and Aquila. ¶ It should rather be read from Paul as "Acyla" with a "y" (upsilon). However, our writers commonly write this name as "Aquila" <note>the Latin word for 'eagle'</note>. **Paul:** <note>original: "ἀσπάσασθε Πρίσκαν καὶ Ἀκύλαν"</note> salute Prisca and Akylas. ¶ **Vulgate edition.** Salute Epaenetus, my beloved, who is the first-fruits of Asia in Christ JESUS. ¶ From Paul, it is "Epaenetus"; and he is the "first-fruits of Achaia," not "Asia"; that is, he who first believed and was won for Christ in Achaia. And "Jesus" is not found in Paul, but only "in Christ." **Paul:** <note>original: "ἀσπάσασθε Ἐπαίνετον τὸν ἀγαπητόν μου, ὅς ἐστιν ἀπαρχὴ τῆς ἀχαΐας εἰς χριστόν"</note> salute Epaenetus my beloved, who is the first-fruits of Achaia unto Christ. ¶ **Vulgate edition.** Salute Mary, who has labored much among you. ¶ It should be said in the first person, "among us," or "toward us." **Paul:** <note>original: "ἀσπάσασθε μαριάμ, ἥτις πολλὰ ἐκοπίασεν εἰς ἡμᾶς"</note> salute Mary, who labored much for us. ¶ **Vulgate edition.** Salute Andronicus and Julia. ¶ here the Greek has "Junia." And Paul calls them "kinsmen," having <term>συγγενεῖς</term> <note>syngeneis</note>, that is, of the same lineage or race, meaning they were Jews. **Paul:** <note>original: "ἀσπάσασθε Ἀνδρόνικον καὶ Ἰουνίαν"</note> salute Andronicus and Junia. <margin>B</margin> ¶ **Vulgate edition.** Salute Ampliatus, most beloved to me in the Lord. ¶ It should be read "Amphias," my beloved in the Lord. <margin>135</margin> **Paul:** <note>original: "ἀσπάσασθε Ἀμπλίαν τὸν ἀγαπητόν μου ἐν κυρίῳ"</note> salute Amplias my beloved in the Lord. ¶ **Vulgate edition.** Salute Urbanus, our helper in CHRIST JESUS, and Stachys, my beloved. ¶ Paul has only "in Christ." And "Stachys" is written with a "y" (upsilon). **Paul:** <note>original: "ἀσπάσασθε οὐρβανὸν τὸν συνεργὸν ἡμῶν ἐν χριστῷ καὶ στάχυν τὸν ἀγαπητόν μου"</note> salute Urbanus our fellow-worker in Christ and Stachys my beloved. ¶ **Vulgate edition.** Salute those who are of Aristobulus' household. ¶ "Household" is not expressly there, but the sense requires it of Paul, who says "salute those who are of the [people] of Aristobulus" (or "Aristoboli," both are commonly said). **Paul:** <note>original: "ἀσπάσασθε τοὺς ἐκ τῶν ἀριστοβούλου"</note> salute those of [the household] of Aristobulus. ¶ **Vulgate edition.** Salute those who are of Narcissus' household, who are in the Lord. ¶ As before, he expressed "household" for clarity. And "Narcissus" should be written with a double "s," not "sc." And the phrase "who are in the Lord" means the same as "believers in the Lord." **Paul:** <note>original: "ἀσπάσασθε τοὺς ἐκ τῶν ναρκίσσου, τοὺς ὄντας ἐν κυρίῳ"</note> salute those of [the household] of Narcissus, those being in the Lord. ¶ **Vulgate edition.** Salute the most dear Persis. ¶ It should rather be said "Persida" or "Persis," "beloved" with an "e" <note>dilectam</note>, maintaining the third declension. **Paul:** <note>original: "ἀσπάσασθε περσίδα τὴν ἀγαπητήν"</note> salute Persis the beloved. ¶ **Vulgate edition.** Salute Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermes, Patrobas, Hermas. ¶ It should be read "Asyncritus" with the second syllable as a "y" (upsilon) and the third with a thin "e" and a Latin "i." And "Phlegonta" or "Phlegon" with an "e," not "Phlegontam" with an "a," so it is recognized as the third declension. And in the first place "Hermas" with an "a," and in the second place "Hermes" with an "e." **Paul:** <note>original: "ἀσπάσασθε ἀσύγκριτον, φλέγοντα, ἑρμᾶν, πατρόβαν, ἑρμῆν"</note> salute Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermas, Patrobas, Hermes. ¶ **Vulgate edition.** And his sister, and Olympas. ¶ It should be read "Olympas" with a "y" (upsilon). **Paul:** <margin>C</margin> <note>original: "καὶ ἀδελφὴν αὐτοῦ καὶ ὀλυμπᾶν"</note> and his sister and Olympas. ¶ **Vulgate edition.** And through sweet words and blessings, they seduce the hearts of the innocent. ¶ Paul speaks in the singular. <note>The author likely means singular concepts rather than plurals like 'blessings'</note>. **Paul:** <margin>136</margin> <note>original: "καὶ διὰ τῆς χρηστολογίας καὶ εὐλογίας ἐξαπατῶσι τὰς καρδίας τῶν ἀκάκων"</note> and through <term>chrestologia</term> <note>smooth or kind speech</note> and <term>eulogia</term> <note>fine speaking or flattery</note> they deceive the hearts of the simple. ¶ **Vulgate edition.** For your obedience has been published in every place. ¶ "To all [people]" rather than "in every place." **Paul:** <note>original: "ἡ γὰρ ὑμῶν ὑπακοὴ εἰς πάντας ἀφίκετο"</note> for your obedience has reached unto all. ¶ **Vulgate edition...**

<header>COMMENTARY</header>

<margin>20. 2. 137 D</margin> **May the God of peace crush Satan under your feet swiftly.** <note>original Latin: "Deus autem pacis conterat sathanā sub pedibus vestris velociter."</note> ¶ One should read "he will crush" <note>conteret</note> in the future indicative, not as a wish <note>optative</note>, but as an assertion and a prophecy; as one who had received the gift of prophecy as well as other charisms of the Holy Spirit. Paul writes: *And the God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet.* <note>original Greek: "ὁ δὲ θεὸς τῆς εἰρήνης συντρίψει τὸν σατανᾶν ὑπὸ τοὺς πόδας ὑμῶν ἐν τάχει."</note> ¶ **I, Tertius, salute you.** <note>Tertius means "Third" in Latin.</note> ¶ "Tertius" is a Roman name which Paul inserted among the Greek names while writing to the Romans. Therefore, Tertius—that is, in the third place. He gave the first place to Timothy; the second to his kinsmen Lucius, Jason, and Sosipater; and the third to himself. But because "Tertius" is a foreign word to the Greeks <note>original: "hellenibus"</note>, the Greeks write it as a proper name, as they do not easily find this passage accessible. Paul writes: *I, Tertius, salute you.* <note>original Greek: "ἀσπάζομαι ὑμᾶς ἐγὼ τέρτιος."</note> ¶ **Vulgate edition: Gaius, my host, and the host of the whole church, salutes you.** ¶ In Paul's text, "Gaius" is written with a 'G' <note>The Vulgate often uses 'C' for 'Caius'</note> and "of the whole church" is in the genitive singular, so that he is understood to be both my host and the host of the entire church. Paul writes: *Gaius, host to me and to the whole church, greets you.* <note>original Greek: "ἀσπάζεται ὑμᾶς γάϊος ὁ ξένος μου καὶ τῆς ἐκκλησίας ὅλης."</note> ¶ **Vulgate edition: Erastus, the Treasurer of the city, salutes you, and Quartus, a brother.** ¶ I believe the word "Treasurer" <note>term: *Arcarius* — literally a keeper of the chest or ark</note> is corrupted, as are many other things in this chapter—not so much by the fault of the translator, but by the long passage of time and the ignorance of scribes. It should have been "Exchequer" <note>term: *Aerarium* — the public treasury</note>, as he was a faithful man entrusted with the care of the public treasury for public expenses. For who would have been more faithful than a Christian man, especially in the primitive church? Paul, however, has "Steward of the city" <note>term: *oeconomum* — a manager or administrator</note>, that is, a public dispenser. And he was of such goodness that Paul named "Quartus" <note>Quartus means "Fourth" in Latin</note> as a brother, using a name foreign to the Greeks but known to the Romans. For he placed himself in the third place (as said before) and admits this man in the fourth place. Indeed, I believe if he had been writing to the Gauls, Germans, or Spaniards—whom he held in his heart as those living at the farthest ends of the earth according to the understanding of Holy Scripture—he would have inserted Gallic, German, or Spanish words. For what languages did Paul not know? He says: "I thank God that I speak in the tongues of you all," or as it is in Greek: *speaking in tongues more than you all.* <note>Reference to 1 Corinthians 14:18</note> There are also those who think "Quartus" is a proper name. Paul writes: *Erastus, the steward of the city, greets you, and Quartus, the brother.* <note>original Greek: "ἀσπάζεται ὑμᾶς ἔραστος ὁ οἰκονόμος τῆς πόλεως, καὶ κούαρτος ὁ ἀδελφός."</note> And among the Greeks, the subscription is held: *Written to the Romans from Corinth. Sent by Phoebe the deacon.*
