# SECOND BOOK OF THE COMMENTARIES ON THE EPISTLES OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PAUL, WHICH IS ON THE FIRST EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS. CHAPTER I

<margin>1</margin>
<image-desc>Large historiated woodcut initial 'F' depicting a figure, likely Saint Paul, seated at a desk and writing in a book, set within a room with classical architectural features like a vaulted ceiling and a view out a window.</image-desc>AT the beginning of the first epistle to the Corinthians, the apostle sets forth this holy greeting. ¶ Paul, called to be an apostle of JESUS CHRIST through the will of God, and Sosthenes our brother: to the church of God which is at Corinth, to those sanctified in CHRIST JESUS, called to be saints with all who call upon the name of our Lord JESUS CHRIST in every place of theirs and ours: grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord JESUS CHRIST. ¶ From the unfolding <note>original: "enucleatione"</note> of the greeting of the epistle to the Romans, this greeting can be immediately understood, as well as the way they aptly speak the word after the phrase "in every place of theirs and ours," which is understood implicitly. And because Paul says he is called and summoned as an apostle of Jesus Christ through the will of God, he makes the divine will the cause of this vocation—so salvific for the whole world—and he prefers the honor of all good to it (as is right). He teaches that in all things the divine will is to be honored first, and that it, rather than himself, is to be looked upon in all good things. Because if this is so, thanks must be returned for all good things to that supreme good will, the chief cause and author of all blessings. Paul does this regarding the gifts of grace poured out upon the Corinthians, saying:

<margin>2</margin>
¶ I give thanks to my God always for you, for the grace of God which is given to you in CHRIST JESUS. Because in everything you are made rich in him: in all knowledge. Thus the testimony of CHRIST is confirmed in you, so that you lack no gift, waiting for the revelation of our Lord JESUS CHRIST, who will confirm you until the end blameless <note>original: "inoxios," meaning harmless or beyond reproach</note> in the day of our Lord JESUS CHRIST. God is faithful, through whom you were called into the fellowship of his son, JESUS CHRIST our Lord. ¶ The revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ is twofold: particular and universal. Particular: it is revealed to every faithful person who has lived faithfully after the course of this gliding and transitory life. Universal: when he shall appear on the last day to everyone, both good and evil, faithful and unfaithful. Paul can be understood regarding both. And in all things—whether in all speech, or in knowledge, or in the confirmation of good works and spiritual gifts—he teaches the Corinthians not to look to themselves but to God who gives grace, speech that is learned and suited for edification, and right knowledge that never deviates from the truth. It is He who confirms and stabilizes until the end. ¶ For if anyone looks to himself, and believes that grace, edifying speech, and knowledge that does not waver from the truth come from himself, and that he can stabilize himself in the good as he wishes: he attributes to himself the glory he owes to God, and has exchanged true glory for empty glory. And when he believes himself to be rich in himself, he is most poor. For he does not have riches in himself, but ought to have sought them in Christ the Lord. And therefore, when he believes he can be stable of his own accord, not recognizing the author of that status and firmness, he is often abandoned to himself. Then he is puffed up by his own sense, is wise in his own conceit, looks down on others, becomes empty, and quite often (as the truth of the matter holds) becomes delirious and foolish. There were some such people among the Corinthians, concerning whom Paul warns them.

<margin>3</margin>
And with flaming charity he exhorts them not to be such, showing what they ought to do, saying: ¶ Now I beseech you, brothers, by the name of our Lord JESUS CHRIST: that you all say the same thing, and that there be no schisms <term>schisms: divisions or formal separations within a religious body</term> among you. But be perfect: in the same mind and in the same judgment. ¶ For it has been declared to me concerning you, my brothers, by those who are of Chloe <note>Chloe was a Christian woman in Corinth; the "those of Chloe" likely refers to her family members or servants who traveled to visit Paul.</note>, that there are contentions among you. Now I say this: that each of you says, "I am indeed of Paul," "I am of Apollo," "furthermore, I am of Cephas <note>Cephas is the Aramaic name for the Apostle Peter.</note>," "but I am of CHRIST." Is CHRIST divided? Was Paul crucified for you, or were you baptized in the name of Paul? I give thanks to God that I baptized none of you except Crispus and Gaius, lest anyone should say that I baptized in my own name. But truly I also baptized the household of Stephanas; otherwise, I do not know if I baptized any other. ¶ Those who are Christians ought to feel the same, to live with the same mind, understanding, and judgment. And that is especially true in those things which regard religion. For there is only one religion, one foundation of religion, one goal of religion, and one head: Jesus Christ, blessed above all forever. There are, however, different states and degrees of religion. For some remain in the world <note>original: "in sæculo," referring to secular life or life outside of a monastery.</note> serving Christ. Others, fleeing the world, shut themselves away in caves and cloisters for the sake of Christ. Yet all, whether remaining in the world but not living according to the world's ways, or taking flight from the world and shutting themselves in solitudes, call themselves religious followers of Christ.

<summary>This page begins the commentary on 1 Corinthians, where Paul addresses the congregation in Corinth, emphasizing that spiritual gifts and status come from God's will rather than human merit. Paul strongly rebukes the emerging factions and "schisms" within the church, where members were pledging loyalty to specific teachers like Apollo or Peter instead of remaining unified in Christ.</summary>
<keywords>1 Corinthians, Paul, Sosthenes, divine will, grace, spiritual gifts, revelation, schisms, Chloe, Apollo, Cephas, baptism, religious life, unity</keywords>

# COMMENTARY.

<margin>
...to resist, many with the sword of their own error. <note>Gregory the Great, *Letters*, Book 3, Letter 35. This refers to the duty of leaders to combat heresy.</note>
...the most wicked depravity... your excellence... Known. These people, therefore, whom the distinction of our faith and laws condemns as worldlings, the audacity of the Donatists <note>The Donatists were a breakaway Christian sect in North Africa who believed that only "pure" clergy could administer sacraments; they were famous for rebaptizing converts.</note> has so grown that they reject the authority of the Church... not only priests of the faith, but those whom the true water of regeneration <note>A technical term for Baptism.</note> had washed, they rebaptize. <note>Gregory the Great, *Letters*, Book 3, Letter 12.</note>
...your [excellence] has so poured forth into the African province... that the devious sects should in no way be restrained with priestly fervor. And a little after: Although therefore heresy [is present], and we desire all heretics [to be returned] to the Catholic [faith] by the vigor of moderation... looking closely, they entirely terrify us... things which were done among you, by the hands of others, which may the Lord turn away... <note>Gregory the Great, *Letters*, Book 4, Letter 47.</note>
...the hearts of heretics in the insanity of a perverse sense... yet in the time of the orthodox emperor they do not presume to speak what they feel, so that we see fulfilled that which is written: "He gathered the waters of the sea as in a bottle." <note>A reference to Psalm 33:7.</note> For the water of the sea is gathered in a bottle because the bitter malice of heretics, whatever hatred it perversely feels, it suppresses in the breast, and does not presume to speak openly. <note>Gregory the Great, *Letters*, Book 4, Letter 10.</note>
...your [excellence] in hostile wars in this... has made to shine with the light of victories, so to meet all the enemies of His Church with all the liveliness of the body, so that from both...
</margin>

...one ought to [follow], since the religion of Christ is one: who alone is to be attended to / alone to be looked upon / alone to be named. For as it is written: there is no salvation in any other / nor is there any other name under heaven given to men / in which it is necessary for us to be saved. <note>original: "non est in aliquo alio salus..." citing Acts 4:12.</note> And no one can lay another foundation: except that which has been laid / which is Christ Jesus. Therefore, let us keep our remaining observations of life under the name of Christ: and having heard the name of Christ—who unites all things—we shall keep the truth toward all, without which no religion stands. No one will dare to think himself better than another / or to judge another servant of his Lord / but he finally shall be thought better whom Christ the Lord (to whom alone the eyes of all shall be intent) shall have accepted more / or rather, shall have made better. For services do not glorify the servant: but after the services, the goodness of the Lord glorifies him. He who judges a servant better than himself: usurps for himself the judgment of the Lord. And that is a matter of pride: since nevertheless the humility of the servants is pleasing to the Lord himself.

---

For he says:
> For Christ did not send me to baptize / but to preach the gospel in the wisdom of speech / lest the cross of CHRIST be rendered void. For the word of the cross / to those who are perishing is foolishness: but to us who are being saved / it is the power of God. For it is written: I will destroy the wisdom of the wise / and the prudence of the prudent I will reject. Where is the wise man / where is the scribe / where is the searcher of this age? Has not God made the wisdom of this world void? After the world did not know God through wisdom in the wisdom of God: it pleased God through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe. For indeed the Jews seek a sign / and the Gentiles seek wisdom: but we preach CHRIST crucified / a scandal indeed to the Jews / but foolishness to the Gentiles / but to those who are called, both Jews and Gentiles, CHRIST the power of God and the wisdom of God. Because the foolishness of God is wiser than men: and the weakness of God is stronger than men. <note>A translation of 1 Corinthians 1:17–25.</note>

Therefore, he who wishes to be saved: let him meditate on the cross of Christ / let him cling to the cross / let him carry it with him / mortifying the members of his body, that is, his lusts. And having followed Christ in this world when He was in the world: he shall follow the same outside the world, living for ages of ages / living also himself for ages of ages. And this is the single and truest <term>theorem</term> <note>In this context, a "theorem" refers to a fundamental principle or established truth of the faith.</note> of the universal religion: whether for those remaining in the world / or those fleeing the world. The wisdom of worldly philosophy does not preach this / the commentaries of philosophers do not contain it / nor do those who probe secret nature, the hidden things—what spirit shakes the lands / what contains or impels the winds / what is the thunder in the cloud / what is snow / what is hail / what is cloud / what is mist / what is the rainbow / what are the stars / the threshing floor and the circular crown <note>Likely referring to halos or celestial orbits.</note> / what are the fires vibrating through the air / what are the lights of terrifying eclipses / and innumerable things of that kind. Those who probe those things, I say, do not reveal this / nor do they understand this: namely, the power and wisdom of the cross. Those things which [human wisdom] seeks out: are great by its own judgment / and are called wisdom. This [the cross], however: is called foolish. Those things are strong: this is weak. Truly, with their investigations they have been ignorant of the salvation of men: which is the chief and most worthy of all investigations. This [the cross], however: makes that salvation known. Both they and all their searched-out things: were invalid and powerless for saving. This, however: saves. Wherefore this is wiser than all human and worldly wisdom: and this is stronger than all worldly strength. And what is Christ's cross / if you compare it to eternal wisdom: but a certain lack of wisdom and a certain foolishness? What is Christ's cross / if compared to His omnipotence: but a certain weakness and debility? Truly these—the foolishness and debility of God—when compared to all the wisdom and strength of the world: are spoken of not through deficiency / but through excellence. "Foolishness" indeed: because it is not the wisdom of the world / but superior to all the wisdom of the world. And "weakness": because it is not the strength of this world / but superior to all the strength of this world. For from whom does anything have that it might be wise or strong: except from that form of wisdom and strength / which is Christ God? But the cross: [is] of the highest wisdom and superior...

<summary>This page explores the unity of the Christian faith centered on Christ, contrasting divine wisdom (the "foolishness" of the cross) with human natural philosophy and heresy. It includes extensive marginal references to Gregory the Great’s letters regarding the Donatist heresy in Africa.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the First Epistle to the Corinthians, specifically expanding on Paul’s discussion of the Cross as the intersection of divine power and wisdom. It follows the previous page's focus on the unity of faith.</meta>

# II 1 Corinthians.

...united to strength. Who therefore could hesitate to believe that in the knowledge and imitation of Him <note>Referring to Christ.</note> there is greater wisdom and strength than in all the wisdom and strength of the world? For what can worldly strength do against spiritual powers and the demons themselves? But the Cross of Christ <note>original: "Crux autem Christi"</note> has power: it has both opened the heavens and shattered the depths of hell <note>original: "tartara"</note>, being higher than heaven and deeper than the underworld. The Jews seek a sign and the Greeks seek wisdom. Let them attend to the Cross alone. Let them behold our Lord Jesus crucified: and both shall have what they seek. The Jews shall have a sign—indeed, a most wonderful sign—even though they spoke against it; a most powerful sign, and a sign which is one and the same with Truth. For no sign can be more powerful or more true. The Greeks <note>original: "gentiles"</note> shall have wisdom: but a wisdom that so surpasses all worldly and secular knowledge as the wisdom that created all things surpasses the world itself. And both shall recognize with us that Christ crucified is the power and wisdom of God. For he who is now Christ, God and the Son of God, blessed forever, is no other than He who was crucified for us; then and now all-powerful and all-knowing. In Him alone everyone ought to place all their wisdom, their strength, and their glory, and in Him alone they should boast. And for this reason, God chose the foolish, the weak, the ignoble, the contemptible, and those things which were not, so that they would have no cause to boast in human wisdom, power, nobility, or honor; instead, they should refer the whole cause of their glorying to God and look to Him alone, from whom they received wisdom, strength, nobility, glory, and their names written in the book of life, so that they might boast in Him alone and not in themselves. Paul makes this manifest to us by the example of the Corinthians, saying:

> <margin>,, ,,</margin> "For you see your calling, brothers: that not many are wise according to the flesh, not many are powerful, not
> <margin>,,</margin> many are noble. But God has chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God has chosen 
> <margin>,,</margin> the weak things of the world to confound the strong. And the ignoble things of the world and the despised
> <margin>,,</margin> has God chosen, and those things which are not, to destroy those things which are: so that no flesh
> <margin>,,</margin> should glory in the sight of God. But from Him you are in CHRIST JESUS, who has become for us 
> <margin>,,</margin> wisdom from God, and justice, and sanctification, and redemption: so that, as it is written,
> <margin>,,</margin> let him who glories, glory in the Lord." <note>1 Corinthians 1:26–31</note>

The Apostle does not deny that some wise, powerful, or noble men among the Corinthians believed in Christ; but he denies that, if there were such men, they were many. And he says nothing here about others besides the Corinthians. For even Christ the Lord chose wise men, as it is written: "Behold, I send to you prophets, and wise men, and scribes; and some of them you will kill and crucify, and some you will scourge in your synagogues and persecute from city to city." <note>Matthew 23:34</note> But even if that testimony of Christ were said concerning those wise according to the spirit and not according to the flesh, who would deny that Dionysius the Areopagite, Hierotheus, and (as Athanasius <note>St. Athanasius of Alexandria, a 4th-century Church Father.</note> holds) Antipatus, Clement, Apollos of Alexandria, and many such men were wise even according to the flesh? Yet they valued that worldly wisdom as nothing <note>original: "floccifacientes," literally "valuing at a tuft of wool."</note> because of the surpassing knowledge of Christ, glorying in Christ alone. So too, those powerful men who were chosen esteemed earthly power as a loss for the sake of Christ. Take, for instance, Abdon and Sennen <note>Persian princes martyred in Rome c. 250 AD.</note>: whom Rome—then the mistress of things and conqueror of the world—marveled at when they were adorned with gold and precious stones sought from the Indian Sea and the East, yet they valued the chains of Christ more than royal power. And who will deny that these same men were noble according to the flesh? Joseph of Arimathea was also noble by the testimony of the Scriptures. Noble too was Sosthenes, the ruler of the synagogue and Paul’s companion. And in the Acts of the Apostles, when Paul and Silas were preaching in Thessalonica, a great number of noble women were added to the ranks of the faithful. Truly, these people preferred the ignominy and despicability of Christ over earthly nobility and honor. And even before the coming of Christ, those who were the foolish and weak things of the world, the ignoble, the despised, and those who "were not," were none other than the Gentiles <note>The non-Jewish nations.</note>, of whom Moses spoke with a prophetic mouth: "I will provoke them with those who are not a people, and I will anger them with a foolish nation." <note>Deuteronomy 32:21</note> Which is the foolish nation, if not the Gentile people? Foolish because they did not know God and lacked the knowledge of God. Weak because they had no remedy for their infirmity, by which they were rushing into eternal destruction. They were ignoble and despised, as if abandoned by God. They "were not" because they were not written in the book of life. But by contrast, the Hebrew nation was wise because it possessed the knowledge of God. It was strong because the medicine of the Law and circumcision had been applied to its disease. It was noble and not despised because it was accepted by God and descended from the holy fathers according to the flesh. It "was" because it was inscribed in the book of life. But because it forgot its God, and looking at itself began to boast according to the flesh—and not in God alone as was proper—therefore God despised its wisdom, power, nobility, and honor, and confounded them; and those who "were," He blotted out of the book of life, so that no flesh should glory in His sight. For the boasting of the flesh, wherever it comes from—whether from power, riches, lineage, honor, beauty, or knowledge—is an abomination before God. As it is said in the prophet Jeremiah: "Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, and let not the strong man glory in his strength, and let not the rich man glory in his riches; but let him who glories glory in this: that he knows me. For I am the Lord who exercises mercy, judgment, and justice on the earth." <note>Jeremiah 9:23–24</note> We, therefore, glory...

It provides historical examples of high-status converts like Dionysius and Abdon to show that while nobility exists in the Church, it must be surrendered to the glory of God.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philological and theological commentary on the First Epistle to the Corinthians. ...[let us] boast in our Lord Jesus Christ: who is our wisdom, justice, sanctification, and redemption. Indeed, who is our strength, our nobility, our very being, and our life. To whom be all honor, praise, glory, and thanksgiving, forever. Now to the examination.

# EXAMINATION of several points regarding the literal text.

<margin>A</margin> ¶ **Sosthenes, a brother / to the church of God which is at Corinth.** This Sosthenes, according to the Acts of the Apostles, was a leader of the synagogue. Having disregarded the honor of his leadership, he clung to Christ the eternal King, becoming a companion to Paul for the Gospel of Christ. Because of Christ, all the Jews in Corinth rushed upon him before the tribunal of Gallio, the proconsul of Achaia, <margin>A 1</margin> beating him. <note>Acts 18:12-17 describes Sosthenes being beaten before Gallio's tribunal.</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *In every place of theirs and ours.* <margin>A 2</margin> ¶ According to the better-preserved rule of the Latin language: *In every place, both their own and ours.* <note>original: "in omni loco suorum ac nostro"</note> Paul: <margin>in every place of theirs and ours</margin>. ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *As the testimony of Christ was confirmed in you: so that nothing is lacking to you in any grace.* ¶ It should rather be said: *so the testimony [was confirmed], as [it was]*; following the subsequent particle *so*. And *in any gift* rather than *in any grace*. Paul: <margin>even as the testimony of Christ was confirmed in you, so that you come behind in no gift</margin>. <note>The author distinguishes between 'gratia' (grace) and 'charisma' (spiritual gift).</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *In the day of the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ.* <margin>B</margin> ¶ More appropriately: *unto the day*; so that a progression seems to be indicated, as has been noted elsewhere. Also, the word *coming* is an addition <note>meaning it is not in the Greek source text here</note>. <margin>in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ</margin>. <margin>B 2</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *God is faithful, by whom you were called into the society of his Son Jesus Christ our Lord.* ¶ More correctly: *communion*. For "communion" denotes a community even among unequals, whereas "society" <term>societas</term> suggests more of an equality. For who would call himself a "social peer" or equal to the Son of God? However, nothing prevents one from being called a "communicant" or a participant in his goodness or united to his body. Paul: <margin>God is faithful, by whom you were called into the communion of his Son Jesus Christ our Lord</margin>. <margin>B 3</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *That you all say that same thing.* <note>original: "idipsum"</note> ¶ Better: *that you all say the identical thing.* <note>original: "idem"</note> Paul: <margin>that you all say the same thing</margin>. ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *In the same sense and in the same opinion.* ¶ Rather: *in the same mind, and in the same judgment.* Paul: <margin>in the same mind, and in the same judgment</margin>. ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Except Crispus and Caius: lest any man should say that you were baptized in my name.* ¶ In Paul it is *Gaius* with a 'G' and *I baptized* <note>original: "baptizavi"</note>, not *you were baptized*. Paul: <margin>except Crispus and Gaius, lest any should say that I baptized into my own name</margin>. <margin>C 3</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Moreover, I know not if I baptized any other of yours.* ¶ The word "yours" is superfluous. Paul: <margin>besides, I know not whether I baptized any other</margin>. <margin>C 4</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *But to those who are being saved, that is to us, it is power.* <margin>D 4</margin> ¶ The particle *that is* is not found in Paul. And "power" <term>virtus</term> designates a certain effective force and strength. Paul: <margin>but to you who are being saved, it is the power of God</margin>. ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Because that which is foolish of God is wiser than men; and that which is weak of God is stronger than men.* ¶ It can be translated as "the foolishness of God" and "the weakness of God"; the Greeks frequently use concrete neuters where the Latins, not ungracefully, are accustomed to use abstracts, as we have occasionally noted in the first book. Paul: <margin>because the foolishness of God is wiser than men, and the weakness of God is stronger than men</margin>. <margin>D 5</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *For see your calling, brothers.* ¶ It can also be read: *for you see your calling, brothers.* Paul: <margin>for you see your calling, brothers</margin>. ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *In his sight.* ¶ It should read *in the sight of God* according to Paul. Paul: <margin>before God</margin>. ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Who was made for us wisdom and justice and sanctification.* ¶ It should be said: *who was made for us wisdom from God.* For the particle "from God" is missing. And Christ the Son of God was neither "made" as wisdom, nor was he ever "made" wisdom, but he is eternal wisdom—not made, not created, but eternally begotten by the eternal Father. Yet, he was *made for us* wisdom. From this, it follows not at all that he was [essentially] "made wisdom." For so the Prophet says of God: *Lord, you have been made a refuge for us.* And that is indeed pious. But it would surely be impious if he said: *Lord, you have been made.* Yet it is no less impious if we were to say: *the Son of God was made wisdom.* This is said lest some Sophist <note>The author warns against "Sophists"—scholars who used clever but fallacious wordplay—who might use the Latin words for "happening" or "being made" (fit/factus) to trap the reader into heresy regarding Christ's divinity.</note> might perhaps disturb anyone. For naturally, the words *happens* and *is made* have snares for their deceptions (just like a spider's web). But those who are such have nothing to do with Paul and the eternal wisdom of God. Paul: <margin>who was made for us wisdom from God, and righteousness, and sanctification</margin>.

### CHAPTER II

<margin>6</margin> <image-desc>Decorative initial 'C' showing a landscape with buildings and a figure looking towards them.</image-desc> When Paul had disputed at Athens with the Jews, and with the Epicurean and Stoic philosophers, and had converted Dionysius and his wife Damaris, and their household, and many other Athenians to the piety of the faith, he came to Corinth. There he was received into the hospitality of Aquila and Priscilla, and he suffered much contradiction from the Jews, and faced the danger of death. This history is well known from the Acts of the Apostles. He recalls these things to the memory of the Corinthians, saying:

# II

<margin>Co. in right margin</margin>
o.iiij.

[I decided not to] know anything among you except **JESUS CHRIST** and him crucified. And I was with you in weakness, and in fear, and in much trembling. And my speech and my preaching were not in the persuasive words of human wisdom, but in the demonstration of the Spirit and of power: so that your faith might not rest in the wisdom of men, but in the power of God. <note>original: "non in persuasoriis humanae sapientiae verbis"</note> ¶ He did not come to the Corinthians with a parade of words or curled, ornate speech, but in simple and completely unadorned discourse, as befits an apostle of God. For he did not judge himself to know more philosophy, geometry, or oratory than they did; rather, he knew more of our Lord Jesus Christ, and that he was crucified for the life of the world, along with the other mysteries of his wonderful and not only super-worldly, but even super-divine life. And the apostle’s speech and preaching, declaring the saving mysteries of Christ, were not in the persuasive words of human wisdom (for that belongs to orators, not to apostles or prophets, who speak not of themselves but from God and the Spirit of God), but in the demonstration of the Spirit and of power. For he laid on his hands, and when the power-bestowing name of Christ was invoked, they received the Holy Spirit. He possessed the power of health and healing; as we read in the Acts of the Apostles, God performed no small miracles through the hand of Paul. So much so that even handkerchiefs and aprons <note>original: "sudaria & semicictia"</note> were carried from his body to the sick, and their diseases left them, and evil spirits went out from them. For if the faith of Christ had been persuaded by human eloquence and rhetorical art, it might have seemed like something human. But since it was introduced with simple speech, confirmed by signs and powers, what else can it be seen as but something divine? Truly, he remained among them in weakness, and fear, and much trembling. For this was a continuous fear and trembling—specifically the fear and trembling of death, which is a kind of weakness. Let no one dream up intestinal ailments, or kidney stones, or headaches <note>original: "iliacas passiones / aut nephrites / aut cephaleas"</note> and attribute them to Paul. That fear and trembling did not arise because of the Corinthians, but because of his Jewish adversaries. It reached such a point that the Lord himself deigned to comfort him in Corinth, as it is written:

> And the Lord said to Paul in a vision by night: "Do not be afraid, but speak, and do not be silent; for I am with you, and no one will attack you to harm you." <note>Acts 18:9-10</note>

But you will say: Paul says, "I did not come in excellence, nor in the loftiness of speech or wisdom." But when he was evangelizing Christ to the Corinthians—who is the wisdom and power of God—was not that speech both lofty and wise? It was not lofty with the loftiness of this world, nor with the wisdom of this world, but it was superior to all human loftiness and expressed a wisdom greater than all worldly knowledge. For Paul's negations contain the force of excellent affirmations. But who understands this excellence of Paul’s words to be more eminent than the world and the wisdom of the world? Certainly not everyone who hears, but the "perfect"—those who possess the Spirit of God (who is the Spirit of wisdom). For the imperfect judge eminence to be a defect and consider the light to be darkness. <margin>7</margin> But the perfect, on the contrary, judge all things correctly: a defect as a defect, eminence as eminence, darkness as darkness, and light as light. And therefore Paul adds: ¶ But we speak wisdom among the perfect, a wisdom indeed not of this age, nor of the rulers of this age who are being destroyed; but we speak the wisdom of God hidden in a mystery, which God predestined before the ages for our glory. Which none of the rulers of this age knew; for if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory. But as it is written:

> What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man, what things God has prepared for those who love him:

God has indeed revealed them to us through his Spirit. ¶ The Son of God is wisdom hidden in a mystery. In the sacrifices, in the prophets, in types, in enigmas and figures, he remains hidden; he is revealed in the flesh, and even after revelation, he remains concealed. When Paul says "which God predestined for our glory," he is not looking at himself, but at the eminent outpouring of God's goodness upon all believers. For God predestined it for the glory of all believers, so that he might bestow his glory upon everyone. For in Christ alone is our glory, and it is right to boast in him alone, who was predestined by God for the glory of all. Paul does not boast in himself, but in him, and everywhere he teaches that we must boast. And if King Herod, Pilate, and the leaders of the Jews had known him to be God, they would never have crucified him. For he was God; but (as the prophet Isaiah says) truly a hidden God. But who could have thought of those things which God revealed to his apostles concerning that hidden wisdom, concerning the glory and salvation of men, unless he himself had deigned to reveal them through his Spirit? And what wonder is it if he reveals through his Spirit things which neither eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor have entered into the heart of man, since the Spirit of God is to God as the spirit of a man is to a man? The former in truth, the latter in the most distant trace and imitation. Yet the spirit of a man knows the secrets and hidden things of the man. Much more, therefore, does the Spirit of God know the hidden and deep things of God. He, therefore, who has the Spirit of God, knows the hidden and secret things of God, insofar as it pleases that supremely good Spirit to reveal them. And he who has this Spirit is a spiritual and divine man. But he who lacks this Spirit is a natural <note>original: "aialis" (animalis)</note> and human man. The former has power beyond man and judges all things, yet is judged by no one. The latter has power according to man and often below man; he cannot grasp the things of the Spirit of God of himself.

<summary>This page discusses Paul’s rejection of worldly oratory in favor of divine power and explains that the "hidden wisdom" of God is only accessible through the Holy Spirit to those who are spiritually "perfect." Paul clarifies that his "fear and trembling" in Corinth was not due to illness, but a rational fear of persecution that required divine reassurance.</summary>

# COMMENTARY

<margin>5</margin> 
Could you suffice? Like a lion or another mute animal—and even much less so—those things which belong to the spirit of man. But he can: being clothed with power from on high and made a spiritual man from the spirit of God. The apostles certainly possessed this spirit of God, and copiously so (as is plain to see), especially the divine apostle Paul. The same man reveals all these things more divinely and magnificently as he continues concerning the Holy Spirit, saying: ¶ **For the Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God. For who among men knows the things of a man, except the spirit of man which is in him? In this way, also, no one knows the things of God except the spirit of God. Now we have received not the spirit of the world, but the spirit which is from God, so that we may know the things that have been granted to us by God. These things we also speak, not in the learned words of human wisdom, but in the learned words of the Holy Spirit, comparing spiritual things with spiritual. But the natural man does not receive the things of the spirit of God, for they are foolishness to him; and he cannot understand them, because they are spiritually discerned. But the spiritual man indeed judges all things, yet he himself is judged by no one. For who has known the mind of the Lord, that he may instruct him? But we have the mind of CHRIST.** ¶ The "mind of the Lord" and the "mind of Christ" are understood to be the Holy Spirit. And Paul responds with confidence when someone asks: "for who has known the mind of the Lord?"—which indeed, if anyone knew it, they might instruct him—I say he responds confidently: we know the mind of the Lord, for the mind of the Lord has instructed us. He adds the reason for this: because we have the mind of Christ, which is the mind of God and the Holy Spirit. And we speak those things which have been granted to us by God, things which belong to the spirit of God: not in the learned words of human wisdom, but in the learned words of the Holy Spirit, comparing spiritual things with spiritual. And these "learned words of the Holy Spirit" are not the learned words of human wisdom, but are "super-learned," even if the natural man <note>original: "animalis homo," referring to a person living only by their natural soul/reason without divine inspiration</note> judges them to be unlearned. For he judges from himself, not from God, from whom all true judgment comes; whereas judgment from ourselves is false. But in what way can spiritual things be compared and conferred with spiritual things? Truly, without the spirit of God, they cannot; but those who possess the spirit of God are led by it to the understanding of both the Holy Scriptures and the prophets, which are spiritual things, or gifts of the spirit, and they understand them clearly. But do they use that spirit to understand those things? Not at all. Rather and more truly: the Holy Spirit uses *them*, so that they may understand those spiritual things worthily of God, spiritually, and as is fitting. And this is what it means to "confer spiritual things with spiritual." There are, however, some who understand these things through a gift, and some through the Holy Spirit. Those who understand through a gift can use the gift, but they cannot do so once the spirit is gone. Truly, whether with these or those, the Holy Spirit always makes use of them. May He, by His holy grace, make us His instrument for understanding spiritual things spiritually, and for serving Christ without stain, who reigns with the Father and that most good Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

<margin>A 6</margin> ¶ **EXAMINATION of several points concerning the letter.** ¶ The Vulgate edition: *Announcing to you the testimony of CHRIST.* ¶ It should read: *the testimony of God.* Paul wrote: "announcing to you the testimony of God" <note>original Greek: "καταγγέλλων ὑμῖν τὸ μαρτύριον τοῦ θεοῦ"</note>. ¶ The Vulgate edition: *Not in the persuasive words of human wisdom.* ¶ More correctly: *persuading* or *convincing* words. Paul wrote: "not in persuasive words of human wisdom" <note>original Greek: "οὐκ ἐν πειθοῖς ἀνθρωπίνης σοφίας λόγοις"</note>. <margin>B 7</margin> ¶ The Vulgate edition: *In a mystery, which is hidden.* ¶ The old translator could have more accurately said "the hidden [one]." Paul wrote: "in a mystery, the [wisdom] having been hidden" <note>original Greek: "ἐν μυστηρίῳ τὴν ἀποκεκρυμμένην"</note>. ¶ The Vulgate edition: *As it is written.* ¶ The word "but" is missing; it should say, *but as it is written.* Paul wrote: "but as it is written" <note>original Greek: "ἀλλὰ καθώς γέγραπται"</note>. ¶ The Vulgate edition: *What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it ascended into the heart of man.* ¶ It should be read in Latin as: *things which... and they ascended.* This is shown by the speech that immediately follows: "which God has prepared for those who love him." Paul wrote: "Things which eye has not seen, and ear has not heard, and upon the heart of man has not ascended" <note>original Greek: "ἃ ὀφθαλμὸς οὐκ εἶδεν, καὶ οὖς οὐκ ἤκουσεν, καὶ ἐπὶ καρδίαν ἀνθρώπου οὐκ ἀνέβη"</note>. But you will say: Paul has "ascended" in the singular. This is true, because he speaks elegantly; it is an elegant style among the Greeks to join a singular verb to a neuter plural subject. Paul observed this here, as he does everywhere. However, to observe this among the Latins is not elegant, but plainly barbaric. Whether the relative "which" <note>Latin: "quod"</note> is used at the beginning, the old translator committed a barbarism regarding the following "which" <note>Latin: "quae"</note>; or if "which" <note>Latin: "quae"</note> is used, he fell into a barbarism regarding the verb "ascended." Truly, grammar is more wounded here than the conscience. Nevertheless, it is good to restore Paul to Paul. ¶ The Vulgate edition: *But in the doctrine of the Spirit.* <margin>D 8</margin> ¶ In Paul, it is used as an adjective, *but in the learned [words]*, and the word "words" is understood from the preceding phrase. And after "Spirit," the word "Holy" is missing. Paul wrote: "but in the learned [words] of the Holy Spirit" <note>original Greek: "ἀλλ’ ἐν διδακτοῖς πνεύματος ἁγίου"</note>. ¶ *But the natural man.* ¶ Here "natural" <note>Latin: "animalis"</note> is not derived from the word "animal" [beast], but from the word "soul" <note>Latin: "anima"</note>. Just as "spiritual" comes from "spirit"—specifically the Holy Spirit or His God. For there are many degrees among spiritual men. Those who perceive the gifts of the Holy Spirit are indeed spiritual, but less spiritual than those whom the Holy Spirit fills through Himself. And since the soul and reason are one in man, it also happens that the "rational man" does not reach the mysteries and hidden things of God through reason. Rather, reason is "foolish" toward those things, just as a non-mathematician is foolish toward mathematics. For he thinks it foolish if someone says the sun is more than a hundred times larger than the earth, and the moon is two thousand times smaller than the sun...

<meta>This page continues the philological and theological commentary on Paul's First Epistle to the Corinthians. <margin>Corinthians</margin>
four hundred and four times above seventy; that is, 647 <note>original: "quadringies & quater supra septuagesies; id est 647". Note: The Latin phrasing actually totals 474, but the text specifies 647, perhaps referring to a specific mathematical or symbolic calculation in the author's source.</note> because these matters are judged, discussed, and examined mathematically. However, a person who is not a mathematician cannot do this mathematically. So it is with those things which are of the Spirit of God: to the "natural man" <term>natural man: from the Latin 'animalis,' referring to one guided only by the human soul (anima) and reason, without divine inspiration</term>, who follows natural reason, it is foolishness, because he cannot discuss those things spiritually and divinely—just as a non-mathematician cannot discuss mathematics mathematically or according to the rules of the discipline. But you might say: "he will discuss it rationally." Yet what is this, except that he will discuss divine things in a non-divine way, spiritual things in a non-spiritual way, and (if I may say so) wisdom in a foolish way? It is therefore established as true in every respect, as the apostle—made by God and speaking through the Spirit—asserts. Let us therefore become "fools" to reason and according to the natural man, so that we may be wise toward God. As for why the "natural man" is so named from the soul <note>original: "anima"</note>, Paul has it as *psychikos anthrōpos* <note>original: "ψυχικὸς δὲ ἄνθρωπος", meaning a man governed by the natural soul</note>; and the "spiritual man" from the spirit, the same Paul writes as *ho de pneumatikos* <note>original: "ὁ δὲ πνευματικός"</note>. ¶ **The Vulgate edition** <note>The standard Latin Bible of the time.</note> reads: *Because it is spiritually examined. But the spiritual man judges all things: and he himself is judged by no one.* ¶ It must be said: "they are examined" <note>original: "examinantur"</note> is plural, for it refers to those things which are of the Spirit of God; but elegantly in the Greek (as has been said) a singular verb corresponds to a plural subject. Truly, what is here called "examined" and later "judged" is the same word. Paul says: *hoti pneumatikōs anakrinetai, ho de pneumatikos anakrinei men panta, autos de hyp' oudenos anakrinetai* <note>original: "ὅτι πνευματικῶς ἀνακρίνεται, ὁ δὲ πνευματικὸς ἀνακρίνει μὲν πάντα, αὐτὸς δὲ ὑπ' οὐδενὸς ἀνακρίνεται"</note>. It signifies that which is thoroughly judged, discussed, or discerned. ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has instructed him?* In Paul's text: *For who has known the mind of the Lord: which shall instruct him?* For no one can know the Holy Spirit unless the Holy Spirit has instructed him. Paul writes: *tis gar egnō noun kyriou, hos symbibasei auton?* <note>original: "τίς γὰρ ἔγνω νοῦν κυρίου, ὃς συμβιβάσει αὐτόν;"</note> For "who" <note>original: "ὃς" (hos)</note> seems to refer to "the mind" <note>original: "νοῦν" (noun)</note>; but in Greek, the word for "mind" is masculine, whereas in Latin it is feminine.

### CAP. III.

<image-desc>Decorative initial T containing a scene with a figure, possibly a scholar or saint, in a landscape or architectural setting.</image-desc>
**T**o this, one of the Corinthians might have said: "If you, Paul, have the spirit of God and of Christ, why do we not grasp your words through the Spirit?" This certainly happened not through the fault of the speaker, but through the incapacity of the listeners. Were not Christ’s words concerning the spiritual eating of his flesh and the drinking of his blood spiritual? *The words (he said) that I have spoken to you are spirit and life.* Yet the disciples, understanding them in a physical and carnal way, said: "This is a hard saying." To whom the Lord, calling them back from the flesh to the spirit, said: *It is the spirit that gives life, the flesh profits nothing.* He was speaking spiritual things to the disciples, but as if to carnal people. For they were still carnal, and they understood in a carnal way. In this same manner, Paul had spoken spiritual things to the Corinthians, but still as if to carnal people. For how could they be spiritual who had not yet prepared a dwelling place to have the Holy Spirit as an inhabitant? For the Holy One wants a holy, chaste, and clean home. He is kind: he wants a dwelling free from jealousy and envy. He is peaceful: he flees from hatreds and contentions. He is the spirit of unity: and therefore, hating divisions and schisms, he dwells with such people least of all. Yet such had been, and still were, many of the Corinthians 
<margin>9</margin> 
to whom Paul was writing. Therefore, it was not through Paul’s fault, but their own, that he could only speak to them as though to carnal people. Which he himself testifies, saying: *And I, brethren, could not speak to you as to spiritual people, but as to carnal. As to babes in CHRIST, I gave you milk to drink, not solid food. For you were not yet able; but even now you are still not able. For you are still carnal.* "I could not," he says, "speak to you as spiritual." Truly, this inability was not on Paul’s part, but on theirs, because they had been and still were carnal. "You were not yet able," he says, "nor even now are you able." But you will ask, how were they not able? How were they not spiritual, when Paul previously said of them: *In every way you were made rich in him, in all speech and all knowledge. Thus the testimony of Christ was confirmed in you, so that you lack no gift?* I would not deny that there were spiritual people among them, of whom Paul spoke earlier. But there were also many "natural" and carnal people among them, of whom he speaks now. And in the same discourse, he addressed both these and those—as carnal and as spiritual. And what was milk and drink to the former was solid food to the latter. These were like babes and infants; those were like men. These were weak and feeble; those were healthy and strong. Both were receiving the nourishment of life, but these did not grasp what they lived by or from where they lived, while those did grasp it. For they lived by the spirit, which is grasped not by the flesh, but by the spirit. Therefore, capacity turns a drink into food, and incapacity turns food into a drink. And in truth, whatever he either said or wrote to Titus, Timothy, Sosthenes, Luke, Dionysius, Hierotheus, Ignatius, and their like—to them it was food. But to almost everyone of our own 
<margin>10</margin> 
time, it seems to be a weak drink, and perhaps even much more so than to the Corinthians, for they are more carnal. But may God and the Holy Spirit lead the infancy of our times to spiritual manhood, so that we may magnificently understand those things which are more magnificent than all human sense. But why they are carnal, and why Paul’s words are nothing but a drink—and would that they were even still milk and drink—they shall understand the cause from that which Paul assigns to the Corinthians, saying: ¶ **For**

# COMMENTARY

<margin>11</margin>
* "...where there is envy among you, and contention, and dissensions, are you not carnal, and walking according to man? 
* For when someone says, 'I am indeed of Paul,' and another, 'I am of Apollos,' are you not carnal?" 

These people are surely carnal <term>carnal: from the Latin 'carnalis,' meaning fleshly or worldly, as opposed to spiritual</term>. And we ourselves are carnal for these and many other reasons. But are they not also carnal who look toward men, especially when they ought to look toward God? Therefore, he adds:

* "Who then is Paul, and who is Apollos, but ministers through whom you believed, even as the Lord gave to each? 
* I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth. 
* Therefore, neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the growth. 
* He who plants and he who waters are one. And each shall receive his own reward according to his own labor."

He who plants and he who waters are one—that is, they are of the same condition. One is a servant; the other is a servant. One is nothing; the other is nothing. If you look to God himself (as is right), they are nothing in themselves, but the grace of God and the administration they received from God is something within them. Both that grace and God himself should be venerated in them. They do not give the reward themselves; rather, each of them expects a reward from the Lord according to his own labor. This is not a "reward of debt" <note>original: "mercedem debiti". In scholastic theology, a reward of debt is something earned by right, whereas a reward of grace is a gift from God's favor.</note>, but a reward of overflowing grace from the most exuberant goodness of God, who wishes to bestow Himself freely. 

For what debt can be owed to a servant? It is not a debt, but grace and a gift, when the work done is as nothing, yet the reward received is the greatest. It is no different than if you spend mud and receive gold. And if one servant cultivates a field and another builds a structure, the farming is not called the servant's, nor is the building, the house, or the temple called the servant's—they are the Lord's. Indeed, the servants themselves do not belong to themselves, but to the Lord, and they are the Lord's co-workers <note>original: "cooperatores"</note>. Therefore, let no one name himself after a servant, creating division, but rather after the Lord. For there are many servants, but one Lord of all.

<margin>12</margin>
Paul reveals this to the Corinthians, and through them to us, saying:
* "For we are God's co-workers; you are God's husbandry, you are God's building. 
* According to the grace of God which was given to me, as a wise master builder <note>original: "architectus"</note>, I laid the foundation. 
* But another builds upon it. Let each see how he builds upon it. 
* For no one can lay any other foundation than that which is laid, which is JESUS CHRIST."

Paul does not say he is anything of himself; rather, by the grace of God and through divine favor, he was made a wise master builder to lay the foundation—that is, to announce and preach the Gospel, which is the foundation of eternal life, namely Christ Jesus, the son of the thrice-blessed God. Upon this foundation, the church of God and the soul-saving religion must be built. Regarding the foundation, he indicates that no other can be laid upon which a structure for salvation can be constructed. He warns those who build upon it to use great caution and wisdom in building upon such a noble and unshakable foundation. For if they build well, they will receive the reward of grace: eternal salvation. 

<margin>13</margin>
But if they build wrongly, they will receive the reward of justice: the punishment of eternal fire. For he says:
* "If anyone builds upon this foundation with gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, or straw, each one's work will be made manifest. 
* For the Day will declare it, because it will be revealed in fire; and the fire will test what sort of work each has done. 
* If the work anyone has built remains, he will receive a reward. 
* If anyone’s work is burned, he will suffer loss; but he himself will be saved, yet so as through fire."

In the people of God, there are those who build and those who are built upon. The first builders were the apostles, who also laid the foundation. Many who succeeded them built upon that foundation. Those who build with holy and undefiled doctrine are pure and undefiled, like gold, silver, and precious stones. Others build with impious dogmas and the poison of deceptions; these are signified by wood, hay, and straw <note>original: "ligna / fœnum / lapides". While the scriptural quote uses "straw" (stipula), the author here uses "stones" (lapides) in the list of combustible materials, likely a scribal or printing error for "straw."</note>, all of which are fuel for fire. All these people are called "builders." The "built" are the common people and the nations, who receive either the undefiled doctrine or the pestilential virus of false dogmas. 

Just as there are various levels among those who truly build (represented by the distinctions between gold, silver, and gems), so there will be various levels among those built into the holy building of Christ. These will shine among the others: some as undefiled gold, others as silver, and others among the stones of the holy building will be as precious stones. Similarly, there are various levels among those who build badly and perversely, and various levels of those who are perversely built, which the apostle suggests to us through the wood, hay, and straw. 

Both those who build well and those who are well-built will be saved. Conversely, those who build poorly and those who are poorly built will be damned together. Every building, whether good or bad, will be tested and made manifest on the Day of Judgment. For just as the purest gold, silver, and precious stones feel no injury or consumption from fire, so it is with the saints who built well and were well-built. When the Lord comes to judge the world through fire, when the fire precedes Him and sets His enemies ablaze all around, when the engine of the world burns with the fire of vengeance: in that same fire, the good angels will suffer nothing, and the evil ones (who even now fear it in the gloomy air <note>original: "caliginoso aere". In the theology of the time, the "air" or atmosphere was thought to be the dwelling place of demons or fallen angels.</note>) will be most cruelly tortured. In that same fire, the righteous will suffer nothing but will be saved, as if through fire—as if by the judgment of fire—while that same fire of vengeance destroys the wicked.

<vocab>Paul, Apollos, Corinthians, Jesus Christ, foundation, architect (master builder), husbandry (agriculture), building, gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, straw, fire, judgment</vocab>

It details the "testing by fire" that occurs on the Day of Judgment, where good doctrines (gold, silver) endure while false ones (hay, straw) are consumed.</summary>

On the previous page, the author discussed how apostles like Paul and Apollos are merely servants or "planters" in God’s field. Here, the focus shifts to the metaphor of the church as a temple and the distinction between worldly and divine wisdom.</meta>

<page-num>110</page-num>
<header>II</header>

<margin>1 Corinthians</margin>
...revealing it. But the unjust will be wretchedly tortured. Do you not see how the rays of the sun, which are a punishment and a torment to diseased eyes, are perfection and comfort to healthy ones? So it shall be on the last day: the fire of God’s just judgment. This is the mystery <note>original: "sacramentum." In this context, it refers to a sacred mystery or a truth revealed by God.</note> that Paul reveals to us here through the Holy Spirit. For these words are everywhere most profound and full of mysteries. The Corinthians were being "built up," and their teachers were the builders. However, those who followed a Jewish blindness according to the flesh <note>The author is likely referring to "Judaizers," early Christians who insisted on following the literal Mosaic Law rather than the "spirit" of the new faith.</note> and according to the letter were building not according to the spirit. Others, puffed up by human knowledge and looking only to themselves, were also "builders," but they were wise according to the flesh,

<margin>14</margin>
wise according to the world, boasting in themselves and focusing on themselves. In these things, the Corinthians—having fallen away from the spirit—would boast. Paul calls them back to the spirit, saying: **Do you not know that you are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwells in you? If anyone corrupts the temple of God, God will destroy him. For the temple of God is holy, which you are.** This is an admonition to the Corinthians who were being "built," so they would not believe they belonged to the person doing the building; the builders are servants, but the temple belongs to the Lord. Truly, those "super-builders" <note>Those who came after Paul to lead the church.</note> were corrupting the building. Therefore, God will justly destroy and ruin the corrupters of His holy temple. For Paul had left the Corinthians holy and incorrupt when he departed from them after a year and six months. But afterward, new teachers arrived—violators of holy doctrine—who were

<margin>15</margin>
wise according to the flesh and the world. Paul encourages the Corinthians against them in the following warning, saying: **Let no one deceive himself. If anyone among you seems to be wise in this age, let him become a fool so that he may become wise. For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God.** For it is written: *He catches the wise in their own craftiness.* And again: *The Lord knows the thoughts of the wise, that they are vain.* He who is wise in his own eyes, wise in the flesh, or wise in this age—and considers himself to be wise—deceives himself. For in reality, he is a fool. He is a fool before God, who is Truth itself. Therefore, let him be a "fool" to himself, to the flesh, and to the world, so that he may be truly wise. For the wisdom of the spirit, which belongs to God, is foolishness to the flesh and the world; just as the foolishness of the world is foolishness to God. Thus, both types of wisdom—God’s and the world’s—are called "foolishness." But the world's wisdom is called foolishness because of a deficiency <term>deficiency: a lack of true understanding or spiritual light</term>. God's "foolishness," however, is called so not because of a deficiency, but because of its excellence <term>excellence: or "eminence," meaning it is so far above human reason that it appears as its opposite</term>. It is not the wisdom of this world but a "super-eminent" wisdom; it contains the power of an "excellent negation" <note>A philosophical concept where one describes God by saying what He is NOT, because He is beyond all human categories.</note> and coincides with true wisdom. Indeed, the wisdom of this world is called such by a deficiency, as it truly coincides with folly. 

But wait. If someone is not wise in this world, does that automatically mean he is wise toward God? Not at all. For there are the ignorant and lazy who are not wise in this world, and these are also called fools in this world. This is a "common" foolishness, and like the other, it is described as a deficiency. But this common folly is a deficiency of *nature*, whereas worldly wisdom is a deficiency of *spirit and grace*. These two are opposites. Yet, because the worldly-wise person does not lack natural intelligence—which is the foundation for spirit and grace—it happens that the wise of this age, even if they are truly fools, can more magnificently attain the wisdom of the spirit and grace (which is wisdom according to God). It is of such people that Paul says: "let them become fools to this world so that they may be wise." For the wise of this world, by coming to their senses—that is, by leaving behind worldly wisdom and seeking the wisdom of the spirit—can emerge as perfect spiritual men. But the simpletons and the lazy cannot; they remain as they are. If they live, they will live on "milk," never on "solid food" <note>A reference to Paul's earlier metaphor in 1 Cor 3:2 regarding spiritual maturity.</note>. It follows that worldly wisdom has two opposites: spiritual wisdom and ignorance. Deficiency is opposed to deficiency. And because the wisdom of the world is the wisdom of men, those who follow it boast in men. But the wisdom of the spirit is the wisdom of God; therefore, those who follow it boast in God, not in men. For this reason,

<margin>16</margin>
Paul, wise in the spirit, again encourages the Corinthians to seek true wisdom, saying: **Therefore, let no one glory in men. For all things are yours: whether Paul, or Apollos, or Cephas <note>Cephas is the Aramaic name for the Apostle Peter.</note>, or the world, or life, or death, or things present, or things to come. All are yours, and you are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s.** Those wise in the spirit (as has been said) boast in God, not in men. And for this sake—that is, so that the world might be wise in the spirit—God sent apostles, disciples, and wise men. For this reason they lived; for this reason they met a glorious death. For the sake of those wise in the spirit, the current governance of the world exists; and for their sake, that governance continues until the number of the saints is fulfilled and the day of the Lord arrives. For those wise in the spirit belong to Christ, and Christ belongs to God—the Father, I mean. For as will be said later: the end will be when he delivers the kingdom to God the Father. Since, therefore, we must strive to be wise in spirit and not in flesh, so that we may belong to Christ and be part of the kingdom of God, let honor and glory be to Him with the Father and the Holy Spirit until the day of His coming, and after He has come, for infinite ages of ages.

# COMMENTARY

...used by Paul: "not as to spiritual people but as to carnal people, as to infants in Christ" <margin>A 10</margin>, "I gave you milk to drink" <note>original: "ὡς πνευματικοῖς ἀλλ᾽ ὡς σαρκικοῖς, ὡς νηπίοις ἐν χριστῷ, γάλα ὑμᾶς ἐπότισα."</note>. ¶ **Vulgate edition**: *But neither are you able even now.* ¶ In Paul: "but neither are you yet able even now." Paul: "for you are still carnal" <note>original: "ἔτι γὰρ ὑμεῖς σαρκικοί ἐστε."</note>. ¶ **Vulgate edition**: <margin>12</margin> *For since there is jealousy and contention among you, are you not carnal?* ¶ The particle "and dissensions" is missing. Paul: "For where there is jealousy and strife and dissensions among you, are you not carnal?" <note>original: "ὅπου γὰρ ἐν ὑμῖν ζῆλος καὶ ἔρις καὶ διχοστασίαι, οὐχὶ σαρκικοί ἐστε;"</note>. ¶ **Vulgate edition**: *But another [says] I am of Apollos; are you not men?* ¶ It should say: "are you not carnal?" Paul: "and another [says] I am of Apollos; are you not carnal?" <note>original: "ἕτερος δὲ ἐγὼ ἀπολλῶ, οὐχὶ σαρκικοί ἐστε."</note>. **Vulgate edition**: *What therefore is Apollos? What is Paul? Ministers of him whom you have believed.* ¶ It should be read from Paul as follows: "Who therefore is Paul? and who is Apollos? Ministers through whom [you believed]," not "of him whom." The particle "unless" or a similar exception is missing before "ministers." "Apollos" in the nominative and vocative cases retains the final letter 's'; the other cases are "Apollo" <note>original: "ολλῶ"</note> as with "Menelaus." Paul: "Who then is Paul, and who is Apollos? but ministers through whom you believed" <note>original: "τίς οὖν ἐστι παῦλος, τίς δὲ ἀπολλῶς· ἀλλ᾽ ἢ διάκονοι δι᾽ ὧν ἐπιστεύσατε."</note>. For Paul had left Apollos at Corinth when he returned to Jerusalem by way of Ephesus, as is written in the Acts of the Apostles in this manner: "And it happened while Apollos was at Corinth, that Paul, having passed through the upper regions, came to Ephesus." And from the same Acts: "Apollos was a Jew, an Alexandrian by birth, an eloquent man and powerful in the scriptures." For so it is written in Acts: "And a certain Jew named Apollos, an Alexandrian by birth, an eloquent man" <margin>C 12</margin> <note>original: "ἰουδαῖος δέ τις ἀπολλῶς ὀνόματι ἀλεξανδρεὺς τῷ γένει, ἀνὴρ λόγιος."</note>. ¶ **Vulgate edition**: *For we are God's helpers.* ¶ Better "co-workers." For we "help" <term>adiuuamus</term> someone whose strength is insufficient. Who would say this of God? But to "work together" <term>cooperari</term> with the All-Powerful is not forbidden. For this cooperation is a sharing of His power and a certain imitation of Him, so that through the communication and participation of His goodness, being sharers of His power, we may <margin>C 13</margin> imitate Him. Paul: "For we are God's co-workers" <note>original: "θεοῦ γάρ ἐσμὲν συνεργοί."</note>. ¶ **Vulgate edition**: WHICH IS CHRIST JESUS. ¶ It should say "who is Christ Jesus." Paul: "who is Jesus Christ" <note>original: "ὅς ἐστιν ἰησοῦς χριστὸς."</note>. ¶ **Vulgate edition**: *For the day of the Lord shall declare it.* ¶ "Of the Lord" is not found in Paul, but was added for understanding. Paul: "For the day shall make it known" <note>original: "ἡ γὰρ ἡμέρα δηλώσει."</note>. ¶ **Vulgate edition**: <margin>C 14</margin> *If however as if through fire.* ¶ It should say: "so." Paul: "but so as through fire" <note>original: "οὕτως δὲ ὡς διὰ πυρός."</note>. ¶ **Vulgate <margin>D 14</margin> edition**: *If anyone however violates the temple of God, God will destroy him.* ¶ In Paul, "violates" and "will destroy" are the same word <note>phtheirei/phtheirei</note>, and it properly signifies "I corrupt" or "I ruin." Paul: "If anyone corrupts the temple of God, God will corrupt [or destroy] him" <note>original: "εἴ τις τὸν ναὸν τοῦ θεοῦ φθείρει, φθερεῖ τοῦτον ὁ θεός."</note>. ¶ **Vulgate edition**: <margin>15</margin> *For the temple of God is holy, which you are.* It should say: "which [plural] you are." Paul: "For the temple of God is holy, which sort [of people] you are" <note>original: "ὁ γὰρ ναὸς τοῦ θεοῦ ἅγιός ἐστιν, οἵτινές ἐστε ὑμεῖς."</note>. ¶ **Vulgate edition**: *I will catch the wise in their craftiness.* ¶ Better in the present tense: "He who catches." Paul: "He who catches the wise in their craftiness" <margin>16</margin> <note>original: "ὁ δρασσόμενος τοὺς σοφοὺς ἐν τῇ πανουργίᾳ αὐτῶν."</note>. And so it is read in Job: "He who catches the wise in their craftiness." ¶ **Vulgate edition**: *For all things are yours. But you are Christ's.* ¶ This particle "for" is superfluous. Paul: "All things are yours, but you are Christ's" <note>original: "πάντα ὑμῶν ἐστιν, ὑμεῖς δὲ χριστοῦ."</note>.

### CHAPTER IV

---

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut drop cap 'C' illustrating a figure seated under a tree in a landscape.</image-desc>

Since every faithful person belongs to Christ and not to a man, let him not glory in a man. Let him not say: "I am of Paul," "I am of Apollos," or "I am of Cephas." However holy and great a man is or was in whom one might glory, he was nothing but a servant of Christ and an instrument for the distribution of His graces. For that servant did not distribute his own graces, his own goods, or his own gifts; rather, they were the graces, goods, and gifts of Christ. We ought therefore to look to Him to whom the graces belong, to whom the goods belong, to whom the gifts belong, and glory in Him—not in the servant who is an instrument for the master for the distribution of the master’s goods, from whom the master requires wise faithfulness. "Who do you think," says the Savior, "is the faithful and wise servant whom the master has set over his household to give them food in due season?" Neither Peter nor Paul were anything but servants of Christ, <margin>17</margin> and managers <term>oeconomi</term>, stewards, and distributors of the hidden benefits of God. Nor does Paul wish that he, Apollos, Cephas, and the rest of the apostles and other saints be regarded otherwise, saying: ¶ **So let a man regard us: as servants of CHRIST and stewards of the mysteries of God.** Moreover, what is required thereafter in stewards is that a man be found faithful. ¶ God requires faithfulness in His manager <term>oeconomus</term>, that is, the steward of His mysteries. He does not require that those receiving His gifts—leaving Him aside—should glory in the steward, or think of him and call him their head, their "chief centurion" <term>primipilum</term>, or their "field commander" <term>campiductorem</term>. For the Lord is the head of all and the leader of all, both of those who distribute and those for whom things are distributed. And Paul (as is the mark of a good manager) strove to be faithful as much as he could in the management committed to him in the house of the Lord, which is the church of the faithful. Truly, how he was esteemed as a steward by the Corinthians, or by those who seem to excel in the judgment of human knowledge—whether good or bad—he considered of no value. But neither did he judge himself to be either a good or a bad steward; though he was not aware of doing anything wrongly or negligently...

It then transitions into Chapter 4, defining the apostles as "stewards" (oeconomi) who must be faithful to Christ rather than objects of human boasting.</summary>

## 2 1 Corinthians

...committed in his stewardship, nor should his conscience rebuke him in anything regarding his own stewardship. But the judgment of whether a steward and servant of Christ is good or bad, worthy or unworthy, he leaves to Christ, who is the Lord of all. For such a one is (for instance, a good steward or a good servant) only if the Lord has judged him as such and approved him as such. And even if someone’s conscience does not rebuke him, suggesting he has not served his Lord poorly in anything, he is not <margin>18</margin> immediately "good," nor is he thereby justified. For whether a servant is good or just does not depend on his own judgment, but on the Lord's. And for this reason, Paul adds: ¶ *But to me it is a very small thing that I should be judged by you, or by any human court. Indeed, I do not even judge myself. For I am conscious of nothing against myself, yet I am not justified by this. But he who judges me is the Lord.* <margin>1 Corinthians 4</margin> ¶ Whoever judges himself to be good or a worthy servant of God usurps the judgment of his Lord for himself. This is pride; and by that very act, he is a bad and unworthy servant, as it is written: *God resists the proud.* <note>original: "Superbis resistit deus." A reference to James 4:6 and 1 Peter 5:5.</note> But he who does what he ought and can, and yet judges himself as neither good nor bad, but leaves the judgment of himself to God—feeling himself to be whatever God knows him to be, though he himself does not know what God knows of him—this man is humble; he is ready for grace. As it is written: <margin>19</margin> *But he gives grace to the humble.* And to pursue humility and flee the presumption of judgment, Paul exhorts them, saying: <margin>4</margin> ¶ *Therefore, judge nothing before the time, until the Lord comes, who will both bring to light the hidden things of darkness and reveal the counsels of the hearts; and then each one will have praise from God.* ¶ Are not human judgments fallible, since they often judge the best servants as the worst? For this reason, the apostles were beaten, stoned, and suffered every insult for the name of Jesus. And Paul, so often beaten, stoned, handed over to prisons, bound, and finally struck by the sword, returned his faithful soul to his Lord. On the contrary, bad servants are often judged as good and faithful. From this, particular sects arose against the unity of the church. All these things will be known on the day of the Lord: who were the good and who were the bad servants. And many who are now blasphemed by men will be declared good and faithful by God. Thus, it must be understood that this praise ought to come from God, not from men. Conversely, many now judged as good and holy by men will be rejected by God. Thus, every judgment of election or rejection is left to God. However, concerning some, judgment has been left to men—namely, those for whom they have a divine oracle, a revelation, or an effective sign from God. For that is not the judgment of men, but of God. For he who calls the apostles blessed does so not by his own judgment, but by God's. <margin>Matthew 19</margin> *You also,* he said, *shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.* Likewise regarding the martyrs: <margin>Revelation 6</margin> *To each of them,* it says, *was given a white robe, and they were told to rest a little while longer, until the number of their fellow servants and brothers who were to be killed, as they were, should be complete.* And the church follows the judgment of God in defining such matters rather than its own; for the bride honors and prefers the Bridegroom in all things. But Paul returns to the matter at hand. The Corinthians were boasting in men—that is, in the teachers who had created sects among them. These were not Paul, nor Apollos, nor Peter, but were partly those boasting in human sense rather than announcing Christ in the spirit. The apostle spares their names. In those men, I say, they boasted; and one would say (for example), "I am of Marcion," and another, "I am of Apelles." <note>The author uses Marcion and Apelles—famous 2nd-century heretics—as illustrative examples of factional leaders, though they lived after Paul's time.</note> One would say, "I believe what Marcion asserts," and another, "I believe what Apelles feels." But in place of those names, Paul put his own name and the name of Apollos, so that they might come to their senses and recall to memory <margin>20</margin> what he and Apollos (whom he had left with them upon departing) had taught. And in this way, he recalls them to the unity of doctrine, saying: <margin>4</margin> ¶ *Now these things, brothers, I have figuratively applied to myself and Apollos for your sakes, so that in us you might learn not to think beyond what is written, lest one be puffed up for one against another.* ¶ *So that in us you might learn*—that is, by our example, mine and Apollos's, you might learn not to be puffed up against one another. For we are not puffed up one against the other; we do not glory in ourselves, nor in man, but in God. Soon Paul turns his speech to the teachers of the Corinthians, so that they might attend to their works, which judge them and make them manifest. Man does not judge them, but their deeds themselves. For they were boasting in themselves; they were living <margin>21</margin> luxuriously, abounding in riches, and reigning imperiously and haughtily. But that was not truly "reigning." Therefore, Paul adds to them: <margin>4</margin> ¶ *For who judges you? And what do you have that you did not receive? Now if you did receive it, why do you glory as if you had not received it? Now you are full! Now you are rich! You have reigned as kings without us—and I wish you did reign, that we also might reign with you!* ¶ Paul gives a great lesson for fleeing vainglory. If anyone is handsome and reflects that he received that beauty from God, he glories not in his beauty, but in God who gave it. If anyone is strong and reflects that his strength is but a point of divine fortitude, which nothing can resist, and that the point of his own strength flowed from it, he does not glory in his own strength, but looks up to and admires that from which it flowed, and glories in that. And so it is if anyone is wise, if anyone is full of counsel, or if anyone is established in power. Neither...

<summary>Paul addresses the factions in Corinth, arguing that true judgment belongs solely to God and that human pride in spiritual leaders is misplaced. He uses himself and Apollos as examples of humble service to rebuke the arrogance and luxury of the rival teachers in the Corinthian church.</summary>
