<meta>This page continues the commentary on 1 Corinthians 4, transitioning from the requirement of humility in stewardship to a sharp contrast between the worldly pride of certain Corinthian teachers and the sacrificial suffering of the true Apostles.</meta>

COM.

He will be like the peacock, a vain bird: which considers only itself and is filled with pride. Yet, by the sound of its own voice and the sight of its feet, God humbles its pride. <note>Medieval bestiaries often claimed the peacock was shocked into humility by looking at its "ugly" feet or hearing its own harsh cry.</note> And Paul more openly chastises those vain pedagogues <note>term: pedagogues (pædagogi). In the Roman world, these were household slaves who supervised children, distinguished here from "fathers" who have a biological or spiritual bond.</note> of the Corinthians who boast in themselves and look upon themselves like that proud bird, by showing what they themselves are like and what the apostles were like. For they have bellies stuffed with food and drink; but the true apostles are hungry and thirsty. They abound in gold and riches; the true apostles are destitute. They are like harnessed kings ruling in arrogance; the true apostles are dejected, naked, and despised. They live in comfort; the apostles are as those destined for death. They are as the "wise" in Christ; the apostles are as "fools" for Christ’s sake. They are as the strong—but with the strength of this world; the apostles are as the weak. They are as the noble; the apostles as the ignoble. They have a firm dwelling-place in this world; the apostles are as wanderers and seekers. They are idle; the apostles seek life through the labor of their hands. They provoke those who do not flatter or praise them with insults and abuse; the apostles return a blessing for insults and abuse. They live without persecution and avoid it; the apostles endure persecution and have patience in their suffering. They were like the pomp of the world; the apostles were like the refuse underfoot and the dust that is shaken off. Regarding them, the oracle of God has been pronounced: *These are they whom we once held in derision and as a proverb of reproach; we fools esteemed their life madness and their end without honor. Behold how they are numbered among the children of God.* <note>original: "Hi sũt quos aliquando habuimus in derisum..." A quote from the Book of Wisdom 5:3–5.</note> Therefore, by way of contrast, Paul presents them to be recognized, saying:

<margin>22</margin>
> For I think that God has shown us apostles last, as those appointed to death. Because we have been made a spectacle to the world, and to angels, and to men. We are fools for Christ's sake, but you are wise in Christ; we are weak, but you are strong; you are distinguished, but we are without honor. To this very hour we both hunger and thirst, and we are naked, and are beaten, and are wanderers, and we labor, working with our own hands. Being provoked by insults, we bless; being afflicted, we endure; being cursed, we entreat. We have been made as the refuse of the world, the dross of all things, even until now. <note>1 Corinthians 4:9–13.</note>

¶ Paul named the apostles "the last" because the patriarchs, Levites, holy men, and prophets had preceded them in the Old Law. After all these, the apostles were sent. And let it be seen even now by the analogy of opposites whether those who are placed in the church are good or bad pastors and builders. No one discerns them, no one judges them; but their works make them manifest. Judgment concerning the good is difficult, but the works themselves judge the evil, especially when they are manifest and open. However, when he said these things about the pastors of the Corinthians which could strike shame into them, he subsequently encourages and beseeches the Corinthians kindly. For he had said whatever he said—and indeed whatever he was about to say—not with the intention of hurting anyone, but of healing. And with a spirit of kindness and fatherly affection, he added, saying:

<margin>23</margin>
> I do not write these things to shame you, but I admonish you as my beloved children. For although you may have ten thousand pedagogues in Christ, yet you do not have many fathers. For in **CHRIST JESUS**, through the gospel, I have begotten you. I beseech you, therefore: be imitators of me. For this cause I have sent to you Timothy, who is my beloved and faithful son in the Lord, who will bring back to your memory my ways which are in **CHRIST**, just as I teach everywhere in every church. <note>1 Corinthians 4:14–17.</note>

¶ The Corinthians would have been hardened indeed if they had not been softened by this exhortation—in which they are so humanely besought as beloved children by the father who had spiritually begotten them. And when he says "be imitators of me," he proposes himself as an example of imitation, not the object. For Christ the Lord is the object of imitation. The life of a father on earth ought to be a mirror and example for his children to imitate. Paul is as the father on earth; the Corinthians are the children. It is just as if he had said: "By my example, imitate Christ." And he who wishes to be a good imitator ought never to rest in the example itself, but through the example always attend to the Truth and the Object itself. And for this very purpose—so that they might worthily imitate Christ according to the ways of Paul—he sent them Timothy, a faithful son of the church, who might lead them back to the true way from the error of their "new" instructors, who were not so much builders as destroyers and corrupters. But through the Spirit, Paul knew (for what did he not know?) that certain of those instructors, puffed up with pride and swelling with human wisdom and eloquence, were boasting that Paul did not dare to come. He forewarns them so that their pride might be stilled, lest they feel the power of the Holy Spirit dashing pride to pieces and treading upon haughty necks. For he did not wish to contend in the words of human wisdom—which is foolishness and vanity before God—but in power, and indeed the power of the Holy Spirit, by which he had condemned Elymas the sorcerer, the false prophet, to blindness with a single word, leaving him crawling and seeking someone to reach out a hand to him. <note>A reference to Acts 13:8–11, where Paul strikes the magician Elymas blind.</note> By this example they had reason to fear. But Paul’s kindness is so great that he does not wish to come to them with that rod, in that power, but rather exhorts and hopes that they might repent and that he might come to them in love and a spirit of gentleness, saying:

<margin>24</margin>
> As if I were not coming to you, some are puffed up. But I will come to you quickly, if the Lord wills... <note>1 Corinthians 4:18–19.</note>

Paul asserts his spiritual fatherhood over the congregation and warns that he prefers to come to them in gentleness rather than with the miraculous "rod" of discipline.</summary>

...will be: and I will know not the speech of those who are puffed up, but their power. For the kingdom of God consists not in speech, but in power. <note>original: "rit: & cognoscam non sermonem inflatorum / sed potestatem. non enim in sermone est regnum dei: sed in potestate."</note>

¶ What do you wish? Shall I come to you with a rod, or in love and the spirit of gentleness? ¶ The kingdom of Christ is not established by the eloquence of human wisdom, but (as was said before) in the manifestation of the spirit and power. Paul was never deprived of this power from his calling until the end: out of his own goodness and will, he confronts the proud spirits—that is, the spirit of the rod and vengeance for the stubborn, and the spirit of love and gentleness for those who repent.

## EXAMINATION of several points concerning the text.

<margin>A 1</margin>¶ The Vulgate edition: *And the stewards of the ministers of God.* ¶ It should say *of the mysteries*, that is, of secrets and hidden things. For the sacraments of Christ were hidden from all nations and the Jews, except for those whom Christ the Lord had taught and the Holy Spirit had filled. Paul: <note>original: "καὶ οἰκονόμους μυστηρίων θεοῦ"</note>—*and stewards of the mysteries of God.* ¶ The Vulgate edition: *Here it is now required among stewards, that a man be found faithful.* ¶ It is found more accurately in Paul: *moreover, what remains* or *next*, rather than *here now*. Paul: <note>original: "ὃ δὲ λοιπὸν ζητεῖται ἐν τοῖς οἰκονόμοις, ἵνα πιστός τις εὑρεθῇ"</note>—*Moreover, what is required in stewards is that one be found faithful.* And this small part does not seem to be a question, but rather "it is sought," "it is required," or "it is demanded" seems to be the meaning here.

<margin>B 6</margin>¶ The Vulgate edition: *Now these things, brothers, I have transformed in myself and Apollo for your sakes: so that in you, you might learn.* ¶ Rather, it should be *in myself*, and *so that in us*, using the first person. Paul: <note>original: "ταῦτα δὲ ἀδελφοὶ μετεσχημάτισα εἰς ἐμαυτὸν καὶ ἀπολλὼ δι᾿ ὑμᾶς, ἵνα ἐν ἡμῖν μάθητε"</note>—*Now these things, brothers, I have applied in a figure to myself and Apollos for your sakes, so that in us you might learn.* ¶ The Vulgate edition: *That no one be puffed up for one against another above that which is written.* ¶ After "written," the word *to think* is missing. The infinitive *to think* refers back to the preceding verb *you might learn*. Paul: <note>original: "τὸ μὴ ὑπὲρ ὃ γέγραπται φρονεῖν, ἵνα μὴ εἷς ὑπὲρ τοῦ ἑνὸς φυσιοῦσθε κατὰ τοῦ ἑτέρου"</note>—*not to think beyond what is written, so that no one of you be puffed up for the one against the other.*

<margin>8</margin>¶ The Vulgate edition: *You reign without us. And I wish you did reign: so that we also might reign with you.* ¶ In both places, the past tense is used; indeed, it is said *you have reigned*. However, due to the custom of Latin speech, it seemed better to change that past tense into the past optative <note>A grammatical mood expressing a wish.</note> after the particle *would that* or *I wish*. And where Paul says at the end *con-reign with you*, the particle "with" is appropriately drawn back into the preceding word "you" according to Latin custom. Paul: <note>original: "χωρὶς ἡμῶν ἐβασιλεύσατε, καὶ ὄφελόν γε ἐβασιλεύσατε· ἵνα καὶ ἡμεῖς ὑμῖν συμβασιλεύσωμεν"</note>—*You have reigned without us, and I would to God you did reign, that we also might reign with you.*

<margin>C twice 12</margin>¶ The Vulgate edition: *We are cursed, and we bless. We suffer persecution, and we endure it. We are blasphemed, and we entreat.* ¶ Paul presents these elegantly through participles without the connecting word "and." Paul: <note>original: "λοιδορούμενοι εὐλογοῦμεν. διωκόμενοι, ἀνεχόμεθα. βλασφημούμενοι, παρακαλοῦμεν"</note>—*Being reviled, we bless; being persecuted, we suffer it; being defamed, we entreat.*

¶ The Vulgate edition: *The offscouring of all things until now.* ¶ If the Greek word <term>peripsima (περίψημα)</term> was to be kept, since the second-to-last letter is written with an *eta* (η)—which is turned into a long *e* among the Latins—it should have been translated as *peripsema* with the penultimate syllable lengthened. Indeed, *peripsema* signifies <term>scoria</term> <note>refuse from metal smelting</note> and the general dross and scrapings, such as from iron, copper, clothes, shoes, feet, and the rest. Paul: <note>original: "πάντων περίψημα ἕως ἄρτι"</note>—*the refuse of all things until now.*

<margin>D 14</margin>¶ The Vulgate edition: *But I warn you as my most dear sons.* ¶ It is read as *beloved* in Paul. Paul: <note>original: "ἀλλ’ ὡς τέκνα μου ἀγαπητὰ νουθετῶ"</note>—*but as my beloved children I warn you.* ¶ The Vulgate edition: *Be followers of me, as I also am of Christ.* ¶ The phrase *as I also am of Christ* is missing in Paul's text here. Paul: <note>original: "μιμηταί μου γίνεσθε"</note>—*Be followers of me.* And it is immediately followed by *Because of this*.

<margin>17</margin>¶ The Vulgate edition: *Who is my most dear son.* ¶ In Paul: *beloved*. Paul: <note>original: "ὅς ἐστι τέκνον μου ἀγαπητὸν"</note>—*who is my beloved child.* ¶ The Vulgate edition: *Who shall remind you of my ways which are in CHRIST JESUS.* ¶ In Paul, it is read simply: *which are in Christ*. Paul: <note>original: "ὃς ὑμᾶς ἀναμνήσει τὰς ὁδούς μου τὰς ἐν χριστῷ"</note>—*who shall remind you of my ways which are in Christ.*

<margin>18</margin>¶ The Vulgate edition: *As if I would not come to you, so some are puffed up.* ¶ *So* is not found in Paul. Paul: <note>original: "ὡς μὴ ἐρχομένου δέ μου πρὸς ὑμᾶς ἐφυσιώθησάν τινες"</note>—*As though I would not come to you, some are puffed up.*

### CHAPTER V.

<image-desc>Large decorative woodcut drop cap 'F' featuring intricate floral patterns and scrolling foliage.</image-desc>

False shepherds are recognized by the insolence of the flock and the diseases of the sheep. In this matter, the apostle also notes the <term>pedagogues</term> <note>tutors or guardians</note> of the Corinthians, recounting the unspeakable lust of a stepson with his stepmother, saying:

<margin>1</margin>¶ It is actually reported that there is sexual immorality among you, and such immorality as is not even named among the Gentiles—that someone should have his father’s wife. And you are puffed up! Should you not rather have mourned, so that he who has done this deed might be taken away from among you? ¶ There is no doubt that these words are directed to those who were in charge, whose business it was to remove scandals. Is a shepherd not rightly accused of great madness when he is proud—while he carries himself high, boasts, and is extolled—yet a wolf stalks the flock, and slaughters and destroys the sheep? But where those who are present do not keep watch over the safety of the flock, it falls upon those who are absent (following Paul’s example) to intervene wholesomely. He, though absent, provided for this situation: that such a great evil might be removed, and that he might strike that fornicator with the terrible rod of the power of the spirit...

<header>COMMENTARY</header>

...striking, so that those who were leading poorly and were puffed up in themselves might be terrified; striking, I say, that man and delivering him to the power of the demon. This was done so that the body, which he had used wickedly, might be visibly tortured as an example to others, and lest his soul—the image of God—which had been conscious of the evil deed, might perish forever. For who would not be deterred from committing a crime if he saw someone else, having committed a similar act, possessed by a demon and tortured so miserably? And indeed, Paul did this with a saddened heart, as he himself testifies, saying: <margin>26</margin> <gloss>¶</gloss> For I, though absent in body but present in spirit, have already judged—as though I were present—the one who has worked such a thing; that in the name of our Lord JESUS CHRIST, as you and my spirit grieve together, I might deliver him with the power of our Lord JESUS CHRIST to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord JESUS. <note>Paul is referring to a specific case of incest in the Corinthian church. By "delivering to Satan," he likely means excommunication or a physical affliction intended to bring the sinner to repentance.</note>

<margin>27</margin> <gloss>¶</gloss> Now he censures and corrects both the boasting teachers and the Corinthians who boast in those teachers, saying: <gloss>¶</gloss> Your boasting is not good. Do you not know that a little leaven <note>term: "leaven" (fermentum). In the Bible, leaven or yeast is often used as a metaphor for the way a small amount of sin or influence can spread through an entire community.</note> leavens the whole lump of dough? Clean out the old leaven, so that you may be a new lump of dough, just as you are unleavened. For indeed, CHRIST our Passover has been sacrificed for us. Therefore, let us celebrate the feast, not with the old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth. <gloss>¶</gloss> For how could the boasting of those who led the Corinthians be good, when such a foul crime reigned among them due to their negligence? And how could the Corinthians boast in such noteworthy leaders? Therefore, the boasting of both was evil. But they will say: "Only one man among us committed this whole deed." What of it? Vice is like leaven, and the multitude is like the lump of dough; and it does not escape us that a little leaven makes a large amount of flour mixed with water (which they call a <term>massa</term> <note>original: "massam," referring to a lump of dough</note>) ferment. So, by proportion, the vice of one person usually creeps into the whole multitude and finally renders the whole group vicious. Therefore, a person who is manifest in vice is by no means to be tolerated even in a great multitude, but must be immediately cast out and uprooted. Otherwise, one unjust person will make many unjust, one usurer will make many usurers, the incestuous will make more incestuous, the adulterer more adulterers, the greedy more greedy, the blasphemer more blasphemers, the unclean more unclean—and so it goes with other vices, which are the leavens of ancient malice. But did Christ have any such leaven, he who was sacrificed for us? Not at all. He was sincere and free from all sin. How then shall we celebrate Christ, our Passover, if there is any leaven of the old malice within us? How shall we be sincere lumps in the body of Christ? That would truly be impossible. Therefore, to celebrate with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth is to worship Christ in purity and truth, without the leaven which is vice. As a sign of this, the ancient Passover of the Jews was celebrated with unleavened bread. What then shall we do if people are revealed to us who have the leaven of wickedness—such as publicans, or usurers, or adulterers, or the incestuous, or those falling into bestial vice? The Apostle certainly commands the Corinthians that they must not communicate with such people. For they are excommunicated by the spirit of Jesus <note>The following lines are heavily struck through in the original manuscript</note> <unclear>almost beyond this manner: in which Paul himself convicts them of having been. What then did they do in Corinth? Did they cast them out? Not at all. But rather, moved by mercy, they spared them. But certainly, this was an error.</unclear>

<margin>28</margin> <unclear>...</unclear> Which Paul also commands the Corinthians, saying: <gloss>¶</gloss> I wrote to you in a letter that you should not associate with fornicators—and by no means with the fornicators of this world, or the greedy, or robbers, or idolaters, since you ought certainly to have gone out of the world. <gloss>¶</gloss> Paul wrote other letters which we do not possess; there is no doubt they were full of the teaching of the Spirit. If only the grace of Christ would restore them to us! Yet those which survive for us by his grace, and which have been left to us by his mercy, are richly and abundantly sufficient for salvation, if we wish to live spiritually. And when he says that one should by no means communicate with the fornicators of this world, the name "fornication" is understood to mean every public and notable vice, which he himself suggests should be understood by expressing a few examples. And what he added—"since you ought certainly to have gone out"—refers to our transition with Christ, who is our Passover, sacrificed for us. For if the children of Israel, in the figure of the sacrifice of their Passover, went out of Egypt, how much more should we, having the true Passover, have gone out of this world to follow our immaculate Lamb into the mountains of eternity, who grazes among the lilies of paradise until the eternal day without night breathes. We can follow him only by the works of the spirit, not the works of the flesh. But come, you will say: "What does it mean to 'communicate' with such people? Does it mean not to speak with them, or perhaps not to drink or eat with them?" Not yet. For our Lord ate with publicans and sinners, but he did not "communicate" with them, or (to use Paul’s word) he did not "mingle" with them. So also the Apostles did with the Gentiles. To "communicate" and "mingle" with them, therefore, is to consent to their works and to become a participant in any way. For things that are mixed are confused with one another and share in each other's nature. Truly, when the Church decrees that such people are to be removed from the midst, one must neither drink nor...

### II 1 Cor.

...eating, and even hardly any conversation (unless it is for the purpose of pious exhortation or pious correction) should be held with them. For now, the Church itself, through the Holy Spirit from the mouth of Paul, defines those whom it wishes to be removed from their midst: namely, fornicators, the greedy, idolaters, the abusive, drunkards, robbers, and those openly sinning in that manner. For they are not part of the communion of the faithful. This is what Paul adds, saying: <margin>25</margin> ¶ "But now I have written to you: do not associate with them. If anyone who is called a brother is a fornicator, or greedy, or an idolater, or a slanderer, or a drunkard, or a robber: do not even eat with such a person." ¶ But you will say: "Why is it said 'he who is named a brother'?" Paul responds that he does not wish to be anxious about judging those who are outside the Church of Christ and were never its members, but only those who are within the Church. Thus, they themselves ought to judge their own among themselves—not before outside judges who are not of the Church— and remove from their midst the one who had committed such an enormous sin of fornication. And he says: ¶ "For what have I to do with judging those who are outside? Do you not judge those who are within? God will judge those who are outside. Remove the wicked man from your midst." ¶ For if it is not the business of a believer to discuss the controversies of unbelievers and give judgment upon them, he should also not wish his own controversies to be discussed by unbelievers and judged by them. Certainly, Paul did not want the news of that unspeakable fornication to become known to unbelievers by any means, nor other things that happen to Christians out of the weakness of the flesh. For those who are "carnal" <note>This refers to people driven by worldly or physical impulses rather than spiritual ones.</note> are always weak and falling into every abyss of vices. I say he did not wish this (as is only fair) lest unbelievers blame it on the religion to which they are most hostile—or rather, on the head of the religion, Christ, who is blessed above all. He will judge everyone, both those within and those without, with a holy, just, and inescapable judgment. May His holy, just, and true judgment be blessed forever and ever. Amen.

<margin>A</margin> ¶ AN EXAMINATION of several points regarding the literal text. ¶ The Vulgate Edition: *Such as is not even among the nations.* <margin>25</margin> The word "named" is missing. Paul: *which is not even named among the nations.* <note>original: "ἥτις οὐδὲ ἐν τοῖς ἔθνεσιν ὀνομάζεται"</note> ¶ <margin>B</margin> The Vulgate Edition: *He who so works.* ¶ The word "this" is missing. Paul: *he who has worked this thing in this way.* <margin>26</note> <note>original: "τὸν οὕτως τοῦτο κατεργασάμενον"</note> ¶ The Vulgate Edition: *In the name of our Lord JESUS CHRIST, as you are gathered together with my spirit.* It should rather be said, "as you and my spirit grieve together" or "are saddened together." Paul: *in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, as you and my spirit are gathered together.* <note>The author is debating the Greek word "synachthentōn" (gathered) versus "synachthomai" (grieving together). Original: "ἐν τῷ ὀνόματι τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ, συναχθέντων ὑμῶν καὶ τοῦ ἐμοῦ πνεύματος".</note> For the word *achthomai* means "I am saddened," from which the compound *synachthomai* <note>"to grieve with someone"</note> is derived. ¶ The Vulgate Edition: *With the power of the Lord JESUS to deliver such a man to Satan.* ¶ It should say, "with the power of our Lord Jesus Christ," and the word "man" is extra. Paul: *with the power of our Lord Jesus Christ, to deliver such a one to Satan.* <note>original: "σὺν τῇ δυνάμει τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ, παραδοῦναι τὸν τοιοῦτον τῷ σατανᾷ"</note> ¶ The Vulgate Edition: *In the day of our Lord JESUS CHRIST.* ¶ From Paul, only "in the day of the Lord Jesus" is found here. Paul: *in the day of the Lord Jesus.* <note>original: "ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τοῦ κυρίου ἰησοῦ"</note> ¶ The Vulgate Edition: *Do you not know that a little leaven corrupts the whole mass?* <margin>27</margin> ¶ It should say, "leavens the whole mass." Paul: *Do you not know that a little leaven leavens the whole batch?* <note>original: "οὐκ οἴδατε, ὅτι μικρὰ ζύμη ὅλον τὸ φύραμα ζυμοῖ"</note> Regarding this very statement, repeated by Paul in the epistle to the Galatians, Saint Jerome criticizes the ancient translator, saying: "In our books, it is poorly rendered as 'a little leaven corrupts the whole mass'; the translator transferred his own meaning rather than the words of the Apostle." Jerome prefers the word <term>batch</term> <note>original Latin: "conspersio"</note> rather than "mass" <note>original Latin: "massa"</note>. They define a "batch" as flour moistened with water. However, the question is not whether it is called "mass" or "batch," because Paul always uses the word <term>Phyrama</term> <note>A Greek word meaning a mixture or something kneaded.</note>. Indeed, in the previous epistle, which is to the Romans (Chapter 9), the same word is used for clay, where it is said: *Does the potter not have power over the clay to make from the same mass one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?* So Paul: <note>original: "ἢ οὐκ ἔχει ἐξουσίαν ὁ κεραμεὺς τοῦ πηλοῦ ἐκ τοῦ αὐτοῦ φυράματος ποιῆσαι, ὃ μὲν εἰς τιμὴν σκεῦος, ὃ δὲ εἰς ἀτιμίαν;"</note> But it is also said of figs in Daniel, and of lead in Zechariah, where the word "mass" seems to fit more aptly than "batch." Truly, since the verb *phyro* means "to mix," "mass" seems to signify a certain mixture well enough, whether it is made of flour and water, or of clay, or any other things. But let us love peace and the holy understanding of the Apostle more than a dispute over a word. ¶ The Vulgate Edition: *That you may be a new batch.* ¶ The same word *phyrama*, which the ancient translator had just before turned as "mass," he here translates as "batch" (*conspersio*). But Paul’s analogy would have been clearer if the translator had always used the same word as Paul did. Paul: *that you may be a new batch.* <margin>C</margin> <note>original: "ἵνα ἦτε νέον φύραμα"</note> ¶ The Vulgate Edition: *Therefore let us feast.* <margin>27</margin> ¶ Rather, from Paul, "let us celebrate" or "keep the feast day." HEADER: COMMENTARY

...to have gone out or to go out from the world. Paul says: <note>original: "ἐπεὶ ὀφείλετε ἄρα ἐκ τοῦ κόσμου ἐξελθεῖν"</note> "since you would then be thin obligated to go out of the world."
<margin>D 30</margin> **The Vulgate edition** <note>The standard Latin Bible used in the Western Church.</note> says: "If he who is named a brother among you." The phrase "among you" is superfluous; Paul says: <note>original: "ἐάν τις ἀδελφὸς ὀνομαζόμενος"</note> "if anyone being named a brother." The Vulgate edition says: "Take away the evil from yourselves." It is clearer to say: "Take away him who is evil from among yourselves." For it is spoken in the **masculine** gender in Paul’s text. However, as the old translator rendered it, it can create the illusion that "evil" is spoken of in the **neuter** gender, as if we were saying "remove the evil" or "remove the sin" from yourselves. And where it says "from yourselves," it is the same as what is said in more fitting Latin as "from your midst," which is what we have placed in its stead. Paul says: <note>original: "καὶ ἐξαρεῖτε τὸν πονηρὸν ἐξ ὑμῶν αὐτῶν"</note> "And you shall take away the wicked man from among yourselves."

### CHAPTER VI

<margin>31</margin> <image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial C featuring a scholar or saint seated at a desk with an open book, surrounded by foliage.</image-desc> Since, therefore, it belongs to the faithful to discuss the cases and controversies of the faithful: Paul rebukes the Corinthians because they were not doing this, but were instead going before the unfaithful who are ignorant of the justice of God and are therefore unjust. He says: "Does any of you, having a case against another, dare to go to law before the unjust and not before the saints? Do you not know that the saints shall judge the world? And if the world shall be judged by you, are you unworthy of the smallest <term>pretoriums</term> <note>Latin: "praetoriorum." Here referring to low-level courts or judgment seats.</note>? Do you not know that we shall judge angels? How much more the things of this life? If therefore you have courts for the things of this life, do you appoint those who are most despised in the church to sit in judgment? I speak this to your shame. Is it so, that there is not one wise man among you who can judge between his brother? But brother goes to law with brother, and this before the unfaithful?" In all these things, the Apostle rebukes the Corinthians: that brother called brother—that is, a believer called a believer—to judgment before the unfaithful. They were ignorant of the dignity of the saints, who shall judge the world, and not only the world, but even the fallen angels in the judgment. This is a mystical and hidden thing. Therefore, they are much more able to judge concerning the smallest and temporal matters; for he proves his point by arguing from the greater to the lesser. And concerning the judgment of the saints, it is said: "The just shall shine, and shall run to and fro like sparks among the reeds; they shall judge nations, and have dominion over peoples." <note>A reference to the Book of Wisdom 3:7–8.</note> He also accuses them because, although they have "forums"—that is, places for judging—they were appointing some presiding judge who was lazy and held in contempt in the church, as if there were no wise person among them who could have been put in charge. This results in their shame. And because they were appointing an ineffective judge, it happened that people, avoiding his court, would appeal to the judgment of the unfaithful. 

But he adds another accusation: that they have lawsuits among themselves at all, and one summons another to judges (in which brotherly charity is wounded and love for one's neighbor is pierced). He considers it better to suffer injury than to summon a brother to a judge. To suffer injury is not an evil, but to violate charity is a sin. And the more numerous the summons to court, the more it is a sign of numerous injustices. Therefore Paul says:
<margin>32</margin> "Indeed, it is already a total crime among you that you conduct judicial disputes among yourselves. Why do you not rather suffer injury? Why do you not rather endure the loss of things? But you inflict injury and take away spoils, and this to your brothers. Or do you not know that the unjust shall not inherit the kingdom of God?" When there is a great crowd gathered to see doctors in a city, it is a sign of many illnesses. So also, when many lawsuits are brought to the forum, it is a sign (as has been said) of many injustices. And it often happens that he who summons, or he who is summoned as a "just" person, returns from the forum "unjust." For if someone (for example) withholds some money from me against my will, he does me an injury; but in this, there is no sin in me. And it can happen that I still love him, and he also loves me. But if I summon him to law, if I cause him losses which necessarily follow that judicial summons, and if I even manage to have him deprived of the fellowship of the saints and the participation of the whole church as if he were a pagan: how am I not doing an injury, I who seek "justice"? How am I not breaking the commandment of God, I who violate the holy bond of love between me and my brother? Believe Paul, who speaks through the Spirit of God: it is better to suffer injury and endure the loss of things than to conduct judicial lawsuits, brother against brother. Therefore, for all the unjust and those who inflict injury on others, Paul subjoins a terrifying but general and most true lesson, saying:
<margin>33</margin> "Do not be deceived. Neither fornicators, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, nor the <term>effeminate</term> <note>original: "molles." Referring to those who are soft or passive in vice.</note>, nor <term>sodomites</term> <note>original: "cinædi." Referring to practitioners of unnatural lusts.</note>, nor the greedy, nor thieves, nor drunkards, nor the abusive, nor the predatory shall inherit the kingdom of God." But because many of the Corinthians knew that they had once been such people, they might have fallen into the doubt that leads to despair, thinking they would never enter the heavenly kingdom. For this reason, Paul lifts their spirits with the good hope of the eternal inheritance, saying:
<margin>34</margin> "And such were some of you. But you were washed, but you were sanctified, but you were justified: in the name of the Lord JESUS and in the Spirit of our God." Those, therefore, who are sanctified and justified through the mysteries of Christ, whether through the baptism of <term>Illumination</term> <note>original: "Φωτισμῶν" (Photismōn). An early Christian term for baptism as a source of spiritual light.</note> or after baptism through...

the sacrament of reconciliation: no distrust because of previously committed crimes <note>The author suggests that once reconciled to God, one should not live in fear or doubt because of past sins.</note> ought to creep into them. Who, therefore, recognizing himself as a member of Christ, will take himself from the body of Christ, so that through fornication, which is a work of the flesh, he makes himself a member of a prostitute? He who certainly commits fornication is made one flesh with the prostitute, as it is written: "the two shall be in one flesh." For he who is committed to marriage for the unity of the flesh, his act of clinging to a prostitute is a similar act of the flesh. He, therefore, who clings to a prostitute, clings by the flesh. But he who was clinging to Christ, was clinging by the spirit, and was made one spirit. For as the clinging of flesh to flesh leads to unity, how much more does the spirit to spirit. For never are spirits joined for the union of the flesh; instead, "the two," he says, "shall be in one flesh." But for the union of the spirit, even the flesh is united. For we are one body and one spirit in Christ. ¶ Oh, if only we understood this high mystery of the unity of spirit and body—a holy and admirable unity, I say, which is better understood by angels than by men—we would never, for the sake of an ill-fated work of the flesh, dissolve this holy union.

And our members are the temple of God. Therefore, it is fitting for our bodies to be holy. But nothing is more impure than fornication with all its kinds. Therefore, it is most opposed to the sanctity of the body of Christ and the holiness of the temple of God; it most pollutes his holy temple and renders it profane, polluted, and unclean. For this reason, Paul strictly commands that this robber of holiness, this (as I might call it) polluter of God's temple, must be avoided with the greatest effort,
<margin>38</margin> saying: ¶ Flee fornication. Every sin whatsoever a man shall do is outside the body. But he who commits fornication, sins against his own body. Or do you not know that your bodies are the temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you, whom you have from God, and you are not your own? For you were bought with a price. Glorify God therefore in your body, and in your spirit, which are God’s. <note>1 Corinthians 6:18-20</note> ¶ He who commits fornication does not take the matter for sinning from elsewhere except from the very substance of his body. For example, gluttony: in food and drink; envy: in another's happiness; pride: in honors, external power, and things of this sort. What if someone should boast of their own beauty, like Absalom <note>King David’s son, famous for his physical beauty and long hair.</note>, or pride themselves on their own strength, like a certain Milo <note>Milo of Croton, a legendary Greek wrestler of immense strength.</note> or Samson? These are not the body or the substance of the body, but are added things, like certain appendages to the body. What if it is in knowledge? This also in no way pertains to the body. And he who looks closely perceives that every other sin has its matter outside the substance of the body. Only fornication has the substance of the body as its matter, as if more directly dissipating the dwelling place of the Holy Spirit—which indeed is not ours, but belongs to Christ God. For he bought it with his most precious blood. Therefore, that which is not ours but God's, let us not pollute, let us not dissipate through such a foul monster as fornication. But let us glorify God in both body and mind, which are not ours, but are his own. Therefore, let us make a brief epilogue of these few things above. Let us not do the works of the flesh...

even if they are in our power: because we have been washed, sanctified, and justified through the goodness of Christ and through the Holy Spirit. Let us not do [these things]: because they do not bring us any benefit. Let us not do them: because God will destroy both those who do them and the works themselves. Let us not do them: because the body was given for the service of God, and God is the Lord of the body. Let us not do them: because God, who raised up Christ, will also raise up our own bodies. Therefore, since we await a resurrection conformed to the brightness of Christ's body, let us not stain ourselves with the works of the flesh. Let us not do them: because our bodies are members of Christ. Shall we then take the members of Christ and defile them with the filth of a prostitute? Or shall we make them members of a body of sin—which is a dwelling place of the devil—abandoning Christ and the divine light dwelling within us, so that we may receive the devil with his horrendous darkness as our inhabitant? Let us not do [this]: because we are the temple of the Holy Spirit. Let us not do [this]: because this temple, which consists of both body and mind, is not our own; it was bought with a sacrificial victim greater and more powerful than the whole world—namely, by the offering of the soul, body, and blood of the Son of God, with the Divinity both offering and receiving the sacrifice. Let us therefore glorify God, the author of so great a gift, with our whole soul and our whole body; let us recognize that both we, our soul, and our body are His, and let us not use His property except for His glory and honor. To Him be grace, honor, power, lordship, and empire over us forever. Amen. Now follows the examination.

# EXAMINATION of several points regarding the literal text.

<margin>A 31</margin>
¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *And if the world shall be judged by you, are you unworthy to judge the smallest matters?* <note>The "Vulgate" refers to the standard Latin Bible translation used in the Western Church for centuries.</note> ¶ It should rather be said: "Are you unworthy of the smallest courts or forums?" For a "praetorium" <note>a judicial headquarters</note> or a "forum" is the place where a judge sits, and where controversies are settled in the judgment of those contending. Paul [wrote]: <term>καὶ ἐπ' ὑμῖν κρίνεται ὁ κόσμος, ἀνάξιοί ἐστε κριτηρίων ἐλαχίστων;</term> <note>original Greek: "And if the world is judged by you, are you unworthy of the smallest courts?"</note> for the word <term>κριτήριον</term> <note>transliterated: kriterion</note> designates a forum or a place of judgment. And by the saints, or among the saints, the world will be judged. For when their faith is brought forth as an example (as it pleases certain sacred interpreters), the faithlessness of the wicked will be condemned. The saints will therefore condemn and judge as witnesses of divine goodness; but the King, who is Christ Jesus, will act as the Judge.

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *How much more things of this world.* ¶ It could be said: "Are they not also temporal matters?" Paul [wrote]: <term>μήτιγε βιωτικά</term> <note>original Greek: "mētige biōtika" (how much more matters of this life)</note>, for <term>βιωτικά</term> <note>biōtika</note> designates what is temporal, worldly, and pertaining to this life.

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Appoint those to judge.* ¶ It should rather be said "you appoint." For Paul is not commanding this; rather, he is rebuking the Corinthians because they were doing so. And it is more accurate to say "you make them sit" rather than "you appoint" for judgment. However, the latter interprets and explains the former. Paul [wrote]: <term>τούτους καθίζετε</term> <note>original Greek: "toutous kathizete" (these you seat/appoint)</note>.

<margin>B 31</margin>
¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *But brother contends in judgment with brother.* ¶ Rather: "brother is judged with brother." Paul [wrote]: <term>ἀλλὰ ἀδελφὸς μετὰ ἀδελφοῦ κρίνεται</term> <note>original Greek: "alla adelphos meta adelphou krinetai"</note>.

<margin>B 32</margin>
¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *But you do wrong and defraud: and this to the brethren.* ¶ This ought to be spoken in the plural. And "to the brethren" <note>using the dative case in Latin</note> does not fit the translator's words well. For one does not say "you defraud to the brothers," but "you defraud the brothers" <note>using the accusative case</note>. But it should rather have been said: "you do wrong and aim frauds" or something similar, "and this to the brothers." If the word "defraud" must remain, the first part must be changed to "you inflict injury," and the dative case changed to the accusative, weaving the whole speech together in this way: "but you inflict injury and defraud: and these [your] brothers." This is the case in which Paul spoke. Paul [wrote]: <term>ἀλλ' ὑμεῖς ἀδικεῖται καὶ ἀποστερεῖτε, καὶ ταῦτα ἀδελφούς</term> <note>original Greek: "but you yourselves wrong and defraud, and these things [to] brothers"</note>. But enough of these things for now; let us leave the duties of the grammarians to the grammarians.

<margin>C 34</margin>
¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *And such indeed you were at one time.* ¶ It is neither "at one time" nor "indeed" as a conjunction; rather, it is "some" or "certain ones." For he does not accuse all of them, but only some who were such [sinners]. Paul [wrote]: <term>καὶ ταῦτα, τινὲς ἦτε</term> <note>original Greek: "And such were some of you." The author is noting that "tines" (some) was misread or mistranslated as a temporal adverb.</note>.

<margin>C 35</margin>
¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *All things are lawful for me: but not all things are expedient. All things are lawful for me: but I will be brought under the power of none.* ¶ It is more consistent if we say in Latin: "All things are in my power." For what follows—"but I will be brought under the power of none"—uses a word for "power" <note>Latin: *potestate*</note> that is derived from the word used just before for "lawful" <note>Latin: *licent*</note>. "Lawful" is expressed as <term>ἔξεστιν</term> <note>exestin</note>, and "power" as <term>ἐξουσία</term> <note>exousia</note> (it makes no difference whether it is simple or compound); and <term>ἐξουσία</term> designates "power." Therefore, <term>ἔξεστιν</term> means "to be in one's power." Conversely, <term>ἔξεστιν</term> means "it is permitted/lawful." Therefore <term>ἐξουσία</term> means "license" or "liberty." These are "conjugate" words—a concept very well known to logicians. Sacred eloquence almost everywhere consistently translates <term>ἐξουσίαν</term> as "power." Therefore, <term>ἔξεστιν</term> will be consistently translated as "to be in one's power." I have no doubt that this is what Paul intended; he who was at once a logician, a rhetorician, and a philosopher—but he was all these things divinely, super-mundanely, and (if I may say so) transcendentally. Unless, of course, the darkness wishes to pass judgment on the light. Paul [wrote]: <term>πάντα μοι ἔξεστιν, ἀλλ' οὐ πάντα συμφέρει, πάντα μοι ἔξεστιν, ἀλλ' οὐκ ἐγὼ ἐξουσιασθήσομαι ὑπό τινος</term> <note>original Greek: "All things for me are permitted, but not all are beneficial; all things for me are permitted, but I will not be mastered by anything."</note>.

<margin>C 36</margin>
¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Food for the belly and the belly for foods, but God will destroy both it and them.* ¶ It should be said in the plural, just as he immediately said "foods." And in the plural: "and these things." Paul [wrote]: <term>τὰ βρώματα τῇ κοιλίᾳ</term> <note>original Greek: "Foods [plural] for the belly."</note>.

But we remove the word <note>original: "ventrem" (stomach/belly)</note> so that the understanding might be clearer. ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "He who clings to a prostitute: is made one body." ¶ **In Paul it reads:** "is," not "is made." For it is one thing to speak <margin>38</margin> according to the word "shall be" <note>original: "erunt"</note>—where it is said "they two shall be in one flesh." **Paul:** <note>original Greek: "ὁ κολλώμενος τῇ πόρνη ἓν σῶμά ἐστιν"</note> "He who joins himself to a prostitute is one body." ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "For every sin." ¶ The particle "for" <note>original: "enim"</note> is superfluous here. **Paul:** <note>original Greek: "πᾶν ἁμάρτημα"</note> "Every sin." ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "Or do you not know that your members are the temple of the Holy Spirit: who is in you?" ¶ **It should read:** "your bodies." ->CHAPTER VII<-

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut historiated initial "C" featuring a bearded male figure, possibly a scholar or saint, seated at a desk or lectern.</image-desc>

The Corinthians had asked many things of the Apostle through a letter: such as whether they should abstain from their wives. Whether a wife should be taken. If already married: whether it is permitted for a husband to abstain if he wishes, or for a wife if she wishes, and many things of that kind. To which he responds in order. <margin>1</margin> **First.** You are not bound to a wife: it is good if you do not join yourself to a wife, and do not touch a woman at all. <margin>2</margin> **Second.** Lest the opportunity for fornication creep in: let every man be permitted to have his own wife, and every woman to have her own husband. For a "proper husband" <note>original: "proprius vir"</note> is a lawful spouse. <margin>3</margin> **Third.** He who has a wife: it is not permitted for him to abstain if he wishes, but he must render <term>due benevolence</term> <note>A traditional term for the physical intimacy and affection spouses owe to one another.</note> to his wife. And likewise: the wife to the husband. And the reason is: because the husband does not have power over his own body. For it is not his own: but he has given it to his wife for the use of future offspring. Nor does the wife have her own body in her own power. For it is not hers: but it is the husband’s. For she has given it to the husband for the common propagation of offspring. For that which has been given is no longer in the power of the one who gave it, but in the power of the one who received it as a gift. For the woman is like a field; the man is like a farmer; the offspring is like the abundant fruit from the farmer's seed in the field. But a wise farmer does not always sow seed, nor is the field always ready to receive it. So too, the husband should not always demand mutual benevolence from the wife, for she is not always ready; nor the woman from the man. For it is not always the time for sowing. But this must be done reasonably: when neither he nor she has a reasonable impediment. Do you not see: this is not a simple gift, but a mutual one? You are a husband: you holily require the use of your wife's body. You are indeed able, because it is yours, and you have power over her for this purpose—that is, for the use of offspring. But if she herself is indisposed: she can refuse you. For your body is hers, and not yours. And because she is indisposed, she refuses the use of her own thing. For she has as much power over that as you have over the use of her body. Therefore she does not refuse you the use of her body, nor should she; but she does not wish to use that thing which is in her power either to use or not to use. To use it, indeed, if it is consistent with reason. But not to use it if something intervenes by which it would be used less reasonably. And conversely, if the wife holily requires the use of the husband's body: the husband neither justly can, nor should, deny it. For the wife seeks her own thing. But if a reasonable cause intervenes—as perhaps if the husband is sick—he can be unwilling to use his own thing, that is, the wife's body. Not that he denies the wife the use of his own body, but that he is unwilling to use his own thing because it would not be reasonably expedient. Therefore, mutual consent is required for this, just as the gift of their bodies is mutual. But when there is no reasonable impediment for either one: whichever person requests the due benevolence, it must be holily rendered. For when the time is right, and the field is ready, and the farmer is present with his grain: he commits the seed to the earth in God's blessing. And it would be unreasonable if he did not commit it then. How much more holily, purely, and religiously should that seed be committed from which a human being is to be born—the best fruit of the world, into which God <margin>39</margin> breathes His image. And concerning this "due benevolence" to be rendered in this manner: understand the holy Apostle. Let us now hear him, writing these things to the Corinthians in this way.

¶ Concerning the things about which you wrote to me. It is good for a man if he is not joined to a wife. Nevertheless, because of fornications: let each man have his own wife, and let each woman have her own husband. Let the husband render due benevolence to the wife. And similarly the wife to the husband. The wife does not have power over her own body: but the husband. In like manner also, the husband <margin>+</margin> does not have power over his own body: but the wife. ¶ These things are immediately clear. **Fourth.** Is it permitted for a husband and spouse to live separately and privately? It is permitted by the consent of both, and for a time: so that (for example) they may devote themselves to fasting and prayer. At which time, by agreement: they may live together and come together. Not that you should command this...

<margin>40</margin> is allowed: but it is permitted, lest because of the weakness of self-control: one or both be tempted to fornication. ¶ For this reason, Paul adds, saying: ¶ *Do not deprive one another: unless perhaps by consent for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to fasting and prayer; and then come together again, lest Satan tempt you because of your lack of self-control. This I say by way of permission, however, and not as a command.* ¶ And the life of the marriage bed: is good. And the life of those who abstain from the marriage bed: is good. But the life of those who abstain from the marriage bed for the sake of Christ—so that, leading a celibate life in the service of Christ, they may devote themselves more holily and purely to fasting, prayer, works of mercy, the edification of others, or other similar things: is better. Truly, this is not according to each person’s wish: but according to the gift of God. Paul certainly possessed this gift in an eminent degree, as do those who are spiritual like <margin>41</margin> Paul. Therefore, wishing this excellence for all men, he adds: ¶ *For I would that all men were even as I myself. But every man has his own gift from God: one in this manner, and another in that.* ¶ I would certainly believe they are in error (even if they are many and great men) who think that Paul was tempted by the promptings <note>original: "titillationibus," literally ticklings or provocations</note> of the flesh and by the difficulty of self-control. For he possessed the Spirit of God and was truly spiritual. He did not feel those temptations which are frequent and very troublesome to carnal men, even if he frequently transformed the weaknesses of the carnal man within himself, becoming "as the weak to the weak" though he was not weak at all, but so that he might win over the weak. But let us hear what he thinks in the fifth place regarding those <margin>42</margin> who are without a wife and concerning widows who are without a husband, as he says: ¶ *I say to the unmarried and to the widows: it is good for them if they remain even as I. But if they cannot exercise self-control: let them marry. For it is better to marry than to burn.* <note>original: "ignem experiri," literally "to experience the fire," referring to the fire of passion or the fire of hell mentioned later</note> ¶ Celibacy—a life fleeing all carnal contact (in which Paul also lived holily)—whether for men who have not taken a wife, or for women who have not taken husbands, or even for men who once had wives, or for women who likewise had husbands but have them no longer: is far to be preferred to marriage. For it is holier, purer, and more spiritual. But for those who do not have the <term>vow</term> <note>referring here to the capacity or committed state of celibacy</note> of self-control: if they are men, let them take wives; if they are women, let them take husbands. For to enter into marriage is not a sin. But to fail in self-control outside of the marriage bed: is a sin. For that is fornication; and those who commit it will not escape the fire of Gehenna. Therefore, it is better for such people to commit themselves to marriage than to await the danger of Gehenna's fire. In the sixth place: Is it lawful for a man to dismiss his wife, or for a wife to dismiss her husband? What should be answered to this petition is sufficiently known from the words of the Savior in Matthew, teaching thus: *Everyone who dismisses his wife (except for the cause of fornication) makes her commit adultery; and he who marries her who is dismissed: commits adultery.* And in Mark: *Whoever dismisses his wife and marries another <margin>43</margin> commits adultery against her. And if a wife dismisses her husband and marries another: she commits adultery.* A similar sentiment is held in Luke. Therefore Paul adds: ¶ *But to those who are joined in marriage: I command, yet not I, but the Lord. Let the wife not separate from her husband. But if she departs: let her remain unmarried, or be reconciled to her husband. And let the husband not dismiss his wife.* ¶ And in what way can a wife be separated from a husband? The sole cause is fornication, as is known from the Lord. If the husband is a fornicator: the wife has cause to separate herself from the husband, but let her not then marry another. Instead, let her be without a husband, unless a reconciliation is made with her own husband, to whom she may return according to the words of the Apostle. For he can repent and afterwards keep the marriage bed undefiled. Similarly, if the wife commits fornication: the husband has cause for dismissing her. But let him be without a wife, and she without a husband, unless a reconciliation is made and the husband recalls his own wife to himself. For she can repent and afterwards, in greater humility, observance, and subjection to her husband, keep the marriage bed inviolate. And although in the Gospel and in the Apostle such things are not explicitly stated in so many words: yet from what is expressed, such things are understood (unless the light of right <term>Analogy</term> <note>The "Analogy of Faith," a principle of interpretation where unclear passages are understood in light of clear ones</note> is lacking). And these things are said concerning those where both the husband and wife are believers. Now, however, in the seventh place: concerning those where only one is either a believer or an unbeliever, <margin>44</margin> Paul says: ¶ *But to the rest I speak, not the Lord: If any brother has an unbelieving wife, and she consents to dwell with him: let him not dismiss her. And if any woman has an unbelieving husband, and he consents to dwell with her: let her not dismiss him. For the unbelieving husband is sanctified in the woman, and the unbelieving woman is sanctified in the husband. Otherwise your children would be unclean; but now they are holy.* ¶ In the sanctification of the believing woman, the unbelieving husband is sanctified—not in an absolute sense, but regarding the act of procreation. And in the sanctification of the believing man, the unbelieving wife is sanctified—not in an absolute sense, but regarding the duty of procreation from the man. And the infant who is born of a believing mother, begotten of a believing father: is holy. And the infant who is born of a believing mother, begotten of an unbelieving father: is likewise holy. But one who is born of two unbelievers: is unclean. And should this one or that one die...

<margin>1 Cor.</margin>
For this person there is one secret dispensation of God, and for that person another. Regarding this one: as unclean; regarding that one: as clean and holy. Truly, both this uncleanness and this holiness are derivative. <note>original: "deriuatitia," meaning inherited or passed down through the family line rather than personal</note> And this holiness is a certain holiness begun, not perfected. If it should be perfected through baptism, this holiness will be very close to the fountain of holiness and from the Holy Spirit. For such a person, heaven is already opened, in testimony of which: when Jesus, the author of all holiness, was baptized, the heavens were opened to him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and coming upon him. But derivative holiness is not yet sufficient to open heaven. But concerning such people: God will dispose according to his own secret plan, as he does with those who are holy in this way. Nor is it granted to us to know further concerning such things. For we know from Paul here that they are holy—unless he accuses the possibility of those who do not come <note>to the faith</note> out of negligence. For as it is written: *You are righteous, O Lord, and your judgment is right.* <note>original: "Justus es domine: & rectum iudiciū tuū," a quote from Psalm 119:137</note> **Eighthly.** If a believer has an unbelieving bed-partner, and the unbeliever wishes to depart, should not the believer permit it? He certainly should. For if the husband is a believer, he is not subject to such servitude <note>meaning he is not legally or spiritually bound to force the marriage</note> that he should be compelled to retain an unbelieving wife who wishes to leave. Nor is a believing wife subject to that servitude, that she should retain an unbelieving husband who both hates her and desires to desert her. For there would be no peace between them. But God has called us in peace. Nevertheless, let the believing husband not drive away an unbelieving wife who is unwilling to leave, nor a believing wife an unbelieving husband of such a will. For if you are a believing husband, you do not know whether through you God wishes to save your unbelieving wife, and through you, that she may finally become a believer. Nor also, if you are a believing <margin>45</margin> wife, do you know whether through you he wishes your husband to become a believer. For it will be as God has distributed grace to each person. Which Paul testifies, saying: [**If the unbeliever separates, let him separate. A brother or a sister is not subject to servitude in such cases. But God has called us in peace. For how do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband? Or how do you know, husband, whether you will save your wife?** <margin>9</margin> **Nothing, except as God has distributed to each.**] **Ninthly**, he gives a certain general rule to the <margin>46</margin> Corinthians and declares the same, saying: [**As God has called each one, so let him walk. And so I ordain in all the churches. Was anyone called while circumcised? Let him not undo his circumcision. Was anyone called in uncircumcision? Let him not be circumcised. Circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing, but the keeping of the commandments of God.**] [This precept regards God the caller, who chooses some for himself from every condition of men: some free, some slaves, some circumcised, some uncircumcised. Freedom in some does not displease him, nor servitude in others, nor circumcision in some, nor uncircumcision in others; but what pleases him most is the knowledge of his name and the keeping of his commandments. If he even commands circumcision, circumcision as circumcision is nothing toward salvation, but it is the keeping of his precept. And if he commands not to be circumcised, uncircumcision as uncircumcision is nothing toward justification, but it is the keeping of his precept. <margin>10</margin> Therefore, not the sign, but the will of God is chiefly to be attended to. **Tenthly**, that which <margin>47</margin> he discusses is similar to this, yet in a certain way reversed. For the former refers to the one called, but this refers to the Caller. Moreover, the apostle posits and declares it thus: [**Let each one remain in the calling in which he was called. Were you called as a slave? Do not let it be a care to you. Nevertheless, if you can become free, make use of it all the more. For he who is called in the Lord as a slave is the Lord’s freedman.** <note>original: "libertus," a Roman legal term for a former slave who still owes some duties to their former master</note> **Similarly, he who is called as a free man is the slave of CHRIST. You were bought with a price; do not become slaves of men. Brothers, let each one remain with God in the state in which he was called.**] [He who is called in a humble condition, in which even the service of Christ is less free (as in human servitude), should indeed remain in it; but if he can, let him not stay, but rather pass over to a freer state. In what way? By pressing on in his work: by serving better and more faithfully than ever. So that from good and prompt service, and from the utility gained there by the master, freedom may be granted to the slave; so that he who was a slave of a man may be able to be fully a slave of Christ. For as long as he is a slave of a man, he cannot be fully a slave of Christ. For such a slave is Christ’s alone, and serves and attends to Christ alone. Yet because he was called by Christ and spends not a little time serving Christ amidst the services of a secular master, he can be Christ’s freedman, but not yet fully a slave. For it is more to be a slave of Christ than a freedman, and even more than to be a free man of Christ. Christ’s free man pays him nothing. A freedman pays indeed, but little. A slave is entirely Christ’s—not his own, not the world’s, but Christ’s—and he pays everything to Christ. And as among earthly men, the condition of freedom is the highest, most pleasant, and (so to speak) the happiest in this world; then that of freedmen; and the last, that of slaves. So for the spiritual man: spiritual servitude is the highest, most delightful, and happiest; then that of freedmen; but the lowest and most wretched is freedom. Spiritual servitude is so called by way of excellence; human servitude by way of defect. Spiritual servitude as far surpasses human freedom as happiness surpasses misery. Therefore, he who in this world is called by Christ as a free man can be entirely Christ's slave. Let him therefore strive to claim this precious servitude for himself, and in no way become either a slave of the world or a slave of men. For then that entire, eminent...

# COMMENTARY

and above all precious liberty: one should not retain servitude for oneself. And **O** free people of the world: you have been bought at a price even higher than the world. Do not become slaves of men. <margin>11</margin> For here the word of the divinely-inspired apostle pertains to those who were called as free men. ¶ Then, in the eleventh section, he transitions to the status of virgins, giving counsel. ¶ He who is called as a virgin (whether man or woman: it is good) if they remain so. He gives counsel, because the Lord gave no command concerning this specifically, but rather a recommendation. For when the Lord had said to the Pharisees that it was not lawful for a man to dismiss his wife and give her a bill of divorce, and his disciples had said to him, "If such is the case of a man with his wife, it is not expedient to marry," he said to them: "Not everyone can accept this word, but only those to whom it is given." Concerning the diversity of those who do not marry, touching upon the status of virgins as if in a parable through a third category, he added: "For there are <term>eunuchs</term> <note>In this context, the term refers to those who abstain from marriage for religious reasons, not necessarily physical castration.</note> who were born so from their mother’s womb, and there are eunuchs who were made so by men, and there are eunuchs who <margin>48</margin> have castrated themselves <note>original: "castrauerunt," used metaphorically for a vow of celibacy</note> for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. Let him who can accept it, accept it." See, he gives counsel; he does not <margin>></margin> command. So also Paul, saying: ¶ "Now concerning virgins, I have no command of the Lord, <margin>></margin> yet I give my judgment as one who has obtained mercy from the Lord to be faithful. I <margin>></margin> judge therefore that this is good because of the present necessity: that it is good for a man to remain as he is."
¶ The state of virginity is simply "good," whether a man or a woman has "castrated" themselves—that is, maintained themselves purely and holily for the sake of the kingdom of heaven, for the sake of the Son of God who willed to be born of a virgin, and honored virginity above marriage. It is also good because of the necessity of the present life. For in the state of the married, many things are necessary, there is a need for many resources, and there is much anxiety <note>original: "solicitudo," referring to worldly cares and distractions</note> regarding one's wife, children, household, male servants, female servants, and the rest of the dependents. All these are absent from the state of virgins. And this status was especially fitting during the times of the apostles due to necessity. For those who were then called to Christ were poor and lacked all things for Christ’s sake. Or if they did have goods, the unbelievers—once they realized they were Christians—would plunder them. Whence a greater necessity urged them if they had a wife, children, or a family to nourish; and they were frequently seized for the punishments of martyrdom. From this, the tender affection for a spouse, for small children, and for a desolate family could either pull them back or make them undertake martyrdom less spontaneously. Truly, it is not for everyone to lead this life, but only those to whom it is granted by God. But there are virgins, there are the married, <margin>49</margin> and there are those who are celibate and continent after marriage: and all these states are good. Accordingly, <margin>></margin> in the twelfth place, Paul adds: ¶ "Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek a release. <margin>Released 12</margin> <margin>></margin> Are you released from a wife? Do not seek a wife. But if you do marry, you have not sinned. And if a <margin>></margin> virgin marries, she has not sinned. Nevertheless, such will have trouble in the flesh. But I <margin>></margin> spare you." ¶ If a virgin marries, she does not sin. And if a man released from a wife marries a wife, he does not sin. Each has followed the flesh insofar as the law permits, and will be burdened by the flesh. But the wife will feel, when she carries in her womb, when she experiences the pains of birth, when she raises her offspring with much anxiety, and when she studies to please her husband, that the state of virginity was to be preferred to marriage—even though both of these states are good. And the man will no less experience that troubles have increased for him by following the flesh, which he would have lacked if he were released. Truly, these are to be forgiven. They chose a good thing, indeed, but one that is more troublesome, not the one that is more tranquil. So brief and so uncertain is our life in this age that it is foolish to be twisted by anxiety, except for that by which we can please God. <margin>50</margin> This requires tranquility of mind: a calling back into oneself and toward God. And therefore Paul gives this holy teaching to the Corinthians, and through the Corinthians to us: ¶ "But this I say, <margin>></margin> brothers: the time is short. It remains that even those who have wives should be as though they had none; <margin>></margin> and those who weep, as though they wept not; and those who rejoice, as though they rejoiced not; <margin>></margin> and those who buy, as though they possessed not; and those who use this world, as not <margin>></margin> abusing it. For the fashion of this world passes away. <note>original: "figura huius mūdi," meaning the outward appearance or theater of the world</note> But I would have you be without <margin>></margin> anxiety." ¶ Let us consider the brevity of this life, or rather its vanity: all anxiety perishes, except that which looks toward the eternity of the future. But that anxiety consists (in the zeal for pleasing God) in tranquility of mind, whatever happens in this world—whether this or that status, whether weeping or joy, whether wealth or poverty, whether a calling to honor or abandonment. None of these clings to this world because if anything seems either to be or to promise something, it deceives. For nothing lasts for us, but continually slips away. However, that which follows it is eternal and exists forever. Therefore, let us live without the anxiety of the world, content with necessary food and clothing in whatever state we live; and our mind, turned toward God in tranquility, will reflect the true image of God. Do you not see that if water is disturbed and not at all settled and still, it reflects no image? Truly, so that we may live without the anxiety of the world and <margin>51</margin> possess tranquility of mind, one state of life is more suitable than another, as the state of <margin>></margin> virgins is more so than the married. Indeed, even the state of those remaining continent after marriage is better than that of the married. Not without reason, then, opening this to us, Paul adds: ¶ "He who is without a wife is solicitous for the things of the Lord, <margin>></margin> how he may please the Lord. But he who has married a wife is solicitous for the things of the world, how he may [please his wife]..."

<summary>This page analyzes Paul’s preference for celibacy over marriage, arguing that while marriage is not a sin, the "present necessity" of persecution and the inherent anxieties of domestic life distract from spiritual focus. The author uses the metaphor of still water to illustrate how only a tranquil mind can truly reflect the image of God.</summary>

<header>II 117</header>
<sig>A</sig>

<margin>1 Cor. 7</margin>
...how he may please his wife. And there is a difference between a wife and a virgin. She who is without a husband cares for the things of the Lord, that she may be holy in both body and spirit. But she who is married cares for the things of the world: how she may please her husband. I say this for your own benefit—not to cast a snare <note>original: "laqueum"; referring to a trap or a restrictive obligation</note> upon you, but for the sake of what is honorable, and that you may serve the Lord without distraction, clinging to Him steadfastly. ¶ Paul praised virginity not to cast a snare upon the Corinthians—that is, not to bind them in such a way that they could not enter into marriage if they wished, whether men or women. Rather, he said this with a view toward the benefit of those capable of living in such a way, so that (what is most important) they might be able to cling steadfastly to God alone and not to the world. For both men and women are better able to do this in the state of virginity and continence than in the state of marriage. For even though married people sometimes cling to the service of God, they cannot do so entirely or unchangeably; the cares of the world call them back and divide them, so that they are devoted now to the world, now to their spouse. Similarly, wives cannot cling continually and fully to the service of God, for they are called away now by a husband, now by children, now by household affairs, which entangle them in other occupations and cares. But because there are those who do not have the gift for this most perfect state—as the Lord says, "Not all can accept this word, but only those to whom it is given"—Paul therefore offers a judgment concerning those who are in such a position, which he considers to be from the Spirit of God for both the former and the latter, saying: ¶ But if anyone thinks he is acting dishonorably toward
<margin>13</margin>
his virgin <note>In the context of the time, this refers to a father or guardian deciding the future of a daughter or ward.</note>, if she is past her youth <note>original: "superadulta"</note>, and it must be so, let him do what he will; he does not sin if she marries. But he who stands firm in his heart, being under no necessity and having power over his own will, and has determined this in his heart—to keep his virgin—does well. Therefore, he who gives her in marriage does well, but he who does not give her in marriage does better. ¶ This is the thirteenth point for the instruction of the Corinthians. That which follows should be held as the fourteenth. ¶ A wife is bound to the law as long as her husband lives. But if her husband falls asleep <note>A common early Christian euphemism for death.</note>, she is free. Let her marry whom she will, provided it is in the Lord. But in my judgment, she is happier if she remains as she is. And I think that I also have the Spirit of God. ¶ These things do not present much difficulty in being understood. However, regarding the thirteenth point of instruction, this may be
<margin>14</margin>
noted: there are certain adult virgins who have a purpose of continence for the sake of the kingdom of heaven; and fathers act dishonorably and indecently if, having no other necessity, they force them to take husbands against their holy purpose. Conversely, there are also certain adult virgins whose hearts are tickled by a desire for marriage, and then fathers act dishonorably and indecently toward them if they do not provide husbands for such women; for they have a necessary occasion to hand them over to marriage. Furthermore, if anyone who has free power—that is, one who is not a slave but is his own master—has an adult virgin who is indifferent to either path, and he has established a firm purpose in his mind to consecrate her to virginity and keep her a virgin, he does well. Nevertheless, if he joins her in marriage, he does not sin. Yet he does better if he does not join her. For he shows that virginity is to be honored and preferred over the marriage bed, both because of its greater purity and its freer service to God. And what he said for the fourteenth instruction of the Corinthians—concerning the woman who has married, that upon the death of her husband she is released from the law of the husband (which is the marital law)—is clear. But he restricts and narrows the following part, "let her marry whom she will," by what follows: "provided" or "only in the Lord." For she marries in the Lord if she, being a believer, takes a believer. For this apostolic instruction does not permit a believing woman, after her calling, to take an unbelieving husband, nor conversely, a believing man an unbelieving wife. It is otherwise if, before the calling of the believer, either the man or woman already had an unbelieving partner. In that case, the believer is not forced to dismiss the unbeliever; indeed, according to the seventh point, they are commanded to remain together if the unbelieving party is pleased with the marriage bed of the believer. And what he adds—"But she is happier if she remains so"—prefers the life of the continent over the life of the married. That this is so is shown by the freer service of God. Nevertheless, virginity excels all, as it adds greater purity to that freer service. And it is wonderful how Peter and Paul, and those who heard them, had a powerful discourse through the Holy Spirit for inducing the purpose of perpetual virginity. Those who wish to know this even in part should read the exhortation of Nereus and Achilleus <note>Saints Nereus and Achilleus were legendary early Christian martyrs said to be chamberlains to Domitilla.</note>, disciples of Peter and martyrs, to the virgin Domitilla, the niece of Domitian. From this they will also learn how much those who hand themselves over to marriage suffer in the flesh, and with what eminence virginity shines over marriage. And this state of virginity makes one capable of a certain degree of glory in the other life, as the divine word says, speaking thus of such people: "These are they who have not defiled themselves with women, for they are virgins; and they follow the Lamb wherever He goes" <note>A reference to Revelation 14:4.</note>. May the grace of the Savior grant us to one day hear their "new song" before His throne, which no one can sing except the virgins, and to mingle our praises likewise with Jesus, the Author of life.
