<meta>This page continues the linguistic and theological commentary on 1 Corinthians 7. The previous page discussed the distinction between the life of a virgin and that of a married person, emphasizing that Paul’s advice was intended to help believers cling to God without distraction rather than to trap them with restrictive rules.</meta>

<header>COMMENTARY</header>
<meta>Library stamp 71031 at top left corner.</meta>

This speech is permissive, not commanding: as is known from the fifth and following passages. This is better understood in Latin: since the verb has the sense of "let it be permitted to have," it is interpreted this way. Paul says: <note>original Greek: "διὰ δὲ τὰς πορνείας ἕκαστος τὴν ἑαυτοῦ γυναῖκα ἐχέτω"</note> "Because of sexual immoralities, let each man have his own wife."
<margin>39</margin>
¶ **The Vulgate edition:** <margin>A</margin> "Let the husband render the debt to the wife." ¶ We should say not "the debt," but "due benevolence," following Paul. For he speaks modestly and politely. Paul says: <note>original Greek: "τῇ γυναικὶ ὁ ἀνὴρ τὴν ὀφειλομένην εὔνοιαν ἀποδιδότω"</note> "Let the husband render to the wife the benevolence that is owed." 
¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "The woman does not have power over her own body, but the husband." ¶ It is better to say: "The wife does not have power over her own body." For where the old translator here says "woman" <note>Latin: "mulier"</note>, two words earlier he said "wife" <note>Latin: "uxor"</note>; namely here: "and the wife to the husband." In Paul's text, it is the same word. Also, "woman" is a common term for both one who has a husband and one who does not. If she does not have a husband, she has power over her own body, for she has not given her body to anyone; therefore, it is both hers and under her own power. It is better, then, to say "wife," of whom it is more universally true that she does not have power over her own body. Paul says: <note>original Greek: "ἡ γυνὴ τοῦ ἰδίου σώματος οὐκ ἐξουσιάζει, ἀλλ’ ὁ ἀνήρ"</note> "The wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband." 

But what will you say? If a virgin, having the intention of virginity, marries, does the husband then have power over her body? Or does she still have power over her own body? For example: as when Cecilia married Valerian <note>St. Cecilia is a legendary Christian martyr who, despite being married, maintained her vow of virginity</note>; if Cecilia or any such holy virgin marries, she does not have power over her body, nor is the body her own. For she gave it to God, who loves chaste minds. After the marriage, the body is under the husband's power only in regard to protection—not in regard to the spoiling of the virginity which she has consecrated. For virginity belongs to God. Nor does a virgin of this sort have anything of her body to give her husband power over, except for protection alone. Nor could the most blessed Virgin [Mary] give her husband, the righteous Joseph, any other power over her body. <margin>B</margin> Therefore, those married in this way are the same as those unmarried: married in terms of protection, unmarried in the flesh. And thus, this protection is more precious to the husband than a marriage of the flesh (so to speak); since guarding the flesh of God is more precious than guarding one's own flesh. 

<margin>40</margin>
¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "Do not defraud one another." ¶ The word the apostle uses here indicates a "deprivation." They deprive themselves of common society when they separate themselves from the bedchamber or the marriage bed for the sake of fasting and prayer, which the great celebrations of the mysteries of Christ require. Paul says: <note>original Greek: "μὴ ἀποστερεῖτε ἀλλήλους"</note> "Do not deprive one another." 
¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "That you may devote yourselves to prayer." We should say: "That you may devote yourselves to fasting and prayer." The word "fasting" and the connecting word [and] are missing. Paul says: <note>original Greek: "ἵνα σχολάζητε τῇ νηστείᾳ καὶ τῇ προσευχῇ"</note> "That you may have leisure for fasting and prayer." 
¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "And come together again to the same." ¶ It is better to say "together." For that phrase, <note>original Greek: "ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτό"</note> "to the same," as we noted in the Psalms, is usually used to mean "together." From this phrase "come back together," it is understood that by "depriving one another," he meant their separation for a time. <margin>B</margin> Paul says: <margin>41</margin> <note>original Greek: "καὶ πάλιν ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτὸ συνέρχησθε"</note> "And come together again at the same place." 
¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "But I wish you all." ¶ We should say "For I wish all men." And in the Latin manner we can say "I would wish." For the Hebrews express a wish even through the indicative mood, whose custom Paul imitates. The Latins, however, use the optative. <margin>42</margin> Paul says: <note>original Greek: "θέλω γὰρ πάντας ἀνθρώπους"</note> "For I wish all men [to be as I am]." 
¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "For it is better to marry than to burn." ¶ The word Paul uses here means "to be on fire" or "to be tested by fire," as in "silver tested by fire." There are those who want this passage to be understood as the fire of lust. I, however, understand Paul's statement to refer to the fire of Gehenna <note>a term for Hell or a place of fiery judgment</note>, which those who do not practice continence outside of marriage will feel. Nor does Paul predict this in vain. <margin>43</margin> Paul says: <note>original Greek: "κρεῖσσον γάρ ἐστι γαμῆσαι ἢ πυροῦσθαι"</note> "For it is better to marry than to be burned." 
¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "But if she departs, let her remain unmarried." ¶ I would prefer it to be said here: "remain without a husband" rather than "unmarried." For how is she "unmarried" if she has a husband? And to whom, if she is reconciled, she may return as to her own husband? Paul says: <note>original Greek: "ἐὰν δὲ καὶ χωρισθῇ μενέτω ἄγαμος"</note> "But if she should even be separated, let her remain unmarried." <margin>C</margin> Although the Greek word <term>agamos</term> means both "unmarried" and "without a husband," it is more conveniently interpreted here as "without a husband." 
<margin>44</margin>
¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "For to the rest I say, not the Lord." ¶ Rather: "But to the rest I say." Paul says: <note>original Greek: "τοῖς δὲ λοιποῖς ἐγὼ λέγω οὐκ ὁ κύριος"</note> "But to the rest I say, not the Lord." 
¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "For the unbelieving husband is sanctified by the faithful wife." ¶ The word "faithful" is redundant according to the manuscript [of the Greek]. However, it does not obstruct the meaning. Paul says: <note>original Greek: "ἡγίασται γὰρ ὁ ἀνὴρ ὁ ἄπιστος, ἐν τῇ γυναικί"</note> "For the unbelieving husband is sanctified in the wife." 
¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "And the unbelieving wife is sanctified by the faithful husband." ¶ Likewise, here "faithful" is redundant. Paul says: <note>original Greek: "καὶ ἡγίασται ἡ γυνὴ ἡ ἄπιστος ἐν τῷ ἀνδρί"</note> "And the unbelieving wife is sanctified in the husband." 
<margin>45</margin>
¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "But God has called you in peace." ¶ We should say "us" using the first person. Paul says: <note>original Greek: "ἐν δὲ εἰρήνῃ κέκληκεν ἡμᾶς ὁ θεός"</note> "But God has called us in peace." 
¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "From where also do you know, woman." <margin>D</margin> ¶ Rather: "For what do you know, woman." And then, "or what, husband." But these are very small points. <margin>46</margin> Paul says: <note>original Greek: "τί γάρ οἶδας γύναι"</note> "For what do you know, O woman?" 
¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "And as I teach in all the churches." <margin>47</margin> ¶ It can be said: "and so I ordain in all the churches," or "I arrange." Paul says: <note>original Greek: "καὶ οὕτως ἐν ταῖς ἐκκλησίαις πάσαις διατάσομαι"</note> "And so I ordain in all the churches."

¶ It should read: "The wife and the virgin are divided." That is, the wife and the virgin have a distinction and a difference, which he later declares individually. Paul says: <note>original Greek: "μεμέρισται καὶ ἡ γυνὴ καὶ ἡ παρθένος"</note> "The wife and the virgin are also divided." ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "But for that which is honest: and which may give power to pray to the Lord without impediment." Paul, after the manner of the Greeks, uses concrete neuter terms <note>substantives</note> where the Latins appropriately use abstract ones. Indeed, where the old translator previously said "for utility," Paul uses the concrete neuter <term>to sympheron<gloss>the thing that is profitable</gloss></term>. Therefore, by the same right here, he could have translated it simply as "for honesty" <note>or "decency"</note> without a long phrase. And where he says "and which may give power to pray to the Lord without impediment," it is better held as "good perseverance" or "waiting upon the Lord unmovably," without explicitly mentioning "hindrance."

### CHAPTER VIII.

<margin>54</margin>
The Corinthians wrote to the Apostle regarding food that had been sacrificed to idols: claiming they knew enough from their own teachers. For their teachers had defined that matter according to their own understanding, and they were puffed up and boasting in their definitions, retaining neither the love of God nor of their neighbor. To correct them both, the Apostle rebukes them with these words, saying: ¶ "Now concerning foods that are sacrificed to idols: we know that we all have knowledge. Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up. If anyone thinks he knows anything, he does not yet know anything as he ought to know. But if anyone loves God, he is known by Him." ¶ The preceding words are spoken regarding human and fleshly notions. For knowledge is twofold: one sought by human sense, the other from God. The first is human, the second divine. The former puffs up; the latter humbles. The latter is joined to the love of God; the former is not at all. For how does anyone love God in a matter where he attends not to God, but to himself? Such a person thinks he knows, and attributes that glory to himself; but he does not yet know how anything ought to be known. For he knows in a human and fleshly way. But it is necessary to know in a divine and spiritual way; otherwise, it is vanity. Accordingly, Paul discusses these sacrificed things with the Corinthians not by human sense but by divine, not by the flesh but by the spirit,
<margin>55</margin>
saying: ¶ "Concerning therefore the eating of things sacrificed to idols: we know that an idol is nothing in the world, and that there is no other God but one. For although there are those called gods, whether in heaven or on earth, as there are many gods and many lords: yet to us there is one God the Father, from whom are all things and we in Him; and one Lord JESUS CHRIST, through whom are all things, and we through Him. But there is not knowledge in all." ¶ Divine and spiritual knowledge, given from above, consists in knowing that an idol is nothing—that is, it should be esteemed as nothing because it has no divinity or power—and that there is only one God. And although there are many in heaven who are called gods and lords, such as the good angels happy in their perpetual fellowship with divinity, and many gods and lords on earth, such as holy men presiding over sacred functions and administering holy things: yet for those who understand spiritually, there is absolutely only one God and Lord, who is the one Father from whom are all things and we from Him, and one Son our Lord Jesus Christ through whom...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the First Epistle to the Corinthians. Following the previous page’s discussion on marriage and social status, the author now transitions into Chapter 9, where Paul defends his apostolic authority and his right to material support, despite his choice to forgo it.</meta>

# COMMENTARY

"No one shall be set against you to harm you, because I have many people in this city." <note>A reference to Acts 18:10, where God encourages Paul in Corinth.</note> Wherefore, he truly and clearly refutes this deception of detractors who claim he is not an apostle—
<margin>60</margin>
and especially to the Corinthians—saying:
> ¶ Are you not my work in the Lord? If I am not an apostle to others, yet at least I am to you. For you are the seal of my apostleship in the Lord.

¶ For Paul first engraved the image of Christ—that is, the knowledge of Him—upon the minds of the Corinthians. For this reason, he calls them the "seal" of his apostleship, just as if he had impressed Christ into them with a signet ring. And this is a sufficient defense for Paul against those slanderers who claim he was not an apostle. But those "dogs" (for so one may call those who disparage and bark at spiritual men), disparaging not so much Paul as the grace of God, were saying that he was not a "free man" <note>In this context, "free" refers to the status of a recognized apostle who has the right to be supported by the community.</note> because those to whom he preached did not provide for his living; instead, he acquired the necessities of life through the labor of his own hands. They argued this because he did not take a wife along with him, and because he gave himself to everyone while receiving nothing from anyone. Truly, the most noble Paul did this not out of necessity, but by the will of a noble man—indeed, Paul was the most generous of those who are divinely liberal. He held the free power <term>potestas</term><note>Meaning a legal or moral right or authority.</note> to not work with his hands, and he did not sin by not exercising it. Yet, just as necessity makes a slave, so does free power demonstrate a free man. Therefore, he rightly refutes the slanderers who say he is not free, even if for Christ’s sake he made himself a servant to all. For that does not take away his power; rather, it adds an example of humility and a true imitation of Christ, who, though he was Lord of all, came into this world to serve and not to be served. 
<margin>61</margin>
Wherefore, against them, the most blessed and irreproachable apostle prepares such a defense, saying:
> ¶ My defense against those who examine me is this: Do we not have the power to eat and drink? Do we not have the power to take a sister-wife <note>The Latin *sororem mulierem* is often debated; the author interprets this as a believing wife who travels with the apostle.</note> along with us, as the other apostles and the brothers of the Lord and Cephas <note>The Aramaic name for the Apostle Peter.</note> do? Or is it only I and Barnabas who do not have the power to refrain from working? Who ever serves as a soldier at his own expense? Who plants a vineyard and does not eat its fruit? Or who tends a flock and does not drink the milk of the flock? Do I say these things according to human reasoning, or does not the Law say this also? For in the Law of Moses it is written: "You shall not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain." <note>Quoting Deuteronomy 25:4.</note> Is God concerned about oxen? Or does he say it altogether for our sake? Surely it was written for our sake, because he who plows ought to plow in hope, and he who threshes in hope of sharing the fruits of his hope. If we have sown spiritual things for you, is it a great thing if we reap your material things? If others share in this power over you, do we not much more? Nevertheless, we have not used this power, but we endure all things so that we may not give any hindrance to the gospel of CHRIST. Do you not know that those who perform sacred rites eat from the temple? Those who wait at the altar share in the altar? So also the Lord ordained for those who announce the gospel to live from the gospel. But I have used none of these things.

¶ This is an outstanding and sufficient satisfaction against those who would strip Paul of his liberty. And where he says above, "Do we not have the power to eat and drink?" understand this as "receiving from those to whom we preach the gospel," and not as "seeking it through the labor of our hands." He certainly had this right, as the Savior permitted: "Into whatever city you enter and they receive you, eat what is set before you." <note>Quoting Luke 10:8.</note> As for what he adds: "Do we not have the power to take a sister-wife along, as the other apostles and the brothers of the Lord and Cephas?" Ignatius <note>Ignatius of Antioch (c. 35–107 AD), an early Christian writer.</note>, a contemporary of Peter and Paul, testifies that Paul had a wife—a faithful one, and thus a "sister"—but for the sake of the Gospel of Christ, he left her behind for the work of the ministry. Concerning her, we shall add more when we reach the Epistle to the Philippians, if God permits. It is clear from history that other apostles, though not all (for John remained a virgin forever), even by the testimony of the divine Ignatius, had wives: including those called the "brothers of the Lord"—James, Joseph the Just, Simon, and Thaddeus—as well as Peter. This is enough to show that he also had the power to receive food and drink from those to whom he preached. And when he says "and does not eat of its fruit," understand it as "does he not have the power to eat?" and so with similar phrases. For here (as was fitting), he defends the power that asserts his liberty. But following this, with "Do I say these things according to human reasoning?" he shows he had this power not only by human logic but also by arguments taken from divine Law, specifically from Deuteronomy. And here, with "If we have sown spiritual things for you," he uses an "argument from the greater" <note>A logical form: if a greater thing is true (spiritual sowing), then the lesser thing (material reaping) is certainly justified.</note>. Then, with "Do you not know that those who perform sacred rites," he concludes his point with an example. He omits nothing in his defense that belongs to a true dialectician <note>An expert in logic and debate.</note> and a divine orator. I say "true," lest some sophist boast of being a dialectician before Paul. For those of that sort will be the ones to whom it is said, "Lord, Lord, open to us," and the answer will be, "Amen, I say to you, I do not know you." For how shall they be known by the Truth, who refused to know the Truth? And how did they have lamps giving light, who extinguished even those things that were shining? O Christ, the true Light, shine forth, so that they may see the light of your words and, seeing, be saved.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the First Epistle to the Corinthians, specifically focusing on Chapter 9. ...to shatter the darkness. This plague [of detraction] opposes the spirit more than the flesh; it is a more ruinous stain upon the soul. This error had deeply occupied the minds of those who were disparaging the holy apostle of God, denying that he was an apostle and that he was a free man. They even went so far as to deny that he had seen our Lord Jesus Christ, since he had not been with Him while He still lived on earth. Because he had not seen Him then, they ask—is this not a sophisticated trick?—"He did not see the Lord while He lived as a mortal on earth; therefore, he has not seen the Lord?" Has not he who saw the Lord now immortal, clothed in glory and honor, truly seen Him? And is that not a better sight than seeing Him while He was still mortal? Paul does not fail to make a defense <term>apologia</term> <note>From the Greek word for a formal defense of one's position or actions.</note> regarding this; however, he reveals the truth of the matter more fully later on, where he says: "He was seen by Cephas; and after that by the eleven; then He was seen by more than five hundred brothers at once, of whom many remain until now, though some have fallen asleep." And a little later he adds: "Last of all, as to one born out of time <note>original: "abortivo." Paul uses this term to describe his late arrival to the apostolate, appearing like a child born at the wrong time compared to the other disciples.</note>, He was seen by me also." And although (to return to the matter at hand) Paul had the freedom to receive food and clothing from those to whom he preached the kingdom of heaven, and to take a wife with him—and he demonstrated this very thing against those who barked at him—his defense does not aim at this: 

<margin>62</margin>
that he actually wishes to use that freedom (even though he could do so without sin). He testifies to this himself, saying: ¶ "But I have written none of these things, that it should be so done to me. For it were better for me to die, than that any man should make my glorying void. For if I preach the gospel, I have nothing to glory of; for necessity is laid upon me. Woe is unto me if I preach not the gospel! For if I do this thing willingly, I have a reward; but if against my will, a stewardship has been committed to me." 

¶ The necessity of preaching to the Ninevites was laid upon Jonah, whether he was willing or unwilling; otherwise, a curse awaited him for not obeying the divine command. If he had done it willingly, he could have expected a reward—that is, the favor of the one who commanded him. If unwillingly, he nevertheless fulfilled the duty of his office. And he certainly did fulfill it, but unwillingly; therefore, he lacked the expectation of grace for this deed. In the same way, the necessity of preaching the gospel was laid upon Paul, whether he did it of his own accord or unwillingly. Yet he performed the office joined to him willingly and with great readiness; for this reason, he did not lack the expectation of a reward—and by "reward," I mean grace. But he expected grace even more in another respect: namely, that he made manifest the gospel of Christ without expense, without being a burden to anyone, but rather providing relief and consolation to all. He did this so that he might not in any way 

<margin>63</margin>
abuse the office committed to him, or place any obstacle in the way of the gospel's reception. He testifies to this further with great honesty, saying: 

> What then is my reward? That in my preaching, I may make the gospel of CHRIST without charge, so as not to abuse my power in the gospel. For though I was free from all men, I made myself a servant to all, that I might gain the more. And unto the Jews I became as a Jew, that I might gain the Jews; to them that are under the law, as under the law, that I might gain them that are under the law; to them that are without the law, as without the law (being not without law to God, but under the law to CHRIST), that I might gain them that are without the law. To the weak became I as weak, that I might gain the weak; I am made all things to all men, that I might by all means save some. And this I do for the gospel's sake, that I might be a partaker thereof.

¶ What does "What then is my reward?" mean, if not "In what does my reward consist?"—so that we may hear the answer: "in that, while preaching, I set forth the gospel of Christ without charge." For Paul was free to take food, drink, and clothing from those to whom he preached, and to lead about a wife and a household; but in all these things he made himself a servant, so that he might gain more people for Christ. With the Jews, he made himself like them in food and in all things which would not hinder the gospel, so that he might acquire the Jews for Christ. With the Gentiles, he also made himself like them in food and drink and other matters, so that he might join the Gentiles to the flock of Christ. And with those weak in the flesh, he was as one surrounded by the weakness of the flesh—though he was spiritual—in order to lead them toward the spirit. He conformed himself to all where there was no sin, so that he might save all, and above all, so that he might be a partaker of the gospel. For this is the reward he expects from all these things. 

Yet Paul's first and primary intention was to fulfill the will of God; and second, to expect the reward of His grace from the best and most just Lord. But great is the reward that is expected; great is the prize <term>brauium</term> <note>From the Greek 'brabeion,' the prize awarded to the winner of an athletic contest.</note> which the Lord of all offers freely to His servants who 

<margin>64</margin>
contend well in His service. By this He encourages and drives them to serve well: namely, the crown of immortality, which all who are partakers of the gospel shall receive. And therefore Paul adds: ¶ "Do you not know that they which run in a race <note>original: "stadio." Referring to the Greek stadium where athletic games were held.</note> run all, but one receives the prize? So run, that you may obtain. And every man that strives for the mastery is temperate in all things. Now they do it to obtain a corruptible crown; but we an incorruptible."

¶ Those running in the stadium and contending in the struggle abstain from all things which the master of the games forbids, so that they may receive a crown—perhaps of poplar leaves, or let us say of silver or gold—yet it is still a corruptible crown. And not all of them receive it, but only one. How much more, then, should the servants of Christ abstain from all things which...

# COMMENTARY

"no one will be set against you to harm you, because I have many people in this city" <note>original: "nemo apponetur tibi / vt noceat..." This is a reference to God's promise to Paul in Acts 18:10 regarding his safety in Corinth.</note>. Wherefore, 
<margin>60</margin>
he truly and openly refutes this deception of those detractors who claim he is not an apostle—especially to the Corinthians—saying:

> Are you not my work in the Lord? If I am not an apostle to others, yet I am to you. For you are the seal of my apostleship in the Lord.

For Paul first engraved the image of Christ—that is, the knowledge of Him—upon the minds of the Corinthians. For this reason, he calls them the <term>signaculum</term> <note>A Latin term for a seal or signet ring's impression, used here to show that the existence of the Corinthian church is the "official stamp" proving Paul’s authority.</note> of his apostleship, just as if he had pressed the image of Christ into them with a seal. This is a sufficient defense for Paul against those speaking evil of him, claiming he was not an apostle. 

But those "dogs" (for so one may call the detractors and barkers against spiritual men), detracting not so much from Paul as from the grace of God, were saying that he was not a "free man" because those to whom he preached did not provide for his living. Instead, he obtained the necessities of life for himself by the labor of his hands. They also criticized him because he did not take a wife along with him, and because he spent himself for everyone while receiving nothing from anyone. 

Yet, the most noble Paul did this not out of necessity, but by the will of a generous man; the most liberal Paul did this by a divine liberality. He had the free power to not work, nor did he sin by not doing so. But just as necessity makes a slave, so does free power reveal a free man. Therefore, he rightly refutes the slanderers who say he is not free, even if, for Christ's sake, he made himself a servant to all. For that does not take away his power; rather, it adds an example of humility and a true imitation of Christ, who, though He was Lord of all, came into this world to serve and not to be served. 

Wherefore, against them, the most blessed and blameless apostle prepares such a defense, 
<margin>61</margin>
saying:

> This is my defense against those who examine me. Do we not have the power to eat and drink? Do we not have the power to take along a sister, a wife, as do the rest of the apostles, and the brothers of the Lord, and Cephas <note>Peter</note>? Or is it only Barnabas and I who do not have the power to refrain from working? Who ever serves as a soldier at his own expense? Who plants a vineyard and does not eat of its fruit? Or who tends a flock and does not drink of the milk of the flock? Do I speak these things according to human judgment? Does not the Law say these things also? For in the Law of Moses it is written: "You shall not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain." Is it for oxen that God is concerned? Or does He say it altogether for our sakes? Surely it was written for our sakes, because he who plows ought to plow in hope, and he who threshes in hope should be a partaker of his fruit. If we have sown spiritual things for you, is it a great thing if we reap your carnal things? If others have this power to be partakers of you, do we not have it even more?

Nevertheless, we have not used this power; but we endure all things so that we might not give any hindrance to the Gospel of CHRIST. Do you not know that those who perform sacred rites eat from the temple, and those who serve at the altar partake of the altar? So also the Lord ordained for those who announce the Gospel to live from the Gospel. But I have used none of these things. 

This is an excellent and sufficient satisfaction against those who would take away Paul's freedom. And regarding what he says above, 

> "Do we not have the power to eat and drink?" 

understand this as receiving from those to whom we preach the Gospel, rather than seeking it through the labor of our hands; he certainly had this power, as the Savior also permitted. He said: "Into whatever city you enter and they receive you, eat what is set before you." 

As for what he adds: "Do we not have the power to take along a sister, a wife, as the rest of the apostles and the brothers of the Lord and Cephas?" Ignatius <note>Ignatius of Antioch, a late 1st-century church leader.</note>, a contemporary of Peter and Paul, testifies that Paul had a wife—and a faithful one at that, and therefore a "sister"—but for the sake of the Gospel of Christ, he left her separate for the work of the Gospel. Concerning her, we shall add something more in the Epistle to the Philippians, if God permits. It is clear from history that the other apostles—though not all (for John remained a virgin forever)—and even those called the "brothers of the Lord" (James, Joseph the Just, Simon, and Thaddeus) had wives, as did Peter, according to the testimony of the divine Ignatius. And let this suffice: the authority of the apostle in this prominent passage. 

By saying "Who ever serves as a soldier at his own expense?" he shows by natural reason that he also had the power to receive food and drink from those to whom he preached. And when he says "and does not eat of its fruit," understand it as "does he not have the power to eat," and similarly in the other examples. For here (as was fitting), he defends the power which asserts his freedom. 

And following this, with the phrase "Do I speak these things according to human judgment?" he shows that he held this power not only by human reasoning but also by reasons taken from the divine law. For he cites Deuteronomy. And here, in "If we have sown spiritual things for you," he uses an argument from the greater to the lesser. Then, in "Do you not know that those who perform sacred rites," he concludes his proposition with an example. 

He omits nothing for his defense that belongs to a true dialectician <note>A master of logic and debate.</note> and a divine orator. I say "true," lest some sophist boast that he is a greater dialectician than Paul. For such people will be among those who say "Lord, Lord, open to us," to whom it will be said: "Truly I say to you, I do not know you." For how shall they be known by the Truth, who did not wish to know the Truth? 

And how could they have glowing lamps, who extinguished even those things that were shining? O Christ, the true light, shine forth, and [open] these [eyes], so that they may be able to see the light of your words, and by seeing they may be saved...

## II

...shatter the darkness. This pestilence opposes the spirit more than the flesh, and it is a more destructive ruin of souls. It had deeply occupied the minds of those who were disparaging the holy apostle of God, denying that he was an apostle or that he was free. They even denied that he had seen our Lord Jesus Christ, since he had not been with Him while He still dwelt on earth. Because he had not seen Him then, is this not a sophistical argument: "He did not see the Lord while He dwelt as a mortal on earth; therefore, he did not see the Lord"? Did not he who saw the Lord clothed in glory and honor—and now immortal—see Him? And indeed, was it not in a better way than those who saw Him while He was still mortal? And why would Paul not make a defense regarding this here? Nevertheless, he reveals the truth of the matter further down, where he says: 

> He was seen by Cephas, and after that by the eleven; then he was seen by more than five hundred brothers at once, of whom many remain until now, but some have fallen asleep. 

And a little later, he adds: 

> And last of all, as if by one born out of due time <note>original: "tanq̃ abortiuo". Paul uses this term in 1 Corinthians 15:8 to describe his late arrival to apostleship compared to the original twelve.</note>, he was seen also by me. 

And although (to return to the matter) Paul had the liberty to receive both food and clothing from those to whom he preached the kingdom of heaven, and to take a wife with him—and he showed this very thing against his detractors—his defense does not aim at wanting to use that liberty, even though he could do so without sin.

<margin>62</margin>
He himself testifies to this in this way, saying: 
> But I have written none of these things, that it should be so done unto me: for it were better for me to die, than that any man should make my glorying void. For if I preach the gospel, I have nothing to glory of: for necessity is laid upon me; yea, woe is unto me, if I preach not the gospel! For if I do this thing willingly, I have a reward: but if against my will, a dispensation of the gospel is committed unto me. 

The necessity of preaching to the Ninevites was laid upon Jonah, whether he was willing or unwilling; otherwise, a curse awaited him for not obeying the divine command. If he had done it willingly, he could have expected a reward—that is, the favor of the one commanding him. But if unwillingly, he nevertheless fulfilled the province <note>In this context, a "province" refers to an assigned duty or sphere of responsibility.</note> joined upon him. And certainly, he fulfilled it, but unwillingly; and therefore, he lacked the expectation of grace for this deed. In the same way, the necessity of preaching the Gospel was laid upon Paul, whether he performed it willingly or unwillingly. Yet, he fulfilled the duty joined to him gladly and very voluntarily; and for this reason, he did not lack the expectation of a reward—and by reward, I mean grace. But he also expected grace in another way: namely, that he made the Gospel of Christ manifest without expense, without burdening anyone, but rather with the relief and consolation of all. He did this lest he might in some way abuse the office committed to him, or provide some hindrance to the Gospel being received.

<margin>63</margin>
Which he furthermore frankly testifies, saying:
<margin>' ' ' ' ' ' ' ' ' ' ' ' ' ' ' ' ' '</margin>
> What is my reward then? That, when I preach the gospel, I may make the gospel of CHRIST without charge, that I abuse not my power in the gospel. For though I be free from all men, yet have I made myself servant unto all, that I might gain the more. And unto the Jews I became as a Jew, that I might gain the Jews; to them that are under the law, as under the law, that I might gain them that are under the law; to them that are without law, as without law (being not without law to God, but under the law to CHRIST,) that I might gain them that are without law. To the weak became I as weak, that I might gain the weak: I am made all things to all men, that I might by all means save some. And this I do for the gospel's sake, that I might be partaker thereof with you.

What does "What then is my reward" mean, if not "In what does my reward consist?" Let us hear the answer: "In this, that while preaching, I set forth the Gospel of Christ without expense." For Paul was free to take food, drink, and support from those to whom he preached, and to lead a wife and family around; but in all these things, he made himself a servant so that he might gain more for Christ. With the Jews, he made himself like them in food, drink, and all things—those which could not hinder the Gospel—so that he might acquire the Jews for Christ. With the Gentiles, he also made himself like them in food, drink, and other matters, so that he might associate the Gentiles with the flock of Christ. And with those weak in the flesh, he was as one surrounded by the weakness of the flesh, even though he was spiritual, in order that he might save them; and for this reason, furthermore, that he might be a partaker of the Gospel. For this is the reward which he expects from all these things. 

However, Paul’s first and principal intention was to fulfill the will of God; and the second was to expect the reward of His grace from the best and most just Lord. But great is the reward that is expected; great is the <term>brauium</term> <note>From the Greek 'brabeion,' meaning a prize in an athletic contest.</note> which the Lord of all offers freely to His servants competing in His service, by which He encourages and 
<margin>64</margin>
impels them to serve well: namely, the crown of immortality, which all who are partakers of the Gospel will receive. And therefore, Paul adds:
<margin>' ' ' '</margin>
> Do you not know that they which run in a race <note>original: "in ſtadio", referring to the stadium or running track.</note> run all, but one receiveth the prize? So run, that ye may obtain. And every man that striveth for the mastery is temperate in all things. Now they do it to obtain a corruptible crown; but we an incorruptible.

Both those running in the race and those contending in the competition abstain from all things that the master of the games prohibits, so that they may receive a crown—whether of poplar or (if we prefer) let us say of silver or gold—which is nevertheless corruptible. And not all of them receive it, but only one. How, then, shall the servants of Christ not abstain from all things which...

### COMMENTARY

<margin>65</margin>
The eternal King, the Son of God, commands the prize of the goal so that they may receive an immortal and incorruptible crown. Indeed, all should receive it—both those who run according to his commands and those who, in his service, generously strive with a zeal to serve better—not just one alone. That this is certainly how it must be done is gathered by a rational argument from the lesser to the greater. Why, then, did they disparage the apostle, claiming he was not free because he abstained from all things, so that he might run more swiftly toward the gospel of peace, while by doing these things he struggled with a zeal to serve better? O blind, sluggish, and idle men: neither running nor struggling; indeed, not even serving, but rather slandering the <margin>10</margin> servants and the works of the servants of God. Let them learn that they should have done the same for themselves, as Paul most modestly renders his reasoning to them, saying: ¶ **I therefore so run: not as if toward uncertainty. I so fight: not as if beating the air. But I punish my body and bring it into servitude: lest by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should become a castaway.** ¶ For what would it benefit to announce the kingdom of God, to cry out through the scriptures of God that one must run, that the precepts of God must be fulfilled, that one must fight in the spirit and not the flesh, and that the flesh must be mortified so that the spirit may live—if you yourself transgress the commands of God, if you live according to the flesh, and neither run nor struggle, but when you have preached to others, you are found to be a castaway? Therefore, one must act as Paul did: truly running and truly struggling. And more certain than any certainty: Jesus Christ our King, blessed above all, will give us the immortal crown. For he wishes to give it not to one alone, but to all for his own sake, for the treasure of his goodness is infinite. To him be honor, glory, and thanksgiving, forever.

<margin>A 59</margin>
### EXAMINATION of several points regarding the text.
¶ **The Vulgate edition:** <note>original: "Vulgata æditio". This refers to the standard Latin Bible used in the Western Church.</note> **Am I not free? Am I not an apostle? Have I not seen JESUS CHRIST our Lord?** ¶ The old interpreter <note>original: "vetus interpres". Likely referring to the translator of the Vulgate or an earlier Latin version.</note> reads this as an interrogation, but the speech can seem "swelling" <note>arrogant or boastful</note> when attributed to the most mild Paul; perhaps it is not consistent. Truly, it can be read without a question mark: as if Paul were repeating certain words from his detractors for which he wishes to make a defense, as indeed he does. Then the speech is more modest and more consistent with the apostle's character. However, if anyone prefers the interrogation, let him see that he does not read or pronounce it haughtily, but modestly, and as if grieving over the error of his detractors. Also, the order of the phrases is inverted. For in Paul's original Greek, the first phrase is: **Am I not an apostle?** <note>original Greek: "οὐκ εἰμὶ ἀπόστολος" (ouk eimi apostolos)</note>. Paul writes: **Am I not an apostle? Am I not free? Have I not seen Jesus Christ our Lord?** <note>original Greek: "οὐκ εἰμὶ ἀπόστολος, οὐκ εἰμὶ ἐλεύθερος, οὐχὶ ἰησοῦν χριστὸν τὸν κύριον ἡμῶν ἑώρακα;"</note> <margin>A 61</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition: My defense among those who interrogate me is this.** ¶ Better to say **against those** or **toward those who examine me: this is it.** Paul writes: **My defense to those who examine me is this.** <note>original Greek: "ἡ ἐμὴ ἀπολογία τοῖς ἐμὲ ἀνακρίνουσιν, αὕτη ἐστί."</note> For the detractors were examining, discussing, and prying into Paul, carping at his words and deeds. ¶ **The Vulgate edition: Or do only I and Barnabas not have the power to work this?** ¶ It should be read: **Or do only I and Barnabas [not have the power]...** not "or." And **not have the power of not working**, using a negation rather than the pronoun "this." Paul writes: **Or do only I and Barnabas not have the power not to work?** <note>original Greek: "ἢ μόνος ἐγὼ καὶ βαρνάβας οὐκ ἔχομεν ἐξουσίαν τοῦ μὴ ἐργάζεσθαι."</note> He says this because Paul himself and Barnabas performed manual labor to provide the necessities of life for themselves, even if the other apostles did not do so. This is not because he carps at the other apostles. For he did what was permitted to them and what was allowed to them by Christ. Therefore, by a similar and equally compelling reason: it was permitted to him and Barnabas not to work—that is, not to seek the necessities of life by the labor of their hands—but they wished, in addition, to generously endure this labor for Christ. For Barnabas was a servant and a generous soldier of Christ, who was even the first (while the Savior, dwelling on earth, gave the precepts of the life of salvation to mortals) to bring the salvific name of Christ to the Romans, as Clement <margin>B 61</margin> of Rome is the author in the *Recognitions*. <note>original: "i Anagnosi". This refers to the "Pseudo-Clementine Recognitions," an early Christian work.</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition: And he who threshes, in hope of receiving fruit.** ¶ The old interpreter could have said: **the fruit of his hope.** And although Paul only has: **and he who threshes in hope, of participating in his hope**, for Latin understanding, it is good to express the infinitive "to plow" from the sequence of the preceding phrase. Even if the noun "fruit" is added, the sense of the speech is rendered much clearer, which we also have done for this reason. Paul writes: **and he who threshes, to participate in his hope, in hope.** <note>original Greek: "καὶ ὁ ἀλοῶν τῆς ἐλπίδος αὐτοῦ μετέχειν ἐπ᾽ ἐλπίδι."</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition: Do you not know that those who work in the sanctuary eat of the things that are of the sanctuary?** ¶ Rather: **those who perform sacred things eat sacred things.** Paul writes: **Do you not know that those who perform the sacred things eat from the temple?** <note>original Greek: "οὐκ οἴδατε ὅτι οἱ τὰ ἱερὰ ἐργαζόμενοι, ἐκ τοῦ ἱεροῦ ἐσθίουσιν;"</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition: And those who serve the altar participate with the altar.** Rather: **those who sit at the altar share with the altar.** For the Latins use the third declension more than the second in this word <note>referring to the Latin 'altar' vs 'altarium'</note>. <margin>C 62</margin> ¶ Paul writes: **those who wait upon the altar share with the altar.** <note>original Greek: "οἱ τῷ θυσιαστηρίῳ προσεδρεύοντες, τῷ θυσιαστηρίῳ συμμερίζονται."</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition: That anyone should make void my glory.** ¶ **Glory** here signifies boasting, and exultation of the soul, and a certain (so to speak) rejoicing, when someone has done a good thing to which they were not bound. Paul writes: **For it is better for me to die than that anyone should make void my boasting.** <note>original Greek: "καλὸν γάρ μοι μᾶλλον ἀποθανεῖν, ἢ τὸ καύχημά μου, ἵνα τίς κενώσῃ."</note> Similarly, in the following phrase, the old interpreter takes "glory" to mean "boasting."

<margin>D</margin> *I made myself the servant of all.* ¶ It should say *to all* or *among all.* Paul says: <note>original Greek: "πᾶσιν ἐμαυτὸν ἐδούλωσα"</note> "I enslaved myself to all."
<margin>63</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Though I myself was not under the law.* ¶ This little phrase is not found in Paul's original text, though it might not contradict the meaning. For Paul was not under the ceremonial laws. And those who are under the precepts are weak and carnal. Paul, however, is spiritual. Nonetheless, he himself observed the purifications of the Jews when he came from Asia to Jerusalem to see James, as if he had been under the law, though he was not truly under it.
<s>¶ Because he says he became as the law to those under the law, as if he were under the law, that he might gain those under the law</s>
¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *To those who were without the law, as if I were without the law, though I was not without the law of God, but was in the law of CHRIST.* ¶ What the old translator said in two words as "without law" <note>Latin: "sine lege"</note>, we can say in Paul's style with a single word, in this way: *to the lawless as if lawless, though I was not lawless toward God but lawful toward Christ.* Paul says: <note>original Greek: "τοῖς ἀνόμοις ὡς ἄνομος, μὴ ὢν ἄνομος θεῷ, ἀλλ᾽ ἔννομος χριστῷ"</note>. ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *But I do all things for the gospel's sake.* ¶ It should say: *But I do this.* Paul says: <note>original Greek: "τοῦτο δὲ ποιῶ, διὰ τὸ εὐαγγέλιον"</note> "But I do this because of the gospel."
<margin>D</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Everyone, however, who contends in the contest abstains from all things.* ¶ Neither "in" nor "himself" <note>referring to Latin particles "in" and "se"</note> are necessary; the word <term>agone</term><note>The "agon" refers to an athletic contest or struggle, like those in the ancient Greek games.</note> denotes the struggle itself.
<margin>64</margin> Paul says: <note>original Greek: "πᾶς δὲ ἀγωνιζόμενος, πάντα ἐγκρατεύεται"</note> "Every man who strives in the contest exercises self-control in all things." <margin>65</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *But we an uncorrupted [crown].* ¶ Better: *an incorruptible [crown].* Paul says: <note>original Greek: "ἡμεῖς δὲ ἄφθαρτοι"</note> "But we are incorruptible."

### CHAPTER X

And someone will say: We have received the Holy Spirit, we have been baptized in Christ, we have participated in the body and blood of Christ; therefore, we shall be made partakers of the gospel. Therefore, we shall receive the incorruptible crown. But it must not be understood in this way; rather, the truth must be recognized through the "figure" <note>The author uses "figure" (figura) to mean a historical event that foreshadows a spiritual reality.</note>. For if we fall into the evil lusts of the throat (gluttony), or into greed which is idolatry, or into any other species of idolatry, or into fornications, or if we provoke Christ by our unfaithfulness, or if we murmur against his providence and do such illicit and wicked things—even if all those holy mysteries have been performed around us—we shall not receive that crown, and we shall by no means enter the kingdom of God. Just as the children of Israel, who were a figure of us, underwent similar things <margin>66</note> (though as a figure), yet because they fell into similar illicit acts, they did not enter the Promised Land at all. What was done regarding their experience of Christ, who was hidden in the Old Law, the Apostle adds, saying: ¶ **For I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers: that all our fathers were under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea, and all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink (for they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them; and that rock was CHRIST). But with most of them God was not well pleased. For they were laid low in the desert. Now these things were figures for us, so that we should not be led by a desire for evil things, as they were led by desire. Neither become idolaters, as some of them were, as it is written: The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play. Neither let us commit fornication, as some of them committed fornication, and twenty-three thousand fell in one day. Neither let us tempt CHRIST, as some of them tempted him, and perished by serpents. Neither murmur, as some of them murmured, and perished by the destroyer. Now all these things happened to them as a figure; but they were written for our admonition, upon whom the ends of the ages have come.** ¶ Behold, the things that happened to the Hebrews were types and figures. The Hebrews are a figure of the people of Christ; the cloud is the Holy Spirit; the sea is baptism; Moses is Christ as the lawgiver; the manna is the body of Christ as the heavenly bread and food of life; the water flowing from the rock is the blood of Christ as the drink of life; the Rock is Christ as he was pierced on the cross; the desert is the world; the Promised Land is the heavenly kingdom; the serpents are demons; the destroyer is the justice of God; the various penalties are the various eternal punishments; and the end of the times of the Hebrews is the end of the ages. ¶ Therefore, those upon whom the end of the Hebrew times had come were a type and figure of those upon whom the end of the ages will come. For Paul adapts every type to its own truth and calls it back to its own reality; he sees the type in the truth and the truth in the type, just as one sees the shadow in the light and the light in the shadow. For truth is light, and the type is a shadow. This reasoning of Paul from the type to the truth was well known to the first theologians. The more they possessed of the divine light, the more they recognized it. He who could see this in all things and in everyone would have nothing hidden from him, neither in human nor divine matters. However, this benefit of divine light was not granted as abundantly to those who came after. Now let us return to Paul. For he exhorts the Corinthians—who were too confident in the things done around them, as if once they had been initiated, they could not perish and would fail to obtain the heavenly kingdom. And this was a human temptation which they were able to resist, with <margin>67</margin> divine help always present to them. Thus he exhorts them, saying: ¶ **Wherefore let him who thinks he stands take heed lest he fall. No temptation has overtaken you except what is human. But God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you are able; but with the temptation, he will also provide a way out, so that you may be able to endure it.**

Q.j.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the First Epistle to the Corinthians, specifically addressing the transition into chapter 10. The previous page ended with Paul's discussion on making himself "all things to all people" to save some; this page focuses on his warnings against idolatry and the proper conduct regarding food offered to idols.</meta>

<header>COMMENTARY</header>
<sig>A</sig>

<meta>catchword: re.</meta>

re. <margin>68</margin> <note>This "re." likely completes a word or phrase from the bottom of the previous page, leading into the discussion of Paul's warning.</note> This temptation had seized some of the Corinthians: they thought it did them no harm if they sacrificed to idols, as long as all the sacred rites of Christ had been performed for them. Paul disapproves of this and refutes it with a manifest argument, saying: ¶ "Wherefore, my beloved: flee from idolatry. I speak as to wise men; judge for yourselves what I say. The cup of blessing which we bless: is it not the communion of the blood of **CHRIST**? The bread which we break: is it not the communion of the body of **CHRIST**? For we, being many, are one bread and one body, for we all partake of one bread. Consider Israel according to the flesh: do not those who eat the sacrifices communicate with the altar?" <note>original: "Israelem secundum carnem"</note> ¶ It followed that he would say: those who eat things sacrificed to an idol—especially insofar as they are sacrificed—communicate with the idol. But it is impossible to communicate with Christ and an idol at the same time, just as it is impossible to have light and darkness together. Idolatry must therefore necessarily be fled if we are to communicate with Christ. But they will say: "If what is sacrificed to an idol is nothing, and if an idol is nothing, how shall we communicate with the idol?" It is certain that an idol is nothing, nor is the spirit of
<margin>9</margin> idols anything divine to which any cult of veneration is owed; rather, they are demons. Demons, however, are not divine, but enemies of divinity, even if through pride they wish to be called divine. And for that reason Paul adds: ¶ "What do I say then? That an idol is anything, or that what is sacrificed to an idol is anything? No. But the things which the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons, and not to God. I do not want you to communicate with demons. You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons; you cannot partake of the table of the Lord and the table of demons. Do we provoke the Lord to jealousy? Are we stronger than He?" ¶ Since it is impossible for us to partake of both God and a demon (for they are opposites), it further happens that when we communicate with demons through idolatry, we provoke God to anger and vengeance. But shall we be able to escape the vengeance of His jealousy and His indignation? Are we stronger than He? Not at all. It would certainly be madness and fury to think so. Therefore, both so that we may be united to God (for this is what it means to communicate with God) and so that we may avoid His vengeance, idolatry must be fled. Nevertheless, the union with and veneration of God is to be looked to in the first place, and the avoidance of vengeance in the second. And since an idol is nothing, and likewise a sacrifice is nothing, it is permitted to eat sacrificed things, yet not *as* sacrificed things. And
<margin>70</margin> not always: but (as was said before) when it edifies, or does not hinder edification. For this reason Paul adds: ¶ "All things are in my power: but not all things are helpful. All things are in my power: but not all things edify. Let no one seek his own: but each one that which belongs to another. Eat everything that is sold in the meat market <term>macellum<note>A Latin term for a provision market, specifically for meat and delicacies.</note></term>, asking no questions for the sake of conscience. For the earth is the Lord's and the fullness thereof." ¶ For it was permitted for the faithful to eat all those things which were sold in public shops; but to inquire whether those things had been sacrificed to idols or not was not permitted for the sake of conscience—not for the sake of the conscience of those faithful who might have asked, but for the sake of those who were selling or present, whether they were unbelievers or weak. For they might have thought that the buyer, knowing it was a sacrifice, had bought it out of reverence for the idol, even if he had bought it for no such reason. But he knows the idol is nothing, nor does it have any power over the sacrifice: but only the Lord, to whom the earth belongs and all those things that fill the earth. For this reason also, it was not permitted for a believer to sit at a table in an "idolium"—that is, in a temple of an idol—and eat with others who ate sacrificed meats as if they were indeed sacrifices. And by similar reasoning, if the market seller had told the faithful buyer, "this meat has been sacrificed," then it is not [meat]; he ought to take from the non-sacrificed meat, as if despising and detesting the sacrificed meat not as meat, but as a sacrifice.
<margin>71</margin> In private homes, however, nothing prohibited the faithful from eating whatever they wished, as long as it did not hinder edification. Which Paul also joins, saying: ¶ "If any of the unbelievers invites you, and you wish to go: eat whatever is set before you, asking no questions for the sake of conscience. But if someone says to you 'this has been sacrificed to idols': do not eat for the sake of him who pointed it out, and for the sake of conscience (for the earth is the Lord's and the fullness thereof). But I say conscience, not your own, but that of the other. For why is my liberty judged by another's conscience? If I partake with grace: why am I blasphemed for that for which I give thanks? Therefore, whether you eat, or drink, or whatever you do: do all for the glory of God. Be without offense, both to Jews and Gentiles: and to the church of God. Just as I also please all in all things: not seeking my own advantage, but that of many, so that they may be saved." ¶ A holy precept and a holy admonition: whatever we do, do it for the glory of God. It is certain that we must then abstain from all evil. For evil cannot be done for the glory of God. It is also holy to conduct oneself without offense to every man, whether Jew or Gentile. How much more should one conduct oneself without offense toward a fellow believer and the church of the faithful, which is the church of God. And as Paul sought to please all: that pleasing was not worldly, carnal, or flattering, but proceeding from an imitation of divine kindness, flowing from the Spirit, and edifying. For we ought to please only as long as we can edify and procure the salvation of others. May Christ Jesus, the salvation and life of all, grant us this grace of pleasing in the Spirit for the salvation of others and ourselves; who is blessed forever and ever. Amen.

<margin>66.</margin> they were baptized. ¶ It can be said "into Moses" as a two-syllable word following Paul's phrasing. Paul: *and all were baptized into Moses*. <note>original: "καὶ πάντες εἰς τὸν μωσῆν ἐβαπτίσαντο"</note> ¶ The Vulgate edition: *And they drank of the spiritual rock following them.* ¶ It should be said: *For they drank of the spiritual [rock]*. And the word "them" is superfluous. Truly, it can also be said "by the following rock." "Following" indeed, because Christ had not yet come, but was going to come into the world.

<margin>B 66.</margin> Therefore, they drank in a figure from the spiritual rock which was to come. For the Rock was Christ: that is, a type and a figure of the Christ who was then to come; and "spiritual" is feminine and an adjective, for which the substantive is "rock." This is known to have occurred regarding the rock of Horeb from Exodus. Paul: *for they drank from the spiritual rock that followed*. <note>original: "ἔπιον γὰρ ἐκ πνευματικῆς ἀκολουθούσης πέτρας"</note>

<margin>66.</margin> ¶ The Vulgate edition: *Moreover, these things were made our figure.* ¶ From Paul: *rather, for these things were made as figures of us.* But it falls back into the same understanding. Paul: *Now these things happened as examples for us.* <note>original: "ταῦτα δὲ τύποι ἡμῶν ἐγενήθησαν"</note> ¶ The Vulgate edition: *Neither let us tempt CHRIST, as some of them tempted.* ¶ It should be said: *they tempted him*, using the singular accusative referring to Christ. Paul: *Neither let us tempt Christ, as some of them also tempted.* <note>original: "μηδὲ ἐκπειράζωμεν τὸν χριστόν / καθὼς καί τινες αὐτῶν ἐπείρασαν"</note>

<margin>C</margin> ¶ The Vulgate edition: *But they are written for our correction.* ¶ More appropriately, *for our admonition*, or *of us*, so that the relative pronoun may more clearly refer to the plural. Paul: *but they were written for our admonition.* <note>original: "ἐγράφη δὲ πρὸς νουθεσίαν ἡμῶν"</note>

<margin>67</margin> ¶ The Vulgate edition: *Let no temptation apprehend you except what is human.* ¶ It should be said: *it apprehends* <note>The author is arguing for the indicative mood "it has taken you" rather than the optative/imperative "let no temptation take you."</note> using the past tense of the indicative. For Paul does not command, nor does he wish that no temptation—neither human nor non-human—should seize them; rather, he was speaking of that temptation which *had* seized the Corinthians: that as long as the sacred rites of Christ had been performed for them, even if they served idols alongside Christ, they could be saved. For in this way, they would have saved their worldly goods, retained their magistracies, escaped the penalties of martyrdom, and remained in the favor of princes. But it could by no means happen this way. For a participant of an idol cannot at all be a participant of God. Paul: *No temptation has overtaken you except such as is common to man.* <note>original: "πειρασμὸς ὑμᾶς οὐκ εἴληφεν εἰ μὴ ἀνθρώπινος"</note>

¶ The Vulgate edition: *But he will also make with the temptation an issue.* <note>The Vulgate uses "proventum," which can mean an outcome or increase.</note> ¶ This sentence in Paul seems to designate that God, along with the temptation, will provide them a good exit and bring help. For the word *ekbasis*, which Paul uses here, designates an "exit" or a "prosperous outcome." Paul: *but will with the temptation also make a way to escape.* <note>original: "ἀλλὰ ποιήσει σὺν τῷ πειρασμῷ καὶ τὴν ἔκβασιν"</note>

<margin>D</margin> ¶ The Vulgate edition: *Wherefore, my most dear: flee from the culture of idols.* ¶ From Paul: *my beloved.* But that matters nothing, or very little. Paul: *Wherefore, my beloved, flee from idolatry.* <note>original: "Διόπερ ἀγαπητοί μου, φεύγετε ἀπὸ τῆς εἰδωλολατρίας"</note>

<margin>68.</margin> ¶ The Vulgate edition: *The cup of blessing which we bless: is it not the communication of the blood of CHRIST? And the bread which we break: is it not the participation of the body of the Lord?* ¶ What the old translator says here with two words—"communication" and "participation"—is the same word in Paul: *koinōnia*. <note>original: "κοινωνία"</note> This, the holy fathers interpreted as "communion," and it is this very thing which they call the "communion of saints." Those who have not understood this should at least understand it from this passage of Paul. And in both places at the end, it should be "of Christ," not "of the Lord." Paul: *The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ? The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ?* <note>original: "τὸ ποτήριον τῆς εὐλογίας ὃ εὐλογοῦμεν, οὐχὶ κοινωνία τοῦ αἵματος τοῦ χριστοῦ ἐστιν; τὸν ἄρτον ὃν κλῶμεν, οὐχὶ κοινωνία τοῦ σώματος τοῦ χριστοῦ ἐστιν;"</note>

<margin>69.</margin> ¶ The Vulgate edition: *All we who participate of one bread and of one cup.* ¶ It should be said: *For we all participate from one bread.* And the phrase "and of one cup" is an addition. Paul: *for we all partake of the one bread.* <note>original: "ὅτι γὰρ πάντες ἐκ τοῦ ἑνὸς ἄρτου μετέχομεν"</note>

<margin>69.</margin> ¶ The Vulgate edition: *What then do I say? That what is sacrificed to idols is anything, or that the idol is anything?* ¶ The order of the particles is changed. Paul: *What do I mean then? That an idol is anything, or that what is offered to idols is anything?* <note>original: "τί οὖν φημί; ὅτι εἴδωλόν τί ἐστιν; ἢ ὅτι εἰδωλόθυτόν τί ἐστιν;"</note> And the response is more expressive: "No," which Paul understands even if he did not express it; and we have done this so that the understanding might be clearer for Latin readers. ¶ The Vulgate edition: *But the things which the heathens sacrifice.* ¶ It should be said: *But that the things which the Gentiles sacrifice.* Paul: *but that the things which the Gentiles sacrifice.* <note>original: "ἀλλὰ ὅτι ἃ θύει τὰ ἔθνη"</note>

<margin>E 70</margin> ¶ The Vulgate edition: *And I would not that you should become the fellows of devils.* ¶ Rather, *communicants* or *partakers* of demons. Paul: *and I would not that ye should have fellowship with devils.* <note>original: "οὐ θέλω δὲ ὑμᾶς κοινωνοὺς τῶν δαιμονίων γίνεσθαι"</note>

¶ The Vulgate edition: *Because you cannot drink the cup of the Lord.* ¶ Quite a few manuscripts have it this way. But in those that do, the word "because" is superfluous. Paul: *Ye cannot drink the cup of the Lord.* <note>original: "οὐ δύνασθε ποτήριον κυρίου πίνειν"</note>

<margin>F 70.</margin> ¶ The Vulgate edition: *Do we emulate the Lord?* ¶ A more intelligible interpretation: *Do we provoke the Lord to jealousy, or to indignation?* Paul: *Do we provoke the Lord to jealousy?* <note>original: "ἢ παραζηλοῦμεν τὸν κύριον;"</note>

¶ The Vulgate edition: *But that which is another's.* ¶ The particle "each one" is missing. Paul: *but each one the thing of the other.* <note>original: "ἀλλὰ τὸ τοῦ ἑτέρου ἕκαστος"</note>

<margin>G 71.</margin> ¶ The Vulgate edition: *All that comes in the market.* <note>The Latin "macellum" refers to a meat market or shambles.</note> ¶ Here, "comes" (*venit*) is from *veneo*, that is, "it goes for sale" and is sold. Truly, the old translator made the passage ambiguous by an equivocation: whether Paul meant it from *veneo* (to be sold) or from *venio* (to come). <note>In Latin, *venit* (he comes) and *vēnit* (it is sold) are spelled the same in many forms, though they have different vowel lengths and origins.</note> Nevertheless, it ought to be understood as "come for sale" since the market is mentioned in the ablative case. For if it were from *venio* (to come), it would have to be said with the accusative "into the market" (*in macellum*). Yet, he himself does not everywhere observe Latin propriety. Paul: *Everything sold in the meat market.* <note>original: "πᾶν τὸ ἐν μακέλλῳ πωλούμενον"</note>

¶ The Vulgate edition: *For his sake that showed it, and for conscience sake.* Here, after this particle, there is missing: *The earth is the Lord's and the fullness thereof.* ¶ Which was perhaps omitted because it was thought superfluous.

COMMENTARY

...superfluous <note>Latin: "superflu[um]"</note>: since just before, after a similar particle, it had been added. But neither here nor there is it superfluous. For here, this understanding is added: *the earth is the Lord's and the fullness thereof* <note>Psalm 24:1, quoted by Paul in 1 Cor 10:26</note>: so many and such great things are on the earth and are produced by it, which you are able to eat, besides those things which someone might say were offered to idols. For other things will not be lacking to you which you may eat. Truly in that place: it was permitted for them to eat those things because they were the Lord's. For *the earth is the Lord's and the fullness thereof*. It was indeed permitted, provided it did not fail to build up others. Paul: *On account of the one who informed you and for the sake of conscience. For the earth is the Lord's and the fullness thereof.* <note>original Greek: "Δι’ ἐκεινον τὸν μηνὺσαντα καὶ τὴν συνείδησιν. τοῦ γὰρ κυρίου ἡ γῆ, καὶ τὸ πλήρωμα ἀυτῆσ."</note>

<margin>CHAPTER 11</margin>

<image-desc>A large historiated woodcut initial 'C' depicting a scene with several men, some seated and others standing, in an interior setting that resembles a study or meeting room.</image-desc>

Since Paul had said that he did not seek his own advantage but that of many so they might be saved, he exhorts them to do the same by his example. For he himself in this very thing imitates Christ, who did not seek what was profitable for himself in this world, but what was profitable for many so that they might attain eternal salvation. And Paul, by commending the memory of his traditions—or rather, Christ's—strives to stir the Corinthians and make them more eager, saying:

<margin>72</margin>
¶ *Be imitators of me, as I also am of CHRIST. Now I praise you, brothers, that you remember me in all things. And just as I delivered them to you, you hold fast to my traditions.* ¶ Then he instructs them how Christ, even according to his humanity, holds the highest place among all men, having only the divinity above himself; but the man holds the highest place over the woman, that is, the position of leadership. Furthermore,

<margin>73</margin>
he instructs them how a man and how a woman ought to pray or prophesy, saying:
¶ *But I would have you know that the head of every man is CHRIST; and the head of the woman is the man; and the head of CHRIST is God. Every man who prays or prophesies with his head covered dishonors his head. But every woman who prays or prophesies with her head uncovered dishonors her head; for that is even all one as if she were shaven. Therefore, if a woman is not covered, let her be shorn. But if it be a shame for a woman to be shorn or shaven, let her be covered. For a man indeed ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God; but the woman is the glory of the man.* ¶ The man was made immediately by God, as the image and likeness of God for his glory; but the woman was made through the medium of the man, as if a veil were placed between her and God. For a "medium" <term>medium: a middle or intervening thing</term> is like a gap or a certain veil. To designate this mystery, when a man turns himself toward God—which he does most especially when praying or prophesying—he should do so with his head uncovered, as if having no veil between himself and God, offering the honor of his creation to God just as it is. But the woman, with her head covered, acknowledging her creation and offering honor to God as is fitting, does so in the second place, with the glory of the man acting as an intermediary. For the man is the primary and immediate glory of God; the woman is the mediated

<margin>74</margin>
and secondary glory, being the immediate glory of the man, and made for the sake of the man himself. Therefore Paul adds:
¶ *For the man is not from the woman, but the woman from the man. Neither was the man created for the woman, but the woman for the man. For this cause ought the woman to have power on her head because of the angels.* ¶ Both man and the angels were created immediately by God; and therefore the man ought to have no veil as a symbol of this when he turns to God, no differently than the angels. But the woman ought to have one, not only because of the man, but also because of the angels. For it would be pride if she made her creation equal to the angels, since she has this "power" <note>Referring to the head covering as a symbol of authority or being under authority</note> mediated through the man. For what is it for a woman to have power, and indeed to be obliged to have it on her head, except through the mediation of the man, through the mediation of the "head" who is her husband? But it is worthwhile to know this: that just as the first Eve came from the first Adam and for the sake of the first Adam carnally (who are types and figures), so the second Eve—who is the Virgin blessed above all women—comes from the second Adam—who is Christ Jesus, the super-blessed—and for the sake of the second Adam spiritually. And these are the Archetypes <term>Archetypes: the original patterns or ultimate realities</term> and the truths. And just as the first Adam is the head and the first of all carnal men, both men and women (for he is the father of all), so Christ is the father and head of all spiritual people, both men and women (for he is the father of all spiritual ones). And just as the first Adam is the head over all carnal men and women, with the exception of one Adam; so that most blessed of the blessed virgins is above all spiritual ones, both men and women, with the sole exception of Christ, from whom and for whose sake alone she was created. For she is the mother of all spiritual ones. Whence it follows that in Mary, the veil of Eve is laid aside. For between her and Christ the Lord, from whom she is and for whom she is, no medium intervenes. Moreover, Christ is God. Nothing, therefore, prevents her from being not only equal to the angels, but even superior. Equal indeed, for she is immediately from Christ just as the angels are; but superior truly, for she is the Mother of Christ, which none of the angels is, nor can be. Nay, rather, since she was made the Mother of Christ, she was in a certain way made the mother of the angels, to be venerated by all angels and more august than the angels. But other men ought to magnify women. For by divine ordinance, all are born through women. And other women should honor men, for all are (also by God's ordinance) from men. And they ought to honor one another mutually. Let not the man

<margin>75</margin>
despise the woman, or vice versa; nor let the man insolently exalt himself over her, or she against him. Concerning which Paul adds: ¶ *Nevertheless, neither is the man without the woman, nor the woman without the man, in the Lord. For as...*
