<meta>This page continues the commentary on 1 Corinthians 11, specifically following the argument that woman was created from man. It transitions from the natural symbolism of hair and head coverings to the proper conduct required for the celebration of the Eucharist.</meta>

[header]
II 1 Cor.

In the same way that woman came from man, so now also man is born through woman; but all things are from God. <note>original Latin: "omnia autem ex deo," quoting 1 Corinthians 11:12</note>
<margin>76</margin>¶ He placed the divine reason in a more secret mystery: for which cause a woman, when she prays or prophesies, ought to cover her head. But now he insists upon the reason of nature, and as if he were showing the faithful instrument of God itself, he says: ¶ **Judge among yourselves: is it proper for a woman to pray to God unveiled? Does not nature itself teach you that if a man has long hair, it is a disgrace to him, but if a woman has long hair, it is a glory to her? For her hair is given to her for a covering.** ¶ It is certain that more abundant and longer hair grows naturally on women, so much so that sometimes the hair is seen to extend all the way to the heels—more so than in men. And this is given to the woman as an honor. But if hair grew this way on a man, it would be a disgrace to him. Therefore, woman appears veiled by nature when compared to man; thus, with nature as a guide, the woman ought to pray veiled, but the man uncovered. But perhaps some dabbler in human philosophy <note>Latin: "humanæ philosophiæ sciolus"</note> wishing to go further might say that this hair-veil in the woman does not extend for that reason, but because she is "moister" than the man. <note>In ancient and medieval science, women were believed to have a "moist" temperament, which was thought to stimulate hair growth.</note> To whom we could respond: why then, by that reasoning, does she not have a longer beard than a man? Why does this happen only on the head, so that from it she appears totally veiled, while the man does not?
<margin>77</margin>¶ But the Apostle forbids that such contentious tossing-about of words be held, especially regarding divine matters, saying: ¶ **But if anyone seems to be contentious, we have no such custom, nor do the churches of God.** ¶ Not without cause does Paul forbid these kinds of altercations and futile contentions: because they build nothing and profit nothing. Rather, those who stir them up are "little foxes that destroy the vineyards"—that is, the Scriptures of the Bridegroom and the Bride, which is to say, Christ and the Church. For it is not the role of divine philosophy (the philosophy of the faithful) to dwell on the hot, the cold, the moist, and the dry <note>The four primary qualities of Greek natural philosophy</note>, but to dwell in these "traces" and to rise from the trace toward the truth (which Paul did a little above), or to know the trace from the truth (which is a more sublime path). For in divine philosophy, this is like a "demonstration of why" <note>Latin: "demonstratio propter quid," a logical term for proving something from its cause</note>, while the former is like a "demonstration of fact" <note>Latin: "demonstration quod est," proving something from its effects</note>. Paul knew both ways perfectly, but he was often forced to lead us by the hand using the weaker method. However, human philosophy knows little of this wisdom of truth and traces, especially where a contentious education exists. Therefore, those coming out of such education are contentious and should not be received; rather, they must first be educated, unless their habit of arguing does not permit it—as it often does not. For they do not accept traces as traces, but as the things themselves. They savor only the "letter" and not the "spirit"; for the spirit is the type of things and the archetype in truth. Such people are usually rigid and stubborn against the spirit. May God therefore take away fruitless contention—which human or sub-human philosophy, not divine philosophy, produces—from these most divine studies. May He return to His churches the peaceful and consistent wisdom that befits them, whether it flows from Him into signs, or (like a sunbeam bouncing back from earthly things toward the sun) leaps back from signs into Him. And because the consummation of prayer and of every divine gift is union with God <note>Latin: "vnitio"</note>, and that union to God and in God happens through the spiritual taking of the body and blood of Christ: therefore, one must approach that all-consuming participation in the divine body and blood with the greatest reverence, purity, and holiness. Because the Corinthians did not do this—not recognizing the august and deeply venerable divine mystery—Paul rightly rebukes and argues with them, saying:
<margin>78</margin>¶ **In giving this warning, however, I do not praise you: for you come together not for the better but for the worse. First of all, when you come together as a church, I hear there are schisms among you, and I partly believe it. For there must also be heresies among you, so that those who are proven may be manifest among you.** ¶ God occasionally permits schisms and heresies (that is, divisions and sects) to occur for the testing of the good. For just as gold—from which fire takes nothing away, but instead makes it more brilliant—is known to be genuine and not at all counterfeit, so he who is not shaken by schisms and heresies but perseveres firmly in the traditions of the church is proven to be faithful. And because some among the Corinthians were such people, whom neither schisms nor heresies would touch, the Apostle said, "I partly believe it." For not all were schismatics or heretics, but it had happened to them in part because of different "pedagogues" <note>teachers or guardians</note> who were instructing them wrongly. But he also accuses them of another thing. At a set time (which was usually the Lord’s Day in the primitive church), they were supposed to meet together for the taking of the body and blood of Christ, and to eat and drink together in that place in memory of the Lord’s Supper <note>Latin: "cena domini"</note>—when He was with His disciples in the large upper room at the institution of this most wonderful mystery. I say they met to eat and drink together in a public supper which, in memory of the Lord’s Supper, is called the Lord’s Meal. But when they came to that most holy communion, they no longer ate and drank together, neglecting the memory of the Lord’s Supper; instead, they ate and drank in their own homes before they came to the communion. Many of them who were wealthier were distended with food and drink and arrived drunk, while others who were poorer were hungry...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the First Epistle to the Corinthians, moving from the natural order of men and women discussed in chapter 11 to the spiritual gifts and the theology of the Holy Spirit found in chapter 12.</meta>

[header]
COMMENTARY

<image-desc>An ornamental woodcut initial letter 'M' featuring two figures in an interior architectural setting with a tiled floor.</image-desc> **The Apostle has already declared the great mystery of the Son of God, who is the "hidden manna"** <note>original: "manna absconditũ," a reference to Revelation 2:17, signifying the spiritual nourishment of Christ</note>. Now, however, he speaks concerning the gifts of the Holy Spirit, which can only be possessed by those who believe in our Lord. Those who possess these gifts cannot help but confess that Jesus Christ is Lord and God. Those who do not have them blaspheme Jesus Christ and consider him accursed. ¶ This is exactly what those people were doing when, led astray, they followed deaf and mute idols—and what the Corinthians themselves would have done if the grace of the Holy Spirit had not shone upon them. From this, it is clear that those who worship idols do not have the Holy Spirit; for if they did, they would not consider the Lord Jesus accursed. It is regarding these gifts of the Holy Spirit, I say, that he instructs the Corinthians, saying:

<margin>85</margin>¶ **Now concerning spiritual gifts, brothers, I do not want you to be ignorant. You know that when you were pagans, you were led away to mute idols, however you were led. Therefore I make known to you that no one speaking in the Spirit of God says "Jesus is accursed." And no one can say "Jesus is Lord" except by the Holy Spirit.** <note>Latin: "anathema IHESVM," meaning to pronounce a curse or separation from God upon Jesus.</note> ¶ Since, therefore, the faithful Corinthians confessed Jesus to be Lord and God, they possessed the Holy Spirit, who is of the same substance <term>consubstantial|meaning the Spirit is of the same divine "stuff" or essence as the Father and Son</term> as the Spirit of the Father and the Son. He who is Lord, who is God: as he is Spirit, his bestowals are "gifts"; as he is Lord, they are "ministries"; as he is God and the artisan of all, they are "workings" <note>This identifies the Trinity in the three terms used by Paul: Gifts (Spirit), Service/Ministry (Lord), and Working (God).</note>. For these three—the gift of the Spirit, the ministry of the Lord, and the working of the Artisan—maintain a shared harmony among themselves. And so, further instructing them regarding the Holy Spirit, Paul adds, saying:

<margin>86</margin>¶ **There are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit. And there are varieties of ministries, but the same Lord. And there are varieties of workings, but it is the same God who works all things in everyone.** ¶ And just as in the source, or in the cause, the Spirit, the Lord, and God are the same, so in their effects, the gifts, ministries, and workings are the same—though the reasons for them differ here and there. And just as the Holy Spirit divides and distinguishes gifts, ministries, and works in truth, so the evil spirit divides and distributes "gifts," "ministries," and "workings" in lies and falsehood. The things given by the Holy Spirit are useful; they build up and save. The things given by the evil spirit are useless; they build nothing and save nothing, but rather overturn and destroy. In this way, the distributions, inspirations, and breathings of the Holy Spirit are distinguished from the suggestions and deceptions of the evil spirit. And while the Holy Spirit is one and the same, the evil spirits are many and diverse. Accordingly, Paul adds:

<margin>87</margin>¶ **To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good. To one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom; to another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit; to another faith in the same Spirit; to another gifts of healing in the one Spirit; to another the working of miracles; to another prophecy; to another the discernment of spirits; to another various kinds of tongues; and to another the interpretation of tongues. All these are empowered by one and the same Spirit, who apportions to each one individually as he wills.** ¶ The manifestation of the Holy Spirit happens in some through the **word of wisdom**, when they speak of sublime and divine things. Such were Bartholomew <note>One of the twelve Apostles.</note>, Joseph the Just <note>Likely the candidate to replace Judas in Acts 1.</note>, Dionysius, and Hierotheus <note>Dionysius the Areopagite and his teacher Hierotheus were legendary figures in early Christian mysticism.</note> in the primitive Church. In others, it is through the **word of knowledge**, which concerns the things of faith necessary for salvation to those who know them, delivering the mysteries of God in a humbler speech suited even to the unlearned. In others, it is through **faith**, as in the Canaanite woman or the Centurion. In others, through **gifts of healing**, as in Peter or Paul, whose very shadows, garments, and cloths drove away diseases. In others, through the **working of miracles**, who powerfully commanded spirits, overthrew the temples of idols, shattered idols with a single word, and performed wonders. In others, through **prophecy**, knowing hidden and secret things. In others, through the **discernment of spiritual gifts**, distinguishing whether they are from the Holy Spirit or from other spirits; and if from the Holy Spirit, what kind of gift and bestowal it is. If you have a gift of the Holy Spirit, it is also a gift of the Holy Spirit that you recognize and discern that you have it from the Spirit, so that you do not take pride in what is not yours, nor attribute to yourself what belongs to the Holy Spirit. In others, through **kinds of tongues**, when in whatever region they spoke the language of the natives, which they had not learned, for their edification. In others, through the **interpretation of tongues**, so that they might interpret through the Spirit for those who spoke in foreign tongues (which they themselves might not even understand) and for others who had never heard the language. And those who heard them speaking in languages known to them—seeing their neighbors and those raised with them interpreting things beneficial for salvation—recognized that both possessed the Spirit, who manifested himself through the others in a different way. Yet if all had faith, he manifested himself in all through faith. And blessed be He in his holy manifestations, who still deigns to manifest himself to many in our own times, according to the capacity of the times and the hearts of men. And it is not men, nor various spirits that work these things; rather, it is one and the same Spirit who invisibly glides in and works all things in all people—more in some, fewer in others, higher things in some, humbler in others—according to his own goodness and wisdom, and according to the capacity of those who receive him. But...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on 1 Corinthians 12, specifically addressing the distinction between the diverse, deceptive spirits of the pagan world and the unified distribution of gifts by the Holy Spirit within the Body of Christ.</meta>

[header]
II 1 Corinthians

...who distribute deceitfully: these spirits are many and divided, and not one and the same. Hence the Gentiles, deceived by error, thought that Minerva distributed the word of wisdom; Mercury, knowledge; Apollo, the power of healings; Hecate, portents; Phoebus, divination; and again Mercury, languages and interpretations. These were diverse spirits of error, falsely claiming to have visible dwellings in heaven, from whence they had been invisibly cast out. What Minerva inspired was not wisdom, but rather a certain—if I may call it so—"demonology" <note>original: "demonologia"</note> hostile to true wisdom, such as the books of Orpheus, Zoroaster, and certain works of Proclus, Iamblichus, Porphyry, and several other Platonists <note>These were Neoplatonic philosophers and legendary figures whom the author views as sources of pagan error rather than true divine wisdom.</note> contain. The power of Apollo was not true power, but a pretense. The powers of Hecate were not true powers, nor wonders, nor miracles, but deceptions and magical portents, useful for nothing, such as those of Dositheus and Simon Magus <note>Simon Magus is a biblical figure from Acts 8 associated with the origin of "simony" and gnosticism.</note>. The prophecy of Phoebus was not prophecy, but divination, having for the most part an ambiguous meaning in either direction—mere imposture, sophistry, and a device for deception. As for Mercury, the protector of thieves: his were not true languages, nor true interpretations, but the frauds of a crafty eloquence, intended to destroy the body along with the soul. The Gentiles, therefore, could be united neither in body nor in spirit, having so many spirits of error tearing their souls and bodies apart.

But it is not so with the faithful. Because they are one body in the body of Christ and one spirit in the Holy Spirit, do we not see that whatever things are united to one and the same thing are united among themselves? Now all are united to the body of Christ through holy communion—to one and the same body—and all are united to the Holy Spirit through baptism— to one and the same Spirit. And because the Spirit of Christ and his body are not divided: Christ and the Holy Spirit are like the center of a circle; the faithful are like innumerable lines going out from the center and flowing back from the circumference into the center. Moreover, the power of Christ and his Spirit is like the circumference, containing, preserving, and nourishing all things. And just as in lines some are at the top, some in the middle, and some at the bottom, and one is not the other, yet being united in one they constitute one circle; so in the body of Christ some members are highest, some middle, and some lowest, and one is not the other, yet all being united to the body of Christ, they are one body. Which is to say: all the faithful, being with Christ or (if I may put it this way) "concentrated" in Christ, constitute this body. So it is also with the gifts of the Holy Spirit: some are highest, some middle, and some lowest, all converging in the identity of the Spirit, like all solar rays into the same sun; flowing from the same Spirit, as all the lights of the rays from the same sun. And in short, just as in one animal body all members are corporally united and are held together by one soul, and all are mutually necessary, breathing together and having a wonderful agreement among themselves, though performing different functions: so in the body of Christ, those possessing various and varying gifts of the Holy Spirit are united in one body and held together by one Holy Spirit. And by this proportion and 

<margin>88 analogy</margin>

analogy <note>original: "analogia"</note> the most blessed Paul leads us by the hand to understand the body of Christ, saying:

> ¶ **For just as the body is one and has many members, yet all the members of the one body, though they are many, are one body: so also is CHRIST. For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body—whether Jews or Gentiles, whether slaves or free—and we were all given to drink of one Spirit. For the body is not one member, but many. If the foot should say, "Because I am not a hand, I am not of the body," it is not for this reason any less a part of the body. And if the ear should say, "Because I am not an eye, I am not of the body," it is not for this reason any less a part of the body.**

For this reasoning is not valid: "I am not a hand, therefore I am not of the body." "I am not an eye, therefore I am not of the body." Likewise, neither is this: "I am not a prophet, therefore I am not of Christ's body." "I do not have the grace of healings, or of signs and miracles, therefore I am not of Christ's body." For although the foot is not the hand, it is of the body; and although the ear is not the eye, it is of the body. In this same way, he who has faith, even if he is not a prophet, is of the body of Christ. And he who has wisdom or knowledge according to the Spirit, even if he does not have the grace of healings or powers, is of the body of Christ. Nor is it right that all in the body of Christ should be prophets, or all apostles. For the prophets are like the eyes; the apostles are like the hearing. For these latter hear the command of the one who sends them, and the prophets see. But everyone in the body of Christ ought to have faith, hope, and charity, just as all members of the body have a twofold sense of touch and vital heat. For faith is 

<margin>89 Faith, hope, charity</margin>

like the first spiritual touch; hope like the second; and charity is the vital heat. For take away the heat, and the member of the animal is sensibly dead. Take away also charity, and the member is spiritually dead. Indeed, if you take away both types of touch, it is dead. These gifts, therefore, are like particular parts. Concerning which the Apostle here distinguishes in proportion, saying:

> ¶ **If the whole body were an eye, where would the hearing be? If the whole were hearing, where would the sense of smell be? But now God has placed the members, each one of them in the body, just as he willed. If they were all one member, where would the body be? But as it is, there are many members, but one body.**

<summary>This page contrasts the fragmented, deceptive "spirits" of pagan mythology with the unified Body of Christ, where diverse spiritual gifts are harmonized by the Holy Spirit. Using the analogy of a circle's center and the biological body, the author explains how individual believers (the members) are essential to the whole despite their different functions.</summary>

COMMENTARY

<warning>Water damage and staining on the left margin and bottom left corner.</warning>

...[mem]bers in a single animal, arranging them as He willed and indeed most wisely; so too the Holy Spirit distributes as He wills to establish the diverse members of the Body of Christ. For if all the members of an animal were a single member—for instance, a foot—it would not be the body of an animal, for a foot alone is not the whole body of a living creature. Likewise, if all the gifts of the Holy Spirit were one single gift, it would not be the Body of Christ; for having only a single good thing, it cannot constitute the "Body" of Christ <note>The author argues that a "body" by definition requires diversity of parts working together.</note>. For Christ possessed all things eminently <note>term: eminently (Lat. eminenter) — In scholastic theology, this means possessing a quality in its highest, most perfect form, containing all the virtues of the lesser versions.</note>, even as a man, whereas others possess them only in part. This is because He is the head of this mystical body. As God, however, He transcends all things, possessing all things super-eminently. For the head is seen to possess, in a superior way, all the senses that are found in the members, and even more abundantly.

<margin>90</margin>
Lest we think that the lowliest of the faithful in the Body of Christ, or those participating in less remarkable graces of the Holy Spirit, are not necessary to the Body—or that those who have attained moderate or the highest graces do not need the others—Paul adds the following: ¶ *The eye cannot say to the hand: "I have no use for you." Or again, the head to the feet: "I do not need you." But much more, those members of the body which seem to be weaker are necessary. And those which we think to be less honorable parts of the body, we surround with more abundant honor. And our unpresentable parts are dressed with more abundant propriety. But our presentable parts have no such need. But God has tempered the body, giving more abundant honor to that which suffered lack, so that there should be no discord in the body, but that the members should have the same care for one another. And if one member suffers, all the members suffer with it. If one member is honored, all the members rejoice with it.*

Paul provides a very simple teaching for understanding how everyone in the church ought to conduct themselves. Truly, everyone should act as if they were a single animal <note>original: "animal vnum" — here meaning a single living organism.</note> of which Christ is the head and His Spirit is the soul. We are individuals as members of that animal, yet co-members with one another. We should regard the weaker members as more necessary, and strive to bestow even more honor upon the less honorable parts. If there is anything unseemly, we should cover it, adorning it with greater beauty if we are able, because it is a member of Christ. For no one should consider especially what he himself is, or what another is, but rather *whose* he is. For all belong to Christ, and all are members of Christ, and mutually co-members. Let there be no discord in the whole body; rather, if anyone is wounded by sin, let all be sorrowful. And let everyone strive to bring aid to the injured person as a fellow member, as a member of Christ. If anyone rises from sin back to grace, let everyone rejoice, just as the angels also rejoice. If anyone makes progress in grace toward honor and that glory which is according to the spirit, let everyone rejoice with him whom God honors. The honor with which the world or men bestow is vain, empty, and earthly. But the honor which God bestows is the greatest. For the latter, everyone ought to rejoice; for the former, one should often mourn.

<margin>91</margin>
But now Paul reveals his comparison to the Corinthians, saying: *Now you are the body of CHRIST, and members in particular. And God has placed these in the church: First, apostles. Second, prophets. Third, teachers. Then powers <note>original: "potestates" — referring to the working of miracles.</note>. After that, the gifts of healings, helps, governments, kinds of tongues. Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Are all teachers? Are all powers? Do all have the gifts of healing? Do all speak with tongues? Do all interpret? Be zealous for the better gifts.* ¶ The Corinthians were the Body of Christ—not the whole, but a part. They were members of Christ, but a part. Therefore the apostle added the detail: "in part." Then he describes nine members of the Body of Christ, which constitute nine gifts of the Holy Spirit: namely, the gift of apostleship, the gift of prophecy, the gift of teaching (under which the gifts of wisdom and knowledge are contained), the gift of powers in performing wonders and signs, the gift of healings in curing illnesses, the gift of helps in maintaining hospitality and exercising works of mercy, the gift of governments in presidency and the authority of administering justice, the gift of tongues, and the gift of interpretations. We can also add a tenth gift from the preceding sections: namely, the discernment of spirits. We ought to have zeal and fervor for possessing these gifts of the Holy Spirit, but especially for those which are better and more suited to the edification of others. May that immense goodness—which is the diffusive breath of Himself—grant us those gifts which may further cleanse, illuminate, and perfect us; those which make us and others more spiritual for serving Him with august reverence, and for perpetually meditating upon and giving thanks for such great and excellent gifts of His grace. For whichever of these are better are to be more zealously desired and more earnestly entreated.

# 12

...to say that Jesus is Lord; and to "say" this is to assert it and believe it in the mind.
<margin>A 86</margin> The scribes and Pharisees spoke in an evil spirit concerning Christ when they said: "He casts out demons by Beelzebub, the prince of demons." Concerning this spirit—which is the spirit of blasphemy, contrary to the Holy Spirit, and which sins against the Holy Spirit—the Savior says that it is not forgiven in this age nor in the next. However, in the Holy Spirit (which opposes the spirit of blasphemy), a woman immediately cried out from the opposite side: "Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts that nursed you." Those men called Jesus "anathema" <note>Anathema: a Greek term meaning something accursed or handed over to evil.</note>; this woman, however, called Him Lord. Paul says: *calls Jesus accursed, and no one is able to say "Jesus is Lord"* <note>original Greek: λέγει ἀνάθεμα ἰησοῦν, καὶ οὐδεὶς δύναται εἰπεῖν κύριον ἰησοῦν</note>. ¶ The Vulgate edition <note>term: Vulgate (Lat. Vulgata) — The standard Latin translation of the Bible used in the Western Church, which the author is here comparing to the original Greek.</note> reads: *There are indeed divisions of graces.* ¶ It should rather be "of gifts." Paul writes: *There are varieties of gifts* <note>original Greek: Διαιρέσεις δὲ χαρισμάτων εἰσί</note>.
<margin>87 B</margin> ¶ The Vulgate edition reads: *To another, the discerning of spirits.* ¶ This should be read in the plural: "discernings of spirits." Paul writes: *and to another, discernings of spirits* <note>original Greek: ἄλλω δὲ Διακρίσεις πνευμάτων</note>. ¶ The Vulgate edition reads: *To another, the interpretation of speeches.* ¶ It is better to say "of tongues." For nothing prevents someone from having the gift of a tongue but not having the interpretation; or another from having the interpretation through the Holy Spirit but not the tongue. Just as Daniel, through the Holy Spirit, interpreted the writing of an unknown tongue. Paul writes: *and to another, the interpretation of tongues* <note>original Greek: ἄλλω δὲ ἑρμηνεία γλωσσῶν</note>. ¶ The Vulgate edition reads: *Dividing to each one as he wills.* ¶ It can also be read as "dividing separately," "apart," "secretly," or "individually." We, however, have used "individually," because it more closely approaches the Vulgate’s interpretation. Paul writes: *dividing to each individually as he wills* <note>original Greek: Διαιρεοῦν ἰδία ἑκάστω καθώς βούλεται</note>.
<margin>88</margin> ¶ The Vulgate edition reads: *Yet they are one body.* ¶ The particle "yet" is redundant. And it is more elegant to say "it is one body" rather than "they are," just as Paul has it: *it is one body* <note>original Greek: ἕν ἔστι σῶμα</note>. ¶ The Vulgate edition reads: *And we have all been given to drink in one Spirit.* ¶ It is more apt to say "into one Spirit," just as previously it was "into one body." For Paul uses the same preposition in both places. And it is better to say "watered" or "irrigated" than "given to drink." For those who are baptized are irrigated and dipped in the waters, not given them to drink. They are baptized, therefore, into one body and irrigated into one Spirit—that is, for the purpose of forming one body and one spirit. Paul writes: *and we were all irrigated into one Spirit* <note>original Greek: καὶ πάντες εἰς ἕν πνεῦμα ἐποτίσθημεν</note>; for the verb *potizomai* <note>original: ποτίζομαι</note> signifies "I am watered" or "I am irrigated." ¶ The Vulgate edition reads: *They are more necessary.* ¶ One should simply say "they are necessary." For he speaks of this necessity with much greater emphasis; to use the comparative again would be superfluous. And in Paul's text, it is also in the positive degree. Paul writes: *they are necessary* <note>original Greek: ἀναγκαῖά ἐστι</note>. ¶ The Vulgate edition reads: *But the members are concerned for one another into the very same.*
<margin>D 90</margin> ¶ It is better to say "the same." For what does "into the very same" even mean? Paul writes: *but the members should have the same care for one another* <note>original Greek: ἀλλὰ τὸ αὐτὸ ὑπὲρ ἀλλήλων, μεριμνῶσι τὰ μέλη</note>. ¶ The Vulgate edition reads: *Or if one member glories.*
<margin>91</margin> ¶ It can be said: "or if one member is glorified," that is, honored. Paul writes: *or if one member is glorified* <note>original Greek: εἴτε Δοξάζεται ἕν μέλος</note>. ¶ The Vulgate edition reads: *And members of member.* ¶ It should be read "and members in part." It is as if he were saying: "You are the body of Christ in part," that is, a portion of the body of Christ. "You are members of Christ in part," that is, a portion of the members of Christ, but not all the members. For the faithful of Corinth were not the whole body of Christ; indeed, neither Europe, nor Asia, nor Africa is capable of containing the fullness of the body of Christ—the body of Christ, I say, to which our bodies are united in a spiritual manner and (so to speak) "incorporated." This body fills heaven and earth, for it is wherever the Word of God is. For the Word was made flesh; therefore, the Word is nowhere without the flesh, nor is that flesh anywhere without the Word. Take care that your bodily imagination does not deceive you here by multiplying places or stretching out spaces. Neither a multiplication of places nor a distension of spaces is to be understood here, but rather a fullness without place—above every place, below every place, outside and inside everything—without space, above and below all space, outside and inside all space. And the body of Christ exists in that super-spiritual way which is beyond any "way," comparable to nothing, proportionable to nothing. But in the physical way in which He was seen on earth, He is both comparable and proportionable. The latter admits of measure, comparison, and proportion because of the weakness He assumed; the former, however, escapes all measure, comparison, and proportion because of the power of the One who assumed it. Reason joined to imagination cannot grasp this, nor can reason remaining within itself. Indeed, reason speaks and fashions absurdities on both sides. But when reason goes out of itself, into the superior mind by a super-rational and infused power—where neither places, nor spaces, nor number, nor multitude, nor time are contemplated—then it perceives the truth and speaks the truth. It speaks, certainly, in the way that unutterable, incomparable, and disproportionable things can be spoken, which is in a sense unutterably. But more on this matter another time, if God breathes His grace upon us. Paul writes: *and members in part* <note>original Greek: καὶ μέλη ἐκ μέρους</note>. ¶ The Vulgate edition reads: *And indeed God placed some in the church.* ¶ It can be read as "And God placed his own in the church." Paul writes: *and some indeed God placed in the church* <note>original Greek: καὶ οὓς μὲν ἔθετο ὁ θεὸς ἐν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ</note>; for the word *hous* <note>original: οὓς</note> which Paul uses here is often used for "who" or "his own." ¶ The Vulgate edition reads: *Governments. Kinds of tongues. Interpretations of speeches.* ¶ This "interpretations of speeches" is an addition. Paul writes: *governments, kinds of tongues* <note>original Greek: κυβερνήσεις, γένη γλωσσῶν</note>. Then he immediately adds: *Are all apostles?* <note>original Greek: μὴ πάντες ἀπόστολοι;</note>

### CHAPTER XIII.

<image-desc>Decorative historiated woodcut initial 'E' featuring classical architectural elements and a figure.</image-desc>

**E**xcellent are the gifts of the Holy Spirit which were previously listed; but they are particular, and not necessary for every member of the body of Christ for salvation. However, there are three other gifts of the Holy Spirit which are necessary for salvation for every single member of Christ capable of sense and reason: **Faith, Hope, and Charity** <note>Latin: "charitas"</note>, which is also called love <note>Latin: "dilectio"</note>, specifically the love of God. For Faith looks toward God, Hope looks toward God, and Charity, most of all, looks toward God. For by this love, God is loved chiefly for His own sake; and every human is loved because they are God’s creature and God’s image. Every believer, moreover, must be loved not only because they are God’s creature and image, but also because through regeneration they have been made a child of God, a member of Christ, and a brother, having the same Christ as Father as every other believer. And this charity and love—which necessarily draws the love of neighbor along with it, no differently than light draws the shadow of an opaque body—makes us nothing more commendable to God, and nothing is more necessary for salvation. We ought to be zealous for this love of God above all things, prepare ourselves for it with all our strength, and ask it of God with all our heart; it is the most saving gift of the Holy Spirit and the completion of all His gifts. By it we ascend to God and are transformed into God. Concerning this so sublime a gift of the Holy Spirit, which is to be most sought after and most desired, Paul 
<margin>92</margin> admonishes the Corinthians, extolling, celebrating, and praising that same gift of the Holy Spirit, saying: ¶ *And yet I show you a way by excellence. If I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, but have not love: I have become as sounding brass and a clanging cymbal. And if I should have prophecy, and know all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I should have all faith, so that I could move mountains, but have not love: I am nothing. And if I should distribute all my goods for food, and if I should hand over my body to be burned, but have not love: it profits me nothing.* ¶ The gifts of the Holy Spirit are an excellent way to God, such as tongues, prophecy, wisdom, knowledge, faith, helping <note>Latin: "subuectionis"</note>, and power, which Paul lists in order. But Charity is a more eminent way than all these and the rest which were listed in the previous chapter. For those who have those gifts without charity are nothing; those gifts without charity help nothing and profit nothing. But he who has charity, even if he does not have the others, is something. This helps along with the others, and helps by itself. But you will say: it is certain that charity can exist without the gift of tongues, wisdom, science or knowledge, without the gift of prophecy, healings, powers, discernment of spirits, helping, governing, or the interpretation of tongues; but how shall it be without faith? Even if not in this world, charity and love nevertheless exist and help in the other world, because "it does not fall away," 
<margin>93</margin> even when it is without faith. And the same must be said of hope. And Paul lists those things which accompany the love of God, and which do not fall away either in this world or in the next, saying: ¶ *Love is patient, is kind, love does not envy, love does not act inconstantly, is not puffed up, does not work shame, does not seek its own, is not provoked to anger, thinks no evil, does not rejoice over injustice but rejoices with the truth, bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things; love never falls away.* ¶ Just as a pleasant scent, color, and flavor accompany healthy fruit, so do patience, kindness, an absence of malice, constancy and gravity in well-doing, humility, honesty, being an example, gentleness, clemency, sadness over evil, and joy over good, equanimity, right faith toward God in all things, certain hope of all divine promises, the expectation of all things, and an unwithering nature accompany the love of God, the gift of the Holy Spirit. But the other 
<margin>94</margin> gifts of the Holy Spirit wither and fall away; in this they differ from the always-green and unfailing love of God. Which Paul adds, saying: ¶ *But whether prophecies shall be done away, or tongues shall cease, or knowledge shall be taken away.* ¶ Whether these gifts of the Holy Spirit shall be entirely taken away—and the judgment is the same for the rest—charity and the love of God shall never fall away. But those and other gifts of the Holy Spirit shall be taken away. For they are "in part" and imperfect; for example, the gift of knowledge, or rather of wisdom, is now (that is, in the present age) a gift "in part" and imperfect, through figures, types, and enigmas. But in the other age, it will no longer be shadowy, but through...

<summary>This page marks the transition to 1 Corinthians 13, where the author argues that while spiritual gifts like prophecy and tongues are valuable, they are secondary to Charity (Love). He explains that Charity is the only gift necessary for salvation and the only one that persists into the afterlife.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the gifts of the Spirit, moving from the specific miraculous gifts (prophecy, tongues, healing) to the permanent "more excellent way" of Love (Charity) described in 1 Corinthians 13. It contrasts the temporary nature of earthly knowledge with the perfection of the afterlife.</meta>

II 127 1 Corinthians.

...perfect, naked, and open knowledge and wisdom in the archetype—in truth itself—just as there is perfect knowledge of us in God. For He does not know us by mere traces <note>Latin: "ex vestigijs" - hints or footprints of evidence</note>, but in the fullness of truth. Similarly, prophecy now is a certain partial and imperfect knowledge of hidden future things. But then all things will be open, when the immense light that reveals all things arises. There will be no "future" where eternal things are known beyond the constraints of time. Therefore, those temporary gifts will cease.

But will there be any need for the gift of healing where there is no more mourning, no more crying, and no more pain? Or for portents and signs, where the abyss of divinity will surpass every immense miracle? Or for the discernment of spirits, where no craftiness of the ancient serpent <note>The devil</note> will find any place? Or for various kinds of tongues, or their interpretation, where the nods and thoughts of minds will be visible and known? Or for acts of assistance, when no one will be in need? Or for acts of administration <note>Latin: "guberna-tionibus" - often translated as "governments" or "leadership"</note>, when no one will be able to stray? Or even for faith? But faith is of things that are not seen; then all things will be visible. Or for hope? But hope is of things absent; then whatever could have been hoped for will be present. But will there not remain delight and love in those present things, the enjoyment of which will be infinitely pleasant? It will certainly remain, and the rest will pass away. Therefore, although these three spiritual gifts—faith, hope, and charity <note>The author uses "charitas" and "dilectio" interchangeably for "love"</note>—are universal gifts in this age, necessary for all and lasting until the end, the greatest of these is charity, as it is meant to endure both in this age and the next. And is it any wonder if the remaining gifts, being imperfect, do not remain once the perfect age of immortality has come? For the things belonging to children do not remain when the perfect physical age of adulthood arrives. The worldly age is like infancy or a certain childhood compared to the state of immortality, while that future state is like perfect and consummate manhood. Accordingly, Paul adds:

> ¶ For we know in part, and we prophesy in part. But when that which is perfect is come, then that which is in part shall be done away. When I was a child, I spoke as a child, I understood as a child, I thought as a child; but when I became a man, I put away childish things. For now we see through a glass, darkly <note>The Greek term used here suggests a riddle or an enigma</note>; but then face to face. Now I know in part; but then shall I know even as also I am known. And now remaineth faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity.

¶ Let no one wonder if now there are no prophets, if there are no tongues, if there are no gifts of healing, if there are no signs, if there are few who are wise and knowledgeable; for these are not necessary for the salvation of the faithful. Rather, they were necessary for the conversion of unbelievers. What, then, is necessary for the faithful? Faith, hope, and charity. And blessed be God, who does not cease to pour these three necessary things into the faithful until the end of the age. In these gifts of His, may we be so strong to serve in this age, that in the next we may be able to praise Him with unfailing love without end, alongside all the angels and all the saints.

# EXAMINATION of several points regarding the literal text.

<margin>92.</margin>
¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *I am become as sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal.* ¶ The word "as" is redundant, yet it does not hinder understanding. And it could be called a "rejoicing cymbal." "Sounding" refers to the tongues of men, and "rejoicing cymbal" <note>clashing or loud cymbal</note> refers to the tongues of angels, which designates certain secret and ineffable praises and rejoicings they offer to God. To speak with the tongues of men is a great gift of the Holy Spirit; but to speak with the tongues of angels, to praise God and rejoice in an angelic manner, is a far greater gift—yet unless charity is present, it is nothing, and it profits us nothing. Paul writes: <margin>I have become sounding brass, or a clanging cymbal. <note>original Greek: γέγονα χαλκός ἠχῶν, ἢ κύμβαλον ἀλαλάζον</note></margin>

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *And if I should have prophecy.* <margin>L</margin> Although Paul speaks here everywhere using the present indicative, by Latin custom we aptly join the subjunctive everywhere. But just as the old translator <note>the translator of the Vulgate</note> at the beginning changed the present indicative to the present subjunctive by saying, *if I should speak with the tongues of men*, he could have similarly changed the other present indicative verbs here into the present subjunctive and said, *And if I should have prophecy.* Paul writes: <note>original Greek: καὶ ἐὰν ἔχω προφητείαν — "And if I have prophecy"</note>
<margin>B 92.</margin>
¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *And if I should deliver my body so that I burn.* ¶ The word "so" is superfluous; it should simply say "that I may burn," which is the same as saying "to be burned." For this is put for the gift of the operation of powers. For instance, John the Evangelist <note>Tradition holds that St. John was thrown into boiling oil in Rome but emerged unharmed</note> delivered his body to be put into a vat of boiling oil, and that heat of boiling oil did not harm him through the gift of the Holy Spirit. And the virgin Thecla <note>Saint Thecla, a legendary follower of Paul who survived various executions</note> delivered her body to the fire to be burned at Iconium and Alexandria, but that all-consuming and fierce flame spared her virginal flesh consecrated to Christ God. Truly, without charity, the gift of such great power would have profited neither the former nor the latter. I say "profited" <margin>B</margin> in regard to eternal salvation and to being worthy of God. Paul writes: <margin>And if I deliver my body that I may be burned. <note>93. original Greek: καὶ ἐὰν παραδῶ τὸ σῶμα μου ἵνα καυθήσωμαι</note></margin>

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Is not ambitious.* ¶ It can be read as: *it does nothing base or dishonest.* Paul writes: <note>original Greek: οὐκ ἀσχημονεῖ — "does not behave unseemly"</note>

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Seeketh not her own.* ¶ It can also be read as: *the things that are its own.* That is, in all good things, it does not look to itself, but especially to the one whom it loves. Vulgate edition: "But the greatest of these is love." ¶ According to Latin custom, it can be said: "the greatest [maxima] of these is love" or "the greatest [maximum] of these," even though Paul—as the Greek language allows—uses the comparative form. Paul says: "But the greater [meizōn] of these is love" <note>original Greek: μείζων δὲ τούτων ἡ ἀγάπη - *meizōn de toutōn hē agapē*</note>.

### CHAPTER XIV.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'O' with scrollwork and foliage motifs.</image-desc>
Of all the gifts of the Holy Spirit (not only faith and hope), love is the greatest; yet all are great. Therefore, we ought to aspire to love above all things, and to be zealous for the other gifts of the Holy Spirit, especially the better ones, such as prophecy rather than the gift of tongues. For that [prophecy] is better than this [tongues].
<margin>96</margin>
First, because he who speaks in an unknown tongue through the Spirit does not speak to men but to God. For no one who is present will understand the mysteries that he speaks through the Spirit. Wherefore Paul adds: ¶ Pursue love, and be zealous for spiritual gifts, but rather that you may prophesy. For he who speaks in a tongue does not speak to men but to God; for no one hears <note>In this context, "hears" implies "understands."</note>; but in the spirit he speaks mysteries. But he who prophesies speaks to men for edification, and exhortation, and consolation. ¶ As he prophesies, he speaks to men words of edification—sometimes exhorting, sometimes consoling. For the prophets exhort men to follow eternal things, to despise fleeting things, to desire heavenly things, and to look down upon earthly things; and in those things they provide comfort. Second: prophecy is preferable to the simple gift of a tongue. For it is better to build up the church and the multitude of the faithful than only oneself.
<margin>97</margin>
He who prophesies builds up the multitude. But he who has only the gift of a tongue builds up only himself. If he were to build up neither himself nor another, that would be vain, for it would be recognized as coming not from the Holy Spirit but from another spirit. ¶ Prophecy is therefore preferable to the simple gift of a tongue. Paul reveals this, saying: ¶ He who speaks in a tongue builds up himself, but he who prophesies builds up the church. Third. Because he who prophesies is considered greater than he who speaks in tongues, unless he himself can interpret for the edification of the church. But he who has only the gift of a tongue speaks indeed but does not interpret. For the gift of interpretation is something else. ¶ Prophecy is therefore preferable to the gift of tongues, even if the gift of 
<margin>98</margin>
tongues is great and desirable. For who would not want to praise God through the Spirit in every tongue? Therefore, Paul adds: ¶ I would like you all to speak in tongues, but even more that you would prophesy; for he who prophesies is greater than he who speaks in tongues, unless he interprets, so that the church may receive edification. ¶ Fourth: by a clear example, it can be known that prophecy is superior and more powerful than the gift of a tongue. For instance, if I were to go to the Hebrews and speak the 
<margin>99</margin>
mysteries of God through the Spirit in the Carmanian <note>Carmania was an ancient region in modern-day Iran.</note> or Brahman <note>Referring to the languages of India.</note> language, how would I help them? Just as much as inanimate things like flutes, pipes, or harps emit sound. But prophecy would help. Taking himself as an example, Paul asserts this, saying: ¶ But now, brothers, if I come to you speaking in tongues, what will I profit you unless I speak to you either in revelation, or in knowledge, or in prophecy, or in doctrine? ¶ Just like inanimate things emitting a voice, whether pipes or harps. If they do not give a distinction in the sounds <note>Latin: *pthongis*, from the Greek for "musical notes" or "distinct sounds."</note>, how will it be known what is played on the pipe or the harp? ¶ For if the pipe gives a festive sound <note>Though the author uses *tibia* (pipe), the context refers to the biblical "uncertain sound" of a trumpet.</note>, who will prepare himself for battle? ¶ In this same way, unless you give a clear speech through the tongue, how will it be known what is being uttered? For you will be speaking into the air. ¶ You will be "speaking into the air": you will be empty, emitting voices profitable to no one. Fifth. Because since there are so many kinds of languages in the world, none of which is without meaning: he who speaks in some unknown kind 
<margin>100</margin>
will not only seem to his listeners to be shaking the air in vain, but will also seem like a barbarian and a complete fool. And conversely, the listeners will be barbarians to the speaker if he does not know their speech. But he who prophesies does not appear barbarian or foolish to those to whom he prophesies. ¶ Prophecy is therefore preferable to the tongue. Paul reveals this in this way: ¶ There are, it may be, so many kinds of voices in the world, and none of them is without meaning. If therefore I do not know the power of the voice, I shall be a barbarian to him who speaks, and he who speaks will be a barbarian to me. ¶ Because the gift of a tongue, by itself, is small among the gifts of the Holy Spirit, Paul instructs the Corinthians that those who have only this from the Holy Spirit should pray to the same Spirit so that He might grant them the gift of understanding and the interpretation of the tongue for their own greater edification and that of the church. For he who has only the tongue is like Nebuchadnezzar, who had a vision from God but did not understand it. So too does that man speak and not understand; he prays and speaks the proclamation of the Holy Spirit, but the mind does not grasp it. But he who has both the tongue and the interpretation is like Daniel, who both had the vision from God and grasped the understanding of its interpretation. It is good to see visions of God, it is good to pray and to speak the proclamation of God in the Holy Spirit, but it is better to see the visions of God and to grasp them with understanding. To pray in the spirit and to bring forth divine praises, and to grasp them with understanding and the mind—this is what it means to pray both in the spirit and with the mind, and to sing psalms to God both in the spirit and with the mind. ## CHAPTER XIV.

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'O' depicting a seated biblical figure, possibly a prophet, being visited by an angel or divine messenger descending from a cloud.</image-desc>
Of all the gifts of the Holy Spirit (not only faith and hope), the greatest is charity, yet all are great. Therefore, we ought to aspire to charity most of all: and to be zealous for the other gifts of the Holy Spirit, especially the better ones—such as prophecy more than the gift of tongues. For the former is better than the latter. First, because he who speaks through the Spirit in an unknown tongue speaks not to men but to God. For no one present will understand the mysteries which he speaks through the Spirit.

<margin>96</margin> Wherefore Paul adds: *Pursue love, yet be zealous for spiritual things, but especially that you may prophesy. For he who speaks in a tongue speaks not to men, but to God; for no one hears, but in the spirit he speaks mysteries. But he who prophesies speaks to men for edification, and exhortation, and consolation.* When he prophesies, he speaks edifying words to men—sometimes exhorting, sometimes consoling. For the prophets exhort us to follow eternal things and to despise fleeting ones, to desire heavenly things and to look down upon earthly ones; and in these things they find consolation.

Second: prophecy is more powerful than the simple gift of a tongue. For it is better to build up the church and the multitude of the faithful than oneself alone. He who prophesies builds up the multitude. But he who has only the gift of a tongue builds up only himself. For if he built up neither himself nor another, it would be a useless thing; it would be recognized as coming not from the Holy Spirit, but from some other spirit.

<margin>97</margin> Prophecy, therefore, is more powerful than the simple gift of a tongue. Paul reveals this, saying: *He who speaks in a tongue builds up himself; but he who prophesies builds up the church.*

Third. Because he who prophesies is esteemed greater than he who speaks in tongues, unless he himself can interpret for the building up of the church. But he who has the simple gift of a tongue speaks indeed, but does not interpret. For the gift of interpretation is another matter.

<margin>98</margin> Prophecy is therefore more powerful than the gift of tongues, even if the gift of tongues is great and desirable. For who would not wish to praise God through the Spirit in every tongue? Therefore Paul adds: *I would wish you all to speak in tongues, but more so that you might prophesy. For he who prophesies is greater than he who speaks in tongues, unless he interprets, so that the church may receive edification.*

<margin>99</margin> Fourth: by a clear example it can be known that prophecy is superior and more powerful than the gift of a tongue. For example, if I were to go to the Hebrews and speak the mysteries of God through the spirit in the Carmanian or Brahman language <note>historical references to the languages of ancient Persia and India</note>, how would I help them? No more than inanimate things like pipes, flutes, or the lyre emitting sound. But prophecy would help. Taking an example from himself, Paul asserts this, saying: *Now, brothers, if I come to you speaking in tongues, how shall I help you unless I speak to you either in revelation, or in knowledge, or in prophecy, or in teaching? Just like inanimate things emitting a voice, whether flutes or the lyre: if they do not give a distinction in the sounds* <note>original: *pthongis* — musical notes or tones</note>*, how will it be known what is played on the flute or lyre? And indeed, if the trumpet gives an uncertain sound, who will prepare himself for battle? In this manner, you also, unless you give a clear speech through the tongue, how will it be known what is uttered? For you will be speaking into the air.* "You will be speaking into the air" means you will be empty, emitting voices that are profitable to no one.

<margin>100</margin> Fifth. Because since there are so many kinds of languages in the world, none of which is without meaning <note>original: *ineloquibile* — incapable of being expressed or understood</note>, he who speaks in some unknown kind will not only seem to his hearers to be beating the air in vain, but will also seem like a barbarian and be fully foolish. And conversely, the listeners will be "barbarians" to the speaker if he does not know their language. But he who prophesies appears neither a barbarian nor foolish to those to whom he prophesies. Therefore prophecy is more powerful than a tongue. Paul reveals this in this way: *There are, as it happens, so many kinds of voices in the world, and none of them is without meaning. If, therefore, I do not know the power of the voice, I shall be a barbarian to him who speaks, and he who speaks will be a barbarian to me.*

Because the gift of a tongue by itself, among the gifts of the Holy Spirit, is of little value, Paul therefore instructs the Corinthians that those who have only that from the Holy Spirit should pray to the same Spirit so that he might grant them the gift of understanding and the interpretation of the tongue for their own greater edification and that of the church. For he who has only a tongue is like Nebuchadnezzar, who had a vision from God but did not understand it. So also that person speaks and does not understand. He prays and speaks the proclamations <note>original: *pręcentum* — possibly referring to a chanted proclamation or heraldic announcement</note> of the Holy Spirit, yet the mind does not grasp it. But he who has both the tongue and the interpretation is like Daniel, who both had the vision of God and grasped the understanding of its interpretation. It is good to see visions of God, and it is good to pray and speak the heraldry of God in the Holy Spirit; but it is better to see visions of God and grasp them with understanding. It is better...

## II

To pray in the spirit and to bring forth divine praises: and to grasp them with understanding and the mind. For this is what it means: to pray both in spirit and in mind, and to sing psalms to God both in spirit and in mind. ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Builds the church of God.* ¶ "Of God" is superfluous according to the [original] copy. Paul: [English: *builds the church.*] <note>original Greek: ἐκκλησίαν οἰκοδομεῖ</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Yet things without life giving sound.* ¶ Rather: *similarly* or *just as things without life.* For it is a response to the preceding points through a comparison. Paul: [English: *likewise things without life giving sound.*] <note>original Greek: ὅμως τὰ ἄψυχα φωνὴν τὰ διδόντα</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Unless they give a distinction of sounds.* ¶ Rather: *a distinction in the notes* or *tones*, that is, through notes or tones, which is the same thing. And it is better for "given" to be plural, so that it refers to the inanimate things. Paul: [English: *unless it gives a distinction to the notes.*] <note>original Greek: ἐὰν διαστολὴν τοῖς φθόγγοις μὴ διδῷ</note> 
<margin>C 100</margin>
¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *There are so many, for example, so many kinds of tongues in this world, and nothing is without a voice.* ¶ Rather: *so many or such great (as it happens) kinds of voices there are.* And also rather: *and none of them is out of tune*, so that "none" is understood to refer to the "kind" as an adjective. For "out of tune" <note>original: *absonum*</note> is the same as "unspeakable" <note>original: *ineloquibile*</note>. And there are seventy-two kinds of voices—that is, tongues—in the world, and seventy-two nations of people over whom God appointed seventy-two presiding angels, according to the sermons of Peter. Regarding these, Moses says: *When the Most High divided the nations, when he separated the sons of Adam, he established the boundaries of the peoples according to the number of the children of God. But the Lord's portion is his people: Jacob, the cord of his inheritance.* <note>A reference to Deuteronomy 32:8-9, often interpreted in mystical traditions to mean that different nations are governed by specific angels.</note> The twelve apostles before Christ were a sign of the twelve tribes of the children of Israel. Or rather, were the twelve tribes of Israel a sign of them, as Moses was a sign of Christ, and Aaron a sign of Peter? The other seventy-two disciples were sent out "two by two" before his face as a sign of the seventy-two nations, and as a sign of the angels presiding over those nations. For they were good angels, not those who turned the nations toward idolatry. For by "two and two" they are represented, which is a sign of charity and love. And grant that there are seventy-two principal and essential kinds of tongues; each of them also receives many accidental differences within itself, such as Italian, Spanish, or French. There are perhaps those who believe these differ only by accident. But there is no one who does not know that there are very many kinds of languages, none of which is "out of tune" or unharmoniously uttered, even if one is ignorant of the exact number—whether essential or accidental—which is nevertheless well known to God. 
<margin>C 101</margin>
Paul: [English: *There are, perhaps, so many kinds of voices in the world, and none is without voice.*] <note>original Greek: τοσαῦτα εἰ τύχοι γένη φωνῶν ἐσὶν ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ, καὶ οὐδὲν ἄφωνον</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *What is it then?* ¶ This is fine, but I have supplied "to be done" here so that the speech may be more conveniently understood. For when Paul says, "What is it then?", it is just as if he were asking, "What then must be done?" or "What must be said?" ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Who fills the place of the unlearned, how will he say "Amen" over your blessing?* ¶ It should be said at the beginning: *He who*. For the first little word is not asking a question; the sense is: "He who fills the place of the unlearned..."

## II

...unlearned <note>The text begins with the end of the word 'idiotae' (unlearned/laypeople) from the previous page.</note>; that is, one who is ignorant of your speech: how will he confirm your blessing / with which you have blessed / by saying and responding **Amen**? For that is impossible for the unlearned and one ignorant of the language: so that he may know how to do it fittingly.

<margin>101</margin>
Paul. *He who fills the place of the unlearned, how will he say "Amen" at your giving of thanks?* <note>original Greek: ὁ ἀναπληρῶν τὸν τόπον τοῦ ἰδιώτου, τὸν πῶς ἐρεῖ τὸ ἀμὴν ἐπὶ τῇ σῇ εὐχαριστίᾳ.</note> ¶ Vulgate edition. **I give thanks to God / that I speak with the tongues of all of you.** ¶ Thus from Paul: *I give thanks to my God / speaking in tongues more than all of you.* <note>original Latin: gratias ago deo meo / omnibus vobis magis linguis loquens.</note> For Paul spoke in all tongues by the gift of the Holy Spirit: in which both the Corinthians spoke through the Spirit / and others as well. For wherever among the nations he might be: he spoke in the tongues of those with whom he was / not in foreign ones / even though he knew them all. For that (I mean speaking in foreign tongues) pertains to ostentation: and not to edification. Indeed, that the apostles knew all languages was testified even by a demon giving answers to the Indians concerning Bartholomew / who confessed the truth against his will. He said, "One hundred times with bended knees by day / and one hundred times by night he prays to the Lord. His voice is like a powerful trumpet. The angels of the Lord walk with him : who do not permit him to be fatigued / nor to hunger. He always perseveres with the same countenance / the same mind. At every hour he is cheerful : and remains joyful. He foresees all things. He knows all things. He both speaks and understands every language of everyone : and behold, even this which you ask / and the answer I give you about him : he already knows it. For the angels of the Lord serve him : and they announce these things to him." So also Paul : he had received tongues more abundantly (as he himself testifies) through the gift of the Holy Spirit than the Corinthians had.

<margin>D,</margin>
Paul. *I give thanks to my God, speaking in tongues more than you all.* <note>original Greek: εὐχαριστῶ τῷ θεῷ μου, πάντων ὑμῶν μᾶλλον γλώσσαις λαλῶν.</note> ¶ Vulgate edition. **But in the church I want to speak five words with my sense.** ¶ Rather "five speeches," or "prayers," to speak from the mind / or through my mind. You can also understand this better from the preceding part: as I would say "I prefer," or "I rather want."

<margin>102</margin>
Paul. *But in the church I want to speak five words through my mind.* <note>original Greek: ἀλλ’ ἐν ἐκκλησίᾳ θέλω πέντε λόγους διὰ τοῦ νοός μου λαλῆσαι.</note> ¶ Vulgate edition. **Brothers, do not become children in your senses.** ¶ "Senses" here / and a little below: designates parts of reason / as if we were to say "do not become children in mind / or in reason." And therefore in its place we have put "by reason."

<margin>D,</margin>
Paul. *Brothers, do not become children in your minds.* <note>original Greek: ἀδελφοὶ μὴ παιδία γίνεσθε ταῖς φρεσίν.</note> For even if we interpreted it as "do not become children in mind," that also fits with what precedes / and consequently looks back to what he had said a little before: "I prefer to speak five speeches in the church with my mind." ¶ Vulgate edition. **Therefore tongues are for a sign, not to the faithful / but to the unfaithful. But prophecies are not for the unfaithful, but for the faithful.** ¶ It should be said from Paul in the singular: "But prophecy is not for the unfaithful / but for the faithful or the believers."

<margin>103</margin>
Paul. *So tongues are for a sign, not to those who believe, but to the unbelievers. But prophecy is not for the unbelievers, but for those who believe.* <note>original Greek: ὥστε αἱ γλῶσσαι εἰς σημεῖόν εἰσιν οὐ τοῖς πιστεύουσιν, ἀλλὰ τοῖς ἀπίστοις. ἡ δὲ προφητεία οὐ τοῖς ἀπίστοις, ἀλλὰ τοῖς πιστεύουσιν.</note> For who does not know that the prophets Elijah, Elisha, Nathan, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Daniel, Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi / were given to the faithful people of the Hebrews? For then there was only the faith of the Old Law / which they had received and to which they adhered. But when the faith of the New Law arrived, which they ought to have received and did not: then they were unbelievers, and then tongues were given as a sign: so that even thus they might be made faithful / and be drawn to salvation by the new gift of the Holy Spirit. Because they did not understand this: they have remained in unbelief even to the present day.

<margin>104</margin>
¶ Vulgate edition. **Will they not say: why are you mad?** ¶ It should be said "that you are mad."

<margin>E,</margin>
Paul. *Will they not say that you are mad?* <note>original Greek: οὐκ ἐροῦσιν ὅτι μαίνεσθε;</note> ¶ Vulgate edition. **He is convicted by all / he is judged by all.** ¶ It can be said "he is argued against" / or "refuted by all."

<margin>104</margin>
Paul. *He is convicted by all, he is judged by all.* <note>original Greek: ἐλέγχεται ὑπὸ πάντων, ἀνακρίνεται ὑπὸ πάντων.</note>

<margin>G,</margin>
¶ Vulgate edition. **And the spirit of the prophets is subject to the prophets.** ¶ It should be said in the plural: "and the spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets" / or "are subjected," it makes no difference. By this you understand: it is not the Holy Spirit, who is one, that is to be understood here / but the gifts of the Holy Spirit. These are also various in the prophets: and they are subjected to them for use. For they are able to use them (those they have, I mean) when they wish, no differently than someone uses a science they have already learned. But the Holy Spirit in Himself is subject to none, but all things are subject to Him.

<margin>107</margin>

For he puts forward the churches of the saints as an example: in which the peace of God and no dissension reigns. Just like the angelic hierarchies which are the heavenly churches: in which there is the highest peace / and which no dissension ever disturbs.

<margin>G,</margin>

<margin>109</margin>

## II 130 1 Corinthians.
### r. iij.

...more abundantly than the other apostles: he did not attribute the honor to himself / but to God who poured in the grace / which worked within him. He was truly the instrument: and the grace of God the principal architect. Neither he / nor the apostles taught otherwise: concerning those things mentioned above.

But what Hermogenes of Iconium did / asserting that there is no other future resurrection / <margin>112</margin> but the resurrection (he said) has already taken place / and happens continuously in children <note>Hermogenes was an early heretic; the "resurrection in children" likely refers to a belief that one "lives on" only through one's offspring or through a purely spiritual rebirth</note>. Certain impostors did something similar among the Corinthians. Against whose perverse error: Paul adds. ¶ **But if CHRIST is preached as having risen from the dead: how do some among you assert / that there is no resurrection of the dead? If indeed there is no resurrection of the dead: neither has CHRIST risen.** ¶ For it follows naturally: if there is no resurrection from the dead / then Christ did not rise from the dead. But this is the opposite of the faith: which all the apostles preached / and which no one who calls himself faithful: can grant. Therefore Christ rose from the dead. Therefore there is a resurrection of the dead. But he brings in the "inconveniences" <note>In logical terms, an "inconvenience" is an absurd or unacceptable consequence of a false premise</note> / which follow if Christ had not risen from the dead. So that / having turned back and destroyed the absurd <term>symperasmatis</term> <note>original: "symperasmatis", from the Greek *symperasma*, meaning the conclusion of a syllogism</note> which are inserted / he may gather by returning reasoning that Christ rose / and <margin>113</margin> that the resurrection of the dead (as it truly is) exists. And so he continues the reasoning toward the inconveniences. ¶ **But if CHRIST has not risen: then our preaching is empty / and your faith is also empty. We are even found to be false witnesses of God. Because we have testified against God / that he raised CHRIST: whom he did not raise / if the dead do not rise at all.** ¶ This argument returns from the opposite. But we are not false witnesses of God saying against God / that he raised Christ whom he did not raise / because the signs and miracles following those who bear this testimony show it. Neither is your faith empty / nor was our preaching empty. Therefore Christ rose <margin>114</margin> from the dead. Furthermore, he brings in the inconveniences which follow from this / that the dead do not rise: saying. ¶ **For if the dead do not rise: neither has CHRIST risen. But if CHRIST has not risen: your faith is vain / you are still in your sins. Therefore also those who have fallen asleep in CHRIST: have perished.** ¶ By direct but disjointed and leaping argumentation it follows: therefore if the dead do not rise / then you are still in your sins (for what use would the remission of sins be: if the dead do not rise?) therefore those who have fallen asleep in Christ / have perished / like all the saints / and all the martyrs. But these things are most absurd. Therefore the argument is driven back: where nothing absurd accompanies it. Those sleeping in Christ do not perish: therefore being purged in his faith / they are not in sins. Therefore their faith is not vain. Therefore Christ rose. Therefore also the dead rise. Which was the first proposition. Furthermore, if there were no resurrection of the dead: the faithful of Christ who have hoped / would be so only in this life. And if they were only in this life / they would be more miserable than all men. Since in this life they hunger / thirst / are naked / endure persecutions / cast themselves into all accidents and dangers / abstain from every pleasure / fear no punishment / no torment of cruelty / finally no death for the confession of his name. Far be it / however, that they should be unhappier than all men. ¶ For they are those of whom it is said: *Having been troubled in a few things: they shall be well-treated in many.* <note>original Latin: "In paucis vexati: in multis bene habebunt"; a reference to the Book of Wisdom 3:5</note> Because God found them worthy of himself. Therefore they are not only in this life: <margin>115</margin> but they expect another happier one / and certainly / and with all certainty more certain than certainty / they expect it. Therefore there is a resurrection of the dead. And Paul adds this reason: saying. ¶ **If in this life we who have hoped in CHRIST / are only so: we are more miserable than all men.** ¶ The argument returns from the opposite: as before. But we are not more miserable than all men / even from the testimony of the Savior saying: *Blessed shall you be when men hate you / and when they separate you / and reproach you / and cast out your name as evil because of the Son of Man. Rejoice in that day: and exult. For behold / your reward: is great in heaven.* <note>A reference to the Beatitudes in Luke 6:22-23</note> Therefore we are not only in this life. Therefore there is a resurrection. Now, however, he acts by direct argumentation / but by the analogy of the opposite: that Christ rose from the dead / and that there will be a resurrection. For Christ and Adam correspond from the opposite. Through Adam: death. Through Christ: life. Through Adam: the separation of the soul from the body / which is death. Therefore through Christ: the reunion of body and soul / which is the resurrection. Through Adam: the deprivation of justice / which darkness / agitation / and eternal punishment follow. Therefore through Christ <margin>116</margin> : justice / which light / rest / and eternal comfort will accompany. Because of which Paul says: ¶ **But now CHRIST has risen from the dead. He has been made the firstfruits of those who sleep. Since indeed through man came death: and through man the resurrection of the dead. For just as in Adam all die: in this manner / also in CHRIST all shall be made alive / each in his own order.**

<summary>This page provides a logical and theological defense of the physical resurrection of the dead, refuting early heresies and arguing that if Christ did not rise, the entire Christian faith, including the forgiveness of sins, would be void. It concludes by contrasting the death brought by Adam with the life and resurrection brought by Christ.</summary>
