--- Page 342 ---
<meta>The previous page refuted the error of those in Corinth who denied the resurrection of the dead, using Christ’s own resurrection as the logical proof that a return from death is possible. This page continues the argument by defining Christ as the "firstfruits" and explaining the mechanics and order of the coming resurrection.</meta>

<header>COMMENTARY.</header>

<margin>In order. The firstfruits: CHRIST. Then those who were Christ’s at his coming.</margin>

¶ But how has Christ become the "firstfruits of those who sleep," <note>original: "primitiæ dormientium"; "those who sleep" is a common biblical metaphor for the dead</note> when both Adam and such an innumerable multitude before him have fallen asleep? Truly, he is made the firstfruits of those who sleep. For he is the first who was righteous—and indeed righteous with a perfected justice—and not a debtor to death, yet he sought out death. All others who preceded him were debtors to death. Therefore, he is the first of the righteous and the firstfruits of the righteous who sleep. And although this is so, Paul seems to mean here rather that Christ became the firstfruits *of* the sleeping, that is, the firstfruits *from* those who sleep; which his own proof appears to show. 

But you will ask: how can that be, since "firstfruits from the sleeping" and "the first of those rising from the dead" are the same thing? For before Christ, the prophet Elijah raised the son of the widow of Zarephath from the dead; and Lazarus rose, and those whom the Lord raised before his own passion. It is necessary to know that there is a twofold resurrection. This one: perfect. That one: imperfect. This one: the truth. That one: a shadow. This one: with transformation. That one: without transformation. By "transformation" <note>original: "immutatione"; referring to the change from a corruptible body to an incorruptible one</note> I mean when that which was mortal puts on immortality and is made immortal. 

Christ, however, was the first of all to rise from the dead with a complete, true resurrection, which is by transformation. Christ (he says) "rising from the dead, dies no more; death no longer has dominion over him." <note>A reference to Romans 6:9</note> But the others who rose from the dead before Christ rose in an imperfect, shadowy resurrection, and not through transformation. For the widow’s son, and Lazarus, and the rest whom the divine kindness of Christ raised, died again. Therefore, a resurrection of this kind was not true and perfected, but a shadow and figure of the true and perfected resurrection which they will obtain at the end. But Christ rose with a true resurrection; and those nearby who rose with him for his honor, so that they might accompany him as he ascended on high; whom he might lead according to the word, "leading captivity captive." <note>A reference to Psalm 68:18 or Ephesians 4:8</note> This is the resurrection we also expect at the end of the age by the Lord's mercy: one conforming to the resurrection of Christ, not to that of Lazarus or any of the others who rose before Christ the Lord. 

Each in his own order, his own glory, and his own splendor. In the first order are the apostles, and those who were with Christ and adhered to him; the martyrs in their order; the virgins in theirs; and the rest of the holy people likewise in theirs—just as He who is all-knowing and all-powerful both knows and has willed. 

But you will say: will all be made alive in Christ? Certainly: those who *will* be made alive. So also in Adam: all die, who *do* die. For dissolution <note>The separation of soul and body</note> comes from Adam, and this is called death. And the reuniting of the dissolved comes from Christ, which is a certain "making alive" and resurrection. 

Truly, in Adam it happens that one dies in two ways: in one way as those liable and debtors to death, just as those not justified by the righteousness of Christ die in Adam. In another way, not as debtors, but as imitators of the Just One; who, although he owed nothing to death, willed to suffer the dissolution which Adam brought in by his own choice, so that he might undo the loss of death for Adam and all others, and all might return to life. And thus the righteous in Christ die "in Adam." Indeed, even Christ died "in Adam," not by necessity, but by will. We, however, if we have been righteous, die in Adam because dissolution is from Adam; and we die in Christ because we imitate the death of Christ. For this is what it means to die in Christ. Therefore all who die, whether in this way or that, die in Adam. 

What if Christ should wish some not to be dissolved in the body? Such as those who might be found alive at his coming. And likewise, if it pleased him concerning Enoch and Elijah, and if any other is reserved for his coming. 

There is also a twofold "making alive" in Christ. This one: in glory. That one: in punishment. This one: of the righteous. That one: of the unrighteous. This one: for mercy. That one: for the acknowledging of the justice of God. And all, in this way or that, will be made alive by Christ. I say "all" who will be made alive. For nothing prohibits some from having been made alive by Christ already; since we read that the tombs were opened, and many bodies of the saints who had slept arose. And coming out of the tombs after his resurrection, they came into the holy city and appeared to many. We do not read, however, that they returned further to their graves and their dust, but (as has already been said) that Christ "ascended on high and led captivity captive." 

But what follows once this universal 

<margin>117</margin> making alive of all (which is the resurrection, whether to justice or to mercy) has been done, Paul opens to us through the Spirit of God, saying: 

¶ **Afterward the end: when he shall have delivered the kingdom to God, that is the Father, when he shall have abolished all principality, and all authority and power. For he must reign until he puts all enemies under his feet. The last enemy to be destroyed is death. For he has subjected all things under his feet.** 

But when he says that all things are subjected to him, it is clear that this excludes Him who subjected all things to him. But when all things shall have been subjected to him, then the Son himself will also be subject to Him who subjected all things to him, so that [God] may be [all in all]...

<summary>The author distinguishes between "imperfect" resurrections (like Lazarus) and Christ's "perfect" resurrection, explaining that while all die through Adam, all will be raised through Christ in a specific order—some to glory and others to judgment.</summary>

<header>II</header>
<sig>r.iiij.</sig>
<margin>1 Cor. 15</margin>

, God [will be] all in all. ¶ After the resurrection: the end of the age. And then the kingdom of the Father will be complete, which the Son completes through the Gospel: reigning until that time and filling up the number of those to be saved. And he shall hand over the kingdom to the Father whole, with the ruin of the angels restored. <note>Refers to the theological idea that humanity was created to fill the void left in heaven by the fallen angels.</note> Concerning this kingdom, he taught us to pray to the Father: *thy kingdom come*. But he gives the kingdom to the Father in this way: that the Father reigns as Father, and the Son reigns together with him as Son. Indeed, the kingdom of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is one and undivided: in which the Son honors the Father, and the Holy Spirit honors the Father and the Son. What does it mean that "he must reign until he puts all enemies under his feet," <note>original: "oportet eum regnare donec ponat omnes inimicos sub pedibus eius"</note> except that it is necessary to subject the world to the Gospel of the Son until the Father puts all enemies—all rebels and adversaries—under the Son's feet? By these enemies and rebels, we understand both unfaithful and treacherous men as well as spiritual wickednesses. Death, however—the last enemy to be abolished—is the devil, from whom all power and tyranny will be taken away at the end, as he is assigned to the places of punishment and torments. And Hell (it says) and Death were cast into the lake of fire. Neither shall there be any more tyranny, nor any human power outside the kingdom of God, nor any of the spiritual wickednesses. For Christ shall abolish all rule and authority and power. Indeed, even the administrators in the heavens—the principalities, and powers, and virtues—will cease. For they will have fulfilled their function. No longer will the good angels who now preside over places, kingdoms, and persons be ministering spirits, although they will remain everlasting spirits celebrating and praising God with unwearied praise in his completed kingdom. What does it mean that "he must reign until he puts all enemies under his feet"? Regarding the subjection of enemies under the feet of Christ, Psalm 109 <note>Psalm 110 in modern numbering</note> makes mention; and regarding the subjection of all things—heavenly, earthly, and infernal—Psalm 8. This oracle explains that saying of Paul: that all things are subject to the Son. This excludes the one who subjected all things to him: the Father, and whatever is consubstantial <note>of the same substance or essence</note> with the Father. And the Son, according to the dispensation of the flesh, will be subject; but according to the divine hypostasis <note>term: <term>hypostasis</term> — the underlying reality or distinct personhood of the Son within the Trinity</note> and the form of God, he reigns with the Father over all things. Thus the Son of God, who is God, may be all in all: in God he is God and reigning over all things, and in creatures he is a creature and subject to God as a creature, yet one who is the head of every creature. And he is the summit and the beginning of every creature. For how is he not the beginning, who is the first of all, and (so to speak) an uncreatable creature and a creatable creator? And how will he not be all in all, who will be the goodness of all, the life of all, the love of all, the peace of all, the salvation, happiness, and glory—and all these things eminently and super-eminently, finitely and infinitely? For he is finite in the infinite, and infinite in the finite. For since he is infinite in the infinite and finite in the finite (for God is in God, and the creature is in the creature), he would not be all in all if he were not also finite in the infinite, and infinite in those things which are finite. But enough concerning these matters.

Furthermore, he secretly rebukes the error of those whom the Marcionites <note>A 2nd-century sect that rejected the Old Testament and believed in a different God than the creator.</note> followed. From this, however, they ought rather to have confessed the resurrection of the dead than to have denied it. For on behalf of those who had perhaps already died many years ago without baptism, some relative—either a son, or a grandson, or a great-grandson, or a kinsman, or a friend—would go beneath the tomb of the deceased. And being closed inside, he was asked in the name of the deceased: did he wish to be baptized? Upon his responding that he did, he was baptized in the name of the deceased. But if they did not believe that souls survived, for what purpose were they baptized for the dead? If they believed they survived, they ought also to have believed in the resurrection. For they were born to be united to bodies, having a natural inclination and desire for this very thing. God by no means granted them this in vain, for he never does nor has done anything in vain. For why would Judas Maccabeus have sent gifts to be offered in Jerusalem for the dead, unless he had considered that souls survive and that there would be a future resurrection? It would certainly have been vain and superfluous (as the scripture also says). So too it would be vain to be baptized for the dead, unless those who did these things thought that souls likewise survived and that there would be a future resurrection.

<margin>118</margin>
And though this practice contained an error in itself, it nevertheless follows from it that a future resurrection is to be believed. For what prevents true and faithful conclusions from following from false and erroneous things?
<margin>></margin>
And this argument—from the things themselves and the facts themselves against the erring Corinthians—Paul touches upon in this way:

¶ Otherwise, what shall they do who 
<margin>></margin>
are baptized for the dead? If the dead do not rise at all, why are they also baptized 
<margin>></margin>
for the dead? ¶ That would surely seem entirely vain, superfluous, and rashly done. But Paul also proposes himself as an example of faith: how his works and life show that he has a certain and indubitable faith in the resurrection. For having this certainty, he daily exposes himself to dangers, daily to death. Which he testifies by that glorying which he himself had in CHRIST JESUS, in whom alone

He was boasting. Having **this** certainty: he did not avoid the beasts set before him at **Ephesus** <note>Paul refers to "fighting wild beasts at Ephesus" in 1 Corinthians 15:32; scholars debate if this was a literal event in the arena or a metaphor for fierce human opposition.</note>, making nothing of this transitory life for the sake of the future resurrection (which he held as certain), even if he were to be torn apart by them, thus ending this passing life. Nevertheless, his faith and the power of **Christ** overcame them so that they could do him no harm. But how would all this have helped **Paul**, unless he had believed—and indeed believed without doubt—in the future resurrection and the immortal state of souls? Certainly, if he had known that souls were to perish and that there would be no future resurrection, he would have eaten, he would have drunk, and he would not have cheated himself of the pleasure of the present life, thinking perhaps that he would die tomorrow and have nothing thereafter. He by no means acted in this way, because he was (if I may put it this way) more certain than certain of another life. He himself testifies to this in this manner, saying:

<margin>119</margin>
> ¶ Why do we also face danger every hour? I swear by our glorying, which I have in **CHRIST JESUS** our Lord: I die daily. If, in the manner of men, I fought with beasts at **Ephesus**, what is the profit to me? If the dead do not rise: let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die. **Do not be misled. Bad company corrupts good morals. Wake up to what is right, and do not sin. For some have an ignorance of God.** I say this to your shame.

Where he has put forward himself and his own deeds as an example of true faith, he urges them not to listen to talk or admit conversations that corrupt good morals. Truly, all the words of the impious and all those of the fleshly-minded corrupt good morals. **Christ** requires chaste morals. Why should I pour into the ears of youths—into their tender and incorrupt souls—**Tibullus**, **Catullus**, or the madams and pimps of **Terence**? <note>The author is listing classical Roman authors whose erotic poetry or comedic plays were seen as morally dangerous by some Christian educators.</note> Or the soft *Heroines* of **Ovid**, and that kind of poisonous and deadly song of the sirens? A prudent man—all the more a **Christian** man—will avoid all these things like the rocks of a shipwreck. **Do not those who do these things entice the tender souls of youths (who are sealed by the Holy Spirit as the little virgins of Christ) toward corruption?** Nevertheless, for those who corrupt even one of these, it would be better (according to the divine word) that a donkey’s millstone be hung around their neck and they be drowned in the depth of the sea. **Do not be misled. Bad company corrupts good morals.** If you do not wish to believe this because of **Menander** <note>original: "Menandrum"; St. Paul is actually quoting a line from a lost play by the Greek playwright Menander.</note> who said it before, believe it now because of **Paul** who takes it up again. **Christ** wants to have the pious; he wants to have the faithful. For those desiring the study of philosophy, why should I bring in the discourses of **Lucretius**, or **Democritus**, or **Epicurus**? <note>These philosophers were associated with atomism and the belief that the soul dies with the body.</note> Shall we extol the seventh book of **Pliny** with great admiration, or shall I preach **Alexander of Aphrodisias** <note>original: "Aphrodyseum"; a famous commentator on Aristotle who argued against the immortality of the individual soul.</note> as the only authority? This must be said to the shame of our times in many places and among many people. May God grant that they wake up justly, detest these things, and that they all repent and sin no more. May these things—and every filthy and sophistical plague that builds nothing but either destroys or hinders building—be committed to the fire by the healthy decree of the men of **Christ**, who are especially the bishops and primates of the holy church of God, wherever they may be. And let the multitude that harms perish, and let the few who are saved be preserved in every study and every exercise of the souls (which ought to be noble) acquired for **Christ** and God through the washing of rebirth, so that we may obtain a pure and unstained resurrection with the saints. ¶ But the impious, unable to see worldly things clearly, question divine things: "How do the dead rise? With what kind of body does the animated seed come out of the womb? With the kind that the divine order provided for each one. <meta>The previous page concluded with Paul’s argument that if there is no resurrection, Christian faith and suffering are in vain. This page continues that argument by explaining the nature of the resurrected body, using Paul’s metaphors of seeds and different types of flesh to distinguish between the natural body of Adam and the spiritual body of Christ.</meta>

II 1 Cor.
r.iiii.

<margin>120</margin>
A guiding hand is opened for us regarding the restoration of bodies. Paul himself reveals this in the following way, saying: **But someone will say: How do the dead rise? With what kind of body do they return? You fool! What you sow is not made alive unless it dies. And what you sow is not the body that is to be, but a bare grain—perhaps of wheat or of something else. But God gives it a body as He has chosen, and to each of the seeds its own body. Not all flesh is the same: there is one kind for humans, another for beasts, another for birds, and another for fish. There are also celestial bodies and terrestrial bodies; but the glory of the celestial is one thing, and the glory of the terrestrial is another. There is one glory of the sun, another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars; for star differs from star in glory. So it is with the resurrection of the dead.**

¶ When he adds that **there are celestial bodies and terrestrial bodies**, and what follows, he is pointing toward this: that the bodies of the blessed will be different from the bodies of the miserable <note>The "miserable" refers to those who are damned or excluded from heavenly glory.</note>. For the bodies of the blessed will be like celestial bodies: pressed down by no weight, rising to the heights with no resistance and no difficulty, and capable of receiving divine light. The bodies of the miserable, however, will be heavy, inert, dim, and drowned in horrific darkness. Furthermore, the bodies of the blessed will shine with various degrees of happiness according to their own order and capacity: some like the sun, some like the moon, and some like the stars in the sight of God, just as it is written: **Those who have been taught the knowledge of God will shine like the brightness of the firmament, and those who have instructed many in justice will be like stars for all eternity.** <note>original: "Qui scitiã dei docti fuerint... quasi stellæ in perpetuas æternitates." This is a reference to Daniel 12:3.</note> And the Savior says in Matthew: **The Son of Man will send His angels, and they will gather out of His kingdom all causes of sin and those who act lawlessly, and throw them into the fiery furnace. There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father.** <note>Matthew 13:41-43.</note> And the bodies of the miserable will also exist according to various degrees, capable of different punishments—just as the capacity for pain differs in the bodies of men, beasts, fish, and birds. These comparisons do not suggest a difference in the "substance" or essence of the body, but rather degrees of glory or of shameful suffering. For good and evil angels, as spirits, do not differ in their basic substance; nor will the blessed and the unhappy differ in substance as humans.

<margin>121</margin>
The bodies of both will be immortal and incorruptible: the latter for their shame, the former for unfailing glory. Therefore Paul adds: **It is sown in corruption; it rises in incorruption. It is sown in dishonor; it rises in glory. It is sown in weakness; it rises in power. It is sown a natural body; it rises a spiritual body.** <note>The Latin *corpus animale* (natural/soulish body) refers to a body animated by the *anima* (soul) for earthly life, while *corpus spirituale* is animated by the spirit for eternal life.</note> **There is a natural body, and there is a spiritual body. As it is written: The first Adam was made into a living soul; the last Adam into a life-giving spirit.**

¶ It is certain that the bodies of the blessed rise in glory and power. But how will the bodies of the miserable rise in "glory and power"? Certainly, immortality and incorruptibility are "glory" in themselves when compared to what is corruptible and mortal, and in this sense they too shall rise. But in their case, this glory of incorruptibility and immortality will actually work against them: because that which God had ordained for everyone to receive for His glory is, in them (on account of their past unjust lives), assigned to the sustaining of perpetual punishment and the enduring of perpetual darkness—bodies which otherwise would have experienced eternal and all-beneficial light. Therefore, the bodies of the blessed will rise in glory and power in a distinguished and unhindered way to receive the fullness of glory; but the miserable rise in a clouded and hindered glory and power. For their incorruptibility cannot receive the *perfection* of incorruptibility, just as the immortality and incorruptibility of the evil angels cannot reach the perfection for which they were created.

A "natural body" <note>original: "corpus animale"</note> is so called as long as it grows, lives, and feels through a corruptible life and sense. A "spiritual body" exists when it lives by an immortal spirit, life, and sense. The natural body grows: it is nourished, it increases, it decreases, it propagates its own kind, and being subject to a flow of physical change, it never remains in the same state. The spiritual body does not grow, is not nourished, does not increase or diminish, and generates nothing. It is no longer subject to physical change but has been translated from the condition of time into the condition of eternity. The natural body serves the spirit and mind by coming before them in its operations <note>The physical senses react before the mind can process them.</note>; but in the senses of the spiritual body, the mind and spirit serve by being faster in operation. In the natural state, the mind knows through the body; in the spiritual state, the senses of the spiritual body know through the mind. This is especially true for those who will not be addicted to perpetual darkness. In the former, the body absorbed the mind; in the latter, the mind absorbs the body. The first man, Adam, was made as the pattern for all humans living a natural life in a physical body. But the second man, Christ, is the pattern and the truth—through His resurrection—of all who will live a spiritual life in a spiritual body. Therefore, while we all live this mortal life, being nourished and growing while we intend to propagate offspring, we are natural, earthly, and "first men," carrying the image of the first man who was made into a living soul. But after the final day, we shall all be spiritual, men of the second and last type, carrying the image of the second man who came from heaven—the blessed happily, the others unhappily. For to this end the Lord rose in...

> <margin>,</margin> that is to be, but a bare grain, perhaps of wheat or of some other kind.
> <margin>,</margin> But God gives it a body as He has willed, and to each of the seeds its own body. Not all
> <margin>,</margin> flesh is the same flesh: but there is one flesh of men, another flesh of beasts, another
> <margin>,</margin> of birds, and another of fish. And there are celestial bodies, and there are terrestrial bodies: but
> <margin>,</margin> the glory of the celestial is one, and the glory of the terrestrial is another. There is one glory of the sun, another glory of the moon, and another glory
> <margin>,</margin> of the stars, for star differs from star in glory. So also is the resurrection of the dead.

¶ Regarding his addition that "there are some celestial bodies and some terrestrial," and what follows, the point is this: the bodies of the blessed will be different from the bodies of the wretched. For the bodies of the blessed will be like celestial bodies: weighed down by no heaviness, striving upward with no resistance or difficulty, and capable of receiving divine light. The bodies of the miserable, however, will be heavy, sluggish, opaque, and shrouded in horrific darkness. Furthermore, the bodies of the blessed will shine with various degrees of <term>beatitude</term> <note>A state of supreme blessedness or happiness in the presence of God.</note> according to their own order and capacity: some like the sun, some like the moon, and some like the stars in the sight of God, just as it is written:
> Those who have been taught the knowledge of God shall shine like the brightness of the firmament; and those who instruct many unto justice, like the stars for all eternity.

And the Savior says in Matthew:
> The Son of Man shall send his angels, and they shall gather out of his kingdom all scandals and those who work iniquity, and shall cast them into the furnace of fire. There shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth. Then the righteous shall shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father.

The bodies of the wretched will also exist according to various degrees of capacity for punishment, just as the capacity of the bodies of men, beasts, fish, and birds differs. These comparisons do not suggest a difference in <term>substance</term> <note>The underlying essence or "stuff" of which something is made; here, the author argues that humans remain humans in essence even if their quality changes.</note>, but rather degrees of glory or of shameful suffering. For good and evil angels, as spirits, do not differ in substance; nor will the blessed and the unhappy differ in substance as humans. <margin>131</margin> The bodies of both will be immortal and incorruptible—the latter for their shame, the former for unfailing glory. Therefore, Paul adds:
> <margin>,</margin> It is sown in corruption; it rises in incorruption. It is sown in dishonor; it rises in
> <margin>,</margin> glory. It is sown in weakness; it rises in power. It is sown a natural body; it
> <margin>,</margin> rises a spiritual body. There is a natural body, and there is a spiritual body. Just as it is written:
> <margin>,</margin> The first Adam was made into a living soul; the last Adam into a life-giving
> <margin>,</margin> spirit.

¶ It is certain that the bodies of the blessed rise in glory and in power. But how will the bodies of the miserable rise in glory and power? Certainly, "glory" in itself refers to immortality and incorruptibility when compared to what is corruptible and mortal; in this sense, they too shall rise. But in this case, the glory of <term>incorruptibility</term> <note>The state of being unable to decay, age, or die.</note> and immortality will work against them. Because of their past unjust lives, that which God ordained for everyone to perceive His glory is instead assigned to them for the enduring of perpetual punishment and perpetual darkness—whereas they otherwise would have experienced eternal and all-beneficial light. Therefore, the bodies of the blessed rise in glory and power, unimpeded, to receive the fullness of glory; but the wretched rise in a clouded and hindered glory and power. For their incorruptibility cannot receive the *perfection* of incorruptibility, just as the immortality and incorruptibility of the evil angels cannot reach the perfection for which they were created. 

A "natural body" <note>original: "corpus animale," literally an "animal-like body" or a body animated by a soul (anima).</note> is so called because it thrives, lives, and feels through a corruptible life and sense. A "spiritual" one, however, is when it lives by the spirit, life, and immortal sense. The natural body functions through nutrition, growth, and decay; it propagates its own kind and, being subject to a constant flow of substance, never remains in the same state. The spiritual body does not grow, nourish itself, diminish, or generate anything. It is no longer subject to the flux of substance, but has been translated from the condition of time into the condition of eternity. The natural body serves the spirit and mind, with its physical operations coming first. But in the spiritual body, the mind and spirit serve the senses with faster operation. In the former, the mind knows through the body; in the latter, the senses of the spiritual body know through the mind. This is especially true for those who will not be addicted to perpetual darkness. In the former, the body absorbed the mind; in the latter, the mind absorbs the body. The first man, Adam, was made as the pattern for all men living a natural life in a natural body. The second man, Christ, is the pattern and the truth, by His resurrection, for all who will live a spiritual life in a spiritual body. Therefore, while we live this mortal life, we are nourished, we grow, and we intend to propagate offspring: we are natural, earthly, and "first" men, bearing the image of the first man made into a living soul. But afterward, on the last day, we shall all be spiritual, "second," and "last" men, bearing the image of the second man who came from heaven—the blessed unto happiness, the others unto unhappiness. For to this end the Lord rose in...

...he boasted. Having this certainty: he did not avoid the beasts set before him at Ephesus, making nothing of his future resurrection (which he held as certain), even if he were to be torn apart by them, thus ending this transitory life. Nevertheless, his faith and the power of Christ overcame those beasts so that they could not harm him. But what would all this have helped Paul, unless he had believed—and indeed believed without a doubt—in the future resurrection and the state of immortality for souls? Certainly, if he had known that souls were destined to perish and that there would be no future resurrection, he would have eaten and drunk; he would not have cheated himself of the pleasure of this present life, thinking perhaps that he would die tomorrow and have nothing hereafter. He did no such thing, because he was more certain (if I may put it this way) of that other <margin>119</margin> life. He himself testifies to this fact, saying:
<margin>¶ „ „ „ „ „ „</margin> "Why are we also in danger every hour? I swear by our glory, which I have in CHRIST JESUS our Lord: I die daily. If, as a man, I fought with beasts at Ephesus, what is the benefit to me? If the dead do not rise: let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die. Do not be led astray. Bad company corrupts good morals. Wake up to what is right and do not sin. For some have an ignorance of God. I say this to your shame."
¶ Here, where he has set himself and his deeds as an example of true faith, he exhorts them not to listen to talk or admit conversations that corrupt good morals. Truly, all the words of the impious and all those of the fleshly-minded corrupt good morals. Christ requires chaste morals. Why should I thrust Tibullus, Catullus, or the pimps and madams of Terence <note>These are classical Roman poets and playwrights whose works were often considered too erotic or worldly for Christian education.</note> into the ears of adolescents or into their tender and incorrupt souls? Or the soft *Heroides* of Ovid, and that kind of poisonous and deadly siren-song? A wise man—even more so a Christian man—will avoid all these things like the rocks of a shipwreck. Do not those who do these things entice the tender souls of the young (who are sealed by the Holy Spirit as little virgins for Christ) toward corruption? For those who corrupt even one of these, it is better (according to the divine word) that a millstone be hung around their neck and they be drowned in the depths of the sea. Do not be led astray. Bad company corrupts good morals. And if you do not want to believe this because of Menander <note>The apostle Paul is here quoting a line from the Greek playwright Menander.</note> who said it before, believe it now because of Paul who takes it up again. Christ wants to have the pious; He wants to have the faithful. Why, for those seeking the study of philosophy, should I thrust forward the words of Lucretius, or those of Democritus or Epicurus? Why should I extol the seventh book of Pliny <note>Book 7 of Pliny the Elder's *Natural History* contains many skeptical views on the immortality of the soul.</note> with great admiration? Why should I preach Alexander of Aphrodisias <note>A Greek commentator on Aristotle who argued against the soul's individual immortality.</note> as unique? Why should I greatly admire the intellect of Averroes <note>original: *Abeuruſth*. Referencing the medieval philosopher Ibn Rushd, whose theories on the "unity of the intellect" were often seen as a denial of personal resurrection.</note>—mere deceptions? These kinds of insanities have occupied all studies more than spiderwebs occupy neglected houses. Wake up to what is right and do not sin; bad company corrupts pious and faithful morals. And those who sweat over these and similar things have an ignorance of God. This must be said to the shame of our times in many places and among many people. May God grant that they wake up rightly, detest these things, and that everyone repents and sins no more. And let these things—and every filthy and sophisticated plague that builds nothing but either destroys or hinders edification—be committed to the fire by the healthy decree of the men of Christ, especially the bishops and primates of the holy church of God, wherever they may be. Let the multitude that harms perish, and let the few who save be preserved in every study and every exercise of souls (which ought to be noble) acquired for Christ God through the bath of rebirth, so that we may obtain a pure and undefiled resurrection with the saints.

But the impious, unable to see worldly things clearly, question divine things: *How do the dead rise?* and *With what kind of body do they return?*—not believing that a dead person can be brought to life again and return to life. Paul refers their foolishness to the providence of God, to be contemplated in sensible and earthly things. And in his piety, being an imitator of the supremely good God who wishes all men to be saved, he leads them by the hand so that they might become believers. It is as if he questions them in this way, and they answer by the light of reason—or rather with God, the leader and illuminator of reason and nature—and he adds to their answers what is lacking for perfection. Let him ask, I say: How is the seed cast into the earth brought to life? How is the seed in the womb of an animal animated? By the providence of God. Yet first, the seed in the earth dies so that it may be brought to life, and the seed in the womb is decomposed so that it may be animated. Otherwise, seeds would always remain seeds, and only seeds. With what kind of body does the quickened seed come out of the earth, which was placed in the earth naked and without such a body? With what kind of body does the animated seed come out of the womb? With the kind that the divine ordinance provided for each. In such a way, and with such bodies, will the dead rise when brought to life. For the souls and the bodies of the dead are, until the day of judgment, like seeds committed to the earth, or rather like seeds enclosed in maternal wombs, until the time of quickening arrives. And in many other ways, His divine power regarding the resurrection...

...guidance is opened for the restoration of bodies. Paul himself reveals it in this way, saying:
¶ "But someone will say: How do the dead rise? With what kind of body do they return? You foolish man: what you sow is not brought to life unless it dies. And what you sow: you do not sow the body that is to be, but a bare grain, perhaps of wheat or some other kind. But God gives it a body as He willed, and to each of the seeds its own body. Not all flesh is the same flesh: one is of humans, another is the flesh of beasts, another of birds, and another of fish. And there are heavenly bodies, and there are earthly bodies: but the glory of the heavenly is one, and that of the earthly is another. One is the glory of the sun, and another the glory of the moon, and another the glory of the stars. For star differs from star in glory. So also is the resurrection of the dead."

¶ What he adds—that there are heavenly bodies and earthly bodies, and what follows—points to this: that the bodies of the blessed will be of one sort, and the bodies of the wretched <note>original: "miserorum," referring to those who are damned or excluded from salvation</note> another. For the bodies of the blessed will be like heavenly ones: pressed down by no weight, striving upward with no resistance and no difficulty, and capable of receiving divine light. The bodies of the wretched, however, will be heavy, sluggish, opaque, and covered in horrendous darkness. Furthermore, the bodies of the blessed will shine with various degrees of bliss according to their own order and capacity: some like the sun, some like the moon, and some like the stars in the sight of God, just as it is written: "Those who are learned shall shine like the brightness of the firmament, and those who instruct many unto justice shall be like stars for all eternity." <note>Daniel 12:3</note> And the Savior says in Matthew: "The Son of Man will send His angels, and they will gather out of His kingdom all causes of sin and those who do iniquity, and will throw them into the furnace of fire. There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father." <note>Matthew 13:41-43</note> And the bodies of the wretched will be capable of various degrees of punishment, just as the capacity for sensation <note>original: "poenarum capacitas," the capacity for suffering</note> differs in the bodies of men, beasts, fish, and birds. These things, therefore, do not suggest a difference in substance, but degrees of glory or of shameful suffering. For the good and bad angels, as spirits, do not differ in substance; nor will the blessed and the unhappy, as humans, be distant in substance. The bodies of both will be immortal and incorruptible—the latter for shame, the former for unfailing glory. Therefore Paul adds: <margin>121</margin> ¶ "It is sown in corruption: it rises in incorruptibility. It is sown without honor: it rises in glory. It is sown in weakness: it rises in power. It is sown an animal body: it rises a spiritual body. There is an animal body, and there is a spiritual body. As it is written: The first Adam was made into a living soul; the last Adam into a life-giving spirit."

¶ It is certain that the bodies of the blessed rise in glory and power. But how will the bodies of the wretched rise in glory and power? Certainly, "glory" in itself refers to immortality and incorruptibility when compared to the corruptible and mortal; in this sense, they too shall rise. But in this case, the glory of incorruptibility and immortality will work against them. For that which God ordained for all to receive His glory is, in them (because of their past unjust lives), appointed to sustain perpetual punishment and to bear perpetual darkness—bodies which otherwise would have experienced eternal light, and indeed a most beneficial light. Therefore, the bodies of the blessed rise in glory and power, distinguished and unhindered in receiving the fullness of glory; the wretched, however, rise in a clouded and hindered glory and power. For their incorruptibility cannot receive the perfection of incorruptibility, just as the immortality and incorruptibility of the evil angels cannot reach the perfection for which it was born. A body is called "animal" <term>animalis: from the Latin 'anima' (soul), referring to a body animated by a natural soul and subject to physical needs</term> as long as it grows, lives, and feels with a corruptible life and sense. It is "spiritual" when it lives by an immortal spirit, life, and sense. An animal body grows: it is nourished, it increases, it decreases, it propagates its like, and being subject to a substantial flux <note>a philosophical term for the constant changing/decaying of physical matter</note>, it never remains in the same state. A spiritual body neither grows, nor is nourished, nor increases, nor diminishes, nor generates anything. It is no longer subject to substantial flux, but has been translated from the condition of time into the condition of eternity. The animal body serves the spirit and mind, preceding them in action; but to the senses of the spiritual body, the mind and spirit serve, being swifter in action. In the former, the mind knows through the body; in the latter, the senses of the spiritual body know through the mind. And this is especially true in those who will not be addicted to perpetual darkness. In the former, the body absorbed the mind; in the latter, the mind absorbs the body. The first man, Adam, was made as the pattern for all men living an animal life in a natural body. The second man, however, Christ, is the pattern through His resurrection and the truth for all who will live a spiritual life in a spiritual body. Therefore, as long as we live this mortal life, are nourished, grow, and attend to the propagation of offspring, we are "animal," earthly, and like the first man, and we bear the image of the first man who was made into a living soul. But after the last day, we shall all be spiritual, second, and "last" men, bearing the image of the second man who came from heaven—the blessed happily, the wretched unhappily. For to this end the Lord rose in...

It argues that while both the saved and the damned receive immortal bodies, the former experience this as glory and the latter as a capacity for eternal punishment.</summary>

<header>COMMENTARY</header>

...a life-giving spirit <note>original: "spiritum viuificantem"</note>, indeed in a spiritual body that is incorruptible and immortal. This is so that everyone, both the good and the wicked, may bear his image, just as everyone has borne the image of the first Adam: some in temporal happiness, others in misery. Thus, he himself may rule over those in heaven and those in the lower regions. But first, we must bear the image of the first and earthly man, rather than the image of the second and spiritual one. For in this way, God and nature proceed from the imperfect to the perfect, and not the other way around. The speech of the Apostle opens this truth to us, adding these points to what came before:

<margin>122</margin>
• But it is not the spiritual that is first, but the natural <note>original: "animale," referring to a body animated by a soul (anima) but subject to physical needs</note>; then comes the spiritual. The first man: 
• from the earth, made of dust. And the second man: the Lord from heaven. As was the man of dust, so also are those who are of the dust;
• and as is the heavenly man, so also are those who are heavenly. And just as we have borne the image of the man of dust: we shall also 
• bear the image of the heavenly man. This I say, brothers: that flesh and blood cannot 
• inherit the kingdom of God; nor does corruption inherit incorruption. ¶ Everyone in the resurrection 
will receive and bear the image of the heavenly man in this: that they will receive a spiritual, incorruptible, and immortal body. In this state, they will not be called earthly, but heavenly, since they will possess this—whether they be good or evil—not from the earthly man, but from the heavenly one. And when he says, "flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God," it is as if he says that we, in this natural body—which is indeed alive but lacks what it needs for food, drink, and other necessities—cannot possess the kingdom of God. For such a body is corruptible, and the kingdom of God is incorruptible; and corruption does not inherit incorruption. Conversely, flesh and blood will not endure eternal punishments. Rather, flesh and blood will be changed, and in both the just and the unjust, they will be made into a spiritual body: in the just, so they do not succumb to eternal punishments <note>The author likely means that the body is transformed to survive the state of eternity, whether in joy or suffering</note>; in the former, so that eternal joys do not fail. By the names "flesh and blood," therefore, we ought to understand the natural and unchanged parts of the body. Yet, it is the same flesh and substantially the same blood—though no longer natural, but spiritual; not corruptible, but incorruptible and transformed—that will possess the kingdom of God with the spirit in the good, and the everlasting Gehenna <note>original: "gehennam," referring to hell</note> in the evil.

<margin>123</margin>
• But concerning this transformation: let Paul report the mystery of the Holy Spirit, saying: ¶ Behold, I tell you a mystery. We
• shall not all indeed sleep <note>Paul uses "sleep" as a metaphor for death</note>: but we shall all be changed, in an instant, in the twinkling of an eye, 
• at the last trumpet. For it will sound: and the dead will rise incorruptible, and we shall be 
• changed. For this corruptible body must put on incorruption: and this mortal body 
• must put on immortality. But when this corruptible body has put on incorruption, and this 
• mortal body has put on immortality: then shall come to pass the word that is written. Death is swallowed up 
• in victory. Where, O death, is your sting? Where, O hell <note>original: "inferne"</note>, is your victory? The sting of death is 
• sin. And the power of sin is the law. But thanks be to God, who has given us the victory through 
• our Lord JESUS CHRIST. Therefore, my beloved brothers: be steadfast, 
• immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, knowing that your labor is not in vain 
in the Lord. ¶ When he says, "we shall not all indeed sleep," he speaks from a revelation of the Lord in another place. "For this we say to you in the word of the Lord: that we who are alive, who remain until the coming of the Lord, shall not precede those who have fallen asleep. For the Lord himself, at the command, and at the voice of the archangel, and at the trumpet of God, will descend from heaven. And the dead who are in Christ will rise first; then we who are alive, who are left, will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet Christ in the air, and so we shall always be with the Lord." However, those who are caught up alive will not die—for death is the separation of body and soul—and the coming of the Lord will be in a momentary instant. The Lord himself expressed this, saying: "For as lightning comes from the east and appears even to the west, so will be the coming of the Son of Man." And the resurrection happens in a moment. For in an instant (as the Apostle says here), in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet, the dead will rise incorruptible. And concerning those who are caught up to meet Christ, the Savior himself also says: "Two will be in the field: one will be taken, and one will be left. Two women will be grinding at the mill: one will be taken, and one will be left. Two in bed: one will be taken, and one will be left." Those who are taken will be the faithful, and they will be placed at the right hand of God, retaining the primacy of the resurrection in their own order. Those who are left at the sound of the angelic trumpet will be on the left; they will be changed along with the reprobate. For both these and those will be changed. Since flesh and blood, if not changed, are not able to possess the kingdom of God, nor to endure the future punishments of Gehenna. ¶ Moreover, this trumpet—which will sound first for the resurrection of the chosen and then for the reprobate—is called the trumpet of the seventh angel in the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation</note>. And "the angel," it says, "whom I saw standing upon the sea and upon the land, lifted up his hand to heaven and swore by Him who lives forever and ever, who created heaven and the things that are in it, and the earth and the things that are in it, and the sea and the things that are in it: that time shall be no more. But in the days of the voice of the seventh angel, when he shall begin to sound the trumpet, the mystery of God shall be finished, as He has preached through His servants the prophets." And this is the understanding we apply to this passage: "we shall not all indeed sleep, but we shall all be changed." It is surely a great transformation, whether in the good or in the evil: to become immortal from a mortal body, and incorruptible from a corruptible one.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on 1 Corinthians 15, specifically focusing on the mystery of the "transformation" (immutatio) of the living at the end of time and the theological distinction between the two types of death. It picks up from the previous discussion regarding the nature of the resurrection body.</meta>

<page-num>133</page-num>
<header>II</header>
<sig>A</sig>
<meta>110.</meta>

<margin>1 Cor.</margin>

And it is understood concerning those to be changed. For if any have already ascended with Christ having been changed <note>original: "immutati," referring to those who might have undergone the final transformation early</note>, they will not be changed then, because they have already been changed. But perhaps some will refute this understanding, because it is a matter of faith to believe in the "resurrection of the flesh." If, however, not all "sleep" (die), then not all will "rise." Yet it does not follow from this that the resurrection of the flesh should not be believed. For to believe in the resurrection of the flesh is to believe in the resurrection of the dead. I believe, moreover, that all the dead shall rise—I say all dead *men*. This is said lest some twisted sophist, or one infected by the Muhammadan sect <note>A common Renaissance-era reference to Islamic theology, which some Christian commentators incorrectly argued suggested the resurrection of animals</note>, should understand it to include even horses and dogs. But it is not proposed for us to believe that all people will die. What if Christ—who possessed immortality by nature in himself, but voluntarily set it aside for our salvation—granted to John, his beloved disciple, the gift of not dying? I mean, not to be dissolved <note>original: "dissolui," meaning the separation of soul and body</note>, but wishing him to remain without dissolution until He came, and to take hold of the heavenly kingdoms by a change alone? In him, Christ would be showing what the status of humanity would have been if man had not sinned. If I want him (He said) to remain until I come, what is that to you? Nor are we forced to believe that all flesh must rise on that final day. For we believe that some flesh has already risen, the resurrection being completed. Who would deny this concerning the most glorious flesh of Christ, and that of the untainted Virgin from whom Christ’s flesh was taken? And perhaps also concerning those who rose with Christ and ascended on high with him? For was it not a sign of changed flesh—of a spiritual and incorruptible body—that Christ appeared to whom he willed, and was hidden from whom he willed, vanishing by a spiritual invisibility? For if I were able to cover my body with my spirit in the same way that my body now covers my spirit—just as the spirit is now seen in the visibility of the body—then the body would not be seen in the invisibility of the spirit, and it would be, as it were, spiritual and invisible. Could Lazarus do this? Or the son of the widow? Could those who had risen in an "incomplete resurrection" <note>An "incomplete resurrection" refers to those brought back to life in the Bible who were destined to die a second time, unlike Christ</note> do such things? It is therefore in no way absurd that it could be so: "we shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed," as is read in the Greek manuscripts. As for what follows, "then shall come to pass the saying that is written, death is swallowed up in victory" <note>1 Cor 15:54</note>, something very similar is written in the prophet Hosea. But here it must be noted that there is a double death: the first and the second. The first is the dissolution of body and soul. The second is the eternal deprivation of the highest life in the torments of Gehenna <note>Hell</note>. The first entered into the world through the envy of the devil, for God had created man indissoluble. The second, however, is owed in the first place to the devil, who sinned before man and by whose suggestion man sinned; and in the second place, it is owed to those men who imitate the devil. The first death, in the universal resurrection, will be "swallowed up in victory" by the immortality and indissolubility of the soul from the body. For our first parent brought this death into the world. But the second death is not taken away. For this death is not of our first parent, but belongs to the devil. Even before there were men, it was owed to the devil, who sins from the beginning and who is not to be redeemed. For the first death, the "sting" or prick is sin; and the aggravation of sin is the Law—that is, the transgression of the Law. After the resurrection, nothing further will be added that could induce dissolution. There will be no more law that can be transgressed, no more suggestion from the evil one. For all his tyranny, license, and power will be taken away, and at the final judgment, he will be judged to eternal punishments. Therefore, the first death will be entirely removed; harmful sin will be removed; and the Law, the medicine for sin, will be removed. For in the second death, no one is curable. And in the second and eternal life, no one is susceptible to disease. But you will say: if the death of Gehenna is the death of the devil, and was introduced before mankind, then that ought to be called the "first death," and the one consisting in the dissolution of the harmony of body and soul should be called the "second." You speak truly if you are comparing man to an angel—and specifically a rebel angel—but not if you remain focused on man. For in man, dissolution precedes the death of Gehenna, and therefore the former is rightly called the "first death" and the latter the "second." When, therefore, they say they are speaking of the death of man, they want us to look at the state of human beings; and in speaking of man's death, it will be most true that "death is swallowed up in victory. Where, O death, is your sting? Where, O hell, is your victory?" So too, the other life, which we call "second," which consists in the attainment of the highest and eternal life—which John says "was with the Father and appeared to us"—the good angels possessed before us. And even our "first" life, if we contemplate the angels, is much later than theirs. When, therefore, we call it "the second," we are looking only at ourselves. Thus, the reprobate demons will live in the "first life" <note>existence</note> but be forever dead in the "second." The good angels, however, will live perpetually in both lives. I call the "first life" of the angels that which they received in the indissolubility of their own harmony; and the "second" is that which they perceive in the highest life, the Life of lives. May Christ Jesus deign to grant this to us, He who made for us this victory over the death which our first parent brought in, restoring the first life to us in a better way, and, once the first is restored, granting us the second and best life. To Him be honor and thanksgiving from every living thing, both in this age and the next, forever and ever.

<margin>B III</margin> ¶ In the Greek, it is now read: "then the twelve." But I think it more correctly stands as "the eleven," based on the testimony of the Gospels of Matthew and Luke and from the Acts of the Apostles. For the twelfth, Matthias, was added to the number of the twelve after the Ascension <note>original: "assumptioem," referring to Christ being taken up into heaven</note>. This is not because Matthias did not see Him after the resurrection—for he was one of the disciples—but he was not yet of the "number of the twelve." Furthermore, Paul does not speak here of a chronological order, but rather of the instances of the Lord's manifestation, even if Paul does not include all of them here, but only those he had received from those who had seen Him, or knew by revelation. Now in the Greek it is: "then to the twelve" <note>original Greek: "εἶτα τοῖς Δώδεκα"</note>. I think it should say "eleven" <note>original Greek: "ἕνδεκα"</note>. And so I have found it well-written by the ancient translator and well-translated. ¶ The Vulgate edition says: "Who am not worthy to be called an apostle." ¶ It could be said: "sufficient" or "fit" to be called an apostle, Paul says: "who am not fit to be called an apostle" <note>original Greek: "ὃς οὐκ εἰμὶ ἱκανὸς καλεῖσθαι ἀπόστολος"</note>. ¶ The Vulgate edition says: "And his grace in me was not void." ¶ It should be said: "but his grace which is in me." Paul says: "and his grace which [is] toward me, was not made empty" <note>original Greek: "καὶ ἡ χάρις αὐτοῦ ἡ εἰς ἐμὲ, οὐ κενὴ ἐγενήθη"</note>. ¶ The Vulgate edition says: "But the grace of God with me." ¶ It should be said: "but the grace of God which is with me." For Paul attributes everything to the grace of God, for it is the master-builder <note>original Latin: "architectonica," suggesting grace is the primary designer of the work</note>; he himself is only the instrument and the vessel of God's grace, just as the Savior said to the apostles: "It is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you." Even when Paul had said "I labored," he immediately corrects his word as if he had made a slip and says, "not I labored, but the grace of God which is in me," or "the spirit of God in me." Paul says: "but the grace of God which [is] with me" <note>original Greek: "ἀλλὰ ἡ χάρις τοῦ θεοῦ ἡ σὺν ἐμοί"</note>. ¶ The Vulgate edition says: "So we preached: and so you believed." ¶ It should be 
<margin>C 114 115</margin> read: "so we preach" in the present tense. Paul says: "so we preach and so you believed" <note>original Greek: "οὕτως κηρύσσομεν καὶ οὕτως ἐπιστεύσατε"</note>. ¶ The Vulgate edition says: "For you are still in your sins." ¶ The particle "for" <note>original: "enim"</note> is superfluous. Nor does Paul confirm anything here, but rather introduces the negative consequences. Paul says: "you are still in your sins" <note>original Greek: "ἔτι ἐστὲ ἐν ταῖς ἁμαρτίαις ὑμῶν"</note>. ¶ The Vulgate edition says: "If in this life only we are hoping in Christ." ¶ The ancient translator seems to suggest the exclusion of the particle "only" <note>original: "tantum"</note> from "hoping," whereas it ought to be joined with "we are." And certainly, in this life alone we hope. For in the other life, we shall no longer hope, but what we hoped for, we shall see, hold, and embrace. For no one hopes for what he sees. And faith shall cease where the most evident truth shall shine present. And hope shall cease where the most present enjoyment of the highest good is found. However, Charity—the love of that infinite good—as the apostle said in another place, does not fail. And what he said as "hoping" should be explained in the past tense <note>original: "speravimus"</note>. For the sense in Paul is: "we are more miserable than all men, if we who have hoped in Christ are so only in this life." This would follow if there were no resurrection of the dead. For then this life alone would be ours, and there would be no future life. Paul says: "if in this life we have been hoping in Christ only" <note>original Greek: "εἰ ἐν τῇ ζωῇ ταύτῃ ἠλπικότες ἐσμὲν ἐν χριστῷ μόνον"</note>. Nevertheless, the particle "in Christ" should be referred continuously to "having hoped." For Paul's speech is somewhat transposed <term>hyperbatica<span>a rhetorical figure where the natural order of words is changed</span></term>; and he uses this style of speaking frequently. This often happens to those who have quick and excessively fertile minds, and especially to those moved by the swiftness of the Spirit. 
<margin>C 116</margin> ¶ The Vulgate edition says: "And as in Adam all die." ¶ It should be said "For just as," or something similar. Paul: "For just as in Adam all die" <note>original Greek: "ὥσπερ γὰρ ἐν τῷ Ἀδὰμ πάντες ἀποθνήσκουσιν"</note>. ¶ The Vulgate edition says: "Those who believed in his coming." ¶ The word "believed" is not found in Paul. If anything was to be expressed, a substantive verb (as is customary) should have been expressed instead, by saying "were." And "at his coming." This is understood regarding the first coming. For it was not in his second coming—which is yet to be—that there were some who believed in him. Paul says: "then those of Christ at his coming" <note>original Greek: "ἔπειτα οἱ τοῦ Χριστοῦ ἐν τῇ παρουσίᾳ αὐτοῦ"</note>. 
<margin>D 117 119</margin> ¶ The Vulgate edition says: "Lastly, however, the enemy death shall be destroyed." ¶ It can be said: "the last enemy," so that the devil is understood, whose entire power shall be taken away and made void. Paul: "The last enemy to be destroyed is death" <note>original Greek: "ἔσχατος ἐχθρὸς καταργεῖται ὁ θάνατος"</note>. ¶ The Vulgate edition says: "I die daily because of your glory," but it should rather be "by our glorying." Where the old translator put "because of," Paul has a particle of protestation <note>a Greek word used for making a solemn oath or declaration</note>. Yet it should be understood not so much as a legal oath but as a holy protestation. Therefore, we have omitted the particle "by" <note>original: "per"</note>, which is frequently a sign of swearing, and expressed the word "protestation," lest those who freely favor swearing should believe it to be an oath. In this matter, Christ must be heard, not men. Paul: "I die daily, [I swear] by your glorying" <note>original Greek: "καθ’ ἡμέραν ἀποθνήσκω νὴ τὴν ὑμετέραν καύχησιν"</note>. He immediately adds: "which I have in Christ Jesus our Lord." ¶ The Vulgate edition says: "For tomorrow we shall die." ¶ Through the present tense, it says: "tomorrow we die." However, the Latin usage with the adverb "tomorrow" (looking to the future) is rather to join it to a future tense verb. Paul took this proverb from Isaiah, from whom even the Gentiles who lived before Paul seem to have adopted it. Paul: "for tomorrow we die" <note>original Greek: "αὔριον γὰρ ἀποθνήσκομεν"</note>. 
<margin>E 119</margin> ¶ The Vulgate edition says: "Awake, you righteous." ¶ it should be said through the adverb: "righteously." For it is absurd to say "awake," "wake up," or "return to your senses, you righteous." For the righteous are already awake and have no need to return to their senses; rather, it is for those who are erring, such as the apostle argues the Corinthians to have been.

Therefore, he encourages them to wake up and return to their senses for the sake of righteousness. Paul says: "Wake up as is right, and do not sin." <note>original Greek: "ἐκνήψατε δικαίως, καὶ μὴ ἁμαρτάνετε"</note> ¶ The Vulgate edition says: "I speak to your reverence" <note>original Latin: "Ad reuerentiam vobis loquor"</note>. ¶ Because the word "reverence" is usually taken in a positive sense—referring to the honorable fear 
<margin>F 120</margin> owed to parents and superiors—the ancient translator could have more accurately used "shame," "modesty," or something similar. Paul says: "I speak to your shame." <note>original Greek: "πρὸς ἐντροπὴν ὑμῖν λέγω"</note> ¶ The Vulgate edition says: "Unless it first dies." ¶ The word "first" is superfluous here. Paul says: "Unless it dies." <note>original Greek: "ἐὰν μὴ ἀποθάνῃ"</note> ¶ The Vulgate edition says: "He gives it a body as He wills." ¶ Paul used the past tense, "He willed"—meaning He pre-defined it and ordained it from the beginning. For although in eternity there is neither "before" nor "after," nevertheless, the divine ordinations are prior to the world and all things in the world, just as eternal things precede those that are not eternal. Paul says: "He gives it a body as He willed." <note>original Greek: "δίδωσι σῶμα καθὼς ἠθέλησεν"</note> ¶ The Vulgate edition says: "there is one brightness of the sun, another brightness of the moon, and another brightness of the stars." ¶ Here, and in the following lines, the ancient translator could have said "glory" wherever he said "brightness" <note>original Latin: "claritas"</note>. For he had translated the same word as "glory" just a little earlier. Just as Paul does not change the word, the translator should not have changed the vocabulary of the translation—
<margin>E 121</margin> unless he preferred to be called a paraphraser rather than a translator. Paul says: "There is one glory of the sun, 
<margin>122</margin> and another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars." <note>original Greek: "ἄλλη δόξα ἡλίου, καὶ ἄλλη δόξα σελήνης, καὶ ἄλλη δόξα ἀστέρων"</note> ¶ The Vulgate edition says: "The first man Adam was made." ¶ The word "man" is superfluous. Paul says: "The first Adam was made." <note>original Greek: "ἐγένετο ὁ πρῶτος ἀδάμ"</note> ¶ The Vulgate edition says: "But not first that which is spiritual, but that which is animal." ¶ It is more correct Latin to say *spirituale* (spiritual) from the word for spirit. And the word "animal" here is derived from the word for "soul" <note>Latin: "anima"</note>, not from the word for a "beast" <note>Latin: "animal"</note>, as we have noted elsewhere. For those who have attained a spiritual body will no longer eat, drink, or grow; to do so would be to have an "animal" body and not a spiritual one. Paul also uses the simple "first" rather than the comparative "sooner," but it makes no difference to the meaning. Paul says: "But the spiritual was not first, but the soulful." <note>original Greek: "ἀλλ’ οὐ πρῶτον τὸ πνευματικὸν, ἀλλὰ τὸ ψυχικόν"</note> ¶ The Vulgate edition says: "The first man was of the earth, earthly. The second man is from heaven, heavenly." ¶ It should read: "The second man is the Lord from heaven." Paul says: "The first man was from the earth, <term>choicus</term> <note>meaning "of the dust" or "earthy"</note>; the second man is the Lord from heaven." <note>original Greek: "ὁ πρῶτος ἄνθρωπος ἐκ γῆς χοϊκός, ὁ δεύτερος ἄνθρωπος ὁ κύριος ἐξ οὐρανοῦ"</note>
An "earthy" man is one who is subject to that divine sentence which says, "you are ash and to ash you shall return." The "heavenly" man is one who is not subject to it, as Christ undoubtedly was by his nature. However, he willed to carry the likeness of the earthy man in himself until death, though not until the point of dissolving into ash. For it was written of him: "You will not allow your Holy One to see corruption." In this age, we carry the image of the earthy man, being subject to dissolution and return to dust. But in the other age, we shall carry the image of Christ; through him (the power of death having been destroyed), we will no longer be subject to dissolution or returning to the earth—for that would be to die again—but we shall be immortal. ¶ The Vulgate edition says: "Therefore, just as we have carried the image of the earthy, let us also carry the image of the heavenly." ¶ It should say: "just as we have carried the image of the earthy, we *shall* carry the image of the heavenly." I say "shall carry" in the future tense. For Paul is not giving an exhortation here; rather, he is predicting what is to come. As long as we are in this world, we carry the image of the earthy; but in the other world, we shall first carry the image of the heavenly. From the first life, we are able to be scattered into the atoms of the earth, just like the earth itself; from the second life, we are indissoluble, like heaven. For who would say that heaven is resolvable into dust like an earthly body? Now our body bears the condition of the earth; then it shall bear the condition of heaven. Paul says: "And just as we 
<margin>C</margin> bore the image of the earthy, we shall also bear the image of the heavenly." <note>original Greek: "καὶ καθὼς ἐφορέσαμεν τὴν εἰκόνα τοῦ χοϊκοῦ· φορέσομεν καὶ τὴν εἰκόνα τοῦ ἐπουρανίου"</note>
<margin>123</margin> ¶ The Vulgate edition says: "We shall all indeed rise, but we shall not all be changed." ¶ This is what the Latin manuscripts have. But from Paul, as has been said, it should read: "We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed." Truly, I believe the text was altered because people thought the latter was more true than the former, perhaps not understanding the sacred mysteries of these matters. I believe it can stand as it is read in the Greek. They think the bodies of the damned are not changed; but surely it is a great "change" to be made immortal, incorruptible, and indissoluble from a mortal state. They interpret "change" only as a certain transformation into glory and the receiving of divine splendor. But that is an interpretation of convenience, making it necessary to invent an excuse for the altered text. Paul says: "We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed." <note>original Greek: "πάντες μὲν οὐ κοιμηθησόμεθα, πάντες δὲ ἀλλαγησόμεθα"</note> ¶ The Vulgate edition says: "For the trumpet shall sound." ¶ The word "trumpet" is superfluous according to the original text, even if it fits the meaning based on what was said above—unless perhaps "trumpet" is understood as the instrument of the action. Paul says: "For it shall sound," <note>original Greek: "σαλπίσει γὰρ"</note> and immediately adds, "and the dead." ¶ "For this corruptible must put on incorruption," and so forth. ¶ When Paul adds this, he seems to clarify what he meant by "we shall be changed." For if even the damned put on incorruptibility, they are indeed "changed." ¶ The Vulgate edition says: "But thanks be to God." It should be "grace" <note>original Latin: "gratia"</note>, in the nominative singular. So be it: let the verb "be" be understood. Paul says: "But grace to God." <note>original Greek: "τῷ δὲ θεῷ χάρις"</note> ¶ The Vulgate edition says: "Be stable and immovable." ¶ Paul says this without the connecting "and." But perhaps he would judge that detail unworthy of note. Paul says: "Be steadfast, immovable." <note>original Greek: "ἑδραῖοι γίνεσθε, ἀμετακίνητοι"</note>

# COMMENTARY ON CHAPTER 16

**E**aving finished the deeper mysteries, the apostle now pursues more familiar matters: concerning the giving of alms <note>original: "eleemosynis"</note> to the holy poor who were in Jerusalem, who had nothing for the sake of Christ—or rather, who had continually provided whatever they possessed for works of charity, dispensing it until the very end. Those who perform works of charity emulate God’s providence, mercy, grace, and blessing. **Providence**: God’s providence is a single good common to all and to each individual, which God dispenses to everyone in such a way that He seems to wonderfully care for the whole and the individual at the same time. This is also called **mercy**: because every creature is so unworthy in itself that it would immediately fail unless that mercy came to support its needs. It is called **grace**: because it is not a debt, but a gift of pure divine liberality. **Blessing**: because by God's blessing all things abound, all things become joyful, and every need is removed. Here, those who are vigilant in works of mercy are called provident, merciful, liberal, and blessed, obtaining these divine names through imitation. But those who have the means and do not act: what else shall we call them but improvident—despisers of the image of divine providence—unmerciful, greedy, and cursed, children of a curse. 

But they say: "We are not improvident, for we provide for ourselves more than for other men." Yet God's providence is not so called because God provides anything for Himself, but for others. Therefore, what the greedy call "providence" is not an image of providence but its opposite; it regards not the common good but one's own. Thus, they do not have providence, nor are they provident. Therefore, just as this holy operation toward others imitates the work of providence, Paul calls it "communion" (as seen in chapter 15 of the Epistle to the Romans in the preceding book) and, as he does here, a "gathering" or "collection." Just as it imitates God's mercy, it is named <term>eleemosyna</term> <note>Almsgiving or works of charity</note>, that is, mercy. As found in Luke: "Give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you." <note>original Greek: "Δότϵ ϵ̓λϵημοσύνην, καὶ ἰδοὺ πάντα καθαρά ὑμῖν ϵ̓στιν"</note>. Insofar as it imitates divine liberality, it obtains the name of **grace**, as Paul calls it in this chapter. Insofar as it imitates God's blessing, Paul calls it in the second chapter to the Corinthians an <term>eulogiam</term> <note>original Greek: "εὐλογία," meaning a blessing or a bountiful gift</note>, that is, a blessing. So great a work, therefore, obtains so many names. To show the Corinthians how they might perform this more conveniently, he provokes them by the example of the Galatians, saying:

<margin>124</margin> › Regarding the collection that is being made for the holy ones: you should do just as I ordered 
› the churches of Galatia. On the first day of the week, let each of you put something aside, saving up 
› whatever he conveniently can, so that collections are not made only when I come. And when I arrive, 
› whomever you approve by letters, I will send them to carry your grace <note>In this context, the financial gift or favor</note> 
› to Jerusalem. If it is worthy for me to go also, they shall go with me. But I will come 
› to you after I have passed through Macedonia. For I shall pass through Macedonia. 
› Perhaps I will stay with you, or even spend the winter, so that you may send me on my way wherever 
› I go. For I do not wish to see you now just in passing, but I hope to remain with you 
› for some time, if the Lord permits. But I will remain at Ephesus until Pentecost. 
› For a great and effective door has been opened to me, and there are many adversaries. 

¶ See how familiarly the apostle opens the 

<margin>125</margin> heart of his mind to the Corinthians. This is a sign of the charity with which Paul burned toward all men for the sake of God. Now he reveals the pious concern he had for Timothy, his disciple and coworker in the gospel of Christ, saying: 

› If Timothy comes, see that he is with you without fear. For he works the work of the Lord, 
› just as I do. Therefore, let no one despise him. But conduct him on his way, 
› and send him forward in peace so that he may come to me. For I am waiting for him 
› with the brothers. 

¶ These things are about Timothy. Now concerning 

<margin>126</margin> **Apollos**, an eloquent man who had a true zeal for Christ, whom the Corinthians were asking for: Paul writes an excuse for his delays, promising his arrival at another time, God permitting. Saying of him thus: 

¶ Concerning the brother **Apollos**: I strongly urged him 
› to go to you with the brothers, but it was not at all his will to go now; 
› however, he will go when it is a convenient time. 

¶ Since, therefore (by God's disposition), 

<margin>127</margin> Apollos could not conveniently come to them, the apostle’s kindness exhorts them to more careful vigilance, caution lest they fall from the faith, true magnanimity, and spiritual strength which is from Christ—who is our power, our foundation, and our strength—and concerning doing everything in charity, saying: 

¶ Watch, stand firm in the faith, act manfully, be strengthened; let all your affairs be done in love. 

¶ He then commends **Stephanas** and **Fortunatus**, faithful Corinthians and the carriers of the present letter, who had brought letters from the Corinthians to the apostle. Indeed, in this epistle, he has satisfied those letters with apostolic dignity, instructing us that we should never...

and helps our infirmity: let us give him both glory and honor and thanksgiving
forever and ever, Amen.
