### AN EXAMINATION of several points regarding the literal sense. The **Vulgate** edition. Now concerning the collections
<margin>A 114</margin> which are made for the saints. Paul used the **singular** <note>original: "Singulariter"</note>: he did not use the word "are made" or any other. However, the explicit word does no harm. Paul says: <term>concerning the collection for the saints</term> <note>original Greek: "περὶ δὲ τῆς λογίας τῆς εἰς τοὺς ἁγίους"</note>. The **Vulgate** edition says: "Upon the first of the Sabbath." It is said in the plural: "of the Sabbaths." <term>according to the first of the Sabbaths</term> <note>original Greek: "κατὰ μίαν σαββάτων"</note>. And it is just as if we were to say "on the first day of the weeks." The Hebrews had weeks, which they called "Sabbaths," from "rest" <note>original: "a quiete"</note>. For on their Sabbath the Lord rested in the tomb; for it is the day of the Lord's rest. Christians also
have weeks, which are also called Sabbaths. The first day of these, consecrated by the resurrection of the Lord, is called the
Lord's Day <note>Sunday</note>. Therefore, the days ought to be named: the Lord's day, the second day of the week, the third of the
week, the fourth of the week, the fifth of the week, the sixth of the week, the last of the week. But according to ecclesiastical rite, we say the first, second, third, fourth weekday <note>original: "feria"</note>, and so on up to the seventh. But I know not what evil and pagan error has taken hold, so that—excepting the Lord’s Day and the Sabbath—the other days are still named after the gods of the Gentiles. Such as Moon-day from Diana; Mars-day from the demon who incites discord; Mercury-day from the impostor and chief of thieves; Jupiter-day from him whom the Jews call Beelzebub, the prince of demons, whom the sacred scriptures call the prince of this world and the prince of darkness, whom the Lord Jesus cast out. The Gentiles, however, deceived by the great impiety of error, called him the highest of the gods—which comes to the same thing. For all the gods of the Gentiles are demons. Venus-day from the spirit of fornication. How then are Christians not ashamed to name their days with these shameful names? Why do those who have the administration of the Word not teach publicly how they ought to be named? Why is this not commanded to Christians by public edicts, and the other forbidden, so that the word which was spoken may be fulfilled: "their memory shall perish with a noise"? Why are those voices still heard, in which the divinity is so gravely, impiously, and injuriously offended? What shall I say of those who still exist, who, because of the retained names, believe out of pagan superstition that those days are ruled—this one by the moon, that one by Mars, and so on for the rest—and that in those days and their specific hours, the Moon, Mars, Mercury, or Venus have some power? What is this but being Gentiles, and still worshipping the Sun, Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn? But here you will say they mean the stars. The same error and the same superstition! For those demons falsely claimed those to be their seats, and that through them they moderated earthly affairs; they provoked men to the worship of the visible creature against the Creator. Let this impious error, therefore, be gone from every faithful mind. And in the months: what have I to do with two-faced Janus, and two-horned Faunus, and the other masks of demons, when in...

### THE THIRD BOOK OF THE COMMENTARIES ON THE EPISTLES OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PAUL, WHICH IS ON THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS, CHAPTER 1

<image-desc>Large ornamental woodcut initial 'I' decorated with scrolling foliage and floral motifs.</image-desc>

<margin>1</margin> In this second epistle to the Corinthians, Paul puts forth actions first (as is his custom), offering a greeting saying: ¶ Paul, an apostle of JESUS CHRIST by the will of God, and Timothy our brother: to the church of God which is at Corinth, with all the saints who are in all Achaia <note>Achaia was a Roman province in southern Greece, including cities like Corinth and Athens.</note>: grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord JESUS CHRIST. ¶ Having set down this holy and spiritual greeting, he gives thanks to God for both prosperity and for adverse pressures and consolations, both for his own and those of the Corinthians, saying: ¶ Blessed be God, that is, the Father of our Lord JESUS CHRIST, the Father of mercies and the God of all consolation, who consoles us in all our pressure <note>original Latin: "pressura," meaning the crushing weight of affliction or tribulation</note>, so that we also may be able to console those who are in any pressure, through the consolation by which we ourselves are consoled by God; because as the sufferings of CHRIST abound in us, so through CHRIST our consolation also abounds. 

<margin>2</margin> But whether we are pressed for your consolation and salvation, or whether we are consoled for your consolation, which is achieved in the endurance of those same sufferings which we also suffer: even our hope is firm for you, knowing that just as you are sharers of the sufferings, so also of the consolation. ¶ In two ways we imitate Christ our God and our King. First, in enduring sufferings—that is, pressures and tribulations—for his name, and doing so with joy. Otherwise, we would not be imitating him, who, for the joy set before him, endured the cross, despising the shame. Second, when we are delivered from pressures or when they are not present, we bring him who delivers and consoles us with all devotion of soul; he who does not desert us when hard and adverse things are present, nor despise us when they are absent. We rejoice that our pressures are for the salvation of others, shaping them by the example of patience; and we also rejoice that our deliveries and consolations are for the consolation of others. Indeed, we ought not only to rejoice in our own pressures and consolations from God, but also to rejoice in the pressures of the saints because they imitate the sufferings of our Lord with patience, knowing this: that they will also receive consolation from God—I say, to rejoice in their future consolation. ¶ This is a life most full of joys, which neither takes away sad things nor softens happy things—a happy life, a life to be desired, which Paul also had in his pressures and his consolations from being delivered from pressures, and which the pressures and consolations of the saints increased...

<margin>3</margin> ...that is, in both sorrowful and favorable matters, the imitations of Christ. And concerning his own pressures and their deliverances—that is, the consolations from God—Paul adds: ¶ For I do not wish you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning our pressure which came upon us in Asia <note>The Roman province of Asia, in modern-day Turkey, where Paul faced severe rioting and opposition.</note>: that we were burdened excessively beyond our strength, so much so that we were weary even of life. Indeed, we had within ourselves the sentence of death, so that we should not trust in ourselves but in God, who raises the dead; who rescued and delivered us from such a death, in whom we have hoped that he will still deliver us, as you also help together in prayer for us. So that for the gift bestowed upon me through many persons, thanksgivings may be made by many for you. ¶ God loves charity within us; and if he loves it in one, he loves and hears it much more in many. ¶ Therefore Paul asks for their prayers in common to God for him, so that on account of the gift which he will obtain from the prayers of many for their benefit and that of others, many acts of thanksgiving may be performed toward God on behalf of those who obtained it from God by their prayers. For the Lord of all things does not want to have envious servants, but rather those following one another with mutual love, being suppliants toward the Lord and anxious, one for the safety of all and all for the safety of one. Then both the individual glories in service toward the Lord for the good of all, and all glory for the one. Then everyone rejoices in himself, exults, and glories in serving his Lord not simulatedly, not falsely, not with duplicity, but in simplicity and according to the will of his Lord. Indeed, in this he glories most: that his Lord has helped him...

<margin>4</margin> ...and poured out his grace to serve him in this manner. And he does not attribute this glory of serving well to himself, but to the grace of his Lord. Therefore Paul adds: ¶ For our glorying is this:

<margin>5</margin> the testimony of our conscience, that in simplicity and sincerity of God—not in

<margin>6</margin> carnal wisdom but in the grace of God—we have conducted ourselves in the world, and more abundantly...

<summary>This page contains the beginning of the commentary on 2 Corinthians, where the author explains Paul's greeting and his theological reflection on the relationship between suffering (pressures) and divine consolation. Paul emphasizes that the trials he faced in Asia serve as an example of relying on God's power rather than human strength.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the first chapter of 2 Corinthians. The previous page discussed Paul’s sincerity and the shared nature of suffering and comfort between the Apostle and the church. Here, Paul defends himself against accusations of being fickle or unreliable regarding his travel plans.</meta>

<header>COMMENTARY</header>

...[understand] you. For we write no other things to you than what you read or even understand; and I hope that you will understand even to the end, just as you have understood us in part: that we are your boast, even as you are ours in the day of our Lord JESUS. ¶ This simplicity and sincerity in which Paul boasts by the testimony of his conscience, he does not call his own, but the simplicity and sincerity of God—that is, bestowed upon him by the gift and benefit of God. And although this gift of God accompanied him everywhere, he attained it even more abundantly among the Corinthians, so that in this he might boast more toward God on behalf of the Corinthians, and the Corinthians on behalf of Paul toward God: that for the sake of their instruction, he obtained greater graces from God than when he was among others, even though he obtained great graces among all.

<margin>5</margin>
Moved by this confidence—a confidence, I say, of receiving greater grace for their enlightenment—he wished to come a second time to the Corinthians. However, by the ordaining of the Holy Spirit, he did not immediately carry out what he had proposed. He himself testifies to this, saying: ¶ And trusting in this confidence, I wished to come to you first, that you might have a second grace, and to pass by you into Macedonia, and to return again from Macedonia to you, and by you to be brought on my way toward Judea. ¶ But he did not do this. Rather, as is held in the last chapter of the preceding epistle <note>Referring to 1 Corinthians 16</note>, having sent the Corinthians away, he passed through Macedonia, and from Macedonia he sailed into Asia, where he suffered many hardships even unto death, from whence he returned to the Corinthians. But because he wished to come to them sooner and did not, should he not be accused of levity <note>original: "levitatis," meaning fickleness or lack of seriousness</note>? Or is he led by fleshly duplicity, so that in his speech, after the manner of fleshly men, there is now "yes" and now "no"? It is not so at all. For in those who are led by the Spirit of God, whatever is deliberated and promised is certain, but it is put into execution according to the will of the Spirit. Regarding this matter, Paul adds:

<margin>6</margin>
¶ When I therefore deliberated this, did I use levity? Or the things that I deliberate, do I deliberate according to the flesh, so that with me there should be "yes, yes" and "no, no"? But God is faithful, that our word to you was not "yes" and "no." For the Son of God, JESUS CHRIST, who was preached among you by us—namely by me, Silvanus, and Timothy—was not "yes" and "no," but in him was "yes." For however many are the promises of God, in him they are "yes," and in him "Amen," through us to the glory of God. ¶ "Yes" is a mark of affirmation. "No" is a mark of negation. "Amen" is a mark of confirmation. Therefore, this statement "our word to you was not yes and no" is just as if we said: our word to you was not an affirmation and a negation of the same thing. And this "but in him was yes" means that in the Son of God there was affirmation. Furthermore, "however many promises are in him, they were yes": as many as there are promises in the Son of God, they are certainties and affirmations. Likewise, "and in him Amen through us to the glory of God" means that in the Son of God there is confirmation of the promises through us to the glory of God himself. But if the promises of God are confirmed through them to the glory of God, it is God who confirms them, who anoints them by the grace of the Holy Spirit, and who seals them with the Holy Spirit.

<margin>7</margin>
How, then, could they use levity? How could they deliberate according to human standards? How could they affirm one thing now and immediately deny it? Therefore Paul adds: ¶ Now he who confirms us with you in CHRIST, and who has anointed us, is God: who has also sealed us and given the pledge <note>original: "arrabonem," a legal term for a down payment or earnest money that guarantees a contract</note> of the Spirit in our hearts. ¶ And now he adds the cause of why he did not go down to them before entering Macedonia: because he would have afflicted them more by being present, on account of the dissensions that had arisen and on account of the wicked and monstrous incest between a stepson and stepmother that had happened among them. In his absence, however, he tempered everything better and more calmly, and with less disturbance, trouble, and sadness for them. For otherwise, he would have had to come "with a rod" <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 4:21, meaning coming to exercise discipline or punishment</note>, but he desired to come in a spirit of gentleness and mildness. For he possessed the Spirit of God, which is gentle and mild.

<margin>8</margin>
Paul explains the reason in this way, saying: ¶ But I call God as a witness upon my soul, that to spare you, I did not come again to Corinth; not that we lord it over your faith, but we are coworkers of your joy: for you stand by faith. ¶ He does not say "sparing you" because he did not want to be a burden to them; he does not say this because he wished to dominate the Corinthians or their faith (for they were servants of Christ and he a fellow servant). Rather, he said it because he wished to cooperate with the joy of all rather than their sadness. And he also rejoices with them because they keep their faith in Christ steadfastly. May Christ the Lord deign to keep us so steadfast in faith that through it, having perceived eternal joy, we may never cease from his praise and thanksgiving. To him is due all honor for ages of ages.

<sig>A 2</sig>

¶ EXAMINATION of certain points regarding the text. ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *So that we also may be able to console those who are in every pressure, through the exhortation by which we ourselves are exhorted by God.* ¶ The ancient translator <note>Referring to Jerome, the traditional translator of the Vulgate</note> could have said "through the consolation by which we are consoled by God." For where he says "exhortation" and "exhorted" here below, a little earlier he translated it as "consolation" and "console." It was therefore fitting that the same words be used in Paul’s subsequent speech.

<summary>Paul defends his integrity against charges of fickleness, explaining that his change in travel plans was intended to spare the Corinthians from a harsh disciplinary visit. He emphasizes that all God's promises are affirmed in Christ and that his ministry is based on divine sincerity, not human whim.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philological and theological commentary on the first chapter of 2 Corinthians, moving into the opening of chapter 2. It focuses on clarifying the nuances of the Greek text compared to the Latin Vulgate translation, specifically regarding the themes of comfort, Paul's integrity, and his pastoral concern for the Corinthians' emotional state.</meta>

<page-num>137</page-num>
<header>2 Cor. III 137</header>

<margin>B</margin>
...should preserve the same interpretation. Paul writes: <note>original: "εἰς τὸ δύνασθαι ἡμᾶς παρακαλεῖν τοὺς ἐν πάσῃ θλίψει, διὰ τῆς παρακλήσεως ἧς παρακαλούμεθα αὐτοὶ ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ"</note> "so that we may be able to comfort those who are in any affliction, through the comfort with which we ourselves are comforted by God." The usage of Sacred Scripture allows this: sometimes the word "comfort" is used in an active sense, as in "he who comforts us in all our pressure," and sometimes in a passive or neutral sense, as in "blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted." However, if someone does not like the phrasing "through the consolation wherewith we ourselves are comforted by God," let them change the wording and say, "wherewith God comforts us." But these matters involve a grammatical debate. ¶ **Vulgate edition.** "So you shall be [partakers] of the consolation." ¶ No specific verb is found here in Paul’s Greek; it can be understood as either present or future. It is as if he were saying: we know that just as you are sharers of the sufferings, so you are also sharers of the consolation. And just as God comforts us in all our pressure, so God also comforts you in your afflictions. For he is not referring here to that consolation which follows this present life, but to that which is a companion to the pressures of this world. Paul writes: <note>original: "οὕτως καὶ τῆς παρακλήσεως"</note> "so also of the consolation."
<margin>B</margin>
<margin>3</margin>
¶ **Vulgate edition.** "Which happened in Asia." ¶ It should say: "Which happened to *us* in Asia." The word "us" is preferable. Paul: <note>original: "τῆς γενομένης ἡμῖν ἐν ἀσίᾳ"</note> "of that which happened to us in Asia." ¶ **Vulgate edition.** "Who delivered us from so great dangers." ¶ Rather: "from such a death." Paul: <note>original: "ὃς ἐκ τηλικούτου θανάτου ἐῤῥύσατο ἡμᾶς"</note> "who delivered us from so great a death." ¶ **Vulgate edition.** "In whom we hope." ¶ It should be expressed in the past tense: "we have hoped." Paul: <note>original: "εἰς ὃν ἠλπίκαμεν"</note> "in whom we have set our hope." ¶ **Vulgate edition.** "You also helping in prayer for us." ¶ It could be said "serving together" or "supplicating together with us." Paul: <note>original: "συνυπουργούντων καὶ ὑμῶν ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν τῇ δεήσει"</note> "you also joining in helping for us by prayer." ¶ **Vulgate edition.** "That from the persons of many faces, thanks may be given for the gift which is in us, on our behalf by many." ¶ Rather: "that from many persons, because of the gift that is in us, thanksgivings may be offered for *you* by many." Here at the end, he uses the second person <note>referring to 'you' instead of 'us'</note>. Paul: <note>original: "ἵνα ἐκ πολλῶν προσώπων τὸ εἰς ἡμᾶς χάρισμα διὰ πολλῶν εὐχαριστηθῇ ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν"</note> "so that the gift bestowed on us through many persons may be cause for many to give thanks on your behalf."
<margin>3</margin>
<margin>3</margin>
<margin>C</margin>
<margin>4</margin>
¶ **Vulgate edition.** "For our glory is this, the testimony of our conscience." ¶ It should rather be said: "For our boasting." <note>original: "ἡ γὰρ καύχησις ἡμῶν αὕτη ἐστίν, τὸ μαρτύριον τῆς συνειδήσεως ἡμῶν"</note> "For this is our boasting, the testimony of our conscience." However, as noted elsewhere and as will be seen below, the old translator <note>the author of the Vulgate</note> is accustomed to confuse these two nouns, "glory" <term>doxa</term> and "boasting" <term>kauchesis</term> or "pride" <term>kauchema</term>, treating them as the same. Lest we do this, we treat "glory" and "boasting" as distinct things. ¶ **Vulgate edition.** "Which you have read and known." ¶ It can be expressed in the present tense: "which you read or even acknowledge." Paul: <note>original: "ἀλλ᾿ ἢ ἃ ἀναγινώσκετε, ἢ καὶ ἐπιγινώσκετε"</note> "other than what you read or even acknowledge." ¶ **Vulgate edition.** "In the day of our Lord JESUS CHRIST." ¶ In Paul it is simply: "in the day of the Lord Jesus." Paul: <note>original: "ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τοῦ κυρίου Ἰησοῦ"</note> "in the day of the Lord Jesus."
<margin>C</margin>
<margin>D</margin>
<margin>6</margin>
¶ **Vulgate edition.** "As if there were with me 'it is' and 'it is not'." ¶ It can also be said: "'Yes, yes' and 'No, no'." For here Paul places two particles, one affirming and the other denying, and he doubles each. One designates affirmation; the other, negation. The Savior commanded these should be used while forbidding oaths. Paul: <note>original: "ἵνα ᾖ παρ᾿ ἐμοὶ τὸ ναὶ ναὶ, καὶ τὸ οὐ οὔ"</note> "that with me there should be the 'Yes, yes' and the 'No, no'." ¶ **Vulgate edition.** "For however many are the promises of God, in him it is." ¶ As has been said, wherever the old translator puts "is" in this passage, we can put the mark of affirmation, "Yes." But the phrasing remains ambiguous: does it show "Yes" in himself, or does it refer to the Son of God? It is better understood to refer to the Son of God from the preceding discourse, where the Apostle says: "it was not in him 'Yes and No', but in him was 'Yes'." It is certain here that those particles take the place of nouns, which is indicated by the article <note>original: "τὸ"</note> which Paul added to them, and that "in him" refers to the Son of God. Therefore, it seems more accurate that in the following parts, "in him" always refers to the Son of God. These particles should be understood to occupy the place of subjects, and the verb "is" or "are" should be supplied as appropriate. Paul: <note>original: "ὅσαι γὰρ ἐπαγγελίαι θεοῦ ἐν αὐτῷ, τὸ ναί"</note> "For all the promises of God in him are 'Yes'." ¶ **Vulgate edition.** "Therefore also through him is Amen to God for your glory." ¶ "Therefore" is superfluous; it should say: "In him is the Amen." Where "him" refers to the Son of God. And "Amen" is a mark of confirmation, praise, or thanksgiving to God, or something similar, acting here as a noun. And it should not say "for your glory," but "to the glory through us." This passage of Paul is obscure because of these indeclinable particles used in place of declinable nouns, unless one watches over the meaning very attentively. Paul: <note>original: "καὶ ἐν αὐτῷ, τὸ ἀμὴν τῷ θεῷ, πρὸς δόξαν δι᾿ ἡμῶν"</note> "and in him is the 'Amen' to God, for glory through us."

### CHAPTER II

<margin>9</margin>
Sparing the Corinthians from sorrow, Paul had not come to them; and he still proposes that he will not come to them while his arrival would be a sad one, but rather when there will be a joy common to all. And he consoles those whom he might have saddened by his letter, saying: ¶ But I determined this within myself: that I would not come to you again in sorrow. For if I cause you sorrow, then who is there to bring me joy except the one who is saddened by me? And I wrote this very thing to you, so that when I come, I might not be saddened by those from whom I ought to receive joy, having confidence in all of you that my joy is the joy of you all. For out of much pressure and anguish of heart I wrote to you with many tears; not so that you might be saddened, but that you might know the love which I have more abundantly toward you. ¶ He admits that he has saddened some, but they are the ones from whom he most desires to receive joy. For when those who possess a holy purpose and are full of the love of God (as Paul was) sadden or rebuke anyone, they do it for this very purpose...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the first chapter of 2 Corinthians, specifically addressing verses 13 through 24. It bridges the transition from Paul's defense of his integrity to his explanation for why he delayed his promised visit to Corinth.</meta>

<page-num>221</page-num>
<header>COMMENTARY</header>
<sig>A 2</sig>

> ...you. For we write nothing else to you than what you read or even acknowledge. And I hope that you will acknowledge us even to the end, just as you have acknowledged us in part—that we are your glory, even as you are ours on the day of our Lord JESUS.

¶ This simplicity and sincerity in which Paul glories by the testimony of his conscience, he does not call his own, but the simplicity and sincerity of God—that is, conferred upon him by the gift and benefit of God. And although God’s gift accompanied him everywhere, he attained it more abundantly while he was among the Corinthians. Thus, he can glory even more in this toward God for the sake of the Corinthians, and the Corinthians for Paul toward God: namely, that for the sake of instructing them, he obtained greater graces from God than when he was among others, even if he obtained great graces among all. Moved by this confidence—the confidence, I say, of receiving greater grace to enlighten them—he wished to come a second time to the
<margin>5</margin> Corinthians. However, by the ordering of the Holy Spirit, what he had proposed was not immediately carried out. He himself testifies to them of this, saying:

> ¶ And relying on this confidence, I wanted to come to you first, so that you might have a second grace, and to pass through you into Macedonia, and to return again from Macedonia to you, and by you to be helped on my way into Judea.

¶ But he did not do this. Instead, as is held in the last chapter of the preceding epistle <note>referring to 1 Corinthians 16:5-7</note>, having left the Corinthians, he passed through Macedonia and sailed from Macedonia into Asia, where he endured many hardships even unto death, from whence he returned to the Corinthians. But because he wished to come to them first and did not come, is he to be accused of light-mindedness <note>or fickleness</note>? Or is he led by fleshly duplicity, so that in his speech, after the manner of fleshly men, there is now "yes" and now "no"? Not at all. For in those who are led by the
<margin>6</margin> Spirit of God, whatever is deliberated and whatever is promised remains firm, but it is put into execution according to the will of the Spirit. On this matter, Paul adds:

> ¶ When I was deliberating this, did I use light-mindedness? Or the things that I deliberate, do I deliberate according to the flesh, so that with me there is "yes, yes" and "no, no"? But God is faithful, for our word to you was not "yes" and "no." For the Son of God, JESUS CHRIST, who was preached among you by us—namely by me, Silvanus, and Timothy—was not "yes" and "no," but in him was "yes." For however many are the promises of God, in him they are "yes." And in him is the "Amen" through us to the glory of God.

¶ "Yes" <note>original: "Etiam"</note> is a mark of affirmation. "No" <note>original: "Non"</note> is of negation. "Amen" is of confirmation. Therefore, the phrase "our word to you was not yes and no" is the same as saying "our word to you was not an affirmation and a negation of the same thing." And that phrase, "but in him was yes," means that in the Son of God there was affirmation. Furthermore, "however many are the promises in him, they are yes" means that as many as are the promises in the Son of God, they are certainties and affirmations. Likewise, "in him is the Amen through us to the glory of God" means that in the Son of God, the confirmation of the promises is through us to God himself for glory. For if the promises of God are confirmed through them to the glory of God, it is God who confirms them, who anoints them with the grace of the Holy Spirit, and who marks them with the Holy Spirit. How then could they use
<margin>7</margin> light-mindedness? How could they deliberate according to human standards? How could they now affirm one thing and immediately deny it? Therefore, Paul adds:

> ¶ But he who confirms us with you in CHRIST, and who anointed us, is God: who also sealed us and gave the pledge of the Spirit in our hearts.

¶ And now he provides the reason why he did not descend to them before entering Macedonia. It was because, being present, he would have distressed them more due to the dissensions that had arisen, and because of the wicked and monstrous incest between the stepson and stepmother <note>A reference to the scandal in 1 Corinthians 5:1</note> which had occurred among them. In his absence, however, he tempered everything better and more calmly, with less disturbance, trouble, and sadness for them. For at that time, he would have had to come "with a rod" <note>meaning with disciplinary authority</note>; but he himself desired to come in a spirit of gentleness and mildness. For he had the
<margin>8</margin> Spirit of God, which is gentle and mild. Therefore, in this way, Paul provides the cause, saying:

> ¶ But I call God as a witness upon my soul: that sparing you, I did not come again to Corinth. Not that we lord it over your faith, but we are coworkers of your joy: for you stand by faith.

¶ He does not say "sparing you" because he wants to avoid being a burden to them, nor does he say it because he wants to lord it over the Corinthians or their faith (for they were servants of Christ and he was a fellow servant). Rather, he said it because he wants to cooperate with the joy of all rather than their sadness. And he also rejoices with them because they steadfastly keep the faith in Christ. May Christ our Lord deign to keep us so steadfastly in that faith: so that through it, having perceived eternal joy, we may never cease from his praise and thanksgiving. To whom is due all honor forever and ever.

For where he says "exhortation" and "exhorted" here below, a little earlier he translated it as "consolation" and "comfort." It was fitting, therefore, that the same words in Paul and in the following discourse...

<meta>This page continues the philological and theological commentary on Paul's Second Epistle to the Corinthians, moving from the end of Chapter 1 into the beginning of Chapter 2. It focuses on correcting the Latin Vulgate translation against the original Greek, particularly regarding the themes of comfort, boasting, and Paul’s integrity in his promises.</meta>

<page-num>137</page-num>
<header>III 2 Cor. 137</header>

...they should maintain the same interpretation. Paul writes: <note>original: "εις το δύνασθαι ημας παρακαλεῖν τοὺς ἐν πάση θλίψει, διὰ της παρακλήσεως ἧς παρακαλούμεθα αὐτοὶ ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ"</note> **so that we may be able to comfort those who are in any trouble, by the comfort with which we ourselves are comforted by God.** And the usage of the Sacred Scriptures holds this: sometimes it uses the verb "to comfort" in an active sense, as here, "he who comforts us in all our pressure"; at other times it is used passively or neutrally, as in "blessed are those who mourn, for they themselves shall be comforted." <margin>B 2</margin> However, if the wording "through the consolation by which we ourselves are comforted by God" does not please someone, let them change the phrasing and say: "with which God comforts us." But these matters involve a grammatical dispute.

¶ **The Vulgate Edition:** *So you will also be of consolation.*
¶ No verb is found here in Paul’s Greek; it can be understood as much in the present tense as in the future, as if he were saying: "We know that just as you are partakers of the sufferings, so you are also partakers of the consolation." And just as God comforts us in all our pressure, so also God comforts you in your afflictions. For here he is not referring to that consolation which follows this present life, but that which is the companion of the pressures of this world. <margin>B 3</margin> Paul writes: <note>original: "οὕτως καὶ τῆς παρακλήσεως"</note> **so also of the comfort.**

¶ **The Vulgate Edition:** *Which happened in Asia.*
¶ It should be said: *which happened to us in Asia.* The word "to us" is missing. Paul writes: <note>original: "τῆς γενομένης ἡμῖν ἐν ἀσίᾳ"</note> **which happened to us in Asia.**

¶ **The Vulgate Edition:** *Who rescued us from such great perils.*
¶ Rather: *who delivered us from such a death.* Paul writes: <note>original: "ὃς ἐκ τηλικούτου θανάτου ἐρρύσατο ἡμᾶς"</note> **who delivered us from so great a death.** <margin>C</margin>

¶ **The Vulgate Edition:** *In whom we hope.*
¶ It should be expressed in the past tense: *we have hoped.* Paul writes: <note>original: "εἰς ὃν ἠλπίκαμεν"</note> **in whom we have hoped.**

¶ **The Vulgate Edition:** *You also helping in prayer for us.*
¶ It can be said *cooperating* or *supplicating together with us.* Paul writes: <note>original: "συνυπουργουντων καὶ ὑμῶν ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν τῇ δεήσει"</note> **you also helping together for us in prayer.**

¶ **The Vulgate Edition:** *That from the persons of many faces, the gift which is in us may have thanks given for us by many.*
¶ Rather: *so that from many persons, on account of the gift that is in us, thanksgivings may be given for you by many.* Here, at the end, it should be in the second person. <margin>4</margin> Paul writes: <note>original: "ἵνα ἐκ πολλῶν προσώπων τὸ εἰς ημᾶς χάρισμα διὰ πολλῶν εὐχαριστηθῇ ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν"</note> **that from many persons the gift toward us may be given thanks for on your behalf.**

---

<margin>C</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate Edition:** *For our glory is this, the testimony of our conscience.*
¶ Rather it should be said: *For our boasting.* <note>original: "ἡ γὰρ καύχησις ἡμῶν αὕτη ἐστίν, τὸ μαρτύριον τῆς συνειδήσεως ἡμῶν"</note> **For our boasting is this: the testimony of our conscience.** However, as has been noted elsewhere and will be seen below, the ancient translator <note>referring to the author of the Vulgate, traditionally St. Jerome</note> is accustomed to confuse these two nouns *glory* <note>original: "δόξα"</note> and *boasting* <note>original: "καύχησις"</note>, and even *the object of boasting* <note>original: "καύχημα"</note>, as if they were the same thing. So that we do not do this, we use "glory" and "boasting" for different things.

¶ **The Vulgate Edition:** *Than what you have read and known.*
¶ It can be said in the present tense: *you read* or even *you acknowledge.* Paul writes: <note>original: "αλλα η αναγινωσκετε, η και επιγινωσκετε"</note> **but what you read or also acknowledge.**

¶ **The Vulgate Edition:** *In the day of our Lord JESUS CHRIST.*
¶ In Paul it is simply: *in the day of the Lord Jesus.* <margin>D 6</margin> Paul writes: <note>original: "ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τοῦ κυρίου ἰησοῦ"</note> **in the day of the Lord Jesus.**

¶ **The Vulgate Edition:** *That there is with me 'it is' and 'it is not'.*
¶ It can also be said: *'yes, yes' and 'no, no'.* For Paul places two particles here, one affirming and the other denying, and he doubles each one. One designates affirmation, the other negation—the very ones the Savior commanded to be used when he forbade swearing. Paul writes: <note>original: "ἵνα ᾖ παρ’ ἐμοὶ τὸ ναὶ ναὶ, καὶ τὸ οὒ οὔ"</note> **that with me there should be 'yes, yes' and 'no, no'.**

¶ **The Vulgate Edition:** *For as many as are the promises of God, in him it is.*
¶ As has been said, wherever the ancient translator puts "it is" in this passage, we can also put a mark of affirmation, "yes." But the wording still remains ambiguous: whether it demonstrates "yes" in him, or refers to the Son of God. It is better understood to refer to the Son of God from the preceding discourse, in which the apostle says: "it was not in him 'yes' and 'no,' but in him it was 'yes'." It is certain here that those particles take the place of nouns, which is indicated by the article <note>original: "το"</note> which Paul added to them, and that "in him" refers to the Son of God. Therefore, it seems more just that in what follows, "in him" always refers to the Son of God. And those particles should be understood to occupy the place of nouns, with the verb "is" or "are" being supplied as appropriate. Paul writes: <note>original: "ὅσαι γὰρ ἐπαγγελίαι θεοῦ ἐν αὐτῷ, τὸ ναί"</note> **For as many as are the promises of God, in him they are 'yes'.**

¶ **The Vulgate Edition:** *Therefore also through him 'Amen' to God for your glory.*
¶ Therefore it was surplus, and it should be said: *in him 'Amen'.* Where "in him" refers to the Son of God. And "Amen" is a mark of confirmation, of praise, or of thanksgiving to God, or something similar, also performing the role of a noun. And it should not say "for your glory," but "for glory through us." This text of Paul is obscure because of these indeclinable particles <note>words that don't change their endings</note> inserted in place of declinable ones, unless one watches over the meaning very attentively. Paul writes: <note>original: "καὶ ἐν αὐτῷ, τὸ ἀμὴν τῷ θεῷ, πρὸς δόξαν δι’ ἡμῶν"</note> **and in him the 'Amen' to God for glory through us.**

...they look back so that, having been saddened, they may mend their ways and be faithful to God. ¶ Because if they are amended, they change their habits and advance toward the better: those breaking out into thanksgivings toward God are affected by a greater joy than the sorrow they felt from their error. For it is necessary for this new joy, being superior and more effective, to drive out the preceding sorrow. For indeed, Paul had been saddened; but lest all the Corinthians <margin>10</margin> should think they had saddened Paul and be consumed by some grief from that, he adds that not all of them had saddened him: but only some who were erring, and especially he who had committed that unspeakable adultery <note>Paul refers here to the "offender" mentioned in 2 Corinthians 2, often identified with the man who committed incest in 1 Corinthians 5.</note>, and so he says:

> ¶ But if anyone has caused sorrow, he has not saddened me, except in part, so that I might not seem to burden you all. For such a one, that rebuke is sufficient which was inflicted by the many. Therefore, on the contrary, you should rather forgive him and comfort him, lest perhaps such a one be consumed by an even greater sorrow. For which reason, I beseech you: resume your love toward him.

¶ Great is the kindness of Paul, and a sign of the Holy Spirit (who is kind and most kind) dwelling within him: he prays for the one by whom he had been saddened, and by whom the community—that is, the church of the Corinthians—had been scandalized. I say he prays that he be forgiven by all: that he be helped by consolation: that they watch attentively lest from excessive sorrow he fall into death or despair, but instead they should show a more abundant charity toward him because of his repentance. He covers his sin, as if it were deleted before God; nor does he name what it was, instructing us with what charity we ought to behave toward those who have repented of their crimes. For in what way—those sins which God says he has forgiven, covered, deleted, and of which he remembers no more—would you, unhappy man, burdened by your own sins as if with chains, uncover them, remember them, reproach them, and by both his name and your reproach, heap sorrow upon him over whom the angels in heaven had greater joy than over ninety-nine righteous who do not need repentance? Therefore, do not ever again either name or reproach what was done, but embrace love toward him again: or even increase it. And even now, Paul, through that obedience which those who represent the person of Christ owe to the apostle of Christ—just as the king’s legate represents the king—through that obedience, therefore, he asks that they forgive and spare him, that they comfort him, and pursue him with their accustomed charity. Lest, if they maintain their indignation, they be circumvented by Satan under the likeness of zeal, by not forgiving him. For Paul himself, in the person of Christ—or rather Christ in him—forgives him.
¶ For the cunning of the devil is sometimes to foster zeal (which indeed began well and appropriately) in some people more than is right: so that through zeal, which has the appearance of good, he may impede charity, which is both a higher good and more strictly commanded of us. For good zeal is that which is concluded in mercy, kindness, and love, and is an emulator of divine zeal. But it is evil in its perseverance and in that it does not imitate the placability of God at the end. And through this kind of zeal, the cunning of Satan ensnares many <margin>11</margin> who think they are pleasing God, when in this they do not please Him. For how would they please Him in that in which they are unlike God, who is great in forgiving? Therefore, Paul adds:

> <margin>TO</margin> ¶ For to this end also I wrote: that I might make a trial of you, whether you are obedient in all things. But to whom you forgive anything, I also. For I too, if I have forgiven anything to anyone, I have forgiven it for your sakes in the person of CHRIST, so that we may not be circumvented by Satan. For we are not ignorant of the devices of his mind.

¶ After he warned them, therefore, about the indiscreet retention of long-lasting indignation and zeal, which is usually done by the cunning of the serpent to ensnare souls, he now reveals that he went to Troas, which is a maritime city of Asia, hoping to find Titus. Not having found him there, and being affected by sorrow, he sailed from there into Macedonia; and the celebrated name of Christ was made known everywhere through him and Timothy. And this occurred because they preach in the sincerity of God, mixing in nothing of their own, speaking from God and before God. For no others are fit to obtain victory and triumph in preaching the name of God. Therefore, those who preach the word of God for gain through human cleverness are to be rejected and despised. For such as these do not preach in the sincerity of God, nor <margin>12</margin> as before God, but as before men. And they are hucksters <note>original: "cauponatores" — literally "wine-sellers" who were notorious in the ancient world for watering down their wine for profit; used here for those who corrupt or "water down" the Gospel for money.</note> of the word of God rather than preachers of the word of God. For Paul speaks in this manner:

> ¶ Furthermore, when I had come to Troas for the gospel of CHRIST, and a door was opened to me in the Lord: I had no rest for my spirit, because I did not find Titus my brother. But saying farewell to them, I set out for Macedonia. But thanks be to God, who always makes us triumph in CHRIST, and who manifests the odor of his knowledge through us in every place. For we are the good odor of CHRIST to God: among those who are being saved, and among those who are perishing. To these indeed, an odor of death unto death; but to those, an odor of life unto life. And who is sufficient for these things? For we are not (as many) huckstering the word of God: but as if from sincerity, but as if from God, in the sight of God, we speak in CHRIST.

¶ For Paul and apostolic men did not preach from themselves, being eager for new inventions and leaning on the dreams of a cold head so as to hold the people's attention with novelty; but they preached what the Lord Jesus poured into them. They did not conquer by themselves: but God produced the victory in them. He himself manifested His knowledge to the world through them: as a lyre-player through a lyre demonstrates his art; as incense through an incense-burner <note>original: "acerra" — a small box or vessel used for burning incense in Roman religious rituals.</note> demonstrates its sweet smell, an odor indeed good and sweet to God, but to the elect unto life, and to the reprobate unto death. Not indeed because it is of itself unto death: but because they did not receive that odor and rejected it once received. For of itself, it was unto life for all, more than the peaceful time when it is spring and the breaths of the west wind give life to all plants that receive that sweet breath. Therefore—

### CHAPTER III

And when Paul said, *for we are not (as many) peddling the word of God, but as if from sincerity, but as if from God, in the sight of God, we speak in Christ,* someone might perhaps say: "In saying these things, Paul begins to commend himself, to praise himself, and to exalt himself." By no means is it so; rather, he speaks the open and sincere truth, attributing honor not to himself but to God. To God indeed, who was working through him and his affections. And those who commend themselves to strangers do so by imploring the favor of others who are known. For Paul was not a stranger to the Corinthians, nor the Corinthians to Paul; he held them like a letter, inscribed indeed upon his own heart. Thus he followed them with a close and intimate love of the heart. And since the teaching of the Holy Spirit had inscribed their minds, he did not need the support of an external person to be commended to them. To praise oneself and exalt oneself is the habit of carnal and vain men, and those who are without the Spirit of God. Therefore, he does not commend himself, and much less does he praise or exalt himself. And so he says:

<margin>13</margin> > Do we begin again to commend ourselves? Or do we need (as some do) letters of recommendation to you, or letters of recommendation from you? You are our letter, written in our hearts, which is known and read by all men; you are manifested to be a letter of CHRIST, ministered by us, written not with ink but by the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on fleshy tablets of the heart.

See, therefore, how he did not speak the previous words for the sake of self-commendation—though those who understand carnally might strike at them as if they were said for the commendation of his own person. But he reveals with what confidence he said them, saying:

<margin>14</margin> > Such confidence we have through CHRIST toward God. Not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think anything as if from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God, who also has made us sufficient as ministers of a new testament, not of the letter, but of the spirit.

¶ He frankly admits that he is not sufficient to think anything from himself, but grants the glory of sufficiency to God, who made him sufficient—that is, who made Paul and his coworkers sufficient administrators of the New Testament. Is this the behavior of one praising himself or exalting himself? On the contrary, it is acknowledging and praising the benefits of God. And he said "of the new testament," not the old. For the Old Testament is the letter; the New is the spirit. The Old Testament is the first law; the New is the second. The Old is the law of Moses; the New is the gospel of Christ. The Old, if we follow it according to the letter, now kills; the New gives life. The Old, therefore, is the ministry of death; the New is the ministry of life. And just as shadows vanish when the light arrives, so death is removed when life arrives. And by the New Testament, the Old is removed, and by the law of Christ, the Mosaic law. For the mysteries of Christ are truth and light; the mysteries of Moses are traces and shadows. Truth remains forever; the trace is removed. Therefore, concerning the excellence of the New Testament (of which he is an administrator by God's indulgence) over the Old, Paul instructs the Corinthians, speaking thus of the Old and New:

<margin>15</margin> > For the letter kills, but the spirit gives life. But if the ministry of death, formed in letters on stones, was in glory, so that the children of Israel could not look intently at the face of Moses because of the glory of his face—which glory (I say) is passing away—how much more will the ministry of the spirit be in glory? For if the ministry of condemnation was glory, much more does the ministry of righteousness abound in glory. For indeed, that which was glorified in this part was not glorified, because of the glory that surpasses it. For if that which is passing away came through glory, much more that which remains is in glory.

¶ It has been said that the Old Testament is understood by the name of "the letter" and the New by the name of "the spirit," and not by an absurd proportion. For letters, unless they are formed by spirits—that is, by vowels—are vain and useless. And they can do nothing of themselves, but the spirit and the vowels give them all their power. So the Old Testament, unless it is animated by the Spirit of Christ, unless it is informed by the Gospel, is vain and useless. It can do only as much as the Gospel gives it the power to do. The Old Testament is also called the ministry of death, especially now. Although it was never completed...

...could administer justice: but only a shadowy kind, since at that time everyone descended to the underworld <note>original: "inferos"</note>. But what was this, if not a kind of death, or a certain image of death? The New Testament, however, administers a perfected justice, with which someone immediately flies up into the heavens. And therefore, it is rightly called the ministry of the spirit and of justice. Likewise, the Old Testament is the ministry of condemnation, because all who lived solely according to it were condemned to descend to the underworld. From there, Christ the Lord rescued many, specifically those whom he willed; for they were captives, and as a magnificent. conqueror, he led captivity captive. What if even now God has condemned and abolished that very old way, as it is written in Isaiah?

> Offer sacrifice no more in vain. New moons and sabbaths, and your festivals I will not bear. Your calendars and your solemnities my soul has hated. <note>Isaiah 1:13-14</note>

You read in Exodus of the glory of Moses' face during the tradition of the Old Testament; but this glory was not evident insofar as it was old (for there is nothing excellent in it as such), but insofar as the New was shining upon it. For he carried two horns <note>A common medieval/Renaissance interpretation of Exodus 34:29-30. The Hebrew word 'qaran' (to shine) was mistranslated in the Vulgate as 'cornuta' (horned).</note>: one figured the Old, the other the New. Therefore, the horn of the New Law shone upon the horn of the Old. For the Old Law does not shine with any light other than that of the New—just as the moon shines only with the light of the sun. For the New Law is altogether excellent and pre-shining. And everywhere Paul uses an argument based on a prologue familiar to philosophers: "if that which is less" and "that which is more," or if you prefer to call it "from the greater" or "from the lesser." And those who announced the Old Testament had hope in God, but by a much stronger reason, hope ought to grow strong in those who announce the New. For those who announced the Old had a veil over their minds, because Christ had not yet shone upon them. This veil—which signifies ignorance and the darkness of the mind—was symbolized by the veil that Moses placed

<margin>16</margin>
over his face when he spoke to the Jews from the mountain. But those who announce the New Law, the Gospel of Christ, do not have a veil of ignorance placed over their hearts; rather, all things are open to them in the light. Now, the light of the Gospel is Christ. Paul opens these mysteries to us, saying: Having therefore such hope, we use great confidence. And we do not act as Moses did, who put a veil over his face so that the children of Israel would not look intently at the end of that which is passing away—but their minds were blinded. For until this very day, that same veil remains in the reading of the Old Testament, not lifted (because it is taken away in CHRIST); but until this very day, when Moses is read, a veil is placed over their hearts. But whenever they turn to the Lord, the veil shall be taken away. Now the Lord is the Spirit; and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty. But we all, with unveiled face, reflecting the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord. ¶ Because the children of Israel could not look into the brightness of Moses' countenance—which light and brightness signified the end of the Old Law which is being removed, and the end is Christ, the paternal light—therefore Moses placed a veil over his face. And the Jews will have this veil for as long a time as a covering over the eyes of their own minds while reading the books of the Old Law, hiding its brightness and the light of truth, so long as they do not fix the eyes of their minds on Christ through faith. For Christ is the light of the books of their Law.

For just as light is the spirit for every reader, and no one can read without light, just as no one can live without life; so Christ is the spirit for those reading the ancient scriptures, without whom no one is able to understand them. He is the light, he is the spirit, he is the life of all understanding. But those who look toward Christ, illuminated by faith, drink in that glory, that light, and that spirit purely, with an unveiled and uncovered face as if from a mirror; and they are made Christ-formed <note>original: "Christiformes"</note>, marked by the same image—that is, by the seal and knowledge of the Son of God. Some do this more clearly, others more obscurely; not indeed because of any changeability in the truth, but according to the capacity of the mirrors—that is, of minds that are uncovered and not veiled. Indeed, one and the same person rises little by little from a less remarkable to a more remarkable knowledge of divine things. As from light to light, from glory to glory: so acts the Spirit of God, who is the inseparable attendant to the Son of God. To whom, with the Father, the fountain-like and super-ineffable light, praise and glory are due, forever and ever.

### CHAPTER IV

Therefore, just as the face of Moses shone from the glory of God, so from the glory of Christ was the mind of Paul and his fellow workers filled with the light of truth, so that they might grasp a clear, sincere, and open understanding of the law. They received this through the mercy of God to be administered to others. And therefore they did not slip, nor succumb to any evil, nor did they wish or think evil against anyone; instead, they cast far away from themselves all hidden wickedness of the heart and all the unseemly secrets of a lurking conscience, because they had obtained this mercy from God. Walking in simplicity, deceiving no one with the word of God, but manifesting the pure truth, and thus presenting themselves as approved, pure, and upright before God to every human conscience. Paul says it in this way:
<margin>17</margin>
¶Therefore, having this ministry, as we have obtained mercy, we do not lose heart; but we renounce the hidden things of shame, not walking in craftiness, nor handling the word of God deceitfully, but by the manifestation of the truth, commending ourselves to every man's conscience in the sight of God.
¶But someone might say: "If you present yourselves as such, and fear no human conscience that could accuse you, but rather commit yourselves to everyone, how then is the Gospel not known to all?" Certainly, they committed themselves in all truth and before God, because they were in no way accusable or blameworthy before Him. It was not due to a defect in their administration that it was not known to all. Rather, it is because the prince of this world—who is not a prince but a tyrant—the god of this world—who is not God, but the adversary of God—has blinded the minds of those who do not receive the Gospel. He has blinded them, I say, lest the light of the Gospel of the glory of CHRIST should shine upon them; lest Christ should be formed in them, who is the image of God. For He is the character and the consubstantial image of the Father’s substance <note>The author uses technical theological terms "character" and "hypostaseos" to argue that Christ shares the same essence as God the Father.</note>, as the Son: the consubstantial image of the Father. Therefore Paul adds:
<margin>18</margin>
¶But if our Gospel is also hidden, it is hidden to those who are perishing, in whom the god of this world has blinded the minds of unbelievers, so that the light of the Gospel of the glory of CHRIST, who is the image of God, should not shine upon them.
¶But again, those who perhaps listen in a carnal or worldly way will say: "You cast the blame for those who perish, who do not receive the Gospel, away from yourselves. You say you do not fail, that you have no internal wickedness of mind, that you do not walk in craftiness, that you deliver the word of God without deceit in the sole manifestation of truth, making every human conscience a witness before God. But by saying this, you justify yourselves; you preach yourselves." They were by no means justifying themselves, but rather the mercy of God. They were by no means preaching themselves, but the Lord Jesus Christ. In all these things they look to God as the author, not to themselves.
<margin>19</margin>
But carnal men, even in the things of God, look only at men, and are never able to look toward God, just as a blurry eye cannot look at the sun. Therefore Paul adds:
¶For we do not preach ourselves, but CHRIST JESUS the Lord; and ourselves your servants for JESUS' sake. For God, who commanded the light to shine out of darkness, has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the person of JESUS CHRIST. But we have this treasure in earthen vessels <note>term: earthen vessels <gloss>original: "testaceis vasis." Referring to the fragile, mortal human body holding the divine message.</gloss></note> (so that the excellence of the power may be of God and not from us); we are hard pressed on every side, but not crushed; in need, but not destitute; suffering persecution, but not forsaken; cast down, but not perishing; always carrying about in the body the dying of the Lord JESUS, so that the life of JESUS may also be manifested in our body. For while we live, we are constantly delivered unto death for JESUS' sake, so that the life of JESUS may be manifested in our mortal flesh. Therefore death works in us, but life in you.

<header>COMMENTARY</header>

¶ How did they preach themselves—those who preached the Lord Jesus, who called themselves nothing other than the servants of all for the sake of Jesus? In their minds, God—who made heaven and earth, and who commanded light to shine out of darkness (as it is written: *In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth, and darkness was upon the face of the deep. And God said, "Let there be light," and there was light*) <note>original: "In principio creauit deus cœlum & terrā/ & tenebræ erāt super faciē abyssi. Dixitq; deus fiat lux: & facta est lux." See Genesis 1:1-3.</note>—this God, I say, who spoke, commanded, and ordered light to shine out of darkness, has shone in them. He did this so that they, acting in the person of Christ and taking the place of Christ on earth, might illuminate others toward the knowledge of the glory of God. This is the recognition of the truth about God, which is bright and glorious. They carried this treasure of divine knowledge, powers, and signs in a fragile body, in clay-like and soft flesh, so that the "super-excellence" of wisdom, signs, and powers would be understood as belonging to God, and not to those who appeared in a fragile and mortal body. These men (as they themselves testify) could do nothing of themselves; yet God defended them in every trial so that they would not be crushed. When they were in need, He did not abandon them; in persecutions, He did not desert them; when cast down, He did not allow them to perish. He willed for them to be imitators of the sufferings of Christ in enduring tribulations, so that their flesh, by imitating the flesh of Christ, might finally shine with the immortality of Christ. And just as death worked in Christ through the afflictions of life, even unto the shame of the cross and the condemnation of a most foul death, so death worked in them throughout their entire lives, even unto the final punishment of martyrdom. By this imitation of Christ’s all-saving sacrifice, they were offered as a sacrifice to God. But for those who believed in Christ through them, death did not afflict them in every way; rather, they lived in faith, magnifying 
<margin>20</margin>
Christ, awaiting the resurrection of their mortal bodies and the same glory of immortality. Not without reason, therefore, does Paul add: ¶ *But since we have the same spirit of faith, according to what is written, "I believed, therefore have I spoken," we also believe, and therefore we speak; knowing that He who raised up the Lord JESUS will also raise us up through JESUS, and will place us with you. For all things are for your sakes, so that grace, having been multiplied through the thanksgiving of many, may abound to the glory of God.* <note>See 2 Corinthians 4:13-15.</note> Therefore we do not give up. For even if our outward man is decaying, yet the inward man is renewed day by day. For our current trouble, which is light and passing, works for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all measure, while we look not at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen. For the things which are seen are temporary; but the things which are not seen are eternal. ¶ In their punishments they did not succumb or fail, because they felt their soul being perfected day by day and approaching the possession of immortality, even if the body tended toward dissolution. Moreover, what they suffered in the body was light and momentary, but what remained—both for the soul immediately after the body, and from the resurrection when the body is taken up again—is eternal. Therefore, they did not focus on what was momentary, but on what is eternal; not on the things that were seen and are temporary and transitory, but on the things that are not seen, but are eternal and never end. May Christ Jesus, the eternal and invisible king, grant these things to us—He who is blessed by every creature, both visible and invisible, forever and above all. Amen.

¶ EXAMINATION of several points regarding the literal text. ¶ The Vulgate edition: *According as we have obtained mercy.* <note>original Latin: "Iuxta quod misericordiā cōsecuti sumus." 2 Cor 4:1.</note> ¶ Rather: *as*, or *insofar as*. Paul says: <note>original Greek: "κατὼς ἡλεήθημεν."</note> ¶ The Vulgate edition: *Nor adulterating the word of God.* <note>original: "Neq; adulterātes verbū dei." 2 Cor 4:2.</note> ¶ Rather, *neither dealing deceitfully with the word* (or the speech) of God, or *not deceiving with the word of God*. Paul says: <note>original Greek: "μηδὲ Δολοῦντες τὸν λόγον τοῦ θεοῦ."</note> ¶ *In whom the god of this world has blinded the minds of unbelievers.* <note>2 Cor 4:4.</note> ¶ There are those who want "the god of this world" to be understood as the true God, lest they seem to agree with the Manichaean <note>The Manichaeans were a dualistic sect that believed in two gods: one good and one evil. The author is explaining how to interpret "god of this world" without implying a second evil god.</note> in asserting two gods: one of good things, the other of evil. Truly, if it is taken to mean the "prince of this world" <note>The Devil.</note> who blinds the minds of the wicked, this addition of "of this world" diminishes the title and is taken in a bad sense; and to "blind" is used properly and effectively, as when it is said *their own malice blinded them.* If, however, "God" is taken for the true God, the addition "of this world" is taken in a good sense for the present transitory world, and "blinded" is used not effectively, but permissively. For as much as it depends on God, He opens the eyes of all, makes them see, and wants them to breathe in the pure light and come to the knowledge of the truth. We followed the first sense in our exposition, thinking nothing similar to the Manichaean madness, nor going against the custom of the Apostle, who even calls the belly the "god" of gluttons. *Whose god,* he says, *is their belly.* <note>Philippians 3:19.</note> But the belly-god is not God; nor in that way is the "god of this world" God, but rather the opposite of God. ¶ The Vulgate edition: *That the light of the gospel of the glory of CHRIST should not shine.* <note>2 Cor 4:4.</note> ¶ It should say *that the light should not shine to them.* For the relative pronoun "to them" or "to those" or something similar is missing.

### III

Now "face," now "person" is interpreted. But in this place, "person" is more appropriate—referring to Paul. *unto the illumination of the knowledge of the glory of God, in the person of Jesus Christ.* <note>original Greek: "πρὸς φωτισμὸν τῆς γνώσεως τῆς δόξης τοῦ θεοῦ, ἐν προσώπῳ ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ." See 2 Corinthians 4:6.</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *We are perplexed [aporiamur], but not driven to despair.* ¶ It would be better to say "we are in need," but expressed through participles; and indeed, Paul speaks elegantly. "Aporiamur" signifies nothing among the Latins, but *aporia* means "indigence" or "want" in Greek, from which comes the verb *aporoumai*, which among the Greeks means "I am in need." Paul says: *being in need, but not utterly lacking.* <note>original Greek: "ἀπορούμενοι, ἀλλ’ οὐκ ἐξαπορούμενοι." The author is arguing that the Greek implies a state of being at a loss or in want, rather than just psychological perplexity.</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *We are humbled, but not confounded.* <margin>C 19</margin> ¶ This is not found in Paul’s text. ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Always carrying about the dying [mortificationem] of JESUS CHRIST in our body.* ¶ It should be read as "always the dying of the Lord Jesus." Paul says: *always carrying the dying of the Lord Jesus in the body.* <note>original Greek: "πάντοτε τὴν νέκρωσιν τοῦ κυρίου ἰησοῦ, ἐν τῷ σώματι περιφέροντες."</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *That the life of JESUS also might be made manifest in our bodies.* ¶ It should be stated in the singular: "in our body." Paul says: *that also the life of Jesus might be made manifest in our body.* <note>original Greek: "ἵνα καὶ ἡ ζωὴ τοῦ ἰησοῦ, ἐν τῷ σώματι ἡμῶν φανερωθῇ."</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Therefore death works in us.* ¶ It should rather be said: "Wherefore death indeed works in us." Paul says: *wherefore <margin>C 20</margin> death indeed works in us.* <note>original Greek: "ὥστε ὁ μὲν θάνατος ἐν ἡμῖν ἐνεργεῖτε."</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *But having the same spirit of faith, as it is written.* ¶ It can be read: "through whom it is written." For whatever the prophets write, they are written through the Holy Spirit as the one who pours it in—as the principal author. Paul says: *but having the same spirit of faith, according to what is written.* <note>original Greek: "ἔχοντες δὲ τὸ αὐτὸ πνεῦμα τῆς πίστεως, κατὰ τὸ γεγραμμένον."</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Knowing that he who raised up JESUS.* ¶ It should say: "the Lord Jesus." For "the Lord" is missing. Paul says: *knowing that he who raised the Lord Jesus.* <note>original Greek: "εἰδότες ὅτι ὁ ἐγείρας τὸν κύριον ἰησοῦν."</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Will also raise us up with JESUS.* ¶ It should be said: "will also raise us up through Jesus." Paul says: *will also raise us through Jesus.* <margin>D 20</margin> <note>original Greek: "καὶ ἡμᾶς διὰ ἰησοῦ ἐγερεῖ."</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *That grace, abounding through many in thanksgiving, may abound to the glory of God.* ¶ It can be read: "on account of the thanksgiving of many." Paul says: *that grace, having abounded through the many, might increase thanksgiving to the glory of God.* <note>original Greek: "ἵνα ἡ χάρις πλεονάσασα διὰ τῶν πλειόνων τὴν εὐχαριστίαν, περισσεύσῃ εἰς τὴν δόξαν τοῦ θεοῦ."</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *For that which is at present is momentary and light.* ¶ Neither "at present" nor "momentary" is found; but rather a single adverb which signifies "immediately," "transitively," or "in passing." Paul says: *for the lightness of the moment.* <note>original Greek: "τὸ γὰρ παραυτίκα ἐλαφρὸν."</note>

->CHAPTER V<-

<image-desc>Large woodcut ornamental initial E, featuring a stylized foliage and scroll design within a square border.</image-desc>
Our outer man is the mortal flesh; the inner man is the immortal soul. Our earthly house of this habitation—that is, of this present life and sojourn—is again the mortal flesh, which we inhabit as long as we lead this present life. The "building from God, eternal in the heavens" is the spiritual, immortal, and indissoluble body of the resurrection. Our earthly house is opaque; that other house is clear and radiant, for those who shall be worthy to be "clothed over" with that garment. Although our earthly house is from God, as it is written: *Thy hands, Lord, have made me and fashioned me wholly round about,* <note>original: "Manus tuę domine fecerūt me & plasmauerūt me/totū in circuitu." See Job 10:8.</note> yet human labor has intervened. In that heavenly and radiant house, however, only the divine hand is applied. While our soul contemplates this divine, heavenly, and immortal house, it groans and sighs to be clothed over with it. Indeed, the soul shall be clothed over with it if it be found clothed in faith and good works. But if it be found naked, it shall not be clothed with that house, but rather with a darkness suited for torments and a perpetual death that never yields. And the soul is so affected toward that immortal garment that it wishes even this mortal body, while it is mortal, to be immortal. It does not wish to be "unclothed," even though the body weighs it down. If it were possible, without being unclothed and without setting aside the mortal, the soul would wish for it to be changed and to be clothed over with that immortal tunic. Therefore, the fact that the soul is so affected toward the body is not because of the mortal body, but because of the immortal body; God provides this instinct to the soul, even if it does not know in many respects what it affects. Yet in these matters, those who have received the Holy Spirit—the sponsor, or rather the guarantee and <term>earnest</term> <note>original: "arrabonē." From the Greek 'arrabon,' meaning a down payment or deposit that guarantees the full amount later.</note> of this immortal gift—know why they groan and what they desire. And therefore Paul says: ¶ *For we have it explored and certain that if our earthly house of this habitation be dissolved, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens. For in this also we groan, desiring to be clothed over with our dwelling which is from heaven—if indeed we be found clothed and not naked. For we who are in this habitation groan, being burdened, because we do not wish to be unclothed, but clothed over, so that what is mortal may be absorbed by life. Now he who fashioned us for this very thing is God, and he has given us the earnest of the Spirit for this purpose.* ¶ The Holy Spirit gives this certain and indubitable knowledge of the state of the future resurrection to holy men: both concerning the absence of God in the present life, and His presence in the other. Not that we are ever "absent" from God, neither in this life nor the future, for all things are present to Him. But in this life He is absent to us through "appearance" [species], yet present through faith—just as a blind man is equally as present to light, colors, and a mirror as one who sees, yet the light, colors, and mirror are absent to him in appearance, though present in faith. For he believes, and believes without doubt, that light, colors, and mirrors exist. But in the other life, God will be present through appearance. And faith will no longer be in darkness, but in light. And he shall not only believe, but shall also know and perceive most perfectly—as if a man blind until adulthood were then to receive sight: light, color, and mirrors he would then know by appearance. And he shall believe...

¶ In what way did they preach themselves, those who preached the Lord Jesus? They said nothing else than that they were the servants of all for the sake of Jesus. In their minds, God—who made heaven and earth and who commanded light to shine out of darkness (as it is written: *In the beginning God created heaven and earth, and darkness was upon the face of the deep. And God said, let there be light, and light was made* <note>Genesis 1:1-3</note>)—God, I say, who spoke, ordered, and commanded light to arise from the darkness, has shone in them. They, acting in the place of Christ and bearing the person of Christ on earth, were to illuminate others toward the knowledge of the glory of God. This knowledge is the recognition of the bright and glorious truth concerning God. They carried this treasure of divine knowledge, of powers, and of signs in a fragile body, in clay-like and soft flesh. They did this so that the surpassing excellence of wisdom, of signs, and of powers might be understood as being attributed to God, and not to those who appeared in a fragile and mortal body. As they themselves testify, they could do nothing of themselves. In every matter they were pressed down, yet God defended them so they would not be crushed; they were in need, but He did not abandon them; in persecutions, He did not desert them; though cast down, He did not permit them to perish. By enduring these things, He willed them to be imitators of the sufferings of Christ, so that their flesh, in imitating the flesh of Christ, might finally shine with the immortality of Christ. And just as death, through afflictions, worked life in Christ—even to the shame of the cross and the condemnation of a most foul death—so in them, death worked throughout their whole lives, even unto the final punishment of martyrdom. By this devotion to the all-saving sacrifice of Christ, they were offered as a sacrifice to God. However, for those who clung to Christ through faith, death did not afflict them in every way; rather, in life, possessing that same faith, they looked forward with great expectation to the resurrection of their mortal bodies and that same glorious immortality. Therefore, Paul adds with good reason: ¶ *But since we have the same spirit of faith, as it is written: "I believed, therefore I have spoken," we also believe, and therefore we speak; knowing that He who raised the Lord JESUS will also raise us through JESUS, and will place us with you. For all things are for your sakes, so that grace, having been multiplied through the thanksgiving of many, may overflow to the glory of God.* <note>2 Corinthians 4:13-15</note> For this reason, we do not succumb. For although our outward man is decaying, yet the inward man is renewed day by day. For that which is momentary and our tribulation works in us an eternal weight of glory, surpassing all measure, while we look not at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen. For the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal. ¶ They did not succumb in their punishments, nor did they fail, because they felt their soul being perfected day by day and approaching the possession of immortality, even if the body tended toward its dissolution. Furthermore, what they suffered in the body was light and momentary; but what remained—both for the soul immediately after the body, and from the resurrection when the body is taken up again—was eternal. Therefore, they did not pay attention to that which was momentary, but to that which belongs to eternity; not to things that were seen and were temporal and transitory, but to those things which are not seen, which are eternal and never come to an end. May Christ Jesus, the eternal and invisible king, grant these things to us; He who is blessed by every creature, both visible and invisible, forever and above all.

In explaining this, we have followed the first interpretation, thinking nothing similar to the Manichaean madness, nor opposing apostolic custom, since Paul even calls the belly the "god" of gluttons. *Whose god,* he says, *is their belly.* <note>Philippians 3:19</note> But the belly is not truly God. Neither in that way is the "god of this world" God, but rather the opposing demon. ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *That the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ should not shine.* ¶ It should be said: "that the light should not shine **to them**."
