->CHAPTER V<-

Our outer man is the mortal flesh. The inner man is the immortal soul. Our earthly house of this habitation—that is, of this present life and residency—is again the mortal flesh in which we dwell as long as we lead this present life. The building from God, eternal in the heavens, is the spiritual, immortal, and indestructible body resulting from the resurrection. Our earthly house is dark; that other house is bright and shining, at least for those who are worthy to be clothed over with that garment. Although our earthly house is from God, as it is written: *Your hands, O Lord, have made me and fashioned me all around* <note>Job 10:8</note>, human labor nevertheless intervenes. In that heavenly and radiant house, however, only the divine hand is applied. While our soul contemplates this divine, heavenly, and immortal house, it groans and sighs to be "clothed over" with it. It will surely be clothed over if it be found dressed in faith and good works; but if it be found naked, it shall not be clothed with that house, but shall be found dark and suited for torments and a perpetual death that never yields. And the soul is so affected toward that immortal garment that it wishes this mortal body, while it is still mortal, to become immortal. It does not wish to be stripped of it, even though the body weighs it down. If it were possible, without stripping off or putting away the mortal, the soul would wish it to be changed and to be "clothed over" with that immortal tunic. Therefore, the reason the soul is so attached to the body is not because of the mortal body itself, but because of the immortal body; God provides this instinct to the soul, even if it does not know in most cases what it yearns for. Yet in these matters, it does know why
<margin>21</margin>
it groans and what it yearns for: those who have received the Holy Spirit, the sponsor—or rather the guarantor and <term>pledge</term> <note>original: *arrabo*, a Semitic loanword used in Greek to mean a down payment that guarantees the full amount later</note>—of this immortal gift. And therefore Paul says: ¶ For we have found it to be certain that if our earthly house of this habitation be dissolved, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens. For in this we groan, desiring to be clothed over with our habitation which is from heaven—if indeed, being clothed, we shall not be found naked. For we who are in this habitation groan, being burdened, because we do not wish to be stripped, but clothed over, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life. Now he who has prepared us for this very thing is God, who also has given us the pledge of the Spirit. ¶ The Holy Spirit gives this sure and indubitable knowledge concerning the state of the future resurrection to holy men: both concerning the absence of God in the present life, and His presence in the other. Not that we are ever absent from God, either in this or in the future life, for all things are present to Him; but in this life, He is absent from us in "appearance" but present through "faith." Just as a blind man is as physically present to light, colors, and a mirror as one who sees, yet the light, colors, and mirror are absent to him in appearance, though present in faith. <meta>This page continues the commentary on Paul’s Second Epistle to the Corinthians, specifically moving into Chapter 5. The author is exploring the theological distinction between "faith" (believing without seeing) and "sight" (the direct vision of God), using the metaphor of blindness to describe those who lack spiritual belief.</meta>

<header>COMMENTARY</header>

...which he believed; but through an enlightened belief, which is more than simply believing. For to know and to understand most clearly is this: those things which were previously present to him by faith will be present to him by sight. If a blind man were certain that he would receive his sight in a certain year, how he would sigh! How he would pant with his whole soul to see? Why, therefore, ought we not also to sigh and pant, so that we may see God through direct vision, if the blind sigh for nothing more than sensible light and the final spectacles of things? But take away the faith of such things from the blind man: he no longer sighs for them, for he is touched by no desire for them. In the same way, take away faith in divine things: no one sighs for them, and no one is touched by an affection for them—unless perhaps by a certain deaf instinct of nature, which he does not understand, by which he is continually goaded and pricked to breathe for that life which is without goading, pricking, or pain. But he is blind—indeed, worse than blind; deaf—and deafer than the deaf. ¶ O Pliny! ¶ O Lucian! ¶ O senseless Epicurus! <note>The author cites Pliny the Elder, Lucian of Samosata, and Epicurus as representatives of worldly philosophy or skepticism that remains "blind" to spiritual truth.</note> O you deaf and blind ones, and as many as are disciples of this unhappy school in this regard! ¶ You are leaders of the deaf and blind, yet worse than the deaf and blind yourselves. How many instances of blindness, how many are blinded daily! May God turn away this most pitiable plague. Let faith heal what the blind and deaf demon of infidelity has wounded. But whoever has faith—and the more he has it—the more vehemently and ardently he affects that direct vision. For faith increases the instinct and adds a desire that "happily torments" him. And if he who has faith alone is still blind and still deaf <note>In the sense that he does not yet "see" God face-to-face.</note>, he nevertheless sees and hears, and understands the instinct and the stings of that instinct. Here, therefore, is a man who is blind and deaf, yet less blind than the blind man, and less deaf than the deaf man, and better than both. And who had greater

<margin>22</margin> faith than Paul and those like him? Therefore, he truly and most certainly says, and is able to say, that which he subjoined in this manner:
> Therefore we are always confident, knowing that while we are at home in the body, we are absent from the Lord. (For we walk by faith, not by sight.) We are confident, I say, and willing rather to be absent from the body, and to be present with the Lord. Wherefore we labor honorably, that, whether absent or present, we may be accepted by him. For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ; that every one may receive the things done in his body, according to that he hath done, whether it be good or bad. Knowing therefore the terror of the Lord, we persuade men; but we are made manifest unto God; and I trust also are made manifest in your consciences. <note>original: 2 Corinthians 5:6-11</note>

And so, this discourse means the same thing regarding being "absent from the Lord" and "present with the Lord": that as long as we are in the mortal body, we endure the absence of the Lord through the privation of sight, and after the casting off of the body, we possess the presence of the Lord through the apprehension of sight, insofar as God has made us capable of Himself. Even if this discourse seems to be inverted. And there are two things which ought especially to move us to please God. First: the love of contemplating that sight, which is the good above every good and the prize <term>braveium</term> <note>From the Greek 'brabeion,' meaning the prize awarded to a winner in a race or contest.</note> for which we all ought to strive and contend nobly. Second: the fear of the judge, who will judge everyone and condemn those who have not contended, or have not contended lawfully to receive such an ineffable reward. The noble and those who are mentally alert are sufficiently animated to please God, to run, and to contend by the first of these things. But the more ignoble and the lazy are goaded, excited, and plucked to run by the second—the fear of God and of divine judgment—as if by a certain sting. For God wants all, both noble and ignoble, to run and contend to receive the prize; and through those who know His fear, He wishes to announce this to men, and through it to excite even those who are less noble to contend and to please Him. Paul touched upon these two causes. The first, when he said: "we walk by faith, not by sight." The second, when he added: "knowing therefore the fear of the Lord, we persuade men." And he who reads in the spirit knows what kind of man he is. For he is known by God; therefore this knowledge is not so much his own as it is God’s knowledge. But he who reads in the flesh is ignorant of himself. He who thinks he knows, does not know. What wonder? For he is ignored by God. For from the flesh comes ignorance, distrust, and the denial of light. But Paul read in the spirit; therefore he knew himself to be manifest to God. For how could he not know himself to be manifest, he who looked back upon God's light in himself like the cast of a glancing eye? But in the flesh, no brightness of the divine glancing eye appears. Therefore, Paul was also manifest to the Corinthians, if they were looking spiritually and not according to the flesh—which Paul both hoped for and wished well for them. But in saying this, does he wish to flatter the Corinthians? Does he seek to capture favor? Does he seek to commend himself? By no means. For to flatter is a human thing and of the flesh. And he does not need human favor who has divine favor. He does not

<margin>23</margin> need human commendation whom God commends. Therefore he adds:
> ¶ For we commend not ourselves again unto you, but give you occasion to glory on our behalf, that ye may have somewhat to answer them which glory in appearance, and not in heart. <note>original: 2 Corinthians 5:12</note>

¶ Those who are wise according to the flesh seek exterior glory and are ignorant of the true interior glory. They glory in appearance <note>literally "in the face" (facietenus)</note>; they cannot glory in the heart. Against such people, the Corinthians could justly glory through the spiritual words of Paul. In the words of Paul there is excellence; in the words of Paul there is modesty. When there is excellence, it regards God, and the discourse is in the spirit and a certain divine ecstasy <term>extasis</term>. When there is modesty, it regards men, and he accommodates himself to human custom. And charity brings forth both: the charity of God brings forth excellence; the charity of neighbor brings forth modesty. Wherefore he subjoins...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the fifth chapter of Paul’s Second Epistle to the Corinthians. Having discussed the longing for the heavenly dwelling, the author now addresses the transformative power of Christ's love and the nature of the "new creature" in the process of divine reconciliation.</meta>

<page-num>141</page-num>
<header>III 2 Corinthians 14</header>

<margin>24</margin> Paul says: ¶ Whether we are beside ourselves for God, or whether we are of sound mind for you: certainly the love of Christ compels us, discerning this: that one died for all, therefore all have died. And he died for all, so that those who live should no longer live for themselves, but for him who died and rose again for them. ¶ **The Mystery.** If Christ died for all, then truly all have died. And most especially those around whom the mysteries of Christ have been enacted have died through the death of Christ. Therefore, just as all have died through Christ’s death, so they live through Christ’s life, not their own. That life, moreover, is spiritual. Thus, all ought to live spiritually. And no one living in Christ lives carnally <note>original: "carnaliter" — meaning according to the physical or worldly desires rather than spiritual ones</note>, as a person living in Christ. Nor can anyone who is carnal be recognized in Christ, even if they were once carnal. What then shall we say of those who confess Christ but live carnally? We shall say they are no longer living members of Christ’s body, but are either dead, or perhaps cut off from that established body—severed from that pure mass. For life in Christ is a new life and a spiritual life. The old and carnal life has passed away. There is a new creature in Christ. Other things which <margin>25</margin> belonged to the old creature have passed away, unless by the freedom of your will you slide back into them, contrary to the new creature. Accordingly, Paul adds: ¶ Therefore, from now on, we know no one according to the flesh. Even if we once knew Christ according to the flesh, we no longer know him in this way. Thus, if anyone is a new creature in Christ, the old things have passed away; behold, all things have been made new. But all things are from God, who reconciled us to himself through Jesus Christ and gave to us the ministry of reconciliation: namely, that God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, not counting their sins against them. And he placed in us the word of reconciliation. Therefore, we act as ambassadors for Christ, as though God were exhorting through us. We beg on Christ’s behalf: be reconciled to God. For him who knew no sin, he made to be sin for us, so that we might be the righteousness of God in him.

¶ Come now, you will ask: when did we know Christ according to the flesh? We, existing in the flesh and not yet in the spirit, knew Christ when Christ was first announced to us. When we were catechumens <note>original: "cathecumini" — those receiving formal instruction in the Christian faith before being baptized</note>, we received the word of Christ, but were not yet initiated into his sacred rites. This is what it means for us to know Christ according to the flesh. But once we were baptized—because we are a new creature, and old things have passed away, and all things are made new (all things indeed made new by God)—we no longer know Christ according to the flesh, but according to the spirit. That phrase "according to the flesh" is aptly joined to us before our second and spiritual birth. However, it could never be aptly joined to Christ, who never lived according to the flesh, but lived according to the spirit more eminently than all others—indeed, most super-eminently.

But you will add: if someone lived according to the virtues and avoided all vices before regeneration, would they not be living according to the spirit? By no means. For how could one live according to the spirit who does not yet possess the spirit, and has not yet received the spirit? For one receives the spirit in regeneration <note>original: "regeneratione" — referring to the spiritual rebirth through baptism</note>. Therefore, those virtues are not spiritual, but are moral and human—the kind that philosophers preach, not the kind that holy theologians celebrate. I call "theologians" Peter, Paul, John, and the rest of the apostles, and their distinguished disciples Dionysius, Hierotheus, and the like <note>Dionysius the Areopagite and Hierotheus the Theologian were traditionally considered early converts and scholars of the apostolic age</note>, who saw by the light of the divine spirit. They did not despise the light of the human spirit, but they considered it a small thing compared to the contemplation of the divine.

You will ask further: when did God reconcile the world to himself through Jesus Christ? By the name "world," we must understand the people of the world. He reconciled and daily reconciles the world to himself. First: when the children of wrath are made children of God through the washing of regeneration. Second: when children have wandered away and fallen from the spiritual life back to the life of the flesh, and they repent of that carnal life, and return as suppliants to the spiritual Father, saying: "Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you; I am no longer worthy to be called your son." And the pious and merciful Father receives them and brings out for them the first robe, and clothes them in that spiritual righteousness which they had lost, and gives himself as the food of eternal life for a meal while the choirs of angels rejoice and exult. And to this double reconciliation, Paul and other coworkers of the Gospel cry out as legates and orators of God in the person of Christ: "We pray, we beg, we beseech in the person of Christ: be reconciled to God."

O immense kindness of God! Which so sweetly recalls the offense—us who were turned away and willing to perish—and so lovingly invites us. He, whom every creature is too lowly to even petition, instead prays and begs us. Who, then, would not run toward reconciliation? Who would despair of such great mercy? What is this, that he who is supreme made him who knew no sin to be sin for us, and willed him to be fixed to the cross like sin itself? For death was owed to sin. He willed, I say, that he should be fixed to the cross (a punishment owed to the unjust), so that in him, whom he made sin for us, he might make us the righteousness of God. We were sin. He, who for our sake took our sin upon himself—bearing the burden of sin upon his holy and innocent neck—is the righteousness of God. Death was owed to us; life to him. But he, being infinitely good, made an exchange: carrying our heavy weight and accepting death, while bestowing his life upon us and taking up our obligation.

The author emphasizes the divine mercy of God, who through Christ exchanges human sin for divine righteousness.</summary>

<header>COMMENTARY</header>

...and affixing [our sin] to the cross with himself; while liberating us. To him, our invincible liberator, be honor, excellence, glory, and power, unto ages of ages.

### EXAMINATION of several points concerning the literal text.
<margin>A</margin> ¶ The Vulgate edition: *This dwelling be dissolved: that we have a building from God.* <note>original: "Huius habitationis dissoluatur: q edificationem ex deo habemus" — quoting 2 Cor 5:1.</note> ¶ *Which remained.* And the reading "we have" is found. This "have" possesses the meaning of the future tense here, which is frequent in the sacred scriptures. 
<margin>A 21</margin> Paul: *the dwelling being destroyed, we have a building from God.* <note>original: "τοῦ σκήνους καταλυθῆ, οἰκοδομὴν ἐκ θεοῦ ἔχομεν"</note> ¶ The Vulgate edition: *But he who fashions us for this very thing is God.* ¶ Rather, "affected" or "perfected," <note>original: "affecit aut perfecit"</note> for this kind of "affection" is toward the garment of immortality: a certain perfection which God has implanted in our nature. Paul: *Now he who has prepared us for this very thing is God.* <note>original: "ὁ δὲ κατεργασάμενος ἡμᾶς εἰς αὐτὸ θεός"</note> ¶ The Vulgate edition: *Who gave us the pledge of the spirit.* ¶ It should be read: *and* gave. Paul: *and giving* 
<margin>B 22</margin> *to us the pledge of the spirit.* <note>original: "καὶ δοὺς ἡμῖν τὸν ἀῤῥαβῶνα τοῦ πνεύματος"</note> ¶ The Vulgate edition: *Since we are as long in the body: we are on a journey from the Lord.* ¶ Rather: *while present in the body, we are absent from the Lord.* For these respond to each other from the opposite, just as "present" and "absent" do in Latin; and equally so is Paul's vocabulary in Greek. And where the old translator here translates "we are on a journey" <note>original: "peregrinamur"</note>, a little later he translates it as "absent." Why then not also before? And where he translates this as "present," why not also before? It is true that what he translates as "journeying" is usually translated that way because those on a journey are absent from home; but it is more fittingly interpreted everywhere here as being "present" and "absent." From this, the habit of Paul's speech—who frequently responds from opposites—is more readily understood, and the sense is better. Paul: *that being at home in the body, we are away from the Lord.* <note>original: "ὅτι ἐνδημοῦντες ἐν τῷ σώματι ἐκδημοῦμεν ἀπὸ τοῦ κυρίου"</note> And a little below, the old translator says: *whether away, or at home, to be pleasing to him.* <note>original: "εἴτε ἐκδημοῦντες, εἴτε ἐνδημοῦντες εὐάρεστοι αὐτῷ εἶναι"</note> He translates it thus: *whether absent or present, to please him.* If he had followed the prior translation, he would have had to say: *whether journeying or present, to please him.*
<margin>C 24</margin> ¶ The Vulgate edition: *That each one may receive the proper things of the body, according to what he has done: whether good or evil.* ¶ It should rather be said "those things through the body" <note>original: "quæ per corpus"</note> toward what he has done: whether good or evil; that is, whether he did those things toward good or toward evil. Paul: *each one the things through the body, according to what he practiced, whether good or bad.* <note>original: "ἕκαστος τὰ διὰ τοῦ σώματος, πρὸς ἃ ἔπραξεν, εἴτε ἀγαθὸν, εἴτε κακόν"</note> ¶ The Vulgate edition: *For whether we exceed in mind, it is for God; whether we are sober, it is for you.* ¶ What he said as "we exceed" <note>original: "excedimus"</note> is not bad. However, because "excellence" is usually taken in a good sense, while "excess" is often taken in a bad sense—and in this manner "to excel" and "to exceed"—lest "we exceed" should create a fantasy of an evil excess, we preferred to say "we excel" <note>original: "excellimus"</note>. For this excellence (or if you prefer, exceeding), by which hearts made and inspired by God exceed in those things which are of God and transcend human things, is called "ecstasy." For they "exceed" themselves and are "outside" themselves in the divine spirit. It is of this ecstasy and excess that the divine Paul speaks here. Paul: *For whether we were beside ourselves, it is for God; whether we are of sound mind, it is for you.* <note>original: "εἴτε γὰρ ἐξέστημεν θεῷ, εἴτε σωφρονοῦμεν ὑμῖν"</note>
<margin>C 25</margin> ¶ The Vulgate edition: *Therefore we from this have known no one according to the flesh.* ¶ It should be said "from this now," or more appropriately "henceforth." Paul: *so that we from the now, no one* 
<margin>D 25</margin> *know according to the flesh.* <note>original: "ὥστε ἡμεῖς ἀπὸ τοῦ νῦν, οὐδένα οἴδαμεν κατὰ σάρκα"</note> ¶ The Vulgate edition: *Since indeed God was in CHRIST reconciling the world to himself.* ¶ Rather it should be said: *that since God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself*, or in one word, "was-reconciling" to himself. Paul: *how that God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself.* <note>original: "ὡς ὅτι θεὸς ἦν ἐν χρισῷ κόσμον καταλάσσων ἑαυτῷ"</note> ¶ The Vulgate edition: *For CHRIST therefore we perform the duties of an embassy.* ¶ It can be said: *we are appointed as speakers and ambassadors.* Paul: *On behalf of Christ then we act as ambassadors.* <note>original: "ὑπὲρ χριστοῦ οὖν πρεσβεύομεν"</note> ¶ *Him who knew no sin, he made sin for us.* ¶ He does not say that CHRIST committed sin—for that is insane and full of absurd impiety. For (as Peter says and is the truth itself) he is the one who committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth. But it is said: that the Father made Christ "sin" for us, and that "sin" was to be affixed to the cross for us. For our sin was affixed to the cross together with him, extinguished and dead. And God made us "righteousness" in him. For thus that incomprehensible wisdom performed this marvelous exchange <note>original: "mirabile commercium" — a famous theological concept describing Christ taking our sin and us taking his righteousness</note>: making him sin in us, and us righteousness in him; revealing to us the riches of his ineffable kindness and mercy, and meeting the ingenuity and cunning of the evil one in a wondrous and unthinkable way; so that he whom the evil one had deceived through envy, He might liberate through mercy and kindness. To Him again be glory and thanksgiving forever.

Without a doubt, of God: by whose merciful will they had been sent to men, and of whom they were ambassadors and speakers. <meta>This page continues the commentary on the Second Epistle to the Corinthians, specifically moving into Chapter 6. # III 2nd Corinthians

...now if they are rejected: they perish; and they receive that grace of the highest King—the eternal King (who is God)—to no purpose, in vain, and fruitlessly. If someone wanted to take up the cenobitic <note>From the Greek *koinobion*, referring to a communal monastic life as opposed to living as a hermit.</note> life, perhaps someone would describe to them the form of living of that holy congregation which they maintain—not boasting, not commending himself, or thinking of the empty breeze of worldly favor, but setting forth their life and his own as an example of the future life for the other's salvation, if they so desire. In this manner, Paul sets forth his own life and the lives of God’s fellow-workers in the Gospel of Christ; not for the sake of extolling himself or commending his own person, but for the sake of the salvation of the Corinthians and all others, following through on his exhortation: he proposes it to be imitated and adds: 

<margin>27</margin> ¶ We give no offense to anyone, so that our ministry is not blamed, but in everything we show ourselves to be commendable: as ministers of God, in much patience, in pressures, in necessities, in hardships, in stripes, in prisons, in seditions, in labors, in vigils, in fasts, in chastity, in knowledge, in long-suffering, in kindness, in the Holy Spirit, in unfeigned love, in the word of truth, in the power of God, through the armor of righteousness on the right hand and on the left, through honor and dishonor, through ill-report and good-report, as deceivers and yet true, as unknown and yet known, as dying and behold we live, as chastened and not killed, as sorrowful yet always rejoicing, as poor yet enriching many, as having nothing and yet possessing all things. 

¶ How different is the spiritual life from the carnal life, the heavenly from the earthly, the divine from the worldly! The spiritual, heavenly, divine life offends no one ever. By itself, it is commended before God and men. Like light, it reveals itself to every eye; it is beneficial in itself. The spiritual life is strong in pressures, sufficient in necessities, expanding in hardships, healthy in stripes, free in prisons, 

<margin>A</margin> superior to seditions, unbroken by labors, insuperable by vigils and fasts, clean in chastity, provident in knowledge, not vengeful, kind, relying not on its own sense but on the Holy Spirit, truly loving without any simulation, truthful in speech, relying not on its own but on the power of God, steady in prosperity and adversity, never deserting the armor of God's justice, and to which dishonor and ill-report lead to blessedness. 

"Blessed are you," he says, "when men curse you, and persecute you, and say all manner of evil against you, lying because of me." <margin>B</margin> <note>Quoting Matthew 5:11 to support the Pauline paradoxes.</note> What is thought to be a deception in this spiritual life is actually truth and direction toward every good. What is unknown is the knowledge of God. What is death is life. What is chastisement is quickening. What is sadness is joy. What is poverty is riches. What is the destitution of things is the possession of all goods. 

But the carnal, earthly, and worldly life corresponds entirely from the opposite: it is impatient, it is powerless against tribulations. It cannot bear needs, hardships, stripes, or prisons; instead, it forces others to suffer these things. It is seditious, idle, given to sleep and gluttony, intemperate, ignorant, furious in vengeance, harsh, leaning on its own sense, feigned, lying in word, trusting in its own strengths, 

<margin>C</margin> armed with injustices in both fortunes. No glory, no true honor, no good fame. Whether it be honor or dishonor, worldly fame or infamy: it is misery either way. When it seems truthful, it deceives. When known, illustrious, and splendid, it is unknown to God. Its life is death. Its chastisement is the beginning of the future Gehenna <note>The place of final punishment; hell.</note>. Its joy is the perpetual weeping that will follow. Its riches are want. And when it seems to possess all things, in truth it possesses nothing at all. 

But this world—this world blinds the eyes of its own, so that they believe light to be darkness, and think darkness to be light, and they flee from good itself and pursue evil. And do we not see where the frost flourishes, all things are constricted; where there is heat, all things spread themselves out and dilate into the wide? In this way, where there is no love, all things are constricted, capable of no spiritual gift. For the spirit is more ample; it is not captured by these narrow straits, just as heaven is not captured by the earth, nor divinity by the sensible and worldly machinery. 

But charity <note>original: *charitas* — divine, self-giving love.</note> dilates and spreads, so that minds themselves are 

<margin>28</margin> more spacious than the world. For they receive the spirit of God, which he says the world cannot receive. Therefore the apostle exhorts the Corinthians to love, without which they cannot receive this spiritual, divine, and heavenly life, saying: 

¶ Our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians. Our heart is dilated; you are not constricted in us, but you are constricted in your own bowels <note>original: *praecordiis* — literally the area around the heart, used here to mean the internal seat of feelings and capacity for love.</note>. Now for the same recompense (I speak as to children) you also be dilated. 

¶ He who is loved is in the lover. If the lover loves much, he is greatly dilated, and receives the beloved amply and diffusely. But if the beloved loves little in return, he receives the lover narrowly; for he is constricted in himself and poorly capable. Paul, however, loved the Corinthians much; and therefore he received them amply and diffusely in his heart. For he had that fountain-like love of the Holy Spirit in him, which compelled him to love diffusely and divinely. On the contrary, the Corinthians did not love as much in return. Not without reason, therefore, he exhorts them as children that they should strive to dilate themselves, having received the spirit of love, and to repay like with like in loving. But just as the spiritual life and the carnal life cannot cohere, as neither justice and injustice, light and darkness, the angel of light and the angel of darkness (for these are opposites), so neither can the believer with the unbeliever, nor...

# COMMENTARY

<margin>29</margin>
...the worship of Christ with the worship of an idol: nor the temple of God with the temple of a demon. Therefore Paul says to the Corinthians: ¶ Do not be diversely joined <note>original: "varie copulari"; usually translated as "unequally yoked"</note> with unbelievers. For what participation has justice with injustice? And what fellowship has light with darkness? What agreement also has CHRIST with Beliar? <note>original: "beliar"; a variant of Belial, a name for the devil or a personification of wickedness.</note> Or what portion has a believer with an unbeliever? And what conspiracy has the temple of God with idols? For you are the temple of the living God, just as God says: "Because I will dwell in them and walk among them; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people." Wherefore, "come out from the midst of them and be separate," says the Lord, "and touch no unclean thing; and I will receive you. And I will be a father to you, and you shall be sons and daughters to me," says the Lord Almighty. ¶ When Paul says "just as God says," he shows himself to be a prophet, and that God speaks a divine oracle through his mouth. Nor is it always necessary to seek from others what he speaks by way of prophecy. For he himself was a prophet, and one in whom the Holy Spirit spoke as familiarly as in other prophets. Does he not say in another place, prophesying: "But the Spirit manifestly says," subjoining a prophecy concerning the end times? If you look for that in another prophet, you lose your labor. Do not, therefore, strive to seek the present prophecy from another either, although the prophet Isaiah has something partly close to it where he opens the mysteries of Christ, the evangelists, and the apostles. "Depart," he says, "depart; go out from there; touch no polluted thing; go out from the midst of her. Be clean, you who carry the vessels of the Lord." Who does not know that the worship of demons is polluted and unclean, which the Corinthians were forbidden to touch, and so too every sin? And how could they not carry the vessels of the Lord, who were themselves the temples of God? May the Lord Jesus thus deign to make us his temples, and so purify us, that he may deign to dwell in us perpetually, and to walk in us perpetually, and to place in us—and receive from us—hymns and praises of his glory and thanksgivings.

<margin>A 26</margin>
¶ EXAMINATION of several points regarding the literal text. ¶ The Vulgate edition <note>The "Vulgata" refers to the standard Latin Bible translation used in the Western Church.</note> reads: "Helping, however, we exhort." ¶ More appropriately: "Working together, however, we exhort." For we properly say that we "work together" <note>original: "cooperari"</note> with God; however, it is not quite appropriate (as has been noted elsewhere) to say we "help" <note>original: "adiuuare"</note> God. Paul says: *dei synergeountes de parakaloumen* <note>original Greek: συμεργοῦντες δὲ παρακαλοῦμεν; meaning "Working together, we exhort."</note>.

<margin>A 27</margin>
¶ The Vulgate edition reads: "Lest our ministry be blamed." ¶ The word "our" is redundant according to the Greek. But because it makes the speech clearer, we have left that little particle in. Paul says: *hina mē mōmēthē hē diakonia* <note>original Greek: ἵνα μὴ μωμηθῇ ἡ διακονία; meaning "lest the ministry be blamed."</note>. ¶ The Vulgate edition reads: "But in all things let us exhibit ourselves as ministers of God." ¶ It should rather be said in the present tense, "we exhibit," and with the nominative "ministers of God." Ambrose <note>Saint Ambrose (c. 340–397), an influential Bishop of Milan and theologian.</note> observed this in his translation as well. Paul says: *all’ en panti synistōntes heautous hōs theou diakonoi* <note>original Greek: ἀλλ’ ἐν παντὶ συνιστῶντες ἑαυτοὺς ὡς θεοῦ διάκονοι; meaning "but in everything commending ourselves as God’s ministers."</note>.

<margin>B 27</margin>
¶ The Vulgate edition reads: "Through the armor of justice on the right and on the left." ¶ Thus from Paul: "through the armor of justice of the right and of the left." But because this is the same as saying "of favorable and adverse things," and these are perhaps clearer, we preferred to say "of favorable and adverse things" in place of "of the right and of the left." Paul says: *dia tōn hoplōn tēs dikaiosynēs tōn dexiōn kai aristerōn* <note>original Greek: διὰ τῶν ὅπλων τῆς δικαιοσύνης τῶν δεξιῶν καὶ ἀριστερῶν.</note>.

<margin>C 28</margin>
¶ The Vulgate edition reads: "You are not straitened in us, but you are straitened in your own bowels." ¶ It should rather be said: "you are constrained" <note>The author is debating the Latin grammar of "angustiamini" versus "angustamini."</note> in both places. For from "straits" (*angustia*) I am "constrained" (*angustor*), just as from "molestation" (*molestia*) I am "molested" (*molestor*); this seems better said than "narrowed" (*angustior*). But let the grammarians debate these things. Paul says: *ou stenochōreisthe en hēmin, stenochōreisthe de en splanchnois hymōn* <note>original Greek: οὐ στενοχωρεῖσθε ἐν ἡμῖν, στενοχωρεῖσθε δὲ ἐν σπλάγχνοις ὑμῶν.</note>. ¶ The Vulgate edition reads: "Having the same recompense." ¶ The word "having" is not found in Paul. And he seems to intend "by the same recompense," using the accusative in place of the ablative case. This is the same as saying, "paying back in kind, you also be enlarged." For he invites them to an equal return of love; which, however, was not possible unless the Spirit of the Lord were present more abundantly. Paul says: *tēn dē autēn antimisthian* <note>original Greek: τὴν δὴ αὐτὴν ἀντιμισθίαν.</note> and immediately subjoins: "I speak as to children."

<margin>C 28</margin>
¶ The Vulgate edition reads: "of CHRIST to Beliar." ¶ The Greeks write it with an *r* at the end, *Beliar*. Among the Hebrews, they wish this to designate "blindness of light" <note>The author's etymology for Beliar/Belial; historically it is more likely associated with "worthlessness."</note>—a name undoubtedly fitting and accommodated to the angel of darkness. Paul says: *christou pros beliar* <note>original Greek: χριστοῦ πρὸς βελίαρ.</note>.

### CHAPTER VII.

<margin>30</margin>
Since it was said above: "touch no unclean thing and I will receive you, and I will be a father to you, and you shall be sons and daughters to me," says the Lord Almighty: the apostle seems to elucidate what "touch no unclean thing" means, and that it is the same as universally abstaining from every stain of flesh and spirit, saying: ¶ Since we have these promises, therefore, beloved: let us cleanse ourselves from every stain of flesh and spirit, perfecting sanctification in the fear of God. Receive us: <note>original: "Capite nos"; literally "Take us in."</note> we have injured no one, we have corrupted no one, we have defrauded no one. ¶ What is "Receive us" but "Receive our doctrine"? Or rather, not ours, but the doctrine of God, which promises you eternal life. And when he says he has struck no one with injury, corrupted no one, defrauded no one: he does not say this as if reproaching them or noting them in some way, as if he had been defrauded by them or hurt by them in some matter. Therefore he adds: ¶ Not to your condemnation...

### III 143 2 Cor.

...no one, I would by no means wish it said. For I have said before: **that you are in our hearts to die together and to live together.** <note>original: "vt cōmoriar & cō-viuam"; quoting 2 Corinthians 7:3</note> **I have much confidence toward you; I have much boasting on your behalf.** ¶ This is the mildness, this is the gentleness of the spirit: which would be able to draw even carnal people to a desire for the spiritual life. For the spirit is kind. But he reveals from where this confidence and boasting regarding the Corinthians increased for him. It was from the arrival of Titus, who, coming from the Corinthians, narrated their correction to Paul—indeed, he showed all the duties of humanity exhibited toward himself, and that a longing was held by them for Paul, along with **mourning, and wonderful zeal, and the fire of love.** He says, therefore: ¶ **I am filled with consolation; I superabound with joy in all our pressure.** <note>The Latin "pressura" refers to tribulation or distress.</note> **For when we had come into Macedonia, our flesh was given no rest, but we were pressed in every thing: fights without, fears within. But God, who consoles the humble, consoled us by the arrival of Titus. And not only by his arrival, but also by the consolation with which he was consoled by you, reporting to us your longing, your mourning, your zeal for me, so that I rejoice even more.** ¶ Wherever the apostles descended, the machinations of the
<margin>32</margin>
evil one were not lacking—pressures and innumerable tribulations—so that, broken by the pressures of the flesh, they might desist from the publication of the gospel. But the insuperable Spirit who dwelt in them made them superior to all things, victors over all hardships. And as there were many pressures, so were there many consolations: now from God above, now from below through the growth of the faithful. Paul does not deny that this happened to him. Rather, this holy life is so full of joy, so full of consolation, that they find joy and consolation even from sadness. But not from just any sadness: but from that which brings about a conversion to God. For he who sins turns away from God; he who repents turns back to God from that turning away. Therefore, sadness that converts those who have turned away is holy and
<margin>33</margin>
according to God, and deservedly induces spiritual joy, not only in men but even in the Savior, who reveals it to the angels of God. <note>A reference to Luke 15:10 regarding joy in heaven over one sinner who repents.</note> Regarding this, Paul adds: ¶ **Because although I saddened you in my letter, I am not led by regret, even if I did regret it.** <note>Paul expresses the human tension of having to write a harsh letter for the benefit of the recipients.</note> **For I see that even if that letter affected you with sadness for an hour, I now rejoice; not that you were affected with sadness, but that you were affected with sadness unto repentance. For you had sadness according to God, so that you suffered no detriment from us. For sadness according to God works repentance unto salvation which has no regret; but the sadness of the world works death. For behold, this very sadness of yours according to God, how much diligence it has worked in you, and even defense, and indignation, and fear, and longing, and zeal, and vengeance! In every thing you have established yourselves to be pure in the matter.** ¶ He who cures wounds induces pain, but that pain leads to health, which has no pain. And such is the sadness according to God, which is unto salvation. But the pain that leads to disease, and disease to destruction, is likened to the sadness of the world, which leads to death. Suppose someone loses the wealth that fueled his greed; he is saddened, he mourns, he complains, he is indignant, he accuses heaven and God—this is the sadness of the world, and it gives birth to death. Someone else seeks a bishopric <note>The author uses a contemporary example to explain Paul's point.</note> (I am mistaken—not a bishopric, but the pride of that high dignity, or the temporal things which ought to follow spiritual things like a shadow); he is frustrated, he falls from his ambitious hope, he is saddened, he mourns inconsolably, the consolation of friends is desolation to his wounded heart, he curses his enemies, he shuts out his friends—this is the sadness of the world, and it is the herald of a future death that is perpetual. If, however, he should come to his senses and grieve that he had such insane concupiscence, and with rising tears humbly pray for pardon, and choose to lead a poor life without pride and without greed, so that he might not from now on so dangerously offend God (whom he knows is pleased by humility and innocent poverty), for every ambitious man, every proud and arrogant man, and every greedy man is harmful and unjust—this indeed is sadness according to God and a herald of eternal life, not unlike the <term>hypostasis</term> <note>original: "hypostasis"; here referring to the sediment in a person's urine used by medieval and Renaissance physicians to diagnose the return of health.</note> of digested human urine, which is an indication of future health. And indeed the Corinthians were affected by this sadness at the first of Paul’s letters and by his censure, as was appropriate. For here, keeping silent about the name of the crime, Paul calls it a "matter" in which the Corinthians showed themselves chaste, pure, and upright. For they understood well enough. And
<margin>34</margin>
if they did not yet understand from those things which he immediately subjoins, they were able to understand promptly enough. For Paul adds: ¶ **Therefore, although I wrote to you, it was not for the sake of him who did the injury, nor for the sake of him who suffered the injury, but I wrote for the sake of manifesting your diligence, which is for us among you in the sight of God. For this reason we are comforted. And in your consolation we rejoiced much more abundantly in the joy of Titus, because his spirit was refreshed by all of you. Because if I boasted anything to him on your behalf, I am not shamed. But as we spoke all things to you in truth, so also our boasting which was made to Titus was found to be the truth. And his heart is more abundantly moved toward you, as he remembers the obedience of all of you, and in what way with fear...**

### CHAPTER VIII.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration within a decorative rectangular frame depicting an eagle perched on a rocky crag or nest, gazing directly at a radiant sun in the upper right. Beside the eagle are smaller eaglets, representing the classical motif of the eagle testing its young by their ability to gaze at the sun.</image-desc>

He commended the Corinthians for that sorrow which they had undertaken toward repentance and a multifaceted, saving correction. Now he extols the Macedonians with public praise for their liberality and works of charity toward the saints. He does this so that, by their example, he might provoke the Corinthians to pursue a similar virtue, not unlike a father with his sons when he proposes the examples of their ancestors to be imitated, painting before their eyes a life which they ought to look up to and admire. In this way, eagles provoke their chicks to fly; in this way, they defend the unshaken gaze of their eyes against the sun. These things are more useful and more necessary for those being provoked than for those provoking them. So too, to exercise charity and to dispense good things to the poor of Christ is far more useful and worthwhile for those dispensing them than for those encouraging this duty of piety, or even for those receiving it. For in this, the givers become more like God, who bestows all things on everyone freely and receives nothing from anyone, except the thanksgivings of grateful hearts for the benefits received. These thanksgivings are also received by those who are generous toward the saints and the poor—who, because of their mercy and sacred work of liberality, are an image of the Divine—from those holy men. 
<margin>
35
</margin>
Therefore, when Paul encourages and provokes the Corinthians in this manner by proposing the image of others, he thinks chiefly of their own good, not the good of others. Even if his own good and that of others exists equally, it is nonetheless less than theirs. He says, therefore: ¶ **We make known to you, brothers, the grace of God which was given in the churches of Macedonia. For in a great trial of affliction <term>pressure</term>, the abundance of their joy and their deep poverty abounded unto the riches of their simplicity <term>sincerity</term>. For according to their strength, I bear witness, and even beyond their strength, they were spontaneous, asking us with much entreaty that the grace and the fellowship of the ministry to the saints might be done. And not as we had hoped; nevertheless, they gave themselves first to the Lord, and then to us by the will of God. For which reason we asked Titus that, just as he had begun before, so he might also finish this grace among you.** ¶ Titus, a man of great perfection—attained not by human sense but granted by the Spirit of God—is placed in charge of forming virtues, and spiritual ones at that. For earthly people who are being formed toward divine things are like youths who flee from discipline; whatever the teachers labor at for the building up of character, the youths think these are mere schemes, devised not for their own benefit but only for the use of the teachers. But it is not so at all. For God has implanted better things in those who lead. I mean those who lead...

III 144

<margin>2 Corinthians</margin>
...they are: those who truly lead. For to lead is a divine condition. For who would deny that God, and indeed he alone, presides over all things? And therefore, though Paul wishes them to become <note>literally "diviniformes," or god-like in form</note> in this regard and for this grace to be acquired by them, he does not command it, but rather gives counsel. This is lest the Corinthians' bounty toward the saints should appear to be coerced—which is a kind of imitation of divine liberality and grace (than which nothing more free can be imagined)—and lest it should seem to weave some scheme for one’s own benefit or private utility. Yet Paul was most distant from such a suspicion, as one who never ate the bread of idleness. For what does it profit us if we have many imitations of God, yet lack that one which we could have, by which he disposes all things? Since he commands us to be merciful, just as our heavenly Father is merciful, the duty of this virtue must be joined to all things. Wherefore Paul 
<margin>36</margin>
adds: *But as you abound in everything—in faith, and speech, and knowledge, and all diligence, and in your love toward us—so also may you abound in this grace.* <note>original: "gratia," here referring specifically to the "grace" of giving or charity</note> *I say this not as a command, but through the diligence of others, I am testing the sincerity of your love.* This "diligence of others" by which he tests, proves, and provokes the Corinthians was that of the Macedonians. <note>The Macedonians were residents of a neighboring province who had given generously despite their own poverty.</note> Truly, in practicing good deeds, we should attend not so much to human actions as to divine ones; we should be provoked to emulation not so much by men as by Christ. He gave us all things, and he gave himself. And though he was rich and "super-rich," enriching all, he willed to be poor. He did this so that when you give to his poor, he might receive your good gift. *As long,* he said, *as you did it for one of the least of these my brothers, you did it for me.* <note>A reference to Matthew 25:40.</note> Therefore, let these acts of grace be done now, not for the sake of the Macedonians, but for the imitation of Christ; and let us understand that we have given not so much to the poor as to Christ. And let the rich venerate Christ in every poor person, who became poor for us; and conversely, let the poor venerate Christ in every liberal rich person, as the one who enriches the world. For the poverty of Christ is the greatest wealth of the world, and his riches are the fullness of eternal joy and an unfailing, inexhaustible treasury of 
<margin>37</margin>
good. Come then: in this grace of bounty, let Christ provoke us most greatly, with his apostle thus exhorting us in the name of the Corinthians: *For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you through his poverty might become rich.* And I give my judgment in this matter: for this is profitable for you, who began not only to do, but also to be willing since the previous year. But now perform the deed as well, so that just as there is a readiness of will, so there may be a completion out of what you have. For if the readiness is present, it is well-accepted according to what a person has, if he has anything, and not according to what he does not have. ¶ Everyone ought to bestow bounty upon Christ's poor out of what he has and what is his own with a ready will, and this is accepted by God; but not out of what he does not have. For if he distributes another's property as his own, that is surely not acceptable to God. And it often happens that those who have an abundance of earthly goods suffer a penury of spiritual ones; and conversely, those who abound in spiritual goods suffer a lack of temporal ones. Therefore, there ought to be a certain reciprocal compensation, so that a sufficient equality may be achieved. For each excess is insufficient by itself, but the abundance and excess of earthly goods is more so. Therefore, when those who give earthly things are made participants in spiritual things, and those who communicate spiritual things become participants in earthly ones, a certain sufficient equality, pleasing to God, is 
<margin>38</margin>
created. Paul, therefore, wants this mutual response of participation to result in a holy and sufficient equality when he says: *For it is not that others should have relief and you should have distress, but that there should be equality. At the present time, your abundance should supply their need, so that their abundance may also be a supplement for your need, so that there may be equality.* As it is written: *He who gathered much had nothing over, and he who gathered little had no lack.* <note>original: "qui multum, non abundavit: & qui paucum, non minoratus est."</note> ¶ At that time, certainly, the holy poor who were in Jerusalem lacked earthly things, but they abounded in spiritual things. And conversely, those who abounded in riches lacked spiritual things. Both, therefore, both abounded and lacked; and in turn, these filled the lack of those, and those the lack of these, and they supplied what was missing. The figure of the Manna showed that this equality pleases God, as is read in Exodus. ¶ Among those who gathered manna: those who gathered more had no more than those who gathered less; nor did those who gathered less have any less than those who gathered more. It is fitting, therefore, for the saints—and those who are fed by the same manna but in truth, that is, by the body of Christ—to strive to equalize their possessions according to their dignity. For in this, that the highest bestow their duties upon the lower, and the lower return obedience to the higher, the highest are equalized with the lowest and the lowest with the highest without confusion, each remaining in his own grade and order. The influence of the superiors fills the need of the inferiors, and the reflux of the inferiors assists their superiors and those who lead. And in this the apostle commends Titus: that of his own accord (God so moving him), he undertook the duty of soliciting the Corinthians regarding this business. To him, he joined faithful companions who were to receive what had been collected to be carried to the saints in Jerusalem. And so...

# ☛ COMMENTARY

<margin>39</margin> he says. ¶ **But thanks be to God, who put this same earnest care for you into the heart of Titus. For he not only accepted our appeal, but being very diligent, he went to you of his own accord. And we have sent with him the brother whose praise is in the gospel throughout all the churches. And not only that, but he was also chosen by the churches as our traveling companion with this grace <note>The "grace" here refers to the charitable collection for the poor in Jerusalem.</note> which is administered by us to the glory of the Lord himself, and to show our ready mind. We are taking care that no one should be able to blame us in this abundance which is administered by us.**

¶ Who does not know that Luke the Evangelist was a companion of Paul, and that during the time he was with Paul he wrote that holy book titled *The Acts of the Apostles*? However, he was not always with Paul, as is recognized from this passage. Instead, as circumstances required, he was sent to other places. Therefore, it is no wonder if he does not record the countless deeds of Paul which Paul performed while he was absent. For he wrote only those things which he himself saw while present, and which he witnessed while they were happening. But with what great vigilance they took care lest they cause harm by any example (for those who lead cause the most harm by their example).

<margin>40</margin> Paul reveals this more openly, not for his own commendation, but for the instruction of those who lead, and he adds: ¶ **For we provide for good things, not only before the Lord, but also before men. And we have sent with them our brother, whom we have often proved diligent in many things, but now much more diligent, because of the great confidence which he has toward you; whether because Titus is my close companion in my place and a fellow-worker among you, or because our brothers are apostles <note>The term "apostle" is used here in its literal sense of "messenger" or "one sent out" by the local churches.</note> of the churches, who are the glory of Christ. Therefore, show the proof of your love and of our boasting on your behalf toward them in the sight of the churches.**

¶ Who this third brother might be, whom he commends and whom he had as a companion and tent-mate in place of Titus, is perhaps Sylvanus <note>Also known as Silas, a frequent companion of Paul.</note>. But because he does not name him, it is not known for certain who it is. Nevertheless, they were distinguished in the churches and were like apostles—not those first apostles who were tent-mates of Christ and were placed as princes over all the earth, but "second" apostles, or "apostles of the churches." Yet they shone brightly to the glory of Christ. To Him be all honor, all light, splendor, and glory forever. Amen.

<margin>A 35</margin> ¶ **EXAMINATION of several points regarding the literal text.** ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** <note>The Vulgate was the standard Latin Bible translation of the time.</note> *And that in much experience.* ¶ It is redundant; Paul wrote: *that in much testing.* <note>original Greek: ὅτι ἐν πολλῇ δοκιμῇ</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *I speak not as if commanding.* ¶ Rather: *I speak not according to a precept,* or *I speak not commanding.* For the particle *as if* <note>original Latin: "quasi"</note> is in no way found in Paul’s meaning. Paul wrote: *I speak not according to command.* <note>original Greek: οὐ κατ’ ἐπιταγὴν λέγω</note>

<margin>B 36 37</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Because for your sakes he became poor, though he was rich, that through his poverty you might be rich.* ¶ we read in the archetypes <note>The "archetypes" refers to the original Greek manuscripts.</note> in the first person: *for our sakes.* And subsequently in the first person: *that through his poverty we might be rich,* or rather *we might become rich.* Paul wrote: *that for our sakes he became poor, being rich, so that we by his poverty might be enriched.* <note>original Greek: ὅτι δι’ ἡμᾶς ἐπτώχευσεν πλούσιοϛ ὤν , ἵνα ἡμεῖς τῇ ἐκείνου πτωχείᾳ πλουτήσωμεν</note>

<margin>C 39</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *And I give counsel in this.* ¶ It can be said: *and I give my judgment in this.* Paul wrote: *and I give an opinion in this.* <note>original Greek: καὶ γνώμην ἐν τούτῳ δίδωμι</note>

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *But I give thanks to God.* ¶ In the nominative singular it is said: *Thanks be to God.* Paul wrote: *thanks be to God.* <note>original Greek: χάρις δὲ τῷ θεῷ</note>

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *And our destined will.* ¶ Rather: *our promptness* or *our alacrity*, or if you prefer, *our ready mind.* For the ancient translator previously translated the same word as *ready mind* when he said: *for if the will is ready according to what one has, it is accepted.* And in the following chapter, *ready mind*, where he has: *for I know your ready mind.* Paul wrote: *and our readiness.* <note>original Greek: καὶ προθυμίαν ἡμῶν</note>

<margin>D 39</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *In this abundance which is administered by us to the glory of the Lord.* ¶ The phrase *to the glory of the Lord* is redundant here. Paul wrote: *in this abundance which is administered by us.* <note>original Greek: ἐν τῇ ἁδρότητι ταύτῃ τῇ διακονουμένῃ ὑφ’ ἡμῶν</note> And he immediately adds: *for we provide good things.* <note>original Greek: προνοοῦμεν γὰρ καλά</note>

<margin>D 40</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Whether for Titus, who is my companion and a helper among you.* ¶ The words *who is* <note>original Latin: "qui est"</note> are redundant. It should rather be said: *as for Titus, my companion and a fellow-worker among you.* But the ancient translator added *who is* because he perhaps believed the phrase should refer to Titus, not noticing that Paul would then have made a grammatical error <note>a solecism</note>, since the name of Titus in Greek is in the genitive case while *my companion* is in the nominative; it refers rather to the one he is commending, not to Titus. The particle *because* makes the meaning clearer. Paul wrote: *whether on behalf of Titus, my companion, and toward you a fellow-worker.* <note>original Greek: εἴτε ὑπὲρ τίτου , κοινωνὸς ἐμὸς , καὶ εἰς ὑμᾶς συνεργός</note>

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *The apostles of the churches, the glory of Christ.* ¶ Rather in the nominative: *the glory of Christ.* And it does not refer to the "churches," but to the "apostles," as if we were to say: *the apostles, who are the glory of Christ.* Paul wrote: *apostles of the churches, the glory of Christ.* <note>original Greek: ἀπόστολοι ἐκκλησιῶν , δόξα χριστοῦ</note> For if a wise son is the glory of the father, how much more are the apostles—the first offspring and progeny of Christ for bringing new sacraments to the world—the glory of Christ? None have ever been wiser, better, or more admirable than they.

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *And our glory for you.* ¶ Rather: *of our boasting for you.* Paul wrote: *and of our boasting on your behalf.* <note>original Greek: καὶ ἡμῶν καυχήσεως ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν</note>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Second Epistle to the Corinthians. Having finished Chapter 8 regarding the collection for the poor in Jerusalem, the author now begins Chapter 9, where Paul shifts from introducing his messengers to encouraging the Corinthians to follow through on their promised generosity so that they (and Paul) are not embarrassed when the collection is actually gathered.</meta>

### CHAPTER IX

<margin>41</margin>
Now he commends the Corinthians: so that they might not need the provocation <note>In this context, "provocation" means "calling forth" or "inspiring" someone to action.</note> of others; rather, by their own example, others might be inspired to this duty of piety, saying:
¶ **For as touching the ministering to the saints, it is superfluous for me to write to you: for I know the forwardness of your mind, for which I boast of you to them of Macedonia, that Achaia was ready a year ago; and your zeal hath provoked very many.** <note>original: "De ministratione profecto..." 2 Corinthians 9:1-2</note>
¶ Achaia is the region in which Corinth is situated, having the Ionian Sea on one side and the Aegean Sea on the other. And the Apostle adds the reason why he sent the brothers ahead to them: namely, so that the Macedonians—who had been stirred to this work of virtue by the Corinthians' example—would not themselves slacken if they found the Corinthians unprepared or negligent in this duty of piety. For such is the nature of zeal: if it is intense in one, it grows in another; but if it slackens in one, it gradually withers in the other. This can be seen in those who compete with zeal for victory: as in music, the wrestling ground <note>original: "palaestra"</note>, jumping, and similar exercises. In these, the intensity of zeal in the contestants is praised, and slackness leads to reproach, even though the end goal is only empty glory.

<margin>42</margin>
What then, when the contention is for virtue, for a holy zeal, and for perfect glory? Therefore Paul adds: ¶ **But I have sent the brothers, lest our boasting of you should be in vain in this behalf; that (as I said) ye may be ready: lest haply if they of Macedonia come with me, and find you unprepared, we (that we say not, ye) should be ashamed in this same confident boasting. Therefore I thought it necessary to exhort the brothers, that they would go before unto you, and make up beforehand your bounty, whereof ye had notice before, that the same might be ready, as a matter of bounty, and not as of covetousness.** <note>original: "Misi autem fratres..." 2 Corinthians 9:3-5</note>

¶ What is this "substance of boasting," except the participation in the pious distribution to the saints, which results in honor and glory for the givers? Here "boasting" is not taken as vain-glory, but as true glory: for when we see things done for the honor of God, we exult and boast that we can tell these things to others, to the honor of those who performed such noble deeds and to inspire similar actions. When I think of the Kingdom of Baetica <note>original: "Bethicum regnum." This refers to the Kingdom of Granada in Southern Spain, which was finally "restored to Christ" by the Spanish monarchs in 1492.</note> restored to Christ in our own time, my heart leaps, and I boast in extolling the one who brought forth such a magnificent victory for Christ. I call those "holy wars" which make people holy, not those which kill brothers or snatch empires from brothers. I do the same when I hear that several kingdoms of regions unknown for so many centuries have come to Christ the Lord, and that the "Ethiopians" <note>A term often used for people of the Southern Hemisphere or distant lands in the Age of Discovery.</note> now sing hymns to Christ under another pole and another sky. I call that prince happy whom God chose for such illustrious things. And this boasting should be held in the deeds of others rather than one's own, and especially one should boast in Him who grants the grace to perform such outstanding and noble deeds. He alone is to be looked up to, He is to be admired, He is to be invoked for the growth of the family and the undertakings. So also Paul boasted and sought a greater boasting in the Corinthians. What also does it mean for "your blessing to be ready as a blessing, and not as covetousness"?
<margin>A</margin>
Certainly, when every harvest is multiplied and abounds, it is a sign of God's blessing. **Thou shalt bless** (it says) **the crown of the year of thy goodness, and thy fields shall be filled with plenty.** <note>Psalm 65:11</note>
<margin>B</margin>
However, when the harvest fails as a punishment for crimes, it is a sign of a certain curse. **From the face of the curse** (it says) **the earth has mourned; the fields of the desert are dried up.** <note>Jeremiah 23:10</note>
<margin>C</margin>
Thus, a "blessing" is a spontaneous providence, and a "curse" is the withdrawal of providence. Therefore, gifts are given "as a blessing" when they are distributed spontaneously, delightfully, and abundantly. I say "abundantly" according to one's strength and means and with a desire for providence—that is, imitating divine providence.
<margin>D</margin>
They are "as covetousness," however, when they are given either unwillingly, or not abundantly according to one's strength, or without the care of providing. For the covetous person is like the cursed earth, which yields either nothing or very little, as if caring nothing for the providence of those it ought to nourish.
<margin>E</margin>
But the merciful and liberal person is like the blessed earth and the most intent providence of all (by the will of God). What reward shall the covetous receive, except that of covetousness and curse, which is owed to the sterile and unfruitful—just as at the voice of the Lord [the fig tree] withered? And what for the merciful and liberal, except mercy and blessing? Justly does God bring sterility upon the covetous and take away or diminish their means.
<margin>43</margin>
And on the contrary, He multiplies the goods of the merciful and increases their means. For this reason, Paul not without cause adds:
<margin>F</margin>
¶ **But this I say, He which soweth sparingly shall reap also sparingly; and he which soweth bountifully shall reap also bountifully. Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver. And God is able to make all grace abound toward you; that ye, always having all sufficiency in all things, may abound to every good work: (As it is written, He hath dispersed abroad; he hath given to the poor: his righteousness remaineth for ever.)** <note>2 Corinthians 9:6-9</note>
¶ **He who purposes in his heart:** he urges the work more diligently, so that he may carry out what he has well intended in his heart.

The author draws parallels between biblical "blessings" and contemporary events like the Reconquista of Granada and the Age of Discovery to illustrate the nature of true zeal and divine providence.</summary>

# COMMENTARY ON 2 CORINTHIANS

...he has set forth. If he has set nothing forth, he is himself sluggish and remiss in his duties. And he who acts out of sadness is greedy; as far as his own will is concerned, he denies providence. He does not imitate the blessing of God, but the curse of the earth. And he who gives out of necessity—that is, from those things which he himself lacks and which would supply his own want and poverty—usually does so out of sadness. Therefore, Paul does not require that he do this, but leaves it to the sufficiency of his own poverty. However, if anyone is of such perfection that he gives joyfully and voluntarily to the poorer saints even from those things necessary to himself, out of contemplation of Christ, he shall not lack a reward before God. For God commended the woman who gave two small copper coins <note>original: "duo minuta æra," referring to the "widow's mite"</note> out of her own necessities more than all the others. "Truly," he said, "I say to you: this poor widow has put in more than they all. For all these out of their abundance have cast into the offerings of God, but she out of her lack has cast in all the living that she had." What if the things are not necessary for want, but necessary for pleasure? Those are surely not necessary, but superfluous. If you grant those to pleasure, you lose virtue and grace; if you grant them to liberality <note>A term for the virtue of generous giving</note>, you acquire virtue and grace, and you obtain a blessing from God. Instead of fleeting pleasure, you will possess eternal pleasure from those same goods.

¶ Generosity is a most illustrious virtue, for which alone God provides an abundance of earthly wealth. The thanksgivings for His benefits redound <note>overflow or abound</note> not only among men, but also from the saints who receive them toward God. And just as God's providence reaches from the highest things to the lowest, so also this virtue touches the highest things from the lowest. For whom, then, should we hope that fortune, resources, and an abundance of things are present? It is clearly for the merciful and the generous, for whose sake God multiplies good things. Paul therefore prays that God may increase the goods of the Corinthians, who so promptly gird themselves for the duty of generosity, 
<margin>44</margin> 
so that this imitation of divine blessing and providence may be practiced by them more amply and perfectly day by day. This, therefore, is Paul's holy prayer: 

¶ **Now he that ministereth seed to the sower both minister bread for your food, and multiply your seed sown, and increase the fruits of your righteousness; that in every thing ye may be enriched in all bountifulness, which causeth through us thanksgiving to God. For the administration of this service not only supplieth the want of the saints, but is abundant also by many thanksgivings unto God; whiles by the experiment of this ministration they glorify God for your professed subjection unto the gospel of Christ, and for your liberal distribution unto them, and unto all men; and by their prayer for you, which long after you for the exceeding grace of God in you. Thanks be unto God for his unspeakable gift.** <note>2 Corinthians 9:10-15</note>

¶ If anyone should have some eminent or super-eminent grace—such as wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety, or mercy—let him not attribute this to himself, but understand it as something sown from above into his own earth. And (with the spirit-bearing Paul, full of the grace of God, showing us the way to this very thing) let him give immense thanks to God the author for such an ineffable <note>indescribable or beyond words</note> gift. Therefore, for all His ineffable goods, whichever He deigns to bestow, to Him be honor, glory, and thanksgiving forever.

### EXAMINATION of some points regarding the text.

<margin>A 42</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition** reads: "But we sent the brothers." <note>original: "Misimus autē fratres"</note> It is said in the singular, "I sent." Paul: "I sent the brothers." <note>original: "ἔπεμψα δὲ τοὺς ἀδελφούς"</note>

¶ **The Vulgate edition** reads: "That we say not you in this substance." The word "of boasting" is missing; it should be said: "in this substance of boasting." Paul: "lest we should say in this foundation of boasting." <note>original: "ἵνα μὴ λέγωμεν ἡμεῖς ἐν τῇ ὑποστάσει ταύτῃ τῆς καυχήσεως"</note>

<margin>B 42 43</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition** reads: "This promised blessing." The word "your" should be said: "this your promised blessing"; "your" is missing. Paul: "this previously announced blessing of yours." <note>original: "προκατηγγελμένην εὐλογίαν ὑμῶν ταύτην"</note>

¶ **The Vulgate edition** reads: "But this I say." The word "I say" is extra; rather, the verb is to be understood. Paul: "But this [is the point]." <note>original: "τοῦτο δὲ"</note> And immediately there follows: "he who sows," that is, "the one sowing" or "he who is sowing." <note>original: "ὁ σπείρων"</note>

<margin>C 43 44</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition** reads: "As he hath purposed in his heart." Rather: "as he proposes" or "chooses." And the word "his" is extra. Paul: "just as he chooses in the heart." <note>original: "καθὼς προαιρεῖται ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ"</note>

¶ **The Vulgate edition** reads: "His righteousness remains for age of age" <note>forever and ever</note>. The second "age" is extra; it is only found in the original as "for the age" or "into eternity." Paul: "His righteousness remains into the age." <note>original: "ἡ Δικαιοσύνη αὐτοῦ μένει εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα"</note>

¶ **The Vulgate edition** reads: "He will provide and multiply your seed and increase the growth of the fruits of your righteousness." 
<margin>D 44</margin> 
It should rather be said: "may he provide, multiply, increase," so that the words are understood as those of one offering a holy prayer. Paul: "Now may he who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food, supply and multiply your seed and increase the fruits of your righteousness." <note>original: "ὁ δὲ ἐπιχορηγῶν σπέρμα τῷ σπείροντι καὶ ἄρτον εἰς βρῶσιν χορηγήσαι καὶ πληθύναι τὸν σπόρον ὑμῶν καὶ αὐξήσαι τὰ γεννήματα τῆς Δικαιοσύνης ὑμῶν"</note>

¶ **The Vulgate edition** reads: "That in all things being enriched you may abound unto all simplicity." The phrase "you may abound" is extra according to the archetype <note>the original Greek source</note>. Paul: "being enriched in everything unto all simplicity." <note>original: "ἐν παντὶ πλουτιζόμενοι εἰς πᾶσαν ἁπλότητα"</note>

¶ **The Vulgate edition** reads: "Through many thanksgivings in the Lord." It should be said "thanksgivings to God," not "in the Lord." Paul: "Through many thanksgivings to God." <note>original: "Διὰ πολλῶν εὐχαριστιῶν τῷ θεῷ"</note>
