### III 2 Corinthians

...the Vulgate edition <note>original: "Vulgata æditio"</note> reads: *In the obedience of your confession.* ¶ This is how Paul has it, but the phrasing seems reversed, standing in place of *in the confession of your obedience.* We have expressed this meaning accordingly, which Paul also understood in that reversed order. He frequently uses this *hypallage* <term>hypallage: a rhetorical figure where the natural relationship between words is swapped or reversed</term> and alternation of speech. It also frequently happens that what is a "hypallagic" expression in one language is not so in another. ¶ The Vulgate edition reads: *And in the simplicity of your communication toward them.* ¶ The word "your" is redundant here. This "communication"—or "communion," if you prefer—is a single term for pious distribution to the saints. For just as it is called "grace," "blessing," "mercy," and "alms," it is also called "communion." Paul writes: *and for the simplicity of the fellowship toward them* <note>original Greek: "καὶ ἀπλότητι τῆς κοινωνίας εἰς αὐτούς"</note>.

->CHAPTER X<-

The Apostle Peter, for the building up of the church, punished the lie of Ananias and his wife Sapphira with death by his word alone. In Paphos, for the building up of Sergius Paulus, Paul blinded Elymas the sorcerer for a time by his word because he struggled against the ways of the Lord. An adulterer he handed over to Satan, to be afflicted in the body so that his spirit might be saved in the day of the Lord. And the apostle did these things not by human power, but by the power of the Spirit, whom all things obey and who holds all powers in His service. Hence, their weapons are from God and not from men; they are stronger not only than men, but than all spiritual powers. Yet, just as God is kind and clement, preferring to spare and impart grace rather than to punish, so Paul, moved by the Spirit of God and an imitator of divine clemency, prefers to exercise clemency rather than punishment toward certain individuals. These were "false apostles" <term>pseudapostoli: rival teachers in Corinth who claimed apostolic authority but, according to Paul, preached a distorted version of Christ</term> among the Corinthians, announcing Christ falsely and not for the truth, introducing false doctrines against the ways of the Lord and the true traditions of the apostles. He wishes, I say, to spare them if they repent; and he prays much for them so that they might repent. Thus, if they must be struck by a divine plague, they may understand it happened not through Paul’s ill-will or by injustice, but by their own fault. For when God punishes and shows His severity, He does so with no ill-will—He who is benevolent and a benefactor to all—but solely because of the fault of the one being punished. For this reason, God deters us and allures us with promises so that we do not sin, because He does not want to punish but to spare. To deter, to threaten, to coax, and to always entice toward the good is the mark of one who does not wish to punish. Indeed, God no more wants to punish than He wants men to sin; the latter comes first, the former follows as a consequence. And in this way Paul, an imitator of the good God, inclined toward mercy and not punishment, says:

<margin>45</margin>
> ¶ Now I Paul myself beseech you by the meekness and gentleness of CHRIST, who in presence indeed am lowly among you, but being absent am bold toward you; I beseech you, I say, that I may not be bold when I am present with that confidence wherewith I am thought to be bold against some, who reckon us as if we walked according to the flesh. For though we walk in the flesh, we do not war according to the flesh. ¶ The false apostles said that Paul's presence was lowly and easily contemptible, but that he was bold in absence—a boldness he would not dare in person. They thought of nothing but "the flesh" <term>carnem: referring to human weakness or worldly standards as opposed to spiritual power</term>, as if Paul did everything by human effort and not by the Spirit of God. For those who walk according to the flesh measure others by themselves; they judge others to be walking according to the flesh, and since they themselves have nothing of the Spirit, they judge that others have no Spirit either. They prepare human weapons, believing others can use no weapons except human ones. But they are deceived by their own judgment and their own dullness. For even if others walk clothed in a garment of flesh, they do not nevertheless fight with carnal weapons. Which Paul adds, saying:

<margin>46</margin>
> ¶ For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strongholds. We cast down imaginations, and every high thing that exalteth itself against the knowledge of God, and bring into captivity every thought to the obedience of CHRIST; And having in a readiness to revenge all disobedience, when your obedience is fulfilled. You see the things that are according to outward appearance. If any man trust to himself that he is CHRIST's, let him think this again with himself, that as he is CHRIST's, even so are we. ¶ He could have revenged all disobedience even if the Corinthians had remained disobedient; but the apostle preferred, if vengeance were necessary, that they should first come into obedience, and afterwards recognize the danger and efficacy of vengeance upon others. And if there were those among them who were persuaded they belonged to Christ because of the virtues and wonders they performed, they ought to have reflected within themselves; they only saw and judged according to outward appearance. This is a peculiar vice of human infirmity: to judge others based on oneself. But perhaps someone of that sort will say: Paul boasts of that power more than is actually the case or than is fitting. This is a carnal thought, which compares a piece of straw to the strength of an oak, or a gnat to an elephant. For what power of the flesh is equal to the ocean of infinite wisdom? Paul’s speech, therefore, contains less—even without proportion—than the reality of the matter holds in truth. But modesty itself must be maintained for the sake of men; yet ecstasy and excess are entirely toward...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Second Epistle to the Corinthians, specifically focusing on Chapter 10. The previous page established that the weapons of the Apostles' warfare are spiritual and divinely powered, rather than human or worldly.</meta>

<header>COMMENTARY</header>

<margin>47</margin> ...God. Wherefore Paul adds: ¶ **For even if I should boast somewhat more abundantly of our power, which the Lord gave us for building up and not for your destruction, I shall not be ashamed; so that I may not be thought as if scaring you through letters. For "his letters," they say, "are weighty and strong, but his bodily presence is weak and his speech contemptible."** ¶ These were the words of human detractors against Paul—men who judged by the flesh and were puffed up with human wisdom, or more truly, with foolishness. They boasted in human eloquence, and because they fled from divine things, they called his speech "contemptible." ¶ Since they were not approved by God, they approved and commended themselves, seeking human favors and knowing nothing of the divine—considering the divine to be nothing, though it alone is true and to be sought. For this habit is common to all who possess earthly wisdom and nothing of the divine, even if they think they know everything. <margin>48</margin> Paul rebukes them, exposing their behaviors so that they might repent and be corrected, and not rashly think they can measure divine things by earthly standards, saying: ¶ **Let such a person consider this: that such as we are in word by letters when absent, such are we also in deed when present. For we do not dare to approve ourselves or compare ourselves with some who commend themselves. But they, measuring us by themselves and comparing us, do not understand. We, however, will not boast beyond measure, but according to the measure of the rule which God distributed to us, a measure reaching even to you. For we do not overextend ourselves as if we had not reached you. For we reached even to you in the gospel of CHRIST, not boasting beyond measure in other men’s labors.** ¶ Those false apostles boasted that they had announced the truth about Christ to the Corinthians, when in fact it was the labors of others, not their own, that had provided for them. They boasted "beyond measure" in things that were not the standard—namely, in their own traditions and fleshly additions <note>original: "adiuuentionibus," referring to supplementary teachings or 'helps' that the author views as worldly</note>. <margin>49</margin> Therefore, exhorting the Corinthians further regarding what they should truly boast in, Paul adds: ¶ **We have hope, as your faith increases, to be magnified in you according to our rule—preaching the gospel even more abundantly in those regions beyond you, not boasting in another's rule in things already prepared. But he who boasts, let him boast in the Lord. For not he who commends himself is approved, but whom the Lord commends.** ¶ By God's gift, Paul had certain things prepared beyond what the Corinthians had heard, through which he could boast in preaching the gospel according to the measure and norm of Christ’s gift. But this is not boasting in oneself; it is boasting in God who gives. For whoever boasts in something—not because it is from himself, but because it is from another; not for his own sake, but for the sake of the one who bestows it—boasts not in himself but in the Giver. And this boasting is true and holy. May Christ, who is blessed forever, grant this to us; in Him alone let the whole world boast.

***

<margin>A</margin> ¶ **AN EXAMINATION of certain points regarding the text.** ¶ **The Vulgate edition** <note>The standard Latin Bible used in the Western Church</note>: *Absent, however, I am confident in you.* <margin>45</margin> ¶ It should rather be translated here as "I am bold" <note>original: "audeo"</note> rather than "I am confident," as the meaning is better. Paul’s Greek: *though absent, I am bold toward you* <note>original: "ἀπὼν δὲ θαρρῶ εἰς ὑμᾶς"</note>. <margin>B</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Look at the things that are before your face.* <margin>46</margin> ¶ It should rather be said: "You see." For Paul is not giving a command, but making an assertion. Paul’s Greek: *you see the things according to the face/outward appearance* <note>original: "τὰ κατὰ πρόσωπον βλέπετε"</note>. <margin>C</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *For we do not dare to insert or compare ourselves with some.* <margin>48</margin> ¶ It should rather be said: "For we do not dare to approve or compare ourselves with some." Paul’s Greek: *for we do not dare to rank/approve ourselves* <note>original: "οὐ γὰρ τολμῶμεν ἐγκρῖναι ἑαυτοὺς"</note>. For the word *enkrinō* <term>enkrinō: a Greek verb meaning to include in a group or to judge as worthy</term> specifically signifies "I approve." ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *But they, measuring ourselves in us and comparing ourselves to us.* ¶ The old translator <note>referring to the translator of the Vulgate</note> omitted one joining clause: "they do not understand"—unless the manuscript became corrupted after his translation. This passage of Paul is ambiguous because the words for the first and third persons are indistinguishable in certain forms. This whole section can be explained through the third person to mean: "They, measuring themselves by themselves and comparing themselves, do not understand themselves." This is how Augustine understood it. It can also be taken entirely in the first person, which is the sense the old translator followed. However, the verb at the end is then rendered awkwardly, for it is in the third person. In truth, the section can be explained partly through the third and partly through the first person. For there are those who wish to measure others by themselves: what they do not grasp, they believe others do not grasp; the way they walk, they believe others walk. But they do not grasp or understand others within the context of themselves. This is the interpretation we have followed, as it seems more fitting to this passage, unless perhaps it seems otherwise to someone else. Paul’s Greek: *but they, measuring themselves among themselves and comparing themselves with themselves, do not understand* <note>original: "ἀλλὰ αὐτοὶ ἐν ἑαυτοῖς ἑαυτοὺς μετροῦντες καὶ συγκρίνοντες ἑαυτοὺς ἑαυτοῖς οὐ συνιοῦσιν"</note>. <margin>D</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *We, however, will not boast into the immense.* <margin>48</margin> ¶ It could be said: "We will boast in those things which are without measure." Indeed, I understand this to be the same as "beyond measure." Paul’s Greek: *we, however, will not boast in things without measure* <note>original: "ἡμᾶς δὲ οὐχὶ εἰς τὰ ἄμετρα καυχησόμεθα"</note>. <margin>b.</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Even to preach the gospel in those things which are beyond you.* <margin>49</margin> ¶ The word "even" is redundant. And it should rather be said: "above those things which are yours" rather than "beyond you." Paul’s Greek: *to preach the gospel in the things beyond those of yours* <note>original: "εἰς τὰ ὑπὲρ ἐκεῖνα ὑμῶν εὐαγγελίσασθαι"</note>. For the preposition *hyper* <term>hyper: a Greek preposition meaning "over," "above," or "beyond"</term> when it signifies "above," is joined with the accusative case, not the genitive.

<summary>This page concludes a commentary on 2 Corinthians 10, where the author defends Paul’s apostolic authority against detractors who valued outward eloquence over spiritual substance. It includes a detailed philological examination of the Latin Vulgate compared to the original Greek, correcting several translations regarding boasting and self-measurement.</summary>

### CHAPTER 11

<sig>t.iij.</sig>
<meta>Handwritten note in margin: "2 Corinthians"</meta>

It was not only the deceivers of the Corinthians who disparaged Paul—saying that his physical presence was weak and his speech contemptible—but they even called him foolish. They considered that to be a defect which was actually a matter of surpassing excellence. <note>original: "per eminentiam"</note> O you owls, who judge the day to be night! For just as the wisdom of this world is foolishness before God (which is a foolishness of actual deficiency), so the wisdom of God is foolishness to the world—but this is a foolishness of surpassing excellence and an excess of perfection. It is like how light appears as darkness to those with weak eyes, yet it is clear to those who see sharply. Conversely, what is light to those who see clearly appears as darkness to the weak-eyed—yet it is a "darkness" caused by the overwhelming excellence and excess of light. In the same way, the "foolishness" of Paul is light to those who are spiritual and have sight, but to those who are weak-eyed and carnal, it is darkness. And Paul, out of the benevolence of his soul, desires nothing else than for the Corinthians to be capable of receiving that surpassing foolishness; he is like someone who wishes for a weak-eyed person to be capable of the light, which that person currently cannot see because its brilliance exceeds his ability to look at it. It is in this manner that Paul makes his request:

<margin>50</margin>
¶ **Would that you would bear with me a little in my foolishness; but indeed, do bear with me. For I am jealous for you with the jealousy of God. For I have prepared you to present you as a chaste virgin to one husband, to CHRIST.** ¶ To arrange, fit, and harmonize someone in wisdom, and to present them in the purity of the highest wisdom: this can surely only be done through surpassing excellence and a wisdom that transcends human understanding. It is like one who would harmonize the eyes of an owl so that, once purified, they might be presented to the pure light and reflect that light back; this would certainly be the work of someone who sees not in darkness, but in the open light. How is it then that the Corinthians, having been fitted and harmonized in this way, do not bear, tolerate, or grasp this surpassing foolishness?

<margin>51</margin>
If they do not bear, tolerate, or grasp it, this has happened not through any fault in the Apostle’s preparation, but through the seduction of the Evil One, who seduced the virgin Eve and always lies in wait to corrupt chaste minds. Therefore, the Apostle adds: ¶ **But I fear lest, by any means, as the serpent seduced Eve by his craftiness, so your minds should be corrupted from the simplicity that is in CHRIST.** ¶ And he adds the cause of this seduction: because they were "well"—that is, promptly and easily—bearing, tolerating, and admitting those who spoke differently about

<margin>52</margin>
Christ, the Holy Spirit, or the Gospel than what they had heard. It is through this very susceptibility that all heresies and pestilential sects are introduced. And therefore, Paul adds: ¶ **For if he who comes preaches another CHRIST whom we have not preached, or if you receive another spirit which you have not received, or another gospel which you have not accepted, you bear with him well.** ¶ But this is certainly not how things should be done. Indeed, if we do not wish to be deceived, if we do not wish our minds to be corrupted by the serpent’s craftiness, let us listen to the Evangelists, the Apostles, and Paul; and let us reject those who teach otherwise about such things.

<margin>53</margin>
I speak of Paul, who possessed nothing less through revelation than what the twelve Apostles received from the divine mouth while Christ was still dwelling on earth. This he himself testifies, saying: ¶ **For I think I have been in no way inferior to the most excellent apostles. For although I am unskilled in speech, yet I am not in knowledge.**

->**A DEFENSE OF PAUL**<-
<margin>APOLOGIA PRO PAVLO</margin>

¶ Paul grants to his detractors that he may be "unskilled in speech." For they were looking for human eloquence. Those who knew only a single language thought Paul was unskilled, rude, and tongue-tied—he who knew every language! But that "unskillfulness" and "rudeness" was actually an abundance of knowledge. For because Paul was a speaker of all languages, he frequently mixed into his own speech what was proper to another language. For this reason, some thought him a commoner <term>idiota</term> <note>Latin "idiota" here refers to a common person or someone lacking professional rhetorical training.</note> and ignorant in speech, when this did not proceed from ignorance, but from a multifaceted knowledge of languages. Thus, even Paul’s "unskillfulness" is a superabundance of science. For if a Latin speaker who was also a Greek speaker were to impress a Greek form upon his Latin speech, someone who knew only Latin would judge him to be rude and unskilled in the language. But someone who knows both languages would say that his apparent lack of skill is actually an abundance of knowledge. 

And so it certainly happened with Paul: in those instances where he does not seem to favor the customary form of speech, he is borrowing from elsewhere out of his abundant knowledge. I believe, indeed, that if he had wished to observe a pure form of speaking, he could have surpassed Demosthenes <note>The most famous orator of ancient Greece.</note> himself or any of the most eloquent orators of that language. This was also the opinion of Valla <note>Lorenzo Valla (1407–1457), a famous Renaissance humanist and linguist.</note>—otherwise a most sharp critic of languages—when responding to a certain Remigius of our own people who accused Paul regarding the property of his speech. "You do not consult the Greek truth," Valla says, "in which language Paul spoke accurately. He who, in words both proper and ornate, while preserving the majesty of the matter, surpasses Demosthenes himself." These are the words of Valla. 

And Eusebius <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339), an early Christian historian.</note> says: "Paul seems the most learned of all the apostles, powerful both in words and in meanings." And Origen <note>Origen of Alexandria (c. 184–253), an early Christian scholar.</note> says against Celsus: "Explain Paul’s epistles if you can. Whatever fault you find there, I would wish you to try and surpass Paul in speaking." Indeed, Origen attributes such eloquence to Paul that because of it, the Gentiles once believed him to be Mercury <note>The Roman god of eloquence and messages (the Greek Hermes).</note>. Luke also reveals this in the Acts of the Apostles: "When the crowds saw what Paul had done," he says, "they lifted up their voices in the Lycaonian tongue, saying: 'The gods, having become like men, have come down to us!' And they called Barnabas 'Jupiter,' but Paul 'Mercury,' because he was the leader of the word." <note>Acts 14:11-12.</note> Nevertheless, he avoided the empty flowers and charms of the tongue which constitute the ornament of secular speech...

<header>COMMENTARY</header>

...it was something for spiritual minds to avoid. And it is a wonder that Jerome, such a venerable man, believed that Paul was unskilled in speech through some deficiency, <note>original: "per defectum sermonis"</note> and that he even attempted to prove this. It is a wonder he did not instead realize that since Paul was a scholar of various languages, he sometimes mixed the properties and forms of a foreign language into his Greek speech, which is why he was thought to be unskilled in speaking. Yet this "unskillfulness" was actually a multifaceted knowledge of speech; but as the proverb goes, "Even the good Homer sometimes nods." <note>Latin: *Bonus nonnunquam dormitat Homerus*. This means that even the greatest masters make mistakes.</note> Therefore, let us rather side with the more vigilant Origen, Eusebius, and Luke, who were no less knowledgeable in many languages, and let us not perceive Paul as unskilled through any deficiency. For the sea, containing within itself the sweetness of all rivers, appears bitter; so too Paul, being expert in every tongue, appears unskilled in speech. He says, "I thank my God that I speak in tongues more than you all." Let this brief apology suffice regarding Paul’s lack of skill in speech—that it was not by deficiency, but by excellence. <note>original: "non per defectum sed per eminentiam"</note> But what is the use of conducting a longer discourse on this matter, since Paul was well known to all the Corinthians?

<margin>54</margin>
> Paul adds the following, calling certain things back to their memory, saying: "In every way, however, we have been made manifest to you in all things. Or did I commit a sin by humbling myself so that you might be exalted, because I preached the gospel of God to you for free? I robbed other churches by taking a wage from them for your ministry. And when I was present with you and in need, I was a burden to no one. For the brothers who came from Macedonia supplied my need; and in everything, I kept myself from being a burden to you, and I will continue to do so. The truth of CHRIST is in me: this boasting of mine shall not be silenced in the regions of Achaia."

This responds to certain points placed at the beginning of the ninth chapter of the preceding book. He did all these things to provide an example to those who would lead the Corinthians: that they should not glory in a pomp of words, nor in the wisdom of the world, nor in elation and pride, nor in greed by burdening their subordinates. Instead, they should have a simple, truthful, and entirely unadorned speech. They should be wise toward God, not the world; they should be humble, merciful, and generous, seeking their glory in God alone. For such were the apostles of Christ. But those who crept in acted far differently, to the point that they declared themselves to be apostles of Satan, <note>Latin: *Sathanas*</note> who is entirely contrary to Christ. Now, therefore, Paul gives the reason why he conducted himself thus: it was not out of hatred for the Corinthians (for he loved them with the charity of God), but so that those who wished to assert themselves as apostles of Christ when they were not might be recognized by his own life and character—lest they be able to boast that they were apostles of Christ when they were not, being found unlike the true apostles in life and character. Thus, he adds this cause, saying:

<note>The marginal text "GRADATIO" refers to a "rhetorical ladder" or a sequence of steps in an argument.</note>
> "Why? Because I do not love you? God knows. But what I am doing, I will continue to do, so that I may cut off the opportunity from those who desire an opportunity to be found like us in the things they boast about. For such false apostles <note>Latin: *pseudoapostoli*</note> are deceitful workers, transforming themselves into apostles of CHRIST. And no wonder: for Satan himself transforms himself into an angel of light. It is no great thing, therefore, if his ministers also transform themselves as though they were ministers of justice; whose end shall be according to their works."

When the spirit of darkness mocks the curious, he says he is an angel of light and the good spirit of God. For whom would he deceive if he openly confessed to being an evil spirit? Those who possess Pythonic spirits <note>referring to the "spirit of Python" or divination, as mentioned in Acts 16:16</note> (which is the worst kind of idolatry) believe them to be good angels. In this way, they falsely claim to be angels of light, and this is what it means for them to transform themselves into angels of light. So too the workers of iniquity—those who use exorcisms, consecrations, hymns, and incense, along with profanations of divine names—think they are summoning good angels and heavenly powers. Nevertheless, all these serve under the prince of this world and under the rulers of this darkness. Yet they call themselves holy angels and take the names of holy angels for themselves; and this is "transforming themselves into angels of light." Regarding books of this kind of extreme vanity and total madness: as many as possessed them in Ephesus, having been previously led astray by "curious arts" <note>The "curious arts" (*curiosa*) refers to magic and the occult</note> before Paul's teaching, brought their books together and burned them before everyone. And when the price of them was calculated, they found the money amounted to fifty thousand pieces of silver. Would that a vengeful flame might everywhere consume such pure nonsense, such mere impostures, such vain meddling, and such demonic traps, so that every opportunity for Satan to transform himself into an angel of light might be removed, and so that he might have no ministers striving to drag the minds of men down to such nefarious sacrileges. But Satan also measures himself out as an angel of light in certain visions and revelations; as in the prophets of Ahab, King of Israel, he placed a lie in place of the truth, yet they believed him to be the good spirit of God. And also in Montanus, Prisca, and Maximilla—those insane seers—he wished to be seen as the Holy Spirit, though he was a most foul spirit, as he rejoiced in their drunkenness and indecencies. And he transforms himself not only into an angel, but even into God—an error by which he once enveloped an infinite multitude of nations unto perdition. Since, therefore, Paul did not boast in those things in which the ministers of Satan (falsely claiming to be ministers of Christ) boasted, he did not boast in foolishness—

<margin>'</margin> I say: let no one think me a fool. If otherwise, receive me as a fool, that

He by no means willed to be cut off by death through the malice of his enemies. But He gave him life 
then, and so many other times from certain dangers of death, for His own glory and our salvation. 
To Him be honor, and glory, and thanksgiving, forever and ever.

### <margin>A</margin> EXAMINATION of certain points regarding the text.

<margin>50</margin> ¶ The Vulgate edition says: "Would that you would sustain a certain small part of my foolishness." <note>Latin: *Vtinam sustineretis modicū quid infipientiæ meæ*</note> ¶ Better from Paul: "Would that you would sustain me a little in foolishness." Paul wrote: ὄφελον ἀνείχεσθέ μου μικρὸν τῇ ἀφροσύνῃ. <note>original Greek: "O that you would bear with me a little in [my] foolishness."</note> For "foolishness" in Paul’s Greek is in the dative case; among us [Latin speakers] this would be translated into the ablative, but it is more intelligible when 
a preposition is added to it. ¶ The Vulgate edition: "For I have betrothed you to one husband."

<meta>This page continues the philological and theological commentary on the Second Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 11. The translator is comparing the standard Latin Vulgate Bible with the original Greek text to refine the meaning of Paul’s words regarding his ministry and his sufferings.</meta>

### COMMENTARY

<margin>A 51</margin> Paul uses a term that I have translated as "fitted," "arranged," or "harmonized," rather than "betrothed," which is what the Greeks call *memeyka*. <note>original: "designat in Paulo/aptaui/concinnaui/harmonizaui/nõ id quod desponsaui/ quod græci μεμευκα dicunt."</note> Paul says: *For I have fitted you to one husband.* <note>original: "ἡρμοσάμην γαρ ὑμας ἑνι ἀνδρι"</note> ¶ The Vulgate edition says: *So your senses may be corrupted and fall away from the simplicity which is in Christ.* ¶ It should rather be read: *lest [someone] corrupt your senses,* or your minds, or your understandings. And the phrase *fall away* is superfluous. Paul says: *lest somehow your thoughts be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ.* <note>original: "οὑτω φθαρῃ τὰ νοήματα ὑμῶν ἀπὸ τῆς ἁπλότητος τῆς εἰς τὸν χρισόν"</note> 
<margin>A 52</margin> ¶ The Vulgate edition says: *He preaches another Christ whom we have not preached.* ¶ In Greek, this is expressed through a relative pronoun and a following negation, both here and in the following clauses. Truly, it is more suited to Latin speech if it is explained through the word *than* and the following relative. For *than* allows one to understand the negation in a more fitting way; for example, "John the Elder was someone other *than* he who was the Evangelist." This way of speaking is more suited to our language. Therefore, we preferred to explain the above-mentioned particle and the following ones through *than* rather than through *not*. ¶ The Vulgate edition says: *You might rightly suffer.* ¶ It should rather be: *You might easily* or *favorably suffer,* or as the old interpreter previously translated it, *you would endure.* The same word is often translated in various ways according to his custom, as if he were translating something different. And that word "well" does not imply approval here—it is not taken in a positive sense—but rather refers to a certain ease and licentious proneness. For Paul is not approving of them; he is accusing them. Therefore, the particle *rightly* would not be placed appropriately in this spot, because *rightly* implies approval and is taken in a better sense.
<margin>B 53</margin> Paul says: *You bear it well.* <note>original: "καλῶς ἀνέχεσθε"</note> ¶ The Vulgate edition says: *For I think I have done nothing less than the great apostles.* ¶ This passage could be interpreted with more modesty (as Paul himself speaks). ¶ *For I think I have lacked nothing,* or *I have had nothing less than the great or excellent apostles,* or something similar. For Paul does not say here that he has "done" anything, but that he has "not lacked," that is, he did not have less. Paul says: *For I reckon I was not a whit behind the very chiefest apostles.* <note>original: "λογίζομαι γὰρ μηδὲν ὑστερηκέναι τῶν ὑπὲρ λίαν ἀποστόλων"</note> 
<margin>B 54</margin> ¶ The Vulgate edition says: *Or did I commit a sin humbling myself?* ¶ The particle *or* was either superfluous, or the particle *whether* was. One should not say "or" but simply "whether," which is the mark of a question. Paul says: *Did I commit a sin humbling myself?* <note>original: "ἦ ἁμαρτίαν ἐποίησα; ἐμαυτὸν ταπεινῶν"</note> ¶ The Vulgate edition says: *Receiving wages for your ministry.* ¶ In Paul’s text, "wage" is said in the singular. Paul says: *taking a wage for your service.* <note>original: "λαβὼν ὀψώνιον πρὸς τὴν ὑμῶν διακονίαν"</note> 
<margin>C 55</margin> ¶ The Vulgate edition says: *For such false apostles are deceitful workers.* ¶ It should be said with a single five-syllable word, *pseudapostoli* [false-apostles]. Paul says: *For such are false apostles, deceitful workers.* <note>original: "οἱ γὰρ τοιοῦτοι ψευδαπόστολοι ἐργάται δόλιοι"</note> ¶ The Vulgate edition says: *It is no great thing then if his ministers are transformed.* ¶ It should say: *if also his ministers.* But that is a very small point. Paul says: *It is no great thing then if also his ministers are transformed.* <note>original: "οὐ μέγα οὖν, εἰ καὶ οἱ διάκονοι αὐτοῦ μετασχηματίζονται"</note> 
<margin>D 56</margin> ¶ The Vulgate edition says: *I do not speak according to God.* ¶ It is read *according to the Lord.* Paul says: *I speak not according to the Lord.* <note>original: "οὐ λαλῶ κατὰ κύριον"</note> ¶ The Vulgate edition says: *In this substance of glory.* ¶ I preferred to say *matter of boasting* rather than *substance of glory.* For *hypostasis* is a name for *matter*, because it "stands under" [sub-stands]; although this word is various and has multiple meanings. Paul says: *in this matter of boasting.* <note>original: "ἐν ταύτῃ τῇ ὑποστάσει τῆς καυχήσεως"</note> 
<margin>E 57</margin> ¶ The Vulgate edition says: *As if we were weak in this part.* ¶ The particle *in this part* is superfluous. 
<margin>F 59</margin> Paul says: *As if we were weak.* <note>original: "ὡς ὅτι ἡμεῖς ἠσθενήσαμεν"</note> And he immediately joins to it: *In whatever anyone dares,* or *in whatever indeed anyone dares.* <note>original: "ἐν ᾧ δ’ ἄν τις τολμᾷ"</note> ¶ The Vulgate edition says: *A night and a day I have been in the depth of the sea.* ¶ *Of the sea* is redundant. And *I have spent* or *I have made* should be said rather than *I have been.* Therefore, it was enough to have said: *a night and a day I spent in the deep,* that is, in the sea, in the deep water, in the open sea, or I labored in the brine. For I do not understand it to mean that Paul was detained for a day and a night at the bottom of the sea with the bottom-dwelling fish, but that he was tossed among the waves and floods for a day and a night before he reached port. This ambiguity is caused by the word *Bython*: which is sometimes taken for "depth" and sometimes for "the sea," just as among us the word *the deep* [altum] is used sometimes for "altitude" and sometimes for "the sea," as in: *Much was he tossed on both land and the deep.* Because, however, our people usually use *the deep* [altum] for the sea, and others use *the depth* [profundum], we preferred to use the word *the deep* rather than *the depth*. Paul says: *a night and a day I have spent in the deep.* <note>original: "νυχθήμερον ἐν τῶ βυθῶ πεποίηκα"</note> ¶ The Vulgate edition says: *Who is weak and I am not weak? Who is scandalized and I do not burn?* ¶ These clauses could be read as indefinite; for the word Paul uses is usually taken indefinitely, so that "who" is the same as "anyone," and it could be read without any interrogation. Following that interpretation, we added an explanation. They can also be read interrogatively, which is how they are usually read in the Vulgate edition. And then let the sense be: *Who is weakened and I am not weakened?*—as if he were saying: "If anyone is weak, I am not only weak, but even more weak." *Who is scandalized and I do not burn?*—as if he were saying: "You are offended, but if any of you is offended, it is a light thing. I am not only offended in pressures and in enduring troubles, but I am tested as if by a rack or by fire," which can be drawn from the Greek in Psalm 16: *You have tested me with fire,* where the active form of the verb is used, while Paul uses the passive *pyroumai* [I am burned/refined]. ¶ This word *I burn* is explained in that sense which is in frequent use among poets, as when one [is burned] vehemently...

# III
## 2 Cor.

It is used in the sense of "hoping for and nourishing a sterile love," and to attribute this to the apostle is wicked and unworthy; it is the thinking of those who understand things in a passive and carnal way. ### CHAPTER XII.

<image-desc>Historiated woodcut initial 'C' featuring a scene with several figures in a landscape; a central figure appears to be addressing or preaching to a seated group.</image-desc>
Since the apostle has recounted many tribulations, troubles, dangers, and fears of death that were barely overcome, struggled through, and avoided—which do not provide material for boasting according to the flesh, unless one boasts in the weaknesses and pressures of the flesh—so that in enduring these very things he becomes an imitator of Christ and a sharer in his sufferings. This is just as it was written of the apostles when they had been beaten by the magistrates of the temple and the chief priests in the assembly of the Jews: they indeed went away rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they were counted worthy to suffer shame for the name of Jesus. But this boasting is not according to the flesh, but according to the spirit. Paul has long since declared that one should not boast according to the flesh, even if nothing prohibits boasting according to the spirit. And here he still declares this, recounting many things that happened to him that were rare and singular—not because he seeks glory in recounting them, but so that those who hear may be built up and give glory to God. Even if he could have boasted in those things without vanity and not imprudently seeking glory from men, he boasted in God, giving glory not to himself but to God for such great and wonderful works. ¶ Therefore, when he has recounted all these things, he adds: ¶ *It is certainly not profitable for me to boast. For I will come to visions and revelations of the Lord. I know a man in Christ fourteen years ago (whether in the body I do not know, or whether out of the body I do not know: God knows) such a one caught up even to the third heaven. And I know such a man (whether in the body, or whether out of the body I do not know: God knows) that he was caught up into paradise: and heard unspeakable words, which it is not permitted for a man to speak.* For such a thing I will boast; yet for myself I will not boast, except in my infirmities. ¶ *For though I might desire to boast, I shall not be a fool; for I will say the truth.* ¶ It has been said that to boast in infirmities endured for the name of Christ is not to boast according to the flesh. Nor is it boasting according to the flesh if someone boasts in the great works of God, giving glory to God in them, looking not to himself but to God, not vainly seeking glory from men, and not imprudently. And Paul certainly notes in both cases that it is prudent and according to God to boast. But what is it that was said: *he heard unspeakable words, which it is not permitted for a man to speak*? I certainly think this: that those words were of such a kind, and their manner was such, that a mortal man could not utter them. And if Paul revealed any of them, he did not disclose them in that unspeakable way and exactly as he heard them, but speakably and in a human manner. In the same way, the disciple beloved by God <note>The apostle John</note> delivered the holy Apocalypse, not as he heard it (for he heard it in a way impossible for men to speak), but speakably and in a possible way of speaking and representing it. And as often as angels communicate by signs and reveal secrets to minds, it is impossible for men to speak that way. For that would be to speak "angelically" and not humanly. Those things were therefore unspeakable and such as were by no means permitted or possible for a man to speak. Paul could have either written or told the Corinthians in a human way what he had seen and heard; but he refrained, lest they, looking at a mortal man, should attribute more to a mortal man than was fit, and look more to him and less to God than was proper. He declares this, saying: ¶ *But I refrain, lest any man should think of me above that which he sees me to be, or what he hears from me.* ¶ For foolish men, when they see someone by the grace of God either doing works or reporting God’s secrets beyond human grasp, admire him, look up to him, and extol him as if he had such power in himself and from himself. This also happened to Peter when in Jerusalem at the Beautiful Gate, by the power of Christ, he raised a man lame from birth. For those seeing it were filled with wonder and ecstasy, and all the people ran to him and John in the portico called Solomon's. Peter said to them: *Men of Israel, why do you marvel at this, or why do you look at us?* I say they admire them so much that they almost worship them, when they ought to look up to and magnify God, admiring Him in that person. For it is written: *praise the Lord in his saints*, not those saints in themselves as if they had holiness in and from themselves. Paul feared this because of the ignorance and carnality of his listeners, if he had openly revealed his visions, revelations, and (so to speak) his familiarities with God. Moreover, since he was of such perfection by God's doing, lest he be tempted by any carnal pride because of the greatness and excellence of the revelations—lest he boast vainly by looking at himself even a little—there was given a stake <note>original: "pallus". Usually "stimulus" or "thorn".</note> to his flesh, that is, the devil pursuing him, and stirring up against him all bodily pressures, prisons, blows, scourges, beatings, stonings, shipwrecks, daily and nightly...

The author interprets Paul's "unspeakable words" as being expressed in an angelic mode that cannot be replicated in human language.</summary>

...thrice through savage storms, tossings, dangers on journeys, from robbers, from Jews, from gentiles, and other troubles of that kind which he enumerated in the preceding chapter, and innumerable others.

<margin>63</margin> ¶ Therefore he adds: ¶ *And lest I should be exalted by the abundance of the revelations, there was given to me a thorn in the flesh <note>original: "flagellum carnis" — the author uses the word for 'whip' or 'scourge' rather than the more common 'thorn' or 'prick'</note>, a messenger of Satan to buffet me, lest I should be exalted. For this thing I besought the Lord thrice, that it might depart from me. And he said to me: My grace is sufficient for you; for my power is made perfect in infirmity.* ¶ When Paul was distressed by pressures, so that he could scarcely suffice to bear them in the flesh, he "besought the Lord thrice" that he might move Satan far from him, so that such great weights upon the flesh would not be ceaselessly stirred up against him. Truly, he received the answer that the sufficiency for enduring those pressures and for avoiding so many deaths did not come from himself, but that it was the grace of God which was the sufficiency by which he might overcome them; and that the power of God is known in weakness. For when human strengths are not enough but are immensely overwhelmed, yet one nevertheless escapes, it is recognized that the deed was done by divine power and overcome by divine grace. Paul, therefore, recognized the power of God dwelling in him in these types of pressures that are beyond human strength.

<margin>64</margin> He also recognized the grace of God openly through the gifts given for the illumination of others. Therefore he adds: ¶ *Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may dwell in me. Therefore I am of good courage in infirmities, in reproaches, in necessities, in persecutions, in distresses for Christ’s sake: for when I am weak, then am I strong.* ¶ Certainly anyone can call himself powerful then, when he knows himself to be able not by his own power, but by the power of God. Just as Daniel was more powerful in the lions' den than outside of it; for in the lions' den, he was able by the power of God, but outside, by his own. Was it by the power of God or by Daniel's own strength that the ferocity of seven lions and as many days of fasting were tamed? Furthermore, he overcame the hunger of so many days by the power of God, surely, not his own. Indeed, even those lions were more powerful in the den than outside; for by the power of God they were able to endure the hunger of so many days without the madness of ferocity. So also Paul, when he was "weakened"—that is, pressed beyond his own strength—felt himself to be more powerful; for then he was able by God’s power, not his own. But when Paul narrates these things, it could

<margin>65</margin> seem to the Corinthians that he was seeking glory, even if he was not seeking it, and therefore acting in the manner of the foolish who seek glory. For this reason Paul joins this, saying: ¶ *I have become a fool in glorying; you have compelled me. For I ought to have been commended by you; for in nothing was I behind the most excellent apostles, even though I am nothing.* ¶ When he says "I ought to have been commended by you" and "I was in no way less than the excellent apostles," he is looking toward God and God's grace. But when he says "I am nothing," he is looking at himself. That which he adds further, however, regards God. For to perform the signs of apostleship is not the work of a man, but of God. Therefore, even if they ought to have esteemed him as nothing in terms of what he is by himself, they nevertheless ought to have venerated the signs of his apostleship—or more truly, God in those signs—which are from God and can only be from God.

<margin>66</margin> This is easily understood from those things which Paul annexed to the previous points, speaking in this way: ¶ *Truly the signs of an apostle were performed among you in all patience, in signs, and wonders, and mighty deeds. For what is there in which you were less than the other churches, except that I myself was not a burden to you? Forgive me this wrong. Behold, the third time I am ready to come to you; and I will not be a burden to you. For I seek not what is yours, but you. For children ought not to lay up treasures for their parents, but parents for their children. And I will most gladly spend and be spent for your souls, even if the more abundantly I love you, the less I am loved.* ¶ Certainly, the fact that he was not a burden to the Corinthians in incurring expenses is not a "wrong." Therefore, his request that this be "forgiven" or "remitted" to him is a modest irony and a rebuke. However, the things he added reveal his paternal affection toward them and a certain imitation of Christ <note>original: "Christi emulationem"</note>, who said: *Greater love has no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends.* <note>John 15:13</note> Paul does not seek the goods of the Corinthians, but the Corinthians themselves; just as Christ, coming into the world, did not seek the goods of mortals, but mortals themselves, so that he might save them and make them immortal. Fathers lay up treasures for their children, not the other way around; so also Paul wishes to lay up treasure for the Corinthians, not the other way around. Coming to them twice already, he incurred expenses so that he might save them. He is ready a third time to incur expenses for their salvation; and not only to incur expenses, but even to offer himself as the expense and be sacrificed for their souls. But what can be greater than this charity? That since he is the father, they are the children. Since he is the benefactor, they are the ones affected by the benefits. Since he is the architect, they themselves are his work. It follows that he, loving more, is loved less. For love that is direct and descending is greater and more like the divine than love which is reflected, ascending, and springing back. For love is born in the highest; from which, descending all the way to the lowest, it penetrates by providing for them. Love is in the highest, as in the father of all, the maker, and the all-beneficent power, as in a fountain and in its own origin. From that origin, it is vibrated, permeates, and is hurled directly into all things, and indeed with a most powerful and inevitable cast. But who would want to avoid love? In other things, however—such as in children, or in works, or in those affected by a benefit—outside of its own fountain and its own origin, love is reflected and springs back, and indeed springs back weakly. And such was the love of the Corinthians; nor indeed did that happen without a reason. But someone will say, all...

...turning everything to the worse: it is true that Paul paid his own expenses and was a burden to no one by himself; but he did this craftily, so that by sending others, he might receive the collected money for his own costs, and even far more than he had spent himself. These perverse thoughts, as it is written, separate one from God, being born from the weakness of the flesh which judges piety to be a trick, and every virtue and work of virtue to be a vice. By no means were the collections made to provide for Paul’s expenses, nor for even greater gains beyond those expenses, but for works of piety toward the saints and the poor of Christ, to relieve them from want and necessity. And for this very purpose, Titus and Luke—holy men proven in all piety—were commissioned. This yielded no benefit to them nor to Paul, but served only to relieve the poverty of the saints, and for the building up of Christians and their training in the work of the most noble virtue: I mean mercy and piety. In this virtue, those who expect mercy must first be trained. For this reason "blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy" <note>Matthew 5:7</note>. Paul therefore wanted the Corinthians to be practiced in virtue and blessed, not to circumvent them with trickery and craftiness. He asserts this himself, responding to those thinking perversely and slandering a good work, saying:

<margin>'</margin>
> ¶ But be it so, I was not a burden to you; but being crafty, I caught you with guile. Did I take advantage of you by any of those whom I sent to you? I urged Titus to go, and sent a brother with him. Did Titus take advantage of you? Did we not walk in the same spirit? Did we not walk in the same steps? Again, do you think that we are excusing ourselves to you? We speak in the sight of God in CHRIST. But we do all things, dearly beloved, for your edification. <note>2 Corinthians 12:16-19</note>

<margin>¶</margin> Paul foresaw what the detractors and slanderers of good men were going to say: namely, that he was pretending some excuse for the craftiness and trickery of receiving expenses and making a kind of public exaction upon the Corinthians. Those who are led by the spirit of the world do this; not those led by the Spirit of God. Those who look to their own utility do this; not those who look to the public good, nor the good of others and their perfection in virtue. And yet Paul, Titus, and the brother sent with him—whoever he may have been, whether Luke, or Silvanus, or anyone else—walked in the Spirit of God; they looked to the public good, not their own convenience, but to the edification of others. Truly, because there were some such detractors among the Corinthians, perceiving nothing of God or the Spirit but only things of passion and the flesh—slanderers of good things and stirrers of sedition and factions—therefore Paul forewarns them and others who have sinned gravely against discipline, that they might come to their senses and perform penance <margin>67</margin> before his third arrival, lest upon his arrival God take vengeance on them. For Paul was not his own avenger, nor did he take revenge; but it was God who enacted vengeance. Knowing therefore that God (unless they repented) would take vengeance at his arrival, he forewarns and exhorts them to repent. He does this lest, seeing God's vengeance and those he loves with paternal affection being afflicted, he himself might be saddened, mourn, grieve, and be humbled along with those who are brought low through the affection of compassion. <margin>¶</margin> He warns them therefore, and fortifies them by the foresight of things to come, saying:

<margin>68</margin> <margin>'</margin>
> ¶ For I fear lest, when I come, I shall not find you such as I would, and that I shall be found by you such as you would not; lest there be contentions, envies, wraths, strifes, backbitings, whisperings, swellings, seditions; and lest, when I come again, my God will humble me among you, and that I shall bewail many who have sinned already and have not repented of the uncleanness, fornication, and lasciviousness which they have committed. <note>2 Corinthians 12:20-21</note>

<margin>¶</margin> Is it not a sign of paternal affection, and of a heart burning with great love, to fear so much and to fortify them so solicitously, so that they might avoid impending and certain future evils? Certain to happen (I say) unless repentance prevents it. For repentance was the only way they could be avoided. This was the refuge, the only protection, which Paul points out for avoiding the plague of God. For Paul greatly desired that God would have mercy on them and spare them, rather than take vengeance on them; in this he was also an emulator of the good God. For God also absolutely wants to have mercy and to spare; He does not absolutely want to take vengeance except in the coincidence of mercy and vengeance. Therefore, when He takes vengeance, He does so mercifully. And when He has mercy, He does so with justice. For God accepts all repentance in place of vengeance, so that He may finally pour out His mercy upon one who is sufficiently prepared. May God therefore grant us that, through worthy repentance, we may so prepare ourselves to receive His mercy that we may be able to celebrate Him with all the saints, both now and in the future, with eternal praise.

¶ When Paul was being distressed by pressures so great that he could scarcely endure them in the flesh, he prayed to the Lord three times to drive the adversary <note>original: "sathanam"</note> far from him, so that he would not incessantly stir up so many grievances of the flesh against him. But he received the answer that the sufficiency for enduring those pressures and for escaping so many deaths did not come from himself, but that the grace of God <term>grace: the unmerited favor and divine assistance of God</term> was the sufficiency by which he might overcome them. This is because the power of God is recognized in weakness. For when human strengths are not enough but are immeasurably overwhelmed, yet one nevertheless escapes, it is recognized that the deed was done by divine power and overcome by divine grace. Paul, therefore, recognized the power of God dwelling within him in the midst of pressures that were <margin>64</margin> beyond human strength, and he also clearly recognized God’s grace through the gifts given for the illumination of others. Therefore he adds:
> Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my weaknesses, that the power of Christ may dwell in me. Therefore I take pleasure in weaknesses, in injuries, in necessities, in persecutions, in distresses for Christ's sake: for when I am weak, then am I strong.

¶ Certainly anyone can say they are powerful when they know they are capable not by their own power, but by God’s. Like Daniel: he was more powerful in the lions' den than outside of it. For in the lions' den, he prevailed by the power of God; but outside, by his own. Was it the power of God or Daniel’s own ferocity that tamed the seven lions and their hunger during those days? Furthermore, he overcame the hunger of so many days by God's power, certainly not his own. Indeed, even those lions were more powerful inside the den than outside; for by God’s power, they were able to endure hunger for so many days without their natural savage rage. So also Paul, when he was weakened—that is, when he was being pressed beyond his own strength—felt himself to be more powerful. For then he was capable by God’s power, not his own. ¶ When he says "I ought to have been commended by you" and "I was in no way inferior to the excellent apostles," he is looking toward God and God's grace. But when he says "though I be nothing," he is looking at himself. As for what he adds next, it regards God. For to perform the signs of an apostle <term>apostleship: the office and authority of the original messengers of the Gospel</term> is not the work of a man, but of God. Therefore, even if they ought to have esteemed him as nothing (as he is in himself), they nevertheless ought to have venerated the signs of his apostleship—or more truly, to have venerated God in those signs which are from God and can only be from <margin>66</margin> God. And I will very gladly spend and be spent for your souls; though the more abundantly I love you, the less I be loved.

¶ Certainly, the fact that he was not burdensome to the Corinthians regarding his expenses is not an "injury" or "wrong." Therefore, his request that this be "forgiven" or "remitted" to him is a form of modest irony and a gentle correction. Just as Christ, coming into the world, did not seek the goods of mortals, but the mortals themselves, so that he might save them and make them immortal. Parents store up treasures for their children, not the other way around. So also Paul wishes to store up treasure for the Corinthians. Since he is the father, and they are the children; since he is the benefactor, and they are the ones affected by his benefits; since he is the architect, and they are his work. It follows that he, loving more, is loved less. For love that is direct and descending <note>meaning love from a superior to an inferior, like God to man or parent to child</note> is greater and more similar to the divine than love that is reflected, ascending, or bouncing back. For love is born in the Highest, from whom it penetrates everything by descending to the lowest through providence. Love is in the Highest: as in the Father of all, the Creator, and all-beneficent power; as in a fountain and in its own origin. From that source, love is vibrated, permeates, and is thrown directly into all things by a most powerful and inevitable cast. But who would want to avoid love? In other things, however—such as in children, in works, or in those who have received a benefit—away from their own fountain and origin, love is reflected and bounces back, and indeed bounces back weakly. ...turning everything to the worse: they claim it is true that Paul did not charge for his own expenses and was a burden to no one, but that he did this craftily so that, by sending others, he might receive the collected money for his own costs, and indeed far more than he would have spent himself. <margin>67</margin>
> But be it so; I was not a burden to you: but being crafty, I caught you with guile. Did I make a gain of you by any of them whom I sent to you? I desired Titus, and with him I sent a brother. Did Titus make a gain of you? Did we not walk in the same spirit? Did we not walk in the same steps? Again, do you think that we excuse ourselves to you? We speak before God in Christ: but we do all things, dearly beloved, for your edification.

But Paul foresaw what the detractors and slanderers of good men were going to say: namely, that he was offering some excuse for the trickery and craftiness of receiving expenses and for the oversight of the public collection to be made among the Corinthians. This is what those do who are led by the spirit of the world, not those led by the spirit of God. This is what those do who look to their own advantage, not to the public good, nor the good of others and their perfection in virtue. Yet Paul, Titus, and the brother sent with him—whoever he may have been, whether Luke or Silvanus or anyone else—walked in the spirit of God, attending to the public good and not their own convenience, but rather the edification of others. 

But because there were some such detractors among the Corinthians, sensing nothing of God or the spirit but only things of passion and the flesh—slanderers of good men and stirrers of seditions and factions—for this reason Paul warns them, and others who have sinned gravely against discipline, that they should come to their senses and perform penance <unclear>      </unclear> before his third arrival, lest upon his arrival God should take vengeance on them. For Paul was not his own avenger; he did not take revenge, but it was God who performed the vengeance. Knowing therefore that God would punish them (unless they repented) at his arrival, he warns and exhorts them to repent. He does this so that he himself, seeing God’s vengeance and those he loves with fatherly affection afflicted, might not be saddened, mourn, grieve, and—through the affection of compassion—be humbled among those who are brought low. He warns them, therefore, and fortifies them by the foresight of things to come, saying:

<margin>68</margin>
> For I fear, lest, when I come, I shall not find you such as I would, and that I shall be found unto you such as ye would not: lest there be debates, envyings, wraths, strifes, backbitings, whisperings, swellings, tumults: and lest, when I come again, my God will humble me among you, and that I shall bewail many which have sinned already, and have not repented of the uncleanness and fornication and lasciviousness which they have committed.

Is it not a sign of fatherly affection, and of a heart burning with great love, to fear so much and to fortify them so solicitously? He does this so that they might avoid the impending and certain future evils—certain, I say, unless repentance prevents them. For repentance alone was the means by which they could be avoided. This was the refuge, this was the sole protection, which Paul points out for avoiding the plague <note>referring to divine punishment</note> of God. For Paul wanted, and greatly desired, that God would have mercy on them and spare them, rather than take vengeance on them. In this, he was an emulator of the good God; for God also desires absolutely to have mercy and to spare, and does not absolutely desire to take vengeance except in the coincidence of mercy and vengeance. Therefore, when He takes vengeance, He does so mercifully; and when He has mercy, He does so with justice. For God accepts all repentance in place of vengeance, so that He may finally pour out His mercy upon one who is sufficiently prepared. May God therefore grant us that, through worthy penance, we may so prepare ourselves to receive His mercy that we may be able to celebrate Him both now and in the future with eternal praise alongside all the saints.

The same thought: foretelling that he does not wish to glory in these things, and that to glory in that way is not profitable for him. Paul says: *it is not profitable for me to boast* <note>original Greek: "καυχᾶσθαι δὴ οὐ συμφέρει μοι"</note>. There are also manuscripts that have: *it is necessary to boast; it is not profitable for me* <note>original Greek: "καυχᾶσθαι δεῖ; οὐ συμφέρει μοι"</note>. In that case, the word is not an affirmative particle, but a verb, and it is just as if we were speaking through a question and a continuous response: "Is it necessary to boast? It is not profitable for me." And thus I believe the old translator read it: but it is stated without condition.

¶ **The Vulgate Edition.** *Whether in the body, or out of the body, God knows: such a man caught up even to the third heaven.* <note>2 Corinthians 12:2</note>
<margin>,</margin>
¶ It should be said here: "whether in the body, I do not know; or out of the body." The phrase "for the body, I do not know" is missing.
<margin>,</margin>
And this speech suggests: I do not know whether that man was caught up into the third heaven bodily or only spiritually. And Paul, speaking these things about himself, seems through modesty to speak as if of another. It is not that he doubted that his soul was always in his body and had animated the body: but the *manner* of the being caught up—not the event itself—was unknown. For he could have been caught up bodily like Habakkuk <note>A reference to the story of Habakkuk being carried by an angel to Babylon in the book of Bel and the Dragon</note>. He could also have been caught up only in spirit, without however leaving the body: just as John, when he was on Patmos, was caught up in spirit into heaven. He says, "Immediately I was in the spirit, and behold, a throne was set in heaven." <note>Revelation 4:2</note> And what John saw and heard were invisible and ineffable things, like those which Paul saw and heard. But to wish to say anything regarding Paul’s ineffable things—beyond those mysteries he revealed to us concerning the sacraments of Christ—is a matter of human presumption and vanity. And the book titled the *Apocalypse of Paul*, which was published on this subject, was by no means seen as worthy of being received by the Church. But enough of these things. Paul says: *whether in the body, I do not know; or out of the body, I do not know; God knows. Such a man caught up even to the third heaven.* <note>original Greek: "εἴτε ἐν σώματι, οὐκ οἶδα· εἴτε ἐκτὸς τοῦ σώματος, οὐκ οἶδα· ὁ θεὸς οἶδεν. ἁρπάγεντα τὸν τοιοῦτον ἕως τρίτου οὐρανοῦ"</note>

¶ **The Vulgate Edition.** *And he heard secret words, which it is not permitted for a man to speak.*
<margin>,</margin>
¶ Rather: *ineffable words*. And rather *it may not be permitted* or *it would not be permitted*.
<margin>,</margin>
For the word he uses for "permitted" or "would be permitted" is usually explained while it "is possible" or "would be possible." Paul says: *and he heard ineffable words, which it is not possible for a man to speak.* <note>original Greek: "καὶ ἤκουσεν ἄρρητα ῥήματα, ἃ οὐκ ἐξὸν ἀνθρώπῳ λαλῆσαι"</note> Where you should note that these words <term>exesti, exon, exousia: Greek terms relating to authority, power, or legal permission</term> in Paul usually signify the power or faculty of speaking, and not always that which is divinely lawful or permitted.

¶ **The Vulgate Edition.** *But for myself nothing, except in my infirmities.*
¶ It should be said: "But for myself I will not boast, except in my infirmities." Paul says: *but for myself I will not boast, except in my infirmities.* <note>original Greek: "ὑπὲρ δὲ ἐμαυτοῦ οὐ καυχήσομαι, εἰμὴ ἐν ταῖς ἀσθενείαις μου"</note>

¶ **The Vulgate Edition.** *Lest anyone should think of me above that which he sees in me.*
¶ The speech is reversed. It should rather be said: "lest anyone should think *in* me above that which he sees me." As if he were saying: lest anyone fix their attention on me and believe me to be something other than what he sees me to be; for he sees me as a mortal. Lest he believe that divinity is held in me and from me—which is what the Lycaonians had believed about Paul <note>Acts 14:11-13, where the people of Lystra mistook Paul and Barnabas for gods</note>—and because of idolatry they were prone to fix their eye on a creature, which they ought to have fixed on God. By fixing it thus, many were deceived by Dositheus, many by Simon Magus, and finally many by other sorcerers. Paul says: *lest anyone should account of me above that which he sees me.* <note>original Greek: "μή τις εἰς ἐμὲ λογίσηται ὑπὲρ ὃ βλέπει με"</note>

¶ **The Vulgate Edition.** *There was given to me a sting of my flesh, an angel of Satan to buffet me.*
<margin>,</margin>
¶ Immediately after "to buffet," the particle "lest I be exalted" is missing.
<margin>,</margin>
And it should be "to the flesh" in the dative case, not "of the flesh" in the genitive.
<margin>,</margin>
And the word "my" is superfluous.
<margin>,</margin>
Indeed, it rather should have been said a *stake* <term>pallus: a stake or pole</term> or *prick*. And "Satan" rather than "of Satan," so that it is understood as a nominative case and an apposition of speech, so the whole sense is: "there was given to me a stake for the flesh, the angel Satan, who might beat me."
<margin>,</margin>
For that is what "buffet" <note>original: "colaphizet"</note> designates. It is as if we understand it thus: "there was given to me a stake, a pike, a whip, the angel Satan: by which I might be pierced in the flesh, whipped, and beaten." There are those who have understood "there was given to me a sting for the flesh, an angel of Satan to buffet me" as referring to the tickling of lust and the temptation of the flesh. And I believe that among us—that is, the Latins—the old translator provided the occasion for this, because he translated "sting" <note>original: "stimulus"</note> for what was a "stake," "pike," or "whip." And to think this of Paul—so spiritual and holy a man—I consider unworthy and a sin. Nor (I believe) would he have ever written that he did not know it, unless the old translation had twisted their understanding to that sense; and I judge them worthy of pardon. For if they had read Paul in Paul’s own words, because of their piety and mild character, they would have felt differently—even if higher grace had been lacking. For how is a temptation of the flesh of this kind—whether you call it a movement, an impulse, or a tickling—fittingly called a "stake" or a "pike"? For the word <term>skolops: the Greek word Paul uses (σκόλοψ), meaning a pointed stake or thorn</term> which Paul uses does not designate that. How is it an "angel of Satan"? How is it "to buffet," that is, to beat and strike? Furthermore, do we not see that Paul interprets himself? He declares what the "stake" is, what the "pike" is, what the "buffeting of Satan" is, and what that same "infirmity" is, when he says: *Because of which I am content* (or *I am of good courage*) *in infirmities, in insults, in hardships, in persecutions, in distresses for Christ.* And he declares in many places what those things were by which he was beaten and buffeted by the angel of Satan, who wished to hinder him from the announcement of the Gospel of Christ with pressures and troubles. For what else is he doing when he says: *From the Jews five times I received forty stripes (save one), three times I was beaten with rods, once I was stoned, three times I suffered shipwreck, a night and a day I labored in the deep, in journeys often, in perils of rivers, in perils of robbers, in perils...*

[in every] kind: in dangers from the gentiles, in dangers in the city, in dangers in the wilderness, in dangers at sea, in dangers from false brothers. These things he undoubtedly suffered everywhere through the plotting of Satan, just as he himself also testifies when writing to the Thessalonians: *We wanted*, he says, *to come to you—I, Paul, again and again—but Satan hindered us.* <note>1 Thessalonians 2:18</note> But lest I seem to have fashioned this new, or rather (as I believe) most true opinion alone, we could bring the Greeks forward into the midst. Of these, let it now suffice to cite Athanasius <note>Athanasius of Alexandria, a 4th-century Church Father</note> elucidating this passage: "The messenger of Satan," he says, "everywhere incited seditions against Paul, such as Alexander the coppersmith, Hymenaeus, and Philip at Ephesus; so that the most blessed Paul was afflicted in the flesh by various persecutions and tribulations, now by blows, now by lashes, now by imprisonment, and by infinite evils which seemed to be even beyond human endurance." For these things he asked the Lord three times. And so for the rest that follows. Behold, the holy Athanasius, who did not read Paul through an interpreter, feels not differently but the same as we do; or rather, we feel the same as that most blessed man. 

And it is unworthy to hear certain stories—fashioned, I believe, by men lacking both sense and spirit—concerning this passage: new fictions of "infirmities" which never touched Paul. May God grant that those who read these things think on more spiritual and truer matters, and do not judge the "weakness" of spiritual men by the weakness of nature; for this weakness is for the imitation of Christ Jesus, the Savior and Illuminator of all. These things, I believe, were said by me according to the truth and the will of God and the Apostle.

-> CHAPTER XIII. <-

<image-desc>A large decorative historiated initial 'Q' containing a figure in a landscape with buildings in the background.</image-desc>

<margin>69</margin>
That Paul forewarned the Corinthians to repentance—otherwise, in his third arrival, they would be struck by God's vengeance—is not only a threat, but also a prophecy. For it was not he himself who was speaking, but Christ the Lord who was speaking through him. And therefore he adds: ¶ *Behold, I come to you a third time. In the mouth of two or three witnesses every word shall stand. I told you before, and I foretell as if present a second time, and now being absent I write to those who sinned before and to all others: that if I come in the future, I will not spare. Since you seek a proof of Christ speaking in me: who toward you is not weak, but is powerful in you.* ¶ Just as the prophets threaten, so that what they predicted might not absolutely come to pass—for they did not predict it absolutely, but only unless those to whom they spoke changed their ways and reconciled God to themselves—in this same manner Paul also speaks. And what he says: *In the future I will not spare*, he says not because he himself is the avenger, but Christ who was in him. He, however, was the instrument, just as he was also an instrument of powers and signs. And the cause was the unfaithfulness annexed to their sins: of those not believing that Paul could punish, not believing that Christ commanded these things through him. Almost every disease has this quality: that it seeks the "proof" of its own loss.

<summary>The author identifies Paul's "thorn in the flesh" as external persecution based on the Church Fathers and criticizes Vulgate translations of 2 Corinthians 12. He then introduces Chapter 13, emphasizing that Paul's warnings of judgment come from the authority of Christ speaking through him.</summary>
