--- Page 394 ---
<meta>This page transitions from the discussion of Paul's "thorn in the flesh" to the conclusion of the Second Epistle to the Corinthians, focusing on the nature of apostolic power, the necessity of spiritual self-examination, and the final Trinitarian blessing.</meta>

<page-num>13</page-num>
->**COMMENTARY**<-

Nor does one believe before the experience; just as one who suffers from a fever seeks cold water, so one does not believe in an injury until after the danger has been tasted. Such were the Corinthians. But they will say: it is true that Christ is powerful, but the man in him is weak, so that he might show the power of Christ as a testament. This is true: the "man of Christ" <note>Referring to the human nature or the believer in union with Christ</note> is weak in the imitation of the sufferings of Christ in the flesh, but powerful in the virtue of God, by which he lives with him and is capable in the spirit. Just as Elijah was weak in body and in human strength, but powerful by the virtue and power of God in the spirit, by which he was able to draw fire from heaven by his speech and close the heavens by his word. It was not that his speech or word itself drew fire from heaven, or closed the heavens for three years and six months, but it was a sign of the divine power within him, drawing fire from heaven and closing the sky. So also Paul, and the men of Christ, were capable in Christ. Therefore, concerning Christ and those who belong to Christ, the "Christ-bearing" Paul adds:

<margin>70</margin>
> ¶ For although he was crucified out of weakness, yet he lives by the power of God. For we also are weak in him, but we shall live with him by the power of God toward you. Examine yourselves, whether you are in the faith; prove yourselves. Do you not know yourselves, that JESUS CHRIST is in you, unless perhaps you are without proof? <note>Original: *absque probatione*, often translated as "reprobates" or "disqualified," but here meaning "failing the test."</note> But I hope that you know that we are not without proof.

¶ If the Corinthians held the faith, they were able to make a trial from within themselves that Christ the Lord was capable through Paul and the apostles. For Christ the Lord was in them, and they were capable. And they knew this, unless they were without experience and proof. For if they knew it, they undoubtedly ought in no way to be ignorant that Christ was present and powerful in Paul, through whom they held the faith. And even though this is so, Paul nevertheless prays and desires that those who have done evil might be corrected, and those who have not, might do no evil. He desires this so that there might be no need for the proof of that power which he possessed in Christ. He hopes that it might not be necessary to make a trial, but that he might appear as if he were without proof and without the power of making a trial. For all those who threaten the wicked out of the charity of God, and are able to carry out those threats, desire this very thing: they prefer not to execute them and not to make a trial. For the end goal is the correction of character, not the execution of threats. Therefore, they prefer to be seen as being without proof—indeed, without the possibility of proving their threats—on account of the amendment of others. This is the mark of a most kind and merciful nature, and an imitator of God, who threatens not so that he may execute, but so that those who have turned away might be converted and the delinquents amended. He who is omnipotent is always ready and able to punish, yet prefers to restrain his infinite power as if he were in some way powerless, rather than to exercise the vengeance of his threats immediately. For what is it to restrain power and contain power, except in some way to appear unable? So also Paul, the emulator of God, prefers in some way to appear unable, rather than to make a trial of his power. Therefore, with a most kind soul and as an emulator of God, he subjoins, saying:

<margin>71</margin>
> ¶ Now I pray to God that you admit no evil; not that we should appear approved by proof, but that you should do what is good, though we be as if without proof. For we can do nothing against the truth, but for the truth. We rejoice whenever we are weak and you are powerful.

¶ When all live holily and blessedly, there are no wars, no plagues, no pestilence or diseases from contagion, no sterilities. And it pleases God that he should appear weak, as if not prevailing to bring about wars, plagues, diseases, and sterilities, and that the power of men should appear strong, disturbed by no incursions. So also Paul, speaking according to the truth which he emulates, protests that he rejoices that he appears feeble and weak at his arrival, without the strength for taking vengeance. Let them instead be strong against him, fearing no lashes, as if there were none; for it is not the way of an imitator of God to lash the innocent. And for the sake of this, Paul sends ahead this prayer and adds, saying:

<margin>72</margin>
> ¶ And this also we pray for, even for the consummation of your perfection. Therefore I write these things being absent, so that being present I might not use severity according to the power which the Lord has given me for edification and not for destruction.

¶ God gives spiritual power for edification, not for destruction. Therefore, those who wish to strike with spiritual power in any way according to their own lust <note>Meaning "whim" or "arbitrary desire."</note> do not have this power from God, but they presume themselves to have what they do not possess. For that which is of God is ordered; that other is disordered, and therefore not power, but a presumption of power. Therefore, where Paul [addresses] this truth, he greets them holily, saying:

<margin>73</margin>
> ¶ Finally, brothers, farewell. Be perfect, be comforted, be of one mind, live in peace; and the God of love and peace shall be with you. Greet one another with a holy kiss. All the saints greet you. The grace of the Lord JESUS CHRIST, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Spirit, be with you all. Amen.

¶ He concluded his letter by touching upon the mystery of the super-divine TRINITY, attributing love to the Father, grace to the Son, and communion to the Holy Spirit. For the Father so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son. And of the Son it is said: *grace and truth were made through Jesus Christ.* And of the Holy Spirit: *for in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body.* The love of the Father made us sons; the grace of the Son [gave us] the right...

<summary>This page concludes the commentary on 2 Corinthians 13, emphasizing that Paul’s apostolic authority is intended for spiritual building (edification) rather than punishment. It concludes with a Trinitarian analysis of the final benediction, linking the Father to love, the Son to grace, and the Holy Spirit to the community of the Church.</summary>

...the union of the Holy Spirit: undivided. The love of the Father: has drawn us. The grace of the Son: has adorned us. And the union of the Holy Spirit: has joined and grafted us to God. Therefore, to the highest Father, the highest Son, and the highest Holy Spirit—to the one and only God, supreme and overflowing: be the highest honor, the highest thanksgiving, the highest harmony of all praise, and union: forever and ever. # EXAMINATION of some points concerning the text.

<margin>69.</margin>
¶ **Vulgate edition.** *Behold, this third time I am coming to you.* <note>Latin: *Ecce tertio hoc venio ad vos*</note> ¶ It is sufficient if it is said: *behold, the third time I come to you.* The pronoun "this" <note>Latin: *hoc*</note> is redundant, as was also mentioned above. Paul: *Behold, the third time I am coming to you* <note>Original Greek: ἰδοὺ τρίτον ἔρχομαι πρὸς ὑμᾶς</note>.

<margin>A 69, 69.</margin>
¶ **Vulgate edition.** *That in the mouth of two or three witnesses every word shall stand.* ¶ The word "that" <note>Latin: *Ut*</note> is superfluous; it does not help the understanding. Paul: *By the mouth of two witnesses and three, every word shall be established* <note>Original Greek: ἐπὶ στόματος δύο μαρτύρων καὶ τριῶν, σταθήσεται πᾶν ῥῆμα</note>. ¶ **Vulgate edition.** *I told you before, and foretell, as present to you, and now absent to them that sinned before.* ¶ "Therefore" <note>Latin: *ergo*</note> is redundant. And the old translator should have said: *and I foretell as present a second time.* For "a second time" <note>Latin: *secundo*</note> is missing and "to you" <note>Latin: *vobis*</note> is redundant. And furthermore, it should say: *And now being absent I write.* For "I write" <note>Latin: *scribo*</note> is also missing; *to those who have previously sinned,* or *sinned before.* Paul: *I told you before, and foretell, as if I were present the second time; and being absent now I write to them which heretofore have sinned* <note>Original Greek: προείρηκα καὶ προλέγω ὡς παρὼν τὸ δεύτερον, καὶ ἀπὼν νῦν γράφω τοῖς προημαρτηκόσι</note>. ¶ **Vulgate edition.** *Do you seek a proof of Christ who speaks in me?* ¶ It should be said: *since you seek a proof of Christ speaking in me,* or *since you seek a proof, a document, or an approval of Christ who speaks in me.* Paul: *Since ye seek a proof of Christ speaking in me* <note>Original Greek: ἐπεὶ δοκιμὴν ζητεῖτε, τοῦ ἐν ἐμοὶ λαλοῦντος χριστοῦ</note>. ¶ **Vulgate edition.** *But is mighty in you.* ¶ It can be read as *against you* <note>Latin: *in vos*</note>, that is, against and opposite you by taking vengeance; for the Latins are accustomed to use this preposition *in* in this way. Paul: *but is mighty in you* <note>Original Greek: ἀλλὰ δυνατεῖ ἐν ὑμῖν</note>.

<margin>B 70</margin>
¶ **Vulgate edition.** *But he lives by the power of God.* ¶ By "virtue" <note>Latin: *virtute*</note> he means the potency and efficacy of power. Paul: *but he liveth by the power of God* <note>Original Greek: ἀλλὰ ζῇ ἐκ δυνάμεως θεοῦ</note>. ¶ **Vulgate edition.** *But we live with him by the power of God in you.* ¶ And here also "by virtue" means by power. And it seems more appropriate to say at the end *toward you* <note>Latin: *ad vos*</note> or *regarding you* rather than *in you*. Paul: *but we shall live with him by the power of God toward you* <note>Original Greek: ἀλλὰ ζησόμεθα σὺν αὐτῷ ἐκ δυνάμεως θεοῦ εἰς ὑμᾶς</note>. ¶ **Vulgate edition.** *Test your own selves.* ¶ It might be more correct if it were said: *prove yourselves.* Paul: *examine yourselves* <note>Original Greek: ἑαυτοὺς δοκιμάζετε</note>.

<margin>B 71, D 73.</margin>
¶ **Vulgate edition.** *Unless perhaps you are reprobates.* ¶ That word "reprobi" <note>Often translated as outcasts or rejected</note> means "without proof" <note>Latin: *absque probatione*</note>. Just as a "proven" man <note>Latin: *probus*</note> is one who tests, and indeed tests rightly, and has a true sense of things and true experience. An "unproven" man <note>Latin: *improbus*, which the old translator calls *reprobus*</note> is one who does not test, or who does not test as is fitting, who does not attempt the experience of things, or at least not a true one. Furthermore, I do not deny that these terms are also used passively, according to the subject matter. As "proven gold" <note>Latin: *aurum probum*</note>: that which has been tested by experience, and found good and fine. "Unproven gold" <note>Latin: *improbum*</note>: that which experience has shown to be either impure or fake. Here, however, they speak more of action. "Test," he says, "examine": which is to make a trial and a risk of experience. Paul: *unless indeed ye be reprobates* <note>Original Greek: εἰ μήτι ἀδόκιμοί ἐστὲ</note>. ¶ **Vulgate edition.** *Now we pray to God.* ¶ It is said in the singular: *But I pray to God.* Paul: *Now I pray to God* <note>Original Greek: εὔχομαι δὲ πρὸς τὸν θεόν</note>. ¶ **Vulgate edition.** *For the rest, brethren, rejoice.* ¶ Elegantly (as is the custom of letters), the old translator could have said: *farewell.* Paul: *Finally, brethren, farewell* <note>Original Greek: λοιπὸν ἀδελφοὶ χαίρετε</note>. And among the Greeks, the subscription is held: *The second to the Corinthians: written from Philippi, which is in Macedonia, sent by Titus and Luke.*

# COMMENTARIES ON THE EPISTLES OF BLESSED PAUL THE APOSTLE
## BOOK FOUR, WHICH IS ON THE EPISTLE TO THE GALATIANS. CHAPTER I.

<margin>1</margin>
<margin>2</margin>
<margin>3</margin>
<margin>4</margin>
<margin>5</margin>
<margin>6</margin>
<margin>7</margin>
<margin>8</margin>
<margin>9</margin>
<margin>10</margin>
<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'E' depicting a seated figure within an ornate frame of foliage and architectural elements.</image-desc>Writing to the churches of the Galatians <note>The Galatians were a people in central Asia Minor, modern-day Turkey, to whom Paul wrote this stern letter regarding their adherence to Jewish law versus Christian grace.</note>, the apostle (as he is accustomed to do) sets forth a greeting, saying:

> ¶ Paul, an apostle—not from men nor through man, but through JESUS CHRIST and God the Father, who raised him from the dead—and all the brothers who are with me: To the churches of Galatia. Grace to you and peace from God the Father and our Lord JESUS CHRIST, who gave himself for our sins to rescue us from the present evil age, according to the will of our God and Father. To Him be glory forever and ever. Amen.

¶ This is the holy greeting in the grace and peace of Christ, the Son of God, and the eternal Father; it transcends all understanding of this world. For this grace makes us pleasing to the eternal King, and this peace reconciles us to Him and makes us participants in the eternal kingdom, citizens of heaven, and children of God. This holy greeting, I say, first lifts up the hope of our own resurrection by setting before us the true pattern of Christ's resurrection, saying of the Father: *who raised him* (he says) *from the dead.* Truly, Christ also raised Himself, as he said: *Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.* But He (as John says) was speaking of the temple of his body. Yet the Holy Spirit also raised Him from the dead; for it is the Spirit (he says) who gives life. 

For the super-divine Trinity, just as it is one in essence, nature, and power, so too is it undivided in its operation—even if works are referred back to the Father as the "fountain-like" <note>original: *fontanam*; the author uses this to describe the Father as the source or spring from which the other persons of the Trinity and all divine actions flow</note> origin of all movement. *The Father,* he says, *dwelling in me, He does the works.* 

And after the hope of a future resurrection is believed, he places before our eyes the ineffable kindness of Christ toward us and the will of the heavenly Father’s infinite goodness, as well as the malice of the present world. He does this so that we might meditate on Christ’s benefits and not be ungrateful to the one who loves us so much and bestows such great favors. He intends that we be seized by love for the Father—who possesses such piety toward us and such a merciful will that He, who is God over all, desires to be our Father—and that we may praise Him, glorify Him, and hate the world. *Who gave* (he says) *himself for our sins, to rescue us from the present evil age, according to the will of our God and Father.* 

Therefore, if this resurrection of ours (through the meditation on Christ’s resurrection), this kindness of Christ, and this most gracious and paternal will of the Father toward us move us toward hope, gratitude, and a melting love <note>original: *liquefactiuum amorem*; a mystical term suggesting that divine love softens the "frozen" or "hard" heart of the believer</note> (for divine love melts the souls of the pious), then the grace and peace of Christ and of God the Father in the Holy Spirit will surely follow. This is what Paul wishes for the Galatians—indeed, for all people through the Galatians. 

Moreover, a constant divine praise and thanksgiving follows this grace and peace. Paul suggested this as one who, being full of this grace and peace, immediately joins to it the praise of God. 

But come, you will ask: does Paul intend to commend himself? Does he intend to extol and boast of himself when he says: *Paul, an apostle, not from men, nor through man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father*? By no means. Rather, he is like the envoy of some most powerful king crying out to the people: "I come to you from your King, not from another, but sent by Him personally." Though he speaks the truth, his intent in manifesting this truth is to more easily turn the will of the people toward the good of their lord. Does such a servant intend to commend, extol, or boast of himself—especially since he is focused on the person of his lord and not his own? Should he have remained silent about this, or claimed he received such a province from someone lower than the king? Certainly not. For if he had remained silent (as it might have seemed appropriate to some), he would have made the subjects more negligent; and if he claimed a lower authority, he might have made them not only negligent but even contemptuous. I would add that he would also have been a false-speaking interpreter of the king’s will. 

Thus, Paul does not commend himself here; rather, he faithfully and humbly declares the will of the Lord of all majesty, by whom he was truly sent as an apostle to all nations—among whom were the Galatians—so that, knowing clearly by whom he had been sent, they would be neither negligent nor contemptuous. But also, having been led astray by others, they might immediately return to the true Lord who was Christ Jesus and His eternal Father (blessed above all) upon hearing the herald’s proclamation in his own person, not in another's. For they had been led astray by those who were false apostles, who lied by saying they were sent not by God, but through the apostles. For this reason, Paul accuses the Galatians of being so quick to agree with those who testified that they were sent by others and indeed by men; they turned away so easily from the things they had heard from him—who was not sent by man, but by the command of God.

<margin>Gal.</margin>
<margin>2</margin>
yielding <note>original: "cedentes"</note>, that is certainly a marvel. And therefore he adds: ¶ **I marvel that you are so quickly turning away from Him who called you into the grace of CHRIST, into another gospel; which is not another, except that there are some who trouble you and strive to subvert the gospel of CHRIST.** ¶ **But even if we, or an angel from heaven, should preach a gospel to you contrary to what we have preached to you: let him be anathema <note>Anathema is a Greek term meaning "accursed" or "set apart for destruction."</note>. As we have said before, so now I say again: if anyone preaches a gospel other than what you have received: let him be anathema.** For do I now trust in God or in men? Or do I seek to please men? Truly, if I still pleased men, I would not be a servant of CHRIST. ¶ Paul did not trust in, nor did he accommodate himself to men, but to God. And we ought to please men only as long as we believe we can build them up; however, when we see that the desire to please stands in the way of building them up, we must no longer seek to please. Otherwise, we are not servants of Christ. Now, the most blessed apostle saw that if he had studied to please the Galatians and the false apostles at that time, rather than contradicting and opposing them, it would have hindered their spiritual growth. Therefore, he no longer wishes to please them. For that kind of pleasing would be human, carnal, flattering <note>original: "palpatorium"</note>, and harmful. Yet he always wishes to please spiritually. For this is saving and harmless. To please spiritually asserts one's servitude to Christ; to please carnally, however, takes away one's servitude to Christ. And these things are contrary to one another. For the latter belongs to this world, the former to the other. The latter is "civil" according to worldly citizenship; the former is "civil" but pertains to the citizens of the eternal city. The latter is on the surface, the former in the heart. The latter is without true affection and is hypocritical; the former is with holy affection and is not at all feigned. By the former, we please God and the holy angels; by the latter, the world and the malignant powers. The former is truth; the latter, for the most part, gives birth to lies.

<margin>3</margin> Paul, therefore, does not wish to please men, nor the flesh, but the spirit, speaking the truth and adding: ¶ **I make it known to you, brothers: the gospel which was preached by me is not of human origin. For I did not receive it from man, nor was I taught it, but through the revelation of JESUS CHRIST.** ¶ From these words, we ought to be able to clearly understand what Paul’s gospel is, or what was preached by Paul. For it is the "apocalypse" and revelation made to Paul by our Lord Jesus Christ. But is this not the Gospel of Luke? It does not oppose the Gospel of Luke, nor any other gospel; yet it is not the Gospel of Luke, though it harmonizes with all of them. The Gospel of Luke was written not as if immediately from Christ, but as he heard it from men—yet men who were holy and full of God. Just as he himself testifies, saying: *Just as those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and ministers of the word delivered them to us, it seemed good to me also, having followed all things closely from the beginning, to write an orderly account for you, most excellent Theophilus, so that you may know the truth of those words in which you have been instructed.* <note>Quoting the opening of the Gospel of Luke 1:2-4.</note> And how could Paul have received or learned the gospel from men, whom he held as most bitter enemies and whom he dragged to death everywhere? Immediately after he was baptized, before he saw any of the apostles, before he consulted anyone, he preached Christ as the Son of God in the synagogues of the Jews. And in those

<margin>4</margin> places of Arabia where neither the apostles nor the gospel of the Son of God had been heard. This he also adds, saying: ¶ **For you have heard of my former way of life in Judaism: that I persecuted the church of God beyond measure and tried to destroy it. And I advanced in Judaism beyond many of my contemporaries among my people, being more abundantly a zealot for the traditions of my fathers. But when it pleased God—who set me apart from my mother’s womb and called me through His grace—to reveal His Son in me, so that I might preach Him among the gentiles: I did not immediately consult with flesh and blood, nor did I return to Jerusalem to those who were apostles before me, but I went away into Arabia. And again I returned to Damascus. Then after three years, I went back to Jerusalem to visit Peter, and I stayed with him fifteen days. But I saw none of the other apostles except James, the brother of the Lord. Now regarding what I am writing to you: behold, before God, I witness that I am not lying. Afterward, I went into the regions of Syria and Cilicia. I was unknown by face to the churches of Judea which were in CHRIST. They only heard it said: "He who once persecuted us is now preaching the faith he once tried to destroy," and they glorified God in me.** ¶ This is a plain narrative, having no difficulty in being understood. Paul had a zeal for the observations of the ancient law, but not according to knowledge. For he sinned through ignorance, not through the choice of a depraved mind. And he advanced so far in Judaism—that is, in the literal, veiled, and blind observation of the ancient law—that while still a young man, public duties in the persecution of Christ’s churches were entrusted to him. But afterward, because he acted ignorantly in unbelief and not out of certain malice of mind, he obtained the mercy of God; from being a persecutor and blasphemer (as he writes to Timothy), he was placed in the ministry of the gospel. And what does this mean, *who set me apart from my mother’s womb*, except from the womb of Theocrita <note>Theocrita is identified in some early Christian traditions as the name of the Apostle Paul's mother.</note>, as from a carnal mother? For thus Pope Zosimus <note>Zosimus was Pope from 417 to 418 AD.</note> considers the carnal mother of Paul to have been named. And from the womb of the synagogue, as from a mystical mother, into the bosom and breasts of the bride, the Church, which are better than wine and more fragrant than ointments.

a</margin>Writing to the churches of the Galatians (as he is accustomed to do), the apostle first provides a greeting, saying: <term>¶</term> **Paulus, an apostle, not from men nor through man, but through JESUS CHRIST and God the Father who raised him from the dead, and all the brothers who are with me: to the churches of Galatia, grace to you and peace from God the Father and our Lord JESUS CHRIST, who gave himself for our sins, so that he might rescue us from this present evil age, according to the will of our God and Father. To whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.** <term>¶</term> This is the holy greeting in the grace and peace of Christ, the Son of God, and the eternal Father—a greeting that transcends all human understanding. For this grace makes us pleasing to the eternal King, and this peace reconciles us to Him and makes us participants in the eternal kingdom, citizens of heaven, and children of God. This holy greeting, I say, primarily lifts up the hope of our resurrection by setting before us the true model: the resurrection of Christ. Regarding the Father, he says: **who raised** (he says) **him from the dead.** Truly, Christ also raised himself, which he implied when he said: **destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up** <note>John 2:19</note>. But he (as John says) was speaking of the temple of his body. Yet the Holy Spirit also raised him from the dead; for it is the **Spirit** (he says) **who gives life.** <note>original: "spiritus est qui viuificat"</note> For the super-divine Trinity, just as it is one in essence, nature, and power, so it is undivided in its operation—even if works are referred to the Father as the fount-like origin of all movement. **The Father** (he says) **dwelling in me, he does the works.** <note>John 14:10</note> And after the hope of the future resurrection, he places before our eyes the ineffable kindness of Christ toward us, the will of the heavenly Father’s infinite goodness, and the malice of the present world. He does this so that we might reflect on Christ’s benefits and not be ungrateful, but love in return Him who loved us first and granted such great benefits. We should be seized by love for the Father of such great piety and merciful will—who, though he is God over all, wishes to be our Father—and we should praise Him, glorify Him, and hate the world. **Who gave** (he says) **himself for our sins, so that he might rescue us from this present evil age, according to the will of our God and Father.** Therefore, if this resurrection of ours (found in the meditation on Christ’s resurrection), Christ’s kindness, and the most benign and paternal will toward us move us toward hope, gratitude, and a "melting" love (for divine love melts the souls of the pious), then the grace and peace of Christ and of God the Father in the Holy Spirit will surely follow. This is what Paul desires for the Galatians—indeed, for all people through the Galatians. Continual divine praise and thanksgiving follow this grace and peace, which Paul introduced as one who, being full of this grace and peace, immediately joins to it the praise of God.

But come now, you might say: does Paul intend to commend himself? Does he mean to extol and puff himself up when he says: **Paul, an apostle, not from men nor through man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father**? Not at all. Rather, he is like the ambassador <note>original: "legato"</note> of a most powerful king crying out to the people: "I come to you from your king, not from another; I have been sent by his own hand." While telling the truth, his intent through this manifestation of the truth is to more easily turn the people toward the good will of their lord. Does a servant of this kind intend to commend, extol, or puff himself up—especially when he is looking not to his own person but to that of his lord? Should he have kept silent about this, or claimed he received such a province from a subordinate rather than the king? By no means. For if he had kept silent (even if it seemed appropriate), he would have rendered the subjects more negligent; and if he claimed it was from a subordinate, he might have made them not only negligent but perhaps even contemptuous. Add to this that he would have been a false-speaking interpreter of the royal will. Thus, Paul does not commend himself here; rather, he faithfully and humbly declares the will of the Lord of all majesty, by whom he was truly sent as an apostle to all the nations (among whom were the Galatians), so that they, clearly recognizing by whom he was sent, would be neither negligent nor contemptuous. But having been led astray by others, they might immediately return to the true Lord, who was Christ Jesus, and to the proclamation of the Father. For they had been led astray by those who were false apostles, who lied by saying they were sent not by God, but through the [other] apostles. For this reason, Paul accuses the Galatians of so quickly and easily assenting to those who testified that they were sent by others and by men, turning away from those things they had heard from him—sent not by man, but by the command of God re... <meta>The sentence continues on the next page: "re-vealing" or "regarding".</meta>

<header>FOURTH BOOK ON GALATIANS</header>

<margin>2</margin>...preceding points. That is certainly wonderful. And so he adds: ¶ **I marvel that you are so quickly turning away from him who called you into the grace of CHRIST, to another gospel; which is not another, except that there are some who trouble you and want to subvert the gospel of CHRIST. But even if we, or an angel from heaven, should preach a gospel to you contrary to what we have preached to you, let him be accursed** <note>original: "anathema"</note>. **As we said before, so now I say again: if anyone preaches a gospel to you other than what you have received, let him be accursed. For do I now seek the favor of men, or of God? Or do I seek to please men? Truly, if I still pleased men, I would not be a servant of CHRIST.** ¶ Paul did not put his trust in men, nor did he adapt his conduct to suit them, but rather to God. And although we ought to please men for as long as we believe we can edify them, yet when we see that the desire to please stands in the way of and opposes edification—effectively hindering their growth—he no longer wishes to please them. For that kind of pleasing would be human, carnal, flattering <note>original: "palpatorium"</note>, and harmful. However, he always wishes to please in a spiritual way, for this is healthy and harmless. Indeed, to please spiritually confirms one's service to Christ, whereas to please carnally destroys that service. These two are opposites: one belongs to this world, the other to the next. One is "civil" according to worldly conduct; the other is "civil" as a citizen of the eternal city. One is on the surface <note>literally: "on the forehead"</note>, the other is in the heart. One is without true affection and is feigned; the other is with holy affection and not at all counterfeit. In the latter, we please God and the holy angels; in the former, we please the world and malignant powers. The latter is truth; the former for the most part gives birth to lies. Therefore, Paul does not wish to please men—not the flesh, but the spirit—speaking the truth and adding: <margin>3</margin>¶ **I make known to you, brothers, that the gospel which was preached by me is not according to man. For I neither received it from man, nor was I taught it, but through the revelation of JESUS CHRIST.** ¶ From these words, we can clearly determine what we ought to understand as "Paul's Gospel," or that which was preached by Paul. For it is the "apocalypse" and revelation made to Paul by our Lord Jesus Christ. But is this the Gospel of Luke? It is not the Gospel of Luke, nor is it contrary to any other gospel; rather, it is in total agreement with all of them. The Gospel of Luke was written not as something received immediately from Christ, but as Luke heard it from men—though men who were holy and full of God. As he himself testifies, saying: *Just as they delivered them to us, who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and ministers of the word, it seemed good to me also, having followed all things closely from the very beginning, to write an orderly account for you, most excellent Theophilus, that you may know the truth of those things in which you were instructed.* <note>Luke 1:2-4</note> And how could Paul have received or learned the gospel from men, whom he held as bitter enemies and was dragging to their deaths everywhere? Instead, as soon as he was baptized, before he had seen any of the apostles or consulted anyone, he preached Christ in the synagogues of the Jews as the Son of God. He did this even in those <margin>4</margin> regions of Arabia where neither the apostles nor the gospel of the Son of God had yet been heard. This is what he adds, saying: ¶ **For you have heard of my former way of life in Judaism, how I persecuted the church of God beyond measure and tried to destroy it. And I advanced in Judaism beyond many of my contemporaries in my own nation, being more exceedingly zealous for the traditions of my fathers. But when it pleased God, who set me apart from my mother’s womb and called me through his grace, to reveal his Son in me, so that I might preach him among the Gentiles, I did not immediately consult with flesh and blood, nor did I go up to Jerusalem to those who were apostles before me; but I went to Arabia, and returned again to Damascus. Then after three years I went up to Jerusalem to visit Peter, and remained with him fifteen days. But I saw none of the other apostles except James, the Lord’s brother. (Now concerning the things which I write to you, indeed, before God, I do not lie.) Afterward I went into the regions of Syria and Cilicia. And I was unknown by face to the churches of Judea which were in CHRIST. But they only heard it said, "He who formerly persecuted us now preaches the faith which he once tried to destroy." And they glorified God in me.** ¶ This is a clear narrative, having no difficulty in being understood. Paul had a zeal for the observances of the ancient law, but it was not according to knowledge. For he sinned through ignorance, not according to the choice of a depraved mind. He was so advanced in Judaism—that is, in the literal, veiled, and blind observation of the ancient law—that while still a youth, he was publicly entrusted with the task of persecuting the churches of Christ. But afterward, because he acted ignorantly in unbelief and not out of certain malice of mind, he obtained the mercy of God; from being a persecutor and a blasphemer (as he writes to Timothy), he was appointed to the ministry of the Gospel. And what does it mean, **who set me apart from my mother’s womb**? Does it mean from the womb of Theocrita, <note>Apocryphal tradition, sometimes cited by early medieval writers, naming Paul's mother.</note> as from a carnal mother? For so Pope Zosimus <note>Zosimus was Pope from 417-418 AD.</note> believes Paul's carnal mother was named. Or does it mean from the womb of the Synagogue, as from a mystical mother, into the bosom and breasts of the Bride, the Church, which are better than wine and more fragrant than ointments?

<sig>V. i.</sig>

<summary>Paul recounts his miraculous conversion and early ministry to prove that his Gospel came via direct revelation from Christ rather than human instruction. The text contrasts Paul's direct apostolic authority with Luke's historical compilation and interprets Paul's "mother's womb" both literally and allegorically.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians, moving from Paul’s general defense of his ministry to the specific and famous confrontation with Peter (Cephas) in Antioch. It addresses the tension between Jewish Law and the new life in Christ.</meta>

<header>COMMENTARY</header>
<page-num>9</page-num>

<image-desc>A large ornamental drop cap 'P' begins the text with the word 'Petri' (Of Peter).</image-desc>

**P**eter: and others on account of Peter. And Peter sinned not so much for his own sake as for the sake of others, and thus he was to be rebuked. For it was indeed permitted for him not to eat with the Gentiles and to abstain from their foods; however, that **pretending** <note>original: "simulatio"</note> was harmful to others and contrary to their spiritual growth <note>original: "ædificationi," literally "building up"</note>: and therefore he had to be rebuked,

<margin>9</margin>
because neither he nor the others were acting rightly in this matter. And for that reason, Paul adds the manner in which he rebuked Peter’s pretense, in this way: <margin>,, ,, ,, ,, ,, ,, ,, ,, ,, ,, ,, ,,</margin> **But when I saw that they were not walking uprightly according to the truth of the gospel, I said to Peter before everyone: If you, though you are a Jew, live like a Gentile and not like a Jew, why do you compel the Gentiles to live like Jews? We, who are Jews by birth and not "Gentile sinners," knowing that a person is not justified by the works of the law, but only through faith in JESUS CHRIST—even we have believed in CHRIST JESUS, so that we may be justified by faith in CHRIST, and not by works of the law. For this reason, no flesh shall be justified by the works of the law. But if, while seeking to be justified in CHRIST, we ourselves have been found to be sinners, is CHRIST then a minister of sin? Certainly not! For if I rebuild the very things I tore down, I make myself a lawbreaker. For I through the law died to the law, so that I might live for God. I have been crucified with CHRIST. It is no longer I who live, but CHRIST lives in me. And the life I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself up for me. I do not nullify the grace of God. For if righteousness comes through the law, then CHRIST died for nothing.**

To this rebuke, Peter yielded his hands <note>an idiom meaning "to surrender" or "accept correction"</note> for the spiritual growth of both parties. For the truth of the gospel is this: once Christ's baptism and Christ's faith have been received, the old Jewish rites are nothing. Peter was not ignorant of this. For since he was a Jew by birth, he had been living like a Gentile, not observing the Jewish rituals, except for that brief time when he was pretending—fearing to offend those sent from James. That is, he feared for them, lest perhaps by being offended by this, they might fall away from the faith. And this fear was "good" in intent, for he was the Apostle to the Circumcised <note>the Jewish people</note>; but the pretense born from this fear was harmful to the Gentiles who were present, and of whom Paul was the Apostle. Therefore, out of necessity and duty—not rashly, nor out of pride or impudence—Paul rebuked him; not imperiously, not with a haughty brow, nor contentiously, but speaking very kindly and in the fervor of the Spirit of God.

This is made clear by the reasons Paul attaches to his rebuke of Peter. One of these is: that a person is not justified by the works and observations of the Old Law, but justification is poured in through faith in Christ alone. Otherwise, if observance of the Law could justify, they would never have had to flee to the faith of Christ to be justified. Yet all of them had fled to exactly that. Therefore, Jewish ritual is not necessary for justification. Furthermore, through the New Law we are dead to the Old Law: and the mysteries of Christ destroy the observances of the Old Law just as the rising light destroys the darkness. If, therefore, we restore the things which the light of Christ’s mysteries destroys, do we not do wrong and find ourselves to be sinners? How then shall those initiated into the mysteries of Christ observe Jewish rituals? How, through those mysteries, shall they repair what has been destroyed? Will they not sin? But is Christ a minister of sin? Certainly not. Therefore, the Law of Christ does not serve to keep the Jewish rites alive once they have been set aside.

Furthermore, in baptism we are all crucified with Christ, and we die together, and with Him we rise in mystery: and we no longer live our own life, but the life of Christ. For Christ lives in us. Our "carnal" life was destroyed, and now we live a life not our own, which is of the Spirit. For it is not our spirit, but God's. And the Old Law was the law of the life of the flesh; but the New Law, the Law of Christ, is the law of the life of the Spirit. How then shall we live by the law of that life which has been destroyed? Therefore, those who live by the Law of Christ must not observe Jewish rituals. Again, those who think they are justified through the observances of the Law deny the grace of God. For what works provide is not grace, but the "fruit" of works. But those who are justified not by works, but through faith in Christ, affirm God's grace rather than taking it away. And these people are grateful to God, while the others are ungrateful. But how shall we be ungrateful to the Son of God, in whose faith we live, who loved us and gave himself for us? Let the works of the Old Law be gone, then, lest we be ungrateful—lest we consider the grace of Christ (through which alone everyone is saved) to be void, useless, and nothing. Finally, if the works of the Law justify, then Christ died pointlessly. But Christ did not die for nothing or without cause. Therefore, the "Stronger One" <note>Christ</note> arriving took away the weakness of the Law. Therefore, the overcome weakness of Judaism must not be observed alongside the power of the Law of Christ. These are the spiritual arguments which the "Spirit-speaking" <note>original: "spiritiloquus"</note> Paul poured out from the Holy Spirit while correcting Peter's pretense in the sight of all. To these, Peter did not wish to resist, nor were the others able to. And God permitted Peter to slip a little—not so much for himself as for others—so that from that fall, a greater rising might happen for everyone, and a greater good might be born for all. This permission is called a **divine dispensation** <note>a theological term for God's purposeful arrangement of history</note>.

But come now, was Paul not similarly to be criticized when he circumcised Timothy, or when he purified himself for seven days, or when an offering was made for him as he entered the Temple, just as for the others? Did he not know that the circumcision of Timothy was nothing, and likewise the rituals of that purification and the offering of sacrifices?

<summary>This page explains Paul’s public rebuke of Peter in Antioch, arguing that Jewish rituals are obsolete because justification comes through faith in Christ alone. It frames Peter’s error as a "divine dispensation" allowed by God to clarify the supremacy of the Gospel over the Old Law.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Paul's rebuke of Peter, shifting focus toward a theological defense of Paul’s own actions—specifically his "pretense" in following Jewish customs—and a technical comparison between the Latin Vulgate and the original Greek text of the Epistle to the Galatians.</meta>

<header>IIII</header>
<sig>V. iij.</sig>

<margin>Galatians</margin>
to be nothing. If he knew this and yet acted as if it were otherwise, he was undoubtedly pretending <note>original: "simulabat," referring to the act of "simulation" or "dissimulation," which in this context means outward behavior that differs from inward conviction for a specific purpose.</note>. Why then was he not to be rebuked like Peter? This ambiguity has perplexed many. But we say that pretense, as pretense, is not an evil (for even the Lord pretended he was going further <note>A reference to Jesus on the road to Emmaus in Luke 24:28.</note>), but is an indifferent thing that can lead to both good and evil. For if it saves, if it further inflames the heart—just as Christ’s pretense further inflamed the disciples so that they sought his presence—if it builds up <term>edifies (ædificat): the process of strengthening the faith or moral character of others</term>, it is good. If it destroys, if it takes away charity, if it is contrary to edification, it is evil and deserves rebuke. We freely admit that Paul pretended in his observance of Jewish rites, even though he knew they were nothing; but he did so at a time when his example did no harm, and the pretense was actually beneficial. For when he came to Lystra, he circumcised Timothy, whom he had decided to take as a companion on his journey. He did this not so much out of fear of the Jews as out of concern for the Jews through whose lands he was to pass, lest he offend their faith in Christ by bringing an uncircumcised man among them, and lest they grow weak in faith or fall away from it. Furthermore, he was quieting seditions and tumults that might have been stirred up against him for this reason. He knew that by this act he was opening a freer way for the word of God among the Jews. There were similar reasons when he pretended to undergo Jewish purifications in Jerusalem. For these acts were beneficial; they preserved charity and did not hinder the more ready acceptance of the faith of Christ (which is the greatest edification). Therefore, even if he feared and pretended out of fear as Peter did, he is not to be rebuked by the same right as Peter. For Peter was doing harm, while Paul was not. Therefore, "building up" or "doing harm" are the rules by which we judge whether a pretense should be criticized or not. Certainly, all of Paul's deeds, even his pretenses, are spiritual. And he who understands otherwise does not understand Paul, but sins in the flesh against the spirit. May Jesus Christ therefore grant us to understand spiritually, and worthily of himself, those things which he spoke through his apostle Paul, so that we may be able to magnify and glorify his most blessed name forever.

# EXAMINATION of certain points regarding the literal text.

**The Vulgate edition:** *With Barnabas, taking Titus also along.* 
Paul uses the active participle: *taking along Titus as well.* But this matters little. Paul: *with Barnabas, having taken along also Titus* <note>original Greek: "μετὰ βαρνάβα συνπαραλαβὼν καὶ τίτον"</note>.

**The Vulgate edition:** *And I conferred with them the Gospel.*
We could say: *I presented it to them.* In this place, Jerome criticizes the Latin translator. That which the Latin translator previously called "I acquired," he has in this present place translated as "I conferred." He adds: "and (to speak more truly), the Greek word *I laid before/communicated* <note>original Greek: "ἀνεθέμην"</note> means something other than how we understand it; namely, when we confer those things we know with a friend and place them, as it were, into his bosom and conscience." Paul: *and I communicated to them the gospel* <note>original Greek: "καὶ ἀνεθέμην αὐτοῖς τὸ ἐυαγγέλιον"</note>.

<margin>
B
7
</margin>
**The Vulgate edition:** *To those who seemed to be something.*
The phrase "to be something" is superfluous; it is equally expressed by the present tense, as if we said "to those who are esteemed." For in the time of the most blessed apostle Paul, those who had enjoyed familiarity with Christ were held in the highest estimation. Paul himself admits this, and it was reasonable. But the way the old translator speaks seems to diminish the reputation which Paul actually honors and increases. It seems to sound like contempt, where it actually sounds like reverence. The flesh and the spirit make this difference visible: for those who read according to the flesh perceive contempt, but those who read according to the spirit perceive reverence. Paul: *but privately to those of reputation* <note>original Greek: "κατ' ἰδίαν δὲ τοῖς δοκοῦσιν"</note>.

<margin>
A
6
</margin>
**The Vulgate edition:** *But because of the false brothers brought in secretly.*
The word "but" does not seem to fit in this place; however, if one does fit, "indeed" seems better. For if you read "but," it seems as though Titus was not compelled to be circumcised by the apostles, yet was nevertheless circumcised because of the false brothers brought in. Jerome rejects the conjunction "but" <note>original: "autem"</note> and thinks it is superfluous. For, he says, if it is read, it has nothing to which it responds. Paul: *But because of the false brothers brought in* <note>original Greek: "Διὰ δὲ τοὺς παρεισάκτους ψευδαδελφούς"</note>.

**The Vulgate edition:** *To whom we did not yield in subjection for even an hour.*
We might prefer to join this with the word "subjection" in the ablative case <note>A grammatical point regarding Latin case endings</note>. And this passage was corrected from Jerome according to the Greek truth. For (as Jerome says) the Latins previously read it as an affirmation: *to whom we yielded for an hour.* Ambrose also confirms this and defends the affirmation, not based on the circumcision of Titus (whom he admits was not circumcised), but based on the circumcision of Timothy. However, Timothy was not circumcised during that introduction of false brothers, but at Lystra, as Chapter 16 of the Acts of the Apostles testifies. Therefore, to read it with the negation <note>i.e., "we did *not* yield"</note> seems altogether healthier and truer. Paul: *to whom not even for an hour did we yield in subjection* <note>original Greek: "οἷς οὐδὲ πρὸς ὥραν εἴξαμεν τῇ ὑποταγῇ"</note>.

<margin>
A
7
</margin>
**The Vulgate edition:** *But from those who seemed to be something.*
It can be said, as was said before: *those who are esteemed to be something,* or *those who are of some reputation.* Paul: *but from those seeming to be something* <note>original Greek: "ἀπὸ δὲ τῶν δοκούντων εἶναί τι"</note>.

<margin>
B

</margin>
**The Vulgate edition:** *For to me, those who seemed to be something contributed nothing to me.*
The words "to be" and "something" are redundant; it is enough to say: *those who are esteemed.* Paul: *for to me those of reputation added nothing* <note>original Greek: "ἐμοὶ γὰρ οἱ δοκοῦντες οὐδὲν προσανέθεντο"</note>.

**The Vulgate edition:** *Who seemed to be pillars.*
It can be said: *who are esteemed as pillars.* Dionysius does this:

<meta>This page continues the theological argument regarding the transition from the Jewish Law to the grace of Christ. The previous page discussed the concept of "pious pretense" (simulation) in the actions of Peter and Paul; here, the author moves into a formal commentary on the promise made to Abraham and why the Old Law was a temporary necessity before the arrival of the New Covenant.</meta>

<page-num>3</page-num>
<header>COMMENTARY</header>
<language>Latin</language>
<page-type>text</page-type>

¶ In the history of Genesis, it is written that God said to Abraham: *In your seed all the nations of the earth shall be blessed.* <note>original: "in semine tuo benedicentur omnes gentes terre," referencing Genesis 22:18.</note> This is understood, without a doubt, to refer to Christ and the spiritual blessing, which is the truest blessing of all. This certainly could not be hidden from Paul, who, through the Holy Spirit, poured into us an understanding of the Scriptures. And Christ the Lord confirmed this promise by the testament of his death; he was the seed of Abraham according to the flesh, but the divine offspring according to eternal generation. Now, if a testament <term>testament (testamentum): in this context, both a "will" leaving an inheritance and a "covenant" or formal agreement between God and humanity</term> is validated by the death of a man—and though it be validated by a man, no one may void it, cancel it, or add a further order to it—how much less can the promise of the blessing of all nations of the earth (validated and confirmed later by the testament of the death of the Son of God) be made void or have another testament ordered over it? If a man's testament is not made void, how shall the testament of God be made void? For Christ is not only man, but also God. But you will say that the Old Testament was ordained. You speak truly; but it was not "super-ordained" <note>In the sense of being a superior law that replaces the promise.</note>. And it was confirmed not in the death of a man, but in the death of cattle, so that it might be called not so much a testament as a type and figure <note>original: "typus & figura," referring to a symbolic precursor that points toward a future reality.</note> of the testament, and a kind of preparation for receiving the true testament which was yet to come. I say "preparation" because it provided for infirmities and diseases, so that people might be capable of receiving the benefits and the goods of the future testament. Accordingly, the Apostle—overflowing with divine light—satisfies these doubts in a few words, saying:

<margin>15</margin> ¶ Why then the Law? It was added because of transgressions (until the seed should come to whom the promise was made), ordained through angels by the hand of a mediator. Now, a mediator is not of one; but God is one. ¶ The Old Law was arranged by angels for Moses. But Moses was a mediator between the Lord and his servants. For there is a mediator where there are at least two parties. The New Law, however, was arranged through Christ, who is superior to all angels; and he himself, who arranged it, is the mediator between God as Father and men—no longer as servants, but as sons. And the law of the human mediator lasted only until the law of the divine mediator was introduced. For servitude lasts only until liberty is introduced. Therefore, the Old Law was "angelic" by those who arranged it, "human" by its mediator, and for those who received it, it was a law of servitude and (if I may say so) of bondservants. But the New Law is divine and super-angelic from its Ordainer and Mediator, and for those who receive it, it is a law of liberty and of sons. The Old Law did not justify, but prepared servants for justification; the New Law now justifies, taking away servitude and making people free and making them sons. Therefore, the Law was not given in place of the promises, but only as a preparation—like medicines and diets, which are no longer needed once perfect health is reached. The Old Law was given like a tutor <note>original: "pedagogus." In the Roman world, a pedagogue was a trusted slave who supervised a child's conduct and escorted them to school, but was not the primary teacher.</note> for infants

<margin>16</margin> in the raw elements of letters, who is no longer needed when a mature and perfect age arrives. The most blessed Paul opens this to us in this way: ¶ Is the Law then against the promises of God? By no means. For if a law had been given which could give life, truly justification would be from the law. But Scripture has confined all things under sin, so that the promise by faith in JESUS CHRIST might be given to those who believe. But before faith came, we were kept confined under the law for the future faith that was to be revealed. Therefore, the Law was our tutor leading us to Christ, so that we might be justified by faith. But when faith came, we were no longer under a tutor. For you are all sons through faith. ¶ A tutor is one who pre-instructs boys and leads them to their letters. When they are sufficient to hear the excellent Master, they no longer have need of the tutor. When Christ came, the Supreme Master came. Therefore, those who have come to him no longer have need of the tutor. Now, the Law was the tutor that pre-instructed and led them to Christ. Therefore, the Law was no longer necessary, but rather faith—which is superior to the law, just as wisdom is superior to grammar. And just as one who comes to a wise man and listens diligently "puts on" wisdom and is made like the wise man—whoever he may be and of whatever condition, whether Gaul, Scythian, Greek, free, slave, male, or female—he is nothing else and becomes nothing else from the wise man but a wise person. In

<margin>17</margin> this same way, those who come to Christ "put on" Christ, whoever they are and of whatever condition; and they are nothing else but Christ from Christ. And for that reason, Paul adds: ¶ For as many of you as were baptized into CHRIST have put on CHRIST. There is neither Jew nor Gentile, there is neither slave nor free, there is neither male nor female; for you are all one in CHRIST JESUS. And if you are CHRIST’S, then you are the seed of Abraham and heirs according to the promise. ¶ It follows: Christ is the seed of Abraham, and we have put on Christ; therefore, in Christ, we are the seed of Abraham. Again: we are the seed of Abraham in Christ, and in Christ the blessing of all nations was promised, as well as the true inheritance; therefore we are sons of the blessing and heirs of the true promise, whom Christ the King of the heavens has enrolled in the eternal inheritance. Let us rejoice not merely because we are sons of Abraham, but especially because we carry the name and substance of Christ, and because our names are written in heaven, and we are one with Christ.

->To whom be all honor and glory forever and ever.<-

It argues that through faith in Christ, all people—regardless of status or ethnicity—become "clothed in Christ" and are the true heirs of the promise made to Abraham.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philological and theological examination of Paul's Epistle to the Galatians, moving from the specific phrasing of the Vulgate's translation of Chapter 3 into the beginning of Chapter 4, which compares the state of humanity before Christ to that of a minor under the care of guardians.</meta>

<page-num>157</page-num>
<header>IIII 157 Gal.</header>

<margin>A 10</margin> # EXAMINATION of certain matters regarding the literal text.
¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "O foolish Galatians, who has bewitched you not to obey the truth?" <note>original: "O insensati Galatę quis vos fascinauit nō obedire veritati."</note>
¶ It could be said: "O mad or foolish Galatians, who has persuaded you not to be persuaded by the truth or not to yield to the truth?" For he who is persuaded, yields. Thus the words of Paul: "senseless," "bewitched," "to be persuaded" <note>original: "ἀνόητοι, ἐβάσκανεν πείθεσθαι"</note> seem to signify: "mad," "to envy," and "to be persuaded." But even Saint Jerome <note>original: "Hieronymus"</note> omitted this phrase "to obey the truth" because he had not found it translated in the copies belonging to Origen. 
Paul: "O foolish Galatians, who has bewitched you not to be persuaded by the truth?" <note>original: "ὦ ἀνόητοι γαλάται τίς ὑμᾶς ἐβάσκαμεν τῇ ἀληθείᾳ μὴ πείθεσθαι"</note>

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "Before whose eyes Jesus Christ was portrayed, and crucified among you." <note>original: "Añ quorum oculos IHESVS CHRISTVS proscriptus est / & in vobis crucifixus."</note>
¶ The old translator could have expressed this with the dative: "to whom he was also depicted." That is, as if he were represented before their eyes in a painting, since the truth had been narrated to them precisely <term>to the fingernail (ad unguem): a Latin idiom for "perfectly" or "with high precision," referring to a sculptor checking the smoothness of a joint with a thumbnail</term> and as if to the life. In the phrase "and crucified in you," the conjunction "and" is superfluous. 
Paul: "Before whose eyes Jesus Christ was publicly portrayed as crucified." <note>original: "οἷς κατ᾽ ὀφθαλμοὺς ἰησοῦς χριστὸς προεγράφη, ἐν ὑμῖν σταυρώμενος."</note>

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "Are you so foolish?" <note>original: "Sic stulti estis."</note>
¶ Where the old translator says "foolish" <note>original: "stulti"</note> here, at the beginning of the chapter he said "senseless" <note>original: "isensati"</note>. 
Paul: "Are you so foolish?" <note>original: "οὕτως ἀνόητοί ἐσέ"</note>

<margin>11</margin> ¶ "Does this happen from the works of the law or from the hearing of faith? Certainly from faith." <note>original: "An id ex operibus legis fit an ex auditu fidei: certe fidei."</note> We have expressed the response "certainly from faith"—which is nonetheless understood even if suppressed—for the sake of greater and readier understanding. For Paul is quite brief-spoken and often suppresses words, yet he is overflowing with meaning.

<margin>B 12</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "Scripture, however, providing." <note>original: "Prouidens autē scriptura."</note>
¶ More fittingly: "foreseeing" <note>original: "pręuidens"</note>, since that Spirit through whom the Scripture was inspired knows and foresees all things. 
Paul: "The Scripture, foreseeing..." <note>original: "προϊδοῦσα δὲ ἡ γραφή."</note>

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "Because the just lives by faith." <note>original: "Quia iustus ex fide viuit."</note>
¶ It should be spoken in the future tense: "shall live" <note>original: "viuet"</note>, as was already stated in the first chapter of the commentaries on the Epistle to the Romans. 
Paul: "Because the just shall live by faith." <note>original: "ὅτι ὁ δίκαιος ἐκ πίστεως ζήσεται."</note>

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "But he who has done them shall live in them." <note>original: "Sed q fecerit ea: viuet in illis."</note>
¶ It should say: "the **man** who has done them." For the word "man" is missing in the Vulgate. 
Paul: "But the man who does these things shall live by them." <note>original: "ἀλλ᾽ ὁ ποιήσας αὐτὰ ἄνθρωπος, ζήσεται ἐν αὐτοῖς."</note>

<margin>B 13</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "He was made a curse for us, for it is written: 'Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree.'" <note>original: "Factus est pro nobis maledictum quia scriptum est maledictus omnis qui pēdet in ligno."</note>
¶ What the old translator previously called "a curse" <note>the noun *maledictum*</note>, he here calls "cursed" <note>the adjective *maledictus*</note>. But perhaps it is more appropriately said: "He was made a curse" <note>original: "maledictum" or "maledictio"</note> for us, rather than "cursed." Just as in Paul's manner of speaking, "He was made sin for us" rather than "a sinner." To be made sin or to be made a curse for us is for Him to bear our sins and our curse himself. As Peter says: "He himself bore our sins in his body upon the tree." And regarding what Paul brings from Deuteronomy according to the Septuagint version, Saint Jerome disputes the opinion of many that the Hebrew says: "the curse of God is he who is hanged." This fits Paul's meaning, who says he was made a "curse" <note>original: "κατάραν"</note>. It is as if, because it was a punishment with which God wanted to afflict curse and sin along with Christ on the cross, he wanted this grace to be given to all who die on a cross: that their bodies should not remain on the cross until the next day, but be buried on the same day. It is as if the cross before the Cross—that is, before the arrival and recognition of the true Cross—was already working mercy. Paul follows this understanding under the Septuagint translation. 
Paul: "having become a curse for us; for it is written, 'Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree.'" <note>original: "γενόμενος ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν κατάρα. γέγραπται γὰρ ἐπικατάρατος πᾶς ὁ κρεμάμενος ἐπὶ ξύλου."</note>

<margin>B 14</margin> ¶ "Brothers, I speak according to man; yet a man’s confirmed testament..." <note>original: "Fratres secundum hominem / dico tamen hominis confirmatum testamentum."</note> That phrase "I speak" <note>original: "dico"</note> has the force of the particles "even if" or "although" in Paul’s speech, which is shown by the contrasting particle "yet." But because this does not correspond to Latin custom, we have placed the word "although" <note>original: "licet"</note> in place of the word "I speak." According to the usage of Latin speech, the contrasting particle "yet" <note>original: "tamen"</note> responds to it, and the Apostle's meaning is rendered clearer and more lucid to us. 
Paul: "Brothers, I speak in a human way; though it is only a man's covenant..." <note>original: "ἀδελφοί, κατὰ ἄνθρωπον λέγω ὅμως ἀνθρωπου κεκυρωμέμνη διαθήκην."</note>

<margin>14</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "The testament confirmed by God, which the law made four hundred and thirty years later does not make void." <note>original: "Testamētū cōfirmatū a deo: quæ post quadrigētos & trigīta annos facta est lex / nō irritū facit."</note>
¶ One should read: "pre-confirmed" or "previously established" by God in Christ. For the prefix "pre-" or "before" is missing, as is the phrase "in Christ." 
Paul: "A covenant previously ratified by God in Christ, the law, which came four hundred and thirty years later, does not annul." <note>original: "Διαθήκην προκεκυρωμένημ ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ εἰς χριστὸν, ὁ μετὰ ἔτη τετρακόσια καὶ τριάκοντα γεγονὼς νόμος οὐκ ἀκυροῖ."</note>

<margin>C 16</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "Is the law then against the promises of God?" <note>original: "Lex ergo aduersus promissa dei?"</note>
¶ This word "against" <note>original: "aduersus"</note> or "contrary to" seems to imply a substitution rather than an opposition. It is as if one were asking: "Is the law in the place of the promises?" 
Paul: "Is the law then against the promises of God?" <note>original: "ὁ δὲ νόμος κατὰ τῶν ἐπαγγελιῶν τοῦ θεοῦ;"</note>

<margin>D 17</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "For you are all one." <note>original: "Omnes enī vos unū estis."</note>
¶ It should be said "one [person]" <note>original: "vnus," correcting the Vulgate's neuter "unum" to the masculine singular to reflect the Greek "heis"</note>. 
Paul: "For you are all one [in Christ Jesus]." <note>original: "πάντες γὰρ ὑμεῖς εἷς ἐσε."</note>

### CHAPTER 4.

<image-desc>A large decorative initial "O" depicting a seated male figure in academic or religious robes, holding a book, set within a classical arched architectural frame.</image-desc>
Before the coming of Christ, both the nations and the Jews were like small children under tutors, guardians, and stewards. The tutors of the nations were the sophists, instructing them in the false worship of demons. The guardians were liars. For they said they were the guardians and commissioners of God, but they were of the opposing power. They were bad stewards and administrators; for they distributed evil things instead of good, and they squandered the goods of the Lord. But the tutors of the Jews were the Law...

It concludes by beginning Chapter 4, illustrating the spiritual state of humanity before Christ as that of a child under the control of untrustworthy guardians.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians, transitioning from the previous discussion of the law as a temporary guide to the specific metaphors Paul uses in Chapter 4 regarding childhood, inheritance, and the "elements of the world."</meta>

<page-num>4</page-num>
<header>( COMMENTARY )</header>

<margin>4</margin>
They established these things legitimately, preparing for the true worship of God, acting as the true commissioners of the true God and rightly managing the household of God. And both the people of the nations <note>the Gentiles</note> and the Jews were like servants, over whom <term>pedagogues</term> <note>original: "pædagogi," referring to household tutors or guardians who supervised children</note>, deputies, and stewards held authority. However, divine kindness wished to reveal His Son to both groups when they reached adult age. This adult age—the time, so to speak, when the period of guardianship was full and complete—was the coming of Christ, the Son of God and Son of Man, <term>consubstantial</term> <note>sharing the same essential nature or "substance"</note> with both God and us. Then, those who wished to recognize God the Father through the consubstantial Son of God—who deigned to become our brother—were no longer in the servitude of guardians, deputies, and stewards. Instead, as children and free people, knowing the Father and the Father's wisdom, majesty, and beauty, they received the inheritance and the lordship. But those who were unwilling remained servants under guardians, occupied with the <term>rudimentary elements of the world</term> <note>original: "rudia mundi elementa," referring to basic physical rituals and worldly laws</note>, making no further progress toward the wisdom of God and receiving nothing of the inheritance or lordship. For just as the things that guardians teach to children are nothing but certain basic elements and first principles compared to those things to be learned in adulthood (which is the age of maturity), so too the ceremonies and rites of both the Gentiles and the Jews were elements running ahead of the adult age. The former <note>the Jewish rites</note> guided one well by the hand; the latter <note>the Gentile rites</note> did so wrongly; yet both were fleshly and worldly elements. Under these were the Jews, and under those were the Gentiles. But when the perfect age arrived—which is the age of liberty and recognized <term>sonship</term> <note>original: "filiationis"</note>—the pursuit of the flesh and of corporal things no longer helps; rather, it is the teaching of the spirit and of eternal things. The elements of the world become superfluous, their duty performed, just as the rough studies of boys are set aside in older age. Neither the rites of the ancients nor those of the Jews or Gentiles will hold any further place. Nor does this analogy fail. Wherefore Paul adds:

<margin>18</margin>
¶ **I say then, that as long as the heir is a little child, he differs in no way from a servant, though he be the lord of all; but he is under deputies and stewards until the time preordained by the father. In like manner we also, when we were children, were under the elements of the world, bound in servitude. But when the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, made of a woman, made under the law, to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption. And because you are sons, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying out "Abba," that is, "Father." Therefore, he is no longer a servant, but a son; and if a son, then an heir of God through CHRIST.**

¶ This is a great and inexpressible proof of divine kindness toward us: lest we should despair out of our own fragility that we possess such a Father, He sent His own Spirit—the Spirit of His Son—into our hearts, providing confidence to our smallness of soul and instructing us so that we may call God "Father," whom even the angels do not dare to call so. And from where does such great confidence come to us? It comes from the humility of the Son of God, who willed to become consubstantial with us. However, He was not made consubstantial with angels; for He was made flesh, and He was not made an angel. He did not take up the nature of angels, but He took up the <term>seed of Abraham</term> <note>meaning He took on human ancestry</note>. If we are sons—and sons inherit with the father—then we are heirs of God, but through Him by whom we were adopted as sons. In Him, therefore, every soul dissolves <note>in devotion</note>; through Him we are made sons of God and participants in the eternal kingdom. But could either the Gentiles or the Jews, serving under guardians and learning the rough elements of the world, ever have imagined such an inexpressible dispensation of the depths of God’s kindness toward us, which, even when known, turns the whole world to wonder? Why do I say "known"? It is certainly so great that it cannot be fully known, and it escapes every faculty of cognition. If we cannot know it because of its sheer excellence, it is enough—and certainly far better—that He Himself knows us as sons. For what would it benefit anyone to know the king as a father if the king does not recognize the son? Indeed, it is a great good for him who is recognized as a son by the king, even if he did not yet know the father. It is good, however, to know, and better to be known; it is best and most pleasant to know and be known. And therefore, addressing the Galatians, who had been Gentiles, Paul adds:

<margin>19</margin>
¶ **But then indeed, not knowing God, you served those who by nature are not gods. Now, however, knowing God—or rather, being known by God—how is it that you turn back again to the weak and beggarly elements, which you wish to serve all over again?**

¶ These Galatians were like a man who, having been raised among filth, was recognized by the king as his son; having been led out from humble places, he was brought into the sublime royal court of the father, recognizing the father and (what is better) being recognized by the father. Yet, that man, leaving behind that heavenly place of the father, would descend to humble things which might seem less filthy than his previous ones, but having abandoned royal liberty, he would serve again. And that is indeed a servitude which consists in the depression of the spirit and the exaltation of the flesh. But the liberty of a son consists in the exultation of the spirit and the depression of the flesh. Would not the father justly disown him as degenerate and ignoble, and deprive him of the kingdom? So the Galatians had been led from the servitude of demons—which was filthy and lowest—to the sublime worship of God, recognizing God as Father and (what is better) being recognized by God as sons. But from 그 sublime place and the royal liberty of sonship, they wished to descend to Jewish observances, which appeared less filthy but were still situated in a lowly place.

<summary>This page explains Paul's metaphor of the "pedagogue," comparing the religious laws of Jews and Gentiles to a child's temporary guardians who are made redundant once the "adult age" of Christ arrives. It emphasizes the transformation of believers from servants into heirs through the Spirit of adoption.</summary>
<keywords>sonship, inheritance, consubstantial, pedagogue, elements of the world, Galatians, divine kindness, Abba Father, adoption</keywords>
