<meta>This page continues the commentary on Paul's Epistle to the Galatians, Chapter 4. The previous page discussed how the Law served as a temporary "pedagogue" or guardian until the coming of Christ. Now, the author explores Paul's frustration with those who, having achieved the freedom of adulthood in Christ, wish to return to the "childish" rituals of the Old Law.</meta>

<page-num>155</page-num>
<header>IIII 155</header>
<margin>Galatians</margin>

...about to serve again, keeping days, years, months, new moons, and other Jewish observances. Having despised the wisdom of the heavenly court, like children sitting in the dust, they prefer to spend their whole lives on grammatical basics and the useless scraps of petty phrases. The Apostle reveals how they have fallen back from the exalted freedom of Christ into Jewish <term>trifles</term> <note>original: "nenias," meaning nonsense, trifles, or funeral songs</note>. With great kindness, he calls them back through his own concern and example, saying: "*You observe days, and months, and seasons, and years. I am afraid for you, that perhaps I have labored over you in vain. Become as I am, for I also became as you are.*"

"You see," he says, "that I observe no ceremonies according to the Jewish calendar; I do not offer sacrifices, I do not keep the <term>Feast of Tabernacles</term> <note>original: "scenophegia," from the Greek for the Jewish festival of Sukkot</note>, nor do I perform any other of their rites. Be like me, for you are just as free as I am, and I am just as you are. I am a son, and you are sons. Otherwise, I would have labored among you in vain, since you do not wish to hold onto your freedom but instead prefer slavery. For how can it be that you are the children of a King, yet you are slaves—or rather, you *wish* to be slaves? This is beneath the status of a King's children; it is beneath their very spirit."

<margin>21</margin>
Now Paul, burning with the love of God and unable to contain his affection for them—treating them as the children of his own Lord—recalls them to the freedom of sons with the great gentleness of the Holy Spirit, saying: "*Brethren, I beg you. You have done me no wrong. You know that because of physical infirmity I preached the gospel to you at first; and you did not despise or reject the trial I faced in my flesh, but you received me as an angel of God, even as Christ Jesus. Where then was your sense of blessing? For I bear you witness that, if possible, you would have plucked out your own eyes and given them to me. Have I therefore become your enemy by telling you the truth?*"

He now pleads from a place of loving affection, declaring himself their friend, as one whom the Galatians never wronged. On the contrary, they bestowed many kindnesses upon him when he first preached the simpler <note>original: "rudiora," meaning the more basic or unrefined elements of the faith</note> gospel to them because of their <term>infirmity of the flesh</term> <note>often interpreted as either a physical illness or a lack of spiritual maturity</note>, rather than the deep and sublime mysteries. When he suffered many persecutions, poverty, and tribulations among them (for these are the "trials of the flesh," as the Lord says: *'But you are those who have stayed with me in my trials'*), they did not look down on him. Instead, they welcomed him like an angel of God, like Christ the Lord. Back then, they considered themselves blessed if they could show him any kindness—so much so that they would have gladly (figuratively speaking) torn out their own eyes and their very hearts to give to him if they could. How can it be, then, that now—when he speaks to them of the great, difficult, and secret truth of the freedom of the children of God, which they could not grasp before—he has become their enemy? Or how could he have offended them now, when he was such a friend back when he was speaking of small things? This is not consistent; rather, by writing these high mysteries, he ought to become an even greater friend. 

It follows that they ought to love him with an increased and strengthened devotion, for he calls them back to freedom and is <term>zealous</term> for them in what is good, with the zeal of God. They should not love those who call them back from freedom into slavery, and from happiness into misery—those who are zealous for them in evil, with a worldly zeal. These were the Jews, preferring the slavery of the Law to the freedom of Christ. Therefore Paul adds: 

<margin>23</margin>
"*They are zealous for you, but not for good; they want to exclude you, so that you may be zealous for them. It is always good to be zealous in a good thing, and not only when I am present with you. My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you. I wish I could be present with you now and change my voice, because I am perplexed about you.*" 

The Galatians would have been harder than stones and deafer than the sea if the love in these words did not penetrate their hearts: "*My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you.*" To be in labor is to struggle with pain to give birth; this pain is not relieved until the birth occurs. Nor could the Apostle be relieved of this pain until Christ was brought forth into the light. For Christ was that light, to whose likeness he wished to restore the Galatians—from which they had distorted themselves by descending into the old legalities of the Law. For how can the form of a free person be kept in a servant? Certainly no more than the condition of a free person can. The condition of a free person and the condition of a servant are in conflict. But the "form" of Christ is free, while the "form" of the ancient Law is that of a servant. 

When the Apostle wishes to be present with the Galatians, he declares his "lack" —which he feels not for his own sake, but for the sake of the Galatians. He wishes he could change this expression of "needing to be with them." If he were actually with them, he would change it, for he would not lack what he already possessed. If he were with them, he would not *need* to be with them. Then, he could reveal these secrets to them better, more fully, and more clearly. 

<margin>24</margin>
However, since he cannot do this in person, he does what he can in his absence, saying: "*Tell me, you who want to be under the law, do you not hear the law? For it is written that Abraham had two sons, one by a slave woman and one by a free woman. But the son of the slave woman was born according to the flesh; while the son of the free woman was born through the promise. These things are spoken through allegory. For these are the two covenants: one from Mount Sinai, bearing children for slavery, which is Hagar. For Hagar is Mount Sinai in Arabia, and it corresponds to the present Jerusalem, for she is in slavery with her children. But the Jerusalem above is free, and she is the mother of us all.*"

<summary>Paul expresses his deep paternal love for the Galatians, grieving their return to legalistic Jewish customs which he likens to slavery. He employs the allegory of Abraham’s sons to distinguish between the bondage of the Old Law (Sinai/Hagar) and the freedom of the New Covenant (the heavenly Jerusalem).</summary>
<keywords>Galatians, Paul the Apostle, freedom vs slavery, Abraham, Hagar, Sarah, Sinai, allegory, Jerusalem, Jewish rituals</keywords>

# COMMENTARY

...ours. For it is written: *Rejoice, O barren woman who does not bear; break forth and cry out, you who do not labor: for the children of the desolate are more than those of her who has a husband.* <note>original: "Laetare sterilis..." quoting Isaiah 54:1, used by Paul to describe the growth of the Gentile Church.</note> Now we, brothers, are the children of promise according to the pattern of Isaac. But just as then, he who was born according to the flesh <note>Ishmael</note> persecuted him who was born according to the spirit <note>Isaac</note>, so it is now. But what does the scripture say? *Cast out the slave woman and her son, for the son of the slave shall not inherit with the son of the free woman.*

¶ Wonderfully, the most holy Apostle Paul opens to us the <term>mystery</term> <note>original: "sacramentum," here meaning a sacred secret or allegorical meaning</note> of the two testaments—that is, the Old Law and the New Law—through the two sons of Abraham: namely Ishmael and Isaac; the slave woman and the free woman: Hagar and Rebecca <note>The Latin text here and below names Rebecca, though the biblical text of Galatians 4 refers to Sarah. The commentator may be conflating the two matriarchs or following a specific tradition linking the mothers of the two nations.</note>; and the two locations: Sinai and Jerusalem. Hagar represents Mount Sinai and the Old Law. Ishmael represents the people of the Old Law. Rebecca represents Jerusalem and the New Law. Isaac represents the people of the New Law. From Sinai, the Old Law came forth; and the Word of the Lord, which is the New Law, came from Jerusalem. Mount Sinai slopes toward <note>original: "vergit," meaning inclines or tends toward</note> Jerusalem, just as the Old Testament ought to tend toward the New. Even before the coming of Christ, the sons of Isaac according to the flesh prefigured the people of the New Law; and the sons of Ishmael, who proceeded from Hagar, prefigured the people of the Old. Before Christ’s coming, the sons of Isaac according to the flesh were called the children of the free woman, and the sons of Ishmael were the children of the slave. These were servants, and those were the future heirs of the Lord; and all these things were in type and figure. 

But after the coming of Christ, the sons of Isaac according to the flesh who wish to serve the Old Law are now the children of the slave woman. For Hagar is the Old Testament, whose children they choose to remain. But the Gentiles coming to the faith of Christ, which is the New Law, are the children of the free woman, the children of Rebecca and Jerusalem. For this was the New Law. 

But what did Abraham, having two sons, represent? Without a doubt, he represented Christ, who has two testaments and two peoples. He grafts the children of the Synagogue into his own people just as the old Synagogue once grafted <term>proselytes</term> <note>converts to Judaism</note> into itself, and from both peoples one was made, as it were. How much more in Christ does each people become one. And he who is now a son of the slave woman, if he comes to Christ, shall be born again and become a child of the free woman. For one born of the slave cannot inherit with the son of the free woman unless he is born anew. Understanding this only in a fleshly sense, Nicodemus was amazed <note>Referencing John 3:4, where Nicodemus asks how an old man can be born again.</note>. For through the new birth, one is made a child of the free woman, and thus inherits and can enter the kingdom of heaven. 

And before Christ’s coming, many were the children of the desolate—that is, the slave woman—and few were the children of her who had a husband—that is, the free woman. And the children of the desolate persecuted the children of the free. So after the coming of Christ, who is the Bridegroom, there are few children of the Church who is free, and few spiritual children. But there are many fleshly children who are the children of the slave woman, and who in time oppose the spiritual children. But may God grant that the cries of the Church be heard, so that henceforth the free woman may be more fruitful than the desolate, so that the spirit may be known and the flesh condemned. Let both peoples become one, acknowledging Christ as Father and the Church as Mother, and acknowledging themselves as born of the spirit, the spiritual children of the free woman, giving praise, glory, and thanksgiving to Christ the Lord forever and ever. Amen.

<margin>A 18</margin> ¶ EXAMINATION of several matters regarding the literal text. ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *But he is under tutors and actors until the time appointed by the father.* ¶ The ancient translator preserved the speaking habits of legal experts. But the words of Paul sound more like this: *under commissioners and procurators.* Paul says: *but is under guardians and stewards until the time appointed by the father.* <note>original Greek: "ἀλλὰ ὑπὸ ἐπιτρόπους ἐστὶ καὶ οἰκονόμους ἄχρι τῆς προθεσμίας τοῦ πατρός."</note>

<margin>B 18</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *And because you are the sons of God, God sent the spirit of his Son.* ¶ The word "of God" is redundant. Paul says: *And because you are sons, God sent forth the Spirit of his Son.* <note>original Greek: "ὅτι δὲ ἐστὲ υἱοὶ, ἐξαπέστειλεν ὁ θεὸς τὸ πνεῦμα τοῦ υἱοῦ αὐτοῦ."</note>

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Crying, Abba, Father.* ¶ "Father" has been brought back and seems to be held as an explanation. So that this may be understood, and so it is not believed to be a vocative case, we have inserted a particle of explanation. Paul says: *crying, Abba, [which is] Father.* <note>original Greek: "κράζον ἀββᾶ, ὁ πατήρ."</note>

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *And an heir through God.* ¶ It should read: *and an heir of God through Christ.* Paul says: *and an heir of God through Christ.* <note>original Greek: "καὶ κληρονόμος θεοῦ διὰ χρισοῦ."</note>

<margin>B 18</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *To which you wish to serve again.* ¶ It should say: *to which you wish to serve again from above,* for "from above" is missing. For those who transfer from the faith of Christ to legal requirements tumble headlong from the heights, from freedom into slavery. For the freedom of Christ is high, but the slavery of the law is the lowest point. Paul says: *wherefore you wish to serve again from above.* <note>original Greek: "διὸ πάλιν ἄνωθεν δουλεύειν θέλετε." The term "anothen" can mean "again" or "from above."</note>

<margin>B 20</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *I fear you, lest perhaps I have labored in you without cause.* ¶ It is the custom of the Latins to say "I fear for you" <note>original: "timeo vobis"</note> in this sense. Jerome notes this about the ancient translator. He says "I fear you" <note>original: "timeo vos"</note> was placed there instead of "I fear concerning you." Paul says: *I am afraid for you, lest perhaps I have labored for you in vain.* <note>original Greek: "Φοβοῦμαι ὑμᾶς, μήπως εἰκῆ κεκοπίακα εἰς ὑμᾶς."</note>

<margin>B 21</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *But you know that through the infirmity of the flesh...* ¶ It should rather read: *because of the infirmity of the flesh.* This was not Paul's infirmity, but the Galatians', who could not bear the understanding of the mysteries. Paul says: *but you know that [it was] because of the weakness of the flesh.* <note>original Greek: "ὅτι οἴδατε δέ ὅτι δι᾿ ἀσθένειαν τῆς σαρκός."</note>

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *And your temptation in my flesh.* ¶ It should say: *and my temptation in my flesh.* Paul says: *and my temptation, which was in my flesh.* <note>original Greek: "καὶ τὸν πειρασμόν μου τὸν ἐν τῇ σαρκί μου."</note>

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Where then is your blessedness?* ¶ Rather: *what then was your blessedness,* or *what has been.* Paul says: *What then was the blessedness?* <note>original Greek: "τίς οὖν ὁ μακαρισμὸς."</note>

# 4 GALATIANS

...of you: And he responds that this was their <term>blessedness</term> <note>original: "beatitudinem," referring to the joy the Galatians initially felt in the Gospel</note>: if they could have given him their heart or their eyes.

<margin>Q</margin>
¶ The Vulgate edition: *Am I therefore become your enemy, by telling you the truth?* <note>Galatians 4:16</note> ¶ He does not assert this as a fact; rather, through a question, he wishes to infer from the greater point the opposite of what he asks. Therefore, so that the question may be understood, it could be said more appropriately: "Why have I become your enemy?" rather than "Therefore I have become your enemy."

<margin>12</margin>
Paul: *So then, have I become your enemy by telling you the truth?* <note>original Greek: "ὥστε ἐχθρὸς ὑμῶν γέγονα ἀληθεύων ὑμῖν"</note> ¶ The Vulgate edition: *But be zealous for the good in a good thing always.* <note>Galatians 4:18</note> ¶ It should rather be expressed through an infinitive: *it is good, however, to be zealous in a good thing always*; or through a verbal noun: *good is the zeal in a good thing always.* Paul: *It is fine to be objects of zeal in a good thing always.* <note>original Greek: "καλὸν δὲ τὸ ζηλοῦσθαι ἐν καλῷ πάντοτε"</note>

<margin>22</margin>
¶ The Vulgate edition: *For I am confounded in you.* <note>Galatians 4:20; the modern RSV/KJV reads "I am perplexed about you."</note> ¶ Here Jerome notes the ancient translator. In Greek (he says) it is said more properly. For <term>aporia</term> <note>original: "ἀπορία," meaning a state of being at a loss or in doubt</note> does not signify "confusion"—which among the Greeks is called *aischyne* or *entrope*—so much as it sounds of "want" and "poverty." This is the sense, therefore: I wish to be present with you now, and to bring the living voice of letters in person, because *I lack in you*. I have no fruits, which teachers are accustomed to have from their disciples. Thus says Jerome. For this reason we have translated this place: *because I lack being in you*. Truly, it must not be denied on the other hand that in the Sacred Scriptures "confusion" is found translated this way. As in that passage of Luke: *There shall be signs in the sun and stars / and on earth distress of nations for the confusion of the roaring of the sea and the waves.* <note>Luke 21:25</note> That phrase, "for the confusion of the roaring of the sea and the waves," is said there as *in aporia of the sea and the tossing.* <note>original: "ἐν ἀπορίᾳ θαλάσσης καὶ σάλου"</note> Behold where *aporia* is translated as "confusion." Therefore, if the sense of the ancient translator were preserved, it comes back to the same thing, and the sense would be: "I wish to be present with you now and to change my voice"—namely, this voice by which *I am confounded in you*—finding you, of course, walking so rightly that no confusion or shame arises from your life.

<margin>23</margin>
¶ It could be so; and both understandings are good. ¶ *Which things are said through allegory.* <note>Galatians 4:24</note> ¶ <term>Allegory</term> is (says Jerome) that which holds out one thing in words, but signifies another in sense. Things that are handed down in <term>type</term> <note>a "type" is a historical person or event that foreshadows a future spiritual reality</note> and figure are allegorical. Those which are not handed down in figure are not allegorical; nor do they require a sense other than that which is expressed and which the author intended—who for the most part is the Holy Spirit. This is also called the <term>literal sense</term>: because it is without type and figure. But it is also the <term>spiritual sense</term>. For how could a sense not be spiritual whose author is the Spirit? Therefore, for those who understand the writings in another way and apply them to something other than what the Spirit of the prophet intended: that is not the literal sense, but only a Jewish, carnal, and death-dealing one, and it is the "letter that kills." <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 3:6</note> For example, those who apply this passage—*for a child is born to us and a son is given to us* <note>Isaiah 9:6</note>—to King Hezekiah, and the passage *as a sheep led to the slaughter* <note>Isaiah 53:7</note> to Jeremiah, and countless such things: I would deny that sense to be literal, unless it be a Jewish, pseudographical, fabricated, and deceptive sense. Those who follow it rush into death. And the Holy Fathers have noted that four senses are found in Sacred Scripture: the **literal**, **allegorical**, **tropological**, and **anagogical**. <note>The classic "Fourfold Sense" of the Middle Ages: Literal (history), Allegorical (what to believe), Tropological (how to act/morals), and Anagogical (what to hope for/heaven).</note> It is not that these four senses are to be sought everywhere: but in those things which only require the letter, let us seek the literal sense. In those which require allegory: the allegorical. And that which is spoken regarding morals: the tropological. But those which require a divine and transcendent understanding: in those let us seek the <term>anagogy</term> <note>spiritual interpretation leading the mind "upward" to heavenly things</note> and the divine resurrection. Otherwise, if you seek allegory in those things which are not said allegorically, you do an unworthy thing. If you treat human morals where the secrets of divinity are handed down, you stop below the dignity of the subject, and from the brightness of the sun you catch only the evening glow. Therefore, let us not confuse these. But to those things which require the letter: let us grant the letter. To those which require allegory: allegory. To those which require both: let us grant both. Just as the history of Abraham and his sons has both; for here the Spirit intends both the history and the allegory. And those things which are expressed through anagogy: to those alone let us grant anagogical understanding. For it is more unworthy to lead the more worthy things down to the less worthy, than to lead the lower things up to the heavenly. For he who does this leads the obscure into the light; but he who does the former rolls the light back into darkness. But all these things are good, provided they are done according to their dignity. And let these things be said in passing, because Paul spoke of *allegoroumena*, that is, things which are said through allegory.

<margin>1</margin>
Paul: *which things are spoken allegorically.* <note>original Greek: "ἅτινά ἐστιν ἀλληγορούμενα"</note> ¶ *Generating into servitude, which is Hagar.* ¶ That is not translated badly. For the relative pronoun in Latin agrees with the following word. However, so that it may be understood to refer back to "testament," I preferred to say *which*, by saying *which is Hagar*, that is, *which is signified through Hagar*. For the Old Testament designated Hagar, and the New, Rebecca. <note>As noted on the previous page, the author uses Rebecca where the Bible usually names Sarah as the mother of the free child.</note> Yet it refers aptly in Greek: because what we call a "testament" is feminine among them. However, it is missing immediately after: *for this is Hagar*. This explains what was said. Paul: *Which is Hagar. For Hagar...* <note>original Greek: "ἥτις ἐστὶν ἄγαρ. τὸ γὰρ ἄγαρ"</note>

<margin>2</margin>
¶ The Vulgate edition: *Who is joined to the Jerusalem that now is.* ¶ Rather: *who diverges or contends toward that Jerusalem which now is.* For the word which Paul uses here signifies "to proceed in order." Which also serves the mystical understanding of allegory. For the Old Testament is ordered toward the New, and in a right order, as if by a right path, it ought to contend toward it. And Paul used the simple form (of the compound word placed here) in the following chapter, where we translate: *if we live by the Spirit... by the Spirit*

COM.

...and let us proceed. Paul: *it corresponds to the present Jerusalem.* <note>original Greek: "συστοιχεί δὲ τῇ νῦν ἰερουσαλήμ," referring to the earthly Jerusalem as a symbol of slavery to the Law.</note> ¶ The Vulgate edition: *With the freedom wherewith Christ has made us free.* <note>Galatians 5:1</note> ¶ It should be said: "with what freedom therefore." And it seems to belong to the following part, and should be brought back to the following word "stand," which the particle "therefore" <note>original: "igitur"</note> shows. For this reason, we have also begun the following chapter here. Paul: *In the liberty wherewith Christ has made you free, stand fast.* <note>original Greek: "τῇ ἐλευθερίᾳ ᾗ ἡ Χριστὸς ὑμᾶς ἐλευθέρωσεν. στήκετε."</note>

### CHAPTER 5

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'Q' featuring a scene with a figure (possibly a traveler or shepherd) amidst foliage and a tree, enclosed in an ornamental square frame.</image-desc>

**B**ecause therefore Scripture commands the servant-woman and her son to be cast out: Paul encourages the Galatians with a pious exhortation that they should stand in the freedom of Christ. He declares that if they return to the slavery of the ancient law, they are to be cast out and will not be heirs of the kingdom of Christ; moreover, they will make themselves subject to the entire law, which would not benefit them for eternal salvation. By abandoning Christ, they will suffer more bitter punishments in the judgment. As those who did not wish to be free, they will be punished more severely because of that slavery which they chose—whether the law was abandoned or performed negligently. And even if they fulfill the law, which even their fathers were unable to fulfill: they will be justified by the <term>righteousness of the law</term> <note>original: "iustitia legis," refers to being right with God through following rules perfectly</note> and of works, which is the righteousness of a servant, and they will have a milder experience in judgment. Nevertheless, they will not be made partakers of the heavenly kingdom. For the servant-woman and the sons of the servant-woman shall not inherit with the sons of the free woman. Since the righteousness of a servant, however great it may be, does not give freedom: but rather that righteousness which is from faith and the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ. Because (as has been said) Paul piously exhorts the Galatians: he opens with a sacred speech, saying:

<margin>24</margin>
¶ *Stand fast therefore in that liberty wherewith Christ has made us free: and be not held again under the yoke of bondage.* 
<margin>></margin>
*And I, Paul, say to you: that if you be circumcised, Christ shall profit you nothing.* 
<margin>></margin>
*And I testify again to every man circumcising himself, that he is a debtor to do the whole law.* 
<margin>></margin>
*You are made void of Christ, you who are justified in the law; you are fallen from grace.* 
<margin>></margin>
*For we, through the Spirit, wait for the hope of righteousness by faith.* 

¶ Righteousness from the law is the righteousness of slavery; righteousness from faith is the righteousness of liberty. Righteousness from the law is the righteousness of works; righteousness from faith is the righteousness of grace. Righteousness from the law is the righteousness of the flesh; righteousness from faith is the righteousness of the spirit. When Isaac came and grew up a little, Ishmael was cast out from the paternal house. So when Christ came and faith grew up a little, the old law was cast out; and liberty, grace, and the spirit took its place, while slavery, the works of slavery, and the flesh went into exile. 

The reason why Paul does not want the Gentiles to be circumcised is not because <term>uncircumcision</term> <note>original: "præputium," literally "foreskin," referring to the state of being a non-Jew</note> is anything special, but because he does not want them to be slaves and separated from Christ by taking up the slavery of the ancient law. Whether someone is circumcised or not circumcised matters nothing, as long as it is not done as a burden of ancient slavery. But if a Jew who was circumcised under the burden of the law comes to the faith of Christ, is he not—because he is circumcised—still bound to fulfill the whole law? By no means any longer. Because the law of liberty, which is more powerful than slavery (just as light is more powerful than darkness), has set him free. Because a new birth has made him dead to the law. For how could he live a new life unless he first died? But if he still considers himself bound, he is blind; he thinks he is in darkness while in the light, and in slavery while in freedom. If he still pours himself into the ancient law, he has lost freedom, grace, and the spirit. Not because he is circumcised and lacks a foreskin, but because he hopes in the works of slavery and distrusts grace. He confides in the flesh and distrusts the spirit. He embraces darkness, unwilling to look toward the light. And therefore his lot is in darkness, and he will never breathe in the light which is the kingdom of God. 

Therefore, having a foreskin or the removal of it (which is circumcision) does nothing toward death or life; but faith or unbelief does. For the faith of Christ—whether it be with a foreskin or with circumcision, or without both—works life, grace, and the spirit, and the love of God as a Father. For a woman has no less in Christ than a man with a foreskin or circumcision. And unbelief, wherever it may be—whether with a foreskin, or with circumcision, or without either—brings forth death, obligation, and the deeds of the flesh, and makes one always fear God as a Lord and an avenger. And thus one shudders at the thought of Him, so that this fear excludes love. Why? Because he thinks of himself as a servant. Therefore he lacks the spirit and grace by which he might know himself as a son, and know God as the eternal Father and the giver of the inheritance to His faithful children. But it is not the foreskin, circumcision, or the lack of both that does this in these or those people: but (as has been said) faith or unbelief. Which Paul adds, saying:

<margin>25</margin>
¶ *For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision avails anything, nor uncircumcision: but faith which works by love.* <note>Galatians 5:6</note> 

¶ For how would faith, which makes us sons and God our Father, not work through love? It certainly works, both toward us—so that He loves us as sons and does all things concerning us through love—and from us—so that we love God as a Father. Just as He wants to be loved by us because of Christ (into whose sonship we are initiated), so He wants us to do all things through love. Is it not natural for a father to love his children, and conversely, for children to love their father? So much so that no love is more natural to them. Paternal love wins out because it represents the love of God toward us. He, having made us sons out of immense faith, loves us more than we can repay in love. First, the Galatians...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Galatians chapter 5, moving from the legalistic fear of the Old Covenant to the filial love of the New. ### IIII Galatians

<margin>26</margin>
Through love, they ran to God as sons; but now, wishing to be circumcised and to trust in the works of the Law, they wanted to run through fear. And indeed, they ran with that fear which excludes love. For a servant who has transgressed, thinking of his master as a punisher and a terrible figure, cannot help but be shaken by terror, which does not permit love to exist within him. He seeks to flee from his master and would rather be hidden from him than run toward him. But a son, even when he has transgressed, when he thinks of his father—and a favorable father at that—remains confident and does not cease to love. In humility, running to the father, the fountain of mercies, he falls prostrate and begs for pardon. Experiencing the father's goodness, he loves him all the more because many sins have been forgiven him. This love makes him more cautious, so that he may not further offend his most loving father. You see, therefore, confidence and love in sons, but distrust and fear in servants. You see that sons, whether they keep righteousness or transgress, run to God; servants, however, flee from God rather than toward Him. Paul says this to the Galatians in this way: ¶ *You were running well; who hindered you from being persuaded by the truth? This persuasion was not from Him who calls you. A little leaven leavens the whole batch. I have confidence in you in the Lord, that you will think nothing else. Whoever disturbs you shall bear the judgment, whoever he may be.* <note>Galatians 5:7–10</note> ¶ The persuasion by which the Galatians were urged to be circumcised was not from God, nor from Christ, who called them to faith. For He who calls to faith calls to liberty; however, he who urges circumcision calls to slavery. A bad persuasion and a bad doctrine, even if it is small, infects all those to whom it clings. But Paul does not trust in himself; he trusts in God, that He will be their help, so that from now on they may think nothing other than what he has written to them. And he warns the corrupter of the Gospel doctrine that he will either amend himself or feel the judgment of God. Although Paul might have known who the man was, he threatens him through the Spirit of God as if he were unknown, so that the man might mend his ways and not feel God's blow. For what else is it to mix the Old Law with the Gospel of Christ, except to mix leaven and impurity into that which is unleavened and pure? And then the whole becomes leavened and impure, losing the power to lead one to the kingdom of Christ. But those perverse agitators were even persuading the Galatians that Paul himself still preached circumcision. He shows this to be false by the persecutions he endures daily from the Jews because of this very issue, showing that righteousness comes from the cross of our Lord—which is a stumbling block <note>original: "scandalum"</note> to the Jews—and by his own

<margin>27</margin>
example, Paul leads the Galatians not to trust in the righteousness of the Law, but in the righteousness which Christ brought to us through the punishment of the cross, by which He justifies us, having despised the shame. He says: ¶ *But if I, brothers, still preach circumcision, why do I still suffer persecution?* ¶ *In that case, has the stumbling block of the cross been removed? I wish that those who disturb you would even castrate themselves!* <note>original: "amputentur," often translated as "cut themselves off" or "emasculate themselves." Galatians 5:11–12</note> ¶ This follows excellently: if justification is found in circumcision, then the punishment of the cross contributes nothing to justification. And thus, the stumbling block of the cross is removed. But it is expedient, both for their own sake and for others, that those who so disturb people be removed from the midst. For while they live, they increase their own punishment and drag others into ruin. Therefore, desiring the good of both parties, Paul wished they would be cut off and removed from the midst—not out of a spirit of vengeance, nor desiring any revenge, but so that they might escape a greater punishment of damnation and others might not be hindered from their salvation. A spiritual man desires things spiritually; a carnal man, carnally. Those who understand this passage—"I wish those who disturb you would be cut off"—as expressing a desire for vengeance or something more than "an eye for an eye," adapting it to this sense: "I wish those who disturb you would not only be circumcised but even more than that, be completely castrated and cut off," <note>original: "castrati penitus abscindantur," referring to the physical act of emasculation as a jab at those obsessed with circumcision.</note> are giving it a carnal sense which seems poorly suited to Paul, a Christ-like man. Therefore, anyone who reads the epistles of Paul ought to strip off the flesh and put on the spirit given from on high, just as one who commits himself to reading the wedding song <term>epithalamium<explanation>A song or poem written specifically for a bride and groom</explanation></term> of the heavenly groom and bride. Now, Paul, having shown the way of liberty, grace, and the spirit, further instructs the Galatians to perform the works of their calling—that is, of liberty, grace, and the spirit. He tells them to abstain from the works of slavery, sin, and the flesh, so that they may stand in true liberty through love. And so he says: ¶ *For you, brothers, were called to liberty; only do not use your*

<margin>28</margin>
*liberty as an opportunity for the flesh, but through love serve one another. For the whole law is fulfilled in one word: namely, you shall love your neighbor as yourself.* <note>Galatians 5:13–14</note> ¶ What does it mean, "only do not use your liberty as an opportunity for the flesh"? It can have a double meaning. First: Only do not, for any opportunity or cause, exchange your liberty in which you were called for subjection to the flesh, to which those who want you to be circumcised are striving to lead you. Second: You were called to liberty; only for no cause or opportunity should you give liberty to your flesh. Instead, let the flesh be a servant, and the spirit truly free. For your liberty is spiritual, not carnal. And the liberty of the spirit is the slavery of the flesh. Conversely, the liberty of the flesh is the slavery of the spirit. For the flesh and the spirit fight against each other from opposite sides. But how is the whole law fulfilled in this saying, "You shall love your neighbor as yourself"? Certainly, he who loves his neighbor in God and for the sake of God as himself—because he himself is as much the image and likeness of God as his neighbor, and he has been adopted as a son of God and grafted into the body of Christ—has also fulfilled the first and greatest commandment of God. He who does this undoubtedly fulfills the whole law, as is explained more broadly in chapter thirteen <note>referring to Romans 13</note>

### CHAPTER V.

<image-desc>A square decorative initial 'V' containing a woodcut illustration of a bearded man (likely a saint or scholar) seated at a desk with a book, surrounded by floral and leaf patterns.</image-desc>
**Therefore, the way of Scripture** commands that the slave girl and her son be cast out; Paul urges the Galatians with a pious exhortation to stand in the freedom of Christ. He declares to them that if they return to the servitude of the ancient law, they are to be cast out and will not be heirs to the kingdom of Christ. Furthermore, they would be obligated to perform the entire law; and because this does not profit them toward eternal salvation, those who omit any part of it will be given even more bitter punishments in the judgment. Since they refused to be free, they shall be more severely punished for that servitude they chose—whether it was left unfinished or done negligently. And even if they do fulfill the law (which even the fathers under the law were unable to fulfill), they would be justified only by the righteousness of the law and of works—which is the righteousness of a servant—and they might be treated more mildly in the judgment, yet they will not be made partakers of the heavenly kingdom. For the slave girl and the sons of the slave girl shall not inherit with the sons of the free woman. Since the righteousness of a servant, no matter how great, does not grant freedom, only that righteousness which comes from the faith and grace of our Lord Jesus Christ can do so. Piously exhorting the Galatians on this point (as has been said), Paul opens his sacred mouth, saying: <margin>24</margin> ¶ *Stand fast, therefore, in the freedom with which Christ has set us free, and do not be held again by the yoke of slavery. And I, Paul, say to you: if you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing. Again, I testify to every man who is circumcised that he is bound to keep the whole law. You are separated from Christ, you who are justified in the law; you have fallen from grace. For we, through the Spirit, by faith, wait for the hope of righteousness.* ¶ Righteousness from the law is the righteousness of servitude; righteousness from faith is the righteousness of freedom. Righteousness from the law is the righteousness of works; righteousness from faith is the righteousness of grace. Righteousness from the law is the righteousness of the flesh; righteousness from faith is the righteousness of the spirit. When Isaac came and grew up a little, Ishmael was cast out from the paternal house; so when Christ came and faith grew up a little, the old law was cast out. Freedom, grace, and the spirit took their place, while servitude, the works of servitude, and the flesh were exiled. And the reason Paul does not want the Gentiles to be circumcised is not because uncircumcision is anything special, but because he does not want them to be servants, separated from Christ by taking up the servitude of the ancient law. Whether someone is circumcised or not does not matter, as long as it is not done as a burden of ancient servitude. What if a Jew, who was circumcised under the burden of the law, comes to the faith of Christ? Is he not still bound to fulfill the whole law because he is circumcised? By no means anymore, because the law of liberty—which is more powerful than servitude, as light is to darkness—has released him. Because the new birth has made him dead to the law. For how could he live a new life unless the old one had died? ¶ If he still thinks himself bound, he is blind; he is one who thinks there is darkness in the light and servitude in freedom. ¶ If he still toils under the ancient law, he has lost freedom, grace, and the spirit—not because he is circumcised and lacks a foreskin, but because he puts his hope in the works of servitude and distrusts grace. He trusts in the flesh and distrusts the spirit. He embraces darkness, unwilling to look toward the light; and therefore his lot is in the darkness, and he will never breathe in the light which is the kingdom of God. For the faith of Christ—whether it be with a foreskin or with circumcision, or without either—works life, grace, and spirit, and the love of God as a Father. For a woman has nothing less in Christ than circumcision or uncircumcision. And unbelief, wherever it may be—whether with a foreskin or with circumcision, or without both—brings forth death, obligation, and the deeds of the flesh, and it makes one always fear God as a master and an avenger. Just as for the sake of Christ, into whose sonship we are grafted, He wishes to be loved by us and wishes us to do all things through love. Is it not natural for a father to love his children, and conversely, for children to love their father, so much so that no love is more natural than this? #### [Commentary on Galatians]

...love, as sons they used to run toward God. Now, however, by wishing to be circumcised and putting their trust in the works of the Law, they were trying to run through fear—and specifically that kind of fear which excludes love. For a servant who commits a fault, thinking of his master as an avenger and someone terrible, cannot help but be shaken by terror, which does not allow love to dwell within him. He seeks to flee from the master and hide from him rather than run toward him. But a son, even when he commits a fault, when he thinks of his father as a merciful father, remains confident. He does not cease to love, and running in humility to the father, the fountain of mercies, he prostrates himself and begs for pardon. Experiencing the father's goodness, he loves all the more because many sins have been forgiven him. This love makes him more cautious, so that he does not further offend such a most devoted father. You see, therefore, confidence and love in the sons; <margin>26</margin> and in the servants, distrust and fear. Whether the sons maintain their righteousness or fall into fault, they run toward God; but the servants flee from God rather than toward Him. ¶ Paul speaks to the Galatians in this way: 

¶ *You were running well: who hindered you from obeying the truth? This persuasion was not from Him who calls you. A little leaven leavens the whole lump. I have confidence in you in the Lord, that you will feel no otherwise. Whoever disturbs you shall bear the judgment, whoever he may be.* <note>Original Latin: "Currebatis bene... Quicunq; conturbat vos: portabit iudiciu̅." This refers to Galatians 5:7–10.</note> ¶ The persuasion by which the Galatians were persuaded to be circumcised was not from God, nor from Christ, who called them to the faith. For He who calls to faith calls to liberty; however, he who persuades toward circumcision calls to servitude. A bad persuasion and a bad doctrine, even if it is small, infects all who cling to it. But Paul does not trust in himself, but in God, that He will be their help, so that from now on they may feel nothing different from what he wrote to them. And as for the one who corrupts the Gospel doctrine, Paul will either correct him or defend the judgment against him. Even if Paul knew who this person was, he nevertheless threatens him through the Spirit of God as if he were unknown, so that the man might correct himself and not feel the blow of God. For what else is it to mix the old Law with the Gospel of Christ, except to mix leaven <term>fermentum; yeast used here as a metaphor for corrupting influence</term> and impurity with what is unleavened and pure? And then the whole thing becomes leavened and impure, unable to lead into the kingdom of Christ. 

But those perverse impostors were also persuading the Galatians that Paul himself was still preaching circumcision. He shows this to be false by the persecutions which he endures daily from the Jews because of this; showing that righteousness comes from the cross of our Lord, which is a stumbling block to the Jews. And by his own <margin>27</margin> example, Paul induces the Galatians not to trust in the righteousness of the Law, but in the righteousness which Christ brought to us through the punishment of the cross, which He endured for us, despising the shame, saying: ¶ *But if, brothers, I still preach circumcision, why do I still suffer persecution? Then the stumbling block of the cross has been removed. I wish that those who disturb you would even be cut off.* <note>Original Latin: "Si au̅t fratres ego adhuc circu̅cisione̅ prædico... Vtinam et amputetur ij: qui disturbant vos." (Galatians 5:11–12).</note> ¶ A remarkable conclusion follows: if justification is in circumcision, then the punishment of the cross does nothing for justification, and thus the "stumbling block" of the cross is removed. 

But it is expedient, both for their own sake and for others, that those who thus disturb people be removed from the midst. For as long as they live, they increase their own punishment and drag others into ruin. Therefore, wishing well for both sides, he desired that they be "cut off" and removed from the midst—not out of a spirit of vengeance, nor desiring any revenge, but so that they might escape a greater punishment of damnation, and that others might not be hindered from their salvation. A spiritual man desires things spiritually, and a <margin>f</margin> carnal man, carnally. Those who understand this passage as "I wish those who disturb you would be cut off" <note>original Latin: "vtinam abscindantur qui vos disturbant"</note> and give it a sense of desiring vengeance or an even greater retaliation—applying the meaning that those who disturb you should not only be circumcised, but even more so be completely castrated and emasculated—give it a carnal sense that seems very little suited to Paul, a Christ-like man. Therefore, he who reads the letters of Paul ought to strip off the "flesh" and put on the "spirit" given from on high, just as one commits oneself to reading the wedding song of the heavenly bridegroom and bride. 

Now, however, Paul, having shown the way of liberty, grace, and the spirit, further instructs the Galatians so that they might perform the works of their calling—that is, of liberty, grace, and the spirit. And let them <margin>28</margin> abstain from the works of servitude, sin, and the flesh, so that they might stand in true liberty through love. And thus he says: ¶ *For you, brothers, were called to liberty: only do not give liberty as an opportunity for the flesh, but through love serve one another. For the whole law is fulfilled in one word: namely, you shall love your neighbor as yourself.* <note>Original Latin: "Vos enim fratres in libertate vocati estis... diliges proximu̅ tuum sicut teipsu̅." (Galatians 5:13–14).</note> ¶ What does "only do not give liberty as an opportunity for the flesh" mean? It can have a double understanding. First: only do not, for any occasion or any cause, change your liberty into which you were called into a subjection to the flesh, toward which those who want you to be circumcised are striving to lead you. Second: you were called into liberty; only for no cause or occasion should you give "liberty" to your flesh. Instead, let the flesh be a servant, but the spirit be free. For your liberty is spiritual, not carnal. And the liberty of the spirit is the servitude of the flesh; and conversely, the liberty of the flesh is the servitude of the spirit. ¶ For the flesh and the spirit fight from opposite sides. 

But how is the whole law fulfilled in this saying: *you shall love your neighbor as yourself*? Certainly, he who loves his neighbor in God and for God’s sake as himself—because he himself is just as much the image and likeness of God as his neighbor, and his neighbor has been adopted as a son of God and grafted into the body of Christ—has also fulfilled the first and greatest commandment of God. He who does this undoubtedly fulfills the entire law, as is explained more widely in the thirteenth chapter...

COMMENTARY

...as was shown in the letter to the Romans. And by contrast, where there is no love of neighbor, there is the corruption of the whole law. For how can you love Him whose image you cannot see? <margin>29</margin> How will you not freely inflict every injury upon one whom you hate? And for that reason, Paul says that hatred is the greatest hindrance, being the opposite of love for one's neighbor.

¶ **But if you bite and devour one another, take care that you are not consumed by one another. I say then: walk by the spirit, and you will not fulfill the lust of the flesh. For the flesh lusts against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh; these are opposed to each other so that you do not do the things you wish. But if you are led by the spirit, you are not under the law.** <note>Original Latin: "Si autem vos inuicem mordetis... non estis sub lege." This is Galatians 5:15–18.</note>

¶ He who is healthy is not under the rule of a doctor, even if he avoids all those things which the doctor would order a sick man to avoid. This is not because he is under the doctor's rule, but because he possesses health, which is better than a doctor's rule. 

¶ **He who walks by the spirit** possesses the grace and justice of God for doing those things which the law commands, by a far superior law. **But those who are under the doctor’s rule do what the doctor commands out of fear; so also those who** are under the law do what the law prescribes out of fear. For they are sick. If indeed they were entirely healthy, they would not be under the law, but above the law; and what they do, they would do not out of fear, but out of will and love.

¶ Therefore, not everyone who performs the works of the law—that is, who fulfills the ten commandments of God—is under the law. Rather, it is only those who are carnal <term>carnal: focusing on worldly or physical desires rather than spiritual growth</term> and not yet spiritual. Love guides the latter; fear compels the former. These are healthy, these are righteous; the others are not yet so, but are all like patients in a hospital—some improving and some worsening. Therefore, act out of health, out of delight, and out of the love of God: then you are not under the law, but above the law. All who are under the law struggle in the weakness of the flesh. If they follow the works of the flesh, they will not be able to enter the kingdom of God. 

<margin>30</margin>
¶ **Paul enumerates these works of the flesh, saying:**

¶ **Now the works of the flesh are evident, which are: adultery, fornication, uncleanness, lewdness, idolatry, sorcery, hatred, contentions, jealousies, outbursts of wrath, selfish ambitions, dissensions, heresies, envy, murders, drunkenness, revelries, and the like. I tell you beforehand, just as I also told you in time past, that those who practice such things will not inherit the kingdom of God.** <note>Original Latin: "Manifesta autẽ sunt opera carnis... regnum dei non haereditabunt." Galatians 5:19–21.</note>

¶ While health is one thing, the infirmities of the body are many; so it is with the flesh. For the love of God and neighbor is the health of both spirit and flesh. Holiness of the flesh accompanies this health just as beauty accompanies a healthy body. Love clearly removes idolatry, sorcery, hatred, contentions, jealousies, outbursts of wrath, selfish ambitions, dissensions, sects, envy, murders, and things like these. Holiness, however—which is nothing other than the purity of mind and body in imitation of heavenly things—removes adultery, fornication, uncleanness, lewdness, drunkenness, revelries, and everything of that sort. But (so that we may more specifically know what the works of the spirit are) the most spiritual Paul enumerates them in this way, saying:

<margin>31</margin>
¶ **But the fruit of the Spirit is: love, joy, peace, long-suffering, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control; against such there is no law. And those who are Christ’s have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires. If we live in the Spirit, let us also walk in the Spirit. Let us not become conceited, provoking one another, envying one another.** <note>Original Latin: "At vero fructus spiritus est... inuidentes." Galatians 5:22–26.</note>

¶ These are the works of the spirit, all of which are orderly and taken in the best sense: love according to God, joy in the Holy Spirit, peace of mind, a patient waiting for divine promises however long it may be, benevolence toward all, innocence of life, truth in word and deed, and temperance, which is the total purity of mind and body and a certain holiness. Let us long for these fruits in which there is true glory; let us provoke one another toward these, and not in those things which belong to the flesh and empty glory, which are accompanied by jealousies and envy. Let us ask for these to be bestowed by Christ, the giver of spiritual gifts, giving glory, praise, and honor forever and ever. Amen.

x.i.

<margin>19.</margin>
**But I say: walk in the spirit in CHRIST.** <note>original: "Dico autem in CHRISTO spiritu ambulate."</note> ¶ **In Christ**: even if not for the meaning, it is superfluous in the phrasing. For in the Greek it says only: **But I say, walk by the spirit.** Paul says: *But I say: walk by the spirit.* <note>original Greek: "λέγω δὲ πνεύματι περιπατεῖτε"</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition** <note>The "Vulgate" refers to the standard Latin Bible used in the Western Church, largely translated by St. Jerome in the 4th century.</note>: **Which are fornication, uncleanness, immodesty, luxury, the service of idols.** ¶ Here, 17 works of the flesh are enumerated, and just as many in the Greek. However, in the Greek, **adultery** <note>original: "adulterium"</note> is held at the beginning, then **fornication**. And **luxury** in the fourth place has no place there. Jerome’s copy contained only 15; I believe it was either defective, or ours is excessive, for we have had three different versions. Paul says: *Which are adultery, fornication, uncleanness, licentiousness, idolatry.* <note>original Greek: "ἅτινά ἐστιν μοιχεία, πορνεία, ἀκαθαρσία, ἀσέλγεια, εἰδωλολατρεία"</note> ¶ **The Vulgate**
<margin>D</margin>
**edition: But the fruit of the spirit is: charity, joy, peace, patience, long-suffering, goodness, kindness.** ¶ It should be said: **kindness, goodness**. And one of the two—**patience** or **long-suffering**—is redundant. For **long-suffering** and **patience** are exactly the same thing; it signifies the waiting for something for a long time with an even mind. Paul says: *But the fruit of the spirit is love, joy, peace, long-suffering, kindness, goodness.* <note>original Greek: "καρπὸς δὲ τοῦ πνεύματός ἐστιν ἀγάπη, χαρά, εἰρήνη, μάκροθυμία, χρηστότης, ἀγαθωσύνη"</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition: But those who are CHRIST’S have crucified the flesh with its vices and lusts.** ¶ Jerome says it is better that there is one compound word in the Greek, which we can translate as: **recrucifying**. He adds: Where the Latin translator placed "vices," in the Greek we read *pathēmata*, that is, **passions**. <note>The author is debating the best word for internal struggles—"vices," "passions," or "affections."</note> And a little later: And let this be noted: if we follow the common exposition, reading: *but those who are Christ's have crucified their flesh with its vices and lusts*, let us say that they have crucified not the flesh of Christ, but their own. We have carefully reviewed these points from Jerome so that everyone may understand without any cloud of doubt that this exposition, which the churches use everywhere, is not Jerome's, but the one used before Jerome, which was the common version in his time; and therefore, Jerome calls that version the "Vulgate." And it matters little that where the old translator said **vices**, and Jerome says it should be called **passions**, we have said **affections**. This is because Latins prefer to interpret that word as **affections** <note>original: "affectus"</note> rather than **passions** <note>original: "passiones"</note> when it signifies "disturbances." However, it is otherwise when it designates pressures, afflictions, and troubles brought upon the flesh, as in the first chapter of the preceding letter where it is said: *As the passions of Christ abound in us, so through Christ our consolation also abounds.* For then that word is taken in a good sense, and ought to be translated as **passions**, not **affections**. But when it means affection and disturbance, as above, then it is taken in a bad sense. Paul says: *And those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires.* <note>original Greek: "οἱ δὲ τοῦ χριστοῦ τὴν σάρκα ἐσταύρωσαν σὺν τοῖς παθήμασι καὶ ταῖς ἐπιθυμίαις"</note>

### CHAPTER VI

<margin>1</margin>
Here the apostle gives certain holy warnings and precepts to the Galatians, which we can arrange into eight points. **First**: Those who are more spiritual should strive to restore those who are overtaken in faults, instructing them kindly and gently. They will do this easily if they consider themselves, because they too are capable of falling. If they were to fall by some error, they would wish to be instructed in a spirit of gentleness. For this is the law of loving one's neighbor: to measure those things done regarding neighbors by oneself. Therefore, the **second** precept is joined to it: **Consider yourself**, <margin>2</margin>
lest you also be tempted, lest you also slip into a fault, and you yourself be overtaken by a fault. **Third**: **Bear one another’s burdens**; correct one another’s errors in gentleness <margin>3</margin>
and love; forgive one another's offenses, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ. For He says: *If your brother sins against you, go and correct him between you and him alone.* And again: *Forgive, if you have anything against anyone, so that your Father who is in heaven may also forgive you your sins. But if you do not forgive, neither will your Father who is in heaven forgive you your sins.* **Fourth**: Let no one think himself to be something, when in truth he is nothing; otherwise, he deceives himself. This prohibits pride and vainglory and commends humility. An eye that boasts of seeing by itself denies the benefit of light. So also, he who possesses the gifts of God but looks to himself, thinks himself to be something, and extols and boasts of himself, is ignorant of the grace of God—which is "the something," not he himself. He thinks himself the author of that of which God is the author; he deceives himself and is proud. But the humble man considers "something" to be not himself, but God; not what comes from himself, but the grace which comes from God. And he boasts, not in himself, nor in that which comes from himself, but in God and in God's grace. And this humility is true greatness of soul and true **magnanimity**. <note>The author argues that true humility and greatness (magnanimity) are the same thing because both recognize God as the source of all good.</note> This quality is small in the small and greatest in the great, so that it has received a double name: from both smallness and greatness. For it is a **humble magnanimity** and a **magnanimous humility**. And there is no other true humility, no other true magnanimity. Therefore, grace produces true humility and true magnanimity, not works, even if works are not lacking. And that which is preached by the philosophers as coming from works is a certain shadow and thin footprint of this. **Fifth**. <margin>5</margin>

### COMMENTARY

Let each person examine his own work, and then he will have cause for glorying in himself alone, and not in another. Each will bear his own burden—whether a light burden of good works leading to life, or a heavy burden of evil works leading to death. This does not mean that anyone should boast in themselves, but rather that if one weighs their own deeds, they find the matter for glorying only within themselves. Yet, far be it from anyone to boast in such a way; instead, **let him who boasts, boast in the Lord.** <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 1:31.</note> If anyone considers God to be the author of our justification, and if anyone considers grace, he will have cause for glorying not in himself but in another <note>meaning in God</note>. And even if it is in himself (for grace is internal), it is nevertheless not *from* himself. Certainly, if anyone examines his own work, he will see his own imperfections, and find more reason to be ashamed of himself than to boast. Therefore, he will not seek vain glory from another, seeing that in his own work he has cause for shame and a burden that he might dread to carry before the judge’s tribunal. Therefore, this precept does not simply say that one should boast in oneself during the examination of works, but rather, it subtly suggests one should be humbled, since no one is without a fearsome burden to carry. **Sixth.**

<margin>6</margin>
¶ Just as one who is unrefined in the faith and is instructed in the Word by another, he should not deny a share of all his goods to the one who instructs him. A son should not deny a share of his goods to the father who raised him for this earthly life; how much less should a son according to the spirit deny a portion of his goods to the one who forms him for the spiritual life. For the latter makes him a son of light, while the former makes him a son of the world and of darkness. Truly, just as a biological father spares the goods of his sons as much as possible and uses them sparingly, so too ought a 

<margin>7</margin>
spiritual man spare the goods of his "children." **Seventh.** Do not be deceived; do not offer any pretense of simulation or excuse, because **God is not mocked.** <note>original: "deus non irridetur"</note> Whatever humans do—whether good or evil, whether in simplicity or through a facade—they do it in the presence of God, and God knows all things. No one can deceive Him or mock Him. Whatever a person has done, according to that shall he receive. If he lives according to the flesh, he will receive death 

<margin>8</margin>
and eternal destruction. If, however, he lives according to the spirit, he will receive eternal life. **Eighth.** Let us never fail in doing good; let us never grow weary. For in due time we shall receive a good that never fails, which will never be diminished or grow weak. Indeed, it will rather seem to intensify—

<margin>32</margin>
» like one who directs his eye toward the sun: the light does not seem to fade, but rather to continually intensify and increase. And these are the holy admonitions. The Apostle <note>Saint Paul</note> sets them down in this manner: ¶ **Brothers, if a man is overtaken in any sin, you who are spiritual should restore such a person in a spirit of gentleness. Consider yourself, lest you also be tempted. Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of CHRIST. For if anyone thinks he is something when he is nothing, he deceives himself in his mind. But let each one prove his own work, and then he will have reason to boast in himself alone, and not in another. For each will bear his own burden. Let him who is taught the word make the one who teaches a participant in all good things. Do not be deceived: God is not mocked. For whatever a man sows, that he will also reap. For he who sows in his flesh will from the flesh reap corruption. But he who sows in the spirit will from the spirit reap eternal life. Furthermore, let us not fail in doing good. For in due time we shall reap, if we do not faint. Therefore, while we have time, let us**

» **work good toward all, but especially toward those of the household of faith.** ¶ The **household of faith** <note>original: "domestici fidei"</note> are those who, having already been initiated into the sacraments of Christ, have received the faith. One ought to have charity and beneficence toward them first among mortals. But even if we can, let us also do good to those who are not imbued with the faith, and let us strive to bring some light to the blind. It is far better if, by the example of our good conduct and our kindness, we could lead them to the full light, which is Jesus Christ, who is blessed forever and ever. For the love that emulates divine charity does not contain itself within the "domestic walls" but breaks out into the world. Just as light, while remaining in the sun, pours itself out beneficially to the eyes of all. Now, however, Paul invites the Galatians to consider the quality of his letters—what sort they were, whether they were written by his own hand and not forged, or whether they were written by someone else and perhaps fake. So that when they recognized them as written by Paul’s hand (for many among them knew Paul’s handwriting), they would know they were not faked, and contained nothing but the truth 

<margin>33</margin>
against those who wished to cast them down from the kingdom of light into the darkness of the old law. And so he says: ¶ **See with what large letters I have written to you with my own hand. Whoever wants to please in the flesh, they compel you to be circumcised: only so that they may not suffer persecution for the cross of CHRIST. For not even they who are circumcised keep the law of God; but they want you to be circumcised so that they may boast in your flesh.** ¶ Among the reasons why those dogmatic Jews—false teachers and mixers of the old leaven with the unleavened bread of Christ—wanted this, one was because they wished to please according to the flesh. By doing this, they appeared to be preaching Judaism, which was not prohibited by the Emperor or by the courts. <meta>This page continues the commentary on the final chapter of Galatians. The previous page discussed the duty of supporting teachers and personal accountability. #### Fourth [Section] on Galatians

The laws of Augustus were promulgated: that the Jews, who were dispersed throughout the whole circle of the Roman Empire, should live by their own rite and serve their ancestral ceremonies. And furthermore, they pleased the Jews greatly in this and smoothed things over with them. There was another reason [for seeking circumcision]: so that they might escape the persecution of the cross of Christ. For when they performed sacrifices and their accustomed rites, they appeared to be Jews and not Christians, even if they were secretly confessing Christ. In this way, they were not dragged away to share in the sufferings of the Lord's cross along with the Christians who were being sought out everywhere for punishment. A third cause was this: so that they might boast among the carnal Jews that they had led the Gentiles to circumcision and to keeping Jewish rites, as if they had made them not Christians, but 
<margin>34</margin> Jewish proselytes—children of eternal perdition and eternal hell. Truly, one must not boast in such a way; but as the Apostle reveals to us, we must boast as he says: ¶ **But far be it from me to glory, except in the cross of our Lord JESUS CHRIST, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.** For in CHRIST JESUS, neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts for anything, but a new creature. ¶ How can anyone be born again and receive a new spirit unless he is a new creature—not of the creation of this world, but of a heavenly creation? And this "something" is what leads to salvation: not circumcision, nor the lack of circumcision (which is the foreskin). This new creature is crucified with Christ and has breathed again with him from death into life in the mystery of a new birth, being superior to the flesh and the world. If one must boast, it must be only in the cross 
<margin>35</margin> of our Lord Jesus Christ. And for those who understand this law of boasting alone, the Apostle adds: ¶ **And whoever follows this rule, peace be upon them and mercy, and upon the Israel of God. From now on, let no one cause me trouble. For I carry the marks of the Lord JESUS in my body.** The grace of our Lord JESUS CHRIST be with your spirit, brothers. Amen. Written at Rome. ¶ With this holy prayer, the Apostle closes his epistle. And when he says "upon the Israel of God," it is the same as if he said "upon the spiritual people of God." Because he prays that the Galatians no longer bring him trouble, he means that they should no longer struggle over receiving circumcision. For Paul considers circumcision in the body to be nothing, and uncircumcision to be nothing; but he considers the *stigmata* <note>original: "stigmata" — referring to the scars or marks of physical suffering</note> and the insignia of the Lord's passion, which he carries in his body, to be for salvation. He does not say "circumcision," but "I carry the marks of the Lord Jesus in my body." Therefore, let them cease bringing him more labors over this matter. Let them not care to carry circumcision, but let them glory in being marked by the mysteries of the Passion. Indeed, every Christian who is co-crucified with Christ the Lord carries the marks of the Lord Jesus in his body. How then shall the hands that were nailed with Christ to the cross reach out toward crimes, or the pierced feet run toward vices, or the opened side burn with greed or any other evil desire? Every Jew carries circumcision as a sign of the faith of Abraham; we, however, carry the marks of the Lord as a sign of our faith and redemption. To the Lord himself, the author of such great sacraments and mysteries for us: let there be grace, honor, glory, and thanksgiving, for all ages of ages. Amen.

---

<margin>A.</margin> AN EXAMINATION of several points concerning the literal text. <margin>31</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *You who are spiritual, instruct such a one in a spirit of gentleness.* ¶ The word used here [in Greek] means "to perfect," "to fit," or "to repair," rather than "to instruct." Paul says: <note>original Greek: ὑμᾶς οἱ πνευματικοὶ καταρτίζετε τὸν τοιοῦτον ἐν πρεύματι πραότητος — "you who are spiritual, restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness."</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Considering yourself, lest you also be tempted.* ¶ The use of participles in place of verbs is frequent in Paul's writing. It is better to use a verb here than a participle. For those who do not pay attention to Paul’s custom and use the participle might suspect Paul of a barbarism <note>a grammatical error or non-standard usage</note>, assigning a singular epithet to a plural substantive. They would not suspect this if they noticed his frequent habit of using a participle for a verb. The preceding sentence should be read not with a comma, but as a distinct clause. Paul says: <note>original Greek: σκοπῶν σεαυτὸν μὴ καὶ σὺ πειρασθῇς — "looking to yourself, lest you also be tempted."</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Carry one another's burdens.* ¶ The old translator could also have said: "carry your mutual burdens" or "carry burdens in turn." Paul says: <note>original Greek: ἀλλήλων τὰ βάρη βασάζετε — "bear the burdens of one another."</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *He deceives himself.* ¶ Here, Jerome notes that the word from the Greek composition, which the old translator translated as "to deceive" (*seducere*), means not just to lead away, but to lead the mind away. For *phren* means "mind" or "the rational part," and *apatao* means "I fail," "I deceive," or "I lead astray." Paul says: <note>original Greek: ἑαυτὸν φρεναπατᾶ — "he deceives his own mind."</note>
<margin>B.</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *But let him who is catechized in the word communicate with him who catechizes him.* <margin>32</margin> ¶ The old translator fashioned non-Latin words from a foreign word. For the Greeks say *katecheo*, meaning "I teach," "I instruct," or "I educate," from which he fashioned "catechize" and "to be catechized." This refers to those who are still unrefined [in the faith]. Thus they were called "catechumens"—those who were being instructed and educated in the faith but were not yet initiated into the sacred mysteries. Paul says: <note>original Greek: κοιρονείτω ὁ κατηχούμενος τὸν λόγον τῶ κατηχοῦντι — "let the one being taught the word share with the one who teaches."</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *For in its own time we shall reap, not failing.* ¶ Rather: "at the proper time." This is more suited even to Latin speech...
