-># COMMENTARY<-
<meta>image quality: excellent; catchword/footer: by the author Jerome / Caius Caesar / Octavian Augustus / and Tiberius his successor</meta>

Let each man examine his own work: and then he will have glory in himself alone, and not in another. Each will bear his own burden—whether it be the light burden of good works leading toward life, or the heavy burden of evil works leading toward death. This does not mean that anyone should boast in themselves; rather, if someone weighs their own deeds, they find the matter for glory only within themselves <note>original: "gloriandi materiam"</note>. Yet, far be it from anyone to boast in such a way; instead, let him who boasts, boast in the Lord. If someone acknowledges God as the author of our justification, or if someone acknowledges grace, he will find the grounds for glorying not in himself but in another—and even if it is within himself (since grace is internal), it is nonetheless not *from* himself. Certainly, if anyone examines his own work, he will see his own imperfections, which are reasons to be ashamed within himself rather than to boast. Therefore, he will not seek empty glory from others, seeing that in his own work he has reason for shame, carrying a burden he might dread to bring before the judge's tribunal. This precept, then, does not simply say that one should boast in oneself upon examining one’s works, but rather hints that one should be humbled, since there is no one who does not carry a fearsome burden. 

**The Sixth [Precept]:**

<margin>6</margin> He who is unlearned in the faith and is instructed in the word by another should not deny a share of all his goods to the one who instructs him. A son should not deny a share of his goods to the father who formed him for this earthly life; how much less should a spiritual son deny the abundance of his goods to the one who forms him for the spiritual life. For the latter makes him a son of light, while the former makes him a child of the world and of darkness. Truly, just as a biological father spares his children’s goods as much as possible and uses them sparingly, so too should a spiritual man spare the goods of his spiritual children.

<margin>7</margin> **The Seventh.** Do not be deceived; do not offer any pretense or excuse, because God is not mocked. Whatever humans do—whether good or evil, whether in simplicity or in pretense <note>original: "fictè"</note>—they do in the presence of God, with God knowing all things. No one can deceive Him or mock Him. Whatever a man has done, he shall receive according to that deed. If he has lived according to the flesh, he will receive death and eternal destruction; but if he has lived according to the spirit, he will receive eternal life.

<margin>8</margin> **The Eighth.** Let us never fail or grow weary in doing good. For in due time we shall receive a tireless good that will never fade or slacken. Indeed, it will seem to intensify, just as one who fixes his eye on the sun does not see the light fade, but rather sees it continually intensify and increase. And these are the hallowed warnings. The Apostle sets them down in this manner:

<margin>32</margin>
> Brothers, even if a person is overtaken in some sin, you who are spiritual should restore such a person in a spirit of gentleness. Consider yourself, lest you also be tempted. Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of CHRIST. For if anyone thinks he is something when he is nothing, he deceives himself in his mind. But let each one prove his own work, and then he will have reason to glory in himself alone, and not in another. For each will bear his own burden. 
> 
> Let the one who is taught in the word make the one who teaches a participant in all good things. 
> 
> Do not be deceived: God is not mocked. For whatever a man sows, that he will also reap. Because he who sows in his flesh will reap corruption from the flesh. But he who sows in the spirit will from the spirit reap eternal life. Furthermore, let us not fail in doing good. For in the proper time we shall reap, if we do not give up. Therefore, while we have time, let us work good toward all, but especially toward those of the household of faith.

The "household of faith" <note>original: "Domestici fidei"</note> are those who, having already been initiated by the sacraments of Christ, have received the faith. Toward these, one must hold the primary charity and beneficence among mortals. But even if we are able, let us do good to those who are not yet imbued with the faith, and strive to bring some light to the blind. It is far better if, by the example of our good conduct and our kind deeds, we could lead them to the total light, which is Jesus Christ, blessed into all ages and above all ages. For the love that emulates divine charity does not contain itself within the walls of the home but breaks out into the world. Just as the light dwelling in the sun pours itself out beneficently to the eyes of all, so too does this love. 

Now, however, Paul invites the Galatians to consider the quality of his letters—what they were like, and whether they were written by his own hand and not forged, or whether they were someone else's and perhaps false or simulated. When they recognized they were written by Paul’s hand (for many among them knew Paul’s handwriting), they would know they were not fakes and contained nothing but the truth, unlike those who wished to cast them from the kingdom of light back into the darkness of the old law. And so he says:

<margin>33</margin>
> See with what large letters I have written to you with my own hand. As many as desire to please in the flesh, they compel you to be circumcised, only so that they might not suffer persecution for the cross of CHRIST. For not even those who are circumcised keep the law of God; but they want you to be circumcised so that they may boast in your flesh.

Among the reasons why those dogmatic Jews—the false teachers and mixers of the old leaven with the unleavened—wanted this, one was that they wished to please according to the flesh. By doing this, they appeared to be preaching Judaism, which was not prohibited by the Emperor or the courts. For sa—

<meta>This page concludes the commentary on Galatians chapter 6. The previous page discussed the responsibility of the individual to examine their own deeds and the humility required when facing God's judgment. This page explores why some early Christians adhered to Jewish laws to avoid Roman persecution and concludes with a linguistic analysis of the Greek text versus the Vulgate translation.</meta>

->### Galatians, Chapter 3 [sic, refers to Book 3 of the commentary] 162<-
->X.ij.<-

The laws of the Emperors <note>original: "Augusti leges"</note> promulgated that the Jews, who were dispersed throughout the entire world of the Roman Empire, should live by their own rite and serve their ancestral ceremonies. Furthermore, they pleased the Jews greatly in this and smoothed things over with them. There was another reason [for following Jewish rites]: to escape the persecution of the cross of Christ. For when they performed sacrifices and their accustomed rites, they appeared to be Jews and not Christians, even if they secretly confessed Christ. In this way, when Christians were being sought out everywhere for punishment, these people were not dragged away to share in the sufferings of the Lord's cross. A third cause was so that they could boast among the carnal Jews that they had induced the Gentiles to accept circumcision and the observance of Jewish rites—as if they had made them not Christians, but proselytes of the Jews, making them "children of eternal perdition and eternal Gehenna" <note>A reference to Matthew 23:15</note>. But one must not boast in such a way; rather, as the Apostle reveals to us how we ought to boast, saying: **But far be it from me to boast, except in the cross of our Lord JESUS CHRIST, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.** For in CHRIST JESUS, neither circumcision nor uncircumcision <note>original: "praeputium", literally "foreskin"</note> has any power, but only a **new creature**. How can anyone be born again and receive a new spirit unless he becomes a new creature—not of the creation of this world, but of the heavenly creation? And this is what has power for salvation: not circumcision or the lack of it. This new creature is crucified with Christ, and with him, it has breathed again into life from death in the mystery of a new birth, rising above the flesh and the world. If such a person is to boast, he must boast only in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ. And for those who understand only this law of boasting, the Apostle adds: **And as many as follow this rule, peace be upon them and mercy, and upon the Israel of God. From now on, let no one cause me trouble, for I carry the marks <note>original: "stigmata"</note> of the Lord JESUS in my body. The grace of our Lord JESUS CHRIST be with your spirit, brothers. Amen. Written from Rome.**

With this holy prayer, the Apostle closes his epistle. When he says "upon the Israel of God," it is as if he said "upon the spiritual people of God." When he prays that the Galatians no longer bring him trouble, he means they should no longer trouble him about receiving circumcision. For Paul considers circumcision in the body to be nothing, and uncircumcision to be nothing; rather, he considers the **marks** <note>original: "stigmata"</note> and the insignia of the Lord's passion, which he carries in his body, to be what matters for salvation. He does not say "I carry circumcision," but **I carry the marks of the Lord Jesus in my body.** Therefore, let those people stop bringing more labor to him on this matter. They should not care about carrying circumcision; instead, let them boast that they have been marked by the mysteries of the Passion. Indeed, every Christian who is co-crucified with Christ the Lord carries the marks of the Lord Jesus in his body. How then shall the hands, which were nailed with Christ on the cross, reach out toward crimes? How shall the pierced feet run toward vices? How shall the opened side burn with greed or any other evil desire? Every Jew carries circumcision as a sign of the faith of Abraham; we, however, carry the marks of the Lord as a sign of our faith and redemption. To the Lord himself, the author of such great sacraments and mysteries concerning us, be honor, glory, and thanksgiving, forever and ever. Amen.

<margin>A</margin> **EXAMINATION of several points regarding the literal text.**

<margin>32</margin> **The Vulgate edition:** *You who are spiritual, instruct such a person in the spirit of gentleness.*
The word used here actually means *restore, fit together,* or *repair* rather than *instruct*. Paul wrote: <term>you who are spiritual, restore <note>original Greek: "hymas hoi pneumatikoi katartizete"</note> such a person in the spirit of gentleness <note>original Greek: "ton toiouton en pneumati praotētos"</note></term>.

**The Vulgate edition:** *Considering yourself, lest you also be tempted.*
The use of a participle in place of a verb is frequent in Paul's writing. It is better to use the verb here than the participle. For those who do not notice Paul’s habit and use the participle might suspect Paul committed a barbarism by assigning a singular epithet to a plural noun. They would not suspect this if they noticed that he used, according to his frequent custom, a participle for a verb. The preceding sentence should be read not with a comma, but as a full clause. Paul wrote: <term>consider yourself <note>original Greek: "skopōn seauton"</note> lest you also be tempted <note>original Greek: "mē kai sy peirasthēs"</note></term>.

**The Vulgate edition:** *Bear one another’s burdens.*
The old translator could also have said: *carry your mutual burdens*. Paul wrote: <term>bear one another's burdens <note>original Greek: "allēlōn ta barē bastazete"</note></term>.

**The Vulgate edition:** *He deceives himself.*
Here, Jerome notes that the word from the Greek composition which the old translator rendered as "to deceive" <note>original: "seducere"</note> means not just to deceive, but to deceive in the mind. For <term>mind <note>original Greek: "phrēn"</note></term> signifies the mind or the rational part, and <term>to deceive <note>original Greek: "apataō"</note></term> means to fail, trick, or lead astray. Paul wrote: <term>he deceives his own mind <note>original Greek: "heauton phrenapata"</note></term>.

<margin>B</margin> **The Vulgate edition:** *Let him who is instructed in the word communicate with him who instructs him.*
<margin>32</margin> The old translator fashioned non-Latin words from a foreign word. For the Greeks say <term>to teach or instruct <note>original Greek: "katēcheō"</note></term>, from which he fashioned "catechize" and "catechized." This pertains to those who are still unrefined in the faith; hence they were called "catechumens"—those being instructed and trained in the faith who were not yet initiated into the sacred rites. Paul wrote: <term>let him who is instructed in the word share <note>original Greek: "koinōneitō ho katēchoumenos ton logon"</note> with the one who instructs <note>original Greek: "tō katēchounti"</note></term>.

**The Vulgate edition:** *For in its own time we shall reap, if we do not fail.*
Rather: *in its proper time*. This is more suitable even to Latin speech...

<header>COMMENTARY</header>

<margin>1</margin> But the glory of the divine good will, in which will alone he has filled both the apostles and us—whom he filled through them as if through ambassadors of divine goodness—with his grace in his beloved son. In this son, we have everything; in his blood, our sins are forgiven and wiped away. Having been translated from the captivity of the wicked one into the freedom of the eternal kingdom and the children of God, it was God's goodness alone that served as the reason for infusing wisdom and prudence into the apostles. This was done by revealing the mystery <note>original: "mysterium," referring to a divine secret now revealed</note> and secret of his good will, according to his good pleasure. This plan was to collect, unite, and confirm all things, both heavenly and earthly, in Christ as the head, and in him to repair the ruin of both angels and men. Lest this good pleasure be thought of as something new, he predestined it within himself from eternity, to be administered in the fullness of time. Now, the "fullness of time" occurred when the childhood and adolescence of the world had passed; then he sent his son—in whom are all things, both heavenly and earthly—into the world to become consubstantial <term>consubstantial: sharing the same essential nature or "substance" as humanity</term> with us. He did this so that, as brothers through the mystery of the assumed flesh <note>The Incarnation, where God took on human form</note>, he might call us into the fellowship of the eternal inheritance with him. We were predestined according to the foreknowledge of him who works all things through the Son, who is the "Angel of Great Counsel" <note>original: "magni consilii angelus," a traditional title for Christ drawn from the Septuagint version of Isaiah 9:6</note>, the messenger of the great and eternal counsel of the divine good will. Therefore, those who announced these things to us, and those who heard these mysteries from the Son of God, did not announce them so that any mortal might carry away the praise, but so that we might praise the glory of God and his infinite good will. In praising him, let us burn with love; and in burning, let us possess the riches of his propitious goodness within us, never <margin>3</margin> failing in the praises of such great goodness. To acknowledge this, the Apostle exhorts the Ephesians by referencing similar benefits received through faith in Christ, saying:

**In whom you also, believing, were sealed with the holy Spirit of promise, who is the pledge of our inheritance for the redemption of his possession, to the praise of his glory.**

Those who believe in Christ receive a seal from the Holy Spirit. Without this seal, no one will be admitted to the eternal inheritance, which we receive because Christ acquired us in redemption. To him we owe praise and glory. One ought not to contemplate any other cause for our redemption except the good will of the Father, the obedience and prompt execution of the Son, and the generous pouring out of the Holy Spirit's gifts, which are the pledges <note>original: "arrabo," a legal term for a down-payment or earnest money that guarantees a future transaction</note> and seals of future blessedness. The Apostle prays that God may help the Ephesians to be able to understand these things spiritually, making a pious memory of them in his prayers (which is an argument of true love). For through such duties, the grace of God increases, and the gifts of divine distribution are poured out more abundantly—especially in those who, as far as is in them, prepare themselves for divine graces. This is what the <margin>4</margin> Ephesians were doing through faith and love for the saints.

Paul testifies to this, saying: **For this reason, I too, hearing of your faith in the Lord JESUS and your love toward all the saints, do not cease to give thanks for you, making mention of you in my prayers. That the God of the glory of our Lord JESUS CHRIST, the Father, may give you the spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him, the eyes of your heart being enlightened; so that you may know what is the hope of his calling, and what are the riches of the glory of his inheritance in the saints. And what is the exceeding greatness of his power toward us who believe, according to the working of the might of his power, which he worked in CHRIST, raising him from the dead and making him sit at his right hand in the heavenly places, above every principality, and power, and virtue, and domination, and every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the one to come. And he subjected all things under his feet, and gave him as head over all things to the church, which is his body, and his fullness: he who is filled all in all.**

Those whose hearts' eyes the eternal Father enlightens to the knowledge of himself possess the greatest faith in his promises. For they know him to be most true; their hope is most firm because he is most willing to give; and their charity is most fervent because he is the best, and will freely bestow the ineffable riches of his goodness, as one who is the supreme good and with whom are all the treasures of riches. In these three things consist the gift of the spirit of wisdom and his revelation. But consider also those who contemplate the magnitude of the power of the works and signs which the eternal Father granted to the apostles and other believers in him through our Lord, whom he raised from the dead. Furthermore, consider the exaltation of human nature in Christ: for that nature which was raised from the dead, residing at the right hand of the Father, has been placed above every principality, power, virtue, and domination <note>These terms refer to the traditional hierarchy of angelic beings</note>—and lest you disbelieve, even above the Thrones, Cherubim, and Seraphim. He is even above those, and above everything that can be named, not only in this age but also in the future. God alone is ineffable and beyond naming. Every creature is subjected to his feet. And he himself, even according to his assumed humanity, is the summit and head of every creature: a creature (if I may say so) uncreated, and a creator created. Since he is the head in the praise of God—above all praise—he is the head of all things appointed by God, containing in himself the praise of the creators...

<header>THE FIFTH MODE</header>
<margin>Ephesians</margin>

<margin>A</margin>
...connecting, who are the blessed angels and the holy souls of the saints; and who, all together, both the highest and the most exalted, are the body of the head who completes all things—the church—and the fullness of him who is filled in all through all. Do not believe the body of Christ is complete before all things are restored. And then all things will be as one most absolute and perfect living creature <note>original: "animal," used here in the philosophical sense of a "living being" or "unified organism"</note> whose members will be forever in the greatest harmony, praising God together. But even the head itself, the most glorious humanity of Christ, adds above all praise. "I will add," he says, "above all your praise." Therefore, those who consider this exaltation of our nature in Christ, how do they not already leap for joy in the hope of those eternal goods? How do they not burn with the love of such ineffable divine goodness? Beginning their praises in this world, which in the fullness of Christ—which is his body and the assembly of all the saints—they will never stop for eternity, with the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit dwelling in them, one God, simple and undivided. To whom be all power, wisdom, and goodness, fear, love, and honor, for ever and ever.

<margin>B
1
2</margin>
### EXAMINATION of several points concerning the literal text.

¶ **The Vulgate Edition:** *Who predestined us to the adoption of children through JESUS CHRIST.* ¶ It is enough to say, as has been said often elsewhere, "unto adoption through Jesus Christ." Paul: <note>original Greek: "ho proorisas hēmas eis huiothesian dia Iēsou Christou"</note> "having predestined us unto adoption as sons through Jesus Christ." ¶ **The Vulgate Edition:** *According to the purpose of his will.* ¶ It should rather be said "according to the good pleasure of his will." For here the word is not *prothesis* <note>meaning a "setting forth" or "purpose"</note>, which the old translator usually renders as "purpose," but *eudokia*, which is more accurately translated as "good will" and "good pleasure." Indeed, the old translator himself renders it as "good pleasure" a little further down where he says: "to make known to us the mystery of his will according to his good pleasure." It should have been the same here. Paul: <note>original Greek: "kata tēn eudokian tou thelēmatos autou"</note> "according to the good pleasure of his will." ¶ **The Vulgate Edition:** *In which he hath graced us in his beloved son.* ¶ Since the Greek word *charitō* signifies "to fill with grace," the old translator could have more accurately translated it "he filled us with grace" than "he graced us." Also, the phrase "his son" is redundant and not found in the Greek, as the holy Jerome <note>Saint Jerome, the 4th-century translator of the Vulgate</note> also noted. Paul: <note>original Greek: "en hē echaritōsen hēmas en tō ēgapēmenō"</note> "in which he filled us with grace in the Beloved." And immediately he adds: "in whom we have." ¶ **The Vulgate Edition:** *To make known to us the mystery of his will according to his good pleasure.* ¶ I think the old translator should rather have said "when he made known to us" instead of "to make known to us." For God then filled them with all wisdom and prudence when he revealed the mystery and secret of the faith to them. Indeed, that universal wisdom and prudence is nothing other than the opening and unlocking of that divine mystery. And since the old translator said "the mystery of his will," it followed that he should have said "according to his own <note>Latin: "suum"</note> good pleasure" rather than "his" <note>Latin: "eius"</note>, so that the speech would be mutual and reciprocal everywhere, and he would not create the illusion that "his" refers to someone else. Paul: <note>original Greek: "gnōrisas hēmin to mystērion tou thelēmatos autou kata tēn eudokian autou"</note> "having made known to us the mystery of his will, according to his good pleasure." ¶ **The Vulgate Edition:** *To restore [instaurare] all things in CHRIST.* ¶ The holy Jerome wonders why the old translator turned the word *anakephalaiōsasthai* into "restore" and not "recapitulate," since both logicians and orators use that term. At the end of their cases, for the sake of the memory of the judges and those who heard the business, they are accustomed to perform a "recapitulation." For a recapitulation is an epilogue and a summary comprehension of many preceding things. Therefore, we have paraphrased the word toward this understanding. Paul: <note>original Greek: "anakephalaiōsasthai ta panta en tō Christō"</note> "to sum up all things in Christ." ¶ **The Vulgate Edition:** *In whom also we are called by lot [forte].* ¶ The particle "also we" is superfluous. And it seems it should be said "we were called into a lot <note>or "allotment/inheritance"</note> or fellowship" rather than "we were called by chance [forte]," lest the apostle seem to mean by his speech that we were called by luck, fortune, or some kind of lottery—which is as far from divine understanding as attributing anything to chance or rashness. But if it is said "we were called into a lot," it is readily understood as a part, portion, inheritance, fellowship, or something similar, which does not contradict divine and apostolic understanding. Paul: <note>original Greek: "en hō kai eklērōthēmen"</note> "in whom also we were assigned a lot." ¶ **The Vulgate Edition:** *In whom also you, when you had heard the word of truth, the gospel of your salvation, received it.*

<margin>1</margin> But the glory of the divine good will, in which will alone: he filled both the apostles and us—whom he filled through them as if through messengers of divine goodness—with his grace in his beloved son. In him, we have all things; in his blood, our sins are forgiven and wiped away. After we were transferred from the captivity of the evil one into the liberty of the eternal kingdom and of the children of God, God’s goodness alone was the reason for pouring wisdom and prudence into the apostles, by revealing the mystery <note>original: "mysterium," a divine secret revealed to believers</note> and secret of his good will. In what way was it his good pleasure to gather, unite, and confirm all things—both heavenly and earthly—in Christ as the head, and in him to repair the ruin of both angels and men? Lest this good pleasure be thought of as something new: he predestined it from eternity within himself, to be dispensed in the fullness of time. Now, the fullness of time occurred when the childhood and youth of the world had already passed, when he sent his Son, in whom are all things both heavenly and earthly, into the world to become of one substance <note>original: "consubstantialem," meaning of the same essence or nature</note> with us. He did this so that, as brothers through the mystery of the assumed flesh, he might call us into the fellowship of the eternal inheritance with himself. We were predestined according to the foreknowledge of him who works all things through the Son, who is the messenger of great counsel <note>original: "magni consilij angelus," a traditional title for Christ derived from the Greek version of Isaiah 9:6</note>, the herald of the great and eternal counsel of the divine good will. Therefore, those who announced these things to us, and those who heard these mysteries from the Son of God, did not announce them so that any mortal might receive praise, but so that we might praise the glory of God and his infinite good will. Moreover, in praising him, let us burn with love. And burning with love, let us possess the riches of his propitious goodness within us, never 
<margin>3</margin> failing in the praises of such great goodness. To recognize this also from similar benefits received through the faith of Christ, the apostle exhorts the Ephesians, saying: ¶ *In whom also you, believing, were sealed with the holy Spirit of promise: who is the pledge <note>original: "arrabo," a legal term for a down payment or earnest money that guarantees a future transaction</note> of our inheritance in the redemption of his acquisition, to the praise of his glory.* ¶ Those believing in Christ receive a seal from the Holy Spirit, without which seal no one will be admitted to the eternal inheritance. We receive this inheritance because Christ acquired us in redemption, to whom we owe praise and glory. Nor should any other cause for our redemption be contemplated except the good will of the Father, the obedience and prompt execution of the Son, and the generous outpouring of gifts from the Holy Spirit, which are the pledges and seals of future happiness. The apostle prays that God may help the Ephesians to be able to understand these things spiritually, making a pious remembrance of them in his prayers (which is a proof of true love) before God. For by such duties, both the grace of God increases and the gifts of divine distribution are poured out more abundantly—especially in those who, as much as lies within them, prepare themselves for divine graces. This the Ephesians did through both faith and love for the saints. And Paul testifies to this, saying:

V. MOD.

<margin>Ephesians</margin>
...unfolding. These are the blessed angels and the holy souls of the saints: who all together, both the highest and the most exalted, are the body of the head that completes all things—the church—and the fullness of him who is filled in all through all. Do not believe the body of Christ is completed before all things are restored. Then all things will be as one most absolute and perfect living being, whose members will perpetually be in the greatest harmony, praising God together. But the head itself, the most glorious humanity of Christ, adds above all praise. "I will add," he says, "above all your praise." Therefore, those who consider this exaltation of our nature in Christ, how do they not now leap with joy in hope of those eternal goods? How do they not burn with the charity of such ineffable goodness of God? They begin praises in this world which, in the fullness of Christ—which is his body and the assembly of all saints—shall find no end in eternity, as the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit dwell in them: one God, simple and undivided. To whom belongs all power, wisdom, goodness, fear, love, and honor, for ages of ages.

<margin>B</margin> EXAMINATION of some points concerning the text. ¶ **Vulgate edition:** *Who predestined us to the adoption of sons through JESUS CHRIST.* ¶ It is sufficient to say, as has been said often elsewhere, "into adoption through Jesus Christ." Paul says: *who predestined us into the adoption of sons through Jesus Christ* <note>original Greek: "ὁ προορίσας ἡμᾶς εἰς υἱοθεσίαν διὰ Ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ"</note>.

¶ **Vulgate edition:** *According to the purpose of his will.* ¶ It should rather be said "according to the good pleasure of his will." For the word here is not *prothesis* <note>meaning a "setting forth" or "purpose"</note>, which the old translator usually interprets as "purpose" [propositum], but <term>eudocia</term> <note>original Greek: "εὐδοκία," meaning good will, delight, or favor</note>, which is more accurately interpreted as "good will" or "good pleasure." Indeed, the old translator himself interprets it as "good pleasure" [beneplacitum] a little further down, where he says: "that he might make known to us the mystery of his will according to his good pleasure." So he should have done here as well. Paul says: *according to the good pleasure of his will* <note>original Greek: "κατὰ τὴν εὐδοκίαν τοῦ θελήματος αὐτοῦ"</note>.

¶ **Vulgate edition:** *In which he hath graced us in his beloved son.* ¶ Since the Greek word *charitoo* signifies "I fill with grace," the old translator could have more justly rendered it "he filled with grace" rather than "he graced" [gratificavit]. Likewise, the phrase "his son" is redundant, nor is it found in the Greek. Saint Jerome also noted this fact. Paul says: *in which he graced us in the beloved* <note>original Greek: "ἐν ᾗ ἐχαρίτωσεν ἡμᾶς ἐν τῷ ἠγαπημένῳ"</note>. And he immediately adds: *in whom we have* <note>original Greek: "ἐν ᾧ ἔχομεν"</note>.

¶ **Vulgate edition:** *That he might make known to us the mystery [sacramentum] of his will according to his good pleasure.* ¶ I think it would have been better for the old translator to say "when he made known to us" rather than "that he might make known to us." For God then filled them with all wisdom and prudence when he revealed to them the mystery and secret of the faith. Indeed, that all-encompassing wisdom and prudence is nothing other than the disclosure and unlocking of that divine mystery. And since the old translator had said "the mystery [sacramentum] of his will," it followed that he should have said "according to *his own* [suum] good pleasure" rather than "according to *his* [eius] good pleasure," so as to avoid the impression that "his" and "his own" referred to different people, keeping the speech reciprocal throughout. Paul says: *having made known to us the mystery of his will, according to his good pleasure* <note>original Greek: "γνωρίσας ἡμῖν τὸ μυστήριον τοῦ θελήματος αὐτοῦ, κατὰ τὴν εὐδοκίαν αὐτοῦ"</note>.

¶ **Vulgate edition:** *To restore [instaurare] all things in CHRIST.* ¶ Saint Jerome wonders why the old translator turned the word *anakephalaiosasthai* into "to restore" [instaurare] and not "to recapitulate" [recapitulare], since both logicians and orators use that term. At the end of their cases, for the sake of the memory of the judges and the recollection of those who heard the business, they are accustomed to perform a <term>recapitulation</term> <note>original: "recapitulatīonē"; the act of summarizing and bringing all points under one heading</note>. For a recapitulation is an epilogue and a summary comprehension of many preceding things. Therefore, we have used a longer description to capture this meaning. Paul says: *to recapitulate all things in Christ* <note>original Greek: "ἀνακεφαλαιώσασθαι τὰ πάντα ἐν τῷ χριστῷ"</note>.

¶ **Vulgate edition:** *In whom also we are called by lot [forte].* ¶ The particle "also we" is redundant. And it seems better to say "we are called into a lot" [in sortem] or "into a fellowship" [consortium] rather than "we are called by lot" [forte], lest the apostle seem to signify that we were called by "chance," "fortune," or some random "lottery." Such a thought is as far from divine understanding as attributing anything to chance or rashness. But if it is said "we are called into a lot," it is readily understood as being into a part, a portion, an inheritance, a fellowship, or something similar, which does not contradict divine and apostolic understanding. Paul says: *in whom also we were chosen by lot* <note>original Greek: "ἐν ᾧ καὶ ἐκληρώθημεν"</note>.

<margin>C</margin> ¶ **Vulgate edition:** *In whom also you, when you had heard the word of truth, the gospel of your salvation, received it.* ¶ It should rather be said in the first person: "we, when we had heard." And the word "received" is redundant. And where it says "in whom," it seems to mean "from whom." For the apostles and Paul, who hoped in Christ beforehand, heard the gospel of salvation—and indeed of eternal salvation—from Christ. They heard it while he still lived as a mortal on earth; Paul, however, heard it while Christ, robed in the glorious garment of immortality and shining, reigned in the heavens. For he says: "I did not receive it from man, nor did I learn it, but through the revelation of Jesus Christ." Paul says: *in whom also you, having heard the word of truth, the gospel of our salvation* <note>original Greek: "ἐν ᾧ καὶ ὑμεῖς ἀκούσαντες τὸν λόγον τῆς ἀληθείας τὸ εὐαγγέλιον τῆς σωτηρίας ἡμῶν"</note>. And it immediately follows: *in whom also believing* <note>original Greek: "ἐν ᾧ καὶ πιστεύσαντες"</note>.

¶ **Vulgate edition:** *Who is the pledge of our inheritance.* ¶ The word "Who" [Qui] refers to the same person as the previous phrase "in whom"—namely Christ, not the Holy Spirit. This is clearly known from the Greek, for the word for "Spirit" in Greek is neuter, while the relative pronoun "who" is masculine. And the old [translator]...

But we praise the glory of the divine good will, in which will alone he filled both the apostles—and us through them as if through ambassadors of divine goodness—with his grace, in his beloved Son. In this Son, we possess all things; in his blood, our sins are forgiven and washed away. <margin>Concerning goodness</margin> We have been translated from the captivity of the evil one into the liberty of the eternal kingdom and of the children of God. This was the reason for pouring wisdom and prudence into the apostles: by revealing the mystery and secret of his good will. In what way was it his good pleasure to gather, unite, and confirm all things—both heavenly and earthly—in Christ as the head, and in him to repair the ruin of both angels and men? Lest this good pleasure be thought of as something new, he preordained it within himself from the beginning, to be administered in the fullness of time. The fullness of time, however, occurred once the childhood and adolescence of the world were completed: when he sent his Son—in whom all things, both heavenly and earthly, consist—to become consubstantial <note>original: "consubstantialem," meaning having the same essence or substance</note> with us. He did this so that he might call us, who are now brothers through the mystery of his flesh, to a shared partnership in the eternal inheritance. This was predestined according to the foreknowledge of him who works all things through the Son, who is the Angel of Great Counsel <note>A traditional title for Christ derived from the Septuagint version of Isaiah 9:6</note> and the messenger of the great and eternal counsel of the divine good will. Therefore, those who announced these things to us, who heard these mysteries from the Son of God, did not announce them so that any mortal might carry away the praise; rather, they did so that we might praise the glory of God and his infinite good will. And in praising him, let us burn with love; and burning with love, let us possess the riches of his propitious <note>favorably inclined or merciful</note> goodness within us, lest we fail in the praises of such great goodness.

<margin>3</margin> The Apostle also exhorts the Ephesians to recognize this from the similar benefits received through Christ, saying: <margin>In whom also etc.</margin> <margin>4</margin> "In whom also you, having believed, were sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise, who is the pledge <term>arrabo: a Greek/Latin term for a down-payment or earnest money that guarantees a future transaction</term> of our inheritance, toward the redemption of his possession, to the praise of his glory." For those whose eyes of the heart the eternal Father enlightens unto the knowledge of himself, they possess a most immense faith in his promises. For they know him to be most true; they have a most firm hope because he is most willing to give; and they have a most fervent charity because he is the best and will freely bestow the ineffable riches of his goodness, as he is the supreme good and the one with whom all the treasures of riches reside. And in these three things consists the gift of the spirit of wisdom and of his revelation.

# V

<margin>1</margin>¶ AN EXAMINATION of several points regarding the literal text. ¶ **The Vulgate edition.** *Who predestined us for the adoption of sons through JESUS CHRIST.* ¶ It is sufficient to say, as has often been said elsewhere: *into adoption through Jesus Christ.* Paul says: <note>Greek: "ho proorisas hēmas eis huiothesian dia iēsou christou"</note> *the one who predestined us for adoption through Jesus Christ.* ¶ **The Vulgate edition.** *According to the purpose of his will.* ¶ It should rather be said: *according to the good pleasure of his will.* For here we do not find the word *prothesis* <note>Greek for a "setting forth" or "purpose"</note>, which the old translator usually interprets as "purpose" (propositum); instead, we have *eudokia* <note>Greek for "good will" or "delight"</note>, which is more accurately interpreted as "good will" and "good pleasure." Indeed, the old translator himself interprets it as "good pleasure" (beneplacitum) a little further down, where he says: *to make known to us the mystery of his will according to his good pleasure.* He should have done the same here. Paul says: <note>Greek: "kata tēn eudokian tou thelēmatos autou"</note> *according to the good pleasure of his will.* ¶ **The Vulgate edition.** *In which he has graced us in his beloved son.* ¶ Since *charitoō* <note>Greek: "to fill with grace" or "to favor"</note> signifies that one is filled with grace, the old translator could have more accurately rendered it as *he filled with grace* rather than *he graced.* Likewise, the phrase *in his son* is redundant; it is not found in the Greek. Saint Jerome <note>A 4th-century scholar and the primary translator of the Vulgate Bible</note> also noted this. Paul says: <note>Greek: "en hē echaritōsen hēmas en tō ēgapēmenō"</note> *in which he filled us with grace in the Beloved.* And he immediately adds: <note>Greek: "en hō echomen"</note> *in whom we have.*

<margin>2</margin>¶ **The Vulgate edition.** *To make known to us the mystery of his will according to his good pleasure.* ¶ I believe it would have been better for the old translator to say *when he made known to us*, rather than *to make known to us.* For God then filled them with all wisdom and prudence when he revealed the mystery and secret of the faith to them. Indeed, that all-encompassing wisdom and prudence is nothing other than the disclosure and unlocking of that divine mystery. And since the old translator had said *the mystery of his will*, it followed that he should have said *according to his own good pleasure* rather than *according to his* <note>The author is debating the nuances between the Latin reflexive pronoun "suum" and the demonstrative "eius"</note>, so that he might have maintained a consistent phrasing everywhere and not created the illusion that "his" (sua) referred to one thing and "his" (eius) to another. Paul says: <note>Greek: "gnōrisas hēmin to mystērion tou thelēmatos autou kata tēn eudokian autou"</note> *having made known to us the mystery of his will, according to his good pleasure.* ¶ **The Vulgate edition.** *To restore all things in CHRIST.* ¶ Saint Jerome marvels that the old translator rendered the word *anakephalaiōsasthai* <note>Greek: "to bring back under one head" or "to sum up"</note> as *to restore* (instaurare), and not rather *to recapitulate* (recapitulare), since both logicians and orators use that term. At the end of their cases, for the sake of the memory of the judges and of those who have heard the proceedings, they are accustomed to making a "recapitulation" to aid recollection. For a recapitulation is an epilogue, and a summary comprehension of many preceding things. Therefore, we have used a longer phrasing to capture this meaning. Paul says: <note>Greek: "anakephalaiōsasthai ta panta en tō christō"</note> *to sum up all things in Christ.* ¶ **The Vulgate edition.** *In whom also we were called by lot.* ¶ The particle *and we* (et nos) is superfluous. And it seems better to say *we were called into a lot* or *into a partnership* rather than *we were called by lot.* This is to prevent the apostle from appearing to mean that we were called by "luck," "fortune," or some "casting of lots." Such an idea is as far removed from divine understanding as attributing anything to chance or rashness would be. But if it is said *we were called into a lot*, it is readily understood as being called into a "part," "portion," "inheritance," "partnership," or something similar, which does not contradict divine and apostolic understanding. Paul says: <note>Greek: "en hō kai eklērōthēmen"</note> *in whom we also were made heirs.*

<margin>3</margin>¶ **The Vulgate edition.** *In whom also you, when you had heard the word of truth, the gospel of your salvation, received it.* ¶ It should rather be said in the first person: *we, when we had heard.* And the word *received* (recepistis) is superfluous. And when it says *in whom*, it seems to mean the same as *from whom.* For the apostles and Paul, who hoped in Christ beforehand, heard from Christ the gospel of salvation—and indeed of eternal salvation. They heard him while he still moved upon the earth as a mortal; Paul, however, heard him while he reigned in the heavens, clothed and shining in the glorious robe of immortality. For he says: *I did not receive it from man, nor was I taught it, but through a revelation of Jesus Christ.* Paul says: <note>Greek: "en hō kai hēmeis akousantes ton logon tēs alētheias to euangelion tēs sōtērias hēmōn"</note> *in whom also we, having heard the word of truth, the gospel of our salvation.* And immediately there follows: <note>Greek: "en hō kai pisteusantes"</note> *in whom also believing.* ¶ **The Vulgate edition.** *Who is the pledge of our inheritance.* ¶ The "who" (qui) refers to the same thing as the previous phrase "in whom" or "into whom"—namely Christ, not the Holy Spirit. This is clearly recognized from the Greek, for the words for the "Holy Spirit" among the Greeks are neuter, while the relative pronoun "who" (qui) here is masculine. And the old...

Saint Jerome notes that he translated this as a "pledge" <note>original: *pignus*</note>; however, we prefer the term "earnest-money" <note>original: *arrabonem*; a legal term referring to a down payment that guarantees the full amount later</note>. This word is indeed commonly used by Latin writers. For Christ is the <term>earnest<gloss>a security deposit or down payment on a future inheritance</gloss></term> of our inheritance, and so that we might not despair of eternal salvation, the Eternal Father—the Father of mercies and the God of all consolation—gave us His own Son as an earnest. For He did not spare His own Son, but handed Him over for us all. This is an earnest greater than any other, better than all the angels and the entire world. # EPHESIANS.

### V

We have been raised up from the body of Christ, and are already sitting with him in mystery <note>original: *in mysterio*; meaning spiritually or sacramentally rather than physically</note> at the right hand of the Father: which is a symbol of future glory and of the riches of the Father's grace, which in the ages to come will be revealed in us through His ineffable kindness toward us in Christ Jesus. Let us therefore be of a mind always full of thanksgiving toward God; let us be faithful. For by His grace through faith we are saved: not saved by ourselves nor by our works, but by the grace of God. 
<margin>to be created by us</margin>
For grace is a gift, not a work. And lest we should even think the faith by which we are justified is provided by ourselves: even that itself is the gift of God. 
<margin>not from us</margin>
<margin>not from us but from God</margin>
Therefore, we ought to attribute nothing to ourselves, but everything to God, so that we may not boast in ourselves or in our works, but in the grace and mercy of God alone. And that we are, and that we are spiritual, and that we will walk according to the spirit in the future—as in the works of faith, hope, and love—this is <unclear>ours</unclear>. Those things in which we shall walk are not <unclear>our</unclear> doing, for we are His workmanship, a new creature created in Christ Jesus. Created, I say, for those good works which God prepared that we should walk in them. For we are as earth without seed insofar as it is in ourselves; but God sows the good seed in which we may exercise our "earth." We have received the seeds: the rain of grace waters them, and God gives the increase. He who thinks otherwise deceives himself, being ungrateful toward God, the author of all good things—a stubborn work not acknowledging its Maker. Wherefore, Paul, the proclaimer and apostle of God and the asserter of the great divine piety toward us, further rouses the Ephesians to recognize the benefits of God alone, speaking in this manner:

> "Wherefore remember that you, being once Gentiles in the flesh—who were called the 'uncircumcision' by that which is called the 'circumcision' made by hands in the flesh—remember, I say, that at that time you were without CHRIST, being alienated from the legal governance of Israel, and strangers to the testaments, having no hope of the promise, and without God in the world. But now in CHRIST JESUS, you who were once far off have been made near in the blood of CHRIST. For He Himself is our peace, who has made both one, and has dissolved the middle wall of partition—the enmity—in His flesh: He has abolished the law of commandments in decrees, that He might create the two in Himself into one new man, making peace, and might reconcile both to God in one body, killing the enmity in Himself through the cross. And coming, He preached peace to you who were far off, and to those who were near. For through Him we both have access in one spirit to the Father."

<margin>¶ This is the holy exhortation by which Paul rouses the Ephesians to receive the benefits of God: which pertains no more to them than to us and to all coming from the Gentiles.</margin>
For by the Jews, who were circumcised according to the flesh, our ancestors were called the "uncircumcision," the uncircumcised, and the unclean. They were without Christ, without the legal observation of the Hebrew law (which prepared the way for Christ), outcasts from both testaments, having the hope of the promised inheritance neither in type <note>a symbolic foreshadowing</note> nor in truth, being impious and without God in the world. For even if they worshipped many gods, they were not gods but demons—whose worship was not piety, but impiety and an insult to the highest and true God. 
<margin>But what has been done with us by God's mercy?</margin> 
We who were once far off have been made near in the blood of Christ. He is our peace: the peace of angels and men, the peace of Gentiles and Jews. He made both testaments one, and dissolved the middle wall—that is, the difference between Gentiles and Jews that caused enmity—in His death. Likewise, He took away the law of commandments which was contained in ceremonies and edicts, so that He might create the two peoples, Gentiles and Jews, in Himself into one new man, who would no longer be called Jew or Gentile, but would be called Christian after Christ. 
<margin>New: because no longer carnal, but spiritual. No longer under the law, for that is of slavery, but in the law of liberty.</margin> 
Making peace between both peoples, He reconciles both to God. For both Gentiles and Hebrews were transgressors, and both needed reconciliation to God. He reconciled both to God the Father, extinguishing the enmity between God and them in Himself, connecting both in one body—namely, in His own body. Making them fellow members with angels and all the saints, with no more enmities or dissensions remaining. For how could you become a common body with the heavenly angels, holy souls, apostles, prophets, martyrs, the peaceful sons of God, and all the blessed, if you preserved any discord? 
<margin>How could you adhere to Christ your head, the Prince of Peace, if you do not have peace?</margin> 
He who, coming, preached peace to all: both to the Gentiles who were far from God, and to the Jews who were near by God's election and the preparation of the law. 
<margin>If you do not adhere:</margin> 
You are not made alive by His spirit, which is the Holy Spirit. For a member cut off from the body—torn away and separated—no longer lives the life of the body. If you do not adhere to the body, if you do not live by the spirit, you have no access to the Father; you are a child of wrath, excluded from the reconciliation of the Son of God. For all whoever have access to the Father—whom He admits to His presence, whom He accepts as sons—are in one body and live by the same spirit. They live in the body of the Son of God and by the Holy Spirit. Let us not think that if we still live in the flesh, it is according to the flesh; or if we are still against the world, the flesh, and the spirits of the air...

# COMMENTARY

we perform our service: that we are not with the angels and all the saints in the same body, or that we do not live by the Holy Spirit, or that we are not already presented and present to the Father at his right hand. Beyond a doubt, we are. Nor should you believe that there are two churches—one for those in heaven and another for those on earth. There are not two, but one; for there are not two bodies of Christ, but one body; not two spirits, but one spirit. And even if we cannot see these things with carnal eyes, blessed are they who can see such holy and wonderful sights through the spirit. This is not because of their own sight, but because the grace and mercy of God has gathered them, grafted them in, and brought them to life. I say He gathered them when they were strangers and foreigners, and grafted them into that sacred body with the angels and all the saints. He grafted them into Himself, so that together they might become one temple of God, and He gave them life by His Holy Spirit. These things are indeed most true. This is a most certain and wondrous sacrament of divine and ineffable piety, which is able to melt the very souls within us. Because of this, Paul concludes most holily: 

¶ *Therefore you are no longer strangers and foreigners, but fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household, built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Jesus Christ himself being the chief cornerstone. In him the whole building, joined together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord; in whom you also are built together into a dwelling place for God in the Spirit.*

The things the apostle discussed just before regarding the body of Christ, and now regarding the temple of God—whose highest point and chief cornerstone is Christ—are divine spectacles. They are visions of this same holy reality formed in his soul through the Spirit, not mere human thoughts. In the first vision, he saw the glory of Christ in the likeness of a single, all-beautiful living being, reflecting within itself the beauty of all the saints and angels; its head was Christ, a divine and incomprehensible beauty. In the second vision, he saw the glory of Christ in the likeness of the temple of God, likewise containing all beauty within itself. But a marvelous and indescribable beauty exists at the very summit, in the highest corner that binds all things together, which in this symbol is Jesus Christ, received, exalted, and raised high above all things. 

And just as in material buildings everything is connected to the foundation and tends toward the foundation, so in a spiritual building everything is connected to the foundation and tends toward it. But there is this difference: in a material building, the foundation is at the bottom, the lowest part of all; but in a spiritual building, the foundation is above <note>The author uses a common Renaissance theological metaphor: while earthly buildings are held up from below, spiritual ones are suspended from above by God.</note> and is the highest of all. This is not without reason, for all material things tend downward toward their foundation, but all spiritual things tend upward toward their own foundation, which holds all things together from above. The foundation of material things is very broad; the foundation of spiritual things is most narrow, most singular, and most simple. The more a creature is capable of this simplicity, the more blessed it is, and (if I may say so) the more subordinate and united to God. 

And the apostles preached, and the prophets foretold, that highest and simplest foundation, the chief cornerstone. Those who are built in Him are expanded into a holy temple in the Lord, reaching from the heavens to all the spaces of the earth, spread abroad by the Holy Spirit who gives life and sanctifies all things. The Son of God, within Himself as the highest foundation, unites all things and holds all things from above; and God the Father is the foundation of His holy temple, thus sanctified by its Inhabitant. Therefore, to the Sustainer, the Sanctifier, and the Inhabitant of this holy temple—the one God, the maker of all things—be all honor, glory, praise, and power in this His holy temple, for ever and ever. Amen.

### ¶ EXAMINATION of several points regarding the literal text.

**The Vulgate edition:** *doing the will of the flesh and of thoughts.* <note>Latin: *facientes voluntatem carnis et cogitationum*</note>
It is spoken in the plural, "wills" <note>original: *voluntates*</note>; and this is a metaphor signifying "desires." Paul writes: *doing the desires of the flesh and of the minds.* <note>Greek: *ποιοῦντες τὰ θελήματα τῆς σαρκὸς καὶ τῶν διανοιῶν*</note>

**The Vulgate edition:** *Because of his exceeding charity.* <note>Latin: *Propter nimiam charitatem eius*</note>
Paul has "because of his great love," and this designates something massive. Certainly, it is so great and so copious that it cannot be grasped by human intellect any more than the mass of the world could be enclosed in a human fist, or the entire wave of the sea contained in a narrow little jar. Paul writes: *Because of his great love.* <note>Greek: *Διὰ τὴν πολλὴν ἀγάπην αὐτοῦ*</note>

**The Vulgate edition:** *And when we were dead in sins, he brought us to life in CHRIST.* <note>Latin: *Et cum essemus mortui peccatis conv vivificavit nos i CHRISTO*</note>
It can be read: "and us, being dead in sins," or "since we are dead in sins, he brought us to life with Christ." For those who lived in sins must first die to sins in reality, just as darkness is driven out before the air can shine with light. Paul writes: *and us being dead in trespasses, he brought us to life with Christ.* <note>Greek: *καὶ ἡμᾶς νεκροὺς ὄντας ἐν τοῖς παραπτώμασι, συνεζωοποίησε τῷ χριστῷ*</note>

**The Vulgate edition:** *Of his grace in goodness toward us.* <note>Latin: *Gratiae suae in bonitate super nos*</note>
Rather, "in kindness." Paul writes: *of his grace in kindness toward us.* <note>Greek: *τῆς χάριτος αὐτοῦ ἐν χρηστότητι ἐφ' ἡμᾶς*</note>

**The Vulgate edition:** *For it is the gift of God.* <note>Latin: *Dei enim donum est*</note>
The word "for" <note>original: *enim*</note> is redundant. Paul writes: *the gift of God.* <note>Greek: *θεοῦ τὸ δῶρον*</note>

**The Vulgate edition:** *Created in CHRIST JESUS in good works.* <note>Latin: *Creati in CHRISTO IHESV in operibus bonis*</note>
It would be clearer if interpreted as: "unto good works." Paul writes: *created in Christ Jesus unto good
<margin>C 6</margin>
works.* <note>Greek: *κτισθέντες ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ ἐπὶ ἔργοις ἀγαθοῖς*</note> Here the use of the preposition "upon" <note>Greek: *ἐπὶ*</note> seems to stand in for "unto" <note>Greek: *εἰς*</note>.

**The Vulgate edition:** *Who were at that time without CHRIST.* <note>Latin: *Qui eratis illo in tempore sine CHRISTO*</note>
It should be read "that you were," not "who were." Paul writes: *that you were at that time without Christ.* <note>Greek: *ὅτι ἦτε ἐν τῷ καιρῷ ἐκείνῳ χωρὶς χριστοῦ*</note> And for a clearer understanding, from above...

# 5th Section on Ephesians

the previous small part, the word "remember" is taken up again: and "remember, I say" is added.

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Alienated from the conversation of Israel.* <note>original: "Alienati a couersatione Israel"</note>
¶ Where the ancient translator says "conversation" here, Paul’s own word signifies polity, citizenship, and the commonwealth. And indeed, the Jews were citizens of the city and kingdom of God, and hence theirs was a commonwealth. Yet they were not yet the adopted sons of the King, but still servants; however, the Gentiles were citizens not of the city and kingdom of God, but of the devil and his tyranny. They were as alienated from the Hebrew mode of government as those who are under a tyrant and live tyrannically are alienated from the mode of royal government and the best form of a republic. **Paul says:** *alienated from the commonwealth of Israel.* <note>original Greek: ἀπηλλοτριωμένοι τῆς πολιτείας τοῦ ἰσραήλ</note>

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *And strangers to the testaments.* <note>original: "Et hospites testamentorum"</note>
¶ The word Paul uses here signifies a guest, a pilgrim, and a stranger. I have preferred to say "strangers to the testaments" <note>original: "extranei"</note> rather than "guests," <note>original: "hospites"</note> lest the Gentiles seem to have been once received into the testaments. For they were not received; they were entirely foreign and made strangers until the mercy of the Savior called them to the hope of life. At that time, they did not even suspect there would be a future life, but were then continually provoking the Author of life. **Paul says:** *and strangers to the covenants.* <note>original Greek: καὶ ξένοι τῶν διαθηκῶν</note>

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *And without God in this world.* <note>original: "Et sine deo in hoc mundo"</note>
¶ It is enough to say "in the world." **Paul says:** *and without God in the world.* <note>original Greek: καὶ ἄθεοι ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ</note>

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Abolishing the law of commandments in decrees.* <note>original: "Legem mādatorū decretis euacuans"</note>
¶ The ancient translator could also have said "abolishing, taking away, or something similar, the law of commandments in decrees." **Paul says:** *having abolished the law of commandments in ordinances.* <note>original Greek: τὸν νόμον τῶν ἐντολῶν ἐν δόγμασι, καταργήσας</note>

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Killing the enmities in himself through the cross.* <note>original: "Per crucem interficiens inimicitias in femetipso"</note>
¶ Where it says "in himself," it could be said "in it" <note>referring to the cross</note>. It could also be said: "in it" <note>referring to the body</note>. For in Greek, the relative pronoun is ambiguous as to whether it refers to the cross—and then it should be said "in it" [feminine]—or whether it refers to what was said about "one body"—and then it should be said "in it" [neuter]. If it refers to the one "killing," then it should be said "in himself." Yet it signifies "in him" or "in it" rather than "in himself." However, on account of the ancient translation, we have put "in himself." **Paul says:** *having slain the enmity in it through the cross.* <note>original Greek: διὰ τοῦ σταυροῦ ἀποκτείνας τὴν ἔχθραν ἐν αὐτῷ</note>

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *And peace to those who were near.* <note>original: "Et pacem iis qui prope"</note>
¶ The word "peace" is redundant here, but it is understood from the preceding passage. **Paul says:** *and to those who were near.* <note>original Greek: καὶ τοῖς ἐγγύς</note>

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Therefore you are no longer guests and strangers, but you are citizens of the saints.* <note>original: "Ergo iam nō estis hospites & aduenę sed estis ciues sanctorum"</note>
¶ Here too, for the reason stated above, it can be said "strangers and foreigners," but "fellow citizens with the saints." **Paul says:** *So then you are no longer strangers and sojourners, but fellow citizens with the saints.* <note>original Greek: ἄρα οὖν οὐκ ἔτι ἐστὲ ξένοι καὶ πάροικοι, ἀλλὰ συμπολῖται τῶν ἁγίων</note>

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Christ Jesus himself being the chief cornerstone.* <note>original: "Ipso summo angulari lapide CHRISTO"</note>
¶ The word "stone" <note>original: "lapide"</note> is not found here, but only: "the chief corner," or "the highest angular Jesus Christ." **Paul says:** *Jesus Christ himself being the cornerstone.* <note>original Greek: ὄντος ἀκρογωνιαίου αὐτοῦ ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ</note> But the ancient translator or others added "stone" because of the prophecy: *The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner.* <note>A reference to Psalm 118:22</note> And certainly, Christ is that highest and sharp-angled joiner in whom the entire spiritual building is bound together, contained, and supported.

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *In whom you also are built together into a dwelling place of God in the Holy Spirit.* <note>original: "In quo & vos coædificamini in habitaculum dei in spiritu sancto"</note>
¶ The word "Holy" <note>original: "sancto"</note> is redundant, nor is it found in Paul’s text. **Paul says:** *in whom you also are being built together into a dwelling place of God in the Spirit.* <note>original Greek: ἐν ᾧ καὶ ὑμεῖς συνοικοδομεῖσθε εἰς κατοικητήριον τοῦ θεοῦ ἐν πνεύματι</note>

->**CHAPTER III.**<-

Paul recognizes the mystery of such a beautiful body of Christ, of such a wonderful and fair temple of God. In order to aid the construction—so that he, as a servant, might prepare the Gentiles, the Ephesians, the Galatians, the Corinthians, the Romans, and all others of every kind as a temple for God—he fled from no labors, no pressures, no prisons, and no chains. He testifies to this continuously, being even then a prisoner when writing to the Ephesians, saying:

> For this reason I, Paul, am the prisoner of Christ Jesus for you Gentiles. Surely you have heard of the administration of the grace of God which was given to me for you. For by revelation the mystery was made known to me, as I wrote before in few words. By reading this, you can perceive my understanding in the mystery of Christ.

Behold, Paul confesses that he knows the secret from a vision of divine revelation, which he wrote about a little earlier regarding the mystery of the body of Christ and the holy temple of God, bound together in that chief cornerstone which the builders rejected and which became the head of the corner of the celestial building. He knew this, I say, from a vision of divine revelation, just as John knew the same celestial mysteries in the vision of the bridegroom and the bride, the Lamb and the heavenly Jerusalem, in the divine Apocalypse. And Paul further pursues his revelation, saying:

> Which in other generations was not made known to the sons of men, as it has now been revealed to his holy apostles and prophets in the Spirit: that the Gentiles are co-heirs, members of the same body, and partakers of his promise in Christ through the gospel. Of this gospel I was made a servant according to the gift of the grace of God, which was given to me according to the working of his power. To me, the least of all the saints, this grace was given: to preach among the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ, and to enlighten all people as to what is the administration of the mystery hidden for ages in

-># COM.<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut header featuring the word "COM." (short for Commentary) centered within a circular frame, flanked by ornate scrollwork and floral flourishes.</image-desc>

...God, who created all things through JESUS CHRIST. So that now the manifold wisdom of God might be made known to the princes and powers in the heavenly places <note>This refers to angelic or spiritual hierarchies</note> through the church, according to the eternal purpose <note>original: "præfinitionem sæculorum," literally the pre-definition of the ages</note> which he made in CHRIST JESUS our Lord. In him we have boldness and access in confidence through faith in him. ¶ The prophets had foretold that God would reign over the nations and that Christ would be their expectation, and that the nations would one day be saved. However, the *mode* of their salvation—how they were included in the promises of the inheritance made to Abraham (I mean the true inheritance, not the symbolic one <note>original: "non typicę sed verę"</note>)—and in what way, lay hidden for eternal ages in the foreknowledge of God. This mode of saving the nations God first revealed when Christ came, through whom God made all things (for in the beginning, the reason <note>original: "ratio"</note>, wisdom, and Word of all things were with God, and all things were made through him). When Christ, I say, came, God first opened this mode of salvation to his apostles and prophets. Nor is the salvation of the nations and of the Hebrews any different, even if there are various ranks among the holy and the saved, just as there are in the members of a single body and the joints of a single building. But the mode of saving everyone is: co-inheritance, co-incorporation, and co-participation in eternal blessedness in Christ; being grafted in and built together into a holy temple contained in Christ, sanctified in the Holy Spirit, inhabited by the eternal Father, and most full of the whole of God. Since Paul knows these things to be most true and certain—because of which every pressure and trouble of the world is most light to him and of no moment—he urges the Ephesians with great charity that they should by no means waver or falter because of his pressures <note>referring to Paul's imprisonment</note>, but rather grow much stronger to become holy members of Christ's body and be fitted to a more magnificent world, the temple of God. And if the exhortation to them is not effective enough, he knocks at the fountain of all power with prayers, so that He who alone is almighty and all-effective might give them the power and the understanding to do so; and he says:

> ¶ Wherefore I pray: that you do not succumb in my tribulations <note>original: "pressuris"</note> for you, which is your glory. For this cause I bow my knees to the Father of our Lord JESUS CHRIST, from whom all fatherhood <note>original: "paternitas"</note> in heaven and on earth is named. That he would grant you, according to the riches of his glory, to be strengthened with power through his Spirit in the inner man: that CHRIST may dwell through faith in your hearts. That you, being rooted and grounded in love, may be able to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth, and length, and depth, and height, and to know the love of CHRIST which surpasses knowledge, that you may be filled with all the fullness of God. Now to him who is able to do all things more abundantly than we ask or understand, according to the power that works in us, be glory in the Church in CHRIST JESUS unto all generations of the world forever and ever. Amen.

¶ When we look at the sun reflected in water, we do not claim the name "sun" from the image. Rather, the image we see has claimed the name of the sun for itself from the actual sun. In the same way, God does not draw his name from existing beings because he is called "Being" <note>original: "ens"</note>; rather, all other things draw their names from him, who is the highest and only true Being. Thus, regarding his being called "Father": he does not borrow this from earthly things. But from him, who is true Fatherhood <note>original: "paternitas"</note>, fatherhood is named in all others, whether in heaven or on earth. Therefore, "Father" as a name transferred <note>original: "translatitium," meaning a metaphorical or derivative term</note> from worldly things is not the name of God; rather, it is his primary and true name, from which those names that fit creatures are merely derivatives. For in order for things to be true and so named, we must look to the Truth itself. It is not the other way around—that Truth exists and is named through the things themselves—rather, the things are merely his traces. If we emulate the sense of the apostle, we see that he, having holily prayed for power for the Ephesians lest they succumb, asks it to be given from the fountain of omnipotence. So it is concerning faith, concerning love, and concerning knowledge: by which they might comprehend the length, breadth, depth, and height of God, and taste the super-eminent, super-excessive, and ecstatic charity which is in the knowledge of Christ, and thus be filled with all the fullness of God, which is infinity. And this is to pass into God and to comprehend beyond-intelligibly the incomprehensible, and to understand God by no other way than God's own understanding. It is as if you understood light not by the appearance of light but by the light itself existing in the soul—nay, if the light itself apprehended itself and were its own apprehension, your intellection would be light, or rather the very apprehension of the light by which it apprehended itself. And the apostle seeks to praise the supremely and infinitely powerful God: not according to human power, but according to that power which the Almighty himself works, and which will work in him and in the church according to what he works in Christ, and in that age which shall have no end, and which is the world of worlds, and in all generations of the saints who, from the beginning of the world, will possess that age forever. Therefore, such praise befits him above all power, holiness, and wisdom—he who is super-powerful, super-wise, and super-holy <note>The author uses "super-" prefixes to denote God's existence beyond all human categories</note>. It befits him, I say, above all time and age, in eternity and above the eternity of ages.

For he uses a comparative form which implies more than "least." Because we lack such a word in Latin, we have used the superlative, as the old translator did. Paul says: "to me, the less than the least of all saints." <note>original Greek: "ἐμοὶ τῷ ἐλαχιστοτέρῳ πάντων ἁγίων"</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "To evangelize the unsearchable riches of CHRIST." ¶ To more clearly deny the word just as Paul does, we have said "untrackable riches." <note>original: "inuestigabiles"</note> Paul says: "to preach the unsearchable wealth of Christ." <note>original Greek: "εὐαγγελίσασθαι ἀνεξιχνίαστον πλοῦτον τοῦ χριστοῦ"</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "Who created all things: that it might be made known to the princes and powers." ¶ After "created," the phrase "through Jesus Christ" is missing. Paul says: "to the one who created all things through Jesus Christ, so that now it might be made known to the principalities and powers." <note>original Greek: "τῷ τὰ πάντα κτίσαντι Διὰ ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ, ἵνα γνωρισθῇ μῦν ταῖς ἀρχαῖς καὶ ταῖς ἐξουσίαις"</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "Through the church the multiform wisdom of God." ¶ The word Paul uses here means "manifold" or "variegated" rather than "multiform"; however, the meaning remains the same whether it is said this way or in those ways. Paul says: "through the church the manifold wisdom of God." <note>original Greek: "διὰ τῆς ἐκκλησίας ἡ πολυποίκιλος σοφία τοῦ θεοῦ"</note>

<margin>C 10</margin>

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "Wherefore I pray that you faint not in my tribulations for you." ¶ According to the authority of Jerome, it can be read "that I faint not." However, even "that you faint not" works; following this understanding, we have put "that you do not succumb," both because of the old translator and because of what Paul adds next: "that he may grant you according to the riches of his glory to be strengthened with power," where he seems to have prayed for *them* so that they would not fail, rather than for himself. Paul says: "wherefore I ask not to lose heart in my afflictions for you." <note>original Greek: "διὸ αἰτοῦμαι μὴ ἐκκακεῖν ἐν ταῖς θλίψεσί μου ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν"</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "From whom all paternity in heaven and on earth is named." ¶ There are Greek manuscripts that have the singular "in heaven" <note>original Greek: "ἐρ᾽ οὐρανῷ"</note>; there are also those that have the plural "in the heavens" <note>original Greek: "ἐρ᾽ οὐρανοῖς"</note>, which the old translator followed; both convey the same meaning. And regarding the phrase "all paternity": here "paternity" properly means the same as "family" <note>original: "patria"</note> or a household derived from one father. Therefore, every heavenly family and every earthly family is called a "paternal family" from that highest and eternal Father. Paul says: "from whom every family in the heavens and on earth is named." <note>original Greek: "ἐξ οὗ πᾶσα πατριὰ ἐν οὐρανοῖς καὶ ἐπὶ γῆς οὐράζεται"</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "That he would grant you according to the riches of his glory to be strengthened in power." ¶ It should rather be said in the sixth case <note>the ablative case in Latin grammar</note>, "by power" <note>original: "virtute"</note>, that is, "to be strengthened by his authority." Paul says: "that he may give to you according to the wealth of his glory, to be strengthened with power." <note>original Greek: "ἵνα δῴη ὑμῖν κατὰ τὸν πλοῦτον τῆς δόξης αὐτοῦ, δυνάμει κραταιωθῆναι"</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "Height and depth." ¶ The old translator could have said

<margin>D 10</margin>

"depth" <note>original: "profunditas"</note>, just as he had used "height" <note>original: "sublimitas"</note> in a similar expression. And the order is changed: for in Paul, the word "depth" comes first and "height" follows. Paul says: "depth and height." <note>original Greek: "βάθος καὶ ὕψος"</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "But to him who is able to do all things." ¶ Paul adds the word "beyond" <note>original Greek: "ὑπὲρ"</note>, which we have referred back to "the powerful one" <note>original: "potens"</note>; this both increases and designates not only "being able," but more abundantly and more than "being able." For the power of God is immense, infinite, and beyond understanding—it is "more than power." If you do not wish to refer this preposition back to "the powerful one," it must be read: "to him who is powerful above" or "beyond doing all things," and so forth. Paul says: "but to him who is able beyond..." <note>original Greek: "τῷ δὲ δυναμένῳ ὑπὲρ"</note>
