<header>->COMMENTARY<-</header>

...to do all things. ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "Superabundantly <note>original: 'superabundanter'</note> above what we ask." ¶ The Latin particle requires that it should rather be expressed by the comparative "more than abundantly" <note>original: 'superabundantius'</note> so that the property of the language is preserved. Or, if we interpret it through the positive, it should be read as "those things which" <note>original: 'quae'</note> rather than "than" <note>original: 'quam'</note>, as Paul also has it: "beyond the abundance of what we ask or think." <note>original Greek: 'ὑπὲρ ἐκ περισσοῦ ὧν αἰτούμεθα ἢ νοοῦμεν'</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "To him be glory in the church and in Christ Jesus." ¶ Because the interpretation "to the one who is able" <note>original: 'τῷ Δυναμένῳ'</note> expresses a relative pronoun, we have substituted "to him" <note>original: 'ei'</note> here; otherwise, we would be using two consecutive relatives contrary to Latin custom, whereas Paul uses only one. And as for what is said "in the church and in Christ Jesus," the conjunction "and" <note>original: 'et'</note> is redundant. Paul says: "to him be glory in the church in Christ Jesus." <note>original Greek: 'αὐτῷ ἡ δόξα ἐν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ ἐν χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ'</note>

### CHAPTER IV.

N<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'N' featuring a human figure within an ornamental square frame.</image-desc>ow Paul descends to the teachings by which everyone can be prepared: so that one may be grafted as a member into the body of Christ, fitted to the temple of God, and finally, in that unity, transcend into the state where God, dwelling and moving within, administers to all the saints the abyss of his infinite fullness, and where God is all and works all in all. Moreover, we are prepared for that future blessedness—for that union which consumes all things—through modesty of feeling (not relying on our own prudence and attributing nothing to ourselves), through gentleness of character, through a patient expectation of eternal goods (however great the delay may be, and however much adversity may press in the meantime), and through mutual support in love according to God, by preserving all unity. Thus, by gradually preserving these unities, we may finally reach that supreme and all-consuming unity. For this unity, the Savior prayed to the Father, speaking first of the disciples: "I do not pray for these only, but also for those who will believe in me through their word, that they all may be one, even as you, Father, are in me and I in you, that they also may be one in us." <note>A reference to Jesus's "High Priestly Prayer" in John 17:20-21.</note> The unity of the Spirit must be kept in the bond of peace: the unity of the body of Christ (which is the one holy Catholic Church), the unity of the hope of eternal goods, the unity of the Lord, the unity of faith, and the unity of baptism. From the preservation of these unities, one reaches that which is the consummation of all: that unity which God alone grants in himself and in his infinite unity. Therefore, Paul exhorts and teaches the Ephesians in this manner:

<margin>11</margin>
> I therefore, a prisoner in the Lord, beseech you to walk worthily of the calling to which you have been called, with all humility of sense and gentleness, with patience, supporting one another in love, striving to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. May you be one body and one spirit, just as you were called in one hope of your calling. One Lord, one faith, one baptism. One God and Father of all, who is over all, and through all, and in us all.

¶ Now God is in us all, who works all things through the Son and perfects them in the Holy Spirit. He is hidden by his essence, which will be revealed in the supreme union, but manifest through the various distribution of graces, according to the various offices that befit the holy temple of God and the various members in the sacred body of Christ. Paul, the knower of God's mystery, adds this, saying:

<margin>12</margin>
> But to each one of us grace has been given according to the measure of Christ's gift. Therefore he says: "Ascending on high, he led captivity captive, and gave gifts to men." Now, what does "he ascended" mean, except that he also first descended into the lower parts of the earth? He who descended is the same one who ascended above all the heavens, that he might fill all things.

¶ The measure of Christ’s gift is the Holy Spirit, filling each person with spiritual gifts <note>original: 'charismatibus'</note> as he wills, knows, and sees fit. What does "he led captivity captive" mean—or rather, as Paul’s words sound, "he captivated captivity" <note>original: 'captivavit captivitatem'</note>—if not that he led us out of captivity? To those he brings out, he bestows the gifts of his Spirit. This is what the mercy of Christ performs with us daily: when we receive his faith, he leads us out of captivity, leads us with him from the left hand to the right, grafts us into his body, bestows the gifts of the Holy Spirit, and makes us a temple of God. Do not believe that Christ is absent from us (even if we are still upon the earth, or if we were being purified among the dead in the lower regions). For he who descended to the dead in the lower parts of the earth was also above all the heavens. And he who ascended above all the heavens did not desert his presence among those below—even if those below, obstructed by their own darkness, did not then, and do not now, understand his presence. For Christ fills all things. The world was made through him, and he was in the world even before he came into the world. For he came into the world immovably; he was already where he began to appear to men. And in his immovability, he immovably transfers us to his right hand and leads us to the heights, even if we do not yet have an understanding of this secret mystery concerning us. Those caught up in the spirit see this, no longer seeing with the senses of the flesh (which are blind and inept regarding spiritual things), but with the sense of the spirit which is most powerful for them. The spirit sees those things that seem cast down to the sense of the flesh as being exalted in the spirit—not by its own power, but by the Spirit of God. It sees that what is below is actually above; what lies on earth among wild beasts and mute animals, in the spirit is already dwelling in the heavens; and these...

...to have the fellowship of angels. These beings, if they fall into sin—for they are still capable of falling—could be seen by you if you were caught up in the spirit; you would perceive someone falling from the heavenly fellowship no differently than if a star were falling from heaven. Therefore, in a bodily sense—which pertains to what is from ourselves—our **way of life** <note>original: 'conuersatio'; in a biblical context, this refers to one's citizenship or conduct</note> is on earth. But in a spiritual sense—which pertains to what is from God—our way of life is in the heavens. Indeed, we dwell and exist infinitely more truly in the heavens and above the heavens, if it pleases God, and if He transfers us into His own immovability, than we exist on earth; for it is far more true to exist in the spirit than to exist in the flesh. It is, therefore, no small ruin that sin brings: for in the spiritual state, it hurls one down from heaven, or from above heaven, to the depths. But leaving aside these matters which, while we live, require being caught up in spirit and revelation <note>original: 'apocalypsin'</note>, let us return to the graces of Christ’s gift. Paul enumerates some of these here, though he spoke of them more broadly before to the Corinthians, saying:

<margin>13</margin>
> And he himself gave some indeed to be apostles, some prophets, others evangelists, others pastors and teachers, for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the building up of the body of CHRIST; until we all meet in the unity of faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, unto a perfect man, unto the measure of the age of the fullness of CHRIST: that we may no longer be children, tossed to and fro and carried about by every wind of doctrine in the wickedness of men, in craftiness for the schemes of error. But following the truth in love, let us grow in all things in him who is the head, CHRIST. From whom the whole body is joined together and united through every joint of its nourishment, according to the operation in the measure of every part, making increase for the building up of itself in love.

¶ A marvelous and beloved builder and architect of the body of Christ (if I may put it so) is **Love** <note>original: 'charitas'</note>—not our love but God’s; not a reflected love but a direct one, which alone allows the rays of love reflecting into the buildings of the body of Christ to enter. This Love will not cease to build up men through the gifts of the Holy Spirit until that body is finished and perfect. For as long as our body grows and takes increase while we live this life of the senses, we do not yet bear the name of a "perfect man." Similarly, while the spiritual body of Christ takes increase, it is still being built; it is not yet perfect, it does not yet feel the name of a "perfect man," nor does it yet possess the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ. But then it will have the full measure of Christ's age: when nothing more shall be added, but the whole divine building shall be constructed. This will not happen before the end of the age, which shall be closed by the age of ages. For this reason, we ought no longer to be little children, tossed and carried about by every wind of human doctrine—our navigation toward God in this sea of the world being disturbed by the craftiness of Satan, who lays these snares of error for us. Instead, we must follow the true doctrine, which is of God and not of men, which is of the Holy Spirit and not the spirit of error. We must, I say, follow it in love, which is the likeness of the Architect, Love. And we must daily increase that body of which Christ is the head. From him indeed the entire body takes its harmony, its connection, and its union through every measure of various members for various functions: until each member takes its own increase and its own measure, which pertains to that building for its edification in love. One part and member are the apostles, another the prophets, another the evangelists, another the pastors, another the teachers, another the martyrs, confessors, virgins, celibates, widows: and in each lot of life (which creates the distinction between members) are the saints. And in all these, if the number is not already full in some, it is necessary that the number be fulfilled, which is known to God. And happy is he who shall not be excluded as a reprobate from the number of any member of the building. For when that building is finished, it will remain in honor forever. It is built daily from those who walk not according to their own sense, but according to the spirit. And therefore, sighing for the completion of this building of supreme beauty, Paul adds, saying:

> ¶ This, therefore, I say and testify in the Lord: that you must no longer walk as the other Gentiles walk in the vanity of their mind, having their understanding darkened, being alienated from the life of God through the ignorance that is in them, because of the blindness of their heart. Who, feeling no pain, have given themselves over to lasciviousness, to the working of all uncleanness with greediness. But you have not so learned CHRIST. If indeed you have heard him and have been taught in him, as the truth is in JESUS: that you must lay aside the **old man** according to your former way of life, who is corrupted according to the snares of desire, and be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the **new man**, who according to God is created in justice and the truth of holiness.

### CHAPTER IV.

<meta>This page continues the philological and theological commentary on Ephesians 4. It focuses on comparing the Latin Vulgate translation with the original Greek text, specifically examining grammatical choices and metaphors regarding the body of Christ and the moral failings of the Gentiles.</meta>

Ephesians.
y. i.

# V

<margin>[to keep] the unity of the Spirit.</margin> <note>original: "θεῖν τὴν ἑνότητα τοῦ πνεύματος"</note> ¶ Vulgate edition: One body and one spirit, <margin>11</margin> even as you are called in one hope of your calling. <note>original: "Unum corpus & unus spiritus sicut vocati estis in una spe vocationis vestrae"</note> ¶ A clearer understanding is reached if, immediately after "one body and one spirit," the word "you are" <note>Latin: "sitis"</note>, which was suppressed by Paul, is expressed; we have done this for the sake of a more lucid understanding. Paul: One body and one spirit, just as you were called in <margin>i</margin> one hope of your calling. <note>original: "ἓν σῶμα καὶ ἓν πνεῦμα καθὼς καὶ ἐκλήθητε ἐν μιᾷ ἐλπίδι τῆς κλήσεως ὑμῶν"</note> ¶ Vulgate edition: Who is over all, and through all, and in us all. <note>original: "Qui super omnes / & per omnia / & in omnibus nobis"</note> ¶ Since the old translator used the masculine "over all" <note>Latin: "super omnes"</note>, he could have equally translated the same word as masculine consistently and said "through all" <note>Latin: "per omnes"</note>, lest he seem to vary the use of the same word without reason. Or he could have expressed the first part in the neuter: "who is over all things [super omnia] and through all things." For Paul’s speech is indifferent <note>term: "indifferent" | here meaning grammatically ambiguous, as the Greek "panton" can be masculine (people) or neuter (things)</note>, unless you prefer to interpret it as masculine everywhere, because in the last place "in all" [omnibus] is masculine, which is suggested by the added phrase "in us" [nobis]. Paul: "who is over all, and through all, and in us all." <note>original: "ὁ ἐπὶ πάντων, καὶ διὰ πάντων, καὶ ἐν πᾶσιν ἡμῖν"</note> ¶ Vulgate <margin>12</margin> edition: He led captivity captive. <note>original: "Captiuam duxit captiuitatem"</note> ¶ This could have been said with one word, "he captivated," as if to say "he captivated captivity"; and thus, in Psalm 67, the Septuagint <note>The Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> edition has it, from which Paul cites this testimony. For in his time, there was no other edition of the sacred scriptures among the nations. But to "captivate captivity" is to liberate captivity from captivity. For that which is liberated is no longer captive. Paul: "he led captivity captive." <note>original: "ἠχμαλώτευσεν αἰχμαλωσίαν"</note> ¶ Vulgate edition: That he might fulfill all things. <note>original: "Ut adimpleret omnia"</note> ¶ Paul does not use a compound verb, and it sufficed to say "fill" [impleret]. For "to fulfill" [adimplere] means to complete and perfect, whereas the simple "to fill" [implere] does not necessarily mean that, but also speaks of a fullness whose presence and power excludes absence. Paul: "that he might fill <margin>C</margin> all things." <note>original: "ἵνα πληρώσῃ τὰ πάντα"</note> ¶ Vulgate edition: In the wickedness of men. <note>original: "In nequitia hominum"</note> ¶ Rather: "in the confusion of men." Paul: "in the trickery [kybeia] of men." For the word *kybeia* <note>original: "κυβεία"</note> with the first syllable as an *upsilon* and the second as a diphthong, speaks rather of confusion and disturbance, from *kykein* <note>original: "κυκεῖν"</note> which means to mix, confuse, and disturb, rather than "malice" which is called *kakia* <note>original: "κακία"</note> with an *alpha* in the first syllable and an *iota* in the second. However, I would not deny that this confusion and disturbance of men proceeds from wickedness, just as the rippling, tossing, and disturbance of waves arises from the origin of the winds. ¶ Vulgate edition: Let us grow in him <margin>13</margin> through all things. <note>original: "Crescamus in illo per omnia"</note> ¶ The old translator could have said: "let us increase all things in him." For whether the martyrs make up one member, virgins another, confessors another, and widows and the continent another, their number must increase until the final day, so that the perfection of the body of Christ is fulfilled. Or, if the prudent and wise in the spiritual understanding of the law are the eyes; explorers in secret examinations to correct any deviations are the ears; the discreet are the teeth; teachers and preachers are the lips; the firm and constant are the neck; those strongly bearing burdens for Christ are the shoulders; the strong warriors of faith are the arms; the active and merciful are the hands; those supporting the Church as the bride are the legs; and those running the course of the common people according to the precepts of the Gospel of peace are the feet—we ought to increase all these in Christ for the salvation of all. And if the exterior parts are beautiful, the interior parts ought to be even more so. As it is sung in the song: "Your eyes are like doves, besides that which lies hidden within; your teeth are like flocks of shorn sheep coming up from the washing; your lips are like a scarlet ribbon, and your speech is sweet." <note>Quoting Song of Solomon 4</note> And the rest which is said about the members of the Bride, who are the members of Christ’s body. Paul: "let us grow into him in all things." <note>original: "ἀυξήσωμεν εἰς ἀυτὸν τὰ πάντα"</note> ¶ Vulgate edition: In the measure of every <margin>D</margin> member. <note>original: "In mēsurā vniuscuiusq⁹ mēbri"</note> ¶ According to Paul, it should be said: "of every part." Paul: "in the <margin>14</margin> measure of each individual part." <note>original: "ἐν μέτρῳ ἑνὸς ἑκάστου μέρους"</note> ¶ Vulgate edition: This I say therefore, and testify in the Lord, that you walk no more as also the Gentiles walk. <note>original: "Hoc igit dico & testificor i dño vt iā nō ābuletis sicut & gētes ābulant"</note> ¶ More correctly by an infinitive as in Paul, and more suited to Latin speech if resolved as "that there must be no more walking." And it should say: "the other or remaining Gentiles." Paul: "This therefore I say and testify in the Lord, that you no longer walk as the rest of the nations [walk]." <note>original: "τοῦτο οὖν λέγω καὶ μαρτύρομαι ἐν κυρίῳ, μηκέτι ὑμᾶς περιπατεῖν καθὼς καὶ τὰ λοιπὰ ἔθνη"</note> ¶ Vulgate edition: In the vanity of their sense. <note>original: "In vanitate sēsus sui"</note> ¶ I preferred to say above: "no more" [non amplius], and here "of their mind" [mentis suae], because in this way we seem better to follow the divine-speaking Paul’s meaning. Paul: "in the vanity of their mind." <note>original: "ἐν ματαιότητι τοῦ νοὸς αὐτῶν"</note> ¶ Vulgate edition: Through the ignorance that is in them. <note>original: "Per ignorātiā qđ est i illis"</note> ¶ It should be said: "because of [propter] ignorance." Paul: "because of the ignorance being in them." <note>original: "διὰ τὴν ἄγνοιαν τὴν οὖσαν ἐν αὐτοῖς"</note> ¶ Vulgate edition: Because of the blindness of their heart. <note>original: "Propter cæcitatē cordis ipsorū"</note> ¶ The word which Paul uses here signifies persistence, obstinacy, and blindness. And if the relative "their" [ipsorum] is properly to be referred to the "nations" [gentes, which is feminine in Latin], it should have been "of them" [ipsarum]. For since God's kindness was sent to enlighten all, I think those alone remained blind who were obstinate and persistent. Thus, obstinacy is the cause of that blindness and ignorance. Whence it follows that both are well said: "because of the blindness of their heart" and "because of the obstinacy of their heart," but "obstination" seems to sound somewhat more (if I may say so) causal. Paul: "because of the hardening [porosin] of their heart." <note>original: "διὰ τὴν πώρωσιν τῆς καρδίας αὐτῶν"</note> ¶ Vulgate edition: Who despairing, have given themselves up to lasciviousness. <note>original: "Qui desperantes: semetipsos tradiderūt impudicitiæ"</note> ¶ We have always referred the relative to the Gentiles, so that it might better observe the form of Latin speech. And as for what the old translator calls "despairing" [desperantes], Jerome prefers it to be called "feeling no pain" [indolentes]. For Paul has it así: "who, having become callous [apelgekotes], gave themselves over to licentiousness." <note>original: "οἵτινες ἀπηλγηκότες ἑαυτοὺς παρέδωκαν τῇ ἀσελγείᾳ"</note> For *algeo* <note>original: "ἀλγέω"</note> means "I feel pain."

<meta>This page continues the line-by-line commentary on the Epistle to the Ephesians, moving from the description of the Gentiles' spiritual blindness to the specific moral transformations required of the "new man" in Christ. It bridges the theological shift from internal renewal to outward ethical conduct.</meta>

COMMENTARY.

They are ignorant of God: because of the obstinacy of their hearts, which is a hardening in evil, they fall into ignorance of God. And we, having been made truly eager in spirit, ought to give ourselves over to chastity in the practice of all holiness and in abundance; for by walking in such a way—namely, by the opposite path to that which the Gentiles walk—we have learned Christ. For the way of Christ is bright and radiated by heavenly light, while that of the Gentiles is full of darkness. But it is a wonder: so great is the light of Christ that it even shines in the darkness, even if the darkness does not perceive it. For those who live a new life put off the **old man** <note>The "old man" refers to the unregenerate human nature prone to sin.</note> of the former life, who is corrupted by the allurements of the desires of the flesh, and they are renewed in the spirit of the mind, putting on the **new man**: who is created according to God <margin>15</margin> in justice and the truth of holiness. But nothing is so contrary to truth as falsehood. And anger prevents the perception of truth. Therefore, joining these together, Paul forbids those things and says: ¶ *Because of this, putting away falsehood, speak the truth every man with his neighbor, because we are members one of another. Be angry, and sin not. Let not the sun go down upon your wrath.* ¶ If he commends the truth of words so greatly, he intends to commend the truth of deeds even more. If you say that one must not commit fornication, must not steal, and must not inflict injuries on others, you speak the truth, and it is the truth of words. But if you commit fornication and steal, and if you bring injury to others, this is a falsehood of deeds; and the apostle commands that this falsehood—both of words and of deeds—must be entirely put away, so that we may be truthful in every part. But he who is not truthful in words is even less so in deeds; therefore, he expressed the former, without which the other cannot exist. And in all these things we ought to contemplate Christ: because both we and our neighbors are members of the body of Christ, in which no falsehood is fitting, but rather truth in every part. And as for what he joins to this—*Be angry and sin not, let not the sun go down upon your wrath*—he partly permits, partly commands, and partly uses a parable. *Be angry*: he permits. *Sin not*: he commands. *Let not the sun go down upon your wrath*: this is a parable. We are sometimes angry in the night—that is, when we see the blindness and malice of men, which is also said of the Lord. And looking around at them with anger (says Mark), being grieved over the blindness of their hearts, he said to the man: stretch out your hand. And such anger is permitted; indeed, nothing prevents it even if it is commanded. Yet one must never sin. The reason is the eye. Truth is the sun and its light; anger, which is evil and leads to sin, is a dark cloud preventing truth from being perceived and (like a black night) obscuring reason. When this anger is present, the sun sets upon the wrath; for truth no longer illuminates the eye of the mind, but sets for it, leaving the darkness of falsehood in the mind. But it is not enough to abstain from that which causes the sun to set; one must also abstain from all things that are the ways of the devil. Christ dwells in the day, and the ways of Christ are bright; the perception of truth creates the day. All the ways of the day are, in the first place, those infused by the Holy Spirit; in the second, those acquired by our own diligence. The devil dwells in the night, and his ways are dark. Night is falsehood, which is created by ignorance and the hiding of truth. The ways of the night are all individual vices: in the first place, those which the ancient serpent inspires, and those are for the most part bestial and tragic; in the second place, the vices which human fragility contracts from its own weakness, preferring to yield to the infirmity of the flesh rather than to obey reason. And just as Christ, the shepherd of souls, enters through bright ways—especially those illuminated from above—so conversely the devil, the plunderer of souls, enters through nocturnal and dark ways, and especially those he inspires with a Stygian <note>Stygian: referring to the River Styx in the underworld; here meaning hellish or demonic.</note> breath. Wherefore <margin>16</margin> the apostle forbids us all such ways of darkness, whether in deed, word, or mind, saying: ¶ *Give no place to the devil. He who stole, let him steal no more, but rather let him labor, working with his hands that which is good, so that he may have something to contribute to those suffering in want. Let no corrupt speech proceed from your mouth: but if any be good for the use of edification, that it may give grace to the hearers, and do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you are sealed for the day of redemption. Let all bitterness, and fury, and anger, and clamor, and blasphemy be taken away from you, with every vice. But be kind to one another, merciful, forgiving one another, even as God in CHRIST has forgiven you.* ¶ From these things we can understand the ways in which a place is given to the devil in deed, word, and mind, so that we may flee from them. But we cannot flee from those things in the darkness unless we do so by a clear light. The light, however, is the ways of Christ in deed, word, and mind, which (as I am not hindered from knowing) we can understand from these things which Paul brings forward here and in many other places, so that we may embrace them, with the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, the inhabitant and eternal king of the region of light, to whom be honor and glory without end. Amen.

Paul: *with all humility of mind and gentleness.* ¶ Vulgate edition: *Careful to keep the unity of the Spirit.* ¶ Rather: "striving to keep the unity of the Spirit." Paul: *striving for the* <note>The text cuts off here, continuing the philological comparison of the Greek verb "spoudazontes" (striving/being diligent) against the Latin "solliciti" (anxious/careful).</note>

<margin>2.</margin>
<margin>ii.</margin> <term>To keep the unity of the Spirit</term>. <note>original Greek: "τηρεῖν τὴν ἑνότητα τοῦ πνεύματος"</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *One body and one spirit, just as you were called in one hope of your calling.* ¶ A clearer understanding is achieved if the word "are" <note>Latin: "sitis"</note>—which was suppressed by Paul—is expressed immediately after "one body and one spirit." We have done this for the sake of a more lucid understanding. **Paul:** *One body and one spirit, just as you were called in one hope of your calling.* <note>original Greek: "ἓν σῶμα καὶ ἓν πνεῦμα καθὼς καὶ ἐκλήθητε ἐν μιᾷ ἐλπίδι τῆς κλήσεως ὑμῶν"</note> <margin>3.</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Who is over all, and through all, and in all of us.* ¶ Since the ancient translator used the masculine "over all" <note>Latin: "super omnes"</note>, he could have translated the same word consistently as masculine and said "through all" <note>Latin: "per omnes"</note>, so as not to appear to vary the use of the same word without reason. Or, he could have expressed the first part as a neuter: "who is over all things" <note>Latin: "super omnia"</note>. For Paul’s speech is indifferent here, unless you prefer to interpret it as masculine everywhere, because "in all" in the last position is masculine, which is suggested by the added particle "us." **Paul:** *Who is over all, and through all, and in all of us.* <note>original Greek: "ὁ ἐπὶ πάντων, καὶ Διὰ πάντων, καὶ ἐν πᾶσιν ἡμῖν"</note> <margin>13.</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *He led captivity captive.* ¶ This could have been said in one word, "he captivated," so that it read "he captivated captivity." This is how the Septuagint version of Psalm 67 <note>Modern Psalm 68:18</note> has it, from which Paul cites this testimony; for in his time, there was no other edition of Holy Scripture among the nations. But to "captivate captivity" means to "liberate captivity from captivity." For that which is liberated is no longer a captive. **Paul:** *He led captivity captive.* <note>original Greek: "ᾐχμαλώτευσεν αἰχμαλωσίαν"</note> <margin>C</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *That he might fulfill all things.* ¶ Paul does not use a compound verb; it would have sufficed to say "fill." For "to fulfill" <note>Latin: "adimplere"</note> means to complete and perfect, but the simple "to fill" <note>Latin: "implere"</note> does not necessarily mean that, but also speaks of a fullness which excludes the absence of presence and power. **Paul:** *That he might fill all things.* <note>original Greek: "ἵνα πληρώσῃ τὰ πάντα"</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *In the wickedness of men.* ¶ Rather: *In the confusion of men.* **Paul:** *In the trickery of men.* <note>original Greek: "ἐν τῇ κυβείᾳ τῶν ἀνθρώπων"</note> For the word *kybeia* <note>Referring to "dice-playing" or "sleight of hand"</note>—with the first syllable spelled with a *ypsilon* and the second with a diphthong—refers to confusion and disturbance, coming from the verb *kykein*, which means to mix, confound, and disturb. This is distinct from "malice," which is called *kakia*. I would not deny, however, that this confusion and disturbance of men proceeds from wickedness, just as the rippling, tossing, and disturbance of waves arises from the origin of the winds. ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Let us grow in him through all things.* ¶ The ancient translator could have said: *Let us increase all things in him.* For whether the martyrs make up one member, the virgins another member, the confessors another, and the widows and the continent yet another: their number ought to be increased until the last day, so that the perfection of the body of Christ may be fulfilled. Or, if the prudent and wise in the spiritual understanding of the law are the **eyes**; the **ears** are the scouts who correct deviations through secret examinations; the **teeth** are the discerning; the **lips** are the teachers and preachers; the **neck** consists of the firm and constant; the **shoulders** are those strongly carrying burdens for Christ; the **arms** are the brave warriors of the faith; the **hands** are the active and merciful; the **shins** are those supporting the Church, the Bride; and the **feet** are the holy common people running according to the precepts of the Gospel of peace—then we ought to increase all these things in Christ for the salvation of all. And if the external parts are beautiful, the internal parts ought to be even more beautiful. As it is sung in the Song of Songs: *Your eyes are as doves, besides that which is hidden within; your teeth are like flocks of shorn sheep coming up from the washing; your lips are like a scarlet ribbon, and your speech is sweet.* And so with the rest that is said concerning the members of the Bride, which are the members of the body of Christ. <margin>14.</margin> <margin>δ.</margin> **Paul:** *Let us grow into him in all things.* <note>original Greek: "αὐξήσωμεν εἰς αὐτὸν τὰ πάντα"</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *In the measure of every member.* ¶ According to Paul, it should say: *of every part.* **Paul:** *In the measure of every single part.* <note>original Greek: "ἐν μέτρῳ ἑνὸς ἑκάστου μέρους"</note> <margin>D</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *This I say therefore and testify in the Lord, that you no longer walk as the Gentiles walk.* ¶ It is more correctly expressed by an infinitive, as in Paul, and more suited to Latin speech if it is resolved as "that there must be no walking." And one should say: "the rest" or "the remaining" Gentiles. **Paul:** *This therefore I say and testify in the Lord, that you no longer walk as the remaining Gentiles.* <note>original Greek: "τοῦτο οὖν λέγω καὶ μαρτύρομαι ἐν κυρίῳ, μηκέτι ὑμᾶς περιπατεῖν καθὼς καὶ τὰ λοιπὰ ἔθνη"</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *In the vanity of their sense.* ¶ I preferred to say above: "no longer" <note>Latin: "non amplius"</note>, and here "of their mind" <note>Latin: "mentis suae"</note>, because in this way we seem better to reach the meaning of the divinely-spoken Paul. **Paul:** *In the vanity of their mind.* <note>original Greek: "ἐν ματαιότητι τοῦ νοὸς αὐτῶν"</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Through the ignorance that is in them.* ¶ It should be said: *On account of the ignorance.* **Paul:** *On account of the ignorance being in them.* <note>original Greek: "Διὰ τὴν ἄγνοιαν τὴν οὖσαν ἐν αὐτοῖς"</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *On account of the blindness of their heart.* ¶ The word Paul uses here signifies pertinacity, obstinacy, or blindness. And if the relative "their" <note>Latin: "ipsorum"</note> must properly refer to the "Gentiles" <note>Latin: "gentes," a feminine noun</note>, it should have been "of them" <note>Latin: "ipsarum"</note>. Since God's kindness sent the apostles to enlighten everyone, I believe those alone remained blind who were obstinate and pertinacious. Thus, obstinacy is the cause of that blindness and ignorance. Hence, it is well said either way: "on account of the blindness of their heart" or "on account of the obstinacy of their heart," but "obstinacy" seems to sound somewhat more (if I may say so) causal. **Paul:** *On account of the hardening of their heart.* <note>original Greek: "Διὰ τὴν πώρωσιν τῆς καρδίας αὐτῶν"</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Who despairing, gave themselves up to impurity.* ¶ We have always referred the relative back to the Gentiles, so that it follows the form of Latin speech more closely. And whereas the ancient translator says "despairing," Jerome prefers it to be said "feeling no pain" <note>Latin: "indolentes"</note>. For Paul has it thus: *who, having become callous, gave themselves up to licentiousness.* <note>original Greek: "οἵτινες ἀπηλγηκότες ἑαυτοὺς παρέδωκαν τῇ ἀσελγείᾳ"</note> Indeed, *algeo* signifies "I feel pain."

<summary>This page contains a philological critique of the Vulgate translation of Ephesians 4, using the Greek text to clarify concepts of spiritual unity, the growth of the Church as a body, and the nature of Gentile "hardening of heart." The author employs allegorical imagery to describe different roles within the Church as specific body parts, such as the eyes, teeth, and hands.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philological commentary on the Epistle to the Ephesians, Chapter 4. The author continues to compare the Greek original and the Latin Vulgate, specifically addressing the transition from the "old man" of sin to the "new man" in Christ, with a focus on linguistic nuances and rhetorical figures like hypallage.</meta>

<header>COMMENTARY</header>

...from which, when the privative particle is added, the compound word *apelgēkotes* <note>original Greek: "ἀπηλγηκότες," meaning "having become callous" or "ceased to feel pain"</note> seems to be formed, for which we say "nothing in itself," intending the same sense. For it does not seem possible for it to have a composition derived from the word for "hope" <note>original: "ἐλπίζω"</note>. ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Unto the working of all uncleanness, unto avarice.* ¶ Why should we not say here "in abundance" or "in excess"? Since "avarice" seems to sound among the Latins as <term>philargyria</term>—that is, the greed for silver and money—which is a specific vice, like a fever or dropsy is a specific disease. Here, however, a general term is used, designating "having more than is proper," which is nothing other than a superfluous abundance, an excess, and (if I may say so) a certain insatiable greed. For the further anything recedes from its goal, the less it can be satisfied; for everything finds rest in its own goal. Therefore, everything is "unclean" which is as far removed from its goal as possible. ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *If so be that you have heard him, and have been taught in him.* ¶ This particle (as was said of some previous instances) we have preferred to explain as an assertion rather than a doubt under a condition. For here and elsewhere the particle is the same in Paul's writing. **Paul:** *If indeed you have heard him, and have been taught in him.* <note>original Greek: "εἴγε αὐτὸν ἠκούσατε, καὶ ἐν αὐτῷ ἐδιδάχθητε"</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *To put off, according to the former conversation, the old man.* 

<margin>E 14</margin>It must be spoken more clearly through an infinitive or a gerund, and it is joined to what was said: "you have heard and were taught." **Paul:** *That you put off, according to the former manner of life, the old man.* <note>original Greek: "ἀποθέσθαι ὑμᾶς κατὰ τὴν προτέραν ἀναστροφὴν τὸν παλαιὸν ἄνθρωπον"</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *According to the desires of error.* ¶ According to the custom of the Roman <note>Latin</note> language, this speech seems to contain a <term>hypallage</term> <note>a rhetorical figure where the natural relations of two words are reversed</note>; it is as if we were to say "according to the error of desires." Regarding this matter, in accordance with this understanding, we have translated it as "according to the allurements of lusts." For often a way of speaking is correct in one language but appears changed in another. ¶ Therefore, also, when a speech translated into another language seems to contain a <term>hypallage</term>, we transfer it to a more direct form while preserving the meaning of the eloquence. This is not because Paul’s form of speaking is not more perfect. For just as Hebrew writing is more perfect than ours (for it proceeds from the right toward the left, imitating the movement of nature, while ours, in a way contrary to nature, inclines from the left to the right), so the Hebrew form and Paul’s form of speech are more perfect than ours. For our language is turned around in many ways. Consequently, when we look at our own, we judge his to be a <term>hypallage</term>. But when we reduce it to our own form of speaking, it is clearer and more familiar to us, and we change "right-handed" speech into "left-handed." And indeed, the "right-handed" speech of Paul, which he uses in this chapter, is: First, *according to the lusts of allurements*; Second, *in justice and holiness of truth*; Third, *unto the edification of utility*. Because these seemed as if they were reversed, we have translated them into a speech more fitting for us as: *according to the allurements of lusts*; *in justice and the truth of holiness*; and *unto the utility of edification*. And this speech of ours is "left-handed." Therefore, Paul's speech is better and wiser; our speech is inferior, but more known and common to us. Yet these speeches are the same, differing not at all in meaning, but only in the form of speaking. Our form of speaking—that is, the Latin—is by nature a <term>hypallage</term> and contains a figure of speech; Paul’s form, however, is direct and without figure, even if we judge it to be the opposite. And this is said for the dignity of the speech of the [divine] oracles above all other modes of speaking, even if the censors of languages judge otherwise. But enough of these things; a few words on the occasion of the property of languages have stirred up a great and inextricable battle of tongues. **Paul:** *according to the desires of deceit.* <note>original Greek: "κατὰ τὰς ἐπιθυμίας τῆς ἀπάτης"</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *And of the holiness of truth.* ¶ Paul has it this way as well. But to Latin usage, it seems to commit a <term>hypallage</term>. Therefore, for the reason just mentioned above, we have translated the speech as

<margin>G 16</margin>we said: *and the truth of holiness*. **Paul:** *and in the holiness of truth.* <note>original Greek: "καὶ ὁσιότητι τῆς ἀληθείας"</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Let no evil speech proceed from your mouth.* ¶ The word Paul uses here seems to signify "rotten" rather than "evil." And we understand "rotten speech" as that which will bring no fruit, no edification to anyone; for a rotten thing is limp and unfruitful. **Paul:** *Let every rotten word not proceed out of your mouth.* <note>original Greek: "πᾶς λόγος σαπρὸς ἐκ τοῦ στόματος ὑμῶν μὴ ἐκπορευέσθω"</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *But if any be good to the edification of faith.* ¶ It should be said "unto the edification of utility," or "unto the utility of edification," lest it appear as a <term>hypallage</term> as already stated. **Paul:** *but if any is good for the building up of the need.* <note>original Greek: "ἀλλ' εἴτις ἀγαθὸς πρὸς οἰκοδομὴν τῆς χρείας"</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *All bitterness, and anger, and indignation.* ¶ Rather "all bitterness, and fury, and anger." **Paul:** *all bitterness, and fury, and wrath.* <note>original Greek: "πᾶσα πικρία, καὶ θυμὸς, καὶ ὀργή"</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *And be ye kind one to another.* ¶ Here the priest Jerome prefers that it should be said "be ye sweet one to another," so that it might more clearly reflect, by way of opposition, that which was said about "bitterness." For this reason we also said "sweet." For what things are more clearly opposed than sweetness and bitterness, sweet and bitter? **Paul:** *And become kind to one another.* <note>original Greek: "γίνεσθε δὲ εἰς ἀλλήλους χρηστοί"</note> For thus *chrēstos* <note>kind/useful</note> is interpreted as "sweet" in Psalm 24, where the translator of the Psalms says: "Sweet and righteous is the Lord." <note>original Greek: "Χρηστὸς καὶ εὐθὺς κύριος"</note>

The author re-evaluates specific terms like "rotten speech" and "avarice" to better capture the original Greek nuances and the theological contrast between vice and virtue.</summary>

# V

### CHAPTER V.

<margin>17</margin>
Paul proceeds to open up more fully to the Ephesians, and thus to us, the bright ways of Christ and the dark ways that oppose them, saying: <note>Large decorative initial A featuring intricate floral and scrollwork designs</note> ¶ **Be therefore imitators of God, as beloved children. And walk in love, even as Christ also loved us, and gave himself up for us as an offering and a sacrifice to God for a sweet-smelling savor. But fornication, and all uncleanness, or covetousness, let it not even be named among you, as becomes saints; nor filthiness, nor foolish talking, nor jesting, which are not fitting; but rather the giving of thanks.** <note>original: "gratiosus sermo," literally "gracious speech" or "thanksgiving"</note> ¶ Our entire good consists in the imitation of Christ. For his life is our exemplar; his love is the form and the very idea of our own love. Just as he loved us, we should love one another for his sake, so much so that we would rather die than offend our neighbor—who is a member of Christ in whom Christ is formed, and who lives by the Spirit of Christ. Where this imitation of Christ and this love are present (for Christ is entirely love and entirely affection), not only will there be no fornication, no uncleanness of any kind, no covetousness, filthiness, foolish talking, or jests that seek the pleasures of the world, but these things will not even be spoken of, as is right for saints and befits the conversation of holy people. Truly, every word will be seasoned with grace and will strive to follow Christ’s own speech, since it flows from his grace. But how wretched will they be who, lacking that love which emulates the love of Christ, fall into those evils. The Apostle reveals what these evils are and from whom we must turn away, saying:

<margin>18</margin>
¶ **For know this: that no fornicator, nor unclean person, nor covetous man, who is an idolater (that is, a servant of idols), has any inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God.** ¶ The kingdom of God is everything that is good. He who does not inherit the kingdom of God is deprived of every good thing. And he is not only deprived, but like a worthless servant, he is thrust down into every evil and every punishment from which there is no rescue. Nor should we listen to the impious, who say that God cares little for these human matters—the things souls do through their bodies while they are bound to them for a time—and that he forgives and easily grants pardon once the soul is stripped of the body. But how can they say he does not care, or cares little, if he sends such heavy scourges upon them—plagues, famines, and the like—as if they were unworthy of his providence? One must never think in such a way. ¶ Therefore, the Apostle adds:

<margin>19</margin>
¶ **Let no one deceive you with empty words. For because of these things the wrath of God comes upon the children of disobedience. Therefore, do not be partakers with them. For you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. Walk as children of light. For the fruit of the Spirit is in all goodness, and righteousness, and truth. Prove what is well-pleasing to God; and have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness, but instead even reprove them.** ¶ The "children of disobedience" <note>original: "filij diffidentiæ," literally children of mistrust or lack of faith</note> are those who do not urge themselves toward the ways of God, but rather turn away from them; they disbelieve and judge the opposite ways to be good and worth following. These people are darkness, and they walk in the ways of darkness. Not a darkness that can be felt by the senses, but a darkness of the spirit. When the darkness of the physical night is added to this, existing as they do in the darkness of the spirit and the darkness of the world, they dare to say and think things that are horrendous. Their works are not to be imitated, but are to be refuted and eliminated by the illumination of the Spirit. For they are works of darkness and works without fruit, consisting of all wickedness, injustice, and falsehood. Just as, on the opposite side, the works of the Spirit are works of light and are fruitful, consisting of all goodness, righteousness, and truth. The former are children of darkness; the latter are children of light. These latter, as those who are in the light and the day, they stand, they watch, they live, and they behold the light. The former lie down, they sleep, and they are exiled from life and light. But though they do such wicked things, though they are darkness, though they are prostrate, though they sleep—nay, though they are dead—how great is the piety of God, how great is his mercy! The Holy Spirit, through itself, rouses them and cries out: **Arise, you who sleep, and rise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you.** <note>Paul quotes a fragment of an early Christian hymn or liturgical text here</note> He desires everyone to breathe again into true life and true light. Paul reveals to us how the piety and mercy of God are brought to those who are dead, saying:

<margin>20</margin>
¶ **For the things that are done by them in secret it is a shame even to speak of. But all things that are reproved are made manifest by the light; for everything that is made manifest is light. Therefore he says: Arise, you who sleep, and rise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you.** ¶ As long as it is night, the world and the air are dark and are not made manifest. But that which makes them manifest is the light, which refutes, scatters, and expels the darkness. As soon as the light rises, the world and the air are made manifest; they become light and partakers of the light. For how could they be made manifest, and how could they have light within them, if the darkness were not scattered? In this same way, those who are in the spiritual night are not made manifest except by the light—and indeed, a spiritual light. However much they may be in deep night, if the light of Christ rises upon them, they are immediately made manifest as their darkness is reproved, refuted, and scattered; and they immediately become light and partakers of the spiritual light. And this is the <term>justification of the ungodly</term> <note>original: "iustificatio impij," a central Reformation-era theological concept referring to God making a sinner righteous</note>, which happens suddenly by the light of Christ, not by works. Why then do we not all—insofar as the Holy Spirit is within us, rousing, helping, and giving us life—arise to receive with reverence the rising of that divine light within us, which justifies us?

y. ij.

COM.

which transfers us from the confusion of darkness into the kingdom of light! This is the light! by which one is known to God; if this light has not risen, we are unknown to God. ¶ For what can be more "unknown," or what more unmanifest, than that which is unknown and unmanifest to God (from whom nothing is hidden, nor can be hidden)? Therefore, we must live with great diligence and great caution, namely by avoiding all things that belong to darkness, lest as that divine light departs, we become unknown and unmanifest to God once again. Instead, we must carefully persist in the works of the Holy Spirit, which in private consist of psalms, hymns, spiritual songs, and thanksgivings to God for all good things, both our own and those of others. In common and in public, they consist of: mutual love, subjection, assistance, and works of life shining before men, so that they may glorify the Father of all who is in heaven. For this reason, Paul subjoins, saying: ¶ **See then how you walk accurately: not as unwise, but as wise. Redeem the time: because the days are evil. Therefore, do not be imprudent: but understand what the will of God is. And do not be drunk with wine, in which is unhealthiness <note>The Latin 'insalubritas' suggests not just physical illness but a lack of moral or spiritual health; often translated in Bibles as 'debauchery.'</note>: but be filled with the Spirit, speaking to yourselves in psalms, and hymns, and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your hearts to the Lord. Giving thanks always for all things: in the name of our Lord JESUS CHRIST to God and the Father. Submitting yourselves to one another in the fear of CHRIST.** ¶ When there is a "dearth" <note>The author plays on the Latin word 'caritas,' which means both 'Christian love' and 'high price' or 'scarcity.'</note> and a penury of goods, then men labor more vigilantly to obtain whatever they can of the grain supply <term>annona</term> <note>The 'annona' refers to the yearly harvest or the regulated price of grain in a city.</note>. Likewise, when times are evil, when there are few good people who perform anything good in their time, but very many who do evil, the Apostle persuades us to buy for ourselves whatever time we can (as if in a time of high prices), working well at all hours. For what else is "buy for yourselves time because the days are evil" than "buy for yourselves life because the days are dear"? For when seed cast into the earth perishes, it causes a high price; likewise, when time perishes, it causes the malice of the days. But when men work evil, does not that time perish for them, and they do not regain it? Only the good, therefore, acquire time, and it does not perish for them. For just as a high price for grain is the result of sterility, so the malice of the days is the sterility of time. But by what means do the good acquire time for themselves? Surely by good works, flowing from the fecundity of divine grace. If all men intended these works, they would remove all sterility of time just as dew and heavenly rain remove the high price of grain. Only the good, therefore, are rich in time; the evil are truly destitute, as those who buy no time for themselves, nor have they the means by which they might buy it. Time is a truly precious thing: it is bought by virtue, watered by heavenly dew, and by good works. ¶ Would that we all studied to be merchants of time rather than merchants of riches; though I estimate nothing to be more precious than time, nor is anyone in this world richer than he who is rich in time. For he who is rich in time in this world will be rich in eternity in the other. He who gains and buys time should not be imprudent, but understanding of what the good will of God is. He does not seek to be filled with wine, in which filling there is unhealthiness, but he seeks to be filled with the Holy Spirit, in whose filling is the perfect health of body and mind. He sings psalms, he sings hymns, he sings spiritually, he gives thanks for all things; as a superior, he submits and humbles himself to his inferiors for their instruction, and as an inferior, he submits to his superiors. Now, however, the Apostle arranges more specific duties: of wives to husbands and of husbands to wives. Between them, there ought to be a bond of love such as exists between Christ and the Church. For in Paradise, Adam represented Christ; Eve represented the Church. The formation of Eve from the bones and flesh of Adam represents the formation of the Church from the flesh and bones of Christ. And the betrothal of Adam and Eve represents the betrothal of Christ and the Church, for the sake of which the world was made. And therefore the sacrament of betrothal between husband and wife is so great in the Exemplar—that is, in Christ and the Church—that a man should leave father and mother and cleave to his wife, and conversely: the wife her father and mother, and cleave to her husband. So sublime and so high did God wish the bond of Christ and the Church to be declared to us, that it is tighter than that between father and mother, or any kind of kinship. We who are carnal do not see the sacred mysteries being carried out around us, yet nonetheless great sacraments are performed concerning us. Every bridegroom is a sign <note>original: 'signaculum'</note> of Christ, the true and eternal bridegroom. And every bride is a sign of the Church, the immaculate bride. Therefore, let every man see that he does not defile his imitation. And let every wife see that she herself does not represent the Church impurely or unworthily. See also that he who, with a bride, cleaves to Christ as the bridegroom, should cleave to Him far more than to father and mother. For He is the truth. For whose sake it was said: *For this reason a man shall leave his father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife,* showing us the great and ineffable love which Christ has for his Church. What love then can we, who are members of the Church, return to Christ, other than the love of cleaving to Him? Certainly, we ought to cleave to Him more than to father and mother, more than to wives and children, so that we never seek to be separated. For God made this union infinitely tighter than that between man and woman. For this is the shadow; that is the light. This is the footprint; that is the truth. And for the sake of this imitation, it is not permitted for a man to dismiss his wife, nor a wife her husband. And these things (as has been said) are great mysteries in Christ, as in the Exemplar. Because of which the Revealer of mysteries, the Apostle, adds, saying: ¶ **Wives, be subject to your own husbands as to the Lord: because the husband is the head of the wife, as also CHRIST is the head of the church, and he is the savior of the body <note>The page ends mid-sentence; the catchword indicates the word 'body' is completed here.</note>.** ¶ Therefore, just as the church is subject to CHRIST: in this way also let wives be to their [husbands]...

# Ephesians

-> V <-

<margin>2</margin> ...to husbands in every matter: Husbands, love your wives, even as **CHRIST** also loved 
<margin>3</margin> the Church, and gave himself up for her, so that he might sanctify her, purifying her by the washing of water in the word: 
<margin>4</margin> that he might present her to himself as a glorious Church, not having spot or wrinkle, or any 
<margin>5</margin> such thing, but that she should be holy and without blemish. In this way, husbands ought to love their own wives 
<margin>6</margin> as their own bodies. He who loves his wife loves himself. For no one ever hated his own flesh, 
<margin>7</margin> but nourishes and cherishes it: even as the Lord does the Church. Because we are members of his 
<margin>8</margin> body: of his flesh, and of his bones. For this cause shall a man leave his father and 
<margin>9</margin> mother, and shall be joined unto his wife: and they two shall be one flesh. This is a great mystery: but I 
<margin>10</margin> speak concerning **CHRIST** and the Church. Nevertheless, let every one of you in particular so love his 
<margin>11</margin> wife even as himself; so that the wife also may reverence her husband. ¶ The Apostle has opened a mystery <note>original: 'mysterium'; referring to a hidden truth revealed by God</note> that is seen not 
with carnal, but with spiritual eyes. Just as Christ is the savior of his body, which is the 
Church: so a husband ought to strive for the salvation of his wife, who is his body, while he is the head. And if 
it were even necessary, he ought to offer himself for his wife, so that he might have her holy and pure. But no 
one approaches the love of the true Bridegroom. For Christ the Bridegroom offered himself for his bride, the 
Church, so that he might sanctify her, purifying her by the washing of the water of baptism in the word, which is the 
invocation of the name of the eternal Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Indeed, he purified her in the perennial fountain 
of the grace of the Holy Spirit, poured out upon her generously and superabundantly: and in the approach of the highest 
inhabitants—the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. But also the remaining things which Paul inserted with divine meaning 
are immediately known to the spiritual man. May God increase the Spirit in us to worthily 
contemplate and know these mysteries, and add grace to live worthily according to the dignity of those things 
which have been made known. To him, however, from us and from every creature, by an indissoluble bond, be 
all honor and glory, for all ages of ages. Amen.

<margin>A 17</margin> ¶ AN EXAMINATION of several points regarding the literal text. ¶ The Vulgate edition says: *As most dear children.* <note>original: 'Sicut filij charissimi'</note>
¶ It should be said: *beloved children.* For Paul never uses the word that designates "most dear" or "dearest," 
but always "beloved" or "lovable." Paul says: <term>as beloved children</term> <note>original Greek: 'ὡς τέκνα ἀγαπητά' (hōs tekna agapēta)</note>. ¶ The Vulgate edition says: *In an odor of sweetness.* <note>original: 'In odorem suauitatis'</note> 
¶ Paul has it thus: but we translate it so that, according to the custom of the Latins, it performs a "hypallage" <note>A rhetorical figure where the natural relation of two words is reversed; here, perhaps meaning 'a sweet-smelling odor'</note>. Paul says: <term>for an odor of fragrance</term> <note>original Greek: 'εἰς ὀσμὴν εὐωδίας' (eis osmēn euōdias)</note>. ¶ The Vulgate edition says: *As becomes saints.* <note>original: 'Sicut decet sanctos'</note> ¶ Since the old translator <note>Jerome, the traditional author of the Vulgate</note> had said "in you" just before, he could have subsequently said "as becomes saints" without 
reproach of speech, and more in conformity with Paul. Paul says: <term>as is proper for saints</term> <note>original Greek: 'καθὼς πρέπει ἁγίοις' (kathōs prepei hagiois)</note>. ¶ The Vulgate edi-
tion says: *Or scurrilousness which does not pertain to the matter.* <note>original: 'Aut scurrilitas quæ ad rem non pertinet'</note> ¶ It should be said in the plural and the neu-
ter: *which things do not pertain to the matter.* And Paul here has a word which, among the philoso-
phers, pertains even to the honorable joking of words. Although human virtue may admit this, 
it nevertheless very little becomes holy and spiritual men. In which matter—that is, in pleasantry and 
wit—if any are skillful, they will be judged more human than divine, more carnal than spiritual. 
If, therefore, "eutrapelia" <note>The term 'eutrapelia' refers to refined wit or urbanity, which the author argues is still too worldly for the saintly life</note> is barred from the life of holy and truly spiritual men, 
how much more scurrilousness and all licentious talkativeness? Paul says: <term>or wit, the things not fitting</term> <note>original Greek: 'ἢ εὐτραπελία, τὰ οὐκ ἀνήκοντα' (ē eutrapelia, ta ouk anēkonta)</note>. ¶ The Vulgate edition says: *But rather giving of thanks.* <note>original: 'Sed magis gratiarum actio'</note> ¶ Here the holy Hieronymus <note>Saint Jerome</note> prefers—and 
skilfully indeed, given the context and the subject matter—that the word <term>eucharistia</term> <note>original Greek: 'εὐχαριστία'</note> 
be interpreted as "gracious speech" rather than "giving of thanks." Even if, depending on the place, it cannot be denied 
that it can sometimes be interpreted as "giving of thanks." For it is a homonym <note>A word with multiple meanings</note>. ¶ Which we have indeed observed 
in this place. Paul says: <term>but rather graciousness/thanksgiving</term> <note>original Greek: 'ἀλλὰ μᾶλλον εὐχαριστία' (alla mallon eucharistia)</note>. And this "gracious speech" 
is to be understood not from human and carnal grace, but from spiritual grace. But is that which is philosoph-
ical also "gracious"? Certainly: but it is human, and though it may contain the highest perfection in that part, 
it is not yet spiritual. But that which is "super-philosophical" from the sacred elocutions is 
truly gracious (for it is made by the Spirit who is the giver of graces) and now also spiritual. But 
<margin>B 18</margin> not everyone—the direct and the oblique rays—are good judges of this. ¶ The Vulgate edition says: *For know this, knowing.* <note>original: 'Hoc enim scitote cognoscentes'</note> ¶ It was enough to have said: *for know this* or *be knowing.* 
¶ Paul says: <term>for this you are knowing</term> <note>original Greek: 'τοῦτο γὰρ ἐστὲ γινώσκοντες' (touto gar este ginōskontes)</note>. ¶ The Vulgate edition says: *Or a covetous person, which is the service of idols.* <note>original: 'Aut auarus quod est idolorum seruitus'</note> ¶ It should be said: *or a covetous person, who is a servant of idols,* in the masculine gender, not 
there in the neuter, nor here in the feminine. Paul says: <term>or a covetous man, who is an idolater</term> <note>original Greek: 'ἢ πλεονέκτης ὅς ἐστιν εἰδωλολάτρης' (ē pleonektēs hos estin eidōlolatrēs)</note>. ¶ The Vul-
<margin>B 19</margin> gate edition says: *For because of these things comes the wrath of God upon the children of diffidence.* <note>original: 'filios diffidentiæ'; usually 'children of disobedience'</note> ¶ Here also Hiero-
nymus prefers it to be said: *upon the children of unpersuadableness.* And wherever in Paul the old translator 
placed "children of diffidence," understand "unpersuadable children," who do not wish to believe 
nor to receive those things which are for their salvation, but stubbornly resist the truth. Paul says: <term>For because of these things comes</term>
<margin>C</margin> <term>the wrath of God upon the children of disobedience</term> <note>original Greek: 'Διὰ ταῦτα γὰρ ἔρχεται ἡ ὀργὴ τοῦ θεοῦ, ἐπὶ τοὺς υἱοὺς τῆς ἀπειθείας'</note>. ¶ The Vulgate edition says: *For the fruit of light is.* <note>original: 'Fructus enī lucis est'</note> ¶ It should be said: *For the fruit of the Spirit is.* Paul says: <term>for the fruit of the Spirit</term> <note>original Greek: 'ὁ γὰρ καρπὸς τοῦ πνεύματος' (ho gar karpos tou pneumatos)</note>. 
¶ The Vulgate edition says: *Proving what is well-pleasing to God.* <note>original: 'Probātes quid sit beneplacitū deo'</note> ¶ It should be said: *to the Lord.* And Paul used 
a participle, "proving," instead of a verb, according to his custom. Which, reduced to the verb "prove," makes it more suitable for us...

<header>COMMENTARY</header>

<margin>S....</margin> ...a more suitable expression. Paul: Testing what is pleasing to the Lord <note>original Greek: "Δοκιμάζοντες τί ἐστιν εὐάρεστον τῶ κυρίω"</note>.

¶ Vulgate edition: *But rather reprove them.* It should be said: *But rather [and] reprove.*

<margin>D 20</margin> ¶ Paul: *But rather even reprove.* <note>original Greek: "μᾶλλον δὲ καὶ ἐλέγχετε"</note> Vulgate edition: *All things that are reproved are made manifest by the light.* Since the old translator had said a little earlier, "For you were once darkness but now light in the Lord; walk as children of light," it was consistent that he should translate the same word as "light" everywhere here, lest he create a fantasy of different words in Paul’s writing when Paul always uses the same term. Paul: *But all things being reproved are made manifest by the light.* <note>original Greek: "τὰ δὲ πάντα ἐλεγχόμενα, ὑπὸ τοῦ φωτὸς φανεροῦται"</note> For everywhere Paul uses this word *phos, photos* <note>meaning "light"</note>.

¶ Vulgate edition: *And Christ shall enlighten thee.* It could also be said here (on the authority of Jerome) "and Christ shall arise for you," or "and Christ shall shine upon you." But because the current sense agrees with the understanding of the old translator, we have not bothered to change the translation. Paul: *And Christ will shine upon you.* <note>original Greek: "καὶ ἐπιφαύσει σοι ὁ χριστός"</note>

<margin>D 21</margin> ¶ Vulgate edition: *See therefore, brethren, how cautiously you walk.* "Brethren" is redundant <note>meaning it is not in the original Greek source</note>. And it should rather be said "exactly," "diligently," "accurately," or something similar rather than "cautiously." Paul: *See then how accurately you walk.* <note>original Greek: "Βλέπετε ὄυν πῶς ἀκριβῶς περιπατεῖτε"</note>

¶ Vulgate edition: *Redeeming the time.* Rather "buying." And there is nothing wrong if we change the participle into its own verb. Paul: *Buying up the opportunity.* <note>original Greek: "ἐξαγοραζόμενοι τὸν καιρόν"</note>

¶ Vulgate edition: *And be not drunk with wine, in which is luxury.* There are those who prefer it to be said "in which is unhealthiness" <note>the Latin *insalubritas*</note>. Paul: *And be not drunk with wine, in which is debauchery.* <note>original Greek: "καὶ μὴ μεθύσκετε όινω, ἐν ὦ ἐστὶν ἀσωτία"</note> Since *asotia* <note>debauchery/prodigality</note> comes from the noun *sos*, which means "safe," or *soos*, which means both "safe" and "preserved," one might rightly interpret *asotos* as "unhealthy" and *asotia* as "unhealthiness." Or is it a metaphorical translation when the former is interpreted as "luxurious" and the latter as "luxury"? For the luxurious are usually faint and sickly, seeing as when they sin against their own body, they squander and dissipate their own substance. But let us leave this battle over the word to the grammarians, who search for the origins of words more curiously than philosophers search for the source of the Nile.

¶ Vulgate edition: *Singing and making melody in your hearts to the Lord.* In the Greek it is singular: "in your heart." And perhaps not without reason, because there ought to be one heart and one soul for all those existing in the body of Christ. However, for the sake of euphony <note>pleasantness of sound</note>, I preferred to translate it with the old translator as "in your hearts to the Lord" rather than "in your heart to the Lord." Also, because the singular made it ambiguous whether it should be understood as "in your heart" or "to your Lord." Both of these—the clashing of sounds and the ambiguity of speech—are removed by using the plural number. Paul: *Singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord.* <note>original Greek: "ἄδοντες καὶ ψάλλοντες ἐν τῆ καρδία ὑμῶν τῶ κυρίω"</note>

<margin>D 22</margin> ¶ Vulgate edition: *Wives, be subject to your husbands.* It should rather be said "to your own husbands," and the command "be subject" should be in the second person. Paul: *Wives, submit yourselves to your own husbands as to the Lord.* <note>original Greek: "αἱ γυναῖκες τοῖς ἰδίοις ἀνδράσιν ὑποτάσσεσθε ὡς τῶ κυρίω"</note>

<margin>E 22</margin> ¶ Vulgate edition: *He is the savior of his body.* It should be said "and he is the savior of the body." "His" is redundant, and one should not say "of his" [eius] but "of his own" [sui]. Paul: *And he is the savior of the body.* <note>original Greek: "καὶ ἀυτός ἐσι σωτὴρ τοῦ σώματος"</note>

¶ And immediately he subjoins: *but as,* or something similar. <note>original Greek: "ἀλλ᾿ ὥσπερ"</note>

<margin>F 22</margin> ¶ Vulgate edition: *To their husbands in all things.* It is held as "to their own husbands in everything" or "in every matter," in the singular. Paul: *to their own husbands in everything.* <note>original Greek: "τοῖς ἰδίοις ἀνδράσιν ἐν παντί"</note> But that is a very small point.

¶ Vulgate edition: *Cleansing her with the washing.* The word "her" is expressed redundantly here, but it is sufficiently understood from the previous part of the sentence. Paul: *Having cleansed [it] by the washing.* <note>original Greek: "καθαρίσας τῶ λουτρῶ"</note>

¶ Vulgate edition: *For this cause shall a man leave his father and mother.* Paul has "his father and the mother." Paul: *For this cause shall a man leave his father and the mother.* <note>original Greek: "ἀντὶ τούτου καταλείψει ἄνθρωπος τὸν πατέρα ἀυτοῦ καὶ τὴν μητέρα"</note>

<margin>G 22</margin> ¶ Vulgate edition: *And let the wife fear her husband.* "Her" is redundant. And she should rather "reverence" the husband, so that this fear is understood as a fear of reverence and a noble fear, not an ignoble and servile one, which ought not to exist between a husband and wife, nor between parents and children. For "to fear" is common to both types, but "to reverence" is specific. And in this place also, Paul uses the common term for the specific one, as the Greeks are accustomed to do in this manner. Paul: *that she should fear the man.* <note>original Greek: "ἵνα φοβῆται τὸν ἄνδρα"</note> That is, so that she reverences the husband.

---

->CHAPTER VI.<-

**N**ow the Apostle has unlocked for us the mystery of the closest bond; let him now relate others to us. And first, concerning the bond of the father and the children. For "Father" refers back to the Creator, and "children" are the likeness of creatures. The earth signifies the heavenly homeland, and longevity signifies eternity. Therefore, in the symbol, children obeying the father and honoring the father represents creatures obeying the Creator and honoring the Creator. But this is much more so, insofar as the Creator is the Truth and the father is the likeness. And in the trace and the promised likeness—longevity upon the earth for children honoring their fleshly fathers—there is, in the pattern and in truth, promised eternity in the heavenly homeland for those honoring God. And this is a great bond between God and the creature, yet a less close bond than that between Christ and the Church. For the distance of nature is greater between God and the creature than between Christ and the Church; so much so that the creature, because of its departure, scarcely seems to cling to God.

<meta>This page continues the exposition of the Epistle to the Ephesians, moving from the mystical union of marriage discussed at the end of Chapter 5 into the social hierarchies of Chapter 6. The author interprets these human relationships (parents/children and masters/servants) as earthly mirrors of the divine order between the Creator and the soul.</meta>

# Ephesians V & VI

...to Christ especially. Therefore, concerning this bond, Paul adds: <margin>23</margin>

> **Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is just. Honor your father and mother (which is the first commandment with a promise) so that it may be well with you and you may live long upon the earth. And fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up in the discipline and admonition of the Lord.**

¶ What does it mean to "obey your parents in the Lord" except to do so in imitation of that obedience which you owe to the Lord your Creator? For this is an imitation of divine justice. This is the sense of the Spirit. And fathers toward their children ought to imitate the Creator of all, who provides for His creatures sweetly; He does not embitter them but directs them toward the best. For He disposes all things pleasantly, and into all those capable of knowing His goodness, He pours a sweet knowledge of Himself. Such should be the father's kindness, providence, and direction toward his children: so that in it, as in a seal, divine kindness, providence, and the constant guidance toward the best may shine forth. Great and arduous are the mysteries of the Spirit in every matter concerning us; we ought to imitate them through our senses as best we can, according to their dignity.

Now he deals with the third bond, which is less tight than the second: that of masters toward servants. For servants cling less to a master than children to parents. And if we recall all things to spirit and truth: the Church clings more to Christ than the creature to the Creator; and the creature, as a creature, clings more to God as Creator than a servant-creature clings to God as Lord. For the Fall and sin made the creature a "servant" <note>The author uses 'servus' which can mean both servant and slave; in this context, it refers to the spiritual bondage caused by sin</note>. For where do threats and punishments come from, if not because of sin and offense? Where also does the fear and trembling of the creature toward God come from, if not because of transgression and offense? For the one who has always obeyed and always venerated as they ought does not dread, does not shrink, and does not tremble. 

Therefore, an earthly master is to his servants as the Lord of all is toward sinners. Servants, however (even if they have not sinned), are a likeness of sinners. But just as God is kind, merciful, patient, and inclined to many for forgiveness, so an earthly master—who carries within himself a trace of the eternal Lord—ought to be kind, merciful, and prone to forgiveness. Likewise, servants ought to be suppliants, which the "fear and trembling" of their masters indicates. They should be obedient, and in this likeness conduct all things toward their masters as sinners wishing to deserve God's mercy <margin>24</margin> and grace. For all things around us pass by as a figure. And concerning this final bond, Paul also brings forth the divine sentence, saying: <margin>A</margin>

> **Servants, obey your earthly masters** <margin>E</margin> **with fear and trembling, in the simplicity of your heart, as if to CHRIST; not with eye-service as if pleasing men, but as servants of CHRIST, doing the will of God from the heart, serving with goodwill as if to the Lord and not to men. Not being ignorant of this: that whatever good thing anyone does,** <margin>H</margin> **he will receive this back from the Lord, whether he be a servant or a free man. And masters, render the same to them, giving up threats, knowing that both your master and theirs is in heaven; and with Him there is no** <margin>E</margin> **partiality of persons.**

¶ These are the three bonds by which the lower world is contained in image: <margin>R</margin> the marital, the paternal, and the masterly. And the superior world is contained in truth by three similar ones. The first and highest bond is that of the Bridegroom and Bride: Christ and the Church. The last and lowest is that of the Lord and sinners. The middle is that of the Creator and his creatures. 

And let these matters be explained as the Lord has given. The things contained under the last bond are weak—so much so that not even the demons are excluded from this bond, as wicked servants. But the things contained in the highest and middle bond are strong, provided they recognize from where their strength hangs, and with what arms they ought to battle against the wicked servants. For those two bonds are bonds of peace, as far as they are in themselves. But the third bond stirs up war, which is likened to the war made in heaven when the good angels achieved victory against the evil ones. And therefore, in the third bond and for the sake of the third, armor must be taken up—not earthly, but heavenly; the struggle must be fought not in one's own strength, but in the divine. For even the good angels do not conquer otherwise; rather, they refer the cause of victory and the glory to God, saying: 

> Salvation, and strength, and the kingdom of our God and the power of his Christ have come. 

<margin>25</margin> Wherefore Paul turns to the exhortations of spiritual warfare, saying:

> **Finally, my brothers: be strengthened in the Lord, and in the power of his might. Put on the whole armor of God, so that you may be able to stand against the deceits of the devil. Because our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the cosmic rulers** <note>original: "cosmocratoras"</note> **of the darkness of this age, against spiritual wickedness in high places. Therefore take up the whole armor of God, so that you may be able to resist in the evil day, and having done all, to stand. Stand therefore, having girded your loins in truth, and having put on the breastplate of righteousness, and your feet shod in the preparation of the gospel of peace; in all things taking up the shield of faith, with which you can extinguish all the fiery darts of the wicked one, and take the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the spirit, which is the word of God. Through all prayer and supplication, praying at all times in the spirit: and watching in this very thing with all service and intercession for all the saints, and for me, that speech may be given to me in the opening of my mouth, to dare to make known the mystery of the gospel, for which I act as an ambassador in chains: so that in it I may dare to speak as I ought.**

¶ If we were to see a carnal man with spiritual eyes: his loins are filled with falsehood, for this is the place of false pleasure. His heart is full of injustice. He is with bare and weak feet, with which...

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "But rather reprove them." ¶ It should be said: "But rather even expose them." Paul says: <note>original: "μᾶλλον δὲ καὶ ἐλέγχετε"</note> **but rather even expose.**

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "But all things that are reproved are made manifest by the light."
