This prevents creating a false impression of a variation in Paul’s vocabulary when Paul consistently uses the same word. Paul says: <note>original: "τὰ δὲ πάντα ἐλεγχόμενα, ὑπὸ τοῦ φωτὸς φανεροῦται"</note> **But all things, when they are exposed, are made manifest by the light.** For Paul everywhere uses this word <term>phos</term> <note>light</note>.

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "And Christ shall enlighten thee." ¶ It could also be said here (on the authority of Jerome), "And Christ shall rise upon you," or "Christ shall shine upon you." However, because this agrees with the understanding of the ancient translator, we have not bothered to change the translation. Paul says: <note>original: "καὶ ἐπιφαύσει σοι ὁ χριστός"</note> **and Christ shall shine upon you.**

<margin>D 21</margin>
¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "See therefore, brethren, how you walk cautiously." ¶ The word "brethren" is redundant here. And it is better to say "exactly," "diligently," "accurately," or something similar, rather than "cautiously." Paul says: <note>original: "βλέπετε οὖν πῶς ἀκριβῶς περιπατεῖτε"</note> **See then how accurately you walk.**

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "Redeeming the time." ¶ Rather "buying up." And there is nothing wrong if we change the participle into its own verb. Paul says: <note>original: "ἐξαγοραζόμενοι τὸν καιρόν"</note> **buying up the opportunity.**

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "And be not drunk with wine, wherein is luxury." ¶ There are those who prefer it to be said "wherein is unhealthiness." Thus, <term>asotos</term> is rightly translated as "unhealthy ones" and <term>asotia</term> as "unhealthiness." Or perhaps the translation is metaphorical, when the former is translated as "luxurious" and the latter as "luxury" <note>meaning excess or debauchery</note>? For the luxurious are usually weak and sickly, since those who sin against their own body squander and dissipate their own substance. But let us leave this dispute over a word to the grammarians, who search for the origins of words more curiously than the philosophers seek the source of the Nile.

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "Singing and making melody in your hearts to the Lord." ¶ In the Greek, it is singular: "in your heart." However, for the sake of euphony <note>pleasing sound</note>, I preferred to translate it with the ancient translator as "in your hearts to the Lord" rather than "in your heart to the Lord." Also, because the latter made it ambiguous whether it should be understood as "in your heart" or "to your Lord," both of which—the awkwardness of the sounds and the ambiguity of the speech—are removed by using the plural number. Paul says: <note>original: "ᾄδοντες καὶ ψάλλοντες ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ ὑμῶν τῷ κυρίῳ"</note> **singing and psalming in your heart to the Lord.**

<margin>D 22</margin>
¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "Let women be subject to their husbands." ¶ It is better to say "to their own husbands," and to use the second person: "be subject." Paul says: <note>original: "αἱ γυναῖκες τοῖς ἰδίοις ἀνδράσιν ὑποτάσσεσθε ὡς τῷ κυρίῳ"</note> **Wives, submit yourselves to your own husbands as to the Lord.**

<margin>E 22</margin>
¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "He is the savior of his body." ¶ It should be said: "And he is the savior of the body." ¶ The word "his" is redundant. And one should not say "his" [of another] but "its" [of himself]. Paul says: <note>original: "καὶ αὐτός ἐστι σωτὴρ τοῦ σώματος"</note> **And he is the savior of the body.** And he immediately adds: <note>original: "ἀλλ᾿ ὥσπερ"</note> **but as**, or something similar.

<margin>F 22</margin>
¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "To their husbands in all things." ¶ It is found as "to their own husbands in everything," or "in every matter," in the singular. Paul says: <note>original: "τοῖς ἰδίοις ἀνδράσιν ἐν παντί"</note> **to their own husbands in everything.** But this is a very small point.

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "Cleansing it by the washing." ¶ The word "it" is redundantly expressed here, but it is sufficiently understood from the preceding part of the sentence. Paul says: <note>original: "καθαρίσας τῷ λουτρῷ"</note> **having cleansed by the washing.**

<margin>G 22</margin>
¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "For this cause shall a man leave his father and mother." ¶ Paul has "his father and mother." Paul says: <note>original: "ἀντὶ τούτου καταλείψει ἄνθρωπος τὸν πατέρα αὐτοῦ καὶ τὴν μητέρα"</note> **Because of this a man shall leave his father and his mother.**

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "And let the wife fear her husband." ¶ "Her own" is redundant. And it is better to say "let her reverence her husband," so that this fear is understood as <term>reverence</term> and a "noble fear," not an "ignoble and servile fear," such as should not exist between a husband and wife, nor between parents and children. For "to fear" is common to both types, but "to reverence" is specific. And in this place also, Paul uses the common term for the specific one, as the Greeks are accustomed to do in this manner. Paul says: <note>original: "ἵνα φοβῆται τὸν ἄνδρα"</note> **so that she might fear her husband.** That is, so that she might reverence the man.

# CHAPTER VI.

The Apostle has unlocked for us the mystery of the closest bond; now let him relate others to us. And first, concerning the bond of father and children. For the Father represents the Creator, and children are the likeness of the creatures. The earth signifies the heavenly fatherland, and long life signifies eternity. Therefore, in the symbol, children obeying the father and honoring the father represents creatures obeying the Creator and honoring the Creator—but this much more so, inasmuch as the Creator is the Truth and the father is the likeness. And in the trace and likeness promised to children honoring their fleshly fathers—long life upon the earth—there is, in the original pattern and in truth, the promised eternity in the heavenly fatherland for those honoring God. And this bond between God and creature is great, but it is a less tight bond than that between Christ and the Church. For the distance of nature is greater between God and the creature than between Christ and the Church; so much so that the creature, because of its falling away, seems scarcely to cling to God.

It then begins Chapter 6, explaining how the relationship between parents and children serves as an earthly mirror of the relationship between God and His creation.</summary>

<margin>23</margin>
...but to Christ most of all. Regarding this bond, Paul adds:
> › Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right. Honor your father and mother—
> › which is the first commandment with a promise—that it may be well with you, and that you may live long upon the earth.
> › And fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up in the discipline and admonition of the Lord.

¶ What does it mean to "obey your parents in the Lord," if not an imitation of that obedience which you owe to the Lord your Creator? For this is the imitation of divine justice. This is the meaning of the Spirit. And fathers, in turn, ought to imitate the Creator of all things toward their children; He who provides gently for His creature, does not embitter them, but directs them toward what is best. For He "disposes all things sweetly" <note>A reference to Wisdom 8:1</note> and pours a sweet knowledge of Himself into all who are capable of knowing His goodness. Such should be the father's kindness, providence, and direction toward his children: so that in him, as in a seal, divine kindness, providence, and the constant leading toward the best may shine forth. Great and arduous are the mysteries of the Spirit in every matter concerning us; we ought to imitate them sensibly, as best we can, according to their dignity. 

Now he deals with the third bond, which is less tight than the second: that of master to servants. For servants are less closely attached to a master than children are to parents. And if we call all things back to spirit and truth: the Church is more closely attached to Christ than the creature is to the Creator; and the creature, as a creature, is more closely attached to God as Creator than a servant creature is attached to God as Lord. For the Fall and sin made the creature a servant. For from where do threats and punishments come, if not because of sin and offense? From where also comes the fear and trembling of the creature toward God, if not because of transgression and offense? For the one who has always obeyed and always shown due reverence does not dread, does not shrink back, and does not tremble. 

Therefore, an earthly master stands toward servants as the Lord of all stands toward sinners. Servants, however (even if they have not sinned), are a likeness of sinners. But just as God is kind, merciful, patient, and ready to forgive many, so the earthly master—who carries within himself the footprint of the Eternal Lord—ought to be kind, merciful, and prone to forgiveness. Likewise, servants ought to be suppliant, which the "tremor and fear" of their masters indicates. They should be obedient and conduct all things toward their masters in likeness to how sinners, wishing to merit His mercy
<margin>24</margin>
and grace, conduct themselves toward God. For all things around us pass by in a figure <note>original: "in figura"—meaning as a symbolic representation or type</note>. And regarding this final bond, Paul also brings forth a divine sentence, saying:
> › Servants, obey your carnal masters with fear and trembling, in the simplicity of your heart, as unto CHRIST; not with eye-service
> › as pleasing men, but as servants of CHRIST, doing the will of God from the heart, serving with good will
> › as to the Lord and not to men. Knowing this: that whatever good thing anyone does,
> › he shall receive this back from the Lord, whether he be a servant or free. And masters, do the same things toward them, giving up threats: knowing that both your and their Lord is in heaven, and with Him there is no respect of persons.

¶ These are the three bonds by which the lower world is contained in an image: the conjugal <note>marriage</note>, the parental, and the master-servant. And by three similar bonds, the higher world is contained in truth. The first and highest bond is that of the Bridegroom and Bride: Christ and the Church. The last and lowest is that of the Lord and sinners. The middle is that of the Creator and creatures. And let these be explained as the Lord has given. The things contained under the last bond are weak—so much so that even demons are not excluded from this bond, being like wicked servants. But those things contained in the highest and middle bonds are strong, provided they recognize from whence their strength hangs, and with what arms they ought to battle against the wicked servants. For those two former bonds are bonds of peace, insofar as they are in themselves. But the third moves to war: which is likened to the war made in heaven, when the good angels achieved victory over the evil ones. And therefore, into the third and for the sake of the third, arms must be taken up—not earthly, but heavenly. They do not rely on their own strength, but refer it to God, saying: "Salvation, and strength, and the kingdom of our God, and the
<margin>25</margin>
power of His Christ has come." <note>A reference to Revelation 12:10</note> Wherefore Paul, exhorting us to an imitation of spiritual warfare, says:
> › Finally, my brethren, be strong in the Lord, and in the power of His might. Put on the whole armor of God, that you may be able to stand against the snares of the devil. For our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the world-rulers <note>original: "cosmocratas"—rulers of the world</note> of the darkness of this age, against spiritual wickedness in high places. Therefore take up the whole armor of God, that you may be able to resist in the evil day, and having done all, to stand. Stand therefore, having your loins girt about with truth, and having on the breastplate of justice, and your feet shod in the preparation of the gospel of peace; in all things taking the shield of faith, with which you can extinguish all the fiery darts of the wicked one, and take the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the spirit, which is the word of God. Through all prayer and supplication, praying at all times in the spirit: and watching in this very thing with all service and intercession for all the saints, and for me—that utterance may be given to me in the opening of my mouth, to boldly make known the mystery of the gospel, for which I act as an ambassador in a chain: that in it I may dare to speak as I ought to speak.

...may be considered good. He has no shield: with which he might blunt the burning desires which the evil one hurls like darts <note>Refers to the "fiery darts of the wicked" in Ephesians 6:16</note>. He has no protection for his head, for he does not cling to Christ, who is the head. His tongue is an incurable poison. Entirely unarmed and a captive, the adversary pushes him wherever he wishes, and wounds the unarmed man from whatever side he chooses. No part of him would be free from blows and wounds—a miserable spectacle to God and the angels, and even to the world, if the world were not blind. When you look, and by looking you feel desire: the evil one has wounded your eyes. When you are soothed by the flatteries of a siren: he has enchanted your ears. When you disparage, when you blaspheme: he has poisoned your tongue. Therefore, all our members must be armed against the crafts of the evil one. 

The loins with truth as a belt and girdle: against the falsehood of desires. The heart with justice <note>Often translated as "righteousness"</note> as a breastplate or thorax. The feet with the peace of the works of God: as swift footwear for the expedition of announcing the gospel of Christ. Against the darts of desires: let us oppose the strength of faith as a shield. Let Christ, who is our salvation, be for us a helmet. Let us arm the tongue with the word of God as a most sharp sword: with which we may pierce our wicked enemy, the ancient serpent, and avoid all his poisons. And in all these things, let us not think we can prevail by our own strength, but by that obtained from the Lord, who is the virtue of all those fighting spiritually. These are the spiritual arms; this is the soldier of Christ, whom God and the angels value, whom they help toward victory, and whom they crown as victor. He, however, lays down the crown of victory before the throne of God, attributing the glory of the victory to God. These things are carried out around us in the spirit every day (unless we are unarmed, unless the evil one has disarmed us). And while we live on earth: in the heavens and against spiritual wickednesses, we are victors. But for the sake of the watch, lest our enemy catch us unaware: prayer ought to be vigilant and intent toward God. For he who saw Satan seeking us, so that in this war he might sift us like wheat, said: "Watch and pray, so that you do not enter into temptation." <note>Luke 22:31-46</note> 

Truly, so that he might show the Ephesians that they could not prevail by our strength, but by the strength of God, he who was an Apostle—who had the power of signs, who had prophecy, and the grace of healings, and the remaining gifts of the Holy Spirit—asks that that grace by which he might prevail be obtained for him from God through their prayers. He used this as an argument in humility: if he, who was an apostle and who was so powerful with such great graces, could do nothing by his own strength and trusted nothing to them: how much less could they, and how much less ought they to trust in their own strength.

<margin>26</margin> ¶ But he also sent Tychicus with the Letter: so that by the familiar consolation in the spirit, they might understand by the oracle of a living voice those things which were being done concerning him, as he was faithfully fighting for our Lord Jesus Christ. And so he says:

<margin>10</margin>
> But so that you also may know the things which are happening with me, and what I am doing: Tychicus, the beloved brother and faithful minister in the Lord, will make everything known to you. I have sent him to you for this very purpose, that you may know the things concerning us, and that he may comfort your hearts. Peace be to the brothers and love with faith from God the Father and the Lord JESUS CHRIST. Grace be with all who love our Lord JESUS CHRIST in incorruptibility. Amen. Written at Rome; sent by Tychicus.

¶ Just as he fixed a holy greeting to the front of the letter, so he closes the letter with a holy farewell: namely, with an imprecation of peace, of God, of love, and of faith—not such as the world gives, but such as God the Father gives, and in His spirit our Lord Jesus Christ. And moreover, with a holy imprecation of grace for all those loving Christ in incorruptibility. The works of the flesh are corruptible; but the works of the spirit are incorruptible. Therefore, those who love our Lord Jesus Christ in incorruptibility: they love in the Holy Spirit. Therefore, to the eternal Father and our Lord Jesus Christ, and to the Holy Spirit, who are one, from whom we expect that peace, and love, and faith, and every grace: be undivided honor, and glory, and thanksgiving for all ages of ages. Amen.

<margin>23</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Honor your father and your mother: which is the first commandment.* <note>original Latin: "Honora patrem tuũ & matrem tuam: quod est mandatum primũ."</note> ¶ The word "your" <note>tuam</note> after "mother" is redundant. Paul says: *Honor your father, and the mother, which is the first commandment.* <note>original Greek: "τίμα τὸν πατέρα σου, καὶ τὴν μητέρα, ἥτις ἐστὶν ἐντολὴ πρώτη."</note>

<margin>B 23</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *But bring them up in the discipline and correction of the Lord.* <note>original Latin: "Sed æducate illos in disciplina & correptione domini."</note> ¶ It should rather be said: *and the admonition of the Lord.* Jerome also notes this against the old translator. Paul says: *but nourish them in the discipline and admonition of the Lord.* <note>original Greek: "ἀλλ᾿ ἐκτρέφετε αὐτὰ ἐν παιδείᾳ καὶ νουθεσίᾳ κυρίου."</note>

<margin>B 24</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Not serving to the eye.* <note>original Latin: "Non ad oculum seruientes."</note> ¶ It can equally be said: *not with eye-service*, or *not with service to the eye.* Paul says: *not according to eye-service.* <note>original Greek: "μὴ κατ᾿ ὀφθαλμοδουλείαν."</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Serving from the heart with good will.* <note>original Latin: "Ex animo cum bona voluntate seruientes."</note> ¶ Paul says: *from the soul with benevolence.* "From the soul" indeed, as also in Deuteronomy: *You shall love the Lord your God from all your heart, and from all your soul.* But the custom of the Latins, in similar apostolic speech, is "from the heart" <note>ex animo</note>; we say "from the heart" more so with the old translator. Paul says: *serving from the soul with benevolence.* <note>original Greek: "ἐκ ψυχῆς μετ᾿ εὐνοίας δουλεύονtes."</note>

<meta>This page concludes the scholarly comparison between the Greek text of the Apostle Paul and the Latin Vulgate translation for the Epistle to the Ephesians. It focuses specifically on the final chapter regarding spiritual warfare and the closing benediction.</meta>

# V Ephesians

...is in heaven. Paul: <note>original: "ὑμῶν αὐτῶν ὁ κύριος ἐστὶν ἐν οὐρανοῖς"</note> their own Lord is in heaven. ¶ Vulgate edition: *And there is no respect of persons with God.* ¶ It should be read relatively as "him" rather than "God": for it refers to the "Lord" mentioned in the previous part / your own Lord is in heaven.
<margin>25</margin> Paul: <note>original: "καὶ προσωποληψία οὐκ ἔστι παρ’ αὐτῷ"</note> and there is no partiality with him. ¶ Vulgate edition: *Finally, brethren, be strengthened in the Lord.* ¶ "My" is missing after "brethren." Paul: <note>original: "τὸ λοιπὸν ἀδελφοί μου ἐνδυναμοῦσθε ἐν κυρίῳ"</note> Finally, my brethren, be strengthened in the Lord. ¶ Vulgate edition: *And in the power of his virtue.*
<margin>B</margin> ¶ Rather "of his strength" <note>Latin: *fortitudo*</note>: which even Saint Jerome notes. Paul: <note>original: "καὶ ἐν τῷ κράτει τῆς ἰσχύος αὐτοῦ"</note> and in the power of his might. ¶ Vulgate edition: *Clothe yourselves [with] armor.* ¶ "Yourselves" is redundant. And the word Paul uses is universal and signifies "full armor" <note>Greek: *panoplia*</note>. Paul: <note>original: "ἐνδύσασθε πανοπλίαν"</note> put on the full armor. ¶ Vulgate edition: *But against princes and powers, against the world-rulers of these darknesses.* ¶ There are those who prefer to say "principalities" rather than "princes" here. And "against powers," with the conjunction omitted before it. And also "of the darkness of this world" rather than "of these [darknesses]." And regarding what the old translator <note>The author refers to the translator of the Latin Vulgate</note> calls "world-rulers," which is expressed by a single word in Paul <note>the word *kosmokratōr*</note>: I prefer to retain Paul’s word, so that we do not seem to disjointly and awkwardly add two substantives, namely "of the world" and "of these darknesses," to "rulers." And so that astrologers may understand—those who annually appoint some "Lord of the year," either Saturn, or Jupiter, or Mars, and so on for the rest, whom they call *cosmocrator* <note>Greek: "world-ruler"</note>, and some also *cronocrator* <note>Greek: "time-ruler"</note>—how heathenishly they speak. And who is this *cosmocrator* but some prince of darkness? Who, from that ancient ruin of the angels, still exercises a principality—that is, a harsh tyranny—over those who do not fight back with the weapons of God and true faith, and achieve victory through the protection of the good angels. For against the children of light, they can do nothing. For such principalities and powers belong to the darkness of this world. Far be it, therefore, that Christians, who are children of light, should either appoint or name for themselves such "Lords of the year." For we have a Lord, Jesus Christ: who is Lord of all time and eternity. Paul: <note>original: "ἀλλὰ πρὸς τὰς ἀρχάς, πρὸς τὰς ἐξουσίας, πρὸς κοσμοκράτορας τοῦ σκότους τοῦ αἰῶνος τούτου"</note> but against the principalities, against the powers, against the world-rulers of the darkness of this age. ¶ Vulgate edition: *Against the spiritual [forces] of wickedness in high places.* ¶ It can also be said "against the spiritual forces of wickedness against the heavenly [ones]"; though because of the old translator we have said "in high places." I say "against the heavenly ones" because such spiritual wickednesses are no longer heavenly; they are not in heaven. Nor (says the Scripture) "was a place found for them any longer in heaven" <note>A reference to Revelation 12:8</note>. But having been cast down into gloom and profound darkness, they continually oppose the heavenly ones. Therefore it seems in no way absurd if it is translated with the accusative and said "against the spiritual forces of wickedness against the heavenly ones," or "against the spiritual wickednesses against the heavenly ones": which would mean the same thing. For in this way we clearly express that they are spiritual wickednesses against the truly heavenly ones, whose conversation <note>meaning "citizenship" or "way of life"</note> is in heaven. And so they are opposed to those heavenly ones (I speak of heavenly men while they are pilgrims on earth) because they sometimes cast some down from that heavenly state into the confusion of their own darkness. Paul: <note>original: "πρὸς τὰ πνευματικὰ τῆς πονηρίας ἐν τοῖς ἐπουρανίοις"</note> against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places. ¶ Vulgate edition: *Therefore take up the armor of God.* ¶ As has been said, Paul's word signifies the "full armor" <note>Greek: *panoplia*</note>, lest we seem to retain any of the devil’s weapons with which he attacks spiritual things. Paul: <note>original: "διὰ τοῦτο ἀναλάβετε τὴν πανοπλίαν τοῦ θεοῦ"</note>
<margin>C</margin> therefore take up the full armor of God. ¶ Vulgate edition: *All the darts of the most wicked one.* ¶ Rather "of the evil one" than "of the most wicked one." Paul: <note>original: "πάντα τὰ βέλη τοῦ πονηροῦ"</note> all the darts of the evil one. ¶ Vulgate edition: *And take the helmet of salvation.* ¶ Rather "of the Savior's [helmet]," and Paul speaks using the infinitive "to receive," not "take." Paul: <note>original: "καὶ τὴν περικεφαλαίαν τοῦ σωτηρίου δέξασθαι"</note> and to receive the helmet of salvation. ¶ Vulgate edition: *And watching in it.* ¶ It should be read: "and in this very thing." Paul: <note>original: "καὶ εἰς αὐτὸ τοῦτο ἀγρυπνοῦντες"</note> and watching unto this very thing. ¶ Vulgate edition: *In all instance and supplication.* ¶ Rather "in all service." Paul: <note>original: "ἐν πάσῃ προσκαρτερήσει, καὶ δεήσει"</note> in all perseverance and petition. For the verb *proskartereo* <note>meaning to persist or persevere</note>
<margin>D</margin> aptly signifies "to serve" or "to attend to." ¶ Vulgate edition: *For which I perform an embassy in this chain.* ¶ "This" is redundant. Paul: <note>original: "ὑπὲρ οὗ πρεσβεύω ἐν ἁλύσει"</note> for which I am an ambassador in a chain. And he immediately adds: <note>original: "ἵνα ἐν αὐτῷ παρρησιάσωμαι"</note> that in it I may speak boldly / that is, that I may dare in him.
<margin>26</margin> ¶ Vulgate edition: *From God our Father and the Lord JESUS CHRIST.* ¶ In Greek it is read only "from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ." The word "our" is redundant in our [Latin] manuscripts. Paul: <note>original: "ἀπὸ θεοῦ πατρὸς, καὶ κυρίου Ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ"</note> from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. ¶ Vulgate edition: *In incorruption.* ¶ The Greek word says "incorruptibility" rather than "incorruption." And many Latin manuscripts have "in corruption" without the negating particle, which is read far more corruptly than "in incorruption" with the privative and negating particle. Paul: <note>original: "ἐν ἀφθαρσίᾳ"</note> in incorruptibility. And among the Greeks, the subscription says: *Written to the Ephesians from Rome. Sent by Tychicus.*

<margin>A</margin> ¶ EXAMINATION of several points concerning the literal text. ¶ **The Vulgate edition**: <note>Latin: *Honora patrem tuū & matrem tuam: quod est mandatum primū.*</note> *Honor thy father and thy mother: which is the first commandment.* "Thy" after mother is redundant. <margin>23</margin> <margin>B</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition**: <note>Latin: *Sed æducate illos in disciplina & correptione domini.*</note> *But bring them up in the discipline and correction of the Lord.* It should rather be said "and admonition of the Lord." Which Jerome <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the scholar responsible for the bulk of the Latin Vulgate translation</note> also notes against the old translator. Paul: <note>original: "ἀλλ’ ἐκτρέφετε αὐτὰ ἐν παιδείᾳ καὶ νουθεσίᾳ κυρίου"</note> "but nourish them in the training and admonition of the Lord."
<margin>23</margin> <margin>B</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition**: <note>Latin: *Non ad oculum feruientes.*</note> *Not serving to the eye.* It can equally be said: "not with eye-service," or "not with service to the eye." Paul: <note>original: "μὴ κατ’ ὀφθαλμοδουλείαν"</note> "not according to eye-service."
<margin>24</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition**: <note>Latin: *Ex animo cum bona voluntate seruientes.*</note> *Serving from the heart with good will.* Paul says "from the soul with benevolence." Indeed, "from the soul" is also used in Deuteronomy: "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul." But it is the custom of the Latins, in a similar apostolic phrasing, to say "from the heart" <note>Latin: *ex animo*</note>; we have said "from the heart" more often with the old translator. Paul: <note>original: "ἐκ ψυχῆς μετ’ εὐνοίας δουλεύοντες"</note> "serving from the soul with good will."
¶ **The Vulgate edition**: <note>Latin: *Vester dominus est in cœlis.*</note> *Your Lord is in heaven.* Rather, "your own Lord..."

...Master is in heaven. Paul: "your own Lord is in heaven" <note>original Greek: "ὑμῶν αὐτῶν ὁ κύριος ἐστὶν ἐν οὐρανοῖς"</note>. ¶ Vulgate edition: "And there is no respect of persons with God." ¶ It should be read relatively to "him" rather than
<margin>B</margin>
"God": it refers to the "Lord" mentioned in the previous part—"your own Lord is in heaven." Paul: "and there is no partiality with him" <note>original Greek: "καὶ προσωποληψία οὐκ ἔστι παρ' αὐτῷ"</note>. ¶ Vulgate edition: "Finally, brothers, be strengthened in the Lord." ¶ The word "my" is missing after "brothers." Paul: "for the rest, my brothers, be strengthened in the Lord" <note>original Greek: "τὸ λοιπὸν ἀδελφοί μου ἐνδυναμοῦσθε ἐν κυρίῳ"</note>. ¶ Vulgate edition: "And in the power of his virtue."
¶ Rather "of his strength": which Jerome <note>St. Jerome, the 4th-century scholar who translated the Latin Vulgate</note> also notes as being more sacred. Paul: "and in the strength of his might" <note>original Greek: "καὶ ἐν τῷ κράτει τῆς ἰσχύος αὐτοῦ"</note>.
<margin>25</margin>
¶ Vulgate edition: "Put on the armor." ¶ The word "you" [vos] is redundant. And the word Paul uses is universal, signifying "all armor" <note>the Greek "panoplia" refers to the full kit of a heavy-armed soldier</note>. Paul: "put on the full armor" <note>original Greek: "ἐνδύσασθε πανοπλίαν"</note>. ¶ Vulgate edition: "But against princes and powers, against the world-rulers of these darknesses." ¶ There are those who prefer to say "principalities" here rather than
"princes." And "against powers," without the preceding joining word [and]. And also "of the darkness of this age" rather than "of these [darknesses]." And where the old translator says "world-rulers" <note>Latin: mundi rectores</note>, which is expressed in one word by Paul: I have preferred to retain Paul's word <note>the Greek term "cosmocratores"</note>, lest we seem to clumsily and disjointedly add two nouns to "rulers," namely "of the world" and "of these darknesses."
And let the astrologers—who every year appoint some "lord of the year," either Saturn, or Jupiter, or Mars, and so on for the rest, whom they call <term>cosmocrator</term> <note>ruler of the world</note> and some even <term>chronocrator</term> <note>ruler of time</note>—understand how paganly they speak. For who is that "cosmocrator" but some prince of darkness? Who, from that ancient ruin of the angels, still exercises a principality—that is, a harsh tyranny—over those who do not fight back with the weapons of God and true faith, and who do not achieve victory through the protection of the good angels. For they have no power against the children of light. For principalities and powers of this kind belong to the darkness of this age. Far be it, therefore, from Christians—who are children of light—to either appoint for themselves or name such "lords of the year." For we have a Lord, Jesus Christ: who is the Lord of all time and eternity. Paul: "but against principalities, against powers, against the world-rulers of the darkness of this age" <note>original Greek: "ἀλλὰ πρὸς τὰς ἀρχάς, πρὸς τὰς ἐξουσίας, πρὸς κοσμοκράτορας τοῦ σκότους τοῦ αἰῶνος τούτου"</note>. ¶ Vulgate
<margin>C</margin>
edition: "Against spiritual wickedness in high places" <note>literally: in the celestials</note>. ¶ It can also be said "against spiritual forces of wickedness against the heavenly ones": though on account of the old translator we have said "in the heavenly places." I say "against the heavenly ones" because spiritual wickednesses of this kind are no longer "heavenly," they are not in heaven. Nor (as the Scripture says) was a place found for them any longer in heaven. But having been cast down into gloom and profound darkness, they continually oppose the "heavenly ones" <note>meaning the faithful</note>. Therefore, nothing seems absurd if it is translated using the accusative case as "against the spiritual forces of wickedness against the heavenly ones," or "against spiritual wickednesses against the heavenly ones": which would mean the same thing. For in this way we express more clearly that these are spiritual wickednesses against the true "heavenly ones," whose citizenship is in heaven. And thus they are opposed to those heavenly people (I speak of heavenly men: while they are pilgrims [on earth]) whom they sometimes cast down from that heavenly state into the confusion of their own darkness. Paul: "against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places" <note>original Greek: "πρὸς τὰ πνευματικὰ τῆς πονηρίας ἐν τοῖς ἐπουρανίοις"</note>. ¶ Vulgate edition: "Therefore take up the armor of God." ¶ As has been said, Paul's word signifies "all armor": lest we seem to keep for ourselves any of the devil’s weapons with which he attacks spiritual things. Paul: "because of this, take up the full armor of God" <note>original Greek: "διὰ τοῦτο ἀναλάβετε τὴν πανοπλίαν τοῦ θεοῦ"</note>. ¶ Vulgate edition: "All the darts of the most wicked one." ¶ Rather "of the evil one" than "of the most wicked one." Paul: "all the darts of the evil one" <note>original Greek: "πάντα τὰ βέλη τοῦ πονηροῦ"</note>. ¶ Vulgate edition: "And take the helmet of salvation." ¶ Rather
<margin>D</margin>
"of the savior," and Paul speaks through an infinitive "to receive," not [the imperative] "take." Paul: "and receive the helmet of the savior" <note>original Greek: "καὶ τὴν περικεφαλαίαν τοῦ σωτηρίου δέξασθαι"</note>. ¶ Vulgate edition: "And watching in it." ¶ It should be read: "and in this very thing." Paul: "and watching unto this very thing" <note>original Greek: "καὶ εἰς αὐτὸ τοῦτο ἀγρυπνοῦντες"</note>. ¶ Vulgate edition: "In all instance and supplication." ¶ Rather "in all perseverance." Paul: "in all perseverance and supplication" <note>original Greek: "ἐν πάσῃ προσκαρτερήσει, καὶ δεήσει"</note>. For the word "proskartereo" <note>προσκαρτερέω</note> properly signifies to serve or to devote oneself to. ¶ Vulgate edition: "For which I am an ambassador in this chain." ¶ "This" is redundant. Paul: "for which I am an ambassador in a chain" <note>original Greek: "ὑπὲρ οὗ πρεσβεύω ἐν ἁλύσει"</note>. And he immediately adds: "that in it I may speak boldly" <note>original Greek: "ἵνα ἐν αὐτῷ παρρησιάσωμαι"</note>.
<margin>26</margin>
¶ Vulgate edition: "From God our Father and the Lord JESUS CHRIST." ¶ In the Greek it is read only "from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ." The word "our" is redundant in our [Latin] codices. Paul: "from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ" <note>original Greek: "ἀπὸ θεοῦ πατρὸς, καὶ κυρίου ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ"</note>. ¶ Vulgate edition: "In incorruption." ¶ The Greek word signifies "incorruptibility" rather than "incorruption." And many Latin codices have "in corruption" because the [negative] particle was not correctly preserved; which is read far more depravedly than "in incorruption" where the particle is properly applied. Paul: "in incorruption" <note>original Greek: "ἐν ἀφθαρσίᾳ"</note>. And among the Greeks the subscription has: "Written to the Ephesians from Rome; sent through Tychicus."

# SIXTH BOOK OF THE COMMENTARIES ON THE EPISTLES OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PAUL, WHICH IS ON THE EPISTLE TO THE PHILIPPIANS, CHAPTER I.

<margin>1</margin> The Apostle, writing to the Philippians—who are located in the inland parts of Macedonia near the people of Amphipolis <note>Amphipolis was a major city in eastern Macedonia; Paul visited it on his second missionary journey</note>—prefixes a holy greeting (as is his custom), saying: <image-desc>Large decorative woodcut initial 'P' featuring a seated figure at a desk writing, within a square architectural frame.</image-desc> **Paul and Timothy, servants of JESUS CHRIST: to all the saints in CHRIST JESUS who are at Philippi, with the bishops and deacons: grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord JESUS CHRIST.** This is a holy, chaste, and spiritual greeting; it is accompanied by an act of thanksgiving, a fervent love for God and for one’s neighbor in God, and prayer—which is a holy lifting of the mind to God within that same love. Paul expresses these three companions [thanksgiving, love, and prayer] in the following speech with pious affection, saying:

> **I give thanks to my God in every remembrance of you, in every prayer of mine for all of you, making my prayer with joy for your fellowship in the**

<margin>2</margin> **gospel from the first day until now, having this very confidence: that he who began a good work in you will complete it until the day of CHRIST JESUS. Just as it is right for me to feel this about all of you, because I have you in my heart, both in my chains and in the defense and confirmation of the gospel, since you are all sharers with me in grace.**

> **For God is my witness, how I long for you all with the affection of JESUS CHRIST** <note>original: "in visceribus," literally "in the bowels," a common idiom for deep, inward compassion or tender mercy</note>. **And this I pray: that your love may abound more and more in knowledge and all perception, so that you may approve the things that are better; that you may be sincere and blameless on the day of CHRIST, filled with the fruit of righteousness through JESUS CHRIST, to the glory and praise of God.**

The "Day of Christ" is twofold: the particular day for each person at death, and the universal day on the final day. In the *particular*, each person is judged by a <term>particular judgment</term> <note>the theological belief that a soul is judged immediately upon death</note> on the day of their death. In the *universal*, each will be judged by a universal judgment before everyone, whether for glory or for eternal confusion. In the particular, the soul receives judgment without the body; in the universal, judgment is received with the soul and body together. Both are "Days of Christ": dreadful for the wicked, but to be desired by the good—indeed, greatly to be desired. And what is it that the apostle says: "because I have you in my heart in my chains"? Does he mean the iron chains with which he was bound for the truth of the gospel? However precious those chains might be—which I wish I were allowed to kiss, as they touched those holy feet equipped for the journey of the gospel of peace—it can also be understood as the bonds of love, by which all members of Christ ought to be bound. These bonds are more precious than all other chains, and even now we do not lack them. Nevertheless, from the

<margin>3</margin> first [physical] chains he adds in the following speech, saying:

> **But I want you to know, brothers, that the things concerning me have actually turned out for the advancement of the gospel, so that my chains have become manifest in CHRIST throughout the whole praetorium** <note>the imperial guard or the governor's palace</note> **and to all the rest. And many of the brothers in the Lord, gaining confidence from my chains, have dared more abundantly to speak the word of God without fear. Some, indeed, preach CHRIST out of envy and rivalry, but others out of goodwill. Those out of rivalry announce CHRIST not purely, thinking they bring distress to my chains; but those out of love, knowing that I am appointed for the defense of the gospel. What then? Only that in every way, whether by pretext or in truth, CHRIST is announced; and in this I rejoice, and will continue to rejoice. For I know that this will result in my salvation through your prayer and the provision of the spirit of JESUS CHRIST, according to my expectation and hope, that I shall be put to shame in nothing. But with all boldness, as always, so now also CHRIST shall be magnified in my body, whether through life or through death. For to me, to live is CHRIST, and to die is gain. But if living in the flesh is my lot, this means fruitful labor for me. And what I shall choose, I do not know. For I am hard pressed between the two, having a desire to be released and to be with CHRIST, which is far, far better; yet to remain in the flesh is more necessary for your sake.**

Why did they speak of Christ out of envy? So that when the reason for Paul being thrown into chains was heard, a sedition might arise, and Paul would be pressured all the more as the head and author of that "novelty" <note>early Christianity was often viewed by Roman authorities as a "new and mischievous superstition" or "novelty" rather than an established religion</note>. They were doing a good thing—for it is good to announce Christ—but they were doing it not purely, not cleanly, not holily. But those who preached, wishing to supply what Paul could not carry out because of the hindrance of his chains, knowing that he had been ordained by God for...

<header>VI 174 Philip.</header>

the gospel was to be preached; he had been thrown into chains for the defense of the gospel and was being held there. These people indeed performed a good work and acted rightly, and their intention was holy, chaste, and pure; and these preached in truth. But others did so out of opportunity—and a bald-faced opportunity at that—but such was the protection of Christ that whether they did it out of opportunity and pretense, or in truth, the faith always advanced, and the number of those to be saved increased. For this reason, Paul rejoiced on every side. They had cast chains upon him to cast down the faith of the gospel; yet, seeing Paul’s constancy and alacrity, the faith grew stronger and more fortified in the hearts of others. And whatever they plotted to extinguish it, they instead only kindled it more, providing it with growth and increase. Just as if you wished to extinguish a fire, and it instead conceived greater flames from the water thrown upon it—would that not be beyond nature? Would not a divine power be perceived therein? So too in these events, they ought to have perceived a divine power, and that this was not within human control. And for one who sees divine power overcoming all adversaries, how could he not rejoice? Certainly, therefore, in the contemplation of divine power overcoming all things, Paul rejoiced; and he testifies that he will always rejoice. How could he not rejoice, he who knew that whether he lived or died, whichever occurred, it would result in his salvation? For him, life is Christ; death is gain. Both are Christ, and both are gain. And clearly he was in doubt as to which he ought to prefer: life or death. If he looks to his own gain, death is to be preferred. For he will be with Christ, having laid aside the tunic of mortality; and no longer knowing Christ through a mirror and a riddle <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 13:12: "For now we see through a glass, darkly (in aithnigma); but then face to face."</note>, but face to face. This is far better than knowing Christ in corruptibility and under an obscure veil. Life to him is Christ, death is Christ; but life is (so to speak) Christ veiled, and death is Christ revealed. Again, life is sleep; death is wakefulness. Christ is like the possession of knowledge <note>original: "habitus scientiæ." In medieval philosophy, a 'habitus' is a stable disposition or quality, like a skill one has even while sleeping, whereas 'act' is the exercise of that skill.</note>. For just as one truly possesses the quality of knowledge whether sleeping or waking, he only possesses it through presence and action while waking. So also Paul, both living and dying, truly possessed Christ; but in death, he possessed Him through presence and action. And this was his own personal gain. But if he looks to the gain of others, life is to be preferred. For as long as he lived, he edified many and brought many to Christ. and this was a gain for others. Behold, therefore: death is gain; life is gain. But death is personal; life is for others. Death is for one; life is for innumerable people. Truly, while he is reserved for the gain of others, he did not lose his own—which is to see Christ in His true form and eternal life—but it was merely deferred. Thus, both gains remained: one present, the other future. So life was to be preferred by him, not simply for its own sake, but because of the joining together of gains, for which the good of others had the greatest necessity. Death, however, did not join both together. And therefore, knowing that life, which joins many good things, is still granted to him by God, he knows through the spirit of prophecy that he will yet see the 

<margin>4</margin>
Philippians. And who would not have a sacred heart burning and desiring to be dissolved, sighing for the presence of Christ? 
<margin>, ,</margin>
Yet he does not despise life, so that he may benefit many and lead them to a similar life of immortality. And therefore he adds, saying:

<margin>, ,</margin>
> ¶ **And having this certainty, I know that I shall remain and continue with all of you for your progress and the joy of faith. That your glorying may abound in CHRIST JESUS in me, through my presence with you again. Only conduct yourselves in a manner worthy of the gospel of CHRIST: so that whether I come and visit you, or be absent, I may hear of your affairs, that you stand fast in one spirit, with one mind striving together for the faith of the gospel, in nothing terrified by your adversaries.** ¶ **Which to them is a sign of perdition, but to you of salvation. And this from God. For unto you it is given for CHRIST, not only to believe in Him, but also to suffer for Him: having the same conflict which you saw in me, and now hear of me.**

¶ The Philippians could glory, and glory more abundantly, not in themselves but in Christ; because for the sake of their grace and that of other faithful ones, Paul was preserved in life. Nor could Satan—who envied his life because of its manifold fruit—prevail against him by any art, any cleverness, or any pressures; he who, though bearing the appearance of a mortal, was already as if immortal. For it is not forbidden to glory in good things; but it is commanded to glory in the Lord, as it is written: *Glory, all you who are upright in heart.* <note>Psalm 32:11</note> Christian affairs are conducted well, and the governance <note>original: "politia." This refers to the conduct of citizens or the administration of a commonwealth, here applied to the Church.</note> in the body of Christ is upright, when there is no distrust among the members, but they live by one spirit—not scattered or cast down, but standing and raised toward the heights—with one soul and one will, striving to fulfill the holy gospel, yielding to no adversaries, neither the pressures of the world, nor the desires of the flesh, nor the snares, suggestions, and evil infusions of the wicked one. And just as to the unbelievers, and those who condemned the Lord of our life to the cross, the cross is a sign of death and perdition, but to us who believe it is a sign of perpetual life and salvation: so also the afflictions and pressures inflicted by the wicked upon the good—especially when for Christ’s sake—are at once a sign of death and life, of perdition and salvation. Death and perdition to the wicked, but life and salvation to the good. And as in other matters, so in these: both Paul and the Philippians, suffering many pressures for Christ, held the sign of life. Which signs, even if they did not have—

<header>COMMENTARY V</header>

...we are not worthy in our own time to suffer for Christ. May he not exclude us from his mercy, he who is greater than all praise and glory, and worthy to be praised above all by every generation. <margin>A 1</margin>
# EXAMINATION of several points regarding the literal text.
<note>This section begins a "scholia" or critical notes section where the author compares the standard Latin Bible (Vulgate) with the Greek source text.</note>

¶ The Vulgate edition: **"To all the saints in Christ Jesus who are at Philippi, with the bishops and deacons."** <note>Philippians 1:1</note> ¶ Since the apostle was addressing the Philippians, it is better to translate it (as was said in previous epistles) as "who *you* are at Philippi." And it should be said: "and with the ministers" <note>Latin: *diaconis*</note> rather than "deacons" <note>Latin: *diaconibus*</note>. For in the nominative singular, it is called *diaconos* in Greek; and I do not believe that *diaco* or *diacon*—from which the inflection *diacones* would have to be derived—is ever read in either Greek or Latin. Paul writes: <note>original Greek: τοῖς οὖσιν ἐν Φιλίπποις σὺν ἐπισκόποις καὶ Διακόνοις</note> "to those being in Philippi with the overseers and servants."

<margin>A 2 B 2</margin>
¶ The Vulgate edition: **"Being confident of this very thing."** <note>Philippians 1:6</note> ¶ Here also it can be said more suitably: "having this very thing as a persuasion," "discovered," "certain," or something similar. Paul writes: <note>original Greek: πεποιθὼς ἀυτὸ τοῦτο</note> "having been persuaded of this very thing." ¶ The Vulgate edition: **"That you all are partners of my joy."** <note>Philippians 1:7</note> ¶ One should read "of grace" rather than "of joy." Paul writes: <note>original Greek: συγκοινωνόυσμου τῆς χάριτος πάρτας ὑμᾶς ὄρτας</note> "you all being fellow-sharers of my grace."

¶ The Vulgate edition: **"That you may be sincere in the day of Christ."** <note>Philippians 1:10</note> ¶ It seems it can equally be said: "unto the day of Christ." For here, a delay does not seem to be intended, but rather that you may be pure and upright when you stand before the judgment seats of Christ on the day of judgment. Paul writes: <note>original Greek: ἵρα ἦτε ἐιλικρινεῖς καὶ ἐις ἡμέραν χρισοῦ</note> "that you may be pure and for the day of Christ." Nor should it be a concern that Paul, using this preposition "unto" <note>Greek: εἰς</note>, joins it to the accusative case; for he is accustomed to using "unto" <note>εἰς</note> and "in" <note>ἐν</note> interchangeably. ¶ But if one prefers to use the accusative: let it be understood as a duration and succession, just as if we were to say "up until the day of Christ," which is the day of judgment, both the particular and especially the universal one.

<margin>B 3</margin>
¶ The Vulgate edition: **"So that my bonds became manifest in Christ in all the praetorium."** <note>Philippians 1:13; the Praetorium refers to the imperial guard or the governor's palace.</note> ¶ Rather: "in the *whole* praetorium." Paul writes: <note>original Greek: ὥστε δεσμουςμου Φαρεροὺς ἐν χριστῷ γενέσθαι, ἐρ ὅλῳ τῷ πραιτωρίῳ</note> "so that my chains became manifest in Christ in the whole praetorium."

<margin>C 3</margin>
¶ The Vulgate edition: **"That many of the brothers."** <note>Philippians 1:14</note> ¶ One should read: "And," not "that." Paul writes: <note>original Greek: καὶ τοὺς πλείορας τῶν ἀδελφῶν</note> "And most of the brothers." ¶ The Vulgate edition: **"Some indeed out of charity, knowing that I am set for the defense of the gospel. But some out of contention preach Christ not sincerely, thinking that they raise up affliction for my bonds."** <note>Philippians 1:15–17</note> ¶ Here the clauses are swapped. In the first place, those who act out of contention are described; in the second place, however, are those who act out of charity or love. And at the head of both clauses, one should read "whereas" or "since" rather than "certain." Thus, in the first clause, we should say "those, however, out of contention." Paul writes: <note>original Greek: ὁι μὲν ἐκ ἐριθείας τὸν χρισον καταγγέλουσιν, ὀυκ ἁγνῶς, ὀιόμεροι θλίψιμ ἐπιφέρειμ τοῖς Δεσμοῖςμου· ὁι δὲ ἐξ ἀγάπης ἐιδότες ὅτι ἐις ἀπολογίαν τοῦ ἐυαγγελίου κειμαι</note> "The ones indeed from selfish ambition proclaim Christ, not purely, thinking to bring pressure upon my chains; the others, however, from love, knowing that I am appointed for the defense of the gospel."

¶ The Vulgate edition: **"While in every way."** <note>Philippians 1:18</note> ¶ Paul has: <note>original Greek: πλὴν παρτὶ τρόπω</note> "except that in every way," which seems to mean "moreover" or "unless," and it makes the sentence more intelligible than when it is explained as "while." For it is aptly understood: "For what [does it matter]? Except that I rejoice and also will rejoice in whatever way Christ is preached."

¶ The Vulgate edition: **"Because in nothing I shall be confounded."** <note>Philippians 1:20</note> ¶ Lest "because" <note>Latin: *quia*</note> should seem to be causative, it seems better to say "that in nothing I shall be confounded." Paul writes: <note>original Greek: ὅτι ἐμ ὀυΔερὶ ἀισχυνθήσομαι</note> "that in nothing I shall be ashamed."

¶ The Vulgate edition: **"For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain."** <note>Philippians 1:21</note> ¶ Paul seems to use "to live" and "to die" as nouns. This is known from the articles attached to them as if they were names. To suggest this, we translate them as the nouns "life" and "death." Paul writes: <note>original Greek: ἐμοὶ γὰρ τὸ ζῆμ Χρισὸς, καὶ τὸ ἀποθανεῖμ κέρδος</note> "For to me, the living is Christ, and the dying is gain."

<margin>D 4</margin>
¶ The Vulgate edition: **"And having this confidence, I know."** <note>Philippians 1:25</note> ¶ Here also it can be said: "and having this as a certainty," or something similar. Paul writes: <note>original Greek: καὶ τοῦτο πεποιθὼς ὀιδα</note> "and having been persuaded of this, I know."

¶ The Vulgate edition: **"That your congratulation may abound in Christ Jesus in me."** <note>Philippians 1:26</note> ¶ It should rather be said "your glorying" <note>Latin: *gloriatio*</note>. Paul writes: <note>original Greek: ἵρα τὸ καύχημα ὑμῶν περισσεύῃ ἐν χρισῷ ἰησοῦ ἐρ ἐμοί</note> "so that your boasting may abound in Christ Jesus in me."

¶ The Vulgate edition: **"Through my coming."** <note>Philippians 1:26</note> ¶ It can be said indifferently as either "coming" or "presence." Paul writes: <note>original Greek: Διὰ τῆς ἐμῆς παρουσίας</note> "through my presence."

¶ The Vulgate edition: **"Only let your conversation be worthy of the gospel of Christ."** <note>Philippians 1:27</note> ¶ It is more intelligible and more fitting to Latin speech if it is said "according to the dignity" <note>Latin: *pro dignitate*</note> [of the gospel]. And that word "conversation" <note>Latin: *conuersamini*</note> signifies "citizenship," "governance," and the administration of both private and public affairs. Paul writes: <note>original Greek: μόρον ἀξίως τοῦ ἐυαγγελίου τοῦ χρισοῦ, πολιτεύεσθε</note> "Only worthily of the gospel of Christ, conduct yourselves as citizens."

¶ The Vulgate edition: **"I may hear of you that you stand in one spirit with one mind striving together."** <note>Philippians 1:27</note> ¶ Rather: "I may hear the things concerning you." And the old translator <note>The author of the Vulgate</note> frequently uses "because" <note>Latin: *quia*</note> instead of "that" <note>Latin: *quod*</note>. And where he says "with one mind" <note>Latin: *vnanimes*</note>, it can be said "with one soul" or "with one spirit." Also, where he says "striving together" <note>Latin: *collaborantes*</note>, it should rather be expressed as "contending together." Paul writes: <note>original Greek: ἀκούσω τὰ περὶ ὑμῶν, ὅτι σήκετε ἐρ ἐρὶ πρεύματι, μιᾶ ψυχῇ συραθλοῦρτες</note> "I may hear the things about you, that you stand in one spirit, with one soul contending together."

¶ The Vulgate edition: **"And in nothing be terrified by the adversaries."** <note>Philippians 1:28</note> ¶ Paul uses a participle, not a verb; specifically a participle that signifies being "disturbed" or "shaken." Paul writes: <note>original Greek: καὶ μὴ πτύρομεροι ἐμ μηΔερὶ ὑπὸ τῶν ἀρτικειμέρωρ</note> "and not being frightened in anything by those who oppose." And Paul uses a double negative, which negates more abundantly. But according to the custom of the Latins and especially for [...]

VI 175 Philippians.

For the sake of the more contentious dialecticians <note>scholars who focused on logic and formal debate, often criticized for hair-splitting</note> who seek everywhere not understanding but strife, it is enough to provide one example. ¶ The Vulgate edition: **"Which is to them a cause of perdition."** <note>Philippians 1:28</note> ¶ It is not called a "cause of perdition" in Paul's text, but rather a "showing" or "indication." Paul wrote: <note>original Greek: ἥτις αὐτοῖς... ἔνδειξις</note> "which is to them an indication." ¶ The Vulgate edition: **"And now you have heard of me."** <note>Philippians 1:30</note> ¶ It should be read: "and now you *hear* in me." Paul wrote: <note>original Greek: καὶ νῦν ἀκούετε ἐν ἐμοί</note>, where one preposition is used for another, or it should be said "in me."

### CHAPTER II.

<image-desc>Large decorative initial letter 'P' featuring intricate floral patterns and the figure of a long-necked bird (heron or peacock) nestled within the loop of the letter.</image-desc>
The Philippians possessed the signs of salvation in common with the apostle, suffering pressures for Christ's sake; they loved Christ and preserved the unity of the spirit, cultivating mutual love. And this was the apostle’s joy. But if they remained steadfast until the end, his joy would be greater and made full. For this reason, he exhorts them—and indeed exhorts them vehemently—adjuring them by the graces and the immense benefits of God to persevere, not falling back into carnal things. Furthermore, those who are greater in any state should imitate Christ and the example of his humility. Though he was God, he took on the "form of a servant" so that he might be for us a pattern of true humility, he who is the truth of glory. And this exhortation to the Philippians proceeded from his vehement and burning affection of love.

<margin>></margin> and under the earth. And that every tongue should confess that the Lord is JESUS CHRIST, to the
<margin>></margin> glory of God the Father. ¶ When Christ the Lord came into this world, he did not consider
what was his own, but what belonged to others, and what were to be our future goods. And he who was by nature the Lord of all came not to dominate, but to serve, a servant by nature. The Son of man (he says) came not to be ministered unto, but to minister. ¶ You who are servants by nature, yet harder than stones, deafer than an asp, blinder than darkness: you who do not know how to be humbled by the humility and the great melting of hearts of your Lord and God! By his own humility, he prepared this exaltation for all the humble: so that all the humble might be exalted and named above all other names, in that name of divine humility exalted above all things, which is the super-sweet and super-blessed name of Jesus. This name the heavens venerate, the earth worships, and hell trembles at; to which all things bow the knees of veneration and obedience. And there is nothing that can resist humility, seeing as it resides on the same throne with the highest majesty. But how was he "made in the likeness of men," he who was truly made man and who, according to nature, exceeds all other human reality? ¶ How was he "found in fashion as a man," of whom Adam and other men were nothing but a type and a figure? Christ truly has two natures in himself: the divine and the human. The divine is the "form of God." The human is the "form of men." The divine is the truth. The human is the image and likeness of the divine. The divine is the <term>archetype</term> <note>the original model or pattern</note> and exemplar. The human is the figure. And that the human form is the image and likeness of the divine, what else does the divine word testify when it introduces God speaking and saying, "Let us make man in our image and likeness"? ¶ How then is Christ—who joined the human form to the divine form, who existed in the truth and the exemplar of God—not found as a man in likeness and in figure? And even if he is a true man compared to another man or to inferior things, yet compared to God he is but a likeness and a resemblance; compared to the exemplar, he is but a figure. But in Christ, it is not a "bare likeness" or a "bare figure" as it is in us; rather, it is a true likeness and an exemplary figure—indeed, that which is the truth and the archetype. For the man Christ is truly God. And now, to the glory of the eternal Father, let every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord and God. For it would not be to the glory of God the Father to have a Son who was not God. Therefore, having reviewed these things concerning both forms of Christ according to the apostle, he proceeds with his exhortation to the Philippians, saying:

God, therefore, works both the will / and the energy / the act and the operation in spiritual matters. And they, as blameless, simple, and immaculate children of God without any reproach, have received from him the ability to be and to shine in the world like luminaries and stars in heaven. Without these (just as the heaven without luminaries and stars), the whole world would be in darkness. So too, the entire assembly of men would be foul, opaque, and covered in the thickest darkness without divine light. Such a state perhaps now exists among the Ethiopians, the Gymnosophists <note>term used for "naked philosophers," often referring to ascetic groups in India or Africa</note>, and the Cannibals <note>original: "Anthropophagos"</note>: upon whom the light of Christ has not yet shone, even though they live under the midday region of heaven where the sun of the physical world always passes. For they do not lack that light: but rather the light of Christ, so that the dark state of their life may be illuminated. Those people show what the entirely carnal man is: but the grace of Christ shows what the spiritual man is. Both of these are extremes: and both are simple <note>meaning "unmixed" or "pure" in their nature</note>. But between these and those are the middling ones: who are spiritual in appearance and on the surface / but carnal in secret. But are these the children of God? Not at all. For it is necessary for the children of God to be whole and simple. These, however, are neither wholly spiritual nor wholly carnal: they are not simple, but "double" <note>original: "duplices," meaning hypocritical or two-faced</note>. And by the same right, those are excluded from the true spiritual ones and children of God who are carnal in appearance, but chaste and spiritual in mind; for they are "double," and such people are not whole: but are transgressing the command of God's herald [Paul]. Through him, God mandates that we ought to be blameless, whole, and simple, immaculate and without reproach, shining, and not dark. And so that men might be such, we ought to willingly spend our souls, so that we might be imitators of Christ: who died for us so that we might be such: and offered himself as a victim and an oblation to God the Father for us, sacrificed on the cross. The Christ-like Paul would willingly and joyfully imitate him: undertaking a sacrifice for those whom he was acquiring for Christ—or rather, those whom Christ was acquiring for himself through him. For he who burns with the spirit, returning the good odor of life for the salvation of many: is immolated and sacrificed to God as an odor of sweetness. And he rejoices and exults in that very hour of his offering, like the holy martyrs: and by his own odor of life, he invites other men to joy and exultation. Paul did this daily, like incense placed in a censer. But now he descends to humbler matters, leaving behind the high counsel of God and disclosing his own affairs (that is, the duties of humanity: which are not 

<margin>7</margin> contrary to the spirit, but rather agreeable to it), as if descending from a great ship with many oars into a small boat / 
<margin>,</margin> but one which always stays close to the great ship, and says: "I hope in the Lord JESUS / 
<margin>,</margin> to send Timothy to you shortly: so that I also may be of good heart, having been made more certain of those things 
<margin>,</margin> which are happening around you. I have no one of a more like mind: who will sincerely care for those things which concern 
<margin>,</margin> you. For all seek their own interests: not those of JESUS CHRIST. 
<margin>,</margin> But you know the proof of him: that as a son with a father, he has served with me in the 
<margin>,</margin> gospel. I hope, therefore, to send him immediately: as soon as I see how things will go with me. I trust, 
<margin>,</margin> however, in the Lord: that I myself will also come quickly." <note>Philippians 2:19-24</note> This is a commendation of the faithfulness and integrity of Timothy by Paul: in every proof of charity toward the Philippians. Unless he visits them in person, his mind will not be satisfied. Thus love and true affection require the presence of the beloved. Paul often bore the chains of Christ in Rome: and often Christ freed him so that he might go from there wherever he wished, and wherever the spirit directed him. And although Paul was then bound: having been made certain by the spirit of God, he knew he was to be released and would travel to them. For he could have crossed the Adriatic from Rome, or by a land journey, wandering through many lands of Europe, descend to the Philippians and the Macedonians. And the Prussians <note>original: "Pruteni"</note> and a certain race of barbarians closer to the frozen pole still contend that Paul completed that journey. Although perpetual ice and frost constrain them: Paul nevertheless attempted to warm them with the life-giving and inextinguishable fire of Christ. To these people, nothing is sweeter than to hear the name of their guest Paul, the apostle of the most high God. These, therefore, are signs that Paul fulfilled what he promised concerning his own visitation. But he also sends ahead Epaphroditus, the "apostle" <note>meaning messenger or envoy</note> of the Philippians: who, having been sent by the Philippians to Paul, relieved his needs while he was held in chains, and fulfilled every duty of humanity. He who properly instructed the Philippians in the faith, and they also loved him as...

### VI

...of light and salvation / and a guide to the true life which is to know Christ / and having known Him, to follow Him as the bringer of all salvation; and by relieving Paul’s needs, he fulfilled the role of the Philippians. The apostle congratulates them: that out of the greatest and most desperate weakness, the kindness of Christ granted him life / which was still <margin>S</margin> necessary for many others / and indeed for the Philippians themselves. And he commends the man in a holy manner (for virtue is not commended except in a holy way) and adds: ¶ But I thought it necessary to send to you Epaphroditus, my brother and co-worker and fellow soldier / but your apostle / and the minister to my need: since he was indeed longing for all of you, and was distressed / for the very reason that you had heard he had labored with ill health. Indeed, he labored nearly to death. But God had mercy on him: and not only on him but also on me / so that I would not have sorrow upon sorrow. Therefore, I sent him more diligently: so that seeing him again you might rejoice / and I might be less sorrowful. Receive him, therefore, in the Lord / with all joy: and hold such as he is in honor. Because for the sake of the work of CHRIST he approached even unto death: by deliberate choice / ready to lay down his life / to fulfill toward me that which was lacking in your service. ¶ From these things we understand that Epaphroditus did not fall into a sickness so near to death from any excess / nor by chance: but from the insults and pressures which he endured for the name of Jesus / not content only to have endured those / but ready to endure such things again. And if it were necessary, to lay down his life: so that he might assist Paul, cast into chains and delivered to a harsh prison / and relieve his needs, filling the place of all the Philippians. Him, almost restored from death / for the comfort of all the Philippians: the apostle, an imitator of the God of consolation, sends ahead with this holy epistle. Therefore, let there be thanks to Christ the King <margin>A</margin> of glory: who grants us to be faithful / calling back even from death those whom He consoles unto eternal life. Amen.

<margin>S</margin> ¶ EXAMINATION of several points regarding the text. ¶ Vulgate edition: *If there be any fellowship of the spirit.* <note>original: "Si qua societas spiritus"</note> ¶ It can be said: *if there be any communion of spirit.* Paul [says]: <note>original: "εἴ τις κοινωνία πνεύματος" — eí tis koinōnía pneúmatos</note>.
¶ Vulgate edition: *If any bowels of mercy.* <note>original: "Si qua viscera miserationis"</note> ¶ Here also it can be said: *if any mercy and compassions.* Paul [says]: <note>original: "εἴ τις σπλάγχna καὶ οἰκτιρμοί" — eí tis splánchna kaí oiktirmoí</note>. For what else is <term>splánchna</term> <note>a Greek term for the internal organs, used metaphorically to mean deep-seated, visceral compassion</note> than 'bowels' or (if I may say so) 'viscerality' and mercy? ¶ Vulgate edition: *That you may be of the same mind.* <note>original: "Vt idē sapiatis"</note> ¶ 'To be of a mind' <note>original: "sapiatis"</note> is the same word which among the Latins is more commonly translated as 'to feel' <note>original: "sentire"</note>: and which in the immediately preceding chapter the old translator interpreted as 'to feel,' where he said: *It is right for me to feel this for all of you.* And of which / immediately after / he translates the participle as 'feeling' when he says *feeling the same thing.* And not much later the same word *feel* where he says: *for feel this in yourselves.* Wherefore here also it was fair that he should translate the same word as 'you may feel.' Paul [says]: <note>original: "ἵνα τὸ αὐτὸ φρονῆτε" — hína tó autó phronēte</note>. ¶ *Feeling the same thing.* ¶ Rather: *feeling one thing.* Paul [says]: <note>original: "τὸ ἓν φρονοῦντες" — tó hén phronoúntes</note>. ¶ Vulgate edition: *Nothing through contention / nor through vainglory.* ¶ The second part is specifically denied in Paul, but it is separated. Paul [says]: <note>original: "μηδὲν κατὰ ἐρίθειαν ἢ κενοδοξίαν" — mēdén katá erítheian ē kenodoxían</note>. ¶ Vulgate edition: *But in humility.* ¶ Here is the word which we said above shows 'humility of sense,' which is a certain good simplicity of reason. For if men / whether men or women / are so affected in mind and reason / in the way a sheep or a dove is in body and appetite: they are those having simplicity of mind. Paul [says]: <note>original: "ἀλλὰ τῇ ταπεινοφροσύνῃ" — allá tē tapeinophrosýnē</note>. ¶ Vulgate edition: *Thinking others superior to themselves.* ¶ It seems better to speak in the second person / and to say *to yourselves*: from that which he said above: *fulfill my joy* / and no less from this which he joins: *for feel this in yourselves.* Paul [says]: <note>original: "ἀλλήλων ἡγούμενοι ὑπερέχοντας ἑαυτῶν" — allēlōn hēgoúmenoi hyperéchontas heautōn</note>. ¶ Vulgate edition: *Each one not considering the things that are his own.* ¶ Here also one should speak through the second person: *the things which are yours* / or *be yours.* And it should be said through the verb *consider.* Paul [says]: <note>original: "μὴ τὰ ἑαυτῶν ἕκαστος σκοπεῖτε" — mē tá heautōn hékastos skopeíte</note>. ¶ Vulgate edition: *He thought it not robbery to be equal to God.* ¶ The 'himself' <note>original: "se"</note> is redundant. Paul [says]: <note>original: "οὐκ ἁρπαγμὸν ἡγήσατο τὸ εἶναι ἴσα θεῷ" — oúk harpagmón hēgēsato tó eínai ísa theō</note>. ¶ Vulgate edition: *And in habit found as a man.* ¶ The Greek figure of speech is retained. Paul [says]: <note>original: "καὶ σχήματι εὑρεθεὶς ὡς ἄνθρωπος" — kaí schēmati heuretheís hōs ánthrōpos</note>. For this word <term>schēma</term> <note>referring to outward appearance or form</note> is usually explained in many different ways: now as figure, form, appearance, outward look, manner, and sometimes even habit. ¶ Vulgate edition: *Of things in heaven / on earth / and under the earth. And let every tongue confess that the Lord JESUS is in the glory of God the Father.* ¶ It should be said: *of things in heaven and on earth.* And the phrase *let every tongue confess* and what follows can have a double meaning. One is that expressed by the old translator: so that the verb 'is' is understood after 'glory.' But both angels and all saints are in the glory of God the Father / even if that is by a very wide distinction from Christ. For Christ the Lord is in the form of God in equality of glory with God the Father; others, however, neither angels nor saints, can be in that equality of glory. Another sense is expressed here in the letter: so that the verb 'is'...
