<meta>This page continues the philological analysis of the Epistle to the Philippians, chapter 2. Having discussed the narrative of Epaphroditus on the previous page, the author now shifts into a technical comparison between the Greek source text and the Latin Vulgate translation, identifying errors in the Latin tradition and proposing more accurate renderings based on Greek grammar and vocabulary.</meta>

<header>COMMENTARY</header>

...is understood after "Lord." For to say that Christ is the Son of God, and is Lord, and is God: is to the glory of God the Father. Since He is both God and Lord, He begat both God and Lord equal to Himself by an eternal fruitfulness. And either sense is both pious and acceptable. Paul left this possibility of dual meaning to us because he did not express a specific word through which we might recognize either one sense or the other more clearly. Paul <note>original Greek: ἐπουρανίων καὶ ἐπιγείων καὶ καταχθονίων· καὶ πᾶσα γλῶσσα ἐξομολογήσηται ὅτι κύριος ἰησοῦς χριστὸς, εἰς δόξαν θεοῦ πατρός</note>: "of things in heaven, and things on earth, and things under the earth; and that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father."

<margin>B</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition.** <note>Philippians 2:12</note> "Therefore, my most dear ones, as you have always obeyed: not as in my presence only." ¶ It should read: "my beloved." And why did the ancient translator not say "in my presence" <note>original Latin: in praesentia mea</note> as he immediately after says "in my absence"? Either logic demands the use of the noun "of me" <note>mei</note> in both places, or the possessive "my" <note>mea</note> in both places. Paul <note>original Greek: ὥς τε ἀγαπητοί μου καθὼς πάντοτε ὑπηκούσατε, μὴ ὡς ἐν τῇ παρουσίᾳ μου</note>: "Wherefore, my beloved, as you have always obeyed, not as in my presence."

¶ **The Vulgate edition.** <note>Philippians 2:13</note> "Who works in you both to will and to accomplish." ¶ Because Paul uses infinitives in place of nouns, nothing seemed inappropriate if we were to use nouns, which are more customary to Latin speakers than using infinitives as nouns. Furthermore, Paul's vocabulary says "to work" rather than "to accomplish." Paul <note>original Greek: ὁ ἐνεργῶν ἐν ὑμῖν καὶ τὸ θέλειν καὶ τὸ ἐνεργεῖν</note>: "He who works in you both the willing and the working." And why, indeed, when they are so close together, does the ancient translator interpret "the one working" <note>original Greek: ὁ ἐνεργῶν</note> as "who works," but then renders "to work" <note>original Greek: τὸ ἐνεργεῖν</note> as "to accomplish"?

¶ **The Vulgate edition.** <note>Philippians 2:14</note> "But do all things without murmurings and hesitations." ¶ It is sufficient to say "do all things." And where the ancient translator said "hesitations," it could be called "disputations" or "discussions"—that is, with much debate. For it does not befit earthly servants to murmur, nor to refuse to do the commands of their masters unless they have debated them. How much less would these things befit spiritual servants, who boast that they have a Lord, not on earth but in the heavens, who is a most sharp observer of all their deeds and words, and from whom no thought can escape. Paul <note>original Greek: πάντα ποιεῖτε χωρὶς γογγυσμῶν καὶ διαλογισμῶν</note>: "Do all things without murmurings and reasonings."

¶ **The Vulgate edition.** <note>Philippians 2:15</note> "Without reproach, in the midst of a crooked nation." ¶ It can also be said here at the beginning: "spotless." Paul <note>original Greek: ἀμώμητα ἐν μέσῳ γενεᾶς σκολιᾶς</note>: "blameless in the midst of a crooked generation." Indeed, they are accustomed to interpret <term>amōmon</term><note>Greek: ἀμώμον, meaning without blemish or spot</note> as "spotless" as well. This is not without reason, for he who is without spot is deservedly irreproachable.

<margin>C</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition.** <note>Philippians 2:17</note> "But even if I am envied upon the sacrifice and service of your faith." ¶ It should read: "I am sacrificed" <note>immolor</note>, not "I am envied" <note>emulor</note>. I suspect it happened through the fault of scribes that it is now read as "envied" in many manuscripts. <note>The translator notes that the Latin words "emulor" and "immolor" are visually similar, leading to a long-standing error in the Latin Bible.</note> Paul <note>original Greek: ἀλλ’ εἰ καὶ σπένδομαι ἐπὶ τῇ θυσίᾳ καὶ λειτουργίᾳ τῆς πίστεως ὑμῶν</note>: "But if I am even poured out as a drink offering upon the sacrifice and service of your faith."

¶ **The Vulgate edition.** <note>Philippians 2:18</note> "And for that same thing, you also rejoice." ¶ Regarding that phrase "that same thing," I think it could more properly be said in Latin custom as <term>itidem</term> <note>meaning "likewise" or "in the same way"</note> (that is, "that very same," but the 'd' changes to 't' among grammarians for the sake of pleasant sound) or <term>identidem</term> <note>meaning "repeatedly" or "again and again"</note>. Paul <note>original Greek: τὸ δ’ αὐτὸ καὶ ὑμεῖς χαίρετε</note>: "And in the same way, you also rejoice."

¶ **The Vulgate edition.** <note>Philippians 2:20</note> "For I have no one so like-minded who with sincere affection is solicitous for you." ¶ It does not say "with sincere affection" in the Greek, but only a single adverb which signifies "genuinely," "nobly," "peculiarly," or something similar. Paul <note>original Greek: οὐδένα γὰρ ἔχω ἰσόψυχον, ὅστις γνησίως τὰ περὶ ὑμῶν μεριμνήσῃ</note>: "For I have no one of like soul, who will genuinely care for your affairs."

¶ **The Vulgate edition.** <note>Philippians 2:21</note> "For all seek the things that are their own." ¶ The effort of those who "seek" is not concerned with what they already have, but mostly with what they wish to have. Therefore, it seems it should equally or rather be said in the future or optative mood: "for all seek what *might* be their own," rather than in the present indicative "are." Paul, however, did not express a specific verb here. And it said "of Christ Jesus." Therefore, the order in the Vulgate edition has been changed. Paul <note>original Greek: οἱ πάντες γὰρ τὰ ἑαυτῶν ζητοῦσιν, οὐ τὰ χριστοῦ ἰησοῦ</note>: "For they all seek their own things, not the things of Christ Jesus."

¶ **The Vulgate edition.** <note>Philippians 2:22</note> "But know the proof of him." ¶ This can equally be interpreted through the present indicative. Paul <note>original Greek: τὴν δὲ δοκιμὴν αὐτοῦ γινώσκετε</note>: "But you know his proven character."

¶ **The Vulgate edition.** <note>Philippians 2:22</note> "Because as a son with a father he has served with me in the gospel." ¶ So that "me" and "father" are said in the same case, just as they are said in the same case in Greek: I took "with" from the following part and prefixed it to "father." For in this way the speech seems better suited to Latinity. Paul <note>original Greek: ὅτι ὡς πατρὶ τέκνον σὺν ἐμοὶ ἐδούλευσεν εἰς τὸ εὐαγγέλιον</note>: "that as a child with a father, he has served with me for the gospel."

¶ **The Vulgate edition.** <note>Philippians 2:23</note> "As soon as I shall have seen what things are around me." ¶ It seems it should rather be understood as the future tense, and therefore expressed as "will be" rather than "are." Paul <note>original Greek: ὡς ἂν ἀπίδω τὰ περὶ ἐμέ</note>: "as soon as I see how things go with me."

<margin>D</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition.** <note>Philippians 2:27</note> "For indeed he was sick even unto death." ¶ It does not say "even unto" <note>usque ad</note>; rather, the word placed here speaks more of "nearness." Paul <note>original Greek: καὶ γὰρ ἠσθένησε παραπλήσιον θανάτῳ</note>: "For indeed he was sick, neighbor to death."

¶ **The Vulgate edition.** <note>Philippians 2:28</note> "And I may be without sorrow." ¶ He seems to be expressing a reduction here, as if we were to say "less sorrowful" or "less sad." Paul <note>original Greek: κἀγὼ ἀλυπότερος ὦ</note>: "and I may be less sorrowful."

¶ **The Vulgate edition.** <note>Philippians 2:30</note> "He approached even unto death, delivering up his soul." ¶ He "drew near" rather than "approached." The word "unto" <note>quam</note> at the end is redundant. And the ancient translator, in saying "delivering up his soul," expresses less than what the Greek intends, which designates not just delivering up the soul, but doing so by will, of one's own accord, and by deliberation. Paul <note>original Greek: μέχρι θανάτου ἤγγισε, παραβουλευσάμενος τῇ ψυχῇ</note>: "He drew near to death, having risked his life."

<meta>This page transitions from the narrative of Epaphroditus’s journey to the theological warnings contained in Chapter 3 of the Epistle to the Philippians. Having established the context of the messenger's return, the author now interprets Paul’s stern warnings against those who would force Christian converts to follow Jewish ritual laws.</meta>

### VI 177 CHAPTER III. Philippians

Now there were certain things about which Epaphroditus, after the shared joy of his arrival, was to warn the Philippians, as well as things pertaining to the office of the apostle; here Paul reveals them. Those warnings were these: that they should not be led astray by the old <term>leaven</term> <note>original Latin: "fermento"; a biblical metaphor for influence or corruption</note> of the Jews, be circumcised, and submit their necks to the slavery of the Law, whom the grace of Christ had made free, and made so freely. For when the firstborn son of some earthly king enters a place, the captives and those condemned to heavy labor are released for free. And whoever imposes slavery or other burdens upon those released by grace (unless something else occurs) does an injury to the king’s son. 

In the same way, when the Son of the eternal King illuminated this world with His holy arrival, when He entered the prison of this world, shining with the splendor of His glory upon those who were in darkness and in the shadow of death: He freely liberated all captives and those condemned to the harsh commands of death. And he who wishes to subject those liberated to slavery does an injury to the grace of Christ our Liberator—as if the grace of Christ were not so great that it could fully liberate and make them free. It is as if the Son of the eternal King, being Himself eternal, were not great enough that by His arrival in the very city He Himself founded, He could give complete freedom to the captives and the oppressed. 

You Jews, who deny the grace of the Son of God and dishonor His holy arrival into the world: repent! To wish to reduce the free into slavery is to envy their freedom. Circumcision was a seal of faith before the liberation from burdens. If a male pressed by the yoke of slavery lacked this, his soul was cut off. He says, "The male whose flesh of his foreskin is not circumcised: that soul shall be deleted from his people." <note>A reference to Genesis 17:14</note> Therefore, what you now do in the flesh is no longer circumcision (for the definition no longer fits), but is a certain <term>concision</term> <note>original Latin: "concisio"; Paul uses a pun here, contrasting "peritome" (circumcision) with "katatome" (mutilation or "concision")</note> opposed to circumcision. For whoever is "cut" in this way and (so to speak) <term>unskinned</term> <note>original Latin: "recutitus"; a derogatory term for those circumcised</note>, his soul shall be cut off, unless he returns to the grace of the Savior and places his salvation in that alone. 

Therefore, those who persuade others to be circumcised do not circumcise, but rather they "concise" and skin them. They envy salvation; they do not save. They waste effort; they do not truly labor. But by what name are such people more aptly called than "dogs," whose nature is to love slavery and to envy all strangers? For this reason, Paul—lifting the minds of the Philippians toward heavenly joy and fortifying them against such people, making them cautious—adds the following:

> For the rest, my brothers, rejoice in the Lord. To write the same things to you is not tedious for me, and for you it is safe. Beware of the dogs, beware of the evil workers, beware of the <term>concision</term>. For we are the circumcision, we who worship by the Spirit of God and glory in CHRIST JESUS, and have no confidence in the flesh. Although I myself might seem to have confidence in the flesh. If anyone else seems to be able to trust in the flesh, I more so: circumcised on the eighth day, of the race of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew of Hebrews; according to the law, a Pharisee. According to zeal, I persecuted the church; according to the righteousness which is in the law, I became blameless. But what things were gain to me, these I have counted as loss for the sake of CHRIST. But indeed, I count all things as loss because of the excellence of the knowledge of CHRIST JESUS my Lord. For whose sake I have treated all things as <term>worthless wool</term> <note>original Latin: "floccifeci"</note> and consider them to be dung, that I may gain CHRIST, and be found in Him, not having my own righteousness which is from the law, but that righteousness which is from God through the faith of CHRIST. That in faith I may know Him, and the power of His resurrection, and the fellowship of His sufferings, being conformed to His death, if by any means I may attain to the resurrection of the dead.

Paul was circumcised on the eighth day according to the precept of the old law, of the race of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew of Hebrews, a Pharisee by sect (which seemed more religious and observant of legal matters), who had such zeal for the ancient law that he persecuted the church, becoming blameless in the observances of the law—Paul, I say, who was such a man, trusts in these things not at all, and considers all these things as nothing. How then should the Gentiles—who are neither circumcised on the eighth day as the law commands, nor are of the race of Israel, nor of any tribe, nor Hebrews, nor of any sect, without any zeal for the law, without any observation of circumcision and the legalities of the Hebrews—how should they trust in these things? How can they think those things will benefit them? If they have any reason at all, they certainly should not. 

Paul used this "argument from the greater" to show that human things must align with divine ones. Truly, just as Christ is the true Paschal Lamb, so is the Baptism of Christ the true circumcision. For it is a seal of faith; if anyone lacks it, his soul will be cut off. He says, "Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God." <note>John 3:5</note> How then is it not the true circumcision, since the definition of the truth of circumcision fits it? In Baptism, we die with Christ, circumcised in all our flesh by the Rock which is Christ, so that we may be entirely spirit. For how, having been made spiritual, are we not circumcised in the flesh? We rise with Christ, so that being thus "Christ-formed," we may attain to the final resurrection of the dead. And so great is the excellence of the knowledge of Christ, of grace, and of His mysteries compared to the righteousness of the old law and its observances: as great as light is to darkness, freedom to slavery, gain to loss, the precious to dung, and the divine to the earthly. But who, when offered—

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Philippians Chapter 3, specifically interpreting Paul’s shift from rejecting the Jewish Law to describing the spiritual race toward Christ. It maintains the theme of moving from "shadows" to "reality."</meta>

# COMMENTARY

Light, liberty, gain, the precious and the divine: Paul does not merely disregard and count as nothing the darkness, slavery, loss, the dung-heap, and the earthly; rather, the knowledge of Christ, His righteousness, and His grace were to be esteemed so highly, so remarkably and preeminently, that the righteousness of the Law—with its ritual observances and works—was to be considered worthless, vile, and cast aside. 

But someone might say: "Since you value it so much, Paul, and you possess such an eminent knowledge of Christ, have you already grasped it? Are you already blessed? Have you already attained that perfection which others expect at the resurrection?" 

Paul excellently refutes this. For he still runs in hope, not yet in full enjoyment. He runs in certain hope, always stretching himself toward what is ahead and what is better; he is not yet resting at the finish line—which is the state of being *in* Christ, rather than the race *toward* Christ. That state is the enjoyment of Christ, not the hope and desire of enjoying Him. It is the act, not the habit; the day, not the night; the face, not

<margin>10</margin>
the veil; the truth, not the footprint. For this reason, Paul adds: 

¶ Not that I have already grasped it, or have already been perfected: but I pursue it, if I may also grasp that in which I was grasped by CHRIST JESUS. Brothers, I do not yet consider myself to have grasped it. One thing I do: forgetting what is behind, and stretching myself toward what is ahead, I pursue the goal for the prize of the upward call of God in CHRIST JESUS. Therefore, as many of us as are perfect, let us think this way. And if you think otherwise in anything, God will reveal this to you also. Nevertheless, to what we have reached, let us lean upon the same rule, let us think the same thing. 

¶ What is that in which Paul was grasped by Christ Jesus, if not the truth, the <term>archetype</term> <note>original: "archetypus"; the original model or reality that symbols point toward</note>, and the pattern? Therefore, he was pursuing and running so that he might grasp the truth, the archetype, and the pattern, wishing to leave behind the mere likenesses, <term>types</term> <note>original: "typos"; symbolic foreshadowings found in the Old Testament</note>, and footprints. 

What are those things that are behind, and those that are ahead? 
**Behind:** the Old Law, legal observances, likenesses, types, and figures. 
**Ahead:** the New Law, the mysteries of Christ, the truth, the archetype, and the pattern. 

Yet, as long as we live, the mysteries of Christ—which are the realities behind the Hebrew types—are nonetheless still "types" of the heavenly truths. These heavenly truths will first be revealed when we grasp that in which we were grasped, and when we no longer see through a veil, but face to face. Paul especially pursues those "naked" truths, no longer covered by a sacred veil or shadowed. Toward this goal—that is, the sign and the predefined finish line—he has Christ as his target. Just as those who aim all their arrows at a target to receive the prize, so he directs all his actions toward Christ, never turning his eyes away from Christ, so that he might attain the heavenly palm of eternal life in that very truth. This prize is not one that merit or works produced, but one which the grace of the "upward call" imparts. 

The Philippians were meant to think this way. But if they thought otherwise, being deceived by error, Paul predicts that God will reveal the truth of this to them, just as he has opened the goal of divine truth. Nevertheless, in this state which we have reached (for we have reached the symbols of Christ, the light that replaces the Hebrew shadows, but not yet the final grasping), let us lean upon the same rule and think the same thing. Our rule is the Gospel of Christ, held in all harmony and identity of thought. For where there is diversity, where there is a sect or a heresy, there is no identity or truth in thinking. I speak of symbolic truth, which also has a higher "pattern"—the goal and the predestined finish line toward which Paul, a runner and knower of the divine way, always intended to proceed. Therefore, he offers himself as an example to the Philippians, so that they might reach the ultimate Pattern. He offers himself as an example in the manner of those who, having climbed first, know the paths to the 

<margin>11</margin>
heights; and he accuses those who prepare pitfalls for those wishing to climb. The Pattern, however, is higher than heaven, while the pitfall is deeper than the abyss. Therefore, Paul, our leader under the Eternal Leader, says: 

¶ Join with others in following my example, brothers, and consider those who walk according to the pattern you have in us. For many walk, of whom I have often told you (and now tell you even weeping) that they are enemies of the cross of CHRIST. Their end is destruction; their god is their belly; and their glory is in their shame, for they mind earthly things. For our <term>republic</term> <note>original: "respublica"; often translated as "citizenship" or "commonwealth," implying the community to which a person truly belongs</note> is in heaven, from which also we await the Savior, our Lord JESUS CHRIST, who will transform the body of our humility so that it becomes conformed to the body of His glory, according to the working of His power, by which He is able to subject all things to Himself. 

¶ When Paul invites the Philippians to imitate him, he is calling them to the imitation of the *Exemplar* (the Pattern), who is Christ, and to fix their eye on Christ. But when he tells them to look to him, he does not call them to the *Exemplar*, but to the *type* and the *example*. For an example is a "type," whereas the Pattern is the "archetype." Anyone who imitates another as if they were the final end of imitation, rather than Christ, imitates poorly. Even Paul says he is nothing but a "type" of imitation, from which one must immediately pass to the Pattern. This is not without reason. For the Church of Christ, even while it dwells on earth, borrows the order of its governance and function from heavenly patterns. Even the things it does for the time being are "types"; the "patterns" themselves are in heaven. 

Therefore, in truth, our republic is in heaven; that which is on earth is symbolic. Is the republic not wherever the King is? Our King, Christ, blessed above all, is in heaven. From there we await His arrival, when He will come in His majesty with all His angels. Then we will be changed; and for those who are worthy of that region of light, He will transform their bodies into the likeness of His own glorious body, according to His omnipotence, by which He can subject all things to Himself. Then the types [will end]...

<summary>Paul distinguishes between his current "race" of faith and the future "fruition" of heaven, using the metaphor of a runner aiming at Christ as the target. He defines Christian life as moving away from Old Testament "shadows" toward the heavenly "archetype," urging believers to view their true citizenship as being in heaven where Christ the King resides.</summary>

# EXAMINATION of several points concerning the literal text.
¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *See the concision* <note>Philippians 3:2</note>. It could have been translated as "bruising" or "crushing," but since it is translated as "concision" <note>original: *concisio*, meaning a cutting-up or mutilation</note>, the wordplay on the name "circumcision" is better. In Latin, "bruising" does not play upon the word "circumcision" as it does in the Greek. Paul writes: *blepete tēn katatomēn* <note>original: βλέπετε την κατατομήν</note>. For when one says *peritomēn* <note>circumcision</note> and *katatomē* <note>mutilation/concision</note>, the names play upon each other. 

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Who serve God in the spirit*. It would be better to say: *who worship God in the spirit*, or *who hold worship*, so that "God" is joined with "worship" rather than "serve." For the word used in this passage signifies "worship" <term>cultura: religious veneration or service</term> and requires a dative case in Greek. However, in Paul’s text, "of God" is written in the genitive, not "to God" in the dative. Paul writes: *hoi pneumati theou latreuontes* <note>original: οἱ πνεύματι θεοῦ λατρεύοντες; "who by the Spirit of God worship"</note>.

<margin>B</margin>
¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Though I also might have confidence in the flesh*. This could also be translated according to Paul's meaning, while preserving the proper nature of the Latin language, in this way: *nevertheless, I too would have confidence in the flesh, if anyone else seemed to trust in the flesh*. Or, as explained above from the Greek text. For in this way, he seems to assert it less strongly than if it is said: *although I too have confidence in the flesh*. But how could Paul assert that he has confidence in the flesh, when immediately before he said: *and we glory in Christ Jesus, and have no confidence in the flesh*? 

<margin>9 test. 9 lived</margin>
Paul writes: *kaiper egō echōn pepoithēsin kai en sarki* <note>original: καίπερ ἐγὼ ἔχων πεποίθησιν καὶ ἐν σαρκί; "though I myself am having confidence also in the flesh"</note>. 

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Lived without reproach*. It should rather be read: *became blameless*. Paul writes: *genomenos amemptos* <note>original: γενόμενος ἄμεμπτος</note>. 

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *These things I have counted losses for Christ*.

<margin>C dung: addition.</margin>
¶ Paul uses the singular: *loss* or *damage*. Paul writes: *tauta hēgēmai dia ton christon zēmian* <note>original: ταῦτα ἥγημαι διὰ τὸν χριστὸν ζημίαν; "these things I have counted, because of Christ, a loss"</note>. 

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *For whom I have suffered the loss of all things, and count them as dung, that I may gain Christ and be found in him*. Instead of "suffered the loss," one could say "regarded as a penalty," which is more than simply "valuing at nothing." Paul therefore valued all things—especially legal observances—as nothing for the sake of Christ, and even more than nothing: as a "loss" and an "impediment" that hindered the acquisition of Christ. As for the phrases *as dung* and *that I may be found*: here the "that" <note>original: *ut*</note> is redundant. And after "dung," the word "to be" is missing. Paul writes: *Di' hon ta panta ezēmiōthēn, kai hēgoumai skubala einai, hina christon kerdēsō, kai heurethō en autō* <note>original: Δι’ ὃν τὰ πάντα ἐζημιώθην, καὶ ἡγοῦμαι σκύβαλα εἶναι, ἵνα χριστὸν κερδήσω, καὶ εὑρεθῶ ἐν αὐτῷ</note>. 

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *But that [righteousness] which is from the faith of Christ Jesus, which is the righteousness from God*. The word "Jesus" is extra according to the Greek manuscripts. And "righteousness" at the end should be said in the accusative case. Paul writes: *alla tēn dia pisteōs christou tēn ek theou dikaiosynēn* <note>original: ἀλλὰ τὴν διὰ πίσεως χριστοῦ τὴν ἐκ θεοῦ δικαιοσύνην</note>. But this is excusable in the ancient translator, as he changed the accusative article into the nominative. Therefore, he also changed that to which the article belonged into the nominative, and said "righteousness" <note>original: *iustitia*</note> in the nominative case. Truly, this is a very small point. 

¶ **The Vulgate edition:**
<margin>edition</margin>
*And the fellowship of his sufferings*. It can be called "communion," "communication," or something similar. For whenever anyone dies for Christ, a communion of His sufferings is understood here. Is He not the head of the whole body and of all its members? When the members suffer, He suffers with them all; and when they die, He dies with them. In Himself, He is indeed immortal; but in His members, with whom He fills the earth, He is mortal until the last day. This precious death is fulfilled daily in deeds, and most of all in the glorious martyrs for His name. 

We have seen this happen even in our own age in the case of **Little Simon of Trent** <note>Simon of Trent was a boy whose death in 1475 was falsely attributed to the Jewish community, leading to a "blood libel" trial. He was venerated as a martyr at the time this was written</note>, a boy scarcely three years old. In him, the faithless Jews re-crucified Christ the Lord of glory as much as they could. They stretched out his arms, pierced his hands and feet, opened his side, and inflicted insults, mockery, and reproaches upon him as if upon Christ, finishing him with a most cruel death. But Christ, recognizing and showing His own passion in him, in memory of the infant in whom He had suffered, gave light to the blind, made the deaf hear, the mute speak, cleansed lepers, raised the dead, and performed every sign by which He is truly recognized to be Christ, who alone does great and stupendous things. 

In the year 1500, which was a Universal Jubilee, I saw the body of the blessed infant; with those marks, he shall meet the judgment more radiant than the stars. I also saw then the infant's mother, not yet forty years old in my estimation, through whom I commended myself to God with the holy prayers of the martyr. 

And so that this "communication of the sufferings of Christ" in the martyrs may be even better understood in practice, let us hear Linus—or rather Christ Himself—speaking in the *Passion of the Apostle Peter* <note>referring to the apocryphal *Acts of Peter* attributed to Linus, Peter's successor</note>. For when Peter was about to suffer, and being overcome by the tears of many, was declining martyrdom by fleeing for the safety of the survivors, Linus writes: "While he was going," he says, "the bandages fell from his leg, having been loosened by the shackle. But as he wished to go out of the city gate, he saw Christ coming to meet him, and adoring Him, he said: 'Lord, where are you going?' <note>The famous phrase *Quo vadis?*</note> Christ answered him: 'I am coming to Rome to be crucified again.' And Peter said to Him: 'Lord, are you being crucified again?'"

<meta>This page continues the philological and theological commentary on the Epistle to the Philippians, specifically transitioning from the "fellowship of sufferings" in Chapter 3 to the exhortations for steadfastness and heavenly citizenship in Chapter 4.</meta>

<header>COMMENTARY</header>

The Lord said to him: "Yes, I am to be crucified again." But Peter said: "Lord, I shall return and follow you." And when these things were said, the Lord ascended into heaven. Peter, however, followed him with a long gaze and most sweet tears. After this, returning to himself, he understood that this was said concerning his own passion <note>original: *passione*; here meaning suffering or martyrdom</note>, in that the Lord was to suffer within him. Thus says Linus <note>Saint Linus, traditionally the second Pope, to whom an account of Peter’s martyrdom is attributed</note>. This is the fellowship of the sufferings of Christ. And since the members of Christ are more closely joined to Christ than our own hand or foot is to us, who can doubt that whatever is inflicted upon a member of Christ is inflicted upon Christ himself? For indeed, whatever is inflicted upon our hand or foot is also inflicted upon us. When the hand suffers, we suffer; when the foot suffers, we suffer; so much more when a member of Christ suffers, Christ also suffers. Whatever shall be brought upon a member of Christ—whether good or evil, whatever it may be—it shall be accounted as done to Christ. Therefore, let this fellowship of Christ and his members make all people cautious: lest while they believe they are offending a mere man, and see nothing else but a man, they might offend Christ himself, the Lord, King, and Judge of all. But enough of these matters. Paul says: *and the fellowship of his sufferings* <note>original Greek: καὶ τὴν κοινωρίαν τῶν παθημάτων αὐτοῦ</note>.

<margin>c 9</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *If by any means I may attain to the resurrection which is from the dead.* This is the same as if we were to say: "that by some means I may reach the resurrection of the dead." For Paul’s usage and habit of speaking is sometimes to use the particle "if" <note>Latin: *si*</note> in place of "so that" <note>Latin: *vt*</note>; not expressing doubt, but rather making an assertion, as in the present passage.

<margin>C 10</margin> Paul says: *if by any means I might attain unto the resurrection of the dead* <note>original Greek: εἴπως καταντήσω εἰς τὴν ἐξανάςασιν τῶν νεκρῶν</note>.

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Brethren, I do not count myself to have apprehended.* It should read: *not yet* <note>original: *nondum*</note> I count. Paul says: *Brethren, I count not myself yet to have apprehended* <note>original Greek: ἀδελφοὶ ἐγὼ ἐμαυτὸν οὔπω λογίζομαι κατειληφέναι</note>.

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *I press toward the mark, for the prize of the high calling of God.* Where the ancient translator says "the mark" <note>original: *destinatum*</note>, it designates that which we have especially fixed in our mind as an intent and (so to speak) the object and end toward which we direct all our acts as the nearest goal to be achieved. Once this is achieved, we have obtained the heavenly prize <note>original: *brauium*, from the Greek *brabeion* meaning a prize in an athletic contest</note>. Just as archers set a target for themselves, at which they always aim; and as they hit it as closely as possible, they shall obtain the prize. Christ, however, is our target <note>original: *scopus*</note>; we ought not to look toward any other when we perform any work or abstain from anything, but toward him alone with the greatest attention. Otherwise, we shall be like bad archers who shoot their arrows at random, worthy of no prize, but rather of disgrace and ignominy. Paul says: *I press toward the mark for the prize of the high calling of God* <note>original Greek: κατὰ σκοπὸν Διώκω ἐπὶ τὸ βραβεῖον τῆς ἄνω κλήσεως τοῦ θεοῦ</note>.

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *And this God hath revealed unto you.* It should be read in the future tense: *shall reveal*. Paul says: *and this God shall reveal unto you* <note>original Greek: καὶ τοῦτο ὁ θεὸς ὑμῖν ἀποκαλύψει</note>.

<margin>D 10</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Nevertheless, whereto we have attained, let us mind the same thing, and let us remain in the same rule.* The order of the particles is changed. And where it is said "that we may mind the same thing," the word "that" <note>Latin: *vt*</note> is redundant. Paul says: *Nevertheless, whereto we have already attained, let us walk by the same rule, let us mind the same thing* <note>original Greek: πλὴν εἰς ὃ ἐφθάσαμεν, τῷ αὐτῷ στοιχεῖν κανόνι, τὸ αὐτὸ φρονεῖν</note>. Nevertheless, to that which we have reached: the same rule must be leaned upon, the same thing must be felt. And it is the same if the infinitives are resolved into the subjunctive mood.

<margin>D 11</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Brethren, be followers of me.* Paul says: *be co-imitators of me* <note>original: *coimitatores*</note>. But what is "co-imitators of me" except "imitators together with me"? Paul says: *Brethren, be followers together of me* <note>original Greek: συμμιμηταί μου γίρεσθε ἀδελφοί</note>.

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *As you have our form.* It can be said: *as you have us for an example*. Paul says: *as you have us for a pattern* <note>original Greek: καθώς ἔχετε τύπον ἡμᾶς</note>.

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *But our conversation is in heaven.* It seems better to say here: *for our commonwealth is in heaven*, rather than "conversation" <note>original: *conversatio*; in the 16th century this meant conduct or way of life</note>. For our daily conduct is not yet in heaven, but our true commonwealth <note>term: *respublica*: citizenship or political community</note> is in heaven. For we are still occupied in the world and among the symbols of things, and not yet among the truths of the symbols. Therefore, in the governing of lower things, the heavenly governance must be attended to, so that all things may be done in imitation of the true commonwealth which is in heaven. There, symbols do not exist, but rather the truths of the symbols. Paul says: *for our citizenship is in heaven* <note>original Greek: ἡμῶν γὰρ πολίτευμα, ἐν οὐρανοῖς</note>.

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *From whence also we look for the Savior, our Lord JESUS CHRIST, who shall reform the body of our lowness, made like to the body of his glory.* Where it says "from whence also," the Greek has "from which things also." The word "our" is redundant. "Who shall reform" would be better as "who shall transfigure." "Made like" means "conformed." "Of his clarity" <note>original: *claritatis*</note> means "of his glory." Paul says: *from whence also we look for the Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, who shall change our vile body, that it may be fashioned like unto his glorious body* <note>original Greek: ἐξ ὧ καὶ σωτῆρα ἀπεκδεχόμεθα κύριον ἰησοῦν χριςὸν, ὃς μετασχηματίσει τὸ σῶμα τῆς ταπεινώσεως ἡμῶν, εἰς τὸ γένεσθαι αὐτὸ σύμμορφον τῶ σώματι τῆς δόξης αὐτοῦ</note>.

<margin>12</margin> Expressing the great kindness of Christ the Savior in both deed and word, the Apostle prays for the Philippians that they might so stand fast in Christ, caring nothing for circumcision and legal shadows—which, by the illumination of the first coming of the Savior, go into nothingness, as darkness does when the sun rises. And so, moved by the spirit of God’s kindness, he says to the Philippians: ¶ *Therefore, my dearly beloved brethren and longed for, my joy and crown, so stand fast in the Lord, my dearly beloved.* ¶ And not only does the spirit of the fervor and love of Christ take care for men, but also for women: lest they should permit or persuade their sons to be circumcised, but rather that they might think the same concerning the faith of Christ as the men do. <meta>This page continues the commentary on the Epistle to the Philippians, moving into Chapter 4. It addresses Paul’s personal exhortations to specific members of the Philippian church and his famous discourse on peace, virtue, and contentment.</meta>

# VI 169 Philippians.

<margin>13</margin> Eusebius and the Greek commentators <note>original: *Græci*; referring to the Eastern Church Fathers</note> record that Paul does not remain silent regarding his own wife, to whom he commends other women, especially so that she might be of assistance to those who labored in the gospel. In this farewell portion of the letter, he greets her along with the others, adding what follows: ¶ **I urge Euodia and I also urge Syntyche to be of the same mind in the Lord.** <note>original: *Euodiam rogo/ etiam Syntychen rogo: idem sentire in domino*</note> **I also urge you, noble spouse** <note>original: *ingenua coniunx*; this refers to the "loyal yoke-fellow" mentioned in Phil 4:3, which this author interprets as Paul's wife</note>, **help these women who have struggled with me in the gospel, along with Clement and the rest of my co-workers, whose names are in the book of life. Rejoice in the Lord always; again I say, rejoice. Let your gentleness be known to all people. The Lord is near.** <note>original: *Dominus prope est*</note> **Be anxious for nothing, but in every prayer and petition, with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God. And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, shall guard your hearts and your minds in CHRIST JESUS.** ¶ Behold, he called upon two by name—Euodia and Syntyche—and he requested and greeted his own wife, wishing her a holy farewell. He demanded that both men and women appear mild and gentle before everyone. He announced that the Lord is near. He taught that we should have no other anxiety except for praying, petitioning, and seeking the kingdom of God, his justice, and the necessities of life from God with thanksgiving. 

But what does it mean that "the Lord is near"? It is certain that this temporal life is short, and its end is death. When death is present, the Lord is also present. We have run the race-course; at the finish line stands Christ the Lord, the judge of either life or punishment. Therefore, if it is clear to anyone that death is near and that they lead a short and uncertain life, it is also clear that the Lord is near. To him, at that moment, a strict and particular account of our actions must be rendered. But when the apostle wants us to set aside all anxiety except for prayer, petition, thanksgiving, and the like, does he want us to be idle? By no means. For those who do these things are not idle. Rather, he wants them to work, cooperating with God's providence for the necessities of life, to cherish honesty, and to perform all the duties of virtue. For they had seen Paul working so that he would not eat bread for free, which is a matter of integrity. For this reason, he adds: ¶ **Finally, brothers: whatever is true, whatever is honorable, whatever is just, whatever is pure, whatever is lovely, whatever is commendable, if there is any virtue and if there is any praise: think on these things. What you have learned and received and heard and seen in me: do these things. And the god of peace will be with you.** ¶ Behold how he wants us to be truthful, serious, just, temperate, and devoted to each of the virtues that the philosophers recommend. It is not that our righteousness consists in these things, but they prepare us to receive it, and they preserve it once it is held. For an image is not formed except in a clean and polished mirror, nor is the divine likeness formed except in a soul that is, in a sense, prepared, polished, and clean. He who devotes himself to no virtue and no honorable thing is like a dead tree trunk, which is not brought to life by the arriving rays of the sun. Likewise, such a person is not brought to life by the rays of Christ's grace, which shine in all and over all. But as soon as one begins to perform some work of virtue, they are known to be coming to life, just as a tree first puts forth leaves. 

<margin>15</margin> ¶ Therefore, having recognized the work of virtue among the Philippians, Paul congratulates them, saying: ¶ **I rejoiced in the Lord greatly that at last you have flourished again** <note>original: *reviruistis*; literally "to grow green again," like a plant in spring</note> **to care for me. In this you were indeed concerned, but you lacked opportunity. Not that I speak because of need; for I have learned to be content in whatever state I am. I know how to be brought low, and I know how to abound in every thing. In all things I am instructed: both to be full and to be hungry, both to abound and to suffer need. I can do all things in CHRIST who makes me strong.** ¶ Paul had admonished the Philippians to the work of piety toward the saints, but they had been slow to provide that help, as if they lacked the sap and moisture of life, or were not of the same mind as the apostle in extending their hands in the duty of piety. But at last they "flourished again," taking up the sap of virtue once more through the fertilizing grace of Christ. For this, Paul exults in the Lord with a great spirit, and simultaneously excuses them (such is his kindness) by saying they were not slow because they lacked the will to do the work of piety, but because they had not yet had the opportunity or the means. Indeed, Paul equally excuses himself, noting that he did not do this because of his own poverty. For in whatever was present, whether much or little, he knew how to have sufficiency. He knew how to endure prosperity and adversity equally. And that he could do this in all things, remaining unconquerable—this was not his own power, but the power that Christ administered to him, in whom he could do all things, and who is the source of all power. Truly, the Philippians were so devoted to the work of piety that they were vigilant not only for the common needs of the saints, but even sent help for Paul's private needs. And who would not know that Paul could not truly lack? For how can he who has Christ in his heart—who is the sum of all good—be in need? How can one who is great-souled by the greatness of the true Christ be in need? For him, poverty for Christ’s sake is wealth; pressures and troubles are joy. He who counts the riches and honors of this whole world as nothing, considers the grace of Christ alone to be his wealth and sufficiency, with which he is abundantly filled and overflowing.

# Commentary

...gives; who then would not know that Paul was in need? Even if he were in the greatest of prisons and pressures, he was in want. Nevertheless, he gives thanks to God for the Philippians because, once and again, when they understood him to be in distress, they sent support for his personal necessities to Paul as he was departing from Macedonia to Thessalonica; and afterward, they sent aid through Epaphroditus. Other churches had neglected to do this. In this, he commends the Philippians—not looking at the gifts themselves, but at the **affection** of the giver and the **fruit of virtue** in those giving. This preparation allows for the more generous and abundant reception of the illuminating and life-giving grace of Christ.

For the angels who descended to Abraham <note>Referring to the story in Genesis 18 where Abraham hosts three divine visitors.</note> did not stand in need of the washing of feet, the cakes, the butter, or the cooked calf; rather, they accepted the grace of hospitality as a fruit of Abraham's virtuous goodwill. In this same way, Paul—the herald and angel of the most high God—did not stand in need of the Philippians' gifts, even if he greatly <margin>16</margin> approved of them doing so. This was not because of the gifts themselves, but because of the virtue they were acquiring for themselves, which is acceptable and well-pleasing. For this reason, he adds: 

¶ **Nevertheless, you have done well by sharing in my distress. And you yourselves know, O Philippians, that in the beginning of the gospel when I set out from Macedonia, no church shared with me in the matter of giving and receiving except you alone. For even in Thessalonica, you sent aid for my needs once and again. Not that I seek the gift, but I seek the more abundant fruit for your account. I have received everything and have plenty. I am filled, having received from Epaphroditus the things sent by you: a fragrant aroma, an acceptable sacrifice, well-pleasing to God. But my God will supply your every need according to his riches in glory, in CHRIST JESUS. To our God and Father be glory forever and ever. Amen.**

¶ In the duty of **generosity** <note>original: *liberalitas*; the virtue of being free and noble in giving.</note>—which is called by many names according to persons and places (for it is "hospitality" in receiving guests, "communion" in community, "mercy" toward the needy, and "grace" in all things due to the affection of the giver)—there are two accounts: one of **giving** and the other of **receiving**. Many, as much as was in their power, gave to Paul, but Paul did not receive from them. In those cases, there was an account of giving, but no account of receiving. However, the Philippians gave to Paul, and Paul received. Here, those two accounts met, which Paul rarely permitted elsewhere. The "account of receiving" belonged to Paul; the "account of giving" belonged to the Philippians. In this, there is a more abundant fruit of virtue, since it is "more blessed" and more emulative of divine bounty "to give than to receive." 

Paul sought this fruit in them, not the benefit he held in the account of receiving. For the latter is small and modest, but the former is abundant, distinguished, well-pleasing, and accepted by God—just as Abel’s sacrifice was accepted by God because of the spirit of the one offering and giving. For God is full and overflowing; he needs to receive nothing. Yet if he "receives," he does not seek fruit in the object, but in the givers and offerers, through a certain imitation of his own goodwill and all-bestowing nature. 

Nevertheless, what they bestowed upon Paul, he poured out and offered to God as a sacrifice and oblation on their behalf. He proclaims that they will receive a good reward: the riches of eternal glory in Christ, the beloved Son of the eternal Father. Therefore, he also gives thanks to God the heavenly Father. Having done this, according to his custom, he asks for the greetings of the saints in his name and offers the common greetings of the faithful. He specifically mentions those who were of **Caesar's household** <note>The Roman Emperor's staff and slaves.</note>—who at that time was **Nero**—so that they might rejoice and understand that even those in the houses of Kings do not disdain to serve Christ. He prays for the grace of our Lord upon them, which is more desirable than any empire or human dignity. And so he says:

¶ **Greet every saint in CHRIST JESUS. The brothers who are with me greet you. All the saints greet you, especially those from Caesar’s household. The grace of the Lord JESUS CHRIST be with all of you. Amen. Written at Rome. Sent by Epaphroditus.**

¶ There are those who maintain that **Seneca** and **Lucan** <note>Seneca the Younger (philosopher) and Lucan (poet), high-ranking Romans under Nero.</note>, and many from Caesar's family, had a friendship with Paul and became lovers of Christ and Christians. Indeed, it is found in certain ancient records that Seneca even dedicated a "Book of Virtues" to Paul, the apostle of Christ. If that book does not carry that title now, they believe it was done through the malice of the enemies of Christ. 

However that may be, blessed are all those—whether from private houses or the houses of kings—who have believed in Christ, the King of Glory, of whom it is said: *Let all the angels of God adore him, and all the kings of the earth shall adore him.* Even the cruel Nero, along with other kings and tyrants, shall adore him on the left hand, placed beneath his feet. Meanwhile, all faithful kings who lived and died in faith shall lay down their crowns beneath his feet, recognizing what is written on his garment and on his thigh: **King of kings and Lord of lords**. They shall adore him as the only King, along with all the heavenly host, living and reigning over all forever. To him, from now and forever, be all honor, splendor, power, dominion, and majesty, into and above all ages of ages. AMEN.

# Philippians, Section 6
### z, iiii.

...most dear and most longed-for / my joy and my crown. So stand fast in the Lord, most dear. ¶ Paul does not use superlatives here, but simple names: beloved, longed-for. 

**Paul:** <note>original Greek: "ὥστε ἀδελφοί μου ἀγαπητοὶ καὶ ἐπιπόθητοι, χαρὰ καὶ στέφανός μου, οὕτως στήκετε ἐν κυρίῳ ἀγαπητοί"</note> *Therefore, my brothers, beloved and longed-for, my joy and crown, so stand fast in the Lord, beloved.* 

¶ **The Vulgate Edition:** *I ask Euodia and I entreat Syntyche to be of the same mind in the Lord.* 

¶ It should be read as "Euodia" using 'u' and 'o' as the fifth and fourth vowels following each other. I believe this word was corrupted in the Latin manuscripts by the fault of the scribes. And "Syntyche" should be written with a double 'y'—a thin 'i' sound—and an aspirated 'ch'. Regarding what the old translator calls "I ask and entreat," Paul uses the same word for both: *parakalō* <note>original: "παρακαλῶ," meaning to urge, exhort, or comfort</note>. As for "to be of the same mind" <note>original: "sapere"</note>, it could be translated no less appropriately as "to feel the same." 

**Paul:** <note>original Greek: "ἐυοδίαν παρακαλῶ, καὶ συντύχην παρακαλῶ τὸ αὐτὸ φρονεῖν"</note> *I urge Euodia, and I urge Syntyche to think the same thing.* 

¶ **The Vulgate Edition:** *And I ask you also, true companion.* 

¶ What is said here as "also" is an affective particle in Paul's writing. And where the old translator says "and you, true companion" <note>original Latin: "germane compar"</note>, it seems rather that Paul is speaking to a woman instead of a man. This can be understood from what follows immediately after: he commends these women to be helped as if they were female companions living together. Clement, Eusebius, and a good portion of the Greeks understand this passage to refer to Paul’s own wife, whom Paul addresses so familiarly and affectionately. Following their opinions, we have translated it: *I also ask you, noble spouse.* For what the old translator called "true" <note>original: "germane"</note> more specifically signifies "noble," "special," or "one's own." Truly, "companion" <note>original: "compar"</note> is most appropriately translated as "spouse" <note>original: "coniunx"</note>. For so it is held. 

**Paul:** <note>original Greek: "καὶ ἐρωτῶ καὶ σὲ σύζυγε γνήσιε"</note> *And I ask you also, true yoke-fellow.* 

But many will perhaps object to this interpretation. This is especially true based on the sayings of Jerome to Eustochium on the preservation of virginity, to whom he writes saying: "Concerning virgins (says the Apostle), I have no commandment from the Lord. Why? Because he himself, though he was a virgin, was so not by command, but by his own will." Jerome makes these points. I would not deny that the Blessed Paul was a virgin, and was a great and distinguished herald of virginity, for which cause he suffered bonds and imprisonment at Iconium <note>A reference to the apocryphal "Acts of Paul and Thecla," where Paul's preaching on virginity leads to his arrest.</note>. 

However, it is difficult to find this in the author's own words. Nor could Jerome be the definitive authority on this matter, writing so many years after Paul’s memory. For it does not follow that because he was a distinguished preacher of virginity—inducing men and women everywhere to the vow of white virginity—that he was therefore a virgin himself. For according to the author Linus <note>Referring to the legendary first bishop of Rome after Peter, to whom various apocryphal works were attributed.</note>, Peter did the same, yet he had a wife and children. And he did so in such a way that, because of his preaching on virginity and the chastity he introduced to Roman women through his holy and chaste words of exhortation, he was dragged to the punishment of martyrdom. 

So too did the other apostles, who announced the virgin Christ, born of a virgin. For they knew that the virginal purity was most pleasing to the virgin Lord, the son of a virgin mother, and born eternally of an "ultra-virgin" Father. But does not Paul place himself among the virgins when he says to the Corinthians, *I wish all men were even as I am*? And when he says again: *I say to those who are without a wife and to widows, it is good for them if they remain even as I.* 

Is it not clear? For in the first place, he is speaking of those who had wives, who could not be like Paul in terms of virginity. But in this respect only: that even if they had a marriage bed, they might remain continent for the sake of prayer, the continual service of God, and the imitation of Christ the eternal King. Just as Paul, for the same reasons, abstained from all female contact. In the second place, he speaks of those who are without wives—which applies to bachelors and widowers—and of women who are single and widows. 

Thus, from these passages, we do not find that he places himself among virgins any more than among those who are continent within marriage, or among those who are single after marriage. What if Paul’s wife—who remained continent for Christ's sake—was instructing the young women of Philippi in the vow of virginity, and had preceded Paul to Christ through martyrdom or some other way? Would Paul then not be numbered among the unmarried and those single after marriage? 

But some say it is a "wicked thing" <term>piaculum<explanation>In this context, an act requiring atonement or a religious crime/sin.</explanation></term> to say Paul had a wife. But how is it a wicked thing, when neither he who does not marry sins, nor he who does marry? For neither is an evil thing. How much less is it to have married a woman who was holy and perpetually continent for the sake of Christ the Lord? 

Moreover, do not Clement, Bishop of the Alexandrians, and Eusebius Pamphili, and many other ancients, wish this passage in Paul’s *Apologia* to the Corinthians—*do we not have the power to lead about a sister, a wife, as do the rest of the apostles and the brothers of the Lord and Cephas?* <note>1 Corinthians 9:5. "Cephas" is the Aramaic name for the Apostle Peter.</note>—to be understood as referring to his own wife? So that their opinion might be more evident, we have translated that passage: *do we not have the power to lead about a sister, a wife?* For the word placed there by Paul is usually interpreted as both "wife" and "woman." For thus in the *Ecclesiastical History* of Eusebius, when he enumerates those who had wives from the *Stromata* of Clement, he adds: "But even Paul," he says, "the apostle, does not hesitate in a certain epistle to make mention of and send a greeting to his companion, whom he says he does not lead about for this reason: so that he might be more unencumbered for the preaching of the Gospel." Where does he make mention of his companion? Certainly it is in this place. Where he denies that he...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the fourth chapter of Philippians, specifically addressing the identity of the "true companion" mentioned in the previous verse and launching into a significant theological debate regarding whether the Apostle Paul was ever married.</meta>

# COMMENTARY

<margin>
Unless this was added to Ignatius from elsewhere: for some ancient copies do not have Paul’s name among the others.
</margin>

...to lead about [a wife]? This is established in the passage from the Epistle to the Corinthians cited previously. However, Jerome, writing to <term>Eustochium</term><note>Eustochium (c. 368–420 AD) was a disciple of St. Jerome and a leader of a monastic community for women in Bethlehem.</note>, asserts the opposite, saying: "For they are not to be heard who imagine that he had a wife." I frankly confess that Jerome held that opinion—namely, that Paul did not have a wife. But those who defend the opposite view will enter into the assembly [to argue] that they are not "imagining" that Paul had a wife. Should Paul himself not be heard, who seems to say this (as they clearly show)? Should the divine Ignatius not be heard, who was a contemporary of Paul and who saw Paul in the flesh? In his <term>Epistle to the Philadelphians</term>, Ignatius places Paul among the married men. He says: "I do not disparage the other blessed ones who were joined in marriage, whom I now remember. For I pray to be found worthy of God, following in their footsteps in his kingdom. Just as Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; as Joseph, Isaiah, and the other prophets; as Peter and Paul and the rest of the apostles who were joined in marriage. They had wives not for the sake of lust, but for the sake of continuing their lineage." So says Ignatius.

What, then, shall we do? We will gladly grant Jerome that Paul was a lover of <term>chastity</term> and a virgin. Yet it is not so easy to grant that he never had a wife, as the authority of the elders cries out against it—and they do so not without reason. Furthermore, Jerome’s statement seems to have neither the authority of the elders, nor the faith of eyewitnesses (such as the divine Ignatius was, by no small favor), nor the reasoning of Scripture. Rather, it seems to be an arbitrary bit of persuasion and an oratorical way of speaking. For writing to a tender virgin, he wished to strengthen her resolve for virginity by the example of such a great man, and likewise to draw her toward a more fervent love of the Apostle. Thus, he persuaded her both that Paul was a virgin and that he had no wife. <gloss>That</gloss> it was enough to have persuaded her of the first part.

Indeed, the queen of virgins [Mary] had a husband and remained a virgin forever. No less is the virginity of <term>Cecilia</term><note>Saint Cecilia, a 2nd-century martyr, is said to have converted her husband Valerian to Christianity and a life of celibacy.</note> praised because she had a husband whose virginity she also consecrated to God. If a virgin has no husband, we look up to and admire that person more. <term>Ursula</term>, the leader of a host of virgins, had a husband and consecrated her virginity to God. Do they not even more admire the virginity of the noble Roman <term>Alexis</term><note>Saint Alexius (or Alexis) of Rome reportedly fled his marriage on his wedding night to live as a beggar and ascetic.</note>, who married a tender, beautiful, and most noble young woman, whom he also led to a similar vow [of celibacy]? If he had been a virgin without having a wife, through whom would he have done this?

Thus, in Paul’s case, his virginity is no less to be celebrated—indeed, it is more to be admired—even if he did take a wife. Rather, it is to be admired in both: in Paul and in his virgin wife. And to admire this is a gift of God; it is the grace of God in anyone who admires it. Therefore, it does not immediately follow that "he had a wife, therefore he is not a virgin." For we see so many famous men had wives, and conversely, most famous women had husbands, and there was no loss of virginity to either this group or that; indeed, it brought them greater glory. And what wonder is it if Paul, being of noble birth (as <term>Sophronius</term><note>Likely referring to Sophronius of Jerusalem or a contemporary hagiographer.</note> writes), was betrothed to a virgin according to the custom of his country? And when as a young man he was called to Christ, he had not yet touched her by the time of his calling; but once called, he consecrated his virginity not only to the Lord Christ, but also to his companion, who, though betrothed, was still untouched. Should we not admire Paul as a virgin, a spouse, an apostle, a prophet, and a most full vessel of election of every grace?

But perhaps these things have drawn us too far afield on the occasion of Saint Jerome, which has lured many into a contentious dispute. But I think that neither Jerome disagrees much with us, nor do we with Jerome, though it may seem so. For he was writing a private letter to a particular virgin, to whom it was more expedient to write in such a way that he made no mention of marriage. For if mention of marriage or betrothal were made, the virgin might fall into a suspicion that her own virginity was not being preserved. If, however, he had written a universal letter, or had thought it would come into everyone's hands, he might perhaps have discussed the truth of this matter more fully and investigated it differently. But enough of these things, perhaps even more than was necessary.

# VI 181 Philippians

<margin>B 15</margin>
One reads: "whatever things are chaste." Paul says: "whatever things are pure, whatever things are lovely." <note>original: "ὅσα ἁγνά, ὅσα προσφιλῆ"</note> The **Vulgate edition** says: "If there be any virtue, if any praise of discipline." It should be read as: "if there be any virtue, and if there be any praise." The word "discipline" is superfluous. Paul says: "if there be any virtue, and if there be any praise." <note>original: "εἴ τις ἀρετὴ, καὶ εἴ τις ἔπαινος"</note> And it immediately follows: "think on these things." <note>original: "ταῦτα λογίζεσθε"</note> And when it is said, "if there be any virtue," Paul used that name in the same way the **philosophers** use it to refer to moral excellence. ¶ The **Vulgate edition** says: "But I rejoiced in the Lord vehemently." It could also be said: "magnificently." <note>original: "ἐχάρην δὲ ἐν κυρίῳ μεγάλως"</note>

<margin>C 15</margin>
¶ The **Vulgate edition** says: "I know also how to abound; everywhere and in all things I am instructed." It is not "everywhere," but rather "in every matter." Paul says: "I know also how to abound in everything, and in all things I have been initiated." <note>original: "οἶδα καὶ περισσεύειν ἐν πάντι, καὶ ἐν πᾶσι μεμύημαι"</note> ¶ The **Vulgate edition** says: "I can do all things in him who strengthens me." This word "strengthens" in Paul means "provides power" and "makes one grow strong." And the specific word "Christ" is missing in some versions. Paul says: "I can do all things in Christ who empowers me." <note>original: "πάντα ἰσχύω ἐν τῷ ἐνδυναμοῦντί με χρισῷ"</note>

<margin>16</margin>
¶ The **Vulgate edition** says: "In the account of giving and receiving, but you only: for even to Thessalonica you sent once and again for my use." From this passage, it is clearly recognized that the **Philippians** are **Macedonians**. And it can be phrased: "in the matter of giving and receiving." Paul says: "in the account of giving and receiving, except you only; for even in Thessalonica, both once and twice, you sent for my need." <note>original: "εἰς λόγον δόσεως καὶ λήψεως, εἰ μὴ ὑμεῖς μόνοι ὅτι καὶ ἐν θεσσαλονίκῃ καὶ ἅπαξ καὶ δὶς, εἰς τὴν χρείαν μοι ἐπέμψατε"</note>

<margin>D 16</margin>
¶ The **Vulgate edition** says: "But I have all things and abound." It should rather be said: "But I receive all things." Paul says: "I have received all, and I abound." <note>original: "ἀπέχω δὲ πάντα, καὶ περισσεύω"</note> ¶ The **Vulgate edition** says: "Having received from Epaphroditus the things which you sent, an odor of sweetness." It should rather be read as: "receiving from Epaphroditus," or "through Epaphroditus." Neither is the verb "you sent" present in the Greek; rather, the verb "are" is understood, as if we were saying "receiving through Epaphroditus the things which are from you." Paul says: "having received from Epaphroditus the things from you, a fragrant odor." <note>original: "δεξάμενος παρὰ ἐπαφροδίτου τὰ παρ' ὑμῶν, ὀσμὴν εὐωδίας"</note>

<margin>17</margin>
¶ The **Vulgate edition** says: "But may my God fill every desire of yours." It can be read as: "He will fill." And "necessity" or "indigence" rather than "desire." Paul says: "But my God will fulfill your every need." <note>original: "ὁ δὲ θεός μου πληρώσει πᾶσαν χρείαν ὑμῶν"</note> ¶ "Especially those who are of Caesar’s household." **Caesar** at that time was **Nero**, whose teacher and instructor is known from history to have been **Annaeus Seneca**. From this passage, people speculate that Paul knew **Seneca**. Indeed, there are many witnesses who cannot be easily refuted claiming that Seneca was most dear to Paul. If he spoke of Seneca here, it would be established that Seneca was a Christian, for he speaks of "saints." He says: "All the saints salute you, especially those who are of Caesar’s household." I do not think they would be named "saints" unless they belonged to the religion and had been initiated into the <term>sacraments</term><note>Here meaning the sacred mysteries or rites of the early Church.</note> of Christ. If it does not please someone to understand this as referring to Seneca (concerning whom more will be brought forward in the thirteenth book), nevertheless, from the writings of <term>Linus</term><note>Traditionally regarded as the second Bishop of Rome after Peter.</note>, there is no doubt that many others from Caesar’s house were accustomed to go to Paul, believing in the Lord Jesus. Although their names are unknown on earth, they are nonetheless much more happily inscribed in heaven. For Linus, a contemporary of Peter and Paul, says when speaking of Paul: "A great crowd also from Caesar’s house came to him, of those believing in the Lord Jesus Christ; and the great joy of the faithful increased daily." Therefore, there is no doubt that the Apostle spoke of those who were faithful, believing in the Lord Jesus Christ—already "saints" and brothers of the saints, whoever they were. Among them, some were known to the Philippians, and they themselves were known to the Philippians, for they prayed for their health.

<margin>D 17</margin>
¶ The **Vulgate edition** says: "The grace of our Lord JESUS CHRIST be with your spirit. Amen." The word "our" is superfluous. And the final phrase "with your spirit, amen" is not read that way in the Greek now, but rather "with all of you. Amen." Paul says: "The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen." <note>original: "χάρις τοῦ κυρίου ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ, μετὰ πάντων ὑμῶν. ἀμήν"</note> And among the Greeks, the subscription is held to be: "To the Philippians, written from Rome, sent through Epaphroditus."

# ¶ SEVENTH BOOK OF THE COMMENTARIES ON THE EPISTLES OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PAUL, WHICH IS ON THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS. CHAPTER I.

<image-desc>A large decorative historiated woodcut initial 'S' depicting classical figures entwined with scrolling foliage and architectural motifs.</image-desc>

<margin>1</margin> When Paul writes to the Colossians—who are Phrygians, a people of Asia Minor situated between Galatia and Lycaonia—he first greets them in his usual holy manner, saying: ¶ **Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ by the will of God, and Timothy our brother: to the saints and faithful brothers in Christ who are at Colossae. Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.** ¶ This holy greeting of Paul is not unlike his method of greeting which he observes in his other epistles. <margin>2</margin> He then adds a thanksgiving and reveals his love for them through his concern in praying for them, and he commends Epaphras their apostle, who was sent by Paul to them and announced Christ to them. And he says: ¶ **We give thanks to God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, always praying for you since we heard of your faith in Christ Jesus and the love you have toward all the saints, because of the hope laid up for you in heaven. You heard of this before in the word of the truth of the gospel, which has come to you just as it has in the whole world; and it is bearing fruit and growing, even as it has in you from the day you heard and knew the grace of God in truth. Just as you learned from Epaphras, our beloved fellow-servant, who is a faithful minister of Christ for you, and who also indicated to us your love in the spirit. For this reason, since the day we heard it, we do not cease to pray for you and to ask that you may be filled with the knowledge of his will in all wisdom and spiritual understanding, so that you may walk worthily, pleasing the Lord in all things: bearing fruit in every good work and increasing in the knowledge of God; strengthened with all power according to the power of his glory, in all patience and long-suffering; giving thanks with joy to the Father, who has made us worthy to share in the inheritance of the saints in light. He has delivered us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love, in whom we have redemption and the remission of sins.**

¶ These words clearly contain a pure account from a holy heart, showing what things ought to be asked from God in the spirit and prayed for on behalf of others. These are: the fulfillment of the knowledge of the divine will; all wisdom and spiritual understanding; walking with dignity to please the Lord in every way; bearing fruit in every good work and taking an increase in the knowledge of God; being able to act in all power—not according to human strength, but according to the power of divine glory. And this means being able to act in all spiritual truth, such as being empowered in faith, in hope, in charity, and in all patience and long-suffering. It means rejoicing in the spirit—that is, to rejoice in God and his benefits. It means giving thanks to God the Father, who rescued us from the power of darkness and brought us into the region of light to participate in the inheritance of the saints; and from a dark tyranny he transferred us into the bright kingdom of his beloved Son. He has redeemed us and forgiven us our sins, and through him and because of him the heavenly Father willed for us to be redeemed and for our sins to be forgiven. These are the highest things that should be prayed for among men and asked of God. If these things were in the world, the whole world would be in light; and immediately upon departing from the light of this life, one would pass to the eternal light. For then every <term>type<note>In this context, a "type" refers to a symbolic representation or an earthly shadow of a greater heavenly reality.</note></term> passes away. However much light there may be in this life, it is a "type" of the other life; but in that other life, it is no longer a type, but the true light. ¶ And this is not from ourselves, who were made from nothing and had perished after being made—no longer appearing in the light of God, and thus being as nothing once again—but it is from the Son of God, who sought us out in the darkness and drew us out from nothingness again into the creation of light.

<margin>3</margin> But who is this Son of God, so beloved, so powerful, so kind, and so wonderful? He who cannot be defined (for he defines all things and is the definition of all things), Paul defines as best he can, saying: ¶ **Who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature. For in him all things were created in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or principalities or powers: all things were created through him and in him. And he is before all things, and in him all things consist. And he is the head of the body, the church, who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, so that he himself might hold the primacy in all things. For it pleased the Father that in him all fullness should dwell, and through him to reconcile all things to himself, making peace through the blood of his cross, whether things on earth or things in heaven.** ¶ When the Apostle says, "who is the image of the invisible God," he indicates <term>consubstantiality<note>The theological concept that the Son is of the same "substance" or essence as the Father (original Latin: consubstantialitatem).</note></term>...

<vocab>Paul, Colossians, Epistle to the Colossians, Epaphras, Christ, image of God, firstborn, redemption, grace, wisdom, spiritual understanding</vocab>

The author emphasizes the transition from the "darkness" of sin to the "light" of Christ's kingdom, defining Christ as the creator and sustainer of all things.</summary>
