<meta>This page continues the theological commentary on the first chapter of the Epistle to the Colossians. The author is mid-argument, establishing the unique nature of Christ’s relationship to God the Father using the concept of "consubstantiality"—the idea that the Son is of the same "stuff" or essence as the Father.</meta>

<header>Colossians</header>

->VII<-

he suggests. For the Son is the image of the Father: but he is a **consubstantial** <note>Having the same essential nature or substance.</note> image. For you cannot properly call someone a "son" who is not of the same substance, and specifically of the same substance in a particular way. You would not call your reflection in a mirror your "son"; for although it is a natural image, it is not consubstantial. Therefore, the Son of God is the image of the Father and a consubstantial image. And since he is the Son in the highest degree, he is consubstantial in the highest degree. Moreover, the highest consubstantiality is the most spiritual, found in the greatest identity of the same substance and nature. For you would never say a wolf-cub <note>original: "leuculum," likely a diminutive for wolf or a specific hybrid.</note> is the son of both a wolf and a dog. For although both are of the same general "animal" substance, they differ too much in their specific substance. Likewise, a leopard-cub is less the son of a lion than a lion-cub is. For the former enjoys less identity of nature with the lion than the latter does, and is a less "natural" image. So too a wolf-dog <note>original: "lycisca," a term for a hybrid animal or a specific breed of hound.</note> is less the son of a dog than a puppy is; and a mule <note>original: "hemionos," a half-ass.</note> is less the son of a donkey than a young donkey is, because of the lesser identity of nature. For these hybrids seem to be neither "one-substanced" <note>original: "unisubstantialia"</note> nor "different-substanced," but "two-substanced" and "two-natured," not constituting a simple species, but a composite one in a certain way. Indeed, a mule lacks neither the substance of the mare (since it is the son of a mare) nor the substance of the donkey (since it is the son of a donkey). The condition of "sonship" requires consubstantiality to such an extent that even if something is called a son of two different species, it must possess the consubstantialities of those differing species.

But what do these lowly examples show (unless such great Majesty shrinks from comparison with such weak things) except that the Son of God is maximally consubstantial with the Father? Truly, just as he is also truly called the "Son of Man," he is also truly a consubstantial man; he is truly "two-substanced" and "two-natured" <note>Refers to the doctrine of the Hypostatic Union: Christ being fully God and fully man.</note>. However, in the Son of God, all things are spoken of with the greatest dignity; in a creature, dignity does not correspond in the same way, even if there is some remote shadow of imitation of this consubstantiality. For the Son is consubstantial, and a consubstantial image. 

But regarding what is added about the same person being the **firstborn of all creation**: what else does this indicate but his eternal generation? For if he were not begotten, he would not be a son; and if he were not eternally before every creature, he would not be eternal. For what is "the firstborn of all creation" except he who was begotten most "prior" to every creature, begotten most "before" every creature? And what is "most" except "immensely"? For if it were not immense, there could be something "more" or "prior." Truly, since age, time, and life-spans are created things, and before these there is only eternity: he was begotten "most"—that is, immensely—prior to every creature; he was begotten immensely before every age, time, and every era. His generation is eternal. 

And Paul sufficiently suggests that he intends this understanding of "the firstborn" through the reasoning he attaches: **because in him all things were created.** And what he adds afterward: **and he is before all things.** And what he adds about him being **the head of the church**: I think this is sufficiently understood from what came before. 

Indeed, there is also this: he calls him the **firstborn from the dead**. This is because he rose before all others in the truth of the resurrection, and that which was mortal (the sting of death having been swallowed up) put on immortality and incorruptibility. For those who had risen before him did not rise in the "truth" of the resurrection; their mortality was not swallowed up, they were not perfectly transformed, but they went into death again. Such was the son of the widow whom Elijah raised, the son of the widow whom the Lord raised, and Lazarus, and whoever else was raised before. But he was the first of all to be raised by a true resurrection, holding the priority in all things—he who is before all things, and after all things, the Alpha and the Omega <note>original: "alpha et ω"</note>, the first and the last. 

And that all things were created so that the fullness of things might dwell in him, affecting his body: his good will and pleasure alone brought this about. That he reconciled all things in himself, both heavenly and earthly: this was his pleasure alone, and he chose the manner of reconciliation by his own pleasure—namely, for the sake of this reconciliation, his own death on the cross, so that he might reveal his immense love to every creature in heaven and on earth. All people trust in love. Who, then, would distrust the King of Glory, who loves us (whom he himself made) so vehemently? Who is there who, considering that he is joined to the holy angels in that harmony by which the members of the same body work together, would not praise and magnify with all the efforts of his soul that mercy of infinite pity and the incomprehensible kindness of the immense God toward his creature? Who will not keep the faith? Who will not hold onto hope? Who will not consider sufferings sweet for the sake of imitating the sufferings of Christ, the Son of God? Therefore, Paul adds:

<margin>
4
</margin>
> ¶ **And you, though you were once alienated and enemies in your mind through evil works: yet now he has reconciled you in the body of his flesh through his death, to present you holy, and unspotted, and blameless in his sight, if indeed you remain in the faith, grounded and firm and unmovable from the hope of the gospel which you have heard, which has been preached to every creature under heaven, of which I, Paul, have been made a minister. Now I rejoice in my sufferings for you, and in my turn I fill up what is lacking in the afflictions** <note>original: "pressurae," meaning pressures, tribulations, or heavy burdens.</note> **of CHRIST in my flesh for his body (which is the church). Of this church I have been made a minister according to the dispensation of God, which was given to me toward you, that I might fulfill the word of God, the mystery hidden from ages and generations.**

It concludes with Paul's call for the Colossians to remain firm in faith following their reconciliation through Christ's death.</summary>

# THE SEVENTH BOOK OF COMMENTARIES ON THE EPISTLES OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PAUL: THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS. CHAPTER I.

<margin>1</margin>
<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'P' featuring a landscape with a bridge or building and foliage.</image-desc>
**Paul Writing** Paul writes to the Colossians, who are Phrygians <note>An ancient people of central Asia Minor.</note>, a people of Lesser Asia situated between Galatia and Lycaonia. First, as is his holy custom, he greets them, saying: **Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ by the will of God, and Timothy our brother: to the saints who are at Colossae and the faithful brothers in Christ: grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.** ¶ This holy greeting of Paul is not at all unlike his manner of greeting which he observes in his other epistles. He follows this by joining a thanksgiving, revealing his love for them through his concern in praying for them, and he commends Epaphras, their apostle, who was sent by him to them and announced Christ to them. And so he says: ¶ **We give thanks to the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, always praying for you, since**

<margin>2</margin>
**we heard of your faith in Christ Jesus, and the love you have toward all the saints, because of the hope laid up for you in heaven. You heard of this before in the word of the truth of the gospel, which has come to you, as it has into the whole world; and it brings forth fruit and increases, even as it does in you, from the day you heard and knew the grace of God in truth. Just as you learned from Epaphras, our beloved fellow-servant, who is a faithful minister of Christ for you; who also declared to us your love in the spirit. For this reason, we also, from the day we heard it, do not cease to pray for you and to ask that you may be filled with the knowledge of his will in all wisdom and spiritual understanding; that you may walk worthily, pleasing the Lord in all things: being fruitful in every good work and increasing in the knowledge of God; strengthened in all power according to the might of his glory, in all patience and long-suffering; giving thanks with joy to the Father, who has made us worthy to share in the inheritance of the saints in light. He has delivered us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love, in whom we have redemption, the remission of sins.** ¶ These clear words contain a pure narration from a holy heart, showing what things should be asked from God in the spirit and prayed for on behalf of others. These are: the fulfillment of the knowledge of the divine will; all wisdom and spiritual understanding; walking with dignity to please the Lord in every way; bearing fruit in every good work and taking increase in the knowledge of God; being capable in every power, not according to human strength but according to the power of divine glory—and this means being capable in all spiritual truth, such as being capable in faith, in hope, in charity, in all patience and long-suffering. To rejoice in the spirit—that is, to rejoice in God and his benefits. To give thanks to God the Father, who rescued us from the power of darkness and adopted us into the region of light, into a participation in the inheritance of the saints; and from the tyranny of the dark enemy, he transferred us into the bright kingdom of his beloved Son, who redeemed us and forgave us our sins, and through whom and for whose sake the heavenly Father willed us to be redeemed and our sins to be forgiven. ¶ These seven things are to be prayed for on behalf of men and asked from God. If these were present in the world, the whole world would be in light; and immediately upon departing the light of this life, one would pass into the eternal light. For then every type <note>original: "typus"; a symbolic foreshadowing or representation of a higher reality.</note> passes away. Moreover, whatever the light of this life may be, it is a type of that other life; there it is no longer a type, but the true light. And this is not from ourselves, who were made from nothing, and having been made, had perished, no longer appearing in the light of God—and thus we were nothing once again. Rather, it is from the Son of God, who sought us in the darkness and drew us out of nothingness again into the creature of light. But who is this Son of God, so beloved, so powerful, so kind, so

<margin>3</margin>
wonderful? He who cannot be defined (for he defines all things and is the definition of all) is defined by Paul as best as he can be, saying: ¶ **Who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature. For in him all things were created that are in heaven and that are on earth: visible and invisible, whether thrones, or dominions, or principalities, or powers: all things were created through him and in him. And he is before all things, and in him all things consist. And he is the head of the church, who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, so that in all things he might hold the primacy. For it pleased the Father that in him all fullness should dwell; and through him to reconcile all things, making peace in himself through the blood of his cross, whether things on earth or things in heaven.** ¶ When the apostle says "who is the image of the invisible God," he refers to consubstantiality <note>original: "consubstantialitatem"; the theological doctrine that the Son is of the same essential substance as the Father.</note>

<header>Colossians</header>

### VII

He suggests this. For a son is the image of his father: but specifically a <term>consubstantial</term> <note>original: "consubstantialis," meaning of the exact same substance or essence</note> image. Indeed, you could not properly call someone a son if he were not consubstantial, and specifically so. You would not, for example, call your own image in a mirror your "son"; for although it is a natural image, it is not consubstantial. Therefore, the Son of God is the image of the Father and a consubstantial image. And since he is the Son in the highest degree, he is consubstantial in the highest degree. This supreme consubstantiality is most spiritual, found in the greatest identity of the same substance and nature. For you would never call a hybrid of a wolf or a dog a "son" in the proper sense. For although both share a substance, they differ too much in the specifics of that substance. A leopard-cub is less the "son" of a lion than a lion-cub is. For the former enjoys less identity of nature than the latter, and is a less natural image. So too a <term>lycisca</term> <note>A term used by ancient writers like Virgil for a hybrid between a wolf and a dog</note> is less the son of a dog than a puppy is; and a mule <note>original: "hemionos"</note> is less a son of a donkey than a young ass is, because of the lesser identity of nature. For these seem to be neither "of one substance" nor "of different substances," but of dual substance and dual nature; they do not constitute a simple species, but a sort of composite one. Indeed, the mule does not lack the substance of the mare, since it is the offspring of a mare, nor the substance of the donkey, since it is the offspring of a donkey. The condition of sonship requires consubstantiality to such an extent that if anything were said to be the son of things differing even in species, it would necessarily have to possess the consubstantialities of those different species. But what do these lowly examples show—unless such great majesty shrinks from comparison with such weak things—except that the Son of God is consubstantial with the Father in the highest degree? Truly, since he is also truly called the Son of Man, he is also truly consubstantial with man; he is truly of two substances and two natures <note>A reference to the "hypostatic union," the Christian doctrine that Jesus is both fully God and fully man</note>. In the Son of God, however, all things are spoken of with dignity and in the highest sense; in a creature, however, dignity does not correspond in the same way, even if there is a certain remote shadow of imitation regarding consubstantiality. For the Son is consubstantial, and a consubstantial image. But regarding what is added about him—that he is the **firstborn of every creature**—what else does this indicate than his eternal generation? For if he were not begotten, he would not be the Son. And if he were not eternally prior to every creature, he would not be eternal. For what is the "firstborn of every creature" except one begotten most prior to every creature, begotten most before every creature? And what is "most" if not "immensely"? For if it were not immense, there could be something greater and more prior. Truly, since age, and time, and era are created, and before these there is only eternity: he was begotten immensely prior to every creature, begotten immensely before every age, and time, and every era. His generation is eternal. Paul sufficiently suggests that he intends this understanding of the "firstborn" through the reasoning he joins to it: **because in him all things were created.** And also by what he adds later: **and he is before all things.** And that he adds that he is the head of the church; I think this is sufficiently understood from the preceding points. Truly, there is also this: that he calls him the **firstborn from the dead.** This is because he rose before all others in the truth of the resurrection, and that which was mortal (the sting of death having been swallowed up) put on immortality and incorruptibility. For those who had risen before him did not rise in the truth of the resurrection; their mortality was not swallowed up, they were not perfectly transformed, but they went into death again. Examples include the son of the widow whom Elijah raised, the son of the widow whom the Lord raised, and Lazarus, and whoever else was raised before. But he was the first of all raised in a true resurrection: holding the priority in all things, he who is before all things, and after all things, the Alpha and the Omega, the first and the last.

And that all things were created so that the fullness of things might dwell in him, affecting his body: his good will and pleasure alone brought this about. That he reconciled all things in himself, both heavenly and earthly: this was his pleasure alone, and he chose the manner of reconciliation according to his pleasure—namely, his death on the cross for this reconciliation, so that he might reveal his immense love to every creature both in heaven and on earth.

All people trust in love. Who, then, will distrust the King of Glory, who loves us (whom he himself made) so vehemently?

Who is there who, considering himself joined to the holy angels in that harmony by which the members of the same body work together, would not praise and magnify with all the efforts of his soul that mercy of infinite pity, and the incomprehensible kindness of the immense God toward his creature?

Who will not keep the faith? Who will not hold onto hope? Who will not consider sufferings sweet for the sake of imitating the sufferings of Christ, the Son of God? Therefore Paul adds:

<margin>4</margin> **And you, although you were once alienated and enemies in your mind in evil works: now certainly he has reconciled you in the body of his flesh through his death, so that he might present you holy, and unspotted, and blameless in his sight, if however you remain in the faith, grounded, and firm, and unmoved from the hope of the gospel which you have heard, which has been preached to every creature under heaven: of which I, Paul, am made a minister. Now I rejoice in my sufferings for you: and in his place I fill up what is lacking in the afflictions of CHRIST in my flesh for his body (which is the church). Of which I am made a minister according to the dispensation of God, which is given to me toward you: that I may fulfill the word of God, the mystery hidden from ages and generations.**

<margin>1</margin>
...[among the Gen]tiles <note>The text begins with a fragment of the word "gentibus" (Gentiles) carried over from the previous page</note>; but now it has been made manifest to his saints, to whom God willed to make known the riches of the glory of this mystery among the Gentiles, which is Christ in you, the hope of glory. We announce him, admonishing every man and teaching every man in all wisdom, so that we may present every man perfect in Christ Jesus. To this end I also labor, striving according to his working, which works in me with power. ¶ He makes himself an enemy to understanding and truth who does the opposite of what understanding and truth command; and he who devotes himself to evil works does that very thing. ¶ Why is it said that the Gospel was preached to every creature under heaven, if not because divine mercy freely willed to save all through the Gospel, which was the announcement of the death of Christ, the savior of all? And such is the goodness of Christ that, not only did he, who is the head, wish to be afflicted, to suffer, and to die for the sake of saving the body (which is the church), but he also sent his own representatives—his disciples and apostles—to endure pressures, tribulations, and finally death in his place for the love of the church, thus dying again in them. Paul, acting in the place of Christ <note>original: "vices Christi gerens"</note>, suffered these things willingly. And by this very fact, Christ suggests to us that he would still willingly die for us in his own person, if he—who is now in every way immortal—were permitted to die, so that we might not perish. What can we repay him for such great benefits, for such ineffable mercy, for such incredible love? Truly, we can do nothing worthy. Yet, as much as we are able and as much as he helps us, let us give him praise, honor, glory, and thanksgiving. Let us keep ourselves holy, pure, and unstained for him as members of his body, and present our hearts to him inflamed with love (for such a gift is fitting for the Lord of love). ¶ May he himself inflame our hearts and deign to accept them—he who is the first of lovers and the true love of those who love: the Son of God, blessed above all things.

### EXAMINATION of some points regarding the literal text.

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** <note>original: "Vulgata editio"</note> *To those who are at Colossae, the saints and faithful brothers in Christ Jesus.* ¶ Since the Apostle addresses the Colossians (as was said in the preceding epistles), the translation could have been made in the second person, saying: *to the saints and faithful brothers in Christ who are you Colossians.* This is also shown by the following segment: *grace to you and peace.* And at the end, the name "Jesus" is superfluous. **Paul:** <note>The author uses "Paulus" to refer to the original Greek text</note> *To the saints in Colossae and faithful brothers in Christ.* <note>original: "τοῖς ἐν κολοσσαῖς ἁγίοις καὶ πιστοῖς ἀδελφοῖς ἐν χριστῶ"</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Grace to you and peace from God our Father.* ¶ A segment should be added: *and the Lord Jesus Christ.* <margin>A</margin> **Paul:** *Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.* <note>original: "χάρις ὑμῖν καὶ εἰρήνη ἀπὸ θεοῦ πατρὸς ἡμῶν, καὶ κυρίου ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ"</note> <margin>2</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Hearing your faith.* ¶ This can be explained through the past tense. **Paul:** *Having heard your faith.* <note>original: "ἀκούσαντες τὴν πίστιν ὑμῶν"</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *And the love which you have toward all the saints.* ¶ What the old translator <note>The author refers to the traditional translator of the Latin Vulgate, often thought to be St. Jerome</note> here renders as "love" <note>original: "dilectionem"</note>, he usually renders elsewhere as "charity" <note>original: "charitatem"</note>. Also, the verb "you have" is not found in the Greek; rather, he could have said *which is toward all the saints*, or even without the relative pronoun, simply *and the love toward all the saints.* **Paul:** *and the love toward all the saints.* <note>original: "καὶ τὴν ἀγάπην τὴν εἰς πάντας τοὺς ἁγίουσ"</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Which you heard in the word of truth.* ¶ It should be read as *which you heard beforehand* or *heard earlier.* **Paul:** *which you heard beforehand in the word of truth.* <note>original: "ἣν προηκούσατε ἐν λόγῳ τῆς ἀληθείας"</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *And it has come to you.* ¶ The word "it" refers to the Gospel, not the "word." This ambiguity would have been removed if the old translator, where he said "in the word," had said "in the speech." **Paul:** *of the [Gospel] present among you.* <note>original: "τοῦ παρόντος εἰς ὑμᾶς"</note> For *present* <note>original: "παρόντος"</note> is a genitive adjective modifying *Gospel* <note>original: "εὐαγγελίου"</note>, which immediately precedes it. ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *As it is also in the whole world.* ¶ The word "is" is superfluous; one should rather say *into the whole world*, which refers back to the preceding verb *has come.* **Paul:** *as also in all the world.* <note>original: "καθώς καὶ ἐν παντὶ τῷ κόσμῳ"</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *And it brings forth fruit and grows.* ¶ This refers to the Gospel, not the "word." We know this because Paul uses the neuter gender. However, the term *logos* <note>original: "λόγος"</note>, which means "word" or "speech," is masculine. Regarding what the old translator calls *grows*, some Greek copies have *increasing* <note>original: "αὐξανόμενον"</note>, and many have nothing at all that corresponds to it, but only this: **Paul:** *and it is bearing fruit, just as also among you.* <note>original: "καὶ ἔστι καρποφορούμενον, καθώς καὶ ἐν ὑμῖν"</note> Nevertheless, I have included the word because of the old translator, even if it is found only in rarer copies. ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *As you learned from Epaphras, our most dear fellow-servant.* ¶ It should be read as *beloved fellow-servant.* **Paul:** *just as also you learned from Epaphras our beloved fellow-servant.* <note>original: "καθώς καὶ ἐμάθετε ἀπὸ ἐπαφρᾶ ἀγαπητοῦ συνδούλου ἡμῶν"</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Who is a faithful minister of Christ Jesus for you.* ¶ "Jesus" is superfluous. **Paul:** *who is a faithful minister of Christ on our behalf.* <note>original: "ὅς ἐστι πιστὸς ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν διάκονος τοῦ χριστοῦ"</note> And it follows immediately: *who also indicated...* ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *That you may walk worthily of God, pleasing him in all things.* ¶ It should say *Lord*, not *God*. And the meaning is doubtful: whether *Lord* refers to the preceding part *worthily*, or to the following part *pleasing*. If to the preceding, the sense is: *that you may walk worthily of the Lord* (that is, according to the dignity of the Lord and as becomes the Lord) *unto all well-pleasing.* Nor is it said "in all things," but "all" is used as an adjective. For it means "all well-pleasing" or...

<meta>This page continues the philological and theological commentary on Paul's Epistle to the Colossians, specifically focusing on the descriptions of Christ's divinity and his relationship to creation. It follows the previous discussion on Christ as the image of God.</meta>

# VII Colossians

"Well-pleasing" <note>original: "beneplacentia"</note> is used by Paul to mean "those who are pleasing." If it is read into the following clause, the meaning is: "that you may walk worthily, according to all the well-pleasing of the Lord." For here, Paul uses the genitive case "of the Lord." We have accepted this according to the sense, for the sake of conforming to the old translator <note>The "old translator" refers to the author of the Latin Vulgate, traditionally St. Jerome</note>, even though the first reading represents the Greek more closely. Paul says: *that you walk worthily of the Lord unto all pleasing* <note>original Greek: "περιπατῆσαῖ ὑμᾶς ἀξίως τοῦ κυρίου εἰς πᾶσαν ἀρεσκείαν"</note>.

<margin>1</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *And increasing in the knowledge of God, strengthened in all virtue.*
<margin>2</margin> ¶ The old translator could have said "in the recognition of God," and "powerful in all power"—that is, "being strong" and "full of strength." Paul says: *increasing in the knowledge of God, being empowered with all power* <note>original Greek: "αὐξανόμεροι εἰς τὴν ἐπίγνωσιν τοῦ θεοῦ ἐν πάσῃ δυνάμει δυναμούμενοι"</note>.

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *According to the power of his brightness.*
¶ It could be said "of his glory." Paul says: *according to the might of his glory* <note>original Greek: "κατὰ τὸ κράτος τῆς δόξης αὐτοῦ"</note>.

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Who has made us worthy for a share in the lot of the saints.*
¶ Where the old translator says "made us worthy," it signifies "he sufficed" or "made us sufficient." Paul says: *to him who made us sufficient for the portion of the lot of the saints* <note>original Greek: "τῷ ἱκανώσαντι ἡμᾶς εἰς τὴν μέριδα τοῦ κλήρου τῶν ἁγίων"</note>.

<margin>1</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *In whom we have redemption and the remission of sins.*
¶ The word "and" is superfluous. However, let "the remission of sins" be understood as being placed as an explanation for "redemption." Paul says: *in whom we have redemption, the remission of sins* <note>original Greek: "ἐν ᾧ ἔχομεν τὴν ἀπολύτρωσιν, τὴν ἄφεσιν τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν"</note>.

<margin>B</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature.*
<margin>3</margin> ¶ I preferred to say "firstborn *before* every creature"—that is, having a generation prior to every creature, just as eternal things are prior to those that are not eternal. I say I preferred to speak this way rather than "firstborn of every creature," lest he should seem to be numbered among the rest of the creatures. This was the view of the insane Eunomius, Photinus, and Arius <note>These are early Christian heretics; Arius, for example, argued that Christ was a created being rather than co-eternal with God the Father</note>, who did not attend to the Apostle’s meaning but brought forward the presumption and madness of their own thinking. For if they had attended to what Paul immediately added to explain his words—*and he is before all things*—they would have understood his saying without great difficulty. When he says "firstborn of every creature," it is the same as "begotten before every creature," "begotten prior to every creature," for he is eternally begotten. No creature, however, is eternally begotten. They are either eviternally <note>A philosophical term meaning "having a beginning but no end," often applied to angels or the heavens</note>, temporally, or in time. Creatures above time are begotten eviternally. The heavens are begotten temporally. Those things below the heavens, such as all sensible things, are begotten sub-temporally and within an age. And because the sense of that divine saying of Paul—"begotten before every creature"—offers and represents itself more clearly when we speak in the ablative case, we have therefore preferred to interpret that saying through the ablative rather than the genitive. Likewise, this removes the illusion of him being numbered among them. For Paul does not number him among creatures, whom he places *before* every creature, through whom all things were created, and for whom all things were created. Yet he is before every creature as the one begotten; just as the Father is before every creature as the one begetting; and as the Holy Spirit is before every creature as the one proceeding. For the Father eternally begat; the Son was eternally begotten; the Holy Spirit eternally proceeds. And these three are before all things as such. Wherefore, as the Son is the "first-begotten" of all, the Father is the "first-begetter" of all, and the Holy Spirit is the "first-proceeding" of all; and these three are beyond numbering with creatures. Before all things, they are one unnumberable and immense thing, which is neither counted in its distinction nor confused in its distinction. It is above all and in all, unnamable and incomprehensible by every creature. Of this, nothing is known, nothing is said, and nothing is affirmed that does not fall infinitely short of the dignity of such a great matter. Therefore, it is better worshipped in silence than in words. Let there be, therefore, a holy silence in heaven and on earth for the first-begetter of all, the first-begotten of all, and the first-proceeding of all: the one God, exalted and set apart above all, blessed and most-blessed forever and ever. Amen. Paul says: *who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation* <note>original Greek: "ὅς ἐσιν εἰκὼν τοῦ θεοῦ ἀοράτου, πρωτότοκος πάσης κτίσεως"</note>.

<margin>3</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Because in him all things were founded.*
¶ The old translator could have said "all things were created." For the same word which he here translates as "founded" <note>original: "condita"</note>, he translates a little later as "created" <note>original: "creata"</note>, where he says: "all things were created through him and in him." Why, then, "created" here and "founded" there, when the word is the same in both places, even if "founded" and "created" are to be understood as the same? Paul says: *because in him all things were created* <note>original Greek: "ὅτι ἐν αὐτῷ ἐκτίσθη τὰ πάντα"</note>.

<margin>3</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *And he is before all.*
¶ Better: "before all *things*." For the logic of the speech requires this, since he placed "all things" immediately before and places "all things" immediately after. Nor is there anything to which you might aptly refer "all" <note>original: "omnes," masculine plural</note> as an adjective. Paul says: *and he is before all things* <note>original Greek: "καὶ αὐτόσ ἐσι πρὸ πάντων"</note>.

<margin>3</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *And all things consist in him.*
¶ It could be said in the past tense: "they were established." Paul says: *and all things consist in him* <note>original Greek: "καὶ τὰ πάντα ἐν αὐτῷ συνέσηκε"</note>.

<margin>3</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Because in him it has well-pleased that all fullness should dwell.*
¶ If one looks to the Father, whose good pleasure it was that all fullness should dwell in Christ: then the phrases "in him," "of him," and "before him" are correct here and in what follows. But if one looks to the Son, whose good pleasure it was to assume a human body and for all fullness to dwell in himself in the form of man: then it should rather be said "in himself," "of his own," and "before himself" (or "in his own sight"), so that a mutuality and reciprocity (so to speak) may be recognized. Since therefore...

### COMMENTARY

<margin>1</margin>
...but now it has been made manifest to his saints, to whom God willed to make known what are the riches of the glory of this mystery among the Gentiles: which is CHRIST in you, the hope of glory. Him we announce, admonishing every man and teaching every man in all wisdom, so that we may present every man perfect in CHRIST JESUS. To this end I also labor, striving according to his working, which works in me in power. ¶ They make themselves enemies of understanding and truth who do the opposite of what understanding and truth prescribe; and he who devotes himself to evil works does this very thing. ¶ What does it mean that the gospel was preached "to every creature under heaven," <note>referring to Colossians 1:23</note> unless it means that divine mercy freely willed to save all through the gospel, which was the announcement of Christ’s death as the savior of all? And such is the goodness of Christ that, for the sake of saving the body—which is the church—he, who is the head, willed not only to be afflicted, to suffer, and to die himself, but he also sent his <term>vicars</term> <note>From the Latin *vicarius*, meaning a substitute or deputy acting in the place of another</note>, the disciples and apostles, to endure pressures, tribulations, and finally death in his stead for the love of the church, dying in them once again. This is what Paul, acting in Christ's stead, willingly endured. And by this very act, Christ suggests to us that he would still willingly die for us in himself if it were permitted for him—now immortal in every part—to die, lest we should perish. What shall we be able to repay him for such great benefits, for such unspeakable mercy, and such incredible love? We can certainly do nothing worthy. Yet, what we can do, insofar as he helps us, is to give praise to God, and honor, and glory, and thanksgiving; and let us keep ourselves for him as holy, pure, and uncontaminated members of his body, presenting to him our hearts inflamed with love (for such a gift is fitting for the Lord of love). May he himself, who is the first of lovers and the true love of those who love, the Son of God blessed above all, inflame us and deign to accept it.

<margin>A 1</margin>
### EXAMINATION of several points concerning the literal text.

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *To those who are at Colossae, the holy and faithful brothers in CHRIST JESUS.*
¶ Since the apostle is addressing the Colossians, as was said in the preceding epistles, the interpretation could be made in the second person, saying: "to the holy and faithful brothers in Christ, you who are at Colossae." This is also shown by the following part: *grace to you and peace.* And at the end, the name "Jesus" is redundant. <note>original: "Ihesu abundat"</note> Paul says: *to the saints and faithful brothers in Christ who are in Colossae.* <note>original Greek: "τοῖς ἐν κολοσσαῖς ἁγίοις καὶ πιστοῖς ἀδελφοῖς ἐν χριστῷ"</note>

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Grace to you and peace from God our Father.*
¶ There is a missing phrase that should be added: *and the Lord Jesus Christ.* Paul says: *grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.* <note>original Greek: "χάρις ὑμῖν καὶ εἰρήνη ἀπὸ θεοῦ πατρὸς ἡμῶν, καὶ κυρίου ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ"</note>

<margin>A 2</margin>
¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Hearing your faith.*
¶ This can be explained by the past tense. Paul says: *having heard your faith.* <note>original Greek: "ἀκούσαντες τὴν πίστιν ὑμῶν"</note>

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *And the love which you have toward all the saints.*
¶ What the old translator <note>The author of the Latin Vulgate</note> renders here as "love" <note>original: "dilectionem"</note>, he usually renders elsewhere as "charity" <note>original: "charitatem"</note>. And the verb "you have" is not found in the Greek; rather, he could have said *which is toward all the saints*, or even without the relative pronoun, simply *and the love toward all the saints.* Paul says: *and the love which is toward all the saints.* <note>original Greek: "καὶ τὴν ἀγάπην τὴν εἰς πάντας τοὺς ἁγίους"</note>

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Which you heard in the word of truth.*
¶ It should be read as *which you heard beforehand* or *heard previously*. Paul says: *which you heard beforehand in the word of truth.* <note>original Greek: "ἣν προηκούσατε ἐν λόγῳ τῆς ἀληθείας"</note>

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *And it has come to you.*
¶ The word "it" refers to the gospel, not the "word." This ambiguity would have been removed if the old translator, where he said "in the word," had said "in the speech." Paul says: *which is present among you.* <note>original Greek: "τοῦ παρόντος εἰς ὑμᾶς"</note> For "present" <note>original: "παρόντος"</note> is a genitive adjective referring to "gospel" <note>original: "εὐαγγελίου"</note> which is contained in what precedes.

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *As it is also in the whole world.*
¶ The verb "is" is redundant. It should rather be said "into the whole world," referring back to the preceding verb "it has come." Paul says: *just as also in the whole world.* <note>original Greek: "καθὼς καὶ ἐν παντὶ τῷ κόσμῳ"</note>

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *And it brings forth fruit and grows.*
¶ This refers to the gospel, not the word. We know this because Paul uses the neuter gender; however, *logos* (which is translated as "word" or "speech") is masculine. And where the old translator says "grows," some Greek copies have *auxanomenon* <note>meaning "increasing"</note>, though many have nothing that corresponds to it, but only this: *and it is bearing fruit, just as also among you.* <note>original Greek: "καὶ ἔστι καρποφόρουμενον, καθὼς καὶ ἐν ὑμῖν"</note> Nevertheless, I have included the word on account of the old translator, even if it is found only in rarer copies.

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *As you learned from Epaphras, our most dear fellow-servant.*
¶ It should be read as "our beloved fellow-servant." Paul says: *just as you also learned from Epaphras, our beloved fellow-servant.* <note>original Greek: "καθὼς καὶ ἐμάθετε ἀπὸ ἐπαφρᾶ ἀγαπητοῦ συνδούλου ἡμῶν"</note>

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Who is a faithful minister of CHRIST JESUS for you.*
¶ "Jesus" is redundant. Paul says: *who is for us a faithful minister of Christ.* <note>original Greek: "ὅς ἐστι πιστὸς ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν διάκονος τοῦ χριστοῦ"</note> And there follows immediately: *who also made known* <note>original Greek: "ὃ καὶ δηλώσας"</note>—that is, "who also indicated."

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *That you may walk worthily of God, pleasing in all things.*
¶ It should say "of the Lord," not "of God." And the meaning is doubtful: whether "of the Lord" should be referred back to the preceding word "worthily," or forward to "pleasing." If to the former, the meaning is "that you may walk worthily of the Lord"—that is, in accordance with the dignity of the Lord and as befits the Lord—unto all well-pleasing. Nor is "in all things" <note>original: "per omnia"</note> used; rather, "all" is used as an adjective. For it means "all well-pleasing" or...

### VII 183 Colossians

"Well-pleasingness" is used by Paul rather than "those who please." If we look at the following clause, the meaning is: "that you may walk worthily, according to the Lord’s full well-pleasingness." For here Paul uses the <term>genitive</term> <note>A grammatical case usually indicating possession or relationship, in this case "of the Lord."</note> of "Lord." We have accepted this according to the sense, out of conformity with the old translator <note>The "old translator" refers to the author of the Vulgate, traditionally identified as Saint Jerome.</note>, although the former version represents the Greek more accurately. Paul says: *that you walk worthily of the Lord unto all pleasing* <note>original: περιπατῆσαι ὑμᾶς ἀξίως τοῦ κυρίου εἰς πᾶσαν ἀρεσκείαν</note>. ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *And increasing in the knowledge of God, strengthened in all power.* ¶ <margin>2</margin> The old translator could have said: "in the recognition of God, being powerful in all potential"—that is, being strong and full of strength. Paul says: *increasing in the knowledge of God, being strengthened with all power* <note>original: αὐξανόμενοι εἰς τὴν ἐπίγνωσιν τοῦ θεοῦ ἐν πάση δυνάμει δυναμούμενοι</note>. ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** <margin>3</margin> *According to the power of his brightness.* ¶ It could be said: "of his glory." Paul says: *according to the might of his glory* <note>original: κατὰ τὸ κράτος τῆς δόξης αὐτοῦ</note>. ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Who has made us worthy for a share in the lot of the saints.* ¶ Where the old translator says "he made us worthy," it signifies "he sufficed" or "he made us sufficient." <margin>4</margin> Paul says: *to him who has made us fit for a share of the lot of the saints* <note>original: τῶ ἱκανώσαντι ἡμᾶς εἰς τὴν μερίδα τοῦ κλήρου τῶν ἁγίων</note>. ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *In whom we have redemption and the remission of sins.* ¶ Here, "and" is redundant. Let it be understood, however, that "the remission of sins" is added as an explanation of "redemption." <margin>5</margin> Paul says: *in whom we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins* <note>original: ἐν ᾧ ἔχομεν τὴν ἀπολύτρωσιν, τὴν ἄφεσιν τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν</note>. ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature.* ¶ <margin>6</margin> I preferred to say "firstborn [prior to] every creature"—that is, having a generation prior to every creature, just as eternal things are prior to non-eternal things. I say I preferred to speak thus rather than "firstborn *of* every creature," lest he should seem to be numbered among the rest of the creatures. This was the view of the insane **Eunomius**, **Photinus**, and **Arius** <note>These were ancient theologians whose views—collectively known as Arianism or its variants—suggested that Christ was a created being rather than eternally co-existent with God the Father.</note>, who did not attend to the Apostle’s meaning, but brought forth the presumption and madness of their own thought. For if they had attended to what Paul immediately added to explain his words—*and he is before all things*—they would have understood his saying without great difficulty. When he says "firstborn of every creature," it is the same as being "begotten before every creature" or "begotten prior to every creature," for he is eternally begotten. No creature, however, is eternally begotten, but rather <term>eviternally</term> <note>From *aeviternus*, referring to a duration that has a beginning but no end, often applied to angels or the soul.</note>, or temporally, or age-specifically. Creatures above time are begotten eviternally. The heavens were begotten temporally. Those things beneath the heavens, like all sensible things, are begotten sub-temporally and within an age. And because the sense of that divine saying of Paul—"begotten before every creature," "begotten prior to every creature"—offers and represents itself more clearly when we speak in the <term>ablative</term> <note>The author is arguing that the Latin grammar should imply "born [starting from/before]" rather than "born [as part of]."</note>, we therefore preferred to interpret that saying through the ablative rather than the genitive. Likewise, the illusion of being "numbered among" them is removed. For Paul does not number him among the creatures, he whom he places before every creature, through whom all things were created, and for whose sake all things were created. Yet he is before every creature as the one begotten; just as the Father is before every creature as the one begetting; and as the Holy Spirit is before every creature as the one proceeding. For the Father eternally begat; the Son is eternally begotten; the Holy Spirit eternally proceeds. And these three are before all things as such. Wherefore, as the Son is the First-Begotten of all, the Father is the First-Begetter of all, and the Holy Spirit is the First-Proceeding of all. These three are incalculable relative to creatures; and before all things they are one incalculable and immense Being, which is neither divided by number, nor is the distinction within it confounded. It is above all and in all, unnamable and incomprehensible by every creature. Of this Being, nothing is known, nothing is said, and nothing is affirmed that is not immensely deficient relative to the dignity of so great a thing. Wherefore, it is better worshiped in silence than in words.

->Therefore, let there be a holy silence in heaven and on earth for the First-Begetter of all, the First-Begotten of all, and the First-Proceeding of all: the one God, exalted and set apart above all, blessed and most-blessed unto all ages of ages. Amen.<-

Paul says: *who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation* <note>original: ὅς ἐστιν εἰκὼν τοῦ θεοῦ ἀοράτου, πρωτότοκος πάσης κτίσεως</note>. ¶ <margin>7</margin> **The Vulgate edition:** *Because in him all things were founded.* ¶ The old translator could have said "all things were created." For the same word that he translates here as "founded," he translates a little later as "created," where he says: *all things were created through him and in him.* Why then "created" there and "founded" here, since the word is the same in both places, even if "founded" and "created" are to be understood as the same thing? <margin>8</margin> Paul says: *because in him all things were created* <note>original: ὅτι ἐν αὐτῶ ἐκτίσθη τὰ πάντα</note>. ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** <margin>9</margin> *And he is before all [men].* ¶ It is better "before all [things]." For the sequence of the discourse demands this, since he placed "all things" immediately before and places "all things" immediately after. Nor is there anything to which "all [men]" as an adjective can aptly refer. <margin>10</margin> Paul says: *and he is before all things* <note>original: καὶ αὐτός ἐστι πρὸ πάντων</note>. ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** <margin>11</margin> *And all things consist in him.* ¶ It could be said in the past tense: "they were established." Paul says: <margin>12</margin> *and all things consist [or hold together] in him* <note>original: καὶ τὰ πάντα ἐν αὐτῶ συνέστηκε</note>. ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Because in him it well-pleased [the Father] that all fullness should dwell.* ¶ If it refers to the Father, whose good pleasure it was that all fullness should dwell in Christ, then "in him," "his," and "before him" are used correctly here and in the following. If, however, it refers to the Son, whose good pleasure it was to assume a human body and for all fullness to dwell in himself in the form of men, then one should rather say "in himself," "his own," and "before himself" (or "in his own sight"), so that a certain mutuality and reciprocity (if I may say so) might be recognized. # VII 183 Colossians

"Well-pleasing" is used by Paul to mean "those pleasing." If we look at the following phrase: "intelligence is such that you may walk worthily unto every well-pleasing of the Lord." For here, Paul uses the genitive case <note>original: "genitivo domini"</note> "of the Lord." We have accepted this according to the sense, out of conformity with the old translator: <margin>1</margin> although the first version reflects the Greek more closely. Paul says: "that you walk worthily of the Lord unto all pleasing." <note>original: "περιπατῆσαί ὑμᾶς ἀξίως τοῦ κυρίου εἰς πᾶσαν ἀρεσκείαν"</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "And increasing in the knowledge of God: strengthened in all power." <margin>2</margin> ¶ The old translator could have said: "in the recognition of God: powerful in every power," <margin>3</margin> that is, strong and full of strength. Paul says: "increasing into the knowledge of God, being strengthened in all power." <note>original: "αὐξανόμενοι εἰς τὴν ἐπίγνωσιν τοῦ θεοῦ ἐν πάσῃ δυνάμει δυναμούμενοι"</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "According to the power of his clarity." ¶ It could be said "of his glory." Paul says: "according to the might of his glory." <note>original: "κατὰ τὸ κράτος τῆς δόξης αὐτοῦ"</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "Who made us worthy for the part of the lot of the saints." ¶ What the old <margin>1</margin> translator calls "made us worthy," actually signifies "sufficed" or "made us sufficient." Paul says: <margin>2</margin> "to the one who made us sufficient for the portion of the lot of the saints." <note>original: "τῷ ἱκανώσαντι ἡμᾶς εἰς τὴν μερίδα τοῦ κλήρου τῶν ἁγίων"</note> <margin>3</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "In whom we have redemption and the remission of sins." ¶ The word "and" is redundant. However, let it be understood <margin>B</margin> that "remission of sins" is added as an explanation of "redemption." Paul says: "in whom we have the redemption, the remission of sins." <note>original: "ἐν ᾧ ἔχομεν τὴν ἀπολύτρωσιν, τὴν ἄφεσιν τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν"</note> <margin>1</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "Who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature." <margin>2</margin> ¶ I preferred to say "firstborn *to* every creature" <margin>3</margin>—that is, having a generation prior to every creature, just as eternal things are prior to non-eternal things. I say I preferred to speak this way <margin>4</margin> lest he should seem to be numbered among the rest of the creatures, as it seemed to the insane <margin>5</margin> Eunomius, Photinus, and Arius <note>These were historical figures deemed heretics for their views on Christ's nature; Arius, for instance, taught that Christ was a created being rather than co-eternal with God.</note>. They did not attend to the Apostle’s meaning, but brought forth the presumption and madness of their own thought. For if they had attended to what Paul immediately added for the understanding of his words—"and he himself is before all things"—they would not have found it so difficult to understand Paul’s saying. When he says "firstborn of every creature," it is the same as being "begotten before every creature," "begotten prior to every creature," for he is eternally begotten. No creature, however, is eternally begotten. They are begotten either "eviternally" <note>term: eviternally (original: "aeuiterne") — referring to a state of being that has a beginning but no end, such as that of angels, existing outside of human time.</note>, or temporally, or within an age. Creatures above time are begotten eviternally. The heavens were begotten temporally. Those things below the heavens, like all sensible things, are begotten sub-temporally and in an age. And because the sense of that divine word of Paul—"begotten before every creature" and "begotten prior to every creature"—offers and represents itself more clearly when we speak in the ablative case <note>The author is arguing that using a different grammatical case prevents the reader from thinking Christ is just "the first of many creatures" instead of "prior to all creation."</note>, we have therefore preferred to interpret that saying through the ablative rather than the genitive. Likewise, the illusion of numbering him among creatures is removed. For Paul does not number him with creatures; he places him before every creature, through whom all things were created, and for whom all things were created. Yet he is before every creature as one begotten; just as the Father is before every creature as the one begetting; and as the Holy Spirit is before every creature as the one proceeding. For the Father eternally begat; the Son was eternally begotten; the Holy Spirit eternally proceeds. And these three are before all things as such. Wherefore, as the Son is the first-born of all, the Father is the first-begetter of all, and the Holy Spirit is the first-proceeding of all; and these three are beyond numbering with creatures. Before all things they are one, innumerable and immense, which is neither numbered in distinction, nor confounded in distinction. This is over all and in all, unnamable and incomprehensible by every creature. Of this, nothing is known, nothing is said, nothing is affirmed that is not immensely deficient for the dignity of such a great matter. Wherefore, it is better worshipped in silence than in words. Therefore, let there be a holy silence in heaven and on earth to the first-begetter of all, the first-born of all, the first-proceder of all, the One exalted and set apart above all, the blessed and super-blessed God for all ages of ages. Amen. Paul says: "who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation." <note>original: "ὅς ἐστιν εἰκὼν τοῦ θεοῦ ἀοράτου, πρωτότοκος πάσης κτίσεως"</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "Since in him were all things founded." ¶ The old translator could have said "all things were created." For the same word which he translates here as "founded" <note>original: "condita"</note>, he translates a little later as "created," where he says: "all things were created through him and in him." Why, therefore, "created" here and "founded" there, when the word is the same in both places, even if the same thing is to be understood by both? Paul says: "because in him all things were created." <note>original: "ὅτι ἐν αὐτῷ ἐκτίσθη τὰ πάντα"</note> <margin>1</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "And he is before all." <margin>2</margin> ¶ Better: "before all things." For the logic of the speech requires this, since he placed "all things" immediately before, and also places "all things" immediately after. Nor is there anything to which you might aptly refer "all" <note>original: "omnes"</note> as a masculine adjective. Paul says: "and he himself is before all things." <note>original: "καὶ αὐτός ἐστι πρὸ πάντων"</note> <margin>3</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "And all things consist in him." <margin>4</margin> ¶ It can be said in the past tense: "they have consisted." Paul says: "and all things in him have consisted." <note>original: "καὶ τὰ πάντα ἐν αὐτῷ συνέστηκε"</note> <margin>5</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "Because in him it well-pleased all fullness to inhabit." ¶ If this refers to the Father, whose well-pleasing it was that all fullness should dwell in Christ, then "in him," "his," and "before him" are correct here and in what follows. But if it refers to the Son, whose well-pleasing it was to assume a human body and that all fullness should inhabit in himself in the figure of men, then it should rather be said "in himself," "of his own," or "before himself," or "in his own sight," so that (if I may say so) a mutuality and reciprocity might be recognized. This is what Paul, acting in the place of Christ, gladly endured. And by this very act, Christ suggests to us that he would still gladly die for us in his own person if it were permitted for him to die now—even though he is in every respect immortal—lest we should perish. What can we possibly repay him for such great benefits, for such ineffable mercy and such incredible love? Truly, we can do nothing worthy. Yet, as much as we are able and as much as he helps us, let us give him praise, and honor, and glory, and thanksgiving. Let us keep ourselves for him as holy, pure, and undefiled members of his body, and let us present our heart to him, set on fire with love (for such a gift befits the Lord of love). ¶ May he himself ignite it and deign to accept it, he who is the first of lovers and the love of true lovers: the son of God, blessed above all.

# VII Colossians

...pleasing <note>original: "beneplacentia"</note> is used by Paul to mean "those who are pleasing." If it is read in the following phrase, the meaning is: "that you may walk worthily, according to every pleasure of the Lord." Here, Paul uses the genitive case "of the Lord." We, following the sense and for the sake of consistency with the ancient translator, have accepted this, <margin>1</margin> although the first reading represents the Greek more closely. Paul says: *to walk worthily of the Lord unto all pleasing.* <note>original: "περιπατῆσαι ὑμᾶς ἀξίως τοῦ κυρίου εἰς πᾶσαν ἀρεσκείαν"</note>

<margin>2</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *And increasing in the knowledge of God, strengthened in all virtue.* ¶ The ancient translator could have said: *in the recognition of God, being powerful in all power*—that is, prevailing and full of strength. Paul says: *increasing into the knowledge of God, being strengthened in all power.* <note>original: "αὐξανόμενοι εἰς τὴν ἐπίγνωσιν τοῦ θεοῦ ἐν πάση δυνάμει δυναμούμενοι"</note>

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *According to the power of his brightness.* ¶ It could be said: *of his glory.* Paul says: *according to the might of his glory.* <note>original: "κατὰ τὸ κράτος τῆς δόξης αὐτοῦ"</note>

<margin>3</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Who made us worthy for a share in the lot of the saints.* ¶ What the ancient translator calls "made us worthy," actually signifies "he sufficed" or "made us sufficient." Paul says: *to him who made us sufficient for the portion of the inheritance of the saints.* <note>original: "τῶ ἱκανώσαντι ἡμᾶς εἰς τὴν μέριδα τοῦ κλήρου τῶν ἁγίων"</note>

<margin>2</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *In whom we have redemption and the remission of sins.* ¶ The word "and" is superfluous here. Let it be understood instead that "remission of sins" is added as an explanation of "redemption." Paul says: *in whom we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins.* <note>original: "ἐν ᾧ ἔχομεν τὴν ἀπολύτρωσιν, τὴν ἄφεσιν τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν"</note>

<margin>B</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature.* <margin>3</margin> ¶ I have preferred to say *firstborn before every creature*—that is, having a generation prior to every creature, just as eternal things are prior to those that are not eternal. I say I preferred to speak this way—rather than "firstborn of every creature"—lest he should seem to be numbered among the other creatures. This was the view of the insane <term>Eunomius, Photinus, and Arius</term> <note>These were early Christian theologians whose views were later condemned as heresies; they generally argued that Jesus was a created being rather than eternally co-existent with God the Father.</note>, who did not attend to the Apostle’s meaning, but brought forth the presumption and madness of their own thinking. 

For if they had attended to what Paul immediately added to clarify his words—*and he is before all things*—they would not have found it so difficult to understand Paul’s statement. When he says "firstborn of every creature," it is the same as saying *begotten before every creature*, or *begotten prior to every creature*, for he is eternally begotten. No creature, however, is eternally begotten. They are begotten either "ever-terminally" <note>original: "æuiterne," referring to things that have a beginning but no end, like angels.</note>, or temporally, or within an age. 

Creatures above time are begotten "ever-terminally." The heavens were begotten temporally. Those things below the heavens, such as all sensible things, are begotten "sub-temporally" and within an age. And because the meaning of that divine statement of Paul—*begotten before every creature, begotten prior to every creature*—presents and represents itself more clearly when we speak in the <term>ablative case</term> <note>The author is arguing that using the Latin ablative ("prior to creation") avoids the ambiguity of the genitive ("of creation"), which might imply Christ is part of the created order.</note>, we have preferred to interpret that saying through the ablative rather than the genitive. Likewise, this removes the illusion of him being numbered among them. 

For Paul does not number him among the creatures; he places him before every creature, as the one through whom all things were created, and for whose sake all things were created. Yet he is before every creature as the *begotten*. Just as the Father is before every creature as the *begetter*. And as the Holy Spirit is before every creature as the one *proceeding*. For the Father eternally begat; the Son is eternally begotten; the Holy Spirit eternally proceeds. And these three are "before all things" as such. 

Therefore, as the Son is the "first-begotten" of all, the Father is the "first-begetter" of all, and the Holy Spirit is the "first-proceeding" of all; and these three are incommensurable with creatures. Before all things they are the one, the un-numerable and the immense, which is neither counted in its distinction nor confused in its distinction. This is above all and in all, unnamable and incomprehensible by any creature. Of this, nothing is known, nothing is said, and nothing is affirmed that is not, in comparison to the dignity of such a great thing, immensely deficient. 

Therefore, it is better worshipped in silence than in words. Let there be, then, a **Holy Silence** in heaven and on earth for the First-Begetter of all, the First-Begotten of all, and the First-Proceeding of all—the one God, exalted and set apart above all, blessed and super-blessed forever and ever. Amen. 

Paul says: *who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation.* <note>original: "ὅς ἐστιν εἰκὼν τοῦ θεοῦ ἀοράτου, πρωτότοκος πάσης κτίσεως"</note>

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Because in him all things were founded.* <note>original: "condita sunt"</note> ¶ The ancient translator could have said "all things were created." For the very same word that he translates here as "founded," he translates a little later as "created," where he says: *all things were created through him and in him.* Why, then, "created" there and "founded" here, when in both places it is the same word? Although "founded" and "created" are to be understood as the same thing. Paul says: *because in him all things were created.* <note>original: "ὅτι ἐν αὐτῷ ἐκτίσθη τὰ πάντα"</note>

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *And he is before all [men/people].* ¶ It is better to say *before all things.* For the logic of the discourse demands this, since he has just placed "before all things" and immediately after also places "all things." Nor is there anything to which you could aptly refer "all" as a masculine adjective. Paul says: *and he is before all things.* <note>original: "καὶ αὐτός ἐστι πρὸ πάντων"</note>

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *And all things consist in him.* ¶ It could be said in the past tense: *they were established.* Paul says: *and all things consist in him.* <note>original: "καὶ τὰ πάντα ἐν αὐτῷ συνέστηκε"</note>

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Because in him it has well-pleased that all fullness should dwell.* ¶ If this refers to the Father, whose good pleasure it was that all fullness should dwell in Christ, then it is well said here and in the following "in him," "his," and "before him." If, however, it refers to the Son, whose good pleasure it was to assume a human body and for all fullness to dwell in himself in the form of men, then it should rather be said "in himself," "of his own," or "before himself"—that is, "in his own sight"—so that a certain mutuality and reciprocity (so to speak) might be recognized. Since therefore...

# COMMENTARY

We translate that as "good pleasure"; we understood it to refer to the Son, of whom it is read in a certain place that he says: "and my delights were to be with the sons of men." <note>A reference to Proverbs 8:31, often interpreted as the pre-existent Christ.</note> However, the ancient translator understood it to refer to the Father, to whom <margin>c</margin> he attributed that good pleasure. Neither this nor that is poorly understood, for it pleased the Father and it <margin>4</margin> pleased the Son. Paul's speech is indifferent to either sense. Paul: *because in him it pleased all the fullness to dwell.* <note>original Greek: "ὅτι ἐν αὐτῷ εὐδόκησε πᾶν τὸ πλήρωμα κατοικῆσαι"</note>

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *And enemies in sense.* ¶ It could also be said: *and enemies in understanding.* Paul: *and enemies in the mind.* <note>original Greek: "καὶ ἐχθροὺς τῇ διανοίᾳ"</note>

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** <margin>d</margin> *Of his flesh through death to present you holy.* ¶ The ancient translator should have said: *through his death.* The word "his" is missing. But we, who always look to the Son, to Christ: *through his own death.* <margin>4</margin> Paul: *of his flesh through his death to present you holy.* <note>original Greek: "σαρκὸς αὐτοῦ διὰ τοῦ θανάτου αὐτοῦ παραστῆσαι ὑμᾶς ἁγίους"</note>

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Who now rejoice in the passions for you.* ¶ The "who" is redundant. What is missing is "my." Paul: *now I rejoice in my sufferings for you.* <note>original Greek: "νῦν χαίρω ἐν τοῖς παθήμασίν ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν"</note>

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *And I fill up those things that are wanting of the sufferings of Christ.* ¶ The word Paul uses here <term>antana-plerō: to fill up in turn</term> seems to signify a reciprocity or an alternation of fullness. It is as if we were to say: *I supply the turns* by filling up the subsequent pressures of Christ in my flesh, for his body, which is the church. It is as if Christ is still suffering in his representatives on behalf of all. For the word that follows the word for "fullness" also signifies a certain subsequence. This sense is placed close to the literal meaning. Paul: *and I fill up in turn the things lacking of the afflictions of Christ.* <note>original Greek: "καὶ ἀνταναπληρῶ τὰ ὑστερήματα θλίψεων τοῦ Χριστοῦ"</note>

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *To whom God would make known the riches of the glory of this sacrament.* ¶ Rather: *to make known what are the riches.* Paul: *to whom God willed to make known what is the wealth of the glory of this mystery.* <note>original Greek: "οἷς ἠθέλησεν ὁ θεὸς γνωρίσαι, τί τὸ πλοῦτος τῆς δόξης τοῦ μυστηρίου τούτου"</note>

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Which is Christ in you, the hope of glory.* ¶ It should be read in the masculine gender, "who is." Paul: *who is Christ in you, the hope of glory.* <note>original Greek: "ὅς ἐστι χριστὸς ἐν ὑμῖν, ἡ ἐλπὶς τῆς δόξης"</note>

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Correcting every man.* ¶ Rather *admonishing.* Paul: *admonishing every man.* <note>original Greek: "νουθετοῦντες πάντα ἄνθρωπον"</note>

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *And teaching in all wisdom.* ¶ It should be said: *and teaching every man.* For "every man" is missing. Paul: *and teaching every man in all wisdom.* <note>original Greek: "καὶ διδάσκοντες πάντα ἄνθρωπον ἐν πάσῃ σοφίᾳ"</note>

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Which he works in me in virtue.* ¶ That word "virtue" signifies power, potential, and force. And it should be said, "working in me," or "which works in me" using the nominative rather than the accusative "which he works in me." For "works" refers to the operation, not to Christ. Paul: *the operation working in me in power.* <note>original Greek: "τὴν ἐνεργουμένην ἐν ἐμοὶ ἐν δυνάμει"</note>

## CHAPTER II.

<image-desc>A large decorative initial 'C' featuring a crane or similar long-necked bird standing in a landscape with stylized foliage and architecture in the distance.</image-desc>
When those who only act as representatives urge a task with great sharpness and flee from no labor, sustaining every struggle, it is a sign that the business is of great concern to the Lord and has been most strictly enjoined by him. For this reason, Paul wishes that the Colossians and the Laodiceans—who are peoples of Asia not very distant from the Colossians—would understand his struggle and vehement zeal. He hopes that from this, <margin>5</margin> they might rise to understand the will of the supreme Father and the love of Christ, and rejoice in spirit in the Lord, to whom they are of such great concern. And he adds:

¶ *For I would have you know what manner of struggle I have for you, and for those who are at Laodicea, and for as many as have not seen my person in the flesh; that their hearts may be comforted, being instructed in love, and unto all riches of the full assurance of understanding, to the acknowledgment of the mystery of God the Father and of Christ; in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.*

¶ If you think you know anything worthy of weight and consideration besides the knowledge of God the Father and the mystery of Christ, you deceive yourself. For in this knowledge are stored all the treasures of wisdom and science; in this knowledge, the highest happiness and eternal life consist. "And this," he says, "is eternal life: that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent." Indeed, to know all things (this one thing excepted) is to know nothing. For do you not know poorly—indeed, are you not ignorant—when by knowing these things you rush into eternal death? For if you knew the truth, it would lead you to the truth, yet it leads you to the opposite of truth. For truth is life, and eternal life. And to know this one thing—that is, the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ—even if you are ignorant of everything else, is to know all things. This leads you to the truth, which is eternal life. Here are our treasures and our riches. This is the certain light of understanding, following which we cannot err. Therefore, the Apostle exhorts the <margin>6</margin> Colossians—indeed, everyone—to be attentive and cautious in this knowledge against those who, by crooked paths, would wish to turn us away from this certainty of life, deprive us of such light, and rob us of such ineffable treasures. And he says:

¶ *Now this I say, that no one may deceive you with persuasive speech.* <note>The Latin text uses "paralogizet," a Greek loanword meaning to lead astray with false reasoning or sophistry.</note> *For though I be absent in the flesh, yet am I with you in the spirit, rejoicing and beholding your order, and the steadfastness of your faith which is in Christ. As therefore you have received Christ Jesus the Lord, walk in him, rooted and built up in him, and confirmed in the faith, as you have been taught, abounding in it with thanksgiving.*

<meta>This page continues the philological and theological commentary on the second chapter of the Epistle to the Colossians. The author focuses on Paul’s warning against false philosophy and the Jewish "elements" of the law, contrasting them with the spiritual reality found in Christ.</meta>

<header>VII 184</header>
<margin>Colossians</margin>

, See to it that no one takes you captive through philosophy and empty deceit: according to human tradition, according to the elements of the world, and not according to CHRIST. <note>original: "Videte ne quis vos deprædetur per philosophiā & inanem fallaciam..." Colossians 2:8</note> ¶**To paralogize**: <term>Paralogize</term> <note>From the Greek 'paralogizomai,' meaning to reason falsely or mislead with fallacious arguments.</note> this is a term well known to <term>dialecticians</term> <note>Logic experts or those who study the art of reasoning.</note>. It means to reason wrongly, and to circumvent the truth through crooked, twisted arguments and (as it were) "horned" syllogisms—things that do not truly exist but only appear to—distorting the truth and bringing as much slander as a fallacy can manage. ¶The **twisted serpent**, crawling in crooked coils, seven-tongued, breathes out these paralogisms; he is the father of sophists. ¶The **sevenfold Holy Spirit**, however, channels the truth to his people through the seven rivers of heavenly grace; He is the father of the truthful. He roots, builds up, strengthens, and places thanksgivings in the hearts of his people. The devil, however, and those who study his art, do the opposite: they uproot, destroy, empty out, and make people arrogant and ungrateful. They deprive them of the gifts of the Holy Spirit and prefer the inventions of men—or often (what is more miserable) of demons—over heavenly doctrine. They call this bilge-water of ignorance "philosophy," using a false name; for it is not philosophy, but as Paul explains, an **empty deceit**. For true philosophy catches its light from heavenly wisdom, which is Christ, and is reflected back into Him, just as the light that comes from the sun is reflected back to the sun. ¶Therefore, those who believe they give light to the truth through paralogisms and clever follies (or foolish cleverness) are in error. Night does not bring the day; rather, it is the light which shines from above. Truly, those empty philosophers against whom Paul now contends were Jews who "philosophized"—or rather, more truly, "paralogized"—based on the signs and elements that had been handed down to the Jews, to which they added their own feelings rather than divine ones. For circumcision, and the Passover, and the lamb, and the sprinkling of blood, and the red heifer, and things of that kind, which were like letters and "elements" to the Hebrews—yet **elements of the world**—find their truth in Christ. Divinity does not dwell in those elements as if in its own body; but in Christ, the **fullness of divinity dwells bodily**. Indeed, the body of Christ, of which He is the head, is most full of divinity. Through His mercy, He has made us—as members of His body—bodily participants in this divine fullness.

<margin>7</margin>
¶Paul opens these mysteries to the Colossians, adding: ¶*Because in him dwells all the fullness of divinity bodily. And you are filled in him, who is the head of every principality and power. In whom also you were circumcised with a circumcision not made by hands, in the stripping away of the body of the sins of the flesh, in the circumcision of CHRIST; buried with him in baptism, in which you also rose again through faith by the working of God, who raised him from the dead. And when you were dead in your sins and the uncircumcision of your flesh, he brought you to life together with him, forgiving you all your sins, blotting out the handwriting of the decrees that was against us, and which was contrary to us. And he took it out of the midst, fastening it to the cross; despoiling the principalities and powers, he led them away boldly, triumphing over them in himself.* <note>Colossians 2:9-15. The "handwriting" (chirographum) refers to a legal bond or record of debt.</note> ¶What does "and you are filled in him" mean, if not that you are filled with divinity in Christ, who is the head of the church? If you are of the church, you are of the body of Christ. If you are of the body of Christ, you are filled with divinity. For the fullness of divinity dwells in Him bodily. Oh, if only men could perceive how sublime and how divine it is to be of the body of Christ! How chaste, pure, and holy they would keep themselves for divinity! They would consider all the luxury and glory of the world to be ignominy and disgrace compared to the eternal glory (which is hidden from the senses of the flesh). Other mysteries from other previous passages, as God has permitted, have already been revealed. For these mysteries contain such great dignity that unless someone saw them in the spirit with the eyes of Paul—not attending to what is outside, but what is inside, entirely stripped of the condition of the flesh, like the divine spectacles of the Revelations—no one would be sufficient to declare them, and still he would be an insufficient narrator. For writing only expresses the voice remotely, nor does the voice express the concept; and much more so, human speech does not reach the mysteries of the spirit. And truly we have been brought to life with Christ, even if this life-giving remains hidden from us, especially if we are not yet able to perceive it by the spirit. Our sins have been dismissed from the memories of the devil and from the book of death in which all the sons of darkness are written. Our certificate and obligation <note>original: "diploma & obligatio nostra"</note> has been taken away by the Son of God; He fastened it to the cross and blotted it out and wrote us in the book of the living. And not that alone: but the tyrant of death and his satraps, despoiled as a sign of victory and bound behind his chariot (which is "ten thousand times ten thousand" of the joyful), He triumphed over them under the victorious banner of the cross, and gave them as a spectacle of ignominy to all the rejoicing angels. For this is what "to lead away" means: that is, to make an example of, and a common spectacle of mockery. For thus the heavenly Father wished to triumph in His Son: so that he who had wanted to mock God through His creature might be mocked by the Craftsman of that creature. For the Son is the all-crafting Reason of God, and the Word through which all things were made.
