<header>COMMENTARY</header>

...either Christ as the head, or the body of Christ. But to demonstrate this would be more laborious than the present passage can allow. Nevertheless, leaning on this opinion, Bishop Claudius <note>Likely Claudius of Turin (d. 827), a bishop known for his biblical commentaries and opposition to the use of images.</note> wished to show this in those commentaries which he wrote on the "spirit of the letter." Truly, the superstition of certain people was to introduce the worship of angels, as if it were necessary to be brought to God through them as mediators. The Apostle <note>Saint Paul</note> forbids these libations, invocations, and sacrifices of angels as if they were profane. For many, having been deceived by curiosity, have let evil spirits take the place of good ones, with the spirits lying and claiming to be angels of light. When people cling to these, they are severed from the Head <note>Christ</note> and become 
<margin>9</margin> dead members—just as in a physical body, those members into which no life-force flows from the head are dead. Therefore, the divine Apostle forbids such a wicked superstition and says: >**Let no one disqualify you, insisting on self-abasement and worship of angels, dwelling on things he has not seen, puffed up without reason by his sensuous mind, and not holding fast to the Head, from whom the whole body, nourished and knit together through its joints and ligaments, grows with a growth that is from God.**< <note>Colossians 2:18-19. The word "disqualify" (Latin: "ad bravium vocet") literally refers to being cheated of the "bravium" or the prize at the end of a race.</note> Like those who are about to receive a prize, and something greater and more magnificent than others, these superstitious people call out to those who are simple and of humble wisdom. They call them to the "religion of angels," to private prayers, rites, and sacrifices; and they approach things which they themselves have not seen and which they do not know. But what Paul advises, he has both seen and known; and in it there can be no fraud, no trickery, and no fallacy. These things are made manifest by the figures <note>Types or symbols in the Old Testament.</note>, the prophets, the holy ones, and the Holy Spirit. Furthermore, he gives the Colossians a general instruction to abstain from all the "elements of the world" <note>The basic principles or elementary rules of religious life.</note>: whether they were handed down to the Gentiles for the worship of demons, to the Jews 
<margin>10</margin> for ancient ceremonies, or to the superstitious for magical delusions and the mocking of souls, all of which work toward universal corruption. He says, therefore: >**If with Christ you died to the elemental spirits of the world, why, as if you were still alive in the world, do you submit to regulations? "Do not handle, Do not taste, Do not touch," referring to things that all perish as they are used, according to human precepts and teachings. These have indeed an appearance of wisdom in promoting self-imposed piety, humility, and severe treatment of the body, but they are of no value in stopping the indulgence of the flesh.**< <note>Colossians 2:20-23.</note> <margin>11</margin> Those who live in this world must seek the doctrines of the world, although it would be better not to seek them through the mortification of the world. Those who live for Christ ought to seek the doctrines of Christ, and no longer those things which belong to the world. As for what is added—"do not touch, do not taste, do not handle"—this is a specific sentiment. Even if it were an old saying, there is nothing preventing it from being attributed to the Holy Spirit, who forbids such things.

<margin>Job</margin> ["And the ancient seniors are among us."] Because all heretics have gone out from the holy universal Church, as John testifies when he says: "They went out from us, but they were not of us." But in order to commend the things they assert to the dull minds of men, as if they were from antiquity, they claim to have the ancient Fathers on their side, and they call the very Doctors of the Church the masters of their own profession. While they despise present-day preachers, they glory with false presumption in the mastery of the ancient Fathers, so that they may claim the Ancient Fathers held the same views they do—to the end that what they are unable to prove by right reason, they may confirm as if by the authority of the ancients. All arrogant people have this specific trait: that when they perceive something right or even a little truth, they puff themselves up in this one act of elation. Thus, because they become higher in their own eyes through their intellect, they fall from there into the pit of pride through their swelling vanity. They consider themselves more learned than the learned, demand reverence from their betters, and contend to teach those who are holier as if from a position of authority. And a little later: Because heretics are sometimes put to shame regarding their condemned Fathers, and yet they bring their opinions forward as if with authority, they are rightly reproved by the very folly of those heretics, as it is said: "The wise confess, and do not hide their fathers." Book 12 of the *Morals*, chapter 18.

...my person. We have translated this as "person." Paul [writes]: *and as many as have not seen my face.* <note>original Greek: "kai hosoi ouch heōrakasi to prosōpon mou"</note> ¶ **Vulgate edition:** *That their hearts might be comforted, being instructed in charity, and unto all riches of the fullness of understanding.* ¶ It would be better to say "of them being instructed," so that the adjective and noun agree in their case, just as they do in Paul's text. And "in all riches" should use the ablative case, just as the ancient translator previously used that case for "in charity." Perhaps it says even more: if the word "fullness" does not fully explain the force of the Greek word, which also signifies "full certainty." <note>The Greek "plērophoria" implies a state of being fully persuaded or having total assurance.</note> Paul [writes]: *that their hearts might be knit together in love, unto all riches of the full assurance of understanding.* <note>original Greek: "autōn symbibasthentōn en agapē, kai eis panta plouton tēs plērophorias tēs syneseōs"</note> ¶ **Vulgate edition:** *In the knowledge of the mystery of God the Father and of CHRIST JESUS.* ¶ "Jesus" is redundant here. One should say "of God and the Father," and it is held as an explanatory phrase. Paul [writes]: *unto the knowledge of the mystery of God, and of the Father, and of Christ.* <note>original Greek: "eis epignōsin tou mystēriou tou theou kai patros kai tou christou"</note> And it follows immediately: *in whom are...*
<margin>b
6</margin>
¶ **Vulgate edition:** *That no man deceive you by loftiness of words.* ¶ What the ancient translator calls "loftiness of words," Paul uses to designate the persuasion or "winningness" of eloquence. Paul [writes]: *lest any man should beguile you with enticing words.* <note>original Greek: "hina mētis hymas paralogizētai en pithanologia"</note> ¶ **Vulgate edition:** *As therefore you have received JESUS CHRIST our Lord.* ¶ One should say "Christ Jesus." And "our" is redundant. Paul [writes]: *as therefore you have received Christ Jesus the Lord.* <note>original Greek: "hōs oun parelabete ton christon iēsoun kyrion"</note> And it follows immediately: *in him.* ¶ **Vulgate edition:** *As also you have learned, abounding in him in thanksgiving.* ¶ It is better to say "you were taught." And "in it" (using the feminine) rather than "in him" (masculine); for it refers back to "faith." <note>In Latin and Greek, "faith" is a feminine noun, so the pronoun should match.</note> Paul [writes]: *as you have been taught, abounding in it with thanksgiving.* <note>original Greek: "kathōs edidachthēte, perisseuontes en autē en eucharistia"</note> ¶ **Vulgate edition:** *Lest any man deceive you.* ¶ Here it could be translated as "plunder you." Paul [writes]: *Lest any man spoil you.* <note>original Greek: "mētis hymas estai ho sylagōgōn" – literally, to carry off as a captive or booty.</note>
<margin>c
7</margin>
¶ **Vulgate edition:** *In the stripping away of the body of the flesh.* ¶ One should say "of the sins of the flesh," or "from the sins of the flesh." The small word "sins" is missing. Paul [writes]: *in the stripping away of the body of the sins of the flesh.* <note>original Greek: "en tē apekdysei tou sōmatos tōn hamartiōn tēs sarkos"</note> ¶ **Vulgate edition:** *In whom also you are risen again by the faith of the operation of God.* ¶ Rather: "you have been raised up together." And it seems nothing is out of place if we resolve the genitive into the ablative case and say "by the operation of God"—and this is when it is referred back to "raised up together." If, however, it refers to "faith," it should be explained by the genitive, since faith is an "operation of God" within us. Paul [writes]: *in whom you are also risen together through faith in the operation of God.* <note>original Greek: "en hō synēgerthēte dia tēs pisteōs tēs energeias tou theou"</note>
<margin>d
7</margin>
¶ **Vulgate edition:** *Blotting out the handwriting of the decree that was against us.* ¶ It should be in the plural ablative: "by the decrees" or "from the decrees." Paul [writes]: *blotting out the handwriting that was against us in the decrees.* <note>original Greek: "exaleipsas to kath' hēmōn cheirographon tois dogmasin"</note> ¶ **Vulgate edition:** *And despoiling principalities and powers, he led them confidently, openly triumphing over them in himself.* ¶ The word "And" is redundant. And that word "to lead" <note>Latin: "traducere"</note> means to make an example of shame; it is a term well known to historians and legal experts. One could also say: "in confidence." "Openly" is redundant. ¶ What the ancient translator says as "in himself" has an ambiguous meaning in the Greek. For if the relative pronoun refers back to the "cross," then one should say "in it" [the cross]. If, however, the speech is understood to be about the Father, and the relative refers to Christ, then one should say only "in him" or "through him." If it refers to Christ, such that Christ is understood to be the one triumphing, it can be said "in himself," so that it is understood as reflexive speech, even if the Greek is not reflexive. Therefore, we have explained it without the reflexive, as if the Father were triumphing in the Son, having conquered the evil powers and removed the document of our debt. Just as Vespasian <note>Roman Emperor, 69–79 AD.</note> triumphed over the Jews in [the person of] his son Titus. Paul [writes]: *And having spoiled principalities and powers, he made a show of them openly, triumphing over them in it [the cross/himself].* <note>original Greek: "apekdysamenos tas archas kai tas exousias edeigmatisen en parrēsia, thriambeusas autous en autō"</note> ¶ **Vul-**

8</margin>
**gate edition:** *Let no man judge you in meat or in drink, or in respect of a festival day.* ¶ This discourse concerns the foods, drinks, and festivals of the Jewish observance. These were "elements" and "figures" <note>Symbols or prefigurations.</note> of Christ, who has now been offered and is expiating our sins, now satisfying us and feeding us with heavenly and <term>super-vital nourishment</term> <note>Nourishment that sustains more than just biological life.</note>. The <term>New Moons</term>—that is, the new months, which were reckoned from the silent and new moon—prefigured the new time of the Church. The Hebrew people celebrating at the newness of the month [prefigured] the people of Christ celebrating a new era; which faithful people are indeed the body of Christ. Who then ought to judge us, blame us, or accuse us if we do not observe those foods, drinks, festivals, or new moons as they do, since we now possess all these things in their Truth? The body and blood of Christ contain the Truth of every food and drink. The festivities of Christ are the Truth of all Jewish celebrations. The Passion of Christ fulfills every sacrifice. The body of Christ is the Church, always celebrating in newness. These things are the whole; those things of the Jews, however, were "in part." The festival was partial and imperfect; the food and drink were partial; and everything of the Jews was partial and imperfect. Let us therefore leave behind

He who knows how to do this would see the New in the Old, and the Old in the New; he would see the light in the shadow, and the shadow in the light; he would see the Truth in the figure, and the figure in the Truth. <meta>This page continues the philological and theological commentary on the second chapter of Paul’s Epistle to the Colossians. The author remains focused on refining the Latin Vulgate translation by comparing it to the original Greek, while transitioning into a deeper meditation on "Christiformity"—the spiritual process of being reshaped into the likeness of Christ.</meta>

<header>COMMENTARY</header>

<margin>D 9</margin> Paul and Timothy understood [this] through the sacred imposition of Paul's hands. Neither man, nor reason, nor human study is able to give this sense; rather, it is infused from above, or taken from those who have been infused from above. Whatever is done without these, such as the human study of authorities in these matters, is presumption and rashness. Many sail in this deceitful sea. But enough of these things for now. ¶ **Vulgate edition:** *Let no man seduce you.* <note>Colossians 2:18</note> ¶ The word used here rather signifies "to stir up" and "to call toward the prize," <note>The author is discussing the Greek word "katabrabeuetō," which implies a judge disqualifying someone from a prize.</note> rather than simply "calling to the worship and veneration of angels." The prize is won (for neither do the angels give the prizes to believers, nor do they propose them; rather, the good angels merely assist the worshippers, while the evil ones hinder them however they can), but some were calling people to this kind of worship, observances, and religious rites—or more truly, superstitions—as if those who worshipped in such a way would receive a prize. They did not understand that Christ is the head, the one who both proposes the prizes and distributes the rewards to the authors. Paul [writes]: *Let no one disqualify you from your prize.* <note>original Greek: "mēdeis hymas katabrabeuetō"</note> ¶ **Vulgate edition:** *In humility and religion of angels.* ¶ It should be said, "in humility of sense." <note>The author suggests "humility" here refers to a lowly or misguided way of thinking.</note> Paul [writes]: *in humility and the worship of angels.* <note>original Greek: "en tē tapeinophrosynē kai thrēskeia tōn angelōn"</note> ¶ **Vulgate edition:** *Puffed up by the sense of his flesh.* ¶ It could be said "by the mind." And this mind belongs to the flesh—a carnal mind, unchaste according to the flesh, and leaning upon its own prudence. Paul [writes]: *Puffed up by the mind of his flesh.* <note>original Greek: "physioumenos hypo tou noos tēs sarkos autou"</note> <margin>D 10</margin> ¶ **Vulgate edition:** *Why do you yet, as if living in the world, make distinctions?* <note>Colossians 2:20</note> ¶ It could be said: "do you dogmatize," "are you burdened with dogmas," "do you seek dogmas," or something similar. For dogmas are the inventions of men and the curious doctrines of men, and for the most part, they are vain and superstitious. Paul [writes]: *Why, as if living in the world, do you submit to decrees?* <note>original Greek: "ti hōs zōntes en kosmō, dogmatizesthe"</note> ¶ **Vulgate edition:** *Touch not, taste not, handle not: which all are unto destruction by the very use.* <note>Colossians 2:21-22</note> ¶ Paul speaks in the singular. And these are the words of the Spirit speaking through him. "Unto destruction" in the fourth case <note>the accusative case in Latin grammar</note>, that is, *toward* destruction, seems better said than "in destruction" in the sixth case <note>the ablative case</note>. and "by misuse" <note>original: "abusu"</note> rather than "by the very use." Paul [writes]: *Do not handle, nor taste, nor touch; all of which are for destruction in the consuming.* <note>original Greek: "mē hapsē, mēde geusē, mēde thigēs ha estin panta eis phthoran tē apochrēsei"</note> ¶ **Vulgate edition:** *And humility, and not sparing the body.* ¶ It should be said (as before) "humility of sense." And where the ancient translator says "and not sparing the body," Paul uses a privative noun, as if we might say "unsparingness," which is a certain cruelty and (as it were) a harsh affliction of the body. Paul [writes]: *and humility, and severity to the body.* <note>original Greek: "kai tapeinophrosynē, kai apheidia sōmatos"</note>

### CHAPTER II

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'N' featuring a robed figure, likely a prophet or saint, seated in a landscape with clouds above.</image-desc> Let us not follow the precepts and <term>dogmas</term> <note>human-made rules or decrees, often contrasted here with divine truth</note> of men, which have no foundation in the light that shines from above. Instead, let us consider that Christ died for us all: life was offered to all sources in exchange for the death of the infant; <note>This may be a metaphorical reference to Christ's humility or a specific theological paradox regarding the "newborn" state of the soul.</note> life was given to the unjust in exchange for the death of the Just; and life was bestowed upon sinners in exchange for the death of Him who committed no sin. He who died was infinitely—indeed, more than infinitely—good, and His death was powerful enough to give life even to more than infinite evils, if such a plurality of infinity were possible. Indeed, whoever comes to Him dies in His death and rises in His resurrection. For they would not rise unless they had first died. In this way, they are made <term>Christiform</term> <note>original: "Christiformes," meaning shaped or molded into the form of Christ</note> so that they may fit His body. For it is necessary for the members of the whole body to have conformity to the head; otherwise, it would be a monster. In other things, this conformity is called ratio and proportion; but in the body of Christ, it is called **Christiformity**. Therefore, since they rise in the resurrection of Christ, they also live the life of Christ. For from where would the members live—and with such an excellent life—if not from the head? But if they live the life of Christ, and Christ is above (for He is sitting above at the right hand of the Father), they ought to seek the things that are above and feel the things that are above, not the doctrines of men and those things that are upon the earth. For even now, we dwell in heaven in a spiritual state, even if the dying members of our flesh crawl upon the earth. Though this spiritual state cannot be seen by the eyes of the flesh, it is manifest only to those to whom <term>visions</term> <note>original: "orases," from the Greek "horasis"</note> are given—that is, spectacles in the spirit. This happened most frequently to Paul, and it is the way he was taught by Jesus Christ, from which he also teaches us. Certainly, when I read Paul—I who am nothing—I seem to behold the vision itself: he clearly, but I (as is fitting) and as God wills, see it as through a shadow. Who, I say, could see with eyes of flesh that divine state and the manner by which we are even now inserted into a body full of divinity? In this very thing our life, by which we live in the spirit, is hidden. It will be made manifest with Christ, who is our life and eternal life; that inspiration will be made manifest to us. It will be manifested individually to each person in the "coming" which is near—at the laying down of the veil of our flesh—and universally to all in the Universal Coming. Whether that be near or <margin>11</margin> far, only He knows who knows the times and moments which the Father has placed in His own power. Paul opens all these things to the Colossians divinely, yet succinctly and in few words, saying: *If then you have risen with CHRIST, seek the things that are above, where CHRIST is sitting at the right hand of God.*

# VII Colossians

...seeking the things that are above; set your mind on things that are above, not on things on the earth. For you have died, and your life is hidden with CHRIST in God. When CHRIST, who is our life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory. ¶ These are not the doctrines of men, but celestial instructions. And just what kind of "mortification" <note>original: "mortificationem"; a technical term for the spiritual "killing off" of sinful habits or worldly desires</note> of the earthly limbs and the carnal members <margin>12</margin> that are upon the earth the Lord of both flesh and spirit wants from us, that divine herald and interpreter of the divine will, Paul, explains more clearly, saying: ¶ Mortify, therefore, your members which are upon the earth: fornication, uncleanness, lust, evil concupiscence, and greed, which is the worship of idols. Because of these things, the wrath of God comes upon the children of unbelief, in which you also once walked when you lived in them. But now, you also put away all these: anger, fury, malice, blasphemy, and filthy language from your mouth. Do not lie to one another. Strip off the old man with his deeds, and put on the new man, who is renewed in knowledge according to the image of him who created him. Where there is neither Gentile nor Jew, circumcision nor uncircumcision, barbarian, Scythian, slave, or free; but CHRIST is all and in all.

<insert>
The members of Christ are spiritual. The members of the flesh are carnal, such as carnal affections, fornications, uncleanness, lusts, evil concupiscences, and greed. And these must be mortified along with their deeds—that is, in one day and two nights. <note>The author uses a complex allegory here: Christ’s time in the tomb (the Triduum) symbolizes the process of spiritual death and rebirth.</note> For the twelve hours of the day are to the twenty-four hours of the two nights as a single measure is to a double measure. And indeed, the twelve daylight hours, being single, correspond to the death of our Redeemer. But the twenty-four nighttime hours pertain to our own divine death. By a great sacrifice, he lay in the tomb for one day and two nights, which joined the single light of justice to the double darkness of our death.
</insert>

<insert>
...minds: because, without doubt, he rests in dark and simultaneous consciences, and he does not delight in the lascivious and the luxurious. ¶ Then he says, "I will return to the house from which I came": <note>A reference to the parable in Matthew 12:44 about an unclean spirit returning to a house.</note> that is, "I will seek the heretic whom I lost in baptism." This verse is greatly to be feared, for the guilt we believed was forgiven us, through our neglect while we are idle, [returns] <unclear>...</unclear> And coming, he finds <unclear>...</unclear> among which...
</insert>

...indeed spiritual things, which hold the highest and chief place for this victory of the mortification of carnal affections (as if they were the "members" of the flesh), are the love of God and the love of neighbor. For that flame burns up all the harmful affections of the flesh, just as a fire set to the fields burns the stubble. But Paul also adds the specific ways <margin>13</margin> in which they are mortified, commending love above all else, and says: ¶ Put on, therefore, as the holy elect of God and beloved, the bowels of mercy, kindness, humility of mind, gentleness, and patience; bearing with one another and forgiving one another, if anyone has a complaint against another. Just as CHRIST has forgiven you, so you must also do. But above all these things, put on love, which is the bond of perfection. And let the peace of God hold the palm of victory in your hearts, into which you were also called in one body; and be joyful. Let the word of CHRIST dwell in you abundantly in all wisdom, teaching and admonishing yourselves with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs in grace, singing in your hearts to the Lord. And whatever you do, whether in word or in work, do all things in the name of the Lord JESUS, giving thanks to God the Father through him. ¶ These are the spiritual tools with which we fight against the members of the flesh (that is, carnal affections) and deliver them to destruction.

But come, you will say: are the macerations of the flesh—such as fasts, vigils, nakedness, poverty, and hardships—to be considered nothing? By no means would I say that. Rather, when it is appropriate, they are to be applied to the flesh in many ways. Sometimes they are like a spur to a rebellious horse, lest the flesh become wanton. Yet, just as a horse is not fed by the strikes of the spurs, so you will not perceive your rewards because of those strikes, but from the grace of Christ, into whom you are grafted through conformity. Sometimes, too, they are not used as a spur. For even if the flesh is not wanton, I would not deny that these should be applied. For the Apostle [Paul] chastised his own body in this way, lest he be found not fully conformed to Christ in every part, and thus be excluded from his company. "I chastise my body," he says, "and bring it into servitude, lest when I have preached to others, I myself should become a castaway." <note>1 Corinthians 9:27</note> But in those chastisements, he did not place the summit of his salvation, but in the grace of Christ; he believed he was conformed to Christ through them, imitating him and offering himself as a model of imitation to others, whose target and truth is Christ.

But you will say: "I am a sinner; I wear a hair shirt, I fast, I abstain, I receive lashings, I pray, I pour out tears abundantly, I roll myself in the dust so that God may have mercy on me." You do well. But you do best when, doing all these things, you look not at yourself, nor at your works, but at God—except when you call yourself a sinner. For in this [self-reliance], you are contrary to Christ God. If, therefore, you wear a hair shirt: wear it because Christ also deigned to wear it for you. "I was clothed," he says, "in sackcloth." <note>Psalm 35:13</note> Furthermore: "I made sackcloth my clothing." <note>Psalm 69:11</note> If you fast: fast for the sake of Christ, because Christ fasted for you. "I humbled my soul with fasting," he says. <note>Psalm 35:13</note> And again: "And I covered my soul with fasting." <note>Psalm 69:10</note> If you abstain: abstain, because Christ also abstained for you, for which he was mocked by those who did not abstain. "They who drank wine," he says, "sang against me." <note>Psalm 69:12</note> Likewise: "My flesh is changed because of the oil." <note>Psalm 109:24</note> If you receive lashings: receive them, because Christ our King was beaten with whips for you. "And I have been scourged all day long," he says, "and my chastisement is in the morning." <note>Psalm 73:14</note> If you pray: pray, because our Lord prayed for us, and was heard...

### COMMENTARY

...was added out of reverence. ¶ They spoke against me (he says), but I gave myself to prayer. <note>original: "Detrahebant michi: ego autem orabam"; a reference to Psalm 109:4</note> and elsewhere: "My prayer is directed to you, Lord." Pray: because Christ taught us to pray. Pray: because he commanded us to pray. When you pray (he says), say... <note>referring to the Lord's Prayer in Luke 11</note> And again: Pray that you enter not into temptation. If you shed tears: do not merely weep for yourself and your sins (for then you would be looking primarily at yourself), but weep especially because you have offended God your creator and the infinite Goodness, whom heaven and earth obey, to whom all things bow, and to whom all owe <gloss>of</gloss> obedience. Even if you do not feel sins within yourself: weep, because Christ, who is God, wept for you. I am weary (he says) with my groaning; every night I wash my bed; I water my couch with my tears. <note>Psalm 6:6</note> Furthermore: You have put my tears in your sight. If you roll prostrate in the dust: do this because Christ was also cast down upon the ground for you. I (he says) ate ashes like bread, and mingled my drink with weeping. If you do penance: do it because Christ said, "Repent" <note>original: "pœnitentiam agite"; also translated as "do penance"</note>; for he himself deleted our sins by his own penance.

<margin>
Heretics neglect Catholics and [other] heretics.
It is the duty of priests to win them over by the force of reason. He always acts with reason, lest they perish through their own [actions]—let the heretics be silenced. Isaiah 32.
In the time of an Orthodox Emperor, let the heretics be silenced.
Gregory, Gennadius, the Life of the Lord, and the Exarch of Africa... <note>Gregory the Great and Gennadius were early Church fathers; the Exarch of Africa refers to a high-ranking Byzantine official involved in suppressing the Donatist heresy.</note>
The case of the brothers—to see [the case] of the heretics is now commonplace.
Here it must be noted that it is considered more harmful [to neglect them]: in whose time the heretics are brought to a confession of God through the reasoning of our teaching, which things are touched upon. For the Donatists <note>The Donatists were a rigorous schismatic sect in North Africa that clashed with the mainstream Church.</note> [leave] the churches whole: and others whom the law condemns as perfect [wickedness]: not only of heretics but of divine laws—among whom is iniquity, as we have learned from them.
</margin>

¶ This is a good imitation: but that one is better which consists in the imitation of mercy, dignity, spiritual humility, gentleness, patience, mutual support, the forgiveness of offenses if any occur, fiery love, and the peace of God in a spiritual place; in the word of Christ which is the gospel of eternal peace; in wisdom, <term>doctrine</term> <note>original: "doc[trina]"</note>, and spiritual encouragement; and in a certain way a struggle and zeal for winning in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs; in the grace of God, with a heart rejoicing in God; and doing nothing in either word or deed except in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, giving thanks through him to God the Father. Both are imitations. And happy is he who is worthy to imitate Christ in both: to become <term>Christ-formed</term> <note>original: "Christiformis"; the process of being spiritually reshaped into the likeness of Christ</note> both within and without. After these things, the holy apostle speaks briefly on the duties of the married: where there is a most tight bond because of the bond between Christ and the Church, of which it is a symbol. Then the bond of father and children: which is a close bond after the former, representing the bond of God and the creature. And thirdly, of master and servants, where there is a lesser bond, like that of God and the sinner. Yet providence does not desert him, but by its very benefit it makes its sun to rise upon the good and the bad, and rains upon the just and the unjust. For thus he is good and merciful: whom masters ought to imitate toward their servants. But regarding these duties and these bonds in chapters 5 and 6 of the fifth book, which is on the Epistle to the Ephesians, much has been said: here the discourse must be shortened, and from those earlier writings it may be understood more subtly and spiritually.

<margin>14</margin>
> Paul, who says: ¶ Wives, be subject to your husbands (as is fitting) in the Lord. Husbands, love your wives and do not be bitter toward them. Children, obey your parents in all things: for this is well-pleasing to the Lord. Fathers, do not provoke your children: lest they be discouraged by sadness. Slaves, obey in all things your earthly masters, not with eye-service <note>original: "seruitijs ad oculũ"; serving only when the master is watching</note> as though pleasing men, but in simplicity of heart, fearing God. And whatever you do, work at it from the soul as for the Lord, and not for men: knowing that from the Lord you will receive the reward of the inheritance. For you serve the Lord CHRIST. But he who does an injury will receive back what he has done in injury; and there is no respect of persons.

¶ In all things Christ is to be looked upon: and in all things, he is discerned with spiritual eyes. By a woman, Christ is to be looked upon in her husband: as in the head and in majesty. By a husband, Christ is to be seen in the woman: as in the Church. By a child, Christ is to be seen in the father: in the majesty of his creation. In children, Christ is to be seen: as in creatures, preserving them with wonderful care and love. In a master, Christ is to be seen: as exalted in his power. In slaves, Christ is to be seen: as in his justice, punishing evils and injustices, yet with mercy and reason. So that Christ may be all in all to us. All things are types: Christ is the truth of all things. Who in all things and by all things, be blessed and most blessed: without end, and beyond. Even as divinity, goodness, providence, and majesty demand. AMEN.

# VII

<margin>Colossians</margin>

<a></a> with CHRIST. ¶ It is enough that it be said: "if you have risen with Christ," or in our way of speaking: "if you rose together with Christ." Paul: <note>original: "ει ουν συνηγερθητε τω χριςω" (If then you have been raised with Christ)</note>. ¶ **The Vulgate Edition:** *Mind the things that are above.* <note>Colossians 3:2</note> ¶ Here "mind" [sapite]: this comes from a word that they prefer to translate as "set your heart on" or "feel" [sentite]. Paul: <note>original: "τα ανω φρονειτε" (Set your minds on things above)</note>. ¶ **The Vulgate Edition:** *For you are dead.* ¶ This refers to a past state; to express this more clearly, we preferred to say "you have been" rather than "you are." Paul: <note>original: "απεθανετε γαρ" (For you died)</note>. ¶ **The Vulgate Edition:** *When CHRIST shall appear, who is your life.*

<margin>12</margin> ¶ It is read as "our life" using the first-person derivative pronoun, not the second-person. Paul: <note>original: "οταν ο χριςος φανερωθη η ζωη ημων" (When Christ, our life, appears)</note>. ¶ **The Vulgate Edition:** *Lust, evil concupiscence.* ¶ Where the old translator says "lust" [libidinem], in Paul we find "passion" [pathos], which they are accustomed to call an affection or a disturbance of our nature. Paul: <note>original: "παθος, επιθυμιαν κακην" (passion, evil desire)</note>. ¶ **The Vulgate Edition:** *And avarice, which is the service of idols.* ¶ What the old translator calls "the service of idols," Paul says in one word: "idolatry," that is, the worship of idols. For who doubts that the greedy prefer their gold, silver, or merchandise to God out of love? And this is to worship a creature and (so to speak) to commit idolatry. Paul: <note>original: "και την πλεονεξιαν ητις εςιν ειδωλολατρεια" (and greed, which is idolatry)</note>. ¶ **The Vulgate Edition:** *Upon the children of unbelief.* ¶ That word "unbelief" is what the old translator elsewhere called "distrust," and what we have said designates "unpersuadableness," when they refuse to be persuaded to truly follow the good; even if they confess it with their mouth, they show by their works that they do not believe, are not persuaded, and do not trust. Paul: <note>original: "επι τους υιους της απειθειας" (upon the sons of disobedience)</note>. ¶ **The Vulgate Edition:** *But now put you also all away: anger, indignation.* ¶ It should rather be said: "anger, fury." Paul: <note>original: "νυνι δε αποθεσθε και υμεις τα παντα. οργην, θυμον" (but now you also put them all away: anger, wrath)</note>. ¶ **The Vulgate Edition:** *Where there is neither male nor female, Gentile and Jew.* ¶ The phrase "male and female" is superfluous <note>Meaning it is an addition not found in the Greek text of this specific verse, though found in Galatians 3:28</note>. Paul: <note>original: "οπου ουκ ενι ελλην και ιουδαιος" (where there is no Greek and Jew)</note>. ¶ **The Vulgate Edition:** *Barbarian and Scythian, bond and free.*

<margin>β 12</margin> ¶ In Paul, these are spoken with the conjunctive particle "and." Paul: <note>original: "βαρβαρος, σκυθης, δουλος, ελευθερος" (Barbarian, Scythian, slave, free)</note>. ¶ **The Vulgate Edition:** *The bowels of mercy, humility, modesty, patience.* 

<margin>b 13</margin> ¶ Rather: "the bowels of compassion," and subsequently "humility of mind" <gloss>of feeling</gloss>, "gentleness." Paul: <note>original: "σπλαγχνα οικτιρμου, χρησοτητα, ταπεινοφροσυνην, πραοτητα, μακροθυμιαν" (bowels of mercy, kindness, lowliness of mind, meekness, longsuffering)</note>. ¶ **The Vulgate Edition:** *As the Lord also hath forgiven you.* 

<margin>c 13</margin> ¶ It should read "as Christ." Paul: <note>original: "καθως και ο χριςος εχαρισατο υμιν" (even as Christ forgave you)</note>. ¶ **The Vulgate Edition:** *But above all these things have charity, which is the bond of perfection.* ¶ Paul expressed no verb here, but he understood the verb "put on" from the previous verses; therefore, if any verb was to be expressed, "put on" should have been expressed rather than having a new verb which Paul did not use. And it should rather be said "which is" (referring to the feminine 'charity') as shortly after, rather than "that which is." Paul: <note>original: "επι πασι δε τουτοις, την αγαπην, ητις εςι συνδεσμος της τελειοτητος" (and over all these things, love, which is the bond of perfection)</note>. ¶ **The Vulgate Edition:** *And let the peace of CHRIST rejoice in your hearts.* ¶ It should read "of God," and where the old translator says "rejoice" [exultet], Paul’s word signifies to obtain the palm of victory or the prize, or to call to the prize. Paul: <note>original: "και η ειρηνη του θεου βραβευετω εν ταις καρδιαις υμων" (and let the peace of God rule in your hearts)</note>. ¶ **The Vulgate Edition:** *And be ye thankful.* ¶ It can also be said: "and be ye cheerful." For the word placed here signifies both being thankful and being pleasant, but with a holy and spiritual joy and grace. For those who have the peace of God in their hearts cannot but be sincerely cheerful and rejoice; and this joy and exultation in God is great and immense, above all the sweetnesses that earthly men have tasted in their delights, they who are the children of "disobedience" <note>original: "απειθειας"</note> and "unpersuadableness." Paul: <note>original: "και ευχαριςοι γινεσθε" (and be thankful/grateful)</note>. ¶ **The Vulgate Edition:** *In psalms, hymns.* ¶ It should read: "in psalms and hymns." Paul: <note>original: "εν ψαλμοις και υμνοις"</note>. ¶ **The Vulgate Edition:** *In your hearts to God.* ¶ It should read "in your heart" <gloss>singular</gloss> "to the Lord." Paul: <note>original: "και καρδια υμων τω κυριω"</note>. ¶ **The Vulgate Edition:** *And whatsoever you do in word or in work, all things in the name of our Lord JESUS CHRIST, giving thanks to God.* ¶ It should say "may you do." And the understanding is clearer if we express "through" for all things. And the words "our" and "Christ" are superfluous; for as the old translator placed it, the sense is intelligible, which among the Greeks is rightly understood. Paul: <note>original: "και παν οτι αν ποιητε εν λογω, η εν εργω, παντα εν ονοματι κυριου ιησου ευχαριςουντες τω θεω" (and whatever you do in word or deed, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God)</note>. 

<margin>D 14</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate Edition:** *Wives, be subject to your husbands.* ¶ The old translator immediately follows with: "husbands, love your wives." He used the same word for "wives" here that he previously translated as "women." But why here rather than there? Why did he not translate it consistently in both places, since Paul is only speaking of those who have a husband? For he does not command women to be subject to men in any other way. Therefore, it should rather be said "wives" in both places, so that the letter may be less open to the slander of those who do not wish to understand correctly. Paul: <note>original: "αι γυναικες υποτασσεσθε τοις ανδρασιν" (Wives, submit yourselves to your own husbands)</note>. ¶ **The Vulgate Edition:** *Husbands, love your wives.* ¶ The word "your" is superfluous. Paul: <note>original: "οι ανδρες αγαπατε τας γυναικας" (Husbands, love the wives)</note>. ¶ **The Vulgate Edition:** *Fathers, provoke not [your children] to indignation...*

<meta>This page continues the philological commentary on Paul’s Epistle to the Colossians. <header>COMMENTARY</header>
<meta>catchword: to you</meta>

...to love your children: so that they do not become faint-hearted. ¶ Where the old translator <note>The Latin Vulgate</note> says "to provoke to indignation," Paul says it in one word, which signifies the same as "to irritate." For those who correct others ought not to irritate them. To correct is one thing; to irritate is another. For those who correct do so in such a way that those being corrected understand that the rebuke is a medicine for them, and for their own good. But when they irritate, they do not do this at all; neither those who irritate nor those who are irritated feel it to be a medicine or for their good, but only the indignation of the one irritating. And in this, fathers and teachers often tend to sin, for they do not know how to correct, and (if they are rebuking someone) they do not know how to distinguish between correcting and irritating. Hence, children and students are wasted by sadness and hate those who irritate them, whereas they would truly love those who correct them. In a corrector, love is recognized; in an irritator, hatred. But how could love, once recognized, not be loved? And how could hatred ever be loved? This holy precept of Paul must be noted above all by all fathers—both of biological descent and of doctrine and education. And regarding what the old translator says, "lest they become faint-hearted," Paul says in one word what signifies "to be saddened," specifically that sadness which takes away the spirit for doing any good. For indeed, he who is irritated, or who thinks he is being irritated, is dejected in spirit, and has no mind to perform any good work. Let us therefore study to correct prudently, not to irritate. Paul: **"Fathers, do not provoke your children, lest they be discouraged."** <note>original Greek: "οἱ πατέρες μὴ ἐρεθίζετε τὰ τέκνα ὑμῶν, ἵνα μὴ ἀθυμῶσιν"</note>. ¶ **The Vulgate Edition:** *Not serving to the eye.* ¶ Paul does not use a participle, but a noun, as if we were to say "in eye-service," or "service to the eye," or something similar. Paul: **"not in eye-service."** <note>original Greek: "μὴ ἐν ὀφθαλμοδουλείᾳ"</note>. ¶ **The Vulgate Edition:** *Whatsoever you do, work from the heart.* ¶ It should be said: "And everything whatsoever you do." And "from the heart" [ex animo] means "from the soul" [ex anima]. For "animus" <term>animus: the rational mind or will</term> is taken here for "anima" <term>anima: the vital soul or life-force</term>, not for "animosity" or mere "emotion." Paul: **"And whatever you do, work from the soul."** <note>original Greek: "καὶ πᾶν ὅ τι ἂν ποιῆτε, ἐκ ψυχῆς ἐργάζεσθε"</note>. ¶ **The Vulgate Edition:** *Serve the Lord CHRIST.* ¶ It should be said: "for you serve the Lord Christ." Paul: **"for you serve the Lord Christ."** <note>original Greek: "τῷ γὰρ κυρίῳ χριστῷ δουλεύετε"</note>. ¶ **The Vulgate Edition:** *For he who does injury.* ¶ Rather: "But he who acts unjustly." ¶ **The Vulgate Edition:** *And there is no respect of persons with God.* ¶ The phrase "with God" is superfluous. Paul: **"and there is no partiality."** <note>original Greek: "καὶ οὐκ ἔστι προσωποληψία"</note>.

->CHAPTER 4<-

<margin>15</margin> <image-desc>Decorative drop-cap "Q" with an illustration of a figure seated at a desk within an architectural frame.</image-desc> **P**aul has unfolded how servants should behave toward their masters; now he reveals how masters must behave toward their servants, and says: ¶ *Masters, provide justice and equity to your servants: knowing that you also have a master in heaven.* ¶ What is more characteristic of justice than those who represent God—either by correcting or punishing evils, yet granting mercy and clemency to all who are corrected. What he subjoins concerning common prayer, which ought to be done by attending to it with a watchful mind, pertained to all the Colossians. He also requests the support of their prayers to be made for him before God. For God wishes to give for His own sake, but He requires certain preparations in us—possibilities within us, always with His help. For do we not see <margin>16</margin> (with the Head <note>Christ</note> administering strength) the members helping other members, and helping as much as they can to receive the influence of the Head? Therefore, what Paul says is this: ¶ *Be devoted to prayer, watching in it with thanksgiving, praying at the same time for us also: that God may open to us a door for the word to speak the mystery of CHRIST, for which I am also in chains: that I may make it manifest, as I ought to speak.* ¶ Paul believes himself to be made more ready to receive God’s grace more abundantly for the manifestation of the gospel through their prayers; indeed, he believes others are made more ready to receive the word of life. But he also admonishes them regarding how they should behave toward those who are still unbelievers, outside the body of Christ and outside the church, so that they may be drawn to life by the fragrance of wisdom and holiness, and be made members of the church. Over these, the angels in heaven rejoice, and every celestial building taking its increase. He says, therefore: <margin>17</margin> ¶ *Walk in wisdom toward those who are outside: redeeming the time. Let your speech always be in grace, seasoned with salt: knowing how you ought to answer each one.* ¶ What it means to "buy time," and who they are who buy it, we have already said in the commentaries on the epistle to the Ephesians. Where benevolence and love do not appear in speech, it lacks grace. And it is "seasoned with salt" when it is brought forth wisely, when it is savory to the listeners, and draws toward incorruption, and preserves the one who admits it as incorrupt. For this is the property of spiritual salt, which physical salt imitates. What he adds are the familiar duties of a dear friend, naked and open. For it is fitting for friends in the love of Christ to lay bare their souls even to the smallest details. Thus he says: <margin>18</margin> ¶ *Concerning the things regarding me: Tychicus, a beloved brother, and a faithful minister, and a fellow servant in the Lord, will make you certain of everything. I have sent him to you for this very purpose: that he may know the things that concern you, and comfort your hearts, with Onesimus, a faithful brother, who is one [of you]. All things indeed...*

<meta>This page concludes the commentary on the final chapter of Paul’s Epistle to the Colossians. It transitions from the historical details of Paul's companions to a discussion of the "lost" Epistle to the Laodiceans, providing a copy of an apocryphal version the author found in various European libraries.</meta>

<header>Colossians</header>

...will make known twice: what things are here. ¶ **Dorotheus** <note>Dorotheus of Tyre, a traditional author of a list of the seventy disciples of Christ</note> writes that **Tychicus** was the bishop of Colophon. Moreover, **Onesimus** is known from the Apostle to be a Phrygian and to have been of Colossae. But from what place they were sent by the Apostle: if we look at the Latin argument, they were sent from the city of Ephesus; if we believe the Greek subscription, they were sent from the city of Rome. Afterward, the Apostle specifically sets down several greetings from the holy ones. He commends **Epaphras**, from whom the Colossians had also heard the word of God, and who at last, having been crowned with martyrdom among them, rested in Christ. Those whom he names in the greetings are these: **Aristarchus**, **Mark**, **Jesus Justus**, **Epaphras**, **Luke** my physician, and **Mark** the cousin of **Barnabas** (concerning whom you received instructions: if he comes to you, that you should receive him), and **Jesus** surnamed **Justus**, who are of the circumcision. These alone are coworkers for the kingdom of God, who have been a comfort to me. **Epaphras**, who is one of you, greets you; a servant of **CHRIST**, always striving for you in prayers, so that you may stand perfect and complete in every matter, by the will of God. For I bear him witness: that <note>original abbreviation: "$\phi$" for "quod"</note> he has much zeal for you, and for those who are in **Laodicea**, and those in **Hierapolis**. **Luke**, the beloved physician, greets you, and **Demas**. ¶ **Laodicea**: is a city of Maeonia situated above the Lycus river, neighboring Colossae. And **Hierapolis**, which is also called the "sacred city": is near Laodicea, diverging slightly toward the east and south according to **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century geographer</note>. Now, however, **Paul**, in his own name and that of the saints, asks that the brothers of the Laodicean church be greeted, and that the present letter be sent to them and read in their church. Indeed, he asks that the letter which he himself had written to the Laodiceans be read in turn among the Colossians. He commands that **Archippus** be reminded of his diligence: who was performing the office of the apostolate in those places. In place of a farewell, he does not pray for the absence of anything, but rather prays for and desires the presence of the grace of God for them; and he says: ¶ Greet the brothers who are in Laodicea, and **Nympha**, and the church in her house. And when the letter has been read among you, see that it is read in the church of the Laodiceans. And that you read the one that is of the Laodiceans. And he says to **Archippus**: see to the ministry which you have received in the Lord, that you fulfill it. The greeting: by my own hand, Paul's. Remember my chains. Grace be with you. Amen. Written at Rome. Sent by Tychicus and Onesimus. ¶ The letter which Paul sent to the Laodiceans is not currently contained among his epistles. However, I have found one distinguished by the title of "Paul to the Laodiceans" in four places. First, in **Padua** in the monastery of Saint John of the Greenery <note>San Giovanni di Verdara</note>. In **Cologne** among the **Brothers of the Common Life**, and in **Paris** in the libraries of Autun and the Sorbonne. Since I observed that it contains nothing but piety, it would also be nothing alien to piety if we insert it in this place; so that those who are students of Paul (as all Christians ought to be) may read it, and that those reading it may also be comforted. It is of this sort:

### THE EPISTOLA OF THE MOST BLESSED PAUL THE APOSTLE TO THE LAODICEANS.

<margin>EPISTLE TO THE LAODICEANS</margin>
Paul, an apostle not from men, nor through man, but through **JESUS CHRIST**: to the brothers who are at Laodicea, grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord **JESUS CHRIST**. I give thanks to **CHRIST** through all my prayer: that you are remaining and persevering in good works, awaiting the promise on the day of judgment. And let not the vain speech of certain people disturb you, who attack the truth so that they might turn you away from the truth of the gospel which is preached by me. And now God will act: so that those who are of me may be serving toward the perfection of the truth of the gospel, and performing the kindness of works which belong to the salvation of eternal life. ¶ And now my chains are manifest, which I suffer in **CHRIST**: in which I rejoice and am glad. And this is for me unto perpetual salvation: which was brought about by your prayers, with the Holy Spirit administering. Whether through life or through death: for me, to live is life in **CHRIST**, and to die is joy. And he himself will perform his mercy in you: that you may have the same love and be of one mind. ¶ Therefore, most beloved: as you have heard of the presence of the Lord, so perceive and act in fear, and you will have life for eternity. For it is God who works in you. And do whatever you do without sin. ¶ And what is best, most beloved: rejoice in the Lord **JESUS CHRIST**. And beware of all filth in every gain. Let all your petitions be manifest before God. Be firm in the mind of **CHRIST**: and those things which are upright, and true, and modest, and chaste, and just, and lovable, do them. And what you have heard and received, retain in your heart: and peace will be with you. Greet all the brothers with a holy kiss. All the saints greet you. The grace of our Lord **JESUS CHRIST** be with your spirit. Amen. Have this read to the Colossians, and the one of the Colossians read to you. ¶ This is the letter I found under the name of Paul and the Laodiceans. And I rejoiced in finding it, and read it most willingly once found, with pleasure because of the name of Christ and his apostle. If it is short: what prevents the apostle from having composed sometimes short, sometimes long letters? That one which is to [the...] is also short.

For those who reprove <note>original: "corripiunt"</note> ought not to irritate. It is one thing to reprove; it is another to irritate. Afterward, the Apostle lists several greetings from the saints specifically. He commends Epaphras, from whom the Colossians had heard the word of God, and who was finally crowned with martyrdom among them and rested in Christ. Those whom he names as sending greetings are these: Aristarchus, Mark, Jesus called Justus, Epaphras, Luke the physician—who is also the evangelist and author of the Acts of the Apostles—and Demas, who later apostatized <note>Demas is mentioned in 2 Timothy as having deserted Paul because he "loved this present world."</note>. These, therefore, are those specific greetings. ¶ Aristarchus, my fellow prisoner, greets you, as does Mark, the cousin of Barnabas (concerning whom you received instructions: if he comes to you, welcome him), and Jesus, who is called Justus, who are of the circumcision <note>original: "ex circumcisione"; this refers to Jewish Christians.</note>. These alone are my fellow workers for the kingdom of God, who have been a comfort to me. Epaphras, who is one of you, greets you; a servant of CHRIST, always struggling for you in prayers, that you may stand mature and fully assured in everything that is the will of God. For I bear him witness that he has great zeal for you and for those in Laodicea and those in Hierapolis. Luke, the beloved physician, and Demas greet you. ¶ Laodicea is a city of Meonia <note>original: "Meoniæ"; an ancient name for the region of Lydia in Asia Minor.</note> situated upon the Lycus river, near Colossae. And Hierapolis, which is also the "Sacred City," is near Laodicea, diverging slightly toward the east and south according to Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century Greco-Roman geographer and astronomer.</note>. Now, however, Paul, in his own name and that of the saints, asks that the brothers of the church of Laodicea be greeted, and that the present letter be sent to them and read in their church; and likewise, that the letter which he himself had written to the Laodiceans be read among the Colossians. He commands that Archippus, who was performing the office of the apostleship in those places, be encouraged to diligence. In place of a farewell, he prays for and desires the presence of the grace of God for them, rather than the absence of anything else, and says: ¶ Greet the brothers who are in Laodicea, and Nympha, and the church in her house. And when the letter has been read among you, see that it is also read in the church of the Laodiceans, and that you read the letter that is from the Laodiceans. ¶ And say to Archippus: "See to the ministry that you have received in the Lord, that you fulfill it." The greeting is by my hand, Paul's. Remember my chains. Grace be with you. Amen. ¶ Written at Rome; sent by Tychicus and Onesimus. ¶ The letter which Paul sent to the Laodiceans is not currently contained among his epistles. However, I found one entitled "To the Laodiceans" under the name of Paul in four places: First, in Padua in the monastery of Saint John of Viridario; in Cologne among the Brothers of the Common Life; and in Paris in the Edunense and Sorbonne libraries. Because I observed that it contained nothing but piety, it would not be alien to piety if we were to insert it in this place, so that those who are students of Paul (as all Christians ought to be) may read it and even be comforted while reading. It is of this sort:

Paul, an apostle, not from men, nor through man, but through JESUS CHRIST, to the brothers who are at Laodicea: grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord JESUS CHRIST. I give thanks to CHRIST through all my prayer, because you are permanent and persevering in good works, awaiting the promise on the day of judgment. Neither let the vain talk of certain people disturb you, who undermine the truth so that they might turn you away from the truth of the Gospel which is preached by me. And now God will bring it about that those who belong to me <note>or "those who follow my lead"</note> may be serving toward the perfection of the truth of the Gospel, and performing the kindness of works which belong to the salvation of eternal life. ¶ And now my chains are manifest, which I suffer in CHRIST: in which I rejoice and am glad, and this is to my perpetual salvation, which was brought about by your prayers and the administration of the Holy Spirit. Whether through life or through death, for me to live is life in CHRIST, and to die is joy. And He himself will perform His mercy in you, so that you may have the same love and be of one mind. Therefore, most beloved, as you have heard of the presence of the Lord, so think and act in fear, and you shall have life for eternity. For it is God who works in you. And do whatever you do without sin. ¶ And what is best, most beloved: rejoice in the Lord JESUS CHRIST, and beware of all filth in every kind of gain. Let all your petitions be made known before God. Be firm in the mind of CHRIST: and those things which are whole, and true, and modest, and chaste, and just, and lovable, do them. And what you have heard and received, retain in your heart, and peace shall be with you. Greet all the brothers with a holy kiss. All the saints greet you. The grace of our Lord JESUS CHRIST be with your spirit. Amen. Have this read to the Colossians, and that of the Colossians to you. ¶ This is the letter I found under the name of Paul and the Laodiceans. And I rejoiced in finding it, and because of the name of Christ and his apostle, I read the found work very gladly with pleasure. Even if it be short: what prevents the apostle from having composed short letters at some times and long ones at others? Even that one which is to [Philemon] is short...

<header>COMMENTARY</header>
<warning>Page has a large hole/tear on the right side of the lower half, obscuring significant portions of text.</warning>

care for your children: so that they do not become faint-hearted. ¶ Where the <note>original: "vetus interpres"</note> Old Interpreter says "to provoke to indignation," Paul uses a single word that signifies the same as "to irritate." For those who correct others should not irritate them; for correction is one thing, and irritation is another. Those who correct do so so that those being corrected may understand that the correction is a medicine for them and for their own good. However, when they irritate, they do not do this at all; neither those who irritate nor those who are irritated feel the medicine or their own good, but only the indignation of the one irritating. And in this, fathers and teachers often tend to sin: those who do not know how to correct and (if they are reproving someone) do not know how to distinguish between correcting and irritating. Hence, children and students are consumed by sadness and hate those who irritate them, whereas they would truly love those who correct them. In a corrector, love is recognized; in an irritator, hatred. But how could known love not be loved? And how could hatred be loved? And this holy precept of Paul must be noted above all by all fathers—both of biological generation and of doctrine and education. And regarding what the Old Interpreter says, "lest they become faint-hearted" <note>original: "pusillo animo fiant"</note>, Paul uses a single word which signifies "to be saddened," and indeed by that sadness which takes away the spirit for doing any good. For indeed, he who is irritated, or who thinks himself irritated, is dejected in spirit and has no spirit to perform any good work. Let us, therefore, prudently strive to correct, not to irritate. Paul writes: <note>original: "οι πατερες μη ερεθιζετε τα τεκνα υμων, ινα μη αθυμωσιν"</note> "Fathers, do not provoke your children, so that they do not lose heart." ¶ The Vulgate edition says: "Not serving to the eye." ¶ Paul does not use a participle, but a noun, as if we were to say "in eye-service," or "service to the eye," or something similar. Paul writes: <note>original: "μη εν οφθαλμοδουλεία"</note> "not in eye-service." ¶ The Vulgate edition says: "Whatever you do: work from the heart." It should be said "And everything whatsoever you do." And "from the heart" <note>original: "ex animo"</note> means "from the soul" <note>original: "ex anima"</note>. For "mind/heart" here is taken for "soul," not for "animosity or mere emotion." Paul writes: <note>original: "και παν ότι αν ποιητε, εκ ψυχης εργαζεσθε"</note> "And all that you do, work from the soul." ¶ The Vulgate edition says: "Serve the Lord CHRIST." It should be said: "for you serve the Lord Christ." Paul writes: <note>original: "τω γαρ κυριω χριστω δουλευετε"</note> "for you serve the Lord Christ." ¶ The Vulgate edition says: "For he who does an injury." Rather: "But he who..." Paul writes: <note>original: "ο δε αδικων"</note> "But he who does wrong." ¶ The Vulgate edition says: "And there is no respect of <unclear>persons</unclear> with God." ¶ The phrase "with God" is superfluous. Paul writes: <note>original: "και ουκ εστι προσωποληψία"</note> "and there is no respect of persons."

For do we not see <margin>16</margin> (with the head administering strength) the members of the body helping one another, and helping as much as they can to receive the influence of the head? What Paul says, therefore, is this: ¶ Persevere in prayer, being watchful in it with thanksgiving, praying at the same time for us also, that God may open for us a door of the word to speak the mystery of CHRIST, for which I am also bound, that I may make it manifest, as I ought to speak. ¶ Paul thinks he is made more ready to receive God’s grace more abundantly for the manifestation of the gospel through their prayers; indeed, he thinks others are made more ready to receive the word of life. But he also warns how they ought to behave toward those who are still unbelievers, outside the body of Christ and outside the church, so that they may be drawn to life by the scent of wisdom and holiness, and be made a member <margin>17</margin> of the church. For these, the angels in heaven rejoice, and every heavenly edifice takes on growth. He says, therefore: ¶ Walk in wisdom toward those who are outside, redeeming the time. Let your speech always be in grace, seasoned with salt, knowing how you ought to respond to each one. ¶ What it means to "buy time," and who those are who buy it, we have already said in the commentaries on the Epistle to the Ephesians. Where benevolence and love do not appear in speech, it lacks grace. And it is seasoned with salt when it is brought forth wisely, when it is savory to the listeners, and draws them toward incorruption, and preserves the one who receives it as incorrupt. For this is the property of spiritual salt, which physical salt imitates. What he adds are familiar things, and the <margin>18</margin> naked and open duties of a friend. For it befits friends in the love of Christ to lay bare their souls even to the smallest details. Thus he says: ¶ Tychicus, the beloved brother, and faithful minister, and fellow servant in the Lord, will make you certain of all things that concern me. I have sent him to you for this very purpose: that he may know the things that are with you, and comfort your hearts, with Onesimus, the faithful brother, who is one [of you]. All things...

¶ EXAMINATION of several points regarding the literal text. ¶ Vulgate edition: *Continue in prayer.* <note>original: "Orationi instate."</note>
<margin>16</margin>
¶ It can be said: "be devoted to" or "serve." Paul says: <term>be devoted to prayer</term> <note>original Greek: "τῇ προσευχῇ προσκαρτερεῖτε"</note>. ¶ Vulgate edition:
<margin>A</margin>
*Redeeming the time.* <note>original: "Tempus redimentes."</note> ¶ We can say: "buying up the time," and that seems to be sufficient.
<margin>17</margin>
Paul says: <term>buying up the opportunity</term> <note>original Greek: "τὸν καιρὸν ἐξαγοραζόμενοι"</note>. ¶ Vulgate edition: *Tychicus, most dear brother.*
<margin>B</margin>
¶ It should be said: "beloved brother." Paul says: <term>Tychicus the beloved brother</term> <note>original Greek: "τυχικὸς ὁ ἀγαπητὸς ἀδελφός"</note>. ¶ Vulgate
<margin>18</margin>
edition: *With Onesimus, most dear and faithful brother.* ¶ Here also it should be said "beloved," but with the
order of the words changed in a certain way. For it should be said: "with Onesimus, the faithful and beloved
brother." Paul says: <term>with Onesimus the faithful and beloved brother</term> <note>original Greek: "σὺν ὀνησίμω τῶ πιστῶ, καὶ ἀγαπητῶ ἀδελφῶ"</note>. ¶ Vulgate
<margin>C</margin>
edition: *These alone are my helpers.* ¶ Rather: "Co-workers in the kingdom of God." The word "My" is
<margin>19</margin>
superfluous. It also seems possible to say "co-workers for the kingdom of God." Truly, I believe both can be said. For the present church, although it is not the whole kingdom of Christ (who is the same God), is nevertheless a part of the kingdom of Christ and therefore the kingdom of God. But he who is in a part of the kingdom of any king is said to be in the kingdom of that king. Therefore, if we are truly faithful, we are already in the kingdom of God, and we live and work in the kingdom of God. Let us see to it, therefore, that we never do anything unworthy of such a kingdom and such a king, and let us always attend to what befits such a kingdom and such a king. That the state of the present church is called the "kingdom of God" is also testified by sacred authors. "We must know," says the holy Gregory <note>Pope Gregory the Great, an influential 6th-century theologian.</note>, "that in sacred speech the kingdom of heaven is often called the church of the present time." And what is the kingdom of heaven but the kingdom of God? And the Savior said to those believing in him: "Behold, for the kingdom of God is within you." Behold, therefore, how they can be called co-workers in the kingdom of God who also build in this world. But the "kingdom of God" is also called the state of the blessed who already enjoy the revealed Christ-God, which will be completed on the last day. Concerning this, the Savior also says to the unbelieving Jews: "There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth when you see Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob and all the prophets in the kingdom of God, but you yourselves cast out. And they shall come from the east and west, from the north and south, and shall sit down in the kingdom of God." And of the same kingdom it is said in the Acts: "that through many tribulations we must enter into the kingdom of God." This kingdom is the future one; that other is the present one. This one has the open revelation and presence of the eternal King; the other has a veil and a hidden presence. And those who build in this world toward life and co-operate with the Gospel are not yet co-workers in the kingdom of God in this second sense, but they are co-workers *toward* the kingdom of God. Behold, therefore, if the "kingdom of God" is taken in the second sense, it would be aptly translated "co-workers toward the kingdom of God." Truly, all who are co-workers in the present kingdom of God are all co-workers toward the future kingdom of God, which is the end, completion, and consummation of the present. Paul says: <term>these alone are co-workers for the kingdom of God</term> <note>original Greek: "οὗτοι μόνοι συνεργοὶ εἰς τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ θεοῦ"</note>. ¶ Vulgate edition: *A servant of Christ JESUS, always solicitous for you.* ¶ "JESUS" is superfluous. And rather: "striving" than "solicitous." Paul says: <term>a servant of Christ, always striving for you</term> <note>original Greek: "δοῦλος Χριστοῦ πάντοτε ἀγωνιζόμενος ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν"</note>. ¶ Vulgate edition: *Who has much labor for you.* ¶ In Greek it is: "much zeal," that is, he has a very great and exceeding desire. And certain Greek codices have <term>longing</term> <note>original Greek: "πόθον"</note>, which clearly signifies desire. Paul says: <term>that he has much zeal</term> <note>original Greek: "ὅτι ἔχει ζῆλον πολύν"</note>. ¶ Vulgate edition: *Luke the most dear physician.* ¶ As in other places: "Luke the beloved physician."
<margin>D</margin>
Paul says: <term>Luke the beloved physician</term> <note>original Greek: "λουκᾶς ὁ ἰατρὸς ὁ ἀγαπητός"</note>. ¶ Vulgate edition: *And that which is of the Laodiceans, let it be read to you.*
<margin>20</margin>
¶ Rather: "so that you also may read it." Paul says: <term>and the [letter] from Laodicea, so that you also may read it</term> <note>original Greek: "καὶ τὴν ἐκ λαοδικείας, ἵνα καὶ ὑμεῖς ἀναγνῶτε"</note>. ¶ Vulgate edition: *The grace of our Lord JESUS CHRIST be with you. Amen.* ¶ The expression "of our Lord Jesus Christ" is superfluous, even if it is understood. Paul says: <term>grace be with you, amen</term> <note>original Greek: "ἡ χάρις μεθ' ὑμῶν, ἀμήν"</note>. And among the Greeks, the subscription is held: "To the Colossians, written from Rome, sent through Tychicus and Onesimus."

<header>VIII 189 1 Thessalonians.</header>

## BOOK EIGHT OF THE COMMENTARIES ON THE EPISTLES OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PAUL, WHICH IS ON THE FIRST EPISTLE TO THE THESSALONIANS, CHAPTER I.

<image-desc>A large historiated woodcut initial 'S' depicting a figure (likely Saint Paul) seated at a desk and writing in a book, set within a classical interior with architectural details and foliage.</image-desc>Paul, writing this first epistle to the Thessalonians—who are Macedonians living on this side of Mount Athos, which is now called the "Holy Mountain" <note>Mount Athos, or Agion Oros, remains a major center of Orthodox monasticism in Greece</note>, where even in our own time the inhabitants live almost in the manner of the <term>Essenes</term> <note>An ancient Jewish sect known for asceticism and communal living; the author compares them to Christian monks</note>, calling upon the name of Christ there day and night, even though the Turks and the blasphemy of the first beast revealed in the <term>Apocalypse</term> <note>The Book of Revelation; 16th-century authors often identified the Ottoman Empire with apocalyptic figures</note> occupy everything in the surrounding region—writing, therefore, this epistle to the Thessalonians, he begins with a holy greeting according to his custom, starting in this way: ¶ **Paul and Silvanus and Timothy: to the church of the Thessalonians in God the Father and the Lord JESUS CHRIST, grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord JESUS CHRIST.** ¶ This is the holy greeting. To this he joins a giving of thanks, in memory of God's graces which he recognizes are situated within them. And he adds: ¶ **We give thanks to God always for all of you, making mention of you in our prayers, being unceasingly mindful of the work of your faith, and the labor of your love, and the endurance of the hope of our lord JESUS CHRIST, before our God and Father.** ¶ He who gives thanks demonstrates, as much as he can, a grateful soul. He who does not, shows himself ungrateful. Now, a benefactor seeks nothing so much from those upon whom he freely bestows benefits as gratitude; he hates nothing so much in those he helps as ingratitude.
<margin>1</margin> 
<margin>,</margin> 
<margin>,</margin> 
<margin>,</margin> 
<margin>2</margin> 
<margin>,</margin> 
<margin>,</margin> 
<margin>,</margin> From this it follows that we owe nothing to God so much as the giving of thanks. To perform this task, the apostle—that cultivator and preparer of spiritual grace—instructs us in all his epistles, and almost always right near the beginning. For he who sows is God; but Paul himself plowed the furrows with the plowshare of the word of God, which the Holy Spirit also provides. But there is nothing that so obstructs gratitude as the neglect of remembering benefits. For just as the fern that must be burned <note>original: "urenda filix"</note> grows in neglected fields, so ingratitude creeps into our minds unless remembrance is present. Ingratitude, I say, which is to be burned with eternal fires. For this reason, Paul brings to the Thessalonians' memory those first benefits of divine illumination, and says: ¶ **You know, beloved brothers, your election by God: because our gospel was not among you in word only, but also in power, and in the Holy Spirit, and in much fullness of certainty. Just as you know what kind of men we were among you for your sake. And you became imitators of us, that is, of the Lord, receiving the word in much pressure, with the joy of the Holy Spirit. So much so that you became an example to all believers in Macedonia and Achaia. For from you the word of the Lord has been sounded abroad, not only in Macedonia and Achaia, but also in every place your faith toward God has spread. So much so that it is not necessary for us to say anything. For they themselves report about us, what kind of entrance we had among you, and how you turned to God from idols, to serve the living and true God, and to wait for His Son from heaven (whom He raised from the dead), JESUS, who rescues us from the coming wrath.** ¶ The fact that Paul was engaged with the Thessalonians in the grace of speech, in the power of signs, in the Holy Spirit, and in the full certainty of the harvest to be gathered and stored in the Lord's barn—this he does not attribute to himself, but to the Thessalonians. For they, with God's help, were preparing themselves to receive divine graces while the ministers were opening the way. For the power to perform signs, heal diseases, the grace of speech, and spiritual things of that kind were not always given to the apostles; rather, they were given when the Spirit of God knew the grace of God would not be in vain. Therefore, when it was given, it was not given for the sake of the one who performed the signs, but for the sake of those who were being saved and who perceived the new light of divine radiance for their salvation. Indeed, our Lord, who is powerful in Himself and almighty, did not perform signs and powers where they would have been made void. "And he could not," it says, "perform any miracle there" <note>Referring to Mark 6:5, regarding Jesus' visit to Nazareth</note>. Not that He was absolutely unable (for there is nothing He cannot do), but there would have been no fruit from the deeds, since the unbelievers would by no means have given glory to God. This kind of "inability," therefore, was not on the part of the Doer, but of the lack of preparation and the incapacity of those who would receive it. For a fire sent down from heaven burns nothing there nor can it burn; but this kind of impossibility arises not from the part of the agent, but from the part of the recipient. The power of burning is given to the fire, therefore, not for its own sake, but for the sake of those things that are capable of being burned. So too are the gifts of the Holy Spirit: for the sake of those who would receive life-giving from them. **You know** (he says) **what kind of man I was among you for...**

<summary>This page introduces the commentary on 1 Thessalonians, beginning with a historical context of the region and a theological meditation on the necessity of gratitude toward God. The author explains that spiritual miracles and the "power" of the Gospel depend as much on the readiness and faith of the recipients as they do on the power of the ministers.</summary>
