...for your sake. And when he could not perform signs and miracles: this inability belonged to those among whom he lived. For he was not without the spirit of God. For would that all-creating Spirit <note>original Latin: "omnifator spiritus," a rare term likely meaning the Spirit who creates or makes all things</note> sow his seed at random, yielding no fruit, like an unskilled farmer? It is a sin either to ask or believe such a thing. When he says, "who rescues us from the wrath that is coming," he designates a wrath that is nearby, as if it were at the doors. Death is at everyone's door; wrath is in death. But Christ frees us from that wrath which already hangs over us, which is imminent: and not only from this nearby wrath, but also that whose distance is unknown, which is to come on the final day. Jesus is the deliverer now; he is the deliverer then. Jesus is our near peace; he is our far-off peace. May he be blessed above all for ages of ages. Amen.

<margin>A 1</margin> **EXAMINATION of several points regarding the literal text.** ¶ VULGATE EDITION: *To the Church of the Thessalonians in God our father and the Lord JESUS CHRIST.* ¶ "Our" is redundant. PAUL: <note>original Greek: "τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ Θεσσαλονικέων ἐν θεῷ πατρὶ, καὶ κυρίῳ ἰησοῦ χριστῷ"</note> *To the church of the Thessalonians in God the father and the Lord Jesus Christ.* ¶ VULGATE EDITION: *Grace to you and peace.* ¶ The small phrase is missing: *from God our father and the Lord Jesus Christ.* <margin>2</margin> PAUL: <note>original Greek: "χάρις ὑμῖν, καὶ εἰρήνη, ἀπὸ θεοῦ πατρὸς ἡμῶν, καὶ κυρίου ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ"</note> *Grace to you and peace from God our father and the Lord Jesus Christ.* ¶ VULGATE EDITION: *And of labor, and of charity, and of patience.* <margin>B 3</margin> ¶ It should be said: *of labor, of charity* without the conjunction "and." PAUL: <note>original Greek: "καὶ τοῦ κόπου τῆς ἀγάπης, καὶ τῆς ὑπομονῆς"</note> *and of the labor of love and of patience.* ¶ VULGATE EDITION: *Knowing, my beloved brothers, by God.* ¶ We have said it is Paul’s custom, or rather a frequent practice of the Greeks, to use participles where the Latins, according to the proper nature of their language, use verbs. Hence, we have changed that word "knowing" <note>original: "scientes"</note> into the verb "you know" <note>original: "scitis"</note> so that it might better suit Latin speech. PAUL: <note>original Greek: "εἰδότες ἀδελφοὶ ἠγαπημένοι ὑπὸ θεοῦ"</note> *Knowing, brothers beloved by God.* ¶ VULGATE EDITION: *In power and in the Holy Spirit and in much fullness.* ¶ It could be said: *in authority* and *in the fullness of certainty.* For the word placed here <note>Referring to the Greek "plerophoria" (πληροφορία)</note> (as noted in another place) is not sufficiently explained by the word "fullness" alone. <margin>C 3</margin> PAUL: <note>original Greek: "ἐν δυνάμει καὶ πνεύματι ἁγίῳ, καὶ ἐν πληροφορίᾳ πολλῇ"</note> *In power and in the Holy Spirit and in much full-assurance.* ¶ VULGATE EDITION: *So that you were made a form.* ¶ This word "form" is called *typos* in Greek <note>original Greek: "τύπῳ"</note>, which translators are also accustomed to render as "example" or "model" in sacred texts. PAUL: <note>original Greek: "ὥστε γενέσθαι ὑμᾶς τύπους"</note> *So that you became examples.* And though Paul says "examples" in the plural, it seems more fitting to Latin speech if it is said in the singular and uniquely as an "example." ¶ VULGATE EDITION: *For from you the word of the Lord was defamed.* <note>The Latin "diffamatus est" in the Vulgate can imply being "spread abroad," but by the 16th century, it strongly meant "slandered." The author argues this is a poor choice for "resounded."</note> ¶ The ancient translator used a quite unsuitable word, "defamed," instead of "rang out" or "was made public." For "defamed" is usually taken in another sense and in a bad way. And Remigius <note>Remigius of Auxerre, a 9th-century commentator</note> pinned this impropriety of speech upon Paul, as if he had been unskilled in speech through some defect; in this matter (as he has been noted by others, and not without reason), Remigius revealed himself to be the one unskilled through defect. For Paul speaks both elegantly and most appropriately. PAUL: <note>original Greek: "ἀφ᾿ ὑμῶν γὰρ ἐξήχηται ὁ λόγος τοῦ κυρίου"</note> *For from you the word of the Lord resounded.* ¶ VULGATE EDITION: *In every place your faith, which is toward God, has gone forth.* ¶ It should be said "into every place," and at the end: "has arrived," "has gone out," "has been carried," <margin>D 3</margin> or something similar. PAUL: <note>original Greek: "ἐν παντὶ τόπῳ ἡ πίστις ὑμῶν ἡ πρὸς τὸν θεὸν, ἐξελήλυθεν"</note> *In every place your faith toward God has gone forth.* ¶ VULGATE EDITION: *For they themselves report of us.* ¶ Latins are more accustomed to say "for us" <note>original: "pro nobis"</note> as if it had been said in Greek *hyper hēmon*, although there it is said *peri hēmon* <note>original Greek: "περὶ ἡμῶν," meaning "concerning us"</note>. PAUL: <note>original Greek: "αὐτοὶ γὰρ περὶ ἡμῶν ἐπαγγέλουσιν"</note> *For they themselves report concerning us.* ¶ VULGATE EDITION: *How you turned from idols to serve the living and true God.* ¶ The ancient translator, speaking according to the custom of the Latin language, could have resolved the infinitive "to serve" into a gerund and said "for serving" <note>original: "ad serviendum"</note>. And similarly regarding the following infinitive, "to wait." PAUL: <note>original Greek: "πῶς ἐπεστρέψατε πρὸς τὸν θεὸν, ἀπὸ τῶν εἰδώλων δουλεύειν θεῷ ζῶντι καὶ ἀληθινῷ"</note> *How you turned to God from idols, to serve the living and true God.* ¶ VULGATE EDITION: *Who snatched us from the wrath to come.* ¶ It can be said in the present tense: *who snatches.* And "from the wrath that is coming" or "which is about to come." For they are accustomed to translate *erchomenon* <note>original Greek: "ἐρχόμενον"</note> as both "coming" and "about to come." PAUL: <note>original Greek: "ῥυόμενον ἡμᾶς ἀπὸ τῆς ὀργῆς τῆς ἐρχομένης"</note> *Who delivers us from the coming wrath.*

He does not commend his own person, but declares the truth of God’s grace by which he came to them. For it is not Paul’s habit to look at himself, but at grace, and at God the author of grace. He says therefore: **For you yourselves know, brothers, our entrance which was among you, that it was not in vain. For our exhortation was not from error, nor from impurity, nor in deceit: but as we were approved by God to be entrusted with the gospel, so we speak. Not as pleasing men, but God who proves our hearts.** ¶ His entrance was not in vain, because many of the believers...

# VIII 190 1 Thessalonians

<margin>1</margin>
...there was fruit. When a farmer sows and a great crop sprouts, the plowing of the earth was not in vain. Paul plowed; God sowed. Much fruit sprouted. Paul broke the field of the soul with the word of God; God poured in grace. For the word of God is both a plowshare, a sword, and a seed.
<margin>2</margin>
But if you call it seed: Paul sowed, but God gave the fruit and the increase. Philippi (as was already mentioned in some way at the beginning of the sixth book) is a city of the Philippians situated in the inland parts of Macedonia; between it and Amphipolis lies Thessalonica, from which the Thessalonians received their name. In this city of the Philippians, therefore, the chosen apostle, worthy of God, suffered many things. But just as the palm tree rises up against a weight <note>The author refers to the ancient belief that palm wood grows stronger and arches upward when weighted down, making it a symbol of resilience and victory.</note> and exults as a victor, in this same way God made Paul and his ministers stronger in the midst of pressures, making them exult as victors, so that in them it might be understood that He is the one who conquers all things. Thus, he was more powerful than a thousand thousands; being superior to whoever opposed him, he subjugated all of Europe to Christ. Having conquered Philippi, and indeed conquered it happily, he descended to Thessalonica and achieved a victory for Christ. Yet it was no less a blessed victory for one who looks back on those who were "well-conquered." For he did not conquer them through error, nor through uncleanness, nor through deceit, nor through bloody conflict: but through the exhortation of the Holy Spirit, through truth, through holiness, and through the faith of Christ, which holds no deceit but manifests all things in the light. He had been approved by God, who proves, discusses, and examines hearts. And to one so approved were committed the words of the Lord—pure words, like silver examined by fire, tested in the earth, and purified seven times over. But against those so approved, it was necessary for the prophecy to be fulfilled which says: *The assembly of bulls among the cows of the people, so that they may exclude those who have been tested by silver.* <note>A difficult quote from the Latin Vulgate of Psalm 67:31 (Psalm 68 in modern bibles). It refers to the "tested" or "approved" (probati) standing firm against the powerful of the world.</note> Silver signifies the purity and sanctity of life. Thus, among those approved was Paul: like that young Benjamin in an ecstasy of mind, he had been tested and examined by God. <note>Benjamin is mentioned here in reference to Psalm 68:27, often interpreted by commentators as a figure for Paul, who was from the tribe of Benjamin.</note>

<insert>
<image-desc>A rectangular block of printed text from a Bible (Ezekiel 29), rotated 90 degrees clockwise and placed across the left margin and body text.</image-desc>
...forty years. I will make the land of Egypt a desert in the midst of deserted lands, and its cities in the midst of subverted cities, and they shall be desolate for forty years. And I will scatter the Egyptians among the nations and disperse them through the lands. For thus says the Lord God: At the end of forty years I will gather the Egyptians from the peoples among whom they were scattered. And I will bring back the captivity of Egypt and place them in the land of Pathros, the land of their origin. And they shall be there a lowly kingdom. And among the other kingdoms it shall be the lowliest. And it shall no longer be exalted above the nations, for I will diminish them so they do not rule over the nations. And they shall no longer be a source of confidence for the house of Israel, teaching iniquity so that they look back and follow them; and they shall know that I am the Lord God. And it came to pass in the twenty-seventh year, in the first month, on the first day of the month, the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon made his army undergo a great service against Tyre; every head was made bald and every shoulder was peeled. And there was no reward for him... <note>This is a fragment of Ezekiel 29:12-18 from a printed Latin Vulgate Bible, likely used as a bookmark or reinforcement in the manuscript.</note>
</insert>

<margin>3</margin>
Truly, what is so characteristic of those who are tested by earthly examination as flattery? <note>original: "assentatio," meaning fawning or sycophancy.</note> For they wish to please men, and flattery is the primary instrument for this. Indeed, shears are not as necessary for garment cutters, nor razors for barbers, nor nails and oars for sailors, as adulation is for those wishing to please men—to please them, I say, in a human way. But do not those who wish to please men in this manner desire to create a worldly estimation of themselves? For who would please the world if the world considers them as nothing? But how can they create that estimation of themselves unless they strive for the accumulation of temporal things, so that outward glory might shine before the world, and from that, they might in turn receive glory back from the world? This, however, does not happen without the desire for "having more," which is avarice. For they strive to please the world, neither through human virtues which are moral (concerning us and from us), nor through divine virtues which are spiritual (above us and from us). They do not seek the latter because they are internal, while the world sees only external things; and also because these virtues are opposed <margin>4</margin> to those they use to please the world. If anyone has these vices—I mean human flattery and avarice—he has not been approved by the examination of God. And therefore Paul adds: ¶ *For neither were we ever in the speech of flattery, as you know, nor in the pretext of avarice: God is witness.*
<margin>5</margin>
*Nor seeking glory from men: neither from you, nor from others.* ¶ Because the yoke of the Lord is sweet, and his burden is light. This burden is heavy to no one, and that yoke is bitter to no one; rather, they make people meek and humble of heart. Such are those who have been approved by God: truthful and found faithful. For those who are not found truthful and faithful are not approved, but rejected. Yet they can be purged so that at some point they might be approved. For those who smelt silver frequently purge that which was rejected. And when it is pure, sincere, true, and simple: then for the first time it is "approved." So it is with us. Thus Paul, being approved, was pure, sincere, true, and simple, bearing the sweet yoke of the Lord and his light burden. Because it was a burden, he humbled himself, and was quiet and like a little child. Because it was light, he burdened no one. Because it was a yoke, he bound them with charity—but with a motherly, spiritual charity.
<margin>6</margin>
Because it was sweet, he cherished, educated, and nourished them in all the sweetness and pleasantness of spiritual kindness. Hence that holy soul, most approved by God, adds: ¶ *Although we could have been a burden as the apostles of Christ, yet we became quiet in the midst of you, as if a nurse were cherishing...*

<summary>In this commentary on 1 Thessalonians 2, the author explores Paul's integrity, comparing his ministry to a farmer's labor and a mother's care. He contrasts Paul's divine "approval" with the worldly "flattery" and "avarice" used by those who seek human glory.</summary>

# COMMENTARY

<header>COM.</header>

expressed thus, it seems more like a hypallage <note>A figure of speech where the natural relations of two words are reversed (original: "hypallagica").</note> than direct speech. Paul writes: "But we, brothers, having been made orphans <note>original Greek: ἀπορφανισθέντες (aporphanisthentes), conveying a sense of bereavement.</note> from you for a short time." ¶ Vulgate edition <note>The standard Latin Bible used in the Western Church (original: "Vulgata æditio").</note>: "We hastened more abundantly to see your face." ¶ The word placed here signifies both "to hasten" and "to strive," and to exert diligence. However, Paul did not "hasten" in the sense that he actually saw them, but rather he "strove" and applied diligence. ¶ Therefore, it seems more appropriate to translate it as "we have endeavored" <note>original: "studuimus"</note> rather than "we have hastened." Paul writes: "We endeavored more abundantly <note>original Greek: περισσοτέρως ἐσπουδάσαμεν (perissoterōs espoudasamen)</note> to see your face." ¶ Vulgate edition: "I indeed, Paul, both once and again." ¶ It should rather be said "both once and twice." Paul writes: "I indeed, Paul, both once and twice" <note>original Greek: καὶ ἅπαξ καὶ δίς (kai hapax kai dis).</note>. ¶ Vulgate edition: "Either joy, or a crown of glory." ¶ It should rather be said in this place: "of boasting" <note>original: "gloriationis"</note>. Paul writes: "Either joy, or a crown of boasting" <note>original Greek: ἢ χαρὰ ἢ στέφανος καυχήσεως (ē chara ē stephanos kauchēseōs).</note>. Where he says a little later, "For you are our glory," he does not use the same word in both places; here it is called "glory" <note>Greek: δόξα (doxa)</note>, but there it is "boasting" <note>Greek: καύχησις (kauchēsis)</note>. The former signifies splendor and honor, while the latter signifies exultation in God from the consciousness of a good work. ¶ Vulgate edition: "Are you not [our glory] before our Lord JESUS CHRIST at his coming?" ¶ "Christ" is redundant here. And the connecting particle for the interrogation is missing. For Paul asks in this way: "Is it not also you?" Paul writes: "Or is it not also you <note>original Greek: ἢ οὐχὶ καὶ ὑμεῖς (ē ouchi kai hymeis)</note> before our Lord Jesus at his coming?" CHAPTER III.

<margin>11</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'A' containing a landscape with a building and mountains.</image-desc>
**BUT** what did Paul do when, wishing to set out to see the Thessalonians, he was delayed by impediments (which Satan, pursuing him everywhere but everywhere yielding, was devising)? Immediately he sent Timothy to them, and others whom he had with him at Athens, and preferred to remain alone. And Timothy had already returned from them when Paul composed this present letter to them. He sent him, I say, to them so that he might keep them firm and constant in the faith, lest the cunning of the Malignant One—whom no one is able to resist by their own strength—should force them to waver. For does a sheep ever resist a wolf by its own strength? Does a mouse resist a cat? A dove a hawk? ¶ Why is it to be feared when a contest is permitted with one's own enemy, unless a superior power is present to liberate? But Paul, since he was a prophet, had foretold to them through the spirit of prophecy the pressures they would suffer; so that, like foreseen arrows, they might do less harm and be more strongly repelled. Thus Paul says why, since he did not go himself, he sent Timothy ahead, in this manner: ¶ "Therefore, bearing it no longer, we were willing to be left alone in Athens. And we sent Timothy our brother, and God’s minister, and our co-worker in the gospel of CHRIST, so that he might strengthen you and comfort you in your faith, so that no one might yield to flattery <note>original: "adulationi"; the author interprets the temptation to renounce faith as a form of "flattery" from the world.</note> in these pressures. For you yourselves know that we are appointed to this. For even when we were with you, we foretold to you that we must suffer pressures, just as it has happened, and you know. For this reason, bearing it no longer, I sent to know your faith, lest by some means the tempter has tempted you, and our labor be in vain." ¶ If flatteries and the allurements of the flesh—of fathers, mothers, children, brothers, relatives, and friends—ever have power, they have the most power when one is deciding about the danger of life, or when a lasting mark of infamy is brought upon one's family or country. Yet in the opinion of men, those who confessed Christ in that storm were in such danger. Even so, those who endured were a "good odor of life" until the end of the world, destined to remain for eternal ages. Nevertheless, the apostle feared lest anyone yield to flattery, or succumb through the fear of infamy—though it be a vain fear. For he who loves father or mother, son or daughter, or any other thing more than Christ, is not worthy of Christ. But what does it mean, "you yourselves know that we are appointed to this," except that we are stationed in the militia of Christ <note>A common metaphor in early Christian writing, viewing the Christian life as "military service" (militia) for God.</note> to suffer pressures? Lest they be ignorant of this, the apostle had foretold it to the Thessalonians, just as they saw it come to pass. For what else is it that Christ, the leader of our militia and the author of life, says: "He who does not take up his cross and follow me is not worthy of me"? And in another place: "In the world you will have pressure; but trust, I have overcome the world." Therefore, there ought to be great hope for those struggling in the world, if they look not at themselves, but at the victor of the world. For the world is conquered. Christ has conquered. Let us trust, let us look to him, let us acclaim the victor; and without a doubt, we shall conquer in his strength. For no power could conquer the world except the strength of Christ. The Thessalonians conquered, but in faith, which way of conquering Paul had shown them. And for that reason they desired Paul, and desired to see his face; and the reason for these desires was Christ. It was the true love of God which makes one conquer the world.

<margin>12</margin>
All these things Timothy reported to Paul upon returning from them. Wherefore Paul, exulting in the Lord, prays; his soul cannot contain what thanks he might give to God, even if it were otherwise most capable. In no way hiding this, he opens it to them, saying: ¶ "But when Timothy recently came to us from you, and reported to us your faith and love, and that you have a good memory of us, always desiring to see us, just as we also desire you: for this reason, brothers, we were comforted in you through your faith in all our pressure and..."

VIII 152 1 Thessalonians.

...in our necessity. For now we live: if you stand firm in the Lord. For what thanksgiving can we render to God for you, in all the joy with which we exult because of you in the presence of our God: praying exceedingly night and day that we may see your face, and perfect those things which are lacking in your faith?

¶ These words have a clear meaning and show true love in God. But no less do the words that follow, imploring divine help so that he might be able to see them; and that he might bring about increases in all spiritual graces—especially love (which draws with it all the perfections necessary for salvation)—in confirming their hearts without any mark of reproach, until the day of the coming of the Lord, when he shall come in majesty with all his angels and saints. These things, I say, suggest no less the love of his spiritual heart. For the charity of God was poured out in the hearts of those who acquired us for Christ. Therefore, let us return love to those whom the love of Christ has restored.

<margin>13</margin>
But now, under the prayer of our teacher Paul, let us hear the entreaty of love; for he prays in this way with the flaming spirit of God:

> ¶ Now may God himself, and our Father, and our Lord Jesus Christ direct our way to you. And may the Lord make you to have more, and make you abound in mutual love, and toward all, just as we also do toward you: to confirm your hearts irreproachable in holiness before God and our Father, at the coming of our Lord Jesus with all his saints.

<margin>B</margin>
¶ What is this, "may he make you abound in mutual love," or "toward one another and toward all, just as we also toward you," except "just as we abound in love toward you"? This is (says the Lord) my commandment: that you love one another as I have loved you. And Paul says: love one another, just as I love you. But I love you as Christ loved us. Therefore, he follows the footprint by calling back to the pattern: love one another just as Christ also loved us. For the pattern of love is the love of Christ. At the sight of which our hearts may be so inflamed and kindled that we may be able to praise him in songs of love with all his saints forever.

<margin>11 A</margin>
### EXAMINATION of several points regarding the literal text.

¶ Vulgate edition: "It pleased us to remain at Athens alone" <note>original: "Placuit nobis remanere Athenis solis"</note>. ¶ It is better to speak with a personal verb, as Paul does. And "alone" should be said in the nominative case rather than the dative <note>The author argues for "soli" instead of "solis" to avoid confusion with the location</note>, lest it seem to refer to "Athens." Paul: "We were pleased to be left in Athens alone" <note>original Greek: Εὐδοκήσαμεν καταληφθῆναι ἐν ἀθήναις μόνοι (eudokēsamen katalēphthēnai en Athēnais monoi)</note>. ¶ Vulgate edition: "Timothy our brother, and minister of God in the gospel of Christ." ¶ After "God," a small part is missing: "and our fellow-worker." Paul: "Timothy our brother, and minister of God, and our fellow-worker in the gospel of Christ" <note>original Greek: τιμόθεον τὸν ἀδελφὸν ἡμῶν, καὶ διάκονον τοῦ θεοῦ, καὶ συνεργὸν ἡμῶν ἐν τῷ εὐαγγελίῳ τοῦ χριστοῦ</note>.

<margin>B</margin>
¶ Vulgate edition: "That no one be moved in these tribulations." ¶ Rather: "no one be flattered," or "yield to flattery." Paul: "that no one be shaken/fawned upon in these tribulations" <note>original Greek: τὸ μηδένα σαίνεσθαι ἐν ταῖς θλίψεσι ταύταις</note>. For the word *sairo* <note>original: σαίρω</note> signifies "I flatter" or "I wag the tail" <note>The author is discussing the Greek verb 'sainesthai', which can mean both being disturbed and being seduced by flattery</note>.

<margin>C</margin>
¶ Vulgate edition: "That we were to suffer tribulations." ¶ From Paul: "that we were bound to be pressed," or "suffer pressure." But it comes to the same thing. Paul: "that we are destined to be afflicted" <note>original Greek: ὅτι μέλλομεν θλίβεσθαι (hoti mellomen thlibesthai)</note>.

<margin>12</margin>
¶ Vulgate edition: "As also we also you." ¶ "Also" is redundant. Paul: "just as also we [do] you" <note>original Greek: καθάπερ καὶ ἡμεῖς, ὑμᾶς</note>.

<margin>D</margin>
¶ Vulgate edition: "But may God himself and our Father, and the Lord Jesus Christ, direct our way to you." ¶ It should say: "and our Lord Jesus Christ." For "our" is missing in this place. Paul: "But may God himself and our Father, and our Lord Jesus Christ, direct our way to you" <note>original Greek: αὐτὸς δὲ ὁ θεὸς, καὶ πατὴρ ἡμῶν, καὶ ὁ κύριος ἡμῶν ἰησοῦς χριστὸς, κατευθύναι τὴν ὁδὸν ἡμῶν πρὸς ὑμᾶς</note>. ¶ Vulgate edition: "May the Lord multiply you." ¶ What the old translator <note>A common way for Renaissance scholars to refer to the author of the Vulgate</note> calls "multiplying" is understood from Paul as "having more"—I say, having more of divine gifts and graces. Paul: "But may the Lord make you increase" <note>original Greek: ὑμᾶς δὲ ὁ κύριος πλεονάσαι (hymas de ho kyrios pleonasai)</note>. ¶ Vulgate edition: "At the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ." ¶ Rather "into the coming" <note>Latin: "in aduentum"</note>: so that a progression is understood, which is either motion or is not without motion. And "Christ" at the end is redundant. Paul: "at the coming of our Lord Jesus" <note>original Greek: ἐν παρουσίᾳ τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν ἰησοῦ</note>. ¶ Vulgate edition: "With all his saints. Amen." ¶ "Amen" is not expressly held in the Greek codices, but only: "with all his saints." And it immediately subjoins: "Furthermore then, brothers" <note>original Greek: τὸ λοιπὸν οὖν ἀδελφοί</note>. CHAPTER 4.

**D**uring the time the Apostle first prayed: that he might increase the grace of love in the Thessalonians, and make them abound in love toward one another and toward all—that is, universal love. For first the craftsman must be looked upon, then the craftsman's work. And if love were particular <note>In the sense of being exclusive or limited to a small group</note>, it would poorly imitate the fountain of love, which is most universal, who made all things in love, and loves all things that are, and hates nothing of what he has made. Therefore, particular love is not enough; one must have a universal imitation of love. But now he prays for the Thessalonians themselves: that they may prepare themselves more and more for this abundance of divine infusion. For it is necessary that God be the author. For when you hold your hand against the sun, and it shines and grows warm: you are wrong if... <note>The text ends here on a catchword "erras si" (you are wrong if), meant to lead into the next page</note>

### COMMENTARY

You believe your hand shines and grows warm by itself, and you do not recognize the sun as the author of these things. In the same way, when your mind is dark and cold without love, and it is presented to the sun of love: if you feel it glowing—no longer possessing or even thinking of filth—and if you feel it growing warm with love, you err if you believe you shine and are good by your own power. You err if you think you are warm and full of affection by your own strength, failing to recognize that there is a power above you and your own abilities which is the author of these things.

<margin>14</margin> Paul therefore exhorts the Thessalonians: both to walk, to work, and to observe everything; not so that they might become such by their own works, but so that they might be able to become such <note>The author distinguishes between doing good works to earn salvation versus doing them to become a receptive vessel for God's grace</note>. And he says:

> Finally then, brothers, we ask you and urge you in the Lord JESUS: just as you received from us how you ought to walk and please God, so you should abound more.

For what does it matter whether one speaks in this way or that: "we ask and urge you in the Lord Jesus: as you received from us how you ought to walk and please God, so walk and please God, so that you may abound more, so that God—who gives the increase—may make love and his other graces abound in you"? What difference does it make, I ask, except that this manner of speaking is more expressive? For Paul, according to his custom, uses a concise, brief, and sharp style of speech. But if the words "walk and please God" do not satisfy as an implied instruction, then the phrase *so that you may abound more* must be understood as: "so that you may walk more and please God more," and it returns to the same meaning. For the more we abound in walking and striving to please God, the more we receive the operations of divine power within us. 

For just as a beryl <note>A transparent gemstone</note> or a crystal is better prepared, polished, and wiped, so much more—when placed against the sun—does it receive the sun’s impression to burn and ignite those things which are behind it. 
**The Sun:** God. 
**The Crystal:** The mind. 
**Those things behind the crystal:** The soul and the body. 
The divine power, as if in a mirror suited for igniting or in a crystal, is collected and united in the mind; it then inflames and burns the soul and the body, provided we dispose ourselves to receive those divine movements. From our own selves, there can be nothing but preparation. But how shall we prepare ourselves? If we do those things which the divine precepts command to be done, and abstain from those which the same precepts forbid. For God’s will is to sanctify us. But his holiness is so great that he wishes to place it in a pure and clean vessel, to be preserved with all honor and dignity. Furthermore, Paul brings to the memory of the Thessalonians what precepts he gave them—not from himself, but the Lord speaking through him—saying:

<margin>15</margin>
> For you know what instructions we gave you through the Lord JESUS. For this is the will of God: your sanctification. That you abstain from fornication. That each of you know how to possess his own vessel in sanctification and honor, not in the passion of lust, like the Gentiles who do not know God. That no one overreach or circumvent his brother in any matter, because the Lord is the avenger of all these things, as we told you before and solemnly testified. For God has not called us to impurity, but to holiness.

This is God’s will: that he sanctify us. These are the precepts of Christ. First: that we abstain from fornication, not only of the flesh, but also of the spirit. For whoever clings to another’s flesh, that is fornication of the flesh. And whoever clings to another spirit other than Christ’s spirit, that is fornication of the spirit <note>original: "fornicatio spiritus"</note>. This precept is for you: adulterers, those who commit incest, molesters, and fornicators of the flesh—you who hold the vessel of the flesh in impurity and disgrace. Because of this, you have become exiles from holiness and the kingdom of heaven. This precept is also for all you: idolaters, the greedy, sorcerers, mages, those with a "pythonic" spirit <note>A reference to the Pythia/Oracle of Delphi, meaning soothsayers or those possessed by divining spirits</note>, enchanters, and fornicators of the spirit. Because of this, you have been made exiles from holiness and deprived of the inheritance of the kingdom of heaven. 

Holiness does not admit any foreign defilement. Do not cling to foreign flesh; do not follow a foreign spirit; and you will be a virgin, chaste in mind and body, knowing nothing of the corruption of fornication, and you will be vessels prepared to receive the holiness of God. The second precept: Let each of us know how to possess our own vessel in sanctification and honor. Our **vessel** <note>original: "vas nostrum"</note> consists of an interior part and an exterior part. The interior: the mind and the soul, which are of immense capacity. The exterior: of modest capacity, unless through the interior...

### VIII 1 Thessalonians

<warning>Top line of text is heavily struck through and difficult to read.</warning>

<insert>
<del><unclear>Therefore, as we said above, it is spoken concerning the love of a brother and concerning...</unclear></del>
</insert>

<margin>3</margin>
¶ The third precept is: that no one should trip up, trample upon, or circumvent his brother in any matter. This commandment forbids all injustice toward one's neighbor, into which no one falls if he possesses a brotherly love toward his neighbor according to God’s will. Therefore, the fourth commandment is joined to it, concerning
<margin>4</margin>
brotherly love—that is, love of neighbor—which we are taught as it was brought forth from the mouth of the Lord in the Gospel. "This is,"
<margin>16</margin> he says, "my commandment: that you love one another as I have loved you." <note>original: "Hoc est præceptũ meũ vt diligatis inuicẽ: sicut dilexi vos." quoting John 15:12</note> For these are the Lord’s commandments, which it is not lawful to despise. Therefore Paul adds: ¶ "Therefore, he who despises, does not despise man, but God, who also gave his Holy Spirit in you." Concerning brotherly love, however, you have no need for me to write to you. For you yourselves have been taught by God to love one another; for indeed you do this toward all the brothers who are in Macedonia. ¶ In this fourth commandment of the Lord concerning the love of neighbor, he commends the Thessalonians. This is no small commendation in its consequence; for he who has this love has fulfilled the law—that is, every commandment of God. And concerning brotherly love, which both is and is called "brotherhood according to the spirit," it is understood not to be that brotherhood which is according to the flesh. For in Christian neighbors alone is this manner of speaking applied, so that whoever is a neighbor is also a brother, and whoever is a brother is also a neighbor. For they are the children of the same Father, God, and children of the same Mother, the Church. For they are not called brothers by this generation through men, nor by the will of the flesh, nor by the will of man, but were born of God. And how could those not be neighbors who are not only brothers, but also members of the same body? And perhaps nothing prohibits others who are not even Christians from being neighbors; but they are not brothers. For they have not been reborn by the fruitful virginity of the Bridegroom and the Bride <note>The "Bridegroom and Bride" refers to Christ and the Church</note> in the holy kiss of the Holy Spirit. ¶ O, wonderful brotherhood! ¶ A "Christ-likeness" <note>term: Christiformitas. The state of being formed into the image of Christ</note> of inestimable price! We who are all children of the Virgin Mother, just as Christ is the son of a virginal and undefiled womb; we who are all conceived by the Holy Spirit, just as the Virgin, pregnant with God, conceived by the overshadowing power of the Holy Spirit. How then can we neglect the love of such a beautiful brotherhood, especially since our Mother is herself the Mother of "Beautiful Love"? <note>The author personifies the Church or Divine Wisdom as the "Mother of Fair Love," a title often drawn from the Book of Sirach 24:18</note> Therefore, let the love of the world, blind love, and quivered Cupid <note>original: "cupido pharetratus" — a reference to the pagan god of lust, contrasted here with Christian love</note>—shameful and insane love—be gone, and let us never cease to love with beautiful love. For our Father is Love, even the highest Love; and our Mother is the Mother of Beautiful Love. But these things concern the commandments of the Lord, in which we ought to improve daily as much as we can. Now Paul adds a few other things,
<margin>17</margin>
saying: ¶ "But we urge you, brothers, that you abound more, and that you consider it an honor to lead a life in silence, to attend to your own business, and to work with your own hands, just as we commanded you; so that you may walk honestly among those who are outside, and that you may have need of nothing."
<margin>5</margin>
¶ This is the fifth exhortation or fifth commandment to the Thessalonians: that they should abound more, that is, that they should progress more and more daily by fulfilling the commandments of God, doing these things and fleeing those.
<margin>6</margin>
The sixth: that they should strive and consider it a matter of glory and honor to lead a life in quiet and silence. For if you wish to pray, to sing psalms, to contemplate, or to give effort to any holy study, it is necessary that you choose a life in silence and quiet. The same applies if you wish to provide the necessities of life for yourself through some honest labor. The seventh: that they take care
<margin>7</margin>
to do their own business. For those who care for their own affairs can better provide for their own needs and the needs of their neighbors, and can bring help to one another. But those who meddle in the affairs of others, doing nothing of their own, choose a difficult and turbulent life, which they can by no means spend in silence and quiet.
<margin>8</margin>
The eighth: that they should work with their own hands. A hand that does not work is a "lazy work of God," which is by no means acceptable to God. For God made the hand for us as the "instrument of instruments" <note>term: organum organorum. A classical philosophical definition of the human hand as the tool that makes all other tools possible</note> and, in a certain way, the master-craftsman of all things, so that we might live by the work of our hands, or at least not be idle with them. When we pray, it is the hand that is stretched out to God, struck together, or raised up—and this is its first duty. When we contemplate, it records things meditated upon, even the holy oracles of the prophets, holy visions, and all the utterances of God—and this is the second. If you are brave, you are brave in war by your hand. If you are temperate, your hand also flees every dishonest touch. If you are merciful and generous, the hand also works that which you may spend, and offers what has been made. It is the instrument of prayer, the instrument of contemplation, the instrument of action. But it is also the instrument of every craft, even the mechanical ones, for warding off the poverty of life. It tills the fields, sows the harvests, gathers the fruit, digs gardens, plants paradises, grafts trees, builds cities and oratories, whether they be proud or humble temples in which God is worshiped, and innumerable things of this sort. And although this manual, artistic duty of the hand may be the last, it is nonetheless most necessary for us, as it was granted by God for life and so ordained. He lives with great confidence and without a scruple of conscience who lives by the work of his own hands. "Blessed are you," he says, "for you shall eat the labors of your hands." <note>Psalm 128:2</note> But if you have given counsel, whether for recovering health or for fleeing a false accusation, and you live from that, you do not live with the same security. He lives with great security who lives justly by the work of his hands. And even if one lived in a religious order, he ought not to be idle, following the example of the saints. For even Paul, full of Christ and the Holy Spirit, and Timothy...

--- Page 504 ---
<meta>This page continues the commentary on the First Epistle to the Thessalonians, Chapter 4. The author shifts from the topic of brotherly love to the dignity of manual labor and the Christian perspective on death and mourning, contrasting these with pagan "antiquity."</meta>

->COM.<-

[Timo]theus and Barnabas prayed, preached, contemplated, performed works of virtue, and worked with the labor of their hands. These men were (if I may say so with everyone's permission) holier than all the religious men whom the world now holds; superior and more sublime than all who are now bishops and even the apostolic senators. But to work with one's hands lowers one in the honor of the world, yet it exalts one in the divine.

**And** what is the honor of the world except the pride of life? Believe Paul. Whatever your status may be, work at something with your hands. For the All-Artisan God does not want this instrument [the human body] to be idle; so much so that he who has not learned to work at things that are honest will even work at shameful things, which is worse than idleness. Such as throwing dice, plotting with dice-towers and dice-boxes, committing to gambling (which is time owed to works of piety), competing in games with a thousand tricks, playing the "insane little dog" <note>original: "insanam caniculam" — the lowest, most losing throw in Roman dice games</note>, and countless such things which the devil has opposed to honest manual labor, in which he has demented the minds of many, even of the great.

**In what way**, then, did Paul—who was a prophet and saw through the Holy Spirit what was to come as if it were present—not rightly command that one must work with one's own hands? He was not looking for worldly gain, but for what was necessary for the perfection of a Christian. And to live this way in that time was especially fitting for the Thessalonians, so that they might serve as an example to the infidels among whom they lived, and might display all honesty (as befits children of God) before everyone, nor have need to ask for anything.

**Oh**, how beautiful, how holy, how orderly the life of the saints ought to be! But the Thessalonians had one additional thing: they still mourned their dead in the manner of the gentiles <note>The author uses "gentile" to refer to non-Christian or pagan customs</note>, which the apostle forbids. When someone good and holy dies, we should by no means mourn him, whom we know passes from the darkness and obscurities of this death to light and life, and from a thousand dangers to eternal security. Instead, we should rather mourn ourselves and the rest whom he shaped while living by his example of piety and holiness of life, because we are deprived of the edification of his presence.

**He who** mourns them has a heart blocked by infidelity, as if not believing and having no hope that they will pass to a better life. Or if he weeps not for the soul but for the body committed to the earth, this too is faithless; as if he does not know that he will receive the immortal for the mortal, the incorruptible and impassible <note>Incapable of suffering or being affected by external pain</note> for the corruptible and passible, the splendid and noble for the obscure and vile.

<margin>18</margin>
**Therefore**, the apostle warns them not to imitate the infidels in this, and says:
> But we do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning those who are sleeping, so that you may not be saddened as others are who have no hope. For if we believe that JESUS died and rose again, in this way God will also bring with JESUS those who have fallen asleep. <note>original: "Nolumus autē vt vos ignoretis fratres de dormientibus: vt nō contristemini/ quemadmodũ & cæteri qui spem nō habēt. Si enĩ credimus qđ IHESVS mortē oppetijt & resurrexit: hūc in modū deus & eos qui dormierūt/ per IHESVM secũ adducet." — 1 Thessalonians 4:13-14</note>

**He calls** dead men "sleeping" because they are to be awakened from death. For there is a sleep of the senses, and there is a sleep of life. We sleep in our senses when naturally the senses are not in function but are capable of being awakened to vigilance. We sleep in life when life is not in function and the machine of life is dissipated, yet we are capable of being awakened to life, and indeed to a better life. For the immortal is superior to the mortal, even if for some this future state may be worse. For the suffering which some will be forced to undergo eternally does not come from immortality, but from sin and disorder. But when other animals are dead, they are only dead and do not sleep, for they are not capable of being awakened to life again. Those who did not understand the resurrection of bodies and did not know the lives of souls, being destitute of hope for both, mourned souls as if extinguished and lamented the gifts of the body as if they would perish forever into dust and nothingness. It was insane and wretched to see their mourning.

**And** it is a wonder that the Venetians, otherwise a prudent and Christian people, have not expelled this pagan ritual from their city, according to the apostle's opinion. For when I happened to be there in the year they call the Great Jubilee—either seeking the dwellings of the apostles and martyrs in Rome or returning from them—while I was there, a funeral was carried out. And behold, a professional mourning woman <term>præfica: a woman hired to lead the wailing at a funeral</term>, joined by several other little women in mourning clothes, accompanied the funeral; she shouts, vociferates, wails, beats her breast, tears her cheeks, and pulls her hair. The others imitated her mimicry. She proclaimed the gifts of the soul and the gifts of the body—beautiful eyes, rosy cheeks, smooth eyebrows, a noble forehead, the mouth, chin, neck, and the dexterity of all members. She even complained about the earth, which would bury such great gifts forever, as if no hope were left for a better state for either the soul or the body. And then, although I perhaps did not remember Paul's sentence, I frankly confess I detested the pagan imitation, if it should not more truly be called insanity. But someone will say: "Antiquity pleases me." **Nevertheless**, Christ makes all things new. Therefore, if the things of Christ please us, it is necessary that the old things displease us. And just as the things of Christ are most wise, so the things of antiquity are most foolish.

**For what** is more foolish than to perform those mournings, which display despair, for the love of antiquity? And to write above the memorials of the dead: "To the divine shades"? <note>original: "dijs manibus" — the common Roman funerary abbreviation D.M., dedicating the tomb to the spirits of the deceased</note>. I would believe it to be just the same as if it were inscribed "to all the devils and every demon." When such lovers of antiquity die, hell seethes, and the prince of death awaits them, to strike them on a hard anvil and consume them with bitter tortures. Behold what that curiosity for ancient imitation and contempt for the new creation brings forth. For we are a new creature, not an old one. However, whether those who follow old things or those who follow new things...

<meta>This page concludes the commentary on Paul's first letter to the Thessalonians, chapter 4. The author continues discussing the distinction between those who follow God and those who do not, focusing on the Christian hope of the resurrection and the specific language used by the Apostle Paul in the Greek text compared to the Latin Vulgate.</meta>

They belong to God. These are children of peace, those are children of wrath. These are for mercy, those for justice. For no one can escape; for His justice penetrates the deepest things, and His mercy overcomes the highest. God wishes that everywhere all things be formed according to the examples and precepts of the saints, for they have a holy and spiritual consolation in God.

Therefore, the Apostle commands that consolation should not be sought in those pagan imitations (for that provokes the wrath of God) but in spiritual instructions which call us to the peace of God and His mercy. Accordingly, he adds: *For this we say to you in the word of the Lord: that we who are alive, who remain until the coming of the Lord, will not precede those who have fallen asleep. Because the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a command, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trumpet of God: and the dead in Christ will rise first. Then we who are alive, who remain, will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and so we shall always be with the Lord. Therefore, comfort one another with these words.*

Behold the tokens of novelty: in these, the faithful ought to be consoled over their dead—not simply dead, but "sleeping"—and not in mourning after the manner of the pagans. And when the Apostle says "in the word of the Lord," he shows it to be a revelation of God, not his own assertion. We should believe it all the more firmly as God is greater and more truthful than man. And as for what he adds at the end, *and so we shall always be with the Lord*: understand this to mean we shall be living with the Lord forever, though a transformation of our bodies will have taken place. For (as was said in the second book) we shall all be changed, and we shall all put on immortality and incorruptibility.

But will those who are then found alive not die? This divine oracle does not express that; rather, it says they are caught up to meet Christ in the air. Nor does it oppose the article of faith <note>The Apostles' Creed</note> left to us through the Holy Spirit, which says: *from there he shall come to judge the living and the dead*—if we understand the "living" as those who will then be living, and the "dead" as those who will rise from the dead. For since all men come to a predefined limit of death, it is appointed for all to die once. What wonder then, if for those who have not reached that limit (which by God's decree cannot be bypassed), it is granted by Christ's presence that they do not die? But because this was discussed more extensively in chapter 15 of the second book of this work, we will conclude our discourse here. Praying for this one thing from the eternal Father: that we may meet the Lord in the resurrection and, in the shining garment of immortality with which he will clothe his lambs, we may celebrate him and praise him with all the saints for all eternity. Amen.

## EXAMINATION of certain points regarding the literal text.

**The Vulgate edition:** *In what way you ought to walk and please God: so also walk, that you may abound more.*
The phrase "so also walk" is redundant. Paul writes: <note>original Greek: πῶς δεῖ ὑμᾶς περιπατεῖν καὶ ἀρέσκειν θεῷ, ἵνα περισσεύητε μᾶλλον</note> "How it is necessary for you to walk and please God, so that you might abound more."

**The Vulgate edition:** *For you know what precepts I gave you.*
Paul speaks in the plural: "we gave," or "we have given," it makes no difference. Paul writes: <note>original Greek: οἴδατε γὰρ τίνας ἐπαγγελίας ἐδώκαμεν ὑμῖν</note> "For you know what instructions we gave to you."

**The Vulgate edition:** *Not in the passion of desire.*
Rather: "in the affection or disturbance of desire." For *pathos* <note>original Greek: πάθος</note> here signifies a sickness of the soul in a general sense; Latin interpreters prefer to translate this as "affection" or "disturbance" rather than "passion," as we have noted elsewhere. Paul writes: <note>original Greek: μὴ ἐν πάθει ἐπιθυμίας</note> "Not in the passion of lust."

<margin>B 15</margin>
**The Vulgate edition:** *And let no one overstep nor circumvent.*
We preferred to say here: "supplant, nor circumvent." For what else is "overstepping" one's brother than to trample and supplant him? It is the Latin custom to use the words "supplant" or "trample" in this sense rather than "overstep." For we aptly say, "do not supplant your brother," but we do not say, "do not overstep." What Paul meant he expressed in the following word when he added: "and circumvent." One should say "and circumvent," not "nor circumvent." It seems the word "and" is used here for explanation. Paul writes: <note>original Greek: τὸ μὴ ὑπερβαίνειν καὶ πλεονεκτεῖν</note> "Not to overstep and take advantage of."

<margin>B 16</margin>
**The Vulgate edition:** *Therefore, he who rejects these.*
The word "these" is redundant. Paul writes: <note>original Greek: τοιγαροῦν ὁ ἀθετῶν</note> "Therefore, the one rejecting."

**The Vulgate edition:** *Who also gave his Holy Spirit in us.*
It should read: "in you," using the second person. Paul writes: <note>original Greek: καὶ δόντα τὸ πνεῦμα αὐτοῦ τὸ ἅγιον εἰς ὑμᾶς</note> "And who gave his Holy Spirit to you."

**The Vulgate edition:** *But concerning the love of brotherhood, we have not had necessity to write to you.*
It should rather be said in the second person and the present tense: "you have no necessity." Paul writes: <note>original Greek: περὶ δὲ τῆς φιλαδελφίας οὐ χρείαν ἔχετε γράφειν ὑμῖν</note> "But concerning brotherly love <term>philadelphia: the love of brothers</term>, you have no need for one to write to you."

<margin>C 17</margin>
**The Vulgate edition:** *For you yourselves have learned from God.*
Rather: "teachable by God" or "you are taught or instructed by God." Paul writes: <note>original Greek: αὐτοὶ γὰρ ὑμεῖς θεοδίδακτοί ἐστε</note> "For you yourselves are taught-by-God." <note>The Greek term used is *theodidaktoi*</note>

**The Vulgate edition:** *And give effort that you may be quiet, and that you may do your business.*
Rather: "strive," that is, consider it a matter of honor. And when the old translator <note>The translator of the Vulgate</note> says, "and that you may do your business," he acts more as a paraphraser than a translator. For in Paul's text "your business" is not found, but "one's own," that is, "one's own affairs." Paul writes: <note>original Greek: καὶ φιλοτιμεῖσθαι ἡσυχάζειν καὶ πράσσειν τὰ ἴδια</note> "And to aspire to be quiet and to do one's own things."

**The Vulgate edition:** *That you may desire nothing of anyone.*
Rather: "and that you may have need of no one." Namely, so that there would be no need, due to poverty, to beg for what is lacking from the pagans. Paul writes: <note>original Greek: καὶ μηδενὸς χρείαν ἔχητε</note> "And that you may have need of no one."

**The Vulgate edition:** ...

<margin>20</margin> The Thessalonians had already been sufficiently instructed concerning the day of judgment: that it would certainly come, but as to when, it is known to no one except God. Concerning that day (he says) and the hour, no one knows, not even the angels of heaven, but only the Father. But as a thief in the night, so shall be the coming of the Lord. Thus the Lord compares his coming to a thief, who comes unexpectedly when he is least expected. Wherefore Paul adds to them: *But concerning the times and moments, brothers, you have no need for anything to be written to you. For you yourselves know perfectly that the day of the Lord will come just as a thief in the night.* For when they shall say "peace and security," then sudden destruction will come upon them, just as the labor pains of a woman in childbirth, and they shall by no means escape. ¶ Just as on that day the good will be caught up to meet Christ in glory, the evil will be left with the evil for punishment, and will be placed on the left for condemnation. That day (says Zephaniah) <note>The author uses the name Sophonias, the Latin form of the Hebrew name Zephaniah.</note> is a *day of wrath, a day of tribulation and anguish, a day of calamity and misery, a day of darkness and gloom, a day of cloud and whirlwind, a day of the trumpet and crying out against the fortified cities and high corners.* In the day of the fire of the Lord's jealousy, the whole earth shall be devoured; for he shall make a speedy end to all who dwell on the earth. Concerning this day of the Lord, Peter also wrote in the spirit: *But the day of the Lord will come like a thief, in which the heavens will pass away with a great rush, and the elements will be dissolved with heat, and the earth and the works that are in it will be burned up.* How then, for the wicked who will be there and are not struck by the terror of judgment toward repentance and the intent of good works—but instead mocked it and thought it a fable—how, he asks, will destruction not come upon them unexpectedly and suddenly? Just as in the days of Noah for those who mocked the threats of the flood and thought it was a fable. But even if this final and universal coming of the Lord is "as a thief," his particular coming—which is near to those of us living in security and is already at the doors—is also "as a thief." Otherwise, the Lord, warning the "angel" <note>In the Book of Revelation, "angels" often refer to the leaders or bishops of the seven churches.</note> of the church of Sardis about the works of this present life, would not have said: *if you do not watch, I will come to you like a thief, and you will not know at what hour I will come to you.* Because it is necessary for us to be watchful, lest the coming of the Son of God find us in darkness—not the darkness of this world, but spiritual darkness—which rises from the mists of the flesh and the blasts of the evil one. Let us not be sleeping when the Lord comes: not with the sleep of the eyes (which is necessary for the restoration of strength to human necessity), but with the sleep of the spirit. Let us not be caught in the night: not that night which the absence of the sun of the world creates, but the spiritual night which the absence of the grace of Christ creates. Christ and his oracles warn us that we must fear this darkness, this sleep, this night. For Christ always comes to the wicked in the night, but to the good he always comes in the day. Wherefore his final coming will be in the brightest day and the deepest night at the same time. Let us therefore be always watchful, always in the light, always in the day: expecting both comings of the Lord in fear. And all these things are according to the spirit. But in the day, let us hold fast the armor of light and of the day, which are the weapons of the spirit, about which more was said <margin>21 chapter 6 of the fifth book.</margin> extensively. For those who sleep, sleep at night, and those who are drunk, are drunk at night. <meta>This page continues the commentary on the First Epistle to the Thessalonians, Chapter 5. ->VIII 1 Thessalonians<-
<sig>B.iiij.</sig>

...whether they pass from this world through death, they might live with him. For if he used the words **wake** and **sleep** here at the end to mean **live** and **die**, perhaps nothing would seem absurd. He prefers to call our temporal death a "sleeping" <note>original Latin: "dormitio"</note> rather than "death," so that from the very name we may always have an understanding of being awakened and resurrected. And our present life, since it is interrupted by the sleep of death, ought to be called a "watching" <note>original Latin: "vigilia," meaning a state of being awake or on guard</note> rather than "life." He has done this most appropriately, as he surpasses the wise men of this age in the fitness of his speech. For **waking** and **sleeping** are opposites. But the life which is not interrupted is simply **life**, and no longer just a **watch**. Therefore, he called the life which the saints live with Christ simply "life." From this it follows that those who belong to Christ live eternal life even in this world. For the life he gives them is not interrupted by temporal death. *My sheep,* he says, *hear my voice; and I know them, and they follow me, and I give them eternal life.* And elsewhere: *He who believes in me, even if he dies, shall live; and everyone who lives and believes in me shall never die.* Therefore, the life Christ gives is not interrupted by temporal death, but that which was hidden is revealed. That which we consider life in this world is not life, but a **watch** and a certain shadow of life. And what we consider temporal death is not death; rather, for the good, it is the rising of the full day and the manifestation of life. For the wicked, however, it is the foreshadowing of death and the opening of total death.

¶ If men understood these mysteries, how they would rejoice—that even while they dwell upon the earth, while they provide for the needs of the flesh and serve others, they know they are immortal. But you will say that the Lord promises eternal life in the world to come. Indeed, he promises it as hidden in the present, and as manifest in the future. For have we not heard the Apostle saying to the Colossians: *Your life is hidden with Christ in God? When Christ, who is our life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory.* Again, when Paul said, *let us not sleep as others do, but let us watch,* he understood "sleeping" and "watching" according to the spirit. It would not be absurd if in this place also, whether we **wake** or **sleep**, the words are taken in a similar sense. For whoever says this, the great mercy and kindness of God toward us is understood: that he wishes those of us who have "slept" in spirit and existed in sin to be awakened before his coming. For it is difficult to complete this course of transitory life without nodding off or sometimes falling asleep, whether we are wise or foolish—which Christ the Lord showed us by the example of the ten virgins. But let us be awakened before Christ's coming, and let us be instructed and prepared, so that we may live with him, who wants us—whether we **wake** or **sleep**—to live together with him in the future. If it is the sleep of death, it is not yet death in the simple sense, as we can still be awakened from it to life. Therefore, the Holy Spirit cries out through the Apostle: *Rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you.* And John says: *If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.* Behold how he wishes us—whether we **wake** or **sleep**—to live together with him. If this is so, and he wants all to be saved and to live together with him, whether they be good or evil, this is a great occasion for us, out of such a merciful and kind will of God toward us, to exhort one another toward salvation and to build one another up, so that we may cooperate with divine goodness.

<margin>22 Paul.</margin>
Paul therefore adds: ¶ **Wherefore exhort one another: and build each other up, just as you are doing.**

¶ In this he commends the Thessalonians, because they were mutually exhorting one another to pursue the good and to flee from evils, so that they might please Christ. But he also added the precepts that follow, inviting them to do these things with a sweet prayer, saying:

<margin>23</margin>
¶ **We beseech you, brothers: that you know those who labor among you and are over you in the Lord, and who admonish you. And that you esteem them more abundantly in love because of their work. Be at peace with them. And we entreat you, brothers: admonish the disorderly. Comfort the faint-hearted. Help the weak. Be patient toward all. See that no one renders evil for evil to anyone: but always pursue what is good both for one another and for all. Always rejoice. Pray without ceasing. In everything give thanks: for this is the will of God in CHRIST JESUS for you. Do not quench the Spirit. Do not despise prophecies. But examine all things: hold fast to what is good. Abstain from every form of evil.**

¶ In about fifteen short sentences, he has encompassed as many holy precepts.

<margin>1</margin>
First: Let us know <note>meaning "recognize" or "acknowledge"</note> those who are over us. But how shall we know them, unless we cherish them, listen to them, and obey their words and ordinances?

<margin>2</margin>
Second: Let us pursue those who are over us with greater love. If we are commanded to pursue with greater love and honor the parents who are over us carnally and naturally, how much more those who are over us spiritually and supernaturally. For the spirit is above nature. Such are those whom the Apostle commands to be held in the highest esteem of love.

<margin>3</margin>
Third: That we be at peace toward those who are over us. For even the ancient legal sanctions forbade children to be caught up in litigation against their parents. Thus they wanted children to conduct themselves peacefully toward their carnal fathers. How much more, then, is it fitting and right for us to observe peace and all things that belong to peace toward our fathers according to the spirit.

<margin>4</margin>
Fourth:

<header>COMMENTARY</header>

...to admonish the disorderly <note>original Latin: "inordinatos," referring to those who live without discipline</note> and those of unruly character. For not all men are prone to all vices, but different men to different ones. Therefore, they should be admonished in those areas where they fail, so that they might correct themselves and set their lives in order. For all things that are of God are ordered, harmonious, and right. However, those things that are disordered, inharmonious, and crooked are against God. **Fifth.** That we console the faint-hearted <note>original Latin: "pusillanimes," literally "small-souled"</note>, namely those who are of a small spirit, not having the strength in themselves to be consoled by the goodness of God, by the love he has toward us, by the riches of his mercies, and the multitude of his benefits. Instead, focusing only on themselves, they are desolate, sad, possessing little confidence in their own salvation, and almost failing because of the sadness of their souls. Such are the faint-hearted, whom it is necessary to console with the goodness, the grace, and the mercy of God; in the redemption that has been won for us through the Son of God, not by our own works; and in the forgiveness of sins which has been granted to him on our behalf—we who turn to him seeking pardon and acknowledging the fountain of mercy which waters all converted souls. Why are you afraid? Why do you lack faith in the middle of the sea, as if water might fail you? You are dry, you are cold, there is no hope in you; you cannot save yourself, and you cannot find joy in yourself. Turn your eye to Christ: he is a sea of mercy. He is fire and infinite love. He is the hope of all the ends of the earth; in him is your salvation and your joy. In him, be watered, be warmed, and hope for your salvation; rejoice in the greatness of God. Be large-hearted <note>original Latin: "magnanimus"</note>, and do not be faint-hearted in your smallness alone. This is the way of the spirit. **Sixth.** Let us help the weak. This commends the works of bodily mercy, just as the preceding point commended those of the soul. For through these, let us understand the rest: for just as works of mercy for the soul please Christ, so do those for the body. For he took up both body and soul for our sake. And he who neglects those duties toward the body will be judged unworthy of mercy on the day of the Lord’s coming, and will hear the harsh reason for his condemnation spoken against him: *I was hungry, and you gave me nothing to eat; I was thirsty, and you gave me nothing to drink; I was a stranger, and you did not welcome me; naked, and you did not clothe me; sick and in prison, and you did not visit me.* <note>A direct reference to Matthew 25:42-43</note> He who denies works of mercy to others does not realize that he and those he denies are members of one another in Christ—and that what he denies to them, he denies to Christ. Do you not know that a benefit denied to your own suffering eye is denied to yourself? That what is denied to your foot is denied to you? Or rather, that what is denied to a wounded nail or the smallest part of your body is denied to you? So it is with the body of Christ. See to it, therefore, that you fulfill the Apostle's precept and deny nothing to Christ (as much as is in your power) when he is in need. **Seventh.** Let us be patient toward all. This patience is called long-suffering <note>original Latin: "longanimitas," the quality of enduring for a long time</note>, which is a calm and long expectation, whether in times of evil or good. In this way, Christ is also patient and long-suffering toward us. If we are evil, he lures us to repentance by his kindness, not immediately broken or discouraged by our wicked deeds. He even applies scourges <note>meaning divine discipline or hardships</note> and sometimes deprives us of earthly things when the diseases of the soul are curable, until we recover our health. Thus, it is necessary to imitate him in patience and long-suffering: do not be immediately overcome by impatience toward others, even if they are evil, nor cease trying to correct them. This may be done through gentleness and kindness (which sometimes applies to equals among themselves or to those looking toward their superiors) or through gentleness, kindness, and sometimes through severity and punishment (both of which belong to superiors). For theirs is the power and the authority—not that of equals among themselves or of inferiors toward superiors. Christ, being long-suffering, waits for us to do good. Let us also wait for others with long-suffering to do good. Truly, if you expect some good from others—especially spiritual things, such as a right way of living or a knowledge of divine things—and you do not obtain it immediately, do not let yourself be overcome by impatience, which is a smallness of spirit, but be long-suffering. In this way, we shall follow the Apostle’s precept: to be long-suffering toward all, both the evil and the good, and especially toward Christ in the expectation of eternal blessings. **Eighth.** Let us not return evil for evil, but always pursue the good. To return evil for evil is to pour back gall for gall and poison for poison. This is only for those who are children of the ancient serpent, or who have some of his sting in them. We are children of the dove of the Church, which lacks gall <note>A common medieval and Renaissance belief was that doves had no gall bladders, symbolizing their lack of bitterness or malice</note>. Let us not repay gall for gall, but recognize our mother’s nature. We are children of Christ, not of the ancient serpent; let us not pour back poison, but the sweetness of the honeycomb that drips from his lips, and let us recognize Christ as our father and our head. Let us imitate Christ our father, who, when he was cursed, did not curse in return. And how could he have cursed, who is the blessing of all? Since, therefore, we are children of blessing, let us bless all people. Thus, we shall return evil for evil to no one, but in all things (as the Apostle, or rather Christ through the Apostle, commands) we shall pursue the good. **Ninth.** Let us always rejoice. This joy is spiritual. We ought to rejoice not in ourselves, but being caught up in the contemplation of the goodness of Christ, and we should rejoice always. He who ponders that ineffable goodness—redemption, the remission of sins, justification, the infinite treasury of graces, and finally the free gift of salvation and eternal life (for he himself is all those things to us)—he, I say, who sees these things in the spirit and does not rejoice, does not love Christ and lacks the fire of love. Yet even if he asks for it from him, he will obtain it, because he himself is love and charity. And then he will always rejoice, whether things are sad or joyful. For those external things are not strong enough to suffocate that internal fire of love. For everyone who is without the love of God is colder than marble, and everyone who is warmed by it is hotter than fire. Indeed, the fire of the world...

## VIII

...if you compare [worldly things] to that [divine fire], it is coldness. For to the martyrs of Christ, those [torments] were warming: they were a refreshment, not a torture. Let us therefore always be warm; let us always love: so that according to the apostle's precept, we may rejoice always. For joy accompanies love just as a scent follows a rose, or a flavor follows a fruit.

<margin>10</margin>
**Tenth.** Let us pray constantly. Whatever we do, whatever we say, we ought to pray to God in our hearts. Nor should we ever be without a silent invocation of divine help and direction; and this is to pray constantly. And concerning this secret prayer of the heart, by which we feel the presence of God, is the apostle’s precept. It is not concerning open prayer—which occurs in man-made oratories <note>places of prayer</note> by voice, psalms, hymns, kneeling, prostrations, clapping of hands, lifting of hands to God, and similar things. For he who does not pray in that [inner] way does not feel the presence of God. Let us therefore pray constantly (as the apostle commanded) so that we may constantly feel the presence of God with us.

<margin>11</margin>
**Eleventh.** In everything, let us give thanks to God. Whether prosperity flows or adversity presses, we ought to give thanks to God, who governs the world now with serenity, now with stormy weather; now calms the sea with tranquility, now stirs it with gales and whirlwinds; now rules the world's reins with day, now with darkness. If he visits you with some new light of his knowledge: give thanks, and praise the holy day of his visitation. If nothing shines for you: give thanks to him, who says that light shines out of the darkness, who governs through the night as through the day. If prosperity flows: give thanks, praising his mercy, which causes its serenity to rise around you. If adversity: give thanks, praising his justice, which stirs up whirlwinds and movements for the governing of the world. And in all things, acknowledge the providence of God. 

But if sins occur—adulteries, fornications, impurities, blasphemies, and every kind of injustice—in these you should not give thanks, because they are not "things" <note>original Latin: "res"; the author argues that evil is a lack of being rather than a created thing</note>, and are not included under the name of a "thing." For he commands to give thanks in every *thing*. But every thing is a creature <note>a created being</note>. He, however, who created, is above all things. And in whatever and from whatever we give thanks: all things possess a reason for their ordering. For creatures also provide a certain understanding of the creator. For so holy Job used to say: "If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, why should we not endure evil things?" <note>Job 2:10</note> And in all things he gave thanks to God. "Naked," he said, "I came out of my mother's womb, and naked I shall return there. The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it was done. Blessed be the name of the Lord." <note>Job 1:21</note> Let us imitate that holy soul, and follow the apostle's precept, and in every thing let us give thanks to God, considering all things as if they were God's gifts. Moreover, thanksgiving ought always to accompany gifts.

<margin>12</margin>
**Twelfth.** Do not quench the spirit. If anyone has faith, hope, love, or devotion, which are gifts of the Holy Spirit, we ought not to quench them, but rather, if we can, increase them. For the graces of God, wherever they are found, are to be magnified, and God is to be venerated in them. If anyone has the gift of wisdom and understanding, he ought not to quench it, but exercise himself in it, magnifying God and giving him thanks. And so it is concerning any other spiritual endowments. Neither those who have them, nor others (according to the apostle's opinion) ought to quench them.

<margin>13</margin>
**Thirteenth.** Let us not despise prophecies. For prophecies are for edification. And those who despise prophecy despise the Spirit of God, the author of prophecy, who searches the depths of God and speaks mysteries through the prophets. And the prophecies which especially must not be despised are those, above all, which the Old and New Testament contain. And they are full of the light of Christ, as much of past times as of future times. Truly many other things have been introduced as if they were prophetic which are not prophetic, and they possess not a little of the delusions of a wicked spirit. Therefore he joins the fourteenth precept: which indeed is...

<margin>14</margin>
**That we should examine all things:** and whatever is truly good and a true prophecy, let us retain. Indeed, I have known not a few in this our time who followed spirits of error; from my first encounter with those who were being led, I was in suspense as to whether the spirit was good or evil. But gradually through many encounters, where individual things were more openly uncovered, to me—weighing and examining each thing—illusions appeared. Concerning which matter I also warned those who, even through the examinations of others, and some even by their own danger, found it to be so. For they had arrived at that evil through their own curiosity. Therefore when these things happen, they must be tested, proved, examined. If you are not sufficient to examine them, trust yourself to the examination of others, whom the fear and love of God drive, and by no means a vain curiosity. And by examination (as will be fit, and as God will grant it done), if you find what is good, according to the apostle's opinion, retain it. If otherwise: reject it. For here are dangers full of much horror and dread.

<margin>15</margin>
**Fifteenth.** That we abstain from every species <note>original: "specie," meaning form, appearance, or kind</note> of evil. The "species" of evil is not a true form, but is an informity <note>a lack of proper shape or order</note>. He who therefore commands this, deters us from all informity, and forbids every sin. Truly if something is a "species" <note>an appearance</note>, it is not evil [in itself], but it can create a suspicion of evil. And to abstain even from things of that kind, lest others be scandalized, is not an evil thing. Truly the apostle does not so much forbid those things which have only a suspicion of evil as he forbids, in truth, all evils and sins. Let us therefore abstain (according to his opinion) from every evil and every sin. And also for the sake of the edification of our neighbor, as much as lies in us: from everything that would seem or be suspected to be sin. 

These fifteen precepts having been set down, Paul piously prays for the Thessalonians: and he prays for good things for them from God. And he asks for mutual prayer from them for himself to God.

->B.iiij.<-
