<header>COMMENTARY</header>

* ...speaking in prayer. **May the God of peace himself sanctify you, making you entirely complete; and may your whole spirit, soul, and body be kept without blame until the coming of our Lord JESUS CHRIST.**
* **He who calls you is faithful, and he will do it. Brothers, pray for us.** Having placed this dear and holy prayer, and having asked for the reciprocal return of prayer, 
<margin>45</margin>
* he asks that the holy brothers be greeted in his name. He commands that the letter be read in their midst with the binding force of an oath; and he offers a farewell with a prayer for the grace of God, saying: **Greet all the brothers with a holy kiss. I adjure you by the Lord that this letter be read to all the holy brothers. The grace of our Lord JESUS CHRIST be with you. Amen. Written at Athens.**
* What is better in this world than the grace of Christ? Through it, he dwells hidden within us in this world, to be revealed in the next age. He is the entirety of our good. Therefore, may the eternal Father, and our Lord, and his Spirit—one God—deign to make us partakers of this grace along with the Thessalonians, with the blessed apostle Paul also interceding for us before Him. May He hear his holy apostle and, by His grace, place His praises within us: so that we may be able to praise Him without end, who exceeds all praise and is greater than any glory. AMEN.

<margin>A 20</margin>
¶ EXAMINATION of several points regarding the literal text. ¶ The Vulgate edition: *That we write to you.* <note>Latin: "Ut scribamus vobis"</note>
* The text speaks through an infinitive <note>The Greek "γράφεσθαι" (graphesthai) is a passive infinitive</note>, which does not specify a person. Therefore, we have said *that it be written.* Likewise, it speaks through the passive voice. Paul wrote: <note>original Greek: ὑμῖν γράφεσθαι</note> "to be written to you." ¶ The Vulgate edition: *Just as pain in the womb of one having [a child].* <note>Latin: "Sicut dolor in utero habentis"</note>
* "Pain" <note>Latin: "Dolor"</note> does not express the full force of the vocabulary; rather, one should say "the pain of childbirth" <note>Latin: "dolor partus"</note>. And it should not be in the genitive case, but the dative: "to one having in the womb," as was said to them previously. And this phrase—"to one having in the womb"—might not be poorly translated as "to one in labor" <note>Latin: "parturienti"</note> for clearer understanding. For to her who has a child in the womb, a sudden, unexpected, and most vehement pain comes upon her. When it is present, she labors until she either dies or gives birth. Paul wrote: <note>original Greek: ὥσπερ ἡ ὠδὶν τῇ ἐν γαστρὶ ἐχούσῃ</note> "just as the birth-pang to the woman having [a child] in the womb." For the word *odin* <note>Greek: ὠδὶν</note> specifically designates the pain of childbirth. ¶ The Vulgate edition:

<margin>A 21</margin>
* *For you are all children of light.* The word "For" <note>Latin: "Enim"</note> is superfluous here. Paul wrote: <note>original Greek: πάντες ὑμεῖς υἱοὶ φωτός ἐστε</note> "You are all children of light."

<margin>B 22</margin>
* ¶ The Vulgate edition: *And build up one another, just as you are doing.* The old translator could have said: *and build up even to the last one,* that is, build each other up until the very last person, omitting no one. For those who go through numbers "to the last one" <note>Latin: "ad unum usque"</note> omit no number; they even reach unity itself, which precedes every multitude. Paul wrote: <note>original Greek: καὶ οἰκοδομεῖτε εἷς τὸν ἕνα</note> "and build up one the other."

<margin>C 23</margin>
* ¶ The Vulgate edition: *That you may have them more abundantly in love.* One could say *consider,* *estimate,* or *repute.* Paul wrote: <note>original Greek: καὶ ἡγεῖσθε αὐτοὺς ὑπὲρ ἐκπερισσοῦ ἐν ἀγάπῃ</note> "and esteem them beyond measure in love."

<margin>D 23</margin>
* ¶ The Vulgate edition: *We ask you, brothers, reprove the restless.* It is better: *admonish the disorderly.* <note>Latin: "admonete inordinatos"</note> Paul wrote: <note>original Greek: παρακαλοῦμεν δὲ ὑμᾶς ἀδελφοὶ, νουθετεῖτε τοὺς ἀτάκτους</note>. For the word *noutheteo* <note>νουθετέω</note> means "I admonish," and *ataktos* <note>ἄτακτος</note> refers to that which is "disordered" or "unregulated." ¶ The Vulgate edition: *In all things give thanks.* 

<margin>23</margin>
It is said: *in every,* meaning "in every matter." Paul wrote: <note>original Greek: ἐν παντὶ εὐχαριστεῖτε</note> "in everything give thanks."

<margin>D 24</margin>
* ¶ The Vulgate edition: *Abstain yourselves from every evil kind.* The word "yourselves" <note>Latin: "vos"</note> is superfluous, contributing neither to the harmony of the sentence nor to the understanding. Paul wrote: <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ παντὸς εἴδους πονηροῦ ἀπέχεσθε</note> "Abstain from every kind of evil."

<margin>D 25</margin>
* ¶ The Vulgate edition: *May the God of peace himself sanctify you through all things: so that your spirit be whole.* It should rather be said: *sanctify you totally,* or *entirely perfect,* or something similar. And one should also say: *and your whole spirit,* not "so that." Paul wrote: <note>original Greek: αὐτὸς δὲ ὁ θεὸς τῆς εἰρήνης ἁγιάσαι ὑμᾶς ὁλοτελεῖς, καὶ ὁλόκληρον τὸ πνεῦμα</note> "And may the God of peace himself sanctify you wholly, and [may] your whole spirit..."

* ¶ The Vulgate edition: *In the coming of our Lord JESUS CHRIST.* I would prefer it said here: *unto the coming* <note>Latin: "in adventum"</note> of our Lord Jesus Christ, to suggest a continuation—that is, "all the way until the coming" of our Lord Jesus Christ. Paul wrote: <note>original Greek: ἐν τῇ παρουσίᾳ τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ</note> "at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ."

<margin>D 25</margin>
* ¶ The Vulgate edition: *That this letter be read to all the holy brothers.* The word "this" is superfluous. Paul wrote: <note>original Greek: ἀναγνωσθῆναι τὴν ἐπιστολὴν πᾶσι τοῖς ἁγίοις ἀδελφοῖς</note> "that the letter be read to all the holy brothers." ¶ In the Greek codices, this subscription is found: *The First to the Thessalonians: written at Athens.*

# THE NINTH BOOK OF COMMENTARIES ON THE EPISTLES OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PAUL, WHICH IS ON THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE THESSALONIANS, CHAPTER I.

<image-desc>A large historiated woodcut initial 'S' featuring a figure in academic or clerical robes, possibly St. Paul, seated at a lectern reading a book. The scene is framed within a classical architectural arch decorated with floral and foliate patterns.</image-desc>

<margin>1 2 3 2 3</margin>
The apostle begins this second letter to the inhabitants of Thessaloniki with a holy greeting, as is his custom, and says: ¶ **Paul and Silvanus and Timothy: to the church of the Thessalonians in God our Father and the Lord JESUS CHRIST: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord JESUS CHRIST.** ¶ This is the holy greeting. And it is the same as the greeting in the first letter. The people of Israel were one people in Jacob, and the Edomites <note>The descendants of Esau, often contrasted with Israel in biblical tradition.</note> were one people in Esau. So the church, which is a holy assembly and gathering, is one church and one assembly in God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ, in whom the Holy Spirit remains and eternally rests. All Israelites according to the flesh are from Jacob—or rather, from Abraham and Isaac through Jacob—and the Edomites are from Esau. So also the church is born from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ in the Holy Spirit. Therefore, it is rightly called in the greeting "the church of the Thessalonians in God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ." And if the Holy Spirit is not explicitly mentioned here, he is nonetheless not excluded; for immediately, under the name of "grace," the understanding of Him is added. For grace is a gift and a "consubstantial" <note>original: "consubstantiale," meaning of the same essence or substance as God.</note> <term>charisma</term> <note>A Greek word for a gift of grace or a spiritual favor.</note> of God. And the grace which is given to us by God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ is given in the Holy Spirit. "If I do not go," He says, "the <term>Paraclete</term> <note>The "Comforter" or "Advocate," a title for the Holy Spirit.</note> will not come to you; but if I go, I will send him to you." <note>John 16:7</note> It is easy to see, therefore, that in his greetings the most blessed apostle always hints at the understanding of the thrice-blessed and "super-divine" <note>original: "superdiuinæ"</note> Trinity, and greets the churches in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, in whom they were created and re-created, born and born again. For no one, unless he is born again, can see the kingdom of God.

<margin>2 3 3 2 3</margin>
Following this holy and divine greeting is the apostle's giving of thanks for the gifts of God's grace among the Thessalonians, which is as follows: ¶ **We ought always to give thanks to God for you, brothers, as is fitting, because your faith is growing abundantly, and the love of every one of you for one another is increasing. Therefore we ourselves boast of you in the churches of God for your patience and faith in all your persecutions and the afflictions that you are enduring—a sign of the righteous judgment of God, that you may be made worthy of the kingdom of God, for which you are also suffering.**

¶ Paul boasted in the churches of God regarding the faith, love, and patience of the Thessalonians during their persecutions and pressures. And this boasting was a kind of provocation of holy emulation <note>A "holy competition" or desire to imitate a good example.</note> for other churches of God, to constantly and with an unbroken spirit imitate the faith, love, and patience of the Thessalonians. And invincible patience, unbroken and inviolable constancy, has consecrated—that is, prepared—the holy martyrs for us, so that they might be made holy by God with perpetual glory and honor. On one hand, faith, love, and patience were a sign, a judgment, and a manifestation of the righteous judgment of God: that they themselves, according to God's just judgment, would become participants in the kingdom of God, for which kingdom they were indeed suffering and maintaining patience and constancy with equanimity <note>Calmness and composure.</note> in the faith and love of God. On the other hand, the persecutions and pressures which others were unjustly inflicting were likewise a sign, an indication, and a manifestation of the righteous judgment of God upon those who were unjustly afflicting them: that God, by a just judgment, would strike them with worthy vengeance. For when we see the righteous oppressed by the unrighteous, we have on both sides an indication and a sign of God's righteous judgment: of severe divine punishment for the latter, and for the former, a sign of kind consolation in eternal goods; so that those who were troubled in a few things will be well-disposed in many. Others, conversely, showing their wickedness for a short time, will be tormented in many things. This and that both result from the righteous judgment of God.

<margin>8 9</margin>
Therefore Paul adds: ¶ **Certainly it is just in the sight of God to repay with affliction those who afflict you, and to give rest to you who are afflicted, along with us, at the revelation of the Lord JESUS from heaven with his mighty angels, who in flaming fire will inflict vengeance on those who did not know God and who did not obey the gospel of our Lord JESUS. They will suffer the punishment of eternal destruction, away from the face of the Lord and from the glory of his might, when he comes to be glorified in his saints and to be marveled at in all those who have believed, because our testimony was believed among you on that day.**

¶ The apostle expresses the righteous judgment of God both in those who will be saved—who, for a few labors on earth, will enjoy eternal rest in the heavens—and in those who will perish—who, for the wickedness of a short time, will be affected by the punishment of the lower regions with eternal destruction. He who raises his eye upward to God...

<note>The text cuts off here as it nears the bottom of the page.</note>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the first chapter of 2 Thessalonians, specifically reflecting on God's final judgment and the nature of the Trinity, before transitioning into a philological "Examination" (EXAMINATIO) where the author compares the Latin Vulgate translation with the original Greek text.</meta>

->COM.<-
->1. T<-

mercy: who would not be able to be consoled and to sigh for eternal rest? Who also, casting their eye down toward the justice of God, would not be terrified and afraid, and sigh lest they be given over to eternal destruction? But let us be carried where the spirit leads. For he leads to the heights, where Christ, the just judge of all, is; who will also come to take vengeance in a flame of fire, and to burn up his enemies—the high and proud angels. I say angels, though not of God, even if they are spirits and creatures of God; rather, they are the angels of Satan, the king of pride and tyrant of all wickedness, who stood as rebels against God and wished to be worshipped in place of God, along with all men, the sons of pride, who did not know the true God. He will also come to be glorified in all the angels of light and the saints whom he chose out of the world. When he was seen in the world, he appeared wonderful because of the inexpressible glory of his majesty to all who believed the testimony of the holy apostles, even though that task had been committed to them by God. Yet he will appear glorious, admirable, and to be feared with a majesty more than august to all, both the good and the bad. But the wicked—neither angels nor men—will not endure the glory and the power of his majesty; instead, it will be to them a torment and eternal destruction. The good, however, will endure it, and it will be to them health and eternal life. For consider: is not the glory and the vastness of the sun's light a torment, a source of loss, and perpetual blindness to a sick eye? <note>This is a common philosophical analogy: just as the sun heals a healthy eye but pains a diseased one, God's presence is joy to the righteous but agony to the wicked.</note> Yet to a healthy eye, is it not health and a strengthening of its power? So it shall be before the face of the majesty of the glory and power of the Lord. If the demons see anything now, they will be tormented by the power of the Lord's glory, they will be deprived of sight, and they will be struck blind by eternal darkness. Then there will be perfect "outer darkness." Then the night will be complete, which the prince of darkness shall occupy—a night which even now the spirit of wickedness dreads. How is it that even now wicked men do not shudder at it, do not fear it, and do not throb with trembling, when even the demons shudder at it? O you who are blind before the time of eternal blindness: rise up, breathe again, flee to Christ! It is Christ who gives light to the blind. Then there will be absolute day, which will never decline toward the sunset, which Christ will illuminate. Then the vision that makes the soul blessed will never fail. Then the sea of love from which praise emerges will never be diminished. Then the presence of the Divinity, upon which immortality depends, will never be taken away. By this: the memory. By that: the will. By the other: the happy intelligence. <note>The author is referencing St. Augustine’s "Psychological Image of the Trinity," where the human mind's Memory, Will, and Intelligence reflect the Father, Spirit, and Son.</note> By this [memory] we are brought into the eternal Father; by that [will] into the Holy Spirit; and by the other [intelligence] into the Son, the Word and Wisdom of God. By these three, we are brought into the unique unity of God and into the distinct distinction [of the persons]. By presence, I say, by love, and by vision: but in a manner (if there is "manner" in these things which exceed all measure) that is for us entirely inexpressible and unknown. And lest these inexpressible things be lost, Paul once prayed for the Thessalonians, that they might not be deprived of such great happiness.

<margin>4</margin>
And even now he prays for us, who through him believe in Christ, the Lord of inexpressible glory: that we might not lose these same inexpressible goods; and so he says:

> Wherefore we also pray always for you: that our God would make you worthy of his calling, and fulfill all the good pleasure of his goodness, and the work of faith with power. That the name of our Lord JESUS CHRIST may be glorified in you, and you in him, according to the grace of our God and the Lord JESUS CHRIST.

We cannot be worthy of ourselves or respond to the divine calling, nor have the fullness of a good will, nor work powerfully in faith, unless God works in us, brings that calling to effect, gives the power, and suggests the strength by which we may glorify him. Otherwise, we would not be able to glorify him (as is fitting), and we are glorified in his gifts. For in those things which are our own—whether they be works, or character, or human knowledge—we are not glorious, except in a kind of shadow and (so to speak) a certain vanity of glory. But the graces of God make the one who glorifies God in them glorious. Let us therefore glorify God, so that he may more abundantly bestow graces upon us for glorifying him; not so that we ourselves may be glorious (for he who looks at himself loses glory), but so that we may glorify him to whom all glory is fitting and more than fitting, forever and ever.

<margin>☞ B 2</margin>
¶ THE EXAMINATION of several points regarding the literal text. ¶ The Vulgate edition: **Which you endure for an example of the righteous judgment of God.**

¶ The old translator <note>The "old translator" refers to the traditional author of the Latin Vulgate (St. Jerome).</note> could have said "evidence" [exemplum] without a preposition. For those pressures which the righteous suffer unjustly from the impious and unjust are an indication of the righteous judgment of God, who will leave no evil unpunished. Paul: *hoion endeigma tēs dikaias kriseōs tou theou* <note>Original Greek: οἷον ἔνδειγμα τῆς δικαίας κρίσεως τοῦ θεοῦ. The author is noting that the Greek word 'endeigma' means a plain indication or proof.</note>.

<margin>C 3</margin>
¶ The Vulgate edition: **For which also you suffer.** And that is indeed correct. But the phrasing is clearly ambiguous among Latin speakers: to what does "which" refer? To "God" or to the "Kingdom"? But we ought to understand it as referring to the Kingdom (for the Kingdom of God is that He should be known, desired, and loved by all, and glorified in all). This is clearly recognized from the Greek, where the phrasing is not ambiguous, because the relative pronoun is feminine, which can only refer to the noun to which it corresponds—"kingdom"—which is likewise feminine among the Greeks. Paul: *hyper hēs kai paschete* <note>Original Greek: ὑπὲρ ἧς καὶ πάσχετε. The feminine pronoun 'hēs' matches the feminine 'basileia' (kingdom), resolving the Latin ambiguity.</note>.

¶ The Vulgate edition: **If yet it is just with God.**
¶ What is said here, "if yet" [*si tamen*], can be an assertive particle, and is more suited to Paul’s understanding. He proposed nothing in doubt, but as one making certain and asserting, as one who had been made more certain and instructed by the Holy Spirit. Paul: *eiper dikaion para tō theō* <note>Original Greek: εἴπερ δίκαιον παρὰ τῷ θεῷ. The author argues that 'eiper' functions here as "since indeed" rather than expressing doubt.</note>.

### 2nd Thessalonians

<margin>¶</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *With the angels of his power.* <note>original: "Cum āgelis virtutis eius"</note> This "of his power" is the same as "of his might." **Paul:** *with the angels of his power.* <note>original Greek: "μετ’ ἀγγέλων δυνάμεως αὐτοῦ"</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *In a flame of fire giving vengeance.* <note>original: "In flamma ignis dantis vindictam"</note> ¶ Lest "giving" be misunderstood as referring to the fire, rather than to Christ, it seemed better to resolve the speech through a relative pronoun and a verb; then the phrasing would appear far less ambiguous. **Paul:** *in a flame of fire, giving vengeance.* <note>original Greek: "ἐν πυρὶ φλογὸς, Διδόντος ἐκδίκησιν"</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:**
<margin>D</margin> *Who shall suffer eternal punishments in destruction.* <note>original: "Qui pœnas dabunt in interitu æternas"</note> ¶ What is said here concerns the revelation of Christ and the Holy Spirit.
<margin>3</margin> The ancient translator <note>The "ancient translator" refers to the traditional author of the Latin Vulgate, often identified with St. Jerome.</note> should have said *in eternal destruction* rather than *eternal punishments*. For in the Greek, "eternal" is an adjective modifying "destruction." He also should have expressed "punishment" and "destruction" in the same case without a preposition. **Paul:** *who shall pay the penalty of eternal destruction.* <note>original Greek: "οἵτινες δίκην τίσουσιν ὄλεθρον αἰώνιον"</note> This is as if we said: *who pay the penalty of everlasting destruction*, for the punishment by which they are consumed is itself everlasting destruction.
<margin>D</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *And from the glory of his power.* <note>original: "Et a gloria virtutis eius"</note> Here it should be said *of his strength*. **Paul:** *and from the glory of his strength.* <note>original Greek: "καὶ ἀπὸ τῆς δόξης τῆς ἰσχύος αὐτοῦ"</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:**
<margin>4</margin> *That our God may count you worthy of his calling.* <note>original: "Vt dignetur vos vocatione sua deus noster"</note> The word "his" is redundant, though it does not hinder understanding. **Paul:** *that our God may count you worthy of the calling.* <note>original Greek: "ἵνα ὑμᾶς ἀξιώσῃ τῆς κλήσεως ὁ θεὸς ἡμῶν"</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *And the work of faith in power.* <note>original: "Et opus fidei in virtute"</note> Here too, by "power," he means authority. We can also turn the accusatives into ablatives, so that we understand: *may our God fill you with every desire for goodness and with the work of faith.* **Paul:** *and the work of faith in power.* <note>original Greek: "καὶ ἔργον πίστεως ἐν δυνάμει"</note>

### CHAPTER II

<margin>5</margin> <image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'D' featuring a seated figure at a desk, surrounded by architectural motifs.</image-desc> Regarding the day of the Lord's revelation, when fire shall go before him and set his enemies on fire round about: the apostle has already offered some initial thoughts. He knew that the Thessalonians were somewhat afraid and troubled regarding this matter, as if the great and terrible day of the Lord were imminent. Therefore, lest they be terrified more than is proper by what he previously wrote, he restrains their empty fear. For the day of the Lord will not come before the number of the elect is fulfilled—which is known to God—and before the "man of sin" is revealed, the "son of perdition," who is the Antichrist. And in this manner he
<margin>a</margin> says:
> ¶ Now we beseech you, brothers, by the coming of our Lord JESUS CHRIST,
> <margin>b</margin> and our gathering together in him: that you be not quickly shaken in mind, nor troubled,
> <margin>c</margin> neither by spirit, nor by word, nor by letter, as if from us: as if the day of
> CHRIST were at hand. <margin>d</margin> Let no one deceive you in any way. For that day shall not come unless the apostasy comes first, and the
> <margin>e</margin> man of sin is revealed, the son of perdition, who opposes and exalts himself above all
> <margin>f</margin> that is called God, or an object of worship; so that he sits in the temple of God as God, showing himself
> <margin>g</margin> that he is God. Do you not remember that when I was still with you, I told you these things? And now you know what
> <margin>h</margin> restrains him, so that he may be revealed in his own time. For the mystery of iniquity is already at work.
> <margin>i</margin> Only he who now restrains will do so until he is taken out of the way: and then the lawless one will be revealed, whom the Lord shall
> <margin>k</margin> slay with the breath of his mouth, and shall destroy with the brightness of his coming: whose coming is according to the
> <margin>l</margin> working of Satan, in all power, and signs, and lying wonders, and in all
> <margin>m</margin> deceivableness of unrighteousness in those who perish. Because they did not receive
> <margin>n</margin> the love of the truth, that they might be saved. And for this reason God shall send them a strong delusion, that they should believe a
> lie: that all might be judged who did not believe the truth, but had pleasure in un-
<margin>righteousness.</margin> ¶ This is Paul's revelation concerning the coming of the Antichrist: veiled and obscure. And the Apocalypse of John reveals two Antichrists by the names of the first and second beasts. The first beast has already come: and that was Muhammad <note>original: "mahumetes"</note>, who appeared under the Emperor Heraclius, and whose sect still endures—though by God's mercy it shall soon utterly perish. The second beast has not yet appeared, of whom the apostle seems rather to speak. This is not surprising, for at the coming of the first beast, the "apostasy" was not yet complete. "Apostasy" is interpreted as a falling away, a repudiation, or a rebellion. Athanasius <note>A 4th-century Church Father and Bishop of Alexandria.</note> interprets this apostasy in this passage as the falling away of the Roman monarchy. Jerome does the same in his writing to Algasia, who proposed eleven questions to him from the apostle, and in the eleventh, sought the understanding of this very place. Furthermore, the first beast did not sit in the temple of God showing himself as if he were God; rather, he called himself only a prophet and messenger of God. Again, although his coming was in falsehood, it was not as one who, full of the spirit of Satan, lied about the angels of God and his familiarity with God, claiming his own elevation from the holy city up into heaven even to the throne of God, and the knowledge of heavenly secrets, and innumerable such things unworthy of narration. And indeed, this was done with a false ecstasy where he was led fantastically by a diabolical beast of burden even to the prince of demons. By the touch of whose hand (as he himself says) he felt a lethal cold, as if the prince was declaring himself even in this to be the prince of death. Him he worshipped as the true God, accompanied by an angel of darkness who transformed himself into Gabriel, an angel of light. He was led, I say, on a beast of burden (for such a beast suited both the prince of bestiality who sent him and the bestial man to whom he was sent) through fictitious realms of darkness...

### COMMENTARY

...the heavens through many-headed, many-tongued, monstrous, and multiform apostate angels paying their punishments, who even feigned that they stood in need of his help. And—O, horrendous crime! Unspeakable crime!—in that sacrilegious vision, one of them transfigures himself into Christ, as if he were lacking help and demanding his prayers. He sees chains; he sees punishments. He thinks he is giving praise to God while they speak blasphemies, attributing to the <term>Prince of Darkness</term><note>A common title for Satan.</note> those things which are owed to the Lord, the inhabitant of total majesty and immense light. And while he sees the secrets of the deep night, he thinks them to be heavenly mysteries. This is the truth and the true interpretation of that vision and diabolical stage-play. And those who worship the god of Muhammad worship the prince of darkness; he is their god. For it was he whom Muhammad adored, and he was the messenger of him alone. 

Nor should anyone marvel at these fictitious heavens and their fabricated, vast magnitude. For (as **Philo**<note>Philo of Alexandria, a Hellenistic Jewish philosopher.</note> relates) some of the children of Israel, tempted by diabolical curiosity, were deceived by similar fictions by the Canaanites, believing that in the middle of the night they truly saw the sun. And having abandoned the true Creator of the sun, they worshipped him as the true god who had made that fictitious sun appear. 

Do not marvel either at the fictitious angels and the Christ simulated by the cunning of Satan, since it is known from the history of **Heraclides**<note>Likely referring to Heraclides Ponticus or a similar hagiographical source.</note> that something similar happened to the monk **Valens**. A demon (he says), transfigured into the likeness of the Savior, came to him at night with a certain choir of a thousand (as he had feigned) angels holding lit lamps, and with a flaming wheel in which he had simulated the Savior sitting. One of them preceded him, saying these things to him: "Go out from your cell, and do nothing else but this: when you see him coming from a distance, hasten to bow down and adore him; then you shall return to your own dwelling." Having gone out of his cell, and believing himself to see the divine offices of the heavenly ministry, and all things glowing with the brightness of the lamps, and the **Antichrist** himself positioned no more than a single <term>stadium</term><note>An ancient unit of distance, roughly 185 meters.</note> away, he immediately fell prone on the ground and adored him whom he believed to be the Lord. Thus says Heraclides. 

Behold how, having left the true Christ, the puffed-up and foolish Valens adored the adversary as Christ, accepting a simulated phantom and a lying image instead of the truth. For the works of God are truth for the sake of salvation; but the works of the devil are the appearance of truths for the sake of damnation. Therefore, the coming of that beast and of the first Antichrist was in the spirit of Satan and in a lie; yet he did not perform signs and wonders, as he himself testifies of himself. But the *second beast* shall have the power of signs. *And he seduced* (it says) *those dwelling on the earth, because of the signs which were given to him to perform.* <note>A reference to Revelation 13:14.</note> Nevertheless, the first beast and the first Antichrist have a great similarity with the second (as is known from the **Apocalypse**) and he runs before him, so that the second may say he was announced by the first, and that he is the one whom the first commanded to be adored. For he will give spirit to the image of the beast, and the spirit of the image of the beast will be in the spirit of Satan. 

**Moses** and **Christ**: man, and man above man through the fullness of God. The first and second beast: beast, and beast below every beast through the fullness of the wickedness of Satan. Just as Christ came when the empire of the Greeks was utterly removed, so the second beast, who is the Antichrist, will come when the Roman empire is likewise thoroughly removed. Therefore, the **Thessalonians** did not have as just a cause for fear as we do, who ought to fear the near arrival of the **Man of Sin** and the **Son of Perdition**, when, at the signal of **Paul**, we turn our eyes to the Roman monarchy. Where now, I ask, is that monarchy? Where is he who, within it, rules the reins of the world?

But since Muhammad is the "beast of the beast" and the "Antichrist of the Antichrist," it would not be absurd if almost everything the Apostle brought forward were seen to apply to him. Who will deny that he is the **Man of Sin** and the **Son of Perdition**, who withdrew from the kingdom of Christ and of God—unto eternal perdition—Africa, Asia, and a great part of Europe, and who caused such a great apostasy from the Roman Empire across such a vast breadth of the earth? Who ever rose up as such an adversary to Christ? Who is so exalted *above all that is called God*? The Father is called God, and truly is; the Son is called God, and truly is; the Holy Spirit is called God, and truly is. And these three are in truth God, and one God. But he denies the Father as God, he denies the Son as God, he denies the Holy Spirit as God. He denies the Three, and he denies Christ as God. And he exalts himself above Christ; he exalts himself above the angels. Instead of Christ, and instead of the suppliant angels and even the demons, he lies that he prayed as their superior. Is he not therefore exalted above all that is in truth called God? And since he is above the angels and demons, he is even above those who were held to be gods in opinion; there is no need to make mention of idols. 

For he condemned every carved image. Yet the foolish and beast-like people venerated his idol alone—that is, the **hanging sarcophagus**<note>A reference to the medieval legend that Muhammad's coffin was suspended in the air at Mecca by powerful magnets.</note> full of unhappy bones, and more destructive than many idols. He calls the place of veneration in "Happy Arabia"—or rather, in that very unhappy place—**Mecca**. But just as Christ shall dissolve and destroy the future [Antichrist] with the spirit of his mouth, so has he already uncovered that idol (if those things are true which I have heard told, and have read written after hearing them) with a lightning-like spirit, while the machine of the world stands ready to serve whatever he wishes. I myself saw the man...

<meta>This page continues the polemical commentary on the Second Epistle to the Thessalonians. Having previously discussed the "sacrilegious visions" and the rise of the "god of Muhammad," the author now recounts a specific anecdote about a Christian ascetic to illustrate the perceived downfall of this "Antichrist" power.</meta>

About twenty years have now passed (if I am not mistaken) since his time. He was clothed in sackcloth, always walking with a bare head and bare feet, girded with a twisted vine, carrying a wooden cross in his hand. Shuddering at no cold and no snows (which were then very great), he would run from shrine to shrine; where if the doors were not open, he would bend his knees in the snow and pray. His food was vegetables and bread after many days of fasting; his drink, water; his bed, the earth. They say that this man endured seven years of slavery in Constantinople in the confession of the name of Christ. After that time, he set out for **Mecca**<note>The holy city of Islam, which the author portrays through a lens of Christian polemic.</note> with Turkish merchants who recognized him and favored him for his simplicity of character and the faithfulness of his service. 

When they entered the temple, he entered along with them. And as they bent their knees before the **bier of the beast**<note>A derogatory reference to the tomb of Muhammad.</note>, he also bent his. They worshipped the beast, but he, in silent prayer, worshipped Christ. He prayed then with tears that Christ might show a sign of His power and cast down that body which had seduced so many peoples into perdition, and that He might illuminate that land with the light of His grace, so that men might know Him and give glory to the true God, who alone is worthy of glory. 

As he was leaving the temple, scouts seized him so that they might cut him in half with a **wooden saw**<note>Original: *serra lignea*. A common legendary punishment for non-believers entering sacred Islamic spaces in medieval European literature.</note>. For this is the punishment for those who dare to enter the temple who belong to a sect other than the **Mahumatean**<note>Followers of Muhammad; Muslims.</note>. He, however, exulting, patiently awaited being cut asunder for the name of Christ. But the merchants moved the authorities to mercy with their prayers and recovered him unharmed by means of a gift; for he had provided much service to them and their camels on the road. 

As they were departing, a bolt of lightning sent from heaven (just as he had asked for a sign of power from the Lord) struck, shattered, and diminished the bier. I have both heard these things and read them in writing. From this, even the Turks suspect that their law will soon come to an end. 

Behold (if these things are true) he who sat as a **type**<note>A "type" is a person or thing in the Old Testament or history believed to foreshadow a later reality, in this case, the Antichrist.</note> in the temple and was worshipped as a god, and was exalted above Christ and everyone who is called god, has now been cast down; he has already fallen, struck down by the spirit of Christ. His coming had been according to the working of Satan, with all false signs and wonders for the seduction of unrighteousness in those who perish. For that sign was a lie which swept many away to destruction: namely, seeing that **hanging sarcophagus**<note>A reference to the popular medieval myth that Muhammad's coffin was suspended in mid-air by magnets to trick pilgrims into thinking it was a miracle.</note> and thinking it was supported by divine power. I say "hanging in the air" because the simple people did not know how to recognize the cause of it; or if they were not simple, they did not dare to think otherwise because of superstition. Thus, for both the simple and the wise, it was a lying sign and wonder for the perdition of souls. 

But now, after the lightning-strike and the most unhappy conflagration of the bones, they say his body is in **Medinatabi**<note>Medina (Madinat al-Nabi), the burial place of Muhammad.</note> of desert Arabia, where his shrine is visited—100 units long and 80 wide, supported by four hundred columns, with hanging lamps perpetually burning to the number of 3,000. But does he not also seem here to be exalted above the sacred **object of worship**<note>Original: *sebasma* (Greek: σέβασμα), meaning an object of veneration or a sanctuary.</note>, above the Holy of Holies which is truly worshipped, and above every truly holy **rite**<note>Original: *teletam* (Greek: τελετή), a religious rite or initiation.</note> and consummation to which honor and reverence are due? Does such a peak of veneration appear to the twin nations? For those admitted to this funeral spectacle, their eyes are plucked out—and justly so, as those who are never to see God.

¶ What then remains, except that when the **apostasy**<note>The "falling away" predicted in 2 Thessalonians 2:3.</note> and the failing of the **Roman monarchy**<note>Refers to the *translatio imperii* or the historical belief that the Antichrist would appear after the fall of the Roman Empire.</note> have been completed, the second beast should come—the second man of sin and son of iniquity of whom Paul speaks here? To him is given the power of signs, in whom all these things will be more manifest than in the first beast (who was a type of this malice). The Lord Jesus shall strike him down with the spirit of His mouth and destroy him by the brightness of His coming, when the Gospel of peace has been preached in the whole world, truly known, and received. Happy are those who shall then be the chosen ministers of such great happiness from God! Great also is the happiness for those who shall stand immovable in the faith of Christ, both in life and in confession; nor, while those times press upon them, shall they be moved from their minds or disturbed, but they shall firmly adhere to Christ as to an immovable mountain, retaining His peace and serenity, and always giving thanks to Him for the great mercy of God toward them.

> ¶ But we ought always to give thanks to God for you, brothers beloved by the Lord, because God has pitied you unto the salvation of the **firstfruits**<note>The first converts or the elect of the early church.</note>, in the sanctification of the Spirit and faith in the truth. To this He called you through our Gospel, into the acquisition of the glory of our Lord JESUS CHRIST. Therefore, brothers, stand firm, and hold the traditions which you were taught, whether by word or by our epistle. Now may our Lord JESUS CHRIST Himself, and God our Father who loved us and gave us eternal consolation and good hope in grace, comfort your hearts and confirm you in every good word and work.

¶ Whoever the men are who have been saved, are being saved, and will be saved: it is by the mercy of God alone, which is followed by salvation, the sanctification of the spirit, and faith in the truth. And this is especially for those called who are the firstfruits, in their successors, and in the final times of the ages. For mercy encompasses all times and all ages; and not only does it encompass them, but it also wishes to be grasped. Some do not...

IX 199 2 Thessa.

It has now been nearly twenty years (if I am not mistaken) since that time. That man was clothed in sackcloth, with a bare head and bare feet, always walking about girt with a twisted rope, carrying a wooden cross in his hand. He feared no cold and no snows (which were very great at that time), hurrying from chapel to chapel; and where the doors were not open, he would bend his knees in the snow and pray. His food was herbs and bread; and after many days of fasting, his drink was water and his bed was the earth. They say this man endured seven years of slavery in Constantinople in the confession of the name of Christ. After that time, he set out for Mecca with Turkish merchants who recognized him and, because of the simplicity of his character and the faithfulness of his service, took him along. When they entered the temple, he entered with them. And as they bent their knees before the tomb of the beast <note>Referring to the tomb of Muhammad, whom the author identifies with the "Beast" of Revelation.</note>, he also knelt. They adored the beast, but he, in silent prayer, adored Christ. He then prayed with tears that Christ would show a sign of His power and cast down that body which had seduced so many peoples into perdition, and that He would illuminate that land with the light of His grace so that men might know Him and give glory to the true God, who alone is worthy of glory. As he was leaving the temple, guards seized him so that a wooden saw might cut him in half. For this is the punishment for those who dare to enter the temple who belong to a sect other than the Muhammadan one. He, however, exulting for the name of Christ, patiently awaited the sawing. But the merchants, moved by his rigor, pleaded for him and received him back unharmed as a gift; for he had provided much service to them and their camels on the road. Therefore, as they were departing, a lightning bolt sent from heaven struck down, shattered, and diminished the tomb (as a sign of the Lord’s power, granted to his patient servant). I have both heard these things and read them in writing. From this, even the Turks surmise that their law will soon come to an end.

Behold (if these things are true) he who sat as a type in the temple and was adored as if he were a god, and was exalted above Christ and everyone who is called god, has now been cast down; he has already fallen, struck down by the spirit of Christ. His coming had been according to the working of Satan, with all false signs and wonders for the seduction of unrighteousness in those who perish. For that sign was a falsehood which snatched many away to destruction: those who saw that hanging sarcophagus and thought it was supported by divine power. I say "hanging" in the air, a thing for which the simple folk did not know how to recognize the cause; or if they were not simple, they nevertheless did not dare to think about it because of superstition <note>This refers to the medieval legend that Muhammad's iron coffin was held suspended in the air by powerful magnets in the ceiling and floor.</note>. Thus, for both the simple and the non-simple, it was a lying sign and wonder leading to the perdition of souls. Now, however, after the lightning-strike and the burning of that wretched tomb and its bones, they say his body is in Medina <note>Original: "Medinatalabi," a corruption of Madinat al-Nabi, City of the Prophet.</note> in the deserts of Arabia. There, his shrine is seen, 100 paces long and 80 wide, supported by four hundred columns, with hanging lamps perpetually lit to the number of 3,000. But does he not also seem here to be exalted above the most holy object of worship <note>original: "sebafma," from the Greek "sebasma," something held in awe or worshipped.</note>, above the Holy of Holies which is truly worshipped, and indeed above every holy rite <note>original: "teletam," referring to a religious initiation or mystery.</note> and consummation to which honor and reverence are due, when such a height of veneration appears for this twofold people? To those admitted to this funeral spectacle, their eyes are gouged out—and rightly so, as those who are never to see God.

To him is given the power of signs, in whom all these things will be more manifest than in the first beast, who was a type of this malice. The Lord Jesus will strike him down with the spirit of His mouth and destroy him with the brightness of His coming, once the Gospel of peace has been preached in the whole world, known in truth, and received. Happy are those who will then be the ministers elected by God for such great happiness; great also is the happiness for those who will stand immovable in the faith of Christ, both in life and in confession. Nor, when those times press upon them, will they be moved from their minds or disturbed, but they will adhere firmly to Christ as to an immovable mountain, retaining His peace and serenity, and always giving Him thanks for the great mercy of God toward them.

Thus, those who worship the god of Muhammad worship the Prince of Darkness; he is their god. For it was him that Muhammad adored, and of him alone was he the messenger.

Nor should anyone marvel at the fictitious heavens and their fashioned, ample magnitude. For (as Philo narrates) <note>Philo of Alexandria, a Jewish philosopher; the author likely refers to his accounts of idolatry or celestial delusions.</note> several of the sons of Israel, tempted by diabolical curiosity, were deceived by similar fictions from the Canaanites, believing that they truly saw the sun in the middle of the night. Having abandoned the true Creator of the sun, they adored as the true God the one who had made a fictitious sun appear. Do not wonder, either, at fictitious angels and at a Christ simulated by the cunning of Satan, since it is known from the history of Heraclides <note>Heraclides of Cyprus, mentioned in the *Lausiac History*, a 5th-century collection of lives of desert monks.</note> that a similar thing happened to the monk Valens. A demon (he says), transformed into the likeness of the Savior, came to him by night with a certain choir of a thousand (as he had feigned) angels holding lit lamps, and with a flaming wheel in which he had simulated the Savior's presence. One of them preceded him, saying: "Go out therefore from your cell, and do nothing else except, when you see him coming from afar, hasten to bow and adore him; then you shall return to your own dwelling." Having gone out of his cell, and believing himself to see the divine offices of the heavenly ministry—all things glowing with the brightness of lamps—and the Antichrist himself positioned no more than a furlong's distance away, he immediately fell prone on the ground and adored him whom he believed to be the Lord. Thus says Heraclides.

Behold how, having left the true Christ, the puffed-up and foolish Valens adored Christ’s adversary, and embraced a simulated phantom and a lying image instead of the truth. For the works of God are truth unto salvation, but the works of the devil are the appearance of truth unto damnation. The arrival of that beast, the first Antichrist <note>Referring to Muhammad.</note>, was in the spirit of Satan and in lies, yet he did not perform signs and wonders, as he himself testifies of himself. But the second beast <note>The final Antichrist described in the Book of Revelation.</note> will have the power of signs. "And he seduced," it says, "those dwelling on the earth because of the signs which were given to him to perform." Yet the first beast, the first Antichrist, has a great similarity with the second (as is known from the Apocalypse) and runs before him, so that the second may say he was announced by the first, and that he is the one whom the first commanded to be adored. For he will give spirit to the image of the beast, and the spirit of the image of the beast will be in the spirit of Satan. For Moses and Christ were man, and man above man through the fullness of God. The first and second beasts are beast, and beast below every beast through the fullness of the wickedness of Satan. 

Just as Christ came when the empire of the Greeks was utterly removed, so when the Roman Empire is likewise completely taken away, the second beast—who is the Antichrist—will come. Therefore, the Thessalonians did not have as just a cause for fear as we do, who must fear the nearby arrival of the "man of sin" and "son of perdition," when, at the signal of Paul, we turn our eye to the Roman monarchy <note>In 2 Thessalonians 2, Paul speaks of a "restrainer" holding back the Antichrist. # IX 2 Thessalonians

It is now nearly (unless I am mistaken) twenty years since this happened. He was clothed in sackcloth, always walking with a bare head and bare feet, girded with a twisted vine-shoot, carrying a wooden cross in his hand. Fearing no cold and no snows (which were then very great), he hurried from shrine to shrine; and if the doors were not open, he would kneel in the snow and pray. His food was herbs and bread; after many days of fasting, his drink was water and his bed was the earth. They say this man endured seven years of slavery in Constantinople for the confession of the name of Christ. After that time, he set out for Mecca with Turkish merchants who knew him and respected him for his simple character and faithful service. When they entered the temple, he entered with them. And when they knelt before the bier of the beast <note>original: "feretrum bestiæ"; a polemical reference to the tomb of Muhammad.</note>, he also knelt. They adored the beast, but he, in silent prayer, adored Christ. He then prayed with tears that Christ would show a sign of His power, cast down that body which had seduced so many peoples to destruction, and illuminate that land with the light of His grace so that men might know Him and give glory to the true God, who alone is worthy of glory. As he was leaving the temple, guards seized him to cut him in two with a wooden saw. For this is the punishment for those who dare to enter the temple who belong to a sect other than that of Muhammad. He, however, exulted; for the name of Christ, he patiently awaited the execution. But the merchants softened the guards' severity with prayers and received him back unharmed as a gift. For he had provided much service to them and their camels on the journey. As they were departing, a lightning bolt sent from heaven (as a sign of power from the Lord) struck the bier, shaking it and breaking it. These things I have both heard and read in writing, from which even the Turks conjecture that their law will soon come to an end.

Behold (if these things are true) he who sat in the temple as a figure and was adored as if he were a god, and was exalted above Christ and everyone who is called god, has now been cast down. <header>COMMENTARY</header>

...inviting everyone with great sweetness, saying: "Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you." <note>Matthew 11:28</note> He who says "all" wishes none to be excluded. Therefore, let us follow the holy Gospels and embrace the holy instruction of Paul; and let this holy prayer come upon everyone: that our Lord Jesus Christ and our Father, who loved us (for if He had not loved us, how would He have called us?) and gave us the consolation of the Spirit and the hope of eternal good things—than which nothing better can be, nor even be imagined— <insert>He gave indeed not from our works or our merits, but through His grace</insert> may comfort the hearts of all and confirm them in every word and good work. Thus, being made like the good angels, confirmed in every good thing, let us give glory and perpetual praise to Him, who is most kind, most pious, and most merciful toward all and over all who call upon His name. Amen.

<margin>A 5</margin>
EXAMINATION of several points regarding the literal text. ¶ The Vulgate edition: *And of our gathering together in him.* <note>original Latin: "Et nostræ congregationis in eo"; 2 Thessalonians 2:1</note> ¶ It should rather be said: *and our gathering together in him,* so that it is understood to refer back to the word "by," making the sense: "we beseech you by the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ and by our gathering together in him." For would we say "by the coming of our gathering in him"? Certainly, the "coming of Christ" is aptly said, but the "coming of our gathering" is not so apt. A hallucination occurred to the old translator <note>The "old translator" refers to the traditional author of the Latin Vulgate, often identified as St. Jerome.</note> because in the Greek, "of our gathering" is in the genitive case. But even then, he ought to have noticed the preposition **concerning/by** <note>original Greek: **ὑπὲρ** (*hyper*)</note> which he translated as "by" <note>Latin: *per*</note>; just as **through** <note>original Greek: **Διὰ** (*dia*)</note> requires the genitive, "by" <note>Latin: *per*</note> among us requires the accusative. Paul says: **and our gathering together unto him.** <note>original Greek: **καὶ ἡμῶν ἐπισυναγωγῆς ἐπ' αὐτόν**</note> as if he were saying **and concerning** or **through** <margin>’</margin> **the gathering.** ¶ The Vulgate edition: *That you be not easily moved from your sense.* <note>2 Thessalonians 2:2</note> ¶ "Your" is redundant. And it should be said "from your mind" rather than "from your sense." Paul says: **that you not be quickly shaken from your mind.** <note>original Greek: **εἰς τὸ μὴ ταχέως σαλευθῆναι ὑμᾶς ἀπὸ τοῦ νοός**</note> ¶ The Vulgate edition: *Nor by letter as if sent by us, as if the day of the Lord were at hand.* ¶ "Sent" is redundant. And at the end, it should say "of Christ," not "of the Lord." And he says "by letter as if by us" because in the previous chapter he made mention of that terrible day. For this reason, the Thessalonians <margin>’</margin> ought not to have been terrified, as if that universal day of the Lord were imminent. And how many lying spirits have been found in the mouths of those who wished to predict that day! They would not have been deceived by a lying spirit if they had wished to follow this precept of Paul. Paul says: **nor by letter as if through us, as though the day of Christ were at hand.** <note>original Greek: **μήτε δι' ἐπιστολῆς ὡς δι' ἡμῶν, ὡς ὅτι ἐνέστηκεν ἡ ἡμέρα τοῦ Χριστοῦ**</note> ¶ The Vulgate edition: *For unless there come a falling away first.* <note>2 Thessalonians 2:3</note> ¶ Here <margin>’</margin> Paul has *apostasia*. And this "apostasy" is understood as the falling away from the Roman Empire, which began most greatly when Muhammad, the man of sin, came. And a great apostasy was likewise made from Christ. For he is the first beast and the dragon speaking blasphemies and lies, who was shown in the Apocalypse. May God grant that in a short time both these wounds of apostasy be mended, both of the Empire and of the Faith. Paul says: **unless the falling away comes first.** <note>original Greek: **ὅτι ἐὰν μὴ ἔλθῃ ἡ ἀποστασία πρῶτον**</note> ¶ The Vulgate edition: <margin>’</margin> *And is lifted up above all that is called God, or that is worshipped.* <note>2 Thessalonians 2:4</note> ¶ It is better in the masculine gender: "above everyone who is called God." And "that which is called / that which is worshipped" can be expressed by one word: an object of worship. Although <term>sebasma</term> <note>From the Greek *sebasma*, meaning an object of veneration or holiness.</note> properly signifies everything to which the honor and reverence of veneration is due; and thus among us, the altar of Christ, the holy chrism, the Holy of Holies covered by visible signs in the most august sacrament of the Eucharist, and the cup of blessing containing the price of the whole world under sacrosanct veils—these are truly *sebasmata*. Above these things, the impure nation <note>A reference to the Ottoman Empire or Muslims in the author's contemporary context.</note> exalts the memory of the impure Antichrist, the man of sin, and the son of perdition; and those most ignorant of doctrine exalt the most lying Quran <note>original Latin: "Alchoranum"</note> above the most holy and true Gospel. <margin>’</margin> Paul says: **above everyone called God, or an object of worship.** <note>original Greek: **ἐπὶ πάντα λεγόμενον θεὸν, ἢ σέβασμα**</note> ¶ The Vulgate edition: *So that he sits in the temple of God.* <note>2 Thessalonians 2:4</note> ¶ The particle "as God" is missing. It should be said: *so that he sits in the temple of God as God.* Paul says: **so that he himself sits in the temple of God as God.** <note>original Greek: **ὥστε αὐτὸν εἰς τὸν ναὸν τοῦ θεοῦ, ὡς θεὸν καθίσαι**</note> ¶ The Vulgate <margin>B 5</margin> <margin>’</margin> edition: *Do you not retain?* <note>2 Thessalonians 2:5</note> ¶ That word "retain" designates "you have in memory" or "you remember." Paul says: **Do you not remember?** <note>original Greek: **οὐ μνημονεύετε**</note> ¶ The Vulgate edition: *For the mystery of iniquity already works.* <note>2 Thessalonians 2:7</note> ¶ "Works" is taken passively. This is just as if it were said: "the mystery is already being perpetrated, is being done, is being admitted." But because the word "work" is rarely taken passively among us, I preferred to say "is perpetrated," which has a strictly passive and unambiguous meaning. Paul says: **for the mystery of lawlessness is already at work.** <note>original Greek: **τὸ γὰρ μυστήριον ἤδη ἐνεργεῖται τῆς ἀνομίας**</note> ¶ The Vulgate edition: *Only he who now holds, let him hold, until he be taken out of the way.* <note>2 Thessalonians 2:7</note> ¶ "Let him hold" is redundant. And Paul, in his judgment, <margin>’</margin> uses an obscure expression. For concerning the falling away of the Roman Empire—which was the sign of the coming of the son of perdition, the man of sin, and the very notable Antichrist (for there are many antichrists)—it was not safe to speak openly, nor was it the will of the Holy Spirit, even though he had prophesied many things about them to them in person. Through these things, they were able to understand Paul's rather obscure delay regarding the same. Paul says: **only he who now restrains, until he comes from the midst.** <note>original Greek: **μόνον ὁ κατέχων ἄρτι, ἕως ἐκ μέσου γένηται**</note> ¶ The Vulgate edition: *Whom the Lord JESUS shall kill with the spirit of his mouth.* <note>2 Thessalonians 2:8</note> ¶ "Jesus" is redundant. Paul says: **Whom the Lord shall consume with the spir...** <note>original Greek: **ὃν ὁ κύριος ἀναλώσει τῷ πνεύ...**</note>

# IX

...by the breath of his body. ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *In all power and signs and lying wonders.* ¶ **Power:** he means authority. And **of a lie:** the old translator <note>The "old translator" refers to Jerome, the traditional author of the Latin Vulgate.</note> could have said this, for in the Greek it is held in the neuter singular genitive. Paul: "in all power and signs and wonders of a lie." <note>original: "ἐν πάσῃ δυνάμει καὶ σημείοις καὶ τέρασι ψεύδους"</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *In that they received not the love of the truth.* ¶ **It should be said:** "because of which they did not receive the love of truth"—referring to the signs and lying wonders I mentioned. Paul: "because they received not the love of the truth." <note>original: "ἀνθ᾽ ὧν τὴν ἀγάπην τῆς ἀληθείας οὐκ ἐδέξαντο"</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *But consented to iniquity.* ¶ **The old translator** used the word "iniquity" <note>Latin: *iniquitas*</note> in three places in this chapter: first, "the mystery of iniquity is already at work"; second, "in all seduction of iniquity"; and here, "but they consented to iniquity." However, the word is not the same in Paul's text. In the first instance, it is called **lawlessness** <note>original: "ἀνομία" (*anomia*)</note>, but in the two latter instances, it is **unrighteousness** <note>original: "ἀδικία" (*adikia*)</note>. The former is everywhere "iniquity," while the latter is generally translated as "unjustice" or "unrighteousness." For this reason, we preferred to vary the terms as Paul did, saying "iniquity" in the first place and "unrighteousness" in the following places. Paul: "but taking pleasure in unrighteousness" <note>original: "ἀλλ᾽ εὐδοκήσαντες ἐν τῇ ἀδικίᾳ"</note>; "but being well-pleased in unrighteousness," which is not far from saying "acquiescing to unrighteousness." ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Brethren beloved of God: that God hath chosen us.* ¶ **It should be said:** "by the Lord." and rather "that God had mercy on you" using the second person. Paul: "brethren beloved by the Lord, because God chose you." <note>original: "ἀδελφοὶ ἠγαπημένοι ὑπὸ κυρίου ὅτι εἵλετο ὑμᾶς ὁ θεόσ"</note> There are also Greek manuscripts that have "us" in the first person: "chose us." <note>original: "εἵλετο ἡμᾶσ"</note> Both interpretations are applicable. For the apostles were truly the firstfruits—among whom were Paul and the disciples of the Lord—who are understood if "us" is said in the first person. ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *In which also he called you.* ¶ **Rather:** "to which" or "unto which" he called you, for it is a neuter singular relative. "To which [thing]," namely, salvation through sanctification of the spirit and faith in the truth. If you wish for it to have an antecedent—that is, something specific to refer back to—it would refer to the "Spirit," the word for which is neuter among the Greeks. But among us, it would be masculine, and one would have to say: "in whom also he called," namely, in the Holy Spirit. Therefore, it should not be "in which" (feminine), but "in whom" (masculine). Paul: "to which he called you." <note>original: "εἰς ὃ ἐκάλεσεν ὑμᾶσ"</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *And hold the traditions which you have learned.* ¶ **Rather:** "which you have been taught." Paul: "which you were taught." <note>original: "ἃς ἐδιδάχθητε"</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *May he exhort your hearts.* ¶ The old translator could have said "may he comfort your hearts," since a little earlier he had used the word "consolation" <note>original: "παρακλησιν" (*paraklesin*)</note> from the same root when he said "and gave eternal consolation." It would follow that he should use the same root to say "may he comfort" <note>original: "παρακαλέσαι" (*parakalesai*)</note>. Paul: "may he comfort your hearts." <note>original: "παρακαλέσαι ὑμῶν τὰς καρδίας"</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *In every good work and word.* ¶ In the Greek, the words are transposed: "word" comes first, and "work" follows. Paul: "in every good word and work." <note>original: "ἐν παντὶ λόγῳ καὶ ἔργῳ ἀγαθῷ"</note>

### CHAPTER III.

<image-desc>An ornate square woodcut initial 'U' depicting a seated figure, possibly a scholar or biblical figure, in a room with a window.</image-desc>Just as the limbs help each other in the body of an animal, and one limb is concerned for another, so in the body of Christ the faithful ought to assist one another and be mutually concerned for each other. ¶ For this reason, Paul also requests the prayer of the Thessalonians toward God: that the building up of the body of Christ may grow through the free course of the Gospel; and he demonstrates his own concern for them through God, saying: ¶ *Finally, brethren, pray for us, that the word of the Lord may run and be glorified, even as it is with you; and that we may be delivered from unreasonable and evil men: for not all have faith. But the Lord is faithful, who will strengthen you and keep you from evil. And we have confidence in you in the Lord, that the things which we command you, you both do and will do. And may the Lord direct your hearts into the love of God and into the patience of Christ.* ¶ What then are the things he commands them, which he is confident they observe and will observe? One is the love of God, which contains the first commandment and connects the second to itself. For how do you love him whose image you hate? How do you love the Father if you hate the Son? The second is the patience and the expectation of Christ. For we all ought to be like men waiting for their Lord when he returns from the wedding; with loins girded, always ready to depart this world, holding in our hands the lamps of good works shining before God and men, to meet the eternal Bridegroom coming from the heavenly wedding. He will appear to us first not through heraldic symbols, but by himself, and will approve us as good and watchful servants, or accuse us as evil and lazy ones. May his mercy grant that he finds us watchful and ready at that coming of his. But there are also other things which the Apostle is confident the Thessalonians will observe, which he immediately follows up by saying: ¶ *And we charge you, brethren, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you withdraw yourselves from every brother walking disorderly, and not according to the tradition which they received from us. For you yourselves know how you ought to imitate us: because we were not disorderly among you, nor did we eat any man’s bread for free, but worked with labor and toil night and day, so that we might not be a burden to any of you; not because we did not have the right...*

> ...authority: but that we might present ourselves as an example to you, so that you might imitate us. For even when we were with you, we commanded this to you: that if any will not work, neither let him eat.

¶ Other things he commands are not in his own name, but in the name of Christ; we should understand these mandates not as his own, but as the mandates of Christ. First, indeed, that we should turn away from the company of those who live **disorderly**. <note>The Latin *inordinate* refers to living outside the established "order" or "rule" of the Christian community.</note> Now, those live disorderly who despise following the form of living prescribed for them by the apostle—or rather, by the gospel of Christ. This is especially done by those who live in idleness, doing no work. Indeed, even if men are of such great fortune that they are able to live off their own wealth and income, they still ought not to live disorderly and idle lives. Instead, they should focus on actions in the practice of virtues: whether in private, such as works of generosity and the duties of managing a household well, or in public, such as in some governance of the city and the administration of public justice and other civic virtues. For those who watch over the good management of their own affairs, or who properly apply themselves to public matters which look to the good of all, do not walk disorderly at all, nor do they live idly eating their bread for free. Rather, they live honorably, imitating Abraham and the holy fathers who were wealthy men and judges. For even if you have goods from the very "ample hand of God" which provides for all, He does not want you to use them for free and in idleness, but wants you to imitate Him. If His hand were idle in even the smallest degree, all things would fail. Therefore, those who work are the children of providence. Those who are idle, however, reveal themselves as degenerate and unworthy of providence. And it is necessary to turn away from such people.

Second: Not only should we turn away from the idle, but we ourselves should take care not to be idle, even if we are capable in those things which pertain to household matters and our own livelihood. For if you attend to public directions, whether human or—what is better—divine, although you may live off public support, it is nevertheless more perfect if, while attending to those things, you live off your own household resources. The apostle Paul, Barnabas, and those who were with them taught this by their own example; they worked in turns day and night. For who doubts that when Paul was engaged in public works, others were at home attending to and working on private matters? Paul worked more by night than by day, and they did this in shifts. Everyone, according to his strength when it was permitted, attended to public institutions and the best things of all (namely, divine things). When they were not exercising these, they attended to private matters. This was not because it was not lawful for them to live off public support, but so that they might present themselves as an example of why an idle life should be utterly fled. For this is the will of Christ, this is the mandate of Christ: that no one should live idle. Now, he is idle who attends neither to public directions—whether human or divine—nor to any private <margin>9</margin> occupations in order to live. The apostle had received word that some such people were among the Thessalonians. And therefore he adds:

> ¶ For we hear that there are some among you walking disorderly, working not at all, but living aimlessly. <note>original: "superflue degentes" — literally "living superfluously," often translated in this context as "meddling" or being "busybodies."</note> Now, to those who are such, we command and we beseech them through our Lord JESUS CHRIST: that working with silence, they may eat their own bread. But you, brothers: do not cease to do good. And if any man does not obey our word by this letter: note him, and do not keep company with him, so that he may be ashamed. Yet do not count him as an enemy, but admonish him as a brother.

¶ Even if a member of the body is sick, or numb, or sluggish and idle, it must not be abandoned immediately. Instead, it must be kindly helped by the other members, in case it might become useful again and have its own proper duty with the rest of the members, and by no means remain inactive and idle. So it must be done with the members of the body of Christ. If any member appears idle, one must try to lead it back to some work, so that it may be useful to the body of Christ and have a use along with the other members. But if at last it cannot be led back to any work, it is dead; and it is to be feared that it might be cut off from that sacred body by an invisible power. Nevertheless, with all diligence, he must be helped not as an enemy but as a friend and brother, so that he does not perish. For this is how Christ wants those who are, or who were, members of His body to be treated. Let us always have regard for the Head, and for the fact that we are members of one another's body. One baptism has made us all one body, so that we might also live by one spirit, and that there might be mutual love and friendship among all, and toward no one should there be hatred or enmity. One who regenerates us has made us all brothers to one another. Now, concord and peace most befit brothers—and especially those brothers whose father is Peace itself, the author and Lord of peace. Therefore, having set down this admonition of brotherly love, he wishes a holy prayer of divine peace for the Thessalonians as a farewell. And he added the mark of his own writing, which he was accustomed to use with his own hand, so that they might have a more certain <margin>10</margin> letter and by no means think it was falsely attributed. <note>The author explains that Paul signed his letters personally to prevent forged letters from circulating in his name.</note> Indeed, from this, if any were forged in the apostle's name, they would be able to recognize and repudiate them. He says, therefore:

> ¶ Now may the Lord of peace himself: give you peace always, in every way. The Lord be with you all. The greeting: by my hand, Paul's. Which is the sign in every letter. So I write. The grace of our Lord JESUS CHRIST be with you all. Amen.

The Second [Epistle] to the Thessalonians, written from Athens.

IX 201 2 Thessalonians.

...read those things which were written. For the originals and the <term>archetypes</term> <note>The primary manuscript written by the author or their direct scribe.</note> possessed that [mark]; however, those copies which were taken from those archetypes did not, even if they were transcribed most faithfully. This is how it usually happens with other writings: whatever is taken from any originals that retain the authors' own unique handwritten signs of authenticity. And the grace of God, which is the beginning and the end of our perfection, is prayed for by Paul at the conclusion of the letter, according to his custom. May Christ the Lord, the giver and author of all this grace, make us partakers: who was begotten before all ages in the splendor of all the saints; may he be blessed and most blessed, as he is, was, and shall be by all the saints for all ages to come. AMEN.

**EXAMINATION of several points regarding the literal text.** ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Finally, brothers, pray for us: that the word of God may run and be clarified.* <note>original: "De cætero fratres orate pro nobis: vt fermo dei currat & clarificetur."</note> ¶ It should be said: *of the Lord.* <note>original: "domini."</note> And it can be said: *be glorified.* And it means the same thing: *be honored, magnified, or illuminated.* **Paul:** *Finally, brothers, pray for us, that the word of the Lord may run and be glorified.* <note>original: "τὸ λοιπὸν προσεύχεσθε ἀδελφοὶ περὶ ἡμῶν, ἵνα ὁ λόγος τοῦ κυρίου τρέχῃ, καὶ δοξάζηται."</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *And that we may be delivered from importunate [men].* <note>original: "Et vt liberemur ab importunis."</note> ¶ This word is derived here from a "place": as if we were to say: *from those who have no place/standing, who are absurd and irrational.* **Paul:** *and that we might be delivered from the absurd [unreasonable] ones.* <note>original: "καὶ ἵνα ῥυσθῶμεν ἀπὸ τῶν ἀτόπων."</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *But we have confidence concerning you, brothers, in the Lord.* <note>original: "Confidimus autem de vobis fratres in domino."</note> ¶ It could be said: *we are persuaded concerning you.* And the word "brothers" is redundant here. **Paul:** *But we are persuaded in the Lord toward you.* <note>original: "πεποίθαμεν δὲ ἐν κυρίῳ ἐφ᾽ ὑᾶς."</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *That whatever we command, you both do and will do.* <note>original: "Quoniam quæcūq; præcipimus & facitis/ & facietis."</note> ¶ The word *to you* is missing. One should say: *whatever we command or mandate to you.* And this last part is more gentle and kind. **Paul:** *that what we command you, you both do and will do.* <note>original: "ὅτι ἃ παραγγέλλομεν ὑμῖν, καὶ ποιεῖτε, καὶ ποιήσετε."</note>

Why translate the same word so differently and so close together? He could have said: *we mandate* or *we denounce* in the first place. **Paul:** *Now we command you, brothers.* <note>original: "παραγγέλλομεν δὲ ὑμῖν ἀδελφοί."</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Because we were not restless among you.* <note>original: "Quoniā nō inquieti fuimus inter vos."</note> ¶ It should rather be said: *we did not behave in a disorderly way among you.* **Paul:** *for we did not behave in a disorderly manner among you.* <note>original: "ὅτι οὐκ ἠκτήσαμεν ἐν ὑμῖν."</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Neither did we eat bread for free from anyone.* <note>original: "Neq; gratis panē manducauimus ab aliquo."</note> ¶ If it were "we ate" or "we consumed bread," it would be better to say *at someone's house.* Nor should it bother you that the Greek word <note>original: "παρὰ"</note> takes the genitive and not the dative case, for those are sometimes confused. But in some copies it has: *neither did we receive bread for free from anyone,* in this way: *neither did we take bread for free from anyone.* <note>original: "οὐδὲ δωρεὰν ἄρτον ἐλάβομεν παρά τινος."</note>

In others, however, it is *we ate.* <note>original: "ἐφάγομεν."</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** ¶ *Not as if we did not have authority.* <note>original: "Nō quasi nō habuerim⁹ potestate."</note> ¶ It should be said: *not that we do not have* or *had not had authority.* However, the verb in Paul is in the present indicative. **Paul:** *not that we do not have authority.* <note>original: "οὐχ ὅτι οὐκ ἔχομεν ἐξουσίαν."</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *For we have heard that some among you are walking restlessly.* <note>original: "Audiuimus enim inter vos quosdã ambulantes inquiete."</note> ¶ It should be said: *we hear* in the present tense. And *inordinately* [disorderly], as was noted in the previous chapter. **Paul:** *For we hear that some are walking among you in a disorderly way.* <note>original: "ἀκούομεν γάρ τινας περιπατοῦντας ἐν ὑμῖν ἀτάκτως."</note> ¶ And that *disorderly* means: idly and doing no work; which the apostle indicated through the particle he subjoined. ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *To those who are of such a kind: we denounce and beseech in the Lord JESUS CHRIST.* <note>original: "Ijs autē qui eiusmodi sunt: denūciamus & obsecramus in dño IHESV CHRISTO."</note> ¶ In the second part, we have added "them" [as an object]: because *we denounce* or *mandate* on one hand, and *we beseech* on the other, do not require the same case among Latin speakers. <note>The author is noting that in Latin, "denounce/command" takes a dative case, while "beseech/exhort" takes an accusative case. To make the sentence grammatically correct in Latin, the pronoun must be repeated or adjusted.</note> Therefore, repeating the relative pronoun (even if it is not repeated in Paul’s Greek) is more suitable for Latin speech. And it should rather be said: *through the Lord.* **Paul:** *Now such persons we command and exhort through our Lord Jesus Christ.* <note>original: "τοῖς δὲ τοιούτοις παραγγέλλομεν, καὶ παρακαλοῦμεν Διὰ τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ."</note>
