# COMMENTARY

> ...power: but that we might offer ourselves as an example to you, so that you might imitate us. For even when we were among you, we commanded this to you: that if anyone does not want to work, neither let him eat.

¶ Other things they command are not in their own name, but in the name of Christ; so that we may understand these commands to be not his own, but the commands of Christ. First indeed, that we should avoid the company of those who live in a disorderly fashion. Now, those live in a disorderly way who despise following the form of living prescribed for them by the apostle—indeed, by the Gospel of Christ. This is especially done by those who live idly, doing nothing. But even if men are of such fortune that they can live from their own wealth and rents <note>original: "censu & redditibus" — referring to income from property, investments, or taxes</note>, they still ought not to live in a disorderly and idle manner. Instead, they should focus either on actions in the exercise of virtues—whether in private, such as works of liberality and the duties of managing a household well—or in public, as in some civic governance and the administration of public justice and other civil virtues. For those who watch over the good management of their own affairs, or who properly apply themselves to public matters which look toward the good of all, do not walk in a disorderly way at all, nor do they live idly by eating their bread for free, but honorably. Imitate Abraham and the holy fathers who were wealthy men and judges. For even if you have goods from that generous hand of God which provides for all, He does not want you to use them for free and in idleness; rather, He wants you to imitate Him. If His providence were idle in the slightest degree, everything would fail. Therefore, those who work are children of providence. Those who are idle, however, prove themselves to be degenerate and unworthy of providence. And such people must be avoided.

Second: Not only should we avoid the idle, but we ourselves should take care not to be idle, even if we are able to provide for our household and our own food. For if you focus on public directions—whether human or, what is better, divine—though you might be allowed to live off public funds, it is more perfect if, while focusing on those things, you live from your own family estate. The apostle Paul, Barnabas, and those who were with them taught this by their own example, working in turns day and night. For who doubts that while Paul was engaged in public work, others were focusing on and working at private matters at home, and that Paul worked more by night than by day? And they did this themselves by turns: everyone, according to his strength, focusing on public institutions and the best things of all (namely, divine things) when it was possible. When they were not exercising those, they focused on private matters. This was not because it was not lawful for them to live off public support, but so that they might provide themselves as an example of utterly fleeing an idle life. For this is the will of Christ, this is the command of Christ: that no one live idly. Now, he is idle who focuses neither on public directions—whether human or divine—nor on any private occupations in order to live.

And if anyone does not obey our word through this letter, note this person, and do not associate with him, so that he may be ashamed. And do not consider him as an enemy, but admonish him as a brother. ¶ A member of the body, even if it is sick, or if it is numb, sluggish, and idle, must not be immediately abandoned. It transitions from discussing the physical evidence of Paul’s authorship (his signature) to a scholarly linguistic examination of the Latin text compared to the original Greek.</meta>

...read what was written. For the originals and the <term>archetypes</term> <note>original: "archetypę" — refers to the original manuscripts written or dictated by the author himself</note> possessed that [signature], but those copied from the archetypes did not, even if they were copied most faithfully. For this is how it usually happens with other writings: copies taken from any originals retain the author's unique handwritten marks. Paul, according to his custom, prays for the grace of God—which is the beginning and the end of our perfection—at the conclusion of the letter. May Christ the Lord, the author and giver of all grace, make us partakers of it; He who was begotten before all ages in the splendor of all the saints, may He be blessed and most highly blessed, as He is, was, and shall be by all the saints for all ages of ages. AMEN.

<margin>A 7</margin> **EXAMINATION of certain points regarding the text.**

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *For the rest, brothers, pray for us: that the word of God may run and be clarified.*
¶ It should be said: *of the Lord*. And it can be said *be glorified*. It is the same thing: to be honored, magnified, or illustrated. Paul: *Finally, pray, brothers, for us, that the word of the Lord may run and be glorified* <note>original Greek: τὸ λοιπὸν προσεύχεσθε ἀδελφοὶ περὶ ἡμῶν, ἵνα ὁ λόγος τοῦ κυρίου τρέχῃ, καὶ δοξάζηται</note>.

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *And that we may be delivered from importunate men.*
¶ This word is derived here from "place," as if we were to say: *from those who have no place, who are absurd, and irrational.* Paul: *and that we might be delivered from the absurd* <note>original Greek: καὶ ἵνα ρυσθῶμεν ἀπὸ τῶν ἀτόπων — the word "atopos" literally means "out of place" or "unusual," hence "absurd"</note>.

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *But we trust in you, brothers, in the Lord.*
¶ It can be said: *we are persuaded concerning you.* And the word *brothers* is extra. Paul: *But we have confidence in the Lord regarding you* <note>original Greek: πεποίθαμεν δὲ ἐν κυρίῳ ἐφ' ὑμᾶς</note>.

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Because whatever we command, you both do and will do.*
¶ The word *you* is missing. It should say *whatever we command or mandate to you.* The latter is milder and more kindly. Paul: *that what we command you, you both do and will do* <note>original Greek: ὅτι ἃ παραγγέλλομεν ὑμῖν, καὶ ποιεῖτε, καὶ ποιήσετε</note>.

¶ **The Vulgate edition:**
<margin>B 8</margin> *But we denounce to you, brothers.*
¶ Here is the same word which the old translator rendered as *we command* just a little before. Why translate the same word so differently and in such close proximity? He could have said *we mandate* or *we denounce* in the first place. Paul: *But we command you, brothers* <note>original Greek: παραγγέλλομεν δὲ ὑμῖν ἀδελφοί</note>.

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Since we were not restless among you.*
¶ Rather it should be said: *we did not conduct ourselves in a disorderly manner among you.* Paul: *that we were not disorderly among you* <note>original Greek: ὅτι οὐκ ἠτακτήσαμεν ἐν ὑμῖν — the OCR "ἠκτάσαμεν" is a misspelling of the Greek verb for being out of order</note>.

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Neither did we eat bread for free from anyone.*
¶ If it were *we ate* or *consumed bread*, it should rather be said *at someone's house*. Nor should it bother anyone that the Greek preposition *para* takes the genitive case and not the dative, for these are sometimes confused. Indeed, in some copies it has, *neither did we receive bread for free from anyone*, in this way: *nor did we receive bread for free from anyone* <note>original Greek: οὐδὲ δωρεὰν ἄρτον ἐλάβομεν παρά τινος</note>. In others, however, it is *we ate* <note>original Greek: ἐφάγομεν</note>.

¶ **The Vulgate edition:**
<margin>C 8, C 9</margin> *Not as if we did not have power.*
¶ It should be said: *not because we did not have*, or *might not have had power.* However, in Paul the verb is in the present indicative. Paul: *not that we do not have authority* <note>original Greek: οὐχ ὅτι οὐκ ἔχομεν ἐξουσίαν</note>.

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *For we have heard that there are some among you walking restlessly.*
¶ It should be said *we hear* in the present tense. And *disorderly*, as was noted in the previous chapter. Paul: *for we hear that some walk among you in a disorderly way* <note>original Greek: ἀκούομεν γάρ τινας περιπατοῦντας ἐν ὑμῖν ἀτάκτως</note>. And that *disorderly* means idly and doing nothing, which the Apostle indicated by the small phrase he added.

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *But to those who are of this sort, we denounce and beseech in the Lord JESUS CHRIST.*
¶ In the second part, we have repeated the reference to "them," because *denounce* (or *mandate*) and *beseech* do not require the same grammatical case among Latin speakers. One requires the accusative, the other the dative. Therefore, repeating the relative pronoun (even if it is not repeated in Paul’s Greek) is more suitable for Latin speech. And it should rather be said *through the Lord*. Paul: *But to such ones we command and beseech through our Lord Christ* <note>original Greek: τοῖς δὲ τοιούτοις παραγγέλλομεν, καὶ παρακαλοῦμεν Διὰ τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Χριστοῦ</note>.

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *But correct him as a brother.*
¶ It can be said: *but admonish him.* Paul: *but admonish him as a brother* <note>original Greek: ἀλλὰ νουθετεῖτε ὡς ἀδελφόν</note>.

¶ **The Vulgate edition:**
<margin>D 9, D 10</margin> *May he give you everlasting peace in every place.*
¶ In Greek it is held: *May he give you peace always, in every way.* Paul: *May he give you peace always in every way* <note>original Greek: Δῴη ὑμῖν τὴν εἰρήνην Διὰ παντὸς ἐν παντὶ τρόπῳ</note>. And among the Greeks, there is a subscript: *The Second to the Thessalonians, written at Athens.*

<header>COMMENTARY</header>
<page-num>7</page-num>

...I give to you, son Timothy: that according to the preceding prophecies concerning you, you might wage a good warfare in them; having faith and a good conscience, which some, having rejected, have made shipwreck regarding the faith. Among whom are Hymenaeus and Alexander: whom I have handed over to Satan so that they may learn not to blaspheme. ¶ Timothy received from the Lord both the charge that Paul commends to him and the gift of prophecy. The gift of prophecy is twofold. One kind is for predicting future events for the salvation and building up of others. But the other kind is for understanding the writings of the prophets. Therefore, the prophecies which Timothy possessed, and which were more necessary for building up the church, were the understanding of the past prophets concerning Christ and concerning the holy faith in Him for the salvation of all nations. For these prophecies belonged to the faith. What else do we think happened to the apostles when the Lord opened their minds so that they might understand the scriptures, except that He breathed into them the spirit of prophecy, through which they all might understand the prophets? Regarding Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom he handed over to Satan: **Chrysostom** <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), an influential Early Church Father known for his preaching and biblical commentary.</note> understands this as excommunication and cutting them off from the body of Christ, so that there would be no communion of the faithful with them, and no sharing in spiritual support. And this kind is a hidden handing over to Satan, occurring without the destruction and torment of the flesh. However, that case involving the incestuous Corinthian <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 5:5.</note> was manifest, involving a terrifying destruction and torment of the flesh. And this was done not so that they might perish, but so that from this cast-out state from the society of the saints, they might learn not to blaspheme—that is, not to speak evil of Christ and His faith—and that by coming to their senses and performing worthy penance, they might again be grafted into the body of Christ. For whoever is separated from it is like a sheep separated from the flock, and with the wolf present, he is immediately under the wolf’s power; so too is such a person immediately under the power of Satan (who is the devil and the ancient serpent). From whose ways only Christ rescues us; may He always protect, defend, and rescue us, the King of ages, blessed for all ages. Amen.

<margin>A 1</margin>
¶ **EXAMINATION of certain points regarding the text.** ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *To Timothy, my beloved son in faith: grace, mercy, and peace.* <note>1 Timothy 1:2</note> ¶ The word which the old translator here renders as "beloved," he renders as "genuine" in Philippians chapter 4, where he says: *I also ask you, genuine companion.* It properly designates someone who is legitimate, one's own, and special, as **Jerome** <note>St. Jerome, the primary translator of the Latin Vulgate Bible.</note> also confirms. And these words—grace, mercy, peace—are read in Paul without a conjunction. Paul: *To Timothy, my genuine son in faith: grace, mercy, peace* <note>original Greek: τιμοθέω γνησίω τέκνω ἐν πίσει , χάρις , ἔλεος , εἰρήνη</note>. ¶ **The Vulgate edition:**

<margin>A 2</margin>
¶ *As I asked you to remain at Ephesus.* <note>1 Timothy 1:3</note> ¶ It should be read as "So" rather than "As." For he is not making a likeness or a comparison, but rather he intends: "So, in this manner, or on this condition I asked you to remain at Ephesus, that you might charge certain people not to introduce various doctrines," and the rest which the apostle expressed. Paul: *Just as I exhorted you to remain in Ephesus* <note>original Greek: κατὼς παρεκάλεσάσε προσμεῖναι ἐν ἐφέσω</note>. ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Lest they teach otherwise.* ¶ Rather: *variously*. Paul: *not to teach different things* <note>original Greek: μὴ ἑτεροδιδασκαλεῖν</note>. ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Which provide questions rather than the edification of God, which is in faith.* <note>1 Timothy 1:4</note> ¶ One should rather say: *than the dispensation* or *governance*. Paul: *which provide questions rather than the stewardship of God which is in faith* <note>original Greek: αἵτινες ζητήσεις παρέχουσι μᾶλλον , ἢ οἰκονομίαν θεοῦ τὴν ἐν πίσει</note>. For what is this <term>stewardship</term> <note>original: "œconomia" — the management or administration of a household; here, the "house of God" or the Church.</note> if not the distribution, rule, and governance of the house of God, in the nourishment of the right faith?

<margin>B 4</margin>
¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *If anyone uses it lawfully, knowing this, that the law is not set for the just.* <note>1 Timothy 1:8-9</note> ¶ It should be said in the singular, *knowing*, and it refers back to *anyone*, not to us. Therefore, lest any confusion occur, we have resolved it through the relative "who" and the verb appropriately for the speech: *knowing [the one] who does it*. Paul: *if anyone uses it lawfully, knowing this, that the law is not laid down for a righteous person* <note>original Greek: ἐὰν τις αὐτῶ νομίμως χρῆται , εἰδὼς τοῦτο , ὅτι Δικαίω νόμος οὐ κεῖται</note>. And what wonder is it if the law is not set for the just? Since the Savior says: *Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick.* ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *For the wicked and contaminated, for patricides and matricides, for murderers, for fornicators, for those who lie with males, for kidnappers, for liars, and for perjurers.* <note>1 Timothy 1:9-10</note> ¶ One should rather say: *for those who strike their father and mother*. For regarding the striking of father and mother, the law is clearly expressed in **Exodus**: *He who strikes his father or mother* (it says) *shall surely be put to death.* <note>Exodus 21:15</note> Concerning "patricide" and "matricide" <note>The actual killing of a parent.</note>, the law is not explicitly stated, as if such a thing were so enormous and so abhorrent to nature that it ought never to happen. And regarding every kind of shameful person whom Paul names, you will find explicit laws there if you wish to search diligently. And <term>plagiarii</term> <note>original: "plagiarij" — from the Latin "plagium," meaning kidnapping or man-stealing, not the modern sense of stealing words.</note> are thieves and snatchers of men, so called because they bind their feet and cast them into chains while they sell them into slavery, or perhaps so they might ransom themselves. Many such thieves of men happen to exist in times of war. This Greek term expresses the meaning more than our Latin one does. And it is said without a conjunction: *liars, perjurers*. Paul: *for the unholy and profane, for strikers of fathers and strikers of mothers, for manslayers, for fornicators, for sodomites, for kidnappers, for liars, for perjurers* <note>original Greek: ἀνοσίοις , καὶ ἀβεβήλοις , πατραλοίαις , καὶ μητραλοίαις , ἀνδροφόροις, πόρνοις , ἀρσενοκοίταις , ἀνδραποδισαῖς , ψεύσαις , ἐπιόρκοις</note>. ¶ **The Vulgate**

<margin>B 5</margin>
**edition:** *Which was committed to me.* ¶ The phrasing is inverted, for it is read: *with which I have been entrusted.* But it comes to the same thing. Paul: *which I was entrusted with* <note>original Greek: ὃ ἐπιστεύθην ἐγώ</note>. ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *I give thanks to him who strengthened me in CHRIST JESUS our Lord.* ¶ It should be said: *And I give thanks*. Although in Greek it is held as: *And I have grace*. For Latin custom has this when we speak of God. And that "strengthened" designates that He provided strength or made one grow strong. And as for what he says "in Christ Jesus our Lord," it should be said without a preposition and in the same case...

<meta>This page continues the philological and theological commentary on the First Epistle to Timothy, specifically concluding the analysis of Chapter 1 and beginning the instructions for the church in Chapter 2. It compares the Latin Vulgate text with the original Greek and offers an interpretation influenced by Early Church Fathers like Cyprian.</meta>

<header>1 Timothy</header>

## X

<margin>6</margin>...to be with him; for it is He to whom Paul gives thanks, and who made him grow strong, and who supplied him with strength and fortitude. Paul says: <note>original Greek: "καὶ χάριν ἔχω τῷ ἐνδυναμώσαντί με χριστῷ ἰησοῦ κυρίῳ ἡμῶν"</note> "And I give thanks to Christ Jesus our Lord, who has strengthened me."

<margin>C</margin> **The Vulgate edition** reads: "But I have obtained the mercy of God." The word "God" <note>original: "Dei"</note> is superfluous here, even if it does not hinder the understanding of the passage. Paul writes: "He came into the world."

<margin>D</margin> **The Vulgate edition** reads: "That Christ Jesus might show." The order of the words has been changed, for it should say "Jesus Christ." Paul says: <note>original Greek: "ἐνδείξηται ἰησοῦς χριστός"</note> "Jesus Christ might show."

<margin>7</margin> **The Vulgate edition** reads: "Now to the King of ages, immortal, invisible, the only God." It ought to say: "to the only **wise** God," for the word "wise" is missing. Paul says: <note>original Greek: "τῷ δὲ βασιλεῖ τῶν αἰώνων, ἀφθάρτῳ, ἀοράτῳ, μόνῳ σοφῷ θεῷ"</note> "Now to the King of ages, incorruptible, invisible, the only wise God."

Just as He is "only wise" because He alone possesses nothing mixed with ignorance, so He is the "only King of ages" because He alone is Lord of all. He is "only immortal" because He alone absolutely cannot perish, whereas all other things can. He is "only invisible" because all other things can be comprehended—for to be "comprehended" is, in a certain way, to be "seen"—but He alone cannot be comprehended. And as the holy **Cyprian** <note>Cyprian of Carthage (c. 210–258 AD), an Early Christian bishop and writer.</note> says: "He cannot be seen: He is brighter than sight. He cannot be comprehended: He is purer than touch. He cannot be estimated: He is greater than sense. And therefore we only estimate Him worthily when we consider Him inestimable." Therefore, when Jacob or Moses are said to have "seen God," it does not mean they apprehended God, but rather that they touched some "footprint" <note>original: "vestigium"</note> or certain sign of God, and not that incomprehensible nature and substance itself which, being incomprehensible, apprehends all things.

## CHAPTER II

<margin>8</margin><image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'N' featuring a figure seated in a landscape with a tree in the foreground and a distant city skyline.</image-desc>Now the Apostle instructs Timothy on how the churches are to be established for public piety, saying: ¶ "I desire, therefore, first of all, that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made for all men: for kings, and for all who are in high positions; that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and honesty. For this is good and acceptable in the sight of God our Savior, who desires all men to be saved, and to come to the knowledge of the truth."

¶ He desires public piety to take precedence over all things, and that this is pleasing and acceptable to God, who wants all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. ¶ If they were to come to this, all men could lead their lives in great peace and tranquility. If they were to come to it, I say, by the very effect of the knowledge of the truth. For there are those who confess it in word but deny the truth in deed; these have not yet sufficiently reached perfect knowledge so as to lead a quiet and peaceable life, nor do they live in all godliness and honesty. There are others who know the truth neither by word nor deed—I mean the truth which is necessary for salvation. And this is not God’s will, but rather the turning away of their own will from the light of truth. 

For those who do not know the one God, and do not confess that the one Christ our Lord underwent death for the salvation of all, and that He is the **mediator** <term>mediator: a go-between; here referring to Christ as the bridge between God and humanity</term> between God and men—the one through whom all men who are to be saved must be saved—these have not yet come to the knowledge of the truth, even if they had explored all the science of the philosophers, the magi, and the **gymnosophists** <note>original: "gymnosophistarū"; a term used by the Greeks for Indian "naked philosophers" or sages who practiced asceticism.</note>. For to know all these things, if you compare it to that knowledge, is to know nothing. One who knows all those other things falls into the immense darkness of ignorance and is at last rendered perpetually ignorant. But one who knows this truth is lifted up to the immense light of wisdom and is made to know all things—knowing them indeed with the treasures of life and wisdom, of whose riches there is no end. For the others, there will be an unending heap of ignorance in the poverty of death.

<margin>9</margin> Therefore Paul explains this rich wisdom, which is greater than all the wisdom of the world, in these few words, saying: ¶ "For there is one God... and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus: who gave himself as a ransom for all. To which testimony I am appointed a herald and an apostle (I speak the truth in Christ, I do not lie), a teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth." 

¶ For the testimony of that most wealthy wisdom which provides life and salvation to souls in the mansions of eternal light, at the fullness of time defined by God, Paul was appointed a preacher and an ambassador—not by himself (for no apostle, no ambassador, is such by himself) but by Him whose ambassador he is. Thus he was appointed by God and Christ, by whom he was also made a teacher of the Gentiles—not for any worldly discipline which does nothing for salvation, but for the heavenly doctrine, the doctrine of the Spirit which alone saves, and which the angels magnify and would teach if they were to teach anything. "A teacher," he says, "of the Gentiles in faith and truth." What does this mean, "in faith and truth," except in the true faith, in the faith of the truth, in the faith of the Son of God, who is the way, the truth, and the life? He does not, therefore, exalt himself or boast when he says "I speak the truth, I do not lie: I am appointed a teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth," but he renders testimony to the truth, giving glory to Him who made him His herald, apostle, and teacher of the Gentiles. Since, therefore, he has been appointed by God as a teacher of the Gentiles, and it is the office of a teacher to teach, <margin>10</margin> let us now hear what he teaches both men and women. Thus he first teaches the men in this manner, saying: ¶ "I will therefore that men pray in every place, lifting up holy hands, without wrath and contention." 

¶ What is "in every place," except in every church wherever in the world Christ is known? "Without wrath and contention." For the Lord also commands: "If you offer your gift at the altar, and there..."

Therefore, so that no confusion should arise, we have resolved it through the relative pronoun "who" and the verb appropriately for the speech: "knowing what he is doing." Paul wrote: <term>ean tis auto nomimos chretai, eidos touto, hoti dikaio nomos ou keitai</term> <note>original Greek: "ἐάν τις αὐτῷ νομίμως χρῆται, εἰδὼς τοῦτο, ὅτι Δικαίω νόμος οὐ κεῖται"; translated: "if anyone uses it lawfully, knowing this: that for a righteous person the law is not laid down."</note>. And what wonder is it if the law is not set for the just, since the Savior says: "It is not those who are healthy who need a physician, but those who are sick"? ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "For the wicked and contaminated, for murderers of fathers and murderers of mothers, for manslayers, for fornicators, for those who lie with males, for kidnappers, for liars, and for perjurers." ¶ **It should rather be said:** "for strikers of father and mother." For regarding the striking of a father and mother, the law is clearly expressed in Exodus: "He who strikes his father or mother shall surely be put to death." Regarding "parricide" and "matricide" <note>the actual killing of a parent</note>, a law was not explicitly expressed, as if the act were so enormous and so abhorrent to nature that it ought never to happen. And regarding every kind of shameful person whom Paul names, you will find explicit laws there if you wish to search diligently. And "kidnappers" <note>original: "plagiarij"</note> are thieves and stealers of men; so called because they bind their feet and cast them into chains while they sell them into slavery, or perhaps so they may ransom themselves. Many such thieves of men are found in times of war. This Greek term expresses the meaning more clearly than our Latin one. And it is said without a conjunction: "liars, perjurers." Paul wrote: <term>anosiois, kai abebelois, patraloiais, kai metraloiais, androphonois, pornois, arsenokoitais, andrapodistais, pseustais, epiorkois</term> <note>original Greek: "ἀνοσίοις, καὶ ἀβεβήλοις, πατραλοίαις, καὶ μητραλοίαις, ἀνδροφόνοις, πόρνοις, ἀρσενοκοίταις, ἀνδραποδισταῖς, ψεύσταις, ἐπιόρκοις"; a list of lawless behaviors including unholy, profane, parent-strikers, murderers, etc.</note>. ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "Which was committed to me." ¶ **The phrase is reversed:** for it reads: "to whom I was entrusted." But

<margin>
B
5
</margin>
it amounts to the same thing. Paul wrote: <term>ho episteuthen ego</term> <note>original Greek: "ὃ ἐπιστεύθην ἐγώ"; "which was entrusted [to] me."</note>. ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "I give thanks to Him who strengthened me in Christ Jesus our Lord." ¶ **It should be said:** "And I give thanks," although in Greek it is "and I have grace." For Latin custom has it this way when we speak of God. And that word "strengthened" designates that He provided strength or made one grow strong. And what he says, "in Christ Jesus our Lord," should be said without the preposition and in the same case...

### X

...to be with him; for it is He to whom Paul gives thanks, and who made him grow strong, and who supplied him with strength and fortitude. Paul writes: *And I thank Christ Jesus our Lord, who has strengthened me.* <note>original Greek: "καὶ χάριν ἔχω τῷ ἐνδυναμώσαντί με χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ κυρίῳ ἡμῶν"</note> <margin>C</margin> ¶ The Vulgate edition says: *But I have obtained the mercy of God.* ¶ <gloss>'Of God': this is redundant,</gloss> <margin>D</margin> although it does not hinder understanding. Paul writes: *but I was shown mercy.* <note>original Greek: "ἀλλὰ ἠλεήθην"</note> ¶ The Vulgate edition says: *He came into <margin>5</margin> this world.* ¶ <gloss>It is enough to say: 'into the world.'</gloss> Paul writes: *He came into the world.* <note>original Greek: "ἦλθεν εἰς τὸν κόσμον"</note> ¶ The Vulgate <margin>6</margin> edition says: *Christ Jesus might show.* ¶ <gloss>The word order is changed; for he says</gloss> *Jesus Christ.* Paul writes: *Jesus Christ might show.* <note>original Greek: "ἐνδείξηται Ἰησοῦς χριστός"</note> ¶ The Vulgate edition says: *Now to the King of the ages, immortal, invisible, the only God.* ¶ <gloss>One should say: 'to the only wise God.' For the word 'wise' is missing.</gloss> Paul writes: *Now to the King of the ages, incorruptible, invisible, the only wise God.* <note>original Greek: "τῷ δὲ βασιλεῖ τῶν αἰώνων, ἀφθάρτῳ, ἀοράτῳ, μόνῳ σοφῷ θεῷ"</note> Just as He is "only wise" because He alone possesses nothing mixed with ignorance, so He is "only King of the ages" because He alone rules over all. He is "only immortal" because He alone absolutely cannot perish, while all other things can. He is "only invisible" because all other things can be perceived (for to be perceived is, in a certain way, to be seen), but He alone cannot be perceived. And as <term>Cyprian</term> <note>St. Cyprian of Carthage (c. 210–258 AD), an early Christian writer and bishop.</note> says: "He cannot be seen: He is brighter than sight. He cannot be grasped: He is purer than touch. He cannot be estimated: He is greater than the senses. And therefore we estimate Him worthily only when we consider Him inestimable." Therefore, when Jacob or Moses are said to have seen God, it does not mean they perceived God's nature, but that they touched upon some "footprint" or certain sign of God—not that incomprehensible nature and substance of God which, being itself incomprehensible, perceives all things.

### CHAPTER II

<image-desc>A large historiated woodcut initial 'N' set within a square frame, depicting a robed figure seated at a desk or lectern, likely representing a scholar or apostle.</image-desc>

<margin>8</margin> **N**ow the apostle informs Timothy how the churches are to be established for public piety, saying:
> I exhort therefore, first of all, that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and giving of thanks be made for all men; for kings, and for all who are in authority; that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and honesty. For this is good and acceptable in the sight of God our Savior, who will have all men to be saved, and to come unto the knowledge of the truth.

¶ Above all things, he wishes public piety to take precedence, and that this is pleasing and acceptable to God, who wants all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. ¶ If they were to "come," all men would be able to live their lives in great peace and tranquility—if they were to come, I say, in actual effect to the knowledge of the truth. For there are those who confess with words but deny the truth by their deeds; these have not yet come to a perfect and sufficient knowledge for leading a quiet and peaceful life, nor do they live in all piety and honesty. There are others who know the truth neither in word nor in deed—I mean the truth that is necessary for salvation. And this is not God's will, but rather the turning away of their own will from the light of truth. For those who do not recognize the one God, and do not confess that the one Lord Christ died for the salvation of all, and that He is the mediator between God and men—acting as the means through which all who are to be saved must be saved—these have not yet come to the knowledge of the truth, even if they had explored all the science and philosophy of the <term>magi</term> or the <term>gymnosophists</term> <note>Ancient Indian philosophers who practiced asceticism and went naked; used here as a symbol of worldly, non-Christian wisdom.</note>. For to know all these things, if you compare them to that one Truth, is to know nothing. One who knows all these worldly things falls into the immense shadows of ignorance and is ultimately made forever ignorant. But one who knows that Truth is lifted up into the immense light of wisdom and is made to know all things—knowing them with the treasures of life and wisdom, of whose riches there is no end. For the others, there will be an unending heap of ignorance and every kind of poverty in death.

<margin>9</margin> Therefore, Paul explains this wealth of wisdom, which is greater than all the wisdom of the world, in these few words, saying:
> For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus; who gave himself a ransom for all, to be testified in due time. Whereunto I am ordained a preacher, and an apostle (I speak the truth in Christ and lie not); a teacher of the Gentiles in faith and verity.

¶ As a testimony to that most rich wisdom which offers life and salvation to souls in the mansions of eternal light, in the fullness of time defined by God, Paul was appointed as a preacher and legate—not by himself (for no apostle or legate comes from himself) but by Him whose legate he is. Thus, he was appointed by God and Christ, by whom he was also made a teacher of the Gentiles—not for that worldly discipline which does nothing for salvation, but for the heavenly doctrine, the doctrine of the Spirit which alone saves and which the angels magnify. He says he is a "teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth." What does "in faith and truth" mean, if not in the true faith, in the faith of the truth, and in the faith of the Son of God, who is the way, the truth, and the life? He does not, therefore, exalt himself or boast when he says "I speak the truth, I lie not; I am appointed a teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth," but he renders testimony to the truth, giving glory to Him who made him His herald, apostle, and teacher of the Gentiles.

<margin>10</margin> Since, therefore, he has been appointed by God as a teacher of the nations, and it is the office of a teacher to teach, let us hear what he now teaches both men and women. He first teaches the men in this manner, saying:
> I will therefore that men pray every where, lifting up holy hands, without wrath and doubting.

¶ What does "in every place" mean, if not in every church wherever Christ is known on earth? "Without wrath and doubting." For the Lord also commands: if you offer your gift at the altar, and there...

<header>COMMENTARY</header>

...if you remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift before the altar and go first to be reconciled to your brother; then, coming back, offer your gift. <note>A reference to the Gospel of Matthew 5:23–24.</note> For how do you dare present yourself to the Lord of Peace when you do not have the sign of peace in your mind, but rather the opposite sign, which is discord? Therefore, let no one dare to pray—especially in public prayer—with an angry or agitated mind, nor one who has a disagreement with another. However, nothing prohibits one from praying in private so that God may help, so that the disagreement may be settled and cease, and that He may restore His peace. For such a person acts like a sick man toward a doctor, revealing his weakness and imploring help. And this is not "public prayer," which is called intercession (which must be offered to God without anger or contention), but rather private prayer and—if you prefer to put it this way—a certain confession and self-accusation. He also teaches women, saying: ¶ Likewise, let women adorn themselves in clean clothing, with shamefastness and modesty, not with braided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly dress, but as becomes women professing divine piety through good works. Let a woman learn in silence with all subjection. But I do not permit a woman to teach, nor to have authority over a man, but to be in silence. For Adam was formed first, then Eve. And Adam was not seduced, but the woman was seduced and was in the transgression. Yet she shall be saved through the bearing of children, if they remain in faith, and love, and sanctity with modesty. ¶ This is the teaching of the holy apostle regarding women. Let the clothing of women be clean, not expensive. Let the ornament of women be shamefastness and modesty, or chastity. For such an adornment becomes spiritual women, joined with good works, through which they may be seen to profess divine piety. In all women, because of the disobedience of the first woman, there ought to be an innate shamefastness to draw them back from committing forbidden evils, toward which they are prone by nature in imitation of their first parent. And from the Virgin—the repairer of the fault of our parent Eve—the love and desire for virginity ought to be in all women. If they cannot have this along with fruitfulness, they should nevertheless strive to have a "fruitful chastity," which is the closest rival to virginity. Therefore, from their first birth they should have shame, and from their second, virginity or at least chastity. Following this is <term>theosebia</term> <note>original: "theosebia"; meaning divine piety or the pure and sincere worship of God</note>, while the former leads to caution and the flight from evil. A woman should not think her ornament lies in braided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly clothing—the sort of luxury that occupies many in our time, both elsewhere and in the cities of Insubria <note>The region of Lombardy in Northern Italy.</note>, if one happens to travel there. These women can clearly be judged as "daughters of Belial" <note>An Old Testament term for worthless or wicked people; here used to contrast with "daughters of Christ."</note> rather than daughters of Christ, unless one’s eyes are deceived and fascinated. If a woman is compared to a man, who is the head, she is like the appetite, while he is like reason. But it is not permitted for the appetite to teach, but for reason. So it is not permitted for the woman, but for the man, especially in public. Appetite is formed and learns from reason; so too the woman ought to learn from the man. I speak of the woman who is a wife. And all women in the public place of prayer can hear in silence from the man who holds the office of informing everyone. Let young girls not come forward rashly to the mouth of the public teacher to ask questions; let them ask their fathers or mothers, or the wiser matrons, who were better able to understand the public voice than they. Let a woman never dare to take authority over a man—that is, to dominate her own husband. For this resists the divine ordinance and the will of Him who placed her under the power of the man and made the man the master. "You shall be under the power of the man," He says, "and he shall rule over you." <note>Genesis 3:16.</note> O, how many foolish women has the insolence of their lineage or the wealth of their dowry produced! They claim the authority of men for themselves, ignorant of themselves, their sex, and the will of God. They are proud, foolish, and insane, however high they may think of themselves; they are rebels not against men, but against God. For whoever resists the divine ordinance resists God and is a rebel against God, like the Angel of Darkness who for this reason fell from heaven into the abyss. And that a woman ought to defer to a man is evident from creation itself. For man was created first, claiming the honor of the firstborn for himself; but the woman in the second place. And the woman was seduced, not the man. For she was persuaded by the serpent, not the man. While her husband was absent, she plucked the forbidden fruit, ate it, and offered it to her husband to eat while he was ignorant of the matter. He ate what was offered; whence the wretched contagion of death crept into our race. Nevertheless, although she was held more liable for the fault than the man, God nonetheless willed that salvation be common to both the man and the woman. To the woman indeed through the procreation of children (for she is necessary to the man for that purpose), and especially while the man and woman remain in faith, love, and sanctity with modesty and chastity. For they have a chaste bed as long as neither he nor she divides their flesh through fornication. Otherwise, if faith is not present, nor love, nor holiness, nor purity of life and chastity of the bed, the procreation of children will not save the woman. For faith, love, sanctity, and chastity are more precious pledges for salvation than carnal offspring. May our Lord, the Savior of all, grant this; He who was, and is, and shall be blessed without end, forever and ever. AMEN.

...and they are accustomed to interpret "honesty" <note>Latin: *honestatem*</note> according to the context. Paul writes: "in all godliness and dignity." <note>original Greek: ἐν πᾶσι εὐσεβεία, καὶ σεμνότητι</note>
<margin>8</margin>
¶ The Vulgate edition says: "Whose testimony was confirmed in its own times: in which I am appointed." ¶ It should rather be said: "for which testimony." And the phrase "was confirmed" is redundant. Paul writes: "the testimony in its own times, for which I was appointed." <note>original Greek: τὸ μαρτύριον καίροις ἰδίοις εἰς ὃ ἐτέθην ἐγώ</note> For I have traced that word "for which" back to the head of the sentence.
<margin>9</margin>
¶ The Vulgate edition: "I speak the truth, I do not lie." ¶ The Greek codices have: "I speak the truth in Christ." Paul writes: "I speak the truth in Christ, I do not lie." <note>original Greek: ἀλήθειαν λέγω ἐν χριστῶ, οὐ ψεύδομαι</note>
<margin>10</margin>
¶ The Vulgate edition: "Lifting up pure hands without anger and dispute."
¶ There are some who wish to say the word used here signifies "doubt" or "hesitation." But if it comes from the verb *dialegomai* <note>to converse or argue</note>, it signifies not poorly "dispute," "disputation," "dissension," or a certain "contention." And when we hold anger and contention toward one another, then our hands should not be lifted to God; this is a precept of the Savior. He says: "If you offer your gift at the altar, and there you remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go first to be reconciled to your brother: and then coming, you shall offer your gift." <note>A reference to Matthew 5:23–24.</note> For when we present ourselves pure to the divine sight, He hears us according to His mercy—He who wishes to hear, to listen, and to listen exceedingly, as is right and fitting for those who are prepared. Paul writes: "lifting up holy hands, without anger and disputing." <note>original Greek: ἐπαίροντας ὁσίους χεῖρας, χωρὶς ὀργῆς καὶ Διαλογισμοῦ</note>
<margin>11</margin>
¶ The Vulgate edition: "Adorning themselves with shamefastness and sobriety." ¶ What the old translator here calls "sobriety," can more commonly be called "modesty." Saint Jerome also wishes it to be called "chastity" and "modesty." Paul writes: "with modesty and sobriety to adorn themselves." <note>original Greek: μετὰ αἰδοῦς καὶ σωφροσύνης κοσμεῖν ἑαυτάς</note> ¶ The Vulgate edition: "But as becomes women professing piety through good works." ¶ It should have said "those who" <note>feminine</note> rather than "that which" <note>neuter</note>. For this relative pronoun refers back to "clothing," which is known from the Greek where it is masculine, referring to the masculine word for "clothing." <note>Greek: ἱματισμῶ</note> And the general name for "piety" is not used, but a specific one that designates piety toward God alone. Paul writes: "but as becomes women professing the worship of God through good works." <note>original Greek: ἀλλ' ὃ πρέπει γυναιξὶν ἐπαγγελλομέναις θεοσέβειαν δι' ἔργων ἀγαθῶν</note> ¶ The Vulgate edition: "Nor to dominate a man, but to be in silence." ¶ Rather: "nor to have authority over a man." Paul writes: "nor to have authority over a man, but to be in silence." <note>original Greek: οὐδὲ αὐθεντεῖν ἀνδρός, ἀλλ' εἶναι ἐν ἡσυχία</note> Truly, "to have authority over a man" and "to dominate a man" can mean the same thing. But how many matrons are there, swollen with pride from their lineage or wealthy from their dowries, who now hold authority over their husbands? They make the judgment of God void because of the wind of fortune—a fortune more vain than the wind itself. ¶ Blind fortune: which is not only blind, but has blinded the entire age, and with which the apostolic truth cannot shine. ¶ The Vulgate edition: "If she remains in faith, and love, and sanctification with sobriety." ¶ And here also it can be said "with modesty" or "chastity," as was said in the first examination of this chapter. And at the beginning of the clause it should be said in the plural: "they remain" or "if they shall remain." For Paul is looking toward both together: both the man and the woman. Paul writes: "if they remain in faith, and love, and sanctification, with sobriety." <note>original Greek: ἐὰν μείνωσιν ἐν πίστει, καὶ ἀγάπη, καὶ ἁγιασμῶ, μετὰ σωφροσύνης</note>

---

->CHAPTER III.<-

<margin>12</margin>
**A**s the teacher of the nations, the apostle has taught men and women who are parents according to the flesh; now he teaches <term>bishops</term> <note>from the Greek *episkopos*, meaning "overseer"</note>, who are spiritual parents. He shows both what kind of people they ought to be and what their duties are. For they are called "bishops" from the duty of "superintending." I say "superintending" in all spirituality of life, which he accordingly says is a holy work and duty. ¶ A faithful saying: If any man desires the office of a bishop, he desires a good work. A bishop, then, must be: blameless, the husband of one wife, vigilant, chaste, orderly, hospitable, a teacher, not given to wine, no striker, not a follower of filthy lucre; but mild, not a brawler, not covetous, one that rules well his own house; having his children in subjection with all honesty (for if a man knows not how to rule his own house, how shall he take care of the church of God?) not a novice: lest being lifted up with pride he fall into the judgment of the devil. Moreover, he must have a good testimony from them who are without; lest he fall into reproach and the snare of the devil. ¶ "Bishopric": the visitation, intending, and observation of the bishop toward his own is so called. Just as a bishop is a scout, an intender, an observer, and a guardian, like a shepherd of the flock, or like a watchman of the city on a high tower. It is surely a beautiful name, but the execution of the name's reality is more beautiful, which is the duty of the bishop. Since this is so beautiful and venerable, the bishop who is set over that duty and that work must be blameless. "Reproach" runs through all vices: pride, anger, envy, sloth, gluttony, lust, and greed. If he is marked by any of these vices, or any of the innumerable types that exist, he is not blameless. Therefore, he is not at all worthy to be committed to this office. A <term>bigamist</term> <note>one who has been married twice</note> who has taken two wives is not considered fit for the bishopric. For he has divided his flesh and has not kept the unity in the symbol, which represents the unity of Christ and the Church. Therefore, in that unity, the saints decreed that he should not be appointed.

<header>COMMENTARY</header>

...who has violated unity in the image; that is, one who has violated the likeness of that spiritual unity. If a bigamist <note>one who has been married twice</note>, who has divided unity in marriage and the chaste marriage bed, is rejected and judged unworthy of this foresight, what then should be said of those who have divided their flesh in fornications? These are not merely "twice-fornicators," but those who (miserable to say) have perhaps polluted themselves with the fornications of a hundred different mistresses, so many times dividing their own flesh and miserably tearing apart the unity of their own body.

Indeed, who would place a negligent and sluggish scout upon the watchtower <note>Latin: *specula*</note> to ensure no incursion lies open to the city? Who would safely commit his flock to a lazy and sleepy shepherd? A city is much more committed to the scouting and vigilance of a bishop, and the flock more so to his pastoral care. Therefore, he who is not vigilant, attentive, and exceedingly diligent must not be committed to this office, this good and holy work. Let him, therefore, be vigilant; let him also be chaste. For shepherds who are not chaste are less watchful over the flock. And if he who is placed to keep watch is not chaste, the city is placed in danger. Therefore, let the bishop be chaste, both so as not to violate the likeness of divine unity in that great sacrament <note>The "great mystery" of the union between Christ and the Church</note> of Christ and the Church, and for the sake of vigilance.

Let him be adorned. The ornaments of the soul are the virtues and graces, more precious than all gems. In a certain way, we acquire virtues for ourselves, but graces are poured into us from the divine light. And as gems are in darkness, so are our virtues without heavenly grace; as gems in a ray of sunlight, so are virtues illustrated by the rays of divine graces. Therefore, a bishop ought to be conspicuous with this kind of shining adornment of the mind; he must be "adorned." 

But external adornment should not be lacking either, which may represent the internal disposition. Shorn hair <note>A reference to the tonsure</note> displays the cutting away of all superfluity and carnality, and external cleanliness often reflects internal purity. The surplice <note>Latin: *suparus*</note> made of the whitest linen signifies chastity, and the purity and holiness of body and soul. But to run through every single part of external adornment would be too laborious and perhaps less suited to this place. Let the bishop, therefore, be adorned in mind, nor let the external adornment be a lie regarding the internal. Otherwise, he is a "whitewashed wall" and a "decorated sepulcher" <note>An allusion to Matthew 23:27, describing hypocrisy</note>.

While we live, we are all pilgrims, hoping at last to reach the heavenly city. Therefore, mindful of our condition, we ought to be hospitable and willingly receive strangers for the sake of Christ, who willed to be a pilgrim for us in this world, so that He might finally receive us into the hospitality of eternity. And it befits a bishop most of all to be such a man, that he might most closely represent Christ. 

He must be teachable <note>Latin: *docilis*</note>. For if he were dull of wit and did not easily grasp the understanding of the law, he would not be fit to sit in that place to which the knowledge of the entire law pertains—not to be examined in a carnal or coarse sense, but in a spiritual and purer one. Let him therefore be teachable or "able to be taught," that is, one who is easily instructed: even with divinity shining from above, penetrating the understanding of sacred things by his own labor.

He must not be given to wine or reveling in banquets. For it is necessary to be blameless, vigilant, chaste, adorned, hospitable, and teachable. However, this drunkenness and (so to speak) frequency of drinking bouts and revelry is opposed to all these things and closes off the understanding of divine and human matters. Let him therefore be sober and, as far as possible, abstemious. 

Not a striker. But who would choose a striker and a maimer as a shepherd of the flock? So much less should a bishop, the shepherd of a human flock, be a striker, a fighter, or a maimer. For he is the vicar <note>representative</note> of the Eternal Shepherd, who feeds and does not destroy; who heals the broken and does not wound; who is the author of peace, not war; who restores what is dislocated and unites all things in himself, sweetly cherishing the sheep in his bosom, and even on his own sacred shoulders leading them back to the unity of the flock if they wander. He does not maim; he does not crush. Such then should the bishop be—a shepherd established under that Great Shepherd—gentle, mild, and peaceful. Not only not striking in deed, but not even in word, for the strike of the tongue is harsh and wounding, not healing. Concerning this, Paul says below: "Do not rebuke an elder" <note>original Greek: πρεσβυτέρῳ μὴ ἐπιπλήξης</note>. But here he says "not a striker" <note>original Greek: μὴ πλήκτην</note>. Wherefore this passage can also be applied to the striking that is done with the tongue. 

He must not be a seeker of filthy lucre. It does not befit a bishop to be a seeker of filthy lucre, neither from the flock committed to him nor from others in the manner of merchants and usurers <note>Latin: *danistarum*, moneylenders</note>. For the Eternal Shepherd gives, and gives all things freely, and does not receive. If any bishop gives his money to the money-changers so that "money may give birth to money," if he gives to his own for interest, if he practices commerce—does he not seek filthy lucre? And if it is filthy, it is also unjust. For justice is the most beautiful ornament of the soul; how then [can he have] this ornament?

<header>1 Timothy</header>

# X

...lacking [greed] and putting on virtue in its place: he will be an adornment that befits a bishop. Therefore, let him not pursue dishonest gain <note>original Latin: *turpe lucrum*</note>; but on the contrary, let him be generous. Let him also be one who is known to have presided well over his own family, having raised his children (if he has any) in subjection and all integrity. For he who knows not how to preside over his own family, much more will he not know how to preside over the church. For he who knows not how to rule a few: how shall he rule many? He who knows not a house: how shall he rule a city?

<insert>
<note>The following text is written vertically in a separate block and appears to be a fragmented commentary or cross-reference to Ezekiel 31, using the allegory of the Cedar of Lebanon to warn against pride.</note>
A
Just as bees love flowers, so [did they love] its branches. And it is rooted in moist rocks and shady [places] of the earth, and it will leave her; all dwelt in its branches. It was in its height... nor shall they place their height among the leafy and fruitful [trees]... they will be in their height... the waters which all... from those who descend to the lowest earth. Thus says the Lord God: In the day when he descended to hell <note>original Latin: *infernum*</note>, I brought mourning; I held back the rivers, and Lebanon was covered over him, and they were in the pit. At the sound [of his fall], he moved the nations... And they were comforted in the land of consolation... in Lebanon, all the choice trees... they were watered by the waters. For they also went down to hell with him.
</insert>

Furthermore, he who is appointed bishop: let him not be a novice <term>neophytus</term> <note>Literally "newly planted"; a recent convert to the faith.</note> to honors. For he who has never held administration: unless they ascend having been tested step by step, they are usually overcome by glory. When one is a newcomer, and the poisonous spider weaves its web, and the wind of pride blows: he falls into its snares. This may be observed even in small matters. For those who are granted the doctoral laurel: when they are newcomers, they hardly recognize themselves. Thus a certain empty swelling <note>A metaphor for vanity or pride.</note> occupies them (I do not say all, but some). As the years pass, however, that swelling gradually recedes. So that when they are now veterans, and much honor is rightly owed to them, they then estimate themselves as nothing, adorned with humility, though in their novitiate an empty elation had deformed them. Therefore, a novice should not be chosen for that sublime oversight.

Nor is it enough to have a good testimony in one place if he has a bad one in others. For even if he himself perhaps does not fall into the devil's net, yet by this occasion either outsiders or some of his own could fall. For the spider there—that ancient poisonous serpent—stretches its threads. Therefore, as far as possible, let him be chosen for this province and committed to this sacrosanct function: he who has a good testimony from all, and is pleasing and acceptable to all. For just as the light of the sun is pleasing to the eyes of all, so also true virtue is pleasing to the minds of all, even to many of those who are "sick" <note>Metaphorically, those who are morally or spiritually weak.</note>. As the teacher of the gentiles <note>St. Paul</note>—granted this laurel not by men but by Christ—taught bishops, he thereafter also teaches deacons, who are the ministers of the bishops. From their number, if they conduct themselves worthily in the function of their ministry, they are taken up into the office of bishops by a legitimate path. Wherefore, setting aside the highest authority and the primary sacred faculty, the duties of these and those are almost the same, and most functions of both are in common. But these hold them in the lower rank of serving, while those hold them in the highest rank of presiding. And therefore Paul adds this teaching concerning deacons and their families, and their wives, saying:

<margin>13</margin>
> Deacons likewise must be chaste, not double-tongued in speech, not given to much wine, not followers of dishonest gain, holding the mystery of the faith in a pure conscience. And let these also first be tested; then let them serve, provided they are without crime. Their wives in like manner must be chaste, not slanderers, vigilant, faithful in all things. Let deacons be the husbands of one wife, presiding honestly over their children and their own houses. For those who minister well purchase for themselves a good degree, and great confidence in the faith which is in CHRIST JESUS.

For the institution of a bishop, he had numbered seventeen [qualities]: blamelessness, monogamy, vigilance, chastity, orderliness, hospitality, teachability, not being given to wine, no tendency toward violence, no pursuit of dishonest gain, gentleness, peaceableness, generosity, good presiding over family matters, subjection of children in all honesty, not being a novice, and a good testimony both from those over whom he is to be set and from outsiders. 

But for the institution of deacons, he enumerates nine. <margin>1</margin> First: that they be chaste. This prohibits the division of the flesh, and much more of the spirit, which is caused by idolatry and the worship of any other than the true God. <margin>2</margin> Second: that they be not liars. For what else are they who are "double-tongued" <note>original: *sermone duplices*</note> but liars? Let deacons therefore be truthful, so they may be ministers of the truth, which is Christ the Lord. <margin>3</margin> Third: they should not be given to wine. For those who are devoted to much wine, and gorge and drench themselves more than is right, we call drunkards, wine-bibbers, and revelers. While this is always shameful, it is most shameful when they do not shrink from taverns, where a public example of drunkenness and revelry is provided. Therefore, whether a reveler be private or public—that is, one given to much wine—he is not, according to the precept of the apostle (or rather of Christ, from whom he took this teaching), to be taken as a minister for the sacred altars. Let him therefore be sober and abstinent, or at least temperate in food and drink, whoever is to be designated for this office. <margin>4</margin> Fourth: Let him not be a pursuer of dishonest gain. This prohibits all dishonest profit, such as whatever might come from gambling, or from usury...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the qualifications for church leadership in 1 Timothy 3. The previous page discussed the requirements for a bishop (overseer), emphasizing moral integrity and family management. This page shifts focus to the requirements for deacons, specifically addressing their financial dealings, manual labor, and domestic lives.</meta>

<header>COMMENTARY</header>

<margin>3</margin>
...[not] from trade. Even if trade can be honorable for some, it is not so for deacons. However, honest profit is not forbidden, such as that which comes from one’s own lands. For that increase of goods comes from God’s blessing and providence, for He is generous toward all. Such profit is therefore noble <note>original Latin: *liberale*</note>; it ought to be received with much thanksgiving, to be used for works of generosity, for the affairs of the church if necessary, for the family, for the poor, and for hospitality—that is, for receiving strangers who display piety, welcoming them in the likeness of Christ. This does not mean it is a deacon’s job to till the earth and plant trees; such cares should be entrusted to the common faithful <note>original Latin: *idiotis*, meaning laypeople or those without specialized clerical roles</note>. What if they intend to do some honest manual work and seek profit from it for food, clothing, and works of generosity? That is not forbidden either. 

<margin>4</margin>
For indeed Paul, who was greater than all bishops and greater than all deacons, worked with his hands, leaving us an example of a life well-pleasing to God. Therefore, let a deacon not pursue dishonest gain <note>original Latin: *turpe lucrum*</note>; nor should he even pursue honest and noble profit so much as to use it generously once it is obtained. For he who clings to heaven and heavenly ministries ought no longer to cling to the earth, but rather to provide for it. For even the angels provide for the earth, yet they do not cling to the earth, but to the Heavenly Father, whose face they always behold. 

<margin>5</margin>
Fifth: They should have a pure conscience while ministering the sacred mysteries <note>original Latin: *sacramenta*</note> of God. It is the role of the High Priest to celebrate the sacred mysteries; it is the role of the deacons to assist and, once the rites are performed, to distribute them. But if they do not have a pure conscience, how shall they rightly distribute the sacred mysteries? This, therefore, commands an adornment, especially an internal one, which consists in the purity of conscience. Let every deacon, therefore, be adorned with a pure conscience. 

<margin>6</margin>
Sixth: He must not be a novice. For those who have not been tested by long use in a matter are novices. Let their suitability, therefore, be proven before they are granted the honor of the diaconate. For it is no small honor to serve at the Lord’s table: first to feed the holy people of Christ with the Gospel reading, and then, having been fed himself by the bread of eternal life, to reverently hold out with his own hands that same truly heavenly bread—indeed, "beyond-substantial" <note>original Latin: *supersubstantialem*, a term referring to the Eucharist as bread that transcends earthly substance</note> bread—to the people, which is the office of the deacon. The fact that they are commanded to be tested first, and only accepted once well-proven, both excludes novices and mandates blamelessness. For only when they are neither novices nor reprehensible for any vice can they be placed in the holy ministry. 

<margin>7</margin>
Seventh: If a deacon has not chosen virginity, let him have a chaste wife, not a slanderer, but vigilant and faithful in all things, as befits a holy minister. If she has "divided the flesh" <note>likely referring to a previous divorce or remarriage</note>, she is not considered chaste, even if she is now in a marriage with another man; much less so if it happened through fornication. Therefore, the woman whom it was permitted for a future deacon to take as a wife had to be a virgin, adorned with holy character rather than a large dowry. Greed is an unhappy and ill-omened matchmaker. Chastity, however, along with kind speech, diligence, and faithfulness in every matter, is a woman’s greatest dowry. Without these, he who was to be a deacon—and even more so he who was to be a bishop—should never have admitted even a virgin to his bed. Let fortune always hold the last and lowest place, while virtue holds the supreme. Just as heaven holds the highest place, so wealth is dug out from the hidden caverns of the earth, as if from the lowliest of places. Here is the seat of fortune; here is its palace. Let the deacon’s wife, therefore, be distinguished by such integrity. 

<margin>8</margin>
Eighth: If deacons are not virgins, let them be only "once-married" <note>original Latin: *monogami*</note>. For it is not permitted for a twice-married man to be accepted as a deacon, much less a thrice-married or a polygamist. Christ has but one Church, and the Church has none but Christ. There is one Groom and one Bride. It is fitting for the ministers of the Church to be like this in imitation. And let those who preside not believe themselves to be the grooms. They are not the grooms, but the representatives <note>original Latin: *vicarii*</note> of the groom. Indeed, neither Peter nor Paul was the groom; they were the friends of the groom and his faithful stewards <note>original Latin: *oeconomi*</note>. Those who preside, and preside well, are granted the name of "steward" along with Paul. There is but one Groom, for whose sake all grooms and brides from the beginning of the world run in His image. Blessed are they who do not violate the image of the heavenly wedding feast <note>original Latin: *epithalamij*</note> amid the praises of the angels. 

<margin>9</margin>
Ninth: If they have children and do not know how to manage their household affairs properly, they are unworthy to be accepted to manage the ministries of God.

# X

<margin>a</margin> ...the pillar and foundation of truth. And by common confession, great is this mystery of piety: God was
<margin>b</margin> manifested in the flesh, justified in the spirit, seen by angels, preached among the
nations, believed in the world, taken up in glory. ¶ Just as Moses possessed a more distinguished grace
than the seventy-two elders who received from his spirit, so Paul possessed more than Timothy
and his other coworkers. For Paul was chosen as the universal architect, while the others were
co-laborers. Both Paul and Timothy were prophets, but Paul was more distinguished in
discerning through the Holy Spirit who was fit to be appointed as a bishop <note>original: *episcopus*, meaning overseer</note> or chosen
as a minister. They did not require external experience, for they knew the interior and
innermost parts of hearts—not of themselves, but from the Holy Spirit. Therefore, when he instructs Timothy
during his absence, a greater grace instructs a lesser one, and a greater light shines upon a smaller one. A bishop is not
appointed to preside over an earthly house, nor is a deacon chosen to serve in an earthly house;
rather, the former is to preside as a steward <note>original: *oeconomus*</note> in some part of the church of God, which is a spiritual house and
the house of the living God, and the latter is to serve in that same house. And now he compares the church to a
pillar—but a spiritual pillar extended from the earth all the way to the highest heavens, on whose summit
sits Truth, who is Christ, blessed above all. This is the representation of the church in its likeness.
But when he spoke of the church which is the bride, he immediately adds concerning the bridegroom who sits upon the
pillar. For He is the God who was manifested in the flesh; for the Word was made flesh. He was
justified in the spirit. For the Spirit of the Lord rested upon him (even inseparably): the
spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety,
and the spirit of the fear of the Lord. And from the fullness of his justification, we have all received. For no
one can be justified except by His justification, just as there is no daylight except from the source of the
sun's light. He was seen by angels. For he was announced by angels. And once born in the flesh, he was immediately
<margin>LUKE</margin> proclaimed by angels. For the more eminent angel said to the shepherds surrounded by the brightness of God,
stewardship by a great multitude of angels: "Do not fear. For behold, I bring you news of
great joy, which shall be for all people. For today is born to you a Savior, who is Christ
the Lord, in the city of David." And where he gave them the sign of the infant—born before all ages
and then born in time, He who had also made time—suddenly there was with the angel a multitude
of the heavenly host praising God and saying, "Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace,
goodwill toward men." He was preached among the nations. For he himself had commanded the apostles:
"Go," he said, "and preach the gospel to every creature." And their sound went out into all the earth,
and their words to the ends of the world. He was believed in the world, just as it was written in prophecy:
"A people whom I have not known has served me; at the hearing of the ear they obeyed me." He was
taken up in glory. And as they were looking on, he says, he was lifted up, and a cloud received him from
their eyes. And Stephen, the first witness and the crown of martyrs, saw his glory. "Behold,"
he said, "I see the heavens opened, and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of the power of God." This is He
who sits upon the firmest and unshakable pillar until the day of judgment, when the
powers of heaven shall be moved. And all these things are for us a great and ineffable sacrament of His piety.
As he entered into the world, the angels of God adored him, and Him now and forever
all the host of heaven adores. To Him be honor and glory, surpassing all glory
and honor, for all ages of ages. Amen.

<margin>11.</margin>
<margin>12.</margin> ## EXAMINATION of certain points concerning the letter.

¶ The Vulgate edition. ¶ If anyone desires the office of a bishop <note>original: *episcopatum*</note>,
he desires a good work. ¶ I preferred to say "oversight" <note>original: *episcopen*</note> here, and to use Paul's word, so that
"superintendence" and the "office of the bishop" might be better understood here, rather than the thing itself to which one is committed.
For foolish men are now accustomed to ask: "How much is this or that bishopric worth?"—looking at the
temporal fruits which are received from subjects. But if they understood that "oversight" and the
spiritual superintendence of a good bishop were of such great value, they would be like Simon the
Magician or the unhappy Ananias, thinking that the gift of the Holy Spirit can be valued with money; yet
that value is inestimable. If, however, a bishop is negligent, the office is nothing; it
cannot be valued. Therefore, earthly things, which those with good intentions follow, are not the value or the price
of that holy superintendence, but a kind of physical foundation <note>original: *hypostasis*</note> of spiritual works, just as the
sensible world is the foundation of spiritual and intellectual things; and in the small measure of the subjects,
those who rule well, watch, and superintend, administer light, and the shadow of the light is the foundation.
In the shadow they find refreshment. It is otherwise for those who do not understand the function of their turn.
For these men wish to rest only in the shadow of temporal things, caring nothing that the flock of the
supreme Father of the family perishes in a thousand ways through their sloth in the meantime (while they drowse in the shadow).
These men have never desired "oversight" or the "office of a bishop," but only the shadow of the oversight
and of the office itself, which they call by the false name of "bishopric." Paul says: *If anyone reaches out for oversight, he desires a good work* <note>original Greek: εἴτις ἐπισκοπῆς ὀρέγεται, καλοῦ ἔργου ἐπιθυμεῖ</note>. For *episcope* is the act of intending or looking over...
