<meta>This page continues the philological and theological commentary on the First Epistle to Timothy, specifically chapter 3. The author is comparing the standard Latin Vulgate translation with the original Greek text to refine the definitions of the qualifications for bishops and deacons, as well as the nature of the Church and the incarnation of Christ.</meta>

# Commentary

The work and duty of a bishop. ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "The husband of one wife, sober, adorned, prudent, modest, hospitable, a teacher, not given to wine, no striker, but modest, not litigious, not covetous." ¶ Where the ancient translator here says **sober**: in Greek it is held as *nephalios* <note>original: νηφάλιος</note>, which signifies one who is "watchful" or "vigilant." And where he says **prudent**: in Greek it is *sōphrona* <note>original: σώφρονα</note>, which elsewhere he calls "sober." We, however, would rather say **modest**, **chaste**, and **temperate**. Indeed, using *sōphrōn* to signify *phronimon* <note>original: φρόνιμον</note> (that is, "prudent") is only done metaphorically, because temperance is usually the companion of prudence, and it preserves and saves the judgment of a prudent man. It ought to have held the second place here, being placed before **adorned**. And here **adorned** <note>original: *ornatus*</note> refers to cleanliness in outward appearance. For a bishop is not the bridegroom, but the vicar of the bridegroom, representing the groom. It is fitting, therefore, for him to always present himself in a simple and chaste habit before the eyes of the chaste and virginal bride <note>The "bride" refers to the Church</note>. **Modest** <note>original: *pudicum*</note> is redundant here. ¶ Where the ancient translator says **a teacher**: it rather designates one who is **teachable** <note>original: *docilem*</note> and apt for teaching. For how could he teach others who could not even be taught himself? We understand **given to wine** or **winy** as one who, being devoted to wine, is almost driven to a Bacchic frenzy. It is said among the Greeks <note>original: *paroinos* (πάροινος)</note> because he always sits beside his wine. While this is shameful for every Christian, it is especially to be avoided by a bishop. After **no striker**, one term is missing which Paul includes: *aischrokerdēs* <note>original: αἰσχροκερδῆ</note>. If usage allowed, we would say it with one composite word, **filthy-lucre-seeker** <note>original: *turpilucrum*</note>; but because this is little used among the Latins, we must use a circumlocution and say **greedy for base gain** or **a follower of filthy lucre**. And what the ancient translator calls **modest**, signifies **mild** and **clement**. What he calls **not covetous** specifically designates one who is not **avaricious** or **greedy for silver**. Paul: *vigilant, temperate, orderly, hospitable,*

<margin>
B
13
</margin>

*apt to teach, not a drunkard, no striker, not greedy for base gain, but mild, not a brawler, not a lover of money.* ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "Likewise deacons <note>original: *diacones*</note> must be modest, not double-tongued."

<margin>
C
13
</margin>

¶ It should be said: **deacons** <note>original: *diaconos*</note>. For "diacon" is not said, but "diaconus." Paul: *Deacons likewise must be grave, not double-tongued.* ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "Sober, faithful in all things." ¶ Here also it can be said: **watchful**, where he says "sober." Paul: *watchful, faithful in all things.* ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "Let deacons be the husbands of one wife, who rule their children well." ¶ It should be said **deacons** <note>original: *diaconi*</note>. And "sufficiently" is redundant. And when he says "let deacons be the husbands of one wife," any sophist would be delirious, most vain, and an annoying chatterbox if he understood this collectively and not separately and individually. It is as if we were saying: "let each deacon be the husband of one wife." For such people, caviling at everything with a distorted eye of the mind, are as far from the Spirit as Satan is from the assembly of the holy angels—they are one-eyed monsters, or entirely blinded **Polyphemi** <note>A reference to the one-eyed Cyclops from Greek mythology, implying the critics have no depth of spiritual perception</note>. Paul: *Let deacons be the husbands of one wife, ruling their children well.*

<margin>
D
14
</margin>

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "These things I write to you, my son Timothy, hoping that I shall come to you quickly." ¶ The phrase **my son Timothy** is redundant. Paul: *These things I write to you, hoping to come to you sooner.* ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "Which is the church of the living God, the pillar and firmament of truth." ¶ Rather **seat** or **foundation** <note>original: *sedes* or *fundamentum*</note> than **firmament**. Truly, I preferred to say "seat" rather than "foundation," lest "foundation" be thought to be used here as it is when it is said: "for no other foundation can anyone lay than that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ." For that applies to Christ, not to the Church, which is founded and built upon, not the foundation itself. Christ is the foundation of the Church. For the foundations of spiritual things are above, not below in the manner of earthly things ("His foundations," he says, "are in the holy mountains"), and the foundation which is spoken of most preeminently is above all. Therefore, when he compares the Church to a pillar, that which is on the earth is not the beginning, but the end and the extremity. For those foundations that are nearer are prior. Just as the supreme heavenly virtues are placed nearest to the foundation, and the holy mountains in the vision of the spirit, upon which God also sits. Therefore, it seemed more consistent, and not without reason, to treat the "seat" as the summit rather than as the foundation. For that is more fitting for the Church, inasmuch as God sits upon its summit, as if on the summit of a pillar raised from the earth to the highest heavens. Paul: *Which is the church of the living God, the pillar and seat of truth.* ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "And evidently great is the sacrament of piety, which was manifested in the flesh, was justified in the spirit, appeared to angels, was preached to the Gentiles, was believed in the world, was taken up in glory." ¶ It should be said **undeniably** <note>original: *pro confesso*</note> rather than **evidently**; it signifies something certain and explored, with all the fog of doubt driven away. And one should say **God was manifested**, not "which was manifested." And the other following neuter adjectives should be converted to the masculine, saying: **He was justified**, **He was preached**, **He was believed**, **He was taken up**, so that all may refer to their substantive, **God**. Paul: *And without controversy, great is the mystery of godliness: God was manifested in the flesh, justified in the spirit, seen by angels, preached among the nations, believed on in the world, received up into glory.* Now we must pass on to what follows.

<summary>This page provides a philological critique of the Vulgate translation of 1 Timothy 3, refining the moral requirements for church leaders and offering a theological interpretation of the Church as a spiritual pillar whose "foundation" (Christ) is in heaven.</summary>

### CHAPTER IV.

<margin>15</margin>
<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial letter 'H' showing two figures within an ornate architectural frame.</image-desc>This having been done, and the great mystery of piety having been unlocked: Paul prophesies to Timothy concerning those errors which were to come regarding abstinence from foods and marriage, as if these things were evil in themselves. This error appeared later: it was the error of the **Encratites** <note>An early Christian sect that practiced extreme asceticism, forbidding marriage and meat</note>, and those whom they call **Cataphrygians** <note>Another name for the Montanists, a prophetic movement from Phrygia</note>; and it was expedient for the Asians to be fortified by prophecy, because that error spread greatly among them. Paul says therefore: ¶ **But the Spirit says clearly: that in later times some will depart from the faith, giving heed to deceitful spirits and doctrines of demons, of those who speak lies in hypocrisy, having their own conscience seared with a hot iron, forbidding to marry, commanding to abstain from foods which God created to be received with thanksgiving by those who believe and know the truth, because every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected that is received with thanksgiving; for it is sanctified by the word of God and prayer.** ¶ This is the prophecy concerning the Encratites and the heresy of the Phrygians. For who does not know that the delusional **Montanus** <note>The founder of Montanism, who claimed to receive direct revelations from the Holy Spirit</note>, speaking foreign things, and the insane prophetesses **Priscilla** and **Maximilla**, and others—either authors or supporters of these errors—gave heed to deceitful spirits and spoke countless lies? They feigned piety while having a wounded conscience, penetrated by the devil's branding iron so that the scar could never be removed. If anyone desires to know more of these shadows (which the apostle wishes to dispel), let him read **Epiphanius** <note>Bishop of Salamis (c. 310–403), who wrote the 'Panarion', a famous encyclopedia of heresies</note>. However, the eye that loves light has no desire to be turned toward these shadows, unless necessity urges their dispersal and the restoration of the day of true light. Otherwise, curiosity is to be feared: and from curiosity comes a certain lack of preparation for admitting the light more purely, and an easier admission for the entry of the malignant one. ¶ What, then, does he command Timothy? That he preach: that every creature which God established is good, and every **rational food** <note>original: "esca rationabilem"</note> is good for man, and nothing is to be excluded which is received with thanksgiving; and that marriage is good. He warns that those will come who, following the doctrines of demons (which are destructive heresies), teach otherwise so as to lead people away from the true piety of the Creator. For indeed, all rational foods and marriage are sanctified through the word of the Lord. I say "rational," for serpents, poisonous things, human flesh, and many things of that kind—though they are good creatures of God—are nevertheless not rational food. Nor is a marriage rational if a woman is joined to a eunuch, or a woman to a man who wishes to pervert nature, holding the use of his own marriage in mockery. For neither are those foods, nor are these marriages; rather, they are brutalities—both regarding the foods of nature and the worst demonic mockery regarding marriage—which do not receive sanctification. For all things fit for sanctification are orderly. Therefore, Paul adds to Timothy: <margin>16</margin> ¶ **Admonishing the brothers of these things, you will be a good minister of JESUS CHRIST, nourished by the words of faith and the good doctrine which you have followed.** ¶ He gives, moreover, other doctrines which are necessary for anyone wishing to instruct others and to exercise himself in the duties of piety. The first is that when he undertakes the instruction of others, he should not mix in profane and old wives' tales. For the eloquence and the sayings of the holy and pure writers (if anything is to be inserted into a discourse) provide a most ample field. Thus he says: <margin>17</margin> ¶ **But avoid profane and old wives' tales.** ¶ Certainly, in the instruction of those seeking higher things: profane, defiling, and old-womanish words are to be avoided entirely, and not only publicly, but they are to be avoided altogether in private. By the word of the Lord, the adornment of the world came forth, and the beauty of the stars; so whatever comes from our mouth—we who are the children of the word of God—ought to be adorned and beautiful, sprinkled with the light of eternal virtue and grace like twinkling stars. But now, through worthless fables, through soft elegies, through pimps, through the smooth words of harlots, and the parasites of comedies, the minds of adolescents are so softened from an early age that when they reach adulthood, nothing pleases them unless it is profane, soft, and intemperate, or fabulous—things more unworthy and destructive than the ravings of old women. Christ has his own authors: his own hymn-singers, his own epic poets, and (if I may say so) <term>σεμνοποητάς</term> <note>original: "semnopoetas", meaning "venerable poets" or "makers of serious things"</note>, his own historians, his own philosophers and wise men. Those who are instructed in these things bring back pure minds, open to the light of the Holy Spirit and his words, until the eternal day rises for them. They are not corrupted and made unchaste in a thousand ways before puberty through soft little stories about Venus, Cupids, comedies, and satires—which in most cases reprehend shameful things so shamefully that it is as if someone praising chastity before virgins were to strip bare their private parts (which is shameful even to mention now), or as if someone blaming sorcery were to mix poisons before those he blames. Such a person would be a poisoner, who before the crime of poisoning was known, did not know at all what poison was. These are the fascinations of demons; these are profane things: to be avoided at the voice of Paul, the most high herald, and kept far away from every <margin>18</margin> **gymnasium of Christ** <note>A metaphor for a place of Christian training or a school of faith</note>. For those other things belong to the gymnasium of idols, which is opposed to that which is of Christ. The second doctrine he places here concerns exercise unto piety, and it is this: ¶ **Exercise yourself...**

### COMMENTARY

...train yourself in godliness. For bodily exercise is useful for little, but godliness is profitable for all things, having the promises of life, both the present and the future. ¶ Bodily exercise is the movement of the body which preserves health and strength when it is adapted and tempered. But godliness <term>pietas: a word meaning both "piety" and "godliness," referring here to a mind oriented toward God</term> is the movement of a mind turned toward God, which knows no excess, preserving both the present and the eternal life. The latter is valid for eternity; the former only for the present life. The present life, if you compare it to the future, is but a point compared to an infinite line. Therefore, bodily exercise, which pertains only to the present life, is useful for little. But the exercise of the mind according to the movement of godliness is useful for many things—indeed, for all things. For it pertains both to the present and to the future, which contains every good. And to the godly, God promises both lives, the present and the future, through the mouth of the <unclear>apostle himself</unclear> <note>original: "psu [ipsius] apostoli"</note>. A godly and religious mind is like an eye always turned toward the sun, drawing from that light whatever it does, or leading everything back to that light. And all the works of a godly person are bright and luminous. For how can one who turns toward the sun do anything that is not illuminated? <margin>3</margin> The third teaching is that we should hope for salvation from God and from no other reality. For he himself is the savior of all men. For who in this world saves all men, if not he who grants life to all men and provides the means by which it is preserved? But he is especially the savior of faithful men. For he saves them in this world through his providence, and in the other through glory and eternal life. However, he saves the unfaithful only in this world; in the other world (as is just), he deprives them of the glory of eternal life through justice. Therefore, providence is common to both the good and the bad. But glory and eternal life are proper only to the good. Ignominy, extreme confusion, and eternal death belong to the bad. Glory, I say, is proper to the good—that is, those who are faithful. But eternal confusion is for the bad—that is, those who are unfaithful. This applies either simply, as to those who do not even believe the word, or in their works, as to those who have the words of faith but attack that faith with their deeds. For those who say one must not commit adultery yet do so, or that one must not steal yet they steal: the portion of these people is with the unfaithful. And as long as they live in this way, they are included under the name of "unfaithful." If, however, they return to honoring God whom they dishonored, to loving him whom they offended, and to cultivating the justice which they transgressed (for the commandments of God contain all justice), they will change their name and will again become faithful instead of unfaithful. <margin>19</margin> Paul says therefore: 

> The saying is faithful and worthy of all acceptance. For to this end we both labor and suffer reproach: because we have hoped in the living God, who is the savior of all men, especially of the faithful.

¶ He who places his entire hope for salvation in God easily tolerates all labor and the reproaches of the world. Because he hopes in him who saves or condemns. When a farmer sows, whether the day is clear or stormy, he hopes neither in his own work nor in the serenity or adversity of the present time (for hope is of the future), but in the providence of God alone, which alone can either multiply the harvest or, if he wills, destroy it. Nevertheless, he did what he could as a faithful farmer. For if he had not plowed the field, if he had not cast the seed, he would not hope. In a similar way, he who works well in favorable times casts the seed of salvation in the serenity of God. But he who works in adverse times and when hardships press down casts the seed of salvation in the turbulence of God. But he ought not to trust in favorable times, nor in adverse ones, nor in his own works; but in him alone who can make the cast seeds grow into salvation. For God does not grant salvation to works in any other way than he gives life to seeds cast into the earth.

The fourth teaching: That we should illuminate others with the light of the aforementioned teachings. And thus, let us establish ourselves as an example of life in speech, in conduct, in love, in spirit, in purity, and in faith, so that no one can despise us. And let us learn this even from youth. For if we <margin>20</margin> live so that no one despises us as youths, they will be even less likely to despise us when we are old. Therefore the apostle says:

> Command these things and teach them. Let no one despise your youth, but be an example to the faithful in speech, in conduct, in love, in spirit, in faith, and in purity.

¶ What he commands Timothy, he commands to all, especially those who are appointed to preside over others. For to command and to teach belong to the superior toward the inferior. For the lowest things do not illuminate the highest; rather, the highest things send the rays of their illumination into the lowest, and the lowest are made "high-formed" (as much as they can grasp) through the reception of those rays. And so the lesser ones, following the examples of the greater, ought to become "greater-formed" through imitation in speech, in conduct, in love, in the works of the spirit, in faith, and in purity. For these things ought to shine from the superiors into the inferiors just as all lower things appear luminous from the sun and are "light-formed." The fifth teaching, although it seems peculiar to Timothy in some way, can also be understood as universal, and it is this: We ought to attend to divine reading, exhortation, and doctrine; we must not neglect whatever gift of God has been given to us, and we must dwell in these things. For in doing this, we adapt ourselves to the salvation of God, and we likewise lead those with whom we live and who hear us to the port of salvation. He does not command us to attend to impure reading (far be it from us to read Plautus, Terence, Martial, Tibullus, or that player of tender loves <note>Referring to Ovid</note>, who is in truth a deluder of souls), but to holy reading. It is a sacred breast in which holy things dwell...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the First Epistle to Timothy, Chapter 4, where the author provides instructions to Timothy on personal conduct, the exercise of spiritual gifts, and the definition of the office of the "presbyter" or elder.</meta>

[page 208]

1 Timothy
X

If you have written gospels, or if you hold the pure doctrine of Paul, or whatever doctrine does not oppose the Spirit—if you are not capable of exhorting others from holy reading, then exhort yourself. If you are not capable of teaching others, then teach yourself. Do not neglect the gift of God. There is no one whom He does not gift with some blessing. One who neglects this gift seems to despise the Giver; and by this very act, he makes himself unworthy of other gifts. He who remains in these teachings, who exercises himself in them, exercises himself toward godliness, which is powerful for all things—for his own salvation and that of others, and for both the present and the future life. Therefore, <margin>21</margin> these three supreme teachings also open up a second way, making it clearer and more suitable.

Paul therefore adds to Timothy in this manner: ¶ Until I come, attend to reading, exhortation, and doctrine. Do not neglect the gift that is in you, which was given to you through prophecy, with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery. Meditate on these things; be occupied in them, so that your progress may be manifest to all. Attend to yourself and to the doctrine. Persist in them. For in doing this, you will save both yourself and those who hear you. ¶ *Presbyteros*—which among the Latins is called *presbyter* or "senior" <note>original: "senior"</note>. The *presbyterium* <term>presbyterium: the council or office of elders</term> was the function and power of the elders, who laid hands on the heads of those being initiated, purified, or perfected, pouring out sacred prayers and imploring divine help. When they laid hands on Timothy, he received the gift of prophecy—the gift of understanding the prophets and the holy scriptures. And the one who laid holy and unstained hands on him was Paul—as will be known from the following book—who also poured forth holy prayers, obtaining the gifts of the Holy Spirit from God for him. 

But now we use this name "presbyter" <term>presbyter: literally 'elder,' but used here as a title for a priest</term> not to denote age, but rank. Thus, even if a man has not yet reached his twenty-fifth year, if he possesses the senses of the mind and the prudence of the spirit, and has been perfected for this by the sacred office of the ancestors, he is called a "presbyter" or "senior." For this is a rank—not merely an initiation, but a kind of consummation. But such a rank is owed only to those who are gray-haired in mind, to whom greater reverence is due than to gray hair of the body. For they perform those mysteries which are more venerable than all others. And just as in earthly matters, those who hold the highest and most absolute power are earthly kings, so also these, holding the highest and absolute power over divine things, are kings of the sacred rites. 

There lives still (unless rumor deceives me), leading a holy and unstained life (as I believe), a certain man of very harsh life <note>original: "asperrimę vitę," referring to a life of strict asceticism or penance</note>, to whom as a young boy the ministry of angels regarding the divine office of the presbytery was revealed for many years. Never did he see the sacred rite performed without a certain celestial crown appearing over the presbyter's head from the time of consecration, remaining as long as the Lord’s body and blood were being received. Then that crown would vanish, becoming invisible. I believe this to be true, and that a man of this kind is still held by Mantua. But what is this, if not a sign that the priesthood is truly royal—an absolute and mystical power, which the angels of God assist and revere? 

Therefore, all you priests: meditate on these things, be occupied in them. Your promotion is manifest to the angels, not only to men. Save yourselves, as far as it is in you, and those who hear you, and those who assist you. For it is in your power to prepare, to adapt, and to arrange; but it is God's part to complete. Give Him eternal thanks, who made you kings for an immortal work—He who is the King of kings, and who alone creates earthly and spiritual kings. To Him be honor, majesty, glory, and power, over all the kingdoms of those who reign, and this for all ages of ages. Amen.

<margin>4</margin> ### EXAMINATION of several points regarding the literal text.
¶ The Vulgate edition: *But the Spirit manifestly says that in the last times.* <note>original: "Spiritus autem manifeste dicit: quia in nouissimis tēporibus"</note> ¶ What the old translator calls "manifestly" is an adverb signifying "speakably" or "audibly" <note>original: "loquibiliter"</note>, as if we were to say: "the Spirit speaking says." We are little accustomed to using this adverb. And in Paul, it is not said "in the last times" in the superlative degree, but he uses the comparative <note>original: "in nouissimis" vs "in posterioribus"</note>. Thus, the prophecy could have been fulfilled not long after Paul's time, when a great crowd of heretics rose up, falling away from the true faith. Paul says: *But the Spirit expressly says that in later times* <note>original: "τὸ δὲ πνεῦμα ῥητῶς λέγει , ὅτι ἐν ὑστέροις καιροῖς"</note>.

¶ The Vulgate edition: *Of those speaking lies.* <note>original: "Loquentium mendacium"</note> ¶ Lest "of those speaking" should seem to refer to "demons," it seemed better that that genitive and those following be converted into nominatives, so that it clearly refers to "certain ones" <note>original: "quidam"</note> mentioned above. Then the Latin speech is altogether more accessible to readers. Otherwise, let *pseudologon* <term>pseudologon: a Greek term for one who speaks lies</term>—that is, "the lie of those speaking"—be understood to refer to demons. <margin>5</margin> For demons speak lies in a simulation of holiness and religion, by which they may more easily deceive simple men and those of humble or low understanding. We have taken the first sense by referring it to men; the old translator perhaps took the second by referring it to demons. I would reject neither this one nor that one. For the things which such men speak in simulated piety are the very same things which the deceitful demons speak. Paul says: *of speakers of lies* <note>original: "ψευδολόγων"</note>.

¶ The Vulgate edition: *And to those who have known the truth: because every creature of God is good.* <note>original: "Et ijs qui cognouerunt veritatem: quia omnis creatura dei bona est"</note> ¶ It should rather be said "that every creature of God is good." Lest "because" <note>original: "quia"</note> seem to be a confirmation or a rendering of a cause, whereas it seems rather to be explanatory. For to know "that every creature of God is good," and that nothing is to be rejected which is received with thanksgiving, is to know...

### COMMENTARY

<margin>B 15</margin> ...to know the truth. Paul says: *and for those who have known the truth, that every creature of God is good.* <note>original Greek: "καὶ ἐπεγνωκόσι ἀλήθειαν, ὅτι πᾶν κτίσμα θεοῦ"</note> ¶ The Vulgate edition: *For it is sanctified by the word of God and prayer.* ¶ Rather: *and speaking*, or *supplication*. For the word used here is not *proseuchē* <note>original: "προσευχὴ"</note>, which is commonly translated as "prayer"—as at the beginning of the second chapter of this book, where it says: "I desire therefore first of all that prayers/intercessions be made." Instead, a word is used that the old translator rendered there as "petitions." Paul, Chapter 4: *For it is sanctified through the word of God and supplication.* <note>original Greek: "ἁγιάζεται γὰρ διὰ λόγου θεοῦ, καὶ ἐντεύξεως"</note> <margin>B 16</margin> ¶ The Vulgate edition: *Proposing these things to the brothers, you will be a good minister of CHRIST JESUS, nourished in the words of faith and of the good doctrine which you have followed.* ¶ Rather: *admonishing the brothers of these things*. And *of Jesus Christ*. One could also say *nourishing*, as he is speaking in the present tense, even though it has a passive form. And it should be said, according to some Greek manuscripts, *and by good doctrine* in the sixth case <term>sixth case: the ablative case in Latin grammar, used here to show the means or manner of nourishment</term>; for in the Greek, it is in the same case as what the old translator called "words," not "of faith." Therefore, it ought to be translated in the same case. Paul: *Suggesting these things to the brothers, you will be a good servant of Jesus Christ, being nourished by the words of faith and of the good doctrine.* <note>original Greek: "ταῦτα ὑποτιθέμενος τοῖς ἀδελφοῖς, καλὸς ἔση διάκονος Ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ, ἐντρεφόμενος τοῖς λόγοις τῆς πίστεως, καὶ τῆς καλῆς διδασκαλίας"</note> There are also Greek manuscripts that have this final part as: *and of the good doctrine*. In that case, it should be said in the genitive case, <margin>C 19</margin> *and of good doctrine*, which is how the old translator read it. For this reason, it can also be read that way. ¶ The Vulgate <margin>C 20</margin> edition: *Because we hope in the living God.* It should rather be said: *we have hoped*, using the past tense. And *in the living God*, or *the one who lives*. Paul: *because we have hoped in the living God.* <note>original Greek: "ὅτι ἠλπίκαμεν ἐπὶ θεῷ ζῶντι"</note> ¶ The Vulgate edition: *Let no one despise your youth.* ¶ This command is given to Timothy himself, not to others. To emphasize this more, we thought it worthwhile to say: *see to it that no one despises your youth.* Paul: *Let no one despise your youth.* <note>original Greek: "μηδείς σου τῆς νεότητος καταφρονείτω"</note> <margin>D 21</margin> ¶ The Vulgate edition: *In conduct, in charity, in faith, in purity.* It should say *in charity, in spirit*, for *in spirit* is missing after "charity." Paul: *in conduct, in love, in spirit, in faith, in purity.* <note>original Greek: "ἐν ἀναστροφῇ, ἐν ἀγάπῃ, ἐν πνεύματι, ἐν πίστει, ἐν ἁγνείᾳ"</note> ¶ The Vulgate edition: *Do not neglect the grace that is in you.* ¶ In the Greek, the word that is commonly translated as "gift" <term>gift: refers to 'charisma,' a spiritual endowment</term> is used, not "grace," even if in reality and meaning (as has been said elsewhere) it accords with grace. Paul: *do not neglect the gift that is in you.* <note>original Greek: "μὴ ἀμέλει τοῦ ἐν σοὶ χαρίσματος"</note> ¶ The Vulgate edition: *Attend to these things.* ¶ That "attend" <note>Latin: "insta"</note> signifies *remaining within*. It seems to refer back to what was said before: "meditate on these things, be occupied in them." *Remain in them*, that is, stay in them, contain yourself within them, and do not wish to wander off to foreign things. Although this command is most to be observed in sacred speech, if it were also observed in other human disciplines—by meditating, persisting, and remaining in those things handed down by approved authors—we could acquire all disciplines in a short time. From those, we could be transferred by a certain legitimate path to divine things: from the world of the senses to the intellectual world, from the human spectacle to the divine theater (if I may put it that way). But because the teachers of our time, whether of the young or of the mature, do not meditate on the sayings of approved authors, they are not "in them" and do not "remain in them." Instead, they are driven away to foreign pastures, more barren than the Libycan solitudes or the Arabian wilds. They are never able to attain even one human discipline as they ought; yet when they presume to know everything, they are remarkably delusional. When they are hunting gnats, they think they have captured elephants. To them, all divine oracles are lighter than Sybilline leaves <note>Sybilline leaves: a reference to the prophecies of the Cumaean Sibyl, which were written on leaves and easily scattered by the wind, becoming illegible or meaningless</note>. If only we, who wish to be called theologians, would at least meditate on the sacred Scriptures, insist upon them, remain in them, and be contained as if within the walls of paradise! We should not be snatched away to foreign things, which the Apostle forbids. Until this happens, both in human and divine matters, the divine light (even if it shines upon us) will never be grasped. Let all things exotic, barbarian, foul, and stinking be gone—everything that contains any impurity or filth (no matter how much it is cloaked in elegant speech)—so that the divine light may be received. For one must be just as wary of those who use elegant speech to hold a wicked opinion, however festive the oration, as one is of barbarians who, by clamoring harshly and poorly, drag one toward foreign things. Paul: *Persist in them.* <note>original Greek: "ἐπίμεπε ἑαυτοῖς"</note>

### CHAPTER V.

<margin>12</margin> The Apostle further instructs Timothy on how to maintain decorum in every duty and how to adapt himself to various persons with all integrity. And he says: ¶ *Do not rebuke an elder, but entreat him as a father; young men as brothers; old women as mothers; young women as sisters, in all purity. Honor widows who are truly widows.* ¶ If he requires such gentleness and the grace of humanity in teaching and correcting from one who is a leader, then how little do those understand who, having no preeminence of superiority over either individuals or groups, criticize with such severity—as if they themselves were the ones who send people to hell, thinking that by this very act they are righteous. Let them learn the form of teaching and gentleness from the Apostle, and let each recognize his own rank. Let them entreat elders as fathers (even if they are bishops like Timothy), equals as brothers, and those much younger in age either as brothers or as sons. Old women as mothers; young women...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the First Epistle to Timothy, specifically concluding the advice on treating members of the congregation and moving into the detailed instructions for the care and conduct of widows (Chapter 5:1-11). It reflects the author's focus on defining "true" widowhood as a spiritual vocation rather than just a social status.</meta>

# 1 Timothy

...as sisters. Let them see to it, however, that in doing so, they do not feel impure motions of the flesh. For they would then be weak, and perhaps more in need of doctrine and medicine themselves than those for whom they were preparing doctrine and medicine. Therefore, let this be done in all chastity and purity, which no one can do—or only with great difficulty—unless he is spiritual. But to be spiritual is not within everyone's power, however much they may value themselves; rather, it is a gift of God.

¶ Honor widows who are truly widows. <note>original: "Viduas quæ vere viduæ sunt: honorēt"</note> They are truly widows who, like turtledoves lacking a mate, wish to cling no longer to any mortal man, but to cling to Christ alone for the rest of their lives and to please Him alone, bearing a dove-like simplicity within themselves and preserving a turtledove-like chastity. But because he has spoken of widows, he follows up further. For those who are widows either have sons or grandsons, or are left alone, equally deprived of a husband, sons, and the comfort of grandsons. Now, however, regarding the one who has sons or grandsons, he sets down this precept: Let sons or grandsons rule the house with piety and return a mutual exchange of care to their widowed mother. Thus, Paul says: ¶ But if any widow has children or grandchildren, let them first learn to care for their own homes religiously and to give back a mutual exchange to their parents. For this is acceptable before God. 

<margin>23</margin> <margin>2</margin> It is certain that this precept holds its place when the sons or grandsons are of such an age that they can already govern the house and handle external cares, while the widow handles the internal ones, as she who long ago learned to be a mistress of the house. She is a widow, but not to such an extent a "true" widow. For in place of a husband, she has the relief and comfort of sons or grandsons; and she often lives occupied with household affairs just as if she had a husband, unless daughters-in-law <note>original: "nurus"</note> relieve her of the care of internal matters. 

<margin>24</margin> But as to who should be called altogether and simply a true widow, Paul adds, saying: ¶ But she who is truly a widow and remains alone has hoped in God and continues in prayers and supplications night and day. ¶ He wants her to be called a "true widow" who, left alone, has hoped in God, and ceases not from prayers and supplications neither by day nor by night. I say she hoped more in God than she did in her husband while he lived; and she adheres to God in spirit more than she adhered to her husband in body. Therefore, by praying more, she serves God both day and night more than she ever did an earthly and mortal spouse. Although she seeks the comfort of neither sons nor grandsons, she is comforted more in her soul than she could be by any service <term>famuletio: a term for the service or attendance provided by household members or family</term> of offspring or relatives. Whoever is of this kind is altogether, simply, and truly a widow. 

<margin>25</margin> But concerning her who is not at all a true widow, the apostle adds, saying: ¶ But she who lives in luxury is dead while she lives. ¶ Luxuries <note>original: "deliciæ"</note> nourish the flesh and extinguish the spirit. But the life of the flesh is the death of the spirit. Moreover, the death of the spirit is true death. Therefore, even if a widow of this kind is dead in spirit, though living in the flesh, she is in truth dead. 

But from the teaching on widowed women, we are taught what should be felt regarding widowed men—both true and not true widows. The life of those joined in marriage is one of action. But the life of true widows, both men and women, ought to be contemplative. Even if not at the highest level, at least at the lowest, where prayer and supplication are placed in humility and simplicity. 

<margin>26</margin> <margin>3</margin> The apostle commands that everyone should take care of their own widows, whether a father has a widowed daughter, or a son a mother, or a grandson his grandmother. And he says: ¶ And command these things, that they may be blameless. But if anyone does not provide for his own, and especially those of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an infidel <note>original: "infideli deterior" - meaning one who does not believe in the Christian faith</note>. ¶ Why has he denied the faith? Because pure and undefiled religion before God the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their tribulation, even if they are nothing to those visiting. How much more, then, must care be taken for one's own and domestic widows? He who does not do this has denied the faith and religion. It is certain that he has denied the faith by his actions. But even if he says it is nothing to him to provide for them, he has denied the faith both in word and in deed, and is worse than an infidel. For many infidels provide for their own. And if they do not provide, they do not cast off the faith, which they never received. 

¶ He sets down a fourth precept concerning widows who are to be provided for by the church and who are to be fed from the table of the church; and he adds: ¶ Let a widow be chosen not less than sixty years old, who has been the wife of one husband, having testimony in good works, if she has brought up children, if she has been hospitable, if she has washed the feet of the saints <note>A traditional act of humble service and hospitality</note>, if she has helped the oppressed, if she has followed every good work. 

<margin>27</margin> <margin>4</margin> Those who had such recommendations of probity were judged worthy of being helped from the sacred funds. For although it is good to dispense the goods of the church to orphans, widows, and the poor, it is better that sacred things be dispensed to the more sacred, and better things to the better people. 

Wherefore, in the following precept, he commands that young women are not to be chosen in this way, even if they were the wives of only one man. For it often happens that after they have enjoyed the luxuries of Christ’s goods, they want to marry. In this very thing they have sin: that they violate the faith of widowhood which they had promised to Christ through a second marriage <note>original: "bigamiam" - here referring to marrying again after the first husband's death</note>. Moreover, when they are nourished by sacred things, they learn to be idle, to go about from house to house, being talkative and meddlesome, and speaking things that are not proper. 

<margin>28</margin> Therefore, Paul gives this fifth precept concerning them, saying: ¶ But avoid the younger widows. For when they have become luxurious against Christ, they want to marry, having judgment because they have cast off their first faith. And at the same time, being idle, they learn to go about from house to house; and not only idle, but also talkative and meddlesome, speaking things that are not proper. ¶ There are those who understand these last two precepts as referring to priest...

<margin>5</margin>

### Commentary

...and to presbyters <term>presbyteris; meaning elders or leaders in the early church</term> for managing domestic affairs, it is permitted to choose widows no younger than sixty years. But Paul seems to say nothing here regarding the family affairs of presbyters, especially since at that time presbyters had their own wives to care for the family matters within the home. Why then was there a need to speak of "outside" women who would handle their domestic and family business? Therefore, he is speaking of those who were provided for from the sacred treasury. What does it mean, **"when they have grown wanton against Christ"**, <note>original: "quando Christo deliciatę fuerint"</note> except when they have used the "delights of Christ"—which are to pray, to be present at church and sacred things, and to be brought up in holy deeds. When they have tasted these delights, younger widows frequently begin to loathe them and prefer to marry. Thus they make their first "faith" <note>referring to their vow of widowhood</note> void, and moreover, they cause a scandal to the church. For the sake of such younger widows, Paul gives the following precept, not so much commanding as <margin>29</margin><margin>6</margin> making a concession. And so he says:

¶ **I will therefore that the younger women marry, bear children, manage the household, and give no occasion to the adversary to speak reproachfully. For some have already turned aside after Satan.**

What is "I will," if not "I permit"? This precept, therefore, is one of permission. It is better for the younger women to marry than to request sacred nourishment <note>church-funded support</note> while promising a faith of widowhood, only to later wish to marry and make that faith void. For such women are frequently rebuked; and the devil, taking occasion from this rebuke, ensures that those who fear the reproach of a broken vow do not marry, but instead he drags them toward worse things and secret fornications. And so, turned away from Christ, they go after Satan and rush into the pit of perdition. Using the example of some who have perished in this way, he warns Timothy not to receive such women, but <margin>30</margin> to allow them to marry. Regarding those widows who, even if they are younger, do not wish to marry and have fathers, mothers, fathers-in-law, or daughters-in-law: Paul hands down a seventh precept, saying: <margin>7</margin> **If any faithful man or woman has widows, let them provide for them sufficiently, and let not the church be burdened, so that it may be enough for those who are truly widows.**

¶ These things concern widows; thus far <margin>31</margin> is the Apostle’s determination. Now, concerning the presbyters—that is, the elders—who lead well by word and example (that is, by speech and deed), he adds the following precept, saying:

¶ **Let the presbyters who rule well be held worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in the word and doctrine. For the Scripture says: "Thou shalt not muzzle the ox that treadeth out the corn." And: "The laborer is worthy of his reward."** <margin>8</margin>

"Double honor" refers to both spiritual and earthly honor. Spiritual: by revering and venerating them. Earthly: by nourishing them and relieving them of every bodily necessity. For the more spiritual they are, the more they are content with fewer earthly things. Indeed, it is more like God to have self-sufficiency and to need very little. Those who are earthly, however, are insatiable for wealth, and the heat of "having" always grows. Especially to be honored are those who lead and labor well in the word of faith and in doctrine. For they are the architects, while others are like those carrying out the architect's orders. In this way, Christ and the Apostles (the imitators of Christ) have brought us to salvation through the labor of the word. And he confirms that they are to be supported by the authority of the Sacred Scriptures—both of the Old and New Law, of the "shadow" and the "truth." He places a ninth precept concerning the same men, <margin>32</margin><margin>9</margin> saying:

¶ **Against a presbyter, do not admit an accusation, except under two or three witnesses.**

For it is not likely that those of such an age and placed in such a high rank would easily slip into sin; and especially in that time, in which the Holy Spirit presided in their hearts. For in all who lead spiritually, the Holy Spirit presides. For they are driven by the Spirit. And let us act as if comparing a small thing to a great one: if someone is in charge of youths and instructs them in morals and life, an accusation against him ought not to be easily admitted. How much less against an elder who leads the people, striving to form them <margin>33</margin><margin>10</margin> toward piety by word and example. He joins a tenth precept, saying:

¶ **Those who sin, rebuke before all, so that the others also may be struck with fear.**

The subject matter requires this to be said of the presbyters. Just as an accusation against them is more difficult to admit, so once convicted and guilty of a crime, they ought to be rebuked more severely before all the other presbyters (for the talk here is of presbyters), so that the rest may be terrified. For the higher the rank they hold, the more horrific the fall, and the more it ought to be a cause for fear. And for this reason, the reproof and the deterrence are greater. Those who understand this universally <note>applying it to everyone, not just elders</note> do not attend to the subject at hand; that could only and primarily have a place among publicans and public sinners. ¶ Therefore, let it be understood as regarding convicted priests, as is consistent. But the <margin>11</margin> eleventh point especially looks to the Bishop. Just as he is the most honorable of those who lead, so to him belongs the labor of the word and doctrine, and the example of life, and the entreaty, exhortation, approval, or rebuke of each person according to their dignity—but just as the established commands were made. Wherefore, he strictly commands Timothy, even with an oath, that he observe the aforementioned things, and do nothing except what has been <margin>34</margin> pre-judged, pre-defined, and pre-ordered, [not] moved by the advocacy or patronage <margin>11</margin> of others.

¶ **I charge thee before God and the Lord JESUS CHRIST and the elect angels, that thou keep these things without prior judgment <note>prejudice</note>, doing nothing through partiality.**

What is "without prior judgment" except that which has been pre-judged, pre-defined, and pre-ordered by the Holy Spirit and the leaders of the Church?

1 Timothy

## X

...who was it? One of whom was the great Paul: in whom Christ and the Holy Spirit spoke. What is meant by "through advocacy" <note>original: "per aduocationem"</note> if not through human grace and favor? This is how the holy Athanasius <note>Athanasius of Alexandria (c. 296–373), a prominent Greek Church Father and defender of orthodoxy.</note> interprets it. For human patrons or advocates strive to win the favor of the judge, whether they are accusing or defending someone. If a bishop judges otherwise than what has been pre-ordained by holy decrees, he is guilty of violating a holy oath before God, the Lord Jesus Christ, and the elect angels. Oh, how the necessity of judging rightly weighs upon bishops! How harshly their officials now exercise their roles, and how they ought to fear the furnace of Gehenna <note>a valley near Jerusalem used as a metaphor for hell or eternal punishment</note> and the unquenchable oven. I shudder while reporting this.

<margin>12</margin>
The twelfth precept also pertains to the bishop: it is his duty to lay on hands, to pour out sacred prayers, and to perform the other mysteries for the perfecting of priests <term>presbyteros; the Greek term for elders or priests</term>. These are called "kings of sacred things" <note>original: "reges sacrorum"</note>. Indeed, it is not fitting for the Eternal King, the Son of the Eternal King, to be handled familiarly at the altar except by "kings." And these are kings by excellence—even if not in common opinion—whom the angels crown, and whose crowns angels, not men, carry. Regarding them, this is true: ¶ **And all the kings of the earth shall adore him.**

¶ **Therefore** <note>original: "Ergo"</note> priests are not to be made rashly or quickly, lest someone wicked be gifted with such great dignity, than which none on earth is more sublime or more venerable.
<margin>35</margin>
Lest one who is wicked and impure be admitted to the service of the Eternal King. Otherwise, he who ordains them will be held guilty of their sins, just as if he were a partner in their crimes. Therefore, Paul adds: ¶ **Lay hands suddenly on no man, neither be partaker of other men's sins.** ¶ Those who grant their own duties to others share in their works. Just as a judge, if he commits his duties to someone wicked and unjust, is himself held equally guilty of the injustices committed by his substitute. So too a bishop, in handing over to another the sacred duty of handling the most venerable mystery <note>likely referring to the Eucharist or the Sacraments</note>: if that person is filthy and unclean, the bishop will be held as a partner and guilty of his indignities whenever he approaches that mystery in a filthy and unclean manner. Likewise, if a pastor appoints a vicar over his sheep who, like a wolf, devours, maims, and scatters them, he will be considered a sharer in his sins and held guilty of the same offense. Similarly, if a judge commits his office to another who perverts judgment, he will communicate in the sins of others and be guilty of the perverted judgment. And because a bishop can do much and can share his power with others in various ways, he must be very vigilant and direct the sharp edge of his mind toward what the Apostle, full of God, says: **neither be partaker of other men's sins.** For these are the words of the Spirit.

<margin>13</margin>
The thirteenth precept concerns everyone in common, since all children of regeneration <note>those who have been baptized</note> are called to holiness and purity; but it especially befits the bishop, who holds the highest place among them, to be chaste—that is, pure, clean, and holy.
<margin>36</margin>
After him, the priests; then the deacons; down to the lowest state of the holy common people. Therefore Paul says: ¶ **Keep thyself chaste.**

¶ **But** <note>original: "Verum"</note> because temperance and abstinence from foods and drinks that cause the flesh to become wanton and petulant contribute much to maintaining chastity and purity—such as eating much meat, broths, and things prepared too delicately, sumptuously, and (if I may say so) in the manner of Apicius <term>Apiciane; referring to Marcus Gavius Apicius, a famous Roman gourmet known for excessive luxury and gluttony</term>, or excessive drinking from a foaming cup and too free a draft of wine.
<margin>37</margin>
Therefore Paul adds to Timothy: ¶ **Drink no longer water, but use a little wine for thy stomach's sake and thy frequent infirmities.**

¶ **Therefore** wine, and those things which in healthy people make the flesh grow wanton, are to be used in place of medicine, and only when nature requires them for health, not for lust. For it is certain that the custom of the holy man Timothy was to drink water; otherwise the Apostle would not have said, "drink no longer water." This implies "no longer only water," yet he forbids much wine, because it contributes neither to health nor to the chastity and purity of life. And such ought all to be, especially bishops and all priests. If they use wine, they ought to use a little. ¶ But what shall we say of the many who drench themselves immoderately, and with full and swelling veins lose the purity of the flesh and the spirit alike? They pursue the enticements of gluttony in every way, so that it seems some demon of intemperance has mixed the fuel of the throat, the belly, and the kidneys in the tavern to destroy chastity and purity.
<margin>38</margin>

¶ **What**, I ask, shall we say of such men, except what Paul adds, saying: ¶ **Some men's sins are open beforehand, going before to judgment; and some men they follow after. Likewise also the good works of some are manifest beforehand; and they that are otherwise cannot be hid.**

¶ **What** does "and some men they follow after" mean, if not that the sins of some are only uncovered at the end? What does "and they that are otherwise cannot be hid" mean, if not that the good works which were not manifest before will not be hidden at the end? And these good works, whether manifest beforehand or known at the end, lead to the judgment of life. Likewise, evil works (unless they are expiated), whether they are manifested at the beginning or the end, lead to the judgment of death. For neither light nor darkness escapes our eye. It is foolish, therefore, to think that any things, whether good or evil, can be hidden from God, the greatest eye of the universe—an eye existing everywhere and present to all things. For he sees...

D.ij.

# COMMENTARY

...all things; nor can anything escape him. Let us therefore strive to live so that our good works are always manifest before him, even if they are hidden from the world—though in the end, they will not be able to remain hidden from the world. Let us live so that we may please him; for since he is supremely good, he is a lover of all things that are good. And let us serve him, whom all the good shall praise without end. To him, from this moment now, be all praise, glory, and honor, forever and ever.

<margin>A 22</margin> **EXAMINATION of certain points regarding the literal text.** ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Honor widows: who are truly widows.* <note>1 Timothy 5:3</note> ¶ **Truly:** this is an adverb here, not a noun. Paul wrote: <note>original Greek: χήρας τίμα, τὰς ὄντως χήρας - "chēras tima, tas ontōs chēras"</note> "Honor widows who are truly widows." And thus the word "truly," wherever it is joined to the word "widow" in this chapter, is to be understood in this sense.

<margin>A 23</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Let her first learn to rule her own house, and to repay mutual recompense to parents.* <note>1 Timothy 5:4</note> ¶ **It should be said:** *let them learn* in the plural. For Paul gives this precept to children and grandchildren who are of a sufficient and adult age, not to the widow who has been deprived of her husband’s comfort. This is suggested by the phrase: *and to return mutual recompense to parents,* for that duty pertains to children and grandchildren. Furthermore, where the old translator uses "to rule" <note>Latin: regere</note>, the meaning is better understood as: *to cherish piously and religiously.* For *Eusebia* <term>Eusebeia; a Greek term for "piety" or "godliness," referring to the fulfillment of duties toward God, family, and country</term> refers to the care one owes to God, to parents, and to one's fatherland. Paul wrote: <note>original Greek: μανθανέτωσαν τὸν ἴδιον οἶκον εὐσεβεῖν, καὶ ἀμοιβὰς ἀποδιδόναι τοῖς προγόνοις - "manthanetōsan ton idion oikon eusebein..."</note> "let them learn to show piety to their own house and to give back a return to their ancestors."

<margin>A 24</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *But she who is truly a widow and desolate: let her hope in God, and persist in supplications.* <note>1 Timothy 5:5</note> ¶ This word **desolate** signifies one who remains solitary. And it should rather be said "she has hoped" and "she continues" or "persists" in prayers. Because she has placed her hope [in God], she remains alone willingly and persists in constant prayers. Even if the Latin says "she hopes in God and continues in prayers" (because the joining word "and" usually requires the same tense in Latin), it does not much hinder the understanding or the flow of speech, even though in the Greek "hoped" is in the past tense and is the more fitting expression. Paul wrote: <note>original Greek: ἡ δὲ ὄντως χήρα, καὶ μεμονωμένη, ἤλπικεν ἐπὶ τὸν θεὸν, καὶ προσμένει ταῖς δεήσεσι - "hē de ontōs chēra... ēlpiken epi ton theon..."</note> "But she who is truly a widow, and left alone, has hoped in God, and continues in petitions."

<margin>A 26</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *But if any man has not care of his own, and especially of his domestics: he has denied the faith.* <note>1 Timothy 5:8</note> ¶ It should rather be said: "of his own women" and "of his domestic women," using the feminine gender. For Paul is speaking here specifically about widows. Indeed, those who do not care for their mothers, or daughters, or kinswomen who are widows, but allow them to live licentiously as they please and to waste away in luxuries and pleasures—women who would otherwise have been upright and honest widows if their kin had provided for them—these men are worse than infidels who never acknowledged the faith, and they will endure a harsher judgment. Paul wrote: <note>original Greek: εἰ δέ τις τῶν ἰδίων, καὶ μάλιστα τῶν οἰκείων οὐ προνοεῖ, τὴν πίστιν ἤρνηται - "ei de tis tōn idiōn..."</note> "If anyone does not provide for his own..." Because the gender in Paul’s Greek is ambiguous (being a common form), our Latin translator chose the masculine as the least doubtful option, but it seems less fitting for the specific subject matter. He should have left the speech ambiguous in the translation just as he found it, as we have done, so that the reader’s discretion could distinguish the meaning as required.

<margin>B 28</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *For when they have grown wanton: they want to marry in CHRIST.* <note>1 Timothy 5:11</note> ¶ It seems it should rather be said: *they have grown wanton against Christ.* And when Paul said "avoid younger widows," I believe he was looking not so much at their chronological age as at the instability and inconstancy of their character. For if they are "young" in their behavior and inconstant, they may wish for a time to remain alone like "true widows" and persist in prayers and supplications; but when they have grown wanton against Christ after a short while in this way of life, they begin to feel weary and wish to marry. Truly, because of this inconstancy—being "young" in their ways—even if they choose the delights of Christ (which are found in spending time in prayers, supplications, and fasts), they immediately become bored and stop. They remain idle, learn to wander from house to house, become talkative, and say things that are not fitting. Such women are to be avoided; they should not be bound to the service of Christ in cloisters by bishops, even if they or their parents request it. Sustenance from the goods of the church is certainly not owed to such people. But Paul’s precept is little observed now, and such women are rarely avoided. In this passage, the old translator changed the meaning or made the phrasing tasteless and unworthy. For since the word "Christ" refers back to the preceding verb in Paul’s text, it is tasteless to say "wanton in Christ." What is "wantonness" <note>Latin: luxuriatæ</note> here if not "fornication"? No one would say "fornicated to Christ" or "in Christ." For this reason, having changed the sense, they added a preposition to "Christ" and attached it to the following verb "to marry," thereby altering the meaning. Paul wrote: <note>original Greek: ὅταν γὰρ καταστρηνιάσωσι τοῦ χριστοῦ, γαμεῖν θέλουσιν - "hotan gar katastrēniasōsi tou christou, gamein thelousin"</note> "For when they grow wanton against Christ, they desire to marry."

<margin>C 29</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *I will therefore that the younger marry.* <note>1 Timothy 5:14</note> ¶ It should be said: *I will therefore.* For here he concludes what should be done regarding these "younger" women—younger in character rather than age—whom he previously ordered to be avoided regarding the delights of Christ. Paul wrote: <note>original Greek: βουλόμαι οὖν νεωτέρας γαμεῖν - "boulomai oun neōteras gamein"</note> "I will therefore that the younger [widows] marry."

<margin>C 30</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *If any faithful man has widows: let him minister to them.* <note>1 Timothy 5:16</note> ¶ It should rather be said: *if any faithful man, or if any faithful woman.* For the word "faithful" <note>Latin: fidelis</note> is first in the masculine, and the feminine is subsequently joined to it. Paul wrote: <note>original Greek: εἴ τις πιστὸς ἢ πιστὴ ἔχει χήρας, ἐπαρκείτω αὐταῖς - "ei tis pistos ē pistē..."</note> "If any man or woman who is a believer has widows, let them assist them." Truly, if we merely said "if any faithful [man] or faithful [one] has widows," the gender of the second person would not be understood as clearly as it is in the Greek; therefore we added "if any woman." In the Greek, the gender is clearly understood in both the first and second instances through the use of the article, without needing such an addition.

The author argues that "younger widows" refers to those with inconstant character rather than just young age and emphasizes the duty of families to support their own widowed kin.</summary>

It then transitions into the commentary for Chapter 6, which deals with the duties of Christian servants toward their masters.</meta>

# 1 Timothy

->X<-

...in the phrasing: as if we were saying "if any faithful man or faithful woman has widows," but "faithful" <note>Latin: *fidus*</note> does not express the word as aptly as "believing" <note>Latin: *fidelis*</note>. ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *That the church may not be burdened.* <note>1 Timothy 5:16</note> ¶ **It should be read** with a joining mark: *and* let the church not be burdened. Paul wrote: <margin>38</margin> <note>original Greek: καὶ μὴ βαρείσθω ἡ ἐκκλησία - "and let the church not be burdened"</note>. ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *I charge you before God and Christ Jesus.* <note>1 Timothy 5:21</note> ¶ **It should be said:** *and the Lord Jesus Christ.* The word "Lord" is missing and the order of the speech is changed. Paul wrote: <note>original Greek: Διαμαρτύρομαι ἐνώπιον τοῦ θεοῦ, καὶ κυρίου ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ - "I solemnly charge you before God and the Lord Jesus Christ"</note>. ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *That you observe these things without prejudice, doing nothing.* <note>1 Timothy 5:21</note> ¶ **The phrase** "without prejudice" <note>Latin: *sine praeiudicio*</note> should be referred to the following part. And "without prejudice" does not mean what is commonly understood—namely, "without detriment or loss"—but it means without a previous, prior, or preceding judgment. For it designates "pre-judgment": a prior or preceding judgment. Blessed Ambrose, in his exposition of this passage, followed this understanding quite skillfully; and indeed, the logic of the word demands it. Paul wrote: <note>original Greek: ἵνα ταῦτα φυλάξῃς, χωρὶς προκρίματος μηδὲν ποιῶν - "that you keep these things without prejudging, doing nothing [by partiality]"</note>. ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Declining to either side.* <note>1 Timothy 5:21</note> ¶ **It should rather be said:** *by partiality* <note>Latin: *per advocationem*</note>. For the Greek word *prosklesis* <note>πρόσκλησις</note> does not mean "declining," but "summoning" or "invitation," which is the same as acting through the patronage of others who either accuse or approve of something. For the word *clisis* <note>κλίσις</note>, when it means "declining," is written with an *iota* (that is, *i*, the ninth letter); but when it means "calling" or "summons," it is written with an *eta* (that is, *η*, the seventh Greek letter). Here, however, it is written with the *eta*, the seventh letter. Perhaps the similarity of the words caused the old translator to hallucinate, leading him to use a long-winded circumlocution and paraphrase rather than a direct translation. Paul wrote: <note>original Greek: κατὰ πρόσκλησιν - "according to partiality"</note>. ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Some men's sins are manifest.* <note>1 Timothy 5:24</note> ¶ **It should rather be said:** they are *manifest beforehand* <note>Latin: *praemanifesta*</note>. Paul wrote: <note>original Greek: τινῶν ἀνθρώπων αἱ ἁμαρτίαι πρόδηλοί εἰσι - "of some men the sins are manifest beforehand"</note>. ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Similarly also good deeds are manifest.* <note>1 Timothy 5:25</note> ¶ **Here too it should be said:** they are *manifest beforehand*. Paul wrote: <note>original Greek: ὡσαύτως καὶ τὰ καλὰ ἔργα, πρόδηλά ἐστι - "likewise also the good works are manifest beforehand"</note>.

### CHAPTER VI.

<margin>39</margin> <note>Decorative initial 'D'</note> In the preceding chapter, Paul set down precepts concerning widows, elders, and bishops. Now he sets down this precept concerning servants, saying: ¶ **Whosoever are servants under the yoke: let them count their own masters worthy of all honor, lest the name of the Lord and his doctrine be blasphemed.** <note>1 Timothy 6:1</note> ¶ This precept is understood to apply to those servants who were under the yoke of servitude to unbelieving masters. For who doubts that if masters knew their servants had become Christians and then served them less—and were then held in less honor by them—they would blaspheme the name and doctrine of Christ? They would ask: what kind of servants are those who believe in him, and what kind of doctrine has imbued them, if they have become so wicked, rebellious, proud, and contemptuous? Therefore, the negligence and contempt of the servants would fall back as an insult upon Christ and his doctrine, unless the servants served (as is right) and considered their masters worthy of all honor. And they should do this for the sake of Christ, who is the Lord of lords. 

<margin>40</margin> He gives another precept concerning those servants who have believing masters, saying: ¶ **But they that have believing masters: let them not despise them because they are brothers, but rather serve them because they are faithful and beloved, who are partakers of the benefit.** <note>1 Timothy 6:2</note> ¶ Believing servants who have believing masters ought not, as servants, to focus solely on their spiritual condition. For according to their spiritual condition, by which they are Christians, they are not servants but brothers; and the masters, according to their spiritual condition, are not their masters but brothers. But the servants ought to attend to their condition of the flesh, by which they are indeed servants, and their masters are masters. And it makes no difference whether they were bought, or born in the house, or are servants by human law. For I call this the "condition of the flesh," which is not from the spirit but from elsewhere. And the condition of the spirit does not abolish this, because it is not a sin, and one can be in such a state without sin. Both the servant serves without sin, and the master rules without sin. Neither serving nor ruling is, in itself, a sin. 

What then should such servants attend to? Surely the condition of the flesh in serving, humbling themselves in every way, and subjecting themselves. And they should attend to the condition of the spirit in order to love equally and to execute their service more diligently. <margin>2</margin> For how will they not love those whom they know to be brothers according to this spiritual condition? How, when they attend to the condition of the flesh and of fortune—or perhaps to some secret divine judgment—will they not serve more promptly those whom they know to be beloved? But beloved by whom? By Christ, the eternal king and Lord of all. There is certainly much more reason for them to serve such masters than to serve unbelieving masters; for although unbelieving masters bear the mark of power and lordship (for all power is from the Lord God), they are nonetheless not beloved by the Lord. This doctrine is of the spirit. 

<margin>41</margin> Therefore, he gives a mandate to Timothy—indeed, through Timothy to every herald of God—that he should teach thus, saying: <margin>3</margin> ¶ **These things teach and exhort. If any man teach otherwise and consent not to the sound words of our Lord JESUS CHRIST, and to that doctrine which is according to godliness: he is proud, knowing nothing.** <note>1 Timothy 6:2-4</note> But he is sick concerning questions and strifes of words, from which arise envy, contention, blasphemies, evil suspicions, and conflicts...

### COMMENTARY

...of men of corrupt minds and destitute of the truth, who think that godliness is a means of gain. ¶ The precepts set forth by Paul—who speaks the words of Christ <note>Latin: *Christiloquus*</note> and speaks the words of the Spirit <note>Latin: *spiritiloquus*</note>—and the things he commands to be taught and urged upon men, he says are not his own words. Rather, they are the words of the Spirit and the words of our Lord Jesus Christ. Those who teach otherwise boast in vain of their doctrine, for they know nothing, even if they think they know something. And so that we may recognize them, he gives us manifest signs. 

They are those who suffer from a diseased obsession with questions and <term>logomachies</term> <note>From the Greek *logomachia*, meaning "battles of words" or "verbal disputes."</note>, that is, battles over subtle phrasing. From these things bubble up envy, contention, and blasphemies. For when one man asserts something concerning divine matters, another immediately denies it; therefore, if one has spoken well, the other blasphemes. Their suspicions are evil, for as they contend with one another, they frequently suspect each other of holding wrong views regarding the faith. They are the "clashings of men of corrupt minds," for just as those with corrupted physical appetites fly at each other with nails and hands or even lethal weapons, so those with corrupt minds clash in vain and useless verbal battles for the sake of empty glory or profit. And how could they not be corrupt in mind, being destitute of the truth and thinking that godliness is a business? For truth is the very life of the mind. Why is it that they either utterly reject the doctrine of the Spirit, or interpret it in a fleshly way—or even lower than the dignity of the flesh? Would that our own times produced no such men, and that the present age were free from such monsters!

<margin>42</margin>
¶ But if such men shall exist—as the Apostle, seeing far off through the Spirit, teaches us what must be done—he says: ¶ **Stay far away from such people.** Truly, godliness with <term>sufficiency</term> <note>Latin: *sufficientia*; often translated as "contentment," meaning being satisfied with what is enough.</note> is a great gain. For we brought nothing into this world, and it is certain that we can take nothing out. Having food and covering, let us be content with these. ¶ Let us leave behind empty battles of words, which undoubtedly produce nothing but words; they are mere words and pure wordiness. Otherwise, they would not be called "empty." Let us instead follow the doctrines of godliness, which are the doctrines of the Spirit. From those things full of verbal battles and conflict, let us not seek empty glory or the profit of greed. Instead, by following the doctrine of godliness, we shall attain godliness itself—a gain that is truly great and sufficient in itself. Or at least it is a gain that lacks very little—not for its own sake, but for the sake of the flesh. Because of the flesh, it requires food (not much, but a moderate amount) and clothing by which the covered body may be defended from harm. One should not clothe oneself proudly in the manner of a peacock, a bird which bears upon itself the image of an angel turned inward, falling from heaven <note>A traditional moral allegory suggesting the peacock's beauty is a reminder of the pride of Lucifer.</note>. 

But why do you glory in external goods—in clothes or in riches—even if they are present for you through divine blessing and your own efforts without greed, as they were for Job, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob? When you consider that you brought nothing of all those things with you into this world, and you will take nothing of them with you when you leave, what else is left for you to boast in? Unless you are captured by the eye of reason, which is far inferior to the eye of the Spirit. ¶ But if you do not abound in riches, and you have no means to receive them through God's blessing and providence, why do you pant after them—things you cannot possess without greed? How can you think you possess them without greed when that very appetite of yours is the "greed of a corrupt reason"? Therefore, in your pursuit of godliness, be content with food and clothing. Do not desire to become rich, even if resources are present—and even less so if they are not. Hear the Apostle commanding and saying: ¶ **For those who want to become rich fall into temptation and a snare, and into many irrational and harmful desires, which drown men in destruction and perdition. For the root of all evils is the love of money.** <note>1 Timothy 6:9-10</note> Some, desiring this, have wandered from the faith and entangled themselves in many sorrows. 

<margin>43</margin>
¶ It is clear that <term>philargyria</term> <note>Greek for "love of silver" or "love of money."</note>—that is, the love and craving for silver and money—is the root of all evils. For it turns one away from the love of God. It deflects a love that is celestial by its very nature and holds it down to the earth, not unlike how the grease of a candle holds down the heavenly flame, acting as a greedy fuel for the lower parts. If the flame tries to flash upward, it is immediately extinguished. So it is with the mind of a greedy man: if it wishes to reach upward toward the love of God, it cannot, for being immersed in earthly things, it cannot live in the heights. 

The love of money, therefore, extinguishes the love of God, which is the greatest and chief evil. It extinguishes love for one’s neighbor; for the greedy man envies those with greater fortunes, or pants after the goods of one with moderate means. If a neighbor is entirely poor, the greedy man finds him a nuisance, fearing he might ask for or consume any of his things. To avoid losing any earthly profit, he violates the Sabbath and thinks it nothing to lose the profit of eternal life. If his parents are alive and wealthy, their life becomes a weariness to him; he longs for the death of both father and mother so that he may possess their riches and increase the pile of his unhappy greed. See how such people dishonor their parents! But how many now, because of the love of money, have violated the sacrament of the marriage bed, both men and women? I believe their wailing among the damned is most wretched. 

From where do thefts come? From where comes the longing for the wealth of others, if not from an insane love of money? How many people now seek after magistracies and honors just so they can become rich, because their purses are never full enough with coins? There is no species of evil that this venomous root, which the devil planted, does not produce. Thus, it is absolutely certain what the Spirit spoke through Paul: that the love of money is the root of all evils. Money itself is not that evil; it is not the root. Rather, it is the *desire* for money, which one must flee with the utmost effort. Nor is it enough merely to flee it, unless we also follow those things which the Apostle, the herald of God, here commands us to follow...
