# 1 Timothy

<insert>X</insert>

But you, O man of God: flee these things. Pursue: justice, piety, faith, love, patience, and gentleness. Fight the good fight of faith. Lay hold on eternal life, to which you are also called, and have confessed a good confession in the sight of many witnesses.

<margin>6</margin>
Timothy’s "fight" was against falsehood and against a lack of faith; by conquering and uprooting these, he was rewarded with eternal life, for this was the good will of God. Timothy confessed a good confession in the sight of many witnesses; for he publicly acknowledged our Lord Jesus as the Savior of all, born of a virgin, seen on earth, dead for our sins, and risen from the dead for our glory—along with all other things that are consistent with the most holy faith. Now Paul most strictly commands Timothy to keep what has been entrusted to him without violation. In the same way, every bishop ought to keep this command inviolably, as one who must give an account of these matters on the day of the Lord’s coming. He whom He—who alone is blessed, powerful, invisible, and immortal, the King and Lord of all—will visibly manifest in His own time. Therefore he says:

<margin>7</margin>
I charge you before God, who gives life to all things, and Christ Jesus, who testified a good confession under Pontius Pilate: that you keep the commandment immaculate and without reproach, until the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ. Which, in His own time, the blessed and only powerful King of kings and Lord of lords will show; He who alone has immortality, dwelling in inaccessible light, whom no man has seen, nor can see. To Him be honor and eternal power. Amen. Just as God gives "being" to all things, so He gives "living" to all who live. For He alone is the <term>essential being</term> <note>Latin: *entitas*</note> and the life of all things. But consider: what "good confession" did our Lord, the Savior and life-giver of all, testify under Pontius Pilate? "I am a king. For this was I born, and for this I came into the world: that I should bear witness to the truth. Everyone who is of the truth hears my voice." <note>A reference to John 18:37</note> Truly He is our King and the King of all, who came into this world and taught us all the truth that is to be valued, as well as all those who follow Him because they have heard His voice and obey His commands. He is the King of kings and Lord of lords, as the beloved disciple of God saw in a sacred vision. "He was clothed," he says, "in a garment sprinkled with blood, and His name was called the Word of God." And he adds: "And He has on His garment and on His thigh written: King of kings and Lord of lords." <note>A reference to Revelation 19:13-16</note> Furthermore, these titles—and that phrase "the blessed and only powerful"—He holds in common with the Father and the Holy Spirit; they relate to <term>affirmative theology</term> <note>Latin: *theologicam cataphasim*. Affirmative or "cataphasic" theology describes God by what He *is* (e.g., God is good, God is powerful).</note>. However, the things understood from what follows—"alone immortal," "inaccessible," "invisible," and "impossible to be seen"—pertain to a "sacred ignorance" concerning Him, a sacred silence not only on earth but also in heaven. This pertains to the theology which the leader of those who philosophize on sacred things, Dionysius, calls <term>negative theology</term> <note>Latin: *apophaticam*. Negative or "apophatic" theology describes God by what He is *not*, acknowledging that His nature exceeds human language and understanding.</note>. All these things apply to God absolutely and without limit. If any of these apply to others—such as blessedness, power, majesty, dominion, immortality, or invisibility—they apply only by "participation" and in a limited <note>Latin: *contracte*, meaning "contracted" or "drawn down" into a specific, finite form.</note> way. But things that participate compare to the absolute, and the limited to the unlimited, just as the finite compares to the infinite. For sight in a body is like a "limited" intellect, and physical desire is like a "limited" will. But just as physical sight is not the same as the intellect, and physical desire is not the same as the will, so if you compare angels and men to God in His absolute state—or rather, by an infinite degree more—they are neither blessed, nor powerful, nor do they even "exist," nor can they "exist." Yet they do exist and have power in their own way. For each thing's "way" of being is its limit. Therefore, God is "such a way" absolutely, without any limit, and above every limit. And just as the intellect is limited in various ways—appearing one way in a vision and another way in the imagination—so blessedness, power, and other things of that kind which are attributed to creatures only in a limited way, are limited differently in an angel than in a man. But (as is right) the Apostle attributes all these things in their unlimited state to God alone. 

But leaving aside these matters which pertain to the highest mode of philosophizing about God, he returns to giving Timothy a command for the rich of this world. For even they can be saved, if they turn their eyes and their hope. When they focus on earthly things, they become proud; let them be all the more humbled by focusing on heavenly things, which they are currently losing. They look to riches because they are "good"; let them look to God, because He is the Supreme Good and exceeds every other good. They love riches because they are delightful; let them love God much more, because He is the Supreme Delight. They trust in riches because they free them from needs in this world; let them turn and trust in God, because He truly frees them from all needs, not only in this world but also in the next, and He alone can free them. He alone gives true sufficiency; once possessed, the soul is no longer twisted or tortured by the desire to have more. His goods are most constant, most certain, and cannot be snatched away, providing life not for a short time, but for eternity.

<margin>8</margin>
Therefore, for such people, the Apostle sets down this holy and salvific command (if they will listen), saying: Command the rich of this world that they not be haughty, nor trust in the uncertainty of riches, but in the living God, who provides us all things richly for our delightful use; that they do good, that they be rich in good works, that they distribute easily, being ready to communicate, laying up in store...

# COMMENTARY

...laying up for themselves a good foundation for the future: that they may take hold of eternal life. <note>original: "sibijpsis fundamentum bonum in futurum: ut æternam vitam appræhendant," quoting 1 Timothy 6:19</note> This precept encompasses many things at once. First: that the wealthy should not be high-minded or proud. For pride usually accompanies the riches of this world; unless it is repressed through humility of heart, they cannot produce good fruit, nor come to life. Therefore, that opinion of thinking highly of oneself must be uprooted above all else. Second: that they should not hope in the uncertainty of their riches. It is uncertain how long their riches will last for them—or rather, how long they themselves will last for their riches. How then can they hope in things so uncertain on both sides? Instead, let them trust in the living God, the giver of all riches for truly delightful use. He is not an uncertain "good"; He lasts forever for everyone, and everyone will last forever for Him, either in the enjoyment of eternal blessings or in the hell of torments. Third: that they should do good with their riches. God did not make the sun to be idle; likewise, He did not make riches to be idle. He made all those things for use. A rich man who does not use his goods shuts a lit lamp in a chest; even with the lamp lit, he always has night. The liberal man, by contrast, always has his light in the open, just as if he were in the sun, never perceiving the night. For you know that He who dwells in heaven has no turn of nights and days, but is always in the day. Fourth: that they should be rich in good works. For gold, silver, income, and possessions are not true riches; rather, good works are the greatest riches, for they accompany divine graces. Next are the virtues of our own diligence and their works. Fifth: they should be easy and ready in contributing, and contributing well. For those who do so reluctantly and with difficulty still languish in the lethargy of avarice; the desire for money, which is the root of all evils, has not yet been cut away. Sixth: the wealthy should be "communicative" <note>This refers to the Greek term *koinonikous*, meaning a willingness to share or create community.</note>. For in this way they better understand to whom they should worthily impart the benefits of their goods. And by doing these things, they will be truly rich, storing up for themselves a good foundation for the future life in eternal edification.

<margin>47th point</margin>
He sets the final precept before Timothy: that he should guard the talent entrusted to him, the grace deposited with him, and that he should overturn and destroy heresies. And in this, he says farewell with a holy and pious valediction, as is his custom. He says: "O Timothy, guard the deposit: overturning profane vanities of words, and oppositions of knowledge <note>original: "gnoseos"</note> falsely so-called. Which some promising, have erred concerning the faith. Grace be with you. Amen." <note>1 Timothy 6:20-21</note> The first letter to Timothy was written from Laodicea.

It is the duty of bishops to instruct the faithful and convert those who have turned away. From the unfaithful, they must establish the faithful; they must overturn heresies and utterly uproot all vain learning, following the (albeit distant) imitation of the holy apostles who did all these things sublimely and powerfully. This the apostle commands Timothy to do here regarding the vanity of the Gnostics. For the Gnostics, according to Irenaeus <note>St. Irenaeus of Lyons (2nd century), an early Christian theologian who wrote "Against Heresies."</note>, flowed forth from Simon Magus <note>A figure mentioned in Acts 8 who tried to buy the power of the Holy Spirit; traditionally considered the first heretic.</note>. They took their name from *gnosis*, that is, "knowledge" or "science," but it was a name falsely given (as the apostle says). The "Gnostics" were also named falsely, for they call themselves "the ones who know," and yet they know nothing. They promise the science of faith, and they err from the faith. And their terms, like those of Simon Magus, are *cenophoniae* <note>original Greek: "kenophonias," meaning "empty sounds."</note>, that is, vain voices, empty of the reality they signify—much more so than the "Chimera" or "Hippocentaur" <note>Mythical creatures used here as examples of things that have names but no real existence.</note>. Simon Magus proposed a fiction: a certain power superior to the founder of the world, whom he called "God." The "God" of Simon Magus is an empty name; he denies the name of the true God so that he may attribute it to a fiction. Such are the fictions among the Gnostics: *Barbelo* <note>A major figure in Gnostic cosmogony.</note> as a masculine power, and *Ennaea* <note>Thought/Idea</note> as feminine, and an entire offspring: *Prognosis* <note>Foreknowledge</note>, *Aphtharsia* <note>Incorruptibility</note>, *Zoe* <note>Life</note>, *Phos* <note>Light</note>, *Nus* <note>Mind</note>, *Logos* <note>Reason/Word</note>, and *Thelema* <note>Will</note>. What "Barbelo," the fiction of their supreme power, actually sounds like is uncertain. The rest can be said in English: intelligence, foreknowledge, incorruptibility, life, light, mind, reason, will. These are certainly beautiful words, but (as they use them) they are utterly vain and fictitious. For they deny them to true things so that they may attribute them to fictions—things which are nothing and can be nothing. Even their "marriages" are fictions of demons: between *Ennaea* and *Logos*, *Aphtharsia* and *Phos* (whom they call Christ), incorruptibility and light, life and will, mind and foreknowledge. And the *Aeons* <note>original: "æones," meaning "ages" or "eternal beings" in Gnostic thought.</note>, that is, all their ages, are diabolical fictions. The names are indeed magnificent and curious, but no reality corresponds to them according to their understanding, nor can anything correspond, even if they think it does. Thus the devil mocked them with fictions. This chaff of magnificent names deceived not only the Gnostics and those seduced by them, but also many Platonists regarding "the One," "the Idea," and "the Soul of the World." These things, according to the understanding of the Platonists (to use Paul's word), are *cenophoniae*—voices empty of reality. (I would have said this with their peace, but I prefer the peace of Christ.) I wish them all well, and that they follow the teaching of the Holy Spirit. But that divine Socrates asserted these things. I might call him "divine" if it pleases anyone to call one "divine" who was taught by a *daemon* <note>A reference to the "daimonion" or inner voice Socrates claimed to follow.</note>. But what else would a demon teach concerning divine matters, except to lead one toward fictions through things that are most difficult and magnificent? For he hates true divinity, and rejoices to introduce the false and the feigned, mocking the more noble senses with a magnificent apparatus of words. But the multi-tongued hydra <note>A metaphor for a persistent and many-headed argument or opponent.</note> hisses that Augustine celebrated the "Idea."

The author critiques Gnostic and Platonic terminology as "empty voices" and fictions that distract from the true peace of Christ.</summary>

--- Page 549 ---
<meta>This page concludes the theological discussion of Christ as the "Idea" of God and transitions into a philological examination of 1 Timothy 6:2-4, specifically targeting the dangers of intellectual pride and "word-battles."</meta>

So be it. But clearly (as a holy man) he attributes the name of "Idea" to Christ, the Son of God, according to the Catholic <note>original: "catholicam," here meaning the universal or orthodox Church</note> understanding, not that of the Platonists. Porphyry, Plotinus, Iamblichus, Proclus, and the rest of the Platonist crowd <note>These were famous Neoplatonist philosophers who often opposed Christian doctrine</note> do not merely deny Him; they persecute Him and oppose His teaching. Their books are even now carried to the stars by more recent Platonists. And like Augustine, I also celebrate intelligence, incorruptibility, life, light, mind, reason, and the divine will—not according to a Gnostic <note>An early mystical sect deemed heretical</note> understanding, but according to a Christian, holy, and pious one. For the sin is not in the words, but in the understanding of the words and the adaptation of the mind. Therefore, let us leave these and those, and all empty-talkers, to their own devices; let us overturn all obstacles against the faith by repelling them from us at once, like snakes thrown within our borders. And let us follow Christ our King with true cognition and knowledge: celebrating Him through the study of sacred eloquence and never departing from the path of the Holy Spirit through vain curiosity or presumption of mind, confessing one God in substance, and three in hypostatic <note>original: "hypostaticis," referring to the individual persons of the Trinity</note> beatitudes. To whom belongs the perennial praise of all creatures, immortal honor, venerable power, the kingdom of all ages, and incomprehensible glory: for ever and ever. Amen.

<margin>40</margin>
### EXAMINATION of several points regarding the literal text.

¶ The Vulgate edition: *Because they are partakers of the benefit.* <note>original Latin: "Quia beneficij participes sunt," quoting 1 Timothy 6:2</note>
<margin>A</margin>
¶ It should read: *who [are] partakers of the benefit.* Paul wrote: *those who partake of the benefit.* <note>original Greek: "οἱ τῆς εὐεργεσίας ἀντιλαμβανόμενοι"</note>
<margin>A</margin>
¶ The Vulgate edition: *He is proud, knowing nothing, but languishing about questions and battles of words.* <note>original Latin: "Superbus / nihil sciens / sed languēs circa quæstiones & pugnas verborum," 1 Timothy 6:4</note> ¶ What the ancient translator calls "proud," in Paul’s writing is a verb in the past tense which signifies to be arrogant and to boast in vain. For those who taught otherwise than the apostles had handed down were arrogant in their teaching—daring and presuming things that should not be taught. In vain they boasted that they knew things they did not know. ¶ How many there are today who, having abandoned the doctrines of the apostles, are arrogant concerning divine matters: boasting in vain things, wasting away over questions and battles of words. These are among those whom the Spirit of the Lord showed to a certain religious man, Brother Robert, in a spiritual vision, as gnawing on a large, oblong stone. From this stone, the heads of two serpents protruded, with flickering tongues thrust out. I believe this vision is true, so that readers might recover their senses from such empty, frivolous, and fruitless studies. ¶ It is certainly best to contain oneself within the doctrine of the Sacred Scriptures and to insist upon an understanding of them that is not sought through human presumption, but through the inspiration of the Divine Spirit—or to follow the opinion of Peter in Clement <note>referring to the *Pseudo-Clementine Recognitions*, a work once attributed to Clement of Rome recording the deeds of St. Peter</note>. He said: "It must be diligently observed that when the law of God is read, it is not read according to the understanding of one's own ingenuity. For there are many words in the divine scriptures that can be pulled toward whatever sense each person has willfully presumed for himself. This ought not to happen. For you should not seek a foreign and strange sense brought in from the outside to confirm it by the authority of the scriptures; rather, you must take the sense of truth from the scriptures themselves. And therefore one must learn the understanding of the scriptures from him who keeps it as it was handed down to him by his elders according to the truth, so that he himself can competently assert the things he has rightly received." For when someone has received the whole and firm rule of truth from the divine scriptures, it will not be absurd if he also brings something from common education and the liberal studies (which he perhaps touched upon in his youth) to the assertion of true dogma. Provided, however, that where he has learned the truth, he shuns what is false and feigned. These are the words of Peter. Furthermore, the Sacred Scriptures are the most delicate bread, and the sacred spiritual understanding is the best celestial wine; both are the vital and most healthy food for our soul. Those who abandon this for empty battles of words are undoubtedly gnawing on a snake-bearing rock (profiting nothing for their life), similar to those whom Prudentius—a man worthy of God—execrates in his *Apotheosis* <note>a poem by the 4th-century Christian poet Prudentius defending the divinity of Christ</note>, saying:

> They loosen and bind the chains of questions
> Through twisted syllogisms.
> Woe to the deceptive tricks of the sycophants!
> Woe to the shifty cunning!

But if Paul, the apostle of Christ our God and Eternal Wisdom; if the Spirit of God in the prophetic vision; if Peter, the pillar of the church; if Prudentius—indeed, if no prudent man is listened to—how will our advice prevail? Unless Christ certainly raises them up, their minds are prostrate, rolling themselves of their own accord into the deepest hiding places and empty nonsense. And we know that for those who itch with that scabies <note>a metaphorical "itch" or disease of the mind</note>, our warnings do not please them, no differently than the antidotes of doctors and healthy medicines displease the sick. But a doctor does not stop giving warnings for that reason, and even heals if he can. We envy no one, we wish ill to no one; but if we can, we wish a great and healthy good. Paul wrote: *he is conceited and understands nothing, but is sick with questions and word-battles.* <note>original Greek: "τετύφωται μηδὲν ἐπιστάμενος, ἀλλὰ νοσῶν περὶ ζητήσεις καὶ λογομαχίας"</note> ¶ The Vulgate edition: *From which arise envies, contentions.* <note>original: "Ex quibus oriuntur inuidiæ / contentiones," 1 Timothy 6:4</note> ¶ According to Paul it is said in the singular: "is," "happens," "is produced," or "envy, strife, or contention arises." Paul wrote: *from which...* <note>original Greek: "ἐξ ὧν"</note>

<summary>This page concludes a defense of Christ as the divine "Idea" and begins a textual critique of 1 Timothy 6, warning against the "word-battles" and intellectual pride of those who ignore apostolic tradition.</summary>

...envy and strife arise. <note>original: "γίνεται φθόρος, ἔρις"</note> ¶ **Vulgate edition.** "Supposing that godliness is a means of gain." <note>1 Timothy 6:5</note> It is, however, a great gain. ¶ Immediately after "godliness," an entire short phrase is missing: "withdraw yourself" or "be far from such people." Paul says:
> "supposing that godliness is a means of gain; withdraw yourself from such people. But godliness is a great gain." <note>original: "νομιζόντων πορισμὸν εἶναι τὴν εὐσέβειαν, ἀφίστασο ἀπὸ τῶν τοιούτων, ἔστι δὲ πορισμὸς μέγας"</note>

¶ **Vulgate edition.** "They fall into temptation and the snare of the devil and many desires." ¶ "Of the devil" is redundant <note>It is an addition not found in the earliest Greek manuscripts of this specific verse</note>, even if it does not hinder the understanding of the passage. Paul says:
> "they fall into temptation, and a snare, and many desires." <note>original: "ἐμπίπτουσιν εἰς πειρασμὸν, καὶ παγίδα καὶ ἐπιθυμίας πολλάς"</note>

¶ **Vulgate edition.** "Useless and harmful." ¶ It would be better said as "senseless" or "irrational" and harmful. Paul says:
> "senseless and harmful." <note>original: "ἀνοήτους καὶ βλαβεράς"</note>

¶ **Vulgate edition.** "For the root of all evils is greed." ¶ "Greed" <note>original: "cupiditas"</note> expresses the idea more generally than what Paul says. For Paul’s word specifically designates the love of silver, money, and coin <note>original: "philargyria"</note>. It is this passion for which those who wish to become rich burn most intensely; our people name this foul disturbance of the soul with the single word "avarice." Paul says:
> "For the love of money is the root of all evils." <note>original: "ῥίζα γὰρ πάντων τῶν κακῶν ἐστὶν ἡ φιλαργυρία"</note>

<margin>
C
45
</margin>
¶ **Vulgate edition.** "Until the coming of our Lord JESUS CHRIST." ¶ Paul here uses "appearance" or "manifestation" rather than "coming." Paul says:
> "until the appearance of our Lord Jesus Christ." <note>original: "μέχρι τῆς ἐπιφανείας τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ"</note>

¶ **Vulgate edition.** "King of kings and Lord of lords." ¶ The old interpreter could have said "King of those reigning" <note>original: "rex regnantium"</note> just as he said "Lord of those dominating." Why did he not, by the same logic, translate the first part with a participle, as he did immediately in the second part? Paul says:
> "the King of those who reign, and Lord of those who rule." <note>original: "βασιλεὺς τῶν βασιλευόντων, καὶ κύριος τῶν κυριευόντων"</note>

¶ **Vulgate edition.** "And inhabits inaccessible light." ¶ Because the old interpreter changed a participle into a verb, he added a conjunction <note>the word "and"</note> to those things which Paul utters without that particle. Paul says:
> "dwelling in light inaccessible." <note>original: "φῶς οἰκῶν ἀπρόσιτον"</note>

¶ **Vulgate edition.** "But neither can be seen." ¶ It is better expressed in the active sense: "to see." Paul says:
> "whom no man has seen, nor is able to see." <note>original: "ὃν εἶδε οὐδεὶς ἀνθρώπων, οὐδὲ ἰδεῖν δύναται"</note>

<margin>
D
46
</margin>
¶ **Vulgate edition.** "Command them not to be high-minded, nor to hope in the uncertainty of riches." ¶ It has been stated elsewhere that our translators prefer to say "not to feel loftily" rather than "to be wise" <note>The Latin word "sapere" can mean both to be wise and to have a particular "flavor" or "mindset"</note>. And certainly, even in the abstract, it is called "uncertainty." Paul says:
> "Charge them... not to be high-minded, nor to have hoped in the uncertainty of riches." <note>original: "παράγγελλε μὴ ὑψηλοφρονεῖν, μηδὲ ἠλπικέναι ἐπὶ πλούτου ἀδηλότητι"</note>

¶ **Vulgate edition.** "Who provides us all things abundantly for enjoyment." <note>original: "ad fruendum"</note> ¶ For those who shrink from saying that we "enjoy" things bestowed even by divine providence, it will be borne with less anxiety if it is translated "for delightful use" or "delightful usage." And certainly, even spiritual men, participating in the good things of God, "enjoy" them—yet not so much the things themselves as God, the giver of the things. For when I consider that God dispenses all things so sweetly, how could I not take delight in the property of my Lord, especially since it belongs to my Lord who provides for every single thing so kindly and sweetly? And this is what it means to "enjoy" in this world; and for such enjoyment, God supplies us with all things. There is, however, another manner of "enjoying" in the world to come, of which this is not the subject. This word is clearly a homonym <note>A word that sounds the same but has different meanings</note> for both this and that manner of enjoyment. Paul says:
> "to the one providing us all things richly for enjoyment." <note>original: "τῷ παρέχοντι ἡμῖν πάντα πλουσίως, εἰς ἀπόλαυσιν"</note>

<margin>
D
47
</margin>
¶ **Vulgate edition.** "To communicate, to treasure up for themselves a good foundation for the future, that they may lay hold of the true life." ¶ In the beginning, Paul uses nouns and participles, not verbs. And there are manuscripts which, at the end, have "eternal life" rather than "true life." Paul says:
> "being generous, storing up for themselves a good foundation for the future, so that they may take hold of eternal life." <note>original: "κοινωνικούς, ἀποθησαυρίζοντας ἑαυτοῖς θεμέλιον καλὸν εἰς τὸ μέλλον, ἵνα ἐπιλάβωνται τῆς αἰωνίου ζωῆς"</note>

¶ **Vulgate edition.** "Avoiding profane novelties of words." ¶ It could be said: "turning away." And the word Paul uses signifies "vain and empty voices" rather than "new voices" or "novelties of words." Paul says:
> "turning away from profane, empty chatter." <note>original: "ἐκτρεπόμενος τὰς βεβήλους κενοφωνίας"</note>

¶ **Vulgate edition.** "And oppositions of knowledge falsely so called." ¶ What the old interpreter here calls "knowledge" <note>original: "scientiae"</note> is called *gnosis* by Paul—from which the "Gnostics" are named—which is wrongly and falsely named *gnosis*. For it is the very opposite of *gnosis* and indeed of true *gnosis*. Paul says:
> "and oppositions of knowledge falsely so called." <note>original: "καὶ ἀντιθέσεις τῆς ψευδωνύμου γνώσεως"</note>

And among the Greeks, the subscription is found: "The First to Timothy, written from Laodicea."

# THE ELEVENTH BOOK OF THE COMMENTARIES ON THE EPISTLES OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PAUL, WHICH IS ON THE SECOND EPISTLE TO TIMOTHY, CHAPTER I.

<margin>

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'I' featuring a vertical column or vine design within a square frame.</image-desc>

In this second epistle to Timothy, the apostle, according to his custom, provides this holy greeting, saying: ¶ **Paul, an apostle of CHRIST JESUS by the will of God, according to the promise of life which is in CHRIST JESUS our Lord.** ¶ To this holy greeting, as is his habit, he adds a thanksgiving and says: ¶ **I thank God, whom I serve from my forefathers with a pure conscience, that without ceasing I have remembrance of thee in my prayers night and day; greatly desiring to see thee, being mindful of thy tears, that I may be filled with joy; when I call to remembrance the unfeigned faith that is in thee, which dwelt first in thy grandmother Lois, and thy mother Eunice; and I am persuaded that it is in thee also.** ¶ Love does not permit forgetfulness, especially when it is the kind of love that longs for one who is absent. Paul was moved by such love toward Timothy, which made him mindful of him in his prayers. And in return, Timothy repaid Paul with a reciprocal love; there was a mutual and alternating love in both their holy hearts, more beautiful than that of **Pythias and Damon** <note>Pythias and Damon: Famous figures from Greek legend who represent the ultimate model of devoted friendship.</note>, for the faith of Christ and the mutual love of Christ united their affection. As evidence of Timothy’s true and unfeigned love, Paul notes the abundant tears which Timothy shed when leaving Paul due to the necessities of the Gospel—not to see him again until the end, after long hardships. For it was necessary for them to be separated, and they knew by a prophetic spirit what was to come. For Paul was a prophet, and Timothy was a prophet. So also, when Paul was at **Miletus** <note>A city on the coast of Asia Minor; this refers to the events in Acts 20.</note> and had called the elders of the church, he foretold to them that they would see his face no more in Asia, and he revealed what would happen to them (so that they might be cautious). And now, he said, **"behold, I know that ye all, among whom I have gone preaching the kingdom of God, shall see my face no more."** For which cause (as Luke testifies) there was great weeping among them all, and they fell on Paul's neck and kissed him, sorrowing most of all for the words which he spoke, that they should see his face no more. True love for the saints produced those tears and that weeping. So it was also in the faithful Timothy, who had both a grandmother and a mother commendable for their faith in God and their fervor; their names are written in blessing not only in this epistle, but also in the **Book of Life**. For this reason, he exhorts Timothy that—according to the gift of grace and the understanding of the prophecies and scriptures given to him through the laying on of Paul’s holy hands—he should stir up his fervor, boldly announce Christ, and reveal the truth of the doctrine. And in this manner Paul says:

<margin>
3
.
>
>
>
>
>
>
.
.
.
</margin>

¶ **For which cause I admonish thee that thou stir up the gift of God, which is in thee by faith and the putting on of my hands. For God hath not given us the spirit of fear, but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind** <note>original: "castimonie," often translated as sobriety or self-discipline</note>**. Be not thou therefore ashamed of the testimony of our Lord, nor of me his prisoner: but be thou partaker of the afflictions of the gospel according to the power of God; who hath saved us, and called us with an holy calling, not according to our works, but according to his own purpose and grace, which was given us in CHRIST JESUS before the world began; but is now made manifest by the appearing of our Savior JESUS CHRIST, who hath abolished death, and hath brought life and immortality to light through the gospel: whereunto I am appointed a preacher, and an apostle, and a teacher of the Gentiles. For the which cause I also suffer these things: nevertheless I am not ashamed.** ¶ When anything is committed to a person by God, if they possess timidity, coldness in their work, or a lack of confidence, this timidity, lukewarmness, and distrust are not from the Spirit of God. Rather, they arise from the fragility of human nature, which does not sufficiently commit itself to the Spirit and requires a "stirring up" <note>The Latin "exuscitet" suggests re-kindling a fire that has died down to embers.</note> to rouse the Spirit by overcoming one's own lethargy and the cowardice of one's own weakness. For the gifts of the Spirit are powerful and strong, not timid; they are fervent, not cold; they are trustful, not despairing. But because the burden committed by God to Timothy had been somewhat encroached upon by natural weakness—and because he did not retain the same love for saving souls, nor the same zeal and fervor as before—the Apostle rouses him with this holy and salutary admonition. Likewise, whoever possesses any gift of God, if they feel lethargy or some cowardice creeping in from themselves, they ought to immediately invoke divine help and, as much as they can, stir up the gift of God and rouse His grace. For Timothy used to preach and teach the office as usual, yet it was as if he were either afraid...

<header>COMMENTARY.</header>

<insert>2 Timothy 1</insert>

<margin>1</margin>
...should shrink back or be ashamed of the gospel of Christ and of Paul his teacher. Instead, Paul sets before him his own chains, which he bears willingly and joyfully for Christ, and the benefits of Christ: who has called us to the fellowship of angels and to all holiness—not because of the works we have done, but through his own predestination, which is his good and eternal will, and through his grace. This he preordained, predefined, and pre-willed before all ages. He manifested this good will and good grace through the appearance in the flesh of our Lord Jesus Christ. This was his first glorious coming, and by death he took away death from us—specifically, eternal death and the death of darkness—and he illuminated us with eternal life (the opposite of death), which is spiritual, radiant, and eternal, through the preaching of the gospel. Paul was appointed to this office by God as a preacher, a legate <note>original: "legatus"; a representative or ambassador</note>, and a teacher to the Gentiles. It was for the faithful execution of this office that he was cast into chains. But he was by no means confounded by these chains; rather, even in the midst of them, without any fear, he announced the name of the Lord, he labored, and he performed the work of an apostle. Therefore, seeing the noble struggle and the unconquered spirit of his teacher and father, Paul, how could Timothy not be stirred to fight bravely? This example ought to stir every bishop even now to perform the work of a bishop fearlessly and bravely, so that he may instill the holy gospel and the love of Christ—which alone gives life—into the hearts of the sheep entrusted to him. If this is not enough to stir one up, let Christ stir him, who stirred Paul, and who is powerful enough to save what has been entrusted to each person,

<margin>4</margin>
and to return a crown to every man who fights well, and punishment and disgrace to the one surrendered to laziness. For who could be confounded who fights under such and so great a prince? Therefore Paul adds: <margin>></margin> **For I know whom I have believed: and I am certain that he is able to keep my deposit <note>original: "depositum"; the "treasure" of faith or the gospel entrusted to a minister</note> until that day.** <margin>></margin> ¶ Neither Paul nor Timothy was able, by their own power, to preserve the grace entrusted and credited to them by God, nor to guard the fruit that depended on it for very long. Only Christ, who had entrusted the burden to them, was able to keep it—not only while they survived and worked, but even until the day of judgment. This he does even to the present day in countless faithful people who follow his doctrine through the teacher and steward Paul; and by his mercy he will do so until the last day, just as he who is truly faithful promised elsewhere, saying: *Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age.* But then is not the time to be sluggish, when the wolf attacks the sheepfold, when he rages in the fold, when he prowls. For at that time, the authors of sects and the impostors of deadly doctrine were becoming prominent. For this reason, the apostle exhorts Timothy

<margin>5</margin>
to be more stirred and vigilant than ever, and to remember the sound institutions <note>sound teachings or principles</note> which he received from him, <margin>></margin> saying: ¶ **Hold the form of sound words which thou hast heard from me in faith and love, which is in CHRIST JESUS. Keep the good deposit by the Holy Spirit who dwells in us.** <margin>></margin> ¶ What does it mean to "hold the form of sound words," if not to retain the words of sound doctrine which you received from me as a pattern and formula of the Holy Spirit? Who ought to change the "type" <note>The Greek word "typos" refers to a pattern, mold, or standard</note> of words which the Holy Spirit handed down? If anyone changes it, he mints an adulterated coin of doctrine and not a legitimate one—which is exactly what the heretics did. But what was deposited with Paul? What was committed to him, and also to Timothy through the Spirit, if not the "coin" and the faithful distribution of the "coin" of doctrine, whose fruit and profit would endure until the end of the ages? And at that time, the necessity of guarding the grace of the Holy Spirit and faithful doctrine was most pressing,

<margin>6</margin>
as was said: because many in Asia fell away from the faith and were corrupters of true <margin>></margin> doctrine. The apostle reveals this, saying: ¶ **This thou knowest, that all they which are in Asia be turned away from me; of whom are Phygellus and Hermogenes.** <margin>></margin> ¶ Phygellus and Hermogenes, having abandoned the true doctrine of Christ, followed the insanities of Simon the Samaritan (who is also Simon Magus) and of the Gnostics <note>Gnostics: A diverse group of early heretics who claimed special "gnosis" or secret knowledge</note>, opposing the holy institution of the apostle. Paul had also predicted this to the Asians when he was leaving for Jerusalem, knowing he would not see them again, so that he might instruct them through prophecy to beware of such things in the future. For he had predicted: *I know that after my departure ravaging wolves will enter among you, not sparing the flock; and from among your own selves men will arise speaking perverse things to lead away disciples after them. Therefore be vigilant.* But concerning Simon, Menander, Saturninus, Basilides, Harpocrates, Cerinthus, Ebion, Nicolaus, Cerdon, Marcion, Phygellus, Hermogenes, the Gnostics, and such hateful names and demonic madnesses: if anyone wishes to know more, let them read Irenaeus and Epiphanius <note>Irenaeus and Epiphanius: Early Church Fathers famous for writing extensive catalogs and refutations of various heresies</note>. They will find nothing of doctrine there, but will hear only the poisonous hissings of the twisted serpent. It is better to hear the piety of one alone than to have scanned the books of all the heretics—unless one carries with him such a strong antidote of faith that he can struggle against every

<margin>7</margin>
poison. Therefore, after censuring these men of impiety, Paul commends Onesiphorus of <margin>></margin> Ephesus, a man full of piety and integrity. And he says: ¶ **The Lord give mercy unto the house of Onesiphorus; for he oft refreshed me, and was not ashamed of my chain. But, when he was in Rome, he sought me out very diligently, and found me. The Lord grant unto him that he may find mercy of the Lord in that day: and in how many things he ministered unto me at Ephesus, thou knowest very well.** <margin>></margin> ¶ Behold, how...

XI 2 Timothy.

Godly men: they are not deprived of the prayers of the holy toward God. And what does it mean when it says, "may the Lord grant him to find mercy from the Lord" <note>2 Timothy 1:18</note>, except "may Christ Jesus grant him to find mercy from his Father!" With whom and the Holy Spirit he lives, reigns, and is glorified, for 
<margin>A</margin> all ages to come. Amen.

### EXAMINATION of certain points concerning the literal text.

<margin>1</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "To Timothy, my most dear son." ¶ **It is said:** "to my beloved son." Paul writes: <note>original Greek: "τιμοθέω τέκνω," meaning "to Timothy, my child"</note>. ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "From God our Father and CHRIST JESUS our Lord." ¶ **It should be said:** "from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord." In the first instance, the word "our" is redundant <note>it is added in the Latin but not present in the earliest Greek manuscripts</note>. Paul writes: <note>original Greek: "ἀπὸ θεοῦ πατρὸς καὶ Χριστοῦ Ἰησοῦ τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν," meaning "from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord"</note>. ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "I give thanks to my God, whom I serve from my forefathers with a pure conscience." ¶ Paul has "I am grateful," but the Latin custom is more commonly to say to God, "I give thanks." Also, the words "my" <note>referring to God</note> and "my" <note>referring to forefathers</note> are redundant. Paul writes: <note>original Greek: "χάριν ἔχω τῷ θεῷ, ᾧ λατρεύω ἀπὸ προγόνων ἐν καθαρᾷ συνειδήσει"</note>.

<margin>2</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "Recalling that faith which is in you, unfeigned, which also dwelt first in your grandmother Lois." ¶ **It can be said:** "of unfeigned faith," so that it refers back to the faith itself. Paul writes: <note>original Greek: "ὑπόμνησιν λαμβάνων τῆς ἐν σοὶ ἀνυποκρίτου πίστεως ἥτις ἐνῴκησε πρῶτον ἐν τῇ μάμμη σου Λωΐδι"</note>. ¶ There are also some manuscripts that have "recalling the unfeigned love and faith that is in you"—that is, "when I remember the unfeigned love which is in you, and the faith," and the rest that follows. Here, however, we have followed the manuscripts that agree with the ancient translator. ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "For which cause, I admonish you that you stir up the grace of God which is in you." ¶ **It can be said:** "the gift of God which is in you." Paul writes: <note>original Greek: "δι' ἣν αἰτίαν ἀναμιμνήσκω σε ἀναζωπυρεῖν τὸ χάρισμα τοῦ θεοῦ, ὅ ἐστιν ἐν σοί"</note>.

<margin>3</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "A spirit of fear, but of power, and of love, and of sobriety." ¶ **It can be said:** "a spirit of cowardice, but of authority." Paul writes: <note>original Greek: "πνεῦμα δειλίας, ἀλλὰ δυνάμεως, καὶ ἀγάπης, καὶ σωφρονισμοῦ"</note>. ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "According to the virtue of God, who has delivered us and called us with his holy calling." ¶ **It should rather be said:** "according to the power or authority of God, who has saved us and called us with a holy calling." Paul writes: <note>original Greek: "κατὰ δύναμιν θεοῦ, τοῦ σώσαντος ἡμᾶς, καὶ καλέσαντος κλήσει ἁγίᾳ"</note>. ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "But according to his own purpose." ¶ The word used here, "purpose," is usually explained this way, but it signifies the same thing as "will": that which pre-ordained and pre-willed all things even before they were created. Therefore, "according to his purpose" and "according to his will" mean the same thing, but this latter term is perhaps clearer. For this reason, we have used it; indeed, in another place, Paul says of God, "Who wills all men to be saved." Paul writes: <note>original Greek: "ἀλλὰ κατ' ἰδίαν πρόθεσιν," meaning "but according to his own plan/purpose"</note>.

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "But it has now been made manifest through illumination." ¶ **Equally, "through the appearance."** Paul writes: <note>original Greek: "φανερωθεῖσαμ μῦν διὰ τῆς ἐπιφανείας," meaning "made manifest now through the epiphany/appearing"</note>. ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "Life and incorruption." ¶ **It can be said:** "life and incorruptibility." Paul writes: <note>original Greek: "ζωὴν καὶ ἀφθαρσίαν"</note>. ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "Hold the form of sound words."

<margin>6</margin> ¶ **The ancient translator** <note>referring to the author of the Vulgate</note> says "form" here; yet in the first chapter of the preceding epistle, he says "instruction" <note>original: "informationem"</note> where he says, "For the instruction of those who are to believe." Why did he not also translate it as "instruction" here? Paul writes: <note>original Greek: "ὑποτύπωσιν ἔχε ὑγιαινόντων λόγων," where "hypotypōsin" suggests a sketch, pattern, or model</note>. ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "For you know this, that they have turned away from me." ¶ The word **"For"** is redundant. Paul writes: <note>original Greek: "οἶδας τοῦτο, ὅτι ἀπεστράφησάν με"</note>.

### CHAPTER II.

<image-desc>Woodcut decorative initial N depicting a figure in a landscape within a square frame</image-desc>
<margin>8</margin> Now Paul exhorts Timothy to grow strong and regain his strength in the execution of that grace which he obtained from Christ the Lord, and in those things which he heard from Paul himself, confirmed by the testimony of many prophets and others. He says, therefore: ¶ **"You therefore, my son, be strong in the grace that is in CHRIST JESUS: and the things that you have heard from me through many witnesses, these commend to faithful men, who shall be fit to teach others also."** ¶ What does "commend to faithful men" mean, except to hand over and communicate! It is the duty of bishops to grow strong both in public—not slackening in their labor—and in private discernment, possessing a more eminent grace of a purer life and a greater example of humanity and love toward men. It is their duty to instruct them and to commit to them the care of preaching in various places, and not to allow just anyone who wishes to do so. For those whose lives are despised ought to be barred from this kind of office. For in such people, as one of the saints says, nothing remains except for the sermon to be held in contempt; or rather, that the word of God, which is taken up through the mouths of such men, should be deprived of its due honor. Let him also bar those who hawk the word of God <note>original: "cauponantur," implying those who treat the Gospel like a retail business for profit</note>, preaching for gain and not out of zeal for saving souls; for such men are neither suitable nor sufficient.

...counterfeit: but neither ought we to be ashamed of the **word of truth**. <note>original: "verbum veritatis"</note> For whoever is ashamed of it is also ashamed of Christ, who is Truth itself. For it is not handled correctly if you transfer it to something else or apply it to those of whom it was not spoken—and even less so if you empty the divine voices into fictions <note>referring to imaginative or allegorical inventions that depart from the literal sense</note> and your own personal opinions. Therefore, Paul adds a third precept, saying: <margin>3</margin> ¶ **But resist profane and empty babbling.** For otherwise, they will progress further toward impiety, and their speech will spread like gangrene <note>literally "cancer" in the Latin text</note> seeking fodder. Among these are **Hymenaeus and Philetus**, who have wandered away from the truth, saying that the **resurrection has already happened**, and they have subverted the faith of some. Nevertheless, the **solid foundation of Christ** <note>original: "CHRISTI solidum stetit fundamentum"</note> stands firm, having this seal: The Lord knows those who are His. ¶ "The future resurrection" is a holy and beautiful name, which Hymenaeus and Philetus hold in vain, saying that what the apostle preached was nothing, and that the resurrection has already happened—claiming that our fathers have already risen in their children, and we rise in our children, and that the resurrection is nothing other than the procreation of offspring. See how they took the name of resurrection according to the custom of the sacred scriptures and made it empty. Moreover, although the name of resurrection was not a fiction (for the procreation of children is not a fiction), they applied it to something other than what was intended and transferred it elsewhere. In the case of **Saturninus** <note>A second-century Gnostic teacher from Antioch who taught that marriage and procreation were from the devil</note>, the devil condemns marriage, saying it is evil and the work of Satan. But in **Hymenaeus and Philetus**, he lays snares for chastity and modesty, and indeed the state of virginity itself, as if it were evil, and he denies true immortality—which cannot come to us without a true resurrection—filling everything with lies, as he is the father of lies. But the truth shall conquer; the foundation of faith laid by Christ has stood firm, and you have this seal—that is, the true resurrection—engraved and impressed upon it. <margin>A e</margin> ¶ And though this seal did not remain with everyone, it nevertheless remained with those who are faithful. For these are they whom God knows; the others He does not know, because they are not His, but belong to the side of the malignant one, with whom is all injustice and every lie. ¶ And how did they dare to name the name of Christ, being of such a sort? For He Himself is Justice and Truth. <margin>14 Truth.</margin> Therefore, the apostle adds a fourth precept, saying: <margin>4</margin> ¶ **And let everyone who names the name of the Lord depart from injustice.** <margin>15</margin> ¶ But someone will say: How does Christ sustain among His own some who name His name unworthily (even if they ought not to), how, I ask, does He sustain such just-appearing liars and idle talkers? Paul satisfies this question, saying: ¶ **In a great house, however, there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and clay; and some indeed are for honor, while others are for dishonor.** <margin>a r</margin> If anyone, therefore, cleanses himself from these, he will be a vessel for honor, sanctified and useful to the Lord, prepared for every good work. <margin>o t</margin> ¶ The house of Christ is a great house. For He is the King of kings and Lord of lords, in which there are various vessels: precious and not precious. The precious ones are true, faithful, radiant, and holy. The not-precious ones are false, unfaithful, dark, and unclean. But He sustains these (which is His own goodness) so that they might cleanse themselves from falsehood, infidelity, darkness, and uncleanness; so that, having received truth and faithfulness, they might shine and be holy, of great use to the King for every good work, for the use of grace and mercy. Otherwise, they will be assigned to uses of dishonor, serving divine justice in the places of torment. For all men were created to be vessels of mercy, even if not all attain their end; yet they cannot escape being a vessel either of mercy or of justice. And what does "If anyone therefore cleanses himself from these, he will be a vessel for honor" mean, unless <margin>16</margin> it means if he cleanses himself from the errors of Hymenaeus and Philetus, and other errors and injustices, he shall become a vessel sanctified for honor? <margin>5</margin> Paul adds a fifth precept, saying: ¶ **Flee also youthful desires. But pursue justice, faith, love, and peace with those who call upon the Lord from a pure heart.** ¶ This forbids all lusts, especially those that draw one toward every pleasure and the softening of the soul. For the young follow these most of all: such as banquets, games of all kinds, dice, ball games, hunting, dogs, birds, bows, care for one's physical appearance, more curious displays of clothing, and that sort of thing, which ought least of all to be pursued by a consecrated man, but rather fled. And he sets down this precept not so much for the sake of Timothy, whom he knew to be a holy man, but for the sake of the others who would attain a similar rank of dignity. For in Timothy and Titus, he instructs every bishop and ecclesiastical man. Oh, how unbecoming it is to see a bishop soliciting drinking companions, intent on games, handling dice, gaming-towers <note>original: "pyrgos," a device used to prevent cheating with dice</note>, or tokens, occupied with dogs and birds and fowling, howling at the capture of a jackdaw or a wild beast, entering the women's quarters <note>original: "gyneceum"</note>, holding young girls in his lap, mixing soft words with kisses, and nearly drawing out the wool <note>a metaphor for engaging in feminine domestic tasks or wasting time in idle, effeminate luxury</note>, or if not drawing the threads, yet breaking them. ¶ They are worthy of a punishment greater than that of **Sardanapalus** <note>A legendary Assyrian king who became a symbol of extreme luxury, decadence, and effeminacy</note>. These youthful desires are too much, and they are surely unworthy of such a rank—indeed, of any ecclesiastical status, even the lowest. Instead, let them pursue things worthy of a man. These are manly things and worthy of a man: to follow justice, which are the works of the divine law; to follow faith, love, and peace with all the faithful who are truly faithful. For they are those who [call upon the Lord] from a pure [heart].

[mili]tes **Jesus Christ**. <note>The text begins mid-word, likely completing "milites," meaning soldiers.</note> No one who serves as a soldier entangles himself in the business of life, so that he may please the one who chose him for service. <margin>14</margin><margin>4</margin>¶ **And let everyone who names the name of the Lord depart from injustice.** <margin>15</margin>¶ But someone might ask: How does Christ sustain such people—the unjust, the liars, and the empty talkers—among His own, who name His name unworthily (even though they should not)? Paul satisfies this question, saying: ¶ **In a great house, there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and earthenware; and some are for honor, but others for dishonor. If anyone, therefore, purges himself from these, he will be a vessel for honor, sanctified and useful to the Lord, prepared for every good work.** ¶ The house of Christ is a "great house," for He is the King of kings and Lord of lords. In it, there are various vessels: precious and not precious. The precious ones are the true, faithful, radiant, and holy. The non-precious are the false, unfaithful, dark, and unclean. But He sustains these (which is His own goodness) so that they might purge themselves from falsehood, infidelity, darkness, and uncleanness; so that, having received truth and faithfulness, they might shine and be holy, of great use to the King for every good work, in the service of grace and mercy. Otherwise, they will be assigned to uses of dishonor, serving divine justice in the places of torment. For all men were created to be vessels of mercy, even if not all attain their end. Yet they cannot escape being a vessel of either mercy or justice. And what does it mean, "if anyone purges himself from these, he will be a vessel for honor," except that if he purges himself from the errors of Hymenaeus and Philetus, and from other errors and injustices, he will become a vessel sanctified for honor? 

Paul adds a fifth precept, saying: <margin>5</margin>¶ **Flee youthful desires. But pursue justice, faith, love, and peace with those who call on the Lord from a pure heart.** ¶ This forbids all concupiscence, especially those things that lead to every pleasure and the softening of the soul. For young men follow these things most of all, such as banquets, games of all kinds, dice, ball-games, hunting, dogs, birds, bows, concern for appearance, more curious displays of clothing, and that sort of thing—which are the least to be pursued by a consecrated man, but rather fled. And he sets down this precept not so much for Timothy, whom he knew to be a holy man, as for the others who would attain a similar rank of dignity. <margin>S</margin>For in Timothy and Titus, he instructs every bishop and man of the Church. 

Oh, how unseemly it is to see a bishop stirring up drinking companions, intent on games, handling dice, dice-boxes, or tokens, occupied with dogs and birds and fowling, shouting at the capture of a crow or a wild beast, entering the women's quarters, <note>original: "gyneceū"</note> holding young girls in his lap, mixing soft words with kisses, and almost drawing out the wool-spindles <note>A metaphor for effeminate or domestic behavior unsuited to the office.</note>—or if not drawing them, at least breaking the threads. ¶ They are worthy of a greater punishment than Sardanapalus. <note>Sardanapalus was a legendary king of Assyria, often cited in classical literature as the ultimate symbol of luxury and effeminacy.</note> These desires are far too youthful and certainly unworthy of such a rank, or indeed of any ecclesiastical state, even the lowest. Instead, let them pursue things worthy of a man. These are the manly things: to follow justice, which are the works of the divine law; to follow faith, love, and peace with all the faithful who are truly faithful. And those are the ones who [act] from a pure [heart]...

<header>COMMENTARY</header>

17 ...who call upon the name of our Lord from a [pure] heart: and do all things in his name. Paul adds a sixth precept, saying: ¶ **Avoid foolish and unlearned questions: knowing that they breed quarrels. But the servant of the Lord ought not to quarrel, but be mild toward all, apt to teach, patient, with modesty correcting those who resist: if perhaps God may give them repentance to know the truth: and they may recover themselves from the snare of the devil, by whom they are held captive at his will.** <note>This passage translates 2 Timothy 2:23–26.</note> ¶ It is not only unbecoming for a bishop or any man of the Church to stir up foolish questions that contribute nothing to Christian discipline, but it is also unbecoming to even struggle and argue with those who do stir them up. For the apostle strictly forbids these kinds of "battles of words." For both the bishop and men of the Church are servants of God and those who approach most closely to the Lord—who is most mild, most wise, and most merciful; who teaches all men knowledge, and who wishes to save rather than to destroy. It is therefore not fitting for his servants to engage in these kinds of word-battles. Instead, they should show the mildness and teachability of the Lord, mercy, and a gentle correction even of those who resist wisdom and discipline through such foolish and unlearned ways. For in this way it may happen that God touches the hearts of opponents and leads them to repentance, giving them wisdom instead of folly and discipline instead of lack of restraint. Thus, they may be freed from the snare of the devil, who holds them at his whim while they still lead this mortal life. But if you fight with these same foolish and unlearned men with words, you do not untangle them from that snare; rather, you entangle them further, and yourself along with them. From which may the Lord Jesus, the eternal wisdom and discipline of peace, defend us and all people—He who is the King of Peace, blessed in all things and above all ages. Amen.

<margin>A 9</margin>
¶ **EXAMINATION of several points regarding the literal text.** ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** <note>The "Vulgate" refers to the standard Latin Bible translation used in the Western Church.</note> *Labor as a good soldier of CHRIST JESUS.* ¶ **Rather:** *Therefore, you must endure fatigue, be busy, and apply yourself as a good soldier of Jesus Christ.* Paul [says]: <note>original Greek: σὺ οὖν κακοπάθησον ὡς καλὸς στρατιώτης Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ</note> "You therefore suffer hardship as a good soldier of Jesus Christ." ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *No one soldiering for God entangles himself in secular business, so that he may please him to whom he has proven himself.* ¶ [The words] "For God" and "himself" are redundant. And it should rather be read this way: *No one who serves as a soldier is entangled in the business of life, so that he may please the one who chose him for military service.* Paul [says]: <note>original Greek: οὐδεὶς στρατευόμενος ἐμπλέκεται ταῖς τοῦ βίου πραγματείαις, ἵνα τῷ στρατολογήσαντι ἀρέσῃ</note> "No one serving as a soldier entangles himself in the affairs of life, that he may please the one who enlisted him." ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *For even he who strives in a contest shall not be crowned.* ¶ [The words] "In a contest" are redundant. And "but" should be said rather than "for." Also, "is crowned" should be in the present tense; and in this way it should be read: *But if anyone also competes, he is not crowned [unless he competes lawfully].* Paul [says]: <note>original Greek: ἐὰν δὲ καὶ ἀθλῇ τις, οὐ στεφανοῦται</note> "And if anyone also competes, he is not crowned." There are also manuscripts that have <note>original Greek: ἀθλητής</note> "athlete" or "pugilist." Then it would have to be read: "but if he is also a pugilist." I think that the manuscripts which have it in this latter way are 
<margin>B 10</margin>
faulty, and have conflated one word—"athlete"—out of two words—"if anyone competes"—having been misled by the similarity of the sound and the accent. <note>The author is performing "textual criticism," arguing that a scribe accidentally merged two Greek words into one similar-sounding word.</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Be mindful that JESUS CHRIST has risen from the dead.* ¶ [The word] "that" is redundant. Paul [says]: <note>original Greek: μνημόνευε Ἰησοῦν χριστὸν ἐγηγερμένον ἐκ νεκρῶν</note> "Remember Jesus Christ, raised from the dead." ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *In which I labor even to bonds like an evildoer.* ¶ Not "evildoer" <note>original: male operas</note> but rather "criminal" <note>original: maleficus</note> it should have. Paul [says]: <note>original Greek: ἐν ᾧ κακοπαθῶ μέχρι δεσμῶν, ὡς κακοῦργος</note> "In which I suffer hardship even to bonds, as a criminal." ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Which is in CHRIST JESUS with heavenly glory.* ¶ In the Greek it is read: *with eternal glory.* Paul [says]: <note>original Greek: τῆς ἐν χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ μετὰ δόξης αἰωνίου</note> "Which is in Christ Jesus with eternal glory." ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *If we shall sustain, we shall also reign with him; if we shall deny, he also will deny us.* ¶ What the old translator said as "we shall sustain" and "we shall deny" [in the future tense] are in the present tense in Paul. Why then did he not make them present, just as in the phrase he immediately added, "if we do not believe, he remains faithful"—why this one rather than the others? Paul [says]: <note>original Greek: εἰ ὑπομένομεν, καὶ συμβασiλεύσομεν, εἰ ἀρνούμεθα, κἀκεῖνος ἀρνήσεται ἡμᾶς</note> "If we endure [present], we shall also reign with him; if we deny him [present], he also will deny us." 
<margin>C 11</margin>
¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Remind them of these things, testifying before the Lord: do not contend in words.* ¶ It should rather be said: *not to contend in words*, that is, so that *they* do not contend in words. For "to contend" <note>original: contendere</note> is an infinitive, and it refers back to the preceding verb "remind" or "admonish." Nor is it said concerning Timothy, but concerning those who are being admonished, so that Timothy might give that precept to those for whom his care of admonition was intended. Paul [says]: <note>original Greek: ταῦτα ὑπομίμνησκε διαμαρτυρόμενος ἐνώπιον τοῦ κυρίου μὴ λογομαχεῖν</note> "Remind them of these things, testifying before the Lord not to fight about words." ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *For it is useful for nothing, except for the subversion of the listeners.* ¶ "For" and "except" are redundant. And the neuter concrete is turned into an abstract in fit speech, after the custom of the Latins. And when the old translator says "it is useful for nothing, except," he seems to leave some utility to the battle of words. Which Paul neither leaves nor seems to leave; but rather this meaning: *admonish them not to contend in words to the subversion of the listeners, for no utility.* 
<margin>C 13</margin>
Paul [says]: <note>original Greek: εἰς οὐδὲν χρήσιμον, ἐπὶ καταστροφῇ τῶν ἀκουόντων</note> "To no useful purpose, for the ruin of the hearers." ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *But avoid profane and empty babblings.* ¶ "And" and "babblings" are redundant. And what the old translator calls "empty babblings" <note>original: vaniloquia</note>, he calls "novelties of voices" near the end of the previous epistle, where he says: *O Timothy, guard the deposit, avoiding profane novelties of voices.* We, however, have said that the word designates "vanities of voices" rather than "novelties." Which this same translator also hints at here, when he translates the same word as "empty babblings," which is more correctly "vanities."

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Second Epistle to Timothy, Chapter 2. Following the previous discussion on the conduct of God's servants, the author now provides a detailed linguistic critique of the Latin Vulgate Bible by comparing it to the original Greek text, before moving into a prophetic warning about the "last days" in Chapter 3.</meta>

<margin>a</margin>
I would believe we should say "voices" or "the vanities of voices" (as we have already said). Paul writes: **Avoid profane babblings.** <note>original Greek: "τὰς δὲ βεβήλους κενοφωνίας περιίστασο"</note> ¶ The Vulgate edition says: *For they profit much toward ungodliness: and their speech spreads like a cancer.* ¶ It should rather be said: "they will progress," using the future tense—that is, they will move forward and gain momentum. And at the end, it should not say "spreads like a cancer," but "will have pasture like a cancer." For a "cancer" is a disease that consumes the limb upon which it settles; it is called **gangrene** <term>gangræna: a localized death of body tissue</term> by the Greeks. Paul writes: **For they will progress further in ungodliness, and their word will have pasture like gangrene.** <note>original Greek: "ἐπὶ πλεῖον γὰρ προκόψουσιν ἀσεβείας, καὶ ὁ λόγος αὐτῶν ὡς γάγγραινα νομὴν ἕξει"</note>

<margin>b c</margin>
¶ The Vulgate edition says: *But the firm foundation of God stands.* ¶ It should be said "of Christ stood," not "of God stands." Paul writes: **Nevertheless, the solid foundation of Christ has stood.** <note>original Greek: "ὁ μέντοι στερεὸς θεμέλιος τοῦ χριστοῦ ἕστηκεν"</note> ¶ The Vulgate edition says: *Everyone who invokes the name of the Lord.*

<margin>14</margin>
¶ Here it is better to have "who names" rather than "who invokes." For if it were to be said "who invokes," Paul would have written here **invoking** <note>original Greek: "ἐπικαλούμενος"</note>, as he does near the beginning of the First Epistle to the Corinthians, and a little further down where it is written "with those who invoke the Lord from a pure heart." But now he does not have it so, but rather **naming** <note>original Greek: "ὀνομάζων"</note>, which is aptly translated as "naming" or "he who names." Paul writes: **Everyone who names the name of the Lord.** <note>original Greek: "πᾶς ὁ ὀνομάζων τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ κυρίου"</note>

<margin>d 16 17</margin>
¶ The Vulgate edition says: *But follow justice, faith, hope, and charity, and peace.* ¶ "Hope" and the double use of the conjunction "and" are superfluous additions here. Paul writes: **Pursue righteousness, faith, love, peace.** <note>original Greek: "Δίωκε δὲ δικαιοσύνην, πίστιν, ἀγάπην, εἰρήνην"</note> ¶ The Vulgate edition says: *With modesty correcting those who resist the truth.* "The truth" is a superfluous addition. Paul writes: **In meekness instructing those who oppose themselves.** <note>original Greek: "ἐν πραότητι παιδεύοντα τοὺς ἀντιδιατιθεμένους"</note> And immediately there follows **lest perhaps** <note>original Greek: "μή ποτε"</note>, "if peradventure," or "lest by any means." ¶ The Vulgate edition says: *By whom they are held captive.* ¶ It should rather be said "who were held captive or conquered by him," using the imperfect past tense. And the Greek word contains something a little more. For **I am taken alive** <note>original Greek: "ζωγρέομαι"</note> signifies being held captive and bound, and indeed something more: for it means being taken "alive." It is, therefore, as if we were to say: "who were held bound alive by him," that is, by the devil. For there are some over whom the devil has no power while they are still in this life; but if one does not recover one's senses before the moment of death, after the fates of this life are paid, they are held captive and bound by the devil—but not while they lived. But regarding those of whom Paul speaks: even while they live, they are held bound by the devil, and yet, always with the help of divine aid, they can recover their senses unto repentance; otherwise the apostle would not have said: "lest perhaps God give them repentance to the acknowledgment of the truth." What then of those over whom the devil was granted no power while they lived, so as to be conquered by him? Would they not find a place for repentance and recovery much more easily? How many now has the grace of the Prince freed from the executioner after they were bound? In how many was no power granted to the executioners even while they lived, but it was granted after they died, because the same stubbornness that accompanied life also accompanied death? But God is the Prince of Princes, and above all principalities; whose power is recognized nonetheless in every power ordained by a prince, just as visibility is in every color through the power of light (through which all things are seen). For the power of God is that through which all power exists, and without which no power can act, just as without light, no color can be seen. Paul writes: **Having been taken captive alive by him.** <note>original Greek: "ἐζωγρημένοι ὑπ' αὐτοῦ"</note>

<margin>22</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative initial E featuring a figure of a person standing amidst foliage.</image-desc>The apostle sets down a prophecy concerning the last times, so that Timothy might recognize those who will exist in the last times and flee from them; thus he prophesies, saying: ¶ **But know this, that in the last days perilous times shall come. For men shall be lovers of their own selves, covetous of money, boasters, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, unthankful, unholy, without natural affection, truce-breakers, false accusers, incontinent, fierce, despisers of those that are good, traitors, heady, high-minded, lovers of pleasures more than lovers of God; having a form of godliness, but denying the power thereof: from such turn away.** ¶ Since we see all men everywhere to be such as these, especially those who are in positions of leadership, let us suspect that we have come into the times of which the apostle prophesies. These times will not be healed until men—by the mercy of God, through many plagues and tribulations (as the holy Apocalypse shows)—are converted to opposite ways of living. And then there will be "easy times" for finding salvation. For then men will be lovers not of themselves, but of God; not covetous of money or earthly things, but of heavenly things; esteeming themselves as nothing but being humble; pious in speech; obedient to parents and elders; thankful, and continually giving thanks to God; holy; tenacious of faith and covenants; falsely accusing no one; continent; mild; lovers of good things; not at all deceitful, but of good faith and simple; reverent; modest; not followers of pleasures, but rather chastening the flesh and rejoicing in the imitation of the sufferings of Christ; having the true form of piety and religion, and demonstrating its power. ¶ O easy times for salvation! And how happy are those who happen to be born in these times. ¶ How difficult are our own times, and how difficult it is for salvation to be found in ours. But in all things let God be blessed, who with his own hands pulled Peter—who was of little faith and doubting—out of the abyss of destruction. Even now he walks upon the waters, so that he may pull out those who do not trust in themselves, but cry out to him from such great dangers. No other hope of salvation is left. Which surpasses...

->HEADER: COMMENTARY<-

They say: <note>original: "ferunt"</note> they indicate future things. But God alone knows the times—as do those to whom He deigns to reveal them. Moses indicated Christ. The miracles of Moses indicated the miracles of Christ. Aaron indicated Peter. The magicians of Pharaoh indicated Simon Magus, Dositheus, Hermogenes, and others who, by the power of Christ, succumbed to the apostles.

¶ In the time of Paul and Timothy, hypocrites who feigned religion—
> <margin>19</margin> while remaining ignorant of its power, or rather, denying and attacking it, and introducing a false and feigned version—were a sign of the hypocrites of the last times. ¶ Therefore Paul adds: **For of this sort are they who creep into houses, and lead captive silly women laden with sins, who are led away with diverse desires. Who are always learning, and never attaining to the knowledge of the truth. Now as Jannes and Jambres resisted Moses, so these also resist the truth, men corrupted in mind, reprobate concerning the faith. But they shall proceed no further, for their folly shall be manifest to all, as theirs also was.** <note>Paul references Jannes and Jambres, who according to Jewish tradition were the names of the Egyptian magicians who opposed Moses (Exodus 7:11).</note>

¶ And the madness and impotence of Dositheus, Simon Magus, Hermogenes, Harpocras, and other magicians—who opposed the true doctrine of Christ with deceit, and performed false signs and false wonders instead of true signs and virtues—was made open, just as the impotence of Pharaoh's magicians, whom the apostle names, was made open. Nor should one ask here where he took their names; for he who asks this seems to be ignorant of what it means to prophesy. For he who prophesies receives names from the Holy Spirit. Thus Isaiah the prophet named Cyrus long before he was born. And just as all heresies and hypocrites were made manifest before the end of the apostles and disciples, so also the heresies and pretenders of religion in the last times shall be made manifest; the truth will be open, as will the understanding of the spirit. The fictions of doctrines shall cease, as will the inventions of men and the false miracles and signs. Then the glory of the martyrs and the true saints shall be clear and open in the one faithful Witness in heaven, the Holy of Holies. The gain of foolish piety will be recognized as impiety and a trap of avarice. In Paul, in the apostles, and in the disciples, there was true doctrine, true character—or more truly, true divine graces (which transcend character)—true imitations of Christ's passions, true signs, and true powers:

> <margin>20</margin> all of which Timothy followed. In these things the apostle also praises him, so that he may be confirmed in perseverance, saying: ¶ **But you have fully known my doctrine, manner of life, purpose, faith, longsuffering, love, patience, persecutions, and afflictions which came to me at Antioch, at Iconium, and at Lystra; what persecutions I endured, and out of them all the Lord delivered me. And all who will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution. But evil men and seducers shall grow worse and worse, deceiving and being deceived.**

What does it mean that they "shall grow worse," except that they shall lead many to destruction, being themselves the first to go toward destruction? Truly, in the end, they shall not succeed; it shall not go for them according to the wickedness of their depraved will, but (as was said) their uncovered crimes shall lie open. For God permits malice and falsehood to grow strong up to a certain point; but when it reaches its limit, it is suddenly ruined, and goodness 
> <margin>21</margin> and truth exult as victors, which never perish, even if they suffer from malice and falsehood.

¶ Paul therefore exhorts Timothy to persevere in these things, saying:

> <margin>¶</margin> **But continue in the things which you have learned and have been assured of, knowing from whom you have learned them, and that from a child you have known the holy scriptures, which are able to make you wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus. All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness: that the man of God may be perfect, thoroughly furnished unto all good works.**

¶ For the things Timothy had learned, he learned from Paul and from the influence of the Holy Spirit, through which he had obtained the gift of prophecy from his youth, as well as an understanding of the holy scriptures. It was in no way fitting for Timothy to be ungrateful or unmindful of this great benefit of the Holy Spirit. The apostle suggests that Timothy received his understanding of the holy scriptures from the Holy Spirit by what he added concerning divinely inspired scripture, which is inspired only for good, utility, and edification. For to this end the Holy Spirit inspired the understanding of the holy scriptures and the prophets: that it might teach the knowledge of God to those who do not know it; that it might convict, confute, and reprove the falsehood that opposes divine knowledge; that it might direct those who wander; that it might instruct in divine justice; and that the man of God might be perfect and complete, prepared for every good work. "The man of God" can be said of any faithful person, whether he is in authority or is one who must be perfected and completed through the doctrine, direction, and instruction of his superiors. Therefore, it is necessary first for the superiors to be completed in every grace and in an eminent degree of goodness. For how could one who is not completed and perfect be able to perfect and complete others? Truly, no one can be purged, or illuminated (as is right), and much less perfected for salvation, except through faith in our Lord Jesus Christ. Who, with the Father and the Spirit, purging, illuminating, and perfecting all things in heaven and on earth, reigns over 
<sig>A</sig> all things, and in all things, and through all things, for ever and ever. Amen.
