XI 218 2 Timothy.

**Lovers of themselves / covetous.** ¶ In the beginning: the particle "for" <note>original: "enim"</note> is not just a connective word, but explains the reason for the preceding statements, and should be added. And here, **covetous** <note>original: "cupidi"</note> is not a general name naming every kind of desire, but a specific one concerning money, for those people are specifically called **avaricious**. Paul says: *For men shall be lovers of self, lovers of money.* <note>Greek: ἔσονται γὰρ οἱ ἄνθρωποι φίλαυτοι, φιλάργυροι</note> ¶ The **Vulgate** edition says: **Lovers of pleasures more than of God.** ¶ The word "lovers" can be repeated to say: "and lovers of God." Paul says: *Lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God.* <note>Greek: Φιλήδοροι μᾶλλον ἢ φιλόθεοι</note> ¶ The **Vulgate** edition says: **Now as Jannes and Mambres resisted Moses.**
<margin>B</margin>
<margin>19</margin>
**Jannes**: should be written with a double "n" in the middle, like the word *annus* (year), not "mn" like *omnis* (all). And **Iambres** with an "i" at the beginning. For both of these names in Paul's text begin with the third vowel (i). Each is three syllables long. But this is a necessity of the Greek language. Among the Latins, however, nothing prevents both from being three syllables or both being two syllables, just as "Jason" can be three or two syllables. Paul says: *In the manner that Jannes and Jambres resisted Moses.* <note>Greek: ὃν τρόπον δὲ Ἰανρῆς καὶ Ἰαμβρῆς ἀντέστησαν μωϋσεῖ</note>
<margin>C</margin> <margin>T A M H I I V U A I</margin>
¶ The **Vulgate** edition says: **For their folly shall be manifest in all.** ¶ The word "in" is redundant.
<margin>19</margin>
Even without the preposition, the speech is better according to Roman custom. Paul says: *For their folly shall be manifest to all.* <note>Greek: ἡ γὰρ ἄνοια αὐτῶν ἔκδηλος ἔσται πᾶσιν</note> ¶ The **Vulgate**
<margin>C</margin>
edition says: **What things happened to me at Antioch, at Iconium, at Lystra.** ¶ The ancient
<margin>20</margin>
translator could have said: "what sorts of [sufferings] were made for me," so that the adjective "what sorts" <note>original: "quales"</note> would refer to what is closer, namely "passions" or "sufferings," and that would indeed be elegant. This is what Paul seems to have done. For "sufferings" <note>Greek: παθήμασιν</note>, the nearest noun in Greek, was neutral, and he used a neutral adjective for it. However, in our Latin language, the noun is feminine. Therefore, since its gender was changed, the gender of the adjective should also have been changed accordingly. But that is a matter for the grammarians' forum. If you wish to know in part what persecutions and sufferings the apostle endured at Antioch, Iconium, and Lystra, read the 14th chapter of the **Acts of the Apostles**. Paul says: *What things happened to me in Antioch, in Iconium, in Lystra.* <note>Greek: οἷάμοι ἐγένετο ἐν ἀρτιοχεία, ἐν ἰκονíω, ἐν λύστροις</note>
<margin>D</margin>
¶ The **Vulgate** edition says: **Erring and sending into error.** ¶ Rather: **deceiving and being deceived.**
<margin>20</margin>
If the ancient translator preferred to interpret it by the word "erring," the sentence should have been reversed to say "making to err and erring." For in the first place, that which has an active meaning is placed, and in the second, that which is passive. Paul says: *deceiving and being deceived.* <note>Greek: πλανῶντες καὶ πλανώμενοι</note>
<margin>D</margin>
¶ The **Vulgate** edition says: **Which can instruct thee unto salvation.** ¶ The word "instruct"
<margin>21</margin>
explains less than what the Greek text contains. For the word placed here in Greek means **to teach wisdom** or **to instruct wisely**. Paul says: *the things which are able to make you wise unto salvation.* <note>Greek: τὰ δυνάμενα σοφίσαι εἰς σωτηρίαν</note> ¶ The **Vulgate** edition says: **That the man of God may be perfect, instructed unto every good work.** ¶ What the previous words say through verbs—teaching, reproving, correcting, and training—Paul says through nouns: **teaching, reproof, correction, training.** <note>Greek: διδασκαλίαν, ἔλεγχον, ἐπανόρθωσιν, παιδείαν</note> And what is called "perfect" here rather signifies **complete** or **upright**. And what is at the end called "instructed" rather means **perfected**. Paul says: *that the man of God may be complete, having been perfected for every good work.* <note>Greek: ἵνα ἄρτιος ᾖ τοῦ θεοῦ ἄνθρωπος, πρὸς πᾶν ἔργον ἀγαθὸν ἐξηρτισμένος</note>

---

->### CHAPTER IV.<-

*Large woodcut ornamental initial 'U' showing figures in a pastoral landscape with a city in the distance.* So that Timothy might render the men of God "perfected" for every good work, Paul strictly adjures him regarding the office of a bishop to be exercised vigilantly; in which, likewise, all bishops are adjured through the Holy Spirit. For He fills all times and foreknows all things, and in one man He addresses all. And Paul prophesies about the turning away of future people from the truth of the faith of Christ through **fabulous doctrine**, promising the pleasures of the flesh and desires. For the rot of this kind of doctrine tickles the "itching ear" and fascinates the senses of carnal men, drawing them to destruction. By this insane and fabulous doctrine, the **heresy of the Arabs** <note>A common early modern reference to the rise of Islam, often characterized as a "fable" by Christian commentators.</note> is clearly recognized, which has now corrupted almost the entire world. Oh, how great was the necessity of the Word of God to healthily meet those madnesses! How great it would be now to overturn them! But they do not endure sound doctrine; rather, they furiously persecute it with sword and fire. Which pestilential doctrine would undoubtedly never have prevailed if, according to the adjuration of the Spirit, each of the bishops had kept watch over his flock with all care and diligence, and had fed them with healthy doctrine, reproving them in season and out of season, rebuking these, beseeching those, as was necessary for each one, in all patience and all doctrine. This, therefore, is Paul's adjuration against this kind of pestilential heresy.
<margin>22</margin>
¶ I charge thee therefore before God, and the Lord **JESUS CHRIST**, who shall judge the living and the dead at his appearing and his kingdom: preach the word; be urgent in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine. For the time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine; but after their own lusts shall they heap to themselves teachers, having itching ears; and they shall turn away their ears from the truth, and shall be turned unto fables. But watch thou, endure in all things, do the work of an evangelist, fulfill thy ministry. ¶ Blessed by the Lord are those who, when they have undertaken the ministry of this established function, have done so as the apostle commands. Like **white swans** migrating from this world, they shall fly forth to the palaces of immortality. Great is their security.

# Commentary

certainty: one passes from this world to the Lord of all, who crowns his faithful servants. They follow Paul, who leads the way with great security and certainty. For what good and faithful servant could fear or doubt his super-good and super-faithful Lord? Therefore, since the most blessed Paul, through the spirit of prophecy, recognized—as a soul sacred and pleasing to God—that through the palm of martyrdom he would soon glorify God and pass from this world, he inserted his testament into this letter to his dearest son Timothy, saying:

<margin>
Paul’s
Testament
23
</margin>

> For I am now ready to be poured out <note>The Latin *libor* refers to a libation or drink offering, symbolizing Paul's blood being shed in martyrdom.</note>, and the time of my departure is at hand. I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith. Henceforth there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, shall give me at that day: and not to me only, but unto all them also that love his appearing. Do your diligence to come shortly unto me: For Demas has forsaken me, having loved this present world, and is departed unto Thessalonica; Crescens to Galatia, Titus unto Dalmatia. Only Luke is with me. Take Mark, and bring him with you: for he is profitable to me for the ministry. And Tychicus have I sent to Ephesus. The cloak <note>original: *Phelonem*, referring to the *paenula* or traveling cloak.</note> that I left at Troas with Carpus, when you come, bring with you, and the books, but especially the parchments. Alexander the coppersmith did me much evil: the Lord reward him according to his works: of whom you should be aware also; for he has greatly withstood our words. At my first defense no man stood with me, but all men forsook me: I pray it be not laid to their charge. Notwithstanding the Lord stood with me, and strengthened me; that by me the preaching might be fully known, and that all the Gentiles might hear: and I was delivered out of the mouth of the lion. And the Lord shall deliver me from every evil work, and will preserve me unto his heavenly kingdom: to whom be glory for ever and ever. Amen.

¶ This is Paul’s testament. What does "I am now poured out" mean, if not "I am now sacrificed" and offered as a sacrifice to God? "In that day" refers to the day of his death and departure, which was already looming close. "Those who love his appearing" are those who love the coming of the Lord, who has already appeared to us in humility, but will yet appear in venerable majesty. The cloak: it was a memorial he wished to leave to someone before his death. He had Luke with him. He commands Mark to be brought, and earnestly requests the parchments that were with Carpus to be delivered. But for what purpose, if not to leave them to Luke and Mark—the divine scribes chosen by the Holy Spirit—so they might use them to record the holy Gospel? Regarding what he says of Alexander, the worker in the iron forge <note>original: *ferrarię officinæ opifici*</note> who turned to evil deeds, "the Lord reward him according to his works": he does not call down a curse upon him, but leaves the judgment and vengeance to the Lord. He prays for those who, out of fear of death, did not dare to stand by him in his first defense; he prays, I say, that God may not hold it against them. He acknowledges the benefit of God, who then delivered him from the "mouth of the lion," both visible and invisible. The invisible lion was Satan, who envied the fruit of life. The visible lion was Nero, who was a living and visible instrument of Satan. But according to the divine secret, his preaching—which all nations were to hear for their salvation—was not yet fulfilled; therefore, neither the fury of the malignant one nor the rage of Nero could take him away before then. Yet the time was near when his preaching would reach its end, and he himself would receive the heavenly inheritance with Christ, whom he had long since desired with all his soul. He who blesses with his whole heart is already beginning the life that the whole choir of saints lives, praising God forever and ever. To this holy arrangement of his final days, he adds pious greetings and farewells to his dear ones through the letter, saying:

<margin>
24
</margin>

> ¶ Salute Priscilla and Aquila, and the household of Onesiphorus. Erastus stayed at Corinth, but Trophimus I left at Miletus sick. Do your diligence to come before winter. Eubulus greets you, and Pudens, and Linus, and Claudia, and all the brethren. The Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. Grace be with you. Amen. The second letter to Timothy, written from Rome, when Paul was to be presented for the second time to Nero, the Emperor of the Romans.

¶ The words he adds—"Grace be with you. Amen"—look back equally to Timothy and all those he ordered to be greeted: Priscilla, Aquila, Onesiphorus, and his family. And just as Paul is not accustomed to beginning a letter without a prayer for Christ's grace, so he is not accustomed to ending one without that same holy prayer. And what wonder? For what is better, more desirable, or more salutary for us than the grace of Christ and our God? May Jesus Christ—king, lawgiver, and savior, the only truly blessed one—deign to grant this grace to us all and preserve it once granted, through the holy intercessions of his most blessed Apostle Paul. He who lives and reigns with the eternal Father and the Holy Spirit, one God, blessed for all ages and above all ages. AMEN.

### EXAMINATION of several points regarding the text.

¶ The **Vulgate** edition: *And by his coming.* The "And" is superfluous. And it is better to say "by his appearing" <note>Latin: *apparitionem*</note> here than "by his coming" <note>Latin: *adventum*</note>, even though "appearing" and "coming" mean the same thing. Paul says: *according to his appearing* <note>original Greek: κατὰ τὴν ἐπιφάνειαν αὐτοῦ</note>. ¶ The **Vulgate** edition: *But according to their own lusts shall they heap to themselves teachers, having itching ears.* "Itching" <note>Latin: *prurientes*</note> is in the nominative case and refers to the listeners, not to the teachers. For this reason, we have used the word "tickled" <note>Latin: *titillati*</note> so that this may be understood more clearly. And one should say "hearing" rather than "ears," for it is the same word that...

<meta>This page concludes the commentary on the Second Epistle to Timothy. On the previous page, the author introduced Paul’s "testament" as he prepared for martyrdom. This final section focuses on philological corrections to the Latin Vulgate translation by comparing it to the original Greek, while also warning against heretical "fables."</meta>

# Book 11: 2 Timothy

The old translator <note>The "old translator" refers to the author of the Vulgate, traditionally St. Jerome.</note> immediately adds when he says: *they will indeed turn away their hearing from the truth.* But who are those who tickle and, so to speak, make the ears itch? Truly, they are vain and curious teachers who teach heresies and dogmas in secret and in private, as if they were certain mysteries more august than those which are made public. These are fables and mere trifles—even worse than trifles, for they are diabolical. Read the Talmud; read the Alcoran <note>The Quran</note>; read the books of the Indians (even in this age of ours) which concern the worship of evil spirits <note>original: *cacodæmonolatria*</note>: and you will always encounter diabolical fictions, the hissings of the ancient serpent by which souls are swallowed up, just as little birds are ensnared by the song of a deceptive fowler. These are deadly fables which poison the hearing, and at the first touch of desire and a certain madness, cause it to itch with an insane and irrational curiosity. But where the poison has crept in deep, they kill utterly, sinking the soul into the abyss of eternal falsehood, which is the "outer darkness." For the truth of faith dwells in light, even the highest light; therefore, the falsehood opposed to it dwells in the highest darkness. Paul says: *but according to their own desires they will heap up for themselves teachers, having itching ears.* <margin>B 22</margin> The Vulgate edition says: *Fulfill your ministry. Be sober.* <margin>B 23</margin> The phrase *be sober* is superfluous here <note>The author argues this phrase does not appear in the most authentic Greek manuscripts of this specific verse.</note>. Paul says: *fulfill your ministry.* And he immediately adds: *for I am already being poured out* <note>original: *ego enim iam libor*; Paul uses the metaphor of a drink offering or libation to describe his upcoming execution.</note>. The Vulgate edition says: *But also to those who love his coming.* <margin>C</margin> It should read: *but also to all.* The word *all* is missing. And (as stated above), it should be *appearing* rather than *coming.* Paul says: *but also to all those who have loved his appearing.* The Vulgate edition says: *For Demas has left me, loving this world.* It should rather be said: *the present world.* For in this place, the adverb *now* <note>original: *nunc* / Greek: *νῦν*</note> is used, designating the present time, not a demonstrative pronoun. Paul says: *For Demas has forsaken me, having loved the present age.* The Vulgate edition says: *Take Mark and bring him with you.* In the Greek, it is without a conjunction: *Taking Mark, bring him with you.* Paul says: *taking Mark, bring him with you.* The Vulgate edition says: *The cloak that I left at Troas with Carpus, when you come, bring it, and the books.* What the old translator calls a *penula* <note>a heavy traveling cloak</note>, Paul calls a *Phelonên*; it is a masculine noun. Grammarians define a *penula* as that type of garment worn over other clothes when it rains. Therefore, when it rains, there is a need for a cloak; if it does not rain, there is no use for it. The ancients made them of leather <note>original: *scorteam*</note> against the winter cold. In the heat, however, they used a *gausapina*—that is, one made of silk—because it was very light. I believe the one the blessed Apostle was asking for was of the lighter kind, so that it would not have caused Timothy a great burden of weight as he traveled with the parchments. Paul says: *the cloak which I left at Troas with Carpus, when you come, bring it, and the books.* And take note here: those who call a volume of both Laws <note>The Old and New Testaments</note> "the Bible" <note>original: *bibliam*</note> using the first declension feminine singular act barbarously. For *biblia* is a neuter plural of the second declension, like "documents" or "monuments"; it designates "the books." But by a figure of speech <note>original: *antonomasiam*</note>, the Sacred Books are so designated. Therefore, one should say: "Genesis is the first book of the *biblia* [the books]," not "of the *biblia* [the Bible]." It is written "in the *bibliis* [the books]," not "in the *biblia* [the Bible]." I have compared "the *biblia* [the books]," not "the *bibliam* [the Bible]." If we are not believed, let Paul at least be believed when he says: <margin>C 13</margin> *bring also the books* <note>original: *biblia*</note>. Let this be said as the occasion allows. The Vulgate edition says: *The Lord delivered me from the mouth of the lion.* It should be said: *And the Lord will deliver me*, in the future tense, with the preceding conjunction. Paul says: *and I was delivered from the mouth of the lion, and the Lord will deliver me.* <margin>D 24</margin> The Vulgate edition says: *Eubulus, and Pudens, and Linus greet you.* It is said in the singular: *he greets you*, but that is a very small matter. Paul says: *Eubulus, and Pudens, and Linus greet you.* And among the Greeks, the subscription is held: *The second to Timothy, written from Rome: when Paul was presented a second time before Nero, Caesar of the Romans.*

# COMMENTARIES ON THE EPISTLES OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PAUL
# BOOK TWELVE, WHICH IS ON THE EPISTLE TO TITUS. CHAPTER 1.

<margin>

<image-desc>Large historiated drop-cap initial 'I' decorated with intricate floral patterns, strapwork, and geometric motifs within a square frame.</image-desc>IN THIS epistle to Titus, the bishop of the Cretans and his own disciple, the most blessed Paul prefixes a holy greeting according to his custom, beginning thus: *Paul, a servant of God and an apostle of Jesus Christ, according to the faith of God’s elect and the knowledge of the truth which is according to godliness, in the hope of eternal life, which God, who does not lie <note>original: "non mendax deus"</note>, promised before eternal ages, but has manifested his word in due time through preaching, which was committed to me according to the command of God our Savior: To Titus, my special <note>original: "peculari" – meaning a son uniquely his own in a spiritual sense</note> son in our common faith, grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ our Savior.* This is the holy greeting in which Paul manifests for what purpose he was an ambassador and apostle of Jesus Christ. For he was an ambassador to bring faith to the elect of God and to pour in the knowledge of truth, with the certain hope of eternal life to be expected. And how could eternal life not be expected with the most certain hope, since God, who cannot lie, promised it—and indeed promised it eternally before the ages of the world shone forth? For God is immutable, and whatever He manifests in time, He has ordained from eternity. However, He manifests the promise of eternal life through the word of the Gospel and preaching in time—and indeed in the proper time: namely, from the time of Christ's coming until the end of the world. Therefore, He ordained the promise of eternal life from eternity. But to ordain the promise of eternal life from eternity is to promise eternal life from eternity and before the ages of the world. And what does it mean when he says *to which I was entrusted according to the command of God our Savior*, except that I was committed to this preaching according to the order of Christ our Savior, who is God? For the Lord said: *This man is a chosen vessel unto me, to bear my name before kings, and nations, and the children of Israel. For I will show him how great things he must suffer for my name's sake.* He called Titus his "special," "own," and "natural" <note>original: "ingenuum"</note> son because Paul was the author of his rebirth in the faith, and Titus obeyed him as a father. And in the greeting, he places three attributes: mercy, peace, and grace. Although these generally suit all the persons <note>original: "hypostasibus"</note> of the divine nature, mercy is nevertheless uniquely attributed to the Father, for He is the *Father of mercies*. Peace is attributed to the Son, for *He is our peace, who has made both one*. And grace is attributed to the Holy Spirit. As it says: *The faithful of the circumcision who had come with Peter were astonished, because the grace of the Holy Spirit was poured out even upon the nations.* Therefore, in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—one and simple God—and in the harmonious and united distribution of His gifts, is this

<margin>2</margin>holy greeting. Now the holy apostle of God reminds Titus of the cause for which he had left him in Crete, saying: *For this reason I left you in Crete: that you might correct the things that are wanting, and appoint elders <note>original: "presbyteros"</note> in every city in the way I ordained for you: if any man be blameless <note>original: "infons"</note>, the husband of one wife, having faithful children, not accused of luxury or rebellious. For a bishop must be blameless, as a steward <note>original: "dispensatorem"</note> of God; not stubborn, not irritable, not given to wine, no striker, not greedy for filthy lucre; but hospitable, a lover of good men, modest, just, holy, temperate, holding fast the faithful word which is according to doctrine: that he may be able both to exhort in sound doctrine and to convince the gainsayers.* These things have already been made clear from the third chapter of the tenth book <note>The author refers to his previous commentary on 1 Timothy 3</note>. For where it was said there that a bishop must be "irreproachable," here it says he must be "blameless" <note>original: "infontem"</note>, which means "without crime." He who is certainly without crime is undoubtedly irreproachable. And here he adds "not stubborn" <note>original: "pertinacem"</note>, that is, one who thinks everything is permitted to him at his own whim; for that is what Paul’s term designates. For such people fall into pride and into the snare of the devil. For this reason, in that other place, he also rejected "neophytes" <note>recent converts</note> from being chosen for such a high degree of sublimity, because such people might especially be stubborn and licentious. Where he says here "a lover of good men," in that other place he called him "gentle" or "equitable and good." Whoever wishes to pay attention will easily perceive the harmony of all these things. For the Spirit of God is not a spirit of discord or dissonance, but of all harmony and total agreement. And how fitting it would be for bishops to often read "Timothy" and "Titus"—that is, the epistles of the most blessed Paul to both—and how fitting, I say, for those who undertake pastoral care to often recall to memory the reason why they undertook such a burden, and that they are <term>stewards (original: *œconomos*): managers of a household or estate on behalf of the master</term> in that house of which Christ is the Father of the family. Let them not, when called to His tribunal which no one can escape, be proved before the angels of light to have been not "dispensers" but "dissipaters," and let them not blush with confusion and hear that terrible voice—

“Bind them hand and foot and cast them into the outer darkness.” <note>original: "ligatis pedibus & manibus / mittite eos in tenebras exteriores" — a reference to Matthew 22:13</note> For he who takes up the burden of this sacred leadership but does not live blamelessly, who does not steward divine matters as he ought, but is instead stubborn, prone to anger, addicted to wine, a striker with either tongue or sword, gaping after shameful gain, caring nothing for hospitality, rejoicing in a crowd of evil-doers, and surrounded by kidnappers and soldiers in the manner of a tyrant—inflated, unjust, impure, and intemperate—having no word with which he can teach every rank toward piety or refute those contradicting the truth which Paul teaches and the holy Gospel mandates: such a man is the star that fell from heaven in the holy vision of the Apocalypse. <note>original: "stella est quæ in sancta apocalypseos visione de cœlo cecidit" — referring to the fallen star in Revelation 9:1</note> His lot is with the angels who fell from heaven and lost their angelic dignity because they did not keep their own principality. These things are true. Therefore, terror and horror ought to shake him so that he might come to his senses, if by chance he might find mercy and, with light restored, shine again as a star in heaven. For as long as he lives this life, he is not utterly extinguished. The mercy of God is like oil which, when applied to a flame not yet fully out, causes it to burst forth into a great and high-flying light. In the time of Paul, there was a great necessity for bishops to be such men; otherwise, they certainly would not have been bishops at all. And in our own time, the necessity for this is no less.

But why such a necessity had pressed in the time of Paul, he adds, saying:

**OF THE CHURCH**
It is a fact that the soul is more precious than the natural limbs of a man. Indeed, divine functions manage all things. Thus, in the body of the Church, there are diverse orders and common gifts: the Spirit is in all members of Christ, and they expect the same inheritance. Here, the weak are nourished by sweet histories. The parts of the human body are happier when they are used for service. Here, the prophet openly reveals that mortals either do not approach the church or even depart from it. Those who swell with honors are like camels with humps, as is written. And from sweet histories, they are made into these things, insofar as they are moved toward the good. Therefore, they would rather live among dogs and swine than be in a holy place. These are the foolish ideas of Basiliades, Marcion, and others; if any consequence follows, it is that they kindle eternal fire and merit Gehenna <note>Hell</note>. Therefore, it is best to be among the sheep of the Church, written in the Book of Life: those who, though they fall into great evils, do not wish to be removed from the fellowship, but rather to profess penance.
</insert>

¶ Those who do these things and are slow to do what is right ought to be rebuked by the bishops, and those doctrines which are for profit rather than for piety must be overturned. Many are like the Cretans: who receive lies rather than sound doctrine, "evil beasts, devoted to their bellies"—that is, to gluttony and luxury—wishing to do no work, whom it is necessary to rebuke thoroughly. The Apostle taxes all of them under the name of the Cretans, saying:

> One of themselves, even a prophet of their own, said: "A Gnosian is always a talker, an evil beast, slow bellies." <note>original: "Gnosius vsq; loquax / mala bestia / viscera pigra" — This is a reference to the famous "Cretan Paradox" attributed to Epimenides of Knossos.</note>

¶ This testimony is true. For which cause, rebuke them sharply, that they may be sound in the faith, not giving heed to Jewish fables and commandments of men who turn away from the truth.

¶ Paul used in this place a pentameter verse of the poet Epimenides. In this, he proves the poet spoke the truth, so that they might strive all the more to amend the evil to which they are most prone, and not listen to the fables of the Jews. He who does not know these fables seems never to have even heard the name of the **Talmud** <note>original: "Talmuth" — The central text of Rabbinic Judaism</note>. They claim this work is older than the New Law. But such things should be called figments of men rather than the precepts of God; they belong to those men who turn away from the truth and are contrary to the precepts of life. But to whom can such "infancy" do no harm? Surely to those who are sound in the faith. However, to those who err in the faith and are weak, such things are accustomed to harm them unto eternal destruction. Therefore Paul adds:

<margin>
5

•
•
</margin>
¶ To the pure, all things are pure. But to those who are defiled and unbelieving, nothing is pure. But even their mind and conscience are defiled. They profess that they know God, but in works they deny him, being abominable, and disobedient, and to every good work reprobate.

¶ Behold how infidelity makes men defiled and unclean. Although they say they know God, they do not know Him at all, but deceive their listeners. They are like robbers who say they know the paths they do not know, and lead people into trackless wastes; and those who are led away are slaughtered and perish. Their deeds are contrary to their words. But faithfulness makes men pure, who admit nothing but what is pure. For their mind and conscience are pure, just as those of the others are impure. In word, they truly say they know God, and they prove it by deed, leading those who seek God toward Him by word, deed, life, and example. May Christ our Lord, the author of faith and the lover of the faithful and the pure, deign to grant this to us; He who is blessed for all ages and forever.

### COMMENTARY

...the sixth case <note>original: "sextum casum" — referring to the ablative case in Latin grammar</note>. If, however, it does not refer back to what was manifested above, it should be left as an accusative, as in Paul's writing, and then the sense is: "God manifested his word in my preaching, in the preaching to which I was entrusted." From this, the Apostle gives us to understand that the word of his preaching is not his own, but God's. For the Savior also said: "The word which you have heard is not mine, but the Father's who sent me." Both interpretations are good. The old translator <note>The "old translator" refers to the author of the Vulgate, traditionally Saint Jerome, though here the author distinguishes between the Vulgate and Jerome's specific commentaries.</note> rendered the phrase as "which was entrusted to me," whereas the Greek more accurately says: "to whom I was entrusted."

**Paul:** *But in his own time he manifested his word through preaching, to which I was entrusted.* <note>original Greek: "ἐφανέρωσε δὲ καιροῖς ἰδίοις τὸν λόγον αὐτοῦ ἐν κηρύγματι, ὃ ἐπιστεύθην ἐγώ"</note>

**The Vulgate edition:** *To Titus, my beloved son.* Jerome notes here that the old translator did not express in Latin what is said in the Greek. For the word here is the same one that, in the fourth chapter of Philippians, he translates as "genuine" <note>original: "germane"</note>, where he says, "I also ask you, genuine companion." But here he uses "beloved." We have said that this word rather signifies "innate," "special," "proper," or "assigned," following the opinion of the blessed Jerome.

**Paul:** *To my genuine child.* <note>original Greek: "γνησίῳ τέκνῳ"</note>

<margin>B 2</margin> **The Vulgate edition:** *And appoint elders throughout the cities.* In the Greek, it is stated in the singular as "through the city."

**Paul:** *And appoint elders city by city.* <note>original Greek: "καὶ καταστήσῃς κατὰ πόλιν πρεσβυτέρους"</note>

**The Vulgate edition:** *Not proud, not quick-tempered.* Where the old translator says "proud," it is perhaps more appropriately called "stubborn" <note>original: "pertinax"</note>; such a person is one who wants everything to be permitted to himself. For the Greek word *authades* <note>αὐθάδης</note> implies this, being derived from *auto* (self) and *adeia* (license), which signifies license and liberty.

**Paul:** *Not stubborn, not quick-tempered.* <note>original Greek: "μὴ αὐθάδη, μὴ ὀργίλον"</note>

**The Vulgate edition:** *But hospitable, benign, prudent, sober, just, holy.* Where it says "benign" here, it designates only a "lover of good things." And where the old translator says "prudent," it does not please the holy Jerome; he says the old translator was misled by the ambiguity of the word and translated "prudent" instead of "chaste." "Sober" is redundant—unless perhaps you say the old translator rendered *sophrona* <note>σώφρονα</note> as "sober," just as he translates the word in the second letter to the Corinthians as "being sober," where he says "whether we are sober for you," in which case "prudent" would be the redundant word. Nevertheless, as was said, holy Jerome thought he had translated *sophrona* as "prudent." I would not deny this, since at the beginning of the following chapter he translates the same word as "prudent" where he says: "That the old men be sober, chaste, prudent."

**Paul:** *But hospitable, a lover of good, level-headed, just, holy.* <note>original Greek: "ἀλλὰ φιλόξενον, φιλάγαθον, σώφρονα, δίκαιον, ὅσιον"</note>

<margin>C 3</margin> **The Vulgate edition:** *That he may be able to exhort in sound doctrine.* It should read: "that he may be able *both* to exhort *in* sound doctrine." The words "both" and "in" are missing, but that matters little.

**Paul:** *That he may be able both to exhort in sound doctrine.* <note>original Greek: "ἵνα δυνατὸς ᾖ καὶ παρακαλεῖν ἐν τῇ διδασκαλὶᾳ τῇ ὑγιαινούσῃ"</note>

**The Vulgate edition:** *Vain talkers and deceivers.* "Deceivers" does not express the full force of the Greek word; rather, the word designates "deceivers of minds," as has been noted elsewhere. This term is more specific, while the other is more general. For there are deceivers of bodies and deceivers of minds and souls. If you compare the former to the latter, they are of little consequence. Yet both are to be avoided as those who oppose the Spirit, especially these latter ones. For impurity, intemperance, and unchastity produce the first kind. But the second kind are produced by heresy, impiety, infidelity, and everything that opposes sound doctrine.

**Paul:** *Vain talkers and mind-deceivers.* <note>original Greek: "ματαιολόγοι, καὶ φρεναπάται"</note>

**The Vulgate edition:** *Especially those who are of the circumcision, who must be reproved.* It is more fitting to say: "those *from* the circumcision." And where it says "reproved," it rather designates "stopping the mouth" or "muzzling."

**Paul:** *Especially those from the circumcision, whose mouths must be stopped.* <note>original Greek: "μάλιστα οἱ ἐκ περιτομῆς, οὓς δεῖ ἐπιστομίζειν"</note>

<margin>C 4</margin> **The Vulgate edition:** *One of them, their own prophet, said.* That was Epimenides of Crete, who accused them of lying. For they pointed out the tomb of Jupiter among them; and in this, they were not lying <note>Epimenides' famous paradox "All Cretans are liars." The author argues that while Cretans claimed Jupiter was buried in Crete, which was true to their local tradition, it was "lying" in the sense that a god cannot die.</note>. Yet they said he was the supreme god, and in this, they were lying. Even if Epimenides perhaps believed their lie was reversed and denied the tomb of Jupiter—as if he argued: "Jupiter is the supreme of the gods; therefore, the tomb of Jupiter is by no means in Crete." But as the conclusion is false, so too is the premise. Truly, he should have argued thus: "The tomb of Jupiter is in Crete; therefore, he is by no means the supreme of the gods." Thus he would have inferred truth from truth and would not have been a liar like the rest. But his own prophecy is verified concerning himself as well as the others: for just as the nations were deceived, so too were their prophets deceived.

Why does he accuse them, calling them "evil beasts," except that they follow irrationality, being devoted to gluttony and the belly, and moreover brought harm to others? Why "lazy bellies," except that they were unwilling to work, yet wished to fill their bellies? From this, it certainly follows that they were "evil beasts." For those who will not work and crave to glut their bellies are predatory beasts, meditating on only one thing: where they can snatch food and live by the injury of others.

The Apostle calls such people "superfluous dwellers," as if they were redundant to the world, not at all necessary, but to be removed. If the Cretans are no longer such today, they owe thanks to Christ through His holy Apostle. Those who admit His worship first become men from beasts. Then, if they proceed with the Spirit as their guide, they become angels from men. For the men of Christ are angels and above men—indeed, much more so than the men of old and now, who, devoted to the worship of demons, are beasts and below men.

What of the people of Calicut? <note>original: "Calecutianis" — A reference to the people of Calicut in India, often used in the 16th century to discuss the "primitive" state of newly encountered peoples in the light of Christianity.</note> What of...

# XII
### Ti.

...of the Taprobane <note>original: "Taprobanitis" — Taprobane was the ancient Greek name for the island of Sri Lanka.</note> and that type of idolater in India: they are quite bestial. They think the God of heaven should be pursued with no honor; they bestow all the worship of veneration upon the Malignant One <note>The Devil</note>, believing it is owed to him, and they celebrate him by that name. They bow their knees to a deformed statue, many-horned, with teeth protruding in the manner of a beast's tusks, and horrific with long claws like those of a rapacious griffin. Souls are feigned to be its food; some of these it crushes with its teeth, others it snatches with its claws. To this statue, I say, they bend their knees, burn incense, and offer blood sacrifices. For public trade, they stamp their bronze coins with such a horrendous image. They perform funeral rites for the dead surrounded by such monsters, and many people disguised in such masks make a noise around the bier. The more numerous and deformed they are, the more joy they add to the foolish people, increasing the funeral pomp. It is as if it were their greatest pleasure: that the departing soul will have many such companions. With such angels as guides, they think themselves blessed. They do not know the marriage bed unless it has first been violated—and that by those who demand it and are willing. They pursue the veneration of fools—that is, the "Moriones" or those who have been powerless of reason throughout their lives—as if they were saints.

They are, without a doubt, beasts. But let them come to Christ (and I pray they come); they will first be made into men, and many of them will pass into the company of angels even in this life. Thus Christ saves all; thus he illuminates, thus he wipes clean the reason, and thus he radiates the mind. Once the darkness of the Malignant One is driven out, the mind can immediately discern the pure truth, which for so many centuries they could never see. Happy are the Christians, if they would only acknowledge their own happiness and from whence it hangs! Blessed, and truly blessed, are those who know Christ and, once known, follow Him. To Him be praise, honor, glory, and thanksgiving, who deigned to exercise such piety toward us—we who, in our ancestors, were entirely like those people, worshipping that same prince of darkness.

**The Vulgate edition:** *Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, slow bellies.* Thus it is in Paul. But so that it may be recognized that there is a song in Paul—a hexameter verse <note>A form of poetic meter used in Greek and Latin epic poetry.</note> as in Epimenides—we have also translated the song here, as closely as we were able, in this manner: *The Knossian is ever talkative, an evil beast, a lazy gut.* The law of the poem forced the use of singulars for plurals, the general word "talkative" instead of "liar," and "guts" instead of "bellies." Let the same meaning be understood, therefore, as is found through the words of the old translator.

<margin>2</margin> **Paul:** *Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy bellies.* <note>original Greek: "Κρῆτες ἀεὶ ψεῦσαι, κακὰ θηρία, γαστέρες ἀργαί"</note> For Paul does not seem to have been ignorant of poetry or human literature, even if he chiefly cherished and cared for the divine. Truly, he who tastes divine things, even if he is not ignorant of human things, nevertheless cares little for them. Why do you boast of human riches to me if you have heavenly ones? Why do you marvel at the earth if you inhabit heaven?

<margin>3</margin> Why do you marvel at darkness if you are in the light? Paul was not "multifaceted" because he knew human things, but because he knew the greatest divine things. To lead us by the hand toward those divine things, he sometimes descended to human things.

**For which reason, rebuke them sharply.** That "sharply" signifies truncated, fundamentally, or thoroughly—in the manner of those who cut away and prune a wound.

<margin>4</margin> **Paul:** *For which cause rebuke them cuttingly.* <note>original Greek: "δι᾿ ἣν αἰτίαν ἔλεγχε αὐτοὺς ἀποτόμως"</note>

**And to the mandates of men who turn themselves away from the truth.**

<margin>D</margin> The word "themselves" is redundant. And one should rather say "opposing the truth" than "away from the truth." For men oppose the truth when they struggle against it and resist it.

<margin>5</margin> **Paul:** *And to the commandments of men turning away from the truth.* <note>original Greek: "καὶ ἐντολαῖς ἀνθρώπων ἀποστρεφομένων τὴν ἀλήθεια"</note>

**All things are clean to the clean.** It should be said: *All things indeed are clean to the clean.* **Paul:** *All things indeed are clean to the clean.* <note>original Greek: "πάντα μὲν καθαρὰ τοῖς καθαροῖς"</note>

**Since they are abominable and incredible.** I would prefer it to be said: "since they are abominable and unbelieving" or "unpersuadable." Just as the translator below turns the same word into "unbelieving" where he says: "For we were also once unwise, unbelieving, erring." **Paul:** *Being abominable and disobedient.* <note>original Greek: "βδελυκτοὶ ὄντες, καὶ ἀπειθεῖς"</note>

### CHAPTER II.

<image-desc>A large decorative historiated initial 'N' depicting a landscape with classical architecture and towers in the distance.</image-desc>

<margin>6</margin> The previous discourse has made it manifest that one must not pay attention to fables and the fluid opinions of men. And just as the Apostle forbids that, so he commands that one must apply oneself to **sound doctrine**, which bishops ought to sow everywhere and preserve once sown. Therefore he adds to Titus: *But you, speak the things that befit sound doctrine: that the old men be vigilant, chaste, modest, sound in faith, in love, and in patience.*

**Sound doctrine** is that which relates the right faith and the mysteries of faith, and which hands down the precepts containing the building up of salvation and the preparation for eternal life. Here, therefore, he places certain precepts of sound doctrine. The first of these is already set forth concerning the older men: that they ought to keep watch over the family and the youthful habits of others, as those whom experience has taught what dangers loom over the younger ones unless they watch cautiously and diligently. For youthful flesh seeks nothing but corruption. But in grave and composed old men, the opposite is entirely true. Let him, therefore, be vigilant. Let them be **chaste**. By the name of chastity, we understand all honesty and gravity of character, by which they are perfected in themselves—grace assisting them like the polish of mirrors reflects the light sent into them—and by which they shine as an example to outsiders, because of which the younger ones revere and fear them. Let them be **modest**. Modesty keeps us within ourselves and does not allow us to be carried away or to think highly of ourselves, but makes us humble ourselves before God and attribute glory to Him alone. Let them be **sound**. But how shall old men be sound, when old age is itself a certain...

# COMMENTARY

...is old age a natural disease? Certainly, it is a disease of the natural body, because the body naturally tends toward corruption. But it is not a disease of the soul, which is not measured by years, is immortal, and does not grow old. "Their hearts," he says, "shall live forever and ever" <note>original: "vivent corda eorum in saeculum saeculi" — a reference to Psalm 22:26</note>; by the name "hearts," you should understand "souls." Therefore, Paul—who perceived nothing except in the spirit—does not say that they should be healthy in body or possess bodily health, but that they should be "sound in faith, in love, and in patience" <note>Titus 2:2</note>. This is exactly as if he had said: they should be sound in faith, charity, and hope. For "patience" refers to "hope." Indeed, the perfect health of the soul consists in these three things. For the soul is three-formed—whether you call it <term>tri-potential</term><note>Having three powers or capacities</note> or <term>tri-hypostatic</term><note>Existing in three distinct substances or persons</note>—a mirror of eternity, wisdom, and love.

**Memory** is nourished by eternity through **hope**. And this nourishment is called **patience**. This is the health of the memory—I mean the innermost, mental memory, not the memory in the sensory part of the head, at the back of the skull, which receives the compresses of doctors.

**Intellect** is nourished by **wisdom**. And this nourishment, as long as we lead this mortal life, is called **faith**. This is the health of the intellect itself.

**Will** is nourished by **love**, which is called **charity**; and it does not change its name in the next world. This is the health of the will. Therefore, a soul that is healthy in faith, hope, and charity is entirely healthy and blessed—as much as is possible in this world—and is, if I may say so, "tri-healthy" <note>original: "trifana"</note> and "tri-blessed." For hope and patience are the blessedness of memory; faith is the blessedness of intelligence; and charity is the blessedness of the will. Having first set down this precept concerning old men, he sets down the second concerning elderly matrons, saying:

<margin>7 2</margin>
¶ "Likewise, let the aged women be in a state
» that is decent, not false accusers, not enslaved to much wine. Let them be good teachers, that they
» may cause the young women to think modestly, to be lovers of their husbands,
» to love their children, to be modest, chaste, keepers at home,
» good, and subject to their own husbands, lest the word of God be
» blasphemed." ¶ Those duties which the older men have in the first place toward the family, and especially toward the males, these same duties the elderly matrons must have in the second place toward the internal family, and especially toward the girls.

For they ought to be vigilant and attentive, honorable, modest, and sound in faith, hope, and charity, in a state and habit befitting holy religion. They must especially abstain from reproachful words and slanders, to which—on account of the weakness of their reason and the volatility of their nature—they tend to be more prone than men. For women are like turbulent water, always in motion; a man is like calm and tranquil water. For do you not see how the moon stirs the waters, while the sun calms them? Thus in a woman, there is a natural commotion of the <term>humors</term><note>Ancient medical theory held that bodily fluids or 'humors' governed health and temperament</note> designed for childbearing and the physical formation of offspring, which a man neither has nor needs. For he does not form the body of the fetus, but (like the sun) concurs in its formation. And the woman (like the moon) concurs in its physical embodiment. Hence there is a certain greater inconstancy in woman (even by divine ordinance) than in man—a mobility and a swiftness of slipping substance.

Let them not, therefore, be false accusers on account of a vice of nature (if indeed that natural mobility and inconstancy can be called a vice). Let them not be enslaved or serve much wine. For though they are old, much wine nevertheless displaces the mind and even overturns reason in the strong; how much more so in those whom nature has fashioned weak and infirm. Younger virgins and the unmarried ought to abstain from wine entirely. For for them to drink wine is to move fire toward oil. And how could fire moved toward oil not blaze up? Moreover, that heat and that flame is the concupiscence of lust. And where have we ever seen heat and flame where blackness and soot do not occur? If, through the flame of concupiscence and irrational appetite (even if unfulfilled), the minds of young women are already blackened, where is the brightness of virginity? Where is the snowy virginity and the lily of brightness? Therefore, let young women, especially those who do not have a husband, abstain from wine. And if the old women use it because of the feebleness of their age, let them not use much.

Let the old women be "good teachers." Care must be taken for teaching both at home and abroad. The doctrine which is delivered abroad is perceived very well and fruitfully if private instruction at home has preceded it. But how will they be good teachers privately at home? For they are forbidden from teaching publicly abroad. Certainly, it is by pre-teaching the young women whom they have with them in private—if they are unmarried, having the intention of marriage, teaching them how they ought to spend their future life (if God grants them a marriage bed); if they are already daughters-in-law and married, let them teach them to spend their present life with their husbands and children, by respecting and loving their husbands, cherishing their children, preserving modesty and chastity, staying at home, observing goodness, and showing themselves subject and obedient to their own husbands. Otherwise, the reproach of their lives would strike against the doctrine of Christ, when infidels see those who profess themselves Christians living wickedly—and perhaps more wickedly than the infidels live themselves.

<margin>8</margin>
The third precept regards the young men and those who live below the age of seniority, who are
» to be instructed in a similar fashion, as the apostle adds, saying: ¶ "In the same way, exhort the
» younger men to think modestly, showing yourself in all things an example of good
» works, in doctrine showing incorruptibility, chastity, immortality,
» and sound, irreproachable speech, so that he who is an adversary may be
» put to shame, having no evil thing to say against us."

¶ Then the old and the young, both men and women, will strive for all modesty and honesty and the prescribed forms of living when the pastor who is over them presents himself as an example of good...

### Titus Chapter 2

...an example of works / and in teaching, word, and deed, he displays incorruptibility / all integrity / immortality / and possesses speech beyond reproach / as one who never aims for anything corruptible, faulty, or mortal / nor says anything that can be criticized. One who leads in this way: in teaching he offers the immortality of his life / chastity—that is, universal integrity / incorruptibility / and speech beyond reproach—that is, speech which cannot be criticized or condemned / even by those who are on the opposing side and strive as adversaries. A life according to the spirit and spiritual teaching / is so pure, healthy, and whole: that carnal people have no grounds to babble anything against it / just as the enemies of knowledge have nothing against the primary concepts of the mind / which they cannot deny in their hearts. Likewise, carnal people cannot blame a spiritual life or doctrine according to their conscience: even if they sometimes do so with their mouths, but these are very few: who (as they say) "have rubbed their forehead" <note>original: "frontem perfricuerunt" — a Latin idiom meaning to cast off all shame or to be brazen</note> / whom neither shame / nor conscience / nor any sense of honor restrains.

<margin>9</margin>
¶ The apostle adds a fourth precept concerning servants <note>The Latin "servis" can mean both slaves and servants in this context</note>, saying: ¶ Servants should be subject to their own masters in all things / pleasing them well / not talking back / not stealing / but showing all good faith, so that they may adorn the doctrine of our savior / God: in all things. 
<margin>4</margin>
This doctrine which Paul gives: is the doctrine of Christ. Those who follow it / and strive in all things to conduct themselves with dignity / the old as befits the old / the young as befits the young / masters as befits masters / and servants as befits servants / rulers as befits rulers / and subjects as befits subjects: they adorn the doctrine of our savior / God. He came into the world for this purpose: though he was Lord of all / rich toward everyone / taking the form of a servant and a poor man / being born of virginal purity / teaching in all incorruptibility of life and healthy, irreproachable speech: so that he might instruct masters and servants / the old and the young / men and women / rulers and subjects / the rich and the poor in this purity of life and holiness. Therefore, Paul adds, saying:

<margin>10</margin>
¶ For the saving grace of God has appeared / to all men / instructing us: that renouncing ungodliness and worldly desires / we should live modestly / and justly / and piously in the present age / awaiting the blessed hope and the appearance of the glory of the great God and our savior JESUS CHRIST. Who gave himself for us: that he might redeem us from all iniquity / and cleanse for himself a <term>peculiar people</term><note>original: "populum peculiarem" — meaning a people who are God's own special possession</note> / a follower of good works.
¶ What is this "saving grace of God has appeared to all men" / except that he came / so that by his gift / by his grace he might save all men? For what purpose does the sun rise: except to illuminate all eyes / even if it does not illuminate all? And that is certainly not the fault of the sun: but it happens according to the will of those things that have eyes. And he did not only appear: but by appearing in life and word, he taught beyond any example / and more than by example. For he himself was not a <term>type</term><note>A symbolic representation or shadow of something to come</note> or a mere example: but the <term>exemplar</term> and <term>archetype</term><note>The original model or perfect form upon which others are based</note>. And what did he teach? To renounce ungodliness / and all the lusts of the world: and to live chastely / and holily / and justly / and religiously / by awaiting the blessed fruit of our hope / and the coming of the great God / who is the very same Lord Jesus Christ / who both appeared in this way / and taught us thus. And he not only appeared and taught: but he gave himself for us unto death in that part of him which was mortal / as a victim / and a sacrifice: so that he might redeem us from all iniquity / that is, from the offense and transgression of the divine law / and cleanse us in the blood of his own testament / and make for himself a peculiar people / devoted / and his own just like his own substance / having zeal for nothing other than good works. For works are good: which are done in imitation of him / and by his command. Know this well: whatever Peter / John / James / Jude / Matthew / Mark / Luke / or Paul commands / these things Christ commands. If I live as they command / my works do not redeem me / they do not cleanse me / my own cleanings do not wipe me clean: but the precious blood and the clean and immaculate offering of the sacrifice of our Lord Jesus Christ. This sacrifice was always: purer than the angels / and superior to the angels. Yet our works: cooperate with the grace of God toward this cleansing / wiping away / and washing. "If I do not wash you," he said, "you shall have no part with me" <note>John 13:8</note>.

<margin>11</margin>
And this is the doctrine of life and spirit. ¶ Therefore, he strictly commands Titus / and anyone else who performs the office of teaching: to teach these things / to exhort / and to rebukingly command those who might think otherwise / or who oppose him. Furthermore, he must live in such a way while teaching, exhorting, or rebuking the opposition: so that he cannot be despised. And he says:
<margin>5</margin>
¶ Speak these things / and exhort: and rebuke with all authority. And see to it: that no one despises you. ¶ He who teaches something and lives contrary to that teaching: is despised while teaching / and mocked while rebuking. Therefore, whoever is in charge / must live in such a way: that no one can despise him. Lest it be cast against him: "You who teach another, do you not teach yourself? You who preach against stealing, do you steal? You who say one must not commit adultery, do you commit adultery? You who detest idols, do you commit sacrilege? You who glory in the law, do you dishonor God through transgression of the law?" <note>A paraphrase of Romans 2:21-23</note> And let him not fall under this proverb: "If the salt loses its flavor: with what shall it be salted?" <note>Matthew 5:13</note> May Christ the Lord, the King of all ages, grant such leaders to his Church: who teach according to the spirit / exhort / rebuke / and whom no one can despise. So that all with one voice may be able to glorify, praise / and bless our Lord Jesus Christ / living and reigning...

<meta>This page continues the philological and theological commentary on the second chapter of Paul’s Epistle to Titus. Having established the requirements for older men and women, the author now turns to a meticulous comparison between the Latin Vulgate translation and the original Greek, often citing St. Jerome to argue for more precise vocabulary concerning sobriety, modesty, and the nature of Christ’s body.</meta>

**COM.**

<margin>A</margin> ...reigning for all ages of ages. Amen.
<margin>6</margin> ¶ EXAMINATION of several matters regarding the letter. ¶ The Vulgate edition: Older men: that they be **sober, chaste, and prudent**. ¶ Where the ancient translator said **sober and prudent**, it should rather be said **watchful and chaste**, or **modest**. And this is also what Jerome wishes. Paul: <note>original: "πρεσβύτας, νηφαλίους εἶναι, σεμνούς, σώφρονας"</note> **Older men, to be sober, grave, and self-controlled.** ¶ The Vulgate edition: **Older women likewise in holy attire.** ¶ Here, Jerome says, the Greek is better. For what the ancient translator calls **holy**, signifies **that which is fitting for the sacred**. He wishes them, therefore, to be of such attire, state, and condition as becomes sacred women, not profane ones. For they are members of the body of Christ, which nothing but the sacred becomes; far be from it anything profane. They are members of the body of Christ just as men are, in which they retain a name no weaker than men. For in Christ there is neither male nor female (for these are names of the weak flesh), but they obtain a more sublime name: one and the same, firm, robust, and strong. For what is more "one," what is more "the same," than that which is bound by the highest unity and the highest identity? What is more firm, valid, and stronger than that which is supported by the highest stability and defended by omnipotence? For all these things—highest unity, highest identity, highest stability, firmness, and omnipotence—are the Son of God. He unites, identifies, firms, contains, supports, strengthens, and fortifies His own body, making it grow strong and prevail against every power. Paul: <note>original: "πρεσβύτιδας ὡσαύτως ἐν καταστήματι ἱεροπρεπεῖς"</note> **Older women likewise in behavior becoming holiness.** There are also Greek codices <note>A codex is an ancient manuscript in book form</note> which have <note>original: "πρεσβύτιδας ὡσάντως σεμνὰς ἐν κατάστηματι"</note> **older women likewise chaste in their behavior.** And then it should be read: **Let the older women likewise be chaste in a sacredly-becoming state**, that is, in the sacred-becomingness of their state, attire, and condition. ¶ The Vulgate edition: **Teaching well: so that they may teach prudence.** ¶ For the same reason as above, where the ancient translator says **so may they teach prudence**, it can be said: **so that they may cause them to feel modestly**. To this, the continued sentence **young women** should be joined. For these are the ones whom the apostle adds that they must cause to feel modestly. Paul: <note>original: "καλοδιδασκάλους, ἵνα σωφρονίζωσι"</note> **Teachers of good things, that they may train [the young women]**. ¶ The Vulgate edition: **Prudent, chaste, sober, having care of the house.** ¶ Here also (as above) it can be said: **modest, chaste**. **Sober** is redundant. Paul: <note>original: "σώφρονας, ἁγνάς, οἰκουρούς"</note> **self-controlled, pure, workers at home.** ¶ The Vulgate edition:
<margin>8</margin> **In all things show yourself an example.** ¶ And here it can be said **concerning all things**. But that falls back into the same understanding. Paul: <note>original: "περὶ πάντα σεαυτὸν παρεχόμενος τύπον"</note> **concerning all things, showing yourself a model.** ¶ The Vulgate edition: **In doctrine, in integrity, in gravity, a sound word, irreproachable.** ¶ After that "in doctrine," the ancient translator used the ablative case instead of the accusative. And what he says "in integrity," signifies **incorruptibility**. And since he previously translated <term>semnous</term> <note>original: "σεμνούς" — meaning grave or dignified</note> as **chaste**, why does he not also turn <term>semnoteta</term> <note>original: "σεμνότητα" — dignity or gravity</note> into **chastity** here? Although I would not deny that <term>semnon</term> <note>original: "σεμνὸν"</note> signifies a man who is grave and honored for his virtue. The word **and** is missing after the word **incorruptibility**. Paul uses two words which are usually translated among us as **incorruptibility**. Because we had translated the first instance as **incorruptibility**, we said **immortality** in the second, intending the same thing, so that we would not repeat the same word twice under the same sound. Paul: <note>original: "ἐν τῇ Διδασκαλίᾳ ἀδιαφθορίαν, σεμνότητα, ἀφθαρσίαν, λόγον ὑγιῆ, ἀκατάγνωστον"</note> **in teaching, incorruptness, gravity, incorruptibility, sound speech that cannot be condemned.**
<margin>9</margin> ¶ The Vulgate edition: **Servants being subject to their own masters, pleasing in all things.** ¶ It is ambiguous whether **in all things** refers to what precedes it or what follows. I have referred it to what precedes; the ancient translator seems to refer it to what follows. In truth, neither sense is bad. Paul: <note>original: "Δούλους, ἰδίοις Δεσπόταις ὑποτάσσεσθαι ἐν πᾶσιν, εὐαρέστους εἶναι"</note> **Servants, to be subject to their own masters in all things, to be well-pleasing.** ¶ The Vulgate edition: **But in all things showing good faith.** ¶ Rather: **but showing all faith**. Paul: <note>original: "ἀλλὰ πίστιν πᾶσαν ἐνδειγνυμένους ἀγαθήν"</note> **but showing all good faith.** ¶ The Vulgate edition:
<margin>10</margin> **For the grace of God our Savior has appeared to all men.** ¶ It should be said **saving** or **salutary**, not **of the Savior**. For it is the feminine nominative and an adjective of the preceding noun **grace**. So that this might be better recognized, I preferred to say **salutary** rather than **saving**. For that word **salutary** would have been ambiguous, whether it was the nominative or the genitive adjective for the word **God**. **Our** is redundant. Paul: <note>original: "ἐπεφάνη γὰρ ἡ χάρις τοῦ θεοῦ ἡ σωτήριος πᾶσιν ἀνθρώποις"</note> **For the grace of God that brings salvation has appeared to all men.** ¶ The Vulgate edition: **And worldly desires, let us live soberly, and justly, and piously in this world.** ¶ That word **secular** signifies **worldly**; and in Paul, it is derived from **world**, not from **age**. Paul: <note>original: "καὶ τὰς κοσμικὰς ἐπιθυμίας σωφρόμως καὶ, Δικαίως, καὶ εὐσεβῶς ζήσωμεν ἐν τῷ νῦν αἰῶνι"</note> **and worldly lusts, we should live soberly, righteously, and godly in this present age.** ¶ The Vulgate edition: **And the coming of glory.** ¶ And here **appearing** is held. Paul: <note>original: "καὶ ἐπιφάνειαν τῆς Δόξης"</note> **and the appearing of the glory.** ¶ The Vulgate edition:
<margin>10</margin> **And he might purify for himself an acceptable people, a follower of good works.** ¶ Regarding what is called here <term>periousion</term> <note>original: "περιούσιον" — a special or chosen possession</note>: Jerome prefers it to be the same as **genuine**, and that it should be translated as **peculiar** or **special** rather than **acceptable**. For they are his own and special people. And furthermore, it should rather be said **a zealot** or **imitator of good works** than a **follower**. Paul: <note>original: "καὶ καθαρίσῃ ἑαυτῷ λαὸν περιούσιον καὶ ζηλωτὴν καλῶν ἔργων"</note> **and he might purify for himself a special people, zealous for good works.** ¶ The Vulgate edition: Neither...

...let no one despise you. <note>original: "nemo te contemnat"</note> ¶ We have said this paraphrastically: see to it that no one despises you, so that we may more easily grasp the meaning which Jerome wants to convey. Paul says: <note>original: "μηδείς σου περιφρονείτω" — "Let no one think around/despise you."</note>

### CHAPTER III.

<margin>12</margin>
Furthermore, Paul gives Titus a precept regarding how he should admonish the Cretans in the conduct of their lives—how they should behave toward their superiors and among themselves—saying:

<margin>6</margin>
> ¶ Remind them: to be subject to magistrates and powers, to obey princes, to be ready for every good work, to slander no one, to avoid fighting, to be gentle, showing all mildness toward all men.

¶ This subjection toward superior powers was discussed more extensively in chapter 13 of the first volume of these commentaries. Subjects ought to obey them in this way: as an image of divine power and divine ordinance; for he who resists the power, resists God. But just as good men love God, while in the wicked the fear of deserved punishment extinguishes love, in the same way, the good love magistrates, powers, and princes. The wicked, on the contrary, looking upon the punishment for their crimes and dreading it, hate them. Therefore, he commands subjects to be ready for every good work, and not to "blaspheme" <note>Here used in the sense of slandering or speaking ill of human authority.</note> any superior power, whether magistrate or principality. They are to be "without fighting," which means not to provoke one another with mutual lawsuits and accusations under the princes and powers, but to be gentle with one another, easily forgiving mutual offenses (if any should occur through error), and to be mild and patient toward all. For just as among flocks, a flock of sheep is peaceful and most pleasing, and is very easily led by the shepherd because it is mild and gentle, so a mild and gentle people is most pleasing and peaceful to the superior powers, and is most easily led. Such ought to be the people of Christ—a people washed from every stain of sin through the "laver of regeneration" <note>The "laver of regeneration" refers to the ritual of baptism, viewed as a spiritual bath that gives new life.</note> in the water and blood of the redemption of our Lord Jesus Christ. For one of the soldiers opened his side with a spear, and immediately there came out blood and water. That is the blood and that is the water in which we are wiped clean and washed from every stain of sin, of which our baptismal washing is the mystery and symbol. And furthermore, once washed, we are adorned with *charismata*, that is, the gifts of the Holy Spirit.

<margin>13</margin>
¶ Because of this reality, Paul adds:
> For we ourselves were also once without understanding, unbelieving, wandering, serving various desires and pleasures, living in malice and envy, hateful, and hating one another. But when the kindness and humanity of our Savior, God, appeared, not by works of justice which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us through the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out upon us richly through JESUS CHRIST our Savior; so that being justified by his grace, we might be made heirs according to the hope of eternal life.

All those who have not been illuminated by heavenly light and grace were "without understanding"—they were foolish and senseless, unbelieving, wandering, serving insane and numerous lusts and pleasures, occupied in malice and envy, worthy of hatred, and provoking one another with mutual hate. Therefore, that we have obtained the understanding of God, have become masters of our minds and wise, have been illuminated by faith, walk in the right path of life, serve the spirit, and have conquered the allurements and insanities of the lusts of the flesh—all this must be attributed to the kindness and "humanity" <note>The author uses the Greek term *philanthropia* to explain "humanity" as God's love for humankind.</note> of Christ. He saved us through his mercy, not because of our works, but through his grace and mercy, so that praise and thanksgiving may be owed to him alone. Thus, in the contemplation of his kindness, we are swept up into his love, but in the contemplation of ourselves, we are humbled and confounded. For the contemplation of his kindness creates exultation, hope, and confidence, and inflames a love that breathes for high things. But looking at ourselves brings sadness, distrust, and fear, in which that love cannot live which is fed on "celestial ambrosia" <note>A poetic metaphor for divine sustenance or grace.</note> and the nourishment of contemplation. This nourishment the goodness, kindness, mercy, and grace of God are accustomed to provide to those who understand that they are redeemed and saved not by the works they have done, but by God’s grace and mercy. Nevertheless, they perform good works as delightfully as they can, doing the will of the eternal Father; and they patiently endure adversity and hardship, so that they may be imitators of God—or rather, imitators of our "super-good" and "super-kind" Redeemer. He came into the world doing all good works and most patiently enduring the harshest things when we were without understanding, without obedience and faith, wandering in errors, entangled in the pleasures and desires of death, malevolent, envious, and (as far as concerns our own selves and our works) hateful to God and hating one another. He did this so that we might understand the ineffable piety and kindness of God toward us, which then made light shine out of our darkness. Not from our works, but *against* our works, he saved us by his sole mercy through the holy washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit, which he poured out richly and opulently upon the faithful. Thus, justified by his grace, they may participate in the eternal kingdom and inherit eternal life. And this is the truth of the faith. ¶ Therefore Paul continues, immediately adding another precept for those who are in charge, saying:

It emphasizes that redemption comes not through human works but through God's "philanthropy" and the cleansing power of the Holy Spirit in baptism.</summary>
