<meta>This page continues the commentary on Paul’s Epistle to Titus, moving from the duties of subjects into the specific exhortation for believers to focus on "good works" rather than "foolish questions." The author emphasizes that true wisdom is a divine light that brings concord, contrasting it with the contentious debates of "sects" or "heresies."</meta>

# COMMENTARY

<margin>14</margin> <margin>7</margin>
**This is a faithful saying.** <note>original: "Fidelis sermo." Paul uses this phrase to emphasize the absolute reliability of the teaching that follows.</note> And concerning these things I want you to be constant: so that those who have believed in God may be careful to excel in good works. These things are good and profitable for men. What does he mean by *and concerning these things I want you to be constant*, if not: "I want you to hold the things I have said, and those I shall add, with a firm and steady mind, so that by your example other faithful people who lead may be careful to excel in good works"? Moreover, they will excel in good works—that is, in doing well—if they speak the things that befit sound doctrine; if they instruct the old men, the young men, the old women, the young women, and if they establish every state of life according to the rules previously set down. They should also illuminate the minds of men with wisdom—which is a ray of God <note>original: "dei radius"</note> that turns the mind toward itself and fixes the turned mind within itself. These things, certainly, are good and lead toward salvation for men.

<margin>15</margin> <margin>8</margin>
**But avoid foolish questions, and genealogies, and contentions, and strivings about the law; for they are unprofitable and vain.** He gave a similar precept to Timothy, as can be seen more extensively in the second chapter of the previous book. Just as the pious and profitable method of correctly establishing and teaching according to the apostolic precepts is useful, so too is that contentious and (if I may say so) "argumentative" <note>original: "quæstionarius," referring to the overly academic or Scholastic method of debating every point.</note> method useless, impious, and vain. I call it *useless* because it does not build up. *Impious*, truly, because it does not lift the soul to God; it does not "melt" the soul when the Beloved speaks <note>A reference to the Song of Solomon 5:6, often used to describe the emotional response of the soul to God's word.</note>, which is what true piety is. *Vain*, because it does not reach the goal, which is perfected love and the fruit of eternal life. How does he build up, who makes men noisy, contentious, and ambitious for victory—defending this point and attacking that—so that they fight for victory rather than for truth? Where is the person who, while protecting the truth, entangles his opponent in a web of clever arguments? Does he exult in victory as much as someone who actually refutes a falsehood? Where is the person who, when faced with the truth of the Gospel, mocks it with the volubility of his speech and wit? Does he applaud himself as much as the one who accepted the truth? Indeed, much more. For to have accepted the truth might mean that he himself was proven wrong. But it is more "worth the effort" <note>original: "operæpreciū"</note> to the contentious to refute the truth, or to twist it to a foreign meaning, than to be seen as refuted in the problem they are defending.

Where, then, is piety in such things? Where is the fruit? And it is a wonder that those who have chosen only the "argumentative" method for training in things regarding the divine law have not read Paul's precept to Titus: *Avoid foolish questions, and genealogies, and contentions, and strivings about the law; for they are unprofitable and vain.* If the struggles over the Old Law are useless and vain when they are dragged into contention and a desire for victory, how much more so are the contentions and struggles over the New Law, which have their concord in light and spirit without any dissonance? Therefore, struggles are outside the light and the spirit; they create alien meanings and exist outside the harmony of the spirit. The Holy Spirit teaches through harmony, not through fighting. And just as the eye sees light without a struggle, so truth is present to the mind. If that truth is somewhat obscure and requires reasoning—just as colors and tiny writing require light—then it ought to be understood through reasoning without contention. 

Therefore, if someone in the church is ignorant of anything and asks a man of knowledge, whether he hears a simple assertion, a denial, or a reason added to it, he should not immediately (even if he does not understand) contend and struggle, but like a gentle animal, he should "ruminate" on what he has heard. <note>The author uses the metaphor of a "gentle animal" (like a cow) to suggest peaceful, internal meditation on a teaching.</note> If he contends, then neither the teacher nor the listener will profit at all (so true is the apostle’s sentence); indeed, every discipline is learned without contention. Even if someone comes to a geometer (I mean a skilled geometer) and immediately argues against the geometer's words, he can no longer be taught; he will make a thousand difficulties with the geometer, and perhaps the geometer will say: "It is not our custom to bicker and contend, but to admit well-spoken things and to reason from them skillfully and peacefully." How much more does contention disgrace the study of the holy law! I do not say that nothing should be asked regarding divine things; indeed, there are countless things that may be worthily asked, and countless worthy questions. But they must be asked without contention and fighting. Questions that are by their very nature contentious are to be avoided because they generate nothing but lawsuits. This is what the apostle commands. But what follows from these kinds of struggles over the law, if not sects and heresies in the law?

<margin>16</margin> <margin>9</margin>
Therefore, regarding those who have fallen into sects out of contention, Paul connects the following precept, saying: **A man that is a heretic, after the first and second admonition, avoid; knowing that he that is such is subverted, and sins, being condemned by himself.** In human disciplines, there are "sects" <note>Here used in the sense of "schools of thought."</note>, both good and bad; these are of little consequence or danger. The *good* ones are those who adhere closely to the original authors. For instance, I would believe those to be better geometers who adhere to Euclid; more learned mathematicians <note>original: "arithmeticos"</note> who follow Nicomachus and Jordanus; <note>Nicomachus of Gerasa and Jordanus de Nemore were famous historical authorities on arithmetic.</note> philosophers who follow Aristotle (with this one problem refuted: his insistence on the eternity of the world and time, and the consequences drawn from that); and more skilled doctors who follow Galen and Hippocrates, and so on for the rest. But the *wicked* sects are those who have handed down their own ideas instead of the author's, and are furthest from the authors. If the authors themselves were presented to these people in the form of clear explanations (the very knowledge they claim to possess), they would understand them about as well as if you handed them a Gordian knot to untie. <note>A "Gordian knot" is an ancient metaphor for an unsolvable or extremely complex problem.</note> Even if they begin to interpret them after long study, they will drag the text toward their own "dreams," or they will utterly bark against <note>original: "obganniēt"</note> whatever does not seem to agree with their sect. Thus the perverse Marcion <note>Marcion of Sinope (c. 85–160 AD) was an early heretic who rejected the Old Testament and edited the New Testament to fit his views.</note> utterly refuted whatever in the Gospels and Epistles did not support his sect. Therefore, just as it happens in human things, so too in divine things there are sects, both good and bad.

<summary>Paul warns Titus to avoid academic and legalistic bickering, which the author compares to "sects" in fields like geometry or medicine that twist an author's true meaning. The text argues that divine truth is received through peaceful "rumination" and spiritual harmony rather than aggressive debate.</summary>

<keywords>Titus, good works, contention, heresy, sound doctrine, Euclid, Aristotle, Marcion, Gordian knot, Scholasticism, wisdom, Holy Spirit</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Epistle to Titus, specifically addressing the definition of a heretic and the concluding verses of the letter where Paul gives final instructions to Titus regarding his travels and fellow workers.</meta>

# XII
Ti.

and both of these are of great importance, leading either toward salvation or toward the danger of eternal perdition. Now, "sects" are good when they cling to God and yield to divine intelligence; but they are bad when they are cut off from God and oppose divine intelligence (which belongs to the Holy Spirit). The sect of the Sadducees was perverse. But the sects of the Essenes and the Pharisees, as far as most were concerned, were good. For the prophets were of the sect of the Essenes or Pharisees; and Nathanael was a Pharisee by sect, of whom the Savior said: *Behold, a true Israelite, in whom there is no guile.* <note>John 1:47</note> Truly, as long as something is not cut off from the foundation, it is not so much called "cut" <note>original: "sectum," the root of "sect"</note> as it is called "united." However, that which is cut off from those things that cling to the foundation—cast far away—is entirely "cut" and not joined. Therefore, a true sect is not so much called a sect as it is a "non-sect." For those who belong to it cling to God, who is the foundation, and to the intelligence of the Spirit. They are not, therefore, cut off, but united and clinging. But a bad sect (which is the same as a false one) is entirely "cut." For those who belong to it are cut off from those who cling to the foundation, being split apart and cast far away. For all who received the washing of regeneration <note>Baptism</note> were joined and united. Therefore, we do not call a man who lives holily in the true sect a "heretic." For he is not "cut" <note>original: "sectus"</note>; rather, he is grafted and united to the foundation, as much by the holiness of his life as by the integrity of the Holy Spirit's intelligence. We call only him a "heretic" and "cut" who is cut and divided in both ways from the foundation and from those things connected to it. For such a man has fallen away from both God and the intelligence of the Holy Spirit; he both is, and can be called, a heretic.

If impurity of life alone made a heretic—such as the man whom Paul handed over to Satan for an abominable crime <note>1 Corinthians 5:5</note>—he would be called only a sinner and an apostate. But if he is also "cut" by an intelligence contrary to the Holy Spirit, which is also contrary to the faith, he is no longer called only a sinner or only an apostate, but a "heretical man." For a "cutting" <note>original: "sectio"</note> on account of an intelligence contrary to the faith is what most makes one called a heretic. If someone comes to me, not agreeing with the immortality of the soul, but piling up arguments of impiety against me—perhaps from the seventh book of Pliny, from Colotes, or from some follower of Democritus or the Epicureans <note>Pliny the Elder, Democritus, and Epicurus were classical authors often associated with the view that the soul dies with the body</note>—I will admonish him with all piety once and a second time to repent from such snares of demons and yield to the Holy Spirit and to the sacred words, rather than the destructive opinions of men (however eloquent). Afterward, if he does not repent, I shall avoid his company and the man himself, as one who condemns himself by his own speech and judges himself by his own mouth. If every faithful person ought to do this, how much more is a bishop bound to do so, who above all others must strive to be most faithful.

But come, you might say: "Is one who agrees with Pliny, Democritus, or Epicurus in those things regarding God and the soul a heretic? Are not Pliny, Democritus, and Epicurus therefore heretics?" Not at all. For they are not "cut" <note>secti</note>, as they never clung to God, either by the law of circumcision or by the grace of regeneration. Nor does it automatically follow that if someone agrees with Pliny and Epicurus, he is therefore a heretic; for perhaps he is a Jew, an Arab, or a Tartar who agrees with them. But if he had been initiated into the sacraments of Christ and afterward agreed with them, he would truly be a heretic, "cut off" from Christ to whom he once clung. Others, however, are simply called infidels <note>original: "infideles," meaning those without faith or unbaptized</note>. And I would not wish to deny that a heretical man is an infidel, as one who thinks perversely regarding the faith; but he is an infidel *from* the faith. For the washing <note>Baptism</note> makes everyone faithful.
<margin>17</margin>
But others are entirely infidels, such as those who were never faithful. But enough regarding the heretical man. Having set down these precepts, Paul mandates more familiar matters to Titus, saying:

> When I shall send Artemas to you, or Tychicus, hasten to come to me at Nicopolis: for there I have determined to winter. Send Zenas the lawyer and Apollos on their journey diligently, that nothing be wanting to them. And let ours also learn to excel in good works for necessary uses, that they be not unfruitful.

<margin>.</margin>
Nicopolis is a city which the holy Athanasius assigns to Thrace. Nicopolis (he says) is a city of Thrace, overlooking the river Ister <note>The Danube</note>. However, the subscription <note>The note at the end of the epistle</note> records it as being in Macedonia. But why did he command that Zenas the lawyer and Apollos of Alexandria be sent ahead? Both were faithful to Christ, having been experts in the Hebrew law. He revealed the reason when he said, *that nothing be wanting to them*—namely, nothing of spiritual intelligence in the faith of Christ. For he was calling them so that he might further inform and perfect <note>original: "consummaret"</note> them. And once perfected, he might set them over the churches in good works. For they were powerful in word and zeal once they had obtained sufficient intelligence, as is clear from the Acts of the Apostles, especially regarding Apollos. That he wished to set them in authority is sufficiently hinted by what he added: *and let ours also learn to excel in good works for necessary uses, lest they be unfruitful.* For he was summoning them for this very purpose: that they might learn to lead and to gather a manifold harvest. Of what value is a shepherd to the father of the family if no fruit is received from the flock? Of what use is a farmer if no harvest is gathered by the father of the family? Everyone who leads, and leads well, is a good shepherd and a good farmer; and for this very purpose, those
<margin>18</margin>
who lead have been appointed. As for what remains, he adds the greetings and farewell according to his custom at the heel of the letter, saying:

> All that are with me salute thee. Greet them that love us in the faith. Grace be with you all. Amen. Written to Titus, the first chosen bishop of the church of the Cretians, from Nicopolis of Macedonia.

<margin>.</margin>
*Greet them,* he says, *who love us in the faith.* Faith—and indeed the faith of Christ—ought to be the cause and the incentive of love. Christ, moreover, is the reason for all love. And those who thus love all the faithful in the faith of Christ are worthy of the apostolic greeting.

<page-num>3</page-num>
<header>COMMENTARY</header>

...and by the inspiration of the grace of Christ, which Jesus Christ, the author of our faith, may deign to bestow upon us, <margin>A 12</margin> with the Father and the Holy Spirit, one God, blessed for all ages and above all ages. Amen.

EXAMINATION of several points regarding the text. **The Vulgate edition** <note>The "Vulgata" was the standard Latin translation of the Bible used in the Western Church, largely credited to St. Jerome.</note> says: *Admonish them to be subject to princes and powers.* The holy Jerome prefers it to be said "to principalities" <note>Latin: "principatibus"</note> rather than "to princes" <note>Latin: "principibus"</note>. Indeed, that name also extends to magistrates; and what the Greeks call "the authorities" <note>original: "τὰς ἀρχὰς" (tas archas)</note>, our translators are accustomed to render sometimes as "magistrates," sometimes as "principalities," and sometimes as "powers." Paul writes: *Remind them to be subject to authorities and powers.* <note>original: "ὑπομίμνησκε αὐτοὺς ἀρχαῖς καὶ ἐξουσίαις ὑποτάσσεσθαι"</note> **The Vulgate edition** says: *To obey the word: but to be ready for every good work.* Where the old translator <margin>A 13</margin> says "to obey the word" <note>Latin: "dicto obedire"</note>, it more likely means "to obey the rulers," as the composition of the word shows. Paul writes: *to be obedient, to be ready for every good work.* <note>original: "πειθάρχειν πρὸς πᾶν ἔργον ἀγαθὸν ἑτοίμους"</note> **The Vulgate edition** says: *For we were also once foolish, incredulous, erring.* Where the old translator here says "foolish" <note>Latin: "insipientes"</note>, that word—which in the third chapter of Galatians is called sometimes "senseless" and sometimes "unwise"—designates those who are <margin>B 13</margin> out of their minds and without understanding. Paul writes: *For we ourselves were once foolish, disobedient, led astray.* <note>original: "ἦμεν γάρ ποτε καὶ ἡμεῖς ἀνόητοι, ἀπειθεῖς, πλανώμενοι"</note> **The Vulgate edition** says: *But when the kindness and humanity of God our Savior appeared: not by works of justice which we have done.* We can say: *the works of justice which we performed.* And "humanity" here describes the affection by which someone is moved by love and fondness for men, which is called *philanthropy* <note>original: "φιλανθρωπία"</note>. Its opposite is *misanthropy* <note>original: "μισανθρωπία"</note>: when someone maintains such a hatred of men as did Timon of Athens. And here, he does not mean the same thing as when the Savior appeared in a human body; but as has been said: when his love and fondness appeared toward all men—as one who willed to die for everyone so that they might not all die, but that all might become children of God and all be called to eternal kingdoms. Paul writes: *But when the goodness and philanthropy of God our Savior appeared, not from works in righteousness which we did.* <note>original: "ὅτε δὲ ἡ χρηστότης καὶ ἡ φιλανθρωπία τοῦ σωτῆρος ἡμῶν θεοῦ, οὐκ ἐκ ἔργων τῶν ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ ὧν ἐποιήσαμεν ἡμεῖς"</note> <margin>C 15</margin> **The Vulgate edition** says: *But avoid foolish questions, and genealogies, and contentions, and strivings about the law.* That "avoid" <note>Latin: "devita"</note> means to observe and to block them, lest they crawl about and cause harm by their crawling. For it is not enough merely to abstain from evil doctrines; they must also be watched and, as it were, hemmed in by barriers so they do not have the power to break out among others. Toward this end, the authority of elders and superiors is effective, not debates and battles of words. For rational people can be led by reason; irrational people cannot, just as you could not persuade a brute beast. But by authority, they can be easily repressed to the great benefit of all. Paul writes: <margin>C 16</margin> *But avoid foolish questionings, and genealogies, and strifes, and fightings about the law.* <note>original: "μωρὰς δὲ ζητήσεις καὶ γενεαλογίας, καὶ ἔρεις, καὶ μάχας νομικὰς περιΐστασο"</note> **The Vulgate edition** says: *Avoid a heretical man after a first and second correction.* The holy Jerome prefers it to be called "admonition" <note>Latin: "commonitionem"</note> rather than "correction" <note>Latin: "correptionem"</note> here. And this admonition is the instruction of true doctrine. Paul writes: *A heretical man after a first and second admonition, refuse.* <note>original: "αἱρετικὸν ἄνθρωπον μετὰ μίαν καὶ δευτέραν νουθεσίαν, παραιτοῦ"</note> **The Vulgate edition** says: *Since he is condemned by his own judgment.* The word placed here is more usually interpreted as: *condemning himself.* For heretics condemn themselves with their own mouths. It is no different than when someone said to the supreme king in the parable: *I know you are a harsh man, taking up what you did not lay down and reaping what you did not sow.* And immediately he heard: *By your own mouth I judge you, you wicked servant.* <note>Luke 19:21-22</note> So heretics <margin>D 17</margin> condemn themselves and are judged out of their own mouths. Paul writes: *being self-condemned.* <note>original: "ὢν αὐτοκατάκριτος"</note> **The Vulgate edition** says: *Hasten to come to me at Nicopolis.* It seems it should rather be said using the accusative: *Nicopolin.* Paul writes: *Make haste to come to me at Nicopolis.* <note>original: "σπούδασον ἐλθεῖν πρός μὲ εἰς νικόπολιν"</note> **The Vulgate edition** says: *And let yours also learn to excel in good works.* It should be said as a possession of the first person ["ours"]. Even if it were "yours," it would merely repeat what he said a little while before: *Let those who believe in God be careful to excel in good works.* And this follows from the sequence of the speech: having nothing to do with the preceding sentence regarding Zenas the lawyer and Apollo, whom you are to send ahead in haste. Therefore, it must be read as "our people." <margin>D 18</margin> Paul writes: *And let our people also learn to maintain good works.* <note>original: "μανθανέτωσαν καὶ οἱ ἡμέτεροι καλῶν ἔργων προΐστασθαι"</note> **The Vulgate edition** says: *The grace of God be with you all. Amen.* The word "God" is redundant, though it does no harm to the understanding. Paul writes: *Grace be with you all. Amen.* <note>original: "χάρις μετὰ πάντων ὑμῶν. ἀμήν"</note> And among the Greeks, the subscription is held: *To Titus, the first chosen bishop of the church of the Cretans. Written from Nicopolis of Macedonia.*

<page-num>225</page-num>
<header>XIII 225 Philemon</header>

### THE THIRTEENTH BOOK OF THE COMMENTARIES ON THE EPISTLES OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE PAUL, WHICH IS ON THE EPISTLE TO PHILEMON. CHAPTER I.

<image-desc>A large historiated drop cap letter 'A' depicting a landscape with a central tree and a bird, enclosed within a square frame with classical motifs.</image-desc>

<margin>1</margin> Writing a letter to Philemon of Colossae—one that is both personal and full of dutiful service in recommendation of Onesimus the carrier—Paul begins with his usual holy greeting, saying:

> ¶ Paul, a prisoner of CHRIST JESUS, and Timothy our brother: to Philemon our beloved and fellow worker, and to Apphia our beloved, and to Archippus our fellow soldier, and to the church in your house: grace to you and peace from God our Father, and the Lord JESUS CHRIST.

¶ To this holy greeting, he adds a thanksgiving toward God for the faith and (by divine grant) the virtues of Philemon, and says:

> ¶ I give thanks to my God, always making mention of you in my prayers: as I hear of your love and the faith which you have toward the Lord JESUS, and toward all the saints. So that the communication of your faith may be effective in the knowledge of every good thing which is in us in CHRIST JESUS.

<margin>2</margin> ¶ Philemon held love toward Christ and toward all the faithful; but toward the faithful, he declared his love and faith to be effective through the sharing of his goods. He was one who considered and recognized that every good thing in them did not come from themselves, but from the Lord Jesus Christ, the granter of all good that exists in the saints and that ought to be valued. Moreover, that Philemon shared his goods with the saints as a manifestation of his faith and love is declared by Paul in the following discourse, saying:

<margin>3</margin>> ¶ For we have much grace and consolation in your love: because through you, brother, the hearts <note>original: "viscera" - literally "bowels" or "entrails," used in the Bible to signify the seat of deep emotion and mercy.</note> of the saints have been refreshed.

¶ For what is this but saying: "We give you the greatest thanks, and your love affects us with consolation, because you have aided the necessity of the saints; because you have fed, cherished, and restored those who have a heart of mercy toward all, who wish good for all, and who implore God's mercy for all?" For these are the "hearts of the saints": breasts full of faith, love, piety, and the pleading of God’s mercy toward all. Since, therefore, Philemon is such a man toward all the faithful on account of the love of Christ and His saints, he will show himself all the more compliant to the petitions of Paul. Paul, for the sake of Christ's love, has now grown old through infinite tribulations, pressures, filth, and prisons; and for love of Him, he carries chains that are harsh to the body but sweet to him—sweet chains which are usually a burden to others. Though he could command as an apostle of Christ, he does not command, but supplicates and asks. And for whom does he ask? For Onesimus, Philemon’s servant, whom he himself won for Christ while in chains. Therefore, having sent ahead the greeting and the narrative in thanksgivings toward both God and men, he shows his petition to be reasonable. He adds it, saying:

<margin>4</margin>> ¶ Wherefore, though I have much confidence in CHRIST to command you what is fitting: I beseech you rather for love's sake. Being such a one as Paul the aged: and now also a prisoner of JESUS CHRIST. I beseech you for my son, whom I have begotten in my chains, Onesimus: who was once useless to you: but now is very useful to you and to me, whom I have sent back. But you, receive him, that is, my own heart <note>original: "viscera mea" - my own flesh and blood/inner self.</note>.

¶ Because of the love Philemon bore toward Christ, there was no need for a command; a mere supplication seemed sufficient to achieve what Paul desired. For superiors, when they understand that supplications will not prevail with inferiors, use commands, by which they extort even from the unwilling what they want. But the way of supplication and exhortation is more human and more suited to charity; Paul shows by his own example that it is to be preferred. He confesses the sin of Onesimus. He shows Onesimus converted to Christ, grieving much for the injury done to his master Philemon and confessing it—for Paul knew this only from Onesimus’s confession, though he might have known it otherwise through the Holy Spirit. Paul makes Onesimus as dear to himself as a son; he omits nothing, like a divine orator, to bend Philemon toward mercy and toward forgiving Onesimus, who was being sent back to his master with this letter. ¶ love ¶ charity: a rival to the love and charity of Christ. He who receives Onesimus receives Paul—indeed, receives Paul’s very heart. So he who receives the least of Christ's followers receives Christ and Christ’s heart. Onesimus, when he had been a Gentile, [was] an useless servant to his master...

<sig>F.i.</sig>

Paul uses a rhetoric of "sweet chains" and brotherly love rather than apostolic command to urge Philemon to show mercy.</summary>

<header>COMMENTARY</header>

...confessed that he had been <note>original: "fuisse fassus est"</note>: and that having taken money which belonged to his master, he had fled. But when he was illuminated by the light of Christ: he repented of his crime: and desired to subject himself to his master in all humility: and to wash away his fault through diligent service toward the world and to redeem his offense. For satisfaction had already been made to God, for the grace of Christ had remitted both the fault and the punishment. For the grace and mercy of Christ make satisfaction to God for all the faithful and the penitent: even if, frequently, satisfaction has not yet been made to the world. For Onesimus had not yet made satisfaction.

And certainly, so that he might make satisfaction to the world: Paul sent him back. Otherwise, he would have gladly kept him in his own service, which he also adds: saying.

<margin>5</margin>
¶ Whom I would have wished to retain with myself, that he might minister to me in your stead in the bonds of the gospel: but without your counsel I would do nothing, that your good deed might not be as it were of necessity: but voluntary. ¶ It certainly would have been good: if Onesimus, in the place of Philemon his master, had ministered to Paul while he was placed in prison and bonds. But since it was not in Philemon’s power to have used his servant otherwise, nor had it happened according to his counsel and will: it would surely have been a matter of necessity, and outside Philemon’s power, and not a voluntary good. But a good that is necessary to someone—that is, which happens to someone by force and is no longer in their power—is of little benefit to them. However, that which is done by counsel and a cheerful will: is both profitable to him and acceptable to God. Therefore the holy apostle wished that if he were to use any good thing of Philemon’s, it should be by his will and counsel, so that it might be a voluntary good for him, not coerced, not necessary. But someone will say: How was a servant who had fled a "good" to me? The apostle responds: That which is evil is very often, by God’s providence, the occasion for a greater good. And therefore, since such great good followed from his flight—that from a slave of the devil <note>A common patristic metaphor for the state of sin before conversion.</note> he was made a son of Christ, and from a mortal man an eternal one, inserted into the lineage of those who shall inherit eternal life instead of death—therefore Philemon ought to consider his flight not so much an evil as a good. For he receives in exchange for a bad servant both a brother and an excellent servant; for death, life; for vice, virtue; for vile mud, the most precious gold.

<margin>6</margin>
Therefore Paul adds a solution to a silent question and a satisfaction for the accusation in this manner: and he says. ¶ For perhaps he therefore departed for a season: that you might receive him forever, no longer as a servant, but above a servant, a beloved brother, especially to me. But how much more to you: both in the flesh, and in the Lord? If therefore you count me a partner in fellowship <note>original: "communionis participem"</note>: receive him as myself. ¶ To both Paul and Philemon, Onesimus is a brother by the <term>second generation</term> <note>referring to the "new birth" or spiritual regeneration in baptism</note>: not a servant, but above a servant, and something greater and more excellent than a servant, even if by the condition of the first and carnal generation, he was Philemon’s servant and not Paul’s. Thus, by the second generation, Philemon received a brother just as Paul did: and in addition, by the first generation, he received a servant and his own good according to the flesh. Therefore, by a stronger right, he ought to belong to Philemon than to Paul: since he was a greater good to him, both according to the flesh and according to the spirit. Yet, satisfaction was not made to Philemon for the injury inflicted, nor for the money consumed, nor for the loss which Philemon himself suffered from his flight. Who knows if Philemon was not so morose, not so difficult as to not remit the injury and the debt to Onesimus? Nevertheless, Paul wishes the injury to be cast upon himself, and to make satisfaction for the debt; and he plays with him amicably, promising satisfaction by giving his own letter as a <term>caution</term> <note>a formal security or promissory note</note>, written with his own hand. And he says:

<margin>7</margin>
¶ If he has wronged you in anything, or if he owes you anything: put that to my account. I, Paul, have written it with my own hand, I will repay it: not to say to you, that you owe even your own self to me. ¶ It is no wonder if a good imitator of a good God wishes both injuries and debts to be imputed to himself. For Christ the Lord willed that for us: and he made satisfaction for us, useless and runaway servants. But regarding Paul’s satisfaction: they think this was said more jokingly than in earnest. And that which he added: "I, Paul, have written it with my own hand: I will repay it." For in truth, Philemon did not only owe Paul so small a thing that he should forgive the servant's debt: but he owed his very self. For Paul had acquired him for Christ: and through him he lived for God. Therefore, making him mindful of the benefit of his calling to God: he now seriously adds.

<margin>8</margin>
¶ Yes, brother, let me have joy of you in the Lord: refresh my heart <note>original: "viscera mea," literally "my bowels," a metaphor for the seat of deep emotion</note> in the Lord. Having confidence in your obedience I wrote to you: being certain that you will do even more than I say. But at the same time: also prepare a lodging for me. For I am led by the hope: that through your prayers, I shall be given to you. ¶ What is "let me have joy of you in the Lord" except "let me acquire you in the Lord"? Revive, recreate, refresh my heart: receive my son with all kindness and tranquility, whom I love just as much as one I had begotten from my own vitals; although the vitals of love and divine charity are greater than the vitals of blood and flesh. By the preparation of a lodging, he brings joy to Philemon: and raises the hope of his face being seen yet again in the flesh.

<margin>9</margin>
But I think: that he did not see Paul anymore, except in the dwelling-place of eternity. He gives the final greetings and farewell: and says. ¶ *Epaphras*, my fellow prisoner in CHRIST JESUS, greets you, as do *Mark*, *Aristarchus*, *Demas*, *Luke*: who are my fellow workers. The grace of our Lord JESUS CHRIST be with your spirit. Amen.

->Written to Philemon from Rome. Sent by Onesimus the servant.<-

<meta>This page concludes the commentary on Paul's Epistle to Philemon and introduces a series of letters purportedly exchanged between the Apostle Paul and the Roman philosopher Seneca. The previous page discussed the return of the escaped servant Onesimus to his master Philemon.</meta>

# XIII 226 Philemon.

¶ He placed Epaphras, the minister of the Colossians, in the first place among those sending greetings: implying by this very fact that Philemon was a Colossian, as Athanasius <note>Athanasius of Alexandria (c. 296–373), a prominent Greek Church Father.</note> believes. Furthermore, this was done in commendation of the faithfulness of Epaphras: as one who, for the sake of Christ, bore chains and prisons with an equal mind alongside the apostle. As for what he adds at the end, "with your spirit": Paul refers to Philemon, Apphia his wife, Archippus the bishop and instructor of the Colossians, and the church in Philemon’s own household. Upon all of them he invokes the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ: may the same Christ Jesus, our Lord and Savior, grant this grace to us together with them through the intervention of his most blessed apostle Paul; he who is God together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, blessed above all things, and for all ages.

¶ And here is the end of the epistle of Paul to Philemon: which some were hardly willing to attribute to Paul, because it seemed less serious and appeared to contain little instruction. But it is one thing when Paul writes "Catholic" <note>original: "catholicas"; here meaning universal or general epistles addressed to the whole Church.</note> epistles, and another when he writes "Familiar" <note>original: "familiares"; meaning personal letters to individuals.</note> ones. The Catholic epistles contain matters pertaining to everyone. The Familiar ones, however, concern one or a few people. The Catholic epistles are universal, serious, and of great weight; such as those explained in the twelve preceding books. Of such a kind also is the one to the Hebrews: which is to be clarified in the following book through the grace of Christ. Familiar epistles are specific, less formal, and of lesser significance; such as the present one, and six others which they say Paul wrote in the Latin language in response to Seneca. <note>These letters between Paul and Seneca the Younger were widely read in the Middle Ages and Renaissance but are now considered apocryphal by modern scholars.</note> Neither did Saint Jerome deny this fact, nor did Linus <note>Referring to a work attributed to Linus, traditionally the second Pope, regarding the martyrdom of Paul.</note> of that time in the small book he wrote concerning the martyrdom of the most holy Paul.

The apostle composed the other preceding letters in the Greek language. However, the following one, which is to the Hebrews: he wrote in the native tongue of the Hebrews. And would that we were so fortunate that we might possess the archetype <note>original: "archetypum"; the original manuscript written by the author's own hand.</note> of that most divine following epistle to the Hebrews, out of reverence for Paul, the most worthy apostle of Christ, just as we have for the present and all preceding ones. But enough of this. However, because this book, containing only the exposition of this epistle to Philemon, does not seem to contain an equal or sufficient mass: therefore, to bring it to fullness, let us seem to have done nothing beyond our duty if we subjoin the familiar letters of Seneca to Paul and the familiar responsive letters of Paul to Seneca, so that there be no lack for the lovers of Christ and Paul of insight into both styles of the most blessed Paul’s letters—the universal as well as the personal. In the universal: he is more lofty and majestic. In the personal: he is more humble and relaxed, as one who, from some grave and sublime business, relaxes his efforts toward something light, descending in a certain way for the sake of refreshing the mind. For the mind wishes, at times, to be loosened from heavier studies by means of lighter ones. There are eight letters from Seneca to Paul, and six from Paul to Seneca. And Paul writes to Seneca not as to one who is reborn and fully a believer: but as to a friend, and one who pursued the Christians not so much with hatred as with benevolence, and who approved of their discipline. But let us first hear what Saint Jerome thinks of these letters. For speaking in his book *On Illustrious Men* <note>original: "libro virorum illustrium"</note> concerning Annaeus Seneca, he says: "I would not," he says, "place him in the catalog of saints, unless those letters prompted me, which are read by many, from Paul to Seneca and from Seneca to Paul, in which, although he was the most powerful man of that time, he says he wishes he held the same place among his own people that Paul holds among the Christians." Thus says Jerome.

¶ And Linus, speaking of Paul and Seneca, says: The tutor of the emperor was joined to him in such friendship, seeing in him divine knowledge: that he could scarcely restrain himself from conversation with him. Wherefore, if he was not able to speak to him face to face: he might enjoy his sweetness and amicable conversation and counsel through frequent letters given and received. Thus says Linus.

<margin>
Seneca
Paul
</margin>

For who else is read as being the tutor of the Emperor Nero, if not Seneca of Cordoba? And it seems that Seneca somewhat obscured and disguised his style. And I think this was done by industry <note>i.e., on purpose.</note>: so that if by chance the letters had come into other hands (even if inscribed with Seneca's name), they might nevertheless appear not to put Seneca in danger. For there was danger, and it was then against the emperor’s edict, to enjoy the familiarity of a Christian or a Jew.

But now let us come to the matter of the first letter. For Seneca announces to Paul that he has read his letters in a certain secret retreat, in which some Christians had accompanied him along with many who had joined themselves to him. From the reading of these, both he and others took a great deal of consolation. And he considers the discipline "moral" which is more than moral. For he who does not grasp Paul beyond a moral sense, does not grasp Paul at all. For Paul's discipline does not exclude the moral, but it also transcends it by far. For it is grace, a transcendence of morals: even if it is called by the same names by which morals are called. And Seneca was dazzled by that transcendence: and therefore he says that Paul did not speak of himself, but that a certain power superior to man spoke through Paul. And this is true: but it is not therefore "moral discipline," but more than moral, far more eminent than this. For the latter is a shadow, but the former is light. The latter (moral, I mean) is obtained by human industry: the former requires supernatural infusion. The unbeliever has the latter; only the believer can have the former. To the former, the latter has a great resemblance. For the latter is a footprint <note>original: "vestigium"</note>, while the former is the truth. Therefore, since Seneca possessed the latter and was moral, in terms of morals...

COMMENTARY.

...a lover and student of this discipline (which is known from the study of his books) wonderfully extols it at the end of his letter. Here, then, is his first letter.

### SENECA GREETS PAUL
<margin>•</margin>
<margin>•</margin>
<margin>•</margin>
<margin>•</margin>
<margin>•</margin>
<margin>•</margin>

I am reporting back to you, Paul, the conversation we had yesterday with Lucillius <note>Lucillius was the friend to whom Seneca addressed his famous *Moral Letters*.</note> regarding the Apocrypha <note>original: "Apocryphis"; referring here to "hidden" or "secret" teachings rather than the biblical books.</note> and other matters. Some companions of your teachings were with me, for we had retired to the Sallustian gardens. <note>The Gardens of Sallust were a famous landscaped estate in Rome, originally owned by the historian Sallust.</note> In that place, those of whom I spoke, while heading elsewhere, joined us upon seeing us. I would certainly have you know that we longed for your presence. After reading your pamphlet—that is, some of the many letters you directed to a certain city or provincial capital, containing a wonderful exhortation to the moral life—we were thoroughly refreshed. I do not think these sentiments were produced *from* you, but *through* you; or certainly, sometimes both from you and through you. For such is the majesty of those things, and they shine with such nobility, that I think the lifespans of men will hardly suffice to perfect and complete those instructions. I wish you well, brother. ¶ This is Seneca's first letter. And regarding what he says about "apocrypha": that is, about hidden things or teachings. Generally, whatever things come from a higher spirit, whose author cannot be recognized, people are accustomed to call "apocrypha." Nor is this term usually taken in a bad sense in the sacred scriptures. For the divine Paul also calls the treasures of wisdom and knowledge in Christ "apocryphal," that is, hidden. Thus he writes in chapter 2 of the Epistle to the Colossians: <note>original Greek: "ἐν ᾧ εἰσὶ πάντες οἱ θησαυροὶ τῆς σοφίας καὶ τῆς γνώσεως ἀπόκρυφοι"</note> "in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge." Nor does Seneca use this word in a bad sense here, but rather for the teachings of the Christians, whose hidden power and author were superior to men. Furthermore, the teachings of the Christians were "hidden" because they did not dare to go out into public on account of the edicts of the emperors and praetors. There are also "Apocrypha" in a bad sense: such as magic, the sorcerous arts, and the meddling of heretics, of which the evil spirit is the author; these do not dare to come into public because they are prohibited as crimes. But these have nothing to do with the sacred Apocrypha. ¶ The argument of the first responsive letter of Paul to the first letter of Seneca depends on Seneca's letter itself. For Paul writes familiarly, first excusing himself for the somewhat late response. This was because it was not safe, both for Paul's sake and for Seneca's danger, if his letters had been brought to him unless they were entrusted to a secure messenger. For if some informant had accused him—Seneca, I mean—not only of receiving a letter from Paul but from any Christian, or of sharing information with anyone, he would have been held guilty of the admitted crime of high treason <note>original: "læsæ maiestatis"; Lèse-majesté, a crime against the dignity of the emperor or the state.</note>. Furthermore, the apostle describes his own happiness—speaking, however, of earthly happiness in a human and civil manner—because his letters were well received by Seneca, Lucillius, and those who were joined with them in the Sallustian gardens. He also approves that Seneca spoke the truth regarding the letters and their deep sentiments: that they are not from himself, but from a higher power. Now follows this first responsive letter of the most holy Paul.

### PAUL GREETS SENECA

I received your letter yesterday with joy. I could have written back to it immediately if I had possessed the presence of the young man whom I was going to send to you. For you know when, and through whom, and at what time, and to whom anything ought to be given or entrusted. I ask, therefore, that you do not think yourself neglected while I look to the quality of the person <note>Paul explains he was waiting for a trustworthy messenger to ensure the letter's safety.</note>. But because you write that the letters were well received by you all in some place, I consider myself happy in the judgment of such a great man. For you—a censor, a sophist, a teacher of such a great prince and indeed of all—would not say this unless you were speaking the truth. I wish that you may be well for a long time. ¶ This is the letter. As for his calling Seneca a "censor": this regards morals. For he had been given to Nero to instruct his character. As for calling him a "sophist": this is taken in the sense of a title used to mark "philosophasters" and (so to speak) the "apes of philosophers." These are men who, detracting from true philosophers, fill everything with their own dreams. They desperately thrust forward foolish things instead of wise ones, rancid and foul and barbaric things instead of the clever and resonant, new-fashioned things for the old, and dark, grim, and deformed things for the clear, bright, and most beautiful. Such are "sophists" in the bad sense, whoever they are and wherever they are. But Seneca was not such a man. For Seneca was distinguished both as a rhetorician and an orator. As for "teacher": he calls him this from the office of teaching disciplines, for which he had been chosen to instruct Nero. He also calls Nero a "great prince of all," but an earthly one. And he says this truly, without flattery. For he was the monarch of the earthly world and the prince of all. And so prudently and circumspectly did he [write] these things...

# XIII

<note>original: "epistola scripta est"</note> the letter was written in such a way that, should it fall into the hands of an informer, no blame could be pinned upon either Paul for writing it or Seneca for receiving it—except for their names alone, of which one was Gentile and the other Christian. Next, Seneca attaches a second letter to Paul, the tone and subject of which are as follows: Seneca had composed certain books which he had organized by subject, such as his book *On Clemency* <note>Latin: *De Clementia*, a real work by Seneca written to the Emperor Nero, advising him on the virtues of mercy.</note> and *On Virtues*, and similar works. He had decided to read these to Nero; however, before publishing them, he wished to consult with Paul on certain points. Indeed, he wished Paul to be present while he read them to Nero, hoping the Emperor's mind might become more merciful toward the Christians. At that time, Nero’s mind was hostile toward them, and he allowed no one to associate with Christians without punishment. And is it any wonder that Seneca so greatly desired Paul’s judgment, since a spiritual man judges all things, yet is himself judged by no one? <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 2:15.</note> Now, Seneca’s second letter follows.

---

### SENECA TO PAUL. GREETINGS II.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut drop cap 'I' featuring scrolling foliage and vines.</image-desc>
I have arranged certain volumes and established their order according to their divisions. I have also decided to read them to Caesar <note>Referencing Emperor Nero.</note>. If fortune should look kindly upon us and he lends a fresh ear to these things, perhaps you also will be present. If not, I will appoint a day for us to examine this work together. I would not wish to publish this writing before I have consulted with you. If only this could be done without risk, you would know that I would not overlook you. Farewell, dearest Paul.

**This is Seneca’s second letter.** To this, Paul responds briefly, wishing for Seneca’s presence—yet not so much his physical presence as his salvation, which he finally desires for him through the knowledge of Christ. This letter requires no other explanation, and is woven as follows:

### PAUL TO SENECA. GREETINGS II.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut drop cap 'A' with scrolling vines and two small figures at the base.</image-desc>
As often as I hear your letters, I imagine your presence. I think of nothing else than that you are with us at all times. Therefore, as soon as you are able to come, we shall see each other face to face. I wish you good health.

**This is Paul’s**
**response.** To this, Seneca sends another letter, at a time when Caesar was somewhat more mild in his disposition toward the Christians; he did not wish them to be punished without a hearing, but intended to give them an opportunity to be heard and to clear themselves. Let this be the subject and theme of the letter: Paul was being accused before Caesar by both the Jews and the Gentiles. By the Jews, because he had departed from the Old Law, overturning their synagogues and destroying the worship of their fathers contrary to the laws of their country. By the Gentiles, because he had turned many away from the worship of the gods and joined them to his own sect, which was contrary to the gods. Both groups were demanding punishment for Paul at Caesar’s tribunal. Meanwhile, Paul kept himself in seclusion and appeared less in public, avoiding the ill-will of both Jews and Gentiles. Because of this, his long absence tormented the minds of Seneca and Lucillius <note>Seneca’s friend and the recipient of his famous *Moral Letters*.</note>, who was a man of a very pious and well-ordered life. Therefore, Seneca and Lucillius compose a joint letter to Paul, calling him back from his long seclusion. They attribute such wisdom to Paul that they believe once the opportunity to clear himself is open, he will very easily defend himself against both charges before Caesar. The tone of the letter is as follows:

---

### SENECA AND LUCILLIUS TO PAUL. GREETINGS III.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut drop cap 'W' with scrolling floral patterns.</image-desc>
We are distressed by your excessive seclusion. What is it, or what circumstances keep you away? If it is the indignation of the Lord <note>Referring here to the Emperor, often called "lord" (*dominus*).</note> because you have withdrawn from the old rite and sect and converted others in turn, there will be an opportunity to request that he consider this as something done by reason, not out of levity. Farewell, dearest Paul.

**This is the letter.** To which Paul
responds in a "wrapper" <note>original: "inuolucro"; implying a hidden, metaphorical, or coded message.</note>. For through the Holy Spirit, it was becoming known to him what he was about to do. For at that time, the situation did not demand that he request a place for defense or apology from the tribunal. For those who had accused him and those who had issued the edicts were seeking an occasion for indignation and punishment rather than for learning the truth or granting acquittal. And that was the only thing. Moreover, he could not clear himself without speaking the open truth. But the open truth was that the old Jewish rite was no longer to be followed, and the worship of the idols they served as gods was truly abominable. This was the second point that revealed the open truth. But at that time, these things were not to be spoken openly, nor safely committed to paper, except to those upon whom some portion of the living light had already shone. Let this be the hypothesis and argument for the letter. Now follows Paul’s third letter.

### PAUL TO SENECA AND LUCILLIUS. GREETINGS III.

Concerning those things about which you wrote to me: it is not permitted to speak with reed and ink <note>Original: "arundine & atramento." Paul is explaining why he cannot write more explicitly or openly about certain spiritual or political matters.</note>. Of these two things, one marks and designates a matter, while the other shows it clearly. This is especially true since I know there are those "among you"—that is, with you and within you—who understand me. Honor must be shown to all: all the more so because they grasp at every occasion for indignation. If we give them patience, we shall overcome them in every way and from every side, provided they are the kind of people who might feel remorse for their actions. Fare well.

¶ What does it mean when he says: *especially since I know there are those among you—that is, with you and within you—who understand me*, if not that "I know there are some hidden faithful among you, purified by the mysteries of understanding, who understand my words (even if they are veiled and obscure)"? By his silence and his absence, Paul was showing honor to those accusing him—both the Jews and the Gentiles, and Caesar himself before whom he was accused. He did so because he knew they were seeking further opportunity to do harm. He hoped that through his patience, and through the virtues, signs, and benefits of the graces of the Holy Spirit, they might eventually be conquered from every side for their own salvation—if indeed they were the sort who could be led to repentance. Therefore, it was not expedient for Paul to put forward his defense as Seneca and Lucilius <note>Lucilius Junior was the friend to whom Seneca addressed his famous *Moral Letters*.</note> were demanding.

Seneca sends another letter to Paul and Theophilus, the argument of which is as follows: Seneca had recently received into his hands Paul’s letters to the Galatians and the Corinthians (who are indeed in Achaia <note>A Roman province in southern Greece.</note>), which he both read and approved of, being well-affected by the reading of them. He would have wished, however, that the "cultivation of speech"—that is, human eloquence—had not been lacking. Yet it was enough that the cultivation of divine speech and the efficacy of the Spirit were present. And in this, Seneca speaks as one having a "carnal sense," for the carnal man does not perceive the things that are of God. He read these same letters even in the presence of Nero, and he praised Paul with public declarations in order to win for him the favor of the prince. Nero marveled that a man, without much formal instruction from teachers, had arrived at such sublime understanding. Seneca, using a pagan example, hinted to Nero that this was not achieved through human study, but rather through divine inspiration and a gift poured down from heaven. All these things served to commend Paul and to earn the prince's benevolence toward him, if indeed it could be earned by any virtue, innocence of life, or sanctity. Now let the fourth letter of Seneca be heard.

### ANNEUS SENECA TO PAUL AND THEOPHILUS. GREETING IV.

I profess that I am well-affected by the reading of your letters which you sent to the Galatians and the Corinthians of Achaia. And let us live together in such a way that we may fulfill them with divine honor. For the Holy Spirit in you, and upon you, expresses sentiments that are lofty, sublime, and sufficiently venerable. I would wish, therefore, that since you bring forth such excellent things, the refinement of speech <note>Original: "cultus sermonis." Seneca, as a master of Roman rhetoric, is critiquing Paul's simple or "unpolished" prose style.</note> were not lacking to their majesty. And so that I may not hide anything from you, brother, or be burdened by my conscience, I confess that Augustus <note>A title here used for the Emperor Nero.</note> was moved by your sentiments. At the joyful beginning of your virtue in these letters, his word was this: that he wondered how a man who has not been "legitimately imbued" <note>Meaning a man who lacked a formal, classical Greco-Roman education.</note> could think in such a way. To him, I responded that the gods are accustomed to speak through the mouths of the innocent, or those who cannot betray their own teaching. And having given him the example of Vatinius, a simple country man to whom two men appeared in the Reatine field (who were afterwards named Castor and Pollux), he seemed sufficiently satisfied. Farewell.

¶ That which he said, *to the Corinthians of Achaia*, is an epithet. For the Corinthians and the Achaians are the same; they occupy the Isthmus and are neighbors to Hellas, which is called Greece.

*I confess that Augustus was moved by your sentiments.* He means Nero, who rejoiced in novelties. Seneca says he was moved not so much by the speech as by the sentiment; for those who are accustomed to human eloquence (especially if affectation is present) do not receive spiritual speech any differently than those imbued with crooked disciplines admit true philosophy. That Seneca also read the letters of Paul to Nero is proven by Linus <note>Saint Linus, traditionally the successor to St. Peter; here cited as a source for the lives of the apostles.</note>, who says: "For a certain teacher of Caesar [Seneca] read his writings again in his presence, and rendered him admirable in all things."

Moreover, Marcus Antonius Sabellicus <note>A prominent Renaissance historian (1436–1506).</note>, an eminent collector of histories in our time, when discussing Paul and Seneca, cites testimony from this letter. He says: "There exist some letters to Anneus Seneca; and again, Seneca's letters to him. One of these contained this: 'I confess (he said) that Augustus (speaking meanwhile of Nero) was moved by your sentiments.' At the joyful beginning of virtue in you, his word was this: 'That he wondered how one not legitimately imbued could think in such a way.' To which I responded: 'The gods are accustomed to speak through the mouths of the innocent.'" Thus says Sabellicus.

And what does it mean, *at the joyful beginning of virtue in you, his word was this*, if not that for Nero, the beginning of the speech regarding the virtue that is in you was pleasant? That "beginning" regarding Paul's virtue was indeed joyful and pleasant: that he wondered how one not legitimately imbued could think in such a way.

The example of Vatinius is mentioned by Livy, Valerius, and many others. As he was going toward the city in the Reatine field, two young men appeared to him who were believed to be Castor and Pollux. Indeed, what he had received from them he announced to the Senate: that Perseus, the Macedonian king, had been captured on the previous day by Paulus Aemilius <note>Lucius Aemilius Paullus Macedonicus, a Roman general who defeated King Perseus in 168 BC.</note>. But being despised by the Senate, he was thrown into prison. However, after letters were later received in the Senate from Paul stating that Perseus had been captured on that very day, Vatinius was freed from custody and, moreover, was gifted with that field.

Seneca uses the Roman legend of Vatinius and the gods Castor and Pollux to explain how divine truth can be revealed through "uneducated" or "innocent" individuals.</summary>

<header>XIII 228</header>

When Seneca read the example to Nero, Nero appeared sufficiently persuaded that Paul could have been instructed by divine matters. Paul responds to this letter, but he does not quite approve of the fact that his writings were handed over to Nero. Nevertheless, he forgives Seneca, because he did so out of excessive love for him, wishing as much as he could to win the prince's favor for him. However, he warns him and prays that he not do it anymore. Furthermore, he warns him that among Nero’s concubines there is one who holds his name in hatred. Although Paul thinks little of her goodwill or indignation, he nevertheless does not want Seneca to incur her offense on his account. Now follows the fourth letter of Paul.

## PAUL TO SENECA. GREETINGS IV.

<margin>
P
A

</margin>
Although I am not unaware that our Caesar is a lover of wonderful things (whenever they are lacking), you will nevertheless permit yourself to be warned—not lightly, but seriously. For I think you have acted gravely in wishing to bring to his notice something that is contrary to his ritual and discipline. Since he worships the gods of the Gentiles, why did it seem right to you that you should want him to know this, unless I might think you did this out of excessive love for me? I ask you, therefore, not to do so in the future. For care must be taken that, while you love me, you do not cause offense to your master. Indeed, his offense will not hinder me if it continues, nor will it help me if it does not exist. If she is a queen, she will not be indignant; if she is a woman, she will be offended. Fare well.

¶ As for Paul calling Nero "his Caesar," it is no wonder, because Christians obeyed temporal powers in all things—short of offending God—and they acknowledged them. But they acknowledged and venerated them as earthly powers. Nor did they say they had other Caesars or kings than the rest of the people, but rather the same ones in common with others. But Nero was inquisitive. He sought after distant and new things when he heard of them; however, when they were present—even those which were admirable and stupendous—he grew weary of them. So it was with the divine virtues granted to Paul: when they were absent, he praised and loved them; but when they were present and he had seen them, he disparaged them, ascribing them to magic and sorcery. This he did later, as Linus <note>A legendary early Christian author, often identified as the first Bishop of Rome after Peter.</note> writes, regarding the resurrection of the young Patroclus, his favorite cup-bearer. And regarding which concubine or wife Paul speaks of, who might be hostile to him because of informants, it is not known. For one reads that Nero had many queens and many mistresses. Nevertheless, Seneca understood this well enough, and it was sufficient for him to be on his guard. Seneca sends another letter in turn to Paul, the argument of which is briefly this: From the previous letters, Seneca realized that Paul took it poorly that he had re-read his writings in Nero's presence. He asks for pardon, promising that he will not do it again from then on. In addition, he sends Paul a little book "on the abundance of words" <note>Original: "de verborum copia." This refers to a rhetorical manual on style and vocabulary.</note> as a gift; I believe so that Paul might practice his more elegant Latin. These things Paul himself—as one taught by the Holy Spirit—valued as little as children's games or a nurse's trifles. Nevertheless, he highly valued Seneca's friendship and his drawing toward Christ, if he could have done so entirely. Now let the fifth letter of Seneca be heard.

## SENECA TO PAUL. GREETINGS V.

I know that you were moved by the letters I gave you regarding the publication of your writings to Caesar, not so much for your own sake as by the nature of things. This nature so calls back the minds of men from all arts and right morals that I am not surprised today—especially as one who, through many proofs, already holds this as most well-known. Therefore, let us now act so that if anything was done in the past, you may easily grant pardon. I have sent you a book on the abundance of words. Farewell, dearest Paul.

¶ "The nature of things." He seems to be censuring the nature of Nero, which is believed to have been so depraved and inherently warped that it seemed to call him away from every good art and right conduct. This is also clearly testified to by Suetonius where he deals with the robberies, injuries, and other crimes committed by him both secretly and publicly. "His petulance," he says, "his lust, luxury, greed, and cruelty he exercised at first gradually and secretly, as if by youthful error; but even then it was doubtful to no one that those were vices of his nature, not of his age." <note>A quotation from Suetonius's *Life of Nero*, Chapter 26.</note> See how he accuses Nero's nature. Paul does not respond to this letter. For regarding Nero's nature, it was better to remain silent than to make a response on that matter. Instead, he writes a letter in which he both honors Seneca and humbles himself. For in this one, he did not place his name in the second position as he was accustomed to do, saying "Paul to Seneca, Greetings" at the beginning of the salutation; instead, he reserved his name to be placed at the bottom, at the tail of the finished letter. This was a practice often done for the sake of showing honor to the Roman Senate. And the letter, which is Paul's fifth, is as follows:

Lest with perplexity and disgrace I desire to bring about what was of my own will. Farewell. Paul.

<header>COMMENTARY</header>

...signifies [uncertainty], doubt, and confusion. Here, however, Paul uses it to mean confusion. In other respects, the letter is clear. Seneca responds to this, having been taught humility by Paul; from now on, he places his own name after Paul’s name, honoring both Paul and Roman citizenship by this very act. For in those great times, Roman citizenship was a mark of high nobility. We learn from the Acts of the Apostles that Paul was a Roman citizen by birth, but we hardly know if Seneca was also a Roman citizen. The argument of the letter is well understood from this context. Now we add the sixth letter of Seneca.

<margin>11 ¶</margin>
## VI.
## SENECA TO PAUL.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter A featuring a man seated at a desk or table.</image-desc>

Greetings, my dearest Paul. If I were not joined to you and your name in every way—I will not say merely joined, but necessarily mingled—it would be all over for your Seneca. Since you are the summit and the highest peak of all mountains, would you not wish me to rejoice if I am so close to you that I am judged to be another like you? Therefore, do not feel you are unworthy to be named first at the head of these letters <note>Seneca is addressing Paul’s previous concern about social hierarchy by placing Paul’s name before his own in the greeting</note>, lest you seem to be testing me rather than playing with me—especially since you know yourself to be a Roman citizen. For what is mine is yours, and your place among your people, I wish to be my place among mine. Farewell, my dearest Paul.

¶ Jerome <note>original: "Hieronymus"</note> cites this letter as a holy testimony. We do not have a response from Paul to this one, nor is it necessary, for this was Seneca's reply to Paul's previous letter. Seneca writes another letter concerning the persecution stirred up against the Christians and Jews on account of the burning of the city of Rome. Although they were innocent, they were dragged to punishment and given over to death everywhere based on false accusations. Seneca grieves that such innocence is condemned so unjustly, knowing that the fire was set in Rome by Nero; however, it was clearly not safe to write this openly to those who were foolish. He therefore encourages Paul to be of good mind and predicts that the author of these evils will face a future punishment: Stygian fire <note>referring to the fires of the underworld or Hell</note>. Let this serve as the argument for the letter. Now the seventh letter of Seneca follows.

<margin>12 ¶</margin>
## VII.
## SENECA TO PAUL.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter A identical to the one above.</image-desc>

Greetings, my dearest Paul. Do you think I am not saddened and sorrowful that punishment is repeatedly taken upon your innocence? And then, that all the people judge you all so harshly and so liable to guilt, thinking that what happened to the city was done by you? But let us bear it with a calm mind and use the forum that fate has granted, until unconquered happiness puts an end to these evils. Former ages also endured the Macedonian son of Philip <note>Alexander the Great</note>, the Persian Darius, and Dionysius, and our own Caligula <note>original: "Caium Caesarem"</note>, who were allowed to do whatever they pleased. It is manifest from where the burning of the city of Rome often suffers. But if my humility could express the cause, and if it were permitted to speak safely in these dark times, everyone would see everything now. Yet Christians and Jews are usually punished as if they were the plotters of the fire. That marauder, whoever he is, whose pleasure is the executioner’s work and whose veil is a lie, is destined for his own time. And just as one best head is given for the sake of many, so he, given for all, shall be burned with fire. 132 houses and 4 blocks <note>original: "insulae"</note> burned for six days; the seventh day gave a pause. I hope you are well, brother.

¶ What he says here about the Macedonian son of Philip and the Persian Darius, everyone understands well enough as being said of Alexander, King of the Macedonians, and Darius, King of the Persians. But concerning Dionysius and Caligula, this is to be understood of Dionysius who conquered the Indians, and of Caligula; how licentiously he lived is known from the author Suetonius <note>original: "Tranquillo"</note>. Both Suetonius and Cornelius Tacitus, those distinguished historians, testify to the burning of the city. And from this, the first persecution against the Christians was stirred up, by imposing on them the false crime of the fire, of which Nero had been the author, as both Suetonius and Tacitus have recorded. For while he was alive, he sent his chamberlains and set the city on fire. Looking out at the burning of the city from the Tower of Maecenas, happy at the sight of the flames, he sang of the "Destruction of Troy" in theatrical costume, exulting, leaping, and dancing. Behold that marauder, that devil Nero, the killer of Peter and Paul, who burned the city, for whom the execution of the innocent, both Jews and Christians, was a pleasure, and for whom the lie that Christians had set fire to the city was a veil. We do not have Paul’s response to this letter. Seneca sends another letter to Paul concerning certain of his allegorical and enigmatic works. For there is no doubt that in the many years in which he campaigned for Christ—36 years and more, as Sophronius says (which is easily deduced by calculation)—Paul did much more than what has reached us. Among those could be the allegorical and enigmatic works Seneca mentions, which perished through the injury of time. Seneca would have liked to persuade Paul to provide them with rhetorical ornament. Certainly, rhetoricians are as devoted to their style as Lycophron was to the lyre. But in this very matter, Paul had modestly corrected Seneca when he suggested it, saying that many who affect such style corrupt the meaning and weaken the virtues of things, and...

<header>XIII Phile.</header>

(so to speak) to unman and emasculate the speech. And certainly, what makeup <note>original: "fucus" — literally rouge or red dye used to deceive; here it refers to deceptive rhetorical artifice</note> is to a woman, and therefore makes her suspect, this more curious and affected rhetorical ornament in speech is much the same. If we are speaking of human affairs or of softer subjects, and this "makeup" is applied, it is not much blamed (for even superfluous adornment in a somewhat delicate woman is usually pleasing). However, when a discourse is held concerning divine matters—higher, weightier, and altogether chaste—this affectation of speech is entirely unbecoming, no different than makeup on men. For this masculine speech either has, or ought to have, masculine strength and meaning. Therefore, it is no wonder that on this point the apostle did not listen to Seneca, even though Paul could have given his speech this kind of adornment. For he knew that feminine ornament misbecomes a man; it corrupts, softens, and weakens him. Yet Seneca is, in a way, worthy of forgiveness, for he urged this out of a feeling of love. He presumed, however, from the weakness of the flesh over the spirit, believing he could do better than what the Holy Spirit gave to Paul. If Seneca had considered what once happened to the writer Theopompus <note>Theopompus of Chios, a 4th-century BCE historian who, according to legend, was struck with blindness for trying to include sacred Jewish scripture in his profane histories</note>, who, when he had defiled the sacred heights of scripture with a rhetorical style, was suddenly deprived of the light of his eyes, perhaps he would have been more cautious. Now let Seneca’s eighth letter be heard.

<margin>13</margin>
### TO PAUL, SENECA. VIII.

> <margin>
> ,
> ,
> ,
> ,
> ,
> </margin>
> **G**reetings, my Paul. Allegorically and enigmatically, many works are composed by you everywhere. And therefore, so great a force of things and gifts has been granted to you: not to be decorated by the ornament of words, but by a certain cultivation. Do not fear what I remember you saying quite often: that many who affect such things corrupt the meaning and weaken the strength of the subjects. But I would wish you to grant me this: to follow the custom of the Latin language <note>original: "latinitati morem gerere"</note> and to apply a fair appearance to honorable words, so that the granting of your noble gift can be worthily delivered by you. Farewell.

<margin>A</margin>
Behold, he confesses that Paul’s words are fit for the task, but that the speech lacks "appearance" <note>original: "speciem" — outward beauty or polish</note>. And certainly, the words of Paul and others who felt the inspiration of the Holy Spirit in the primitive church were so fitting that men would not know how to speak properly of God unless they borrowed words from them. But what sort of "appearance" does the speech lack, if it is composed of fitting words and honorable terms? What appearance, what cultivation does Seneca wish to apply? Certainly a rhetorical one. As if a tree laden with fruit does not become beautiful unless flowers grow alongside it; or as if a mature crop is not more beautiful than when the stalk is flowering. But nature has provided otherwise. When the fruit is present, there is no need for flowers. Nor indeed did Paul's speech (for it is the fruit) lack the flower that Seneca thought it did. To this letter, Paul
<margin>A</margin>
responds modestly, secretly hinting that he judges his speech to be not human but divine in its sense. He suggests that the things he puts forward are not flowers, but fruit and seeds; not the words of man, but of God. He reveals a good thing: not one that can be acquired by us through our own efforts, but one which, derived from God, takes increase and remains forever. He exhorts Seneca to hold fast to what he reads in his writings and to avoid the observances of the Gentiles and the Jews. And because Seneca was so strongly held by an affection for rhetorical speech, Paul grants him permission to sing the praises of Jesus Christ with rhetorical ornament. Indeed, he may even read them
<margin>A</margin>
to the Prince <note>the Emperor Nero</note>, to his household, and to his faithful friends, who are more enticed by the flower of speech than nourished by the fruit of the journey. For who would not know that Paul’s words would be harsh and unpleasant for believing those things which belong to Jesus Christ? The text of Paul's sixth and final letter, in which he responds to Seneca, follows.

> **T**o you, as you weigh these things, those things have been revealed which the divinity has granted to few. Therefore, I am now certain that I am sowing the strongest seed in a fertile field—not indeed a matter which is seen to be corrupted, but the Word of God, stable, a derivation of the good that grows and remains forever. That which your wisdom has attained must be unfailing, and you must quickly avoid the observances of the Gentiles <note>original: "ethnicorum"</note> and the Israelites. You shall make yourself a new author of JESUS CHRIST; and having obtained the office of a herald, you shall introduce him to the temporal King, and to his household and faithful friends. To them, your persuasion will be harsh and difficult to grasp, since most of them are not at all moved by your teachings. To those whom the Word of God instills a vital benefit, it brings forth a new man without corruption, and an eternal soul, hastening rightly from this place toward God. Farewell, Seneca, most dear to us.

<margin>A</margin>
If Nero, if his household, did not acquiesce to the teachings of Seneca which were human, they were even less likely to show themselves ready to believe those things which were said of Christ—of eternal goods, of regeneration into a new man without corruption, and the rest of the mysteries which are most true, without which human salvation cannot stand.
<margin>X</margin>
And Paul agreed that Seneca should rather read to Nero some things about Christ devised in his own style, rather than the mysteries which he himself had written. For Nero and his household could more likely be led to salvation by the charms of speech than by the higher mysteries, if they showed themselves capable of being cured.
