<meta>This page concludes the discussion of the apocryphal correspondence between Seneca and Paul, shifting focus to a scholarly examination of the Epistle to Philemon. The previous page discussed the stylistic differences between the two men.</meta>

...they might be. But if not, the kindness of God, which called them to repentance and a change of life for the better, was not lacking, so that they themselves might be more severely punished in the future. And whether He did this for Seneca remains hidden from us. However, I do not believe he ever arrived at the true light of Christ, nor received the spirit of regeneration—one who was a lover and admirer of both Paul and Christ. But this love and this admiration remained worldly <note>original: "urbana" — literally "of the city," implying refined, secular, or sophisticated rather than spiritual</note>; for Paul labored much so that it might be effective. For if he were innocent, he would not have slit his veins, nor taken poison to accelerate a slow death on account of the false accusation of the Pisonian conspiracy <note>A plot to overthrow Emperor Nero in 65 AD; Seneca was accused of being a part of it and forced to commit suicide</note>. Nor, finally, when that poison proved ineffective, would he have dissolved himself in the steam of a bath. Rather, he should have waited for all these things from another, rather than ordering them for himself or by another. He ought to have imitated the martyrs of Christ rather than the miserable fate of either Lucretia or Cato <note>Lucretia and Cato the Younger were famous Roman figures who committed suicide to preserve their honor</note>. But we say these things more in sorrow than in disparagement, since in life he had been honored by Paul. Would that he had ended his life in such a way that he could also be honored with Paul!

But perhaps here you will ask why, since Paul in his tenth letter (which is his fifth <note>Referring to the sequence in the apocryphal Paul-Seneca correspondence</note>) did not place his name second, but joined it at the very bottom of the letter after it was finished—why in this letter did he place his name second, rather than adding it to the end as before? To this little question, perhaps one might not unworthily satisfy it by saying: Paul did this because Seneca had requested in his sixth letter (which was the response to that one) that his name be not only joined closely to his own, but (if possible) mingled with it. Therefore, the apostle acquiesced to his petition and joined his name closely to Seneca's. For to join name to name closely in sending a short letter is a sign of friendship and "glued-together" love. To place your name second is to show honor to the one to whom you write and to prefer them to yourself in honor. If, however, you place your name first, you prefer yourself in honor; this is permitted especially when a teacher writes to a disciple, or a superior to an inferior. But if you place your name at the bottom <note>original: "in calce" — literally "at the heel"</note>, it is a sign of greater veneration. And the further it is from the text, the greater the veneration, adjusted almost according to the quality of the persons to whom you write. These things can be understood in a way from Paul’s fifth and Seneca’s sixth letters, which were sent previously. But I frankly confess: these things are confused everywhere in writing, even if reason almost demands this rule. But enough on these humbler matters; by the occasion of the familiar letter to Philemon, our discourse has branched out sufficiently. Now let it return to the business of the following book, with the most blessed Paul obtaining grace for us to fulfill our duty, and Christ truly bestowing it. To whom, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, be all honor, and glory, and thanksgiving, unto all ages of ages. Amen.

## EXAMINATION of certain points regarding the text.

<margin>A 1</margin>
To Philemon our beloved helper, and to Apphia our dearest sister. ¶ *Sister*: is redundant. According to Paul, one should say *Apphia*, with the "ph" aspirated. And *beloved* (feminine). For it is the feminine form of what the translator said just before, *beloved* (masculine). Jerome notes this fact, and that *beloved* <note>original: "dilectum"</note> signifies one who is lovable, or who is worthy and deserving of being loved. Paul: <note>original: "Φιλήμονι τῷ ἀγαπητῷ καὶ συνεργῷ ἡμῶν, καὶ ἀπ-" — To Philemon the beloved and our fellow worker, and Ap-</note>

<margin>A 2</margin>
The Vulgate edition: *Which you have in the Lord JESUS.* ¶ Better: *towards the Lord JESUS.* Paul: <note>original: "ἣν ἔχεις πρὸς τὸν κύριον ἰησοῦν" — which you have toward the Lord Jesus</note>. ¶ The Vulgate edition: *That the communication of your faith may be made evident.* ¶ One should say *effective* rather than *evident*: which the holy Jerome also notes here. Paul: <note>original: "ὅπως ἡ κοινωνία τῆς πίστεώς σου ἐνεργὴς γένηται" — so that the fellowship of your faith may become effective</note>. But I think the ancient translator was misled by the similarity of the words: *eparchēs* <note>meaning evident/manifest</note> with the first vowel in the middle, and *energēs* <note>meaning effective/working</note> with the second vowel in the middle. Of these, the latter signifies "effective and laborious," the former "evident and manifest." Here, however, the word is held with the second vowel in the middle.

<margin>A 3</margin>
The Vulgate edition: *In the acknowledgment of every work which is in us in CHRIST JESUS.* ¶ In most Greek codices, *work* is not found; but simply <note>original: "ἐν γνώσει παντὸς ἀγαθοῦ τοῦ ἐν ἡμῖν εἰς τὸν Χριστὸν ἰησοῦν" — in the knowledge of every good thing that is in us toward Christ Jesus</note>. Truly, a great "good" in Paul and Timothy was the knowledge of the mysteries of the faith of Christ, of which Philemon had also been made a participant. Some codices even have <note>original: "ἐμ γνώσει παντὸς ἔργου ἀγαθοῦ" — in the knowledge of every good work</note>. But what were these "good works" which were in Paul and his followers? Certainly the works of the faith of Christ, and those which they had obtained from the grace of Christ—nay, even what the grace of Christ was working in them. Because of the fullness of his faith, this could by no means be hidden from Philemon.

¶ The Vulgate edition: *For I have had great joy and consolation in your charity.* ¶ We now read *grace* <note>original: "gratiam"</note>, not *joy*. And we have it in the plural and the present tense, *we have*, not the singular past *I have had*. And it refers to both Paul and Timothy, even if it makes no difference if it refers to only one, like Paul, and the sense would be: "We give thanks <note>original: "Gratiam habemus"</note> for your love and moreover are consoled in it." I think, however, the ancient translator read *charan* <note>joy</note> not *charin* <note>grace/thanks</note>, and for this reason translated it as *joy* not *grace*. Paul: <note>original: "χάριν γὰρ ἔχομεν πολλὴν, καὶ παράκλησιν ἐπὶ τῇ ἀγάπῃ σου" — For we have much grace and consolation in your love</note>.

<margin>B 4</margin>
¶ The Vulgate edition: *Wherefore, having much confidence in CHRIST JESUS to command you that which appertains to the matter.* <gloss>Jesus: is redundant.</gloss> And where the translator said *that which appertains to the matter*: it can be said *that which is decent*, or *that which is right*. Paul: <note>original: "διὸ πολλὴν ἐν χριστῷ παρρησίαν ἔχων ἐπιτάσσειν σοι τὸ ἀνῆκον" — Wherefore, having much boldness in Christ to command you what is fitting</note>. ¶ The Vulgate edition: *For*

<meta>This page concludes the scholarly commentary on the Epistle to Philemon, focusing on precise linguistic corrections to the Latin Vulgate translation by comparing it to the original Greek and the writings of Saint Jerome. It marks the transition from the previous page's discussion of the Seneca-Paul correspondence back to canonical scripture.</meta>

### XIII Philemon.
7

<margin>D</margin> **"I beseech you for love's sake, since you are such as Paul the aged, and now also a prisoner of JESUS CHRIST."** <note>Philemon 1:9</note> ¶ It should rather be said in the first person, **"since I am such a person,"** not the second, **"since you are."** What follows, **"as Paul the aged,"** explains what he meant by **"such a one."** It is as if he were saying: **"since I am such a one, namely Paul the aged, and also now a prisoner of Jesus Christ."** For Philemon was not such a person as Paul the aged, or a prisoner of Jesus Christ—that is, a prisoner for the sake of Christ. But this tripped up the translator: because the Greek participle *as* <note>original: "ὡς"</note> is used for any person without distinction. However, he should have noticed that it was in the nominative case, and therefore could not refer to the one to whom the speech is directed, but to the one speaking. Otherwise, it would have had to be in the accusative case, as if it were written: **"I beseech you, being such a one."** <note>original Greek: "παρακαλῶ σε τοιοῦτον ὄντα"</note> But now it is placed in the nominative. Paul says: **"I rather beseech, being such a one, as Paul the aged, and now also a prisoner of Jesus Christ."** <note>original Greek: "μᾶλλον παρακαλῶ, τοιοῦτος ὤν, ὡς παῦλος πρεσβύτης, νυνὶ δὲ καὶ δέσμιος ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ"</note> ¶ The Vulgate edition says: **"Whom I have begotten in bonds, Onesimus."** ¶ The word **"my"** is missing. Paul says: **"whom I have begotten in my bonds, Onesimus."** <note>original Greek: "ὃν ἐγέννησα ἐν τοῖς δεσμοῖς μου ὀνήσιμον"</note> ¶ The Vulgate edition says: **"Whom I have sent back to you."** ¶ The word **"to you"** is redundant. Paul says: **"Whom I have sent."** <note>original Greek: "ὃν ἔπεμψα"</note> ¶ The Vulgate edition says: **"Receive him as my own heart."** <note>The Latin "viscera" literally means "guts" or "bowels," but figuratively refers to the heart or deepest affections</note> ¶ In Paul it says: **"This is,"** which sounds more effective than **"as."** Just as that saying of the Savior: **"Insofar as you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me"** sounds more powerful than if it had been said, "Insofar as you did it to one of these my brothers, you did it *as if* to me." For what does "as if to me" mean, except "like" or "as though to me"? But when it is said **"you did it to me,"** it is as if it were said absolutely: **"you did it to me."** Therefore, Paul's speech is far more effective than the translator's. Paul says: **"that is, receive my own heart."** <note>original Greek: "τουτέστι τὰ ἐμὰ σπλάγχνα προσλαβοῦ"</note> ¶ The Vulgate edition says: **"But without your counsel I would do nothing."** ¶ It could also be said: **"without your opinion."** <note>The Latin "sententia" or "opinion" translates the Greek "γνώμης" (gnomes)</note> Paul says: **"But without your opinion I would do nothing."** <note>original Greek: "χωρὶς δὲ τῆς σῆς γνώμης, οὐδὲν ἠθέλησα ποιῆσαι"</note> 
<margin>D</margin> ¶ The Vulgate edition says: **"For perhaps he departed from you for an hour, that you might receive him forever."** ¶ The phrase **"from you"** is redundant. And the word **"forever"** <note>original: "aeternum"</note> has the force of the adverb **"eternally."** It is as if we were to say: **"For perhaps he withdrew hourly and (so to speak) momentarily, so that you might receive him eternally."** In this way, those who momentarily depart from pleasure for Christ receive pure and sincere pleasure eternally. For what is the whole time of this present life, if not a certain point and moment? As for the word **"perhaps,"** it refers to Paul and Philemon, to whom events might seem accidental. For to God nothing is accidental, but everything is determined by reason. Truly, both the departure of the unbelieving Onesimus and the return of the now-faithful man to remain with him eternally in the body of Christ was accidental to Philemon himself, but directed by a happy and blessed providence. Paul says: **"For perhaps for this reason he was separated for an hour, that you might have him back eternally."** <note>original Greek: "τάχα γὰρ διὰ τοῦτο ἐχωρίσθη πρὸς ὥραν, ἵνα αἰώνιον αὐτὸν ἀπέχῃς"</note> ¶ The Vulgate edition says: **"Now not as a servant, but for a servant a most dear brother."** ¶ It should rather be said, **"above a servant"** rather than **"for a servant."** For the Greek word *hyper* <note>original: "ὑπὲρ"</note> here takes the accusative case, not the genitive. And **"a beloved brother"** <note>original: "dilectum"</note>, not **"most dear."** For Philemon was receiving not only a servant, but more than a servant. For he who receives a servant and a brother receives a servant and "above" or "more than" a servant. For by the condition of the flesh he was a servant; but by the condition of the spirit, which Onesimus had now put on 
<margin>B</margin> from above, Philemon was receiving a brother. Paul says: **"No longer as a servant, but as something above a servant, a beloved brother."** <note>original Greek: "οὐκ ἔτι ὡς δοῦλον, ἀλλ᾽ ὡς ὑπὲρ δοῦλον ἀδελφὸν ἀγαπητόν"</note> ¶ The Vulgate edition says: **"So brother, may I enjoy you in the Lord: refresh my heart."** ¶ Where the old translator says **"so"** <note>original: "ita"</note>, Saint Jerome notes that this is an adverb used for coaxing. We find in Paul that this mark is affirmative, as in the first chapter of the Second Epistle to the Corinthians; and a mark of exhorting and stirring up, as in the fourth chapter of the Epistle to the Philippians. But here it is a mark of a friendly mind, well-wishing and praying for good, which I would rather call it than "coaxing." For to coax, flatter, and stroke is the way of carnal people; but to well-wish, to desire, and to pray for good is the way of the holy and spiritual. Even though it may be an emotional particle, the emotions in carnal and spiritual people are far different and should be expressed by different names. Yet Saint Jerome, when he said this was a mark of "coaxing," followed common usage. And there are perhaps those who would prefer the word **"possess"** <note>original: "potiar"</note> here rather than **"enjoy"** <note>original: "fruar"</note>, because the word "enjoy" should be attributed to divine things rather than human ones. Truly, for those whom the word "enjoy" pleases, one should not strongly object, since Paul does not simply say "I shall enjoy you," but **"I shall enjoy you in the Lord."** To enjoy someone in the Lord is not primarily to take delight in them, but in the Lord, while they provide the occasion for that enjoyment. And the word Paul uses here—*onaimeen* <note>original: "ὀναίμην"</note>—means "may I possess," "may I enjoy," "may I obtain," or something similar, as we learn from Suidas <note>A 10th-century Greek encyclopedia and dictionary</note>. He says: **"May I benefit, may I attain, may I enjoy."** <note>original Greek: "ὀναίμην, ἐπιτύχοιμι, ἀπολαύσω"</note> Paul says: **"Yes, brother, may I have joy of you in the Lord; refresh my heart in the Lord."** <note>original Greek: "ναὶ ἀδελφέ, ἐγώ σου ὀναίμην ἐν κυρίῳ, ἀνάπαυσόν μου τὰ σπλάγχνα ἐν κυρίῳ"</note> ¶ The Vulgate edition says: **"For I hope through your prayers to be given to you."** ¶ The word **"me"** is redundant. Paul says: **"For I hope that through your prayers I shall be granted to you."** <note>original Greek: "ἐλπίζω γὰρ ὅτι διὰ τῶν προσευχῶν ὑμῶν, χαρισθήσομαι ὑμῖν"</note> And in the Greek manuscripts, the post-script is found: **"To Philemon, written from Rome, sent through the servant Onesimus."**

# COMMENTARY

voice. And they all said: "Are you then the Son of God?" He said: "You say that I am." <note>original: "tu ergo es filius dei... Vos dicitis: quia ego sum." A reference to the trial of Jesus in Luke 22:70.</note>

Through the Father’s voice: *This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him.* <note>Matthew 17:5, the Transfiguration.</note>

Through the descent of the Holy Spirit: pouring into the hearts of the apostles all the scriptures concerning the Son of God. Through this Spirit, the Apostle <note>Saint Paul, traditionally considered the author of Hebrews in this period.</note> opens our understanding in this passage concerning the excellence not of just one, but of many names of Christ the Lord, placed above the names of angels—indeed, above all things—saying:

<margin>3</margin>
*For to which of the angels did he ever say: "You are my Son, today I have begotten you"?* <note>Hebrews 1:5, quoting Psalm 2:7.</note>

And again: *I will be to him a Father, and he shall be to me a Son.* And again, when he brings the firstborn into the world, he says: *And let all the angels of God worship him.* And of the angels indeed, he says: *He who makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a flame of fire.* But to the Son: *Your throne, O God, is forever and ever; a scepter of rectitude is the scepter of your kingdom. You have loved justice and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions.* <note>Hebrews 1:5-9.</note>

*And: "You, Lord, in the beginning founded the earth, and the heavens are the work of your hands. They shall perish, but you remain; and they shall all grow old like a garment. And like a cloak you will fold them up, and they shall be changed; but you are the same, and your years will not fail."* But to which of the angels did he ever say: *"Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool"?* Are they not all ministering spirits, sent to serve for the sake of those who will receive the inheritance of salvation? <note>Hebrews 1:10-14.</note>

There are nine names in any of which Christ excels the angels: 1. **Son of God**, begotten in eternity. 2. He to whom **God is Father**, and who is Son to God. 3. One to be **worshipped by angels**. 4. Having an **eternal throne**. 5. **God**, holding the scepter of rectitude and equity of the kingdom. 6. The **Beginning**, in which the earth was founded. 7. The **Hand** that fashioned the heavens. 8. He who **sits at the right hand** of God. When it is said in the second Psalm, *You are my Son, today I have begotten you*: behold the Son of God begotten in eternity. For "today" designates the ever-present "atom of eternity." <note>A scholastic concept where "eternity" is viewed as a single, unchanging "now" rather than a sequence of time.</note> For eternity is the simplest measure, always present to all ages. When it says in the second book of Kings <note>Known today as 2 Samuel 7:14.</note>, *I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son*: behold him to whom God is Father, and who is Son to God.

For this was said of Christ, incarnate from the seed of David. When it says in Psalm 96, *and let all the angels of God worship him*: behold how the name "to be worshipped by angels" befits him. When it is said in Psalm 44, *your throne, O God, is forever and ever; the scepter of rectitude is the scepter of your kingdom*: behold him having an eternal throne. Behold **God**. Behold him holding the scepter of rectitude and the equity of the kingdom. From this passage, the Jews cannot deny that Christ is <term>true man</term>, <term>true God</term>, and an <term>eternal king</term>. For what is said in the same Psalm about the same person, *beautiful in form beyond the sons of men*: behold, he is true man. Because of truth, mildness, and justice: this also pertains to his humanity. But when it says, *your throne, O God, is forever and ever; the scepter of rectitude is the scepter of your kingdom*: behold, the same is God, and behold, an eternal king, whom an eternal throne and the scepter of equity of an eternal kingdom befit. And when it is said in Psalm 101, *and you, Lord, in the beginning founded the earth*: behold the "Beginning" in which the earth was founded. For the Lord himself declared himself to be that "Beginning" when the Jews asked: "Who are you?" He answered: "The Beginning, who also speaks to you." <note>A common Latin interpretation of John 8:25, "Principium, qui et loquor vobis."</note> And when it is added, *and the heavens are the work of your hands*: behold the hand that is the craftsman of the heavens. That it is said in the plural "of hands" is because the Holy Spirit is included. The other parts in the oracle refer to the Father, to whom the divine speech is directed. And finally, when it is added from Psalm 109, *sit at my right hand*: the name of Christ is held as "He who sits at the right hand of God." Behold how magnificent and how excellent is each name of Christ, above the names of both angels and all things. To whom (as is fitting) let all confess: *According to your name, O God, so also is your praise to the ends of the earth.* And again, what is said of the same in Psalm 71, let all confess: *May his name be blessed for ages; his name remains before the sun.* And in him all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed: all nations shall magnify him. Let us therefore magnify him always, and let every creature celebrate, honor, and adore him for all ages of ages. Amen.

### EXAMINATION of several points concerning the letter.

<margin>A 1</margin>
**The Vulgate Edition:** *God, who in times past spoke to the fathers in many ways and in many manners.* <note>Hebrews 1:1.</note> This "in many ways" <note>original: "multifarie"</note> signifies manifoldly and in many parts.

<margin>A 2</margin>
And it should rather be said **"who was speaking"** than **"speaking."** <note>The author is debating the nuance between a participle and a relative clause.</note> The translator of Paul: <note>original Greek: "πολυμερῶς καὶ πολυτρόπως πάλαι ὁ θεὸς λαλήσας τοῖς πατράσι"</note>. **The Vulgate edition:** *Who being the brightness of his glory and the figure of his substance.* <note>Hebrews 1:3.</note> I preferred here to retain the words of the Epistle, saying **"the character of his hypostasis"** <note>original: "character hypostaseos eius"</note> rather than **"the figure of his substance."** Because the former seems to contain more <term>energy</term> <note>spiritual power or vital force</note> than the latter. Also because "figure" and "substance" are widely <term>homonymous</term> <note>terms with many different meanings that can cause confusion</note>. For how do you know, when "figure" is said, whether the old translator meant what is called *schema* <note>original: "σχῆμα"</note> or *typos* <note>original: "τύπος"</note>, both of which the old translator commonly renders as "figure"? When he says "of substance," how do you know whether he means what is called *ousia* <note>original: "οὐσία", meaning essence</note>? Truly, to avoid these ambiguities, if we do not wish to retain the Greek words of the Epistle, we can translate: *Who, being the splendor of glory and the seal of his subsistence.* Where "his" is masculine, referring to the Father. But I think it is also good to retain the original terms for the sake of those who shudder at the name of "hypostasis" being used for the divine persons, lest they further... <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "refor-", likely for "reformident," meaning "dread" or "shrink back."</note>

<meta>This page continues the philological and theological commentary on the first chapter of the Epistle to the Hebrews, specifically focusing on the precise wording of the Greek text versus the Latin Vulgate to defend the eternal nature of Christ against Arian interpretations. <header>Hebrews 14</header>
<sig>B 2</sig>

...[they] see. We have discussed this matter more broadly in our commentaries on the books of Richard of St. Victor regarding the Trinity. <note>Richard of St. Victor (d. 1173) was a prominent medieval theologian known for his work "De Trinitate," which provided a rational defense of the triune nature of God.</note> Paul's Interpreter: *who, being the brightness of his glory and the image of his substance.* <note>original: "ὃς ὢν ἀπαύγασμα τῆς δόξης, καὶ χαρακτὴρ τῆς ὑποστάσεως αὐτοῦ" — Hebrews 1:3.</note>

¶ **The Vulgate edition.** *And upholding all things by the word of his power, making a cleansing of sins.*

¶ It should be said: *when he had by himself made a cleansing of our sins.* For "by himself" and "our" are missing [in the Vulgate]. And where the old interpreter says "making" <note>present tense: "faciens"</note>, it actually signifies a past action. Paul's Interpreter: *and upholding all things by the word of his power, having through himself made a purification of our sins.* <note>original: "φέρων τε τὰ πάντα τῷ ῥήματι τῆς δυνάμεως αὐτοῦ, δι᾽ ἑαυτοῦ καθαρισμὸν ποιησάμενος τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν ἡμῶν."</note>

¶ **The Vulgate edition.** *He sits at the right hand of majesty.*

¶ In the past tense it is said: *he sat.* Paul's Interpreter: *he sat down at the right hand of* 
<margin>2</margin>
*majesty.* <note>original: "ἐκάθισεν ἐν δεξιᾷ τῆς μεγαλωσύνης."</note>

¶ **The Vulgate edition.** *Being made so much better than the angels, as he has inherited a more excellent name than they.*

¶ It should rather be said: *being* <note>existing</note> instead of *made* <note>effectus</note>. For the participle here comes from the substantive verb "to be" <note>referring to the Greek "genomenos" which the author argues implies a state of being rather than a process of creation</note>; it does not descend from the passive "to be made." For it is not fitting to say of the Son of God "he was made," but rather "he is," "he was," or "he has been." 

The interpreter of the Gospel of John fell into a similar error where we read: *this was he of whom I said: he who is to come after me was made before me.* <note>John 1:15. The author is critiquing the Latin "ante me factus est."</note> It should have been said: *he was before me.* For there too, John uses the substantive verb "became" <note>original: "γέγονε"</note>. The unhappy Arius <note>Arius (c. 256–336) taught that the Son of God was a created being, a heresy the author is refuting here.</note> would have wanted no other interpretation than the one we read, so that he might vomit his madness against us and trap us using the translator's words, though he could not do so using the truth. For before John, the Son of God was not yet incarnate—not yet made man from the Virgin. And even though "made" might be applied to him with an addition <note>e.g., "made man"</note>, who would grant that "made" applies to him simply and without qualification?

And where it says "a more excellent name," it also means that which is more primary and more principal. For *diaphoros* <note>original: "διάφορος"</note>, the comparative of which the epistle uses here, signifies both "principal" and "different." And this name, which is more eminent, more excellent, and more principal than all the names of angels, is "Son of God." From this you further understand that it is not fitting to say "he was made." For although he could be called "made" according to the name Jesus, which is the name of the Word incarnate, it cannot be said of him as the "Son of God." For the latter is eternal; the former is new. For this is the one of whom it is said in Psalm 71: *his name remains before the sun.* Or, as some experts in the Hebrew language <term>Hebraicæ linguæ periti<gloss>scholars of Hebrew</gloss></term> prefer, more closely and expressively: *before the sun, "Son" is his name.* And what does "before the sun" mean, if not before the creation of creatures? This name, therefore—whether we say he "attained" it or "inherited" it—he attained and inherited from eternity. Paul's Interpreter: *having* 
<margin>C</margin>
*become as much better than the angels as he has inherited a more*
<margin>3</margin>
*excellent name than they.* <note>original: "τοσούτῳ κρείττων γενόμενος τῶν ἀγγέλων, ὅσῳ διαφορώτερον παρ᾿ αὐτοὺς κεκληρονόμηκεν ὄνομα."</note>

¶ **The Vulgate edition.** *And to the angels indeed he says.*

¶ So it is from the Greek. But the Greek interpreter seems to have used one preposition for another: "to" <note>ad</note> for "concerning" <note>de</note>. Therefore we preferred to use the proper one, which Paul, in my opinion, would undoubtedly have used had he been speaking Greek here. It could have been said consequently: "But concerning the Son." But "to" is also tolerated there because the speech is directed to the Son; previously, however, the speech was not directed *to* the angels but was *concerning* the angels. Paul's Interpreter: *And to the angels indeed...* <note>original: "καὶ πρὸς μὲν τοὺς ἀγγέλους."</note>

<margin>D</margin>
¶ **The Vulgate edition.** *They shall perish, but you shall remain.*

¶ In Greek it is said: *you remain* [present tense]. Paul's Interpreter: *they shall perish, but you* 
<margin>3</margin>
*remain.* <note>original: "αὐτοὶ ἀπολοῦνται, σὺ δὲ διαμενεῖς."</note>

¶ **The Vulgate edition.** *And as a garment you shall change them.*

¶ Rather: *you shall roll them up.* Paul's Interpreter: *and as a mantle you shall roll them up.* <note>original: "καὶ ὡσεὶ περιβόλαιον ἑλίξεις αὐτούς."</note>

¶ **The Vulgate edition.** *But you are the same self.*

¶ In Greek it says only: *you are the same.* Paul's Interpreter: *but you are the same.* <note>original: "σὺ δὲ ὁ αὐτοὸς εἶ."</note>

¶ **The Vulgate edition.** *Sent for ministry.*

¶ It can also be said here in the present tense: *those who are sent.* For angels were sent of old, and now they are sent daily for ministry, and will be sent until the number of those to be saved is fulfilled. I say "for ministry"—not of us, but of God who sends them. For they are ministers of God, not ours. Just as a shepherd is not a servant of the sheep, nor a master a servant of the slaves, but the shepherd is a servant to the head of the household, so also the angels are our directors, shepherds, and established as guardians by divine benevolence. Paul's Interpreter: *sent out for ministry.* <note>original: "εἰς διακονίαν ἀποστελλόμενα."</note>

### CHAPTER II.

The apostle, having the spirit of Christ, has led us magnificently toward the excellence of the names of Christ. Whoever understands these will by no means go astray in other matters. For there are many other divine names, such as in Psalm 23, where he is called *the King of Glory, the Lord strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle, the Lord of Sabaoth*—that is, of powers, of armies, and of heavenly hosts—and so with countless others scattered through the Psalms and the Prophets, through which he is known to be the true God. And therefore, since God is greater than all, he who gave us the law of his grace through himself, Paul adds that we ought to be very vigilant, attentive,
<margin>3</margin>
and circumspect, lest we let any of those things which he commanded for our salvation slip away.

¶ *Therefore we ought to pay more abundant attention to the things we have heard, lest perhaps we drift away. For if the word spoken through angels was made firm, and every transgression and disobedience received a just retribution of reward: how shall we escape if we neglect such great salvation, which, having begun to be spoken by the Lord...*

It transitions into Chapter 2, emphasizing the necessity of heedfulness toward Christ's message given his divine status.</summary>

<header>COMMENTARY</header>

...[the message] which was confirmed to us by those who heard it, God also bearing witness with signs and wonders, with various miracles, and gifts of the Holy Spirit distributed according to His own will. <note>original: "testante deo signis & prodigijs / & varijs potestatibus / & spiritus sancti distributionibus secūdū suā voluntatē" — Hebrews 2:4.</note> ¶ The Apostle here employs an argument from the lesser to the greater <term>a minori ad maius<gloss>a logical method where a truth established in a smaller case is applied with even more force to a larger one</gloss></term>, a technique he frequently uses and which is common throughout the sacred scriptures. He refers to those who transgressed the word of the Old Law, which was spoken through angels to Moses and the prophets. For Stephen, speaking through the Holy Spirit, said to the Jews: *“Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute? And they killed those who foretold the coming of the Just One, whose betrayers and murderers you have now become—you who received the law by the dispensation of angels.”* <note>Acts 7:51-53.</note> I say, those who transgressed a message of this kind did not escape without severe punishment: sometimes they were struck down by the fire of the Lord’s vengeance, sometimes by the bites of serpents, sometimes by famine, by the sword, or by incurable plague. Therefore, how much more shall those who transgress the word spoken by God <note>referring to Christ</note>—neglecting it or making it void—fail to escape vengeance? But what vengeance? That of hellfire, of the most wretched demons, and of every kind of torment. For Christ, the Son of God (as the oracles of the prophets have shown), is God and is over all things, holding those very names. ¶ Therefore, we must not be negligent in guarding His words if we wish to escape the just penalties of Gehenna <note>a historical term for Hell or a place of fiery suffering</note>. Indeed, His words are those which the apostles and disciples heard from His own mouth and, departing for other lands, poured out to everyone, the Lord working with them and confirming His word through the signs that followed. For in His name they cast out demons, they spoke in new tongues, and they received the distributions of the Holy Spirit; neither serpents nor any deadly thing harmed them; they healed the sick, raised the dead, and left the world astonished by many miracles. But should His words not be attended to and observed with great diligence, since God willed the whole world and all things to be subject to Him? If God willed the words of angels—to whom He did not subject all things or the world—to be so strictly observed, how much more so the words of Christ? Certainly with far greater care and diligence. For God did subject the world and all things to Christ, as the oracles of the prophets reveal. For He is the Son of Man whom Daniel saw in a sacred vision coming to the Ancient of Days, to whom was given power, honor, and a kingdom; and all peoples, tribes, and languages shall serve Him. His power is an eternal power that shall not be taken away, and His kingdom is one that shall not be destroyed. <note>Daniel 7:13-14.</note> He is the one whom David saw in the spirit, crowned with glory and honor, with all things subjected under His feet. <note>Psalm 8:5-6.</note> And the Lord said of Himself: *“The Son of Man will be delivered to the chief priests and scribes, and they will condemn Him to death, and deliver Him to the Gentiles to be mocked and scourged and crucified; and the third day He will rise again.”* <note>Matthew 20:18-19.</note> Therefore, Christ is not only God, but also true man, to whom the Father subjected all things. Why then, O Jews, do you attend so much to the Old Law and not rather to the New? Firstly, because the New was not arranged by angels, but by God. Secondly, because even if it was delivered through a man, it was through Him to whom all things are subject. The Old Law, however, was delivered both through angels and through
<margin>5</margin> Moses. For this reason, Paul adds: ¶ *For He has not subjected the world to come, of which we speak, to angels.* But someone has testified in a certain place, saying: *“What is man that You are mindful of him? Or the son of man that You visit him? You made him a little lower than the angels; You crowned him with glory and honor. You put all things in subjection under his feet.”* <note>Psalm 8:4-6 / Hebrews 2:6-8.</note> For in that He subjected all things to him, He left nothing that is not subject to him. ¶ There was an Old Law which passed away, under which was the old world; a New Law has been introduced, and a new world has begun through regeneration in the spirit. This new world God has so subjected to Christ that no one who rejects the New Law and does not submit to Christ shall escape eternal punishment; likewise, no one who receives that law and serves Christ in purity of life shall fail to receive eternal life. How then are all things not subject to Him who has authority over all? Over those in death and those in life; to deliver those who do not obey to eternal death, but to enroll those who obey in eternal life? His kingdom certainly rules over all even now, whether they be infidels or believers: to the latter, for life; to the former, for death. To these in mercy; to those in justice. And *all the tribes of the earth shall wail because of Him.* ¶ Would that men understood the oracles of the Spirit for their salvation! But in what way was He made “a little lower” than God, He who—existing in the form of God—is equal to God? Certainly in this: that He took the form of a servant, He who is Lord of all. For He emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men and found in appearance as a man. <note>Philippians 2:7.</note> But someone might say: *“We do not see all things subjected to Him?”* Even so, though we may not see it now, all things shall be made manifest in the end when the Lord comes with His holy thousands to execute judgment against all who have acted impiously. For now, however, sitting at the right hand of the Father, He is crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death, which He tasted for the sake of liberating everyone from eternal death. Just as He Himself said to the travelers from Jerusalem after His resurrection, who were speaking to Him but did not
<margin>6</margin> recognize Him: *“Was it not necessary,”* He said, *“for Christ to suffer these things and so enter into His glory?”* <note>Luke 24:26.</note> Accordingly, Paul adds: ¶ *But now we do not yet see all things put under Him. But we see JESUS, who was made a little lower than the angels, crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering [of death].*

It explains that while Christ became "lower than the angels" through His human suffering, He is rightfully the ruler of the "world to come."</summary>

<meta>This page continues the exposition of Hebrews Chapter 2, specifically addressing verses 9 through 17. The previous page established the necessity of paying close attention to the message of salvation brought by Christ, who was made briefly lower than the angels to undergo suffering.</meta>

<header>XIIII 233</header>

...of death, so that by the grace of God he might taste death for everyone. <margin>Hebrews</margin> Ignominy and the confusion of death were brought upon Christ the Lord, who had come to the earth for the salvation of all. You have shortened (he says) the days of his time, and you have clothed him with confusion. <note>original: "Minorasti (inquit) dies tẽporis eius: & induisti eũ confusione." Reference to Psalm 89:45 (88:46 in the Vulgate).</note> And behold: he is crowned with glory and immortality above all things. He was dishonored in the world. I honor (he says) my Father, and you have dishonored me. <note>John 8:49.</note> But now all honor is bestowed upon him in heaven, where thousands of thousands say with a loud voice: Worthy is the Lamb who was slain to receive power and divinity and wisdom and strength and honor and glory and blessing. <note>Revelation 5:12.</note> And every creature together joins them in song, <note>The Latin "immaſſonat" likely refers to the chorus of creation echoing or sounding in harmony.</note> saying: To him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb be blessing and honor and glory and power forever and ever. <note>Revelation 5:13.</note> See how he is now honored, he who suffered for all. He suffered indeed for all men since he himself was a man; but he is that man through whom all other men were made, and for whom all others exist. But whose death ought to be valid for the redemption of all: his for whom all men exist, or another for whom no other man exists? Certainly, it is the death of him through whom and for whom men were made. Moreover, Christ himself is the man through whom and for whom all men exist. For according to the first chapter, he is above all: both God and the Son of God. But according to the present chapter, he is the Son of Man to whom all things are subject. Therefore, he is the Man for whose sake all men exist. 

<margin>7</margin> It was fitting, therefore, that since Christ was this man, he should die for all men. This truth Paul relates to us by his sacred eloquence in this manner: For it was fitting for him, for whom are all things and through whom are all things, who brought many sons into glory, to make the author of their salvation perfect through suffering. <note>Hebrews 2:10. The "fittingness" (decuit) of the Incarnation is a major theme in medieval and Renaissance theology.</note> Since both he who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all from one. <note>Hebrews 2:11.</note> Certainly, it was fitting for Christ to suffer if the future salvation of men—which is their sanctification—was to occur; for it could not have been accomplished by any other man suffering. For no other man is the one for whom and through whom all men exist. It was indeed fitting, since he who sanctifies (who works salvation) and those who are sanctified (that is, all men who obtain salvation) are from one man. For what else does this mean: "he who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all from one"? Indeed, if he for whom are all things and through whom are all things had not been a man, he could by no means have suffered. But it is certain that those who are sanctified—that is, who obtain salvation and cleansing from sins through the passion of Christ—are men descended from the one man, Adam. 

<margin>8</margin> But the Apostle confirms by the authority of Scripture that Christ, who sanctifies and cleanses, is a man from that same man <note>referring to the shared human nature of Adam</note> when he adds the following: For which reason he is not ashamed to call them brothers, saying: I will announce your name to my brothers; in the midst of the church I will praise you. <note>Psalm 22:22.</note> And again: I will be trusting in him. <note>Isaiah 8:17.</note> And again: Behold, I and my children whom God has given me. <note>Isaiah 8:18.</note> Since therefore the children partook of flesh and blood, he himself likewise shared in the same, so that through death he might destroy him who had the power of death, that is, the devil, and free those who through their whole lives were subject to slavery by the fear of death. <note>Hebrews 2:14-15.</note> For this reason, namely that Christ the Lord is a man from one man as other men are—with only the capacity for sin removed, but in the true substance and nature of a man—he calls other men "brothers" in the 21st Psalm, saying: I will tell of your name to my brothers. Because he is a true man, as other men are, he hopes in God in the 17th Psalm. My God (he says), my helper, and I will hope in him. <note>Psalm 18:2 (17:3 in the Vulgate).</note> And in the Gospel, he is afraid and weary, and his soul is sorrowful even unto death, because he is a true man, a partaker of flesh and blood just like other men. And in Isaiah, he associates himself as a companion in nature with his disciples, waiting for the Lord who hides his face from the house of Jacob, and he says: Bind up the testimony, seal the law among my disciples; I will wait for the Lord who hides his face from the house of Jacob, and behold, I will wait for him: I and my children whom the Lord has given me for a sign and a wonder in Israel. <note>Isaiah 8:16-18.</note> Whoever thinks of Christ as is proper must believe him to be true God and the same to be true man. God, indeed, as he for whom and through whom are all things. Man, truly, so that through death he might conquer the devil who held the power of death—and I mean eternal death—and might free from the dread of that death those who through every age were debtors to that death and bound by such great slavery to the devil. If the death of this world, which is momentary, is to be feared, with what terror must those have been shaken who were rushing toward eternal death with no remedy? But the death of Christ, if we are willing to follow him, has freed us from this fear and summoned us from the slavery of death into the liberty of life. 

But someone will say: Why did God not rather assume the nature of an angel, so that he might be both God and angel, rather than a man, so that he is both God and man, since an angel is superior and more excellent in nature than a man? The wisdom of God and the divine will are not reached by human wisdom and reason. Nevertheless, to what end would he have assumed an angel, having been made an angel, so that death might conquer death? For an angel cannot die, but a man can. It was therefore more suitable to divine wisdom (which was to bring about human redemption through death) to assume a man who could die rather than an angel who is immune to a mortal lot. 

<margin>9</margin> Indeed, it was in no way appropriate for him to take on an angel. Therefore Paul adds: For surely he does not take hold of angels, but he takes hold of the seed of Abraham. Therefore he had to be made like his brothers in all things, that he might become a merciful and faithful high priest in things pertaining to God, to make atonement for the sins of the people. <note>Hebrews 2:16-17.</note>

### COMMENTARY

<meta>catchword: and those alone</meta>

...twists yours <note>Referring to the human heart or will</note> into a crooked path), but look back to Christ; immerse yourself in his goodness. There, confidence is born, which moves hope toward what is right. For to what end were his hands and feet pierced? To what end was his side opened, dissolving the wall of hostilities? <note>A reference to Ephesians 2:14, where Christ breaks down the "middle wall of partition" between God and man.</note> Are these not signs of love and confidence? To what end does he call the church his bride, saying, "Come, my dove, in the clefts of the rock, in the hollow of the wall," <note>original: "Veni columba mea in foraminibus petræ/ in cauerna maceriæ." From Song of Solomon 2:14, traditionally interpreted as the soul hiding in the wounds of Christ.</note> unless so that in the contemplation of his wounds she might take confidence? "Take heart," he says, "I have overcome the world." <note>John 16:33.</note> And for whom did he overcome it? Not for himself, who was superior to the world, but for us who were held oppressed. Therefore, attending to his goodness and the love with which he loved us, let us cast all our confidence upon him until the end, meditating on how much he loves us—he who suffered so much for us and asks nothing else from us except that we hope in him and glory in him. If another were kinder, more merciful, or more powerful, perhaps one should hope in him; but since he himself is the kindest, most merciful, and moreover the most powerful over all, and the most generous, what else does he want but to show mercy and to give? God placed him as the supreme mediator <margin>13</margin> between himself and our race. How, therefore, would it not be an insult to him to hope more in Moses or anyone else than in him? And so Paul adds: "Therefore, just as the Holy Spirit says:"

> Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts, as in the provocation on the day of testing in the desert, where your fathers tested me, proved me, and saw my works. For forty years, therefore, I was offended by that generation, and I said: they always err in their heart. But they did not know my ways; as I swore in my wrath: they shall not enter into my rest. <note>Psalm 95:7-11 (Psalm 94 in the Vulgate). The author uses this to warn against repeating the Israelites' lack of faith.</note>

These things are from Psalm 94. And as it suffices for the proposal, there are two "days." One is the day of the old law. The other is the day of the new law. In the first day, God was heard through Moses. In the second, God was heard in the Son. The first day is one of exacerbation and provocation of God to anger; the second is one of atonement and reconciliation. A servant <note>Moses</note> did not appease or reconcile the Lord, but the Son truly appeased and reconciled the Father. Of the second day it is said to all those hearing the word of the Gospel (which God has spoken): "Today if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts," just as in the first, they hardened them in the desert, when testing God, they stirred him to anger. And what is it to harden hearts, if not to not believe, not to hope, and not to love with the heart? "They did not believe," he says, "in God, nor did they hope in his salvation." And again: "They loved him with their mouth, and they lied to him with their tongue." <note>Psalm 78:36-37.</note> Therefore, in this day of atonement and reconciliation of the Father through the Son, let us believe, let us hope, and let us love with the heart, lest we be like the men of the day of testing and wrath, with whom God was offended for forty years because of their unbelief and lack of trust; for forty years he spurned, despised, and destroyed them. <margin>14</margin> To whom he also swore in the time of wrath that they would not enter into his rest. This is what the holy herald of God and apostle of Christ, Paul, further exhorts, saying:

> See to it, brothers, lest perhaps there be in any of you an evil heart of unbelief in departing from the living God; but exhort yourselves every single day, as long as it is called "Today," so that none of you may be hardened by the deception of sin. For we have been made partakers of CHRIST, if only we hold the beginning of our substance firm until the end, while it is said: "Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts, as in the provocation." <note>Hebrews 3:12-15.</note>

"As long as it is called 'Today'." This day is surely one of atonement, grace, and peace, concerning which the speech of the Holy Spirit lasts until the end of the world. And if there is no peace for the wicked, this does not happen by reason of the "day." For this entire day belongs to Christ until the consummation of the age, in which there is atonement, grace, and indelible peace for all believing, hoping, and loving him with their heart. Therefore, until the end of the age, let us not cease to admonish, exhort, and provoke one another to this faith, hope, and love. Let us attend to the Holy Spirit saying this to us all through this day: "Do not harden your hearts, as in the provocation, as in the day of provocation and testing." Let this cause move us, so that we do not fall into any sin as far as is possible for us. But if, deceived by error, we should fall into any, let us not harden our hearts, but let us fall down and weep before God and our <term>High Priest</term> <note>original: "pōtificē nostrū." A central theme in Hebrews, presenting Christ as the final priest who mediates for humanity.</note>, whom the Father of mercies willed to both suffer and be tested, so that he might make our sins atoneable by his death and make us overcome temptations by his own temptation. Otherwise, if we harden our hearts, a far worse fate awaits us than those who were laid low in the desert, by as much as we have despised a greater grace and offering of mercy. Indeed, both those who hardened their hearts in the day of testing and those who will harden them in the day of Christ's obedience—both the former and the latter, despised by God—will not enter the <term>Sabbath of God</term> <note>original: "ſabbatum dei." Interpreted here not as a day of the week, but as the eternal rest of heaven.</note> (which is the celebration of the saints in heaven). This is the rest of the saints from all their labors, and God's infinite joy filling the saints. For "he will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither mourning, nor crying, nor pain shall be anymore, for the former things have passed away." <note>Revelation 21:4.</note> This Sabbath of God, this rest of the day—from which, whether in that day or in this day, those alone are repelled who have hardened their hearts. If we do not harden them, having been made partakers of Christ, we shall enter this rest with him. Moreover, we shall not harden them if we hold the "beginning of substance"—that is, of faith (for as will be said in the eleventh chapter of this fourteenth [book], faith is substance) <note>Reference to Hebrews 11:1, "Faith is the substance of things hoped for."</note>—stable and firm until the end. And that those alone...

<margin>
15
XIIII
</margin>
Regarding the Sabbath and the rest of God from which some are excluded, Paul adds: "For some who heard, provoked him; but not all who were led out of Egypt by Moses." <note>A reference to Hebrews 3:16, noting that while many rebelled, a faithful remnant remained.</note> But with whom was he angry for forty years? Was it not with those who sinned, whose bodies fell in the desert? And to whom did he swear that they would not enter into his rest, if not to those who were unfaithful? And we see that they could not enter because of their lack of belief. If on the "day of temptation," "wrath," and "anger," God despised only those who were rebellious and unfaithful, how much more on the "day of obedience," "reconciliation," and "peace" will he not be angry with them, nor will he reject those who are obedient, faithful, and believing. 

And we recognize that there are three types of Sabbaths. The first is in **shadow** alone. The second is in **truth hidden**, and still covered by sacred veils. And the third is in **truth naked** and open. The first belonged to the Hebrews. The second exists in this world for Christians. The third is celebrated in heaven by the saints, and will finally be celebrated by all the elect at the end of the age. This third Sabbath is what is called "the rest of God" here. Into the first Sabbath, both those admitted to rest and those prohibited from God's rest entered. <note>In the Old Testament, the weekly Sabbath was observed by both the righteous and the wicked among the Israelites.</note> Into the second, Christians enter, both good and bad. Into the third, only the faithful and the elect shall enter. 

In the first are contained the stone tables of Moses, the rod of Aaron, and the manna, which were figures <term>figures: symbolic foreshadowings</term> of Christ. In the second, Christ is truly contained, but still covered by a sacramental veil. In the third, the Divinity will be gazed upon naked and open. In the first, the Jews ceased from all servile work, <note>servile work: manual labor forbidden on the Sabbath</note> occupied only with meditations on divine benefits throughout the whole time of the celebration, hearing the divine law and "ruminating" on what they heard. <note>ruminating: a metaphor comparing the study of scripture to a cow chewing cud—repeatedly reflecting on the word.</note> Wherever the Ark was, there they were intent with heart and eye. 

How much more does it befit us in this, our second Sabbath, to cease from all worldly work, intent only on hymns and praises, and occupied with holy confessions of Christ’s benefits, ruminating on his commands, words, and deeds—never departing in eye or soul from our God, who is still covered for us by sacred veils. We do this so that we may be able to see him, once every veil is removed, in the third Sabbath and the complete rest of all the saints. In the seeing of him alone, the eyes of all saints will be fixed. This he grants us for his own sake and the overflowing grace of his own nature: he who, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, is worthy in the celebration of all the saints and in the eternal rest of the saints—more than worthy of the glory, praise, and honor of all saints, for all ages of ages.

¶ EXAMINATION of several points regarding the literal text. ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "The High Priest of our confession, Jesus, who is faithful to him who made him, just as Moses was in all his house." <note>original Latin: "Pontificem confessionis nostræ IHESVM: qui fidelis est ei qui fecit illũ/ sicut & Moyses in õni domo eius." Refers to Hebrews 3:1-2.</note> 
¶ It should say: "Jesus Christ." The word "Christ" is missing. Furthermore, the context requires saying "appointed" rather than "made." For we more aptly say he "appointed him over the house" than he "made him." If one prefers to say "made," let us understand it as "made him High Priest," not simply "made him" <note>This is a theological distinction to avoid the suggestion that Christ was a created being rather than the eternal Son.</note>. For what does "he made him High Priest" mean other than "he appointed him"? And what follows—"just as Moses in all his house"—refers back to the previous part, "who is faithful." And it should be said "in the whole house" rather than "in every house." 
**The Greek text of Paul:** <note>original: "ἀρχιερέα τῆς ὁμολογίας ἡμῶν ἰησοῦν χρῖσο̃ν, πισὸν ὄντα τῷ ποιήσαντι αὐτὸν, ὡς καὶ μωσῆς ἐν ὅλῳ τῷ οἴκῳ αὐτοῦ."</note> "The High Priest of our confession, Jesus Christ, being faithful to the one who made [appointed] him, as also was Moses in all his house." 
<margin>A 11</margin> 
¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "By as much as the house has more honor than he who built it." <note>Refers to Hebrews 3:3. The translator argues the Latin grammar here is confusing.</note> 
¶ The old translator made the phrasing unintelligible. He should have said: "By how much more honor he has than the house," converting the Greek genitive into a Latin ablative, as the nature of comparisons in Latin requires. Instead, he translated it with the Latin genitive *domus* (of the house), which is ambiguous. Those who read it do not know if it is a genitive or a nominative; whether it is one or the other, they can extract no sense from it. That genitive should have been resolved by him through an ablative (as was said) or into a nominative with the particle "than" (quam) added; thus saying "by how much more honor he has than the house, he who made it." Then the interpretation would be correct and intelligible. 
**The Greek text of Paul:** <note>original: "καθ' ὅσον πλείονα τιμὴν ἔχει τοῦ οἴκου, ὁ κατασκευάσας αὐτόν."</note> "Inasmuch as he who built it has more honor than the house." 
<margin>B 12</margin> 
¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "Which house we are." 
¶ It should say: "Whose house we are." And "whose" refers to the Son. 
**The Greek text of Paul:** <note>original: "οὗ οἶκός ἐσμεν ἡμεῖς."</note> "Whose house are we." 
<margin>B 13</margin> 
¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "They proved and saw my works for forty years." <note>Refers to Hebrews 3:9.</note> 
¶ It should say: "They proved me." The word "me" is missing. 
**The Greek text of Paul:** <note>original: "ἐδοκίμασάν με, καὶ εἶδον τὰ ἔργα μου."</note> "They tested me and saw my works." 
<margin>B 13</margin> 
¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "They saw my works for forty years: because of which I was offended by this generation." 
¶ The phrase "for forty years" should be referred to the following part "offended," not to the preceding "they saw." This is known from what follows, where it is asked: "But with whom was he offended for forty years?" For this reason, we preferred to use the conjunction "therefore" (ideo) rather than the phrase "because of which" (propter quod), which is usually used at the beginning of sentences. 
**The Greek text of Paul:** <note>original: "εἶδον τὰ ἔργα μου, τεσσαράκοντα ἔτη Διὸ προσώχθισα τῇ γενεᾷ ἐκείνῃ."</note> "They saw my works for forty years; therefore I was offended by that generation." 
<margin>C 14</margin> 
¶ **The Vulgate edition:** "If only we hold the beginning of his substance firm until the end." <note>Refers to Hebrews 3:14.</note> 
¶ The word "his" is redundant. And "substance" here means "faith," which is the subsistence and foundation upon which the law of Christ is founded. For so it is stated later in chapter 11.

<margin>CHAPTER 4</margin>

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial C depicting a seated figure, possibly a prophet or scholar, in a landscape with buildings in the background.</image-desc>
**W**hen the Holy Spirit says, "Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts, as in the provocation, on the day of temptation," and what follows, "As I swore in my wrath, they shall not enter into my rest": in this prohibition against hardening the heart, there is understood at the same time a promise of entering into the Sabbath of the Lord (which we call the "rest of the Lord") for those who hear the voice and do not harden their hearts, as they did on that other day called the "day of temptation." For a negative statement often implies its own affirmation. For example, if you do not compete lawfully, you will not receive the prize; <note>term: brauiū (the prize of a race or contest)</note> it follows without doubt that if you do compete lawfully, you will receive it. So also here: if you do not hear the voice of the Lord, and you harden your heart and remain unfaithful, you will not enter into the rest of the Lord; but for the second part, it concludes with a promise and affirmation: if you hear the voice of the Lord and do not harden your heart, you will enter into the rest of the Lord. And this promise is not from works, but from faith. Thus, that entry into the Sabbath of the Lord—into a celebration of infinite joy (as it says, "the dwelling of all who rejoice is in you")—is understood as a grace, not a debt. Therefore, to attain this grace of the divine goodness's promise, the blessed apostle exhorts us in this way, saying: ¶ **Therefore, let us fear, lest perhaps while the promise of entering his rest remains, any of you should seem to fall short.** Since the news was preached to us just as it was to them; but the word of hearing did not profit them, because those who heard were not united by faith. For we who have believed shall enter into that rest, as he said: "As I swore in my wrath, they shall not enter into my rest," even though the works were finished from the foundation of the world. For he said in a certain place concerning the seventh day: "And God rested on the seventh day from all his works." And again in this place: "If they shall enter into my rest." ¶ Because of unbelief, the former people were excluded from the rest of the Lord. We, who come after, shall enter that rest through faith. Otherwise, if we hear and do not believe, the word of divine hearing will help us much less than it did them, since it is a greater sin to disbelieve the voice of the Lord than the voice of a servant. Christ is the Lord, and the Lord of all; but Moses was the servant of the Lord. But into what rest shall we enter? Truly into that of which it is spoken in the second chapter of Genesis: "And God completed on the seventh day his work which he had made; and he rested on the seventh day from all the work he had performed." Behold the rest of the Lord in himself—not through a shadow, not through symbols and veils covering him, but in himself, the open and naked glory of eternal celebration. And this rest of the Lord, which is mentioned near the beginning of Genesis, is the rest of which the Holy Spirit speaks in this place—"if they shall enter my rest." The apostle harmonized this when he said, "if they shall enter into my rest," namely, because of the works finished from the foundation of the world; which is indeed the rest with which God rested when the world was finished, as it says in Genesis. In both places, "rest of the Lord" is used in the same way. Therefore, the rest of the Lord is neither taken here for the Jewish Sabbath, nor for the Sabbath of Christians while they still live (where the divinity is covered by sacred veils, even if it is truly present). For God did not rest on the seventh day after the work of the world was finished in either of those ways. Therefore, it is the eternal Sabbath (as was said in the preceding chapter) which will be celebrated in the future life. And this Sabbath, this rest, was not promised on the "day of temptation," but "Today," when the voice of God is heard. For neither Moses, nor Joshua after Moses, could lead even the believers to this rest; they were only led into "Abraham's bosom" <note>A term for the place of repose for the righteous dead before the Resurrection.</note> while waiting for the perfect Sabbath that the Son of God would give; which the Lord deigned to reveal when he spoke of Lazarus and the rich man. And this "Today, if you hear his voice" does not address those who were in the day of temptation and wrath, but those who were to be in the day of reconciliation and peace. This is easily understood from what Paul, understanding sacred things, adds: ¶ **Since therefore it remains that some must enter it, and those...**

# XIII

<margin>Hebrews</margin>
...to whom it was first announced / did not enter because of unbelief: again he limits a certain day / saying "Today" in David after so much time (as was said): **Today if you hear his voice: do not harden your hearts.** <note>A quotation of Hebrews 4:7, referencing Psalm 95:7-8.</note> For if Joshua <note>original: "Iosue." In Latin and Greek, the names Joshua and Jesus are identical. The author here distinguishes between the historical Joshua who led the Israelites into Canaan and Jesus Christ.</note> had provided them rest: he would never afterwards have spoken of another day. Therefore a Sabbath rest remains for the people of God. ¶ And those to whom it was first announced: are those who were present in the "day of temptation" <note>Referring to the wandering in the wilderness.</note>. And what was announced? Was it the rest of the Lord? Not yet: but the Old Law. And those who were under it: because of their unbelief were not yet worthy. But both the New Law / and the rest of the Lord were announced at the same time. ¶ And also "in David" / that is, in the book of the Psalms of David that was written / whose time was still of temptation and wrath: yet not for the time of David / but for a day and time far in the future / that "Today" was spoken. And even if Moses had spoken as an instrument of the Holy Spirit (for there are some who attribute this to his psalms) <note>Some traditions attributed certain Psalms, like Psalm 90, to Moses.</note> he would have accepted that "Today" not for the day of temptation / but for another / which is not the day of temptation / to come after a very long interval of time. Otherwise: he would not have said, "do not harden your hearts today" / as in the day of temptation / if "Today" designated that very day of temptation / and not rather another future one after as much time as passed between him and Christ. In which the voice of God was heard: not through a servant / but through the heir / the free one / and the son. Not through man alone: but through man and God alike. Therefore there remains ¶ this Sabbath rest / this rest of the Lord / this eternal celebration: it is promised and determined for the people of God / the people of whom it was said through the spirit of prophecy: **A coming generation shall be announced to the Lord / and the heavens shall announce his justice / to a people who shall be born / whom the Lord has made.** <note>original: "Annūciabitur domino generatio ventura..." — Psalm 22:31.</note> Who, as soon as he departs from the world (provided he has kept himself unpolluted according to the voice of the Lord) is transferred into the rest of the Lord. But all Jews before the coming of Christ: descended to the underworld <note>original: "inferos." Referring to Sheol or Hades, the place of the dead before the Resurrection.</note> / by no means entering the celebration of the Lord and his holy / and ineffable Sabbath. But Christ descended / so that we might not descend: and so that he might transfer those who had descended into rest / and so that we likewise departing from life might ascend / with all works completed / to enjoy eternal rest. For which reason: Paul adds. ¶ **For he who has entered into his rest: he also has rested from his works / just as God did from his own. Let us hasten therefore to enter into that rest: lest anyone fall into the same example of unbelief. The word of God is living and effective / and sharper than any two-edged sword / and reaching even to the division of soul and spirit / of the joints also and the marrow / and a discerner of the thoughts / and meditations of the heart / and there is no creature hidden in his sight: but all things are naked and open to his eyes / of whom we speak.** <note>Hebrews 4:10-13.</note> ¶ The perfect rest of which the above discourse spoke: is taken in us in a certain proportion to the rest of God. And it is a cessation from all our works / emulating divine quiet / most full of unfailing joy / an occupation with divine things / a drinking from the torrent of God's pleasure / and from the sight of God the glory and fulfillment of all our desires / quieting / saturation: as it is written. **You shall make them drink of the torrent of your pleasure.** <note>Psalm 36:8.</note> And again. **I shall be satisfied when your glory appears.** <note>Psalm 17:15.</note> But this satiety and fulfillment of vows admits no loathing / no weariness: but an immense / and ineffable joy accompanies it. This rest therefore / this Sabbath is for the chosen servants of God: who are admitted to the joy of their Lord / resting completely from all earthly works / and grafted into divinity, to which rest the apostle wonderfully excites us. <margin>at</margin> And what is said "into the same example of unbelief": pertains to the same and similar unbelief / into which they fell in the desert / to whom the Lord swore / because of their unbelief / that they would not enter into his rest. The Word of God of which the apostle also speaks here: is not a passing and vanishing word: which, breathed out / is immediately spread through the air and perishes. But it is an immanent word: not broad / not dispersed / not diffused / but bearing all things / and gathering them. Of which it is said in another place: **For while quiet silence contained all things / and night had her mid-course: your almighty word, O Lord / leaping from heaven out of your royal throne / as a fierce conqueror into the midst of the land of destruction.** <note>Wisdom of Solomon 18:14-15.</note> This same word is he who a little before was called the "voice." **Today if you hear his voice.** An immanent voice / a living voice / a voice through which all things were made. Of which in Psalm 28: **The voice of the Lord is in power: the voice of the Lord is in magnificence.** <note>Psalm 29:4 in modern Bibles.</note> and the same voice: is called the Word of the Lord. which God sent from heaven: for the health of all. This speech / this voice / this word: is Christ the Lord. So living: because he gives life to all. So effective: because he can do all things. So piercing: because he permeates all things. So reaching to the division of soul and spirit: because he is the creator of all souls and spirits / and the distributor of spiritual gifts <note>original: "charismatū."</note> in living beings. So to the division of joints and marrow: because he is the searcher of hearts and kidneys <note>original: "renum." A common biblical metaphor for the innermost thoughts or emotions.</note>. So a discerner of thoughts and meditations: because he knows all things before they happen. So no creature is hidden from him: because nothing can exist / unless he beholds it. For his gaze is: providence / containing and saving all things. Thus all things are naked / and open to his eyes: because he is the paternal light illustrating all—

G.iiii.

...in the same manner and for himself to offer for sins. And no one takes this honor for himself: but he who is called by God just as Aaron was. So also CHRIST did not glorify himself to become a high priest: but he who spoke to him: **You are my son: today I have begotten you.** <note>Quoting Psalm 2:7, applied here to Christ’s appointment.</note> As he says in another place: **You are a priest forever: according to the order of Melchizedek.** <note>Quoting Psalm 110:4. Melchizedek was a mysterious king-priest in Genesis who predated the Jewish priesthood of Aaron.</note> Who in the days of his flesh: offered up prayers and supplications to him who was able to save him from death: with a strong cry and tears: and was heard because of his reverence. And although he was the Son: he learned obedience from the things which he suffered: and having been made perfect: he became the cause of eternal salvation to all who obey him: called by God a high priest according to the order of Melchizedek. ¶ And because of this / namely infirmity <note>original: "infirmitatem." So also, even if there were a hundred diversities of victims: in truth they are one Christ. and in Christ: they are called by one name: but in elements and figures: they have very varied and widely multiplied names.

By this paradigm many things are figured. That Christ is the beginning. That he is the end. That he is the middle. Since in this diagram the beginning is 1, which is unity. The end: 100. The middle: 50. Join the beginning to the end: they are 101. Multiply the middle 50 by the beginning and end, that is 101: you have the <term>enfolding</term> <note>The sum (5050) represents all the individual numbers contained within a single total.</note> of all the numbers gathered together at once. From this same thing you see Christ is before all: because he is the beginning. After all: because he is the end. Within all: because he is the medium. You see him to be the truth of all things: whom all other things explain together in multiple and varied ways: yet none by itself sufficiently or entirely. He truly, uniquely and in truth, enfolds all things. Being more powerful than all together: just as the single number 5050 is more powerful than all the numbers of the diagram together. Which he does not fail to know: who is not ignorant of the 13th proposition of the first book of Jordanus. <note>Referring to Jordanus de Nemore, a 13th-century mathematician who wrote on the properties of numbers and series.</note> and innumerable such things are hidden from many: yet clearly manifest to those able to discern divine things. And the sacrifice of Christ was contained in the ancient rites / but in a shadowy way: as may be observed here. And for the purpose of unshelling these mysteries concerning the true and new priesthood of Christ / a long discourse / and for those who remain fixed to the sense of the letter / with the sort of persistence usually noted in the Jews, it would have to be considered not easily explainable. For all who are fixed to the letter: are weak and sluggish for receiving <term>spiritual understanding</term> / which is solid food. I say spiritual: not that which human intelligence fashions for itself / but that which the divine Spirit has infused. Therefore he chides them: and says. ¶ **Concerning which we have much to say / and not easily interpreted in speaking: since you have become sluggish in hearing.
