<header>XIV</header>

<margin>Hebrews</margin>
...[senses] they have for the discernment of good and evil. <note>original: "boni / malisq; discretionem." This completes the thought from the previous page regarding the maturity of believers.</note> ¶ WHAT is it / about which we have much to say: if not that priesthood and priest according to the order of Melchizedek? <note>Melchizedek was a biblical figure who served as both king and priest; he is used here as a prototype for Christ’s unique priesthood.</note> By the grace of God, for those who are practiced: the word is brief / easy / and immediately accessible. Just as for those practiced in literature: the understanding of the basic elements is accessible; but for the unpracticed: no amount of explanation is enough / however much it may be / to bring them to understanding. For as training in human gyms leads to worldly understanding: so it is in spiritual matters / toward spiritual and divine things. In the former: some worldly teacher [instructs]. But here: the Holy Spirit instructs / as the infuser of divine concepts into prepared minds. The former: requires much time and much labor. This: happens suddenly / and without anxiety. The former: teaches boys. This: teaches men. The former: strikes the ear of the external person. This: strikes the innermost hearing. The former: provides no nourishment of any solidity. This: provides solid food. He who eats of it: is a man / and robust in mind / no longer wishing to touch the soft foods of a mental infancy. These [soft foods] are either human disciplines: or those things which still cling fixed to the shadows and figures of things. Those who cling to these: are of an infantile mind / unable to bear the solidity of spiritual understanding. In this, the divine apostle rebukes some of the Jews: who, although they had fled to Christ / were nevertheless trying too hard to hold onto Judaism / and the elements of the mysteries of God / which are circumcision / sabbaths / solemnities / purifications / and various kinds of sacrifices and offerings. They are like infants: who are nourished by milk. Those who are nourished by milk for too long: are not capable of understanding the law. So too, those who are fed by the shadows of the old law / and neither can nor wish to receive other nourishment: are nourished by milk / being least capable of the words of the new law and of spiritual justice. May Jesus Christ illuminate them and us: so that we may put on a manly mind / prepared by the sacred nourishment of the Holy Spirit / and be fed by that solidity of the scriptures / by which we follow every good to which the Spirit of God calls / and flee every evil from which He repels us: let us give praise to Christ, King of all the world / <margin>A 10</margin> together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, blessed into all ages. Amen.

¶ EXAMINATION of several points regarding the literal text. ¶ The Vulgate edition: **For every high priest taken from among men: is appointed for men in those things which pertain to God.** ¶ The understanding of this passage is somewhat inverted, for there is no doubt Paul wanted it to mean that every high priest is assumed from among men, he who was appointed for men in those things which pertain to God. Therefore, it would be better to place the verb in the first position and the participle in the second, so it would say: "for every high priest is assumed from among men: having been appointed in those things which pertain to God." According to this understanding we have interpreted it / not so much from the Greek as from the understanding which the apostle intended. This must be done in many places in this epistle: because we lack the original archetype. The Interpreter of Paul: <note>original Greek: "πᾶς γὰρ ἀρχιερεὺς ἐξ ἀνθρώπων λαμβανόμενος , ὑπὲρ ἀνθρώπων καθίσταται τὰ πρὸς τὸν θεόν."</note> "For every high priest taken from among men, is appointed for men in things pertaining to God." ¶ The Vulgate edition: **Who can have compassion on those who are ignorant and err.** ¶ The old translator seems by no means to have expressed the force of the Greek word. But rather, he should have said "one who can feel compassion with moderation" or "by mediating." The Interpreter of Paul: <note>original Greek: "μετριοπαθεῖν δυνάμενος τοῖς ἀγνοοῦσι καὶ πλανωμένοις." The term 'metriopathein' implies a balanced or moderate emotional response.</note> "Being able to deal gently with the ignorant and those going astray." ¶ The Vulgate edition: **And therefore he ought, just as for the people: so also for himself to offer for sins.** ¶ One should say "on account of this" [infirmity] or "on account of her" in the feminine singular accusative / not "on account of those things" in the neuter plural accusative. For it refers back to this or that: infirmity. And I believe the old translator said "on account of her" but afterwards the copy was corrupted. For if he had said "on account of this [feminine]": it would not have been so close to being corrupted. The Interpreter of Paul: <note>original Greek: "Διὰ ταύτην ὀφείλει καθὼς περὶ τοῦ λαοῦ οὕτω καὶ περὶ ἑαυτοῦ προσφέρειν ὑπὲρ ἁμαρτιῶν."</note> "Because of this [infirmity] he is obligated, just as for the people, so also for himself to offer for sins." <margin>B 10</margin> ¶ The Vulgate edition: **So also CHRIST did not clarify himself.** ¶ The old translator could also have said "glorified" where he said "clarified." <note>The author is noting that 'clarificavit' and 'glorificavit' are synonymous in this context, though 'glorified' might be more standard.</note> The Interpreter of Paul: <note>original Greek: "οὕτω καὶ ὁ χριστὸς οὐχ ἑαυτὸν ἐδόξασε."</note> "So also Christ did not glorify himself." ¶ The Vulgate edition: **He was heard for his reverence.** ¶ It should be said "and he was heard," with the connecting note preceding it. And "his": is redundant. And equally or even more so, one should say "for his piety" rather than "for his reverence." For "reverence" sometimes signifies bashfulness and confusion / which is not appropriate to say—that he was heard by the Father because of bashfulness. Sometimes it signifies fear and a certain honorable fear which we carry toward superiors. This again does not properly fit when speaking of the Father toward Christ. For Christ, according to the infirmity of the nature by which he cried out to the Father: was not to be revered by the Father in this way. Indeed, not even if the divinity of both is considered: would the nomenclature be apt. But you will say: Christ was not heard because of the reverence by which the Father revered him / but for the reverence by which he himself revered the Father. For according to the nature he assumed, he felt reverence / having fear toward him / a free, filial, and honorable fear, more than all sons toward a father / just as it is written of him: **And the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him.** <note>Quoting Isaiah 11:2.</note> I would not deny that Christ the Lord had that reverence toward the Father, than which none is greater / none more eminent. And if it were understood as being heard for that reverence by which he revered the Father: that would not be bad. But when someone is said to be heard "for reverence" [pro reverentia]: it is more commonly understood as the reverence by which...

21

...[it might be] feared by those who hear it: a sense which we say does not fit. And it is better / if it is translated: "on account of his piety." <note>original Latin: "pro pietate." The author is discussing Hebrews 5:7, where Christ is "heard" because of his godly fear or reverence.</note> Piety is certainly spoken of both regarding superiors toward inferiors and inferiors toward superiors / and for the whole practice of veneration. But what greater piety was there than that of Christ toward the Father as his greater and superior / what greater veneration / obedience / fear / love? And this was piety toward the Father. What piety is also greater than the piety of Christ toward inferiors: that he, the Lord of all, for the sake of his servants who even deserved death / alone willed to die so that they might not die but live forever? This is, in every part, both upward and downward, the ineffable piety of Christ the Lord: for which he was heard by the highest Father, both for himself toward Him and for his servants, so that they might not die / but obtain eternal life instead of death. Add to this that the piety of the Father / toward such an obedient Son of such great piety / and toward us because of him / was equal and the same. It turns out best, therefore: that he is said to have been heard "on account of piety," both his own and the Father's. <note>Paul's translator: "and he was heard because of his reverence [eulabeia]."</note>

<margin>C 21</margin>¶ The Vulgate Edition. *Of whom we have a great word, and hard to be explained.* <note>The Vulgate is the standard 4th-century Latin translation of the Bible. The author is critiquing the specific Latin word used here.</note> ¶ When the old translator says "interpretable" <note>original: "interpretabilis."</note>: he does not fully explain the Greek. For what is called "interpretable": is understood as "explicable." But that is not what the word carries / rather it means "difficult to interpret" / and not having an easy explanation. Especially since the listeners were not capable of such understanding: as those who could not penetrate the mysteries of the spirit. For thinking that they can do this by themselves and by their own sense: they cannot. But when they know that they cannot do it by themselves: when they are clothed with a sense from on high / then they can. And they are hardly ever clothed with that sense: as long as they think they can do it of themselves. For these senses are contrary and do not tolerate being together: and [one must realize] these opposites. Of which one is: as not being able. And the other: truly being able. And this difficulty of interpreting and explaining the discourse: did not depend on Paul’s part (for that discourse was: easy and interpretable) but on the part of the Jews to whom the discourse was held, who could not yet bear spiritual understanding. For they were still using their own "power" / or rather, they were abusing their own impotence: and they had been slow and sluggish to understand the sacred words in the proper way. Which many others still do today: to whom the inner shrines of divinity / every mystery / and spiritual understanding are closed. To which: no one is admitted by their own sense and their own power / but by a higher sense / and a heavenly power. <note>Paul's translator: "concerning whom we have much to say, and it is hard to explain in speech."</note> ¶ The Vulgate Edition. *Since you have become weak in hearing.* ¶ It could be said: "since you have been sluggish in your hearings." That is, slow in understanding the readings of the scriptures / and of the holy prophets. But because the old translator spoke using a gerund / we also have translated it by a gerund "in hearing": wishing for the same thing / as if we had said "in hearings" by a noun. <note>Paul's translator: "since you have become dull of hearing."</note>

<margin>D 21</margin>For if they had made progress in the spiritual understanding of scripture / and the hearings of the prophets: the discourse would have been easily interpretable to them / which was otherwise very difficult for them to interpret. ¶ The Vulgate Edition. *That you be taught.* ¶ In Greek: it is said in the active voice. But that matters little. <note>Paul's translator: "that we teach [you]."</note> ¶ The Vulgate Edition. *Of those who by custom have their senses exercised.* ¶ In the Greek it is held: "of those who because of habit." But that does not vary much from the understanding of the old translator. <note>Paul's translator: "of those who, through habit, have their senses trained [gymnazo] for discernment."</note>

### CHAPTER VI.

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'N' with floral motifs.</image-desc>
**N**ot only did some of the Jews, for whose sake the apostle writes / sin regarding the elements of the old ritual / not understanding what figures they were / and what truth responded to those types: but they even failed immediately at the threshold concerning the beginning of the new law. The "beginning" is: to instruct the unrefined in the faith / to warn of repentance for sins / to teach one baptism for the remission of sins / to lay on hands for the reception of the gifts of the Holy Spirit / to believe in the resurrection / and the final judgment / and the remaining things which the apostles handed down in summary / in that composition which is called the **Apostles' Creed**. <note>The author uses the term "symbolum apostolorum," referring to the fundamental statement of Christian belief.</note> What then were they doing? When they had fallen into the works of the flesh and the errors of sin, which are dead works: they were teaching that one must repent and be baptized again / introducing the doctrines not of one baptism but of various baptisms. Which the apostle absolutely forbids to be done: because it is impossible by this way / to follow after the remission of later sins. Christ died for us once and rose once: so we also die with him once in sacred baptism / are buried with him and rise with him. And it would be not only foolish: but also profane to repeat baptism / as if Christ had suffered and been buried for us not only once / but twice and perhaps frequently: we would be holding this mystery of the passion as a mockery and a public show. Therefore, the remission of sins is impossible by this way. Paul therefore exhorts them: that having left behind <margin>22</margin> those things which belong to the beginning of the new law / they should be carried toward perfection. Nor should they attend to these "doctrines of baptisms": but be carried toward the things that follow. And so he says: ¶ "Therefore, leaving behind the word of the beginning of God: let us be carried toward perfection. Not laying again the foundation of repen—" <note>The text cuts off mid-word ("pæ-" for "pænitentiæ" or "repentance"), following the catchword mentioned in the metadata.</note>

<meta>This page continues the analysis of Hebrews chapter 6. The previous page concluded the discussion on Christ's piety and the transition from basic to mature teachings. Here, the author examines the "foundational" principles of the faith—repentance, baptism, and judgment—and addresses the difficult question of whether those who fall away after baptism can be restored.</meta>

XIV 239 Hebrews.

> ...repentance from dead works, and of faith toward God, of the doctrine of baptisms, and of laying on of hands, and of resurrection of the dead, and of eternal judgment. And this we will indeed do (if God permits). For it is impossible for those who were once enlightened, who have both tasted the heavenly gift and were made partakers of the Holy Spirit, who have also tasted the good word of God and the powers of the age to come, and then fell away: to be renewed again to repentance, crucifying the Son of God again for themselves and making him a public example of shame. <note>original Latin: "nitentiæ ex operibus mortuis... exemplum ignominiæ facientes." This is a translation of Hebrews 6:1–6.</note>

¶ After committing sins, the Hebrews were again laying the foundations of faith, repentance, baptism, the laying on of hands, and the rest, as if they had never been baptized before and had come anew to the knowledge of faith and Christ, the resurrection of the flesh, and eternal judgment. It is called "eternal" for this reason: because those who will be judged by it, whether unto life or unto death, are to remain so forever. Truly, they ought not to do this; instead, they should be carried toward the perfection which we obtain if, from the time of our rebirth, we live not according to the flesh, but according to the spirit. And indeed, those whose will is turned toward Him, and to whom God grants it, do this. For to live according to the spirit is a gift of God for those who are prepared. What does "those who were once enlightened" mean? Certainly, those who were once baptized. For this is called by our ancestors <term>photismatun</term> <note>From the Greek "photismos," meaning illumination or enlightenment; a common early Christian term for baptism.</note>, that is, the sacrament of illumination. They "tasted the heavenly gift": those who received justification from their sins. They were "made partakers of the Holy Spirit": those who, having been grafted into the body of Christ, have now begun to live by the Spirit of Christ. They "tasted the good word of God": those who have obeyed the Gospel of Christ. They also "tasted the powers of the age to come": those who have received the body and blood of Christ, through which the future age can be possessed, and who have received some spiritual gifts of the Holy Spirit. And as for what follows: it is not said simply that it is "impossible to be renewed to repentance," but "impossible to be renewed to repentance while crucifying the Son of God again in themselves and making him an example of shame." This is certainly what those would be doing who, having fallen after their baptismal illumination, thought they could be renewed through a repeated baptism as penance for their falls. For through baptism we die with, are buried with, and rise again with Christ: which can only happen once. For the Lord died once, was buried once, and rose again once. Is it not a great example of shame to crucify Christ a second time within oneself in a second baptism? As if his being once crucified, dead, and buried was not sufficient to redeem the world. Therefore, repentance is not to be repeated in a multitude of baptisms, as if in a multitude of Christ's passions and burials. 

But you will say: If there is not a multitude of baptisms, why does the apostle call it the "doctrine of baptisms" in the plural? He certainly does not mean his own doctrine, nor that of the apostles, but the doctrine of the Jews, which he therefore forbids, saying: "not laying again the foundation of the doctrine of baptisms." For he said this earlier according to his own opinion: "one Lord, one faith, one baptism." <note>A reference to Ephesians 4:5.</note> Do you see, therefore, that he spoke of the other here as coming from someone else? And that human doctrine of baptisms was so prevalent among some that they were washed and bathed daily, thinking that the filth of sins, if they had perhaps contracted any, was wiped away; which is why they were given the name <term>hemerobaptistae</term> <note>Greek for "day-baptizers," a sect that practiced daily ritual washings for purification.</note>. 

But come now, if there is a place for repentance for those who have fallen after baptism, what kind of place is it if it does not happen through the washing of baptism? There is undoubtedly a place for repentance. For if there were not, the apostle would not have handed over the incestuous fornicator to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that his spirit might be saved on the day of the Lord. <note>Reference to 1 Corinthians 5:5.</note> If there were not, the Holy Spirit would not say what is heard in the letter to the Ephesians: "Awake, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you." <note>Ephesians 5:14.</note> For what else is this but to call someone to repentance from dead works? What else does Paul intend when he writes to Timothy: that he should correct those who resist with gentleness, in case God might perhaps give them repentance to know the truth, and they may recover themselves from the snare of the devil? <note>2 Timothy 2:25-26.</note> And in the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation.</note>, almost all the angels of the seven churches—who were the bishops and pastors of those churches—because they had some "dead work," are warned to perform penance. To the first angel it is said: "Remember from where you have fallen, and do penance, and do the first works." <note>Revelation 2:5.</note> And to the third angel, it is said similarly: "Do penance. Or else I will come to you quickly and will fight against them with the sword of my mouth." <note>Revelation 2:16.</note> And to the fifth angel, it is said: "You have a name that you are alive, and you are dead." And it is added: "Be mindful, therefore, how you have received and heard; and observe, and do penance." <note>Revelation 3:1-3.</note> And to the seventh, it is said similarly: "Be zealous, therefore, and do penance." <note>Revelation 3:19.</note> 

Behold how, for the faithful, a place for repentance is undoubtedly left after a fall. But you will say: Since it is not through the washing (for that, as has been said, is impossible and profane to attempt), by doing what then? Undoubtedly, by what was said by Paul in the previous chapter: by approaching the throne of grace with confidence, so that we may receive mercy and find grace in a timely help. If we have sinned after our rebirth in the spirit, and have stained the white robe of regeneration which was washed and wiped clean in the blood of Christ—made whiter than any fuller's clothes—we (according to the command of God's herald), having a great High Priest who has passed into the heavens, Jesus Christ the Son of God, let us hold fast to our confession. For we do not have a High Priest who cannot sympathize with our weaknesses. And John says: "If anyone has sinned, we have an advocate..." <note>1 John 2:1.</note>

<summary>This page argues that while Christian baptism is a unique, unrepeatable event, repentance remains available for those who sin afterward. <meta>This page transitions from the end of a commentary on Hebrews chapter 5 into the beginning of chapter 6. It focuses on the definition of Christ’s "piety," the difficulty of explaining deep spiritual truths to "sluggish" listeners, and the foundational principles of the Christian faith, specifically warning against the repetition of baptism.</meta>

<header>COMMENTARY</header>

...those who hear him might fear him: a meaning which we say does not fit. It is better if it is translated: **for his piety**. <note>original Latin: *pro pietate*. The author is discussing Hebrews 5:7, where the Vulgate says Christ was heard "for his reverence" or "piety."</note> Certainly, "piety" refers both to the devotion of superiors toward inferiors and inferiors toward superiors, and to the entire practice of veneration. But what greater piety was there than the piety of Christ toward the Father, as to one greater and superior? What greater veneration, obedience, fear, and love? This was his piety toward the Father. And what piety was greater than the piety of Christ toward inferiors: that he, the Lord of all, willed to die for his servants—even those who deserved death—so that he alone might not die, but they might live forever? This is the ineffable piety of Christ the Lord in every respect, both upward and downward. Because of this piety—both for himself toward the Father and for his servants, so that they would not die but obtain eternal life instead of death—he was heard. Add to this that the Father’s piety was equal and alike toward such an obedient Son of such great piety, and toward us because of him. It is most fitting, therefore, that he is said to have been heard **for his piety**, both his own and his Father's. The interpreter of Paul: *and being heard because of his reverence.* <note>original Greek: "καὶ εἰσακουσθεὶς ἀπὸ τῆς εὐλαβείας."</note>

<margin>C 21</margin>
¶ **The Vulgate edition.** *Of whom we have a great discourse, and interpretable to say.* <note>Hebrews 5:11. The author is critiquing the Latin word "interpretabilis" (interpretable) used in the Vulgate Bible.</note>

¶ When the old translator says "interpretable," he does not fully explain the Greek. For when something is called "interpretable," it is understood to be "explainable." But the Greek word does not mean that; rather, it means **difficult to interpret**, and not having an easy explanation. This is especially true since the listeners were not capable of understanding it, as they could not penetrate the mysteries of the spirit. For those who think they can do this by themselves and by their own sense, cannot. But those who know they cannot—when they are clothed with a sense from on high—they can. And they are hardly ever clothed with that sense as long as they think they can do it of themselves. For these senses are contrary and do not tolerate each other at the same time: to be able to do these contrary things. One is "not being able," and the other is "truly being able." <note>The author is discussing a paradox of faith: only by admitting one's inability to understand spiritual mysteries can one receive the divine "sense" required to actually understand them.</note> And this difficulty of interpreting and explaining the discourse did not depend on Paul’s part (for that discourse was easily "interpretable" to him), but on the part of the Jews to whom the discourse was held, who could not yet bear spiritual intelligence. For they were still using their own "ability," or rather abusing their own inability; they had been slow and sluggish in understanding the sacred words in the proper way. This is what countless others still do today: those to whom the inner shrines of divinity, every mystery, and spiritual intelligence are closed. To these things, no one is admitted by their own sense or their own power, but by a higher sense and a heavenly power. The interpreter of Paul: *concerning whom we have much to say, and hard to explain,* <note>original Greek: "περὶ οὗ πολὺς ἡμῖν ὁ λόγος, καὶ δυσερμήνευτος λέγειν."</note> *since you have become weak in hearing.*

<margin>D 21</margin>
It can be said: *because you have been sluggish in your hearings.* That is, slow in understanding the readings of the Scriptures and of the holy prophets. But because the old translator spoke using a gerund, we also have translated it as **in hearing** using a gerund, meaning the same thing as if we had said it with the noun "hearings." The interpreter of Paul: *since you have become sluggish in hearing.* <note>original Greek: "ἐπεὶ νωθροὶ γεγόνατε ταῖς ἀκοαῖς."</note> For if they had progressed in the spiritual understanding of Scripture and the hearings of the prophets, the discourse—which was very difficult for them to interpret—would have been easily interpretable. ¶ **The Vulgate edition.** *That you may be taught.* In Greek, this is said in the active voice. But that matters little. The interpreter of Paul: *to teach you.* <note>original Greek: "τοῦ διδάσκειν ὑμᾶς."</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition.** *Of those who, by reason of use, have their senses exercised.* The Greek has: *because of habit,* but that does not vary much from the meaning of the old translator. The interpreter of Paul: *of those who, because of habit, have their senses exercised.* <note>original Greek: "τῶν διὰ τὴν ἕξιν τὰ αἰσθητήρια γεγυμνασμένα ἐχόντων."</note>

### CHAPTER VI.

<note>The letter N here is a large decorated woodcut initial showing a person in a landscape.</note>
<margin>22</margin>
Not only were some of the Jews, for whose sake the apostle writes, sinning regarding the elements of the old rite—not understanding what they were figures of, or how the truth corresponded to those types—but they were also failing right at the threshold regarding the beginning of the New Law. **The Beginning** is: to instruct the unrefined in the faith, to admonish them toward repentance for sins, to teach the one baptism for the remission of sins, to lay on hands for the reception of the gifts of the Holy Spirit, to believe in the resurrection and the final judgment, and the other things which the apostles handed down in summary in that collection called the **Apostles' Creed**. <note>term: "syntagmate quod symbolum appellatur apostolorum." *Syntagma* refers to a systematic arrangement or treatise; *Symbolum* is the traditional term for a Creed or summary of faith.</note> What were they doing? When they had fallen into the works of the flesh and the errors of sin—which are **dead works**—they were teaching that they must again repent and be baptized, introducing not one baptism but doctrines of various baptisms. The apostle completely forbids this from being done, because it is impossible by this route to obtain the remission of later sins. Christ died for us once and rose once; so also we die with him once in holy baptism, we are buried with him, and we rise with him. And it would be not only foolish but profane to repeat baptism, as if Christ had suffered and been buried for us not just once, but twice or perhaps frequently—thereby holding this performed mystery of the Passion up to mockery and display. Therefore, the remission of sins is impossible by this route. Paul therefore exhorts them: that, leaving behind those things which pertain to the beginning of the New Law, they be carried toward perfection. They should not intent upon these doctrines of baptisms, but be carried toward the things that follow. And so he says: ¶ *Wherefore, leaving the word of the beginning of God, let us be carried toward perfection, not laying again the foundation of re-*

# 14th Section on Hebrews

> ...of repentance from dead works, and of faith toward God, of the doctrine of baptisms, and of the laying on of hands, and of the resurrection of the dead, and of eternal judgment. And this we will do, if God permits. For it is impossible for those who were once enlightened, and have tasted the heavenly gift, and were made partakers of the Holy Spirit, and have tasted the good word of God, and the powers of the world to come, and have fallen away: to be renewed again to repentance, re-crucifying in themselves the Son of God, and making him an example of shame. <note>original: *exemplum ignominiæ facientes*. This refers to Hebrews 6:1-6, discussing the danger of apostasy.</note>

¶ After committing sins, the Hebrews were again laying the foundations of faith, repentance, baptism, the laying on of hands, and the rest, as if they had never been baptized before, and were coming anew to the knowledge of faith, of Christ, of the resurrection of the flesh, and of eternal judgment. It is called "eternal" judgment because of those who are involved in it: whether unto life or unto death, they are to remain so forever. Truly, they ought not to do this, but rather be carried toward perfection. We attain this perfection if, from the time of our rebirth, we live not according to the flesh but according to the spirit. And indeed, those whose will is turned toward Him perform this when God grants his approval. For to live according to the spirit is a gift of God for those who are prepared.

What does it mean, **those who were once enlightened**? Certainly, those who were once baptized. For this is called by our ancestors the sacrament of <term>illumination</term> <note>original: *photismatum*. From the Greek *photismos*, a common early Christian term for baptism as a spiritual awakening.</note>. They **tasted the heavenly gift**: those who received justification from their sins. They were **made partakers of the Holy Spirit**: those who, being grafted into the body of Christ, have now begun to live by the spirit of Christ. They **tasted the good word of God**: those who were fed by the Gospel of Christ. They also **tasted the powers of the world to come**: those who have received the body and blood of Christ, through which the world to come can be possessed, and who have received certain spiritual gifts.

And regarding what follows: it is not simply said that it is "impossible to be renewed to repentance," but **impossible to be renewed to repentance while re-crucifying in themselves the Son of God and making him an example of shame**. This is certainly what they would be doing if, having fallen after their baptismal illumination, they thought they could be renewed through a second baptism for their failings. For through baptism we die with Christ, are buried with him, and rise with him: which can only happen once. For the Lord died once, was buried once, and rose once. Is it not a great example of shame to crucify Christ a second time through a second baptism? As if his having been once crucified, died, and buried was not sufficient to redeem the world. Therefore, repentance is not to be repeated through a multitude of baptisms, as if through a multitude of Christ's passions and burials.

But you will say: If there is not a multitude of baptisms, why does the apostle call it the **doctrine of baptisms** (in the plural)? Surely this was not his own saying, nor that of the apostles, but rather the doctrine of the Jews, which he therefore forbids, saying: **not laying again the foundation of the doctrine of baptisms**. For he said earlier, according to his own view: "one Lord, one faith, one baptism." Do you see, therefore, that he said this here based on the opinion of others? That human doctrine of "baptisms" was so strong among some people that they were washed and cleansed every day, thinking that the filth of their sins—any they might have contracted—was wiped away. From this, those people were given the name <term>Daily-Washers</term> <note>original: *hemerobaptistæ*. A Jewish-Christian sect that practiced daily ritual immersion.</note>.

But come now, if there is a place for repentance for those who have fallen after baptism, what kind is it, if it is not through the washing of baptism? There is, without doubt, a place for repentance. For if there were not, the apostle would not have delivered the incestuous fornicator to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that his spirit might be saved on the day of the Lord. If there were not, the Holy Spirit would not say what we hear in the letter to the Ephesians: "Rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you." For what else is this but a call to repentance from dead works? What else does Paul mean when he writes to Timothy that he should correct those who resist with gentleness, "in case God might give them repentance to the acknowledgment of the truth, and they may recover themselves from the snare of the devil"?

And in the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation.</note>, almost all the angels of the seven churches—who were the bishops and pastors of those churches—are warned to perform penance if they had any "dead work." To the first angel it is said: "Remember from where you have fallen, and do penance, and do your first works." And to the third angel it is said similarly: "Do penance. If not, I will come to you quickly and fight against them with the sword of my mouth." And to the fifth angel it is said: "You have a name that you are alive, and yet you are dead." And it is added: "Be mindful, therefore, how you have received and heard, and keep it, and do penance." And to the seventh, it is said similarly: "Be zealous, therefore, and do penance."

Behold how, for the faithful, a place for repentance is undoubtedly left after a fall. But you will say: "Since it is not through a washing (for that, as was said, is impossible and profane to attempt), by doing what?" Without a doubt, it is by doing what was said by Paul in the previous chapter: by "going with confidence to the throne of grace, so that we may receive mercy and find grace in seasonable help." If we have sinned after our rebirth in the spirit, and have stained the white robe of regeneration—which was washed and wiped clean in the blood of Christ, made whiter than any fuller’s cloth—we (according to the command of God's herald), having a great high priest who has passed into the heavens, Jesus Christ the Son of God, let us hold fast to our confession. For we do not have a high priest who cannot sympathize with our weaknesses. And John says: "If anyone sins, we have an advocate..."

<summary>This page explains that while baptism cannot be repeated, repentance after sin is always possible through Christ's intercession. The author clarifies that the "doctrine of baptisms" mentioned by Paul refers to Jewish ritual washings rather than Christian baptism.</summary>

from heaven he stretched out, as if a rope let down and reaching from the throne of God even to us, and again penetrating from us all the way to the inner parts of the heavens and the seat of God. ¶ **EXAMINATION of several matters concerning the literal text.** ¶ **Vulgate edition.** *To be renewed again to repentance: again crucifying for themselves the Son of God.* ¶ Regarding renewal to repentance, or rather *in* repentance: this is understood through baptism, because in that alone are we crucified with Christ, die with him, and rise again. For if he had spoken of another kind of renewal, he would not have immediately added, *again crucifying*—or as it is held in Greek in a single word, *re-crucifying*—the Son of God for themselves. And "for themselves" is the same as "in themselves." And **repentance** <term>pœnitentia: here defined not just as sorrow, but as "re-thinking" (recogitatio) and "coming to one's senses" (resipiscentia)</term> here signifies a rethinking and a change of mind. For when we rethink our prior deeds, detest what we have thought upon, and come to our senses for the future regarding similar things, we repent. Those sacred voices, both of the Precursor <note>John the Baptist</note> and of the Savior, proclaim: *do penance*, *repent and believe the gospel*; that is, rethink your prior ways, and come to your senses from your prior evil works. Not that this repentance, rethinking, or change of mind *renews*, *purges*, or *justifies*—for that is impossible—but it prepares the way for the one who justifies. For the divine entrance and the infusion of divine grace is what renews, purges, and sanctifies. Therefore the divine herald of God said, when he preached repentance: *prepare the ways of the Lord, make his paths straight.* Therefore, to put on a hairshirt, to afflict the body, to beat oneself with whips, to tame oneself with hunger and harsh abstinence from food and drink, or to exhaust oneself with pilgrimages: this is not "doing penance," but these are the **signs** of repentance. And those who are holy, if they do similar things, offer to others a sign of repentance; for they do not have within themselves anything for which they must repent. For what did the Precursor of the Lord, holy from the womb, have in himself that he should rethink, or from which he should come to his senses? Therefore, it was not that he himself was repenting, but he was a form and type of repentance for those who had need of it. And even granted that there are saints who needed repentance, they nevertheless have an "end of repentance for the saints" (as Hermas says). <note>Reference to *The Shepherd of Hermas*, an early Christian work. It suggests that for the truly holy, there comes a point where they move past the need for constant repentance into a state of stable grace.</note> For those who are accustomed to proceed toward what is ahead, with the grace of God leading and providing stability, they forget those things which are behind. And if they have already left them behind, and (as is right) have truly left them, how is it that their repentance is not finished? For after Christ has deigned to place his holy steps into holy minds, and has sanctified his tabernacle, and has turned and fixed those minds upon himself—just as attentive eyes are fixed on the sun—if they behold themselves purged by the grace of God, they no longer have anything to repent of, or to change their minds about; rather, they have cause to give perpetual and perennial thanks to their Sanctifier. It is a great thing to repent; but it is far greater to recognize from whence sanctification descends, and by repenting—that is, by preparing oneself for his grace and justification—to keep an eye, bathed in tears and humbled, fixed upon him, and thus attain that prophetic state: *As the eyes of a maid are on the hands of her mistress, so our eyes are toward the Lord our God, until he has mercy on us.* May Christ the Lord, the bountiful pitier, grant to each one to know how to truly repent, and having completed repentance, to know how to enjoy his mercy in the joy of the Holy Spirit and in inflamed charity. But regarding repentance: only this much for now. In himself, indeed, it is impossible; but in his members, it is possible. When we are initiated into his sacred rites, he immediately grafts us into his own sacred body, and we are a member of Christ and sons of God; indeed, in him we are all one Son of God, needing no repentance. ¶ But if it happens by an evil error that the malignant one detains us, rep...

### 14th Part on Hebrews

...those in need of repentance: he exposes us <note>original: *traducit nos*—literally "leads us across," like a captive in a victory parade</note> and makes us a theater of ignominy and mockery, a wretched spectacle of perdition for the powers of darkness. And behold how we make the Son of God an example of shame within ourselves. O, how harsh it is for those who have been grafted into the sacred body of Christ to sin! Since in them the Son of God must be held in mockery by malignant powers, how heavy and inexpiable this would be, were it not that the same Son of God is of infinite mercy. And the devil, whose pride always rises against God: does he not exult—or rather, does he not exult greatly—not because you as yourself sin in this way, or rush with him into perdition, but because you, a member of Christ, you who are grafted into the Son of God, are sinning? He rejoices greatly not because of the injury to you, but because of the injury to Christ. That he tears away and drags down a member of His: this is a great joy to him; this he considers a distinguished victory; these members he leads forth as a distinguished victor. And although we do not see these public exposures, they nevertheless happen sometimes (and would that it were not so often!) when the saints miserably fall, becoming spectacles for the malignant powers in the spiritual realms. 

And likewise, when the members of the malignant one come to the faith of Christ: with his spoils snatched away, a spiritual triumph is celebrated before the good angels. And these battles, alternating victories, public exposures, and the triumphs of the combatants shall not cease until the end of the world, no differently than those wars we see waged sensibly on earth with eyes of flesh. And this is also one way of "exposing to public shame" and "making the Son of God an example of ignominy"; for another way has already been declared concerning the literal sense. Truly, when the members of Christ are triumphed over by the malignant one in the manner stated here, they become, properly speaking, an "example of ignominy" and are "exposed to shame." For the <term>vessels of honor</term> <note>A biblical metaphor for people chosen for God's purposes</note> have been made into <term>vessels of ignominy and wrath</term>. But when the members of the malignant one are triumphed over by Christ (I speak of those men who are snatched from the evil one), they become an example of mercy and glory. Therefore, they are not so much said to be "exposed to shame" as they are "led out" and liberated from the exposure of the malignant one. For from vessels of wrath and ignominy, they are made into vessels of grace and honor. But enough has been said of these exposures for now.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Epistle to the Hebrews, specifically exploring the metaphors of hope and the spiritual mechanics of repentance. It transitions from the imagery of the anchor and rope to a technical linguistic analysis of the Greek and Latin versions of the scriptures regarding the impossibility of "renewing" those who fall away.</meta>

He reached down from heaven, like a rope <note>original: *funem*</note> let down and reaching from the throne of God all the way to us, and again penetrating from us back to the innermost parts of the heavens and the seat of God. If we hold onto this rope firmly, embrace it, and follow it, this most precious rope will lead us from the earth to the inner sanctuaries of heaven, where the eternal temple of God is. Into this temple, our precursor <note>The "one who runs ahead" to prepare the way, referring here to Jesus.</note> has entered for us: our Lord Jesus Christ, a <term>priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek<note>Melchizedek was a mysterious king-priest in the Old Testament who had no recorded genealogy, making him a "type" or symbol for Christ’s eternal, non-hereditary priesthood.</note></term>. In the temple of God, he is continually offering for us that super-celestial bread and the wine of the true vine—of which the heavenly Father alone was the vine-dresser—sacrificing and offering it to God. For what are we who have fled for refuge to the hope set before us, if not those to whom hope has been previously offered, cast forward, and extended? What did the veil of the physical temple designate in ancient times, if not heaven? What were the inner chambers, if not the secret and hidden depths of heaven, where divinity itself is worshipped openly and without a veil? What did the priest entering as an intercessor and mediator for the people figure, if not the Christ who was then to come? He has transcended the true veil of God’s temple—that is, heaven—and entered the true temple of God as the eternal High Priest. He is always there for us, we who hold the rope of heaven: a hope gleaming with the light of faith, more radiant than the sun, which clings to heaven more firmly than an anchor. He is always, I say, presenting and offering in spirit and truth to the eternal Father the eternal, immortal, and ever-living sacrifice <note>original: *hostiam*</note>, the all-saving and redeeming Lamb of the world. To Him, with the eternal Father and the Holy Spirit, be all praise, grace, honor, and reverence, in all things and above all things, forever and ever. Amen.

<margin>A 22.</margin> EXAMINATION of several points regarding the literal text. ¶ The <term>Vulgate edition<note>The standard 4th-century Latin translation of the Bible used by the Western Church.</note></term> says: *To be renewed again to repentance: crucifying again for themselves the Son of God.* ¶ Regarding the "renewal to repentance," or "in repentance," this is understood to happen through baptism. For in that alone are we crucified with Christ, die with Him, and rise again. For if the author had spoken of another kind of renewal, he would not have immediately added, *crucifying again*—or as it is held in one word in the Greek, <term>recrucifying<note>original Greek: *anastaurountas*</note></term>—the Son of God for themselves. And this "for themselves" is the same as "within themselves." And "repentance" here signifies <term>reflection<note>original: *recogitationem*</note></term> and <term>coming to one's senses<note>original: *resipiscentiam*—a change of mind or heart.</note></term>. For when we reflect on our prior deeds, and detest those things we have reflected upon, we come to our senses and change for the future from similar things: this is how we repent. ¶ Those sacred words, both of the Precursor <note>John the Baptist</note> and of the Savior—*do penance* or *repent and believe the gospel*—put this forward: reflect on your prior deeds, come to your senses from your prior evil works. Not that this repentance, reflection, or change of mind itself innovates, purges, or justifies—for that is impossible—but it prepares the way for the One who justifies. For the divine entrance and the infusion of divine grace is what innovates, purges, and sanctifies. Therefore, the divine herald of God said when he preached repentance: *Prepare the ways of the Lord, make his paths straight.* Therefore, to put on sackcloth, to afflict the body, to strike oneself with whips, to tame oneself with hunger and harsh abstinence from food and drink, or to exhaust oneself with pilgrimages: this is not "doing repentance," but these are <italic>signs</italic> of repentance. And those who are holy, if they do similar things, they offer a sign of repentance to others, for they do not have within themselves anything for which they need to repent. For what did the Precursor of the Lord, who was holy from the womb, have in himself to reflect upon or from which to come to his senses? He did not, therefore, repent for himself; rather, he was a form and model of repentance for those who were in need of it. And even if there are saints who once needed repentance, they nevertheless have an "end of repentance for the saints" (as <term>Hermas<note>An early Christian author, writer of 'The Shepherd of Hermas', a 2nd-century work of apostolic exhortation.</note></term> says). For those who are accustomed to proceeding toward the things that are ahead, with the grace of God leading them and providing stability, they forget the things that are behind. And if they have already come to their senses—and come to their senses as is fitting—how is their repentance not finished? For after Christ has deigned to place his holy steps into holy minds, and has sanctified his tabernacle, and has turned and fixed those minds upon himself (as attentive eyes are fixed upon the sun): if they see themselves purged by the grace of God, they no longer have anything to repent for or to come to their senses from. Instead, they have reason to give constant and perennial thanks to their Sanctifier. It is a great thing to repent; but it is far greater to acknowledge from whence sanctification descends. In repenting—that is, in preparing oneself for His grace and justification—one should keep an eye, humbled and bathed in abundant tears, fixed upon Him, and so attain that prophetic saying: *As the eyes of the handmaid are on the hands of her mistress, so our eyes are toward the Lord our God, until he has mercy on us.* May Christ the Lord, the copious merciful one, grant to each of us to know how to truly repent, and having completed repentance, to know how to enjoy His mercy in the joy of the Holy Spirit and with inflamed charity. But regarding repentance: only this much for now. The Interpreter of Paul <note>The translator of the Greek text into Latin.</note> says: <gloss>to renew again unto repentance, crucifying for themselves the Son of God.</gloss> <note>original Greek: *palin anakainizein eis metanoian, anastaurountas heautois ton huion tou theou*</note> ¶ The Vulgate edition says: *And making him a mockery.* ¶ What the old translator here calls "making a mockery," he translates in the Epistle to the Colossians as "exposed" or "led in triumph," where he says: *He exposed them confidently, openly triumphing over them in himself.* We said in the examinations of the 2nd chapter of the seventh book that "to expose" <note>original: *traducere*</note> designates the same thing as making an example of ignominy. But come now, how would it be possible to make the Son of God an example of mockery and ignominy, He who is the Lord of all majesty and glory? In Himself, it is indeed impossible. But in His members: that is possible. When we are initiated into His sacred mysteries, He immediately grafts us into His sacred body, and we are a member of Christ and of the Son of God; indeed, in Him we are all one Son, needing no repentance. But what if by a evil error it happens that the malignant one detains us, pe— <note>The text cuts off here, continuing the word on the next page.</note>

...needing repentance: he exposes us <note>original: *traducit nos*; here meaning to parade someone in a humiliating public procession</note> as a spectacle of shame and mockery, a miserable sight of perdition to the powers of darkness. And behold how we make the Son of God an example of shame within ourselves. Oh, how hard it is for those who have been grafted into the sacred body of Christ to sin: since in them it is necessary for the Son of God to be held in mockery by malignant powers. How heavy, how inexpiable this would be, unless the same Son of God were of infinite mercy? And the devil, whose pride always rises against God: does he not exult? Does he not exult greatly? Not because you as yourself sin, or fall into perdition with others, but because you—a member of Christ, grafted into the Son of God—sin. He rejoices greatly not because of the injury to you, but because of the injury to Christ. That he tears away and drags down His member: this is a great joy to him; he considers this a distinguished victory; he parades <note>original: *traducit*</note> these members as a famous victor. And although we do not see these parades, they nevertheless occur sometimes (and would that it were not so often) from holy ones who have miserably fallen, in the spiritual spectacles of the malignant powers. 

And even when the members of the malignant one come to the faith of Christ, their spoils being snatched away, they are <term>triumphed<note>Referring to the Roman *triumphus*, a ritual parade for a victorious general. Here, it refers to the spiritual victory where Christ "captures" souls back from the devil.</note></term> over spiritually before the good angels. And these battles, alternating victories, parading of captives, and triumphs of those at war shall not cease until the end of the world, no differently than those we see carried out visibly on earth with eyes of flesh. And this is also one way of parading the Son of God and making Him an example of shame. For another way concerning the literal meaning has already been explained. Indeed, when members of Christ are triumphed over by the malignant one in the manner described here, they properly become an "example of shame" and are properly "paraded." For <term>vessels of honor<note>A biblical metaphor from Romans 9:21 comparing humans to clay vessels shaped by God for different purposes.</note></term> have been made vessels of shame and wrath. But when the members of the malignant one are triumphed over by Christ (I speak of men who are rescued from the malignant one), they become an example of mercy and glory. Therefore, they are not so much said to be "paraded" as to be led out and liberated from the "parade" of the malignant one. For from vessels of wrath and shame they are made vessels of grace and honor. But enough of these "parades" for now.

### CHAPTER VIII

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'P' containing detailed leafy scrollwork.</image-desc>

<margin>36</margin> **B**y those things which are held concerning Melchizedek—as if through the basic elements of the law toward the truth and significance of those elements—the apostle has guided the Hebrews by the hand toward a true, sacred, and God-worthy understanding. Now, as if in an epilogue and summary, he gathers what he intended in the previous discourse: namely, the article of faith that our High Priest <term>pontificem</term> <note>While "pontifex" literally means "bridge-builder," in this context it is the standard Latin term for the Jewish High Priest</note>, Jesus Christ, sits at the right hand of the Father. He is the minister of the heavenly tabernacles and the author of our sacrifices. He offers those things truly worthy of veneration under sacred veils here on earth, and serves openly before the sight of the Divine Majesty, ministering in heaven in that sanctuary of God which no man, but God Himself, fixed and established. He says, therefore: ¶ "Now the main point of what is being said is this: We have such a high priest, who sat down at the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in the heavens. He is a minister of the sanctuary and of the true tabernacle, which God set up, and not man."

¶ The sanctuary of which Christ is the minister is the heavenly and true tabernacle, of which we will speak in the following chapter. This was designated by that which was called the "Holy of Holies." Moses set up a tabernacle in which the priests offered sacrifices and poured out prayers for the people; and this tabernacle was not the "true" one, but a figure of the true. Neither were the victims true victims, nor the rites true rites, but rather shadowy likenesses of the true sacred things. And since the office of every high priest is to offer to God, this eternal High Priest must also have something to offer to God. But it is not the kind of shadowy sacrifice they offered on earth, but a true sacrifice. For He is the consummator of true sacrifices, and not a minister of merely typical ones. Truly, when He was on earth, He offered no such thing, but rather the exemplar of sacrifices, of which he who was greater than the prophets and those born of women <note>A reference to John the Baptist</note> said: <margin>37</margin> "Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world." And therefore, the apostle adds: ¶ "For every high priest is appointed to offer gifts and sacrifices; wherefore it is necessary that this one also have something to offer. But if he were indeed on earth, he would by no means be a priest, since there are priests according to the law who offer gifts, who serve a copy and shadow of the heavenly things. Just as Moses was answered when he was about to complete the tabernacle: 'See,' he said, 'that you make all things according to the pattern shown to you on the mountain.'" ¶ The priests who were appointed by men offered fleshly victims. But He who was appointed High Priest not by men, but by God alone, offers a spiritual and divine sacrifice. It is not one kind on earth and another in heaven: rather, on earth it is still hidden under sacred veils, but in heaven it is revealed. Therefore, in the new priesthood of the eternal Priest, we must no longer sacrifice by serving a copy and shadow of heavenly things (which the old observation of the law held), but in truth—even if that truth is still veiled to us for as long as we lead this mortal life. Therefore, the sacrifices of the Jews have ceased, and the old rite of sacrificing is fulfilled and finished; and now we must insist only on the new. For when the truth is present, what need is there for a figure or a footprint? Since better things have been handed down—indeed, the most perfect and best—why should imperfect and unconsummated things still detain us? You have gold to offer to God; why would you offer Him base metal? The sacrifice of the eternal High Priest surpasses every other sacrifice by an immense degree, which He has already made and willed to be made public to the whole world. Therefore, that which is inferior has ceased. Otherwise, you would be like Cain, who, when he could have offered something better, offered what was worse.

<margin>38</margin> And Paul shows that the old has been taken away, saying: ¶ "But now he has obtained a more excellent ministry, by how much also he is the mediator of a better testament <note>The word "testamentum" translates here as "covenant," a legal agreement between God and humanity</note>, which is established upon better promises. For if 그 first one had been faultless, then no place would have been sought for a second. For finding fault, he says to them: 'Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will complete a new testament over the house of Israel and over the house of Judah; not according to the testament that I made with their fathers in the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt. Because they did not remain in my testament, and I neglected them, says the Lord. For this is the testament that I will arrange for the house of Israel after those days, says the Lord: I will give my laws into their minds, and I will write them in their hearts. And I will be to them a God, and they shall be to me a people. And no one shall teach his neighbor, and no one his brother, saying: Know the Lord. For all shall know me, from the least of them to the greatest of them. For I will be merciful to their injustices, and their sins and their iniquities I will remember no more.' In that he says 'new,' he has made the first one old. Now that which is becoming old..."

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Hebrews Chapter 8. It concludes a theological reflection on the transition from the Old Covenant to the New, followed by a philological "Examination" of specific Latin and Greek terms used in the opening verses of the chapter.</meta>

...it grows old and ages; it is near destruction. **This** oracle regarding the new testament <note>original: "nouo testamento"</note> belongs to the prophet Jeremiah. And Moses wrote the first, old testament on parchments and dead skins. The New, however, was not first written in this way, but in the mind and in living hearts. For Christ did not leave us a written new testament as Moses did the old; rather, he inscribed it by the oracle of a living voice and through the Holy Spirit in the minds of the apostles and disciples, just as the oracle contained, in which he had indeed predicted: "I will give my laws into their minds, and in their heart I will write them."

Thereafter, four from among those who had these laws inscribed in their minds—who were signified in the holy vision of the prophet Ezekiel by the "four living creatures full of eyes before and behind," full of understanding of the Old Law which preceded and the New which followed—left them to us in writing. And this is the New Testament, confirmed by the death of the Son. The witnesses are the apostles and all the disciples and whoever heard the Lord Jesus. The scribes and secretaries are the four evangelists. 

I say the New Testament is so much more excellent by as much as the Son is a more outstanding mediator than Moses. It is so much more excellent by as much as the promises of the New are more powerful than the promises of the Old. "I appoint to you," He says, "as my Father appointed to me, a kingdom." And again: "Where I am, there also my servant shall be." And elsewhere: "The Son of Man must be lifted up, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life. For God so loved the world that he gave his only begotten Son, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life." 

These are the promises of the New: to be in the heavenly kingdom with Christ and to possess eternal life. But what does the Old promise? "But now, Israel, hear," it says, "the precepts and judgments which I teach you, so that by doing them you may live and, entering in, you may possess the land which the Lord the God of your fathers is about to give you." And again: "Every commandment which I command you today, be careful to do, so that you may live and be multiplied, and entering in, you may possess the land for which the Lord swore to your fathers." And elsewhere: "Observe and hear all these things which I command you, that it may be well with you and your children after you." 

How wide a difference there is: the promise of the kingdom of heaven and the kingdom of the Canaanites; to be with Christ and to be in the land promised to the fathers; the promise of eternal life and the promise of a present and momentary life. By so much does the New Testament surpass the Old. And whoever says "New" immediately implies "Old," for the New is called "New" in respect to the Old, as the later in respect to the prior. But what grows old and ages is liable to destruction. Therefore, the Old Testament was destined to perish and has indeed now perished, since the New is known and published everywhere. 

But the New is always new; it always lasts. Indeed, the New will always be new, as that which is later will not have a successor in respect to which it might be considered old. Therefore, the New Testament is an "Eternal Testament," as the Apostle also calls it later, saying: "May the God of peace, who brought back from the dead the great shepherd in the blood of the eternal testament, our Lord Jesus Christ, perfect you in every good work." May we be able to serve and obey Him in this, His eternal testament, so that we may be able to reach the promises of His holy testament, through the gift of the same Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives, reigns, and governs all things, one God in an eternal kingdom. Amen.

<margin>A 36</margin> **EXAMINATION of several points regarding the text.**
¶ **The Vulgate edition.** "The chapter, however, on those things which are being said." <note>original: "Capitulum autē super ea quæ dicitur"</note>
¶ "Chapter" <term>capitulum</term> here signifies a "summary" and a collection in very few words. Therefore, for readier understanding, we preferred to say "the summary" rather than "the chapter."
**The Translator of Paul.** <note>original Greek: κεφάλαιον δέ ἐπὶ τοῖς λεγομένοις</note> "Now the main point of the things being said."

¶ **The Vulgate edition.** "Who sat down at the right hand of the seat of greatness in the heavens." <note>original: "Qui consedit i dextera sedis magnitudinis in cœlis"</note>
¶ We have said "of majesty" <term>maiestatis</term> lest the word "greatness" <term>magnitudo</term>—which is translated by the old interpreter in the first chapter of the fifth epistle (which is to the Ephesians) where he says, "what is the exceeding greatness of his power toward us"—should seem to be the same. For there we find <note>original Greek: μέγεθος</note> "magnitude/greatness," but here we have <note>original Greek: τῆς μεγαλωσύνης ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς</note> "of the majesty in the heavens."
<margin>A</margin> **The Translator of Paul.** <note>original Greek: ὃς ἐκάθισεν ἐμ δεξιᾷ τοῦ θρόνου τῆς μεγαλωσύνης ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς</note> "Who sat at the right hand of the throne of majesty in the heavens."

<margin>37</margin> ¶ **The Vulgate edition.** "Who serve the pattern and shadow of heavenly things." <note>original: "Qui exemplari & vmbrę deferuiunt cœlestiū"</note>
¶ What the true interpreter calls here a "pattern" <term>exemplari</term>, he calls an example and a sketching of something truer which is the <term>archetype</term> <note>The original model from which copies are made</note> and the primary pattern. And what is also named here is such an "example" that it is even a "sub-example," as if it were an example underneath an example. That which is underneath is a "shadow" <term>adumbratio</term>. That which is above is the "pattern" <term>exemplar</term> and its truth and <term>prototype</term>. 

If it exists simply "above," it is simply the truth, the archetype, and the prototype. The ceremonies of the Hebrews were formerly our examples, types, and <term>hypodigmata</term> <note>original: "hypodigmata"; Greek for "sketches" or "indications"</note>. Our ceremonies, however, are the "patterns" <note>original: "exemplaria"</note> and (if I may say so) the "super-patterns" and "hyper-types" of those Hebrew ones. Yet they are not "simply" the patterns, super-patterns, and hyper-types, for they have above them the truths, archetypes, and prototypes. For those truths in the heavens are naked, uncovered, and open. Our things, however, are covered and veiled with sacred coverings. Whence it follows that those heavenly things are the "patterns of patterns." Our things, however, are only "patterns of examples." Those are solely "super-patterns." Ours, however, are patterns and examples, sub-patterns and super-patterns. But regarding these things: enough for now.
¶ **The Translator of Paul.** <note>original Greek: οἵτινες ὑποδείγματι καὶ σκιᾷ λατρεύουσι τῶν ἐπουρανίων</note> "Who serve a copy and shadow of the heavenly things." ¶ **Vulgate—**

<meta>This page continues the philological and theological commentary on the Epistle to the Hebrews, moving from the conclusion of Chapter 8 into the beginning of Chapter 9. The author focuses on the specific Greek terminology used to describe the heavenly "patterns" shown to Moses, contrasting the physical Tabernacle with spiritual reality.</meta>

XIIII 247 Hebrews.

<margin>B. 37</margin> The Vulgate edition says: **“See that you make everything according to the pattern shown to you on the mountain.”** <note>Hebrews 8:5, quoting Exodus 25:40</note>. What the ancient translator calls a **pattern** <note>Latin: "exemplar"</note> here is not the same word he translated as **pattern** just a moment ago when he said, "who serve as a **pattern** and shadow of heavenly things." For in the earlier passage, the Greek word is *hypodeigma* <note>original: "ὑπόδειγμα", meaning a sign or suggestive representation</note>, as seen above. But the word used here is *typos* <note>original: "τύπος", meaning a sketch, strike, or type</note>.

Therefore, so that it does not appear to be the same word in both places, we have called the former an **example** <note>Latin: "exemplum"</note> and the latter a **type** <note>Latin: "typus"</note>. Since a "type" speaks more of a faint sketch than the reality itself, I believe this suggests that it was not the naked truth shown to Moses on the mountain, but a shadow of the truth and a distant idea. Indeed, how could he have seen the truth except through a reflection, unless he had beheld divine things nakedly and revealed—which is not possible for travelers still wandering in this mortal life? Thus, what he saw was a **type**, not yet the truth itself or the **archetype** <note>the original or fundamental model</note>. 

Just as Ezekiel in his sacred vision saw the **type** of the Jerusalem to be rebuilt and of the temple of the Lord, as is known from chapters 40 and 41 of his prophecy; so Moses saw in a sacred vision the **type** of all things God commanded to be made—not the ultimate truths of the type, any more than Ezekiel did. Ezekiel saw everything in a **type** pertaining to Jerusalem and the temple; Moses saw everything in a **type** pertaining to the construction of the tabernacle, the altar, the sacrificial vessels, and all other things. Visions of this kind, whoever receives them, are **typical ideas** <note>conceptual models</note> of sensible and material things that are to be expressed. These typical ideas are signs for both: having a double meaning, one below <note>the material construction</note> and one above <note>the spiritual reality</note>. 

If, therefore, one looks toward the truth as the "pattern" and the shadow as the "copy," then the **pattern** would be the first thing modeled, shown by the example; and the **example** would be the image that displays and points it out. The ancient translator should perhaps have said **example** here rather than **pattern**. Similarly in Exodus. However, authors often confuse these terms, **pattern** and **example**. For instance, they might call the **idea** of a house pre-formed in the mind of an architect the "pattern" of the house. In the same way, since Moses perceived everything that was to be made through an idea in the mind—not one he himself pre-formed, but one infused in a sacred and spiritual vision—nothing prevents us from saying: "you shall make all things according to the **pattern**." All these things are said rightly, provided they are understood appropriately and we do not mistake dreams for truths. *The Translator of Paul.*

<margin>B 38</margin> **“You shall make all things according to the type shown to you on the mountain.”** <note>original Greek: "ποιήσεις πάντα κατὰ τὸν τύπον τὸν δειχθέντα σοι ἐν τῷ ὄρει"</note> 

The Vulgate edition: **“For if that prior one had been faultless.”** <note>Hebrews 8:7</note>. It should say: **“the first,”** for **“first”** and **“second”** correspond to each other, just as **“prior”** and **“later”** do. And where it says **“had been faultless,”** it could be said **“had been irreproachable.”** *The Translator of Paul.* **“For if that first one had been irreproachable.”** <note>original Greek: "εἰ γὰρ ἡ πρώτη ἐκείνη ἦν ἄμεμπτος"</note>

<margin>C 38</margin> The Vulgate edition: **“For finding fault with them, he says.”** <note>Hebrews 8:8</note>. It should rather be said: **“For reproving them, he says to them.”** For that is what "reproving" intends. What is he reproving? Not the first covenant, but he says to them [the people] while finding fault. For it looks back to what was said above: "For if that first one had been irreproachable." *The Translator of Paul.* **“For finding fault with them, he says.”** <note>original Greek: "μεμφόμενος γὰar αὐτοῖς λέγει"</note> 

The Vulgate edition: **“Behold, the days shall come.”** Equally: **“Behold, the days are coming.”** *The Translator of Paul.* **“Behold, the days are coming.”** <note>original Greek: "ἰδοὺ ἡμέραι ἔρχονται"</note>

The Vulgate edition: **“For all shall know me from the least even to the greatest of them.”** <note>Hebrews 8:11</note>. The Greek speech uses positive forms in this way: **“Because all shall know me from their small one even to their great one,”** placing a relative pronoun after both "small" and "great." Therefore, the ancient translator should have said (since he preferred the comparison): **“from their lesser.”** The word "their" is missing. And he used comparatives instead of positives. *The Translator of Paul.* **“Because all shall know me from their small one unto their great one.”** <note>original Greek: "ὅτι πάντες εἰδήσουσί με ἀπὸ μικροῦ αὐτῶν ἕως μεγάλου αὐτῶν"</note>

The Vulgate edition: **“And their sins I will remember no more.”** <note>Hebrews 8:12</note>. It should say: **“And their sins and their iniquities.”** The phrase **“and their iniquities”** is missing. *The Translator of Paul.* **“And of their sins and of their iniquities I will by no means remember anymore.”** <note>original Greek: "καὶ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν αὐτῶν, καὶ τῶν ἀνομιῶν αὐτῶν, οὐ μὴ μνησθῶ ἔτι"</note>

The Vulgate edition: **“He has made the prior old.”** <note>Hebrews 8:13</note>. Here too it should say: **“the first.”** *The Translator of Paul.* **“He has made the first old.”** <note>original Greek: "πεπαλαίωκε τὴν πρώτην"</note>

---

### CHAPTER IX.

The Old Testament, which has grown old, has now been led to its end. It had its own **justifications** <note>legal requirements</note> of divine service and worship, which were the observations of the ancient law. It also had a **sanctuary**. One was the **secular** <note>worldly or earthly</note> room, which was called "holy." This was the first entrance of the whole tabernacle. The other was what was called the **Holy of Holies**, also called in the plural "the Holies of Holies" because of the things contained within it. In it were kept the Ark of the Lord, the tablets of Moses, the mercy seat, the manna, the rod of Aaron, and the censer for incense. 

Truly, the New Testament also possesses all these things in truth. For the observations of the New Law contain the **justifications of God**. Whoever observes them is truly justified by God, and that justification is brought to completion. In the old law, however, they were not yet completed. 

The ancient Tabernacle was a **figure** <note>a symbolic representation</note> of the whole world, both of visible and invisible things. For the entire world is, in truth, the temple of God. Its outer part, open and visible, is called the **worldly and secular holy place**. But the hidden and interior part, which is invisible, is named the **Holy of Holies** and the **Holies of Holies**. As long as we live in this world serving Christ, we worship him in the first holy place. But when the life of this age is finished...

COMMENTARY

those who are worthy pass through to the Holy of Holies, admitted to those divine and ineffable spectacles, already venerating Christ in the Holy of Holies. For there, Christ is worshipped as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit; moreover, as the eternal priest of all sacred functions, he is the **liturgist** <term>liturgus: a minister or leader of public worship</term> and the one who brings them to completion. And concerning those symbolic holy things of the ancient law, where they performed the worship of God according to their own rite, the Apostle adds, saying: ¶ **“Indeed, even the first [covenant] had regulations for worship and a worldly sanctuary. For the first tabernacle was constructed, in which were the lampstands, and the table, and the offering of the loaves, which is called the Holy Place. But after the second veil was the tabernacle which is called the Holy of Holies, having a golden censer and the ark of the covenant covered on all sides with gold, containing a golden urn holding the manna, and the rod of Aaron which had budded, and the tablets of the covenant. Above it were the cherubim of glory overshadowing the mercy seat. Concerning these things, we must not speak in detail here.”** <note>Hebrews 9:1–5</note>. ¶ **“Indeed the first had regulations for worship.”** What was "the first"? Surely the first testament. And he rightly says "it had" <note>Latin: "habuit", in the past tense</note>, because that form of service and mode of veneration has ceased and perished. **“A worldly sanctuary”**: this was said to designate for us this open and lower mode of worship after the coming of Christ. Therefore, those who contaminate this world with sins contaminate the holy tabernacle of God. But the Holy of Holies cannot be contaminated, for it is the super-celestial and invisible tabernacle of God; indeed, nothing defiled enters into it. The **“first holy place”** was the tabernacle after the first veil. And the **“Holy of Holies”** was that tabernacle which was after the second veil. The Apostle has mentioned in a few words what was contained in the first holy place and what was in the second. But he omitted saying what they specifically and individually designated, since this was not the place for explaining those things with exact precision—which is indeed true. Yet I wish it had been, and that he had, as he did with Melchizedek, taken the opportunity to unravel those mysteries for us and restore those images to their true reality. Still, let no one attribute it to arrogance if—having implored divine aid to shine upon us—we investigate in a few words the truth and the models of these symbolic things which the Apostle described.
