The **first holy place** (as has been said) is this lower world, especially where Christ is worshipped. The **lampstands** are the churches, which ought to shine with faith, hope, charity, and good works. The **table** is Christ’s altar. The **offering of the loaves** (that is, the oblation of the bread), which is called holy, designated the Eucharist. The **priests** who entered there daily prefigured the priests of the New Law. The **second veil** is heaven, for the first veil is the covering of the elemental region. The **second tabernacle**, which is also the Holy of Holies, is the super-mundane region of intelligible things. 

<margin>
Second
veil.
Second
tabernacle.
Golden
censer.
Ark.
Manna.
</margin>

The **golden censer** signifies the prayers of the saints. The **ark of the covenant** is Christ as the Lawgiver. Truly, since the ark was gilded inside and out with the purest gold, it indicated the purity of Christ’s humanity—than which none is purer—both externally in word and example, and internally in soul. Nor should you wonder that the ark was made of wood, for Christ is also the **Tree of Life**. The **manna** contained in the golden urn showed the Bread of Life who descended from heaven, who is venerated with all purity in the Holy of Holies—that is, in the celestial region of the blessed. But the other manna which was outside <note>referring to the manna gathered in the wilderness</note> is the Body of Christ by which those who still dwell in the first tabernacle are fed. Yet the manna in the Holy of Holies was not different from that which was outside as **viaticum** <term>viaticum: food for a journey; specifically the Eucharist given to the dying or travelers</term>, but the same. Likewise, the Body of Christ is the same in the super-celestial places as that which is in this world. But there, it exists in all the purity of veneration; here, however, it is neglected enough. And although it could be worshipped here with great dignity and purity, nevertheless men do so less and more negligently than they ought and are able. For he is our one and greatest Holy of Holies. 

<margin>
Aaron's
rod.
</margin>

The **rod of Aaron**, which budded without moisture and without any cultivation, showed the birth of Christ, whom the pure, holy, and unsullied labor of the Virgin brought forth beyond the laws of nature, without a man. This wondrous Virgin, a miracle of the world, had her figure in the Holy of Holies and is numbered among the Holy of Holies. 

<margin>
Tablets.
</margin>

The **second tablets** in the ark are the Gospel of Christ. For the second tablets prefigured the second law, while the first tablets, which were broken, prefigured the old law, which indeed did not enter into the Holy of Holies. For neither did the old law enter, nor was the true Holy of Holies entered through it; but the New Law both entered, and through it, one enters into the sanctuary itself. 

<margin>
Cherubim.
Mercy
Seat.
</margin>

The **cherubim of glory** above the ark represent the heavenly choirs above whom the Divinity sits and is placed, for they are among the first and highest spirits. That the ark appears below them shows the most kind descent of Christ to us. But indeed, the **mercy seat** <note>original: "propiciatorium"</note>, which likewise represents Christ (for Paul says to the Romans: **“whom God set forth as a propitiation through faith in his blood”** <note>original Greek: "ὃν προέθετο ὁ θεὸς ἱλαστήριον διὰ τῆς πίστεως ἐν τῷ αὐτοῦ αἵματι"</note>), is overshadowed by the cherubim of glory; this shows that Christ, having propitiated the Father, even according to his humanity, leaped over all the heavenly choirs and sits above the cherubim in the glory of the Father. For he is the mercy seat, he is the oracle of God, he is the eternal and ineffable truth through which God speaks to both angels and men. Such things, and many more besides, were shown to the Hebrews in figures, as if in certain sacred elements. O happy were they, if they had possessed eyes to understand the mysteries! But those who think they can have such eyes of their own accord...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the ninth chapter of the Epistle to the Hebrews. Having previously listed the physical objects within the Tabernacle—such as the lampstand and the ark—the author now moves into a symbolic and allegorical interpretation of those objects before quoting the Apostle Paul on the high priest's duties and Christ's fulfillment of them.</meta>

### XIII.

<margin>Hebrews</margin>
He is blind who does not have eyes; and he who recognizes that he is blind, sees, or is at least close to seeing. Therefore, regarding the veneration of the holy vessels: **The Rod of Aaron** represents the birth of Christ. **The Ark** represents the giving of the law. **The Tablets** represent the New Testament. **The Manna** represents the institution of the New Sacrament. **The Mercy Seat** <term>propitiatorium: the gold cover of the Ark, seen as the place where God's mercy is dispensed</term> represents Christ's Assumption and his sitting at the right hand of the Father.

<margin>40</margin>
Having touched upon these matters, let us return to the holy things. Let us learn from the Apostle, who speaks in this way, who they were who entered those places. ¶ **“Now when these things had been thus prepared, the priests always entered into the first tabernacle, performing the duties of the ritual. But into the second, only the high priest entered once a year, not without blood, which he offered for himself and for the people’s sins of ignorance. The Holy Spirit was signifying this: that the way into the Holy of Holies was not yet made manifest while the first tabernacle was still standing. This was a symbol for the present time, in which gifts and sacrifices were offered that could not make the worshiper perfect according to conscience, being concerned only with foods and drinks and various washings and fleshly ordinances, imposed until the time of reformation.”** <note>Hebrews 9:6–10</note> ¶ The priests (as has been said) who continually entered the first tabernacle under the Old Law signified the priests of Christ as long as they perform sacred rites in this world. But the High Priest, who alone entered the second tabernacle—that is, the Holy of Holies—once a year, presented an image of the heavenly High Priest. ¶ The phrase **“not without blood”** was a sign: the supreme heavenly priest, who is Christ the Lord, was not going to enter the Holy of Holies except by first shedding blood, with which he himself entered the heavenly kingdom and the hidden tabernacle. As he entered, the heavenly choirs (according to the prophecy) said in wonder:

> **“Who is this who comes from Edom, with dyed garments from Bozrah, this one who is beautiful in his robes, walking in the greatness of his strength?”** <note>Isaiah 63:1. This passage was traditionally interpreted by medieval and Renaissance theologians as a dialogue describing Christ’s return to heaven after the Crucifixion, his garments stained with his own blood.</note>

To whom he, as he entered, replied:

> **“It is I, who speaks in justice, and am a defender to save.”**

And they asked again:

> **“Why then is your clothing red, and your garments like those of one who treads in the winepress?”**

To whom he answered:

> **“I have trodden the winepress alone, and from the nations there was no man with me.”**

Behold, therefore, how he entered the Holy of Holies not without blood. Indeed, because the victim was sacrificed outside the Holy of Holies, and the blood was first shed outside before the High Priest carried it into the Holy of Holies, it signified that Christ also had to die in this world and shed his own blood outside the Holy of Holies, and then enter it with that same blood once he had taken it up again. But as for the fact that the ancient priest, entering the Holy of Holies, offered blood for his own and the people's ignorance: this "parable" or figurative speech regarding "ignorance" did not apply to Christ, but rather to the time of the ancient rite. Through this, the Holy Spirit indicated that they were ignorant of the true holy things, and the way to them was unknown to those who lived in that time. For first, with the coming of Christ, the way to the true holy things was opened, so that the archetypes <term>archetypa: the original spiritual realities that the physical objects merely copied</term> of the types and the truths of the shadowy figures were made known—things which were unknown while the first tabernacle still stood. By the "first tabernacle" here, I mean the entire ancient Tabernacle; not just the first shadowy holy place, but that which embraced both sections, which Moses first pitched and which Solomon's Temple later represented. As for the discussion of gifts, sacrifices, washings, food, and drink, that belongs to the books of Leviticus and Numbers. These were purifications of the flesh and figures of the spiritual purifications and justifications of the New Law. These were established to last until the "time of emendation" <note>original: "tempus emendationis", often translated as "the time of reformation" or "the time of the new order"</note> and correction. Now, the time of emendation, correction, rectification, and change for the better is the time of Christ's coming, who changed all things for the better—indeed, into the best. For this is what it means to emend and correct. And therefore the Apostle adds:

<margin>41</margin>
¶ **“But Christ, having come as a High Priest of the good things to come, through a greater and more perfect tabernacle not made with hands, that is, not of this creation; not through the blood of goats and calves, but through his own blood, he entered once for all into the Holy Place, having obtained eternal redemption.”** <note>Hebrews 9:11–12</note> ¶ The **“good things to come”** are the truly good and heavenly things. The Tabernacle of Moses and the Temple of Solomon were of "this creation" and human construction. Christ, about to perform our redemption, did not enter those. Rather, he was sacrificed under the heavens, as if under the first holy place placed by the hand of God; and with the blood of the sacrifice, he was elevated above all the heavens, entering the "second" holy place which God alone established. Therefore, by his own blood he entered both holy places: the true holy things which God alone placed. Into the first, he entered once as a victim; into the second, once as High Priest, with the blood of his own sacrifice. And by this one entry into the holy places, he found redemption for all, which would have been impossible to find through the infinite entries of the ancient sacrifices and priests. Behold how he corrected and changed for the best that which was ineffective, weak, and powerless. He is, in truth, both the Victim and the High Priest. They were merely figures. Therefore, he who had the reality to offer ought not to have offered goats, calves, and such figures. He who had the most powerful sacrifice ought not to have offered a weak and feeble one. And how much more powerful the sacrifice of Christ is than the sacrifices of the ancient priests, the blessed Paul shows by an argument he often uses, which is called an argument "from the greater." And he adds:

<margin>42</margin>
¶ **“For if the blood of bulls and goats and the ashes of a heifer...”**

The day will come when he will judge the world. But having entered the holy of holies once for all into the heights, he remains present before the face of God, offering himself as an intercessor for all who are to be saved, until the end of the world. And then, when the number of those to be saved is fulfilled, he will be in glory for all the blessed, just as it is written: **And the city does not need the sun, nor the moon, to shine in it; for the brightness of God shall illuminate it, and its lamp is the Lamb.** <note>A reference to Revelation 21:23.</note> And it is added: **Nothing defiled shall enter it, nor anyone practicing abomination or falsehood, but only those who are written in the Lamb’s book of life.** For it is appointed for men to die corporally but once; nor was it necessary for Christ, the destroyer of death, to die corporally more than once. The particular deaths of men serve as the satisfaction of their obligations; but the universal death of Christ serves for the salvation of all. Particular judgments follow particular deaths; but a universal judgment will follow the universal death of Christ. When he comes for that judgment, the particular transitions of all having been fulfilled, he will be seen in glory by those who await him in holiness, for their perpetual happiness; but by the contaminated, he will be seen for their perpetual judgment and eternal damnation. May we ourselves be able to see him among the number of those who await him without sin, as our judge and glorifier, by his mercy toward us and his help for our infirmity. To him, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, is equal honor, power, and glory, forever and ever. AMEN.

# EXAMINATION of several points regarding the literal text.

<margin>¶</margin> The Vulgate edition: **The first indeed also had.** <margin>¶</margin> It is called "the first." Paul’s interpreter <note>The author refers to the Greek text of the Epistle as "Paul's interpreter."</note>: "Even the first indeed had." <note>Original Greek: εἶχε μὲν καὶ ἡ πρώτη</note> There are also Greek manuscripts that have "the first tabernacle." And then it should be said: "certainly the first tabernacle also had," though some understand it as "the first testament." <margin>¶</margin> The Vulgate edition: **Regulations of worship, and a worldly sanctuary.** <margin>¶</margin> It can be said: "and a mundane sanctuary." Paul’s interpreter: "regulations of worship and the worldly sanctuary." <note>Original Greek: δικαιώματα λατρείας τό τε ἅγιον κοσμικόν</note> <margin>¶</margin> The Vulgate edition: **In which was the golden urn holding the manna, and the rod of Aaron that had budded, and the tablets of the covenant.** <margin>¶</margin> Thus it is in the Greek. But it is better to say "with which" rather than "in which," because of the discrepancy <term>diaphoniam: a disagreement or inconsistency between different scriptural accounts</term> found in what is written about this place. The preposition "with" resolves this, whereas "in" causes a conflict. For it is written in the third book of Kings <note>Known today as 1 Kings 8:9.</note>: "In the ark of the Lord, there was nothing else except the two stone tablets which Moses had placed in it at Horeb, when the Lord made a covenant with the children of Israel." And which preposition Paul used, we do not know; for (sadly) we lack the archetype <note>The original manuscript.</note>. For it was in Hebrew, and we know that the Greek interpreter sometimes used a less appropriate preposition for another (as was also said above). If he did so here, he created an apparent dissonance, which any proper preposition, whatever it might have been, would have removed. Paul’s interpreter: "in which was a golden urn, holding the manna, and the rod of Aaron that budded, and the tablets of the covenant." <note>Original Greek: ἐν ᾗ στάμνος χρυσῆ, ἔχουσα τὸ μάννα, καὶ ἡ ῥάβδος ἀαρὼν ἡ βλαστήσασα καὶ αἱ πλάκες τῆς διαθήκης</note> <margin>¶</margin> The Vulgate edition: **Above which were the Cherubim of glory.** <margin>¶</margin> Rather: "and above it the Cherubim of glory," using the feminine relative, referring to the Ark. Paul’s interpreter: "and above it the Cherubim of glory." <note>Original Greek: ὑπεράνω δὲ αὐτῆς χερουβὶμ δόξης</note> <margin>¶</margin> The Vulgate edition: **It is not now the time to speak of these things one by one.** <margin>¶</margin> That "one by one" means "item by item." Paul’s interpreter: "it is not now the time to speak part by part." <note>Original Greek: οὐκ ἔστι νῦν λέγειν κατὰ μέρος</note> <margin>¶</margin> The Vulgate edition: **Completing the offices of the sacrifices.** <margin>¶</margin> It is a paraphrase that the old interpreter said "offices of the sacrifices" for what is "worship." Paul’s interpreter: "performing the acts of worship." <note>Original Greek: τὰς λατρείας ἐπιτελοῦντες</note> <margin>¶</margin> The Vulgate edition: **For his own and the people’s ignorance.** <margin>¶</margin> It should be said: "for himself, and for the ignorances of the people," in the plural. Paul’s interpreter: "for himself, and for the ignorances of the people." <note>Original Greek: ὑπὲρ ἑαυτοῦ, καὶ τῶν τοῦ λαοῦ ἀγνοημάτων</note> <margin>¶</margin> The Vulgate edition: **Which is a parable of the present time.** <margin>¶</margin> A parable is a likeness; for "I throw alongside" <note>Original Greek: παραβάλλω (paraballō)</note> means to liken or compare. And it should be said that it was established—that is, it existed or was—in the time that was then present, rather than "it is of the present time." For that time of which he speaks, and in which the things set before us were a "parable," reached its end in the sacrifice of Christ, which fulfilled the truth of all sacrifices. But of what were those things a parable? Were they a parable of that time and the things that were being done in that time? By no means. But they were a parable of the things that were to come: better, more perfect, and more complete things which Christ the Lord introduced and fulfilled upon his coming. They were therefore a parable *in* that time, but not *for* that time. For a parable and likeness is a parable and likeness of something truer. But consider: if they were still being performed now, would they not be a likeness? No longer. For they were to be a likeness of the future. Where the truth is present, that likeness perishes. Just as the dawn is a parable and likeness of the day—but of the *coming* day. When the day is present, that likeness perishes. Otherwise, if the dawn persisted, it would be a lying sign; for it is a sign of the future, not of the present. So too the old parables of the Hebrews and the old signs of the ceremonies, if they were performed now, they would be lying signs. For they were signs only of things to come, not of things present. Paul’s interpreter: "which is a parable for the time now present." <note>Original Greek: ἥτις παραβολὴ εἰς τὸν καιρὸν τὸν ἐνεστηκότα</note> <margin>¶</margin> was established. <note>Original Greek: κατέστηκε</note> <margin>¶</margin> The Vulgate edition: **According to which gifts and sacrifices are offered.** <margin>¶</margin> It should be said: "according to which [time]." For the relative pronoun refers to the time, not the parable. But because it has passed, I preferred to say in the past tense, "were offered." Paul’s interpreter: "according to which gifts and sacrifices are offered." <note>Original Greek: καθ' ἣν δῶρά τε καὶ θυσíαι προσφέρονται</note> <margin>¶</margin> The Vulgate edition: **To make the worshiper perfect.** <margin>¶</margin> That "worshiper" signi[fies]...

Nor can he ever appear except without sin. Therefore, the phrase "without sin" can be understood to refer to the following word—namely, to those "expecting" him: thus, "to those expecting him without sin," to whom he himself will appear for salvation. The text is somewhat of a <term>hyperbaton</term> <note>a transposition or inversion of normal word order</note>; therefore, to avoid this transposition, we have restored the words to their proper places according to this understanding. "To all" is redundant. The Greek text of Paul: <term>a second time, without sin, he will appear to those who wait for him, unto salvation</term> <note>original: "ἐκ δευτέρου, χωρὶς ἁμαρτίας, ὀφθήσεται, τοῖς αὐτὸν ἀπεκδεχομένοις, εἰς σωτηρίαν"</note>. It is as if we were saying, <term>a second time, he will appear for salvation to those who wait for him without sin</term> <note>original: "ἐκ δευτέρου. ὀφθήσεται εἰς σωτηρίαν, τοῖς χωρὶς ἁμαρτίας ἀπεκδεχομένοις αὐτὸν"</note>. For both the good and the evil await him; both those who are without sin and those with sin. But only to those who await him without sin will he appear for salvation; to the others, however, he will appear for confusion and eternal vengeance. May the kindness of Jesus the Savior grant us that we may be part of those to whom he will appear for salvation and life.

COMMENTARY.
50

<margin>Judah 128</margin>
The Apostle, deterring us with the madness of our condition and indeed with a powerful dread, says: ¶ **For if we sin willfully** <note>original: "Voluntarie enim peccantibus"</note> **after we have received the knowledge of the truth, there is no longer left a sacrifice for sins, but a certain terrible expectation of judgment and the fury of fire which shall consume the adversaries.** ¶ In the Old Law, as often as one had sinned, they were able to have sacrifices which they might immolate with recent slaughter for the legal expiation of sin. To us, however, there is no sacrifice left to be burned if, after the washing of the dismissal of sins <note>original: "post lauacrum," referring to the waters of Baptism</note>, we willfully fall back into vices. For our victim, once offered, remains forever, never to be immolated afterward, even if a memory of his immolation is continually made. What then? Must sinners despair of pardon? It is not so at all. But the fault is to be dismissed in another way than through the offering of a sacrifice. For this mode of purging is reconciliation through repentance and confession. For the Lord says that there will be such joy in heaven over one sinner doing penance as over ninety-nine just who do not need penance. And again: *If your brother sins against you, rebuke him; and if he repents, forgive him. And if he sins against you seven times, and seven times in a day turns back to you, saying "I repent," forgive him.* And to Peter asking, *Lord, how often shall my brother sin against me and I forgive him, up to seven times?* the merciful Lord answered: *I do not say to you up to seven times, but up to seventy times seven.* For which converted sinner would the heart not melt from the abyss of God's mercy? But concerning the sinner who is proud and a contemner of the Church and the power of the priests, he says: *But if he will not hear the Church, let him be to you as a heathen and a tax collector. Amen I say to you, whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven.* <insert><unclear>scribble</unclear> Here therefore</insert>
<margin>50</margin>
is the mode, if sins occur after baptism: the purging is through repentance and confession (*tell it to the Church*, he says) and priestly loosening, which is now called absolution. *Whatever (he says) you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven.* But it is not through the offering of a sacrifice; if you have sinned, no matter how great a sacrifice you offer in remuneration, unless you repent and confess, it profits you nothing, nor is the sin dismissed. Although it is not remitted except in that unique offering of Christ, by which he most fully satisfied for all the sins of the world—those which have been, those which are, and those which are to be. For the priestly offering of the sacrifice is a memory (as has been said) of that all-saving and all-salutary immolation of Christ on the cross, and an act of thanksgiving. Moreover, the receiving <note>the Eucharist</note> is the highest consummation in this mortal life, a union with the divine, and intimate comfort. But illumination and purging precede this consummation, both in heaven and on earth. Therefore, he who approaches this sublime mystery—which in this world is the consummation of all consummations—without being illuminated and purged, offers blind and sick eyes to so great a light, only to suffer more grievously therefrom, aggravating the wounds of his sins, perverting the order of sanctifications, and committing yourself, all too unworthy, into the holy mysteries. Therefore, let everyone strive to have illuminated eyes, and he will attain purging from the <term>mercy</term> <note>original: "mīa," a common abbreviation for "misericordia"</note> of God. For he is of the number of those for whom and by whom the sacred oracle sings that mercy is not to be taken away. For he is among the sons of Christ, of whom the divine word says: *But if his children forsake my law and walk not in my judgments; if they profane my justices and keep not my commandments, I will visit their iniquities with a rod and their sins with stripes. But my mercy I will not take away from him.* Therefore, Christ always has mercy and grace for us whenever we have sinned, and a place is left for repentance and the expiation of sins, as was also shown in the sixth chapter of this work; and the manner of it is manifested both here and there, which the Church has rightly understood through the Holy Spirit. Nevertheless, let it be that we sin as rarely as possible, and least of all willfully. <term>Because</term> <note>original: "Qz," abbreviation for "Quia"</note> if we despise the known truth, which is the true and immaculate law of Christ, and such riches of the kindness and mercies of God toward us, what remains for us but a certain most certain and terrible expectation of judgment, and the zeal of fire which is to devour us—which may the piety and mercy of Christ avert. For zeal adds sharpness; just as one who punishes in zeal does so more sharply and with greater fury, so also that eternal fire, which avenges the contempt of God, avenges both with zeal and (so to speak) with a raging sharpness. And the Apostle sufficiently indicated this terrible and formidable expectation, spoken for sinners who despise, but not for those who turn themselves to the asylum of
<margin>51</margin>
mercy, by comparing the contemners of the Old Law to these, using an argument from the greater <note>an argument "a fortiori"</note> to confirm his saying, and saying: ¶ **A man making void the law of Moses dies without any mercy under two or three witnesses. How much more punishment do you think he deserves who has trodden under foot the Son of God, and has esteemed the blood of the testament as common by which he was sanctified, and has offered an affront to the Spirit of grace?** For we know him who says: *Vengeance is mine, I will repay.* And again: *The Lord shall judge his people.* And *it is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.* ¶ They clearly despised the law of Moses who worshipped idols, or preferred to follow the laws of the nations in contempt of it; concerning whom we read thus in Deuteronomy: *When there shall be found among you, within one of your gates which the Lord your God will give you, a man or a woman who does evil in the sight of the Lord your God and transgresses his covenant, so that they go...*

# XIII. 252 Hebrews.

...they give themselves and serve foreign gods, and adore them—the sun, and the moon, and all the host of heaven—which I did not command. And if this is reported to you, and hearing it you investigate diligently and find it to be true, and that such an abomination has been committed in Israel: you shall lead out the man or woman who committed this most wicked thing to the gates of your city, and they shall be overwhelmed with stones. By the mouth of two or three witnesses, he who is to be killed shall perish. Behold how those who turned away and were despisers died under the Old Law based on two or three witnesses: by a much more bitter punishment will those perish who, spurning the New Law, voluntarily surrender themselves to every sin, just as the New Law is holier and more venerable than the old. Those who consider the blood of Christ, in which they were sanctified, as if it were common—not better, holier, or more powerful than others, but like any other ineffective, defiled, and unholy thing: how do they not offer an insult to the Holy Spirit, when they defile His most radiant grace and drag it through every mire of filthiness? Those whom the love of God does not draw, and whom His benefits do not capture, should at least be deterred by punishment. For they know, or ought to know, what is written in Deuteronomy: *Vengeance is mine: and I will repay in time.* The day of perdition is near, and the times hasten to arrive. *The Lord will judge his people, and will be comforted in his servants.* And again: *A fire is kindled in my fury, and it shall burn even to the lowest hell.* And there is no one who can rescue from my hand. From this it is easy to understand how fearful and dread-inspiring it is to fall into the hand of the Lord. For two hands of the Lord are proposed: the left and the right. The left is justice. And the right is mercy. Those who fall into the right hand are blessed; those into the left would have been more fortunate if they had never been born. And there is no one who can rescue from one or the other; and it is impossible for anyone not to fall into either this one or that one. Therefore, it is the same to say "it is fearful to fall into the hands of the Lord" and "into the hand of the Lord." For that is understood regarding the left hand, and the plural number is used in place of the singular. But to fall into the right hand is not fearful, but most to be desired and beyond choice. Accordingly, when David answered the prophet Gad, he said: *it is better that I fall into the hands of the Lord* <note>original: "melius est vt incidā in manus dñi"</note>; he spoke for both, not understanding only the left. This is also understood from his words when he spoke in this way: *it is better that I fall into the hands of the Lord (for his mercies are many) than into the hands of men.* For what he added regarding the multitude of mercies pertained to the right hand. Thus, he was committing himself to both His mercy and His justice. May Christ the Lord grant us to live so that we may fall into the right hand of God, at which He Himself sits, and escape the fearful left hand of judgment. And how are we, who are Christ’s and on His side at the right, transferred to the left? Let us remember our washing <note>referring to Baptism</note>, our faith, and our first sanctification; let us not be moved from that place by either prosperity or adversity. For without a doubt, 

<margin>52</margin> we are placed at the right hand of God with Christ. The Apostle exhorts the Hebrews to this consideration, so that they do not transfer themselves but always retain their former constancy, saying: ¶ **But call to mind the former days, in which, being illuminated, you endured a great conflict of sufferings. In this, indeed, you were made a public spectacle by reproaches and tribulations; and in that, you became companions of those who were treated in such a way. For you also had compassion on my chains, and you took the plundering of your goods with joy, knowing that you have a better and lasting substance in heaven. Do not, therefore, cast away your confidence, which has a great reward. For you have need of patience, that, doing the will of God, you may receive the promise. For yet a little while, and he who is coming will come, and will not delay. But the just man shall live by faith; but if he withdraws himself, my soul shall not be well pleased in him. But we are not of those who withdraw unto perdition, but of faith unto the acquisition of the soul.** ¶ This is a pious and vehement exhortation. For without a doubt, as long as the illuminated Hebrews—illuminated, I say, by faith—endured the conflicts of suffering for the love of Him, having been made a public spectacle by reproaches and pressures, as associates and sharers with those who were so afflicted for the righteousness of faith, sympathizing with the pressures of others, and thinking nothing of the plundering of their own goods—indeed, rejoicing in the contemplation of the eternal goods they expected from faith—for so long they were at the right hand of God. And what those who are in the right hand of God in this way need, the Apostle, the discloser of the divine will, shows. For to those who retain faith and love, only patience is needed, lest they be broken in such hardships and fail to persevere. Because if they persevere with patience as their driver, they will most certainly receive the promise—that is, the gift of the good will of God, which is eternal life and everlasting joy. Nor is long patience needed. For the life of each person is short; if you compare it to the eternity that follows it, it is even less than a point. Therefore, at the end of this momentary life, Christ will come, and the promise of life will be fulfilled for the faithful. The Apostle confirms this with the oracle of the prophet Habakkuk, which we now read thus: *It will appear at the end, and it will not lie. If it makes a delay, wait for it: because coming it will come, and it will not delay. Behold, he who is incredulous, his soul will not be right in himself; but the just man shall live in his faith.* Where it says *it will appear at the end*, it sounds like *yet a little while*. And to that which says *behold, he who is incredulous, his soul will not be right in himself*, it corresponds to Paul's interpretation: *but if he withdraws himself, my soul shall not be well pleased in him.* Therefore, it is the same thing to "withdraw oneself" as to be "incredulous." For he who is incredulous...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Epistle to the Hebrews, transitioning from the warnings of Chapter 10 to the famous "Hall of Faith" in Chapter 11. The author explores the nature of faith as superior to human reason and begins a chronological survey of Old Testament figures who lived by faith.</meta>

->COMMENTARY<-

Lord, increase our faith <note>original: "domine adauge nobis fidem"</note>, because human reason does not reach it; instead, grace—which is superior to reason—provides it. And what reason provides is obscure and weak, but what grace provides is lucid and strong. He who is truly trusting and faithful commits himself to God, not to the truth of his own logic; he relies on divine truth, not on the limited possibilities of his own imagination. He dwells in a spacious place, not a narrow one. He who refuses to go beyond the possibilities of his own reason shuts himself in narrow straits and in a dark prison, where the sun of grace does not shine and life-giving faith is not contained. O divine faith, wondrous foundation of life, support of hope, and anchor of love! You are a shining rope extended from heaven; by grasping it, we climb to Him who surpasses every height. But now, let us hear the praises of faith from the most blessed Apostle <note>The "Apostle" refers to Paul, traditionally considered the author of Hebrews.</note>.

<margin>54 1</margin>
The first praise is this: by faith, we recognize the true causes and the true origins of things, and understand that all things came forth from nothing by the word of God, bursting forth into a new beginning. This is what he adds, saying:
> ¶ By faith: we understand that the worlds were perfected by the word of God, so that from things not apparent, the things which are seen were made.

¶ Moses believed God when he revealed the genesis <note>The Greek term for "origin" or "beginning," and the title of the first book of the Bible.</note> of the world: how in the beginning He created the heaven and the earth. And He said "Let there be light," and light was made. He said "Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters," and the firmament was made. And so with the rest; it is established from the sacred history of Genesis that they were created by the word of God. By faith, therefore, we know these things which the philosophers could not know. For they proceeded by a narrow and incapable path of reason, not the spacious, lucid path of faith flashing from heaven. Nor could they know it of themselves, for that ray of light is not within our power.

<margin>2</margin>
The second praise of faith: 
<margin>55</margin>
by faith, worship is offered that is pleasing and acceptable to God. The example is Abel, which the Apostle subjoins:
> ¶ By faith: Abel offered a more abundant sacrifice to God than Cain, through which he obtained testimony that he was righteous, God bearing witness over his gifts. And through faith, though he is dead, he still speaks.

¶ That Abel offered to the Lord more precious things because of what he believed is testified by the sacred history of Genesis, saying: *And it came to pass after many days that Cain offered gifts to the Lord from the fruits of the earth. Abel also offered from the firstborn of his flock and from their fat. And the Lord looked upon Abel and his gifts, but toward Cain and his gifts He did not look.* His testimony as a righteous man was attested by our Savior. "Behold," He says, "I send to you prophets, and wise men, and scribes: and some of them you will kill and crucify, and some you will scourge in your synagogues, and persecute from city to city. That upon you may come all the righteous blood shed upon the earth, from the blood of Abel the just, even to the blood of Zechariah son of Barachiah." <note>A reference to Matthew 23:34-35.</note> And that speech of the dead Abel is understood from this passage in Genesis where God speaks to the fratricide <note>One who kills his brother.</note> Cain: "What have you done? The voice of your brother’s blood cries to me from the earth."

<margin>56 3</margin>
The third: by faith, leaving the earth behind, we are transferred to eternal kingdoms. The example is Enoch, which Paul adds:
> ¶ By faith: Enoch was translated <note>Taken up to heaven without dying.</note> so that he should not see death. And he was not found, because God translated him. For before his translation, he received testimony that he pleased God. But without faith, it is impossible to please Him. For he who comes to God must believe that He exists, and that He is a rewarder of those who seek Him.

¶ Concerning Enoch, we read in Genesis: *Enoch walked with God after he fathered Methuselah for three hundred years. He fathered sons and daughters, and all the days of Enoch were three hundred sixty-five years. And he walked with God, and he did not appear, because God took him.* And as for the opinion the Hebrews held regarding Enoch, Jesus Sirach <note>The author of the book of Ecclesiasticus.</note> reveals it: "Enoch," he says, "pleased God, and was translated into paradise." And in another place: <margin>4</margin> "No one was born on earth like Enoch, for he himself was taken up from the earth." The fourth:
<margin>57</margin>
by faith, we avoid coming evils by which the wicked are destroyed forever, and we claim a salvation without end. The example is Noah, faithful and righteous. Of him, the Apostle continues:
> ¶ By faith: Noah received an answer concerning those things which were not yet seen. Moved by fear, he prepared an ark for the salvation of his family, through which he condemned the world, and was made heir of the righteousness which is by faith.

¶ The story of Noah is searched out from Genesis, in which we read: *But Noah found grace before the Lord.* And, *For I have seen you to be righteous before me in this generation.* And God gave one hundred and twenty years to those who lived in that time for repentance, if they had wished to come to their senses. During those years, they even saw the ark being built, by which they themselves were condemned for their unbelief. Seeing and hearing, they by no means believed, nor did they recover from their madness. But Noah and his family believed. For if he had not believed, he would not have prepared the ark and completed every preparation as he had been commanded with all diligence, before any traces of the waters appeared. <margin>5</margin> The fifth: By faith, we recognize that this world is a place of our pilgrimage, and that heaven is our region and the city proper to us toward which we must 
<margin>58</margin>
travel. The figures and examples are: Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. This the divinely-inspired Paul also adds, saying:
> ¶ By faith: he who is called Abraham obeyed to go out into the place which he was to receive as an inheritance. And he went out, not knowing where he was going. By faith, he was a stranger in the land of promise as in a foreign land. He dwelt in tents with Isaac and Jacob, co-heirs of the same promise. For he was waiting for a city having foundations, whose architect and builder is God.

¶ Regarding Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, the history from Genesis is more widely known than can be...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the "Hall of Faith" in Hebrews 11. The previous page discussed the creation of the world by the Word of God and the faith of the early patriarchs. This page focuses on Sarah's faith in conceiving Isaac and Abraham's ultimate test in offering Isaac as a sacrifice.</meta>

# HEBREWS 14 <note>While this text comments on Hebrews chapter 11, the header likely refers to the fourteenth section or "lection" of this specific commentary series.</note>

...it is necessary to cite testimony, for they were figures <note>A "figure" (or "type") is a person or event in the Old Testament believed to foreshadow something in the New Testament.</note> of all the faithful; and the land promised to them was a figure of the celestial habitation. Their pilgrimage was a figure showing that this present life is nothing but a certain pilgrimage toward seeking the future city, which was fabricated not by the hands of men but by the hands of God. Oh, how beautiful and delightful is that city which was constructed by the hands of the Fabricator of all things! For if those things made by the hands of men—which are ultimately nothing—delight us with their beauty and are desirable, how much more so is that city?

<margin>6</margin>**Sixth.** By Faith: we attain the blessing of God and the fruitfulness of every good harvest.
<margin>59</margin>Example: Sarah. This is what Paul subjoins, saying:
¶ By faith also: Sarah herself received the power of succession among women, and even against the timing of her age, she conceived, because she considered him faithful who had promised. Therefore, from one man—and him as good as dead—there were born descendants as numerous as the stars of heaven and as the innumerable grains of sand by the seashore. All these died according to faith, not having received the promises, but seeing and greeting them from afar. And they confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth. For those who say such things indicate that they are seeking a fatherland. And if indeed they had been mindful of that land from which they went out, they would certainly have had time to return; but now they desire a better one—that is, a heavenly one. Therefore, God is not ashamed of them when he is called their God, for he has prepared a city for them.

¶ When Sarah heard the angel saying to Abraham, "I will surely return to you at this time next year, and Sarah your wife shall have a son," she laughed. She knew that at the usual time of conception she had been sterile, and now she was an old woman, for whom the monthly custom of women had ceased, without which women are necessarily unfruitful and sterile. For this reason, she no longer admitted the touch of a man. She laughed, I say, and did not fully offer her faith to the angel, for she believed him to be merely a man. Truly, when she understood the promise of God—from whom nothing remains hidden in secret, and who caught her laughing in private and laid bare the secrets of her heart—and when she recognized the stupendous vengeance upon the cities of Sodom and the liberation of Lot performed by that same one, she understood it was the promise not of a man, but of God. She believed most fully that nothing was difficult for Him, and that she would conceive according to the promise. If she had not believed, the Apostle would not have added "because she considered him faithful who promised." Therefore, those who say that only Abraham believed and not Sarah are not to be heard, as if it follows that because she laughed behind the door of the tent, she therefore did not believe. For Abraham was faithful, and Sarah was faithful. Those who were born from one man—namely Abraham—are children of Abraham not only according to the flesh, but also those according to faith, in whom the promises were fulfilled after Abraham's death and are fulfilled daily. As long as they live in this world, they imitate their faithful father: they live as pilgrims and travelers, providing for food and clothing and being content with the necessities of life, panting with the whole desire of the soul for the supernal city as the destination of this life's pilgrimage.

<margin>7</margin>**Seventh.** By Faith: we transcend nature, and we recognize that things impossible for it are possible.
<margin>60</margin>Example: the sacrifice of Isaac. From him, Abraham nonetheless expected a seed without doubt, in whom all the tribes of the earth would be blessed. This is what the Apostle adds, saying:
¶ By faith: Abraham offered up Isaac when he was tested, and he who had received the promises offered up his only-begotten son, of whom it was said: "In Isaac shall your seed be called." He reckoned that God is powerful enough to raise even from the dead, from which he also received him in a figure <note>original: "in similitudine"</note>.

¶ The history of the sacrifice of Isaac is made manifest in the twenty-second chapter of Genesis. And what is said, "when Abraham was tested," means when he was tested in faith: whether he would doubt the promise of God, which seemed impossible given the death of Isaac. But he held fast to a firm faith like an anchor, nor did he waver, vacillate, or doubt in any way. He believed that even if he sacrificed his only-begotten Isaac, God would raise up a seed from him in whom He would fulfill the promises of blessing, and that God was able to restore the sacrificed one back to life from death. Whence also Abraham received him in a figure. But you will ask: in what figure? Certainly in the figure of both dying and rising again. For what is read in Genesis—that God said to Abraham: "Take your only-begotten son whom you love, Isaac, and go into the Land of Vision <note>original: "terram visionis"</note>, and offer him there as a holocaust upon one of the mountains which I shall show you"—foreshadowed Christ the Lord. The only-begotten son whom Abraham loved, Isaac, figured the only-begotten Son whom the Father loves, Christ the Lord. **The Land of Vision:** Jerusalem, which is also the "Vision of Peace" <note>This is a traditional etymology of the name Jerusalem (Yerushalayim).</note>. **The Mountain Shown:** the place of Calvary. The commanded sacrifice of Isaac figured the true sacrifice of Christ. The receiving of Isaac alive after the commanded sacrifice figured the true resurrection of Christ. Isaac is led to be sacrificed, because Christ is captured at night. Abraham carries the fire and the sword, because Christ is led to his sacrifice with lanterns, torches, and weapons for our sake. Again, the Scripture says: "He also took the wood for the holocaust and placed it upon Isaac his son," because Christ also went out carrying his own cross to the place which is called Calvary. Abraham bound Isaac his son and placed him on the altar upon the pile of wood, because Christ the Lord was to be bound and placed upon the cross to be sacrificed on Mount Calvary. And how did the Jews not recognize the true Isaac and his true sacrifice, they who are so accustomed to glory in the image and so much in the shadow...

# COMMENTARY

...prepared to do with Isaac by his sacrifice; thus Isaac is a likeness and a figure <note>A "figure" or "type" is a person or event in the Old Testament seen as a foreshadowing of Jesus Christ.</note> of Christ, who by his passion reconciled the world to God. As it is written in the book among the Hebrews called *The Ark of the Covenant*, if there had not been the offering of Isaac, no one could have obtained a hearing from God, so inexorable would the rigor of justice have been. This is true not of the offering of the shadowy <note>original: "vmbratilis" - referring to the Old Testament "shadows" of things to come.</note> Isaac, but of Him of whom this is a parable, and of whom Isaac was a likeness. For indeed, the rigor of divine justice would have remained inflexible unless there had been the offering of Christ, in which all things are reconciled, and all confidence of being heard has been placed for us in the most blessed passion of Christ.

<margin>s</margin>
<margin>61</margin>
<margin>8</margin>
¶ **Eighth.** By faith: we receive a blessing from God not only of present goods but also of future things which are eternal. Example: the blessing of Isaac upon Jacob and Esau, and likewise the blessing of Jacob upon the sons of Joseph. The Apostle <note>Referring to St. Paul, traditionally considered the author of Hebrews.</note> testifies to this in this manner, saying: ¶ **By faith: Isaac blessed Jacob and Esau concerning future things. By faith: Jacob, when dying, blessed each of the sons of Joseph, and worshipped, leaning on the top of his staff.** (This is the blessing with which Isaac blessed his son Jacob:

> May God give you of the dew of heaven, and of the richness of the earth, an abundance of grain and wine; and let peoples serve you, and tribes worship you. Be lord over your brothers, and let your mother’s sons bow down before you. Whoever curses you shall be cursed, and whoever blesses you shall be filled with blessings. <note>Genesis 27:28–29</note>

But for Esau, this was the blessing:

> In the richness of the earth and in the dew of heaven from above shall your blessing be. You shall live by the sword and serve your brother. And the time will come when you shall shake off and loosen his yoke from your neck. <note>Genesis 27:39–40</note>

This was fulfilled when the Gentiles <note>The non-Jewish nations.</note> received in Christ—not only from Esau, but from wherever they came—true liberty and the blessing of future goods as firstborn sons of God. Jacob also blessed the sons of Joseph with crossed arms—that is, in the form of a cross. He also worshipped the Lord at the top of his staff. What did the crossed arms show if not the cross of Christ, from which every blessing has been poured out upon us? What was the worship at the top of the wood or his staff—or at the top of the wood that was the headboard of the bed in which he lay—if not that the Lord was to be sought on the wood <note>The "wood" refers to the wood of the Cross.</note> and truly worshipped upon the wood? One who has the heart for it may seek this blessing and these mysteries in the 47th and 48th chapters of Genesis.)

<margin>62</margin>
<margin>9</margin>
**Ninth.** By faith: future things are known as if they were present. Example: Joseph’s command concerning the carrying back of his bones to the land of promise. Paul adds this, saying:
<margin>saying</margin>
¶ **By faith: Joseph, at the end of his life, made mention of the departure of the children of Israel and gave a command concerning his bones.** Near the end of Genesis, Joseph is introduced speaking thus to his brothers:

> After my death God will visit you, and he will make you go up from this land to the land which he swore to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. <note>Genesis 50:24</note>

And when he had adjured them, saying, "God will visit you, carry my bones with you from this place," he died. What is the calling back of the children of Israel to the promised land if not the calling of the faithful, after the harsh exile of this present life, into the kingdom of the blessed? Why did Joseph want his bones to be carried into the holy land, if not because our bones and bodies, which we have carried about in the land of our pilgrimage, are finally to enter into the land of the living, the region of the saints?

<margin>63</margin>
<margin>10</margin>
**Tenth.** By faith: we are liberated from the prince of the tyranny of this world, and in this world. Example: Moses liberated from the tyranny of Pharaoh. Paul hints at this, saying:
<margin>saying</margin>
¶ **By faith: Moses, when he was born, was hidden for three months by his parents, because they saw he was an elegant child, and they did not fear the king’s edict.** For Pharaoh had made an edict that whatever Hebrew of the male sex was born should be thrown into the river. But the parents of Moses kept the infant for three months; and when they no longer dared to hide him, they exposed him to the river in a basket of papyrus smeared with slime and pitch, having faith in God that He would save him. This was indeed done, as the sacred history of Exodus contains. And it is marvelous that the beginnings of the birth of Moses were similar to the birth of Christ; read according to the *Antiquities* of Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, a 1st-century Jewish historian.</note>. It was announced by an angel to Amram the father that Moses would liberate his people from the servitude of the Egyptians. Christ, however, was announced to Joseph, to whom the angel said:

> Joseph (he said), son of David, do not fear to take Mary as your wife. For that which is born in her is of the Holy Spirit. She shall bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus; for he shall save his people from their sins. <note>Matthew 1:20–21</note>

The mother of Moses felt almost no pains in childbirth (according to Josephus). The Virgin Mother of Christ, however, gave birth without pain. Moses was laid in a papyrus basket; Christ in a manger. The sacred scribe indicates to Pharaoh concerning the future birth of Moses, who would humble his kingdom; the chief priests and the scribes of the people indicate to Herod where Christ was to be born. Pharaoh issues an edict that every Hebrew male born from that time should be killed; Herod orders that all the boys in Bethlehem and in all its borders, from two years old and under, should be killed. The three-month-old Moses, for fear of persecutors, was exposed by night and saved by Thermuthis, the daughter of Pharaoh. And the infant Christ, by flight at night, was snatched from death and saved in Egypt. Moses had a nursing mother; Christ a nursing father. For Moses, no milk flowed except that of his own mother; for Christ, none but the milk of his virgin parent. That man, when he grew up, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter. Christ...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Epistle to the Hebrews, specifically chapter 11, moving from the patriarchs to the life of Moses as a "type" or foreshadowing of Jesus Christ, and interpreting the liberation of the Israelites as a symbol of spiritual salvation.</meta>

# XIV Hebrews

...Christ, however, did not say "I am the son of Joseph," but always named his Father who is in heaven. And so great was the harmony, conspiracy, and similarity between Moses and Christ—though the former was the shadow and the latter the truth <note>The author uses "shadow" (original: *umbra*) to mean a symbolic precursor and "truth" (original: *veritas*) to mean the spiritual reality fulfilled in Jesus.</note>—that the Lord said to Moses concerning him: *I will raise up for them a prophet from among their brothers, like you; and I will put my words in his mouth, and he shall speak to them all that I command him.* Thus even the Hebrews, if they had eyes to see, could not have been ignorant of him, given the likeness to Moses or his very origins. For Moses came in likeness, but Christ came in truth.

<margin>rr</margin>
**Eleventh**, by faith: we trample upon the world and its delights, valuing reproaches and passions in imitation of Christ more than the riches of the entire world, knowing him who said: *Blessed are you when men revile you, and persecute you, and say all kinds of evil against you falsely for my sake. Rejoice and be glad, for your reward is great in heaven.* An example: Moses, despising the glory and delights of the Egyptians, who had even been adopted as the son of Pharaoh's daughter. To which Paul adds, saying:

<margin>64</margin>
¶ **By faith: Moses, when he was grown up, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter, choosing rather to be mistreated with the people of God than to enjoy the fleeting pleasures of sin, considering the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures of Egypt; for he looked toward the reward.** ¶ For Moses preferred, in the likeness of Christ, to suffer reproach for the sake of liberating his own nation rather than to possess the kingdom and wealth of the Egyptians. For indeed, Moses came in the figure and likeness of Christ to deliver the Hebrew people from the prince of Egypt; Christ came in truth to deliver the world from the prince of the world's darkness.

<margin>12</margin>
**Twelfth**, by faith: not only are we delivered from the prince of the world's darkness, but we are made superior and more powerful than such a prince of this world. Example: Moses was made superior to Pharaoh. But this also demonstrated that, once the prince of this world was defeated, Christ led us into salvation. For Moses is the figure of Christ, and the Hebrew people are the figure of all the faithful who, following Christ, find life and salvation. Therefore, the Apostle adds:

<margin>65</margin>
¶ **By faith: he left Egypt, not fearing the fury of the king. For he endured as if seeing him who is invisible.** ¶ For Moses endured all things by faith, as if he beheld him who cannot be seen always present, and held him constantly before his eyes. And from Exodus chapter 12, the departure of Moses from Egypt is known.

<margin>13</margin>
**Thirteenth**, by faith: we are delivered from the striking angel <note>Referring to the Angel of Death in the final plague of Egypt.</note> on account of the guilt of our first parent, Adam; we are delivered, I say, through the sacrifice of Christ, who is the truth of the Paschal Lamb. Example: the celebration of the Passover by Moses.

<margin>66</margin>
¶ Which Paul also adds, saying: ¶ **By faith: he kept the Passover and the sprinkling of blood, so that the one who destroyed the firstborn might not touch them.** ¶ This was the last and worst plague of the Egyptians; just as the death of sinners by the devil is the worst death and the final punishment, which no one escapes except through the death and blood of Christ. Concerning this plague, it is written in Exodus: *At midnight I will go out, and every firstborn in the land of the Egyptians shall die, from the firstborn of Pharaoh who sits on his throne to the firstborn of the servant girl who is at the mill, and all the firstborn of the livestock. There shall be a great cry in all the land of Egypt, such as there has never been before nor ever shall be again.* In the first Adam, not only the firstborn but also those born later would have died, had they not been sanctified in the second Adam <note>The "Second Adam" is a common theological title for Jesus, contrasting his life-giving grace with the original sin of the first Adam.</note>, the firstborn of the virginal womb. For he himself, the same first and second, the only-begotten and the firstborn, sanctified all things.

<margin>14</margin>
**Fourteenth**, by faith: through the <term>laver of regeneration</term> <note>A traditional term for Baptism, referring to it as a spiritual washing and rebirth.</note>, we shatter all the power of the opposing forces.

<margin>67</margin>

## COMMENTARY

...shadowy sacrifice of Isaac; thus Isaac was a likeness and figure of Christ: who by his passion reconciled the world to God. As it is written in the book among the Hebrews called the *Ark of the Covenant* <note>original: "arca fœderis". This likely refers to a specific Jewish commentary or traditional text known to the author</note>, had it not been for the offering of Isaac, no one would have been able to obtain a hearing from God, so inexorable would have been the rigor of justice. This is true not merely regarding the offering of the symbolic Isaac, but of him for whom this parable exists; for indeed the rigor of divine justice would have remained inflexible had it not been for the offering of Christ, in whom all things are reconciled, and all confidence of being heard is placed for us in the most blessed passion of Christ.

<margin>61</margin> <margin>8</margin> **Eighth.** By faith: we receive a blessing from God not only of present goods but also of future goods which are eternal. An example: the blessing of Isaac upon Jacob and Esau, and likewise the blessing of Jacob upon the sons of Joseph. The Apostle testifies to this in this manner, saying:
<margin>¶ Faith:</margin> By faith: Isaac blessed Jacob and Esau concerning future things. By faith: Jacob, when dying, blessed each of the sons of Joseph, and worshipped at the top of his staff. This is the blessing with which Isaac blessed his son Jacob:
> May God give you of the dew of heaven, and of the fatness of the earth, an abundance of grain and wine, and let peoples serve you, and tribes bow down to you. Be lord over your brothers, and let your mother’s sons bow down before you. Cursed be everyone who curses you, and may he who blesses you be filled with blessings.
But for Esau, this was the blessing:
> In the fatness of the earth, and in the dew of heaven from above, shall your blessing be. You shall live by the sword, and you shall serve your brother; and the time will come when you shall shake off and loose his yoke from your neck.
This was fulfilled when the Gentiles received in Christ—not only from Esau, but from wherever they came—true liberty and the blessing of future goods through the firstborn Son of God. Jacob also blessed the sons of Joseph with crossed arms; that is, in the form of a cross. He also worshipped the Lord at the top of his staff. What did the crossed arms show, if not the cross of Christ, from which every blessing is poured out upon us? What was the worship at the top of the wood, or his staff, or at the head of the bed where he lay <note>The author is reconciling the different translations of Genesis 47:31 and Hebrews 11:21, where the Hebrew word can mean "staff" or "bed"</note>, if not that the Lord was to be sought on the wood [of the cross], and truly worshipped upon the wood? He who wishes may seek this blessing and these mysteries in the 47th and 48th chapters of Genesis.

<margin>62</margin> <margin>9</margin> **Ninth.** By faith: future things are known as if they are present. An example: Joseph’s command concerning the carrying back of his bones into the land of promise. To which Paul adds, saying:
<margin>¶ Faith:</margin> By faith: Joseph, at the end of his life, made mention of the exodus of the children of Israel and gave a command concerning his bones. Near the end of Genesis, Joseph is thus introduced speaking to his brothers:
> After my death God will visit you: and he will make you go up from this land to the land which he swore to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
And when he had made them swear, saying, "God will visit you, carry my bones with you from this place," he died. What is the calling back of the children of Israel into the land of promise, if not the calling of the faithful, after the harsh exile of this present life, into the kingdom of the blessed? Why did Joseph want his bones carried into the holy land, if not because our bones and bodies, which we have carried about in the land of our pilgrimage, are finally to enter into the land of the living, the region of the saints?

<margin>63</margin> <margin>10** **Tenth.** By faith: we are liberated from the prince of the tyranny of this world, and in this world. An example: Moses liberated from the tyranny of Pharaoh. Paul hints at this, saying:
<margin>¶ Faith:</margin> By faith: Moses, when he was born, was hidden for three months by his parents, because they saw he was an elegant child, and they did not fear the king’s edict. For Pharaoh had made an edict that whatever male born to the Hebrews should be thrown into the river. However, the parents of Moses kept the infant for three months, and when they no longer dared to hide him, they exposed him to the river in a basket of papyrus smeared with slime and pitch, having faith in God that he would save him. This indeed happened, as the sacred history of Exodus contains. And it is marvelous that the beginnings of the birth of Moses were similar to the birth of Christ. Read according to the *Antiquities* of Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, a 1st-century Jewish historian whose works were often used by Christians to supplement biblical accounts</note>:
It was announced to Amram, the father, by an angel that Moses would deliver his people from the servitude of the Egyptians. Christ, however, was announced to Joseph, to whom the angel said:
> Joseph (he said), son of David: do not fear to take Mary as your wife. For that which is born in her is of the Holy Spirit; she shall bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus. For he shall save his people from their sins.
The mother of Moses felt almost no pain (according to Josephus) in childbirth. The Virgin Mother of Christ gave birth without pain. Moses was laid in a papyrus basket. Christ: in a manger. The sacred scribe indicates to Pharaoh concerning the future birth of Moses, who would humble his kingdom. The chief priests and scribes of the people indicated to Herod where Christ was to be born. Pharaoh issued an edict that every Hebrew male born from that time should be killed. Herod: that all the boys in Bethlehem and in all its borders, from two years old and under, should be killed. The three-month-old Moses, due to fear of persecutors, was exposed at night and saved by Thermuthis, the daughter of Pharaoh. And the infant Christ, by night, was snatched from death by flight and saved in Egypt. Moses had a nursing mother. Christ: a nursing father <note>original: "nutritiū patrē" - referring to Joseph as the foster-father</note>. For Moses, no milk flowed except from his own mother. For Christ, none but the milk of his virgin parent. When he grew up, the former refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter. Christ...

COM.
<meta>catchword: tes:</meta>

For this reason, the Apostle used such diligent effort in his encouragement: to hold their souls steady in the faith, showing that they had so far endured much less than was appropriate. For they had not yet resisted sin to the point of death. But even in death itself, one must not give way. He comforts them using the Proverbs of Solomon, and raises their wavering hopes through the testimonies of the Scriptures. From the evidence of their circumstances, he leads them to a true understanding of divine love; instead of being discouraged by the lashes and punishments they received, he uses these very things to lift their spirits. The Lord disciplines even His obedient sons so that they may be conformed to the one into whom they were adopted, bearing the mark of a true son within themselves. He disciplines them so that they may be purer and holier. For good gold is not made worse by fire, but purer; and that which is bad is purified and made good. In the same way, divine corrections—if they are endured with a great soul and as they ought to be—make the good purer and holier, while they purify and mend the wicked, eventually leaving them good. And if they are sorrowful in this world, the fruit that is to come in the future is nevertheless great. Therefore, these trials should be received with great joy and thanksgiving when they are sent, and one must pray that God uses them for the salvation of those being corrected, and that they may endure them to gain knowledge of God and to fulfill His will. For this, one must again pray to God to help their patience and grant them constancy. This He will do because He is good and merciful, if those being corrected (having called for divine help) press on more sharply with righteous works and flee to God as the only one who can heal all their weaknesses. For He strikes in order to heal, not only from the wound He inflicted, but from the scars of sins <margin>74</margin> by which many who are corrected were wounded even unto death. Therefore, Paul continues his holy and life-giving encouragement and adds: ¶ **Wherefore lift up your drooping hands and shaky knees, and make straight paths for your feet: lest that which is lame be turned out of the way, but let it rather be healed.** <note>original: "Quapropter remissas manus..." Quoting Hebrews 12:12-13.</note> ¶ Lest God overturn that which is made lame by our iniquity and cast it into Gehenna <note>An ancient term for a place of spiritual punishment or hell.</note>; but rather, let Him heal it by His mercy and restore it to salvation. "Drooping hands" are when we do not practice good works. "Shaky knees" are when we are immobile toward the good works of faith and piety. We make "straight paths for our feet" <margin>75</margin> when we walk according to the precepts of faith. And now Paul pursues certain precepts. The first of these: that we pursue peace with all and the holiness of life. And he says: ¶ **Pursue peace and sanctification with all, without which no one will see God: looking diligently lest any man fail of the grace of God; lest any root of bitterness springing up trouble you, and thereby many be defiled.** ¶ The peace of God contains all things. Therefore, imitating the peace of God, let us have peace with everyone. Let us imitate Him in holiness, who says: *Be holy, for I am holy.* <note>Quoting Leviticus 19:2, often cited in the New Testament.</note> Without holiness, God cannot be seen, just as pure light cannot be seen by an impure eye. For holiness is the purity of the soul and mind; as the Savior says: *Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.* From this, it is well understood that those who are not holy and pure of heart will not see God—the most unhappy loss and the extreme of all evils. If we do evil, we are abandoned by the grace of God, or rather, we abandon grace. Just as a sick eye leaves the light; it is not left by the light. The "root of bitterness" is the root of sin, and especially of impiety. When it puts forth branches in the open, it infects and corrupts many, like a deadly and pestilential poisonous herb. He wishes, therefore, that each person examine himself diligently against the desires in which the roots of bitterness lie hidden, and explore himself (as the saying goes) "to the fingernail." <note>original: "ad unguem." A Latin idiom meaning "to perfection" or "thoroughly," derived from a sculptor checking the smoothness of a joint with their nail.</note> The second precept: that we avoid all fornication and impurity. <margin>2</margin> <margin>76</margin> For through these, we are deprived of the blessing of God and the heavenly inheritance we were to receive. The example: the intemperate Esau. Paul says: ¶ **Lest there be any fornicator or impure person, like Esau, who for one meal sold his birthright. For you know how afterward, when he desired to inherit the blessing, he was rejected: for he found no place for repentance, though he sought it with tears.** ¶ Regarding the intemperance and impurity of Esau, we read thus in Genesis: *Jacob boiled a pottage. When Esau came from the field weary, he said: Give me some of this red pottage, for I am exceedingly weary. Jacob said to him: Sell me your birthright. He answered: Behold, I am dying. What good will the birthright do me? Jacob said: Swear then to me. Esau swore, and sold his birthright. And so, having accepted bread and a dish of lentils, he ate and drank and went his way, thinking little of having sold his birthright.* <note>Summarizing Genesis 25:29-34.</note> Esau sold the right of the firstborn, to which the chief blessing and inheritance belonged. When he later wished to receive that inheritance and blessing—I mean the chief inheritance and blessing of the firstborn—he was rejected. However, he was not rejected in every sense. For he did receive a blessing (though in an inferior place) and a possession. But his repentance was of no use for that higher status, even though it was held with many tears. This happens daily among the children of Isaac and the children of Christ; many, on account of intemperance and impurities, lose the chief place of inheritance. If they seek the inheritance afterward, they are rejected.

For example, <note>Latin: *Verbi causa*</note> suppose you are a virgin and have lived for a long time untainted in mind and body, blameless in the faith of the Son of God. If you persevere, a primary blessing and inheritance will be given to you, and your place will be among the virgins; you will retain the full right of the firstborn of Christ. But if a wicked error carries you away and you defile yourself with a woman: for the sake of a small and foul pleasure, you have lost that primary inheritance. When you later wish to receive it, you are rejected. No matter how much repentance you perform or how many tears you shed, you will not find that specific place, and your lot will not be among the virgins. However, if you repent in this way, you will not be simply rejected; you will receive a blessing and an inheritance just as Esau did, but not in the same rank as before. For in the heavenly inheritance, there are many places and many mansions. And Isaac had many possessions and many places. For if Esau had not repented and shed tears, he would not have obtained even that blessing from his father. <margin>3</margin> These things happened long ago as a figure <note>A "figure" or "type" is an Old Testament event that foreshadows a New Testament reality.</note>.

**Third.** Our obedience to Christ must be paramount, performed with fear and trembling. For he is a most powerful king and the judge of all, surrounded by thousands of angels at his service. He is the mountain filling all things, to which we draw near. Furthermore, we approach him whose voice is powerful enough to shake heaven and earth. How then shall we escape unpunished if we do not obey? Those who did not listen to Moses—who was merely a mortal man, and only a shadow and figure of the truth—were punished so severely. How shall we escape if we offend that spiritual mountain? For if even a man or a beast touched the physical Mount Sinai, which could be felt with hands, they were put to death. If those people could not bear the sound of trumpets and voices, how shall we bear the final trumpets of the angels and the sentence of the judge condemning us? If they could not endure the physical fire that burns, nor the mist, darkness, and whirlwind, but fainted in terror—how shall we endure the "consuming fire" <note>original: *ignis consumens*</note> that devours all things in its zeal, the outer darkness, and the whirlwinds of the abyss? In all these things, the "argument from the greater" <note>A logical tool: if a rule applies in a lesser case (Moses/Sinai), it applies even more strongly in a greater case (Christ/Sion).</note> holds true. This is the height of misery for those of whom it is said through the prophet: *Let burning coals fall upon them; cast them into the fire; they shall not stand in their miseries.* But what can deliver us? The grace and mercy of the Savior, through obedience offered to him in fear <margin>77</margin> and reverence. And therefore, the divine revealer of saving doctrine, the Apostle, adds:

> *For you have not approached a mountain that can be touched, and a burning fire, and gloom, and darkness, and a whirlwind, and the sound of a trumpet, and a voice of words; those who heard it begged that no further word be spoken to them. For they could not bear what was commanded: "If even a beast touches the mountain, it shall be stoned." And so terrifying was the sight that Moses said, "I am full of fear and trembling." But you have approached Mount Sion, and the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and an assembly of many thousands of angels, and the church of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven, and God the judge of all, and the spirits of the righteous made perfect, and Jesus the mediator of a new covenant, and the sprinkled blood that speaks better than the blood of Abel. See that you do not refuse him who speaks. For if those people did not escape when they refused him who warned them on earth, how much less shall we escape if we turn away from him who warns from heaven? His voice shook the earth then, but now he has promised, saying: "Yet once more I will shake not only the earth, but also heaven." This phrase "yet once more" indicates the removal of those things that are shaken—that is, created things—so that the things that cannot be shaken may remain. Therefore, since we are receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken, let us have grace, through which we may offer service pleasing to God, with reverence and awe. For our God is a consuming fire.*

When the children of Israel received the law, they approached Mount Sinai, which was physical and touchable. We, however, approach the city of God, the heavenly Jerusalem, of which it is said: *The Lord builds up Jerusalem; he will gather the outcasts of Israel.* And again: *I, John, saw the holy city, the New Jerusalem, descending from heaven from God, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband.* The children of Israel approached a gathering and solemnity of men. We approach an innumerable multitude and celebration of angels, of whom it is said: *Thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times a hundred thousand stood before him.* The children of Israel approached a synagogue of the firstborn who were enrolled on earth.
