<meta>This page continues the philological and theological analysis of Hebrews 12. Following the previous discussion on Esau’s loss of his birthright, the author now provides a line-by-line comparison between the Latin Vulgate translation and the original Greek text, arguing for more precise terminology regarding divine discipline and the nature of the New Covenant.</meta>

COM.

The Translator of Paul. <note>original: "pres Pauli," likely an abbreviation for "Interpres Pauli"</note> You have not yet resisted to the point of shedding blood. <note>original Greek: "ὄυπω μέχρις ἅιματος ἀντικατέστητε"</note> $\P$ The Vulgate edition: *My son, do not neglect the discipline of the Lord.* $\P$ The word "My" is extra. *Paideia* <note>The Greek word for education or discipline</note> is defined as discipline, instruction, and correction. It is derived from the word for "boy" <note>Greek: *pais*</note> and not from "disciple" <note>Latin: *discipulus*</note>. Therefore, the care of correction and chastisement is especially applied to children. God does exactly this concerning us: when we live like children, serving youthful desires, we are then "boys" in our behavior and do not yet display the gravity, maturity, or integrity of men. I have preferred to translate this everywhere as "correction" <note>Latin: *correptio*</note> when the speech concerns chastisement, rather than "discipline" <note>Latin: *disciplina*</note>, so that the ambiguity of the word does not deceive. We must avoid the impression that it designates a "lesson" <note>Greek: *mathēma*</note>, which is what "discipline" means when derived from "disciple." It is in that latter sense that the Psalmist says: *Teach me goodness, discipline, and knowledge.* The Translator of Paul: *Son, do not make light of the Lord's discipline.* <note>original Greek: "ὑιὲ μὴ ὀλιγώρει παιδείας κυρίου"</note> And why, even when the true translator renders the verb for "to discipline" <note>Greek: *paideuei*</note> correctly as "he corrects" <note>Latin: *corripit*</note>—where he says: *For what son is there whom the father does not correct?*—why, I ask, does he not also translate *paideia* as "correction"? $\P$ The Vulgate edition: *Persevere in discipline.* $\P$ As I said before, I would prefer "in correction." And that word "persevere" signifies "sustain," "tolerate," "bear patiently," and "do not lose heart." The Translator of Paul: *Endure for the sake of discipline.* <note>original Greek: "ἔις παιδείαν ὑπομένετε"</note> 
<margin>C 73</margin> $\P$ The Vulgate edition: *God offers himself to you as to sons.* $\P$ The word "himself" is extra. Rather, it says "is offered" <note>passive</note>, not "offers" <note>active</note>. The Translator of Paul: *God deals with you as with sons.* <note>original Greek: "ὡς ὑιοῖς / ὑμῖν προσφέρεται ὁ θεός"</note> $\P$ The Vulgate edition: *Therefore you are adulterers and not sons.* $\P$ One should rather say: *adulterini*, meaning "degenerate," "illegitimate," or "bastards." The Translator of Paul: *Then you are bastards.* <note>original Greek: "ἄρα νόθοι ἐσέ"</note> $\P$ The Vulgate edition: *We have had the fathers of our flesh as instructors, and we revered them.* $\P$ Better: "as correctors." And the word "them" at the end is extra. It is strange how the old translator varies the same vocabulary and its derivatives in so many ways: now he says "he chastises," now "he corrects," and now "instructors"—as if the Greek source changed the words, when it always uses the same word and its derivatives. Hence, the meaning is more easily understood in Greek than in Latin. Therefore, we have not varied the terms, just as they are not varied in the Greek, so that the meaning might shine forth more clearly. The Translator of Paul: *We had the fathers of our flesh as correctors and we respected them.* <note>original Greek: "τοὺς μὲν τῆς σαρκὸς ἡμῶν πατέρας ἔιχομεν παιδευτάς καὶ ἐτρεπόμεθα"</note> And immediately there follows: *Shall we not much more?* Place "much more" there. $\P$ The Vulgate edition: *And they indeed for a time of a few days instructed us according to their own will.* $\P$ Where the old translator says "according to their own will," the better reading is: "according to what seemed good to them." And he could have said "they corrected," just as he translated the same verb previously as "he corrects." The word "us" is extra. The Translator of Paul: *For they indeed for a few days disciplined us as it seemed best to them.* <note>original Greek: "ὁι μὲν γὰρ πρὸς ὀλίγας ἡμέρας κατὰ τὸ δοκοῦν ἀυτοῖς ἐπαίδευον"</note> $\P$ The Vulgate edition: *But all discipline for the present indeed seems not to be of joy, but of grief.* $\P$ Here, too, "discipline" is understood as "correction." And when it says "not to be of joy, but of grief," it means it is not dear to the heart, it does not please, but rather displaces, being a mournful and sad thing. Our writers usually express this using the dative case, saying: "this thing is not to my heart," "is not a joy to me," or "is not a solace to me," but is "a sadness and a grief to me." For this reason, to better convey this sense, we have translated it using the dative. The Translator of Paul: *Now no discipline for the present seems to be joyous, but grievous.* <note>original Greek: "πᾶσα δὲ παιδεία πρὸς μὲν τὸ παρὸν ὀυ δοκεῖ χαρᾶς ἔιναι , ἀλλὰ λύπης"</note> 
<margin>D 74</margin> $\P$ The Vulgate edition: *The most peaceful fruit.* $\P$ He speaks in the positive degree <note>i.e., "peaceful" rather than "most peaceful"</note>. The Translator of Paul: *Peaceable fruit.* <note>original Greek: "καρπὸν ἐιρηνικόν"</note> $\P$ The Vulgate edition: *That no one who is limping may wander.* $\P$ Rather: "that he may not overturn the lame." <margin>D 75</margin> The Translator of Paul: *Lest that which is lame be turned out of the way.* <note>original Greek: "ἵνα μὴ τὸ χωλὸν ἐκτραπῇ"</note> $\P$ The Vulgate edition: *Lest any man be wanting to the grace of God.* $\P$ It can also be said here: "lest anyone be abandoned by the grace of God." The Translator of Paul: *Lest any man fail of the grace of God.* <note>original Greek: "μή τις ὑστερῶν ἀπὸ τῆς χάριτος τοῦ θεοῦ"</note> For that signifies: lest anyone lack, be deprived of, or be left behind by the grace of God. $\P$ The Vulgate edition: *He sold his first-things.* $\P$ This is the same as what is called "birthright" <note>Latin: *primogenita*</note>. <margin>D 76</margin> The Translator of Paul: *He sold his birthright.* <note>original Greek: "ἀπέδοτο τὰ πρωτοτόκια ἀυτοῦ"</note> $\P$ The Vulgate edition: *For know that afterward also, desiring to inherit the blessing.* $\P$ Equally: "For you know." The Translator of Paul: *For you know how that afterward, when he would have inherited the blessing.* <note>original Greek: "ἴστε γὰρ ὅτι μετέπειτα θέλων κληρονομῆσαι τὴν ἐυλογίαν"</note> $\P$ The Vulgate edition: <margin>E 77</margin> *For you have not come to a touchable and approachable fire.* $\P$ One should say: "to a touchable mountain." The word "mountain" is missing. And "approachable fire" is not "approachable," but rather [burning], if speaking through participles as in the Greek. The Translator of Paul: *For you have not come unto the mountain that might be touched, and that burned with fire.* <note>original Greek: "ὀυ γὰρ προσεληλύθατε ψηλαφομένῳ ὄρει καὶ κεκαυμένῳ πυρί"</note> $\P$ The Vulgate edition: *For they did not bear that which was said.* $\P$ One reads: "that which was commanded" <note>Latin: *distinguebatur*</note>, that is, those various and prolonged sounds and terrible words. The Translator of Paul: *For they could not endure that which was commanded.* <note>original Greek: "ὀυκ ἔφερον γὰρ τὸ διασελλόμενον"</note> $\P$ The Vulgate edition: <margin>F 77</margin> *And the company of many thousands of angels, and the church of the first-born.* $\P$ What he calls "company" <note>Latin: *frequentiā*</note> designates the gathering of all, the celebration, the praise, and the universal assembly. And regarding "of the first-born": this is what was said before, the "first-begotten." The Translator of Paul: *And to an innumerable company of angels, to the general assembly and church of the firstborn.* <note>original Greek: "καὶ μυριάσιν ἀγγέλων πανηγύρει , καὶ ἐκκλησία πρωτοτόκων"</note> $\P$ The Vulgate edition: *And the spirit of the just made perfect.* $\P$ He uses the plural "spirits." And all these things refer back to "you have come," as if we were to say: "and you have come to the spirits of the just made perfect." The Translator of Paul: *And to the spirits of just men made perfect.* <note>original Greek: "καὶ πνεύμασι δικαίων τετελειωμένων"</note> $\P$ The Vulgate edition: *And the sprinkling of blood.* $\P$ It is also called "the blood of sprinkling." And although it is the same whether we say "the sprinkling of blood" or "the blood of sprinkling," we better say "the blood speaking" rather than "the sprinkling [speaking]," as with the blood of Abel.

### (XIII)

<margin>G 77</margin> The voice, he says, of your brother’s blood cries out to me from the earth. <note>Genesis 4:10</note> **The Translator of Paul.** And to the sprinkled blood. <note>original Greek: "καὶ αἵματι ῥαντισμοῦ" (kai haimati rhantismou). The author is comparing the blood of Abel with the blood of Christ.</note> See how he uses the dative *blood*. However, we have converted all preceding datives into accusatives. ¶ **The Vulgate edition.** Refusing him who spoke upon the earth. ¶ That word "spoke" signifies the administration of justice. For the one he speaks of here is to be understood as Moses; when the Hebrews did not listen to him, God took severe vengeance, as is well known from sacred history. **The Translator of Paul.** Those who refused him who gave divine warnings on earth. <note>original Greek: "τὸν ἐπὶ γῆς παραιτησάμενοι χρηματίζοντα" (ton epi gēs paraitēsamenoi chrēmatizonta)</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition.** Much more we, who turn away from him who speaks to us from heaven. ¶ "Speaks to us" is redundant. And if anything is to be understood, it is rather "administering justice"—that is, as a king or prince establishing his laws, rights, and edicts. **The Translator of Paul.** Much more we, who turn away from him who is from heaven. <note>original Greek: "πολλῷ μᾶλλον ἡμεῖς, οἱ τὸν ἀπ’ οὐρανῶν ἀποστρεφόμενοι" (pollō mallon hēmeis, hoi ton ap' ouranōn apostrephomenoi)</note> And there follows immediately: *whose voice*. ¶ **The Vulgate edition.** Now that he says, "Yet once more," he declares. ¶ It should rather be said "And this." Furthermore, the word "says" is redundant. **The Translator of Paul.** And this "Yet once more" signifies. <note>original Greek: "τὸ δὲ ἔτι ἅπαξ, δηλοῖ" (to de eti hapax, dēloi)</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition.** Through which let us serve. ¶ It is stated in the indicative: "we serve" or "we worship." **The Translator of Paul.** Through which we worship. <note>original Greek: "Δι’ ἧς λατρεύομεν" (Di’ hēs latreuomen)</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition.** With fear and reverence. ¶ Rather, "with reverence and religion," or "piety." **The Translator of Paul.** With reverence and godly fear. <note>original Greek: "μετὰ αἰδοῦς καὶ εὐλαβείας" (meta aidous kai eulabeias)</note>

<margin>CHAPTER XIII.</margin>
<margin>78</margin> <margin>4</margin> Regarding the worship of the new law and the immovable kingdom, in fear, religion, piety, and reverence, the apostle gave his third precept. Now he adds a fourth regarding the preservation of **brotherly friendship** and **hospitality**—that is, the care for receiving travelers—and he says: ¶ Let brotherly friendship persist. Do not forget hospitality; for through this, some who received angels as guests remained hidden <note>or "were kept safe"</note>. ¶ All of us reborn in Christ are brothers, and we ought to preserve a mutual friendship as brothers, since we are all sons of the same infinitely good Father and the same Son. This spiritual brotherhood is far closer and more binding for friendship—beyond any comparison—than carnal brotherhood. Therefore, he who violates it through hatred and envy will be punished more severely than one who violates carnal brotherhood, just as the former is a tighter bond than the latter. But we are wretched: we draw our reason for loving more from the brotherhood of the flesh than from the brotherhood according to the spirit, as if the flesh were something more excellent than the spirit, or as if an affinity from the flesh were greater than that which we have from Christ. Who does not see that we prefer an earthly father to the heavenly and eternal Father, and thus do an injustice to the heavenly Father? Let Christ, therefore, be the chief cause and most powerful reason for this brotherly friendship. And how shall we neglect hospitality, since Christ himself became a traveler for us? Otherwise, we shall hear from him: *I was a stranger, and you did not take me in.* For even now, he travels in each one of his followers. And who are those who remained hidden while receiving angels as guests? Lot, his wife, and his daughters; if the Sodomites could have found them, they would have inflicted great punishment upon them out of their conceived indignation, as is contained in the history of Genesis. But before they went to bed (it says), the men of the city—all the people together, from the young to the old—surrounded his house. They called to Lot and said to him: "Where are the men who came to you tonight? Bring them out here." When he refused to produce them, offering instead his two virgin daughters (for they were angels whom he had received as guests in the form of men, though Lot did not know it), the inhabitants of Sodom said: "We will afflict you more than these," and they pressed violently against Lot. And they were nearly breaking down the doors, but behold, the men reached out their hands, pulled Lot inside to them, and shut the door. And those who were outside they struck with blindness, from the least to the greatest, so that they could not find the door. This is the sacred history. Thus Lot remained hidden by the protection of angels, so that he was not found by those who strove to destroy him. Thus we understand that those who observe hospitality are defended by the guardianship of angels and "remain hidden" in the day of evils, so that evils do not seize them, and they are led out from imminent dangers. But now, in many places (which is to be lamented no small amount), hospitality is either extinct or the greed of the inn-keeper is preferred to it. <margin>5</margin> The fifth precept. He commands concerning the conquered, the incarcerated, and those detained by sickness: that we should help them with all the zeal of piety, and feel compassion for them just as if we were suffering the same things. Paul adds this in this way: ¶ Remember those in bonds, as if you were bound with them. Those oppressed by trouble, as if you yourselves were there in the body. ¶ We ought by right to have compassion for those in bonds, captives, the sick, and those laboring under any oppression. For Christ the Lord also conquered and willed to be captured for us, and to carry the infirmities of all in his most sacred body, as it is written: *Christ the Lord was taken in our sins.* And again: *He himself took our infirmities and carried our sorrows.* And it will be said to those who were unmerciful: *I was sick and in prison, and you did not visit me.* <margin>6</margin> He places the sixth precept concerning marriage in this way: ¶ Let marriage be honorable in all things, and the bed undefiled. For God will judge fornicators and adulterers. ¶ Marriage indeed ought to be honorable, since Christ himself deigned to honor it. For although he was born of a virgin, he nevertheless willed for her to be betrothed in marriage. And he honored marriage with his virgin mother by his presence and by the powerful beginnings of his signs <note>A reference to the Wedding at Cana</note>.

### COMMENTARY

...the presence of Paul. *You have not yet resisted to the point of blood.* <note>Hebrews 12:4; original Greek: "οὔπω μέχρις αἵματος ἀντικατέστητε" (oupō mechris haimatos antikastētē)</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *My son, do not neglect the discipline of the Lord.* <note>Hebrews 12:5</note> ¶ *My*: this word is redundant <note>Latin: "abundat"; indicating it is an addition not found in the Greek</note>. *Paedia* <note>The Greek "παιδεία" (paideia)</note> is called discipline, instruction, or correction. It is derived from the word for "child" <note>Greek: "παῖς" (pais)</note>, not from "disciple," because the care of correction and chastisement is especially applied to children. God does this very thing toward us: when we live like children, serving youthful desires. For we are then children in our behavior, not yet displaying the gravity, maturity, and integrity of men. I have preferred to translate this as "reproof" everywhere here while the discussion concerns chastisement, rather than "discipline," lest the ambiguity of the word deceive. One must not let it seem to designate what is called a "lesson" <note>Greek: "μάθημα" (mathema)</note>, which relates to a "disciple." In that sense, it is said: *Teach me goodness, discipline, and knowledge.* <note>Psalm 119:66</note> **The Translator of Paul:** *Son, do not look lightly upon the discipline of the Lord.* <note>Original Greek: "υἱὲ μὴ ὀλιγώρει παιδείας κυρίου" (huie mē oligōrei paideias kyriou)</note> And why, even when the old translator <note>referring to the Vulgate</note> interprets the verb *paideuei* as "he reproves"—and rightly so—where it says, *For what son is there whom the father does not reprove?* <note>Hebrews 12:7</note>—why, I ask, does he not also translate *paedia* as "reproof"? ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Persevere in discipline.* ¶ As I said before, I would prefer "in reproof." And that word *persevere* designates "sustain," "tolerate," "bear patiently," or "do not lose heart." **The Translator of Paul:** *Endure for the sake of discipline.* <note>Original Greek: "εἰς παιδείαν ὑπομένετε" (eis paideian hypomenete)</note>

</margin>

¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *As with sons, God offers himself to you.* ¶ *Himself*: this is redundant. It should be said "he is offered" in the passive, not "he offers" in the active. **The Translator of Paul:** *God deals with you as with sons.* <note>Original Greek: "ὡς υἱοῖς ὑμῖν προσφέρεται ὁ θεός" (hōs huiois hymin prospheretai ho theos)</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Therefore you are adulterers and not sons.* <note>Hebrews 12:8</note> ¶ It should rather be said: "illegitimate," that is, degenerate or bastards. **The Translator of Paul:** *Then you are bastards.* <note>Original Greek: "ἄρα νόθοι ἐστέ" (ara nothoi este)</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *We have had fathers of our flesh as instructors, and we revered them.* <note>Hebrews 12:9</note> ¶ Rather, "reprovers." And "them" at the end is redundant. It is strange how the old translator varies the same word and its derivatives in so many different ways: 

<margin>
D
73
</margin>

sometimes he says "he chastises," sometimes "he reproves," and now he uses "instructors." It is as if he is trying to vary the Greek vocabulary of the manuscript, even though the Greek always uses the same root and its derivatives. From this, the meaning reveals itself more easily in Greek than in Latin. Therefore, we have not varied our translation, just as the Greek does not, so that the meaning might shine forth more clearly. **The Translator of Paul:** *We had the fathers of our flesh as reprovers and we respected them.* <note>Original Greek: "τοὺς μὲν τῆς σαρκὸς ἡμῶν πατέρας εἴχομεν παιδευτάς καὶ ἐνετρεπόμεθα" (tous men tēs sarkos hēmōn pateras eichomen paideutas kai enetrepometha)</note> And immediately there follows: *Shall we not much more?* <note>Original Greek: "οὐ πολλῶ μᾶλλον" (ou pollō mallon)</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *And they indeed for a time of a few days, according to their own will, instructed us.* <note>Hebrews 12:10</note> ¶ Where the old translator says "according to their own will," it is better held as "according to what seemed right to them." And he could have said "they reproved," just as he had previously translated the same word (as has already been said) as "he reproves." *Us* is redundant. **The Translator of Paul:** *For they indeed for a few days disciplined us according to what seemed good to them.* <note>Original Greek: "οἱ μὲν γὰρ πρὸς ὀλίγας ἡμέρας κατὰ τὸ δοκοῦν αὐτοῖς ἐπαίδευον" (hoi men gar pros oligas hēmeras kata to dokoun autois epaideuon)</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Now all discipline in the present seems to be not of joy, but of sorrow.* <note>Hebrews 12:11</note> ¶ Here too, discipline is understood as "reproof." And what it says, "to be not of joy, but of sorrow," means it is not to one's heart, it does not please, but rather displeases and is a gloomy and sad thing. Our writers are more accustomed to expressing this through the dative case, saying: "this thing is not *to* my heart," "it is not *to* me for joy," "it is not *to* me for comfort," but "for sadness and sorrow." For this reason, to better suggest this meaning, we have translated it using the dative. **The Translator of Paul:** *But all discipline for the present does not seem to be of joy, but of grief.* <note>Original Greek: "πᾶσα δὲ παιδεία πρὸς μὲν τὸ παρὸν οὐ δοκεῖ χαρᾶς εἶναι, ἀλλὰ λύπης" (pasa de paideia pros men to paron ou dokei charas einai, alla lypēs)</note>

# XIIII Hebrews

<margin>G 77</margin> "The voice of your brother's blood," it says, "cries out to me from the ground." <note>Genesis 4:10</note> **The Translator of Paul:** *and to the blood of sprinkling.* <note>Hebrews 12:24; original Greek: "καὶ αἵματι ῥαντισμοῦ" (kai haimati rhantismou)</note> Note how he uses the dative case for "blood" <note>original: "αἵματι" (haimati)</note>. However, we have converted all the preceding datives into accusatives to fit the Latin flow. ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Refusing him who spoke upon the earth.* <note>Hebrews 12:25</note> ¶ That word "spoke" designates the act of pronouncing law; for the one being discussed here is Moses. When the Hebrews did not listen to him, God took severe vengeance, as is well known from sacred history. **The Translator of Paul:** *refusing him who warned on earth.* <note>Original Greek: "τὸν ἐπὶ γῆς παραιτησάμενοι χρηματίζοντα" (ton epi gēs paraitēsamenoi chrēmatizonta)</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *How much more we, if we turn away from him who speaks to us from heaven.* ¶ "Speaks to us" is redundant. And if anything is to be understood here, it is rather "pronouncing the law"—that is, acting as a king or prince who ratifies his laws, rights, and edicts. **The Translator of Paul:** *much more we, who turn away from the one from heaven.* <note>Original Greek: "πολλῷ μᾶλλον ἡμεῖς, οἱ τὸν ἀπ' οὐρανῶν αποστρεφόμενοι" (pollō mallon hēmeis, hoi ton ap' ouranōn apostrephomenoi)</note> And there follows immediately: *whose voice.* <note>Original Greek: "οὗ ἡ φωνή" (hou hē phōnē)</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *Now this, "yet once more," he says, indicates...* <note>Hebrews 12:27</note> ¶ It should rather be said "this, however." And the word "says" is redundant. **The Translator of Paul:** *Now this, "yet once," indicates.* <note>Original Greek: "τὸ δὲ ἔτι ἅπαξ, δηλοῖ" (to de eti hapax, dēloi)</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *By which let us serve.* <note>Hebrews 12:28</note> ¶ This is stated in the indicative: *we serve* or *we worship.* **The Translator of Paul:** *through which let us serve.* <note>Original Greek: "δι' ἧς λατρεύωμεν" (di' hēs latreuōmen)</note> ¶ **The Vulgate edition:** *With fear and reverence.* ¶ Rather *with reverence and religion*, or *piety.* **The Translator of Paul:** *with modesty and godly fear.* <note>Original Greek: "μετὰ αἰδοῦς καὶ εὐλαβείας" (meta aidous kai eulabeias)</note>

### CHAPTER XIII.

<margin>78</margin> <margin>4</margin> <image-desc>Decorative initial E with floral and foliage patterns</image-desc> From the decree of the new law and the immovable kingdom—given in fear, religion, piety, and reverence—the Apostle has provided a third precept. Now he adds a fourth concerning the preservation of brotherly friendship and hospitality (that is, the care for receiving strangers), and he says:
> **Let the friendship of brotherhood persevere. Do not be forgetful of hospitality; for through this, some were hidden who received angels as guests.** <note>Hebrews 13:1–2</note>

All of us reborn in Christ are brothers, and we ought to preserve friendship for one another as brothers; we are all sons of a better Father—indeed, of the one and same infinitely good Son. This brotherhood is spiritual; it is far closer and more binding toward friendship—even beyond any point of comparison—than fleshly brotherhood. Therefore, he who violates it through hatred and envy will be punished more severely than one who violates fleshly brotherhood, just as the former bond is stricter than the latter. But we are wretched: we are led more by the logic of the flesh to love our kin than by the logic of the spirit, as if the flesh were somehow more excellent than the spirit, or as if kinship from the flesh outweighed that which we have from Christ. Who does not see that we prefer an earthly father to the heavenly and eternal Father, and thus do injury to our heavenly Father? Let Christ, therefore, be the chief cause and most powerful reason for this fraternal friendship. And how shall we neglect hospitality, since Christ himself became a stranger for us? Otherwise, we are destined to hear from him:
> **I was a stranger, and you did not take me in.** <note>Matthew 25:43</note>

For even now, he wanders as a stranger in each one of his followers. And who are they who were "hidden," receiving angels as guests? Lot, his wife, and his daughters. If the Sodomites could have found them, they would have afflicted them with great punishment because of the indignation they felt, as is told in the history of Genesis. But before they went to bed (it says), the men of the city—every person together, from the young man to the old—surrounded the house. They called to Lot and said to him: "Where are the men who entered your house tonight? Bring them out here." When he refused to present them, offering instead his two virgin daughters (for they were angels whom he had received as guests in the appearance of men, although Lot did not know this), the inhabitants of Sodom said: "We will afflict you even more than these." And they pressed upon Lot most vehemently. They were already near to breaking the doors when, behold, the men reached out their hands, pulled Lot into the house to themselves, and shut the door. And those who were outside they struck with blindness, from the smallest to the greatest, so that they could not find the door. This is the sacred history. Thus we understand that those who observe hospitality are protected by the guardianship of angels and are "hidden" in the day of evils so that evils do not seize them, and they are led out from imminent dangers. But already in many places (which is to be lamented in no small measure), either hospitality is extinct, or the greed of innkeeping <term>cauponaria cupiditas</term> <note>literally "the greed of the shopkeeper/innkeeper," suggesting turning a duty of care into a mere business transaction</note> is preferred to it. <margin>79</margin> <margin>5</margin> The fifth precept. He commands concerning the conquered, those incarcerated, and those held by sickness: that we should help them with every zeal of piety, and feel for them just as if we were suffering the same things ourselves. Paul adds this in this manner:
> ¶ **Remember those in bonds, as if you were bound with them. The trouble of the oppressed, just as if you yourselves were there in the body.** <note>Hebrews 13:3</note>

¶ We ought by good right to feel for the bound, the captives, the sick, and those laboring under any oppression. For Christ the Lord willed to be bound and captured for us, and to carry the infirmities of all in his most sacred body, as it is written: *Christ the Lord was captured in our sins.* And again: *He himself bore our languors, and he himself carried our sorrows.* <note>Isaiah 53:4</note> And it will be said to those who were unmerciful:
> **I was sick and in prison, and you did not visit me.** <note>Matthew 25:43</note>

<margin>80</margin> <margin>6</margin> He places the sixth precept concerning marriage in this manner:
> ¶ **Let marriage be honorable in all, and the bed undefiled. For God will judge fornicators and adulterers.** <note>Hebrews 13:4</note>

¶ Marriage ought indeed to be honorable, since Christ himself deigned to honor it. For although he was born of a virgin, he nevertheless willed her to be betrothed in marriage. And he honored marriage with his presence and the beginnings of his powerful signs... <note>referring to the Wedding at Cana</note>

<meta>This page serves as a preface by the editor—likely the humanist scholar Jacques Lefèvre d’Étaples—explaining his decision to include the apocryphal accounts of the martyrdoms of Peter and Paul, attributed to Bishop Linus, following his own commentary on the Epistles of St. Paul. It establishes the historical and liturgical rationale for presenting these two apostles together.</meta>

<image-desc>Woodcut decorative initial 'E' featuring floral motifs and stylized foliage.</image-desc>
Now that the labor of the commentaries on the most holy Paul has been exhausted (as God has permitted), most sacred prelate, it seemed not at all out of place if I were to append the records of Bishop Linus <note>Linus is traditionally regarded as the second Bishop of Rome, succeeding St. Peter.</note> concerning the passion of the two apostles worthy of God, Peter and Paul, which were sent to the Eastern churches. I have done this so that by looking upon the end of their way of life, we might also imitate their faith. There was a further reason for doing the same: I have occasionally cited these booklets of Bishop Linus in my commentaries; had I not included them here, the readers might perhaps have felt a lingering desire for them. Just as the absence of a desired thing causes distress while it is away, its presence provides relief. Those who have desired them will therefore be comforted by their presence and will consider their minds satisfied.

These accounts of the apostles' passions are rare to find, especially the one concerning Peter. For even after searching many libraries, even the most ancient, one or two barely ever turn up. I first discovered it in a very old manuscript in the library of the Great Monastery <note>Marmoutier Abbey in France</note>, which was once headed by Martin of Sabaria <note>Better known as Saint Martin of Tours, a famous 4th-century bishop and monk</note>, most famous throughout the world for the holiness of his life and the brilliance of his miracles. The account of Paul is more common, but in many places it is corrupted and full of errors, appearing everywhere without any prefixed title of the author. Therefore, I have revised both according to more corrected examples.

I have placed them in the order in which the Church usually celebrates the apostles: Peter first, because he was called first, was the first to see Christ, confessed him as the Son of the living God, and was appointed prince of the Church by Christ the Lord while he still dwelt visibly on earth; and also because he suffered first, according to the authority of the elders. Paul follows, because he was later in all these things and completed his glorious martyrdom on the annual anniversary of Peter’s passion. For this reason, the Church sings of them: "The glorious princes of the earth; as they loved each other in life, so in death they were not divided," <note>original Latin: "Gloriosi principes terræ/ quo modo in vita sua dilexerũt se/ ita & in morte nō sunt separati"</note> because their celebration is joined on the same birthday <note>In the early Church, the "birthday" of a saint refers to their "dies natalis" or the day of their death/entry into heaven.</note>. And since our purpose here was rather to celebrate Paul, I could not have separated Peter by placing only the passion of Paul and omitting that of Peter, since the Church never celebrates one without the other. This did not seem right or reasonable to us at all. You have, therefore, most wise father, the reasons that compelled me to release both passions and by no means one without the other—reasons which, I think, are not at all unfounded. Now, fulfilling our promise, we append Linus himself.

After many and various teachings on the way of life and salvation, after extraordinary and most famous miracles were shown, and after various struggles for the name of the true Christ against Simon Magus <note>A sorcerer mentioned in the Book of Acts who became a legendary arch-nemesis of Peter in Rome</note> and many other heralds of the Antichrist; after manifold suffering, the bitterness of lashes, and the horrific filth of prisons—while the blessed Peter was exulting in the Lord and giving thanks night and day with the brothers, amidst the crowd of those coming to the faith of God and our Lord Jesus Christ—intent on prayer, doctrine, and other duties of divine piety, especially charity and chastity, he brought grace to the hearts of those listening.

For this city <note>Rome</note>, preferred above the whole world, had lifted itself up in a spirit of pride beyond measure. For very often, where there is pride of mind, there follows the insult of the flesh <note>A reference to sexual immorality or lack of self-control</note>. So much so that many Roman matrons chose to keep their hearts and bodies clean (as much as was in their power) from the union of the marriage bed. Having completed (as God permitted), most holy prelate, the laborious work of commentary upon the most blessed Paul, it seemed in no way out of place if I were to subjoin the records sent to the Eastern churches by Bishop Linus (as the memory of our ancestors has preserved) concerning the passion of the two apostles worthy of God, Peter and Paul. My hope is that by gazing upon the outcome of their conversion, we might also imitate their faith. There was a further reason for me to do this: I have occasionally cited these small books of Bishop Linus within my commentaries; had I not included them here, a longing for them might perhaps remain in the readers' minds. Just as the absence of a desired thing causes distress while it is missing, so does its presence provide relief. Therefore, those who have desired them will be comforted by their presence and will consider their wishes satisfied. Indeed, these accounts of the apostles' passions are rare to find, especially the one concerning Peter. For even after searching through many very ancient libraries, one or two barely ever appear. I first discovered it in a very old manuscript in the library of the Great Monastery <note>original: "Maioris monasterii," referring to the Abbey of Marmoutier</note>, which was once headed by Martin of Sabaria <note>Saint Martin of Tours, born in Sabaria</note>, most renowned throughout the whole world for the holiness of his life and the brilliance of his miracles. The account concerning Paul is more common, but in many places it is corrupted and full of errors, often appearing without any title naming the author. I have, therefore, revised both according to more corrected examples. I have placed them in the order in which the Church is accustomed to celebrate the apostles: Peter first, because he was called first, was the first to see Christ, confessed Him as the Son of the living God, and was appointed prince of the Church by Christ the Lord while He still moved visibly upon the earth; and also because he was the first to suffer, as the authority of the elders maintains. Paul follows, because he was later in all those things, and on the anniversary of Peter's passion, he completed his glorious martyrdom. Thus, the Church sings of them: "Glorious princes of the earth, as they loved each other in their life, so also in death they were not separated," <note>A reference to a traditional liturgical antiphon for the Feast of Saints Peter and Paul</note> because the celebration of their birthdays <note>In early Christian context, "birthday" (natalis) refers to the date of martyrdom or entry into heaven</note> is joined on the same day. And since our purpose here was rather to celebrate Paul, how could I have nonetheless separated Peter, placing only the passion of Paul and omitting that of Peter, when the Church nowhere celebrates one without the other? This did not seem at all right or rational to us. You have, therefore, most wise father, the reasons which compelled me to issue both passions and by no means one without the other—and (as I think) not without reason. Now, fulfilling our promise, we subjoin Linus himself.

## ¶ THE FIRST BOOK OF BISHOP LINUS ON THE PASSION OF PETER, DELIVERED TO THE CHURCHES OF THE EAST AND THEREAFTER TRANSLATED INTO LATIN.

<image-desc>A large decorative drop cap 'P' featuring similar vine and leaf motifs to the first initial, set within a square frame.</image-desc>

After manifold and various lessons on the way and life of salvation, after the exhibition of extraordinary and most celebrated miracles, and after various struggles for the name of the true Christ against Simon Magus <note>A sorcerer mentioned in the Acts of the Apostles who was considered a primary heretic by the early Church</note> and many other heralds of the Antichrist; after manifold suffering, the bitterness of lashes, and the horrific squalor of prisons, the blessed Peter was exulting in the Lord. Spending night and day with the brothers in the crowd of those coming to the faith of God and our Lord Jesus Christ, intent on prayers, doctrine, and other duties of divine piety—especially those of charity and chastity—he brought grace into the hearts of his listeners. He exhorted those believing in Christ to conduct themselves modestly and continently. For this preeminent city <note>Rome</note> had excessively and overwhelmingly raised itself up in a spirit of arrogant pride, and therefore (as is common in wealth and idle security) it was ruled by indecent luxury. For very often, where there is pride of mind, the dishonor of the flesh follows. Thus it happened that through the sermons of the blessed Peter, a great love for chastity was kindled among many women of various ages, status, and nobility. So much so that many Roman matrons chose to keep their hearts and bodies pure from the union of the husband's bed (as much as lay within their power). But as the time drew near when the faith and labors of the blessed apostle Peter were to be rewarded, the head of perdition—namely the antichrist Nero, iniquity personified—took steps to have him confined and held in the most squalid custody...

...he ordered him to be bound by the feet. At that time, four concubines of the prefect Agrippa <note>This Agrippa was the Roman prefect, not to be confused with King Agrippa from the New Testament</note>—whose names were Agrippina, Eucharia, Euphemia, and Cleonis—began to visit him frequently. Hearing from him the discourse on **chastity** and all the commands of our Lord JESUS CHRIST, they began to waste away and feel troubled in Agrippa’s bed. Dedicating themselves to a life of purity, they entered into a mutual pact and, strengthened by our Lord JESUS CHRIST, they resolved that they would no longer submit to his sexual demands. When they withdrew themselves not only from his embrace but from any kind of union with Agrippa, he began to be greatly annoyed and saddened by this. Sending out diligent and clever spies, he learned that they were most eagerly rushing to visit the blessed PETER. When the spies were brought back to him, he said, seized by a most violent madness of love: “I know where you are coming from. That Christian has taught you not to stay with me and to withdraw from your required bed. But I am certain that with his magic arts, he will not be able to weaken your love for me.” Though they were soothed with many flatteries, they did not answer with a single word of love, nor did they look back with an attentive eye upon the fuel of lust, for they were firmly established by the apostolic word.

When the prefect Agrippa saw that they followed the teaching of PETER—unanimously scorning his lust and failing to yield to his flatteries—he began to threaten them with horrific punishments, swearing that he would both burn them alive in a fire and that he would wipe PETER from the memory of men under heaven after afflicting him with the most grievous tortures. But he could never bend them toward defilement, for they said it was more lovely for them to succumb to all torments for the sake of chastity than to refuse CHRIST (to whom they had vowed their purity). Therefore, the prefect Agrippa was indignant, especially toward the apostle; he gnashed his teeth at him, seeking an opportunity to kill him as if he could do so with a rational justification.

Meanwhile, the wife of Albinus (a very close friend of Caesar), named Xandips <note>Commonly known as Xanthippe in other traditions</note>, came to PETER with many other most noble matrons. Receiving from him the word of a chaste life, she rejected not only the marriage bed but even every pleasure of her life. Because of this, Albinus was struck with excessive grief and threatened to inflict many tortures upon PETER. Indeed, he tried to resist his wife Xandips first with insulting words, then with flatteries, and finally with all his effort. Sending a message to the prefect Agrippa, to whom he was joined in friendship, he told him everything he was suffering from PETER regarding his wife, begging that if Agrippa were a friend according to his trust, he would avenge him against PETER; otherwise, he would avenge himself. Agrippa sent back a reply: that he was suffering the same things, and even harsher ones, because of him. Thus it happened that when Albinus went to his bedchamber and had Xandips brought to him, and could obtain a sexual union with her neither by flatteries nor by terrors, he consulted on how he might catch PETER with Agrippa’s hand—like a bird in a snare <note>original: "auem laqueo"</note>—and destroy him as a sorcerer.

However, Xandips, the wife of Albinus, hearing this, sent a most faithful messenger to PETER, urging him to leave Rome and avoid the nearly inevitable traps. Likewise, Marcellus <note>A wealthy Roman convert who features prominently in the apocryphal Acts of Peter</note>—the son of the prefect Marcus, who had fled the pestilential teaching of Simon the Sorcerer <term>Simon Magus: a practitioner of magic who opposed Peter</term> and adhered faithfully and usefully to the apostle in all things—and the brothers also made known to him the conspiracy of her husband and the prefect Agrippa.

On the next day, certain senators rose in the assembly and said: “We suggest to your Greatness, noble men: that for the subversion of the eternal city, PETER delivers marriages to divorce, separates our wives from us, and introduces a new and unheard-of law (we know not what).” Saying these things, they incited others to riot and protest. Then Agrippa rejoiced, because what he desired concerning PETER had come before the senate under this pretext. But this did not escape the notice of PETER and the brothers. Indeed, those who had been among the senators and were enlightened by the Lord through PETER made this known to them by a swift messenger. For this reason, Marcellus and the brothers pleaded with PETER to withdraw.

But PETER said: “It is not right, brothers and sons, to flee from sufferings for the sake of CHRIST the Lord, since He Himself voluntarily offered Himself to death for our salvation.”

But Marcellus and the brothers, with much weeping, said: “Have mercy, merciful father, on the young and those who are raw in the faith; do not leave us or them abandoned among the storms of the unbelievers.”

Then PETER, at their request, said: “You advise that I should flee, and by my example strike fear of suffering into the hearts of the young and the weak; whereas we ought to assert the word of God constantly and preserve the foundations of holy purity which we have laid. You think I should flee to avoid death, which we seek with many sighs and long groans as the entrance to life, through which also, according to His revelation, we ought to glorify the Lord.”

Hearing this, the brothers raised their voices, saying: “O most truthful father, where are the words by which you used to say that you were ready to die for our lives? And now we cannot obtain your consent to live a little longer for our salvation until we are strengthened?” The young men also, whom he himself had carefully guarded in the faith and diligently educated in chastity, took his hands...

# THE PASSION OF PETER
<header>Passion of Peter</header>
<sig>L iiij.</sig>

...stretching their hands toward heaven and throwing themselves before his face, falling to the ground as if suddenly dead, they cried out with great wailing, shouting: “O good **PETER**, father and shepherd, whose mercy is unique after that of your Lord: why do you now expose us to the habits of most cruel wolves? For you recently gave birth to us for the Lord through the sacred font with maternal affection, yet now you leave us with such premature comfort and a cruel spirit, though you never touched us in such a way before.” The matrons also cried out, their heads sprinkled with dust: “Is this the mercy you used to preach regarding your Savior? He was moved by piety to forgive you for eternity for the tears you shed after denying him for a time. And now, despite such rivers of tears, you do not grant yourself to us for even a little while, especially when you could still serve the Lord in the flesh and later receive the eternal crown reserved for you.”

But even the prison guards, **Processus and Martinianus**, <note>Tradition holds that these two guards were converted and baptized by Peter while he was held in the Mamertine Prison.</note> along with the rest of the magistrates and those joined by office, pleaded with him, saying: “Lord, where do you wish to go? For we believe the Emperor has already forgotten you. But that most wicked Agrippa, inflamed by the love of his mistresses and the intemperance of his own lust, hastens to destroy you. If he were attacking you by the Emperor’s command, we would have received a sentence regarding your death from the most illustrious Paulinus, to whom we undertook your custody. For after you baptized us—believers in this nearby prison—by the font brought forth from the rock by prayers and the miraculous sign of the cross in the name of the Holy Trinity, you went freely wherever you pleased, and no one troubled you. Nor would anyone now, if the demonic fire that agitates the city had not more sharply persuaded Agrippa. Therefore, we pray you, minister of our salvation, deign to grant us this exchange: since you have released us from the bonds of sins and demons, depart now—free by our prayer rather than just our permission—away from the prison and the fetters whose cruelty was entrusted to us, for the salvation of such a great multitude.”

Widows and orphans, as well as those heavily worn by old age, tearing at their hair, scratching their cheeks, and baring their chests, said: “You healed others, by whose ministry we were supported, from various ailments, and you even raised them from death itself; yet you withdraw yourself from us, O most pious father? At least send us all before you, lest souls destitute of the teaching of your instruction perish, and those desolate of the comfort of your physical ministry pass away. And so, hasten to go where you desire, lest we, seeing our life die after the Lord and remaining in life, die as wretches.”

Then **PETER**, hearing these things from all sides—who was merciful beyond measure and could never pass by the tears of the afflicted without tears of his own—was overcome by such great weeping and said: “Let none of you come with me; I shall go alone in a changed appearance.” <note>original: "mutato schemate," implying he left in disguise to avoid detection.</note> For on the next night, having celebrated prayer, saying farewell to the brothers and commending them to God with a blessing, he set out alone. And as he went, the bandages fell from his leg, having been worn away by the fetter. As he wished to exit the gate of the city, he saw **CHRIST** coming toward him, and adoring Him, he said: “Lord, where are you going?” <note>original: "Domine: quo vadis?" This is the famous encounter on the Appian Way that led to the construction of the Church of Domine Quo Vadis.</note> **CHRIST** answered him: “I am coming to Rome to be crucified again.” And **PETER** said to Him: “Lord, will you be crucified again?” And the Lord said to him: “Yes, I shall be crucified again.” **PETER** then said: “Lord, I shall return and follow you.” And with these words, the Lord ascended into heaven.

**PETER**, however, followed Him with a long gaze and most sweet tears. And after this, returning to himself, he understood that this had been said concerning his own passion—that the Lord was to suffer in him, He who suffers in His chosen ones through the compassion of mercy and the celebration of glorification. Turning back, he returned to the city with joy, glorifying God and telling the brothers how the Lord had met him and declared to him that He was to be crucified again in him. When he had revealed his passion to them, they all let out weeping and wailing. Everyone grieved and shed tears, saying: “Consider your sheep, O good shepherd; consider those whose faith is weaker and needs to be strengthened by your word. Consider the wavering hearts, which are known to be steadied through you.”

**PETER** said to them: “It is easy for the Lord to strengthen the hearts of His servants even without the word of my humility. For those He has planted, He will make to grow for this purpose, so that they may also be able to plant others. But I, as a servant, must follow the will of the Lord. And if He has decreed that I suffer for His name, and deigns to receive me through passion, I exult and rejoice in His grace.” While he was consoling the minds of the brothers with these and many other words, and they were unable to hold back their tears, **Hieros** arrived with four attendants and ten other men. Seizing him, they snatched him from the midst of the brothers and stood him, bound, before the gaze of Agrippa, the prefect of the city. Agrippa said to him: “Great is your audacity, O wicked man, among the common people whom you circumvent, and among the women who depart from the marital bed by your persuasion. You even dared, to the injury of the Jews, to introduce some 'CHRIST' or other, and to teach I know not what foolish and vain things against the holy Roman rite and against the devotion of the Eternal City.” Then the face of the apostle became bright as the sun, and **PETER**, opening his mouth, said to him: “I see that...”

...you strive: leader of lusts, lover of pollution, inventor of atrocity, persecutor of the innocent, supporter of deceivers, founder of falsehood, dwelling of Satan. For you are ignorant of the glory in which I glory; and therefore you say that my confidence lies in men and women. And **Agrippa** said to him: "Since you know that I am ignorant of what you glory in, make it known to me." And **PETER** said to him: "Let there be no glory for me, except the cross of my Lord **JESUS CHRIST**, whose servant I am." And **Agrippa** said to him: "Do you wish, then, to be crucified, just as your Lord God was crucified?" **PETER** responded: "I am not worthy to make the world a witness to my passion upon an upright cross <note>original: "recta cruce"; Peter traditionally requested to be crucified upside down, feeling unworthy to die in the same position as Christ.</note>; but through any punishment whatsoever, I hope and desire to follow the footsteps of His passion."

Then the prefect, using the accusation of superstition as a pretext for the disease of his own lack of self-control, ordered the apostle to be crucified. And behold, a huge crowd suddenly gathered, of different ages and sexes, of the rich and the poor, of widows, orphans, the weak and the powerful, who shouted with a loud voice: "Why is **PETER** being killed? What crime has he committed? In what way has he harmed the city? It is not lawful to condemn an innocent man. Is it not to be feared that God will avenge the death of such a great man, and command us all to perish?" And the people began to rage against **Agrippa**, striving to snatch him away and preserve **PETER**; and with the tumultuous voices of the common people crying out to one another, Rome was thrown into confusion. Then **PETER** resisted them for a moment, and ascending to a higher place, he beckoned the people to silence with a nod and said: "O men and faithful of God, who serve as soldiers for **CHRIST**. O all you who hope in **CHRIST**: if your charity toward me is true, and you show the inward parts of sincere devotion toward me, do not call back one who is going to the Lord; do not hinder one who is hastening to **CHRIST**. Stand still, therefore, being quiet, rejoicing and glad, so that I may offer my sacrifice to the Lord with joy. For God loves a cheerful giver. <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 9:7.</note>" And with these words, the sedition and the dispute with the prefect were scarcely calmed. For many people were gaping for the chance and desiring to overthrow the prefect, but they feared to grieve the apostle, who followed the example of his Master when He said: "I can ask my Father, and He will provide me now (if I wish) with more than twelve legions of angels."

Finally, together with the apostle and the officers, an infinite number of people arrived at the place called the **Naumachia** <note>original: "Naumachia"; a site for staged naval battles located near the Vatican.</note>, next to the **Obelisk of Nero** on the hill. For there the cross had been placed. And looking back at the weeping people, who were again wishing to stir up a riot, he said in a clear voice: "I beseech you, brothers: do not hinder my offering. Do not rage against **Agrippa**, nor be of a bitter mind toward him. For he is a minister of another's work. As for my condemnation according to the quality of the body, the devil is the author, abusing the Lord's permission because he grieves that the vessels of shame <note>Peter refers to the concubines and others he converted to a life of chastity.</note> have been taken from him through me, and have been made dwellings of continence, temples of **CHRIST**, and homes of honor and grace. Therefore, my brothers and sons, be obedient. For it has been revealed to me by the Lord **JESUS CHRIST** that it would happen thus. The disciple is not above the teacher, nor the servant above his lord. I hasten, therefore, so that, stripped of the flesh, I may be assigned to the Lord. For now is the time in which I shall offer my sacrifice. Remember the signs, wonders, and healings which you saw and felt through **CHRIST**'s work and my ministry. For the infirmities of many were cured so that the souls of all might be saved. Therefore dead bodies were raised so that dead souls might live again. But why do I now endure delays and not approach the cross? Farewell, brothers, and be patient; and keep what you have heard. I commend you to the Lord **JESUS CHRIST**."

Approaching and standing before the cross, he said: "O name of the Cross, hidden mystery! O ineffable grace! For in the name of the cross is peace. O Cross, which has joined man to God and has magnificently separated him from the dominion of the captivating devil! O Cross, which always represents the passion of the Savior of the world and the redemption of human captivity as safe and sound for the human race, accompanied by true faith! O Cross, which daily divides the flesh of the immaculate Lamb to the faithful people, and healthfully drives away the dreadful poisons of the serpent from the people, and unceasingly extinguishes the fiery sword <note>original: "Rhōpheam"; referring to the flaming sword of the Cherubim guarding the entrance to Eden.</note> of paradise for those who believe! O Cross, which daily works peace between earthly and heavenly things, and diligently restores and renews and reforms through a most happy embassy the death of the Mediator—who rose from the dead and now dies no more—to the eternal Father (the Church acting on behalf of her children)! I suffer violence for your sake; and being even now in my final release, I will not rest from manifesting the hidden mystery of God concerning the cross, which my soul once cried out. O you who believe in **CHRIST**: let this cross not be to you what it appears to be. For it is something else, something mystical, within this which appears to you. And now especially, you who are able to hear, as I am in the final hour of this life: set aside all senses, and call away your souls from everything that is visible to that which is invisible; and you shall know that in **CHRIST**, through the cross, the mystery of salvation has been accomplished. It is your debt, **PETER**, to return to the earth the body you received, through those whose task it is to kill the physical body." Then he said to the masters of the executioners: "Why is it that you waste time? Why do you..."

# The Passion of Peter

Hasten, you executioners, and do not allow delays to be woven for me. Fulfill what has been commanded of you; strip me of this mortal tunic, so that I may cling to the spiritual Lord. Indeed, he made his request: and thus addressing the ministers of the executioners, he prayed: "I beseech you, the ministers of my good salvation: that in crucifying me, you place my head downward and my feet upward. For it does not befit me, the last of servants, to be crucified in the same way that the Lord of the Universe was crucified for the salvation of the whole world—He whom it is certain is glorified by my passion. And also, so that I may always be able to behold the mystery of the cross with an intent gaze, so that what I shall say to those standing around may be more easily heard." When this had been done, **PETER** was adored, and he began to console the weeping people from the cross and speak to them in a mystical way, saying:

> Great and profound is the mystery of the cross, and an ineffable and inseparable bond of charity. For through the cross, God has drawn all things to Himself. This is the tree of life <note>original: "lignum vitae"</note>, by which the empire of death has been destroyed. This you have opened to me, O Lord; open also the eyes of all these people, so that they may see the consolation of eternal life.

And with these things said, God opened the eyes of those who were mourning and shedding tears at the passion of **PETER**: and they saw angels standing with crowns of rose and lily flowers, and they saw **PETER** standing at the top of the upright cross, receiving a book from **CHRIST**, and reading from it those words which he was speaking. Seeing this, they began to rejoice and be glad in the Lord, so much so that even those unbelievers and executioners, seeing those whom they had previously seen sad and wailing now exulting and rejoicing, suddenly wasted away in spirit and vanished like smoke. But **PETER**, seeing that his glory had been shown to many who were previously weeping, gave thanks to the Lord **JESUS CHRIST**, saying:

"Worthily do you alone, O Lord, hang crucified with your head raised high, you who redeemed the whole world from sin. I desired to imitate you even in your passion, but I did not presume to be crucified upright. For from Adam, we are born as mere men and sinners. But you are from God: God Himself, and true light from true light before all ages. At the end of ages, you deigned to become man for all without the contagion of man, existing as the glorious redeemer of humanity. You are always upright. You are always exalted. You are always high. We, according to the flesh, are the sons of the first man, who cast his head down <term>demerit in terram: literally 'sank into the earth' or 'brought down to the earth'; referring to the Fall of Adam and the resulting inversion of the natural order</term> into the earth. His fall signifies the nature of human generation. For we are born such that we seem to be poured out prone toward the earth. And what is on the right becomes the left, and what is on the left becomes the right, because in the authors of this life, the condition has been changed. For this world thinks that which is left is right. In this world, O Lord, those whom you found about to perish like the Ninevites <note>The people of Nineveh in the Bible who repented at the preaching of Jonah.</note>, you liberated by your holy preaching. But you, brothers, whose hearing is ready: apply the ears of your heart. And now recognize what must be announced to you: namely, the mystery of all nature and the beginning of every established creation. For the first man, whose race I represent in form, with his head sent downward, showed long ago a lost generation. For his generation was dead and had no vital movement. But the Principle, drawn by His mercy, came into the world through bodily substance to him whom a just sentence had cast down to the earth. And hanging on the cross—through the form of this dreadful calling, namely the cross—He restored and established for us those things which previously had been changed by the wicked error of men. That is, the present things were seen as eternal, and the eternal as present, and the right as left. Indeed, He, glorifying the right, changed all signs back to their proper nature, perceiving as good those things which were not thought good, and as truly kind those which were estimated to be malignant.

Whence the Lord had said in mystery: 'If you do not make the right as the left, and the left as the right, and the things above as the things below, and the things before as the things behind, you shall not know the kingdom of God.' <note>This is an apocryphal saying of Jesus, famously found in the Acts of Peter and also in the Gospel of Thomas.</note> Therefore, I have brought forth this knowledge in myself, brothers. And this is the figure <note>original: "figura"</note> in which carnal eyes behold me hanging. For it is the image <term>Scema: from the Greek 'schema', meaning form, outward appearance, or representation</term> of the first man. But you, my beloved, hearing these things and leading those things you hear toward perfection by converting and living well: just as you have returned from your first error to the most certain station of faith, so persevere in your course, and strive toward the rest of the heavenly calling by living well. For the way by which you must travel there is **CHRIST**. It is necessary, therefore, with **JESUS CHRIST** the true God, to ascend the cross, which is established for us as the sole and living Word. Whence the Spirit also says: **CHRIST** is the Word and the voice of God. Furthermore, the Word signifies this upright wood on which I am crucified. And because the voice properly belongs to the body that receives lineaments, which is not attributed to divinity: the natural parts of the cross are known to represent human nature, which suffered through the error of change in the first man; but through God and man, it has recovered true understanding. For that very key of discipline is bound in the middle: namely, by conversion and conduct, and with the faith of a man’s repentance." And saying these things with a cheerful countenance and a serene face, he cried out thus, breaking into prayer: "You, O Lord **JESUS CHRIST**, have made these words of life known to me: and I give thanks to you who revealed what I have said about the wood I preached. Not with the heart, into which something unseemly often creeps, nor with these lips fixed to the flesh, nor with the tongue through which truth or [falsehood]...

<header>THE LETTER OF LINUS</header>

...falsehood proceeds; nor by a word produced from an articulate and material nature: but with that voice I give thanks to you, O King of Goodness, which is understood through silence; which is not heard in the manifest world; which is not perceived through the organs of a corruptible mouth; which is neither of the earth, nor left in the earth; which is not written in material books, nor moves anyone materially, nor exists as a material thing. With that spirit, I say, Lord JESUS CHRIST, my Lord and teacher, I give thanks to you: by which I believe in you, by which I understand you, by which I love you, by which I hold you; and with the voice by which I address you, by which I call upon you, by which you are intelligible to the whole and modest spirit alone. You are to me, Lord: Father, and friendly creator, and perfecter of salvation. You: my desire. You: my refreshment. You: my satiety. You are everything to me, and all things to me are in you. You are my whole, and all that is: you are to me. You are all things to me. In you: we live, we move, and we have our being. And therefore: we ought to have you as all things, so that you may give us those things which you promised, which no eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man: those things which you have prepared for those who love you. Keep these for your servants. Grant and bestow these. For you are the eternal and supremely good shepherd: the true Son of God. To you I commend the sheep which you handed over to me. Gather them into your sheepfold and preserve them: for you are the door, the sheepfold, and the gatekeeper. You are the pasture and eternal refreshment. To you be glory with the Father and the Holy Spirit: now and for all ages of ages. And as soon as all the people responded with a great voice "Amen": **PETER** gave up his spirit. And immediately Marcellus did not wait for anyone’s sentence: but seeing that the blessed apostle had breathed his last, he took down the holy body from the cross with his own hands and washed it with milk and the best wine. Grinding fifteen hundred <term>minas<note>A 'mina' was a unit of weight roughly equal to one pound; the use of 3,000 pounds of spices emphasizes Marcellus’s great wealth and his devotion, mirroring the burial of Jesus.</note></term> of mastic and aloes, and another fifteen hundred minas of myrrh, leaf <note>original: "folij," referring to nard or malabathrum</note>, and stacte <note>An expensive, high-quality oil of myrrh</note>, along with various other spices: he embalmed him most diligently. He also filled a new sarcophagus with Attic honey <note>Considered the highest quality honey in antiquity, used here as a preservative</note>: and placed the body, smeared with spices, within it. On that very night, while Marcellus was keeping vigil at his tomb and weeping with burning desire for him (for he had resolved in his life never to be separated from the tomb of his most beloved teacher), the blessed **PETER** came to him. When Marcellus saw him, trembling, he quickly rose up to him and stood before him. To whom the blessed apostle said: "Brother Marcellus, have you not heard the voice of the Lord saying: *Leave the dead to bury their own dead*?" And Marcellus said: "Dear teacher, I have heard it." Then **PETER** said to him: "Do not weep, then, lest you seem to have buried a dead man as if you yourself were dead. But as one living, congratulate more greatly him who is living and rejoicing. Leave the dead to bury their own dead. But you: as you have learned through me, go and announce the kingdom of God." Marcellus reported this to all the brothers with much grace. And by the prayers of Saint **PETER**: the faith of the believers was confirmed by God the Father in every part, in the name of our Lord JESUS CHRIST, and in the sanctification of the Holy Spirit. However, when Nero discovered that the blessed **PETER** had died—whom he had ordered to be kept in custody, not killed—he sent for Agrippa the prefect to be arrested, because he had killed **PETER** without his own sentence, whom he had intended to punish with various tortures. For he complained that he had been left desolate by Peter's "tricks" regarding his protector of health, Simon <note>Referring to Simon Magus, the sorcerer who was a favorite of Nero and Peter's rival</note>; and he grieved for the fall of such a great friend who (as he confessed) provided innumerable benefits to himself and the Republic. But through the intervention of friends, Agrippa obtained a pardon so that, though stripped of his prefecture and living as a private and despised citizen, he might stay in his own house. Thus he escaped the fury of Caesar, but he did not escape the vengeance of divine judgment: which he soon experienced terribly and perished. Finally, the most cruel Nero turned his mind to the persecution of those whom he learned had been more closely attached to the blessed **PETER**: so that he might satisfy himself for Peter's death through their punishments. But the blessed apostle made this known to the brothers through a revelation: and suggested how they might avoid the wild beast. Indeed, Nero saw in a vision the holy **PETER** standing by him: and being most severely lashed by someone at Peter's command, he heard: "Stay your hands, most wicked man, from the servants of our Lord JESUS CHRIST, whom you shall not now be able to hold." Whereupon, being not a little terrified, he ceased. The brothers were also together, rejoicing and exulting in the Lord, often comforted by the vision of the blessed apostle **PETER**: glorifying God the Father Almighty, and the Lord JESUS CHRIST with the Holy Spirit. To whom is glory, power, and adoration, forever and ever. AMEN.

II 266 The Passion of Paul

### THE SECOND BOOK OF BISHOP LINUS ON THE PASSION OF PAUL, HANDED DOWN TO THE CHURCHES OF THE EAST AND THEREAFTER TRANSLATED INTO LATIN.

<image-desc>An ornamental woodcut initial 'C' depicting a figure, likely a saint or apostle, holding a book, set within a square frame with floral decorations.</image-desc>

WHEN Luke had come to Rome from Galatia, and Titus from Dalmatia, they waited for PAUL in the city. When PAUL arrived and saw them, he rejoiced greatly. He rented for himself a public granary <note>original: "horreum" — a large storage building or warehouse, here used as a lecture hall</note> outside the city, where he treated the word of life with these men and other brothers. Meanwhile, he began to gather a very great multitude. Through him, many souls were added to the faith by the working of God’s grace, so that the sound of his preaching and holiness was heard throughout the entire city, and his fame went out through the whole region. Indeed, he had already become well known to the Roman world for his signs, wonders, teaching, and his many-faceted and wonderful holiness.

A great crowd also came to him from the house of Caesar <note>The "house of Caesar" refers to the massive staff of slaves, freedmen, and officials serving the Emperor Nero</note>, consisting of those believing in the Lord JESUS CHRIST; and a great joy and exultation increased daily among the faithful. Even the tutor of the emperor <note>Latin: "institutor imperatoris" — this likely refers to the philosopher Seneca, whom medieval legend claimed was a secret friend and correspondent of Paul</note> was joined to him in such close friendship, seeing in him a divine wisdom, that he could hardly restrain himself from talking with him. If he was unable to speak to him face-to-face, he enjoyed his sweetness and friendly conversation and counsel through frequent letters sent and received. And thus his teaching—the Holy Spirit increasing it—was multiplied and loved, so that he now taught freely and was heard most willingly by many. 

He disputed indeed with the philosophers of the Heathens and refuted them; wherefore very many surrendered themselves to his mastery. For a certain teacher of Caesar even read his writings aloud before the Emperor and declared him admirable in all things. Even the Senate thought highly of him, in no small measure. 

Finally, one day, while PAUL was serving his teaching near evening in a high upper room and addressing the crowds, Patroclus—a favorite and the cupbearer of the king <note>A "cupbearer" (Latin: "picerna") was a high-ranking servant responsible for serving wine, often a position of great trust</note>—withdrew himself from the king’s sight and went to the granary where PAUL was staying, so that he might hear the lessons of eternal life. For he had already been invited to this and led in his mind by his companions and the closest friends of Caesar, who, out of their familiar service to him, followed the warnings of PAUL. 

But when he could not enter to reach him because of the multitude of people, he climbed up to a high window and sat beside it, so that he could more easily hear the word of God. For he desired with a fervent soul to be refreshed by the sermons of PAUL. But when PAUL prolonged his sermon at great length and the youth was weighed down by sleep—by the envy of the devil, who grieved over the love of God and of the apostle which the studious young man possessed—the devil made the youth doze for a moment; falling from the very high window of the upper room, he breathed his last <note>original: "spiritum exalauit" — he died</note>. 

When this was soon announced to Nero as he was returning from the bath, he sought the youth he loved with a great crowd, and he was saddened to his very soul over the death of Patroclus. He appointed another in his place for the office of wine, to offer him the cup. 

PAUL, however, knowing through the Spirit shortly after what had happened, said to the people: "Men and brothers, the evil one has found a place to tempt you; but the Lord JESUS CHRIST, in His usual way, will turn his wickedness to His own glory. Go out, therefore, and you will find the favorite youth of Caesar has fallen from on high and now lies lifeless. Lift him up and strive to bring him here to me." 

They, therefore, proceeding with a quick step, immediately brought the dead youth. The crowds wondered how PAUL had known the event in order, though no one had announced it to him. Then PAUL said to the crowds: "Now true faith toward our Lord JESUS CHRIST shall appear. For it is time that the seed of eternal life, falling into good soil, should bear fruit with a hundredfold sowing. Come therefore with full faith to the Lord our God, and let us pray to Him that his soul may be restored into this youthful corpse, and that he may live better than he had lived before." 

And when they had all groaned, prostrating themselves in prayer, PAUL said: "Young man Patroclus, rise!" And he began to glorify God, who gave such power to men. And PAUL dismissed him with the others who were from the house of Caesar; and they all went rejoicing and glad in the Lord, who does the will of those who fear Him and hears their prayers. 

When Nero was lamenting Patroclus and was absorbed by a magnitude of sadness, those standing around said to Caesar: "Lord, let not your greatness be burdened by distress over the death of the youth; for he lives, and is here before the doors." 

But Caesar, when he heard that Patroclus lived—whom he had learned was dead a little while before—was terrified in his heart and refused to let him enter and stand in his presence. But when he had been persuaded by very many of his friends, he ordered him to enter. And seeing him healthy, having no signs of death, he was amazed and said to him: "Patroclus, do you live?" 

But he replied: "Caesar, I live." 

Nero said: "Who made you live?" 

To him Patroclus, cheered in his heart and inflamed with the heat of faith, said: "My Lord JESUS CHRIST, the King of all ages." 

And Nero, troubled by the name of the power of God, said to the youth: "He, then, must...
